Definition: a perishing
BiblicalUsage: This noun for perishing or destruction occurs twice. Job says the fire of lust 'is a fire that consumeth to destruction'; and the proverb pairs it with hell itself — 'Hell and destruction are never full; so the eyes of man are never satisfied'.
TheologicalSignificance: Twice is enough to hear the warning: destruction is a real end, and human appetite is never satisfied on its own. I believe the proverb is honest about my own heart — my eyes are never full either — and that is why I need a satisfaction that comes from outside me.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H11); a destroying angel:--Abaddon.
BiblicalUsage: Abaddon appears once, in Revelation 9:11. The locusts from the bottomless pit have ‘a king over them, which is the angel of the bottomless pit, whose name in the Hebrew tongue is Abaddon, but in the Greek tongue hath his name Apollyon’ — the Destroyer.
TheologicalSignificance: One verse names the king of the pit, and it is enough to know him for what he is: a destroyer, not a ruler to be followed. I believe the naming matters — Scripture does not leave evil anonymous; it names it, shows its end, and sets the Lamb above it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: abstract, a perishing; concrete, Hades
BiblicalUsage: This is the word for destruction itself — the place of ruin, the grave’s shadow. Job says ‘Hell is naked before him, and destruction hath no covering’; Destruction and Death confess they have only heard a rumour of wisdom; and the proverb says ‘Hell and destruction are before the LORD’.
TheologicalSignificance: What strikes me is that destruction is never hidden from God — it is naked before Him, and even Death admits it does not hold wisdom. I believe that is the comfort under the dread: the pit has no secrets from the LORD, and nothing in it is beyond His sight or His reach.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Abagtha, a eunuch of Xerxes
BiblicalUsage: Abagtha is named once, in Esther 1:10, as one of the seven chamberlains who served King Ahasuerus — the king sends him, with six others, to bring Queen Vashti before him wearing the royal crown. He never appears again.
TheologicalSignificance: A one-verse servant carries no doctrine, and I will not invent one for him. What his verse does is set the scene for the whole book: a king's command, a queen's refusal, and the chain of events that puts Esther on the throne — God working through ordinary messengers and palace routines.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to be dense
BiblicalUsage: This verb for growing thick or fat occurs three times. Moses sings that Jeshurun ‘waxed fat, and kicked... thou art grown thick, thou art covered with fatness’ and forsook God; and the young men advise Rehoboam to boast, ‘My little finger shall be thicker than my father’s loins.’
TheologicalSignificance: Both uses warn me the same way — fullness makes people forgetful — and I believe prosperity is a spiritual danger, not just a blessing.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to breathe after, i.e. (figuratively) to be acquiescent
BiblicalUsage: This verb is about willingness — to consent, to yield, to be agreeable. Isaiah promises, 'If ye be willing and obedient, ye shall eat the good of the land'; Moses forbids Israel to consent to an enticer to idolatry; and Pharaoh, again and again, 'would not let them go'.
TheologicalSignificance: Willingness is where obedience starts, and Pharaoh shows what happens when it hardens into refusal. I believe God deals with the will first — His promise in Isaiah is conditional on a willing heart — and I would rather be willing and obedient than right and stubborn.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably to coil upward
BiblicalUsage: This rare verb occurs only in Genesis 32:24: 'there wrestled a man with him until the breaking of the day.' It is the word for the struggle itself — the grappling, the dust-raising contest at the ford of Jabbok where Jacob wrestles through the night.
TheologicalSignificance: One verse, one night, and it changes Jacob’s name and his walk — and I believe the wrestling matters more than the winning, because Jacob holds on and will not let go without a blessing.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: nay, i.e. truly or yet
BiblicalUsage: This little word means ‘truly’ or ‘indeed’ — a word for emphasis, sometimes for contradiction (‘nay’). Joseph’s brothers say, ‘We are verily guilty concerning our brother’; and the widow of Tekoa tells David, ‘I am indeed a widow woman.’
TheologicalSignificance: It is a small word with no doctrine attached, and I will not force one onto it — though I notice where it lands: on guilt confessed and grief stated plainly.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to bewail
BiblicalUsage: This is the verb for mourning — to bewail, to grieve openly. Jacob 'mourned for his son many days' believing Joseph dead; Samuel 'mourned for Saul' after the kingdom was torn from him; and David 'mourned for his son every day' while Absalom was in exile.
TheologicalSignificance: The Bible never rushes past grief: three fathers and a prophet all mourn, and the text simply records it. I believe that is permission — mourning is not unbelief, and God counts the tears of His people rather than telling them to move on.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Abanah, a river near Damascus
BiblicalUsage: The Abanah is named once, in 2 Kings 5:12, when Naaman the leper objects to Elisha's command: 'Are not Abana and Pharpar, rivers of Damascus, better than all the waters of Israel? may I not wash in them, and be clean?' It is one of the two rivers of Damascus, clear and cold from Mount Hermon.
TheologicalSignificance: Naaman's question is still mine whenever God's way looks too plain: why this river, why this simple command, when I know better ones? I believe the Abanah teaches me that healing is not in the water I choose but in obeying the word God speaks — and Naaman had to go down into the Jordan to find that out.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: light particles (as volatile)
BiblicalUsage: This is the word for dust — the fine, light particles that rise and settle. It becomes ‘small dust’ over Egypt and breaks out in boils; and the blossom of the proud ‘shall go up as dust’ in Isaiah.
TheologicalSignificance: Dust is what man was made from and what pride returns to, and in both verses it comes as judgment — a reminder that what looks solid, God can reduce to dust.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to bedust, i.e. grapple
BiblicalUsage: This verb for grappling or wrestling occurs only at the Jabbok, in Genesis 32:24-25: 'there wrestled a man with him until the breaking of the day. And when he saw that he prevailed not against him, he touched the hollow of his thigh.' It is the close, dusty struggle of two men locked together in the dark.
TheologicalSignificance: Jacob wrestled all night and came away limping and blessed — the wound and the blessing in the same encounter. I believe God sometimes meets us this way: not with an answer handed over, but with a struggle that leaves us changed, and a limp that reminds us who won.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {light particles (as volatile)}
BiblicalUsage: This word for dust occurs once, in Nahum 1:3: 'the clouds are the dust of his feet.' It is the fine powder kicked up by a traveller's steps — and Nahum says the clouds themselves are only the dust under God's feet as He marches in the whirlwind and the storm.
TheologicalSignificance: One verse, and it puts everything in its place: the storm clouds that terrify nations are only dust beneath God’s feet.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to cross over; used very widely of any transition (literal or figurative; transitive, intransitive, intensive, causative); specifically, to cover (in copulation)
BiblicalUsage: This is the great crossing-word of the Old Testament — to pass over, go through, or cross to the other side. Jacob says, 'with my staff I passed over this Jordan'; the priests stand firm while 'all the Israelites passed over' on dry ground; and all the people 'passed over' the brook Kidron as David flees Jerusalem.
TheologicalSignificance: Crossing over is the shape of the whole Bible story: from one side to the other, from bondage to promise, from danger to safety. I believe every crossing in Scripture points to the same truth — God makes a way where there is no way, and He goes with His people through the water.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {properly, a region across; but used only adverbially (with or without a preposition) on the opposite side (especially of the Jordan; ususally meaning the east)}
BiblicalUsage: In Aramaic this word means ‘beyond’ or ‘the other side’ — almost always ‘beyond the river’, the Euphrates, the boundary of the Persian province. The accusers warn about the lands ‘beyond the river’; and Darius orders the governor ‘beyond the river’ to leave the builders alone.
TheologicalSignificance: It is a boundary word, and it marks where one power ends and another begins — but in Ezra the real boundary is God’s, and no governor beyond the river can stop what He has decreed.
RelatedEvents: Cyrus's Decree and Return from Exile
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to soar
BiblicalUsage: This verb for flying or soaring occurs once, in Job 39:26, where God asks Job: 'Doth the hawk fly by thy wisdom, and stretch her wings toward the south?' It is the hawk's flight — the lift, the spread wings, the southward journey — set before Job as something he cannot explain or command.
TheologicalSignificance: One question about a hawk, and Job has no answer — and neither do I, which is the point: God’s wisdom runs the world in ways I cannot trace.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a crossing-place
BiblicalUsage: This word for a ford or crossing-place occurs in its clear form once, in 2 Samuel 19:18: 'there went over a ferry boat to carry over the king's household' as David returns across the Jordan. The crossing carries the king's household over, and Shimei falls down before the king as he comes over Jordan.
TheologicalSignificance: A ford is a small thing — a shallow place where a river can be crossed — but David’s whole return turns on it, and I believe God often works at the shallow places.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and G922; weightless, i.e. (figuratively) not burdensome:--from being burdensome.
BiblicalUsage: This Greek word for 'not burdensome' occurs once, in 2 Corinthians 11:9: 'when I was present with you, and wanted, I was chargeable to no man.' Paul is defending his ministry — he worked with his own hands and let the Macedonians supply his need rather than burden the Corinthians.
TheologicalSignificance: One verse shows me Paul’s heart for the churches — he would rather go without than be a weight on the people he served — and it makes me check whether my own service lightens anyone’s load or adds to it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Abarim, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Abarim is the range of mountains east of the Jordan, across from Jericho — the 'mount Abarim' where God tells Moses, 'Get thee up into this mount Abarim, and see the land which I have given unto the children of Israel.' Israel camps 'in the mountains of Abarim, before Nebo', and Moses is told again to climb and view the land he will not enter.
TheologicalSignificance: Moses sees the promise from Abarim and dies without setting foot in it, and that has always moved me. I believe God can show us the land and still say 'not yet' or 'not you' — and faith is trusting Him from the mountaintop, even when the crossing belongs to someone else.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to dry up
BiblicalUsage: This verb for drying up or rotting occurs once, in Joel 1:17: 'The seed is rotten under their clods, the garners are laid desolate, the barns are broken down; for the corn is withered.' It is the locust plague's aftermath — the seed itself rotting in the ground, the storehouses empty, the harvest gone.
TheologicalSignificance: One verse of ruin, and it is total — the seed rots, the barns break, the corn withers — and I believe Joel wants me to feel the weight of it before he offers the hope.
RelatedEvents: The Locust Plague in Joel's Day
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to pawn; causatively, to lend (on security); figuratively, to entangle
BiblicalUsage: This verb for lending on pledge — to take security, to lend — turns up in Moses' promises to Israel: 'thou shalt lend unto many nations, but thou shalt not borrow' is both the blessing of obedience in Deuteronomy 15:6 and of Deuteronomy 28:12. Lending marks the nation that has enough to give; borrowing marks the nation in want.
TheologicalSignificance: It is an economic word, but the promise behind it is spiritual: obedience would make Israel the lender, not the borrower. I believe God still ties provision to obedience — not as a bargain, but as a pattern — and a people who trust Him end up with enough to share.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to interlace, i.e. (figuratively) to pervert
BiblicalUsage: This verb for winding or weaving together occurs once, in Micah 7:3: the prince asks, the judge asks for a reward, the great man utters his mischievous desire — 'so they wrap it up.' The word pictures evil being woven, strand by strand, until prince, judge, and great man have twisted it into one finished scheme.
TheologicalSignificance: One verse shows me how corruption works — not in one bold act, but woven together by many hands — and it warns me to watch for the small threads of compromise in my own life.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a melon (only plural)
BiblicalUsage: The melon is named once, in Numbers 11:5, in Israel's complaint: 'We remember the fish, which we did eat in Egypt freely; the cucumbers, and the melons, and the leeks, and the onions, and the garlick.' It is one item on a homesick menu — the food of slavery remembered as if it were freedom.
TheologicalSignificance: A melon carries no doctrine, but the craving behind it does: Israel remembered Egypt’s food and forgot Egypt’s chains.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Chaldee origin (H2); father as a vocative:--Abba.
BiblicalUsage: Abba is the Aramaic word for father, kept in its own language in the Greek New Testament — a child's word, intimate and direct. Jesus cries it in Gethsemane, 'Abba, Father, all things are possible unto thee'; Paul says believers have received 'the Spirit of adoption, whereby we cry, Abba, Father'; and the Spirit of God's Son cries it in our hearts.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this is the tenderest word in the New Testament: the Son's own word for His Father, given to us. Because Christ prayed 'Abba' in the garden, I can pray it too — not as a slave begging a master, but as a child coming home to a Father who has already adopted me.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {mighty (spoken of God)}
BiblicalUsage: This word for the mighty ones — strong men, bulls, champions — turns up in the songs and the prophets. Deborah sings of 'the pransings of their mighty ones' as the enemy horses flee; the psalm says man ate 'angels' food', the bread of the mighty; and Jeremiah hears 'the neighing of his strong ones' as the invader's horses approach from Dan.
TheologicalSignificance: The mighty ones of earth — the horsemen, the champions, the armies — are strong until God moves, and then their hooves break and their bread fails. I believe the contrast is deliberate: human might makes a fine song until it meets the Lord, and only His strength endures.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Abda, the name of two Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Abda is the name of two Israelites — one the father of Adoniram, who was over Solomon’s tribute, and the other ‘Abda the son of Shammua’, a Levite who served in Jerusalem after the return from exile. Two men, two centuries apart, both named in lists of servants.
TheologicalSignificance: A name in a list is easy to skip, but God does not skip names. I believe Abda matters because the Bible remembers servants: a tribute officer under Solomon and a Levite singer after the exile are both written down, and no faithful service is too small for God's record.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a perishing
BiblicalUsage: This noun for perishing or destruction occurs once, in Esther 9:5: the Jews 'smote all their enemies with the stroke of the sword, and slaughter and destruction, and did what they would unto those that hated them.' It is the word for the ruin that fell on those who had planned ruin for the Jews.
TheologicalSignificance: One verse turns the tables — the destruction Haman planned for the Jews falls on his own party — and I believe Esther’s reversal is the pattern of God’s justice.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Abdeel, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Abdeel is named once, in Jeremiah 36:26, as the father of Shelemiah — one of the officers King Jehoiakim sends to arrest Jeremiah and Baruch after the scroll is burned. The verse is a manhunt: the king commands Jerahmeel, Seraiah, and Shelemiah the son of Abdeel to seize the prophet and his scribe.
TheologicalSignificance: Abdeel himself does nothing in the story; he is known only as someone's father, in a verse about arresting God's prophet. I believe that is worth noting — the Bible names even the bystanders of its great scenes, and a name tied to a king's rage against God's word is a sober place to be found.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Abdiel, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Abdiel is named once, in 1 Chronicles 5:15: 'Ahi the son of Abdiel, the son of Guni, chief of the house of their fathers.' He is a Gadite — the father of a clan chief east of the Jordan, in the genealogy of the tribe of Gad.
TheologicalSignificance: A single line in a genealogy is all we have of Abdiel, and it carries no teaching of its own. What it does show me is the Bible's care for families: a Gadite father and his chief son are remembered by name, and no tribe or household is lost in God's record of His people.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Abdi, the name of two Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Abdi is the name of two Israelites — a Levite, the father of Kish in the singers’ line of Heman, and an ‘Abdi’ among the sons of Elam who had taken foreign wives in Ezra’s day. The same name sits in a worship genealogy and in a repentance list.
TheologicalSignificance: Two men, one name: one in the line of temple singers, one in the list of those who put away foreign wives. I believe that is the Bible in miniature — worship and repentance side by side — and both are written down, because God keeps the record of those who serve Him and those who turn back to Him.
RelatedEvents: Cyrus's Decree and Return from Exile
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Abdon, the name of a place in Palestine and of four Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Abdon is both a place and a person — a Levitical city in Asher, given to the Gershonites, and Abdon the son of Hillel, who judged Israel eight years, had forty sons and thirty nephews who rode on seventy ass colts, and was buried in Pirathon. The name also belongs to a Benjamite in the genealogies.
TheologicalSignificance: Abdon judged Israel eight years and the Bible gives him three verses — a large family, a quiet tenure, an honourable burial. I believe that is a word for ordinary faithfulness: most of God's servants are not Samsons or Gideons, and their eight quiet years matter just as much.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: servitude
BiblicalUsage: This word for bondage or servitude occurs three times, all in the prayers of the returned exiles. Ezra confesses, 'we were bondmen; yet our God hath not forsaken us in our bondage'; and Nehemiah's prayer recalls how the fathers 'appointed a captain to return to their bondage' in Egypt.
TheologicalSignificance: Twice the exiles name their bondage in the same breath as God's mercy — 'yet our God hath not forsaken us in our bondage.' I believe that is the deepest comfort in the word: bondage is real, and so is God's presence inside it, and He does not wait for us to be free before He shows mercy.
RelatedEvents: Cyrus's Decree and Return from Exile; Nehemiah Rebuilds the Wall
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Abed-Nego, the name of Azariah
BiblicalUsage: Abed-Nego is the Babylonian name given to Azariah, one of Daniel's three friends — 'unto Azariah, of Abed-nego.' He is set over the affairs of Babylon, accused of refusing to serve the king's gods or worship the golden image, and thrown into the burning fiery furnace with Shadrach and Meshach.
TheologicalSignificance: His Hebrew name meant 'the LORD has helped'; his Babylonian name praised a foreign god — and he would not bow to it. I believe Abed-Nego's story is about a name you refuse to live by: the world can rename you, but it cannot make you worship what it worships, and the God who helped Azariah walks in the furnace with His own.
RelatedEvents: Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego in the Fiery Furnace; Daniel's Resolve in Babylon
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Abed-Nego, the Babylonian name of one of Daniel's companions
BiblicalUsage: Abed-Nego is the Babylonian name given to Azariah, one of Daniel's three friends — 'unto Azariah, of Abed-nego.' He is set over the affairs of Babylon, accused of refusing to serve the king's gods or worship the golden image, and thrown into the burning fiery furnace with Shadrach and Meshach.
TheologicalSignificance: His Hebrew name meant 'the LORD has helped'; his Babylonian name praised a foreign god — and he would not bow to it. I believe Abed-Nego's story is about a name you refuse to live by: the world can rename you, but it cannot make you worship what it worships, and the God who helped Azariah walks in the furnace with His own.
RelatedEvents: Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego in the Fiery Furnace; Daniel's Resolve in Babylon
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: concrete, something lost; abstract, destruction, i.e. Hades
BiblicalUsage: This word names a lost thing — something that has gone astray and must be dealt with honestly. The law covers the man who finds 'that which was lost' and swears falsely about it; the neighbour's lost ox or garment must be restored; and 'all manner of lost thing' is brought before the judges when two men claim it.
TheologicalSignificance: It is a law word, not a theology word, but the principle underneath it is pure gospel: what is lost is not abandoned, and the finder has a duty. I believe God cares about lost things — lost sheep, lost coins, lost sons — and His law was already teaching His people to seek and restore before Jesus told the parables.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: longing
BiblicalUsage: This word for longing or desire occurs once, in Job 34:36, in Elihu's speech: 'My desire is that Job may be tried unto the end because of his answers for wicked men.' It is one man's stated wish — that Job's testing run its full course.
TheologicalSignificance: A single word for a single wish, and it is not even a kind one — Elihu wants Job tried to the end — and the verse is honest about how people speak into suffering.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Abel of Beth-maakah, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Abel of Beth-maachah is a fortified city in the far north of Israel, near Dan. Sheba flees there when Joab pursues him; a wise woman of the city negotiates with Joab and saves it; Ben-hadad strikes it in Asa's day; and Tiglath-pileser captures it in the fall of the northern kingdom.
TheologicalSignificance: A city known for one wise woman and three invasions: it survives Sheba's rebellion by wisdom and falls at last to Assyria. I believe Abel of Beth-maachah shows both truths — wisdom can save a city, and no wall can save a nation that has left God.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H1893); Abel, the son of Adam:--Abel.
BiblicalUsage: The New Testament remembers Abel as the first righteous man murdered and the first man commended for faith. Jesus says the blood ‘of righteous Abel’ will be required of His generation; Hebrews says ‘by faith Abel offered unto God a more excellent sacrifice than Cain’; and his blood still speaks — set against the blood of Jesus, which ‘speaketh better things than that of Abel’.
TheologicalSignificance: Abel's blood cries for vengeance; Christ's blood speaks forgiveness — and Hebrews puts them side by side on purpose. I believe that is the whole gospel in one contrast: the first murder asks for justice, and the last sacrifice answers it, and the better blood is the one that speaks for me.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a meadow
BiblicalUsage: This word for a meadow — a low, grassy place — occurs once, in 1 Samuel 6:18, in ‘the great stone of Abel, whereon they set down the ark of the LORD’ in the field of Joshua the Bethshemite. It is the ground where the ark comes to rest after its long journey through Philistia.
TheologicalSignificance: A meadow is a plain word for a plain place, and it carries no doctrine of its own; what stays with me is the ground under the story — God meets His people in ordinary fields, not only on mountaintops.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Abel, the name of two places in Palestine.
BiblicalUsage: This is the name Abel on its own — the city in the north where Sheba flees and where Joab besieges him. The verse says Sheba 'went through all the tribes of Israel unto Abel', and the wise woman reminds Joab that Abel was once the place where people said, 'They shall surely ask counsel at Abel.'
TheologicalSignificance: A city remembered for counsel and for one wise woman who stopped a siege with words. I believe Abel's story is a small sermon on wisdom: a city that asked counsel lived, and a woman who spoke well saved it — and that is a better defence than any wall.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Abel hash-Shittim, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Abel-shittim — the meadow of the acacias — is named once, in Numbers 33:49, as the last camp of Israel before the Jordan: 'they pitched by Jordan, from Beth-jesimoth even unto Abel-shittim in the plains of Moab.' It is the camp where the sin of Peor happens and where Moses speaks his farewell.
TheologicalSignificance: The last camp before the crossing holds both sin and promise: Peor's shame and the plains of Moab where Moses preaches Deuteronomy. I believe that is honest about the Christian life — the ground before the Jordan is where we fail and where we hear God's word most clearly, side by side.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Abel-Keramim, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Abel-keramim — the plain of the vineyards — is named once, in Judges 11:33, as the far end of Jephthah's pursuit: he smote the Ammonites 'from Aroer, even till thou come to Minnith, even twenty cities, and unto the plain of the vineyards, with a very great slaughter.' It is the finish line of the victory.
TheologicalSignificance: One place-name, one victory, and then the shadow of Jephthah's vow falls over the chapter. I believe the plain of the vineyards reminds me that victories end and vows remain — and that a triumph won in God's strength can still be followed by a foolish promise made in my own.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Abel-Majim, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Abel-maim — the meadow of waters — is named once, in 2 Chronicles 16:4, when Ben-hadad of Syria, hired by Asa, 'smote Ijon, and Dan, and Abel-maim, and all the store cities of Naphtali.' It is a northern border town, taken in a war Asa bought with temple silver.
TheologicalSignificance: A town whose name means waters, lost because a king trusted Syria instead of God. I believe Abel-maim is a quiet warning: Asa's silver bought a victory and cost him a prophet's rebuke, and the towns of Naphtali paid for a king's unbelief.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Abel-Mecholah, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Abel-meholah — the meadow of dancing — is a town in the Jordan valley. Gideon's enemies flee 'unto the border of Abel-meholah'; it is listed among Solomon's districts; and it is the home of Elisha, 'the son of Shaphat of Abel-meholah', whom Elijah is told to anoint.
TheologicalSignificance: A town where armies flee, a district on a tax list, and the home of a prophet — the same place holds all three. I believe Abel-meholah shows how God plants His servants in unremarkable towns: Elisha was ploughing a field there when the call came, and the call found him working.
RelatedEvents: Gideon's Victory over Midian; Elijah Taken Up in a Chariot of Fire
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Abel-Mitsrajim, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Abel-mizraim — the mourning of the Egyptians — is named once, in Genesis 50:11, when the Canaanites watch Joseph's funeral procession for Jacob: 'This is a grievous mourning to the Egyptians: wherefore the name of it was called Abel-mizraim, which is beyond Jordan.' It is the threshing floor of Atad, renamed by seven days of lament.
TheologicalSignificance: A place gets its name from grief — the Egyptians mourned Jacob for seven days, and the Canaanites could not miss it. I believe Abel-mizraim says something true about mourning: it is public, it is long, and it honours the dead in a way strangers can see.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a meadow
BiblicalUsage: This word for a meadow — a low, grassy place — occurs once, in 1 Samuel 6:18, in ‘the great stone of Abel, whereon they set down the ark of the LORD’ in the field of Joshua the Bethshemite. It is the ground where the ark comes to rest after its long journey through Philistia.
TheologicalSignificance: A meadow is a plain word for a plain place, and it carries no doctrine of its own; what stays with me is the ground under the story — God meets His people in ordinary fields, not only on mountaintops.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H29); Abijah, the name of two Israelites:--Abia.
BiblicalUsage: Abijah is the name of several men and two women. In the Old Testament it is the king of Judah who defeats Jeroboam in battle, the son of Jeroboam who falls sick and dies under Ahijah’s prophecy, and Samuel’s son who judges with his brother and takes bribes; in the New Testament it is the name in Matthew’s genealogy — ‘Roboam begat Abia’ — and the priestly course of Zacharias, the father of John the Baptist.
TheologicalSignificance: One name, four stories — a corrupt judge, a dying child, a warring king, and a priest’s division — and each one shows a different way a life can turn. I believe the name Abijah is a warning and a hope together: a good name does not make a good life, but God still keeps a place for those who return to Him.
RelatedPeople: Samuel; Abijah; Jeroboam; John the Baptist
RelatedEvents: Abijah's Victory over Jeroboam; The Birth of John the Baptist
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H54); Abiathar, an Israelite:--Abiathar.
BiblicalUsage: Abiathar appears once in the New Testament, in Mark 2:26, when Jesus defends His disciples for plucking grain on the Sabbath: 'how he went into the house of God in the days of Abiathar the high priest, and did eat the shewbread.' Jesus reaches back to David's flight to make His point about mercy and the Sabbath.
TheologicalSignificance: Jesus anchors His argument in a priest's name — Abiathar — and a hungry fugitive eating holy bread. I believe the point is mercy over ritual: if David could eat the shewbread in his need, the Sabbath was never meant to starve God's people, and the Lord of the Sabbath knows it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of foreign origin (compare H58); Abilene, a region of Syria:--Abilene.
BiblicalUsage: Abilene is named once, in Luke 3:1, in the careful dating of John the Baptist's ministry: 'in the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar... Lysanias the tetrarch of Abilene.' It is a small district in Syria, listed beside Galilee, Ituraea, and Trachonitis to pin the story to real rulers and real places.
TheologicalSignificance: A one-verse district, named only to date the gospel — and that is exactly the point. I believe Luke lists Abilene because the gospel happened in history, under named rulers, in named places, and the Word did not come to a myth but to a world with a calendar.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H31); Abihud, an Israelite:--Abiud.
BiblicalUsage: Abihud appears in two places and nowhere else. In Chronicles he is a son of Bela and a grandson of Benjamin — ‘And the sons of Bela were, Addar, and Gera, and Abihud’ — and in Matthew he stands in the genealogy of Jesus after the exile, between Zerubbabel and Eliakim.
TheologicalSignificance: One name in a genealogy, with no story attached — and still the line runs through him to Christ. I believe Abihud is there for people like me who feel unremarkable: God keeps His promise through quiet generations too, and a name in the line is enough.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Abiasaph, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Abiasaph is a son of Korah, named in the genealogy of Levi in Exodus 6:24 and in the singers' lines of 1 Chronicles. His descendants are the Korahites — the temple gatekeepers and singers, keepers of the thresholds of the house of God.
TheologicalSignificance: The son of a rebel becomes the father of gatekeepers and singers — that is the story of Abiasaph's line. I believe it shows God's mercy running in families: Korah's rebellion ended in judgment, but his sons were spared, and their children ended up singing at the doors of the house.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Abialbon, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Abialbon the Arbathite is named once, in 2 Samuel 23:31, in the list of David's mighty men. He is one of the thirty — a name among the warriors who stood with David, with no deed recorded beside his name.
TheologicalSignificance: A mighty man with no recorded deed: his name is the whole entry. I believe that is enough — the Bible honours the men who stood with David even when it does not tell us what they did, and God keeps the same kind of record of those who stand with Him.
RelatedEvents: David's Mighty Men and the Philistine Giants
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Abiel, the name of two Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Abiel is the father of Ner and the grandfather of Saul — 'a mighty man of power' whose son Kish fathered the first king. He is also the name of one of David's mighty men, Abiel the Arbathite, in the Chronicles list.
TheologicalSignificance: Abiel stands at the head of two lines: the family that gives Israel its first king, and a warrior who serves the king after God's own heart. I believe the contrast is the lesson — one line rises and falls with Saul, the other stands with David, and God chooses the house He will build.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Abiezer, the name of two Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Abiezer is a Manassite clan name and a man’s name. The clan gets its lot in Joshua 17; when Gideon blows the trumpet, ‘Abiezer was gathered after him’; and Abiezer the Anethothite stands among David’s mighty men.
TheologicalSignificance: The smallest clan in Manasseh gives Israel its judge, and a man of that name stands among David's thirty. I believe Abiezer's story is Gideon's story: God picks the least family and the least man, and the least turns out to be exactly enough.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Abi-Gibon, perhaps an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Abi-Gibon — the father of Gibeon — is named once, in 1 Chronicles 8:29, at the head of the genealogy of Saul's family: 'And at Gibeon dwelt the father of Gibeon; whose wife's name was Maachah.' He is the ancestor through whom Saul's line is traced.
TheologicalSignificance: One verse, one name, and it anchors a whole royal genealogy. I believe the Bible's genealogies are not filler: they show that God's story runs through real families, and even a man named only as 'the father of Gibeon' has his place in the line that leads to a king.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: density, i.e. depth or width
BiblicalUsage: This word for thickness or depth is used of things built to last: the brim of the bronze sea ‘was an hand breadth thick’; and the walls of Ezekiel’s temple are five cubits thick. It measures solidity — how much substance a thing has.
TheologicalSignificance: It is a builder’s word, not a preacher’s word, and it carries no doctrine of its own — though it does show me how seriously God takes the house He orders built: measured, solid, and made to last.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an Abiezrite or descendant of Abiezer
BiblicalUsage: The Abi-ezrite is a descendant of Abiezer — the clan name used of Gideon and his family. The angel finds Gideon 'in Ophrah... which pertained unto Joash the Abi-ezrite'; Gideon builds an altar there; and he is buried 'in Ophrah of the Abi-ezrites'.
TheologicalSignificance: Gideon is introduced by his clan, and his clan is the smallest in Manasseh — and God calls the least man of the least family to save Israel. I believe the Abi-ezrite label is the point: God does not need a great family to do a great work, and He never has.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Abi, Hezekiah's mother
BiblicalUsage: Abi is named once, in 2 Kings 18:2, as the mother of Hezekiah: 'his mother's name was Abi, the daughter of Zachariah.' She is the queen mother at the start of the best king's reign — named in one verse, and never again.
TheologicalSignificance: A mother named once, at the door of her son's reign, and the text moves on. I believe Abi's single verse honours something the Bible does again and again: the mothers behind the kings, named and remembered, even when the story belongs to their sons.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Abijah, the name of several Israelite men and two Israelitesses
BiblicalUsage: Abijah is the name of several men and two women. In the Old Testament it is the king of Judah who defeats Jeroboam in battle, the son of Jeroboam who falls sick and dies under Ahijah’s prophecy, and Samuel’s son who judges with his brother and takes bribes; in the New Testament it is the name in Matthew’s genealogy — ‘Roboam begat Abia’ — and the priestly course of Zacharias, the father of John the Baptist.
TheologicalSignificance: One name, four stories — a corrupt judge, a dying child, a warring king, and a priest’s division — and each one shows a different way a life can turn. I believe the name Abijah is a warning and a hope together: a good name does not make a good life, but God still keeps a place for those who return to Him.
RelatedPeople: Samuel; Abijah; Jeroboam; John the Baptist
RelatedEvents: Abijah's Victory over Jeroboam; The Birth of John the Baptist
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Abijam (or Abijah), a king of Judah
BiblicalUsage: Abijam — also called Abijah — is the son of Rehoboam who reigns three years in Jerusalem, and the text is blunt: ‘he walked in all the sins of his father’; yet ‘for David’s sake did the LORD his God give him a lamp in Jerusalem.’ His wars with Jeroboam are written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah.
TheologicalSignificance: A bad king kept on the throne for David's sake — not his own. I believe Abijam shows me how God's promise outlasts a man's failure: the lamp in Jerusalem burns because of a covenant God made with David, and no son's sin can put out what God has promised to keep.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: green, i.e. a young ear of grain; hence, the name of the month Abib or Nisan
BiblicalUsage: Abib is the month of green ears of grain — the first month, the month of the Exodus. ‘This day came ye out in the month Abib’; and Moses tells Israel to ‘observe the month of Abib, and keep the passover unto the LORD thy God: for in the month of Abib the LORD thy God brought thee forth out of Egypt by night.’
TheologicalSignificance: The year starts with green grain and a night escape — the calendar itself remembers the Exodus — and I believe God marks time by redemption, dating every year after from freedom.
RelatedEvents: The Passover; The Exodus and the Red Sea
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Abida, a son of Abraham by Keturah
BiblicalUsage: Abida is a son of Midian, and so a grandson of Abraham by Keturah — named in the genealogy of Genesis 25:4 and repeated in 1 Chronicles 1:33. He belongs to the sons of the east, the children of Abraham's second family, who are sent away with gifts while Isaac keeps the promise.
TheologicalSignificance: A grandson of Abraham who does not inherit the promise, named and then left in the genealogy. I believe Abida is a quiet reminder that not every child of Abraham is a child of the promise — and that God's blessing runs by His choice, not by bloodline alone.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: labor or business
BiblicalUsage: In Aramaic this word means work or business — the affairs of a province. Daniel asks that his friends be 'set over the affairs of the province of Babylon'; the accusers charge that the three 'are set over the affairs' yet serve not the king's gods; and in Ezra the same word is the work of the house of God, which ceased when the builders were stopped.
TheologicalSignificance: The three friends are faithful in the king's business and faithless to the king's gods — both at once. I believe that is the pattern for God's people in a foreign court: do the work well, serve the king honestly, and refuse the one thing that belongs to God alone.
RelatedEvents: Daniel's Resolve in Babylon; Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego in the Fiery Furnace
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Abidan, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Abidan the son of Gideoni is the prince of Benjamin in the wilderness — named in the census of Numbers 1, in the offerings of the princes in Numbers 7, and in the marching order of Numbers 10. He brings his offering on the ninth day and leads Benjamin’s host when the camp moves.
TheologicalSignificance: A prince named four times, always in his place: counted, camped, offering, marching. I believe Abidan's story is the story of order — God counts His people, sets them in their places, and moves them together, and no tribe marches alone.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Abigail or Abigal, the name of two Israelitesses
BiblicalUsage: Abigail is ‘a woman of good understanding, and of a beautiful countenance’, the wife of the churlish Nabal. When David marches to kill Nabal’s household, she rides out with provisions, bows before him, and talks him out of bloodguilt; after Nabal’s death she becomes David’s wife and follows him to Hebron. A second Abigail, David's sister, is named in 1 Chronicles 2:16.
TheologicalSignificance: Abigail stops a massacre with bread and a wise speech — and David thanks God for her. I believe she is one of the clearest pictures in Scripture of wisdom in action: she sees the danger, she moves quickly, she speaks truth with humility, and a whole household lives because she did.
RelatedPeople: Abigail; Abigail, Daughter of Nahash; King David; Nabal
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Abihail or Abichail, the name of three Israelites and two Israelitesses
BiblicalUsage: Abihail is the name of three men and two women. A Levite prince named Abihail fathers Zuriel; Abihail is the father of Esther and the uncle of Mordecai; and a daughter of Eliab named Abihail marries Rehoboam.
TheologicalSignificance: One name across five lives — a Levite, a Gadite, a king's wife, and the father of a queen. I believe the name Abihail is a reminder that God works through families I barely notice: Esther's father dies before the story starts, and still his name is the root of the rescue.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Abihu, a son of Aaron
BiblicalUsage: Abihu is the second son of Aaron, named with his brothers Nadab, Eleazar, and Ithamar. He goes up the mountain with Moses and sees God; and then, with Nadab, he offers ‘strange fire before the LORD, which he commanded them not’, and fire from the LORD devours them both.
TheologicalSignificance: Abihu stood on the mountain and saw God — and still died for offering strange fire. I believe his story is the sharpest warning in the priesthood: nearness to God is not a licence, and worship is only accepted on His terms, not mine.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Abihud, the name of two Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Abihud appears in two places and nowhere else. In Chronicles he is a son of Bela and a grandson of Benjamin — ‘And the sons of Bela were, Addar, and Gera, and Abihud’ — and in Matthew he stands in the genealogy of Jesus after the exile, between Zerubbabel and Eliakim.
TheologicalSignificance: One name in a genealogy, with no story attached — and still the line runs through him to Christ. I believe Abihud is there for people like me who feel unremarkable: God keeps His promise through quiet generations too, and a name in the line is enough.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Abimael, a son of Joktan
BiblicalUsage: Abimael is a son of Joktan, named in the table of nations in Genesis 10:28 and repeated in 1 Chronicles 1:22. He belongs to the line of Shem that spreads through Arabia — one of thirteen sons of Joktan whose descendants settle the south.
TheologicalSignificance: A name in the table of nations, with no story of his own — and still part of the record of how the earth was peopled after the flood. I believe the table of nations is the Bible's way of saying every people has a place in God's story, even the ones we never hear about again.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Abimelek, the name of two Philistine kings and of two Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Abimelech is the name of two Philistine kings of Gerar — one who takes Sarah and is warned by God in a dream, one who watches Isaac’s wells and makes a covenant with him. It is also the name of Gideon’s son, who murders his seventy brothers, is made king of Shechem, and dies when a woman drops a millstone on his head.
TheologicalSignificance: The same name covers a king God warns in mercy and a son who murders his way to a throne. I believe the two Abimelechs show me the two roads a name can take: one listens when God speaks in a dream, and the other listens to no one — and the end of each road is very different.
RelatedEvents: Abraham and Abimelech; Abimelech's Rise and Fall
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Abinadab, the name of four Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Abinadab is the name of four Israelites. The ark lodges at the house of Abinadab in Kirjath-jearim for twenty years; Jesse’s second son Abinadab is passed over when Samuel anoints David; and Uzzah the son of Abinadab dies touching the ark.
TheologicalSignificance: Four men share the name, and the ark runs through three of them — housed, passed over, and mishandled. I believe Abinadab’s name is tied to the ark because God keeps His presence near ordinary households, and how we treat holy things matters more than how long we have lived beside them.
RelatedEvents: David Brings the Ark to Jerusalem
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Abinoam, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Abinoam is the father of Barak, named in Deborah's call to battle and in her song of victory: 'Hath not the LORD God of Israel commanded, saying, Go and draw toward mount Tabor, and take with thee ten thousand men... Barak the son of Abinoam?' He is known only as a father, in the story of his son's victory.
TheologicalSignificance: A father named only because his son answered God's call — and that is enough. I believe Abinoam's three verses honour the fathers behind the fighters: Barak goes to Tabor, Deborah sings, and the name of the father who raised him is written into the song.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: provocative of desire; the caper berry (from its stimulative taste)
BiblicalUsage: The caper berry is named once, in Ecclesiastes 12:5, in the picture of old age: 'the almond tree shall flourish, and the grasshopper shall be a burden, and desire shall fail.' The caper berry was a stimulant, a spice for appetite — and in old age, even desire fails.
TheologicalSignificance: A spice for appetite, named at the moment appetite dies — the Preacher uses it to say that age takes even our wants, and the time to remember my Creator is now.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: mighty (spoken of God)
BiblicalUsage: This word for the mighty is used only of God — never of men. Jacob blesses Joseph by the hands of ‘the mighty God of Jacob’; David vows to the mighty God of Jacob and will not rest until he finds Him a dwelling; and Isaiah calls the LORD ‘the mighty One of Israel’ who will ease Himself of His adversaries.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word is set apart on purpose: might belongs to God in a way it belongs to no man. The same Scriptures that call Him the Mighty One show kings boasting in their own strength and falling, and I would rather rest in His might than trust my own.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Abiram, the name of two Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Abiram is the name of two Israelites. One joins Korah’s rebellion against Moses and Aaron, and the earth opens and swallows him with Dathan; the other is the firstborn son of Hiel, who dies when his father rebuilds Jericho — ‘he laid the foundation thereof in Abiram his firstborn’, fulfilling Joshua’s curse.
TheologicalSignificance: Two men, one name, and both die for rebellion — one against Moses, one against the word spoken over Jericho. I believe Abiram's name is a double warning: the earth keeps the record of those who rise against God's appointed leaders, and a curse spoken by God does not fade with time.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Abishag, a concubine of David
BiblicalUsage: Abishag the Shunammite is the young woman brought to cherish King David in his old age — 'a very fair damsel' who ministers to him and lies in his bosom, 'but the king knew her not.' After David's death Adonijah asks for her as wife, and Solomon treats the request as a claim on the throne and has him put to death.
TheologicalSignificance: A servant girl caught between two princes, and her body becomes a claim on a kingdom. I believe Abishag's story shows how power uses people — Adonijah wanted her as a step to the throne, and Solomon saw through it — and how a woman with no voice in the matter still ends up at the centre of the kingdom's politics.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Abshalom, a son of David; also (the fuller form) a later Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Abishalom — Absalom — is David’s third son, born to Maacah in Hebron, who murders Amnon for Tamar, flees to Geshur, returns, steals the hearts of Israel, and rebels against his father before he is caught by his hair in an oak and killed by Joab. The fuller form ‘Abishalom’ also names the father of Maachah in the days of Rehoboam.
TheologicalSignificance: Absalom had everything — beauty, a father's love, a kingdom within reach — and he threw it away for revenge and ambition. I believe his story is the saddest in the Bible about a son: David weeps 'O my son Absalom, my son, my son Absalom! would God I had died for thee', and no victory that day could cover the loss.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Abishai, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Abishai the son of Zeruiah is David’s nephew and one of his chief captains — the brother of Joab and Asahel. He goes down with David into Saul’s camp and wants to strike the sleeping king; he leads a third of the army against the Ammonites; and he is chief among the three mighty men who broke through the Philistines to bring David water from Bethlehem.
TheologicalSignificance: Abishai is the loyal man in the shadows — brave, fierce, and always at David's side, even when his counsel is wrong. I believe his story shows me that loyalty is not the same as wisdom: David has to restrain him more than once, and the best service is a loyal heart under a wise king's command.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Abishua, the name of two Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Abishua is the name of two Israelites. One is the son of Phinehas in the high-priestly line — ‘Phinehas begat Abishua’ — in the genealogy of Aaron and of Ezra himself; the other is a son of Bela in the tribe of Benjamin.
TheologicalSignificance: A priest in Aaron's line and a Benjamite with the same name — one carries the priesthood forward, the other simply belongs to the tribe. I believe the two Abishuas show how God's record works: the famous line and the quiet line are written on the same page, and both are His.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Abishur, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Abishur is named once, in 1 Chronicles 2:28, as a son of Shammai of the tribe of Judah: 'And the sons of Shammai were... Abishur, whose wife was Abihail, and she bare him Ahban and Molid.' He is one name in the genealogy of Judah, the tribe of the promise.
TheologicalSignificance: One verse in the genealogy of Judah, with a wife and two sons named beside him — and nothing more. I believe that is enough to matter: Abishur sits in the tribe that leads to David and to Christ, and the Bible does not lose the small names on the way to the great one.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Abital, a wife of King David
BiblicalUsage: Abital is named twice, as a wife of David and the mother of Shephatiah — 'the fifth, Shephatiah the son of Abital' in the list of David's sons born at Hebron, repeated in the Chronicles genealogy. She is one of the wives named only in the family lists.
TheologicalSignificance: A wife named twice, a son named once, and no story of her own. I believe Abital belongs to the quiet women of the Bible whose names are kept even when their stories are not — mothers in the line of David, remembered by God if not by history.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Abitub, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Abitub is named once, in 1 Chronicles 8:11, as a son of Shaharaim by Hushim in the genealogy of Benjamin: 'And of Hushim he begat Abitub, and Elpaal.' He is one name in the Benjamite line, with no deed or story attached.
TheologicalSignificance: A single name in a genealogy is the whole record of Abitub, and it carries no teaching of its own. What it does tell me is that God's book keeps the small names: a son of Shaharaim, in the tribe of Benjamin, written down and never lost.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Abner, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Abner the son of Ner is Saul’s captain and the commander of his army. He introduces David to Saul after Goliath falls; he makes Ishbosheth king after Saul’s death and fights David’s men for years; he defects to David and is murdered by Joab at Hebron — a death David mourns and Joab is never forgiven for.
TheologicalSignificance: Abner is the able man on the wrong side, and then on the right side too late — a general who backs the wrong king, sees the truth, and is killed before he can finish crossing over. I believe his story warns me that seeing the truth is not the same as being safe in it, and that a life of fighting for the wrong cause ends in a grave even David weeps over.
RelatedEvents: David Becomes King; David's War with the House of Saul
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a belt
BiblicalUsage: The abnet is the embroidered sash or girdle — part of the priest’s garments and the royal official’s dress. It is listed among Aaron’s holy garments, woven of fine linen and needlework; and Moses girds Aaron with it at the consecration.
TheologicalSignificance: A sash sounds small, but it is the piece that holds the garments together and marks the man as set apart for service — a picture of readiness, of a priest girded for work.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: work of any kind
BiblicalUsage: This is the noun for work or service — the labour itself, whether Jacob's seven years for Rachel, Egypt's 'rigorous service' laid on Israel, the 'servile work' forbidden on the holy days, or the Levites' 'service of the ministry' in the tabernacle. The same word covers the slave's burden and the priest's duty.
TheologicalSignificance: One word holds both slavery and worship, and the difference is the master. I believe that is the Bible's whole teaching on work: service is not degrading in itself — it is degrading only when the master is cruel, and holy when the Master is God.
RelatedEvents: Jacob and Laban; The Exodus and the Red Sea
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: something intwined, i.e. a string, wreath or foliage
BiblicalUsage: This word names something twisted or interlaced — wreathen chains of pure gold on the high priest’s breastplate, fastened to the ephod, and the ‘wreaths of chain work’ on the capitals of Solomon’s pillars. It is the work of the craftsman, gold and bronze twisted into ornament.
TheologicalSignificance: It is a craftsman’s word, and it carries no doctrine of its own — though I notice where the wreathen work goes: on the breastplate over the priest’s heart and on the pillars of the house, beauty set where God is worshipped.
RelatedEvents: The Tabernacle Is Built; Building of Solomon's Temple
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: intwined, i.e. dense
BiblicalUsage: This adjective for thick or dense is used of trees — ‘the boughs of thick trees’ that Israel is commanded to take for the Feast of Tabernacles, and the branches gathered in Nehemiah’s day to build the booths. In both places the thick branches shelter the feast, a covering God Himself commands.
TheologicalSignificance: The word itself carries no doctrine — it only describes the branches — but it shows me God providing the very covering for the feast He commands, down to the boughs.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a pawn
BiblicalUsage: This is the word for a pledge — something taken as security for a debt. The law forbids taking a millstone as pledge, ‘for he taketh a man’s life to pledge’; and a neighbour’s raiment taken in pledge must be returned by sunset.
TheologicalSignificance: The law guards the pledge because it guards the poor — a man’s millstone is his life, and his cloak is his blanket — and I believe the pledge laws show me God’s heart for the borrower.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: want
BiblicalUsage: This word for woe or want occurs once, in Proverbs 23:29: 'Who hath woe? who hath sorrow? who hath contentions? who hath babbling? who hath wounds without cause? who hath redness of eyes?' It opens the proverb's portrait of the drunkard — six questions, and the answer is the man who tarries long at the wine.
TheologicalSignificance: One word opens a whole portrait of ruin — woe, sorrow, contentions, babbling, wounds, red eyes — and I believe the proverb asks ‘who hath woe?’ so that I will answer honestly and turn away before the woe is mine.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H85); Abraham, the Hebrew patriarch:--Abraham. (In Acts 7:16 the text should probably read Jacob.)
BiblicalUsage: Abraham is the name God gives Abram in Genesis 17:5 — ‘Neither shall thy name any more be called Abram, but thy name shall be Abraham; for a father of many nations have I made thee.’ From there it is the name of the covenant — the birth of Isaac, the binding on Moriah — and the name Paul reaches for when he writes that Abraham’s faith ‘was counted unto him for righteousness’.
TheologicalSignificance: God renames a childless old man ‘father of many nations’ before he has the son of promise — the name is a prophecy before it is a fact. I believe that is how God works with me too: He names me by what He will make of me, and the name is His promise that He will finish what He began.
RelatedEvents: The Call of Abraham; The Binding of Isaac
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Abraham, the later name of Abram
BiblicalUsage: Abraham is the name God gives Abram in Genesis 17:5 — ‘Neither shall thy name any more be called Abram, but thy name shall be Abraham; for a father of many nations have I made thee.’ From there it is the name of the covenant — the birth of Isaac, the binding on Moriah — and the name Paul reaches for when he writes that Abraham’s faith ‘was counted unto him for righteousness’.
TheologicalSignificance: God renames a childless old man ‘father of many nations’ before he has the son of promise — the name is a prophecy before it is a fact. I believe that is how God works with me too: He names me by what He will make of me, and the name is His promise that He will finish what He began.
RelatedEvents: The Call of Abraham; The Binding of Isaac
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Abram, the original name of Abraham
BiblicalUsage: Abram is the name Abraham carries for the first part of his story — the son of Terah in Ur, the man called out in Genesis 12:1, ‘Get thee out of thy country, and from thy kindred, and from thy father’s house, unto a land that I will shew thee.’ He goes out with nothing but the call, and under the stars God promises him a son and a nation before he has either.
TheologicalSignificance: Abram means 'exalted father', and he is an old man with no child when God calls him — the name is almost a joke until God renames him. I believe the Abram years teach me that God calls people before they look like anything: the call comes first, the child comes later, and the land comes last.
RelatedEvents: The Call of Abraham; Abram in Egypt
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: kneel
BiblicalUsage: This word occurs once, in Genesis 41:43, when Pharaoh sets Joseph over Egypt: 'he made him to ride in the second chariot which he had; and they cried before him, Bow the knee: and he made him ruler over all the land of Egypt.' It is the herald's cry — the command for all Egypt to kneel as Joseph passes.
TheologicalSignificance: One cry, and a slave becomes a ruler — ‘Bow the knee’ — and I believe the word points further than Joseph, to the day when every knee will bow.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: something pledged, i.e. (collectively) pawned goods
BiblicalUsage: This word for pawned goods — 'thick clay' in the King James — occurs once, in Habakkuk 2:6: 'Woe to him that increaseth that which is not his! how long? and to him that ladeth himself with thick clay!' It pictures the plunderer loading himself with goods taken in pledge, growing heavier with every stolen weight.
TheologicalSignificance: One verse, and the image is unforgettable — a man loading himself with thick clay until he can barely move — and I believe that is the picture of greed: every unjust gain is weight, not wealth.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: something wrought, i.e. (concretely) service
BiblicalUsage: This word for a body of servants — a household staff — occurs twice. Isaac has 'great store of servants' alongside his flocks and herds, and the Philistines envy him; Job has 'a very great household' alongside his seven thousand sheep and three thousand camels, and he is 'the greatest of all the men of the east'.
TheologicalSignificance: Both men are measured by their households, and both lose them — Isaac by envy, Job by calamity. I believe the word is a quiet warning about wealth: a great household is a sign of God's blessing, and it is also the first thing envy and suffering take aim at.
RelatedEvents: Isaac in Gerar; Job's Suffering and Restoration
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: passed, i.e. kept over; used only of stored grain
BiblicalUsage: This word for stored grain — the old corn of the land — occurs only in Joshua 5:11-12. The day after the Passover, Israel eats 'of the old corn of the land... unleavened cakes, and parched corn in the selfsame day. And the manna ceased on the morrow after they had eaten of the old corn of the land.'
TheologicalSignificance: The manna stops the day Israel eats the old corn — forty years of daily bread ends, and the land feeds them instead — and I believe that is the moment the wilderness ends.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)
