TheologicalSignificance: Lentils are humble food, and the stories they sit in — a birthright sold for pottage, a hero's stand in a lentil field — carry the warning.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to tread out (grain)
BiblicalUsage: To thresh, to tread out the grain — adash appears once: "Bread corn is bruised; because he will not ever be threshing it, nor break it with the wheel of his cart, nor bruise it with his horsemen." The farmer threshes to feed, not to destroy, and he knows when to stop.
TheologicalSignificance: One verse about threshing is a farmer's picture, and the comfort in it is God's limit — He bruises the corn to make bread, not to make dust.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Adajah, the name of eight Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Adaiah is the name of three men: the grandfather of Josiah the reforming king, a priest who backed Jehoiada when Joash was crowned, and a Benjamite in the genealogy of the tribe. Beyond these verses the Bible tells no more of them.
TheologicalSignificance: No doctrine hangs on any of the three. But the first of them sits close to a king who found the Book of the Law and tore his clothes over it — and I hold that as a reminder that reform often runs in families.
RelatedEvents: Josiah Finds the Book of the Law
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Adbeel, a son of Ishmael
BiblicalUsage: Adbeel was a son of Ishmael, named in the record of the twelve princes of Ishmael's line, a desert prince counted among the sons of Abraham's firstborn.
TheologicalSignificance: Ishmael's line is named, counted, and blessed in its own way — I hold that as worth saying. The promise belonged to Isaac, but God did not forget the other son, and He kept his sons' names too.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Addan, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Addan was a place in Babylon from which exiles came up to Jerusalem, whose people could not prove their father's house or whether they were of Israel. As a place, Addan is covered in the Biblical Places collection rather than in a biography.
TheologicalSignificance: There is little doctrine here, and I will not force one. But the record keeps the names of those who could not prove theirs — and I hold that as a kindness: they came home, and they were counted.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Addar, a place in Palestine; also an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Addar is both a man and a place: a son of Bela in Benjamin's line, and a town on the southern border of Judah, where the boundary 'went up to Adar' toward Kadesh-barnea. The man lives on his People profile, and the town is covered in the Biblical Places collection.
TheologicalSignificance: No doctrine hangs on either use. The genealogy keeps the son, and the boundary list keeps the town, and both are kept because the tribe and the land were counted.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: something ample (as a large vine, a wide dress)
BiblicalUsage: A mantle, a wide garment, a robe — addereth is the cloak that marks a prophet. Esau came out "all over like an hairy garment"; Elijah wrapped his face in his mantle at Horeb, cast it on Elisha, and struck the Jordan with it; Elisha took it up when his master was gone; and false prophets are warned not to wear "a rough garment to deceive." The mantle passes from prophet to prophet, and the garment itself is never the point.
TheologicalSignificance: A mantle is cloth, not power, and the lesson is that the Spirit passed with it from Elijah to Elisha because God gives His Spirit to whom He will.
RelatedEvents: Elijah Taken Up in a Chariot of Fire
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably of Hebrew origin (compare H5716); Addi, an Israelite:--Addi.
BiblicalUsage: Addi shows up once, in Luke's genealogy of Jesus, as the son of Cosam and the father of Melchi. Luke lists him without a story of his own, one link in the long chain that runs from Adam to Jesus; Luke's genealogy is the whole of his story, with no fuller profile beyond it.
TheologicalSignificance: A name like this carries no teaching of its own, and I won't pretend it does. Its weight is the weight of the genealogy itself: Jesus was born into a real human line, with real ancestors whose names Luke bothered to record.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: wide or (generally) large; figuratively, powerful
BiblicalUsage: Addiyr is a word for size and majesty — the mighty waters of the Red Sea, the Lord's excellent name, the nobles and princes of the nations. It describes whatever stands tall and commands notice, from a great cedar to a king. Most often it is used of God Himself, whose name and whose power are excellent above all.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that addiyr matters because it gives us a word for God's sheer scale. He is not merely better than the idols or the kings — He is majestic in a way that makes everything else look small, and His name carries that weight wherever it is praised.
RelatedTopics: God's glory; Majesty of God; God's Power
RelatedEvents: The Exodus and the Red Sea
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Addon, apparently an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Addon is one of the towns named in the lists of exiles who came back from Babylon — families returning to a land their grandparents had lost. In Ezra's list the name is spelled Addan; the place itself is covered in the Biblical Places collection.
TheologicalSignificance: There is no doctrine tucked inside this place-name, and I won't invent one. What it does show is how carefully the returning exiles guarded who belonged where — lineage mattered to them, and the record kept the question open rather than guessing.
RelatedTopics: Exile and Return; Return from exile
RelatedEvents: Cyrus's Decree and Return from Exile
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: adverb from G82; uncertainly:--uncertainly.
BiblicalUsage: Paul uses this one word, once, in a picture of himself as a boxer: 'I therefore so run, not as uncertainly; so fight I, not as one that beateth the air.' The adverb describes running without a clear aim — movement that goes nowhere.
TheologicalSignificance: There is no deep theology hiding in this one; it does plain work in its sentence, and the weight lies with the passage, not the word; in this case, the verse is 1 Corinthians 9:26.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and G1212; hidden, figuratively, indistinct:--appear not, uncertain.
BiblicalUsage: Adelos means hidden or indistinct — something you cannot see clearly enough to be sure of it. Jesus used it of unmarked graves that people walked over without knowing, and Paul used it of a trumpet giving an uncertain sound, so no one knew whether to prepare for battle.
TheologicalSignificance: Nothing here asks for a theological system; the word simply does its job in the text, and the passage does the teaching; in this case, the verse is Luke 11:44.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G82; uncertainty:--X uncertain.
BiblicalUsage: Adelotes appears once, in Paul's charge to the rich: do not trust in 'uncertain riches.' The word names what wealth really is — something that cannot be counted on, here today and gone tomorrow. Paul sets it against the living God, who gives richly and can be trusted.
TheologicalSignificance: The word does not preach — the passage does — so I keep the two straight and let this one stay what it is; in this case, the verse is 1 Timothy 6:17.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: feminine of G80; a sister (naturally or ecclesiastically):--sister.
BiblicalUsage: Adelphe is simply 'sister,' used both of blood sisters — Mary and Martha, sisters of Lazarus — and of sisters in the faith, like Phoebe, whom Paul commends to the church at Rome. Jesus stretches the word further still: whoever does the will of His Father is His sister. In the New Testament the word is never small; it names a real bond, whether of birth or of belief.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this word matters because it shows how the gospel remakes family. In Christ, 'sister' is not just a courtesy title — it is a true relationship, with the duties of love and care that belong to family.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a connective particle) and δελφύς (the womb); a brother (literally or figuratively) near or remote (much like G1):--brother.
BiblicalUsage: Adelphos is 'brother,' and the New Testament uses it constantly — for literal brothers like Andrew bringing Simon to Jesus, for fellow Jews, and above all for fellow believers. Jesus says whoever does the will of His Father is His brother, and John says love for the brethren is the mark of having passed from death to life. The word carries the whole weight of belonging to one family under one Father.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that adelphos is one of the great words of the New Testament because it refuses to let faith stay private. If God is our Father, then other believers are truly our brothers, and love for them is not optional — it is the evidence of life in us.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G80; brotherhood (properly, the feeling of brotherliness), i.e. the (Christian) fraternity:--brethren, brotherhood.
BiblicalUsage: Adelphotes is the brotherhood itself — the whole company of believers, named as one body. Peter uses it twice: once in the command to honour everyone and love the brotherhood, and once in the assurance that the same sufferings are being endured by the brotherhood throughout the world. It is the only place the word appears, and both times it gathers scattered Christians into a single family.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this word is a comfort to anyone who feels alone in their faith. The brotherhood is worldwide, and the suffering you face is shared — you are not the only one standing, and you are not standing alone.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a derivative of ἀδέω (to be sated to loathing); to be in distress (of mind):--be full of heaviness, be very heavy.
BiblicalUsage: Ademoneo is distress of mind — heaviness that presses down on the soul. Matthew and Mark use it of Jesus in Gethsemane, sorrowful and very heavy as He faced the cross, and Paul uses it of Epaphroditus, distressed because the Philippians had heard he was ill. The word covers both the Saviour's agony and a missionary's anxious care for his friends.
TheologicalSignificance: This word tells me that heaviness of heart is not unspiritual — Jesus Himself felt it, and Scripture names it plainly. The same Saviour who was very heavy in Gethsemane understands the weight His people carry, and He does not despise them for feeling it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: till now
BiblicalUsage: Aden means 'till now' or 'yet,' and it appears only twice, both in Ecclesiastes 4, where the Preacher weighs the living against the dead and against those never yet born. The living are 'yet alive,' still under the sun and still seeing its evils; the unborn have 'not yet been.' The little word holds the whole comparison together — life as it stands now, under the sun.
TheologicalSignificance: The meaning here is plain and narrow, and the weight of the passage rests on the whole verse, not on this single word; in this case, the verse is Ecclesiastes 4:2.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and a derivative of G1252; properly, undistinguished, i.e. (actively) impartial:--without partiality.
BiblicalUsage: Adiakritos appears once, in James's portrait of the wisdom from above: it is 'without partiality, and without hypocrisy.' The word means undivided, not making distinctions between people. Heavenly wisdom does not pick favourites or play sides; it treats people the same, whether they are rich or poor, friend or stranger.
TheologicalSignificance: I won't build doctrine on a word this small — its job is to hold a sentence together, and the teaching belongs to the passage it sits in; in this case, the verse is James 3:17.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: adverb from G88; uninterruptedly, i.e. without omission (on an appropriate occasion):--without ceasing.
BiblicalUsage: Adialeiptos is 'without ceasing' — Paul's word for prayer and remembrance that never lets up. He tells the Romans he mentions them without ceasing, tells the Thessalonians to pray without ceasing, and tells Timothy he remembers him in his prayers night and day.
TheologicalSignificance: The word itself is a detail, not a doctrine, and the truth it serves belongs to the passage that uses it; in this case, the verse is Romans 1:9.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and a derivative of a compound of G1223 and G3007; unintermitted, i.e. permanent:--without ceasing, continual.
BiblicalUsage: Adialeiptos is the adjective form — 'unceasing' or 'continual.' Paul uses it twice: once of the continual sorrow in his heart for his fellow Jews who have not believed, and once of his unceasing remembrance of Timothy in prayer. One word carries both his grief and his devotion, neither of them switched off.
TheologicalSignificance: This word is a footnote in the story, not a headline, and its value is in the sentence it completes rather than in itself; in this case, the verse is Romans 9:2.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a derivative of a compound of G1 (as a negative particle) and a derivative of G1311; incorruptibleness, i.e. (figuratively) purity (of doctrine):--uncorruptness.
BiblicalUsage: Adiaphthoria appears once, in Paul's instruction to Titus: show yourself a pattern of good works, 'in doctrine shewing uncorruptness, gravity, sincerity.' The word means incorruptness — teaching that has not been spoiled or watered down. A young leader's doctrine is to be sound all the way through, with nothing rotten in it.
TheologicalSignificance: I won't squeeze theology out of a word that was written to name a thing plainly — the verse around it does the teaching; in this case, the verse is Titus 2:7.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G91; a wrong done:--evil doing, iniquity, matter of wrong.
BiblicalUsage: Adikema is a wrong done — a specific act of injustice rather than wrongness in general. Gallio uses it when the Jews accuse Paul, asking whether he has done any 'matter of wrong'; Paul uses it before Felix, challenging his accusers to name his 'evil doing'; and Revelation uses it of Babylon, whose iniquities God has remembered. The word always points at something done, something that can be named and judged.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that this word keeps judgment honest. God does not judge vague badness; He judges deeds — real wrongs, done by real people, with real victims — and the same word that accuses Babylon also promises that every wrong will be answered.
RelatedEvents: Paul Before Felix, Festus, and Agrippa
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G94; to be unjust, i.e. (actively) do wrong (morally, socially or physically):--hurt, injure, be an offender, be unjust, (do, suffer, take) wrong.
BiblicalUsage: Adikeo is the verb for doing wrong or causing hurt — to wrong someone, to injure them, or to suffer wrong yourself. The householder tells the grumbling labourer, 'I do thee no wrong'; Jesus promises His disciples that nothing shall by any means hurt them; Stephen's speech remembers Moses defending a man who suffered wrong; and the risen Christ promises the overcomer shall not be hurt of the second death. The word covers the whole range, from a labour dispute to eternal safety.
TheologicalSignificance: What I take from this word is the promise tucked inside it: those who belong to Christ may be wronged here, but they will not be hurt in the end. The second death has no claim on them, and that is a stronger word than any injury this life can hand out.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G94; (legal) injustice (properly, the quality, by implication, the act); morally, wrongfulness (of character, life or act):--iniquity, unjust, unrighteousness, wrong.
BiblicalUsage: Adikia is unrighteousness — wrongfulness as a quality and as an act, the opposite of what is right before God. Jesus tells of the unjust steward, Paul says God's wrath is revealed against all unrighteousness, and John says all unrighteousness is sin. It is one of the New Testament's broadest words for evil, covering unjust deeds, unjust character, and unjust systems alike.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe adikia matters because it names sin for what it is: not just mistakes, but wrongness — things out of line with God's righteousness. And the same Scriptures that name it also name the cure: Christ, who became our righteousness, so that the unrighteous can stand right before God.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: adverb from G94; unjustly:--wrongfully.
BiblicalUsage: Adikos is the adverb 'unjustly' or 'wrongfully,' and it appears only once: when a servant endures grief, 'suffering wrongfully,' for conscience toward God. Peter is talking about the person who is punished for doing nothing wrong, and who bears it patiently because God sees.
TheologicalSignificance: Its job is finished inside its sentence; the theology, if there is any to find, belongs to the passage as a whole; in this case, the verse is 1 Peter 2:19.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and G1349; unjust; by extension wicked; by implication, treacherous; specially, heathen:--unjust, unrighteous.
BiblicalUsage: Adikos is 'unjust' or 'unrighteous' — the person who is not right before God. Jesus says the Father sends rain on the just and on the unjust; the Pharisee thanks God he is not like other men, 'unjust'; Paul warns that the unrighteous shall not inherit the kingdom; and Peter says Christ suffered, the just for the unjust, to bring us to God. The word draws the line between the two kinds of people, and then the gospel crosses it.
TheologicalSignificance: This word humbles me, because before Christ I stand on the unjust side of that line. I believe the wonder of the gospel is right here in Peter's sentence: the Just One died for the unjust, so that the unjust could be brought to God.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Adiel, the name of three Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Adiel is the name of three different Israelites in Chronicles: a prince of Simeon, a priest named as the father of Maasiai, and the father of Azmaveth, who was over King David's treasures. The name means 'ornament of God,' but Scripture gives us no story for any of the three — only their places in the lists, their families, and their duties.
TheologicalSignificance: A name in a list carries no doctrine, and I won't pretend otherwise. What these three Adiels do show is that God's people were counted and remembered — even the treasurers and the priests whose names never made it into a story.
RelatedPeople: Adiel, Prince of Simeon; Adiel, Father of Maasiai; Adiel, Father of Azmaveth
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: finery; generally an outfit; specifically, a headstall
BiblicalUsage: Adiy is finery — the ornaments and jewellery people wore, and the word carries both beauty and danger. At Sinai the people stripped off their ornaments in mourning after the golden calf; David's lament remembers the daughters of Israel clothed in scarlet with ornaments of gold; Isaiah promises Zion will wear her children as ornaments; and Jeremiah asks how a bride can forget her ornaments — or a virgin her attire — yet Israel forgot God.
TheologicalSignificance: This word does a small, honest job in Scripture, and I won't dress it up as a doctrine — the verse it sits in carries the meaning; in this case, the verse is Exodus 33:4.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Adin, the name of two Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Adin is the head of a family that came back from exile — 454 of his sons in Ezra's list — and one of his descendants, Ebed, came up with Ezra himself. His name also appears among those who sealed the covenant in Nehemiah's day.
TheologicalSignificance: There is no teaching hidden in this name, and I won't invent one. Its value is the record it keeps: whole families came home, signed their names to the covenant, and belonged again to God's people after the exile.
RelatedTopics: Exile and Return; Return from exile; Covenant renewal
RelatedEvents: Cyrus's Decree and Return from Exile
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: voluptuous
BiblicalUsage: Adiyn means voluptuous — given to pleasure, soft and self-indulgent — and it appears only once, in God's judgment on Babylon: 'thou that art given to pleasures, that dwellest carelessly, that sayest in thine heart, I am, and none else beside me.' The word paints a city drunk on its own comfort, certain that nothing can touch it, on the very edge of ruin.
TheologicalSignificance: I won't force this word to carry more than it was written to carry; the teaching lives in its verse, and that is enough; in this case, the verse is Isaiah 47:8.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Adina, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Adina is named once, in the list of David's mighty men: 'Adina the son of Shiza the Reubenite, a captain of the Reubenites, and thirty with him.' That is all Scripture says — a name, a father, a tribe, a rank, and thirty men under him.
TheologicalSignificance: This is a name in a roster, not a teaching, and I won't stretch it into one. Its quiet value is that God counted the captains as well as the kings — thirty men, one captain, and a name the record did not let go of.
RelatedPeople: Adina, Son of Shiza; King David
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: his spear
BiblicalUsage: Adiynow — 'his spear' — appears once, in the list of David's mighty men, where the text names Adino the Eznite, chief among the captains, who 'lift up his spear against eight hundred, whom he slew at one time.' The name itself is bound up with the weapon: the man is remembered by the spear he lifted and the battle he won alone against eight hundred.
TheologicalSignificance: Its contribution is small and specific, and whatever it adds to my faith comes through the passage that uses it; in this case, the verse is 2 Samuel 23:8.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Adithajim, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Adithaim is a town named once, in the list of cities given to Judah in the lowland — between Sharaim and Gederah, in the Shephelah west of Jerusalem. It appears in no story and no battle; it is simply one of the towns that made up Judah's inheritance, marked on the map and then left alone; the place itself is covered in the Biblical Places collection.
TheologicalSignificance: A town named once carries no teaching of its own, and I won't invent one for it. Its place in the list is enough: the land God promised was divided town by town, and even the towns without stories belonged to His people.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Adlai, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Adlai is named once, as the father of Shaphat, who was over David's herds in the valleys. That is the whole record — a father, a son, and a job in the king's service.
TheologicalSignificance: This name holds no doctrine, and I won't dress it up as one. It is a reminder that the kingdom ran on ordinary work — herds in the valleys, men to watch them — and the record kept the names of the families behind that work.
RelatedPeople: Adlai, Father of Shaphat; King David
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Admah, a place near the Dead Sea
BiblicalUsage: Admah was one of the cities of the plain, named beside Sodom, Gomorrah, Zeboiim, and Bela. Its kings went to war against Chedorlaomer, and the city was destroyed with Sodom in the overthrow of the plain; the place itself is covered in the Biblical Places collection.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Admah's story is a mercy as much as a warning. God destroyed it, and then, speaking through Hosea, He says He will not do the same to His people — His heart recoils, His compassions are kindled, and judgment gives way to a love that refuses to let go.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Admatha, a Persian nobleman
BiblicalUsage: Admatha was one of the seven princes of Persia and Media who saw the king's face and sat first in the kingdom. He appears once, in the council Ahasuerus calls after Queen Vashti refuses to come before him.
TheologicalSignificance: A courtier's name carries no doctrine, and I won't pretend it does. His value is in the setting: the empire that could summon seven princes over a queen's refusal is the same empire where God was quietly positioning Esther for the saving of His people.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: reddish (of the hair or the complexion)
BiblicalUsage: Admoniy means reddish — of hair or complexion. Esau came out red all over, like a hairy garment, and the name Edom grew from it; David was ruddy, with a beautiful countenance, when Samuel came to anoint him; and Goliath looked at the boy and disdained him, because he was but a youth, and ruddy.
TheologicalSignificance: A word this rare cannot carry a theme by itself; what it offers is a clear detail inside a verse that does the real teaching; in this case, the verse is Genesis 25:25.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Adna, the name of two Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Adna is the name of two Israelites: one of the sons of Pahath-moab who had taken a foreign wife in Ezra's day and put her away, and a priest, head of the house of Harim, in the days of Joiakim the high priest. The two men share a name and nothing else — one in a list of repentance, one in a list of priests.
TheologicalSignificance: A shared name across two lists carries no teaching, and I won't invent one. Taken together, the two Adnas show the two sides of the return: putting away what God forbade, and keeping the priesthood in order for worship to go on.
RelatedPeople: Adna, Son of Pahath-moab; Adna, of Harim's Course
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Adnah, the name of two Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Adnah is the name of two men: a captain of Manasseh who defected to David at Ziklag, and a captain of Judah under Jehoshaphat, in command of three hundred thousand mighty men of valour. One joined David when he was still an outlaw; the other stood in the ranks of a settled kingdom.
TheologicalSignificance: Two captains, one name, no doctrine hidden in it — I won't pretend otherwise. What I take from them is simpler: God used commanders as well as kings, and the men who brought their thousands to David and to Jehoshaphat are counted among the faithful.
RelatedPeople: Adnah, Captain of Manasseh; Adnah, Captain of Judah
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and G1384; unapproved, i.e. rejected; by implication, worthless (literally or morally):--castaway, rejected, reprobate.
BiblicalUsage: Adokimos is 'rejected' — metal that fails the test, a coin that does not ring true, a life that does not measure up. Paul says God gave those who refused Him over to a reprobate mind, warns that he himself could become a castaway if he does not discipline his body, tells the Corinthians to test themselves lest they be reprobates, and Hebrews says ground that bears thorns is rejected. The word always carries the picture of something tested and found wanting.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this is one of the soberest words in the New Testament, and I take it seriously. It is a call to examine myself, not to despair — because the same Paul who warns of being a castaway also tells us to test ourselves, so that we may know we are in the faith.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle); and G1388; undeceitful, i.e. (figuratively) unadulterated:--sincere.
BiblicalUsage: Adolos appears once: 'As newborn babes, desire the sincere milk of the word, that ye may grow thereby.' The word means unadulterated — milk with nothing mixed into it, no water, no deceit.
TheologicalSignificance: A word like this earns its place by being precise, not by being profound — its meaning is spent inside the verse where it occurs; in this case, the verse is 1 Peter 2:2.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: rosy
BiblicalUsage: Adom is red — the red pottage Esau traded his birthright for, the water in the valley that looked red as blood to the Moabites, and the red in the garments of the Coming One in Isaiah's vision. The word colours hunger, war, and judgment, and each time the red means something is at stake: a birthright, a battle, or the winepress of God's wrath.
TheologicalSignificance: This one is a tool of language, not a theme of Scripture, so I leave the doctrine to the verse and let the word stay small; in this case, the verse is Genesis 25:30.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: the Lord (used as a proper name of God only)
BiblicalUsage: Adonay is 'the Lord,' used as a proper name for God alone — the name Abraham calls on when he asks what God will give him, the name Moses uses when he pleads his slowness of speech, the name the psalmist gives to the One who laughs at the raging nations and stands at the right hand to shatter kings. It is the name of the sovereign Master, spoken with reverence in place of the divine name itself.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Adonay teaches me how to address God: as Lord, as Master, as the One whose authority is total and whose laughter no rebellion can silence. It is a name of submission and of safety at once — the Lord who rules is the Lord who keeps.
RelatedEvents: The Call of Abraham; The Burning Bush
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Adoni-Bezek; a Canaanitish king
BiblicalUsage: Adoni-bezek was the Canaanite king of Bezek, defeated by Judah and Simeon at the start of the conquest. They cut off his thumbs and great toes, and he confessed that he had done the same to seventy kings — and that God had repaid him as he had done.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Adoni-bezek's confession is the point of his story: 'As I have done, so God hath requited me.' It is the law of sowing and reaping, spoken by a defeated king, and it stands as a warning that cruelty comes home.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Adoni-Tsedek, a Canaanitish king
BiblicalUsage: Adoni-zedek was king of Jerusalem when he heard that Joshua had taken Ai and that the Gibeonites had made peace with Israel. In fear he gathered four other kings and besieged Gibeon, and Joshua marched all night to rescue it.
TheologicalSignificance: This king's name — 'my lord is righteousness' — is an irony Scripture lets stand without comment. I believe his story shows that titles do not make a man righteous, and that no alliance of kings can stand against the Lord who fights for His people.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Adonijah, the name of three Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Adonijah was David's fourth son, born at Hebron, who tried to seize the throne while his father was dying. He gathered chariots and horsemen, sacrificed at En-rogel, and had himself proclaimed king — but Nathan and Bathsheba moved first, Solomon was anointed at Gihon, and Adonijah's feast broke up in fear.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Adonijah's story is a warning about grasping for what God has not given. The throne belonged to Solomon by God's word and David's oath, and no feast, no chariots, and no proclamation could take it from him.
RelatedPeople: Adonijah, Son of David; King David; King Solomon
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Adonikam, the name of one or two Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Adonikam is the head of a family that returned from exile — 666 of his sons in Ezra's list — and some of his later sons, Eliphelet, Jeiel, and Shemaiah, came up with Ezra, sixty males in all. His name appears again among those who sealed the covenant in Nehemiah's day.
TheologicalSignificance: No doctrine hides in this name, and I won't look for one. What it keeps is the scale of the return — hundreds in one family alone — and the fact that the same families who came home also put their names to the covenant.
RelatedTopics: Exile and Return; Return from exile; Covenant renewal
RelatedEvents: Cyrus's Decree and Return from Exile
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Adoniram, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Adoniram, son of Abda, was over the levy — the forced labour — under Solomon, and later under Rehoboam. He organised the thirty thousand men sent to Lebanon in monthly shifts to cut timber for the temple, and he was still over the tribute when the kingdom split.
TheologicalSignificance: There is no teaching in this man's name, only a career that ended badly. I take the warning plainly: Adoniram served two kings faithfully and was killed by the people he had taxed, and the kingdom that used him could not save him.
RelatedPeople: Adoniram, Officer of Solomon; King Solomon; Rehoboam
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Adoram (or Adoniram), an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Adoram — the same man as Adoniram — was over the tribute under David, Solomon, and Rehoboam. He is the one Rehoboam sent to the rebellious tribes after Solomon's death, hoping his old authority would calm them, and the people stoned him instead.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Adoram's end shows what happens when a king answers a people with force instead of listening. The man who had collected tribute for forty years became the first casualty of the split, and no title could protect him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: sovereign, i.e. controller (human or divine)
BiblicalUsage: Adown is 'lord' or 'master' — the word Sarah uses of Abraham, the word for the master a servant may choose to serve forever, and the word the psalmist uses when the LORD says to 'my Lord,' sit at My right hand. It covers human masters and the divine Master alike, and the difference is always in who is speaking and who is being addressed.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that adown matters because it teaches me what lordship means: a master who is obeyed, trusted, and loved. And when David's Lord is seated at God's right hand, I know my Master is not only above me but for me — ruling until every enemy is under His feet.
RelatedEvents: The Call of Abraham; The Burning Bush
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Adorajim, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Adoraim was one of the cities Rehoboam fortified after the kingdom split — a fenced city in Judah, stocked with food, oil, wine, shields, and spears. It appears only once, in the list of fifteen cities Rehoboam strengthened to hold what was left of his kingdom; the place itself is covered in the Biblical Places collection.
TheologicalSignificance: A fortified town in a list carries no doctrine, and I won't invent one. Its story is the story of a kingdom shrinking: Rehoboam could wall his cities, but no wall could give back the ten tribes he had lost.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Adrammelek, the name of an Assyrian idol, also of a son of Sennacherib
BiblicalUsage: Adrammelech is two things at once: the god of Sepharvaim, to whom the settlers in Samaria burnt their children in the fire, and the son of Sennacherib who, with his brother Sharezer, murdered his father in the temple of Nisroch and fled to Armenia. The idol and the murderer share a name, and both stand for the same thing — the violence of a world that has turned from the true God.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this name is a warning written twice: a god that demands children in the fire, and a son who murders his father in a temple. Both show what idolatry does to a people, and both fell before the God of Israel, who needs no such worship and permits no such crime.
RelatedPeople: Adrammelech; Sennacherib, King of Assyria; King Hezekiah
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from Ἀδραμύττειον (a place in Asia Minor); Adramyttene or belonging to Adramyttium:--of Adramyttium.
BiblicalUsage: Adramyttenos means 'of Adramyttium' — the ship Paul boarded at Caesarea was a ship of Adramyttium, a port on the coast of Asia Minor, bound for the ports along that coast. Luke names the ship's home the way a sailor would, and it is the only time the word appears; the place itself is covered in the Biblical Places collection.
TheologicalSignificance: This word carries no doctrine — it is a ship's registry, not a sermon, and I won't make it one. Its value is the plain fact it anchors: Paul really sailed, on a real ship, from a real port, on his way to stand before Caesar.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: quickly or carefully
BiblicalUsage: Adrazda is an Aramaic adverb meaning diligently, exactly, with care — and it appears only once, in King Artaxerxes' letter to Ezra: whatever the God of heaven commands 'shall be done diligently' for His house. The Persian king, who did not know this God, still ordered that His temple be supplied without delay and without excuse.
TheologicalSignificance: There is no creed in this word, only a clear meaning in context, and I am content to leave the theology to the verse around it; in this case, the verse is Ezra 7:23.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from Ἀδρία (a place near its shore); the Adriatic sea (including the Ionian):--Adria.
BiblicalUsage: Adrias is the Adriatic Sea — the stretch of water where Paul's ship was driven up and down in the storm, fourteen nights without seeing sun or stars, before it wrecked on Malta. Luke names the sea once, at the darkest point of the voyage, when the sailors suspected they were nearing land; the place itself is covered in the Biblical Places collection.
TheologicalSignificance: There is no doctrine in a sea's name, and I won't pretend there is. What the storm on the Adrias does show is that God's promise to Paul held through fourteen nights of darkness — the ship would be lost, but not one life.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Adriel, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Adriel the Meholathite was the man Saul gave Merab to, though she had been promised to David. Years later, his five sons by Merab were handed over to the Gibeonites and hanged, to atone for Saul's slaughter of Gibeon — and Rizpah, Saul's concubine, guarded their bodies from the birds and the beasts until rain fell.
TheologicalSignificance: This name carries no teaching of its own, and I won't force one onto it. But the story around it is heavy: the sins of one king fell on another man's sons, and a mother's vigil over their bodies is one of the most faithful pictures in all of Scripture.
RelatedPeople: Adriel the Meholathite; King Saul; Merab; Michal
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Adullam, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Adullam was a Canaanite city taken by Joshua, a town in the lowland of Judah — and, most famously, the cave where David hid when he fled from Saul. 'David therefore departed thence, and escaped to the cave Adullam,' and everyone in distress, in debt, and discontented gathered to him there; the place itself is covered in the Biblical Places collection.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the cave of Adullam is one of the kindest pictures in the Bible: a fugitive king in a cave, and the broken and indebted gathering to him — and God made those outcasts into mighty men. If you are in distress, this is where the story says you belong: with David, in the cave, waiting on God.
RelatedTopics: Refuge; God's Protection; Hope; Strength in weakness
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an Adullamite or native of Adullam
BiblicalUsage: Adullamite means a man from Adullam — and in Scripture it belongs to one man, Hirah, the friend of Judah. Hirah was with Judah when he left his brothers, when he married, and when he went up to the sheep-shearing; and it was Hirah whom Judah sent with the kid to pay Tamar.
TheologicalSignificance: A man's hometown carries no doctrine, and I won't pretend it does. Hirah's value is in the company he kept: he stood beside Judah through choices that would shape a tribe, and his presence is a reminder that the friends we keep are part of the story God is writing.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Adummim, a pass in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Adummim was a pass on the road from Jericho up to Jerusalem — the ascent of Adummim, on the border between Judah and Benjamin. It appears twice, both times in lists marking the boundaries of the tribes; the place itself is covered in the Biblical Places collection.
TheologicalSignificance: A mountain pass in a boundary list carries no teaching, and I won't invent one. Its place is on the map: the steep road between two cities, marking where one tribe's land ended and another's began.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G102; to be unable, i.e. (passively) impossible:--be impossible.
BiblicalUsage: Adynateo means to be impossible — and in the New Testament it appears only twice, both times to say that nothing is impossible. Jesus tells His disciples that with mustard-seed faith nothing shall be impossible to them, and Gabriel tells Mary that with God nothing shall be impossible. The word exists in Scripture only to be denied: what cannot be done, God does.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that this word is pure gospel. Twice it appears, and twice it is attached to God's power breaking through human limits — a mountain moved by small faith, a child conceived by the Spirit. What I cannot do, God can, and this word says so twice.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and G1415; unable, i.e. weak (literally or figuratively); passively, impossible:--could not do, impossible, impotent, not possible, weak.
BiblicalUsage: Adynatos is 'unable' or 'impossible' — the word for what human strength cannot do. The rich young ruler hears that with men salvation is impossible, but with God all things are possible; the man at Lystra was impotent in his feet, never having walked; and Hebrews says without faith it is impossible to please God. The word names our limits plainly, so that God's power can be seen clearly.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this word is meant to humble me before it comforts me. Salvation is impossible with men — that is the bad news — but with God all things are possible, and that is the gospel. My inability is the very place where His power shows up.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from an obsolete primary noun (apparently meaning continued duration); "ever," by qualification regularly; by implication, earnestly:--always, ever.
BiblicalUsage: Aei means 'always' or 'ever' — and it is used for things that never stop. Stephen tells the council they do always resist the Holy Ghost; Paul says he is alway delivered unto death for Jesus' sake; the Cretans are 'always liars,' according to their own prophet; and God says of Israel in the wilderness, 'they do alway err in their heart.' The word marks patterns that do not break — for good or for ill.
TheologicalSignificance: This is one of the Bible's small words, and it teaches me only what its sentence teaches — nothing more, and nothing less; in this case, the verse is Acts 7:51.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from ἄημι (to breathe unconsciously, i.e. respire; by analogy, to blow); "air" (as naturally circumambient):--air. Compare G5594.
BiblicalUsage: Aer is the air — the dust the crowd throws into the air, the air into which unintelligible speech is spoken, the realm of the prince of the power of the air, and the air where the saints will meet the Lord at His coming. The word moves from the ordinary sky to the spiritual battleground to the meeting place of the church.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this word reminds me that the air is not empty. An enemy rules there for now, but the Lord will come through it, and His people will meet Him in it — so the same air that carries dust and empty words will carry my hope.
RelatedTopics: Second Coming; Spiritual Warfare; Satan; Hope
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from the same as G109; an eagle (from its wind-like flight):--eagle.
BiblicalUsage: Aetos is the eagle — the bird that gathers where the carcase lies, in Jesus' saying about His coming; the living creature with the face of a flying eagle around God's throne; and the great eagle whose wings carry the woman into the wilderness. Eagles in Scripture mean speed, height, and power, whether in judgment or in deliverance.
TheologicalSignificance: This is a working word rather than a teaching word, and what it means for my faith is decided by the verse it appears in; in this case, the verse is Matthew 24:28.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to breathe after, i.e. to love (sensually)
BiblicalUsage: Agab is lust — inordinate, sensual affection — and it appears only in the prophets' picture of unfaithful Israel. Jerusalem 'doted' on her lovers, the Assyrians and the Babylonians, chasing foreign powers and foreign gods the way a faithless wife chases other men. Jeremiah says her lovers will despise her, and Ezekiel says the very nations she doted on would be the ones to judge her.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this word is a warning about misplaced love. The heart that chases what God forbids always ends despised by what it chased, and the only safe affection is the one fixed on the Lord who never betrays His people.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: love (abstractly), i.e. amorousness
BiblicalUsage: Agabah is the noun for that same inordinate love — amorousness, the lustful affection itself — and it appears only once, in Ezekiel's charge against Jerusalem: her sister Aholibah 'was more corrupt in her inordinate love than she, and in her whoredoms more than her sister in her whoredoms.' The word names the condition, not just the act: a heart given over to craving what God forbids.
TheologicalSignificance: I read this as a plain word doing plain work — its weight, if it has any, is borrowed from the verse around it; in this case, the verse is Ezekiel 23:11.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (compare H2285); Agabus, an Israelite:--Agabus.
BiblicalUsage: Agabus was a prophet from Jerusalem who came to Antioch and foretold a great famine throughout the world — which came to pass in the days of Claudius — and who years later bound Paul's girdle around his own hands and feet, foretelling that the Jews at Jerusalem would bind its owner and deliver him to the Gentiles. Twice he spoke, and twice the word came true.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Agabus shows what a true prophet looks like: he speaks plainly, his words come to pass, and his hardest word is the one that tells a friend he will suffer. Paul listened, thanked him, and went to Jerusalem anyway — and that is what faithfulness looks like on both sides.
RelatedEvents: Relief Sent to Judea in the Famine
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Agag, a title of Amalekitish kings
BiblicalUsage: Agag was the title of the Amalekite kings — Balaam prophesied that Israel's king would be higher than Agag, and centuries later Saul defeated Agag in battle but spared him, against God's command. Samuel had him brought out and cut him in pieces before the Lord at Gilgal, and Saul lost the kingdom for that disobedience.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Agag's story is about obedience that stops short. Saul won the battle and lost the kingdom, because partial obedience is disobedience — and the king he spared became the proof that God's commands are not suggestions.
RelatedPeople: Agag, King of Amalek; King Saul; Samuel; Balaam
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an Agagite or descendent (subject) of Agag
BiblicalUsage: Agagite means a descendant of Agag — and in Scripture it belongs to one man, Haman, the enemy of the Jews in Esther's day. Haman the Agagite plotted to destroy all the Jews, and Esther pleaded against the device he had devised; in the end he was hanged on the gallows he built for Mordecai.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the Agagite's story is the long shadow of Saul's disobedience. The king Saul spared left a line, and that line came back for the Jews in Persia — but God raised up Esther, and the gallows built for Mordecai held Haman instead.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: something revolving, i.e. a wheeled vehicle
BiblicalUsage: Agalah is a cart or wagon — the wagons Joseph sent to carry his father Jacob down to Egypt, the wagons the princes of Israel offered for the tabernacle, the new cart the Philistines built to send the ark home, and the new cart David used to carry the ark, against God's command, until Uzzah died. The word rolls through the story carrying people, offerings, and the ark itself — and the ark's journey shows that even a cart must follow God's way, not man's.
TheologicalSignificance: It names something ordinary — a thing, a place, a manner of speaking — and I take its meaning from the verse, not from the word alone; in this case, the verse is Genesis 45:19.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from ἄγαν (much) and G242; properly, to jump for joy, i.e. exult:--be (exceeding) glad, with exceeding joy, rejoice (greatly).
BiblicalUsage: Agalliao is to jump for joy — exulting, rejoicing greatly. Jesus tells the persecuted to rejoice and be exceeding glad; Mary says her spirit hath rejoiced in God her Saviour; Abraham rejoiced to see Christ's day; and Peter says believers rejoice with joy unspeakable, even though they do not see Him now. The word is always joy that cannot stay still — it leaps.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this word is the sound of real faith. Joy in Christ is not a quiet politeness; it jumps, it exults, it sings — and even suffering cannot keep it down, because the joy is in Him, not in the circumstances.
RelatedTopics: Joy; Joy in hardship; Praise; Worship
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G21; exultation; specially, welcome:--gladness, (exceeding) joy.
BiblicalUsage: Agalliasis is exultation — gladness, great joy. The angel promises Zechariah that John's birth will bring joy and gladness; the baby in Elizabeth's womb leaped for joy at Mary's greeting; the first Christians ate their food with gladness and singleness of heart; and the Messiah is anointed with the oil of gladness above His fellows. The word belongs to births, to fellowship, and to the King Himself.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that this word shows joy is not an extra in the Christian life — it is the atmosphere of it. From a baby leaping in the womb to a church breaking bread together, gladness marks the places where God is at work.
RelatedPeople: Jesus; John the Baptist; Mary, Mother of Jesus
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to be sad
BiblicalUsage: Agam means to be grieved, and it appears only once — in Job's defence of his life: 'Did not I weep for him that was in trouble? was not my soul grieved for the poor?' Job is answering his friends by pointing to the compassion of his past: he wept with the troubled and grieved for the needy, and that grief was the mark of a righteous man.
TheologicalSignificance: On its own it is too small to build on, and I would rather read it honestly in its verse than make it mean more than it does; in this case, the verse is Job 30:25.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a marsh; hence a rush (as growing in swamps); hence a stockade of reeds
BiblicalUsage: Agam is a pool or marsh — standing water, reeds and rushes. Moses stretches his rod over the waters of Egypt and the pools turn to blood; Isaiah says Babylon will become a possession for the bittern and pools of water; and the same prophet promises that the parched ground will become a pool, and the thirsty land springs of water.
TheologicalSignificance: On its own this word carries little theological weight; the meaning that matters lives in the verse around it, not in the word itself; in this case, the verse is Exodus 7:19.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and G1062; unmarried:--unmarried.
BiblicalUsage: Agamos is 'unmarried' — and Paul uses it in his careful teaching on marriage in 1 Corinthians 7. He says it is good for the unmarried and widows to remain as he is, speaks of the unmarried woman's freedom to care for the things of the Lord, and contrasts the married person's divided attention with the unmarried person's single focus. The word is never a judgment; it is a state with its own freedom and its own calling.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this word honours a state the world often pities. Paul does not treat the unmarried as incomplete — he treats singleness as a gift with room for undivided devotion, and marriage as a gift with its own duties, and both as callings from the same Lord.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to debar, i.e. from marriage
BiblicalUsage: Agan means to shut oneself off — to be debarred, in this case from marriage — and it appears only once, in Naomi's bitter question to her daughters-in-law: 'Would ye stay for them from having husbands?' She is telling Ruth and Orpah not to wait for sons she will never have, not to shut themselves away from marriage for her sake.
TheologicalSignificance: On its own it says very little about God or about us; whatever it teaches, it teaches only inside the sentence where God placed it; in this case, the verse is Ruth 1:13.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from ἄγαν (much) and ἄχθος (grief; akin to the base of G43); to be greatly afflicted, i.e. (figuratively) indignant:--be much (sore) displeased, have (be moved with, with) indignation.
BiblicalUsage: Aganakteo is to be greatly displeased, moved with indignation. The ten disciples were moved with indignation against James and John; the disciples were indignant when the ointment was poured out; Jesus was much displeased when they kept the children away; and the ruler of the synagogue was indignant because Jesus healed on the Sabbath. The word covers indignation that is petty, indignation that is wasteful, indignation that is righteous, and indignation that is blind — and the story always shows which is which.
TheologicalSignificance: What this word teaches me is that anger is not one thing. The disciples' indignation was envy, the ruler's was religion without mercy, and Jesus' was love defending little children — and I hold that the difference is everything, because God weighs the heart behind the heat.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G23; indignation:--indignation.
BiblicalUsage: Aganaktesis is indignation — and it appears once, in Paul's joy over the Corinthians' repentance: 'what carefulness it wrought in you, yea, what clearing of yourselves, yea, what indignation, yea, what fear, yea, what vehement desire, yea, what zeal, yea, what revenge!' The indignation here is not against others but against their own sin — a holy anger at what they had tolerated, and the proof that their sorrow was real.
TheologicalSignificance: A single occurrence like this tells me what happened or how something was said — the doctrine, if any, is in the passage, not the word; in this case, the verse is 2 Corinthians 7:11.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: perhaps from ἄγαν (much) [or compare H5689 ]; to love (in a social or moral sense):--(be-)love(-ed). Compare G5368.
BiblicalUsage: Agapao is to love — the great word of the New Testament, used hundreds of times. Jesus commands it toward enemies, John says God so loved the world that He gave His Son, the same apostle commands believers to love one another as Christ loved them, and then states the ground of it all: God is love, and whoever does not love does not know Him. The word covers God's love for us, our love for Him, and our love for each other, and it always means love that acts.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that agapao is the word the whole gospel turns on. God loved, so He gave; Christ loved, so He died; and we love because He first loved us — and any love that does not act is not the love this word means.
RelatedTopics: Love; Love of God; Love for God; Neighbor
RelatedEvents: The Sermon on the Mount; The Crucifixion
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G25; beloved:--(dearly, well) beloved, dear.
BiblicalUsage: Agapetos is 'beloved' — the word for someone dearly loved. The Father speaks it over Jesus at His baptism, 'This is my beloved Son'; Paul writes to the beloved of God at Rome; he tells the Ephesians to walk in love as beloved children; and John warns his beloved not to believe every spirit. The word is used of Christ, of churches, and of individual believers — all of them held dear by the same love.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this word is the gospel in a single adjective. To be beloved is not something I earn — the Father called Jesus beloved before He had done a single miracle, and He calls His children beloved in Christ, before they have done anything to deserve it.
RelatedTopics: Love of God; Identity in Christ; Grace; Assurance
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H1904); Hagar, the concubine of Abraham:--Hagar.
BiblicalUsage: Agar is Hagar, the concubine of Abraham — and Paul uses her name in his allegory of the two covenants. Hagar stands for Mount Sinai and the covenant of bondage, bearing children who are slaves; Sarah stands for the Jerusalem above, the mother of the free.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Paul's use of Hagar is a warning I need to hear: the way of the law is the way of the slave, and it cannot make anyone free. The children of the promise are born of the free woman, and I belong to that line by faith, not by my own efforts.
RelatedEvents: Hagar and Ishmael; The Binding of Isaac
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to harvest
BiblicalUsage: Agar means to gather or harvest — and it appears twice, both in Proverbs, both about the ant and the harvest. The ant 'provideth her meat in the summer, and gathereth her food in the harvest,' and the son who 'gathereth in summer' is wise, while the son who sleeps in harvest brings shame.
TheologicalSignificance: This word carries no doctrine of its own; it simply helps the verse say what it says, and that is its whole work; in this case, the verse is Proverbs 6:8.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a basin
BiblicalUsage: Agartal is a basin — a broad, shallow vessel of gold or silver for the temple service. Cyrus counts out thirty chargers of gold and a thousand of silver for the returning exiles, and Ezra weighs out twenty basons of gold, worth a thousand drams, for the journey to Jerusalem.
TheologicalSignificance: I read it as it stands — a plain term in a particular verse — and I won't make it bear a weight Scripture never put on it; in this case, the verse is Ezra 1:9.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G18 and G2041; to work good:--do good.
BiblicalUsage: Agathoergeo means to work good — to do good as a way of life — and it appears once, in Paul's charge to the rich: 'That they do good, that they be rich in good works, ready to distribute, willing to communicate.' The word is not about a single act but about a habit: a life spent doing good, with open hands and a ready heart.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold this word lightly: it names a thing or a turn of phrase, and any lesson in it comes from the passage, not from the word alone; in this case, the verse is 1 Timothy 6:18.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G17; to be a well-doer (as a favor or a duty):--(when) do good (well).
BiblicalUsage: Agathopoieo is to do good — to be a well-doer, as a favour or a duty. Jesus asks whether it is lawful to do good on the Sabbath; He warns that even sinners do good to those who do good to them; John says he that doeth good is of God; and Peter says it is better to suffer for well-doing than for evil-doing. The word covers doing good as a command, as a mark of belonging to God, and as a reason to suffer.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that this word keeps the Christian life practical. Doing good is not a feeling — it is healing on the Sabbath, it is the mark John gives for knowing God, and it is suffering patiently when the world repays good with evil.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G17; well-doing, i.e. virtue:--well-doing.
BiblicalUsage: Agathopoiia is well-doing — the life of doing good, named as a single thing — and it appears once, in Peter's word to suffering believers: 'let them that suffer according to the will of God commit the keeping of their souls to him in well doing, as unto a faithful Creator.' The word gathers a whole life of good deeds into one act of trust: keep doing good, and leave your soul with the God who made it.
TheologicalSignificance: Its meaning is narrow and practical, and any larger lesson comes from the story or command it appears in, not from the word itself; in this case, the verse is 1 Peter 4:19.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G18 and G4160; a well-doer, i.e. virtuous:--them that do well.
BiblicalUsage: Agathopoios is a well-doer — a person whose life is marked by doing good — and it appears once, in Peter's teaching on government: rulers are sent 'for the punishment of evildoers, and for the praise of them that do well.' The word names the citizen whose life is so plainly good that even the authorities have to praise it. One word, one verse, and a whole ethic of quiet, visible goodness.
TheologicalSignificance: I treat this as vocabulary, not doctrine: useful for reading the verse rightly, but not a truth to build on by itself; in this case, the verse is 1 Peter 2:14.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a primary word; "good" (in any sense, often as noun):--benefit, good(-s, things), well. Compare G2570.
BiblicalUsage: Agathos is 'good' — the commonest word for goodness in the New Testament, used hundreds of times. An evil father still knows how to give good gifts; a good man brings good things out of the good treasure of his heart; the law is holy, just, and good; and Paul tells us to do good unto all men as we have opportunity. The word covers good things, good people, and the good God behind them all.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe agathos matters because it keeps goodness anchored in God. Good gifts come from the Father, and the good heart is the one the Spirit has remade — goodness is not something I manufacture, it is something God grows.
RelatedTopics: Goodness; Fruit of the Spirit; Character
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G18; goodness, i.e. virtue or beneficence:--goodness.
BiblicalUsage: Agathosyne is goodness — virtue, beneficence, the quality of being good and doing good. Paul says the Romans are 'full of goodness,' names goodness as fruit of the Spirit, says the fruit of the Spirit is in all goodness and righteousness and truth, and prays that God would fulfil every good pleasure of His goodness in the Thessalonians. The word is always active: goodness that fills, bears fruit, and overflows.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that this word is the difference between being good and doing good. Goodness as the Spirit grows it does not sit still — it fills a church, it bears fruit, it fulfils God's good pleasure — and that is the goodness I want to be full of.
RelatedTopics: Goodness; Fruit of the Spirit; Character
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: imperative of G71; properly, lead, i.e. come on:--go to.
BiblicalUsage: Age is a command: 'Come on!' or 'Go to now!' — the word you use to call someone to attention. James uses it twice, both times to summon the self-confident to listen: 'Go to now, ye that say, To day or to morrow we will go into such a city,' and 'Go to now, ye rich men, weep and howl.'
TheologicalSignificance: It does its work quietly inside a verse, and I leave the doctrine where it belongs: in the passage, not in the word; in this case, the verse is James 4:13.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Age, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Age is named once, as the father of Shammah, one of David's three mighty men — Shammah the son of Age the Hararite, who stood his ground in a field of lentils when the Philistines came and the army fled. The father never appears; only his son, standing alone in a lentil field, defending it with his life.
TheologicalSignificance: A father's name in a list carries no doctrine, and I won't invent one. But Shammah's stand is the story: one man, one field of lentils, an army fled — and the Lord wrought a great victory through the son of a man we know only by name.
RelatedPeople: Agee, Father of Shammah; King David
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G71 (compare G32); a drove:--herd.
BiblicalUsage: Agele is a herd — and in the Gospels it is always the herd of swine. A great herd of swine feeding on the hillside, two thousand of them, into which the demons begged to go — and the whole herd ran violently down a steep place into the sea.
TheologicalSignificance: A herd of pigs is a detail of the story, not a doctrine — the swine run into the sea, and the word just names what ran.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: figuratively, sad
BiblicalUsage: Agem is an adjective meaning sad — literally 'stagnant,' like still water — and it appears only once, in Isaiah's judgment on Egypt: 'all that make sluices and ponds for fish' — or, as the sense runs, all who work for hire shall be sad of soul. The word pictures a spirit gone flat and still, like water that no longer flows, in a land whose idols and counsellors have failed it.
TheologicalSignificance: Sadness here is the prophet's word for a broken Egypt, and I take it as grief, not as a system — the verse carries the sorrow.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as negative particle) and G1075; unregistered as to birth:--without descent.
BiblicalUsage: Agenealogetos means 'without descent' — unregistered, with no genealogy on record — and it appears once, of Melchizedek: 'Without father, without mother, without descent, having neither beginning of days, nor end of life.' The writer is not saying Melchizedek had no parents; he is saying Scripture records none, and that silence makes him a fitting picture of the Son of God, whose priesthood has no end.
TheologicalSignificance: Melchizedek arrives without a genealogy, and this word only marks the absence — the mystery belongs to the priest, not to the adjective.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as negative particle) and G1085; properly, without kin, i.e. (of unknown descent, and by implication) ignoble:--base things.
BiblicalUsage: Agenes means 'base things' — things without kin, of unknown descent, ignoble in the world's eyes — and it appears once, in Paul's great reversal: 'And base things of the world, and things which are despised, hath God chosen, yea, and things which are not, to bring to nought things that are.' God chooses the nobodies, the things the world calls nothing, and uses them to shame the somethings.
TheologicalSignificance: God chooses the base things of the world, and this word names them — but the choosing is God's doing, and the verse says so.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a bowl (as pounded out hollow)
BiblicalUsage: Aggan is a bowl or basin — a broad, hollow vessel. Moses took half the blood of the covenant and put it in basons at Sinai, sprinkling the rest on the altar; and the Song pictures the beloved's navel as a round goblet that never lacks wine.
TheologicalSignificance: A bowl is a bowl — Moses used it to hold the blood of the covenant, and the vessel is not the message.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: (only plural) wings of an army, or crowds of troops
BiblicalUsage: Aggaph means wings — the wings of an army, or crowds of troops — and it appears only in Ezekiel, always of armies in the day of judgment. God will scatter all who are around the prince 'to every wind,' and all his bands; the fugitives will fall by the sword with all their bands; and Gog's bands will fall on the mountains of Israel.
TheologicalSignificance: Troops scattering is the picture, and the word only counts the wings of the army — the judgment is the Lord's, not the noun's.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: something round, i.e. a ring (for the ears)
BiblicalUsage: Agiyl is a ring — an earring, something round worn on the ear. After the battle with Midian, the officers of Israel brought their gold jewels, chains, bracelets, rings, and earrings as an offering to the Lord; and in Ezekiel's picture of Jerusalem, God puts earrings in her ears and a beautiful crown on her head.
TheologicalSignificance: An earring offered to the Lord is a gift, not a teaching — the gold matters because it was given, and the verse says why.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a bulrush (as growing there); collectively a rope of bulrushes
BiblicalUsage: Agmown is a bulrush or reed — the rush that grows in the marsh, bending in the wind. Isaiah uses it three ways: the Lord will cut off head and tail, branch and rush, in one day; neither head nor tail, branch nor rush, will be able to do anything for Egypt; and true fasting is not bowing the head like a bulrush for a day.
TheologicalSignificance: A bulrush bowing its head is the prophet's picture of a people brought low — the plant is the image, and Isaiah does the preaching.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and the same as G1102; properly, unfulled, i.e. (by implication) new (cloth):--new.
BiblicalUsage: Agnaphos means unfulled — new cloth, not yet shrunk or finished. Jesus uses it in the parable of the patch: no one puts a piece of new cloth on an old garment, for the patch tears away and makes the tear worse.
TheologicalSignificance: New cloth on an old garment is the Lord's own picture, and this word only names the patch — the parable teaches, not the adjective.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G50; a thing ignored, i.e. shortcoming:--error.
BiblicalUsage: Agnoema is an error — a thing done in ignorance, a shortcoming — and it appears once, in the description of the Day of Atonement: the high priest entered the second part of the tabernacle once a year, 'not without blood, which he offered for himself, and for the errors of the people.' The word covers the sins the people did not even know they had committed, and the blood covered those too.
TheologicalSignificance: The high priest carried blood for his own errors as well as the people's, and this word names the errors — the verse holds the mercy, not the noun.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and G3539; not to know (through lack of information or intelligence); by implication, to ignore (through disinclination):--(be) ignorant(-ly), not know, not understand, unknown.
BiblicalUsage: Agnoeo is not to know — through lack of information, or through wilful ignorance. The disciples did not understand the saying about the resurrection and were afraid to ask; the Athenians worshipped in ignorance the God Paul proclaimed; Paul warns the Romans not to be ignorant of the mystery of Israel; and he says of the man who is ignorant, let him be ignorant. The word covers honest not-knowing and the kind that refuses to learn — and Scripture treats them very differently.
TheologicalSignificance: What this word teaches me is that ignorance is not one thing. The disciples' fear and the Athenians' altar are met with patience and preaching — but the ignorance that refuses to know is left alone, and I hold that the difference is the willingness to ask.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G50; ignorance (properly, the quality):--ignorance.
BiblicalUsage: Agnoia is ignorance — the state of not knowing. Peter tells the Jews they crucified Christ through ignorance; Paul tells Athens that God winked at the times of this ignorance, but now commands all men to repent; he says the Gentiles are darkened through the ignorance in them; and he tells believers not to fashion themselves after their former lusts in their ignorance. The word always marks the before — the life before knowing God — and the gospel is what ends it.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that this word is the hinge of the gospel's call. Ignorance was winked at for a time, but now God commands repentance — and the ignorance that once excused us is the very thing Christ came to end, by making Himself known.
RelatedTopics: Repentance; Evangelism; Knowledge of God; Salvation
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as negative particle) and G1108; ignorance (properly, the state):--ignorance, not the knowledge.
