Definition: from ἄλη (vagrancy); braggart:--boaster.
BiblicalUsage: Twice, and both times in a list of what people become without God. In Romans the boasters stand among the haters of God, the inventors of evil things, the disobedient to parents. In Timothy they head the last-days catalogue, lovers of their own selves, covetous, boasters, proud, blasphemers; the word is for the person who talks big about himself.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for a braggart carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the company it keeps, that boasting is listed beside hating God and loving self, and the end of the list is always the same.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G213; braggadocio, i.e. (by implication) self-confidence:--boasting, pride.
BiblicalUsage: Twice, and both times it is the pride that talks. James hears men boasting in their plans, To day or to morrow we will go into such a city, and continue there a year, and buy and sell, and get gain, and calls all such rejoicing evil. John names the pride of life beside the lust of the flesh and the lust of the eyes, and says it is not of the Father but of the world.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for bragging carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the warning, that planning tomorrow as if God had no say in it is not confidence but pride.
RelatedPeople: James, Brother of Jesus; John the Apostle
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a leaf (as coming up on a tree); collectively, foliage
BiblicalUsage: The leaf of a tree, and the Bible uses it at both ends of the story. After the fall Adam and Eve sew fig leaves together and make themselves aprons, the first human cover-up. And the righteous man is a tree planted by the rivers of water whose leaf also shall not wither, green in every season because his roots are in the law of the LORD.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for a leaf carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the two trees, that the leaf sewn to hide shame withers and the leaf rooted by the water does not.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as particle of union) and the base of G3045; to oil (with perfume):--anoint.
BiblicalUsage: To anoint with oil, and the New Testament pours it out in four directions. The twelve anoint many sick with oil and heal them. A sinful woman weeps on Jesus' feet, wipes them with her hair, kisses them and anoints them. Mary takes a pound of costly spikenard and anoints His feet, and the house fills with the smell; and James tells the church to anoint the sick with oil in the name of the Lord and pray the prayer of faith.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe anointing is the body taking part in the prayer, not magic and not medicine alone. Oil on the skin says what words cannot, that this person belongs to God and is being given back to Him for healing. I hold that James keeps it for the church because the sick should never be prayed for alone — the elders come, the oil is poured, and the Lord is asked to raise them up.
RelatedPeople: Mary of Bethany; James, Brother of Jesus
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from ἀλέκω (to ward off); a cock or male fowl:--cock.
BiblicalUsage: Eleven times, and nearly all of them are the same night. Before the cock crow, thou shalt deny me thrice. The cock crows twice in Mark's account, once in the others, and Peter hears it and remembers, and goes out and weeps bitterly; the bird is the clock of the denial.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for a rooster carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the sound it makes, that the cock's crow is the moment Peter's courage failed and grace began.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G220 and G5456; cock-crow, i.e. the third night-watch:--cockcrowing.
BiblicalUsage: Once, in the watch of the night. Jesus tells His disciples to watch, for they do not know when the master of the house comes, at even, or at midnight, or at the cockcrowing, or in the morning. The word is the third watch of the night, the hour before dawn when the cocks cry and the world is still dark.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for the cock's hour carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the command beside it, to watch, because the Master comes at an hour no one can name.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: alas!
BiblicalUsage: Twice, and both times it is a cry of grief. Job says, If I be wicked, woe unto me; and if I be righteous, yet will I not lift up my head. And Micah cries, Woe is me, for I am as when they have gathered the summer fruits, as the grapegleanings of the vintage: there is no cluster to eat; the word is the sound a man makes when there is nothing left to gather.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for alas carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the honesty in it, that the Bible lets a righteous man cry woe over a land with nothing left to eat.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Alemeth, the name of a place in Palestine and of two Israelites
BiblicalUsage: The name belongs to two men and a town. Alemeth son of Becher is counted among the sons of Benjamin, and a later Alemeth is named in the line of Saul, son of Jehoadah; and the town of Alemeth in Benjamin was given to the priests with its suburbs; three uses, and the name is all the Bible says of any of them.
TheologicalSignificance: A name shared by two men and a town carries no lesson of its own. What it shows is how the Bible keeps the record straight, that even the men named only once in a list are counted, and the towns given to the priests are named.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and G2990; true (as not concealing):--true, truly, truth.
BiblicalUsage: True, as not concealing — and John leans on the word harder than anyone. Jesus says His record is true even though He bears witness of Himself, because He knows where He came from and where He goes. The law needs two witnesses, and His witness and the Father's agree. Paul tells the Philippians to think on whatsoever things are true, and John says the anointing teaches all things and is truth, and is no lie.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe truth is not an idea first but a person, and that is why John keeps saying it of Jesus. What is true is what does not hide, and Christ hides nothing — He came from the Father in the open and goes back to Him in the open. I hold that thinking on what is true is not positive thinking; it is fixing the mind on the One who is true, and letting everything false fall away.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G227; to be true (in doctrine and profession):--speak (tell) the truth.
BiblicalUsage: Twice, and Paul uses it both times to say the same thing from two sides. In Ephesians it is speaking the truth in love, so the body grows up into Christ, the head. In Galatians it is the question that stings: Am I therefore become your enemy, because I tell you the truth? The word is truth-telling as a way of life, not just getting the facts right.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe truth without love is a weapon and love without truth is a lie, and Paul will not let me separate them. Speaking the truth in love is how the church grows, and telling the truth can still cost a friendship — Paul lost the Galatians' warmth for it and kept telling it anyway. I hold that is the test of whether I love people: whether I will tell them the truth they do not want to hear, and tell it kindly.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G227; truthful:--true.
BiblicalUsage: The true one, the real thing as opposed to the copy. John calls Christ the true Light which lighteth every man that cometh into the world, and Jesus calls Himself the true vine, and His Father the husbandman. Eternal life is knowing the only true God and Jesus Christ whom He has sent. And the risen Christ writes to Philadelphia as He that is holy, He that is true, who opens and no man shuts.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this word draws the line between the real and the imitation, and the line runs through Jesus. There are many lights and many vines and many gods, and John says there is one true Light, one true vine, one true God. I hold that knowing Him is not one truth among others — it is the truth that makes everything else true, and eternal life is knowing Him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from the same as G224; to grind:--grind.
BiblicalUsage: Twice, in the same saying on two lips. Two women shall be grinding at the mill; the one shall be taken, and the other left. The word is the daily grind, the women's work at the millstone, and Jesus sets the suddenness of His coming against it — ordinary work, and then the separation.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for grinding grain carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the scene it is set in, that the day of the Lord comes on an ordinary working morning and finds two at the same mill.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: adverb from G227; truly:--indeed, surely, of a surety, truly, of a (in) truth, verily, very.
BiblicalUsage: Eighteen times, and it is the word for really and of a surety. Jesus sees Nathanael coming and says, Behold an Israelite indeed, in whom is no guile. And the Samaritans tell the woman at the well, Now we believe, not because of thy saying: for we have heard him ourselves, and know that this is indeed the Christ, the Saviour of the world.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for truly carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the two confessions it carries, that Nathanael had no guile in him and the Samaritans knew for themselves who Jesus is.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from ἀλέω (to grind); flour:--meal.
BiblicalUsage: Twice, in the same parable told twice. The kingdom of heaven is like unto leaven, which a woman took, and hid in three measures of meal, till the whole was leavened. The word is the meal itself, the three measures, the ordinary flour of the house, and the kingdom works through it quietly until the whole lump has risen.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for flour carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the parable it sits in, that the kingdom works like leaven, hidden and slow and unstoppable.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from Ἀλεξάνδρεια (the city so called); an Alexandreian or inhabitant of Alexandria:--of Alexandria, Alexandrian.
BiblicalUsage: A man from Alexandria, the great city of Egypt where the library stood and the Greek Old Testament was translated. In Acts the Alexandrians argue with Stephen in the synagogue of the Libertines, and cannot resist the wisdom and the spirit by which he speaks; and Apollos comes to Ephesus, an eloquent man from Alexandria, mighty in the Scriptures, and Priscilla and Aquila take him aside and explain the way of God more perfectly.
TheologicalSignificance: A name for a man from Alexandria carries no lesson of its own. What it shows is how far the gospel had already travelled, that Jews from Egypt were arguing in Jerusalem and a learned man from Alexandria was preaching Christ in Ephesus, and the Scriptures he knew were the same ones Stephen died for.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from the same as G221; Alexandrine, or belonging to Alexandria:--of Alexandria.
BiblicalUsage: A man from Alexandria, the great city of Egypt where the library stood and the Greek Old Testament was translated. In Acts the Alexandrians argue with Stephen in the synagogue of the Libertines, and cannot resist the wisdom and the spirit by which he speaks; and Apollos comes to Ephesus, an eloquent man from Alexandria, mighty in the Scriptures, and Priscilla and Aquila take him aside and explain the way of God more perfectly.
TheologicalSignificance: A name for a man from Alexandria carries no lesson of its own. What it shows is how far the gospel had already travelled, that Jews from Egypt were arguing in Jerusalem and a learned man from Alexandria was preaching Christ in Ephesus, and the Scriptures he knew were the same ones Stephen died for.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from the same as (the first part of) G220 and G435; man-defender; Alexander, the name of three Israelites and one other man:--Alexander.
BiblicalUsage: Four men share the name, and the Bible keeps them apart by their deeds. One stands with the high priest's kindred against Peter and John; one is the son of Simon of Cyrene, who carried the cross; one is put forward by the Jews in the Ephesus riot and shouted down; and Alexander the coppersmith does Paul much evil, and Paul delivers him with Hymenaeus unto Satan, that they may learn not to blaspheme.
TheologicalSignificance: A shared name carries no lesson of its own. What it shows is the Bible's plain record of opposition, that the gospel met men who fought it with their hands, their words and their crowds, and Paul names them without flinching.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: exultant
BiblicalUsage: Once, in Isaiah's song of the vineyard gone wrong: hell hath enlarged herself and opened her mouth without measure, and their glory and their multitude and their pomp, and he that rejoiceth, shall descend into it. The word is the reveller, the one exulting in the feast while judgment opens its mouth.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for a reveller carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the warning, that the joy that forgets God ends by going down into the pit it laughed at.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: sticks of algum wood
BiblicalUsage: Three times, and always about Solomon's temple. Solomon asks Hiram for algum wood with the cedar and the almug trees, and the king makes of the almug trees terraces for the house of the LORD and for the king's house, and harps and psalteries for the singers. The word is the timber that became music.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for a timber carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is what the wood became, that trees from Ophir ended as steps in the temple and harps in the singers' hands.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from ἀλισγέω (to soil); (ceremonially) defilement:--pollution.
BiblicalUsage: Once, in the letter the apostles send to the Gentiles: that they abstain from pollutions of idols, and from fornication, and from things strangled, and from blood. The word is the ceremonial defilement of idol worship, the stain that clings to food offered to a god who is no god.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for idol-pollution carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the council's wisdom, that the Gentiles were not loaded with the law but were asked to keep clear of idolatry and its table.
RelatedPeople: James, Brother of Jesus; Paul; Simon Peter
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: something lofty, i.e. a stair-way; also a second-story room (or even one on the roof); figuratively, the sky
BiblicalUsage: The upper room, the chamber on the roof, the stairway up. Elijah carries the widow's dead son up into the loft where he abides and stretches himself on the child, and the child's soul comes into him again. And the Shunammite builds a little chamber on the wall for Elisha, with a bed and a table and a stool and a candlestick, so the man of God has a place to turn in; the upper room is where prophets stay, and where the dead come back.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for an upstairs room carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the two rooms, that a widow's son was raised in one and a prophet was sheltered in the other, and both were built by women who made room for God.
RelatedEvents: Elijah and the Widow of Zarephath; Elisha and the Shunammite's Son
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably a crucible (as working over the metal)
BiblicalUsage: Once, in the psalm of pure words: The words of the LORD are pure words: as silver tried in a furnace of earth, purified seven times. The word is the crucible, the vessel the silver is tried in, and the psalm says God's words have already been through the fire and come out pure.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for a crucible carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the comparison, that God's words are not raw ore but silver purified seven times over.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an exploit (of God), or a performance (of man, often in a bad sense); by implication, an opportunity
BiblicalUsage: The doings of God, His exploits, and the Bible calls for them to be told. O give thanks unto the LORD; call upon his name: make known his deeds among the people. Isaiah says the same on the day of salvation: praise the LORD, declare His doings among the people, make mention that His name is exalted; the word is what God has done, and the command is to say it out loud.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for God's doings carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the command with it, that what God has done is not to be kept quiet but declared among the peoples.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: (miraculous) execution
BiblicalUsage: Once, in Jeremiah's prayer over the field he has just bought in a besieged city: God is great in counsel and mighty in work, His eyes open upon all the ways of the sons of men, to give every one according to his ways and according to the fruit of his doings. The word is the mighty working itself, the execution of God's counsel in the world.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for God's mighty working carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the prayer it sits in, that the God who sees every way also acts in every way, and Jeremiah bought the field because of it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: exultation
BiblicalUsage: Once, in Habakkuk's song of the God who marches through the earth: the enemy came out as a whirlwind to scatter him, and their rejoicing was as to devour the poor secretly. The word is their exultation, the joy of the violent over the defenceless, and the song answers it with a God who strikes through their heads with their own staves.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for the enemy's rejoicing carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the answer, that the exultation of the violent is cut short by the God who hears the poor.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: neuter plural of G243; properly, other things, i.e. (adverbially) contrariwise (in many relations):--and, but (even), howbeit, indeed, nay, nevertheless, no, notwithstanding, save, therefore, yea, yet.
BiblicalUsage: The little word that turns a sentence around. God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life; and again, He that spared not his own Son, but delivered him up for us all, how shall he not with him also freely give us all things? Six hundred times the New Testament says but, and the whole gospel turns on it.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for but carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the turn it makes, that where I perish, God gives, and where I have nothing, He delivers His Son for me.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G243; from elsewhere:--some other way.
BiblicalUsage: Once, in the parable of the sheepfold: He that entereth not by the door into the sheepfold, but climbeth up some other way, the same is a thief and a robber. The word is the other way in, the climb over the wall instead of the walk through the door.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for some other way carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the warning, that there is one door and every other way in is a thief's way.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {an oak or other strong tree}
BiblicalUsage: Once, when Joshua sets up the stone of witness under the oak by the sanctuary of the LORD at Shechem, after the people have said, The LORD our God will we serve, and his voice will we obey. The word is the strong tree that stands over the stone, the witness to the promise.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for an oak carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the tree it names, that the promise at Shechem was made under a tree that would outlast the men who made it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Allammelek, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Once, in the border of Asher: the coast turns to Carmel westward, and to Shihor-libnath, and then to Allammelek, and Amad, and Mishal, and reaches to Carmel westward. The name is a town on the boundary line, and the boundary is all the Bible says of it.
TheologicalSignificance: A town named once on a border carries no lesson of its own. What it shows is the care of the record, that even the boundary towns are named, and the inheritance is measured town by town.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G243; to make different:--change.
BiblicalUsage: To make different, to change — and Paul uses it for the greatest change of all. Behold, I shew you a mystery; We shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed, in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trump. The dead are raised incorruptible and the living are changed. And Hebrews says the heavens themselves will be changed like a garment, folded up and laid aside by the One who remains the same.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe change is the promise and the threat both at once: the heavens will be folded up like a worn coat, and my body will be changed in a moment. The difference is who does the changing — God changes what He loves into what it was made to be, and I hold that the twinkling of an eye is not too fast for Him to finish what He started in me.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G243 and ἀγορέω (to harangue (compare G58)); to allegorize:--be an allegory (the Greek word itself).
BiblicalUsage: Once, when Paul reads the story of Hagar and Sarah as an allegory: which things are an allegory, for these are the two covenants, the one from the mount Sinai, which gendereth to bondage, which is Agar. The word is the allegorizing itself, the reading of a history as a picture of something greater.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for allegorizing carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the reading it names, that Paul found two covenants in two mothers and built his whole argument on it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Genitive plural from G243 reduplicated; one another:--each other, mutual, one another, (the other), (them-, your-)selves, (selves) together (sometimes with G3326 or G4314).
BiblicalUsage: One another, each other, mutual — and the New Testament cannot stop saying it. A new commandment I give unto you, That ye love one another; as I have loved you, that ye also love one another. And Paul adds the manner of it: be kindly affectioned one to another with brotherly love; in honour preferring one another; Ninety-four times the word turns the faith outward, toward each other.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for one another carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the direction it gives, that the faith is never a solitary thing but is always practised on somebody else.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (imperative of H1984 and H3050); praise ye Jah!, an adoring exclamation:--alleluiah.
BiblicalUsage: Four times, and all of them in one chapter, the song of heaven. After these things I heard a great voice of much people in heaven, saying, Alleluia; Salvation, and glory, and honour, and power, unto the Lord our God. And again, Alleluia: for the Lord God omnipotent reigneth; the word is Hebrew, praise ye Jah, carried whole into the Greek of Revelation.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for Alleluia carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is where it is sung, that heaven itself answers the fall of Babylon with praise, and the song does not stop.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a second-story room
BiblicalUsage: The upper room, the chamber on the roof, the stairway up. Daniel's windows were open in his chamber toward Jerusalem, and he kneeled upon his knees three times a day and prayed, even after the king's decree made prayer a death sentence; the upper room is where a man prays when no one can stop him.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for an upstairs room carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the praying room, that Daniel prayed there three times a day with his windows open toward Jerusalem.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: exultant
BiblicalUsage: Exultant, and the Bible uses it for the wrong kind of joy as often as the right. God calls His sanctified ones, even them that rejoice in His highness, to execute His anger on Babylon. And Nineveh is the rejoicing city that dwelt carelessly, that said in her heart, I am, and there is none beside me — until she becomes a desolation, a place for beasts to lie down in.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for exultant carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the two cities, that joy in God's highness is commanded and joy in one's own greatness is judged.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G243 and G1085; foreign, i.e. not a Jew:--stranger.
BiblicalUsage: Once, in the story of the ten lepers: There are not found that returned to give glory to God, save this stranger. The word is the foreigner, the one not a Jew, and the only one of the ten who came back to thank Jesus was a Samaritan, a stranger to the promises.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for a stranger carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the sting in it, that the foreigner thanked God while the nine who belonged went home silent.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G243 and G5443; foreign, i.e. (specially) Gentile:--one of another nation.
BiblicalUsage: Once, when Peter explains himself to Cornelius: Ye know how that it is an unlawful thing for a man that is a Jew to keep company, or come unto one of another nation; but God hath shewed me that I should not call any man common or unclean. The word is the foreigner, the man of another tribe, and the sentence that breaks the wall down.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for a foreigner carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the vision behind it, that God showed Peter the sheet from heaven so the gospel could cross into a Gentile house.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: adverb from G243; differently:--otherwise.
BiblicalUsage: Once, in Paul's instruction about elders: Likewise also the good works of some are manifest beforehand; and they that are otherwise cannot be hid. The word is otherwise, differently, the works that are not manifest yet and cannot stay hidden forever.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for otherwise carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the patience in it, that what is done in secret comes out in time, good and bad alike.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a primary word; "else," i.e. different (in many applications):--more, one (another), (an-, some an-)other(-s, -wise).
BiblicalUsage: Another, other, else — and it is everywhere in the Gospels, one hundred and thirty-six times. And other sheep I have, which are not of this fold: them also I must bring, and they shall hear my voice; and there shall be one fold, and one shepherd. And some fell upon stony places, where they had not much earth: and forthwith they sprung up, because they had no deepness of earth; the word is the otherness of the flock and the otherness of the soil.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for other carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the promise in it, that there are other sheep beyond the fold I can see, and the Shepherd is bringing them too.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G245 and G1985; overseeing others' affairs, i.e. a meddler (specially, in Gentile customs):--busybody in other men's matters.
BiblicalUsage: Once, in Peter's list of sufferings that bring no blessing: But let none of you suffer as a murderer, or as a thief, or as an evildoer, or as a busybody in other men's matters. The word is the meddler, the one who oversees other people's affairs, and Peter puts it beside murder and theft.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for a meddler carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the company it keeps, that suffering for sticking your nose in where it does not belong earns no credit at all.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G243; another's, i.e. not one's own; by extension foreign, not akin, hostile:--alien, (an-)other (man's, men's), strange(-r).
BiblicalUsage: Another's, not one's own, foreign. The sheep will not follow a stranger, John says, for they know not the voice of strangers. And Abraham sojourned in the land of promise as in a strange country, dwelling in tabernacles with Isaac and Jacob, the heirs with him of the same promise; the word is the strangeness of a place that is not yet home.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for another's carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the two pictures, that the sheep know the Shepherd's voice from a stranger's and the father of the faithful lived his whole life in a country that was not yet his.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Allon-Bakuth, a monumental tree
BiblicalUsage: Once, under the oak at Bethel: Deborah Rebekah's nurse died, and she was buried beneath Bethel under an oak: and the name of it was called Allon-bachuth, the oak of weeping. The name is the tree and the tears together, the place where the old nurse who raised the family was laid to rest.
TheologicalSignificance: A tree named once for weeping carries no lesson of its own. What it shows is how the Bible marks grief, that the burial place of a faithful nurse is remembered by name for three thousand years.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Allon, an Israelite, also a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: The name belongs to a man and a place. Allon the son of Jedaiah is counted among the princes of Simeon, and Allon is a town on the border of Naphtali, where the coast runs from Heleph to Zaanannim; two uses, and the name is all the Bible says of either.
TheologicalSignificance: A name shared by a man and a town carries no lesson of its own. What it shows is the care of the record, that the men of the tribes and the towns of the borders are named alike.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {an oak or other strong tree}
BiblicalUsage: The oak, the strong tree, and the prophets use it to measure what is left. In Isaiah, when the land is desolate and the tenth is burned, yet the stock remains like a teil tree and as an oak, whose substance is in them when they cast their leaves. And Zechariah cries, Howl, O ye oaks of Bashan, for the forest of the vintage is come down.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for an oak carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the stump in Isaiah, that even when the tree is cut down the substance is still in it, and God can grow it again.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: familiar; a friend, also gentle; hence, a bullock (as being tame; applied, although masculine, to a cow); and so, a chieftain (as notable, like neat cattle)
BiblicalUsage: A familiar friend, a guide, and also the tame ox. The dukes of Edom are amazed and the mighty men of Moab tremble when God brings Israel through the sea. And David's grief is sharper because the betrayer is no enemy: it was thou, a man mine equal, my guide, and mine acquaintance; the same word covers the friend at the table and the ox in the yoke.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for a familiar friend carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the wound in it, that the guide who knew the way turned, and the treachery of a friend cuts deeper than an enemy's sword.
RelatedEvents: The Exodus and the Red Sea
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a lass (as veiled or private)
KeyPassages: Genesis 24:43; Isaiah 7:14; Exodus 2:8; Song of Solomon 6:8
BiblicalUsage: A young woman, a lass, veiled or private — and the word carries the whole story of the virgin birth in one verse. Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel. But the word is older than Isaiah: Rebekah's servant meets a damsel at the well, Pharaoh's daughter sends a maid to call the child's mother, and the Song counts threescore queens and fourscore concubines and virgins without number. The word means a young unmarried woman, and the question the centuries argued is whether Isaiah meant more than that.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Isaiah meant more, and Matthew tells me I am right to read it so: the virgin is Mary, and the child is God with us. The word itself is ordinary, a young woman at a well, a maid by the river, a damsel among the queens — and I hold that is exactly how God works, taking the ordinary word and filling it with the one birth that changes everything.
RelatedBooks: Genesis; Isaiah; Exodus; Song of Solomon
RelatedPeople: Miriam; Mary, Mother of Jesus; Rebekah
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: discarded (as a divorced person)
BiblicalUsage: Once, in the word to Babylon: For Israel hath not been forsaken, nor Judah of his God, of the LORD of hosts; though their land was filled with sin against the Holy One of Israel. The word is discarded, forsaken like a divorced person, and the point is that Israel is not that — God has not cast them off.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for forsaken carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the denial, that a people who sinned against the Holy One are still not forsaken by Him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a widow; also a desolate place
BiblicalUsage: The widow — and the Bible never lets her out of its sight. He doth execute the judgment of the fatherless and widow, and loveth the stranger, in giving him food and raiment. Learn to do well, Isaiah says; seek judgment, relieve the oppressed, judge the fatherless, plead for the widow. God is a father of the fatherless and a judge of the widows in His holy habitation; and Zechariah's charge is plain: oppress not the widow, nor the fatherless, the stranger, nor the poor.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the widow is the test of whether a people knows God, because she has nothing to give back. The law, the prophets, the psalms and the restoration all say the same thing: the widow's cause is God's cause, and a religion that passes her by is not the religion of the Bible. I hold that how we treat the woman with no husband and no income tells the truth about us that our songs cannot hide.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: concrete, a widow; abstract, widowhood
BiblicalUsage: Widowhood, the state of being a widow, and the Bible uses it twice with opposite endings. Tamar puts off her widow's garments and covers herself with a veil, the dress of her widowhood laid aside for the plan that will get her justice. And the restored city is told she shall forget the shame of her youth, and shall not remember the reproach of her widowhood any more.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for widowhood carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the promise with it, that the reproach of widowhood is not the last word — God forgets what He has healed.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an Elamite or inhabitant of Elam
BiblicalUsage: Once, in the letter the enemies of Judah write to Artaxerxes: Rehum the chancellor, and Shimshai the scribe, and the rest of their companions, the Dinaites, the Apharsathchites, the Tarpelites, the Apharsites, the Archevites, the Babylonians, the Susanchites, the Dehavites, and the Elamites. The name is a people from Elam, counted among the settlers planted in Samaria to stop the temple.
TheologicalSignificance: A people named once in a letter carries no lesson of its own. What it shows is the opposition the returning exiles faced, that the land was full of settled peoples who wrote to the king to stop the building.
RelatedEvents: Cyrus's Decree and Return from Exile
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Almon-Diblathajemah, a place in Moab
BiblicalUsage: Once in each of two verses, a camp in the wilderness: they removed from Dibon-gad, and encamped in Almon-diblathaim, and they removed from Almon-diblathaim, and pitched in the mountains of Abarim, before Nebo. The name is a stopping place on the way to the promised land, and the stopping is all the Bible says of it.
TheologicalSignificance: A camp named twice on the march carries no lesson of its own. What it shows is the long road itself, that the way to the promise was measured camp by camp, and none of them was home yet.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: bereavement
BiblicalUsage: Once, in the judgment on Babylon: these two things shall come to thee in a moment in one day, the loss of children, and widowhood: they shall come upon thee in their perfection for the multitude of thy sorceries, and for the great abundance of thine enchantments. The word is bereavement, the loss of children, and it comes on the city that trusted in sorcery.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for bereavement carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the sentence, that the city which dealt in enchantments loses her children in a single day.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: some one (i.e. so and so, without giving the name of the person or place)
BiblicalUsage: So-and-so, without giving the name, and the Bible uses it when the name does not matter or must not be said. Boaz goes up to the gate and says to the nearer kinsman, Ho, such a one, turn aside, sit down here — the man who will not redeem Ruth is not even named. And the king of Syria tells his servants, In such and such a place shall be my camp, and Elisha knows the place before the king gets there.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for so-and-so carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the two scenes, that the man who refused his duty goes nameless and the enemy's secret camp is already known to God.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Almodad, a son of Joktan
BiblicalUsage: Once in each genealogy, a son of Joktan: Joktan begat Almodad, and Sheleph, and Hazarmaveth, and Jerah. The name is a link in the table of nations, one of the thirteen sons whose families spread across the south, and the link is all the Bible says of him.
TheologicalSignificance: A name in a genealogy carries no lesson of its own. What it shows is the spread of the nations after the flood, that the sons of Joktan are counted even though their stories are not told.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Almon, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Once, in the cities of the priests: Anathoth with her suburbs, and Almon with her suburbs; four cities. The name is a town in Benjamin given to the Levites, and the gift is all the Bible says of it.
TheologicalSignificance: A town named once in a list of priestly cities carries no lesson of its own. What it shows is the provision for the Levites, that the tribe with no land of its own was given towns scattered through the land.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: almug (i.e. probably sandle-wood) sticks
BiblicalUsage: Twice, and both times about Solomon's glory: the navy of Hiram brought in from Ophir great plenty of almug trees, and precious stones, and the king made of the almug trees pillars for the house of the LORD, and for the king's house, harps also and psalteries for singers. The word is the timber that came from Ophir and became music in the temple.
TheologicalSignificance: The almug tree is not a doctrine but a delivery, and the delivery is the point: timber from Ophir became pillars in the temple and harps for the singers, and the wood that crossed the sea ended in worship.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from the same as G257; to tread out grain:--thresh, tread out the corn.
BiblicalUsage: To tread out grain, to thresh, and Paul uses it three times to make the same point from the law: Thou shalt not muzzle the mouth of the ox that treadeth out the corn. The ox eats while it works, and Paul says the labourer in the gospel is worthy of his hire, and the elder who rules well is worthy of double honour.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for threshing carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the argument built on it, that the ox is not muzzled and neither is the preacher.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of foreign origin (compare G174); aloes (the gum):--aloes.
BiblicalUsage: Once, in the burial of Jesus: Nicodemus came, which at the first came to Jesus by night, and brought a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about an hundred pound weight. The word is the gum, the fragrant aloes, and a hundred pounds of it went into the tomb with the myrrh.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for aloes carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the man who brought it, that Nicodemus, who once came by night, now comes in the open with a king's weight of spice.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and G3056; irrational:--brute, unreasonable.
BiblicalUsage: Irrational, brute, without reason, and Peter and Jude use it for the same men: these, as natural brute beasts, made to be taken and destroyed, speak evil of the things that they understand not. Jude says the same of the men who speak evil of what they know not, and corrupt themselves in what they know naturally, as brute beasts.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for brute carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the judgment in it, that men who live by appetite and mock what they do not understand have made themselves like beasts.
RelatedPeople: Simon Peter; Jude, Brother of James
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain derivation; a fox, i.e. (figuratively) a cunning person:--fox.
BiblicalUsage: A fox, and Jesus uses it twice. Foxes have holes, and birds of the air have nests; but the Son of man hath not where to lay his head. And to Herod He sends a message: Go ye, and tell that fox, Behold, I cast out devils, and I do cures to day and to morrow, and the third day I shall be perfected; the word is the cunning animal, and in the second use it is the cunning king.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for a fox carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the two sayings, that the Son of man had less shelter than a fox and that a fox of a king could not stop His work.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (compare H2501); Alphæus, an Israelite:--Alpheus.
BiblicalUsage: Once in each list, the father of an apostle: James the son of Alphaeus, named among the twelve in Matthew and in Mark. The name is all the Bible says of the man, and his son is the apostle called James the Less, to tell him from James the son of Zebedee.
TheologicalSignificance: A name that is only a father's name carries no lesson of its own. What it shows is how the apostles are told apart, that two men named James are kept straight by their fathers' names.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a non-rising (i.e. resistlessness)
BiblicalUsage: Once, in Agur's list of things that go well: a greyhound; an he goat also; and a king, against whom there is no rising up. The word is the non-rising, the resistlessness of the king against whom no one can stand, and it closes the proverb with a picture of unchallenged power.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for no rising up carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the picture, that the king walks and no one rises against him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: something bound; a sheaf
BiblicalUsage: A sheaf, something bound, and the Bible binds it into two great scenes. Joseph dreams that they are binding sheaves in the field, and his sheaf stands upright while his brothers' sheaves bow down to it. And the psalm of the return from exile ends with the sower: he that goeth forth and weepeth, bearing precious seed, shall doubtless come again with rejoicing, bringing his sheaves with him.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for a sheaf carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the two harvests, that the sheaf that stood upright was hated for it and the sheaf carried home weeping is the picture of the exile's return.
RelatedPeople: Joseph, Son of Jacob; King David
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: lo!
BiblicalUsage: Lo, behold, four times in Daniel, and always at the unveiling. Thou, O king, sawest, and behold a great image, whose brightness was excellent, stood before thee, and the form thereof was terrible. And Daniel says, I considered the horns, and, behold, there came up among them another little horn; the word is the gasp before the vision.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for lo carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the moment it marks, that the king's dream and the prophet's vision both begin with a behold.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: (only in plural as abstract) adolescence; figuratively, vigor
BiblicalUsage: Youth, adolescence, and figuratively vigour, and the Bible uses it for the strength that returns. The restored city is told she shall forget the shame of her youth, and shall not remember the reproach of her widowhood any more. And Elihu promises the sick man that his flesh shall be fresher than a child's, and he shall return to the days of his youth.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for youth carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the return in it, that shame can be forgotten and flesh can be made fresh again.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: the leech
BiblicalUsage: Once, in Agur's proverb: The horseleach hath two daughters, crying, Give, give. There are three things that are never satisfied, yea, four things say not, It is enough. The word is the leech, the bloodsucker that only takes, and it heads the list of the never-satisfied.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for a leech carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the company it keeps, that the cry of Give, give stands beside the grave and the barren womb and the earth that is not filled with water.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Alush, a place in the Desert
BiblicalUsage: Once in each verse, a camp in the wilderness: they departed from Dophkah, and encamped in Alush, and they removed from Alush, and encamped at Rephidim, where was no water for the people to drink. The name is a stopping place on the way to Sinai, and the stopping is all the Bible says of it.
TheologicalSignificance: Two verses name the camp and nothing more, and the spareness is the point: the way out of Egypt was measured camp by camp, and the next camp had no water at all.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Alvah or Aljah, an Idumaean
BiblicalUsage: Once in each genealogy, a duke of Edom: these are the names of the dukes that came of Esau, according to their families, after their places, by their names; duke Timnah, duke Alvah, duke Jetheth. The name is a chief of Esau's line, counted among the dukes, and the count is all the Bible says of him.
TheologicalSignificance: A duke named twice in the lists carries no lesson of its own. What it shows is the order of Edom, that Esau's chiefs are named by their families and their places.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: moral perverseness
BiblicalUsage: Once, in Hosea's charge against Israel: O Israel, thou hast sinned from the days of Gibeah: there they stood: the battle in Gibeah against the children of iniquity did not overtake them. The word is moral perverseness, the crookedness that has been there since Gibeah.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for perverseness carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the charge, that the sin of Gibeah was not a single crime but a crookedness that never left.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Alvan or Aljan, an Idumaean
BiblicalUsage: Once in each genealogy, a son of Shobal: the children of Shobal were these; Alvan, and Manahath, and Ebal, Shepho, and Onam. The name is a Horite chief in the line of Seir, counted among the dukes of Edom, and the count is all the Bible says of him.
TheologicalSignificance: A chief named twice in the lists carries no lesson of its own. What it shows is the order of Edom, that the sons of Seir are named beside the sons of Esau.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: the stout part, i.e. the fat tail of the Oriental sheep
BiblicalUsage: The fat tail of the sheep, the stout part, and the law takes it for the altar. Take of the ram the fat and the rump, and the fat that covereth the inwards, and the caul above the liver, and the two kidneys, and the right shoulder. And the fat tail of the peace offering is offered whole, with the fat that covereth the inwards; the word is the best part, set aside for God.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for the fat tail carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the offering it names, that the fattest part of the animal belonged on the altar, not on the table.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: comparative of a compound of G1 (as a negative particle) and G3077; more without grief:--less sorrowful.
BiblicalUsage: Once, when Paul sends Epaphroditus home: I sent him therefore the more carefully, that, when ye see him again, ye may rejoice, and that I may be the less sorrowful. The word is more without grief, the comparative of sorrow, and Paul measures his own grief against the Philippians' joy.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for less sorrowful carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the heart in it, that Paul would rather be the less sorrowful himself than keep their beloved messenger from them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and the base of G3081; gainless, i.e. (by implication) pernicious:--unprofitable.
BiblicalUsage: Once, in the charge to obey those who watch for your souls: Obey them that have the rule over you, and submit yourselves: for they watch for your souls, as they that must give account, that they may do it with joy, and not with grief: for that is unprofitable for you. The word is gainless, unprofitable, and the grief of a leader is loss for the whole church.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for unprofitable carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the warning, that making the work of the watchmen a grief costs everyone, not just them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Amad, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Once, in the same border list as Allammelek: the coast turns to Carmel westward, and to Shihor-libnath, and then to Allammelek, and Amad, and Mishal, and reacheth to Carmel westward. The name is a town on the boundary line, and the boundary is all the Bible says of it.
TheologicalSignificance: One mention on a boundary line is all Amad gets, and the care is the point: even the border towns are named, and the inheritance is measured town by town.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {a people (as a congregated unit); specifically, a tribe (as those of Israel); hence (collectively) troops or attendants; figuratively, a flock}
BiblicalUsage: A people, a tribe, a nation gathered together — and in the Aramaic of Daniel and Ezra it is the peoples of the empires. In the days of these kings shall the God of heaven set up a kingdom, which shall never be destroyed, and the kingdom shall not be left to other people. And the Son of man is given dominion, that all people, nations, and languages should serve Him. And Artaxerxes decrees that all they of the people of Israel who are minded to go up to Jerusalem may go.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the peoples of the earth are not an afterthought in Daniel; they are the point. The kingdoms of men rise and are broken, and the kingdom that is not left to another people is given to the saints, and to the Son of man whom all peoples serve. I hold that the end of the story is not one people kept safe but every people gathered, and the decree that let Israel go home is a small picture of the gathering that is still coming.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to load, i.e. impose a burden (or figuratively, infliction)
BiblicalUsage: To load, to impose a burden, and the Bible uses it for the load that breaks and the load that cannot be lifted. Joseph's brothers rent their clothes and laded every man his ass and returned to the city, the silver cup found in Benjamin's sack. And Jerusalem will be made a burdensome stone for all people, that all that burden themselves with it shall be cut in pieces.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for loading carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the two burdens, that the brothers carried their guilt home on their asses and the nations will cut themselves trying to lift Jerusalem.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and G3163; peaceable:--not a brawler.
BiblicalUsage: Twice, and both times in the character of a leader: not given to wine, no striker, not greedy of filthy lucre; but patient, not a brawler, not covetous. And again, to speak evil of no man, to be no brawlers, but gentle, shewing all meekness unto all men. The word is peaceable, not a fighter, and Paul puts it in the list twice because the church needs it twice.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for peaceable carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the place it holds, that the man who leads God's people must not be a man who likes a fight.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Amasjah, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Once, in the army of Jehoshaphat: next him was Amasiah the son of Zichri, who willingly offered himself unto the LORD; and with him two hundred thousand mighty men of valour. The name is a captain who offered himself willingly, and the offering is all the Bible says of him.
TheologicalSignificance: A captain named once for willing himself to the LORD carries no lesson of its own. What it shows is the army of Jehoshaphat, that its captains are counted by their willingness as much as by their thousands.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to shake
BiblicalUsage: Once, in the judgment on Egypt: When they took hold of thee by thy hand, thou didst break, and rend all their shoulder: and when they leaned upon thee, thou brakest, and madest all their loins to be at a stand. The word is to shake, to make totter, and Egypt is the reed that breaks in the hand of everyone who leans on it.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for shaking carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the picture, that a nation leaned on as a staff breaks and leaves the hand torn.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to shake
BiblicalUsage: Once, in the judgment on Egypt: When they took hold of thee by thy hand, thou didst break, and rend all their shoulder: and when they leaned upon thee, thou brakest, and madest all their loins to be at a stand. The word is to shake, to make totter, and Egypt is the reed that breaks in the hand of everyone who leans on it.
