Definition: a maidservant or female slave
BiblicalUsage: A maidservant, a handmaid, and the Bible's great prayers come from her lips. Hannah prays, O LORD of hosts, if thou wilt indeed look on the affliction of thine handmaid, and remember me, and not forget thine handmaid, but wilt give unto thine handmaid a man child. And Ruth says to Boaz, I am Ruth thine handmaid: spread therefore thy skirt over thine handmaid; for thou art a near kinsman.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for a handmaid carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the two women who use it, that Hannah and Ruth both ask as servants and both are answered as daughters.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to toil, i.e. work severely and with irksomeness
BiblicalUsage: To toil, to work severely and with irksomeness, and the Preacher makes it his question: What profit hath a man of all his labour which he taketh under the sun? He looks on all the works that his hands have wrought, and on the labour that he has laboured to do, and behold, all is vanity and vexation of spirit. Jonah is told he had pity on a gourd for which he had not laboured, and the psalm says except the LORD build the house, they labour in vain that build it.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the toil is real and the question is honest: what profit is there in work that ends in vanity? The Preacher's answer is not to stop working but to see whose house it is — the labour is vain when it is mine alone, and it is not vain when the LORD builds with me. I hold that Jonah's gourd is the warning, that I can pity what I did not labour for and resent what God did not give me, and the cure is the same: the work is His, and so is the profit.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: toil, i.e. wearing effort; hence, worry, wheth. of body or mind
BiblicalUsage: Toil, wearing effort, worry of body and mind, and the Bible uses it for the weariness that work leaves behind. What profit hath a man of all his labour which he taketh under the sun? The Preacher keeps his heart from no joy, and his heart rejoices in all his labour, and this is his portion. Job curses the day because it shut not up the doors of his mother's womb, nor hid sorrow from his eyes; and the psalm counts the years: our strength is labour and sorrow, for it is soon cut off, and we fly away.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this word names the tiredness everyone knows and no one can fix by working harder. The labour is the portion and the sorrow is the shadow of it, and the psalm does not hide either — the years are short, the strength is labour and sorrow, and we fly away. I hold that the comfort is not in the toil ending but in the God who counts the years with us, and who gives rest to the labouring that the Preacher could not find under the sun.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Amal, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Once, in the sons of Helem: the sons of his brother Helem; Zophah, and Imna, and Shelesh, and Amal. The name is a son of Asher's line, counted among the heads of the tribe, and the count is all the Bible says of him.
TheologicalSignificance: Genealogies do not preach, and Amal's single mention proves it: the order of Asher is kept straight, and even the brothers of the heads are named.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to droop; by implication to be sick, to mourn
BiblicalUsage: To droop, to be sick, to mourn, and the prophets use it for a land that is dying. The earth mourneth and fadeth away, the world languisheth and fadeth away, the haughty people of the earth do languish. And Hosea says the land shall mourn, and every one that dwelleth therein shall languish, with the beasts of the field and the fowls of heaven.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for languishing carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the land in it, that when the people sin the earth itself droops with them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Amalek, a descendant of Esau; also his posterity and their country
BiblicalUsage: Amalek, the grandson of Esau through Eliphaz, and his people are Israel's first enemy after the Red Sea. Then came Amalek, and fought with Israel in Rephidim, and Joshua discomfited him with the edge of the sword while Moses held up his hands; and Moses commands Israel to remember what Amalek did by the way, when they were come forth out of Egypt, how he smote the hindmost, the feeble, all that were behind.
TheologicalSignificance: A name that is both a man and a people carries no lesson of its own. What it shows is the enmity that runs through the whole story, that Amalek struck the weak at the back of the column, and the LORD swore war with Amalek from generation to generation.
RelatedEvents: The Exodus and the Red Sea
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an Amalekite (or collectively the Amalekites) or descendants of Amalek
BiblicalUsage: An Amalekite, one of the people of Amalek, and they are in the story from the beginning. Abraham's campaign smites the country of the Amalekites at Kadesh, and the spies report that the Amalekites dwell in the valley of the south; and Saul warns the Kenites to get down from among the Amalekites, lest he destroy them with them, for the Kenites showed kindness to Israel when they came out of Egypt.
TheologicalSignificance: A people named across the whole story carries no lesson of its own. What it shows is the long enmity, that the Amalekites are there when Abraham fights and still there when Saul is told to destroy them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to associate; by implication, to overshadow (by huddling together)
BiblicalUsage: To associate, to overshadow by huddling together, and the prophets use it for the tree and the gold. The cedars in the garden of God could not hide him, Ezekiel says of Pharaoh, nor any tree in the garden of God was like unto him in his beauty; and Jeremiah asks, How is the gold become dim, how is the most fine gold changed? The word is the overshadowing and the dimming both at once.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for overshadowing carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the two pictures, that the greatest tree in God's garden could not hide Pharaoh and the finest gold can go dim.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Amam, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Once, in the cities of Judah: Amam, and Shema, and Moladah. The name is a town in the south, counted among the cities of the tribe, and the count is all the Bible says of it.
TheologicalSignificance: A town named once in a list carries no lesson of its own. What it shows is the inheritance measured town by town, that even the small towns of the south are named.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {properly, to build up or support; to foster as a parent or nurse; figuratively to render (or be) firm or faithful, to trust or believe, to be permanent or quiet; morally to be true or certain};
BiblicalUsage: Certain, true, faithful — and in Daniel's Aramaic it is the word for what can be trusted. The dream is certain, and the interpretation thereof sure, Daniel tells the king of the stone cut out without hands. And the presidents could find no fault in Daniel, forasmuch as he was faithful, neither was there any error found in him. And no hurt was found on him in the den, because he believed in his God.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this word is the spine of Daniel's story: the dream is certain, the man is faithful, and the God he believed is sure. Faithfulness is not a feeling but a record — the presidents searched for a fault and found none, and the lions found a man whose trust had already been tested. I hold that the God who makes dreams certain is the same God who keeps faithful men, and believing Him is not a risk but the one sure thing in a foreign court.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to take the right hand road
BiblicalUsage: Once, in the word behind you on the road: thine ears shall hear a word behind thee, saying, This is the way, walk ye in it, when ye turn to the right hand, and when ye turn to the left. The word is to take the right hand road, the turn to the right, and the voice tells you which way to turn.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for the right hand road carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the voice with it, that God does not leave His people to guess the way but speaks behind them as they walk.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an expert
BiblicalUsage: Once, in the song of the bride: the joints of thy thighs are like jewels, the work of the hands of a cunning workman. The word is the expert, the skilled craftsman, and the beauty praised is the work of hands that know their trade.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for a skilled workman carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the praise, that the work of expert hands is itself a kind of beauty.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to take the right hand road
BiblicalUsage: Once, in the word behind you on the road: thine ears shall hear a word behind thee, saying, This is the way, walk ye in it, when ye turn to the right hand, and when ye turn to the left. The word is to take the right hand road, the turn to the right, and the voice tells you which way to turn.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for the right hand road carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the voice with it, that God does not leave His people to guess the way but speaks behind them as they walk.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Amanah, a mountain near Damascus
BiblicalUsage: The name is a river and a mountain. Abana, the river of Damascus, is the water Naaman wants to wash in instead of the Jordan, and he turns away in a rage before his servants talk him back; and Amana is the mountain the bride is called to look from, from the top of Amana, from Shenir and Hermon, from the lions' dens; one name, two places, and the Bible keeps them apart by the story.
TheologicalSignificance: A name shared by a river and a mountain carries no lesson of its own. What it shows is the two scenes, that a proud general nearly missed his healing over a river and a bride is called to look out from a height.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: something fixed, i.e. a covenant. an allowance
BiblicalUsage: Something fixed, a covenant, an allowance, and Nehemiah uses it twice. Now those that sealed were Nehemiah and the priests and the Levites, the sealed covenant after the wall is built. And the singers have a certain portion, due for every day, by the king's commandment; the word is what is fixed and settled, whether a signature or a daily ration.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for something fixed carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the two fixings, that the covenant was sealed in writing and the singers were fed by the day.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G260; properly, to collect, i.e. (by implication) reap:--reap down.
BiblicalUsage: Once, and it is the cry of the unpaid: Behold, the hire of the labourers who have reaped down your fields, which is of you kept back by fraud, crieth: and the cries of them which have reaped are entered into the ears of the Lord of sabaoth. The word is to reap, to gather the harvest, and the wages of the reapers are the charge against the rich.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for reaping carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the cry with it, that the hire kept back by fraud is heard in heaven even when the labourers are not.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to be (causatively, make) deep (literally or figuratively)
BiblicalUsage: To be deep, or to make deep, and Isaiah uses it for the sign and the secret. Ask thee a sign of the LORD thy God; ask it either in the depth, or in the height above — as deep as hell or as high as heaven, the sign is yours for the asking; and woe unto them that seek deep to hide their counsel from the LORD, and their works are in the dark, and they say, Who seeth us? and who knoweth us?
TheologicalSignificance: A word for deep carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the two depths, that God offers a sign from the depth and men dig deep to hide from Him, and neither depth hides anything from the LORD.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {to say (used with great latitude)}
BiblicalUsage: To say, in the Aramaic of Daniel, and the whole book speaks in it. Then spake the Chaldeans to the king in Syriack, O king, live for ever: tell thy servants the dream, and we will shew the interpretation. And the king answered and said to Daniel, Of a truth it is, that your God is a God of gods, and a Lord of kings, and a revealer of secrets, seeing thou couldest reveal this secret.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for saying carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the two speeches, that the Chaldeans spoke to buy time and the king spoke to confess that Daniel's God reveals secrets.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to gather grain
BiblicalUsage: To gather grain, and the law uses it for the thief who gathers men. If a man be found stealing any of his brethren of the children of Israel, and maketh merchandise of him, or selleth him, then that thief shall die. And the psalm of the harvest says the mower filleth not his hand with the grass of the housetops, nor he that bindeth sheaves his bosom; the word is the gathering, whether of sheaves or of stolen men.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for gathering grain carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the two gatherings, that the sheaf-binder's arms are empty on the housetops and the man-stealer dies for treating a brother as a harvest.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: wool
BiblicalUsage: Once, in the vision of the Ancient of Days: I beheld till the thrones were cast down, and the Ancient of days did sit, whose garment was white as snow, and the hair of his head like the pure wool. The word is wool itself, and the hair of the Ancient is white as the wool that has never been dyed.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for wool carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the whiteness, that the Ancient of Days is seen in the colour of purity itself.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to say (used with great latitude)
BiblicalUsage: To say, the commonest verb in the Bible, four thousand times and more. And God said, Let there be light: and there was light. And God said unto Moses, I AM THAT I AM: thus shalt thou say unto the children of Israel, I AM hath sent me unto you; the word is the saying itself, and the Bible begins with God saying and goes on saying until the end.
TheologicalSignificance: Saying is the commonest act in the Bible, and the word itself teaches nothing; the weight is who says it, that when God says, light is, and when God says I AM, Moses has a name to carry into Egypt.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G263; "amaranthine", i.e. (by implication) fadeless:--that fadeth not away.
BiblicalUsage: Once, in the promise to the elders: And when the chief Shepherd shall appear, ye shall receive a crown of glory that fadeth not away. The word is amaranthine, of the flower that does not fade, and the crown is made of it.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for unfading carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the crown, that the shepherds who feed the flock are promised a glory that does not wither.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and a presumed derivative of G3133; unfading, i.e. (by implication) perpetual:--that fadeth not away.
BiblicalUsage: Once, in the inheritance: To an inheritance incorruptible, and undefiled, and that fadeth not away, reserved in heaven for you. The word is unfading, the flower that keeps its colour, and Peter uses it for what is kept for us where moth and rust cannot reach it.
TheologicalSignificance: The inheritance does not fade, and that is the whole weight of the word: what is reserved in heaven keeps its colour the way nothing here does.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and a form of G3144; unattested:--without witness.
BiblicalUsage: Once, when Paul tells the men of Lystra that God did not leave Himself unattested: Nevertheless he left not himself without witness, in that he did good, and gave us rain from heaven, and fruitful seasons, filling our hearts with food and gladness. The word is without witness, and Paul's point is that God is never that — the rain itself is the testimony.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for unattested carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the denial, that the God who gives rain and fruitful seasons has never left Himself without a witness.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Amarjah, the name of nine Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Nine men share the name, and the Bible keeps them apart by their place. Amariah the Levite, son of Hebron, is counted among the heads of the Levites in David's census and again in the courses of the priests; Amariah the chief priest stands over Jehoshaphat's court in all matters of the LORD; and the high-priestly line runs through Amariahs from Meraioth to Ahitub, father to son down the generations.
TheologicalSignificance: A name shared by nine men carries no lesson of its own. What it shows is the order of the priesthood, that the same name recurs in the Levites, the chief priests and the high-priestly line, and each man is counted in his own place.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Amasa, the name of two Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Two men share the name, and both end badly. Amasa son of Jether, Abigail's son and David's nephew, is made captain of Absalom's host, then captain of Judah's host in his place, and Joab greets him with a kiss and stabs him in the belly; and Amasa son of Hadlai is a chief of Ephraim who stands up to the king of Israel and sends the captives home clothed and fed; the name is the same; the men are not.
TheologicalSignificance: Two men, one name, and the contrast is the lesson: one Amasa is murdered by the man he replaced, and the other stops a king's cruelty with mercy.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Amasai, the name of three Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Three men share the name, and the Bible keeps them apart by their errand. Amasai the chief of the captains comes over to David at Ziklag, and the spirit comes upon him, and he says, Thine are we, David, and on thy side, thou son of Jesse; Amasai the priest blows the trumpet before the ark when David brings it to Jerusalem; and Mahath the son of Amasai is a Levite who cleanses the temple under Hezekiah; the name is the same; the men are not.
TheologicalSignificance: The name is the same and the errands are not: one Amasai joins David, one blows the trumpet before the ark, and the third man's son cleanses the house of God.
RelatedEvents: David Brings the Ark to Jerusalem
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Amashsay, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Once, in the priests who came back to Jerusalem: his brethren, chief of the fathers, two hundred forty and two: and Amashai the son of Azareel, the son of Ahasai, the son of Meshillemoth, the son of Immer. The name is a priest counted among the chiefs of the fathers, and the count is all the Bible says of him.
TheologicalSignificance: A name in a list of returning priests carries no lesson of its own. What it shows is the rebuilding, that the priests came back by their fathers' houses and were counted two hundred and forty-two strong.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and G3129; ignorant:--unlearned.
BiblicalUsage: Once, in Peter's warning about Paul's letters: As also in all his epistles, speaking in them of these things; in which are some things hard to be understood, which they that are unlearned and unstable wrest, as they do also the other scriptures, unto their own destruction. The word is unlearned, and Peter puts it beside unstable, the two marks of the man who twists the Scriptures.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for unlearned carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the warning, that hard sayings are not to be wrested by the untaught, and the twisting ends in destruction.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to be alert, physically (on foot) or mentally (in courage)
BiblicalUsage: To be alert, to be strong and of good courage, and the Bible says it to men who are afraid. Be strong and of a good courage, fear not, nor be afraid of them, Moses tells Israel at the Jordan. Have not I commanded thee? Be strong and of a good courage, God tells Joshua at the same river; and David tells Solomon, Be strong and of good courage, and do it: fear not, nor be dismayed: for the LORD God, even my God, will be with thee.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe courage in the Bible is not a temper but a command, given three times at three rivers of fear, and always with the same reason: God goes with you. Moses says it to a people about to fight, God says it to a man about to lead, and David says it to a son about to build. I hold that the courage is not in me but in the company — He will not fail thee, nor forsake thee, and that is the whole of it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Amatsjah, the name of four Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Four men share the name, and the king is the one the story follows. Amaziah son of Joash is twenty and five years old when he begins to reign, and he reigns twenty and nine years in Jerusalem; he gathers Judah, hires a hundred thousand men of Israel for a hundred talents of silver, and is told to send them home; and the other Amaziahs are counted in the lines of Judah and Simeon and Levi, a king's son, a Simeonite prince, a Levite.
TheologicalSignificance: Four men, one name, but only the king's story is told: Amaziah did what was right but not with a perfect heart, and the pride of his victory over Edom was his undoing.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: toiling; concretely, a laborer; figuratively, sorrowful
BiblicalUsage: Toiling, a labourer, and the Preacher hates his own labour for it. Yea, I hated all my labour which I had taken under the sun, because I should leave it unto the man that shall be after me. And the man alone, with neither child nor brother, labours without end, and his eye is not satisfied with riches, and he never asks, For whom do I labour, and bereave my soul of good?
TheologicalSignificance: A word for the toiling labourer carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the question the Preacher never answers, for whom do I labour, when the labour outlasts the man who does it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: languid
BiblicalUsage: Once, in the taunt of Sanballat, who asks what these feeble Jews think they are doing: will they fortify themselves, will they sacrifice, will they make an end in a day, will they revive the stones out of the heaps of the rubbish which are burned? The word is languid, feeble, and the enemy means it as mockery, that the Jews are too weak to build.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for feeble carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the taunt, that the men called too weak to build finished the wall in fifty-two days.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and G3199; to be careless of:--make light of, neglect, be negligent, no regard.
BiblicalUsage: To be careless of, to make light of, to neglect — and the New Testament uses it for the things no one can afford to neglect. They made light of the king's invitation, and went their ways, one to his farm, another to his merchandise. How shall we escape, if we neglect so great salvation? God says of Israel, they continued not in my covenant, and I regarded them not; and Paul warns Timothy, Neglect not the gift that is in thee.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe neglect is the quietest sin in the Bible, and that is why it frightens me. No one sets out to despise the invitation or the salvation or the gift; they make light of it, they go their ways, one to the farm and one to the merchandise, and the door closes behind them. I hold that the opposite of neglect is not effort but attention — to the invitation, to the salvation, to the gift — and attention is the one thing I can give today.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: adverb from G273; faultlessly:--blameless, unblamably.
BiblicalUsage: Faultlessly, unblamably, and Paul uses it twice for the life he lived and the life he prays for. Ye are witnesses, and God also, how holily and justly and unblameably we behaved ourselves among you that believe. And he prays that the whole spirit and soul and body be preserved blameless unto the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for faultlessly carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the two uses, that Paul lived unblamably among the Thessalonians and prayed they would be kept blameless until Christ comes.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and a derivative of G3201; irreproachable:--blameless, faultless, unblamable.
BiblicalUsage: Blameless, without fault, and the New Testament uses it for the life that holds up under inspection. Zacharias and Elisabeth are both righteous before God, walking in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord blameless. Paul tells the Philippians to be blameless and harmless, the sons of God, without rebuke, in the midst of a crooked and perverse nation. And he counts his own record touching the righteousness which is in the law, blameless — before he counts it all loss for Christ.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe blameless does not mean sinless; it means there is nothing to charge, and the charge is the thing that matters. Zacharias and Elisabeth walked blamelessly and still needed a Saviour, and Paul was blameless in the law and still called himself the chief of sinners. I hold that the blameless life is the one that has nothing to hide from men and everything to confess to God, and that is why the same word can describe both the priest and the apostle who threw his record away.
RelatedPeople: Paul; Zechariah, Father of John the Baptist
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H543); properly, firm, i.e. (figuratively) trustworthy; adverbially, surely (often as interjection, so be it):--amen, verily.
BiblicalUsage: Amen, firm, trustworthy, surely — and the word is the seal on everything God has said. All the promises of God in him are yea, and in him Amen, unto the glory of God by us. The whole congregation says Amen at the giving of thanks, and the unlearned man can only say it if he understands what is said. And the Bible ends with it: He which testifieth these things saith, Surely I come quickly; Amen; even so, come, Lord Jesus.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Amen is the shortest creed in the Bible, and the whole faith fits in it: God has spoken, His promises are yes in Christ, and my answer is Amen. The congregation says it together because the promises belong to all of us, and the last Amen of the Bible is a prayer, that He would come quickly. I hold that every Amen I say is a small act of trust, that what God promised He will do, and that the end of the story is not a question but an agreement.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: sure; abstract, faithfulness; adverb, truly
BiblicalUsage: Amen, firm, trustworthy, surely — and the word is the seal on everything God has said. When the curses of the law are read, all the people say Amen, and when David's psalm of thanks ends, all the people say Amen and praise the LORD; and when David names Solomon his heir, Benaiah answers Amen, the LORD God of my lord the king say so too.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Amen is the shortest creed in the Bible, and the whole faith fits in it: God has spoken, and my answer is Amen. The people say it together because the word belongs to all of us, and I hold that every Amen I say is a small act of trust, that what God promised He will do.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: deep (literally or figuratively)
BiblicalUsage: Deep, and the Bible uses it for the speech you cannot understand. Thou art not sent to a people of a strange speech and of an hard language, Ezekiel is told, but to the house of Israel. And Isaiah sees a people of a deeper speech than thou canst perceive, of a stammering tongue, that thou canst not understand.
TheologicalSignificance: Depth is not a doctrine, and the word proves it: a language can be too deep to understand and still be no hiding place from God.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and G3308; not anxious:--without care(-fulness), secure.
BiblicalUsage: Without care, secure, and the New Testament uses it twice for two kinds of freedom. The chief priests promise the soldiers, if this come to the governor's ears, we will persuade him, and secure you — safe from the governor, for a price. And Paul says, I would have you without carefulness, the unmarried man caring for the things of the Lord, how he may please the Lord; the word is the same; the security is not.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for without care carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the two securities, that the priests buy safety with a lie and Paul offers freedom from care to the man who pleases the Lord.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and a derivative of G3334; immovable:--unmovable.
BiblicalUsage: Once, in the verse that closes the resurrection chapter: Therefore, my beloved brethren, be ye stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, forasmuch as ye know that your labour is not in vain in the Lord. The word is immovable, not to be shifted, and Paul sets it at the end of the longest argument in his letters, as if to say, now stand here.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for unmoveable carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the place it stands, that after the resurrection is proved the command is to stand still in it and abound.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and a presumed derivative of G3338; irrevocable:--without repentance, not to be repented of.
BiblicalUsage: Without repentance, irrevocable, and Paul uses it for the two things God will not take back. The gifts and calling of God are without repentance — He does not regret choosing Israel, and He does not regret calling you. And godly sorrow worketh repentance to salvation not to be repented of, the repentance that saves and is never regretted, against the sorrow of the world which worketh death.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for irrevocable carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the two gifts, that God's calling is not regretted by Him and the repentance He gives is not regretted by us.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and a presumed derivative of G3340; unrepentant:--impenitent.
BiblicalUsage: Once, in the sentence on the hard heart: after thy hardness and impenitent heart treasurest up unto thyself wrath against the day of wrath and revelation of the righteous judgment of God. The word is unrepentant, the heart that will not turn, and the wrath is treasured up like money in a storehouse, day by day.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for impenitent carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the picture, that a heart that will not turn is storing up wrath the way a miser stores gold.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and a derivative of G3346; unchangeable, or (neuter as abstract) unchangeability:--immutable(-ility).
BiblicalUsage: Unchangeable, and Hebrews uses it for the two things God cannot do. God, willing more abundantly to shew unto the heirs of promise the immutability of his counsel, confirmed it by an oath, that by two immutable things, in which it was impossible for God to lie, we might have a strong consolation. The word is the counsel that cannot be moved, and the oath that cannot be broken.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for unchangeable carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the consolation, that the heirs of promise have two things that cannot move, and that is why they can hold on.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and a derivative of G3184; the "amethyst" (supposed to prevent intoxication):--amethyst.
BiblicalUsage: Once, in the foundations of the city: the fifth, sardonyx; the sixth, sardius; the seventh, chrysolyte; the eighth, beryl; the ninth, a topaz; the tenth, a chrysoprasus; the eleventh, a jacinth; the twelfth, an amethyst. The word is the stone itself, the purple jewel, twelfth in the wall of the New Jerusalem.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for an amethyst carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the wall it sits in, that the city of God is built on twelve stones and the last of them is purple.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and G3384; motherless, i.e. of unknown maternity:--without mother.
BiblicalUsage: Once, in the portrait of Melchisedec: Without father, without mother, without descent, having neither beginning of days, nor end of life; but made like unto the Son of God; abideth a priest continually. The word is motherless, of unknown maternity, and the point is not that Melchisedec had no mother but that the record gives him none, so his priesthood has no beginning and no end.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for motherless carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the silence, that the priest with no genealogy is the picture of the priest who lives forever.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and G3358; immoderate:--(thing) without measure.
BiblicalUsage: Without measure, immoderate, and Paul uses it twice to say what he will not do. We will not boast of things without our measure, but according to the measure of the rule which God hath distributed to us. And again, not boasting of things without our measure, that is, of other men's labours; the word is the boast that goes past the boundary God set.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for without measure carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the boundary, that Paul will boast only inside the measure God gave him and not in another man's work.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and a derivative of G3392; unsoiled, i.e. (figuratively) pure:--undefiled.
BiblicalUsage: Unsoiled, undefiled, and the New Testament uses it for the things that stay clean. The inheritance is incorruptible, and undefiled, and that fadeth not away, reserved in heaven for you. The high priest is holy, harmless, undefiled, separate from sinners. Marriage is honourable in all, and the bed undefiled; and pure religion and undefiled before God is this, to visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe undefiled is the word for what the world cannot stain, and the four uses agree on what it is: the inheritance kept in heaven, the priest set apart, the marriage bed honoured, and the religion that visits the widow. The world soils by contact, and God keeps by separation — not the separation that hides, but the one that serves. I hold that the cleanest thing in the New Testament is not the man who avoids the world but the one who goes into it to visit the fatherless and comes back unspotted.
RelatedPeople: Simon Peter; James, Brother of Jesus
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H5992); Aminadab, an Israelite:--Aminadab.
BiblicalUsage: Once in each genealogy, a link in the line of the Messiah: Aram begat Aminadab, and Aminadab begat Naasson, and Naasson begat Salmon. Luke counts him the same way, the son of Aram and the father of Naasson, in the line that runs from Abraham to David to Jesus; the name is a link in the chain, and the link is all the Bible says of him.
TheologicalSignificance: A name in the genealogy of Christ carries no lesson of its own. What it shows is the chain itself, that the promise runs father to son through men whose only story is the son they begat.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Amittai, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Once in each verse, the father of a prophet: Jonah the son of Amittai, the prophet, which was of Gath-hepher, by whose word Jeroboam restored the coast of Israel. And the word of the LORD came unto Jonah the son of Amittai, saying, Arise, go to Nineveh, that great city, and cry against it; the name is the father's name, and the son is the prophet who ran.
TheologicalSignificance: Jonah is introduced by his father's name before he is sent anywhere, and that is all Amittai's name does: it places the prophet in a family before it places him in Nineveh.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Ami, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Once, in the children of Solomon's servants who came back from exile: the children of Sotai, the children of Sophereth, the children of Peruda, the children of Jaalah, the children of Darkon, the children of Giddel, the children of Shephatiah, the children of Hattil, the children of Pochereth of Zebaim, the children of Ami. The name is a family among the servants, and the list is all the Bible says of them.
TheologicalSignificance: A family named once in a list of returnees carries no lesson of its own. What it shows is the return itself, that even the servants' families are counted among those who came home.
RelatedEvents: Cyrus's Decree and Return from Exile
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: profound, i.e. unsearchable
BiblicalUsage: Once, in Daniel's praise: He revealeth the deep and secret things: he knoweth what is in the darkness, and the light dwelleth with him. The word is profound, unsearchable, and the deep things are the ones God reveals and men cannot reach alone.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for profound carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the praise, that the deep and secret things are known to the God who dwells in light.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a bunch of grain
BiblicalUsage: A bunch of grain, a sheaf, and the prophets use it for the weight and the gathering. Behold, I am pressed under you, Amos says, as a cart is pressed that is full of sheaves — God bent under the weight of His own people. And Micah says He shall gather them as the sheaves into the floor, the nations gathered for the threshing.
TheologicalSignificance: The sheaf is a weight and a gathering both at once: God is pressed under His people like a cart under sheaves, and the nations are gathered like sheaves for the threshing floor.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a summit (of a tree or mountain)
BiblicalUsage: A summit, the top of a tree or a mountain, and Isaiah uses it for what is left after the shaking. Yet gleaning grapes shall be left in it, as the shaking of an olive tree, two or three berries in the top of the uppermost bough. And the strong cities shall be as a forsaken bough, and an uppermost branch, left because of the children of Israel.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for the uppermost bough carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the gleaning, that after the shaking a few berries are still left at the top.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: companionship; hence (concretely) a comrade or kindred man
BiblicalUsage: Companionship, a comrade, a kindred man — and the law uses it for the neighbour at your elbow. If a soul sin and lie unto his neighbour in that which was delivered him to keep, or in fellowship, or in a thing taken away by violence, or hath deceived his neighbour. Ye shall not steal, neither deal falsely, neither lie one to another. Thou shalt not hate thy brother in thine heart: thou shalt in any wise rebuke thy neighbour, and not suffer sin upon him.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this word is the whole of the second table in one root: the neighbour is not an abstraction but the comrade, the kindred man, the one whose goods are in your keeping and whose sins are your business to rebuke in love. The law does not ask me to love humanity; it asks me not to lie to the man next door, not to steal from him, not to hate him in my heart. I hold that is where love is proved, not in the grand gesture but in the neighbour, and the neighbour is always nearer than I want him to be.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {properly, a mother (i.e. unit of measure, or the fore-arm (below the elbow), i.e. a cubit; also a door-base (as a bond of the entrance)}
BiblicalUsage: A cubit, the forearm, the measure of the builders, and the Bible measures its great things in it. Nebuchadnezzar's image is threescore cubits high and six cubits broad, set up in the plain of Dura. And Cyrus decrees the house of God at Jerusalem shall be threescore cubits high and threescore cubits broad, the foundations strongly laid; the word is the elbow to the fingertip, and empires and temples are both built by it.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for a cubit carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the two buildings, that the king's image and God's house are both threescore cubits high, and only one of them stands.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Ammah, a hill in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Once, in the pursuit of Abner: Joab also and Abishai pursued after Abner, and the sun went down when they were come to the hill of Ammah, that lieth before Giah by the way of the wilderness of Gibeon. The name is a hill on the road to the wilderness, and the sunset there is all the Bible says of it.
TheologicalSignificance: A hill named once at sunset carries no lesson of its own. What it shows is the pursuit itself, that the chase ran until the sun went down and the hill was the mark of how far it had gone.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {properly, a mother (i.e. unit of measure, or the fore-arm (below the elbow), i.e. a cubit; also a door-base (as a bond of the entrance)}
BiblicalUsage: A cubit, the forearm, the measure of the builders, and the Bible measures its great things in it. Nebuchadnezzar's image is threescore cubits high and six cubits broad, set up in the plain of Dura. And Cyrus decrees the house of God at Jerusalem shall be threescore cubits high and threescore cubits broad, the foundations strongly laid; the word is the elbow to the fingertip, and empires and temples are both built by it.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for a cubit carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the two buildings, that the king's image and God's house are both threescore cubits high, and only one of them stands.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Ammiel, the name of three or four Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Ammiel belongs to three men, and the Bible keeps them apart by their sons. Ammiel the son of Gemalli is the spy from Dan who goes up to search the land; Ammiel of Lo-debar is the father of Machir, in whose house Mephibosheth is hidden until David sends for him; and Ammiel is the father of Bathsheba, called Eliam in Samuel, whose daughter becomes the mother of Solomon.
TheologicalSignificance: Three households, one name: one Ammiel sends a spy, one shelters a cripple, and one gives a daughter to the king.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Ammi-Nadib, probably an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Once, in the song: Or ever I was aware, my soul made me like the chariots of Amminadib. The name is read as a man's name, Amminadib, and as a phrase, my noble people, the chariots of my willing people — and the scholars have argued ever since which it is; the verse is the only place the name occurs, and the argument is older than the translations.
TheologicalSignificance: A name that may be a phrase carries no lesson of its own. What it shows is the honesty of the text, that the song leaves the chariots unexplained and the reader must hold both readings at once.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Ammichur, a Syrian prince
BiblicalUsage: Once, in the flight of Absalom: Absalom fled, and went to Talmai, the son of Ammihud, king of Geshur. And David mourned for his son every day; the name is the father of the king who shelters the murderer, and the shelter is all the Bible says of him.
TheologicalSignificance: The father's name is the whole of it, and the refuge is the point: Absalom fled to his grandfather's house in Geshur and stayed there three years.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Ammihud, the name of three Israelites
BiblicalUsage: The name Ammihud belongs to three men, and the Bible keeps them apart by their sons. Ammihud is the father of Elishama, the captain of Ephraim in the wilderness; Ammihud is the father of Shemuel, the prince of Simeon who divides the land; and Ammihud is the father of Talmai, the king of Geshur who shelters Absalom.
TheologicalSignificance: Three sons, three houses, one name: one Ammihud gives a captain, one gives a prince, and one gives a king who hides a fugitive.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Amminadab, the name of four Israelites
KeyPassages: Exodus 6:23; Numbers 1:7; Ruth 4:19; 1 Chronicles 2:10; 1 Chronicles 6:22; 1 Chronicles 15:10
BiblicalUsage: Four men share the name, and the first is the one the story follows. Amminadab is the father of Elisheba, Aaron's wife, and the father of Nahshon, the prince of Judah who leads the march; His name runs through the genealogies of Judah, through Ruth and through the kings, father to son down to David; and the other Amminadabs are counted in the lines of Levi and Judah, a Levite chief and a son of Kohath.
TheologicalSignificance: The line of Judah runs through this name: the prince who leads the march is the son of Amminadab, and the promise runs through his house.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Ammishaddai, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Twice, and both times as a father's name: Of Dan; Ahiezer the son of Ammishaddai. And the captain of the children of Dan shall be Ahiezer the son of Ammishaddai, and the name is the father's name, and the son is the captain of the camp of Dan on the north side.
TheologicalSignificance: Every captain is named by his father, and that is all this name does: it places Ahiezer in the camp of Dan, on the north side, under his father's name.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: strong or (abstractly) strength
BiblicalUsage: Strong, or strength itself, and the Bible uses it for the strength that cannot be matched. Lift up your eyes on high, Isaiah says, and behold who hath created these things, that bringeth out their host by number: he calleth them all by names by the greatness of his might, for that he is strong in power; not one faileth. And Job asks, If I speak of strength, lo, he is strong: and if of judgment, who shall set me a time to plead?
TheologicalSignificance: A word for strong carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the question, that if the strength is His, who will set the time to plead against Him?
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Ammizabad, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Once, in the captains of David: This is that Benaiah, who was mighty among the thirty, and above the thirty: and in his charge was Ammizabad his son. The name is the son of the mighty man, given charge of his father's division, and the charge is all the Bible says of him.
TheologicalSignificance: A name that is only a son's name carries no lesson of its own. What it shows is the army's order, that the divisions pass from father to son, and the mighty man's son holds his father's place.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: perhaps from G260; sand (as heaped on the beach):--sand.
BiblicalUsage: Sand, as heaped on the beach, and Jesus and Paul use it for the two ends of counting. Every one that heareth these sayings of mine, and doeth them not, shall be likened unto a foolish man, which built his house upon the sand. And Isaiah cries concerning Israel, Though the number of the children of Israel be as the sand of the sea, a remnant shall be saved; the word is the sand that cannot be numbered and the sand that cannot hold a house.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for sand carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the two pictures, that the sand is too many to count and too weak to build on.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Ammon, a son of Lot; also his posterity and their country
BiblicalUsage: Ammon, the son of Lot by his younger daughter, and his people are Israel's neighbours and enemies for a thousand years. Ben-ammi, the son of my people, is the father of the children of Ammon unto this day; Moses is told not to distress them, for God has given their land to the children of Lot for a possession; and Jephthah sends messengers to the king of the children of Ammon, asking what he has to do with him, that he comes to fight in his land.
TheologicalSignificance: The children of Lot are given their land by God and still come to fight for it, and that long neighbourhood is the whole story: Israel is told to leave them alone, and they will not leave Israel alone.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an Ammonite or (the adjective) Ammonitish
BiblicalUsage: The Ammonites were Lot's descendants through his younger daughter, and they stayed enemies of Israel for centuries. Nahash the Ammonite besieged Jabesh-gilead and demanded the right eye of every man as the price of peace; centuries later, when the exiles came home, the law was read aloud again — no Ammonite was ever to enter the congregation of God, because they had refused Israel bread and water on the road out of Egypt and hired Balaam to curse them.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the Ammonite story is a warning about how a small refusal hardens into a lasting barrier: they would not give bread and water to tired travellers, and that one unkindness echoed for generations. God remembers how His people are treated, and He also remembers that outsiders like Ruth still found their way in by faith.
RelatedPeople: Nahash, King of Ammon; Tobiah the Ammonite
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an Ammonitess
BiblicalUsage: The Ammonites were Lot's descendants through his younger daughter, and they stayed enemies of Israel for centuries. Nahash the Ammonite besieged Jabesh-gilead and demanded the right eye of every man as the price of peace; centuries later, when the exiles came home, the law was read aloud again — no Ammonite was ever to enter the congregation of God, because they had refused Israel bread and water on the road out of Egypt and hired Balaam to curse them.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the Ammonite story is a warning about how a small refusal hardens into a lasting barrier: they would not give bread and water to tired travellers, and that one unkindness echoed for generations. God remembers how His people are treated, and He also remembers that outsiders like Ruth still found their way in by faith.
RelatedPeople: Naamah, the Ammonitess; Shimeath, the Ammonitess
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a column (as standing); also a stand, i.e. platform
BiblicalUsage: A pillar in the Bible is something that stands — it holds weight and it marks the way. The LORD went before Israel in a pillar of cloud by day and fire by night; the same cloudy pillar came down and stood at the door of the tabernacle while God talked with Moses. In the temple Solomon cast two great pillars of brass, eighteen cubits high, and in the house of Dagon Samson took hold of the two middle pillars and pulled the whole building down.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the pillar is the picture of God's presence going with His people — steady, visible, and impossible to miss. He does not only point the way; He stands in it, ahead of us, so we can follow. And I believe the same God who led by cloud and fire still goes before His people today, even when the pillar looks different than I expect.
RelatedEvents: The Exodus and the Red Sea; Samson and Delilah
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: apparently a primary word; a lamb:--lamb.
BiblicalUsage: John the Baptist saw Jesus coming and said, 'Behold the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world.' The Ethiopian eunuch was reading Isaiah's picture of the same lamb — led to the slaughter, silent before his shearer — and Philip showed him it was Jesus. Peter says we were redeemed not with silver and gold but with the precious blood of Christ, as of a lamb without blemish and without spot.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the lamb is the whole gospel in one word: innocent, offered, and enough. Every lamb in the Old Testament pointed forward to this one, and this one Lamb takes away the sin of the world — not just Israel's sin, and not just mine, but the world's. That is why I can rest: the sacrifice is finished, and the Lamb lives.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Amnon (or Aminon), a son of David
BiblicalUsage: Amnon was David's firstborn son, and his name is tied to one of the darkest stories in the family: he loved his half-sister Tamar, forced her, and then hated her, and two years later Absalom had his servants kill him at a feast, and the news reached David as though all his sons were dead. The Bible tells it plainly, without softening what Amnon did or what it cost.
TheologicalSignificance: What strikes me about Amnon is how fast lust turns to hate and how one sin drags a whole family down with it: David did nothing, Absalom took revenge, and the house never recovered. I believe the story is there so we see sin for what it is — not a private slip, but a fire that burns everyone near it.
RelatedPeople: Amnon, Son of David; Tamar, Daughter of David; Absalom
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from ἀμείβω (to exchange); requital:--requite.
BiblicalUsage: The word appears once, and it is about children and grandchildren repaying their parents: let them learn first to show piety at home, and to requite their parents, for that is good and acceptable before God. Honouring father and mother is not only a command for children — it is a debt the grown children pay back by caring for the ones who cared for them.
TheologicalSignificance: One verse, one duty, and it is plain enough: caring for your own parents is part of serving God, not something separate from it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and a derivative of G3469; unblamable:--blameless.
BiblicalUsage: Peter uses it once, at the end of his letter: seeing that we look for new heavens and a new earth, be diligent to be found of him in peace, without spot, and blameless. The word shares its root with the one for a lamb without blemish — a life with nothing on it that can be blamed.
TheologicalSignificance: One verse carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is Peter's call to live clean while we wait for the day of God.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and G3470; unblemished (literally or figuratively):--without blame (blemish, fault, spot), faultless, unblamable.
BiblicalUsage: God chose us in Christ before the foundation of the world, Paul says, that we should be holy and without blame before him in love — and Christ will present the church to himself glorious, not having spot or wrinkle, holy and without blemish. Peter calls Christ himself the lamb without blemish and without spot, and Jude closes his letter praising the One who is able to present us faultless before the presence of his glory with exceeding joy.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this word holds the whole exchange of the gospel: Christ was without blemish so that we, who are full of them, can be presented without blame. It is not that God lowers His standard — it is that Christ meets it for us, and then His Spirit works the same cleanness into our lives day by day.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H526); Amon, an Israelite:--Amon.
BiblicalUsage: Three men in Scripture carry the name Amon, and the king is the one most people meet first: Amon son of Manasseh took the throne of Judah at twenty-two and reigned only two years, doing evil as his father had done and sacrificing to the carved images Manasseh had made, until his own servants conspired against him and killed him, yet Matthew names him in the genealogy of Jesus — Manasseh begat Amon, and Amon begat Josiah — so the line of the promise runs straight through a wicked king and out the other side. The other two are smaller figures: Amon the governor of Samaria, who held the prophet Micaiah in prison, and Amon among the servants of Solomon whose children came back from exile.
TheologicalSignificance: Amon's two years on the throne tell me that a king can undo nothing and build nothing — he only followed his father's idols and died for it, and his son Josiah had to tear it all down. Yet I believe the genealogy is the point: God's promise did not depend on Amon being good, and the line kept going through him anyway, which gives me hope for families where the middle of the story looks ruined.
RelatedPeople: Amon, King of Judah; Amon, Governor of the City
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: deep (literally or figuratively)
BiblicalUsage: Zophar tells Job that God's wisdom is deeper than hell, beyond man's knowing — and Proverbs says counsel in the heart of a man is like deep water, but a man of understanding will draw it out. The word is used for deep water, deep places, and deep thoughts, and most often in Leviticus it describes a plague that sits deep in the skin.
TheologicalSignificance: Deep is a picture word, not a doctrine: it tells me some things sit below the surface, whether God's wisdom or a man's heart, and I cannot judge them from above.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Amorah, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Gomorrah was one of the cities of the plain, and its name is almost never spoken without Sodom's beside it: the LORD rained brimstone and fire on both cities out of heaven, Moses warned Israel that their land could end up looking like Sodom and Gomorrah if they turned away, and Isaiah told Judah that only a small remnant kept them from sharing the same fate. After Genesis 19 the city is a byword for judgment, not a place anyone goes back to.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Gomorrah stands in Scripture as the warning that judgment is real and sudden, and that mercy is the only reason any of us are not left like it. Isaiah's remnant is the hope in the story: God always keeps a people, even when the cities around them fall.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H531); Amos, an Israelite:--Amos.
BiblicalUsage: The name Amos belongs to three different men, and the Bible keeps them apart by their stories: the prophet Amos was a herdsman from Tekoa whom God sent to Israel with a word of judgment two years before the earthquake, and who told Amaziah plainly that he was no prophet and no prophet's son, only a herdsman and a gatherer of sycamore fruit. In Matthew's genealogy the same Greek name stands for King Amon, son of Manasseh and father of Josiah — the English Bibles spell him Amon — and in Luke's genealogy there is another Amos altogether, the son of Naum and father of Mattathias, an otherwise unknown link in the line of Jesus.
TheologicalSignificance: What I take from the name is that God uses ordinary men — a herdsman with no credentials — and also keeps His promise through kings who failed and ancestors nobody remembers. The prophet's words outlived the kingdoms he spoke against, and the genealogies remind me that every link in the chain mattered, whether the man was famous or forgotten.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of a strong color, i.e. red (others fleet)
BiblicalUsage: The word appears only twice, both times in Zechariah's vision of the four chariots: the fourth chariot has grisled and bay horses, and the bay go forth to walk to and fro through the earth. The colour is a strong red-brown — the same word can mean red — and the horses are part of the patrol God sends out over the whole earth.
TheologicalSignificance: Two verses about the colour of horses carry no teaching of their own; their weight is Zechariah's vision, that God's watchers walk the whole earth and report back to Him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Amos, an Israelite prophet
BiblicalUsage: The name Amos belongs to three different men, and the Bible keeps them apart by their stories: the prophet Amos was a herdsman from Tekoa whom God sent to Israel with a word of judgment two years before the earthquake, and who told Amaziah plainly that he was no prophet and no prophet's son, only a herdsman and a gatherer of sycamore fruit. In Matthew's genealogy the same Greek name stands for King Amon, son of Manasseh and father of Josiah — the English Bibles spell him Amon — and in Luke's genealogy there is another Amos altogether, the son of Naum and father of Mattathias, an otherwise unknown link in the line of Jesus.
TheologicalSignificance: What I take from the name is that God uses ordinary men — a herdsman with no credentials — and also keeps His promise through kings who failed and ancestors nobody remembers. The prophet's words outlived the kingdoms he spoke against, and the genealogies remind me that every link in the chain mattered, whether the man was famous or forgotten.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Amon, the name of three Israelites
KeyPassages: 2 Kings 21:19; 2 Chronicles 33:22; Jeremiah 1:2; 1 Kings 22:26; Nehemiah 7:59; Matthew 1:10
BiblicalUsage: Three men in Scripture carry the name Amon, and the king is the one most people meet first: Amon son of Manasseh took the throne of Judah at twenty-two and reigned only two years, doing evil as his father had done and sacrificing to the carved images Manasseh had made, until his own servants conspired against him and killed him, yet Matthew names him in the genealogy of Jesus — Manasseh begat Amon, and Amon begat Josiah — so the line of the promise runs straight through a wicked king and out the other side. The other two are smaller figures: Amon the governor of Samaria, who held the prophet Micaiah in prison, and Amon among the servants of Solomon whose children came back from exile.
TheologicalSignificance: Amon's two years on the throne tell me that a king can undo nothing and build nothing — he only followed his father's idols and died for it, and his son Josiah had to tear it all down. Yet I believe the genealogy is the point: God's promise did not depend on Amon being good, and the line kept going through him anyway, which gives me hope for families where the middle of the story looks ruined.
RelatedPeople: Amon, King of Judah; Amon, Governor of the City
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a throng of people
BiblicalUsage: The word occurs once, in the list of those Nebuzar-adan carried away to Babylon: the poor of the people, the residue left in the city, those who had fallen to the king, and the rest of the multitude. It is simply a crowd — the leftover people of a fallen city, counted among the captives.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for a crowd in one verse carries no theology of its own; its weight is Jeremiah's account of a city emptied by judgment.
RelatedEvents: Fall of Jerusalem and the Exile
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

It is simply a crowd — the leftover people of a fallen city, counted among the captives.
