Definition: Amok, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Amok was one of the chief priests who came back from exile with Zerubbabel and Jeshua, named among the heads of the priests in the days of Jeshua, and a generation later the list names Eber as the priest of Amok's house. That is all the Bible says of him — a name on two lists, and a house that kept serving.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a name on a list still matters: Amok's house was still serving God a generation after the exile, and the Bible remembers the faithful even when it tells us nothing more about them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Amots, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Amoz is named only as the father of the prophet Isaiah — 'the vision of Isaiah the son of Amoz' — and the phrase follows Isaiah through the book: when Sennacherib threatened Jerusalem, Isaiah the son of Amoz sent word to Hezekiah that God had heard his prayer, and the king and the prophet prayed together and cried to heaven. We know nothing else about Amoz himself, but his son's whole ministry carries his name.
TheologicalSignificance: Amoz matters because of the son he raised: the prophet who stood before kings and spoke for God. I believe that is how most faithful lives work — the name is remembered because of what God did through the next generation.
RelatedPeople: Amoz, Father of Isaiah; Isaiah; King Hezekiah
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G288; a vineyard:--vineyard.
BiblicalUsage: Jesus tells three vineyard stories, and the vineyard is always Israel, or the kingdom, in His hands. A householder hires labourers into his vineyard at every hour of the day and pays them all the same; another plants a vineyard, hedges it, builds a tower, and lets it to husbandmen who beat his servants and kill his son; and Mark's version ends with the same warning — the vineyard will be given to others. The vineyard is God's planting, and the question in every parable is what the tenants do with it.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the vineyard parables are about stewardship, not farming: God plants, God provides, and then He asks what we did with what He gave. The labourers who came late were paid in full because the master is generous, and the tenants who killed the son lost the vineyard because they forgot it was never theirs. Both stories end the same way — with the owner's right to do what He will with His own.
RelatedEvents: The Parable of the Workers in the Vineyard
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably from the base of G297 and that of G257; a vine (as coiling about a support):--vine.
BiblicalUsage: Jesus says, 'I am the true vine, and my Father is the husbandman,' and then, 'I am the vine, ye are the branches: he that abideth in me, and I in him, the same bringeth forth much fruit: for without me ye can do nothing.' At the last supper He says He will not drink again of the fruit of the vine until He drinks it new with His disciples in His Father's kingdom. The vine is not a picture of trying harder — it is a picture of staying joined to Him.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that this is the whole Christian life in one image: I do not produce fruit by effort, I bear it by abiding. Cut off from the vine, a branch does nothing; joined to it, it cannot help but bear. And the promise at the table still stands — there is a day coming when He drinks the fruit of the vine new with us, and that is the hope I live toward.
RelatedEvents: The Vine and the Branches; The Last Supper
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G288 and G2041; a vine-worker, i.e. pruner:--vine-dresser.
BiblicalUsage: The word appears once, in the parable of the fig tree: the owner tells the dresser of his vineyard that for three years he has come seeking fruit and found none, and the tree should be cut down, since it only cumbers the ground. The vinedresser is the one who tends the planting and speaks for it — and in the next verse he asks for one more year to dig about it and dung it.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for a gardener carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the parable's patience — one more year, one more chance to bear fruit.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a compound of the base of G297 and G906; a (fishing) net (as thrown about the fish):--net.
BiblicalUsage: The word appears once: Jesus, walking by the Sea of Galilee, saw Simon called Peter and Andrew his brother casting a net into the sea, for they were fishers. It is a casting net, thrown out over the water and drawn back in — the tool of their trade on the morning Jesus called them to follow Him.
TheologicalSignificance: One net in one verse carries no teaching of its own; its weight is the moment — two fishermen at work, and the call that turned them into fishers of men.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from the base of G297 and ἕννυμι (to invest); to enrobe:--clothe.
BiblicalUsage: Jesus asks, if God so clothe the grass of the field, which today is and tomorrow is cast into the oven, shall He not much more clothe you? And when He speaks of John the Baptist, He asks what the crowds went out to see — a man clothed in soft raiment? The word is used for God clothing His creation and for men dressed in fine clothes, and the contrast is the point.
TheologicalSignificance: Two verses about clothing carry no doctrine of their own; their weight is Jesus' argument — if God dresses the grass, He will dress His people, and soft clothes belong in kings' courts, not in the wilderness where a prophet stands.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from the base of G297 and G4172; a city surrounded by a river; Amphipolis, a place in Macedonia:--Amphipolis.
BiblicalUsage: Amphipolis is named once, as a town Paul and Silas passed through on the road from Philippi to Thessalonica: 'when they had passed through Amphipolis and Apollonia, they came to Thessalonica, where was a synagogue of the Jews.' It was a Roman city on the Via Egnatia, and the Bible says nothing more about it — only that the gospel passed through on its way to the next synagogue.
TheologicalSignificance: A town named once, in passing, still matters to me: the gospel travelled real roads through real places, and Amphipolis was one of the doors it went through on the way to Thessalonica.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from the base of G297 and G3598; a fork in the road:--where two ways meet.
BiblicalUsage: The word appears once, in the story of the colt: the disciples found it tied by the door without, in a place where two ways meet, and they loosed him. It is a fork in the road — a crossroads outside the village — and the detail is there because the colt was waiting exactly where Jesus said it would be.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for a crossroads carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the detail — the colt tied where two ways meet, just as Jesus had told them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: comparative of ἀμφί (around); (in plural) both:--both.
BiblicalUsage: The word simply means both, and it shows up wherever two things are held together: new wine in new bottles, and both are preserved; Jew and Gentile reconciled both unto God in one body by the cross. It appears fourteen times, always joining a pair — both the bottles and the wine, both the peoples, both the sides of a story.
TheologicalSignificance: Both is a small word, and it carries no theology on its own; its weight is in the pairs it joins — especially the two peoples made one in Christ.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: contracted for Latin ampliatus (enlarged); Amplias, a Roman Christian:--Amplias.
BiblicalUsage: Amplias is named once, in Paul's greetings at the end of Romans: 'Greet Amplias my beloved in the Lord.' That is all the Bible says of him — a Christian in Rome whom Paul loved, and whose name has been read in churches ever since, and though tradition says he was one of the seventy, Scripture itself gives us only the greeting.
TheologicalSignificance: One greeting is enough to tell me what mattered: Paul called him beloved in the Lord, and that is the whole of his story in Scripture. I believe God remembers His people by name even when history forgets everything else about them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Amram, the name of two Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Amram was the son of Kohath and the father of Aaron and Moses: he took Jochebed his father's sister to wife, and she bore him Aaron and Moses, and Miriam their sister, and the genealogies name him twice over — in Exodus and in Numbers — with his years counted at a hundred and thirty-seven. There is a second Amram, a son of Bani who had taken a foreign wife in Ezra's day, but the father of Moses is the Amram the Bible remembers.
TheologicalSignificance: Amram's whole story is his children: Aaron the priest, Moses the deliverer, Miriam the prophetess. I believe that is how God often works — a faithful father whose name is carried by what his children do, and whose house shaped the whole history of Israel.
RelatedEvents: The Exodus and the Red Sea
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an Amramite or descendant of Amram
BiblicalUsage: The Amramites were the descendants of Amram, one of the families of the Kohathites, counted with the Izharites, Hebronites and Uzzielites in the census of the Levites. In David's day the Amramites appear again among the treasurers of the house of God, keeping the dedicated things with the other Kohathite families.
TheologicalSignificance: A family name on a census list still tells me something: the children of Amram kept serving in the house of God generations after their father, and God counts the families who keep showing up.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Amraphel, a king of Shinar
BiblicalUsage: Amraphel was king of Shinar, and he appears only in the war of the kings in Genesis 14: he joined Chedorlaomer of Elam, Tidal king of nations, and Arioch of Ellasar against the five kings of the plain, and the four kings won the battle and carried off Lot, until Abram armed his trained servants, pursued them, and brought Lot back. Amraphel's name is never heard again after that chapter.
TheologicalSignificance: Amraphel is a king who won a battle and lost the war, and his whole story is two verses in a chapter about Abram. I believe that is the point: the kings of the earth make their alliances and take their spoil, and God still brings His man home.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, something expansive, i.e. a bag
BiblicalUsage: The word is a sack — the bag Joseph's brothers carried their grain in — and it shows up twelve times in the Joseph story, always at the same point: one brother opens his sack at the inn and finds his money in its mouth; Joseph orders the steward to fill the men's sacks with food and put every man's money in his sack's mouth; and in the last sack, Benjamin's, the silver cup is found. The sack is where the test happens.
TheologicalSignificance: A sack is only a bag, and it carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is Joseph's test — the money in the mouth of the sack, and the cup that proved his brothers' hearts.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: force
BiblicalUsage: The word appears once, and it is strength: the governors of Judah shall say in their heart, 'The inhabitants of Jerusalem shall be my strength in the LORD of hosts their God.' It is the force a people finds in one another when God is their God — the strength of Jerusalem resting in the LORD.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for strength in one verse carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the promise — the people of Jerusalem will be each other's strength because the LORD of hosts is their God.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Amtsi, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Amzi appears twice, both times in lists: once as a Levite in the genealogy of the singers — the son of Bani, the son of Shamer — and once as an ancestor of Adaiah, one of the priests who did the work of the house in Jerusalem after the exile. The two mentions may be the same man or two men of the same name; the Bible gives us only the lists.
TheologicalSignificance: Two list entries are all we have of Amzi, and I believe that is enough: his family sang in the house of God and worked in it, and the lists remember them for it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: middle voice of a primary verb; to ward off (for oneself), i.e. protect:--defend.
BiblicalUsage: The word appears once, in Stephen's speech: Moses saw one of his brethren suffer wrong, and he defended him, and avenged him that was oppressed, and smote the Egyptian. It is the act of stepping in for someone who cannot defend himself — the moment Moses chose his own people over Pharaoh's house.
TheologicalSignificance: One act of defence in one verse carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is Moses' choice — he saw the wrong and stepped in, and that choice set the whole course of his life.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a primary particle, denoting a supposition, wish, possibility or uncertainty:--(what-, where-, wither-, who-)soever. Usually unexpressed except by the subjunctive or potential mood. Also contracted for G1437.
BiblicalUsage: This little word never stands alone in English — it is the particle that turns a statement into a possibility: 'if', 'when', 'whoever', 'whatsoever'. Jesus says not one jot or tittle shall pass from the law till all be fulfilled, and whatsoever ye shall ask in my name, that will I do. It appears over a hundred and fifty times, quietly doing the work of 'if' and 'whatever' in the promises and warnings.
TheologicalSignificance: A particle carries no theology of its own; its weight is in the sentences it shapes — the conditions on God's promises and the certainty behind them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: where?; hence, whither?, when?; also hither and thither
BiblicalUsage: The word is a question — where, whither, how long. The angel asks Hagar whence she came and whither she will go, and David asks the LORD how long He will forget him, and how long He will hide His face. It is the word of someone who does not know where they are or how long the trouble will last, and it is asked straight to God.
TheologicalSignificance: A question word carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the honesty of asking God where, and how long, and trusting Him with the answer.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a primary preposition and adverb; properly, up; but (by extension) used (distributively) severally, or (locally) at (etc.):--and, apiece, by, each, every (man), in, through. In compounds (as a prefix) it often means (by implication) repetition, intensity, reversal, etc.
BiblicalUsage: The word means up, and by extension it means each, or apiece: the labourers hired at the eleventh hour received every man a penny, and the four beasts had each of them six wings. It is a small word that does the work of counting — each one, every man, apiece — and it also carries the sense of 'up' in the compounds built on it.
TheologicalSignificance: A preposition carries no theology of its own; its weight is in the counting — every man a penny, each beast six wings — and in the upward direction of the words built on it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: I
BiblicalUsage: In Aramaic this is simply the word for 'I', and it shows up in Daniel's mouth and in Nebuchadnezzar's: Daniel says the secret was not revealed to him for any wisdom he has more than any living, and the king, walking on his palace roof, boasts of the great Babylon he has built for the honour of his majesty. The same little word carries Daniel's humility and the king's pride in back-to-back chapters.
TheologicalSignificance: One small word for 'I' carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the contrast — Daniel's 'I' that points away from himself, and Nebuchadnezzar's 'I' that points only at himself.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Anab, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Anab was a town in the mountains of Judah, and it is named twice: Joshua cut off the Anakim from Hebron, from Debir, from Anab, and from all the mountains of Judah, and the town is listed again among the cities of Judah's inheritance. It was Anakim country, and Joshua destroyed them utterly with their cities.
TheologicalSignificance: A town named twice still tells the story: Anab was where the giants lived, and Joshua took it. I believe the conquest lists are there so we see God keeping His word town by town, not just in the big battles.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G303 and the base of G939; to go up (literally or figuratively):--arise, ascend (up), climb (go, grow, rise, spring) up, come (up).
BiblicalUsage: No man has ascended up to heaven, Jesus tells Nicodemus, but He that came down from heaven — and after the resurrection He tells Mary, 'I ascend unto my Father, and your Father.' Paul says when He ascended up on high He led captivity captive and gave gifts unto men, and John hears a voice like a trumpet say, 'Come up hither.' The word runs through the whole story of Christ: He came down, and He went up, and He will bring His people up after Him.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the going up is the proof of the coming down: He who descended is the same who ascended, and His ascension is my hope that where He is, I will be too. The gifts He gave when He ascended — apostles, prophets, teachers — are still the way He builds His church, and the voice that says 'Come up hither' is still the last word.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: middle voice from G303 and G906; to put off (for oneself):--defer.
BiblicalUsage: The word appears once: Felix, having more perfect knowledge of the Way, deferred Paul's case and said, 'When Lysias the chief captain shall come down, I will know the uttermost of your matter.' It is a putting off — the governor knew enough to decide and chose to wait instead, and Paul stayed in prison two more years.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for putting off carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is Felix's delay — a man who knew the truth and kept putting the decision off until it was too late.
RelatedEvents: Paul Before Felix, Festus, and Agrippa
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G305 (compare G898); a stairway:--stairs.
BiblicalUsage: The word appears twice, both times on the stairs of the Antonia fortress in Jerusalem: Paul was carried up the stairs by the soldiers for the violence of the people, and then he stood on the stairs and beckoned to the crowd and spoke to them in Hebrew. The stairs are the place where the mob could not reach him — and where he turned and preached to them.
TheologicalSignificance: Two mentions of stairs carry no doctrine of their own; their weight is the scene — Paul lifted above a violent crowd, and using the height to speak the gospel to the very people who wanted him dead.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G303 and a derivative of the base of G939; to cause to go up, i.e. haul (a net):--draw.
BiblicalUsage: The word is used once, in the parable of the net: when it was full, they drew it to shore, and sat down, and gathered the good into vessels, but cast the bad away. It is the hauling in of the catch — the net full of every kind, dragged up onto the beach for the sorting.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for hauling a net carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the parable's ending — the net is drawn in, the good are kept, and the bad are cast away.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G303 and G991; to look up; by implication, to recover sight:--look (up), see, receive sight.
BiblicalUsage: The word does two things: it means to look up, and it means to get your sight back. Jesus looked up to heaven before He broke the bread for the five thousand; the blind man of Jericho heard, 'Receive thy sight: thy faith hath saved thee'; Bartimaeus received his sight and followed Jesus in the way; and the man born blind told the Pharisees, 'A man that is called Jesus made clay, and anointed mine eyes, and I went and washed, and I received sight.'
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the two meanings belong together: looking up to heaven and receiving sight are the same motion. The blind men looked to Jesus and saw; and I hold that is still how it works — sight comes from looking up to Him, not from looking harder at the dark.
RelatedEvents: The Healing of the Man Born Blind
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G308; restoration of sight:--recovery of sight.
BiblicalUsage: The word appears once, in the words Jesus read in the synagogue at Nazareth from Isaiah: the Spirit of the Lord is upon me, to preach the gospel to the poor, to heal the brokenhearted, to preach deliverance to the captives, and recovering of sight to the blind. It is the noun for getting sight back — the thing the blind receive when the Messiah comes.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for recovery of sight carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the promise Jesus read aloud and claimed — the blind see, because He has come.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G303 and G994; to halloo:--cry (aloud, out).
BiblicalUsage: The word appears once, and it is the cry from the cross: about the ninth hour Jesus cried with a loud voice, 'Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani' — My God, My God, why hast thou forsaken me. It is not a quiet prayer — it is a shout, the loudest cry in the whole Bible, and it comes from the Son Himself.
TheologicalSignificance: One loud cry carries more weight than a thousand sermons: the Son of God, forsaken, crying out to His Father — and that cry is what makes it possible for us never to be forsaken.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G306; a putting off:--delay.
BiblicalUsage: The word appears once: Festus tells Agrippa that when Paul's accusers came to Caesarea, 'without any delay on the morrow I sat on the judgment seat, and commanded the man to be brought forth.' It is a putting off — and here the point is that there was none. Festus moved at once, and Paul's case came before the king.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for delay carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the contrast — Festus did not delay, and the gospel got its hearing before Agrippa the same week.
RelatedEvents: Paul Before Felix, Festus, and Agrippa
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: figuratively, to distress
BiblicalUsage: The word appears once, in Nebuchadnezzar's words to Belteshazzar: 'because I know that the spirit of the holy gods is in thee, and no secret troubleth thee, tell me the visions of my dream.' To be troubled by a secret is to be distressed by what you cannot solve — and the king is saying Daniel never is. The word is the worry the king feels, set against Daniel's calm.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for being troubled carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the contrast — the king distressed by a dream he cannot understand, and Daniel untroubled because the God of heaven reveals secrets.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to insist
BiblicalUsage: The word appears once, in the law of Ahasuerus's feast: 'the drinking was according to the law; none did compel: for so the king had appointed to all the officers of his house, that they should do according to every man's pleasure.' In a palace where the king's word was law, this once the drinking was not forced — every man drank as he pleased.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for compelling carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the small mercy in the feast — even in a pagan king's house, no one was forced to drink.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to sigh
BiblicalUsage: Israel sighed by reason of the bondage, the Bible says, and their cry came up unto God — and Isaiah says the new wine mourneth, the vine languisheth, and all the merryhearted do sigh. The word is the sound of a people worn down: not a prayer with words, but a sigh, and God hears it as a cry.
TheologicalSignificance: A sigh is not a doctrine, but it is a prayer all the same: Israel sighed under Pharaoh and God heard, and I believe He still hears the sighs that have no words in them.
RelatedEvents: The Exodus and the Red Sea
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: sighing
BiblicalUsage: David says, 'I am weary with my groaning; all the night make I my bed to swim; I water my couch with my tears' — and Isaiah promises a day when the ransomed of the LORD shall return to Zion with songs, and sorrow and sighing shall flee away. The word is the noun for the sigh itself: David's night of tears on one side, and the day sighing ends on the other.
TheologicalSignificance: Sighing is the sound of sorrow, and Isaiah's promise is that it will flee away: the ransomed come home singing, and I believe that is where every sigh is headed.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Anacharath, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Anaharath is named once, in the list of the towns of Issachar's inheritance: 'And Haphraim, and Shion, and Anaharath.' It was a town in the valley of Jezreel, given to Issachar when the land was divided, and the Bible says nothing more about it.
TheologicalSignificance: A town named once in a list still has its place: Anaharath was part of the inheritance God gave Issachar, and the lists remember every town, not just the famous ones.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: we
BiblicalUsage: In Aramaic this is the word for 'we', and it shows up in the mouths of faithful men: Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego answer the king, 'we are not careful to answer thee in this matter,' and the builders of the temple answer their accusers, 'We are the servants of the God of heaven and earth.' Both times the 'we' is a confession — we belong to God, whatever the king says.
TheologicalSignificance: One small word for 'we' carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the stand it takes — we are God's servants, and we will not bow.
RelatedEvents: Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego in the Fiery Furnace
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: we
BiblicalUsage: The word is simply 'we', and it appears over a hundred times — Joseph's brothers tell the governor, 'We are all one man's sons; we are true men,' and the psalm says, 'we are the people of his pasture, and the sheep of his hand.' It is the word a people uses about itself, whether they are defending their honesty or confessing whose they are.
TheologicalSignificance: A pronoun carries no theology of its own; its weight is belonging — 'we are the people of his pasture' is the confession the whole Bible keeps making.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G303 and G5562; to retire:--depart, give place, go (turn) aside, withdraw self.
BiblicalUsage: The word means to withdraw, to step aside — and it follows both Joseph and Jesus. Joseph took the young child and his mother by night and departed into Egypt, and Jesus, when He heard of John's death, departed by ship into a desert place apart. Fourteen times the word marks a quiet leaving: to Egypt, to the wilderness, to a place apart, and once when Judas himself departed and went and hanged himself.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for stepping aside carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is in the leaving — Joseph slipping away by night to save the child, and Jesus withdrawing to pray before the crowds found Him again.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a compound of G303 and χέω (to pour); properly, effusion, i.e. (figuratively) license:--excess.
BiblicalUsage: The word appears once, and it is excess: Peter says the Gentiles think it strange that you run not with them to the same excess of riot, speaking evil of you. It is a pouring out without restraint — the flood of loose living the old friends still run in, and cannot understand why you have left.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for excess carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is Peter's picture — the old life as a flood, and the strange look you get for stepping out of it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to lace fast
BiblicalUsage: The word means to bind fast, to lace on tight: Proverbs says bind your father's commandment continually upon your heart and tie it about your neck, and Job says he would take his cause upon his shoulder and bind it as a crown to him. In both places the binding is something worn close — a command on the heart, a vindication on the head.
TheologicalSignificance: Two verses about binding carry no doctrine of their own; their weight is the closeness — God's words tied on like a necklace, and Job's innocence worn like a crown.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G303 and G1209; to entertain (as a guest):--receive.
BiblicalUsage: The word means to receive, to take someone in as a guest: Publius, the chief man of Malta, received Paul and his company and lodged them three days courteously — and Hebrews says Abraham, when he was tried, offered up Isaac, he that had received the promises. The same word covers a host opening his house and a father holding on to what God promised.
TheologicalSignificance: Two verses about receiving carry no doctrine of their own; their weight is the welcome — Publius lodging strangers for three days, and Abraham receiving promises he could not yet see.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G303 and G1166; to exhibit, i.e. (by implication) to indicate, appoint:--appoint, shew.
BiblicalUsage: The word means to show, or to appoint: after these things the Lord appointed other seventy also and sent them two and two before His face, and the disciples prayed, 'Thou, Lord, which knowest the hearts of all men, shew whether of these two thou hast chosen.' It is God pointing at the one He has picked — the seventy sent out, and Matthias shown to take Judas's place.
TheologicalSignificance: Two verses about appointing carry no doctrine of their own; their weight is the choosing — the Lord appoints the seventy, and the Lord shows which man He has chosen.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G322; (the act of) exhibition:--shewing.
BiblicalUsage: The word appears once, at the end of the story of John's birth: the child grew, and waxed strong in spirit, and was in the deserts till the day of his shewing unto Israel. It is the showing itself — the day John came out of the wilderness and was presented to the nation he had come to prepare.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for a showing carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the waiting — John growing strong in the desert until the day he was shown to Israel.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G303 and G1325; to hand over:--deliver.
BiblicalUsage: The word appears once: the soldiers who brought Paul to Caesarea delivered the epistle to the governor and presented Paul also before him. It is a handing over — the letter and the prisoner both delivered into Felix's hands, and Paul's case passing to the next court.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for handing over carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the chain of custody — Paul passed from soldiers to governor, and the gospel with him.
RelatedEvents: Paul Before Felix, Festus, and Agrippa
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to be soft or pliable, i.e. (figuratively) effeminate or luxurious
BiblicalUsage: The word means soft, delicate, luxurious — and it is used both ways. Moses warns of the tender and delicate woman who would not set foot on the ground for delicateness, whose eye turns evil toward her own family in the siege; and Isaiah promises that if you delight yourself in the LORD, He will cause you to ride on the high places of the earth. The same softness is a curse in the one place and a delight in the other.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for softness carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the difference between delighting in luxury and delighting in the LORD.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G303 and G1080; to beget or (by extension) bear (again):--beget, (bear) X (again).
BiblicalUsage: Peter uses the word twice, and both times it is the new birth: God 'hath begotten us again unto a lively hope by the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead,' and we are 'born again, not of corruptible seed, but of incorruptible, by the word of God, which liveth and abideth for ever.' It is not a fresh start we manage for ourselves — it is a begetting, a second birth, and God is the one who does it.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe being born again is the hinge of the whole Christian life: my first birth gave me Adam's nature, and my second birth gives me Christ's life. The hope is lively because the resurrection is real, and the seed is incorruptible because it is God's own word — so the new life in me cannot rot the way the old one did.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G303 and G1097; to know again, i.e. (by extension) to read:--read.
BiblicalUsage: Jesus stood up to read in the synagogue at Nazareth, as His custom was; Philip ran to the Ethiopian's chariot and heard him read Isaiah, and asked whether he understood what he read; Jesus asked the chief priests whether they had never read in the Scriptures about the stone the builders rejected; and Revelation blesses the one who reads the words of the prophecy and keeps them. Reading in the Bible is never just sounding out words — it is hearing God speak, and being asked whether you understand.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that reading Scripture is the ordinary way God meets His people: Jesus read it, Philip explained it, and the blessing falls on the one who reads and keeps it. The question Philip asked is still the question for every reader — do you understand what you read? — and the Spirit who wrote it is the one who opens it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: middle voice from G303 and G1107; to make (oneself) known:--be made known.
BiblicalUsage: The word appears once, in Stephen's retelling of Joseph: at the second time Joseph was made known to his brethren, and Joseph's kindred was made known unto Pharaoh. It is the moment the brothers finally recognised the ruler of Egypt as their own brother — the making known that ended years of separation.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for being made known carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the recognition — Joseph revealing himself to his brothers at last.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G314; (the act of) reading:--reading.
BiblicalUsage: The word is the act of reading aloud: Paul tells Timothy, 'Till I come, give attendance to reading, to exhortation, to doctrine,' and in the synagogue at Antioch, after the reading of the law and the prophets, the rulers sent to Paul and Barnabas asking if they had any word of exhortation. Reading was public, out loud, and it was the centre of the gathering.
TheologicalSignificance: Three verses about public reading carry no doctrine of their own; their weight is the practice — the Scriptures read aloud in the assembly, and then explained.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G303 and G71; to lead up; by extension to bring out; specially, to sail away:--bring (again, forth, up again), depart, launch (forth), lead (up), loose, offer, sail, set forth, take up.
BiblicalUsage: The word means to lead up, to bring out, and most often to set sail: Paul and his company loosed from Paphos and came to Perga, and Jesus went into a ship with His disciples and said, 'Let us go over unto the other side of the lake,' and they launched forth. It is the word for a journey beginning — a ship leaving harbour, a prisoner brought up before a court, a sacrifice led up to the altar.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for setting sail carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the going — Paul leaving Paphos for Perga, and Jesus launching out with His disciples into the storm.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to approach; hence, to meet in various senses
BiblicalUsage: The word means to meet, to come upon someone — and it is used for what God allows to happen: if a man lie not in wait, but God deliver him into his hand, then I will appoint a place where he may flee; and the psalm promises that no evil shall befall you, neither shall any plague come near your dwelling. It is not chance — it is what God brings across your path, whether a refuge or a trouble.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for what befalls us carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the hand behind it — nothing meets me except what God has appointed, and the refuge is appointed too.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, to eye or (generally) to heed, i.e. pay attention; by implication, to respond; by extension to begin to speak; specifically to sing, shout, testify, announce
BiblicalUsage: The word means to answer, and it is the whole back-and-forth of Scripture in one verb: in Hebrew it appears over three hundred times, from Abraham answering, 'Behold now, I have taken upon me to speak unto the Lord, which am but dust and ashes,' to the LORD answering Job out of the whirlwind. In Aramaic the same word answers in Daniel's court, where Daniel blessed the name of God and the three friends told the king they were not careful to answer him in the matter of the golden image. A prophet answering a king, a friend answering a friend, God answering man — it is the speaking and the hearing that runs through the Bible.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for answering carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the conversation — God speaks, and men answer, and God answers again, and I believe that is what prayer is.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, to eye or (generally) to heed, i.e. pay attention; by implication, to respond; by extension to begin to speak; specifically to sing, shout, testify, announce
BiblicalUsage: The word means to answer, and it is the whole back-and-forth of Scripture in one verb: in Hebrew it appears over three hundred times, from Abraham answering, 'Behold now, I have taken upon me to speak unto the Lord, which am but dust and ashes,' to the LORD answering Job out of the whirlwind. TheologicalSignificance: A word for answering carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the conversation — God speaks, and men answer, and God answers again, and I believe that is what prayer is.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Anah, the name of two Edomites and one Edomitess
BiblicalUsage: Three people share the name Anah, and the Bible keeps them apart by their fathers: Anah the daughter of Zibeon became one of Esau's wives, Anah the son of Zibeon is the one who found the mules in the wilderness as he fed his father's asses, and Anah the son of Seir is named among the Horite chiefs of Edom. The lists give us the names and the families, and nothing more.
TheologicalSignificance: Three people, one name, and no confusion in the record: the Bible names each Anah by their father and their place. I believe that is how carefully God keeps His people's names — even the ones we only meet in a genealogy.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)
