TheologicalSignificance: I believe the difference matters: Paul's ‘folly’ is a reluctant boast he hates making, while the folly Jesus names is the recklessness of a heart turned inward. One is a shepherd defending his flock; the other is the very thing that defiles a man.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G862; incorruptibility; genitive, unending existence; (figuratively) genuineness:--immortality, incorruption, sincerity.
BiblicalUsage: This is the word for what does not decay — incorruption, unending existence. Paul sets it at the heart of the resurrection in 1 Corinthians 15:53, where this corruptible must put on incorruption, and in 1 Corinthians 15:54, when that putting-on is done, death is swallowed up in victory. Christ has already brought life and immortality to light through the gospel in 2 Timothy 1:10, and Romans 2:7 promises eternal life to those who by patient continuance seek glory, honour, and immortality.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe incorruption is not just living forever; it is living forever without the rot — no decay in the body, no fading in the hope. That is what Christ's appearing has already secured, and what the resurrection will finally put on us. Everything we do now in patient well-doing is aimed at a life that cannot spoil.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and a derivative of G5351; undecaying (in essence or continuance):--not (in-, un-)corruptible, immortal.
BiblicalUsage: The adjective for what cannot decay. At the last trump the dead shall be raised incorruptible in 1 Corinthians 15:52, and Peter says our inheritance is incorruptible, undefiled, and fadeth not away, reserved in heaven in 1 Peter 1:4. We ourselves are born again, not of corruptible seed but of incorruptible, by the word of God in 1 Peter 1:23 — and the word belongs first to God Himself, the King eternal, immortal, invisible in 1 Timothy 1:17.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that this word steadies me when everything around me wears out. Bodies age, goods rust, and even good things fade — but the inheritance, the new birth, and the God who gives them do not decay. If what I am building on is incorruptible, then the life built on it will outlast the grave.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a compound of G575 and G5258; properly, to become awake, i.e. (by implication) to drop (off) in slumber:--fall asleep.
BiblicalUsage: Once, on the lake. As they sailed, Jesus fell asleep — the word means He dropped off into slumber — and then the storm came down and the boat filled with water, and the disciples were in jeopardy.
TheologicalSignificance: The word is only the quiet before the storm; its weight is that Jesus slept through the wind His own disciples feared.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G571; to be unbelieving, i.e. (transitively) disbelieve, or (by implication) disobey:--believe not.
BiblicalUsage: To disbelieve, to refuse the word. The disciples heard that Jesus was alive and had been seen, and believed not in Mark 16:11, and the women's words seemed to them as idle tales and they believed them not in Luke 24:11. Paul asks the harder question in Romans 3:3 — if some did not believe, shall their unbelief make the faith of God without effect? — and answers it in 2 Timothy 2:13: if we believe not, yet He abideth faithful; He cannot deny Himself.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this word draws the line between honest doubt and settled refusal. The disciples' unbelief at the tomb was cured by seeing Him; the unbelief Paul warns about is the kind that calls God's faithfulness into question. But the comfort holds either way: my unbelief cannot undo His faithfulness, because He cannot deny Himself.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G571; faithlessness, i.e. (negatively) disbelief (lack of Christian faith), or (positively) unfaithfulness (disobedience):--unbelief.
BiblicalUsage: Unbelief, and Jesus meets it everywhere. He marvelled because of their unbelief in His own country in Mark 6:6, and did not many mighty works there because of their unbelief in Matthew 13:58. The father in Mark 9:24 shows the other face of it — ‘Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief’ — and Paul gives the warning in Romans 11:20: the branches were broken off because of unbelief, and thou standest by faith; be not highminded, but fear.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that unbelief is not the absence of evidence but the refusal to trust what is in front of us. The father who cried for help against his own unbelief was heard, while the crowds who settled into theirs saw few mighty works. Fear, not pride, is the right posture — I stand by faith, and faith is a gift I did not earn.
RelatedEvents: The Healing of the Demon-Possessed Boy
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and G4103; (actively) disbelieving, i.e. without Christian faith (specially, a heathen); (passively) untrustworthy (person), or incredible (thing):--that believeth not, faithless, incredible thing, infidel, unbeliever(-ing).
BiblicalUsage: The unbelieving person, the one without faith. Paul forbids the unequal yoke in 2 Corinthians 6:14 — what fellowship hath righteousness with unrighteousness? — and yet in 1 Corinthians 7:12 he tells the brother whose wife believeth not to keep her if she is pleased to dwell with him. Jesus speaks straight to Thomas in John 20:27, ‘be not faithless, but believing,’ and Revelation 21:8 puts the unbelieving among those whose part is the lake of fire.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word forces me to hold two truths at once: unbelief is a real and damning condition, and the unbeliever in my own house is still someone to love and live with patiently. Paul does not soften the divide, and he does not command me to widen it by leaving. Faith is the line; love is how I stand on my side of it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a primary particle; "off," i.e. away (from something near), in various senses (of place, time, or relation; literal or figurative):--(X here-)after, ago, at, because of, before, by (the space of), for(-th), from, in, (out) of, off, (up-)on(-ce), since, with. In composition (as a prefix) it usually denotes separation, departure, cessation, completion, reversal, etc.
BiblicalUsage: The little word ‘from’ — off, away, out of — and it carries half the New Testament on its back. ‘From that time Jesus began to preach’ in Matthew 4:17, and Jesus, knowing He was come from God and went to God, in John 13:3: the same small word marks where a ministry begins and where a Saviour came from and returns to.
TheologicalSignificance: No doctrine hides in a preposition, but the whole gospel runs through this one — from God, from sin, from death, and back to God again.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G575 and the base of G939; literally, to disembark; figuratively, to eventuate:--become, go out, turn.
BiblicalUsage: Literally to step off a boat onto the shore, and then, by figure, for a thing to turn out a certain way. The disciples come to land in John 21:9 and find a fire of coals with fish and bread already waiting, and the fishermen in Luke 5:2 have gone out of their boats to wash their nets when Jesus steps in. Jesus promises the persecuted in Luke 21:13 that it shall turn to them for a testimony, and Paul is sure in Philippians 1:19 that his imprisonment shall turn to his salvation.
TheologicalSignificance: I love how this word moves from feet on a beach to the whole shape of a life. What looks like an ending — a night of empty nets, a prison cell, a trial before rulers — turns, in God's hands, into provision, testimony, and salvation. The landing is never the end of the story.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G575 and G906; to throw off; figuratively, to lose:--cast away.
BiblicalUsage: To throw off, to cast away. Hebrews 10:35 commands it of confidence — cast not away your confidence, which hath great recompence of reward — while blind Bartimaeus does it with his garment in Mark 10:50, casting it away and rising to come to Jesus. Romans 13:12 turns the same word on our old life: let us cast off the works of darkness and put on the armour of light.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word teaches me what to drop and what to keep. The garment, the darkness — those I throw off gladly. But confidence in God is the one thing I must not cast away, because the reward attached to it is greater than anything my hands are holding.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G575 and G991; to look away from everything else, i.e. (figuratively) intently regard:--have respect.
BiblicalUsage: Once, about Moses. He esteemed the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures in Egypt, for he had respect unto the recompence of the reward — he looked away from everything Egypt offered and fixed his eyes on what God promised.
TheologicalSignificance: One verse, and the whole of faith is in it: looking away from what is near to look intently at what is coming.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G577; cast off, i.e. (figuratively) such as to be rejected:--be refused.
BiblicalUsage: Once, about food. Every creature of God is good, and nothing to be refused, if it be received with thanksgiving — nothing God made is cast off as unclean once grace and gratitude have received it.
TheologicalSignificance: The word exists to be denied: in Christ, nothing God created is to be thrown away.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G577; rejection; figuratively, loss:--casting away, loss.
BiblicalUsage: Two uses, and in both the loss is not the end. In Acts 27:22 Paul tells the terrified crew there shall be no loss of any man's life, but of the ship, and in Romans 11:15 the casting away of Israel is the reconciling of the world — and what shall the receiving of them be, but life from the dead?
TheologicalSignificance: Loss is real in both verses, and in both it is outweighed: a ship for the lives aboard, a casting away for the reconciling of the world.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G575 and G5562; to go away:--depart.
BiblicalUsage: To go away, to depart. John departs from Paul and Barnabas in Acts 13:13 and returns to Jerusalem, and the spirit in Luke 9:39 hardly departs from the tormented boy. Jesus gives the word its heaviest use in Matthew 7:23, to those who worked iniquity in His name: ‘depart from me, ye that work iniquity.’
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the same going-away can be a desertion, a deliverance, or a judgment, and only the direction tells which. John left the work; the spirit left the boy; the workers of iniquity will be told to leave Him. What matters is not that someone departs, but from whom, and to where.
RelatedEvents: The Healing of the Demon-Possessed Boy
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G575 and G5563; to rend apart; reflexively, to separate:--depart (asunder).
BiblicalUsage: Once, and it splits a friendship in two. The contention between Paul and Barnabas over John Mark was so sharp that they departed asunder one from the other, Barnabas taking Mark to Cyprus — the word is a tearing apart, a rending.
TheologicalSignificance: A single sharp verse, and it refuses to take sides: two faithful men parted, and the gospel went two ways at once.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a compound of G575 and G5530; the act of using up, i.e. consumption:--using.
BiblicalUsage: Once, about man-made religion. Paul dismisses rules about food and touch that perish with the using — commands and doctrines of men, not of God — things that wear out in the very act of being used.
TheologicalSignificance: A word for what is used up carries its own verdict: a religion built on such rules perishes with them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G575 and G1209; to take fully, i.e. welcome (persons), approve (things):--accept, receive (gladly).
BiblicalUsage: To take fully — to receive gladly, to welcome. They that gladly received the word were baptized in Acts 2:41, three thousand souls in a day; the people gladly received Jesus when He returned in Luke 8:40, for they were all waiting for Him. Jesus received the crowds in Luke 9:11 and healed them, and in Acts 28:30 Paul received all that came to him in his own hired house for two whole years.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe receiving is the first act of faith and the first act of love. The crowd receives the word, the people receive Jesus, Jesus receives the people, and Paul receives all who come — the gospel moves by welcome, and a closed door stops it. I want my own house and heart to receive the way Paul's did.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G575 and G1166; to show off, i.e. exhibit; figuratively, to demonstrate, i.e. accredit:--(ap-)prove, set forth, shew.
BiblicalUsage: To show off, to exhibit, to prove by putting on display. Peter tells the men of Israel that Jesus was a man approved of God among them by miracles and wonders and signs in Acts 2:22 — God put the proof where everyone could see it. Paul says the apostles have been set forth last, as it were appointed to death, made a spectacle unto the world in 1 Corinthians 4:9, and the man of sin will sit in the temple of God, shewing himself that he is God in 2 Thessalonians 2:4.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that God proves His servants the same way the enemy proves his — in public, before witnesses. The difference is the proof itself: miracles and wonders for Jesus, suffering and death for the apostles, and a lying display for the man of sin. I am to read the display, not the claim.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G584; manifestation:--demonstration.
BiblicalUsage: Once, and Paul makes it his whole method. His speech and preaching were not with enticing words of man's wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power — the proof was not in the argument but in what the Spirit did.
TheologicalSignificance: The word is a reminder that the gospel does not need my polish; it needs the Spirit's power.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G575 and G1183; to tithe (as debtor or creditor):--(give, pay, take) tithe.
BiblicalUsage: To tithe — to give or take the tenth. The sons of Levi have a commandment to take tithes of the people according to the law in Hebrews 7:5, and the Pharisee in Luke 18:12 boasts that he gives tithes of all he possesses. But Jesus turns the word into a rebuke in Luke 11:42 and Matthew 23:23: they tithe mint and rue and cummin, and pass over judgment and the love of God, omitting the weightier matters of the law.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the tithe was never the problem; the problem was tithing the garden herbs while starving justice and mercy. The tenth belongs to God, and Jesus says so plainly — these ought ye to have done — but a tithe that costs me nothing of my heart is no tithe at all. I hold that giving is measured by what I pass over, not by what I count.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G588; accepted, i.e. agreeable:--acceptable.
BiblicalUsage: Twice, and both times about what pleases God. Prayer for all men is good and acceptable in the sight of God our Saviour in 1 Timothy 2:3, and children who care for their widowed parents show piety at home, which is good and acceptable before God in 1 Timothy 5:4.
TheologicalSignificance: Two quiet duties — praying for rulers and caring for parents — and both are called acceptable to God.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G590; to go abroad, i.e. visit a foreign land:--go (travel) into a far country, journey.
BiblicalUsage: To go abroad, to travel into a far country — and in Jesus' parables it is always the master who leaves. The younger son takes his journey into a far country in Luke 15:13 and wastes his substance with riotous living; the householder plants a vineyard, lets it out, and goes into a far country in Matthew 21:33 and Mark 12:1; and the man travelling into a far country in Matthew 25:14 entrusts his goods to his servants.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the far country is where the story is decided. The master is away, the servants are unsupervised, and what they do with what was left in their hands is the whole test. The son squanders, the husbandmen rebel, the servants trade — and the master always comes back to settle accounts. I live in the far country now, and the question is what I am doing with what He left me.
RelatedEvents: The Prodigal Son; The Parable of the Talents
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G575 and G1218; absent from one's own people, i.e. a foreign traveller:--taking a far journey.
BiblicalUsage: Once, about the Son of man as a man taking a far journey — He left His house, gave authority to His servants and to every man his work, and commanded the porter to watch.
TheologicalSignificance: One parable, one command: the Master is away, the work is assigned, and the porter watches.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G575 and G1325; to give away, i.e. up, over, back, etc. (in various applications):--deliver (again), give (again), (re-)pay(-ment be made), perform, recompense, render, requite, restore, reward, sell, yield.
BiblicalUsage: To give back, to pay over, to render what is due. The Father who sees in secret shall reward openly in Matthew 6:4, and the Son of man shall reward every man according to his works in Matthew 16:27; Revelation 22:12 says the same at the very end — behold, I come quickly, and my reward is with me. Paul turns the word the other way in Romans 12:17: recompense to no man evil for evil.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that this word keeps two accounts straight. God repays — openly, surely, according to works — and that is why I must not. If I take repayment into my own hands, I am collecting a debt that is not mine to collect. My part is to provide things honest in the sight of all men and leave the rendering to Him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G575 and a compound of G1223 and G3724; to disjoin (by a boundary, figuratively, a party):--separate.
BiblicalUsage: Once, about those who separate themselves — sensual, having not the Spirit. Jude's word is for the dividers in the church, who draw their own boundary and stand outside it.
TheologicalSignificance: One verse names the test of every divider: not their arguments, but whether the Spirit is in them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G588; acceptance:--acceptation.
BiblicalUsage: Two uses, and in both Paul stamps a saying as worthy of all acceptation. The first is the heart of the gospel in 1 Timothy 1:15, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom Paul calls himself chief; the second, in 1 Timothy 4:9, is a faithful saying and worthy of all acceptation.
TheologicalSignificance: Paul does not ask me to weigh these sayings; he asks me to receive them whole.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G575 and G1381; to disapprove, i.e. (by implication) to repudiate:--disallow, reject.
BiblicalUsage: To disapprove, to reject after testing — the builders' word. The Son of man must be rejected of the elders and chief priests and scribes in Luke 9:22 and Mark 8:31, and Jesus quotes the psalm against them in Matthew 21:42: the stone which the builders rejected, the same is become the head of the corner. Peter turns it around in 1 Peter 2:4 — the living stone, disallowed indeed of men, but chosen of God, and precious.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this is the great reversal of the gospel. Men examined Christ and rejected Him; God examined the same stone and chose Him, and set Him as the head of the corner. Every builder's verdict is provisional until God gives His. What men disallow, God may have already chosen.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: past participle of a compound of G575 and G1096; absent, i.e. deceased (figuratively, renounced):--being dead.
BiblicalUsage: Once, in the verse that carries the cross. Christ bare our sins in His own body on the tree, that we, being dead to sins, should live unto righteousness — the word is the participle for having died to something, being gone from it altogether.
TheologicalSignificance: To be dead to sins is not to be numb to them; it is to have left them behind the way a dead man leaves a house.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G583; an enrollment; by implication, an assessment:--taxing.
BiblicalUsage: Twice, and both times about a taxing. Luke dates the birth of Christ by the first taxing, when Cyrenius was governor of Syria, in Luke 2:2, and Gamaliel remembers Judas of Galilee, who rose up in the days of the taxing in Acts 5:37 and drew away much people after him.
TheologicalSignificance: The word is a census and a tax roll — Rome counting its subjects — and Luke uses it to date the birth of the King Rome never counted on.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G575 and G1125; to write off (a copy or list), i.e. enrol:--tax, write.
BiblicalUsage: To enrol, to write a name on a list. Caesar Augustus decreed that all the world should be taxed in Luke 2:1, and all went to be taxed, every one into his own city, in Luke 2:3 — Joseph going up with Mary his espoused wife in Luke 2:5. Hebrews 12:23 sets another list beside it: the general assembly and church of the firstborn, which are written in heaven.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the two enrolments are the whole contrast. Rome wrote names on a tax roll to take from its subjects; God writes names in heaven to keep His children. Joseph's journey to Bethlehem put Jesus on Caesar's list, but Hebrews says my name is on a better one — and no emperor can tax it away.
RelatedPeople: Jesus; Joseph, Husband of Mary; Mary, Mother of Jesus
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G601; disclosure:--appearing, coming, lighten, manifestation, be revealed, revelation.
BiblicalUsage: A disclosure, an unveiling — the word the last book of the Bible takes for its title. Paul received his gospel not from man but by the revelation of Jesus Christ in Galatians 1:12, and by revelation God made known to him the mystery in Ephesians 3:3. The Corinthians wait for the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ in 1 Corinthians 1:7, and Revelation 1:1 calls the whole book the revelation of Jesus Christ, which God gave Him to shew His servants things which must shortly come to pass.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that revelation is God pulling back the curtain, not man climbing up to peek behind it. The gospel was not worked out, it was shown; the end was not guessed, it was given. That is why I can trust both — the same God who unveiled the mystery also unveiled the last day.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G575 and G2572; to take off the cover, i.e. disclose:--reveal.
BiblicalUsage: To take off the cover, to disclose. Jesus thanks the Father because He has hid these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them unto babes, in Matthew 11:25 and again in Luke 10:21 — the same words in both Gospels. God has revealed them unto us by His Spirit in 1 Corinthians 2:10, for the Spirit searcheth the deep things of God, and in Romans 1:17 the righteousness of God is revealed from faith to faith.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the uncovering is God's work from first to last. The wise miss it because they look for it with the wrong eyes; babes receive it because they only have to be told. The Spirit does the revealing, faith does the receiving, and my part is to stay small enough to be taught.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a compound of G575 and a compound of κάρα (the head) and G1380 (in the sense of watching); intense anticipation:--earnest expectation.
BiblicalUsage: Twice, and both times about waiting with the head stretched forward. Paul's earnest expectation in Philippians 1:20 is that Christ shall be magnified in his body, whether by life or by death, and the earnest expectation of the creature in Romans 8:19 waits for the manifestation of the sons of God.
TheologicalSignificance: The word is a neck craned toward the horizon; creation itself is watching for what God will do next.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G575 and G2644; to reconcile fully:--reconcile.
BiblicalUsage: To reconcile fully — not a truce but a making of peace. Having made peace through the blood of His cross, Christ reconciles all things unto Himself in Colossians 1:20, and presents us holy and unblameable in Colossians 1:22. Ephesians 2:16 says He reconciled both Jew and Gentile unto God in one body by the cross, having slain the enmity thereby.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe reconciliation is the cross doing what no treaty can: it does not paper over the enmity, it slays it. The blood made the peace, the body holds both sides together, and the result is not a ceasefire but a family — holy, unblameable, and unreproveable in His sight.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G600; reconstitution:--restitution.
BiblicalUsage: Once, in Peter's sermon at the temple. Heaven must receive Christ until the times of restitution of all things, which God hath spoken by the mouth of all His holy prophets since the world began.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for the putting-back of everything — and Peter says the prophets have been promising it since the world began.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G575 and G2525; to reconstitute (in health, home or organization):--restore (again).
BiblicalUsage: To restore, to put back in place. Jesus says Elias truly shall first come and restore all things in Matthew 17:11, and repeats it in Mark 9:12. The disciples ask the risen Lord in Acts 1:6 whether He will at this time restore again the kingdom to Israel, and the writer of Hebrews asks prayer that he may be restored to his readers the sooner in Hebrews 13:19.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that restoration runs from the greatest thing to the smallest: all things, the kingdom, and one man's return to his friends. The same word covers Elijah's coming work and a prisoner's hope of seeing his church again. God restores on every scale, and none of it is beneath Him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G575 and G2749; to be reserved; figuratively, to await:--be appointed, (be) laid up.
BiblicalUsage: To be laid up, reserved, waiting. A crown of righteousness is laid up for Paul in 2 Timothy 4:8, and the hope laid up in heaven in Colossians 1:5. Hebrews 9:27 turns the word sober: it is appointed unto men once to die, but after this the judgment. And the fearful servant in Luke 19:20 kept his pound laid up in a napkin.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word asks me what I have laid up, and where. A crown, a hope, a judgment — all three are laid up and waiting. The servant's pound was laid up too, and it earned him nothing, because he laid it up in fear instead of putting it to work. What is reserved for me depends on what I do with what was given me.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G575 and G2776; to decapitate:--behead.
BiblicalUsage: To behead — four times, and every time about John the Baptist. Herod says in Luke 9:9, John have I beheaded, and in Mark 6:16 he is sure the risen Jesus is John whom he beheaded. Mark 6:27 tells how the king sent an executioner and commanded his head to be brought, and Matthew 14:10 says he sent and beheaded John in the prison.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the repetition is the point: the Gospels will not let Herod's crime fade into the background. Four times the word falls, and four times it names the same prophet, the same prison, the same guilty king. John's death is not a footnote to Jesus' ministry; it is the warning that speaking the truth can cost a man his head.
RelatedEvents: The Death of John the Baptist
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G575 and G2808; to close fully:--shut up.
BiblicalUsage: Once, about a shut door. When the master of the house is risen up and hath shut to the door, those standing outside knock and say, Lord, Lord, open unto us — and He answers, I know you not whence ye are.
TheologicalSignificance: One verse, and the door is the whole sermon: it stands open now, and one day it will be shut.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G575 and G2875; to amputate; reflexively (by irony) to mutilate (the privy parts):--cut off. Compare G2699.
BiblicalUsage: To cut off, to amputate. Jesus commands it twice in Mark 9:43 and Mark 9:45 — if thy hand offend thee, cut it off; if thy foot offend thee, cut it off — better maimed entering into life than whole into hell. Peter does it literally in John 18:10, cutting off the high priest's servant's right ear, and Paul wishes it on the troublers in Galatians 5:12: I would they were even cut off which trouble you.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Jesus' command is not about the hand; it is about how seriously I take the sin the hand serves. Better to lose the thing I love than to keep it and lose life. Peter's sword shows the wrong cutting — violence against another man — while Paul's wish shows the right one: the troublers cut off from the church, so the flock is safe.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G611 (in its original sense of judging); a judicial decision:--sentence.
BiblicalUsage: Once, in Paul's darkest verse. We had the sentence of death in ourselves, that we should not trust in ourselves, but in God which raiseth the dead — the word is a judicial decision, a verdict handed down.
TheologicalSignificance: The sentence was death, and Paul says it was given so that he would stop trusting himself and trust the God who raises the dead.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G575 and κρίνω; to conclude for oneself, i.e. (by implication) to respond; by Hebraism (compare H6030) to begin to speak (where an address is expected):--answer.
BiblicalUsage: To answer — the commonest verb of reply in the Gospels, two hundred and thirty-two times. Jesus answers John the Baptist at His baptism in Matthew 3:15, ‘thus it becometh us to fulfil all righteousness,’ and John answers the priests in John 1:26, ‘I baptize with water: but there standeth one among you, whom ye know not.’ Before Pilate in Luke 23:3 Jesus answers, ‘Thou sayest it,’ and in John 19:11 He answers that Pilate could have no power at all against Him except it were given from above.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word shows me that answering is itself a kind of witness. Jesus answers with a sentence that fulfils righteousness, and with a sentence that gives power back to God, and sometimes He answers with two words and lets them stand. The wisdom is knowing when a word will fulfil righteousness and when silence will.
RelatedPeople: Jesus; John the Baptist; Pontius Pilate
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G611; a response:--answer.
BiblicalUsage: An answer — the noun, four times. The priests demand one of John in John 1:22, that they may give an answer to them that sent them; Pilate asks Jesus whence He is in John 19:9, but Jesus gave him no answer. The boy Jesus in the temple astonishes all who hear Him with His understanding and answers in Luke 2:47, and the spies in Luke 20:26 marvel at His answer and hold their peace.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the answers in these four verses trace the whole range: an answer demanded, an answer refused, an answer that astonishes, and an answer that silences. Jesus gives the answer His hearers need — or withholds the one they have no right to — and either way the questioners are left with nothing more to say.
RelatedPeople: Jesus; John the Baptist; Pontius Pilate
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G613; secret; by implication, treasured:--hid, kept secret.
BiblicalUsage: Hidden, kept secret, treasured away. In Christ are hid all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge, says Colossians 2:3 — hidden not to be kept from us, but kept for us. Jesus promises the reverse in Luke 8:17 and Mark 4:22: nothing is secret that shall not be made manifest, neither anything hid that shall not be known and come abroad.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the two uses belong together. What God hides, He hides in Christ, where seeking finds it; what men hide, God will bring abroad, where nothing stays covered. The word warns me twice: seek the treasure where it is hid, and never trust a secret to stay secret.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G575 and G2928; to conceal away (i.e. fully); figuratively, to keep secret:--hide.
BiblicalUsage: To conceal away, to keep secret. Paul speaks the wisdom of God in a mystery, even the hidden wisdom ordained before the world unto our glory, in 1 Corinthians 2:7 — a mystery hid from ages and generations but now made manifest to His saints, in Colossians 1:26, and hid in God from the beginning of the world, in Ephesians 3:9. Jesus thanks the Father in Luke 10:21 for hiding these things from the wise and prudent and revealing them unto babes.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that God's hiding is not His refusal but His timing. The mystery was hidden for ages so that, when it was made manifest, the whole world would see it was His doing and not man's discovery. And He still hides it from the wise who trust their own wisdom — the cover comes off only for those willing to receive it like children.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G575 and κτείνω (to slay); to kill outright; figuratively, to destroy:--put to death, kill, slay.
BiblicalUsage: To kill outright — seventy times, and almost always about the killing of the righteous. Jesus warns in Matthew 10:28 not to fear them which kill the body but cannot kill the soul, and in Luke 12:5 to fear Him which after He hath killed hath power to cast into hell. Peter charges the Jews in Acts 3:15 with killing the Prince of life, and Jesus tells His disciples in John 16:2 that the time cometh when whosoever killeth them will think that he doeth God service.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word strips every excuse from religious murder. The killers of the Prince of life thought they were serving God; the killers of the disciples will think the same. Killing the body is the worst men can do, and it is not the worst thing that can happen — the soul is beyond their reach, and the Judge beyond their appeal.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G575 and the base of G2949; to breed forth, i.e. (by transference) to generate (figuratively):--beget, produce.
BiblicalUsage: Twice in James, and the two verses are a birth and a birth. Lust, when it hath conceived, bringeth forth sin, and sin, when it is finished, bringeth forth death in James 1:15 — but of His own will God begat us with the word of truth in James 1:18, that we should be a kind of firstfruits of His creatures.
TheologicalSignificance: The same word bears two children, and I must choose which birth I belong to: sin's, which ends in death, or God's, which begins in truth.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G575 and G2947; to roll away:--roll away (back).
BiblicalUsage: To roll away — four times, and every time about the stone at the tomb. The women ask on the way in Mark 16:3, who shall roll us away the stone from the door of the sepulchre, and when they look in Mark 16:4 they see it is already rolled away. They found the stone rolled away in Luke 24:2, and Matthew 28:2 tells how: the angel of the Lord descended from heaven and rolled back the stone and sat upon it.
TheologicalSignificance: I love that the women carried a question they could not answer and found it answered before they arrived. The stone was very great, and it was already moved — the angel did not roll it away to let Jesus out, but to let the women in to see He was gone. Every impossibility I carry to the tomb is already rolled away.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G575 and G2983; to receive (specially, in full, or as a host); also to take aside:--receive, take.
BiblicalUsage: To receive in full — sometimes as a gift, sometimes as a reckoning. The father received his son safe and sound in Luke 15:27 and killed the fatted calf, and Abraham tells the rich man in Luke 16:25 that he received his good things in his lifetime, while Lazarus received evil things. Jesus promises in Luke 18:30 that whoever leaves all for His sake shall receive manifold more, and Paul warns in Romans 1:27 that men receive in themselves the recompence of their error.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word is a ledger word: what I receive in full is what I chose in full. The rich man received his good things and found them spent; the disciple who leaves all receives manifold more, in this present time and in the world to come. I want to be sure of what I am receiving — and from whom.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a compound of G575 and λαύω (to enjoy); full enjoyment:--enjoy(-ment).
BiblicalUsage: Twice, and both times about enjoyment that misleads. The rich are charged not to trust in uncertain riches but in the living God, who giveth us richly all things to enjoy, in 1 Timothy 6:17 — and Moses chose rather to suffer affliction with the people of God than to enjoy the pleasures of sin for a season, in Hebrews 11:25.
TheologicalSignificance: Enjoyment itself is God's gift; the question is only what I enjoy, and for how long.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a presumed derivative of G622; ruin or loss (physical, spiritual or eternal):--damnable(-nation), destruction, die, perdition, X perish, pernicious ways, waste.
BiblicalUsage: Ruin, loss, destruction — the word for the end of the broad way. Broad is the way that leadeth to destruction in Matthew 7:13, and many there be which go in thereat. Judas is the son of perdition in John 17:12, lost while the rest were kept. Paul says of the enemies of the cross that their end is destruction in Philippians 3:19, and Peter says the heavens and earth are reserved unto fire against the day of judgment and perdition of ungodly men in 2 Peter 3:7.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this word is the Bible's plainest warning label. Destruction is not an accident on the broad way; it is the destination the way was built to reach. The narrow gate is strait because it is the only road that does not end in ruin — and the choice of roads is made now, while both gates still stand open.
RelatedPeople: Jesus; Paul; Simon Peter; Judas Iscariot
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G575 and λείχω (to "lick"); to lick clean:--lick.
BiblicalUsage: Once, in the parable of the rich man and Lazarus. The beggar lay at the rich man's gate, desiring the crumbs from his table, and the dogs came and licked his sores — the word is the licking clean of wounds by animals, the only comfort Lazarus received on earth.
TheologicalSignificance: One verse, and the dogs show more mercy than the rich man did.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G575 and G3007; to leave behind (passively, remain); by implication, to forsake:--leave, remain.
BiblicalUsage: To leave behind — and what is left behind tells the story. There remaineth therefore a rest to the people of God in Hebrews 4:9, a rest left over for us after the wilderness generation failed to enter it. But Hebrews 10:26 warns that if we sin wilfully there remaineth no more sacrifice for sins, and Jude 1:6 says the angels which kept not their first estate left their own habitation and are reserved in chains. Paul left Titus in Crete in Titus 1:5 to set in order the things that are wanting.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the word cuts both ways, like everything left behind. A rest remains for me — God has left something good unclaimed, waiting. But the angels left their habitation and found chains, and the wilful sinner finds no sacrifice remaining. What I leave behind decides what remains for me.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from the pagan deity Ἀπόλλων (i.e. the sun; from G622); Apollonia, a place in Macedonia:--Apollonia.
BiblicalUsage: The name is a place on the road, nothing more. Paul and Silas passed through Amphipolis and Apollonia on their way to Thessalonica, where there was a synagogue of the Jews, in Acts 17:1 — Apollonia is one of the towns the gospel walked through without stopping.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the towns the apostles passed through matter too: the gospel was on foot, and every place it passed is part of the road it took.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably from the same as G624; Apollos, an Israelite:--Apollos.
KeyPassages: Acts 18:24; Acts 19:1; 1 Corinthians 1:12; 1 Corinthians 3:6; 1 Corinthians 16:12; Titus 3:13
BiblicalUsage: The name runs through Acts and Paul's letters wherever the church is learning to work together: Apollos came to Ephesus mighty in the Scriptures in Acts 18:24, and was at Corinth while Paul came to Ephesus in Acts 19:1, and the Corinthians divided over him in 1 Corinthians 1:12, saying, I am of Paul, and I of Apollos. Paul answers that in 1 Corinthians 3:6 — I have planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the increase — and years later he is still caring for him, asking Titus to bring Apollos on his journey diligently in Titus 3:13 and telling the Corinthians in 1 Corinthians 16:12 that he greatly desired Apollos to come to them.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Apollos matters because he shows me that the work is shared and the increase is God's. Paul planted, Apollos watered, and neither of them could make anything grow — and the man the Corinthians fought over is the man Paul loved, sent for, and provided for.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G575 and the base of G3639; to destroy fully (reflexively, to perish, or lose), literally or figuratively:--destroy, die, lose, mar, perish.
BiblicalUsage: To destroy fully, to perish, to lose — eighty-four times, and the whole gospel turns on it. God gave His Son that whosoever believeth in Him should not perish in John 3:16, and Jesus says His sheep shall never perish in John 10:28. The lost son was lost and is found in Luke 15:24, and Jesus warns in Matthew 10:39 that he that findeth his life shall lose it, and he that loseth his life for My sake shall find it.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this is the word that makes John 3:16 what it is: perishing is the alternative, and it is real. But the same word that means destruction also means a sheep lost on the hillside and a life laid down — and in both cases the losing is not the end. The son who was lost is found; the life lost for Christ's sake is found again. Perishing is final only for those who refuse the hand that saves.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: active participle of G622; a destroyer (i.e. Satan):--Apollyon.
BiblicalUsage: The name is given once, in Revelation 9:11. The locusts from the bottomless pit have a king over them, the angel of the bottomless pit, whose name in the Hebrew tongue is Abaddon, but in the Greek tongue hath his name Apollyon — the Destroyer.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the two names say the same thing in two tongues: the king of the pit is destruction itself, and his name is his nature.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: middle voice from a compound of G575 and G3056; to give an account (legal plea) of oneself, i.e. exculpate (self):--answer (for self), make defence, excuse (self), speak for self.
BiblicalUsage: To give an account of oneself, to answer for oneself before accusers. Paul counts himself happy to answer for himself before Agrippa in Acts 26:2, and Jesus promises His disciples in Luke 12:11 that when they are brought before synagogues and magistrates they need not plan their answer. Paul says in Romans 2:15 that men's thoughts accuse or else excuse one another, and in 2 Corinthians 12:19 he wonders whether the church thinks he is excusing himself to them.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the word covers two courts: the one before men and the one inside me. Before men I may have to answer, and the Spirit will give the words; inside, my own thoughts accuse or excuse me daily. Paul's answer to both is the same — he speaks before God in Christ, for their edifying, not for his own defence.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from the same as G626; a plea ("apology"):--answer (for self), clearing of self, defence.
BiblicalUsage: A plea, a defence, an answer for oneself — the word our ‘apology’ comes from, though it means the opposite of saying sorry. Peter commands it in 1 Peter 3:15: be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you, with meekness and fear. Paul makes his defence before the Jerusalem crowd in Acts 22:1, counts the Philippians partakers with him in the defence and confirmation of the gospel in Philippians 1:7, and remembers in 2 Timothy 4:16 that at his first answer no man stood with him.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Peter's verse sets the tone for all the rest: ready always, but with meekness and fear. A defence that is loud and proud is no defence at all; the hope itself is the argument, and gentleness is how it is given. Paul stood alone at his first answer and still gave it — and I am to be ready to do the same.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G575 and G3068; to wash fully, i.e. (figuratively) have remitted (reflexively):--wash (away).
BiblicalUsage: Twice, and both times about sins washed away. Ananias tells Paul in Acts 22:16 to arise, be baptized, and wash away his sins, calling on the name of the Lord, and Paul tells the Corinthians in 1 Corinthians 6:11 that such were some of them — but ye are washed, ye are sanctified, ye are justified in the name of the Lord Jesus.
TheologicalSignificance: The washing is baptism's picture and the gospel's fact: the sins are gone, and the washed stand sanctified and justified.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G575 and G3089; to free fully, i.e. (literally) relieve, release, dismiss (reflexively, depart), or (figuratively) let die, pardon or (specially) divorce:--(let) depart, dismiss, divorce, forgive, let go, loose, put (send) away, release, set at liberty.
BiblicalUsage: To free fully — to release, dismiss, or send away. Joseph, being a just man and not willing to make Mary a public example, was minded to put her away privily in Matthew 1:19, and Jesus teaches in Matthew 19:9 that whoever puts away his wife except for fornication commits adultery. Pilate released Barabbas unto the crowd in Luke 23:25 and delivered Jesus to their will, and the Roman examiners in Acts 28:18 would have let Paul go, because there was no cause of death in him.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word shows how the same release can be just, cruel, or corrupt. Joseph's quiet release was mercy; Pilate's release of Barabbas was injustice wearing the robes of law; the Romans' willingness to release Paul was the truth finally being heard. Freedom is not always righteous — what matters is who is set free, and who pays for it.
RelatedPeople: Jesus; Joseph, Husband of Mary; Paul; Pontius Pilate
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a compound of G575 and G3083; (the act) ransom in full, i.e. (figuratively) riddance, or (specially) Christian salvation:--deliverance, redemption.
BiblicalUsage: Ransom in full — the buying back of what was lost. We are justified freely by His grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus in Romans 3:24, and in Him we have redemption through His blood, the forgiveness of sins, in Ephesians 1:7 and Colossians 1:14. Hebrews 9:15 adds the reach of it: by His death, for the redemption of the transgressions under the first testament, they which are called might receive the promise of eternal inheritance.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that redemption is the most personal word in the Bible, because a ransom is paid for someone, not something. Christ did not buy a principle; He bought me, and the price was His blood. The forgiveness is according to the riches of His grace — not the measure of my worth, but the measure of His.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: middle voice from G575 and μάσσω (to squeeze, knead, smear); to scrape away:--wipe off.
BiblicalUsage: Once, in the seventy's commission. Even the very dust of your city, which cleaveth on us, we do wipe off against you — the disciples shake the town's dust from their feet as a testimony, and still add that the kingdom of God is come nigh unto you.
TheologicalSignificance: One sharp gesture, and the warning is plain: a town that refuses the messengers keeps its dust, and loses the kingdom.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G575 and the base of G3551; to apportion, i.e. bestow:--give.
BiblicalUsage: Once, to husbands. Dwell with your wives according to knowledge, giving honour unto the wife, as unto the weaker vessel, and as being heirs together of the grace of life — the word is the apportioning of honour, the deliberate bestowing of it where it is due.
TheologicalSignificance: Honour is not felt but given; Peter commands husbands to bestow it, and says their prayers depend on it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G575 and G3538; to wash off (reflexively, one's own hands symbolically):--wash.
BiblicalUsage: Once, and it is Pilate washing his hands. Seeing he could prevail nothing and a tumult was made, he took water and washed his hands before the multitude, saying, I am innocent of the blood of this just person: see ye to it.
TheologicalSignificance: The water washed his hands and nothing else; the guilt stayed exactly where he left it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G575 and G5342; to bear off (literally or relatively):--bring, carry (away).
BiblicalUsage: To bear off, to carry away. The chief priests bound Jesus and carried Him away and delivered Him to Pilate in Mark 15:1, and the beggar Lazarus died and was carried by the angels into Abraham's bosom in Luke 16:22. Handkerchiefs from Paul's body were brought to the sick in Acts 19:12, and the diseases departed from them, and John was carried away in the spirit to a great and high mountain in Revelation 21:10 to see the holy Jerusalem.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word carries the whole gospel in miniature: Jesus carried away to Pilate, Lazarus carried away to Abraham's bosom, the sick carried away from their diseases, and John carried away to see the city. Being carried is the Christian life — I do not climb to God; I am borne to Him.
RelatedPeople: Jesus; Paul; Lazarus; John the Apostle
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G575 and G5343; (figuratively) to escape:--escape.
BiblicalUsage: To escape — three times, all in 2 Peter, and all about the same snare. By the promises we are partakers of the divine nature, having escaped the corruption that is in the world through lust, in 2 Peter 1:4. But the false teachers allure those that were clean escaped from them who live in error in 2 Peter 2:18, and if after they have escaped the pollutions of the world they are again entangled, the latter end is worse with them than the beginning, in 2 Peter 2:20.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Peter's warning is the sober side of every escape. God has given me a way out of corruption, and it is real — but the escape is not a fence I can never climb back over. Those who return to the pollution they escaped find the second captivity worse than the first, and I am to guard my escape like the gift it is.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G575 and the middle voice of G5412; to unload:--unlade.
BiblicalUsage: Once, on Paul's last voyage to Jerusalem. The ship sailed into Syria and landed at Tyre, for there the ship was to unlade her burden — the word is the unloading of cargo at the end of a leg of the journey.
TheologicalSignificance: A sailor's word, and nothing more: the cargo comes off at Tyre so the ship can go on.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G575 and G5350; to enunciate plainly, i.e. declare:--say, speak forth, utterance.
BiblicalUsage: To speak forth plainly, to utter with a clear voice. They were all filled with the Holy Ghost and began to speak with other tongues, as the Spirit gave them utterance, in Acts 2:4 — and Peter stood up with the eleven in Acts 2:14 and lifted up his voice to declare what it meant. Paul uses the word before Festus in Acts 26:25, answering the charge of madness: I speak forth the words of truth and soberness.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word is the opposite of babble: the Spirit gives utterance, and the utterance is plain, public, and true. Peter's sermon and Paul's defence are the same kind of speech — not ecstasy for its own sake but truth spoken out loud where everyone can hear it. That is the utterance I am to pray for.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G575 and G4098; to fall off:--fall.
BiblicalUsage: A single verse, about scales falling from eyes. Immediately there fell from Paul's eyes as it had been scales, and he received sight forthwith, and arose, and was baptized.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for the moment blindness ends: the scales fall, the sight comes, and the baptism follows.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G575 and G4105; to lead astray (figuratively); passively, to stray (from truth):--err, seduce.
BiblicalUsage: Two uses, and in both someone is led astray. The love of money is the root of all evil, and some coveting after it have erred from the faith in 1 Timothy 6:10; and false Christs and false prophets shall rise and show signs and wonders to seduce, if it were possible, even the elect in Mark 13:22.
TheologicalSignificance: The word is a wandering off the road — and Paul and Jesus agree on where the road bends: money and miracles.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G575 and G4126; to set sail:--sail away.
BiblicalUsage: To set sail — four times, and every sailing is a leg of Paul's journeys. Being sent forth by the Holy Ghost, they sailed to Cyprus in Acts 13:4, and sailed back to Antioch in Acts 14:26, from whence they had been recommended to the grace of God. The voyage to Miletus runs day by day in Acts 20:15, and the last sailing begins in Acts 27:1, when it was determined that they should sail into Italy.
TheologicalSignificance: I love how Luke logs the sailings the way a sailor would: sent forth, recommended, arrived, determined. The gospel travelled by ship, and every departure was either the Spirit's sending or God's determination. My own goings are no less ordered — the winds and the timetables both belong to Him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G575 and G4150; to rinse off:--wash.
BiblicalUsage: Once, on the shore of Gennesaret. The fishermen had gone out of their boats and were washing their nets — the word is the rinsing off of the night's work, the cleaning of the gear before the next cast.
TheologicalSignificance: A fisherman's chore, and the quiet before the miracle: the nets are washed, and then Jesus fills them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G575 and G4155; to stifle (by drowning or overgrowth):--choke.
BiblicalUsage: Twice in Luke, and both times about choking. Some seed fell among thorns, and the thorns sprang up with it and choked it in Luke 8:7; and the herd of swine ran violently down the steep place into the lake and were choked in Luke 8:33.
TheologicalSignificance: The same word chokes a seed and drowns a herd — what grows beside the seed can kill it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G575 and G5594; to breathe out, i.e. faint:--hearts failing.
BiblicalUsage: A single use, about the last days. Men's hearts failing them for fear, and for looking after those things which are coming on the earth — the word is breathing out, fainting, the heart giving way under dread.
TheologicalSignificance: The fear is the point: when the powers of heaven are shaken, men's hearts fail before the blow lands.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a compound of G1 (as a negative particle) and the base of G4198; to have no way out, i.e. be at a loss (mentally):-- (stand in) doubt, be perplexed.
BiblicalUsage: To have no way out, to be at a loss. The women at the tomb were much perplexed in Luke 24:4, and two men stood by them in shining garments; the disciples looked one on another in John 13:22, doubting of whom He spake. Herod heard John gladly in Mark 6:20, yet was perplexed by him, and Paul tells the Galatians in Galatians 4:20 that he stands in doubt of them.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe perplexity is honest ground, and the Bible does not scold it. The women were perplexed and then saw angels; the disciples doubted and then heard the truth; Herod was perplexed and would not act; Paul stood in doubt and wrote to win them back. Being at a loss is not the sin — staying there, when the way out has been shown, is.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from the same as G639; a (state of) quandary:--perplexity.
BiblicalUsage: A single use, and the whole earth is at a loss: upon the earth there shall be distress of nations, with perplexity — the sea and the waves roaring — the word is a quandary with no way out, a whole world at a loss.
TheologicalSignificance: The perplexity belongs to the nations, not the disciples: the world will not know the way out, but those who watch will.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G575 and a derivative of G3737; to bereave wholly, i.e. (figuratively) separate (from intercourse):--take.
BiblicalUsage: Paul uses this word once, for being torn away from the Thessalonians for a short time, in presence but not in heart. It is the language of bereavement, not of a planned goodbye.
TheologicalSignificance: Being kept apart from people you love still hurts, even when the parting is short.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G575 and G4496; to hurl off, i.e. precipitate (oneself):--cast.
BiblicalUsage: The word appears once, when the centurion stops the soldiers from killing the prisoners and orders those who can swim to throw themselves off the ship first and make for land. It is a desperate, all-in leap.
TheologicalSignificance: Sometimes getting to shore takes a leap you cannot take back.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G575 and a derivative of G4632; to pack up (one's) baggage:--take up… carriages.
BiblicalUsage: After the stay at Caesarea, Paul and his company packed up their baggage and went up to Jerusalem. The word is the ordinary business of a journey ending and a harder one beginning.
TheologicalSignificance: Obedience sometimes looks as plain as packing a bag and going where you know trouble is waiting.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a compound of G575 and a derivative of G4639; a shading off, i.e. obscuration:--shadow.
BiblicalUsage: James says the Father of lights has no variableness, neither shadow of turning. The word is a shadow cast by something moving between us and the light, and James says God never shifts that way.
TheologicalSignificance: God does not flicker, and His gifts do not come with a shadow side.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G575 and G4685; to drag forth, i.e. (literally) unsheathe (a sword), or relatively (with a degree of force implied) retire (personally or factiously):--(with-)draw (away), after we were gotten from.
BiblicalUsage: The word means to drag or draw away, and it shows up in three directions at once. Men rise up to draw away disciples after them, Jesus withdraws from His disciples about a stone's cast to pray, and Peter draws his sword in Gethsemane. The same pulling motion can serve ambition, prayer, or violence.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the question is always what is being drawn, and toward whom. Paul warns that some will draw disciples after themselves; Jesus shows the other way, drawing apart to the Father before the cross.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: feminine of the same as G647; defection from truth (properly, the state) ("apostasy"):--falling away, forsake.
BiblicalUsage: Paul says the day of the Lord will not come until the falling away comes first, and the Jews in Jerusalem are told that Paul teaches the Jews among the Gentiles to forsake Moses. In both places the word is a deliberate stepping away from what was once held.
TheologicalSignificance: Falling away is not drifting by accident; it is a decision to walk off, and Scripture names it plainly so we can see it coming.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: neuter of a (presumed) adjective from a derivative of G868; properly, something separative, i.e. (specially) divorce:--(writing of) divorcement.
BiblicalUsage: This is the certificate of divorce, the writing a man gave a woman to send her away. Jesus quotes the old permission in Matthew 5:31 and again in Matthew 19:7, and the Pharisees press Him on it in Mark 10:4. The paper made the break legal, but Jesus pushes past the paper to the hardness of heart behind it.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that a legal paper never settles what God thinks of a marriage. Jesus treats divorce as a concession to hard hearts, not as God's design, and He points us back to what God joined together from the beginning.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G575 and a derivative of G4721; to unroof:--uncover.
BiblicalUsage: When the crowd blocked the door, the four friends uncovered the roof above Jesus and let the paralysed man down through it. The word is that unroofing, the tearing open of a house to get a friend to Christ.
TheologicalSignificance: Faith that will not be stopped finds a way through the roof.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G575 and G4724; set apart, i.e. (by implication) to send out (properly, on a mission) literally or figuratively:--put in, send (away, forth, out), set (at liberty).
BiblicalUsage: To send out on a mission is the heartbeat of this word. God sent His Son not to condemn the world but to save it, Jesus sent His disciples out two by two, and after the resurrection He sent them the same way the Father had sent Him. Sending always carries the sender's authority and purpose with it.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe being sent is not a promotion, it is a commission. We go because we were sent, and the One who sent us goes with the message. That is what makes ordinary people able to carry the gospel anywhere.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G575 and στερέω (to deprive); to despoil:--defraud, destitute, kept back by fraud.
BiblicalUsage: The word means to defraud, to keep back what belongs to someone else. Paul tells the Corinthians they already lose by going to law against each other, because they wrong and defraud their own brothers; married couples are not to defraud one another except by agreement for prayer; and the commandments themselves forbid it.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that defrauding a brother is worse than losing a lawsuit. God sees the quiet keeping-back, in money and in marriage, and He calls it what it is.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G649; commission, i.e. (specially) apostolate:--apostleship.
BiblicalUsage: Apostleship is the commission itself, the office and authority of being sent. Paul received grace and apostleship to bring the nations to obedience, he calls the Corinthians the seal of his apostleship, and the eleven choose Matthias to take the part of the ministry and apostleship Judas left.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe apostleship was never a title to wear, it was a charge to carry. Its seal was not a ceremony but fruit, people brought to faith and obedience by the message.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G649; a delegate; specially, an ambassador of the Gospel; officially a commissioner of Christ ("apostle") (with miraculous powers):--apostle, messenger, he that is sent.
BiblicalUsage: An apostle is one sent with authority, and the word belongs first to the twelve Jesus named after a night of prayer. The church is built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, God set apostles first in the church, and the New Jerusalem itself bears the twelve apostles' names on its foundations.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the apostles matter because they were eyewitnesses the risen Christ chose and sent, not volunteers who appointed themselves. Their foundation still holds the church up, and no new foundation is being laid.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G575 and a (presumed) derivative of G4750; to speak off-hand (properly, dictate), i.e. to catechize (in an invidious manner):--provoke to speak.
BiblicalUsage: After Jesus spoke against them, the scribes and Pharisees began to press Him hard and to provoke Him to speak about many things, trying to catch Him in His own words. The word is that hostile cross-examination, questions fired to trap rather than to learn.
TheologicalSignificance: Questions can be weapons, and Jesus answered them without flinching.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G575 and G4762; to turn away or back (literally or figuratively):--bring again, pervert, turn away (from).
BiblicalUsage: To turn away or turn back covers a wide road. Jesus says do not turn away from the one who would borrow from you, He tells Peter to put his sword back in its place, Paul says the Deliverer will turn ungodliness away from Jacob, and he warns that some will turn their ears away from the truth toward fables.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe turning is the hinge of the whole Bible. Turn away from a needy neighbour and you have turned from Christ; turn away from the truth and you have turned toward a story of your own making.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G575 and the base of G4767; to detest utterly:--abhor.
BiblicalUsage: Paul's command is blunt: abhor what is evil, cling to what is good. The word is utter detestation, the opposite of tolerating evil or making peace with it.
TheologicalSignificance: Love that never hates evil is not love, it is indifference.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G575 and G4864; excommunicated:--(put) out of the synagogue(-s).
BiblicalUsage: This is the word for being put out of the synagogue, excommunicated from the community. The healed blind man's parents feared it because the Jews had agreed to cast out anyone who confessed Jesus as Christ, many rulers believed but would not confess for fear of it, and Jesus warned His disciples that the day would come when being cast out would be counted as service to God.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the fear of being cast out is one of the oldest pressures on faith. The rulers who believed in secret show how costly open confession can feel, and the blind man shows what it looks like to pay the price anyway.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: middle voice from G575 and G5021; literally, to say adieu (by departing or dismissing); figuratively, to renounce:--bid farewell, forsake, take leave, send away.
BiblicalUsage: The word means to say goodbye, to take leave, and by extension to renounce. Jesus says no one can be His disciple without forsaking all he has, a would-be follower asks first to go and bid farewell to his family, Paul takes his leave of the brothers at Corinth, and Jesus sends the crowd away to pray alone.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe farewell is the shape of discipleship. Following Jesus means loosening our grip on everything else, and sometimes the goodbye is the proof that we mean it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G575 and G5055; to complete entirely, i.e. consummate:--finish.
BiblicalUsage: The word means to finish completely, to bring something to its end. James says sin, when it is finished, brings forth death, and Jesus says on the third day He will be perfected, His work brought to its appointed completion.
TheologicalSignificance: What is finished matters: sin finished is death, and Christ's work finished is life.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G659; a repository, i.e. granary:--barn, garner.
BiblicalUsage: A barn or storehouse is where the harvest is kept, and Jesus uses it both ways. The birds do not sow or gather into barns, yet the Father feeds them; the wheat is gathered into the barn while the tares are burned; the rich fool plans bigger barns for a life he will not live; and John says the wheat will be gathered into the garner.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the barn tests what we trust. Hoarding for a future we do not control is folly, and trusting the Father who feeds the birds is not carelessness, it is faith.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: or ἀπώθομαι from G575 and the middle voice of ὠθέω or ὤθω (to shove); to push off, figuratively, to reject:--cast away, put away (from), thrust away (from).
BiblicalUsage: To thrust away, to push off and reject, is what Stephen says Israel did to Moses, and what Paul says the Jews at Pisidian Antioch did to the word of life. Paul then asks whether God has cast away His people, and he warns Timothy that some have thrust away a good conscience and shipwrecked their faith.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that rejection has two directions and only one of them is final. Men thrust God's messengers away, but God has not cast away His people, and the warning stands for anyone tempted to push conscience aside.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G575 and G2343; to treasure away:--lay up in store.
BiblicalUsage: Paul tells the rich to lay up in store for themselves a good foundation for the time to come, treasuring away something that will last. The storing is the same habit as hoarding, turned toward eternity instead of toward self.
TheologicalSignificance: The question is never whether we store up, but what we store, and where.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G659; a laying aside (literally or figuratively):--putting away (off).
BiblicalUsage: The word is a laying aside. Baptism is not the putting away of the filth of the flesh but the answer of a good conscience toward God, and Peter says he must shortly put off this tabernacle of his body, as Christ had shown him.
TheologicalSignificance: Baptism lays aside the old life, and death lays aside the body, and neither is the end of the story.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G575 and G2346; to crowd (from every side):--press.
BiblicalUsage: The word appears once, when Jesus asks who touched Him and Peter answers that the multitude throng and press Him on every side. It is the crush of a crowd, many hands brushing past, and one touch that is different.
TheologicalSignificance: Crowds press, but faith touches, and Jesus knows the difference.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G575 and G2348; to die off (literally or figuratively):--be dead, death, die, lie a-dying, be slain (X with).
BiblicalUsage: To die is the plainest word in the Bible. It runs from Jairus's daughter, whom Jesus says is not dead but sleeping, to Lazarus, whose death Jesus states outright. Paul adds the claim that if we are dead with Christ we shall also live with Him, and the sweeping truth that in Adam all die.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe death is real and it is not the end. In Adam all die, but in Christ the dying itself is remade, so that being dead with Him is the doorway to living with Him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G575 and τινάσσω (to jostle); to brush off:--shake off.
BiblicalUsage: The word is to shake off. Disciples are to shake the dust from their feet against a town that will not receive them, and Paul shakes the viper off his hand into the fire and feels no harm.
TheologicalSignificance: Some things are not to be carried, they are to be shaken off and left behind.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G575 and G5099; to pay in full:--repay.
BiblicalUsage: Paul writes to Philemon about Onesimus and puts his own name to the debt: I will repay it. The word is payment in full, a promise made in writing by a man who means to keep it.
TheologicalSignificance: A debt owned honestly is a debt that can be paid, and Paul shows us how to carry someone else's cost.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G575 and G5087; to put away (literally or figuratively):--cast off, lay apart (aside, down), put away (off).
BiblicalUsage: To put away or lay aside is the Bible's picture of leaving the old life behind.
