BiblicalUsage: Aretas is named once, as the king whose governor kept Damascus with a garrison, desiring to apprehend Paul. Paul was let down in a basket through a window by the wall to escape him.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a king's garrison is no match for a basket and a window when God means a man to get out of a city.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from the same as G730; properly, manliness (valor), i.e. excellence (intrinsic or attributed):--praise, virtue.
BiblicalUsage: The word means excellence, virtue, the manliness of a life well lived. Paul says think on whatever is true and lovely, if there be any virtue and any praise, and Peter says the church is to show forth the praises, the excellencies, of Him who called us out of darkness.
TheologicalSignificance: Virtue is not a private achievement, it is the excellence of God shown forth by His people.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: purple (the color or the dyed stuff)
BiblicalUsage: Purple is the colour of kings and of the sanctuary, the dye of the tabernacle's curtains and the priests' garments. It is also the raiment of the kings of Midian that Gideon takes as spoil, and the clothing of the virtuous woman, silk and purple.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that purple in Scripture is the colour of both worship and wealth, and the difference is who wears it. On the tabernacle it honours God, on a king it honours a man, and on the virtuous woman it honours a life well lived.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a box (as a pannier)
BiblicalUsage: The word is a box or coffer, a pannier, and it appears only in the story of the ark's return. The Philistines put the golden jewels in a coffer by the side of the ark, the ark and the coffer are laid on the cart, and the Levites take down the ark and the coffer at Beth-shemesh.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the coffer beside the ark is the Philistines' apology in gold. It shows that even God's enemies know when they have trespassed and must pay.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G692; to be idle, i.e. (figuratively) to delay:--linger.
BiblicalUsage: The word means to be idle, to linger or delay, and it appears once, when Peter says the judgment of the false teachers does not linger, and their damnation does not slumber.
TheologicalSignificance: God's judgment may seem to linger, but Peter says it does not, and the false teacher's end is already awake.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {purple}
BiblicalUsage: The word is purple, the royal colour of Babylon, and it appears only in the night Belshazzar's kingdom falls. Whoever reads the writing on the wall will be clothed in purple and made third ruler, Daniel is offered the purple, and when he reads the writing, they clothe Daniel in purple the same night the king is slain.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the purple Belshazzar offered was the price of a kingdom already weighed and found wanting. Daniel wore it for one night, and the kingdom fell before morning.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {purple}
BiblicalUsage: The word is purple, the royal colour of Babylon, and it appears only in the night Belshazzar's kingdom falls. Whoever reads the writing on the wall will be clothed in purple and made third ruler, Daniel is offered the purple, and when he reads the writing, they clothe Daniel in purple the same night the king is slain.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the purple Belshazzar offered was the price of a kingdom already weighed and found wanting. Daniel wore it for one night, and the kingdom fell before morning.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Argob, a district of Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Argob is a district of Bashan, the region of the giant king Og, with threescore great cities fenced with high walls. Moses takes all the region of Argob, gives it to the half tribe of Manasseh, and Solomon's officers still list the region of Argob among his twelve districts.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Argob shows that the land of the giants becomes the inheritance of God's people, and the walled cities of Og end up on Solomon's tax list.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and G2041; inactive, i.e. unemployed; (by implication) lazy, useless:--barren, idle, slow.
BiblicalUsage: The word means idle, inactive, unemployed, and by extension useless or lazy. Jesus says men will give account for every idle word, the householder finds men standing idle in the marketplace, James says faith without works is dead, and Paul quotes the Cretans as lazy gluttons.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that idleness is not rest, it is a refusal to work, and the Bible treats it as a sin with an account to give. Faith that does nothing is dead, and words that do nothing will be answered for.
RelatedPeople: Jesus; James, Brother of Jesus; Paul; Titus
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G696; made of silver:--(of) silver.
BiblicalUsage: The word means made of silver, and it appears where silver is worked or kept. Demetrius the silversmith makes silver shrines for Diana, and in a great house there are vessels of gold and of silver, some to honour and some to dishonour.
TheologicalSignificance: Silver can be a shrine for an idol or a vessel in God's house, and the metal is not the problem, the use is.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: neuter of a presumed derivative of G696; silvery, i.e. (by implication) cash; specially, a silverling (i.e. drachma or shekel):--money, (piece of) silver (piece).
BiblicalUsage: The word is silver as money, cash, the price of things. Peter says silver and gold have I none, but what I have I give thee; Simon is told his money will perish with him for thinking God's gift can be bought; Judas covenants for thirty pieces of silver; and Peter says we were not redeemed with corruptible things like silver and gold.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that silver is the Bible's measure of what money can and cannot do. It buys a betrayal, it cannot buy the gift of God, and it cannot redeem a soul, which is why the price of our redemption had to be something else entirely.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G696 and G2875; a beater (i.e. worker) of silver:--silversmith.
BiblicalUsage: The word is a silversmith, one who beats silver into shape, and it appears once, naming Demetrius, who makes silver shrines for Diana and brings no small gain to the craftsmen.
TheologicalSignificance: A silversmith's living depended on the idol, so the gospel sounded to him like bad business.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from ἀργός (shining); silver (the metal, in the articles or coin):--silver.
BiblicalUsage: Silver is the metal itself, shining and weighed out as money. The disciples are told to carry no silver in their purses, Paul tells Athens the Godhead is not like gold or silver or stone graven by art, a man's work may be built on gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, or stubble, and James says the rich man's gold and silver is cankered and will eat their flesh like fire.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe silver is honest about itself: it shines, it weighs, and it rusts. What is built on it will be tried by fire, and only what survives the fire was ever worth building.
RelatedPeople: Jesus; Paul; James, Brother of Jesus
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: the altar of the temple
BiblicalUsage: Ezekiel uses this word twice, both times for the top of the altar in his vision of the temple, the hearth where the burnt offering burned. It is the same word as Ariel, the lion of God, and here it names the place of fire at the heart of worship.
TheologicalSignificance: A single word for the altar's hearth carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the picture, that God's fire burns at the centre of the house where He meets His people.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H7414); Arimathæa (or Ramah), a place in Palestine:--Arimathæa.
BiblicalUsage: Arimathea is named only as the home of Joseph, the rich councillor who asked Pilate for Jesus' body. Each Gospel names the town to place the man, and John adds that Joseph had been a disciple in secret for fear of the Jews.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Joseph matters because he stepped forward when the apostles had scattered, and a town name is all it takes to fix a real man in a real place at the cross.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G712; to take the principle meal:--dine.
BiblicalUsage: To dine is to take the main meal of the day, and the Gospels use it for ordinary meals and one extraordinary one. A Pharisee invites Jesus to dine with him, and after the resurrection Jesus stands on the shore and calls the disciples to come and dine, fish and bread already waiting.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the risen Jesus cooking breakfast says something no sermon could: He is not a ghost or an idea, He is the Lord who feeds His friends. The table is where He meets them, and I hold that He still meets us there, in the ordinary act of eating together.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from the same as G712 and G757; best ruling; Aristarchus, a Macedonian:--Aristarchus.
BiblicalUsage: Aristarchus is the Macedonian who stays with Paul through the worst of it. He is seized in the riot at Ephesus, sails with Paul as a prisoner to Rome, and is still beside him in prison when Paul writes to the Colossians, calling him a fellow prisoner.
TheologicalSignificance: A man named three times for staying put is worth noticing, because faithfulness is mostly that: being there when it costs something, and still being there years later.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: apparently a comparative of the same as G712; the left hand (as second-best):--left (hand).
BiblicalUsage: The left hand is the weaker hand, the second-best side, and the New Testament uses it that way. Jesus tells us not to let the left hand know what the right hand is doing, James and John ask to sit at His right and His left in glory, and Paul speaks of the armour of righteousness on the right hand and on the left.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the left hand matters because Jesus uses it to teach secrecy in giving: true generosity does not keep score, not even with itself. And I believe Paul's armour on both sides says the Christian is armed for every direction the fight comes from.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from the same as G712 and G1012; best counselling; Aristoboulus, a Christian:--Aristobulus.
BiblicalUsage: Aristobulus is named once, and Paul greets his household, not the man himself. Whether he was a believer, dead, or away, we are not told; what we know is that his household in Rome was known to Paul and counted among the saints.
TheologicalSignificance: A household greeted by name tells me the gospel had reached inside a Roman home, and that the church was made of families, not only of famous men.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: apparently neuter of a superlative from the same as G730; the best meal (or breakfast; perhaps from ἦρι ("early")), i.e. luncheon:--dinner.
BiblicalUsage: The ariston is the main meal, dinner or breakfast, and Jesus uses it to teach about the kingdom and about hospitality. A king sends servants to call guests to a dinner already prepared, a Pharisee marvels that Jesus sits down to dinner without washing first, and Jesus tells a host not to invite only friends who can repay the meal.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the dinner table is one of Jesus' favourite pictures of the kingdom, because a meal is invitation, provision and fellowship all at once. And I hold that His rule for hosts still stands: invite those who cannot pay you back, and let God be the one who repays.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G706; to enumerate or count:--number.
BiblicalUsage: To number is to count, and Scripture uses it for the smallest and the largest counts alike. Jesus says the very hairs of your head are all numbered, and John sees a multitude no man could number standing before the throne.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the numbering of hairs is the most tender arithmetic in the Bible: nothing about you is too small for God to count. And the multitude no one could number is the other end of the same truth, that His people are more than any census will ever hold.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G142; a number (as reckoned up):--number.
BiblicalUsage: Arithmos is simply a number, the count of something, and the New Testament counts people, crowds and signs with it. The believers grow to about five thousand men, five thousand sit down to be fed, a hundred and forty-four thousand are sealed, and John names the number of the beast as six hundred threescore and six.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe numbers in Scripture are never just numbers: they mark a people growing, a crowd fed, a remnant sealed, and a counterfeit counted. God numbers His own, and I hold that being counted among them is the only count that finally matters.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Ariel, a symbolical name for Jerusalem, also the name of an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Ariel is the name Isaiah gives Jerusalem, the lion of God, the city where David dwelt, and God says He will distress Ariel until it is brought low. The same name belongs to a chief man Ezra sends for, one of the leaders he gathers before the journey back to Jerusalem.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a name that means lion of God fits a city God chose and then judged: chosen does not mean untouchable. The man who shares the name reminds me that God also calls ordinary leaders by strong names and sends them on hard errands.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: lion of God; i.e. heroic
BiblicalUsage: This word means lion of God, and it is used for men, not places. Benaiah the son of Jehoiada slew two lionlike men of Moab, and both Samuel and Chronicles remember the deed the same way, as the mark of a hero.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for lionlike men carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the picture, that courage in battle was remembered as something lionlike, and God gave such men to Israel.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a lion
BiblicalUsage: The lion is the king of beasts in Scripture, feared and admired in the same breath. Judah is a lion's whelp in Jacob's blessing, David tells Saul he killed a lion that took a lamb, the proverb makes a wicked ruler a roaring lion over the poor, and Amos asks who can but prophesy when the lion has roared.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the lion shows us two things at once: the strength God gives His people, and the strength of the enemies they face. David's lion and Amos's lion are the same animal, and the difference is whose side it is on, which is why I hold that the Lion of Judah is the only lion worth fearing and the only one worth following.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: meal
BiblicalUsage: The arisah is the first of the dough, the lump set aside when bread is made. The law says to offer the first of your dough as a heave offering, Nehemiah's people promise to bring it to the priests, and Ezekiel gives the first of all the dough to the priests in the restored temple.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the first of the dough teaches the same lesson as the firstfruits: God gets the first, not the leftovers. Bread is daily and ordinary, and that is the point, even the ordinary work of the kitchen belongs to Him first.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Arisai, a son of Haman
BiblicalUsage: Arisai is named once, as one of the ten sons of Haman, and he is hanged with his brothers after the Jews defend themselves. The verse gives his name and nothing more.
TheologicalSignificance: A name on a list of the judged reminds me that Haman's house fell whole, and that God keeps the record straight, name by name.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Aridatha, a son of Haman
BiblicalUsage: The book of Esther names Aridatha once, among the ten sons of Haman who were hanged after the Jews defended themselves. His name sits in the middle of the list, and the verse says nothing more about him.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the careful listing of all ten names shows God does not deal in vague judgments: each son of the man who plotted murder is named, and each one falls.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Aridai, a son of Haman
BiblicalUsage: Aridai appears once, in the same list as his brothers, one of the ten sons of Haman hanged after the Jews defended themselves. Like the others, he is named and nothing more is said.
TheologicalSignificance: Ten names, ten hangings, one judgment: the house that rose against God's people fell together, and Scripture keeps the count.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: the sky (as dropping at the horizon)
BiblicalUsage: Isaiah uses this word once, for the skies over a land under judgment. The enemy comes like a roaring sea, and those who look to the land find darkness, with the light dimmed in its heavens.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for the heavens carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the picture, that judgment darkens even the sky above the land.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: bare, i.e. destitute (of children)
BiblicalUsage: To be childless in Scripture is to be cut off from the future, and the word carries that grief plainly. Abram says to God, I go childless, and the heir of my house is a servant; the law makes childlessness the penalty for taking a brother's wife; and Coniah is written childless, a man who will have no son to sit on David's throne.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe childlessness here is more than sadness, it is a sentence: no heir, no throne, no name carried on. And that is why I hold the promise to Abram matters so much, God answers a childless man with a son, and through that son, a nation.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: fearful, i.e. powerful or tyrannical
BiblicalUsage: The terrible ones are the violent, the ruthless who crush the weak, and the prophets name them plainly. Isaiah says God is a refuge from the storm and a shadow from the heat when the blast of the terrible ones beats like a storm against a wall, and that the terrible one will be brought to nought; Jeremiah says the LORD is with him as a mighty terrible one, and his persecutors will stumble.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this word is a warning and a comfort together: the terrible are real, and God sees them. He shelters the poor from them, and He will bring them to nothing, which is why I hold that no tyrant, however terrible, gets the last word.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: length
BiblicalUsage: This Aramaic word means length, and it is used for the lengthening of a king's peace and the lengthening of beasts' lives. Daniel tells Nebuchadnezzar his tranquillity may be lengthened if he breaks off his sins, and the beasts of his later vision have their dominion taken away yet their lives prolonged for a season.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for length carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the mercy in it, that God lengthens days even for kings and beasts, and gives time to turn.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: apparently a primary verb (but probably akin to G142 through the idea of raising a barrier); properly, to ward off, i.e. (by implication) to avail (figuratively, be satisfactory):--be content, be enough, suffice, be sufficient.
BiblicalUsage: To be content is to have enough, to let what is given suffice, and the New Testament presses it hard. The Lord tells Paul His grace is sufficient, Hebrews says be content with such things as ye have, for God will never leave you, and Paul says that with food and raiment we should be content.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe contentment is not settling for less, it is trusting that God's enough is really enough. His grace suffices for a thorn in the flesh, His presence suffices for every lack, and I hold that the person who believes that is richer than the one who keeps grasping for more.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G714; satisfactory:--enough, suffice (-ient).
BiblicalUsage: Enough is enough, and Jesus and Peter both draw the line there. Sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof, says Jesus, and it is enough for the disciple to be as his master; Peter says the time past of our life may suffice us to have wrought the will of the Gentiles.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that 'enough' is one of the kindest words in the Bible. God does not ask us to carry tomorrow's trouble today, or to be more than a disciple, or to keep on in a past we have left, enough is enough, and His grace covers the day in front of us.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an Arkevite (collectively) or native of Erek
BiblicalUsage: The Archevites are named once, among the peoples who wrote to Artaxerxes against the rebuilding of the temple. They are listed with the Babylonians, the Elamites and the rest, a people settled in Samaria who wanted the work stopped.
TheologicalSignificance: A people named once for opposing the temple reminds me that God's work has always had organised opposition, and that the letter-writers are remembered for standing against it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an Arkite or native of Erek
BiblicalUsage: The Arkite is Hushai, David's friend, who meets him on the Mount of Olives when Absalom has taken Jerusalem. Hushai goes back into the city as David's man, and his counsel defeats the counsel of Ahithophel, which is what saves David.
TheologicalSignificance: One man's loyalty carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the reminder that God often saves His people through a friend who stays, and through counsel given at the right hour.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably from G714; a bear (as obstructing by ferocity):--bear.
BiblicalUsage: The bear appears once, in John's vision of the beast from the sea, whose feet were as the feet of a bear. The Greek text behind the King James reads the bear here, while the later Greek text reads the genitive of a different bear-word, so the verse stands on the Textus Receptus reading.
TheologicalSignificance: One mention of a bear's feet carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the picture, that the beast is a mixture of creatures, strong and shambling and made to be feared.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: the knee
BiblicalUsage: This Aramaic word is the knee, and it is used once, for Belshazzar's terror at the writing on the wall. His countenance changes, his thoughts trouble him, and the joints of his loins loosen and his knees smite one against another.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for knees knocking together carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the picture, that a king's strength fails in a moment when God writes on his wall.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H2022 and H4023); Armageddon (or Har-Meggiddon), a symbolic name:--Armageddon.
BiblicalUsage: Armageddon is named once, as the place where the kings of the earth are gathered for the battle of the great day of God Almighty. John says it is called in the Hebrew tongue Armageddon, the mount of Megiddo, the plain where Israel's armies had fought for centuries.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Armageddon matters because it is a real place with a real history of battles, and God chooses it for the last gathering of the kings. The end of the age is not fought nowhere, it is fought somewhere, and the kings who gather there gather against God.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Armoni, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Armoni is named once, as one of the two sons of Saul by Rizpah, and he is handed over with his brother to the Gibeonites, who hang them to settle the bloodguilt of Saul's house. The verse gives his name and his mother and nothing more.
TheologicalSignificance: A son of Saul handed over for his father's sin is a hard verse, and it tells me that bloodguilt in Israel was a family matter, and that even a king's house could not escape the debt it owed.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: the plane tree (from its smooth and shed bark)
BiblicalUsage: The plane tree is a smooth-barked tree, and it is used twice. Jacob takes rods of green poplar, hazel and chestnut and peels white strakes in them for his flocks, and Ezekiel says no tree in the garden of God, plane trees among them, was like the great cedar in beauty.
TheologicalSignificance: One tree named twice carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the picture, that even the finest trees of Eden stood below the cedar God compares to Assyria.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a citadel (from its height)
BiblicalUsage: The palace is the strong place, the citadel of a king, and the prophets speak of palaces burning more often than of palaces standing. Amos says fire will devour the palaces of Benhadad, Isaiah says the palaces will be forsaken and the forts become dens for ever, and Jeremiah says fire will devour the palaces of Jerusalem if the people break the Sabbath.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe palaces burn in the prophets because a palace is where power forgets God. The strongest walls in the land are no shelter when the people inside them will not keep His day or His law, and I hold that no citadel, however high, stands against the fire of His judgment.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Arnan, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Arnan is named once, in the line of David, as a son of Rephaiah, and the chronicler gives his name and his brothers and nothing more. He stands in the genealogy between the exile and the return.
TheologicalSignificance: A name in a genealogy with no story of its own still matters, because God keeps the line of David name by name, even through the generations nobody writes about.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: the hare
BiblicalUsage: The hare is named twice, in the lists of unclean animals. It chews the cud but does not divide the hoof, and so the law says it is unclean to you, and you shall not eat of it.
TheologicalSignificance: One small animal in the food laws carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the lesson, that God's people were set apart even at the table, by what they would and would not eat.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: perhaps from G1 (as a negative particle) and the middle voice of G4483; to contradict, i.e. disavow, reject, abnegate:--deny, refuse.
BiblicalUsage: To deny is to say no to someone you know, and the New Testament uses it for the worst no and the best no alike. Jesus says whoever denies Him before men will be denied before the Father, and that following Him means denying yourself and taking up your cross; Peter denies Him three times before the cock crows, and Paul warns that if we deny Him, He also will deny us.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe denying is the fork in the road of every Christian life: deny yourself and follow, or deny Christ and be denied. Peter's denial is the warning, and his restoration is the hope, and I hold that the same Lord who heard Peter say 'I know not the man' is the one who asked him three times, 'Lovest thou me?'
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: diminutive from G704; a lambkin:--lamb.
BiblicalUsage: The little lamb is John's name for Christ through the whole of Revelation, and once for His people. The risen Jesus tells Peter to feed His lambs, and John sees a Lamb as it had been slain standing in the midst of the throne, the saints washing their robes white in the blood of the Lamb, and the brethren overcoming by the blood of the Lamb.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the Lamb is the centre of the whole Bible's picture of victory: not a lion tearing, but a Lamb slain, standing, and reigning. The blood that washes robes white and the blood that overcomes the accuser are the same blood, and I hold that there is no other way to stand before the throne.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: the Arnon, a river east of the Jordan, also its territory
BiblicalUsage: The Arnon is the river that marked the border of Moab, and Israel's story crosses it again and again. They camp on the far side of the Arnon, Moses commands them to rise up and pass over it against Sihon, and Joshua lists the kings they defeated from the Arnon to Mount Hermon.
TheologicalSignificance: A river that keeps turning up as a border tells me how God measures out the land: here is yours, there is theirs, and the crossing is the moment the promise starts to be kept.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an Aroerite or inhabitant of Aroer
BiblicalUsage: The Aroerite is named once, for Shama and Jehiel, the sons of Hothan, who stand in the list of David's mighty men. The verse gives their father, their town and nothing more.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for a man's hometown carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the reminder that David's mighty men came from real towns, and their names were worth writing down.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a mosquito (from its swarming)
BiblicalUsage: The swarm is the plague of flies, the fourth plague on Egypt, and it comes by God's word and leaves by God's word. The LORD says He will send swarms of flies on Pharaoh and his servants, a grievous swarm fills the houses of Egypt, and the psalm remembers that He sent divers sorts of flies among them which devoured them.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the swarm is a picture of judgment that cannot be fenced out: no house in Egypt was shut against it, except Goshen, where God made a division between His people and Pharaoh's. The same God still makes that division, and I hold that it is His mercy, not our walls, that keeps the swarm out.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: long
BiblicalUsage: Long is used for time and for measure, and the Bible stretches it both ways. The war between the house of Saul and the house of David was long, Jeremiah tells the exiles their captivity will be long, and Zophar says God's measure is longer than the earth and broader than the sea.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe 'long' is honest about how God's work feels: wars drag on, exiles drag on, and God's measure is longer than anything we can pace out. And I hold that the length is not delay, it is God working at His own measure, which is longer than the earth and deeper than hell.
RelatedTopics: Patience; Waiting on God; God's Sovereignty
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G142 (in the sense of sending off scent); an aromatic:--(sweet) spice.
BiblicalUsage: The spices are what love brings to a grave. The women buy sweet spices to anoint Jesus, they rest on the Sabbath and return at dawn with the spices they have prepared, and Nicodemus brings myrrh and aloes to wrap the body with, as the manner of the Jews is to bury.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the spices are the last gift of people who thought He was dead, and that is what makes them so moving: they came to honour a body, and found an empty tomb. Love that brings spices to a grave is not wasted, because the Lord who was buried is the Lord who rose, and I hold that He remembers every gift brought in grief.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G723; to plow:--plough.
BiblicalUsage: To plow is the work of the servant in the field, and it is used twice. Jesus asks which of you, having a servant plowing, would say to him, sit down to meat, and Paul says he that ploweth should plow in hope, and he that thresheth in hope should be partaker of his hope.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for plowing carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the picture, that the work of the field is done in hope, and the labourer who plows in hope has a share in what grows.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from ἀρόω (to till); a plow:--plough.
BiblicalUsage: The plow is named once, in Jesus' warning to the man who wanted to follow Him after saying farewell at home. No man, having put his hand to the plow and looking back, is fit for the kingdom of God.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for a plow carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the picture, that following Jesus is forward work, and a backward look at the furrow ruins the row.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Aroer, the name of three places in or near Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Aroer is the name of three places, and the chief one stands on the edge of the river Arnon. Moses says from Aroer by the river no city was too strong for Israel, Joshua gives it to Reuben as a border town, and Isaiah says the cities of Aroer will be forsaken, left for flocks to lie down in.
TheologicalSignificance: A border town that is taken, given and then forsaken tells me how quickly the map changes: the same walls that marked Israel's edge become sheep pens when judgment comes, and I hold that no border town is safe apart from the God who drew the border.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a juniper (from its nudity of situation)
BiblicalUsage: This word is a shrub of the desert, the juniper or heath that grows alone in the parched places. Jeremiah says the man who trusts in man shall be like the heath in the desert, and tells Moab to flee and save her life, and be like the heath in the wilderness.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for a desert shrub carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the picture, that trusting in man leaves you like a lone bush in a salt land, seeing no good when it comes.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an onager (from his lonesome habits)
BiblicalUsage: The wild ass is named once, in God's answer to Job, and the question is who has sent out the wild ass free and loosed its bands. It is the onager of the wilderness, untamed and alone, and God claims it as His creature.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for a wild ass carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the question, that the creature no man can tame still answers to God.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Arod, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Arod is named once, as a son of Gad, and the census gives his name and his family and nothing more. His descendants are counted among the tribes at the edge of the promised land.
TheologicalSignificance: A name in a census with no story of its own still matters, because God counts His people family by family, and no son of Gad is left out of the number.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an Arodite or descendant of Arod
BiblicalUsage: The Arodites are the descendants of Arod the son of Gad, named twice, once in the list of those who went down into Egypt with Jacob, and once in the census in the wilderness. The name marks a family, and the family is counted both times.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for a family's name carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the record, that the sons of Gad were counted going into Egypt and counted coming out, and none was lost on the way.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: nude, either partially or totally
BiblicalUsage: Naked is used for the body uncovered, and for the soul laid bare, and the Bible is frank about both. Adam and his wife were both naked and were not ashamed, Job says naked came I out of my mother's womb and naked shall I return, and Isaiah says true fasting is to cover the naked when you see him.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe nakedness in Scripture runs from innocence to judgment: unashamed in Eden, stripped by suffering in Job, and clothed again by the mercy of God's people. And I hold that the gospel meets us naked, with nothing of our own to cover us, and clothes us in Christ.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an Edomite (as in the margin)
BiblicalUsage: This word appears once, in the margin of 2 Kings 16:6, as the reading behind the men who came to Elath in the days of Ahaz. Where the text reads Syrians, the margin reads Edomites, the sons of Esau coming to a port on the Red Sea.
TheologicalSignificance: One word in a margin carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the reminder that even the small print of the kings' wars was written down, and that Edom kept pressing at Israel's edges.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a box
BiblicalUsage: The ark is the chest of the covenant, and it goes where God goes. Bezalel makes it of shittim wood overlaid with gold, it goes before Israel into the Jordan, it is taken by the Philistines in battle, and David brings it up to Jerusalem with gladness when he hears God has blessed the house that kept it.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the ark matters because it is the throne of the unseen King in the middle of His people: mercy seat, manna, and the tables of the law all in one box. It could not be handled lightly, and it could not be left behind, and I hold that Christ is the true ark now, God's presence with us, carried into every Jordan we have to cross.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Arpad, a place in Syria
BiblicalUsage: Arpad is a city of Syria, named when empires boast and when prophets judge. Rabshakeh asks where are the gods of Hamath and of Arpad, Assyria says Is not Samaria as Damascus and Arpad as Hamath, and Jeremiah says Damascus is confounded, and Arpad with it, for they have heard evil tidings.
TheologicalSignificance: A city named three times for its gods and its fall tells me that no city's gods can save it, and that the empires which boast over one city will boast over the next until God stops them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Arpakshad, a son of Noah; also the region settled by him
BiblicalUsage: Arphaxad is a son of Shem, born two years after the flood, and the father of Salah. Genesis names him in the table of nations and again at the head of the line that runs through Eber and Peleg down to Abram, and the chronicler keeps his place in the same line.
TheologicalSignificance: A name between the flood and Abram matters, because the promise runs through ordinary fathers and sons, and God keeps the line unbroken from Shem to the father of faith.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H775); Arphaxad, a post-diluvian patriarch:--Arphaxad.
BiblicalUsage: Arphaxad is named once in the New Testament, in the genealogy of Jesus, as the son of Cainan and the father of Sala. Luke carries the line back through him to Shem and to Noah, and on to Adam and to God.
TheologicalSignificance: One name in a genealogy carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the line, that Jesus is the son of Arphaxad and the son of Adam, and the promise given to Shem's house comes home in Him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an Arkite or inhabitant of Erek
BiblicalUsage: The Arkite is a family of the Canaanites, named twice, in the table of nations and in the chronicler's copy of it. The name marks one of the peoples who lived in the land before Israel, descended from Canaan the son of Ham.
TheologicalSignificance: One family name in a table of nations carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the record, that the land had its peoples before Israel came, and God knew them all by name.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H6162); a pledge, i.e. part of the purchase-money or property given in advance as security for the rest:--earnest.
BiblicalUsage: The earnest is a pledge, the first part of the payment given in advance to guarantee the rest. God has sealed us and given the earnest of the Spirit in our hearts, He has wrought us for immortality and given us the earnest of the Spirit, and the Spirit is the earnest of our inheritance until the redemption of the purchased possession.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the earnest is the most comforting word in the New Testament for a doubting Christian: God does not ask us to wait for the whole payment on trust alone, He puts the Spirit in our hearts now as the first instalment. What He has begun He will finish, and I hold that the Spirit's presence in us is the guarantee of it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and a presumed derivative of the same as G4476; unsewed, i.e. of a single piece:--without seam.
BiblicalUsage: The coat without seam is named once, at the cross. The soldiers take Jesus' garments and divide them, but the coat is without seam, woven from the top throughout, so they cast lots for it rather than tear it.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for a seamless coat carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the picture, that even the soldiers saw the coat was too good to tear, and the Scripture was fulfilled over it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: or ἄρσην probably from G142; male (as stronger for lifting):--male, man.
BiblicalUsage: Male is used from the first page to the last, for the way God made us and for the child who rules the nations. He which made them at the beginning made them male and female, every male that openeth the womb shall be called holy to the Lord, Paul says there is neither male nor female in Christ Jesus, and the woman brings forth a man child who is to rule all nations with a rod of iron.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe male and female is God's design from the beginning, not an accident and not a cage: He made them both, He calls the male child holy, and in Christ the division that the world turns into a war is healed without erasing the difference. And I hold that the man child of Revelation is the proof, that God's King is a man, born of a woman, ruling the nations.
RelatedTopics: Creation; Image of God; Unity in Christ
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and the same as G4490; unsaid, i.e. (by implication) inexpressible:--unspeakable.
BiblicalUsage: Unspeakable is used once, for the words Paul heard when he was caught up into paradise. He heard unspeakable words, which it is not lawful for a man to utter, and he came back unable to tell them.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for words that cannot be spoken carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the silence, that some of what God shows His people stays unspoken, and the telling of it is not given to us.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and a presumed derivative of G4517; infirm:--sick (folk, -ly).
BiblicalUsage: The sick are those without strength, and the word is used for the crowds Jesus healed and for the church at Corinth. Jesus went forth and saw a great multitude, and was moved with compassion toward them, and He healed their sick; and Paul says many at Corinth are weak and sickly because they eat and drink the Lord's supper unworthily.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for the sick carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the contrast, that Jesus heals the sick who come to Him, and that the same Lord will let His own people grow sick when they despise His table.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G730 and G2845; a sodomite:--abuser of (that defile) self with mankind.
BiblicalUsage: This word names men who lie with men, and Paul puts it in two lists of sins. The unrighteous shall not inherit the kingdom of God, he says, naming fornicators, idolaters, adulterers and abusers of themselves with mankind; and the law, he tells Timothy, is made for the lawless and disobedient, for the ungodly and for sinners, among them abusers of themselves with mankind.
TheologicalSignificance: One hard word in two lists carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the plain warning, that this sin is named among the sins that shut men out of the kingdom, and that the law names it because God names it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Artachshasta (or Artaxerxes), a title (rather than name) of several Persian kings
BiblicalUsage: Artaxerxes is a title, not one man's name, worn by several kings of Persia, and the books of Ezra and Nehemiah name it for the kings who let the Jews go home. Artaxerxes gives Ezra a letter with silver and gold for the temple, and in the twentieth year of Artaxerxes Nehemiah the cupbearer asks leave to rebuild the wall of Jerusalem.
TheologicalSignificance: A king's title that turns up on both sides of the return tells me God moves the hearts of kings: the same throne that stopped the work lets it go on, and the letters of a Persian king carry the silver for God's house.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: contracted from a compound of G735 and G1435; gift of Artemis; Artemas (or Artemidorus), a Christian:--Artemas.
BiblicalUsage: Artemas is named once, as the man Paul will send to Titus in Crete, or Tychicus in his place. Paul tells Titus to be diligent to come to him at Nicopolis, where he has decided to winter, and Artemas is the one who will take over the work.
TheologicalSignificance: A man named once as a replacement tells me the work of the church goes on by handover: one man comes, another goes, and the gospel stays in Crete either way.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably from the same as G736; prompt; Artemis, the name of a Grecian goddess borrowed by the Asiatics for one of their deities:--Diana.
BiblicalUsage: Artemis is the goddess of Ephesus, Diana of the Ephesians, and her silver shrines feed a whole trade. Demetrius the silversmith stirs up the city because Paul's preaching threatens the craft, the crowd fills the theatre crying Great is Diana of the Ephesians, and the townclerk has to calm them, reminding them the city is a worshipper of the great goddess Diana.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Ephesus shows what idolatry really runs on: not only belief, but business. The goddess has silversmiths and a theatre and a city that worships her, and the gospel threatens all of it at once, which is why I hold that the riot is the honest response of a city that knows what it stands to lose.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a derivative of G737; properly, something ready (or else more remotely from G142 (compare G740); something hung up), i.e. (specially) the topsail (rather foresail or jib) of a vessel:--mainsail.
BiblicalUsage: The mainsail is named once, in the shipwreck of Paul's voyage to Rome. The sailors loose the rudder bands, hoist up the mainsail to the wind, and make toward the shore, and the ship runs aground where two seas meet.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for a sail carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the picture, that men in a storm do the seaman's work and still need God to bring the ship to land.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: adverb from a derivative of G142 (compare G740) through the idea of suspension; just now:--this day (hour), hence(-forth), here(-after), hither(-to), (even) now, (this) present.
BiblicalUsage: Now is the word for this moment, and it is used for the present that will not wait. Jesus tells John to suffer it to be so now, that all righteousness may be fulfilled, and Paul says for now we see through a glass darkly, but then face to face.
TheologicalSignificance: One small word for now carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the tension in it, that now is the time for obedience and for seeing dimly, and then is the time for seeing face to face.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G737 and G1084; just born, i.e. (figuratively) a young convert:--new born.
BiblicalUsage: Newborn babes is Peter's picture for new believers: as newborn babes, desire the sincere milk of the word, that ye may grow thereby. The word is used once, and the picture is of a baby's hunger for milk.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for newborn carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the picture, that the new life in Christ begins hungry, and the milk of the word is what it grows on.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G737; fresh, i.e. (by implication) complete:--perfect.
BiblicalUsage: Perfect here means complete, fitted and furnished, and it is used once, for the man of God. All Scripture is given that the man of God may be perfect, throughly furnished unto all good works.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for complete carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the promise, that Scripture does not leave the man of God half-furnished, but fits him out for every good work.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G142; bread (as raised) or a loaf:--(shew-)bread, loaf.
BiblicalUsage: Bread is the staff of life and the sign of the Life, and the New Testament will not let you forget either. Man shall not live by bread alone, Jesus teaches us to pray for our daily bread, He says I am the bread of life, and at the table He takes bread, breaks it and says this is My body.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe bread is the one food that carries the whole gospel: the daily bread we ask for, the living bread who came down from heaven, and the broken bread of the supper. God feeds His people with bread, and then He gives them Himself as bread, and I hold that no one who comes to Him hungry goes away empty.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Artsa, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Arza is named once, as the steward of Elah's house in Tirzah, and it is in his house that Elah is drinking himself drunk when Zimri his servant conspires against him and slays him. The verse gives Arza's office and his house and nothing more.
TheologicalSignificance: A steward named once because a king was murdered in his house tells me that even the private rooms of a palace are watched, and that a king who drinks himself drunk in his steward's house is already a fallen king.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a presumed derivative of G142; to prepare, i.e. spice (with stimulating condiments):--season.
BiblicalUsage: To season is to make food fit to eat, and Jesus and Paul both use salt for the seasoning. Salt is good, says Jesus, but if the salt have lost his saltness, wherewith will ye season it; and Paul tells the Colossians to let their speech be always with grace, seasoned with salt.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe seasoning is the right picture for Christian speech: not bland and not bitter, but salted with grace, so that the words are worth hearing and the hearer is the better for them. And I hold that salt which has lost its saltness is fit for nothing, which is a warning to every disciple who has gone flat.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: something given as security, i.e. (literally) a token (of safety) or (metaphorically) a bondsman
BiblicalUsage: The pledge is a token left as security, and it is used twice. Jesse sends his son to the camp with ten cheeses for the captain and a pledge from his brothers, that he may know how they fare; and the proverb warns that a man void of understanding striketh hands and becometh surety for his friend.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for a pledge carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the lesson, that a token given in trust is a serious thing, and standing surety for another man is not to be done lightly.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a lattice; (by implication) a window, dovecot (because of the pigeon-holes), chimney (with its apertures for smoke), sluice (with openings for water)
BiblicalUsage: The window is the lattice in the sky, and Scripture opens it for flood and for blessing alike. In the days of Noah the windows of heaven were opened, a lord of Samaria scoffs that even if the LORD should make windows in heaven such a thing could not be, and Malachi promises that God will open the windows of heaven and pour out a blessing there is not room enough to receive.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the windows of heaven say the same thing in judgment and in blessing: heaven is not shut. It opens to flood the earth, and it opens to feed the hungry, and I hold that the God who opens the windows is the same God in both, and His opening is always according to His word.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Arubboth, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Arubboth is named once, as one of the twelve districts that fed Solomon's table, under Benhesed, with Sochoh and all the land of Hepher. The verse gives the officer, the place and nothing more.
TheologicalSignificance: A district named once for feeding a king's table tells me how wide Solomon's provision ran, and that every town in the kingdom had its part in keeping the king's house.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a ration of food
BiblicalUsage: The allowance is the daily ration given to a man in another's power, and it is used for a captive king and for a dinner table. Jehoiachin eats a continual allowance from the king of Babylon all the days of his life, and the proverb says better is a dinner of herbs where love is, than a stalled ox and hatred therewith.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the ration of a captive king is one of the saddest pictures in the Bible: a king of Judah fed day by day from a foreign king's table. And I hold that the proverb answers it, that a small meal with love is better than a fat ox with hatred, because the company at the table matters more than what is on it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: lo!
BiblicalUsage: Lo is Daniel's word for the visions that open before him, and it is used five times in one chapter. Daniel says I saw in my vision by night, and behold, the four winds of the heaven strove upon the great sea; and later, I saw in the night visions, and behold, one like the Son of man came with the clouds of heaven.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for behold carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the wonder in it, that the visions begin with looking, and the looking is given to a man in exile who is told to watch.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: something piled up (as if (figuratively) raised by mental aspiration), i.e. a paterre
KeyPassages: Song of Solomon 5:13; Song of Solomon 6:2; Ezekiel 17:10
BiblicalUsage: The bed is the garden bed, the plot where spices grow, and it is used for love and for judgment. The beloved's cheeks are as a bed of spices, he is gone down into his garden, to the beds of spices, to feed in the gardens; and Ezekiel asks if the vine planted in its beds shall prosper when the east wind touches it.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the garden bed is a picture of tending: spices grow where someone plants and waters them, and a vine in a good bed still withers when the wind of God's judgment touches it. Love grows in a kept garden, and I hold that the same is true of the soul.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: wholeness (literally or figuratively)
BiblicalUsage: Healing here is wholeness restored, and God promises it to His people again and again. Isaiah says when you loose the bonds of wickedness your health shall spring forth speedily, Jeremiah says I will restore health unto thee and heal thee of thy wounds, and again, I will bring it health and cure, and reveal the abundance of peace and truth.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this word is a promise with God's name on it: He is the one who restores health, not the physician and not the nation. The wounds are ours, the healing is His, and I hold that the health He promises is whole, body and land and people together.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: cunning (usually in a bad sense)
BiblicalUsage: Crafty is used for the serpent and for the prudent man, and the Bible makes you tell them apart. The serpent was more subtil than any beast of the field, the wisdom of the prudent is to understand his way, and the prudent man foreseeth the evil and hideth himself, while the simple pass on and are punished.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe craftiness is wisdom twisted: the serpent's subtlety and the prudent man's foresight use the same sharpness, and the difference is whom they serve. One hides himself to escape evil, the other hides to do it, and I hold that God gives His people the second kind, the prudence that sees the trap and steps aside.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Arumah, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Arumah is named once, as the place where Abimelech dwelt after he thrust out Gaal the son of Ebed from Shechem. Zebul his officer drives Gaal out, and Abimelech stays at Arumah, waiting for the next move.
TheologicalSignificance: A town named once as a usurper's waiting place tells me that Abimelech's kingdom was never settled: he holds Shechem by force, loses it, and waits at Arumah for the city to fall again.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: feared, i.e. (concretely) a horrible place or chasm
BiblicalUsage: This word is used once, for the dreadful places where the outcasts of Job's day are forced to live. They dwell in the cliffs of the valleys, in caves of the earth, and in the rocks, driven out from among men and crying under the nettles.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for a horrible hiding place carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the picture, that the poor Job speaks of had nowhere to live but the clefts of the earth.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Arvad, an island-city of Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Arvad is the island city whose men rowed the ships of Tyre and stood on her walls. The men of Arvad were thy mariners, Ezekiel says, and the men of Arvad with thine army were upon thy walls round about, hanging their shields on Tyre's towers.
TheologicalSignificance: A city named twice for the men it lent to Tyre tells me how Tyre's glory was borrowed: rowers from one island, soldiers from another, and when the ships sink, the lenders go down with them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an Arvadite or citizen of Arvad
BiblicalUsage: The Arvadite is named twice, in the table of nations and in the chronicler's copy of it, as one of the families of Canaan the son of Ham. The name marks a people of the coast, and the verse gives the family and nothing more.
TheologicalSignificance: A coastal family counted among the sons of Canaan carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the record, that the peoples of the sea coast were known to God by name.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: nakedness, i.e. (figuratively) impoverishment
BiblicalUsage: This Aramaic word is used once, in the letter the adversaries write to Artaxerxes against Jerusalem. They plead that they have maintenance from the king's palace, and that it is not fitting for them to see the king's dishonour, and the word behind their plea speaks of being laid bare, of living on what the king provides.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for dependence on the king's table carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the picture, that the men who write against God's people justify themselves by the king's salt, and call loyalty to a throne what is really fear for their own place.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Arjeh, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Aryeh is named once, as one of the men slain with Pekahiah the son of Menahem when Pekah conspired against him in Samaria. He is named with Argob, and nothing more is said of him.
TheologicalSignificance: A man named only to die with his king tells me how close the king's men stood to him, and how suddenly a conspiracy ends them all.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {a lion}
BiblicalUsage: The lion in Daniel is the Aramaic lion, and it is the beast of the den and the beast of the vision. Daniel is cast into the den of lions, and in the morning he tells the king that his God has sent His angel and shut the lions' mouths; and in the later vision the first beast is like a lion, with eagle's wings, standing as a man.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Daniel's lions are the proof that God rules the beasts men use to kill His people: the mouths are shut, the man comes out alive, and the empire that fed men to lions is itself the lion in the vision, a beast with wings that will lose them. And I hold that the God who shuts lions' mouths still does, for the people who will not bow.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Arjok, the name of two Babylonians
BiblicalUsage: Arioch is the name of two men, centuries apart, and both stand beside kings. Arioch king of Ellasar goes to war with Chedorlaomer against the kings of the plain, and Arioch captain of the king's guard is sent to slay the wise men of Babylon, but brings Daniel to the king instead.
TheologicalSignificance: A name shared by a king of war and a captain of the guard tells me that God puts His people in the path of powerful men, and that the captain who was sent to kill becomes the one who brings Daniel to the throne room.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: cedar wainscoating
BiblicalUsage: The cedar work is named once, in the ruin of Nineveh. Flocks shall lie down in her midst, the cormorant and the bittern shall lodge in her lintels, and desolation shall be in the thresholds, for He shall uncover the cedar work, stripping the fine panelling from the walls.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for cedar panelling carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the picture, that the richest woodwork of the greatest city ends stripped and roosted in by wild birds.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H609); Asa, an Israelite:--Asa.
BiblicalUsage: Asa is named in the genealogy of Jesus, as the son of Abijah and the father of Jehoshaphat, in the line of kings that runs from David to the exile. The Greek text behind the King James reads Asa here, while the later Greek text reads Asaph, so the verse stands on the Textus Receptus reading.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Asa belongs in the line because he is the king who sought the LORD with all his heart and took away the idols, and his name in the genealogy is a reminder that the King who was promised comes through kings who, at their best, sought God.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Asahel, the name of four Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Asahel is the name of four Israelites, and the chief of them is the brother of Joab, swift of foot as a wild roe. He chases Abner across the field at Gibeon and will not turn aside, and Abner smites him under the fifth rib; and the chronicler names him captain of David's monthly course, his son Zebadiah after him.
TheologicalSignificance: A swift runner who would not turn aside tells me that courage without counsel can kill a man: Asahel's speed was real, and so was the spear that met him, and David's army kept his name on the roster all the same.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to do or make, in the broadest sense and widest application
BiblicalUsage: To do or make is the commonest verb in the Old Testament, and it is used for God's work first of all. God says let us make man in our image, He rests on the seventh day from all His work which He had made, the commandment says in six days the LORD made heaven and earth, and the Preacher says whatsoever God doeth, it shall be for ever.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe 'to make' is the first thing God tells us about Himself: He is the Maker, and everything else is made. His work does not wear out and does not need adding to, and I hold that our making only matters when it answers His, doing what He has given us to do and resting when He rests.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and a derivative of G4531; unshaken, i.e. (by implication) immovable (figuratively):--which cannot be moved, unmovable.
BiblicalUsage: Unmoveable is used twice, once for a ship and once for a kingdom. Paul's ship falls into a place where two seas meet, and the forepart sticks fast and remains unmoveable; and Hebrews says we receive a kingdom which cannot be moved, and should have grace to serve God acceptably.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for unmoveable carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the contrast, that a ship stuck fast is wrecked, and a kingdom that cannot be moved is the one worth receiving.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to press upon, i.e. quarrel
BiblicalUsage: To press upon is to quarrel over what is yours, and it is used once, for the well Isaac digs at Gerar. The herdmen of Gerar strive with Isaac's herdmen, saying the water is ours, and he calls the well Esek, because they strove with him.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for quarrelling over a well carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the picture, that Isaac names the strife and moves on, digging again rather than fighting for the first well.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Asarel, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Asarel is named once, in the families of Judah, as a son of Jehaleleel, with Ziph and Ziphah and Tiria and Asarel his brothers. The verse gives his father and his brothers and nothing more.
TheologicalSignificance: A name in a family list with no story of its own still matters, because God counts the sons of Judah house by house, and no son is left out of the number.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Asarelah, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Asarelah is named once, as a son of Asaph, one of the singers David set over the service of song in the house of the LORD. He is listed among the sons who prophesied with harps and psalteries and cymbals, and the verse gives his father and his office and nothing more.
TheologicalSignificance: A singer named once in a list of musicians tells me that the worship of the temple was a family trade, and that God counts the men who sang His praise by name.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to tithe, i.e. to take or give a tenth
BiblicalUsage: To tithe is to give the tenth, and the Bible uses it for the vow, the law and the practice together. Jacob vows that of all God gives him he will surely give the tenth, Moses commands Israel to truly tithe all the increase of the seed year by year, and Nehemiah's people promise the priest shall be with the Levites when they take tithes.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the tithe teaches what the whole Bible teaches about money: the tenth is the Lord's, and giving it first is how we say so. Jacob vows it before he has anything, the law commands it when the harvest comes in, and I hold that the God who gave the seed is the one who owns the tenth of it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: ten (only in combination), i.e. -teen; also (ordinal) -teenth
BiblicalUsage: Ten is the number inside the counting of Israel, and it turns up in fourteens and twelves and eighteens. The Passover lamb is kept until the fourteenth day, Elim has twelve wells of water, Abram arms three hundred and eighteen trained servants, and Ishmael is promised twelve princes.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe ten is the round number of God's counting: a full set, a complete company, a measure that comes out even. And I hold that the God who counts wells and servants and princes counts His people the same way, and none of the number is lost.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: ten
BiblicalUsage: This Aramaic ten is the ten of Daniel's visions and of the return from exile. The fourth beast has ten horns, and the ten horns are ten kings that shall arise, and at the dedication of the house of God the returned exiles offer twelve he goats for the twelve tribes of Israel.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe ten horns on a beast is a picture of power divided and crowned, ten kings who will rise and fall in their season. And the twelve he goats at the dedication say the other side of it: God's people are counted whole, tribe by tribe, and I hold that His counting outlasts every horn.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Asajah, the name of three or four Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Asaiah is the name of several men, and three of them are worth naming. The king's servant Asaiah goes with Hilkiah to inquire of the prophetess Huldah about the book of the law, a chief of the Levites named Asaiah helps carry the ark to Jerusalem, and another Asaiah of the Shilonites dwells in Jerusalem after the return.
TheologicalSignificance: A name shared by a king's servant, a Levite chief and a returned exile tells me that God's work runs through men of the same name in different generations, and each one is counted in his own place.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and a derivative of G4570; not extinguished, i.e. (by implication) perpetual:--not to be quenched, unquenchable.
BiblicalUsage: Unquenchable is the fire that is never put out, and Jesus uses it for the judgment of the chaff and the worm that dieth not. John says He will burn up the chaff with unquenchable fire, and Jesus says it is better to enter into life maimed than to go into hell, into the fire that never shall be quenched.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe unquenchable fire is the most solemn word in the Gospels, because it says the judgment is not a fire that burns out and lets the sinner out. It is the fire of a holy God against sin, and I hold that the warning is mercy, that we might flee to the One who was baptized with fire for us.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and a presumed derivative of G2192 (in the sense of its congener G4976); properly, shapeless, i.e. (figuratively) inelegant:--uncomely.
BiblicalUsage: Uncomely is used once, for the parts of the body we think less honourable. Paul says those members of the body which we think to be less honourable, upon these we bestow more abundant honour, and our uncomely parts have more abundant comeliness.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for the uncomely parts carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the picture, that God gives more honour to the parts we hide, and the body has no member it can do without.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G809; to be (i.e. act) unbecoming:--behave self uncomely (unseemly).
BiblicalUsage: To behave unseemly is to act in a way that shames, and Paul uses it twice, for a father and for love. If a man thinks he behaves himself uncomely toward his virgin, let him do what he will, he sinneth not; and charity doth not behave itself unseemly, seeketh not her own, is not easily provoked.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for unseemly behaviour carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the contrast, that love never acts the way the word describes, and the man who loves well has nothing to be ashamed of.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G809; an indecency; by implication, the pudenda:--shame, that which is unseemly.
BiblicalUsage: Shame here is the nakedness that ought to be covered, and it is used twice. Paul says men with men working that which is unseemly, and receiving in themselves the recompence of their error; and John says blessed is he that watcheth and keepeth his garments, lest he walk naked, and they see his shame.
TheologicalSignificance: One word for shameful nakedness carries no doctrine of its own; its weight is the warning, that sin strips a man bare, and the blessing is on the one who keeps his garments.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G765; impiety, i.e. (by implication) wickedness:--ungodly(-liness).
BiblicalUsage: Ungodliness is life lived as if God were not there, and the New Testament names it plainly. The wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of men, grace teaches us to deny ungodliness and worldly lusts and live soberly and righteously, and Enoch prophesied that the Lord comes to convince the ungodly of all their ungodly deeds.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe ungodliness is the root sin, deeper than any one deed: it is living without God in the world. Grace does not excuse it, grace teaches us to deny it, and I hold that the wrath revealed against it is the other side of the grace that saves us from it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)
