Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to extend or mark out
BiblicalUsage: This word means to mark out a boundary, and it appears once, in the drawing of Israel's eastern border from Hazar-enan to Shepham. A line on the map, drawn by God's command.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that God cares about boundaries — he gave his people a land with edges, and he gives my life edges too.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to crook, literally or figuratively
BiblicalUsage: This word means to bend or crook — and in Scripture it is almost always moral bending, doing wrong. David says he has done wickedly when he counts the people, Daniel confesses we have sinned and committed iniquity, and God warns David's son that if he commits iniquity he will be chastened. The same root bends a bow and bends a heart off course.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this word is honest about what sin is: not a mistake but a bending away from what is straight. And I hold that the same God who chastens also forgives when we own the bend, the way Daniel and David did.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to extend or mark out
BiblicalUsage: This word means to mark out a boundary, and it appears once, in the drawing of Israel's eastern border from Hazar-enan to Shepham. A line on the map, drawn by God's command.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that God cares about boundaries — he gave his people a land with edges, and he gives my life edges too.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to distort (morally)
BiblicalUsage: Isaiah says that even when favour is shown to the wicked, he will not learn righteousness — in the land of uprightness he will deal unjustly. The word is that unjust dealing, a life lived crooked on purpose.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe kindness alone never straightens a heart that refuses to learn; only repentance does.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to watch (with jealosy)
BiblicalUsage: Saul eyed David from that day forward — watched him with jealous suspicion after the women sang David's praise above his own. One look, and a king's heart turned.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe jealousy starts in the eye, and Saul is my warning that watching a rival too closely can rot a whole reign.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to blind
BiblicalUsage: This word means to blind, and it works two ways in Scripture. A gift blinds the eyes of the wise and perverts the words of the righteous, so Moses forbids judges to take one. And in judgment, Zedekiah's eyes were put out at Riblah after watching his sons killed — blinded in fact because he had been blind in heart.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that bribes blind because they make us see what we are paid to see. Zedekiah's story is the end of that road, and I want my eyes kept clear by refusing the gift.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to wrest
BiblicalUsage: To wrest is to bend justice out of shape — and this word covers every way of doing it. The Preacher says what is crooked cannot be made straight, Elihu insists the Almighty will not pervert judgment, Lamentations says the Lord does not approve when a man's cause is turned aside, and Amos exposes merchants who falsify the balances to cheat the poor.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God notices twisted scales and twisted courts, and I believe that is good news for the poor. No one who wrests justice gets away with it forever, because the Judge himself cannot be wrested.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Aven, the contemptuous synonym of three places, one in Coele-Syria, one in Egypt (On), and one in Palestine (Bethel)
BiblicalUsage: This is not the word for iniquity — it is a place-name, Aven, used with contempt. Amos names the plain of Aven among the places judged with Damascus, and Ezekiel names Aven, the Egyptian On, whose young men will fall by the sword.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that God names the places of false worship one by one, and none of them stands when his judgment comes.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: strictly nothingness; also trouble. vanity, wickedness; specifically an idol
BiblicalUsage: Aven is nothingness that pretends to be something — vanity, trouble, wickedness, and by extension the idol itself. Samuel tells Saul rebellion is as the sin of witchcraft and stubbornness as iniquity and idolatry; Isaiah says God cannot endure the solemn meeting joined to iniquity; Proverbs pictures the naughty person walking with a froward mouth; Habakkuk cries out at the iniquity he sees on every side.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe aven is the right name for sin because sin is empty at its core — it promises weight and delivers nothing. That is why I hold fast to what is solid instead: God's word, which never turns out to be nothing.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a stall
BiblicalUsage: This word means a stall, and it appears once, among Hezekiah's storehouses for cattle — stalls for all manner of beasts, built in a time of peace and plenty.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that even a storehouse can preach: God provided for his king, and provision is one of the quiet ways he shows his care.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: perverse (morally)
BiblicalUsage: Job says God delivered him to the ungodly and turned him over into the hands of the wicked. The word names the perverse, the one who is morally twisted through.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Job's complaint is honest: it hurts most when suffering comes through people who are themselves bent away from God.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: perverse (morally)
BiblicalUsage: Job says God delivered him to the ungodly and turned him over into the hands of the wicked. The word names the perverse, the one who is morally twisted through.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Job's complaint is honest: it hurts most when suffering comes through people who are themselves bent away from God.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Avvith (or Avvoth), a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Avith was the city of Hadad, the Edomite king who defeated Midian in the field of Moab, named in the old Edomite king-list of Genesis and repeated word for word in Chronicles. The name appears only here, as a royal city of Edom before Israel had a king.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the old king-lists matter because they show God was already at work among the nations, keeping records of kings and cities long before Israel's story began.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: perversity, i.e. (moral) evil
BiblicalUsage: Avon is perversity — iniquity with its guilt and its punishment carried together. Cain says his punishment is greater than he can bear, God proclaims himself forgiving iniquity and transgression and sin, Aaron lays the iniquities of Israel on the scapegoat, and Isaiah says the chastisement of our peace was upon him and he was wounded for our transgressions. The word holds the deed and its weight at once.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this is the word that makes the cross necessary and the cross sufficient. My iniquity was laid on him, and because he bore it, I do not have to carry its weight forever.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: overthrow
BiblicalUsage: Ezekiel hears the word of the Lord: I will overturn, overturn, overturn it, until he come whose right it is. One word of overthrow, repeated three times, against a corrupt crown.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God overturns what men build crooked, and he does it until the rightful King comes.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: longing
BiblicalUsage: This word is longing — the soul stretching toward what it desires. God tells Israel that when their soul longs to eat flesh, they may eat it; David is told the king has longed to see him; and Jeremiah pictures Judah as a wild ass in heat, sniffing the wind in her longing, running after other gods. The same longing can be lawful appetite or runaway desire.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that longing itself is not the sin — it is where the longing runs that matters. My soul was made to long for God, and when it runs anywhere else, it runs wild.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: evil (morally)
BiblicalUsage: Avval is the unjust man — morally evil, the opposite of upright. Job says he broke the jaws of the wicked and plucked the spoil from his teeth; he asks whether destruction is not to the wicked; Bildad says such is the dwelling of him that knoweth not God; and Zephaniah says the unjust knows no shame, morning by morning, while the just Lord brings his judgment to light.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this word draws the line plainly: there are the just and the unjust, and God is not confused about which is which. Job's life shows me the unjust do not win in the end, even when they seem to win for a season.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: oppression
BiblicalUsage: Jeremiah cries, O Lord, thou hast seen my wrong — judge thou my cause. The word is oppression, the wrong done to a man by those stronger than him.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God sees every wrong done to his people, and that is why Jeremiah could hand his cause over instead of taking revenge himself.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an Avvite or native of Avvah (only plural)
BiblicalUsage: The Avvites were a people of Avvah, brought by the king of Assyria to settle the cities of Samaria. They made Nibhaz and Tartak, their own gods, and Joshua lists their land among the coasts still to be taken.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that a people is known by the gods it brings with it, and the Avvites are my warning that new neighbours can mean new idols.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Avvim (as inhabited by Avvites), a place in Palestine (with the article prefix)
BiblicalUsage: Avvim was the place where the Avvites lived before the Caphtorim destroyed them, on the coast toward Gaza, and Deuteronomy remembers it in the story of the peoples displaced before Israel. Joshua lists Avvim among the cities of Benjamin's inheritance — a small place, named only twice.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe even two mentions are enough: God remembers small towns and displaced peoples, and his record of the land is exact.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably from ἄγνυμι (to break; compare G4486); an axe:--axe.
BiblicalUsage: The axe is already laid to the root of the trees — John the Baptist's warning in both Gospels. Every tree that does not bring forth good fruit is cut down and cast into the fire.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe John's axe is still laid at the root: God looks for fruit, not leaves, and the time to bear it is now.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G514; to deem entitled or fit:--desire, think good, count (think) worthy.
BiblicalUsage: To count worthy is to judge someone fit for what is asked of them. The centurion did not think himself worthy for Jesus to come under his roof; the Jews at Rome wanted to hear Paul because they knew his sect was spoken against everywhere; Hebrews says Christ was counted worthy of more glory than Moses; and Paul prays God would count the Thessalonians worthy of their calling.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe worthiness is something God counts, not something I earn. Christ was counted worthy of glory, and because of him, God counts me worthy of the calling he gave me.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: adverb from G514; appropriately:--as becometh, after a godly sort, worthily(-thy).
BiblicalUsage: This is the adverb form — walk worthily. Paul begs the Ephesians to walk worthy of the calling they received, and tells the Philippians to let their manner of life be worthy of the gospel of Christ.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that a calling is not just believed but walked, and the walk should match the gospel it belongs to.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably from G71; deserving, comparable or suitable (as if drawing praise):--due reward, meet, (un-)worthy.
BiblicalUsage: Worthy is the word of measuring — is someone or something deserving of what is given? The workman is worthy of his meat, the prodigal says he is no more worthy to be called a son, the elders sing that the Lamb is worthy to take the book and open its seals, and Paul says Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, a faithful saying and worthy of all acceptation.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the prodigal was right about himself and wrong about his father, because worthiness was never the measure of the welcome. And I hold that the Lamb is worthy of everything heaven sings to him, because he was slain and has redeemed us to God by his blood.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Ai, Aja or Ajath, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Ai was the city beside Bethel where Abram pitched his tent, and the city where Israel first failed after Jericho: Joshua sent men to spy it out, the first attack was beaten back because of Achan's sin, and then God told Joshua to take the city without fear. Isaiah later names Ai on the road of the Assyrian's advance toward Jerusalem.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Ai teaches me both sides of the same truth: a small city can defeat a whole army when sin is hidden in the camp, and no defeat is final when God says to rise and take it.
RelatedEvents: The Defeat at Ai and Achan's Sin
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: where? hence how?
BiblicalUsage: Ay is the question word where — and God's first question to fallen man is made of it: where art thou? Cain answers with another where when he asks, am I my brother's keeper? Job asks where wisdom shall be found, and the old prophet's sons ask where their father went when the man of God left. Every where in Scripture is a search, and often a summons.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that God's where is never because he has lost us — it is because he wants us to know we are lost. When he asks where I am, he is calling me out of hiding, the way he called Adam.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to hate (as one of an opposite tribe or party); hence to be hostile
BiblicalUsage: God promises Moses that if Israel obeys his voice, he will be an enemy to their enemies and an adversary to their adversaries. The word is hatred between opposite parties — open hostility, not quiet dislike.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this is a promise with a condition: God's enmity toward my enemies follows my obedience to his voice.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Ajah, the name of two Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Ajah was the son of Zibeon the Horite, the one who found the mules in the wilderness, and the father of Rizpah — Genesis lists him in Esau's family, and Samuel shows his daughter Rizpah watching over the bodies of her sons on the rock through the whole harvest, until water dropped upon them from heaven. One man, named in two stories centuries apart in the telling.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Rizpah's vigil is why Ajah's name survives: a father's name is carried by a daughter who would not leave her dead, and God remembers that kind of faithfulness.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: the screamer, i.e. a hawk
BiblicalUsage: The ayah is a bird of prey — the kite or hawk, named among the unclean birds Israel must not eat. Leviticus and Deuteronomy both list it after its kind, and Job says there is a path no bird of prey knows, not even the eye of the vulture has seen it, speaking of the hidden way to wisdom.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that even an unclean bird can teach me something: the hawk's eye misses the path to wisdom entirely. Only God knows where it lies.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a stag or male deer
KeyPassages: Deuteronomy 12:15; Isaiah 35:6; Song of Solomon 2:9; Song of Solomon 2:17
BiblicalUsage: The stag is the picture of swiftness and sure-footedness. Israel might eat the hart as freely as the roebuck, Isaiah promises the lame man shall leap as a hart when the desert blooms, and the Song pictures the beloved leaping on the mountains like a young hart, coming swiftly over the hills.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God delights in giving his people a hart's feet — not just strength to stand, but joy to leap. The lame leaping is his promise, and I hold him to it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a doe or female deer
KeyPassages: Genesis 49:21; 2 Samuel 22:34; Habakkuk 3:19; Song of Solomon 2:7
BiblicalUsage: The doe is the female deer, and Scripture uses her for grace and sure footing. Jacob blesses Naphtali as a hind let loose, giving goodly words; David sings that God makes his feet like hinds' feet and sets him on high places; Habakkuk says the Lord is my strength and will make my feet like hinds' feet; and the Song adjures by the hinds of the field not to stir up love until it please.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God does not just carry me to the high places — he gives me the feet to stand on them myself. That is the promise I hold when the ground feels steep.
RelatedBooks: Genesis; 2 Samuel; Habakkuk; Song of Solomon
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Ajalon, the name of five places in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Aijalon was a town in the valley where the sun stood still — Joshua cried, Sun, stand thou still upon Gibeon, and thou, Moon, in the valley of Ajalon — and it was also a Levitical city, given to the Kohathites with its suburbs, and a place where Israel pursued the Philistines from Michmash. One name covers several towns, but the valley of Aijalon is the one the whole world remembers.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the day the sun stood still over Aijalon shows me that God will stretch time itself to finish the victory he promised.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably meaning strength
BiblicalUsage: This word seems to mean strength or might, and it appears only twice — Hosea says God will chastise his people when it is his desire, and Isaiah says the Lord will shake his hand over the river with his mighty wind. Strength, used by God against his enemies and for his people.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that God's strength is never wasted: it shakes rivers and chastises nations, and it is the same strength that carries me.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: where?
BiblicalUsage: Ayeh is the question where, asked when someone is missing. The visitors ask Abraham where Sarah is, Isaac asks his father where the lamb is for the burnt offering, Jethro asks his daughters where the man is who helped them, and Gideon asks where all God's miracles are now. The word is always a search for something or someone who ought to be present.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the hardest where in Scripture is Gideon's — where are the miracles our fathers told us of? And I hold that the answer is the same one Isaac received: God himself will provide, and he is never as absent as he seems.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a doe
BiblicalUsage: The ayeleth is a doe, and Proverbs calls the wife of a man's youth a loving hind and pleasant roe, whose breasts should satisfy him at all times. Jeremiah pictures the hind in the field that calves and forsakes her young, because there is no grass in the drought.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the doe in Proverbs is a picture of delight that stays home, and the doe in Jeremiah is a picture of what drought does to a land — both tell me to tend what God gave me.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: languid
BiblicalUsage: Ayeph is weariness that goes to the bone — faint, languid, spent. Esau came from the field faint and sold his birthright for pottage, Gideon and his three hundred were faint yet pursuing, Isaiah promises that none shall be weary in the Lord's army, and God says he will satiate the weary soul and replenish every sorrowful soul.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Esau's bargain is the warning and Jeremiah's promise is the comfort. Weariness makes fools of us when we feed it with the wrong food, but God himself satisfies the weary soul.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: languid
BiblicalUsage: Ayeph is weariness that goes to the bone — faint, languid, spent. Esau came from the field faint and sold his birthright for pottage, Gideon and his three hundred were faint yet pursuing, Isaiah promises that none shall be weary in the Lord's army, and God says he will satiate the weary soul and replenish every sorrowful soul.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Esau's bargain is the warning and Jeremiah's promise is the comfort. Weariness makes fools of us when we feed it with the wrong food, but God himself satisfies the weary soul.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, strength; hence, anything strong; specifically a chief (politically); also a ram (from his strength); a pilaster (as a strong support); an oak or other strong tree
BiblicalUsage: Ayil is strength in several shapes — the ram of sacrifice, the oak, and the chief. God provided a ram caught in the thicket for Abraham in place of Isaac, Daniel saw a ram with two horns pushing westward, northward and southward, Isaiah says the oaks of righteousness are God's planting, and the ram's horns, the breast and the thigh belong to the priest in the consecration offering. Strength, offered back to God, becomes worship.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the ram in the thicket is the whole gospel in one picture: God provides the substitute himself. And I hold that the strength God gives me — like the ram's — is meant to be laid on his altar, not kept for myself.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: where? (only in connection with prepositional prefix, whence)
BiblicalUsage: Ayin in this form is the question word whence — where from? Jacob's sons ask the man at the well whence he is, Job asks whence wisdom comes and where the place of understanding is, Jonah's sailors ask whence he comes, and the king of Israel asks his servant whence he came. The question is always about origins, and the answer always matters.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that whence is the question behind every story: where did this come from, and where is it going? Job asks it of wisdom, and the answer is that wisdom comes from God alone.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an eye (literally or figuratively); by analogy, a fountain (as the eye of the landscape)
BiblicalUsage: The eye is the lamp of the body and the window of the heart. Eve saw the tree was pleasant to the eyes, Samuel learned that man looks on the outward appearance but the Lord looks on the heart, Elisha prayed for his servant's eyes to be opened to the mountain full of horses and chariots of fire, and Proverbs says the eyes of the Lord are in every place, beholding the evil and the good.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God sees what I cannot see, and that is both my comfort and my correction. Elisha's servant needed opened eyes, and so do I — to see the Lord's armies, and to see my own heart the way God sees it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Ajin, the name (thus simply) of two places in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Ain is the name of two towns in the south — one in Judah's inheritance and one in Simeon's — and of a place near Riblah on the northern border, where Joshua lists Ain among the cities and Numbers sets it on the boundary line of the land. The name means a spring or fountain, and the towns sat where water was.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God placed his towns by water on purpose, and I hold that the borders he drew for Israel were drawn with care — every spring counted, every town named.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: where? (only in connection with prepositional prefix, whence)
BiblicalUsage: Ayin in this form is the question word whence — where from? Jacob's sons ask the man at the well whence he is, Job asks whence wisdom comes and where the place of understanding is, Jonah's sailors ask whence he comes, and the king of Israel asks his servant whence he came. The question is always about origins, and the answer always matters.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that whence is the question behind every story: where did this come from, and where is it going? Job asks it of wisdom, and the answer is that wisdom comes from God alone.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, a young ass (as just broken to a load); hence an ass-colt
BiblicalUsage: The ayir is a young ass, a colt just broken to the load. Judah's sons rode on white asses in the days of the judges, Jacob blessed his sons over the foal of an ass, Isaiah pictures the wild asses snuffing up the wind in the desert, and Zechariah promises the King coming to Jerusalem, lowly, and riding upon an ass, and upon a colt the foal of an ass.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the colt matters because the King chose it: he came lowly, riding on an ass's colt. That is the kind of King I can come to without fear.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: the constellation of the Great Bear (perhaps from its migration through the heavens)
BiblicalUsage: Ayish is the Great Bear, the constellation Job names among the wonders God made — Arcturus, Orion and the Pleiades — and which God himself names when he answers Job out of the whirlwind. A star-picture in the northern sky, set there by the same hand that set the Pleiades.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the stars are God's handiwork, not man's fortune-telling, and the Great Bear still turns in its course because he holds it there.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a hawk or other bird of prey
BiblicalUsage: The ayit is a bird of prey — the hawk, the kite, the vulture — and Scripture lets it do God's hard work. The fowls came down on Abram's sacrifice and he drove them away, Isaiah says the birds of prey will be left on the mountains, Jeremiah says God's heritage has become a speckled bird of prey, and Ezekiel calls every feathered fowl to the great sacrifice on the mountains of Israel.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe even the birds of prey serve God's purposes. Abram driving them from his sacrifice is my picture of guarding what God has given me.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: frightful
BiblicalUsage: Ayom means frightful, terrible — the word for what makes the heart quail. Habakkuk says the Chaldeans are terrible and dreadful, and the Song says the beloved is terrible as an army with banners. The same terror, in a lover's face and in a conqueror's army.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that God's people are meant to be terrible to his enemies the way an army with banners is terrible — not by cruelty, but by the sheer weight of being his.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: strong, vehement, harsh
KeyPassages: Exodus 14:21; Numbers 13:28; Judges 14:14; Song of Solomon 8:6
BiblicalUsage: Az means strong, vehement, harsh — strength at full force. The east wind divided the Red Sea, the spies said the people of the land were stronger than Israel, Samson's riddle says out of the strong came forth sweetness, and the Song says love is strong as death, jealousy is cruel as the grave, and its coals are coals of fire.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe love strong as death is the strongest thing in Scripture. I hold that the same strength that split the sea is the strength that holds me.
RelatedBooks: Exodus; Numbers; Judges; Song of Solomon
RelatedEvents: The Exodus and the Red Sea
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: at that time or place; also as a conjunction, therefore
BiblicalUsage: Az is then — at that time, at that place. Then sang Moses and the children of Israel this song, then began men to call upon the name of the Lord, then Joshua spoke to the Lord in the day he delivered up the Amorites, and then the eyes of the blind shall be opened and the lame man shall leap as a hart. The word marks the turning point, the moment everything changes.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God writes then into history again and again: then the song, then the miracle, then the healing. My own life has its thens, and I hold that the next one is coming.
RelatedEvents: The Exodus and the Red Sea
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: goat of departure; the scapegoat
BiblicalUsage: Azazel is the goat of departure, the scapegoat. On the Day of Atonement Aaron cast lots over two goats — one for the Lord and one for Azazel — and the goat for Azazel was presented alive before the Lord to make atonement, then sent away into the wilderness bearing the iniquities of Israel. The word appears only in this ceremony, and only three times.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the scapegoat is the picture of what Christ did: my sins carried away, out of sight, into a land not inhabited. The goat went so that I would not have to.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to kindle; (by implication) to heat
BiblicalUsage: Aza means to kindle, to heat — and it describes Nebuchadnezzar heating the furnace seven times hotter than usual, and the furnace slaying the men who cast in Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego. The fire was made worse, and it still could not touch them.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the hotter the furnace, the clearer the deliverance: the fire that killed the strong men only loosed the bonds of the faithful.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to loosen, i.e. relinquish, permit, etc.
BiblicalUsage: Azab means to loosen, to let go — and in Scripture it is the word for forsaking and for being forsaken, both ways. A man shall leave his father and mother and cleave to his wife, God promises I will never leave thee nor forsake thee, Joshua is told the Lord will not fail him nor forsake him, and Ruth tells Naomi, whither thou goest, I will go, and where thou lodgest, I will lodge.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the whole Bible turns on this word's two directions: men forsake God, and God never forsakes his people. Ruth would not leave Naomi, and God will not leave me — that is the promise I stand on.
RelatedTopics: Covenant; Faithfulness; Love of God; Marriage
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: firm
BiblicalUsage: Azad is the Aramaic word for firm — the king's decree is certain. Nebuchadnezzar tells the wise men the thing is gone from him, and the word is firm: if they do not show the dream, they will be cut in pieces. The king's word, once spoken, does not bend.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe earthly kings love to make their word firm, but only God's word is truly unbreakable — and his is the one I trust.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to depart
BiblicalUsage: This Aramaic word means to go, to depart — and it carries Daniel's story. Daniel went to his house and made the thing known to his companions, he went in to the king and desired time, and the decree went forth to the king's officers. In Ezra it is the same word for the king's command going out and the builders going to Jerusalem.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Daniel's going is my pattern: he went to pray first, and only then went to the king. That order is the whole secret of standing in Babylon.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to go away, hence, to disappear
BiblicalUsage: Azal means to go away, to disappear — like water running off. Moses says the Lord will judge his people and repent himself for his servants when he seeth that their power is gone, Job says the waters fail from the sea and the flood decayeth and drieth up, and Jeremiah says his people have changed their glory for that which doth not profit, going after vanity.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that everything that is not God disappears in the end — power gone, waters dried up, vanity proved empty. Only his mercy stays, and that is what I build on.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to weigh, i.e. (figuratively) ponder
BiblicalUsage: The Preacher gave good heed and sought out and set in order many proverbs, and weighed the words of the wise. One word for pondering — weighing wisdom the way a merchant weighs silver.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe wisdom is worth weighing carefully, and the Preacher is my model: he did not just speak proverbs, he sought them out and set them in order.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to weigh, i.e. (figuratively) ponder
BiblicalUsage: The Preacher gave good heed and sought out and set in order many proverbs, and weighed the words of the wise. One word for pondering — weighing wisdom the way a merchant weighs silver.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe wisdom is worth weighing carefully, and the Preacher is my model: he did not just speak proverbs, he sought them out and set them in order.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Azanjah, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Azaniah was one of those who sealed the covenant in Nehemiah's day, putting his name to the promise that Israel would keep God's law. He appears once, in the list of signers, and his name is enough — he stood and signed.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a signature can be an act of faith, and Azaniah's is one of the quiet ones — he signed the covenant and went home to keep it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to grub over
BiblicalUsage: Isaiah pictures the Lord planting a vineyard on a fruitful hill, digging it, gathering out the stones, and planting it with the choicest vine. The word is that digging over — the hard work of clearing ground for planting.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God digs his vineyard with care before he plants it, and that tells me he does the same hard groundwork in my life.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Azarel, the name of five Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Azarel is the name of five different men — a Benjamite who came to David at Ziklag, a Levite singer, a captain of Dan, a son of Bani who put away his foreign wife, and a priest who helped seal the covenant. The name means God has helped, and it turns up in every corner of Israel's story, from David's outlaws to the priests of the return.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that a name meaning God has helped is a good name to carry, and five men carried it through five different kinds of trouble.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to surround, i.e. protect or aid
BiblicalUsage: Azar is to surround, to protect — to come around someone the way a shield comes around a soldier. God helped the Levites who carried the ark, he helped Israel when the Syrians surrounded them, David says the Lord helped me and my heart greatly rejoiceth, and Isaiah says the Lord God will help me, therefore shall I not be confounded. Help that comes from outside and stands between.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God's help is a surrounding help — not a hint from a distance but a shield that comes around me. Fear not, he says, for I am with thee, and I hold that promise when the enemy is on every side.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to belt
BiblicalUsage: Azar is to belt, to gird — to put strength around the loins for work or war. Hannah sings that the Lord girds the weak with strength, David sings that God girded him with strength for battle, Isaiah says the Lord girds himself with strength, and God tells Job to gird up his loins like a man and answer.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that God girds his people the way a soldier is girded before battle — not for show, but for the work ahead. When he tells Job to gird up his loins, he is telling me to stand ready too.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an inclosure; also a border
BiblicalUsage: The azarah is the court — the enclosed place around the temple where the people stood. Solomon built the great court and the inner court, and Ezekiel measures the court of the house, its borders and its gates, in the vision of the new temple. An enclosure set apart for God's house.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the court matters because it says worship has a place — a bounded, holy space where the people meet their God. No one wanders in by accident.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Azarjah, one of Daniel's companions
BiblicalUsage: Azariah was one of Daniel's three companions, carried into Babylon and given the name Abednego. He went with Daniel to ask the king for time, and he stood with his friends before the golden image and before the furnace.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Azariah's faith is the kind I want: he prayed with his friends first, and then he stood — and the fire could not burn what prayer had already given to God.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Azarjah, one of Daniel's companions
BiblicalUsage: Azariah was one of Daniel's three companions, carried into Babylon and given the name Abednego. He went with Daniel to ask the king for time, and he stood with his friends before the golden image and before the furnace.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Azariah's faith is the kind I want: he prayed with his friends first, and then he stood — and the fire could not burn what prayer had already given to God.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: at that time
BiblicalUsage: Azay means then — at that time. The psalm sings, then they had swallowed us up quick, when their wrath was kindled against us; then the waters had overwhelmed us, the stream had gone over our soul. Three thens in one psalm, and each one is a danger God stopped.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that every then in this psalm is a then that did not happen, because the Lord was on our side — and that is the story of my life too.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Azaz, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Azaz was the father of Bela, a Reubenite chief whose sons dwelt in Aroer and eastward to the entering in of the wilderness. He appears once, in the genealogy of Reuben, as the head of a family that held the eastern border.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the genealogies keep men like Azaz because every family on the border mattered to God, even the ones the story never comes back to.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to be stout (literally or figuratively)
BiblicalUsage: Azaz means to be stout, strong — and it shows up as stubborn strength as often as good strength. The Lord was with Othniel and his hand prevailed against the king of Mesopotamia, the wise man is strong and a man of knowledge increaseth strength, and Proverbs says the wicked man hardeneth his face. Strength, for good or for ill, is a choice of direction.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that strength is a gift with a direction: Othniel's strength delivered Israel, and the wicked man's strength only hardens his face. I want mine aimed the right way.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Azazjah, the name of three Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Azaziah is the name of three men — a Levite musician who played the harp before the ark, a captain of Ephraim in the days of the kings, and a Levite overseer of the offerings in Hezekiah's temple. One name, three servants, all of them set to work in God's house or God's army.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God uses the same name in different generations for the same kind of work, and Azaziah's three bearers show me that musicians, captains and overseers all serve the same Lord.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Azbuk, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Azbuk was the father of Nehemiah the ruler of the half part of Beth-zur, who repaired the wall by the sepulchres of David. He appears once, named only as a father, and his son's work on the wall is his memorial.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that a father is remembered by his son's faithfulness, and Nehemiah son of Azbuk repaired the wall by the tombs of the kings — good work, done in a holy place.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a spade or paddle (as having a broad end)
BiblicalUsage: The azen is a spade or paddle — the tool every Israelite soldier carried on his weapon, to dig a place outside the camp and cover what came from him. God's camp was to be holy, because the Lord walked in the midst of it.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this small tool preaches a large truth: God walks among his people, and holiness reaches into the ordinary, everyday things.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Azekah, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Azekah was a town in the low country of Judah, named in the wars of Joshua, in the muster against the Philistines at Shochoh, and in the last stand of the cities Nebuchadnezzar took before Jerusalem fell. The Philistines camped between Shochoh and Azekah when Goliath came out, and Joshua's men pursued the five kings down to Azekah under the great hailstones.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Azekah's story is the story of a border town that saw both victory and defeat, and I hold that God was in both — the hailstones at Joshua's battle and the long siege at Jeremiah's.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Azgad, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Azgad is the name of a family that came back from Babylon — more than two thousand of them under Zerubbabel, a hundred and ten under Ezra, and one of their sons among those who sealed the covenant. A family that went into exile and came home to rebuild.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that God counts returning families one by one, and Azgad's name in three lists is his way of saying none of them were forgotten.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: manacles
BiblicalUsage: Aziqim are manacles, fetters — and Jeremiah wears them, or is loosed from them. Nebuzar-adan found him bound in chains among the captives at Ramah, and loosed him, saying, behold, I loose thee this day from the chains which were upon thine hand.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God can loose a prophet's chains in the middle of a ruined city, and he can loose mine too.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Aziel, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Aziel was a Levite musician, one of those who played the harps on Alamoth before the ark when David brought it up to Jerusalem. He appears once, in the list of the singers, and his harp is his whole story.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the harp matters as much as the sword in God's kingdom, and Aziel played his part in the day the ark came home.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Aziza, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Aziza was one of the sons of Zattu who had taken a foreign wife, and he put her away in the days of Ezra's reform. His name appears once, in the long list of those who set their houses right.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Ezra's list is hard reading, and Aziza's name in it reminds me that repentance sometimes costs a household everything.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a reminder; specifically remembrance-offering
BiblicalUsage: The azkarah is the memorial portion — the handful of flour and oil and frankincense the priest burns on the altar, so that the whole offering is remembered before God. Leviticus gives it in the meat offering, in the sin offering, and on the shewbread, and Numbers gives it in the jealousy offering. A small part burned, and the whole remembered.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that God remembers his people the way the memorial offering remembers the sacrifice: a handful burned on the altar stands for the whole. My prayers are remembered the same way.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Azmaveth, the name of three Israelites and of a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Azmaveth is the name of three men and a place — a son of Jehoadah in Benjamin's line, one of David's mighty men, the king's treasurer over the storehouses, and a town in Benjamin where the singers lived. The name turns up in the wars, in the court, and in the choir, and each bearer is a different man.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a name that belongs to a warrior, a treasurer and a singer's town is a name that shows how wide God's service is — the same Lord, served in battle, in the storehouse, and in song.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Aznoth-Tabor, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Aznoth-tabor was a town on the border of Naphtali, by Mount Tabor, where the inheritance ran from the sea to the mountain. It appears once, in the drawing of the tribal borders, and then the map moves on.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that God gave every tribe its borders, and even a town named once is part of the promise kept.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (compare H5809); Azor, an Israelite:--Azor.
BiblicalUsage: Azor is a name in the genealogy of Jesus — the father of Sadoc, the son of Eliakim, five generations before Joseph. Matthew lists him between the exile and the birth of Christ, and that is all we know of him: a link in the chain that brought the Messiah.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the links in the chain matter as much as the famous names, because without Azor there is no Sadoc, and without the chain there is no coming of Christ.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H795); Azotus (i.e. Ashdod), a place in Palestine:--Azotus.
BiblicalUsage: Azotus is the Greek name for Ashdod, the Philistine city on the coast, where Philip was found after baptizing the Ethiopian — and from Azotus he preached his way to Caesarea. One city, one verse, and the gospel moving up the coast.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the gospel does not stop at city walls, and Philip walking the coast from Azotus is my picture of a preacher who keeps going.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Azriel, the name of three Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Azriel is the name of three men — a chief of the half-tribe of Manasseh east of Jordan, a captain of Naphtali in David's army, and the father of Seraiah, whom Jehoiakim sent to arrest Jeremiah and Baruch. One name carried by a tribal chief, a royal captain, and the father of a man sent to seize a prophet.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the same name can stand on both sides of the story — Azriel the captain served David, and Azriel's son was sent against Jeremiah — and God kept his prophet safe either way.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Azrikam, the name of four Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Azrikam is the name of four men — a son in the line of Zerubbabel, a Levite who dwelt at Jerusalem after the return, a chief of the house of Elpaal, and the ruler of the king's house who was slain by Zichri the Ephraimite when Pekah invaded Judah. The name runs from the exile to the kingdom, and one of its bearers died defending the king's house.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God keeps the names of men who served in quiet posts — a Levite in Jerusalem, a ruler in the king's house — because faithful service in small places is still service to him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Azubah, the name of two Israelitesses
BiblicalUsage: Azubah is the name of two women — the wife of Caleb, the mother of Jerioth, Jesher, Shobab and Ardon, and the mother of Jehoshaphat, the daughter of Shilhi. One Azubah built a family in the wilderness generation, and the other raised a king who sought the Lord.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe mothers shape kingdoms: one Azubah bore Caleb's sons, and the other bore a king who walked in the ways of his father Asa, and both are remembered by name.
RelatedPeople: Caleb; King Jehoshaphat; Azubah, Mother of Jehoshaphat; Azubah, Wife of Caleb
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: desertion (of inhabitants)
BiblicalUsage: This word means desertion, a land left empty of its people. Isaiah says the forsaking in the land will be great, when the Lord removes men far away and the cities are left without inhabitant.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that desertion is the fruit of turning away: when a people leaves God, the land empties, and only his mercy brings anyone home.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and G2219; unleavened, i.e. (figuratively) uncorrupted; (in the neutral plural) specially (by implication) the Passover week:--unleavened (bread).
BiblicalUsage: Unleavened means without leaven — the bread of the Passover, eaten in haste the night of the exodus, and the feast kept for seven days after. The disciples asked where to prepare the Passover, the chief priests plotted to take Jesus during the feast, and Paul says to purge out the old leaven, for even Christ our passover is sacrificed for us.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe unleavened bread is the picture of a life without the old leaven of malice and wickedness. I hold that Christ, our passover, was sacrificed so I could keep the feast in sincerity and truth.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Azzah, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Azzah is Gaza, the Philistine city on the coast — the border of Canaan's first settlement, the city Samson carried off its gates in the night, and the city Joshua left standing. The prophets judged it too: Gaza shall be forsaken, and the king shall perish from Gaza.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Gaza's long story — from the border of the promise to the night Samson carried its gates — shows God patient with a city for centuries, and still just when the day comes.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Azzan, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Azzan was the father of Paltiel, the prince of Issachar chosen to divide the land among the tribes. He appears once, named only as a father, and his son's work of dividing the inheritance is his memorial.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the men who divided the land are remembered because the inheritance was real, and every tribe's portion was measured by God's command.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an Azzathite or inhabitant of Azzah
BiblicalUsage: An Azzathite is an inhabitant of Azzah, of Gaza. Joshua lists the land of the Philistines still to be possessed, and Judges says the men of Gaza lay in wait for Samson at the gate of the city all night.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the men of Gaza who waited all night for Samson waited in vain, because God had already given his servant strength to leave.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Azzur, the name of three Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Azzur is the name of three men — a prince of the people who stood before Ezekiel in the vision of the temple, the father of the false prophet Hananiah who broke Jeremiah's yoke, and one who sealed the covenant in Nehemiah's day. One name, three very different men: a prince, a prophet's father, and a signer.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the contrast is the lesson: one Azzur's son lied in God's name, and another Azzur signed the covenant to keep it. The name is the same; the choice is what matters.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to gush over, i.e. to swell; (figuratively) to desire earnestly; by implication to ask
BiblicalUsage: Ba'ah means to gush over, to swell — to desire earnestly, and so to ask. Isaiah says the watchman answers, if ye will enquire, enquire ye; he says the mountains shall melt and the waters shall gush at the Lord's presence; and Obadiah says Esau's hidden things shall be searched out. The word is longing that overflows into asking.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that God invites the asking: if ye will enquire, enquire ye. The mountains themselves melt before the God who answers.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Baal-Berith, a special deity of the Shechemites
BiblicalUsage: Baal-berith was the god of the covenant at Shechem — the god Israel made after Gideon's death, and the god in whose temple Abimelech found seventy pieces of silver to hire vain and light persons to kill his brothers. The people forgot the Lord and served the god of the covenant they made with a lie.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Baal-berith is the clearest warning in Judges: a covenant with a false god pays for murder, and the silver from his temple bought seventy graves.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Baal-Chanan, the name of an Edomite, also of an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Baal-hanan is the name of two men — a king of Edom who reigned after Saul of Rehoboth, whose death is recorded in Genesis and Chronicles alike, and an overseer of David's olive trees and sycamores in the low plains. A king and a gardener, both remembered, both named Baal-hanan.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that God records kings and gardeners in the same book, because the olive trees mattered to David's kingdom as much as the throne did.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Baal-Chatsor, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Baal-hazor was the place where Absalom kept his sheep-shearers, and where he invited all the king's sons to the feast — and had Amnon killed. A shearing feast that turned into a murder, and the name of the place is all that marks it.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Baal-hazor shows how revenge dresses itself up as a feast, and Absalom's table is my warning that a grudge served sweet is still poison.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Baal-Chermon, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Baal-hermon is the mountain and the district at the foot of Hermon — the border of the half-tribe of Manasseh east of Jordan, and the limit of the land the Canaanites still held. Chronicles says the Manassites increased from Bashan to Baal-hermon, and Judges names it among the nations left to prove Israel.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the borders God drew were honest borders: he told Israel what was theirs and what was still to be taken, and he left nations there to prove them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Baal-Gad, a place in Syria
BiblicalUsage: Baal-gad was a town in the valley of Lebanon under Mount Hermon, at the northern edge of the conquest — the limit of the land Joshua took, from Baal-gad in the valley to Mount Halak. Joshua names it three times, always as a boundary: the war ended there, and the inheritance began.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the northern boundary matters because it shows the conquest was finished and measured — God gave the land, and he gave it with edges.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a master; hence, a husband, or (figuratively) owner (often used with another noun in modifications of this latter sense)
BiblicalUsage: Baal as a common word means a master, a husband, an owner — the one who has the right to a thing. A married woman has a baal, a man is the baal of his house and his goods, the owner of the ox is its baal, and the master of the dream is the man who holds it. The same word names the lord of the house and, in the next entry, the false god who claimed to be lord of all.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the word itself is not the problem — a husband is a baal, and that is right and good. The problem is when men give the title to a god of wood and stone, and I believe God is the only true Baal, the only true Master, of his people.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Baal, a Phoenician deity
BiblicalUsage: Baal was the Phoenician god of storm and fertility, and Israel's great rival for a thousand years: Elijah stood against his prophets on Carmel and the fire fell, Jehu gathered his worshippers into the temple and destroyed them, and Hosea says Israel forgot God and went after Baal, while Gideon tore down his father's altar to Baal in the night. The name means lord, and the whole fight was over who is Lord.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the fight with Baal is the fight of the whole Old Testament, and Carmel settles it: the Lord, he is God, and Baal is nothing. Seven thousand knees never bowed to him, and I mean to be counted among them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Baal-Hamon, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Baal-hamon was Solomon's vineyard, the place where he let out the vineyards to keepers, each to bring a thousand pieces of silver for its fruit. The Song names it once, as the vineyard of the king himself.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Solomon's vineyard is a picture of the kingdom's wealth, and the beloved's answer — my own vineyard is before me — is the voice of one who keeps what is hers.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Baal-Meon, a place East of the Jordan
BiblicalUsage: Baal-meon was a town east of Jordan, in the land of Reuben — given to the Reubenites and rebuilt with a new name, then named again by Ezekiel among the cities of Moab to be judged. Chronicles says the Reubenites dwelt from Aroer to Baal-meon, and Numbers says it was rebuilt as a city of the children of Reuben.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the towns east of Jordan show the cost of settling short of the promise: Reuben kept Baal-meon, and Moab took it back in the end.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Baal-Peor, a Moabitish deity
BiblicalUsage: Baal-peor was the god of Peor, and the sin at Peor was Israel joining itself to him: the men of Israel yoked themselves to Baal-peor and ate the sacrifices of the dead, Phinehas stopped the plague with his spear, and Moses warned the next generation that their eyes had seen what the Lord did because of Baal-peor. Hosea says they went to Baal-peor and separated themselves to shame.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Peor is the warning that idolatry is never just an idea — it is a yoke, a meal, a shame. And I hold that Phinehas, who stood up and stopped the plague, is the picture of zeal that God honours.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Baal-Peratsim, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Baal-perazim was the place of breakings-through, where David inquired of the Lord and the Lord broke through his enemies like a breach of waters. David named the place himself — the Lord hath broken forth upon mine enemies before me, as the breach of waters — and the Philistines left their images there, which David and his men burned.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe David's habit is my habit to learn: he inquired first, and then God broke through. The place is named for the breakthrough, and I hold that the Lord still breaks through for those who ask him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Baal of Shalishah, Baal-Shalishah, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Baal-shalisha was the place the man came from who brought Elisha twenty loaves of barley and full ears of corn — and Elisha fed a hundred men with it, and there was some left. A small town, one verse, and a miracle of provision.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God feeds a hundred from twenty loaves because he wants his servant to know that the gift is his, not mine — and Baal-shalisha's bread is the proof.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Baal-Tamar, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Baal-tamar was the place where Israel set the ambush against Benjamin in the last battle of the civil war, and where the men of Israel drew the Benjamites out of Gibeah to their destruction. One verse, one ambush, and the end of a tribe's rebellion.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the war at Baal-tamar is the saddest war in Scripture — brother against brother — and it shows what happens when a people will not judge evil in their own midst.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Baal-Tsephon, a place in Eqypt
BiblicalUsage: Baal-zephon was the place by the sea where God told Israel to turn and camp before they crossed — over against Baal-zephon, between Migdol and the sea — and Pharaoh thought they were entangled in the land, so the Egyptians pursued them there, and the sea opened before them. The name is the last landmark before the deliverance.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Baal-zephon is the place where God let Pharaoh think he had won, and then drowned his army. He still turns his people back toward the sea on purpose, so the deliverance is unmistakably his.
RelatedEvents: The Exodus and the Red Sea
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Baal-Zebub, a special deity of the Ekronites
BiblicalUsage: Baal-zebub was the god of Ekron, and Ahaziah sent messengers to enquire of him when he fell through the lattice of his upper chamber; Elijah met the messengers on the road and asked, is it not because there is not a God in Israel, that ye go to enquire of Baal-zebub? The king sent twice more, and the fire of God answered both times.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Ahaziah's question is the question of every age: is there not a God in Israel? Elijah's answer still stands — there is, and he is not to be enquired of through a fly-god.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to be master; hence, to marry
BiblicalUsage: Ba'al as a verb means to be master, to marry — to take a wife and rule a house. God says to backsliding Israel, thy Maker is thine husband, and I will take you, one of a city and two of a family, and bring you to Zion. Malachi says Judah has married the daughter of a strange god, and profaned the holiness of the Lord. The word is marriage itself, in its right and its wrong.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that God calls himself Israel's husband on purpose: marriage is the picture of the covenant, and breaking it is not a small sin. He is the Maker who married his people, and he will not share them with a strange god.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Baalah, the name of three places in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Baalah is the name of three places — the town on Judah's border where the ark was fetched from Kirjath-jearim, the town on the same border toward the sea, and the town in the south of Judah's inheritance. David went to Baalah, to Kirjath-jearim, to bring up the ark of God, and the same town is named in the border lists of Joshua twice over.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Baalah matters because the ark rested there, and David went there to bring it home. A border town became a holy place because God's presence had lodged there.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a mistress
BiblicalUsage: Baalah as a common word means a mistress — the woman who owns or rules. The mistress of the house at Zarephath, whose son Elijah raised, is called the baalah of the house; the witch of Endor is a mistress of a familiar spirit; and Nineveh is called the mistress of witchcrafts, that selleth nations through her whoredoms. One word, three very different mistresses.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the contrast is the whole lesson: the widow of Zarephath was a mistress who trusted the prophet, and Nineveh was a mistress who sold nations. The title is neutral; the heart is not.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Baalath-Beer, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Baalath-beer was a town in the south, in the inheritance of Simeon — Ramath of the south, the town on the edge of the desert. It is named once, in the border list of Joshua.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the towns on the desert edge count as much as the towns in the hills, because God gave Simeon its portion too.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Baalath, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Baalath was a town Solomon built and fortified, in the land he ruled — named with the store-cities and the chariot-cities, and listed again among the towns of Dan's inheritance. A fortified city of the king, on the edge of the hill country.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Solomon's building was real building — cities, walls, storehouses — and Baalath is one of the bricks in the kingdom he was given.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Baale-Bamoth, a place East of the Jordan
BiblicalUsage: Baale-bamoth is a compound name — the high places of Baal — and it comes to us as two words, Bamoth and Baal, joined together: Joshua lists Bamoth-baal among the cities of Reuben on the plain, and Numbers tells how Balak brought Balaam up to the high places of Baal to see the camp of Israel. The name is a place and a warning at once.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the high places of Baal are the picture of worship gone up the hill and away from God, and Balaam standing on them to curse Israel is the picture of how close cursing can come to blessing.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Baale-Jehudah, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Baale-judah is the name David gives for Kirjath-jearim when he goes to bring up the ark of God — the city of Baale in Judah, where the ark had rested in the house of Abinadab. David went there with thirty thousand chosen men, and the ark began its journey home.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the day David went to Baale-judah to fetch the ark is one of the great days of the Bible, because the presence of God was coming home to his people.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Baali, a symbolical name for Jehovah
BiblicalUsage: Baali is the name Hosea says Israel will stop using for God — in that day thou shalt call me Ishi, and shalt call me no more Baali — and the word means my master, which God says is too close to the name of the false god to keep. A new name for a new covenant: my husband, not my master.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that God cares about the names we call him, and Baali had to go because it sounded like Baal. He wants Ishi — husband — and that tells me what the covenant really is.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Baalis, an Ammonitish king
BiblicalUsage: Baalis was the king of the Ammonites who sent Ishmael to kill Gedaliah, the governor Nebuchadnezzar had left over the remnant in Judah, and Johanan warned Gedaliah, but Gedaliah would not believe him — and Ishmael came and slew him at Mizpah. One king, one plot, and the ruin of the remnant.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Gedaliah's refusal to believe the warning is one of the saddest moments in Jeremiah, and Baalis is the name behind it — a foreign king who finished what Babylon started.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Banana, the name of four Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Baana is the name of three men — two of Solomon's twelve officers, one over Taanach and Megiddo and one over Asher, and a wall-builder who repaired the wall in Nehemiah's day with his sons. The king's officers and the wall-builder share one name, and both served the kingdom in their own generation.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that officers who feed a king's table and builders who repair a broken wall do the same work in God's eyes: keeping the kingdom standing.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Baanah, the name of four Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Baanah is the name of four men — the son of Rimmon who murdered Ish-bosheth in his bed and was hanged by David for it, the Netophathite among David's mighty men, and two men who returned from Babylon and sealed the covenant. The same name belongs to a murderer, a warrior, and two men who came home to rebuild.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe David's judgment on Baanah is the line that holds the kingdom together: murder in the king's name is still murder, and the king who will not excuse it is the king God keeps.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to kindle, i.e. consume (by fire or by eating); to be (-come) brutish
BiblicalUsage: Ba'ar means to burn — to kindle, to consume, to set ablaze, and to sweep away like stubble. The bush burned and was not consumed when Moses turned aside to see it, Deuteronomy says the Lord's anger shall burn against the land, Isaiah says the fire shall burn and none shall quench it, and Jeremiah says the word of the Lord shall go forth like a fire in the house of Israel. The same fire warms, judges, and speaks.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe fire is the picture of God himself in this word: the bush that burns without consuming is the God who draws near without destroying. The fire that none can quench is the same God in judgment.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, foot (as consumed); i.e. (by exten.) of cattle brutishness; (concretely) stupid
BiblicalUsage: This word means brutish — the stupid man, the fool who has no understanding. Proverbs says the brutish man knoweth not, and the fool cannot understand, and the psalm says the man that is in honour and understandeth not is like the beasts that perish. A man can have honour and still be a beast, if he will not learn.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the brutish man is the one who refuses correction. I hold that the fear of the Lord is the only cure for a mind that will not learn.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to dig; by analogy, to engrave; figuratively, to explain
BiblicalUsage: Ba'ar means to dig, to make plain — to engrave words so clearly that a runner can read them. Moses was charged to write the law plainly on stones, and Habakkuk was told to write the vision and make it plain upon tables, that he may run that readeth it.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that God wants his word plain — written large on stone, written clear on the tablet — because he wants runners, not scholars, to carry it. That is why I write plainly too.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Baara, an Israelitish woman
BiblicalUsage: Baara was a wife of Shaharaim the Benjamite, named in the genealogy of Benjamin among his wives Hushim and Baara. She appears once, in the list of the sons born to Shaharaim in the country of Moab.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the genealogies keep wives like Baara because families are built by mothers as much as by fathers, and God counts both.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Baasejah, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Baaseiah was a Levite of the house of Merari, named in the genealogy of the singers — the son of Malchiah, the father of Michael, and the ancestor of Asaph's line. He appears once, in the long song of the Levites who stood before the ark.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the singers' genealogies are kept because worship is a family business, and Baaseiah's name in Asaph's line is his share in the song.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to smell bad; figuratively, to be offensive morally
BiblicalUsage: Ba'ash means to stink, to smell bad — and in Scripture a bad smell is a bad reputation. The Philistines made Israel abhorred, the men of Jabesh made themselves odious to the Ammonites, the dead fish of Egypt stank in the river, and the Preacher says dead flies cause the ointment of the apothecary to send forth a stinking savour. A small offence spoils a sweet thing.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that a reputation is like ointment: one dead fly can spoil the whole pot. The wise man keeps the flies out.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to trample down, i.e. (figuratively) despise
BiblicalUsage: Ba'at means to trample down, to kick — and it is the word for despising what God gave. Eli's sons kicked at the sacrifices of the Lord, and Jeshurun waxed fat and kicked when he was full of God's blessing. Trampling is contempt with the foot.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe kicking at God's gifts is the surest way to lose them, and Jeshurun's story is my warning to stay hungry for him even when I am full.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to fear
BiblicalUsage: Ba'ath means to be terrified, to be struck with sudden fear. The evil spirit terrified Saul and his servants said, behold, an evil spirit from God troubleth thee; Daniel fell on his face in fear when Gabriel came near; the waters of the sea terrified the prophet; and Job says the terrors of God set themselves in array against him. Fear that comes like a wave and overwhelms.
