TheologicalSignificance: I hold that there is a fear that comes from God and a fear that comes from the enemy, and Daniel shows me the difference: he fell on his face before Gabriel, and the angel lifted him up. The fear of the Lord does not crush; it raises.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Basha, a king of Israel
BiblicalUsage: Baasha was the king of Israel who conspired against Nadab, took the throne, and reigned twenty-four years in Tirzah, warring with Asa of Judah all their days and building Ramah to shut Judah in. The word of the Lord came against him because he walked in the way of Jeroboam and made Israel to sin, and his house was cut off, as the house of Jeroboam had been.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Baasha's story is the pattern of every king who takes the throne by murder and keeps it by idolatry: God gives the kingdom, and God takes it away, and the house falls exactly as he said.
RelatedPeople: Baasha, King of Israel; King Asa
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a request
BiblicalUsage: Ba'u is the Aramaic word for a request, a petition — and Daniel uses it of the decree the king's men brought to Darius, asking him to sign the law against prayer. The word is a formal asking, made to a king.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the request made to Darius is the contrast to Daniel's own prayers: men petitioned a king who could not save, while Daniel prayed to a God who could — and the lions' den proved which petition was heard.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H1168); Baal, a Phœnician deity (used as a symbol of idolatry):--Baal.
BiblicalUsage: Paul says God kept for himself seven thousand men who have not bowed the knee to Baal. The Greek name for Baal, used once, in the middle of the argument that God has not cast away his people — there is always a remnant, and it belongs to him.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the seven thousand are my comfort in dark days: God always keeps a remnant, and I mean to be counted in it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: something hollowed (as a gate), i.e. pupil of the eye
BiblicalUsage: The babah is the pupil of the eye, the little man in the eye — the apple of the eye. Zechariah says he that toucheth you toucheth the apple of his eye, speaking of Jerusalem, the people God guards as tenderly as the eye guards its pupil.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God guards his people the way an eye guards its pupil — with a flinch before the touch even lands — and that is how close I am to him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {Babel (i.e. Babylon), including Babylonia and the Babylonian empire}
BiblicalUsage: Babel in Aramaic is the name of the city and empire in Daniel's day — the Babylon of Nebuchadnezzar's court, where Daniel served and where the king's wise men could not tell the dream. Daniel's God revealed what Babylon's gods could not, and the king's decrees went out from Babel to all the peoples of the empire.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Babel in Aramaic is the same Babel as in Hebrew, and the lesson is the same: the greatest empire on earth cannot read a dream, but Daniel's God can. That is why I trust him, not the empire.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Babel (i.e. Babylon), including Babylonia and the Babylonian empire
BiblicalUsage: Babel is Babylon — the city of the tower, the city of the exile, the city of the great king. Genesis says its name is Babel because there the Lord confounded the language of all the earth; Isaiah says Babylon the glory of kingdoms shall be as Sodom and Gomorrah; Jeremiah says Babylon is a golden cup in the Lord's hand that made all the earth drunken; and Daniel was carried there as a boy and served its kings with a clear conscience.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Babylon is the city of man's pride from the tower to the exile, and God judges it every time — yet he also keeps his Daniels in it. I hold that I can live in Babylon without bowing to it.
RelatedEvents: The Tower of Babel; Daniel's Resolve in Babylon
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a Babylonian
BiblicalUsage: A Babliy is a Babylonian, and the word appears once, in the letter of the king's officers to Artaxerxes — the Babylonians, the Susanchites, the Dehavites, and the Elamites, all named as the peoples settled in Samaria who wrote against the Jews.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the letter-writers of Ezra are a warning that opposition often comes dressed as administration, and God's work goes on anyway.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H894); Babylon, the capitol of Chaldæa (literally or figuratively (as a type of tyranny)):-- Babylon.
BiblicalUsage: Babylon is the city of the exile and the city of the last days: Matthew counts it in the genealogy — they were carried away to Babylon — Stephen says God removed them into Babylon, and Peter sends greetings from the church at Babylon, while Revelation says Babylon the great is fallen, is fallen. The same city, first as judgment and last as the fall of the world itself.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Babylon falls twice — once to Persia, and once at the end of the age — and I hold that the church which greets me from Babylon in Peter's letter is the proof that God keeps his people even there.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to loath
BiblicalUsage: Bachal means to loathe, to be disgusted with — and it cuts both ways. The sluggard's way is loathsome to the Lord, and Zechariah says God cut off the three shepherds in one month, and my soul loathed them, and their soul also abhorred me. Loathing, met with loathing.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that God loathes what is false, and Zechariah's grief is God's grief: a shepherd who loves his flock and is abhorred for it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a watch-tower
BiblicalUsage: Bachan is a watch-tower, and Isaiah says the pleasant places of the city shall be a place for the watch-tower of the wilderness, where wild asses shall run and flocks shall lie down. A tower for watching, left to the desert when the city falls.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the watch-tower in the desert is the picture of a city that stopped watching, and I mean to keep my own watch.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to test (especially metals); generally and figuratively, to investigate
BiblicalUsage: Bachan means to test — to try metals in the fire, and to try men the same way. God tells the prophet he has set him as a tower and a fortress to know and try the people's way, Jeremiah says the Lord trieth the righteous, Job says when he hath tried me I shall come forth as gold, and Zechariah promises God will refine his people as silver is refined and try them as gold is tried.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God tests his people the way a refiner tests silver — not to destroy them but to burn away the dross. Job's gold is my hope: when he hath tried me, I shall come forth as gold.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, to try, i.e. (by implication) select
BiblicalUsage: Bachar means to choose — to try and then select. God chose Israel above all people on the face of the earth, he chose David his servant and took him from the sheepfolds, Joshua said choose you this day whom ye will serve, and Isaiah says the Lord's servant is mine elect, in whom my soul delighteth. The same word for choosing a king, a people, and a Saviour.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe choosing is the heart of the covenant: God chose Israel when she was nothing, and he chose me the same way. And I hold that my own choosing answers his — choose you this day whom ye will serve, and I choose the Lord.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a Bacharumite or inhabitant of Bachurim
BiblicalUsage: A Bacharumite is a man of Bahurim, and the one named is Azmaveth the Baharumite, among David's mighty men. A man known by his town, and by the king he served.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that God remembers the mighty men by their towns as well as their names, because every one of them stood for the king.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a watch-tower of besiegers
BiblicalUsage: Bachiyn is a watch-tower of besiegers — the tower the enemy builds against a city. Isaiah says the Chaldeans shall set up their towers against Tyre, and the city that trusted in its walls will watch the enemy build higher.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the besieger's tower is the picture of pride's end: the city that trusted its own walls watches the enemy build above them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: select
BiblicalUsage: Bachiyr means chosen, select — the elect. God says, I have chosen thee in the furnace of affliction; Isaiah calls Israel my chosen, and my servant whom I have chosen; David was told to take the chosen men of Israel to fetch the ark; and the psalm says God remembered his covenant with Abraham his servant, and brought forth his people with joy, and his chosen with gladness.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe being chosen is not a prize for being good — God chose Israel in the furnace of affliction, and he chose me the same way, in the middle of my need. That is the grace I hold on to.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an assayer or metals
BiblicalUsage: A bachown is an assayer — the man who tests metals. Jeremiah says God has set the prophet as a tower and a fortress among his people, that he may know and try their way, as an assayer tries silver.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that God sets his prophets as assayers among his people, to know what is real metal and what is dross — and I want my own faith to pass the test.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Bachurim, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Bahurim was a village on the road from Jerusalem to the Jordan, where Shimei came out cursing David as he fled from Absalom, and where Jonathan and Ahimaaz hid in a well to escape Absalom's men. David passed it in tears, and the priests' messengers hid in it, and the town is named in the story of both flights.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Bahurim is the place of the curse and the hiding-place at once, and David's mercy to Shimei there is the picture of a king who forgives what he could have avenged.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, selected, i.e. a youth (often collective)
BiblicalUsage: Bachuwr is a young man in his prime — chosen, strong, at the height of life. Saul stood head and shoulders above the people, a choice young man; the Preacher tells the young man to rejoice in his youth and remember his Creator; Jeremiah says the young men shall fall in her streets; and Proverbs says the glory of young men is their strength. Youth, in its beauty and its danger.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that youth is a gift with a warning attached: rejoice, says the Preacher, but remember your Creator in the days of thy youth. The strength of a young man is glorious only when it is given to God.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: flaxen thread or yarn; hence, a linen garment
BiblicalUsage: Bad is linen — fine flaxen thread, the cloth of the priest's garments. Aaron's sons wore linen breeches, Samuel ministered before the Lord as a child girded with a linen ephod, David danced before the ark in a linen ephod, and Daniel saw a man clothed in linen above the waters of the river. Linen is the cloth of service before God.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe linen is the right picture for service: plain, clean, and worn before God. Samuel wore it as a child and Daniel saw it on the man above the river, and I hold that the same clean cloth is what God gives his servants to wear.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: flaxen thread or yarn; hence, a linen garment
BiblicalUsage: Bad is linen — fine flaxen thread, the cloth of the priest's garments. Aaron's sons wore linen breeches, Samuel ministered before the Lord as a child girded with a linen ephod, David danced before the ark in a linen ephod, and Daniel saw a man clothed in linen above the waters of the river. Linen is the cloth of service before God.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe linen is the right picture for service: plain, clean, and worn before God. Samuel wore it as a child and Daniel saw it on the man above the river, and I hold that the same clean cloth is what God gives his servants to wear.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: flaxen thread or yarn; hence, a linen garment
BiblicalUsage: Bad is linen — fine flaxen thread, the cloth of the priest's garments. Aaron's sons wore linen breeches, Samuel ministered before the Lord as a child girded with a linen ephod, David danced before the ark in a linen ephod, and Daniel saw a man clothed in linen above the waters of the river. Linen is the cloth of service before God.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe linen is the right picture for service: plain, clean, and worn before God. Samuel wore it as a child and Daniel saw it on the man above the river, and I hold that the same clean cloth is what God gives his servants to wear.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: (figuratively) to invent
BiblicalUsage: Bada means to invent — to devise a thing out of one's own head. Jeroboam invented a feast in the eighth month, like the feast in Judah, and set up the calves at Bethel; and Sanballat said Nehemiah invented the rebuilding of the wall out of rebellion. One man invented false worship, and the other was falsely accused of inventing treason.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that invented religion is the oldest sin in the book, and Jeroboam's feast is my warning: if God did not command it, I do not want it, however good it looks.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: separate; adverb, separately
BiblicalUsage: Badad means alone, separate — by oneself. Israel dwelt alone in safety, the Lord alone did lead his people, the city that was full of people sits solitary in Lamentations, and Micah says the Lord will feed his people alone in the wood, in the midst of Carmel. Separation, sometimes as judgment and sometimes as the Lord's own keeping.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God keeps his people separate on purpose — a people that dwells alone, led by the Lord alone. And I hold that even Jerusalem's solitude is not abandonment, because he feeds his flock in the wood himself.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to divide, i.e. (reflex.) be solitary
BiblicalUsage: Badad as a verb means to be solitary, to separate oneself — and Hosea says Ephraim is a wild ass alone by himself, Isaiah says the burden of the wilderness shall be borne alone, and Leviticus commands the leper to dwell alone outside the camp. Solitude can be rebellion, or judgment, or the lonely road of the outcast.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the wild ass alone by himself is Ephraim's picture and mine, whenever I hire lovers and run from God. The leper outside the camp is the other side: solitude imposed by law, until the cleansing comes.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a part
BiblicalUsage: Badal in this form is a part — a portion, a piece. Amos says a shepherd takes out of the mouth of the lion two legs, or a piece of an ear, and so shall the children of Israel be taken out that dwell in Samaria. A scrap saved from the lion's mouth.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the piece of an ear is God's mercy in a hard verse: even when the lion has the flock, he saves a remnant, and I am part of it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to divide (in variation senses literally or figuratively, separate, distinguish, differ, select, etc.)
BiblicalUsage: Badal means to divide — to separate, distinguish, and set apart. God divided the light from the darkness on the first day, he divided the waters from the waters, he separated the Levites from the children of Israel, and he commanded Israel to be separate from the peoples of the lands. The same word that made the world also made his people.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe division is God's first work and his lasting work: he divided light from darkness at creation, and he divides his people from the world by holiness. I hold that separation is not narrowness — it is the shape of being his.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to mend a breach
BiblicalUsage: Badaq means to mend a breach — to repair what is broken in the house of God. Josiah's men were given money to repair the breaches of the temple, to buy timber and stone to mend what had fallen into ruin.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God loves a repaired temple, and Josiah's workmen mending the breaches are my picture of what repentance does in a life.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: food
BiblicalUsage: Bag is food — a portion, a provision. Ezekiel says God will take the spoil of the nations for a prey, and give their food to the beasts of the field. One word for the daily bread that becomes another's spoil in judgment.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that even a man's food is in God's hand, and when a nation is judged, its bread is given to the beasts — a sober reminder that provision is his, not mine.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to cover (with a garment); figuratively, to act covertly; by implication, to pillage
BiblicalUsage: Bagad means to deal treacherously — to act covertly, to cover a wrong with a garment of friendship. Hosea says they have dealt treacherously against the Lord, Isaiah says the treacherous dealers have dealt very treacherously, Malachi says Judah has dealt treacherously with the wife of his youth, and Proverbs says the transgressors shall be taken in their own naughtiness. Treachery is sin that smiles while it stabs.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe treachery is the ugliest sin because it wears a friend's face. I hold that the only cure is the plain dealing Proverbs promises: the integrity of the upright shall guide them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: treacherous
BiblicalUsage: A bagowd is a treacherous one — a dealer in treachery. Jeremiah says Judah was treacherous in turning to idols, and her sister Israel saw it and still did not return. Treachery, named as a person.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Judah's treachery is the warning I take personally: she watched her sister fall and did it anyway, and I must not do the same.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to tremble inwardly (or palpitate), i.e. (figuratively) be (causative, make) (suddenly) alarmed or agitated; by implication to hasten anxiously
BiblicalUsage: Bahal means to be suddenly alarmed — to tremble inwardly, to be troubled in a moment. Joseph's brothers were troubled at his presence when he said, I am Joseph; the chiefs of Edom were amazed and trembling took hold of the mighty men of Moab; Job says his heart trembles at the thunder; and the Preacher says not to be hasty in spirit to be angry. Alarm that comes all at once and shakes the whole frame.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Joseph's brothers had the right reaction: when the one you wronged turns out to be the one who can save you, trembling is the honest response. His grace after it is the whole gospel.
RelatedPeople: Joseph, Son of Jacob; Job; Moses
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: white marble or perhaps alabaster
BiblicalUsage: Bahat is white marble, or alabaster — the pavement of Ahasuerus' court, where the beds were of gold and silver upon a pavement of red, and blue, and white, and black marble. One word, one palace floor, and the splendour of a king who ruled from India to Ethiopia.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the marble floor is worth one verse, because it shows the glory of the court where Esther stood — and the greater glory of the God who used her there.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: shining
BiblicalUsage: Bahiyr means shining, bright — the word for the sky cleared of clouds. Elihu says men see not the bright light which is in the clouds, but the wind passeth and cleanseth them. The brightness is there all along, behind the weather.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the bright light behind the clouds is the picture of God himself: hidden by weather, never gone, and the wind of his Spirit clears the sky.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a diminutive of a derivative probably of the base of G939; a palm twig (as going out far):--branch.
BiblicalUsage: Baion is a palm branch — the word the crowd carried when Jesus entered Jerusalem. They took branches of palm trees and went forth to meet him, and cried, Hosanna, blessed is the King of Israel that cometh in the name of the Lord. The word is the same one the Greeks used for the palm twig, and it is the branch of the King's welcome.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the palm branches were the crowd's way of saying, this is our King — and I hold that I am still called to go out to meet him the same way, branch in hand, crying Hosanna.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: the weeping tree (some gum-distilling tree, perhaps the balsam)
BiblicalUsage: Baka is the weeping tree — the mulberry, or balsam, the tree that weeps gum. David heard the sound of going in the tops of the mulberry trees, and knew it was the sign to go up against the Philistines, because the Lord had gone out before him. The trees were the signal, and the victory followed.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that God still gives his people a sound in the tops of the trees — a sign to move, when he himself has gone out before them. David waited for it, and I mean to wait for mine.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Baca, a valley in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Baca is the valley of weeping — the valley the pilgrims pass through on their way to Zion, making it a well, and the rain filling the pools. One verse, one valley, and the whole pilgrimage in it: they go from strength to strength, every one of them in Zion appeareth before God.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the valley of Baca is the promise for every hard road: the weeping place becomes a well, and the pilgrims go from strength to strength until they appear before God in Zion.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to weep; generally to bemoan
BiblicalUsage: Bakah is weeping — the tears that run through the whole Bible. Hannah wept sore and prayed, the baby Moses wept in the basket and Pharaoh's daughter had compassion on him, David wept when he heard that his son was dead, and Nehemiah wept and mourned and fasted when he heard the walls of Jerusalem were broken down. Weeping, in every generation, before the same God.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God keeps every tear, and I hold that the weeping of Hannah and Nehemiah was heard the same day it was wept. He that soweth in tears shall reap in joy, and my tears are sown too.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to give the birthright
BiblicalUsage: Bakar means to give the birthright — to make the firstborn, and to give the firstborn his double portion. The firstborn of the flock belongs to the Lord, the father shall not make the son of the beloved firstborn before the son of the hated, and Jeremiah hears the voice of a woman in travail, bringing forth her first child. The birthright is the first and best, and it belongs to God.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the firstborn is God's by right. Esau's sale of it is the warning that hangs over this whole word: never trade the first and best for a bowl of pottage.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a first-ripe fig
BiblicalUsage: Jeremiah sees two baskets of figs set before the temple, and the good figs are described as first-ripe, the earliest fruit of the season.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God notices what comes first, and the first-ripe fig is His picture of a people He still calls good.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a Bakrite (collectively) or descendants of Beker
BiblicalUsage: The word names the family of Beker, counted among the sons of Ephraim in the wilderness census.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that God counts families by name, and no clan is too small to be written down in His book.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Baladan, the name of a Babylonian prince
BiblicalUsage: Baladan is named only as the father of Berodach-baladan, the king of Babylon. He sent letters and a present to Hezekiah when he heard the king had been sick.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a name can matter simply because of the son it belongs to, and this one opens the door to Isaiah's hard word about Babylon carrying everything away.
RelatedPeople: Baladan, Father of Berodach-Baladan; Berodach-Baladan, King of Babylon
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, anxiety, i.e. (by implication) the heart (as its seat)
BiblicalUsage: This Aramaic word means the heart, the seat of a person's anxiety, and it appears when the king sets his heart on rescuing Daniel from the lions' den.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that a troubled heart is not a faithless one, and the king's worry that night shows a ruler who wanted to do right and could not find the way.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a Belaite (collectively) or descendants of Bela
BiblicalUsage: The word names the family of Bela, counted among the sons of Benjamin in the wilderness census.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God keeps the record of every family, and the Belaites are remembered because they belonged to Israel.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, a failure; by implication nothing; usually (adverb) not at all; also lest
BiblicalUsage: Bal is the small word for not, nothing, never, lest. It shows up wherever Scripture draws a hard line: the wicked says in his pride that there is no God, the earth is established so it cannot be moved, and the foundations of the world are laid so they will not be removed.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this little word carries enormous weight, because what God says will not happen cannot happen. The psalmist leans on it the way a man leans on a wall: the Lord reigns, the world stands, and no scheming of the wicked can undo what God has fixed.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to make away with (specifically by swallowing); generally, to destroy
BiblicalUsage: Bala means to swallow up, to destroy by swallowing. The earth opens and swallows Korah's company, the sea swallows Egypt's army, and a great fish swallows Jonah, yet the same word turns around in Isaiah, where God promises to swallow up death itself in victory.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that swallowing is the Bible's picture of a power too big to resist, and that is why Isaiah's promise lands so hard. Death has swallowed men whole since Eden, but God will swallow death, and the eater will finally be eaten.
RelatedEvents: Korah's Rebellion; The Exodus and the Red Sea
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H1109); Balaam, a Mesopotamian (symbolic of a false teacher):--Balaam.
BiblicalUsage: Balaam's name reaches the New Testament as a warning, not a biography. Peter says false teachers have followed his way, loving the wages of unrighteousness; Jude says men have run greedily after his error for reward; and the risen Christ says the church at Pergamos holds the doctrine of Balaam, who taught Balak to put a stumblingblock before Israel.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Balaam matters because he knew God's voice and still sold what he knew for money. That is the pattern the apostles hold up, and the reason his name still warns the church: a gift for speaking God's words is worthless if the heart is for sale.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to pinch sycamore figs (a process necessary to ripen them)
BiblicalUsage: Amos says he was no prophet and no prophet's son, but a herdsman and a gatherer of sycomore fruit, and this is the word for that gathering work, pinching the figs so they ripen.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that God delights to call ordinary working men, and Amos's figs are proof that He does not need a title before He speaks.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to break off or loose (in a favorable or unfavorable sense), i.e. desist (from grief) or invade (with destruction)
BiblicalUsage: Balag means to break off, to let go, to desist, and it cuts both ways. Amos says God strengthens the spoiled against the strong, breaking off destruction against them, while Job begs to break off his grief for a moment, to leave off complaining and take comfort before his days run out.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe there is mercy in this word, because God knows when to stop the blow and when to let a weary man rest. Job asked for a little breathing room, and I hold that God hears that prayer even when the answer is slower than we want.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Balah, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Balah is a town named once. It appears in the list of cities given to the tribe of Simeon within Judah's inheritance.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that even a town named a single time mattered to the people who lived there, and God gave them a place by name.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to fail; by implication to wear out, decay (causatively, consume, spend)
BiblicalUsage: Balah means to wear out, to grow old and fail. Moses tells Israel their clothes did not wear out in forty years of wilderness, Nehemiah says the same of their feet, Job says a man wastes away like a rotten thing, and Isaiah says the enemies of God's servant will wear out like a garment.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this word draws the line between what God keeps and what time eats away. Clothes last forty years when God is keeping them, and the proud wear out like moth-eaten cloth when He is done with them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to palpitate; hence, (causatively) to terrify
BiblicalUsage: The word means to terrify, to make the heart beat hard with fear, and it appears once, when the people of the land weakened the hands of Judah and troubled them while they were building.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that fear is the oldest tool against God's work, and the builders in Ezra faced it the same way we do: with hands that had to keep working anyway.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H1111); Balak, a Moabite:--Balac.
BiblicalUsage: Balak's name reaches the New Testament in the risen Christ's letter to Pergamos. There He says the church holds the doctrine of Balaam, who taught Balak to cast a stumblingblock before the children of Israel.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Balak matters because he tried to buy a curse against God's people and could not, yet his name still warns us: a king who cannot curse Israel can still tempt her, and temptation did what cursing could not.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to overflow (specifically with oil.); by implication, to mix; to fodder
BiblicalUsage: Balal means to mix, and it runs from judgment to worship. At Babel God confounds the language of men by mixing it up, so the builders cannot understand one another, while in the law the grain offering is mixed with oil, and the daily offering is mixed with oil and wine before the Lord.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the same mixing tells two stories. At Babel men mixed their plans and God scattered them; at the altar God commands the mixing, and the offering is accepted. The difference is who does the mixing and why.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to muzzle
BiblicalUsage: The word means to muzzle, and it appears once, in the warning not to be like the horse or the mule, whose mouth must be held in with bit and bridle.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God would rather guide us with His eye than muzzle us with a bit, and the psalm is His invitation to be led willingly.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably remotely from G906 (as a depository); a pouch (for money):--bag, purse.
BiblicalUsage: A balantion is a money bag, a pouch for carrying coins, and Jesus tells the seventy to carry no purse on their mission, then later asks them whether they lacked anything when they went without one.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the empty purse was the lesson: the men who carried nothing found they lacked nothing, because the Lord who sent them provided for them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Balak, a Moabitish king
BiblicalUsage: Balak was the king of Moab who feared Israel camped on his border, and he sent for Balaam to curse them. He watched in fury as blessing after blessing came out of the prophet's mouth instead.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Balak's story is God's plain answer to fear-driven scheming: no hired curse can touch a people God has blessed, and the king who tried hardest to stop Israel ended up paying to hear her blessed.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to annihilate
BiblicalUsage: The word means to empty out, to lay waste, and Isaiah uses it when the Lord empties the earth and turns it upside down, scattering its inhabitants.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that a wasted earth is not an accident but a judgment, and Isaiah says it plainly so no one mistakes it for bad luck.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: worn out
BiblicalUsage: Baleh means worn out, and it describes the Gibeonites' trick: old sacks, old wineskins, old shoes and old clothes, all worn out to make it look as though they had come from far away.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the worn-out clothes are a warning about believing appearances, because Israel made a covenant on what they saw and never asked the Lord.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: alarm; hence, destruction
BiblicalUsage: Ballahah is terror, sudden alarm that destroys. Job's friends say terrors take hold of the wicked like waters, the king of terrors drags him from his tent, Isaiah says the enemy is gone by morning, and Ezekiel says Tyre will become a terror and be no more.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that terror is the portion of those who build against God. The prophets use this word the way a man points at a ruin: here is what is left of everyone who trusted in himself.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a primary verb; to throw (in various applications, more or less violent or intense):--arise, cast (out), X dung, lay, lie, pour, put (up), send, strike, throw (down), thrust. Compare G4496.
BiblicalUsage: Ballo is the ordinary word for throwing or casting, and it covers everything from a widow casting two small coins into the treasury to branches cast into the fire and the devil himself cast into the lake of fire. Jesus uses it for plucking out an offending eye and casting it away, and for the net cast into the sea that gathers every kind.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this word forces a choice, because what is cast is either given or judged. The widow cast in all she had and was praised, while the unfruitful branch is cast out and withered, and I hold that the difference is whether a life is cast toward God or away from Him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Bamah, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Bamah is the name Ezekiel gives to the high place itself. God asks what the high place is to which Israel goes, and the name sticks to it.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that God names the sin plainly so His people cannot pretend it is worship, and the place called Bamah stands as a rebuke to every altar He never commanded.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an elevation
BiblicalUsage: A bamah is a high place, an elevation used for worship, and its story is mostly a sad one. Samuel goes up to the high place to bless the sacrifice, Solomon offers a thousand burnt offerings at Gibeon, but the high places become Israel's snare, and Hezekiah finally breaks them down while Ezekiel prophesies against the mountains of Israel and their high places.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the high places show how easily worship drifts from God's command to man's convenience. Solomon could offer a thousand sacrifices at Gibeon and still be told to worship at Jerusalem, and I hold that sincerity never makes a wrong altar right.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Bamoth or Bamoth-Baal, a place East of the Jordan
BiblicalUsage: Bamoth, also called Bamoth-baal, is a place east of the Jordan where Israel camped on the way to the promised land. It is named again when the land was divided among the tribes.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the camps of the wilderness were not wasted miles, and every named stopping place, Bamoth among them, marks a step in God's leading.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to build (literally and figuratively)
BiblicalUsage: Banah means to build, and it runs from the first building in Scripture, when God builds a woman from Adam's rib. It runs on to the tower men built to make a name for themselves, to God's promise that David's son would build a house for His name, and to the proverb that a wise woman builds her house while the foolish tears hers down.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe building is the work God gave us, but the builder decides what the building is for. God builds a woman, men build a tower, and a son builds a temple, and I hold that only the building God orders stands when the testing comes.
RelatedEvents: Creation; The Tower of Babel; Davidic Covenant
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Bani, the name of five Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Bani is the name of five Israelites, and each one is named in a different setting. There is Bani the Gadite among David's mighty men, a Bani in the genealogy of those who returned to Jerusalem, the children of Bani who came up from exile, Rehum the son of Bani repairing the wall, and Uzzi the son of Bani overseeing the Levites.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a name repeated across five different men shows how God keeps His people distinct even when the names repeat, and each Bani is remembered for his own place in the story.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G907; ablution (ceremonial or Christian):--baptism, washing.
BiblicalUsage: Baptismos covers washings of every kind. There is the Pharisees' washing of cups and pots and tables, the doctrine of baptisms listed among the first principles of the faith, the fleshly ordinances of the old covenant, and the burial with Christ in baptism that Paul says raises us with Him through faith.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the washing that matters is the one within, not the one without. The Pharisees washed their cups and missed their hearts, but Paul says true baptism buries us with Christ, and I hold that no amount of outward washing can do what that burial does.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G907; a baptizer, as an epithet of Christ's forerunner:--Baptist.
BiblicalUsage: Baptistes is the title given to John, the Baptist, the man who came preaching repentance in the wilderness and baptizing in Jordan, whom Jesus calls the greatest born of women.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that John's title is his whole message in one word: he baptized with water, and he pointed to the One who would baptize with the Holy Ghost and with fire.
RelatedEvents: The Baptism of Jesus; The Birth of John the Baptist
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a derivative of G911; to immerse, submerge; to make whelmed (i.e. fully wet); used only (in the New Testament) of ceremonial ablution, especially (technically) of the ordinance of Christian baptism:--Baptist, baptize, wash.
BiblicalUsage: Baptizo means to immerse, to dip under completely. It is the word for John's baptism in Jordan, for the baptism Jesus commands His disciples to give in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost, for the three thousand baptized on the day of Pentecost, and for Paul's burial with Christ in baptism.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe baptism is not a sprinkle of religion on a life but a burial and a rising. Paul says we are baptized into Christ's death so we can walk in newness of life, and I hold that every baptism in Scripture points to that same death and that same rising.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a primary verb; to whelm, i.e. cover wholly with a fluid; in the New Testament only in a qualified or special sense, i.e. (literally) to moisten (a part of one's person), or (by implication) to stain (as with dye):--dip.
BiblicalUsage: Bapto means to dip, and it appears in three scenes that could hardly be further apart. Jesus dips the sop and hands it to Judas at the supper, the rich man in torment begs for Lazarus to dip his finger in water and cool his tongue, and the rider on the white horse wears a vesture dipped in blood.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that one small word ties the supper table, the place of torment, and the day of judgment together. A dipped sop marks the betrayer, a dipped finger is denied to the rich man, and a dipped robe marks the Judge, and I believe none of those dippings is an accident.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to cleave; generally, to rend, break, rip or open
BiblicalUsage: Baqa means to split open, to cleave, to break through. The fountains of the great deep are broken up when the flood comes, Moses lifts his rod and the sea is divided, Isaiah says waters will break out in the wilderness, and Zechariah says the Mount of Olives will cleave in the middle on the day of the Lord.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this word belongs to God alone in the end, because only He splits seas and mountains. Men break ground with ploughs, but God breaks open the deep, and I hold that the same hand that opened the sea for Israel will open the mountain for her return.
RelatedEvents: The Exodus and the Red Sea; Noah and the Flood
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to pour out, i.e. to empty, figuratively, to depopulate; by analogy, to spread out (as a fruitful vine)
BiblicalUsage: Baqaq means to empty out, to lay waste, to pour a land out until nothing is left. Hosea says Israel is an empty vine bringing forth fruit to herself, Isaiah says the Lord makes the earth empty and turns it upside down, and Jeremiah says God will make void the counsel of Judah and Jerusalem in the valley of slaughter.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe an emptied land is the fruit of an emptied heart. Israel poured herself out on idols and God poured her out of the land, and I hold that the warning still stands: what we empty ourselves for decides what we are emptied of.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: beef cattle or an animal of the ox family of either gender (as used for plowing); collectively, a herd
BiblicalUsage: Baqar is cattle, the herd, the oxen and cows that carry a household's wealth. Abraham runs to the herd for a tender calf when strangers visit his tent, Pharaoh's cattle are struck in the plagues, the law appoints the herd for burnt offerings, and Job's seven thousand sheep and five hundred yoke of oxen mark him as the greatest man of the east.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe cattle in Scripture are never just livestock, because they measure blessing, feed the altar, and carry the cost of worship. Abraham gave his best calf to guests he did not know, and I hold that generosity with what God gave us is still the mark of a man who knows God.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, to plough, or (generally) break forth, i.e. (figuratively) to inspect, admire, care for, consider
BiblicalUsage: Baqar means to look after, to inspect, to seek out with care. God says He will seek out His sheep as a shepherd seeks out his flock in the day of cloud and darkness, the priest looks carefully at the plague to judge it, and the psalmist says he will dwell in the house of the Lord to behold the beauty of the Lord and to enquire in His temple.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this is the word for God's attention to us. He does not glance at His flock and move on; He seeks, He inspects, He looks after, and I hold that the God who seeks His sheep in the cloudy day is the same God who lets us seek His face in His house.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to search out (by any method, specifically in worship or prayer); by implication, to strive after
BiblicalUsage: Baqash means to seek, to search out, to strive after, and it is the word for seeking God Himself. Moses says if you seek the Lord with all your heart and soul you will find Him, Jeremiah says you will seek Me and find Me when you search with all your heart, the psalm says seek the Lord and His strength and His face continually, and Proverbs says to seek wisdom as silver and search for her as for hidden treasure.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe seeking is the whole of the life of faith in one word, because God promises to be found by those who seek Him with everything they have. He is not hiding from us; He is waiting to be sought, and I hold that every true search ends the same way, with the seeker found by the God he was looking for.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Bakbakkar, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Bakbakkar is a Levite named once. He is among those who returned to dwell in Jerusalem after the exile.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that God remembers the Levites who came back to serve in His house, even when only one verse carries their name.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a bottle (from the gurgling in emptying)
BiblicalUsage: A baqbuq is an earthen bottle, named for the gurgling sound it makes when it is emptied, and Jeremiah is told to take one to the valley of Hinnom and break it before the elders as a sign of how God will break Jerusalem.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the broken bottle is God's plain sermon in clay: a vessel that will not be made whole again is the picture of a city that would not repent.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Bakbukjah, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Bakbukiah is a Levite who led thanksgiving in prayer when the wall was finished. He stood among the gatekeepers at the dedication, and he is named again among those who kept the watches in the days of Nehemiah.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the men who led the praise when the work was done matter as much as the men who built the wall, and Bakbukiah's name is kept because he gave thanks.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Bakbuk, one of the Nethinim
BiblicalUsage: Bakbuk is named among the Nethinim, the temple servants whose children returned from exile with Zerubbabel.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the servants of the house are written down with the rest, and Bakbuk's name is kept because he belonged to the Lord's work.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a looking after
BiblicalUsage: Baqqarah means a looking after, a careful seeking out, and God uses it when He says He will seek out His sheep in the day they are scattered, as a shepherd seeks out his flock.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that God looks after His own the way a shepherd looks after scattered sheep, and no distance or darkness hides them from Him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a petition
BiblicalUsage: Baqqashah is a petition, a request laid before a king. Esther's petition is asked three times at the banquets before she names it, the king offers her half the kingdom if she will only say what she wants, and Ezra is called a ready scribe whose every petition the king of Persia granted him.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a petition is the boldest thing a subject can lay before a king, and Esther shows how it is done: she comes, she waits, she asks. I hold that God still answers the petition that is laid before Him in the right time and the right way.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: the heir (apparent to the throne)
BiblicalUsage: Bar means son, and it appears in the mother's cry to her son in Proverbs and in the psalm's command to kiss the Son lest He be angry.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the Son in the psalm is the King God has set on Zion, and kissing Him is not flattery but submission to the One whose wrath and whose blessing are both real.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: the heir (apparent to the throne)
BiblicalUsage: Bar means son, and it appears in the mother's cry to her son in Proverbs and in the psalm's command to kiss the Son lest He be angry.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the Son in the psalm is the King God has set on Zion, and kissing Him is not flattery but submission to the One whose wrath and whose blessing are both real.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: grain of any kind (even while standing in the field); by extension the open country
BiblicalUsage: Bar is grain, the corn of the field, gathered and stored and sold. Joseph gathers it in Egypt until it cannot be measured, his brothers go down to buy it in the famine, Amos rebukes the merchants who cannot wait for the sabbath to end so they can sell it, and Proverbs says the people curse the man who withholds it and bless the man who sells it.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe grain in Scripture is always about trust, because it is the difference between eating and starving. Joseph stored it by God's wisdom, the merchants sold it by greed, and I hold that what a man does with his grain shows what he believes about God.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: the heir (apparent to the throne)
BiblicalUsage: Bar means son, and it appears in the mother's cry to her son in Proverbs and in the psalm's command to kiss the Son lest He be angry.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the Son in the psalm is the King God has set on Zion, and kissing Him is not flattery but submission to the One whose wrath and whose blessing are both real.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: the heir (apparent to the throne)
BiblicalUsage: Bar means son, and it appears in the mother's cry to her son in Proverbs and in the psalm's command to kiss the Son lest He be angry.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the Son in the psalm is the King God has set on Zion, and kissing Him is not flattery but submission to the One whose wrath and whose blessing are both real.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: (absolutely) to create; (qualified) to cut down (a wood), select, feed (as formative processes)
BiblicalUsage: Bara is the word for create, and it belongs to God alone. In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth, He created man in His own image, Isaiah says He who created Jacob also formed Israel and will redeem him, and David prays for God to create in him a clean heart.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe create is the word that settles who God is and who we are. He made the world out of nothing, He made us in His image, and only He can make a clean heart where sin has ruined one, and I hold that the God who created once is still creating in His people today.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Chaldee origin (H1347 and H5); son of Abba; Bar-abbas, an Israelite:--Barabbas.
BiblicalUsage: Barabbas was a notable prisoner, a robber and murderer held in Jerusalem at the Passover, and the crowd chose him over Jesus when Pilate offered to release one of them. The people cried for Barabbas to be freed and for Jesus to be crucified, and Pilate released the murderer and delivered Jesus to be scourged and crucified.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Barabbas is every one of us standing in the prisoner's place. A guilty man walked free while the innocent One took his cross, and I hold that no picture in the Gospels shows substitution more plainly than that exchange.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to bolt, i.e. figuratively, to flee suddenly
BiblicalUsage: Barach means to flee, to bolt suddenly when danger comes. Hagar flees from Sarai into the wilderness, Moses flees from Pharaoh into Midian, Jonah flees from the presence of the Lord toward Tarshish, and David flees from Saul's house through the window by night.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe fleeing tells the truth about a man's heart, because where he runs shows what he fears and what he trusts. Hagar and Moses fled to the wilderness and found God there, but Jonah fled from God and found a storm, and I hold that the only safe flight is the one that runs toward Him.
RelatedEvents: Moses' Birth and Flight to Midian
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H1296); Barachias (i.e. Berechijah), an Israelite:--Barachias.
BiblicalUsage: Barachias is named once. He is the father of Zacharias, whose righteous blood Jesus says will come upon the generation that rejects Him.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a father's name can carry a son's witness, and Zacharias the son of Barachias stands in Jesus' words as one more righteous man slain by those who would not hear.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: hail
BiblicalUsage: Barad is hail, and it falls as judgment through the whole Bible. The plague on Egypt is hail mingled with fire such as never was in the land, great stones from heaven fall on the Amorites at Gibeon, God asks Job whether he has seen the treasures of the hail reserved for the day of battle, and Haggai says God struck His people with hail and blasting and they still did not turn to Him.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe hail is God's stored weapon, kept for the day He chooses to use it. Pharaoh saw it, the Amorites felt it, Job was asked about it, and I hold that the God who keeps hail in His treasuries is not a God to be trifled with.
RelatedEvents: The Ten Plagues; The Plague of Hail
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to hail
BiblicalUsage: The verb means to hail, to come down like hail, and Isaiah uses it when judgment falls on the forest and the city is brought low.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that God's judgment falls the way hail falls, sudden and heavy, and Isaiah leaves no doubt about which city it falls on.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to select; to feed; to render clear
BiblicalUsage: Barah means to choose, to select, and also to feed, to prepare food for someone. Goliath calls Israel to choose a man to fight him, David's servants beg him to eat bread and he refuses while his child is sick, and Amnon asks for Tamar to come and make food before his eyes.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this word shows how small choices carry great weight, because a chosen champion decides a battle and a prepared meal hides a wicked plan. David would not eat while he pleaded for his son, and I hold that his fasting says more about his heart than any words could.
RelatedPeople: King David; Amnon, Son of David
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Barakel, the father of one of Job's friends
BiblicalUsage: Barakel is named only as the father of Elihu the Buzite, the young man who speaks last in the book of Job. He speaks after the three friends fall silent.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that a father's name is kept here so we know Elihu is a real man with a family, not a voice out of nowhere, and his words carry weight because he waited his turn to speak.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H1301); Barak, an Israelite:--Barak.
BiblicalUsage: Barak's name reaches the New Testament in the roll of faith. Hebrews says time would fail to tell of Gideon, Barak, Samson, and Jephthah, who through faith subdued kingdoms.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Barak is remembered in Hebrews because he went when Deborah told him to go, and faith that obeys a prophet's word is the kind God writes down.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to kneel; by implication to bless God (as an act of adoration), and (vice-versa) man (as a benefit); also (by euphemism) to curse (God or the king, as treason)
BiblicalUsage: Barak means to kneel, and so to bless, and it is the word for God's blessing from the first promise to Abraham all the way to the priestly blessing. God tells Abram He will make him a blessing and bless those who bless him, the priests are told to bless Israel with the Lord's name upon them, and Moses promises blessing in the city and in the field to those who obey.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe blessing in Scripture is God stooping to give, because the word itself begins on bended knee. He blesses Abraham so Abraham can bless the world, and I hold that every blessing we receive is meant to travel onward to someone else.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: lightning; by analogy, a gleam; concretely, a flashing sword
BiblicalUsage: Baraq is lightning, the flash and the gleam of a drawn sword. Thunders and lightnings attend the Lord's descent on Sinai, God says His glittering sword will take hold on judgment, Ezekiel sees the sword sharpened to flash like lightning, and the psalm asks God to cast forth lightning and scatter His enemies.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe lightning is Scripture's picture of a God who cannot be managed, because it comes when He sends it and strikes where He wills. The same flash that lit Sinai still warns us, and I hold that the God of the lightning is the God whose sword is never drawn for nothing.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Barak, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Barak was the captain Deborah summoned to gather ten thousand men at Mount Tabor. He refused to go without her, pursued Sisera's chariots to the river Kishon, and sang with Deborah after the victory.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Barak's hesitation is honest and his obedience is real, because he went, even when he wanted Deborah beside him. God gave the victory to a man who asked for help, and I hold that asking for a godly companion is not weak faith but wise faith.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to lighten (lightning)
BiblicalUsage: The verb means to lighten with lightning, and the psalmist asks God to cast forth lightning and scatter His enemies.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the prayer is bold because it asks God Himself to act, and lightning is the sign that He has answered.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to clarify (i.e. brighten), examine, select
BiblicalUsage: Barar means to make clean, to purify, to separate the pure from the mixed. Daniel says many shall be purified and made white in the time of the end, Isaiah tells those who bear the vessels of the Lord to be clean, Zephaniah says God will turn the peoples to a pure language, and the psalm says with the pure God shows Himself pure.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe purification is God's work and our calling at once, because He cleanses and then commands us to stay clean. Daniel's purified ones are made white by trial, and I hold that the trials God sends are the fire that leaves His people pure.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain derivation; a foreigner (i.e. non-Greek):--barbarian(-rous).
BiblicalUsage: Barbaros means a foreigner, someone whose speech sounds strange to a Greek ear. Paul says he is a debtor to Greeks and barbarians alike, that an unknown tongue makes men barbarians to one another, and that in Christ there is neither Greek nor Jew, circumcision nor uncircumcision, barbarian nor Scythian, while the barbarians of Malta show Paul and his companions uncommon kindness after the shipwreck.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this word exposes the pride of every people that thinks its own speech is the only human one. Paul owed the gospel to the barbarian as much as to the Greek, and I hold that the kindness of Malta's islanders shames every Christian who has ever looked down on a stranger.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a fowl (as fattened on grain)
BiblicalUsage: Barbur is a fowl fattened on grain, named among the daily provisions for Solomon's table.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the king's table shows the peace of his reign, because a land at rest can feed its king so richly.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a Barchumite, or native of Bachurim
BiblicalUsage: The word names a man of Bahurim, listed among David's mighty men.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the mighty men are remembered town by town because each one left his home to follow David, and God kept the record of where they came from.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G926; to weigh down (figuratively):--burden, charge, heavy, press.
BiblicalUsage: Bareo means to weigh down, to press with a burden. Paul says he was pressed out of measure in Asia so that he despaired even of life, and that we who are in this tabernacle groan, being burdened, while Jesus warns His disciples not to let their hearts be overcharged with surfeiting and cares, and finds His own disciples' eyes heavy with sleep in Gethsemane.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this word tells the truth about pressure, because Paul was pressed beyond his strength and did not break. God let the weight fall so Paul would learn to trust the God who raises the dead, and I hold that the heaviest burdens are the ones that teach us we cannot carry ourselves.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: adverb from G926; heavily (figuratively):--dull.
BiblicalUsage: Bareos means heavily, dully, and it describes ears grown dull of hearing, quoted from Isaiah when Jesus and then Paul explain why so many hear the word and do not understand it.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that dull ears are not a hearing problem but a heart problem, and Isaiah's warning still falls on anyone who hears God's word and refuses to let it in.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a gem (as flashing), perhaps the emerald
BiblicalUsage: Bareqeth is a flashing gem, set in the third row of the high priest's breastplate and named again among the stones that covered the king of Tyre in Eden.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the gem's place on the breastplate says what it is for: the stones of God's people are carried over Aaron's heart, and the flashing stone is one more reminder that God sees His people as precious.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Chaldee origin (H1247 and H3091); son of Jesus (or Joshua); Bar-jesus, an Israelite:--Barjesus.
BiblicalUsage: Bar-jesus, also called Elymas the sorcerer, is the false prophet Paul and Barnabas meet on Cyprus. He tries to turn the deputy Sergius Paulus away from the faith.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Bar-jesus shows how a holy name can be worn by an unholy man, because son of Jesus he is called, yet he stands against the gospel, and Paul's blindness upon him is God's answer to a sorcerer who would blind others.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Chaldee origin (H1247 and H3124); son of Jonas (or Jonah); Bar-jonas, an Israelite:--Bar-jona.
BiblicalUsage: Bar-jona is the name Jesus gives Simon when He blesses him. He calls him Simon Bar-jona, the son of Jonah, in the moment Peter confesses that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of the living God.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Jesus names Peter by his father in the very breath that He names him blessed, because the confession did not come from flesh and blood but from the Father in heaven.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: fatted or plump
BiblicalUsage: Bariy means fat, well-fed, plump. It is the word for Pharaoh's fat cows that come up out of the river and are eaten by the lean ones, for the fat sheep the shepherds of Israel feed on while the flock starves, and for Daniel and his friends, who look fairer and fatter in flesh than all the young men who ate the king's meat.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe fatness in Scripture cuts both ways, because Pharaoh's fat cows are eaten and the fat shepherds are judged, while Daniel's health is the fruit of obedience. The difference is never the food; it is whether the fatness came from trusting God or from feeding on His people.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Bariach, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Bariah is named once. He is a son of Shemaiah in the line of David's house.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the genealogies keep names like Bariah's because the line of David is traced person by person, and no link in the chain is forgotten.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a fugitive, i.e. the serpent (as fleeing), and the constellation by that name
BiblicalUsage: Bariyach means a fugitive, one who flees. It is the name for the piercing serpent, Leviathan, whom the Lord will punish with His sore and great and strong sword, while Job says God's hand has formed the crooked serpent and His Spirit has garnished the heavens.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the fleeing serpent is no match for the God who made him, because the same hand that formed him will pierce him. Job marvels at the creature and Isaiah promises its end, and I hold that the serpent's flight is already written: he runs, and God catches him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Chaldee origin (H1247 and H5029); son of Nabas (i.e. prophecy); Barnabas, an Israelite:--Barnabas.
BiblicalUsage: Barnabas, whose name means son of consolation, sold a field and laid the money at the apostles' feet. He took Saul by the hand when the church in Jerusalem feared him, was set apart with Saul by the Holy Ghost for the work in Cyprus, and went up with Paul to Jerusalem to settle the question of the Gentiles.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Barnabas is the friend every believer needs, because he believed in Saul when no one else would and he gave away his field before he ever gave a speech. His life says encouragement is not a soft word but a strong act, and I hold that the church grew because Barnabas kept opening doors for men others had shut.
RelatedEvents: Barnabas and Saul Sent Out from Antioch; Paul and Barnabas Part Ways
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: spotted (as if with hail)
BiblicalUsage: Barod means spotted, speckled like hail, and it describes the speckled goats Jacob sees in his dream and the speckled horses in Zechariah's vision.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the speckled flock is God's answer to Laban's cheating, because Jacob's wages came marked by the hand of God.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably from the same as G939 (through the notion of going down; compare G899); weight; in the New Testament only, figuratively, a load, abundance, authority:--burden(-some), weight.
BiblicalUsage: Baros is weight, a burden, a load to be carried. The labourers in the vineyard complain they have borne the burden of the day, Paul tells the Galatians to bear one another's burdens, the council at Jerusalem lays no greater burden on the Gentiles than what is necessary, and Paul says our light affliction works a far more exceeding and eternal weight of glory.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this word teaches us to tell the weights apart, because some burdens are meant to be shared and some are meant to be laid down. The burden of the day is borne together, the burden of the law is lifted by the council, and I hold that the weight of glory is the one burden no believer will ever regret carrying.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a thorn (perhaps as burning brightly)
BiblicalUsage: Barqan is a thorn, a brier, and Gideon threatens to tear the flesh of the men of Succoth with thorns and briers of the wilderness, and then does it.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Gideon's thorns are a warning to every town that refuses bread to God's men on God's errand, because the judge who was patient with Midian was not patient with Succoth.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Barkos, one of the Nethimim
BiblicalUsage: Barkos is named among the Nethinim, the temple servants whose children returned from exile with Zerubbabel.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Barkos is kept in the record because he belonged to the Lord's work, and the servants of the house are written down with the rest.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Chaldee origin (H1247 and probably H6634); son of Sabas (or Tsaba); Bar-sabas, the name of two Israelites:--Barsabas.
BiblicalUsage: Barsabas is the name of two men. Joseph called Barsabas was put forward with Matthias to take the place of Judas, and Judas called Barsabas was sent with Paul and Silas to carry the council's letter to Antioch.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a name shared by two men is kept twice because each man earned his own place in the story, and neither Joseph nor Judas Barsabas is confused with the other in God's record.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Chaldee origin (H1247 and H8526); son of Tolmai; Bar-tholomæus, a Christian apostle:--Bartholomeus.
BiblicalUsage: Bartholomew, the son of Tolmai, is named among the twelve apostles in every list. He is named again among those who waited in the upper room after the ascension.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Bartholomew's quiet name teaches us that faithfulness is not always loud, because he is named in every list of the twelve and says nothing in the record, yet he was chosen and he stayed.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Chaldee origin (H1247 and H2931); son of Timæus (or the unclean); Bar-timæus, an Israelite:--Bartimæus.
BiblicalUsage: Bartimaeus, the son of Timaeus, is the blind beggar sitting by the roadside at Jericho. He cries out to Jesus, son of David, and receives his sight.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Bartimaeus shows what a cry for mercy can do, because he would not be silenced by the crowd, and Jesus stood still for a blind beggar who refused to stop calling.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Baruk, the name of three Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Baruch is the name of three Israelites, and the chief of them is Jeremiah's scribe, who wrote the prophet's words in a book at his mouth, read them in the house of the Lord, and heard God's own word to him when he grew weary. A second Baruch, the son of Zabbai, repaired a measure of the wall in Nehemiah's day.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Baruch matters because he wrote down words that a king tried to burn, and the words outlived the fire. He was weary and God spoke to him by name, and I hold that the scribe who stays faithful to the prophet's words is remembered with the prophet.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: food
BiblicalUsage: Baruth means food, and it appears once, when the psalmist says they gave him gall for his meat and vinegar to drink in his thirst.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that this single verse is remembered because the cross remembered it, when the same gall and vinegar were offered to the Suffering One.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G926; to burden (figuratively):--overcharge.
BiblicalUsage: Baryno means to weigh down, to overcharge the heart, and it appears in the Textus Receptus reading of Jesus' warning to take heed lest our hearts be overcharged with surfeiting and drunkenness and the cares of this life.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that an overcharged heart is a heart too full of this life to watch for the next, and Jesus' warning is the reason we are told to take heed to ourselves.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from the same as G922; weighty, i.e. (fig) burdensome, grave:--grievous, heavy, weightier.
BiblicalUsage: Barys means heavy, weighty, grievous.
