Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: produce (of the earth, etc.)
BiblicalUsage: bûwl — the produce of the earth — turns up in Isaiah among its 2 occurrences. It is a small word, and it stays in its own lane.
TheologicalSignificance: To me, bûwl is a small window into how precisely God speaks.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Bunah, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Bunah was a son of Jerahmeel, the firstborn of Hezron, named among the sons of Judah's line in the genealogy. He is one of the names that carry the family from Hezron toward David.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that God keeps every link in the chain, and Bunah is remembered because his family line mattered.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

BiblicalUsage: Çᵉgid is the Aramaic word for prostrating oneself in homage, and in Daniel it is the word for what Nebuchadnezzar demanded before his golden image. The king's command was to fall down and worship, and Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego refused. It appears 11 times, all in Daniel, and the word follows the king's court through the whole book.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the demand to bow is still with us. Çᵉgid shows what faithfulness looks like: fall down before God alone, and stand when men demand otherwise.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, shut up, i.e. the breast (as enclosing the heart); also gold (as generally shut up safely)
BiblicalUsage: çᵉgôwr — shut up, the breast, also gold kept safely — turns up in Hosea among its 2 occurrences. It is a small word, and it stays in its own lane.
TheologicalSignificance: To me, çᵉgôwr is a small window into how precisely God speaks.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: wealth (as closely shut up)
BiblicalUsage: When Scripture says çᵉgullâh, it means wealth, closely shut up. That is the sense that runs through its 8 occurrences, from 1 Chronicles to Deuteronomy. The word does not change its meaning to suit the passage; the passage leans on the word.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that çᵉgullâh is worth knowing because God gave us the word for wealth, closely shut up. The word is small; the truth it carries is not.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Secacah, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Secacah was a town in the wilderness of Judah, named among Beth-arabah and Middin in the allotment of the land. It is one of the small wilderness towns that fill out Judah's border.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that God gives His people towns even in the wilderness, and Secacah is one of the names that proves no corner of the inheritance was left out.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: silliness; concretely and collectively, dolts
BiblicalUsage: Here is çekel, the word for silliness, dolts. It turns up in Ecclesiastes, and the meaning is as plain as the word is short.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that çekel is small but not slight: silliness, dolts is part of the picture too.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Sela, the rock-city of Idumaea
BiblicalUsage: Sela was the rock-city of Edom, taken by Amaziah in the valley of salt and renamed Joktheel, and named by Isaiah as the place from which a lamb was to be sent to the ruler of the land. A fortress city, cut into rock, and still a landmark in the prophets' words.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God notices the strong places men trust in, and Sela — a rock city taken by war — shows that no fortress stands against Him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Sela-ham-Machlekoth, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Sela-ham-Machlekoth, the rock of divisions, was the place in the wilderness of Maon where Saul turned back from pursuing David to fight the Philistines. The name marks the moment David escaped, because the enemy's attack divided Saul's purpose.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God can turn an enemy's army into a rescue, and this rock is named for the division that saved David's life.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a craggy rock, literally or figuratively (a fortress)
BiblicalUsage: çelaʻ means a craggy rock, a fortress, and the Bible means it plainly. It occurs 53 times in the Old Testament, in 1 Kings and 1 Samuel and elsewhere, and none of those places bends the word out of shape. What it says in one place is what it says in all of them.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe çelaʻ earns its place. A craggy rock, a fortress is the kind of thing God repeats because His people need to hear it more than once.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Seled, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Seled was a son of Nadab, named in the genealogy of Jerahmeel, and the record adds simply that he died without children. His line ends with him, and Scripture says so plainly.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that God records even the lines that end, and Seled is remembered because his name is part of the family story.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: distortion, i.e. (figuratively) viciousness
BiblicalUsage: çeleph is simply distortion, viciousness. Scripture uses it in Proverbs, and the context leaves nothing to guess at.
TheologicalSignificance: My position is that çeleph is no exception: no word in Scripture is filler.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to ascend
BiblicalUsage: When Scripture says çᵉliq, it means to ascend. That is the sense that runs through its 5 occurrences, from Daniel to Ezra. The word does not change its meaning to suit the passage; the passage leans on the word.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that çᵉliq is worth knowing because God gave us the word for to ascend. The word is small; the truth it carries is not.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: pardon
BiblicalUsage: çᵉlîychâh covers pardon, and the Bible uses it the way ordinary people would. You find it 3 times, in Daniel among other places, and each time it is doing the same steady work. It is a word you understand best by watching where it goes, not by guessing at it.
TheologicalSignificance: My position is simple: pardon is part of how God speaks to us, and çᵉlîychâh is the word He chose for it. That is reason enough to learn it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a vine blossom; used also adverbially, abloom
KeyPassages: Song of Solomon 2:13; Song of Solomon 2:15
BiblicalUsage: The word çᵉmâdar is a vine blossom, abloom. You meet it in Song of Solomon, where it does exactly what it sounds like it should do.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that çᵉmâdar shows God wastes no words — every word He gives, including this one, belongs where it is.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Semakjah, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Semachiah was a son of Shemaiah, one of the strong men of the gatekeepers' families who served in the house of the LORD. He stands in the lists of those who kept the doors and the order of the temple.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God honours the men who kept the gates, and Semachiah's name in that list shows that guarding His house is service too.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a likeness
BiblicalUsage: Scripture uses çemel for a likeness. Across its 5 occurrences the word stays true to that sense, whether it stands in 2 Chronicles or in Deuteronomy. That steadiness is what makes it worth knowing.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that çemel proves nothing in Scripture is filler. A likeness turns up again and again because God wants it noticed.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Senaah, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Senaah was a place whose children returned from exile in large numbers, three thousand six hundred and thirty in Ezra's list, and whose sons built the fish gate in Jerusalem's wall. A town that came home and got to work.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that God counts the returning exiles town by town, and Senaah shows a whole community coming back to build.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a fin (collectively)
BiblicalUsage: Here is çᵉnappîyr, the word for a fin. It turns up in Deuteronomy, and the meaning is as plain as the word is short.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that çᵉnappîyr is small but not slight: a fin is part of the picture too.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Seneh, a crag in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Seneh is the southern crag at the pass of Michmash, the sharp rock on the one side of Jonathan's way up to the Philistine garrison. The name marks the ground Jonathan climbed to reach the enemy.
TheologicalSignificance: To me, Seneh is a reminder that God marks the hard ground His people crossed, and this crag is named because Jonathan climbed it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a bramble
BiblicalUsage: Seneh is the thorn bush, and it is remembered for one blazing moment. Moses turned aside to look at a bush that burned without burning up, and out of the middle of it God called him by name. Years later, when Moses blessed Joseph, he still spoke of the good will of him that dwelt in the bush, as if that fire had never left him.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God chose the lowliest thing in the desert to carry His presence — a thorn bush, not a cedar. That tells me He is not looking for impressive vessels; He is looking for ground that will burn without being consumed.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: pointed; (used with the article as a proper name) Senuah, the name of two Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Senuah means pointed, or bristling. It appears as Hasenuah in the Benjamite genealogy, the father in the line of Sallu, and as Senuah in Nehemiah's list, the father of Judah, who was second over the city. Two records, two spellings, one family name kept on both sides of the exile.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a name kept in two lists is a person God did not lose track of, before the exile or after it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a census
BiblicalUsage: Sephar is a census, a counting of people. Solomon used it to number all the strangers in the land of Israel, counting them the way David his father had counted them before him.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that God counts His people — no one is a number to Him, yet no one is overlooked either.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Sephar, a place in Arabia
BiblicalUsage: Sephar is a place in Arabia, named in the table of nations as the eastern edge of Joktan's sons' dwelling. Their land stretched from Mesha as far as Sephar, a mount of the east. It is a boundary marker, showing how far the family of Shem had spread.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe even a place named once, on the edge of the map, matters — God watched over the spreading of every family.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a book
BiblicalUsage: Sephar is the Aramaic word for a book, and it turns up where records decide things. Enemies of the Jews asked that search be made in the book of the records, Darius ordered a search in the house of the rolls, and the priests were set in their courses as it is written in the book of Moses. In Daniel's vision the books were opened before the throne, and judgment began.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe books matter to God because the truth is written down, not left to rumour. What is recorded can be searched, and what is searched will one day be opened.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Sepharad, a region of Assyria
BiblicalUsage: Sepharad is a place where exiled Israelites were held captive, named once in Obadiah's prophecy. The captivity of Israel would possess the land as far as Zarephath, and the captives of Jerusalem in Sepharad would possess the cities of the south. Its exact site is unknown, but its people were not forgotten.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God keeps track of His people even in places we cannot find on a map.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Sepharvites
BiblicalUsage: Sepharvaim was a city in Syria that the king of Assyria conquered, and its people were settled in Samaria after Israel was carried away. The Sepharvites brought their gods with them, and burned their children in the fire to Adrammelech and Anammelech. When the Assyrian envoys mocked Jerusalem, they named the gods of Sepharvaim among the gods that had failed to save their cities.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Sepharvaim shows what exile does — a people carried off, and their gods carried with them, and neither one able to save.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a Sepharvite or inhabitant of Sepharvain
BiblicalUsage: A Sepharvite is an inhabitant of Sepharvaim, and the one place the word appears is a dark one — the Sepharvites burnt their children in fire to their gods after being settled in Samaria.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this single hard verse is there to show how far a people can fall when they carry their idols into a new land.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a basin (as deepened out)
BiblicalUsage: Sephel is a bowl or basin, deep enough to hold something precious. Jael brought Sisera butter in a lordly dish, and Gideon wrung a bowl full of water from the dew on his fleece.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that ordinary vessels carry the turning points of the story — a bowl of milk before a killing, a bowl of dew before a calling.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: chastisement; also satiety
BiblicalUsage: Sepheq is a rare word, and even the scholars say its meaning is doubtful — something like a stroke, or satiety, or mocking. It appears in Job, where Zophar warns that the wicked man, full of himself, will be struck down, and Elihu warns Job to beware the stroke of God's wrath.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that when a word is uncertain, honesty is the right answer — Scripture does not need me to pretend I know.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, writing (the art or a document); by implication, a book
BiblicalUsage: Sepher is the book — writing, a letter, a record, a scroll — and it runs through the whole Bible. Genesis opens the book of the generations of Adam, God told Moses to write the defeat of Amalek in a book for a memorial, the priest wrote curses in a book in the trial of jealousy, and every king was to write out a copy of the law in a book and read it all his life.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God is a God who writes things down, because His people forget and His promises do not. A book outlasts a memory, and that is why the book outlasts the king.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a (sea-going) vessel (as ceiled with a deck)
BiblicalUsage: Sephinah is a sea-going ship, and it appears once, in the storm that chased Jonah. The mariners were afraid and threw the wares out of the ship to lighten it, while Jonah slept below.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the ship matters because it shows how far a man will run — and that no ship outruns God.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a numeration
BiblicalUsage: Sephorah is a numbering, and it appears once, in a psalm of old age. The psalmist says his mouth will tell of God's righteousness all day long, for he does not know the numbers of it — God's mercies are past counting.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that some things are too many to count, and that is the best kind of arithmetic.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a redundancy
BiblicalUsage: Serach is the excess, the overhanging part — the half curtain left over from the coverings of the tabernacle, which was to hang over the back of it.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe even the leftover curtain had its place, because in God's house nothing is wasted.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Sered, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Sered was the first son of Zebulun, named among the sons who went down to Egypt with Jacob. His family, the Sardites, was still counted in the wilderness census a generation later.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God keeps the family lines straight, and a name in a list is a person He has not forgotten.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an axle; figuratively, a peer
BiblicalUsage: Seren is a lord, a ruler — the title of the five Philistine lords who ruled the coastal cities. They gathered to decide what to do with the ark of God, and they watched it go back to Israel. The same word also means an axle, and it is used for the axles under the great bronze bases in Solomon's temple.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the Philistine lords show the limit of earthly power: five rulers in council could not decide what to do with the ark of God. God lets rulers scheme, and His ark does not answer to them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to conceal; figuratively, to demolish
BiblicalUsage: Sethar is an Aramaic word for hiding — or for tearing down. Daniel praises the God who reveals deep and secret things, and Ezra records the other side of it — how God gave the house into Nebuchadnezzar's hand to be destroyed.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that nothing stays hidden from God, and nothing He hides stays hidden from us for ever.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: winter (as the dark season)
BiblicalUsage: Sethav is winter, the dark rainy season, and it appears once, in the Song — the winter is past, the rain is over and gone, and the time of singing has come.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe winter in Scripture is never the end of the story; it is the season before the singing.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a cover (in a good or a bad, a literal or a figurative sense)
BiblicalUsage: Sether is a covering, a hiding place, a secret — and it cuts both ways. Moses warns of the brother or friend who entices you secretly, Ehud claims a secret errand for the king, Jonathan warns David in secret that Saul means to kill him, and Nathan tells David his sin was done secretly while God's judgment would be done in the open.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the secret is the test of the heart: what we hide, God sees, and what He hides us in, no enemy finds. I hold that His covering is the only secret place that is safe.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Sethur, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Sethur was the son of Michael, the spy sent from the tribe of Asher to search out the land. His name means hidden, and he is named once, in the list of the twelve spies.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a man named once is still known by God, and his name is kept because he walked where God sent him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Seven, a place in Upper Egypt
BiblicalUsage: Syene is a town of Egypt on the frontier of Cush, named by its Hebrew name Seveneh. God says He will make Egypt desolate from Migdol to Syene, and the pride of her power will fall from the tower of Syene.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the far edge of Egypt is still inside God's reach — no border town is beyond His judgment or His knowledge.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to secrete
BiblicalUsage: Chaba means to hide, and its first use is the saddest in the Bible — Adam and his wife hid themselves from God among the trees of the garden. After that it runs both ways: Rahab hid the spies and lived, Abimelech's youngest brother hid himself and lived, and Saul hid himself among the baggage when they came to make him king.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe hiding is the first thing sin teaches us and the last thing God leaves us doing. He finds the hidden man, whether to judge him or to crown him.
RelatedEvents: The Fall; The Walls of Jericho
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, to hide (as in the bosom), i.e. to cherish (with affection)
BiblicalUsage: Chabab is a tender word — to hide in the bosom, to cherish, to love fervently. Moses uses it once, in his blessing: God loved the people, and all His saints are in His hand.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this is the heart of the whole Bible — God does not merely rule His people, He cherishes them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to secrete
BiblicalUsage: Chabah is another word for hiding, and it is usually hiding for a purpose. Rahab told the spies to hide in the mountain for three days, Micaiah warned Ahab's friend he would one day hide in an inner chamber, the king of Samaria suspected the Syrians were hiding in the field, and Isaiah told God's people to hide themselves for a little moment until His anger passed.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe there is a hiding that is fear and a hiding that is faith, and the difference is who told you to hide. When God says hide, it is shelter, not shame.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to ruin
BiblicalUsage: Chabal in Aramaic means to ruin or destroy, and Daniel uses it for the kingdoms of this world. God will destroy any king who lifts a hand against His house, He will set up a kingdom that will never be destroyed, the great tree will be cut down and destroyed, and yet Daniel himself was not hurt — the lions could not destroy a man God had kept.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the kingdoms that destroy are themselves destroyed, and the kingdom that cannot be destroyed belongs to the God of heaven. That is the whole story of Daniel in one word.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to ruin
BiblicalUsage: Chabal in Aramaic means to ruin or destroy, and Daniel uses it for the kingdoms of this world. God will destroy any king who lifts a hand against His house, He will set up a kingdom that will never be destroyed, the great tree will be cut down and destroyed, and yet Daniel himself was not hurt — the lions could not destroy a man God had kept.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the kingdoms that destroy are themselves destroyed, and the kingdom that cannot be destroyed belongs to the God of heaven. That is the whole story of Daniel in one word.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to wind tightly (as a rope), i.e. to bind; specifically, by a pledge; figuratively, to pervert, destroy; also to writhe in pain (especially of parturition)
BiblicalUsage: Chabal in Hebrew covers binding, pledging, and ruining — one root for ropes, debts, and wreckage. The law would not let a man take a neighbour's garment or millstone as a pledge for a debt, Nehemiah confessed that Israel had dealt very corruptly, and Job said his breath was corrupt and his days were nearly spent.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this word warns me twice: do not bind your neighbour in a debt he cannot pay, and do not let your own heart grow corrupt. God hates the pledge that crushes the poor, and He heals the ruin that sin makes.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to clasp (the hands or in embrace)
BiblicalUsage: Chabaq means to embrace, to clasp in the arms. Laban ran and embraced Jacob when he came, Elisha promised the Shunammite woman she would embrace a son, the poor embrace the rock for want of a shelter, and wisdom says to embrace her and she will bring you to honour.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe an embrace in Scripture is never small: it is welcome, promise, shelter, and honour all at once. God embraces His people the way Laban embraced Jacob — running to meet them, not waiting to be asked.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chabakkuk, the prophet
BiblicalUsage: Habakkuk means embrace, and the prophet's name stands at the head of his burden and of his prayer. The burden which Habakkuk the prophet did see opens the book, and his prayer upon Shigionoth closes it.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe his name fits his book: a man who wrestled with God and ended by clinging to Him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an associate
BiblicalUsage: Chabar in Aramaic means a companion, a fellow. When the decree went out to kill the wise men of Babylon, they sought Daniel and his fellows to be slain, and Daniel went home and told the thing to Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah, his companions, so they would pray together for mercy.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God gives His servants companions for the night the decree goes out. Daniel did not face the king's fury alone, and neither do we.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to join (literally or figuratively); specifically (by means of spells) to fascinate
BiblicalUsage: Chabar means to join, to bind together — and joining cuts both ways. The kings of the plain joined together in the vale of Siddim, the curtains of the tabernacle were coupled together into one covering, the law forbids the charmer who joins himself to spirits, and Jehoshaphat joined himself with wicked Ahaziah, who did very wickedly.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe joining is a spiritual act: what you join yourself to, you become. Curtains joined together make a dwelling for God, and a king joined to a wicked king joins himself to the wickedness.
RelatedEvents: Jehoshaphat's Victory by Prayer and Praise
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a streak (like a line), as on the tiger
BiblicalUsage: Chabarburah is a stripe or a spot — the leopard's markings. Jeremiah asks whether the Ethiopian can change his skin, or the leopard his spots, and then turns the question on a people accustomed to doing evil.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the leopard's spots are there to tell us what we cannot do for ourselves — and why we need a God who can.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to wrap firmly (especially a turban, compress, or saddle); figuratively, to stop, to rule
BiblicalUsage: Chabash means to bind on, to saddle, to gird — to get ready. Abraham saddled his ass for the journey to Moriah, Moses girded Aaron's sons with girdles for the priesthood, and Balaam saddled his ass and went with the princes of Moab. The same word is used for binding up wounds, so readiness and healing share one root.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God binds up what is broken and girds up what is sent. Abraham was saddled for obedience, Aaron was girded for service, and the same hands that bind the wound send the servant out.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to knock out or off
BiblicalUsage: Chabat means to beat out, to thresh. The law said to beat the olive tree once and leave the rest for the stranger, Gideon was beating out wheat in a winepress when the angel found him, Ruth beat out the barley she had gleaned, and God promises He will beat off His people one by one and gather them.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe threshing is how God separates what feeds from what does not. Gideon threshed in hiding and became a judge, Ruth threshed what she gleaned and became an ancestor of kings.
RelatedEvents: Gideon's Victory over Midian; Ruth's Loyalty
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chabatstsanjah, a Rechabite
BiblicalUsage: Habaziniah means light of Jehovah, and he is named once, as the father of Jeremiah and the head of a Rechabite family. Jeremiah took his grandson Jaazaniah and the whole house of the Rechabites into the temple to test their vow.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a father whose name means light of Jehovah, and whose children kept their vow, is worth remembering.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably meadow-saffron
BiblicalUsage: Chabatstseleth is a flower of the meadow — a crocus, or a rose. The beloved says she is the rose of Sharon, and Isaiah promises the desert will blossom as the rose.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God plants His roses in the desert on purpose, so no one can say beauty belongs only to gardens.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chabajah, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Habaiah means Jehovah has hidden. His children are named among the priests who came back from exile, in Ezra's list and again in Nehemiah's, a family whose name means God hid them — and kept them.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that God hides His priests sometimes, and hiding is not the same as forgetting.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a partner
BiblicalUsage: Chabbar is a partner, a companion in trade. God asks Job whether the companions will make a banquet of Leviathan and part him out among the merchants.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the question is the point: no partnership of men can carve up what only God can tame.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, bound (with stripes), i.e. a weal (or black-and-blue mark itself)
BiblicalUsage: Chabbuwrah is a bruise, a stripe, a wound. Lamech boasted of a wound he had given, the law answered wound for wound and stripe for stripe, Proverbs says the blueness of a wound cleanses away evil, and Isaiah says the Servant was wounded for our transgressions and with His stripes we are healed.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe every stripe in this word leads to one place: the wounds men give each other, and the wounds Christ took for us. His stripes are the only ones that heal instead of hurt.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an associate
BiblicalUsage: Chaber is a companion, a fellow, one knit to another. All Israel gathered against Gibeah knit together as one man, the King is anointed above His fellows, the man who robs his parents is the companion of a destroyer, and two are better than one because if one falls the other lifts up his fellow.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe companionship is a moral choice: you are either knit to God's people or companion to a destroyer. There is no third company to join.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a consort
BiblicalUsage: Chabereth is a consort, a companion — the wife of your youth, the wife of your covenant, the one the LORD Himself witnessed between you and her.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe marriage is a companionship before it is anything else, and God stands witness to it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: something fried, probably a griddle-cake
BiblicalUsage: Chabeth is a flat cake, a griddle-cake, and it appears once, in the temple duties: Mattithiah the Levite had the set office over the things made in the pans.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God counts the man over the pans among His servants, and no temple duty is too small to be named.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a pawn (as security for debt)
BiblicalUsage: Chabol is a pledge, something held as security for a debt. Ezekiel draws the righteous man twice over: he has restored the debtor's pledge, given bread to the hungry, and spoiled none by violence, while the wicked has withheld the pledge and oppressed the poor. The repentant man proves his change by restoring the pledge and giving back what he robbed.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a pledge is a test of the heart: the righteous man gives it back, the wicked man keeps it, and the repentant man proves his repentance by returning it. God watches what we hold over the poor.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chabor, a river of Assyria
BiblicalUsage: Habor is a river of Assyria, and its name marks the exile. When Samaria fell, Israel was carried away and placed in Halah and in Habor by the river of Gozan, and the tribes beyond the Jordan were carried there too.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a river can be a sentence: the Habor is where God's people lived out the judgment they were warned about for generations.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an associate
BiblicalUsage: Chabrah is a fellow, a companion, and it appears once, in Daniel's vision of the little horn — a horn whose look was more stout than his fellows.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe pride always measures itself against its fellows, and the little horn's pride is the warning.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, overthrown, i.e. (morally) crime
BiblicalUsage: Chabuwlah is a hurtful deed, a crime, a wrong. Daniel tells the king he has done no hurt before God or before the king, and the lions' mouths were shut.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe innocence is not an argument Daniel made — it is a verdict God gave, and the lions agreed.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, perhaps to bow (the neck only in courtesy to an equal), i.e. to be kind; also (by euphemistically, but rarely) to reprove
BiblicalUsage: Chacad means to be kind, to show mercy — and, strangely, it can also mean to be put to shame. David sings it twice over: with the merciful God will show Himself merciful. Proverbs uses the other edge of it, warning that a man who betrays a secret will be put to shame and his infamy will not turn away.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe mercy is the shape of God's dealings: He shows Himself merciful to the merciful, and the man who shows no mercy finds shame waiting for him. The shame in Proverbs is the other side of the same coin: mercy withheld turns to disgrace.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chasadjah, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Hasadiah means Jehovah has been faithful. He is named once, among the sons of Zerubbabel listed after the exile — Hashubah, Ohel, Berechiah, Hasadiah, and Jushab-hesed, five in all.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a boy named Jehovah has been faithful, born to a family that came home from exile, is a promise you can hold in your hand.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to flee for protection; figuratively, to confide in
BiblicalUsage: Chacah means to flee for protection, to trust, to take refuge. Moses asks where the gods are, the rock in whom they trusted; the bramble invites the trees to trust in its shadow; Boaz tells Ruth a full reward will be given her, because she came to trust under the wings of the God of Israel; and David sings that God is his rock, his shield, his high tower, and his refuge.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe trust is not a feeling but a place — under wings, behind a shield, inside a tower. The bramble offers a shadow and gives thorns; God offers His wings and gives shelter.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to eat off
BiblicalUsage: Chacal means to consume, to finish off. Moses warns that Israel will carry much seed into the field and gather little, because the locust will consume it.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the locust is God's arithmetic: much seed in, little harvest out, when His people will not listen.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to muzzle; by analogy, to stop the nose
BiblicalUsage: Chacam means to muzzle, to stop up. The law says not to muzzle the ox when it treads out the corn, and Ezekiel says the burial valley of Gog will stop the noses of travellers passing by.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God muzzles no worker and stops up no honest mouth — but He will stop the road of the proud dead.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to hold in occupancy
BiblicalUsage: Chacan is an Aramaic word for holding, possessing, occupying. Daniel is told the saints of the Most High will take the kingdom and possess it for ever, even for ever and ever.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the kingdom is not rented by the saints — it is theirs to hold, for ever.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, to (be) compact; by implication, to hoard
BiblicalUsage: Chacan means to hoard, to lay up treasure. Isaiah says the merchandise of Tyre will be holiness to the LORD: it will not be treasured nor laid up, but given for food and fine clothing to those who dwell before Him.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe wealth hoarded is wealth wasted, and wealth given to God feeds His people.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a clod
BiblicalUsage: Chacaph is a clod, clay. Nebuchadnezzar's image had feet part of iron and part of clay, and the stone cut out without hands struck the image on those feet of iron and clay.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe clay in a king's statue is the whole story: strength mixed with dust, and dust is what breaks first.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: deficient
BiblicalUsage: Chacciyr means deficient, wanting. The writing on the wall read TEKEL: thou art weighed in the balances, and art found wanting.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God's scales do not lie, and Belshazzar is the warning to every king who thinks his own weight is enough.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: lacking; hence, without
BiblicalUsage: Chacer means to lack, to be without, to fail. Achish asks whether he has need of mad men, David curses Joab's house that it will never fail to have one sick or in need, Pharaoh asks Hadad what he has lacked with him, and Proverbs says the adulterer lacks understanding and destroys his own soul.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe lack is the Bible's plainest teacher: what a man lacks shows what he worships. The house that lacks bread, the king who lacks sense, and the heart that lacks understanding all tell the same story.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: lacking; hence, without
BiblicalUsage: Chacer means to lack, to be without, to fail. Achish asks whether he has need of mad men, David curses Joab's house that it will never fail to have one sick or in need, Pharaoh asks Hadad what he has lacked with him, and Proverbs says the adulterer lacks understanding and destroys his own soul.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe lack is the Bible's plainest teacher: what a man lacks shows what he worships. The house that lacks bread, the king who lacks sense, and the heart that lacks understanding all tell the same story.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a ring for the nose (or lips)
BiblicalUsage: Chach is a ring or a hook — the rings and bracelets the people brought willingly for the tabernacle, and the hook God promises to put in the nose of the raging king of Assyria to turn him back.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God puts a ring in the nose of the proud and a ring on the finger of the willing, and the difference is the heart.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, kind, i.e. (religiously) pious (a saint)
BiblicalUsage: Chaciyd means kind, godly, a saint — the merciful one. Moses calls Levi God's holy one, Hannah sings that He will keep the feet of His saints, David sings that with the merciful God shows Himself merciful, and Solomon prays that God's saints will rejoice in goodness.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a saint in the Old Testament is not a perfect person but a kind one — one God has been kind to, and who shows it back. Kindness is the mark of the godly, and God keeps the feet of the kind.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: the kind (maternal) bird, i.e. a stork
BiblicalUsage: Chaciydah is the stork, the kind or maternal bird, named in the lists of unclean birds — the stork, the heron after her kind, the lapwing, and the bat.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the stork's name is a small mercy in the law: even among the birds Israel could not eat, God names one for kindness.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: the ravager, i.e. a locust
BiblicalUsage: Chaciyl is the ravager, the locust, the caterpillar that eats the harvest. Solomon names it in his prayer for famine and pestilence, the psalm remembers how God gave Egypt's increase to the caterpillar, and Isaiah says the spoil will be gathered like caterpillars swarming over the land.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the caterpillar is God's smallest army: no sword, no siege, only hunger with wings. When the harvest is eaten, the land knows who sent it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, firm, i.e. (by implication) mighty
BiblicalUsage: Chaciyn means firm, mighty, strong — and it appears once, in the psalmist's question: O LORD God of hosts, who is a strong LORD like unto Thee?
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the question answers itself: no one is strong like the LORD, and His faithfulness stands round about Him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: powerful
BiblicalUsage: Chacon means powerful, strong — and both times it falls. Isaiah says the strong will be as tow, burning with his own work, and Amos says God destroyed the Amorite who was strong as the oaks.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe human strength is tow before a spark, and the oak-strong Amorite is the proof.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a shred or scale
BiblicalUsage: Chacpac is a shred, a flake, a small round thing — the manna lying on the face of the wilderness like a small round thing, as small as the hoar frost on the ground.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God feeds His people with flakes, not feasts, because daily bread teaches daily trust.
RelatedEvents: Manna and Quail in the Wilderness
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chasrah, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Chasrah is named once, in the line of Huldah the prophetess: Shallum the son of Tikvah, the son of Hasrah, keeper of the wardrobe. His name survives because his grandson's wife spoke the word of the LORD to the king.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a grandfather's name can be kept by his grandson's wife, and a keeper of the wardrobe can stand in the line of a prophetess.
RelatedPeople: Huldah, Prophetess; Shallum, Husband of Huldah
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: confidence
BiblicalUsage: Chacuwth is confidence, trust — and Isaiah says the strength of Pharaoh will be their shame, and the trust in the shadow of Egypt their confusion.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe confidence is only as good as the shadow it stands in, and Egypt's shadow is a shame.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: as card. one; as article single; as an ordinal, first; adverbially, at once
BiblicalUsage: Chad is the Aramaic word for one — first, single, only. It stands at the head of the letter Rehum wrote against Jerusalem, it marks the first year of Cyrus, the one great image of Nebuchadnezzar's dream, and the one decree hanging over the wise men who could not tell it.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe one is the loneliest number in Daniel: one image, one decree, one God who knows the dream. When everything comes down to one, it comes down to Him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: as card. one; as article single; as an ordinal, first; adverbially, at once
BiblicalUsage: Chad is the Aramaic word for one — first, single, only. It stands at the head of the letter Rehum wrote against Jerusalem, it marks the first year of Cyrus, the one great image of Nebuchadnezzar's dream, and the one decree hanging over the wise men who could not tell it.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe one is the loneliest number in Daniel: one image, one decree, one God who knows the dream. When everything comes down to one, it comes down to Him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: as card. one; as article single; as an ordinal, first; adverbially, at once
BiblicalUsage: Chad is the Aramaic word for one — first, single, only. It stands at the head of the letter Rehum wrote against Jerusalem, it marks the first year of Cyrus, the one great image of Nebuchadnezzar's dream, and the one decree hanging over the wise men who could not tell it.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe one is the loneliest number in Daniel: one image, one decree, one God who knows the dream. When everything comes down to one, it comes down to Him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chadad, an Ishmaelite
BiblicalUsage: Hadad was a son of Ishmael, named in the list of his twelve sons. The King James spells his name Hadar in Genesis and Hadad in Chronicles, but the Hebrew is the same man.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the two spellings are a small reminder to read carefully — one man, two spellings, and the same God keeping the list.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to be (causatively, make) sharp or (figuratively) severe
BiblicalUsage: Chadad means to be sharp, to make sharp, or to be fierce. Iron sharpens iron and a man sharpens his friend, the sword of the LORD is sharpened to make a sore slaughter, and the horses of the Chaldeans are more fierce than the evening wolves.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe sharpening is either friendship or judgment, and the edge is the same. Iron sharpens iron for good, and the sword is sharpened for slaughter — the difference is whose hand holds it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to rejoice
BiblicalUsage: Chadah means to rejoice, to be glad. Jethro rejoiced for all the goodness the LORD had done to Israel, the king is made exceeding glad with God's countenance, and Job turns the word dark — wishing the night of his birth had never been glad, never been counted among the days of the year.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe gladness is the natural sound of a heart that has seen God's goodness, and Job's wish shows what sorrow does to it. Joy is the first thing grief tries to take, and the last thing God restores.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, to be flabby, i.e. (by implication) desist; (figuratively) be lacking or idle
BiblicalUsage: Chadal means to cease, to leave off, to forbear. The builders of Babel left off building the city when God scattered them, Moses said the thunder would cease when he prayed, the man who forbears to keep the passover is cut off, and the poor will never cease out of the land.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe ceasing is God's work and man's duty in turn: He stops the thunder, He stops the tower, and He tells us never to stop opening our hands to the poor. The poor never cease, and neither should our open hands.
RelatedEvents: The Tower of Babel; The Plague of Hail
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chadar, an Ishmaelite
BiblicalUsage: Chadar is a name that lives in a spelling. The King James prints Hadar in the list of Ishmael's sons in Genesis, but the Hebrew text behind it reads Hadad, the same name given in Chronicles. Strong's keeps Chadar as its own entry because some copies read it with an r, and the word itself never stands anywhere else in the Hebrew Bible.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God lets the variant stand without letting it confuse the story — one son of Ishmael, whether the copy says Hadar or Hadad.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, to inclose (as a room), i.e. (by analogy,) to beset (as in a siege)
BiblicalUsage: Chadar means to enclose, to beset, to shut in — and it appears once, in the sword-song of Ezekiel, where the sword of the slain enters into their privy chambers.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a sword that finds the inner chamber is the picture of judgment that cannot be shut out.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: new
BiblicalUsage: Chadash means new. A new king arose over Egypt who knew not Joseph, the feasts brought a new meat offering, the firstfruits were a new offering, and the law excused the man who had built a new house and not yet dedicated it.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe new in Scripture is a mixed word: a new king can mean forgetfulness, a new offering can mean firstfruits, and a new house can mean a blessing not yet enjoyed. New is not good or bad by itself — it depends on whose hands hold it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to be new; causatively, to rebuild
BiblicalUsage: Chadash means to be new, to renew, to rebuild. Samuel called Israel to Gilgal to renew the kingdom, Asa renewed the altar of the LORD, Job complained that God renewed His witnesses against him, and David prayed, Create in me a clean heart, and renew a right spirit within me.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe renewal is God's trade: He renews kingdoms and altars and spirits, and even Job's complaint is answered by it. The only renewal that lasts is the one David asked for — a right spirit, made new inside.
RelatedEvents: David and Bathsheba; Saul Rescues Jabesh-Gilead
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chadashah, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Hadashah was a town in the low country of Judah, named once among the cities of the tribe — Zenan, Hadashah, and Migdal-gad. It is one of the many small towns the book of Joshua records without another word.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the small towns are kept for a reason: Judah's inheritance was measured town by town, and none was left off the list.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: new
BiblicalUsage: Chadath means new, and it appears once, in the order for rebuilding the temple: three rows of great stones, and a row of new timber, paid for out of the king's house.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe new timber for an old house is the whole story of the return — the same God, the same temple, and fresh wood to build it with.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a point
BiblicalUsage: Chadduwd is a sharp point, and it appears once, under Leviathan: sharp stones are under him, and he spreads sharp pointed things upon the mire.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the sharp stones under Leviathan are there to tell Job what he cannot do — no man tames what God made untamable.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: vacant, i.e. ceasing or destitute
BiblicalUsage: Chadel means frail, forsaken, ceasing. The psalmist asks to know his end, that he may know how frail he is; Isaiah's Servant is despised and rejected of men; and Ezekiel is told that he who forbears may forbear, and he who hears may hear.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe frailty and rejection meet in one Man: the Servant was despised and rejected, and the psalmist's frailty is the reason He came. God does not despise the frail — He became forsaken for them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a breast
BiblicalUsage: Chadiy is a breast, and it appears once, in the image of Nebuchadnezzar's dream: the head of fine gold, the breast and arms of silver.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the breast of silver is the second kingdom, and silver is the warning that every kingdom after gold is a little less.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chadid, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Hadid was a town of Benjamin, named with Lod and Ono in the lists of the return — the children of Lod, Hadid, and Ono came back, seven hundred and twenty-five of them, and the town was settled again in Nehemiah's day. It sits in the lists of the return, among the towns Judah's families came home to.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a town that comes home is a promise kept, and Hadid's number is written down because every returning family counted.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chadlai, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Chadlai is named once, as the father of Amasa, one of the heads of Ephraim who stood against bringing the captives of Judah to Samaria. His son's stand is the only thing the record keeps of him, and it is enough.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Amasa's mercy is Chadlai's memorial — a son's stand can be a father's whole story.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chadrak, a Syrian deity
BiblicalUsage: Hadrach is a land named once, in Zechariah's oracle — the burden of the word of the LORD in the land of Hadrach, and Damascus shall be the rest thereof. The oracle names it first, before Damascus, as a place where God's word comes to rest.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God's word rests even on lands we cannot place, and Hadrach is the proof that no border is outside His burden.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a festival, or a victim therefor
BiblicalUsage: Chag is a feast, a festival — and sometimes the sacrifice offered at it. Moses told Pharaoh they would go with young and old to hold a feast to the LORD, the law fixed the feast of unleavened bread in the spring, and the feast of weeks in the summer, each with its offering.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the feasts are God's calendar of joy: He commands His people to eat, to rest, and to remember together. A God who commands feasts is not a God who grudges happiness.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, vertigo, i.e. (figuratively) fear
BiblicalUsage: Chaga is terror, a reeling fear — and it appears once, when Isaiah says the land of Judah will be a terror to Egypt, and everyone who mentions it will be afraid, because of the counsel of the LORD of hosts.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the counsel of the LORD is what makes Judah terrible to Egypt, not Judah's armies.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chagab, one of the Nethinim
BiblicalUsage: Hagab is named once, among the Nethinim who returned — the children of Hagab, the children of Shalmai, the children of Hanan. He is one of the temple servants whose families came home from exile.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the Nethinim are the proof that no servant in God's house is forgotten, even when his name appears once.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a locust
BiblicalUsage: Chagab is a locust, a grasshopper. The law allows the locust to be eaten, the spies said they were grasshoppers beside the giants, God warns that He may command the locusts to devour the land, and the preacher says in old age the grasshopper will be a burden.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the grasshopper is the Bible's picture of smallness: small enough to eat, small enough to fear giants, small enough to be a burden — and big enough, in God's hand, to strip a land bare. Smallness is not safety when God sends it, and it is not shame when He holds it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chagaba or Chagabah, one of the Nethinim
BiblicalUsage: Hagabah is named twice, once in each return list, spelled Hagabah in Ezra and Hagaba in Nehemiah — the children of Hagabah among the Nethinim who came back from exile. Two lists, two spellings, one family that came home.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a name kept in two lists, with two spellings, is a person God brought home twice over.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, to move in a circle, i.e. (specifically) to march in a sacred procession, to observe a festival; by implication, to be giddy
BiblicalUsage: Chagag means to keep a feast, to march in a sacred dance, to celebrate. Moses told Pharaoh to let the people go so they could hold a feast to the LORD in the wilderness, and the law commands the feast of tabernacles and the feast of weeks, seven days of rejoicing before the LORD.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the first thing God asked Pharaoh for was not wages or weapons but a feast. Freedom in the Bible starts with worship, and worship starts with letting go.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to gird on (as a belt, armor, etc.)
BiblicalUsage: Chagar means to gird on — a belt, armour, a sword. Israel ate the Passover with loins girded and staff in hand, Moses girded Aaron with the girdle of the ephod, the spies girded themselves to go up and fight, and Ehud girded a dagger under his raiment on his right thigh.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe girding is the posture of a people about to move: Passover girded for the road, Aaron girded for service, Ehud girded for the deed. God does not call ungirded men.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a rift in rocks
BiblicalUsage: Chagav is a cleft, a rift in the rocks. The beloved is called a dove in the clefts of the rock, and the prophets use the same picture against Edom — you that dwell in the clefts of the rock, whose habitation is high, your pride has deceived you.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the cleft of the rock holds two opposite people: the dove who hides there in love, and the proud man who hides there in pride. The rock is the same; the heart is different.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chaggai, a Hebrew prophet
BiblicalUsage: Haggai was a prophet of the return, and his name is tied to the rebuilding. He prophesied to the Jews in Judah and Jerusalem, the elders prospered through his prophesying and Zechariah's, and his own book opens with the word of the LORD coming by Haggai in the second year of Darius.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Haggai is the prophet for every stalled building: God sends a word, the hands take up the work again, and the house rises.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chaggi, an Israelite; also (patronymically) a Chaggite, or descendant of the same
BiblicalUsage: Haggi was a son of Gad, named among those who went down to Egypt with Jacob, and his family, the Haggites, was counted in the wilderness a generation later. Egypt and the wilderness are two ends of one journey, and his family is counted at both.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a son of Gad who went down to Egypt and a family still counted in the wilderness are one promise kept across two generations.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chaggijah, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Haggiah was the son of Shimea, named once in the genealogy of the Levites — Shimea his son, Haggiah his son, Asaiah his son. His name sits between his father and his son, and that is all the record keeps of him.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a name in a genealogy is never filler: Haggiah is kept because the line was kept, and the line was kept because God keeps His own.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chaggith, a wife of David
BiblicalUsage: Haggith was a wife of David and the mother of Adonijah, named whenever Adonijah is named — the fourth son born in Hebron, the son who exalted himself to be king, and in the genealogy of David's sons. Her name is carried by her son's story, for good and for ill.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a mother's name in a son's rebellion is a sad kind of fame, and Haggith's is kept so we remember the house Adonijah came from.
RelatedPeople: King David; Adonijah, Son of David; Haggith, Wife of David
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a belt (for the waist)
BiblicalUsage: Chagowr is a belt, a girdle for the waist. After the fall, Adam and Eve sewed fig leaves together and made themselves girdles, and Jonathan stripped himself of his robe and gave David his girdle with his sword and his bow.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the girdle tells the whole story twice: man's first covering was sewn by his own hands, and Jonathan's girdle was given away in love.
RelatedEvents: The Fall; David and Jonathan's Covenant Friendship
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: belted
BiblicalUsage: Chagowr means belted, girded. The virtuous woman makes fine linen and sells girdles to the merchant, and Ezekiel sees the Babylonian captains girded with girdles upon their loins, in dyed attire, all of them princes to look to.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a girdle is honest work in one verse and painted pride in the other, and the difference is who is wearing it and why.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a primary verb; to be "cheer"ful, i.e. calmly happy or well-off; impersonally, especially as salutation (on meeting or parting), be well:--farewell, be glad, God speed, greeting, hall, joy(- fully), rejoice.
BiblicalUsage: Chairo means to rejoice, to be glad, and the Gospels use it for gladness of every kind. The wise men rejoiced with exceeding great joy when they saw the star, many would rejoice at John's birth, the friend of the bridegroom rejoices greatly at the bridegroom's voice — and the chief priests were glad when Judas offered to betray Jesus.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe joy is proved by its object: the wise men rejoiced at a star that led to a child, the bridegroom's friend rejoiced at a voice, and the priests rejoiced at a betrayal. Gladness is not good by itself — it depends on what you are glad about.
RelatedEvents: The Magi Visit Jesus; The Birth of John the Baptist
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, to adhere to; hence, to await
BiblicalUsage: Chakah means to wait, to tarry, to hold on. The four lepers said if they tarried till morning light, mischief would come on them; Job says men long for death and dig for it like hidden treasure; the psalm says our soul waits for the LORD, our help and shield; and Isaiah says he will wait on the LORD who hides His face from the house of Jacob.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe waiting is the Bible's hardest work: the lepers waited wrongly, Job waited in darkness, and Isaiah waited on a hidden face. The waiting that saves is the waiting that looks for Him.
RelatedEvents: The Siege of Samaria and the Four Lepers
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chakaljah, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Hachaliah is named twice, both times as the father of Nehemiah — the words of Nehemiah the son of Hachaliah open the book, and his name stands among those who sealed the covenant. Two mentions, and both are about his son.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a father is remembered by his son's work, and Hachaliah's son rebuilt a wall and a people.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: wise, (i.e. intelligent, skilful or artful)
BiblicalUsage: Chakam means wise — intelligent, skilful, artful. Pharaoh called for all the magicians and wise men of Egypt, Moses told Israel to take wise men to be rulers over them, and Sisera's mother listened to her wise ladies while she waited for his chariot.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe wisdom in this word is a skill before it is a virtue: Pharaoh's wise men could copy a wonder, and Moses wanted rulers who were wise and known. True wisdom is known by what it does, not by what it can imitate.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to be wise (in mind, word or act)
BiblicalUsage: Chakam is the verb, to be wise, and it is used for scheming as well as for sense. Pharaoh said, let us deal wisely with the Hebrews, lest they multiply; Moses wished Israel were wise enough to consider their latter end; Solomon was wiser than all men; and Elihu says great men are not always wise.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this word warns me that wisdom can be a weapon: Pharaoh's wisdom was cruelty with a plan, and Solomon's was a gift with a name. The difference is whether wisdom bows to God or uses Him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chakilah, a hill in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Hachilah is the hill in the wilderness of Ziph where David hid from Saul, named when the Ziphites betrayed him to Saul at Gibeah and when Saul camped on the hill itself, before Jeshimon, while David waited in the wilderness. It is a hill of hiding, and of sparing — David hid there, and there he spared the king who hunted him.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Hachilah is the hill of the hunted man: David hid there, Saul camped there, and God kept the one and spared the other.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a hook (as adhering)
BiblicalUsage: Chakkah is a hook, an angle for fishing. God asks Job whether he can draw out Leviathan with a hook, Isaiah says the fishers who cast angle into the Nile will mourn, and Habakkuk says the Chaldeans take up all men with the angle and gather them in their net.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the hook is God's question and man's net in turn: He asks Job if he can hook Leviathan, and the Chaldeans hook whole nations. Only one of them is fishing with God's leave.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: wise, i.e. a Magian
BiblicalUsage: Chakkiym is the Aramaic word for wise men, the Magians of Babylon. The king commanded that all the wise men be destroyed, they sought Daniel and his fellows to be slain, Daniel answered Arioch with counsel and wisdom, and the four friends prayed that they would not perish with the rest of the wise men.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Babylon's wise men show what happens when wisdom cannot answer the king: the whole company is sentenced, and one praying man saves them all. True wisdom is not knowing the dream — it is knowing the God who gives it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: flash (of the eyes); in a bad sense, blearedness
BiblicalUsage: Chakliluwth is redness of the eyes, blearedness — one of the woes of the drunkard, asked in a string of sorrows: who has woe, who has sorrow, who has contentions, who has wounds without cause, who has redness of eyes?
TheologicalSignificance: I believe red eyes are the wine's signature, and the proverb reads them aloud so no one has to guess.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: darkly flashing (only of the eyes); in a good sense, brilliant (as stimulated by wine)
BiblicalUsage: Chakliyl is darkly flashing, red with wine — Jacob's blessing of Judah says his eyes will be red with wine, and his teeth white with milk.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe red eyes in Judah's blessing are abundance, not drunkenness: wine and milk are the promise of the land.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chakmoni, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Hachmoni is a family name among David's mighty men — Jashobeam the Hachmonite, chief of the captains, and Jehiel the son of Hachmoni, who was with the king's sons. Two men carry it, and both stood close to the king.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a family name among mighty men is a place of honour: the Hachmonites stood beside the king and beside his sons.
RelatedPeople: King David; Jashobeam, Son of Zabdiel
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to be sick
BiblicalUsage: Chala means to be sick, and it appears once, of Asa: in the thirty-ninth year of his reign he was diseased in his feet until his disease was exceeding great, yet in his disease he sought not the LORD, but the physicians.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Asa's sickness is the warning that the cure matters less than the turning: he sought the physicians and not the LORD.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: milk (as the richness of kine)
BiblicalUsage: Chalab is milk, the richness of the herd. Abraham set butter and milk before his guests under the tree, God promised a land flowing with milk and honey, and the spies came back saying the land surely flows with milk and honey.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe milk is the taste of the promise: not bread for the journey only, but richness at the end of it. God does not promise His people bare ground — He promises a land that flows.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chalach, a region of Assyria
BiblicalUsage: Halah is a region of Assyria, and its name marks the exile. When Samaria fell, Israel was carried away and placed in Halah and in Habor by the river of Gozan, and the tribes beyond the Jordan were carried there too.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Halah is where the ten tribes went, and the map still remembers what the nation forgot.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, to be rubbed or worn; hence (figuratively) to be weak, sick, afflicted; or (causatively) to grieve, make sick; also to stroke (in flattering), entreat
BiblicalUsage: Chalah means to be weak, sick, worn — and, strangely, to entreat earnestly. Joseph was told his father was sick, Moses besought the LORD after the golden calf, the next generation would see the sicknesses of the land, and Samson said if they bound him with green withs he would be weak as any other man.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe sickness and prayer share one root because they share one posture: worn down, and turning to God. Moses besought because Israel was sick, and Samson was weak because he had forgotten it.
RelatedPeople: Joseph, Son of Jacob; Moses; Samson
RelatedEvents: The Golden Calf; Joseph and His Brothers
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: pierced (especially to death); figuratively, polluted
BiblicalUsage: Chalal means pierced, slain — and, by extension, polluted. Jacob's sons came upon the slain at Shechem, the priest must not marry a profane woman, the man who touches one slain with a sword is unclean, and the law provides for the slain man found lying in the field.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this word joins death and defilement in one root: the slain pollutes, and the profane is counted among the slain. Only God's cleansing touches what death has touched.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, to bore, i.e. (by implication) to wound, to dissolve; figuratively, to profane (a person, place or thing), to break (one's word), to begin (as if by an 'opening wedge'); to play (the flute)
BiblicalUsage: Chalal means to begin — and to profane, to wound, to dissolve. Then began men to call upon the name of the LORD, the altar of hewn stone is polluted if a tool is lifted on it, the name of God must not be profaned by Molech, and Moses told Aaron the plague is begun among the people.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe beginning and profaning share one word because every beginning is a risk: men began to call on God, and men began to profane Him. The same root holds the first prayer and the first pollution.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, to bind firmly, i.e. (by implication) to be (causatively to make) plump; also (through the figurative sense of dumbness) to dream
BiblicalUsage: Chalam means to dream — and, in another sense, to be strong and healthy. Jacob dreamed of a ladder reaching to heaven, the law warns of a prophet or a dreamer of dreams, Gideon's enemy told his fellow a dream of a barley cake, and Job says the young of the wild ass are in good liking and grow up with corn.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe dreams and health share a root because both are gifts that come in the night: God speaks while men sleep, and young creatures grow strong while no one watches. The dreamer of Deuteronomy is the warning that not every night voice is His.
RelatedEvents: Jacob's Dream at Bethel; Gideon's Victory over Midian
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from the base of G5490; to lower (as into a void):--let down, strike.
BiblicalUsage: Chalao means to let down, to lower. The friends let the paralytic down through the roof to Jesus, Jesus told the fishermen to let down their nets for a catch, and Paul was let down by the wall in a basket — twice told, once by Luke and once by Paul himself.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe letting down is the shape of faith here: a roof opened, a net lowered, a basket over a wall. God saves by the ropes of friends and by empty nets let down at His word.
RelatedEvents: The Healing of the Paralytic; The Conversion of Paul
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to pass on (of time)
BiblicalUsage: Chalaph in Aramaic means for time to pass on. All four times it falls in Nebuchadnezzar's sentence: let his heart be changed and let seven times pass over him, till seven times pass over him, until seven times pass over him.
