Amos says God gave cleanness of teeth, want of bread, in all their cities, and Deuteronomy says the disobedient shall serve their enemies in hunger and thirst and nakedness and want of all things, even to eating in secret during the siege.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe want is the fruit of turning from God, and the curse is written plainly so that we will turn back. I hold that the God who sends the want is the same God who promises the return, and that is where hope lives.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chodesh, an Israelitess
BiblicalUsage: Hodesh is a woman of Benjamin, the wife of Shaharaim, named once in the genealogy. She bore him Jobab and Zibia and Mesha and Malcham, and her sons are counted among the heads of the fathers' houses in Jerusalem.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that a mother's name in a genealogy is honour enough, because the families of Israel are carried by women as well as men.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: the new moon; by implication, a month
BiblicalUsage: Chodesh is the new moon and the month, the turning of the moon that sets God's calendar. The Lord tells Moses this month shall be the beginning of months, the law orders offerings at the new moon, Solomon begins the temple in the month Zif, and Esther's twelve months of purifying end in the month of her going to the king.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the new moon teaches me that God marks time for His people, and every month begins with Him. I hold that a calendar set by God is a gift, because it keeps worship at the centre of the year.
RelatedEvents: The Passover; Building of Solomon's Temple
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Choglah, an Israelitess
BiblicalUsage: Hoglah is one of the five daughters of Zelophehad, and her name is tied to the law of inheritance. She stands with her sisters before Moses and Eleazar to claim her father's portion, because he died without a son, and the Lord grants their cause and changes the law for every daughter after them.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Hoglah's claim is the picture of faith asking boldly for what God has promised. I hold that her story shows the law can bend toward justice when God's people plead rightly.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G5522; dusty or dirty (soil-like), i.e. (by implication) terrene:--earthy.
BiblicalUsage: Choikos is earthy, made of dust, and Paul uses it to set the first man against the last. The first man is of the earth, earthy, and as is the earthy so are they that are earthy, but we shall also bear the image of the heavenly, because the last Adam is a quickening spirit.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Paul's earthy man is me by nature, dust that returns to dust, and the heavenly man is me by grace. I hold that the change from earthy to heavenly is the whole hope of the resurrection.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain derivation; a chœnix or certain dry measure:--measure.
BiblicalUsage: Choinix is a dry measure, a day's ration of grain, and it stands once in the opening of the third seal. A voice says a measure of wheat for a penny and three measures of barley for a penny, and the oil and the wine are not to be hurt, a picture of famine with limits set by God.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that even in famine God sets the measure, and scarcity itself obeys His voice.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain derivation; a hog:--swine.
BiblicalUsage: Choiros is a hog, a swine, and the Gospels use it for uncleanness and for a herd's destruction. The demons beg to enter the swine on the hillside, and the whole herd runs violently into the sea, while Jesus warns not to cast pearls before swine.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the swine in these stories show how unclean spirits end, because they rush toward their own destruction. I hold that the man delivered from them is worth more than the whole herd, and Jesus proves it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: wisdom
BiblicalUsage: Chokmah is wisdom in Aramaic, and Daniel uses it for the wisdom that belongs to God alone. Daniel blesses God because wisdom and might are His, the king sees a spirit of wisdom in Daniel, Ezra is told to appoint judges after the wisdom of his God, and Daniel thanks God for giving him wisdom.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the wisdom in Daniel is never man's achievement but God's gift, and that is why the king's wise men fail where Daniel succeeds. I hold that true wisdom begins with knowing the God who gives it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: wisdom
BiblicalUsage: Chokmah is wisdom in Aramaic, and Daniel uses it for the wisdom that belongs to God alone. Daniel blesses God because wisdom and might are His, the king sees a spirit of wisdom in Daniel, Ezra is told to appoint judges after the wisdom of his God, and Daniel thanks God for giving him wisdom.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the wisdom in Daniel is never man's achievement but God's gift, and that is why the king's wise men fail where Daniel succeeds. I hold that true wisdom begins with knowing the God who gives it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: wisdom
BiblicalUsage: Chokmowth is Wisdom herself, speaking aloud in the streets as a woman calling to the simple. Wisdom cries without and lifts her voice in the streets, the psalmist says his mouth shall speak of wisdom, Wisdom has built her house with seven pillars, and every wise woman builds her house.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Wisdom in Proverbs is the voice of God calling in the open, not hiding in a corner. I hold that she is to be heard in the street as well as in the temple, because her call is for everyone.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, exposed; hence, profane
BiblicalUsage: Chol is common, the ordinary and profane set against the holy, and the law draws the line sharply. David asks for bread and is told there is no common bread, only hallowed bread, the priests are charged to put a difference between holy and profane, and Ezekiel says the priests who show no difference have profaned God's holy things.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the line between holy and common is God's own line, and it is drawn for our protection, not our punishment. I hold that when the church blurs the line, it loses the very thing that makes it the church.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G5521; to be bilious, i.e. (by implication) irritable (enraged, "choleric"):--be angry.
BiblicalUsage: Cholao is to be angry, to boil with rage, and it stands once in the words of Jesus at the feast. He asks the Jews whether they are angry at Him because He made a man every whit whole on the sabbath day, as if healing were a crime.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that anger at a healing shows a heart that loves its rules more than its neighbour.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: feminine of an equivalent perhaps akin to the same as G5514 (from the greenish hue); "gall" or bile, i.e. (by analogy) poison or an anodyne (wormwood, poppy, etc.):--gall.
BiblicalUsage: Chole is gall, the bitter bile, and the New Testament uses it for bitterness of soul and for the cross. Peter tells Simon that he is in the gall of bitterness and the bond of iniquity, and the soldiers offer Jesus vinegar mingled with gall before they crucify Him.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe gall is the Bible's picture of a bitterness that poisons from within, and Christ tasted it so that I would not have to drink it.
RelatedEvents: The Crucifixion; Philip Preaches in Samaria
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a weasel (from its gliding motion)
BiblicalUsage: Choled is a weasel, named once among the creeping things the law calls unclean. It runs in the list with the mouse and the tortoise, small creatures that defile by their touch, and the law marks them so that Israel will learn to tell clean from unclean.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that even a weasel in the law teaches me that God cares about the small things of holiness.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: malady, anxiety, calamity
BiblicalUsage: Choliy is sickness, the malady of the body, and Scripture uses it for both judgment and the suffering servant. Ahaziah falls through a lattice and sends to ask whether he will recover of his disease, the Lord promises to take away all sickness from His people, and Isaiah says the servant was a man of sorrows and acquainted with grief.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe sickness in the Bible is never only a body breaking down, because it always asks where we turn for help. I hold that the servant who bore our griefs is the answer to every disease in this word.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: apparently a primary word; "halt", i.e. limping:--cripple, halt, lame.
BiblicalUsage: Cholos is lame, one who halts and cannot walk, and the Gospels use it for the people Jesus heals. The lame walk when John asks whether Jesus is the one to come, the lame man at the Beautiful gate is healed and leaps up, and the blind and the halt lie waiting at the pool of Bethesda.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the lame in these stories are the picture of every sinner, unable to walk until Christ bids them rise. I hold that the healing of the lame is the proof of the kingdom, because it is what the prophets promised.
RelatedEvents: Peter Heals the Lame Man; The Healing at the Pool of Bethesda
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Cholon, the name of two places in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Holon is the name of two towns, one in Judah and one in Moab, and both appear in the lists of judgment and inheritance. Joshua gives a Holon in the hill country to Judah, another Holon is given to the priests as a city of refuge, and Jeremiah pronounces judgment on Holon in Moab.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the two Holons show how one name can stand in promise and in judgment, and the difference is always whether a people obeys God.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: heat
BiblicalUsage: Chom is heat, the warmth of the sun at its strongest, and it marks the turning of the day and the year. The sun is hot by the time the men of Jabesh are delivered, Ish-bosheth is murdered in the heat of the day, God promises that cold and heat shall not cease while the earth remains, and Haggai says the people clothe themselves but there is none warm.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe heat in these verses is the measure of a day, whether it brings deliverance or murder. I hold that God's promise of seedtime and harvest, cold and heat, is the ground of every farmer's hope.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, a bubbling up, i.e. of water, a wave; of earth, mire or clay (cement); also a heap; hence, a chomer or dry measure
BiblicalUsage: Chomer is mortar and clay and a measure, the stuff of building and of weighing, and it carries three senses in one word. The builders of Babel use slime for mortar, Pharaoh makes Israel's lives bitter with bondage in mortar and brick, and Ezekiel fixes the homer as the measure of grain and oil.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the mortar of Babel and the mortar of Egypt are the same word, because man's building and man's bondage are built of the same stuff. I hold that God measures what men build, and His measure is the one that stands.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: the abdomen (as obese)
BiblicalUsage: Chomesh is the belly, the soft place under the fifth rib, and it appears only where a man is struck down in murder. Abner smites Asahel under the fifth rib, Joab smites Abner in the same place, Rechab and Baanah smite Ish-bosheth, and Joab smites Amasa, each blow finding the same fatal spot.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the four murders in one word are a warning about the violence of David's house, because the sword never stayed in its sheath. I hold that the God who forbids murder remembers every blow, even when the histories only record the place of the wound.
RelatedEvents: David's War with the House of Saul
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: the abdomen (as obese)
BiblicalUsage: Chomesh is the belly, the soft place under the fifth rib, and it appears only where a man is struck down in murder. Abner smites Asahel under the fifth rib, Joab smites Abner in the same place, Rechab and Baanah smite Ish-bosheth, and Joab smites Amasa, each blow finding the same fatal spot.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the four murders in one word are a warning about the violence of David's house, because the sword never stayed in its sheath. I hold that the God who forbids murder remembers every blow, even when the histories only record the place of the wound.
RelatedEvents: David's War with the House of Saul
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a lizard (as creeping)
BiblicalUsage: Chomet is a snail, or a lizard that creeps, named once among the unclean creeping things. It stands in the list with the ferret and the chameleon, small creatures that defile by their touch, and the law marks them so Israel will learn to keep clean from what creeps.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that even a snail in the law teaches me that God marks the boundary between clean and unclean with care.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: vinegar
BiblicalUsage: Chomets is vinegar, the sour wine, and it appears in the law, the proverbs, the psalms and the story of Ruth. The Nazarite must separate from vinegar, the sluggard is as vinegar to the teeth, the psalmist is given vinegar to drink in his thirst, and Boaz tells Ruth to dip her morsel in the vinegar.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe vinegar in these verses is sourness itself, and the psalmist drinking it is the picture of Christ on the cross. I hold that Ruth dipping her morsel in vinegar shows God's kindness reaching even into the sour things of life.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: moral filth, i.e. wickedness
BiblicalUsage: Choneph is moral filth, wickedness and hypocrisy, and it stands once in Isaiah's warning. The vile person will speak villany and his heart will work iniquity, to practise hypocrisy and utter error against the Lord, to make empty the soul of the hungry.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that hypocrisy is filth before God, not a small fault, and Isaiah names it plainly.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from the base of G5494; a heap (as poured out), i.e. rubbish; loose dirt:--dust.
BiblicalUsage: Choos is a heap, loose dirt or rubbish poured out, and the Greek text knows it under the spelling for dust. The disciples are told to shake off the dust under their feet against a town that will not receive them, and the merchants of the earth cast dust on their heads weeping over fallen Babylon. The Greek text spells the word as dust rather than the dictionary form, so both verses are cited as a spelling variant rather than an exact match.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the dust shaken off and the dust cast on the head are two sides of one judgment, because the same dust marks rejection and ruin.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to cover (in protection)
BiblicalUsage: Chophaph is to cover in protection, and it stands once in the blessing of Benjamin. The beloved of the Lord shall dwell in safety by Him, and He shall cover him all the day long, and dwell between his shoulders, a single word for a lifetime of shelter.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the covering in this verse is the promise I lean on, because God covers His beloved all the day long.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a fist (only in the dual)
BiblicalUsage: Chophen is a handful, the fistful a hand can hold, and Scripture uses it for ashes, coals and quietness. Moses takes handfuls of ashes and scatters them toward heaven, the priest takes a censer full of burning coals and hands full of incense, the angel fills his hand with coals from the altar, and the preacher says a handful with quietness is better than two handfuls with travail.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the handful in these verses is the measure of a small thing in God's hand, whether it is judgment or worship. I hold that a handful with quietness is the wisdom I need most, because God does not ask me to hold more than my hand can carry.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: something spread loosely, i.e. a carpet
BiblicalUsage: Chophesh is a carpet, a loose covering spread out, and it stands once in the lament over Tyre. Dedan is named as a merchant in precious clothes for chariots, the carpets and cloths that decked the chariots of the rich, one small luxury in the long list of Tyre's trade.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the carpet in Tyre's trade is a picture of wealth spread for show, and it all sinks with the city.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chophni, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Hophni is the elder son of Eli, a priest who profaned the priesthood and died for it. He serves with his brother Phinehas at Shiloh, the Lord promises that both sons shall die in one day as a sign against Eli, and in the battle with the Philistines both are slain and the ark is taken.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Hophni's story is the warning that a priesthood without holiness is worse than no priesthood at all. I hold that God will not let His name be carried by men who despise it, and the ark's capture is the proof.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: exempt (from bondage, tax or care)
BiblicalUsage: Chophshiy means free, exempt from bondage and tax and care, and the law and the prophets both use it for release. The Hebrew servant goes out free in the seventh year, the poor are to be let go free, the king promises the house of Goliath's killer free in Israel, and Isaiah says the fast God chooses is to let the oppressed go free.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe freedom in this word is release from a debt, not licence to do as we please. I hold that the God who frees His people is the same God who frees me, and His freedom always leads to obedience.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: prostration by sickness
BiblicalUsage: Chophshuwth is prostration by sickness, the wasting that keeps a king apart, and it belongs to two leprous kings. Azariah is smitten with leprosy and dwells in a separate house until his death, and Uzziah is a leper to the day of his death and dwells in a separate house, cut off from the house of the Lord.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the separate house is the end of pride, because the king who lifted himself up ends his days apart from his people.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an enactment; hence, an appointment (of time, space, quantity, labor or usage)
BiblicalUsage: Choq is a statute, an enactment appointed by God, and it runs through the covenant from Abraham to the temple. The Lord confirms His word to Jacob for a law and to Israel for an everlasting covenant, He promises Solomon long life if he keeps His statutes, David makes the division of spoil a statute for Israel, and the Lord tells Solomon that keeping His statutes is the condition of the kingdom.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a statute is not a suggestion but an appointment, because God sets the terms of His covenant. I hold that the keeping of His statutes is the proof of love, and David and Solomon both knew the price of forgetting them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chor-hag-Gidgad, a place in the Desert
BiblicalUsage: Hor-hagidgad is a station in the wilderness journey, named twice in the list of Israel's camps. The people journey from Gudgodah to Jotbathah, and from Jotbathah to Hor-hagidgad, one more camp on the long road from Sinai to the promised land.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the stations in the wilderness are God's diary of a journey, and no camp is too small to be remembered.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, white or pure (from the cleansing or shining power of fire; hence (figuratively) noble (in rank)
BiblicalUsage: Chor is a noble, a freeborn man of rank, and the histories use it for the leaders who sign and seal and contend. Jezebel writes letters to the elders and nobles of Naboth's city, the preacher says blessed is the land whose king is the son of nobles, and Nehemiah contends with the nobles who take usury from their brothers.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the nobles in these verses show that rank is no shield from sin, because the nobles can be the worst offenders. I hold that God judges the high and the low by the same law, and that is the comfort of the poor.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: feminine of a derivative of the base of G5490 through the idea of empty expanse; room, i.e. a space of territory (more or less extensive; often including its inhabitants):--coast, county, fields, ground, land, region. Compare G5117.
BiblicalUsage: Chora is a country, a region or a field, and the Gospels use it for the places where the good news travels. Shepherds watch their flocks in the same country, Jesus lifts His eyes to fields white to harvest, the prodigal joins himself to a citizen of that country, and the word of the Lord is published throughout all the region.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the fields in these verses are the world itself, white and ready, and the shepherds are the first to hear. I hold that the gospel was always meant for the whole country, not only for Jerusalem.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain derivation; Chorazin, a place in Palestine:--Chorazin.
BiblicalUsage: Chorazin is a town in Galilee that heard Jesus preach and would not repent, and both Gospels pronounce woe on it. The Lord says if the mighty works done in Chorazin had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would have repented long ago in sackcloth and ashes.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Chorazin is the warning that hearing is not believing, and the towns that saw the most are judged the most. I hold that the woe on Chorazin is meant for every place that has heard the gospel and stayed the same.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, drought, i.e. (by implication) a desolation
BiblicalUsage: Chorbah is a waste place, a desolation, and the prophets use it for Jerusalem's ruin and its repair. Daniel reads that seventy years are accomplished in the desolations of Jerusalem, Ezekiel says God will make the land waste and a reproach, Ezra prays over the desolations God has begun to repair, and Isaiah sees lambs feeding in the waste places of the fat ones.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the waste places in these verses are both judgment and hope, because the same God who desolates also repairs. I hold that the lambs feeding in the waste are the picture of life returning where judgment fell.
RelatedEvents: Fall of Jerusalem and the Exile; Cyrus's Decree and Return from Exile
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Choreb, a (generic) name for the Sinaitic mountains
BiblicalUsage: Horeb is the mountain of God, the other name for Sinai, where Moses sees the burning bush and Elijah flees for his life. Moses turns aside at Horeb to see the bush that burns and is not consumed, the eleven days' journey from Horeb to Kadesh-barnea is measured from it, and Elijah walks forty days to Horeb and hears the still small voice there.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Horeb is holy ground because God meets men there, whether they come in wonder like Moses or in despair like Elijah. I hold that the God of the burning bush is the God of the still small voice, and He is the same in both.
RelatedEvents: The Burning Bush; Elijah at Horeb: The Still Small Voice
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: drought or desolation
BiblicalUsage: Choreb is drought and desolation, the drying up of the land under God's hand, and it appears in the stories of Jacob, Egypt and the prophets. Jacob says the drought consumed him by day, Haggai says God called for a drought on the land, Ezekiel sets Egypt's desolation from Migdol to Syene, and Isaiah promises a covert from the heat.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe drought in these verses is God's hand on the land, and the promise of shelter is His hand on His people. I hold that the same God who dries the land can cover His people from the heat.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a compound of G5525 and G71; to be a dance-leader, i.e. (generally) to furnish:--give, minister.
BiblicalUsage: Choregeo is to supply, to furnish what is needed, and Paul and Peter both use it of God's giving. Peter says if any man ministers, let him do it as of the ability which God supplies, and Paul says He that ministers seed to the sower will multiply the seed sown.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that God supplies both the seed and the strength to sow it, and my giving is only the passing on of His gift.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chorem, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Horem is a fenced city in Naphtali, named once in the list of the tribe's strong cities. It stands among the fortified towns given to Naphtali, one of the walls that guarded the northern border of the land.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the fenced cities of Naphtali were God's provision for a border tribe, and He gives walls to those who live nearest the enemy.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G5561; to be in (give) space, i.e. (intransitively) to pass, enter, or (transitively) to hold, admit (literally or figuratively):--come, contain, go, have place, (can, be room to) receive.
BiblicalUsage: Choreo is to make room, to contain or to receive, and the New Testament uses it for hearts, for vessels and for repentance. Paul asks the Corinthians to receive him, the waterpots at Cana contain two or three firkins apiece, the crowds press so that there is no room to receive them, and Peter says God is not willing that any should perish but that all should come to repentance.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe making room is the heart of the gospel, because God makes room for sinners and asks us to make room for one another. I hold that the room God makes for repentance is the widest room of all, and it is still open.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, the crop gathered, i.e. (by implication) the autumn (and winter) season; figuratively, ripeness of age
BiblicalUsage: Choreph is the winter, the season when the crop is gathered and the cold sets in, and it is also the ripeness of a life. The prophet speaks of winter houses and summer houses, God promises that summer and winter shall not cease, the king sits in his winter house with the fire before him, and Job remembers the days of his ripeness when the secret of God was on his tabernacle.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe winter in these verses is both a season and a stage of life, and God is Lord of both. I hold that the ripeness Job remembers is the autumn of a life lived with God, and it is worth more than the summer.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a fabricator or mechanic
BiblicalUsage: Choresh is a craftsman, a worker in metal and wood, and the first artificer and the temple's bronzesmith share the word. Tubal-cain is the instructor of every artificer in brass and iron, and Hiram of Tyre is a worker in brass, filled with wisdom and understanding to work all works in brass for Solomon's temple.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the craftsman in these verses is honoured by God, because He fills hands with wisdom for His house, and Tubal-cain and Hiram both show that skill is a gift from God, whether it is used for a tool or for a temple.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a forest (perhaps as furnishing the material for fabric)
BiblicalUsage: Choresh is a forest, a wood where men hide and where cities are built, and David knows it well. David abides in the wood in the wilderness of Ziph while Saul seeks him, Jotham builds castles and towers in the forests of Judah, and the prophets use the forest as the image of a proud nation laid low.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the forest in David's story is God's hiding place for a hunted man, and He still hides His people in the woods. I hold that a forest can be a refuge or a ruin, and the difference is whether God is in it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: diminutive of G5561; a spot or plot of ground:--field, land, parcel of ground, place, possession.
BiblicalUsage: Chorion is a field, a plot of ground, and the Gospels and Acts use it for the ground that changes hands. Jacob gives Joseph a parcel of ground, the field bought with the price of blood is called the field of blood, and Gethsemane is a field where Jesus prays while His disciples sleep.
TheologicalSignificance: The fields in these verses are ground where God's story turns, whether it is a gift, a purchase or a prayer. I hold that Gethsemane is the field that matters most, because there the will of God was settled in the dark.
RelatedPeople: Joseph, Son of Jacob; Judas Iscariot
RelatedEvents: The Arrest of Jesus in Gethsemane; Jesus Prays in Gethsemane
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: adverb from G5561; at a space, i.e. separately or apart from (often as preposition):--beside, by itself, without.
BiblicalUsage: Choris means without, apart from, separate, and the New Testament uses it for what we cannot do alone. Jesus says without Him we can do nothing, the writer to the Hebrews says without faith it is impossible to please God, and Paul says the Gentiles were without Christ and without hope in the world.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this little word carries the whole gospel, because apart from Christ we have nothing and in Him we have everything. I hold that every without in Scripture is an invitation to come and be joined to Him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: white bread
BiblicalUsage: Choriy is white bread, and it stands once in the dream of Pharaoh's chief baker. He sees three white baskets on his head, and the birds eat the bakemeats out of the uppermost basket, a dream that Joseph reads as three days to the baker's death.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the white bread in the dream is the baker's own craft turned against him, because the birds eat what he made, and Joseph's reading shows God's hand in every detail, even in a basket of bread.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a Chorite or aboriginal Idumaean
BiblicalUsage: Choriy is a Horite, one of the aboriginal people of Seir, and the histories trace them from the kings to the genealogies. The kings smite the Horites in Mount Seir, the law says the Horites dwelt there before Esau's sons dispossessed them, and the genealogy of Seir the Horite is kept among the sons of Esau.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the Horites are the people who were there before, and their record shows that God keeps the history of the displaced as well as the conquerors. I hold that no people is forgotten in His book, even the ones who lose the land.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a Chorite or aboriginal Idumaean
BiblicalUsage: Choriy is a Horite, one of the aboriginal people of Seir, and the histories trace them from the kings to the genealogies. The kings smite the Horites in Mount Seir, the law says the Horites dwelt there before Esau's sons dispossessed them, and the genealogy of Seir the Horite is kept among the sons of Esau.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the Horites are the people who were there before, and their record shows that God keeps the history of the displaced as well as the conquerors. I hold that no people is forgotten in His book, even the ones who lose the land.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a burning (i.e. intense) anger
BiblicalUsage: Choriy is burning anger, the fierce heat of a wrath that cannot be held back, and it appears in the stories of Jonathan, Moses and the kings. Jonathan rises from the table in fierce anger at his father's shame, the army returns in great anger, Moses goes out from Pharaoh in great anger, and the Lord asks why His anger is kindled against Israel.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe anger in these verses is a fire that must be watched, because it can be righteous or ruinous. I hold that Moses' anger and Jonathan's anger both show a heart that hates what God hates, and that is the only safe anger.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G5561; to place room between, i.e. part; reflexively, to go away:--depart, put asunder, separate.
BiblicalUsage: Chorizo is to separate, to put asunder, and the Gospels use it for the marriage God has joined. Jesus says what God has joined together, let not man put asunder, and Paul says the wife should not depart from her husband, because the bond is God's own making.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word is a guard around marriage, because what God joins is not man's to break. I hold that the separation Paul allows is the exception that proves the bond, and the bond itself is the rule.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chormah, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Hormah is a place in the south where Israel is chased and where kings fall. The Amalekites and Canaanites smite Israel and chase them even to Hormah, Moses warns that the same will happen again, and Joshua's list counts the king of Hormah among the kings he struck down.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Hormah is a place of two memories, a defeat and a victory, and the difference is whether Israel obeyed God. I hold that the same ground can hold both, and God is faithful in each.
RelatedEvents: The Twelve Spies and Israel's Unbelief
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Choronajim, a place in Moab
BiblicalUsage: Horonaim is a town in Moab where the fugitives flee and the cry of destruction is heard. Isaiah sees the fugitives fleeing to Horonaim, and Jeremiah hears the cry of destruction in Horonaim and the weeping going up the ascent of Luhith.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Horonaim is the sound of a nation running from judgment, and the prophets make us hear it so that we will turn back. I hold that the cry in Moab is the warning for every people that forgets God.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a Choronite or inhabitant of Choronaim
BiblicalUsage: The Horonite is Sanballat, the enemy of Nehemiah's wall, and his title is all the name the record gives him. He is displeased when Nehemiah comes to seek the welfare of Israel, he mocks the builders on the wall, and his daughter marries into the priesthood that Nehemiah must cleanse.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Sanballat's title is the mark of an outsider who opposes God's work, and his mockery is the oldest weapon against builders. I hold that the wall went up in spite of him, because God builds through the hands of His people.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Latin origin; the north-west wind:--north west.
BiblicalUsage: Choros is the north-west wind, and it stands once in the voyage that ends in shipwreck. The sailors at Fair Havens decide to sail for Phenice, a haven that lies toward the south-west and the north-west, hoping to winter there, and the storm takes them instead.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that a wind is a small thing in a verse and a great thing in a storm, and Paul's voyage turned on it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain derivation; a ring, i.e. round dance ("choir":--dancing.
BiblicalUsage: Choros is a dance, the round dance of rejoicing, and it stands once in the parable of the prodigal son. The elder brother comes in from the field and hears music and dancing, the sound of a house rejoicing because the lost son has come home.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the dancing in the parable is the sound of heaven itself, because the father's house rejoices over one sinner who repents, and the elder brother standing outside the dance is the warning for everyone who thinks grace is unfair.
RelatedTopics: Joy; God's joy over His people
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G5526; forage, i.e. food:--sustenance.
BiblicalUsage: Chortasma is sustenance, the food that keeps a people alive, and it stands once in Stephen's speech. He tells of the dearth in Egypt and Canaan, when the famine was great and there was no sustenance for the fathers, and they went down to Egypt for corn.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe sustenance in Stephen's speech is the thread that leads Jacob's family to Egypt, because God feeds His people through famine, and the dearth is His way of moving His people where He wants them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G5528; to fodder, i.e. (generally) to gorge (supply food in abundance):--feed, fill, satisfy.
BiblicalUsage: Chortazo is to be filled, to be satisfied with food, and the Gospels use it for the hungry and the blessed. Jesus says the hungry after righteousness shall be filled, the hungry now shall be filled, and the five thousand eat and are all filled with the loaves and fishes.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe being filled in these verses is always God's work, because only He can satisfy a hunger He has put in us. I hold that the filling of the five thousand is the picture of every filling since, because Christ gives and there is always more than enough.
RelatedEvents: The Sermon on the Mount; The Feeding of the Five Thousand
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: apparently a primary word; a "court" or "garden", i.e. (by implication, of pasture) herbage or vegetation:--blade, grass, hay.
BiblicalUsage: Chortos is grass, the green herbage of the field, and Scripture uses it for provision and for the shortness of life. Jesus says the grass of the field, which today is and tomorrow is cast into the oven, is clothed by God, Peter says all flesh is as grass, and James says the rich man shall fade as the flower of the grass.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the grass in these verses is both a promise and a warning, because God clothes it and it still fades. I hold that my life is as grass, and that is why I trust the God who clothes the grass and keeps it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: the dark; hence (literally) darkness; figuratively, misery, destruction, death, ignorance, sorrow, wickedness
BiblicalUsage: Darkness is there from the very first verses, covering the face of the deep before God says let there be light. In Egypt it falls as a plague so thick it can be felt, and at Sinai it wraps the mountain where God speaks. The word moves easily from night to misery, from ignorance to death, because in Scripture darkness is never just the absence of light.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe darkness is the Bible's picture of life without God, and that is why light matters so much in the story. God does not leave His people in it: He speaks into it, leads through it, and promises a day when night ends. My position is simple — wherever darkness is named, I look for what God is doing about it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: perhaps a pocket (as holding the Urim and Thummim), or rich (as containing gems), used only of the gorget of the highpriest
BiblicalUsage: The breastplate is the pouch the high priest wears over his heart, holding the Urim and Thummim and set with twelve stones for the twelve tribes. God gives its pattern on the mountain, and Aaron puts it on when he goes into the holy place. It is not decoration: the names of Israel are carried on the priest's heart whenever he stands before the LORD.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the breastplate shows that intercession is personal, not distant. The priest does not carry a list; he carries names, close to his heart, into God's presence. That is how I understand Christ's priesthood too — He carries His people, by name, before the Father.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a twig
BiblicalUsage: A twig is a small, fresh shoot, and Isaiah uses it for the shoot that grows from the stump of Jesse. Proverbs uses the same picture in reverse, a rod of pride growing from a fool's mouth.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that God delights to bring great things from small beginnings, and the shoot from Jesse is the proof.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a seal
BiblicalUsage: Tamar sends Judah's seal to him as proof, and the seal speaks when she cannot. A seal marks what belongs to its owner, and Judah's own signet convicts him.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God can use the plain evidence of a thing to bring the truth out, even when the person holding it would rather stay silent.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {the bosom (as comprised between the arms)}
BiblicalUsage: The bosom is where a person carries what is closest to them, and Isaiah pictures God carrying His children home in His bosom. Nehemiah shakes out his own bosom as a sign, emptying it of everything he has taken.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that what a person carries close shows what they truly value, and God carries His people close.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain origin; Chuzas, an officer of Herod:--Chuza.
BiblicalUsage: Chuzas manages Herod's household, and his wife Joanna travels with Jesus and supports His ministry from her own means. The steward of a king's house ends up tied to a household that serves a greater King.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the gospel reaches into every household, even the palace staff, and no position puts a person beyond its reach.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a thorn; by analogy, a ring for the nose
BiblicalUsage: A thorn is small, sharp, and good for nothing but catching and tearing, and the kings' fable uses a thistle to mock a king who overreaches. Job says if his land has cheated him, let thistles grow instead of wheat. Proverbs puts a proverb in a fool's mouth like a thorn in a drunkard's hand: dangerous, and wasted.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that thorns in Scripture mark what is useless and harmful, the fruit of the curse rather than the garden. God does not call His people to be thorns; He calls them to bear fruit that feeds others. I believe the contrast is the point — a life given to God stops tearing and starts giving.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: debt
BiblicalUsage: Debt here is what a person owes, and Ezekiel lists the righteous man as one who does not hold back what is due. The word is small and plain, but it carries the weight of obligation.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God counts what we owe to others, and a righteous life pays what is due instead of hiding from it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chobah, a place in Syria
BiblicalUsage: Hobah is the place north of Damascus where Abram's night pursuit of the kings ends. The name appears once, as a marker on the edge of the battle. Abram does not stop at the border of the fight; he follows until his kinsman is recovered.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Hobah matters because it shows how far Abram would go for Lot. Love does not stop at a convenient distance.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: sand (as round or whirling particles)
BiblicalUsage: Sand is the picture of what cannot be counted, and God promises Abraham offspring as many as the sand on the seashore. Moses hides a body in the sand, and Deuteronomy speaks of the treasures hidden in it. Hosea picks the promise up again, telling Israel they will be as the sand of the sea.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God chose sand on purpose: a promise too big to count, given to people who could count everything else. My position is that the promise still stands behind every believer, because the God who counts the sand keeps His word. That is why the same picture returns in Hosea, long after Abraham is gone.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a wall of protection
BiblicalUsage: A wall holds back the sea for Israel at the Red Sea, and it holds up Rahab's house on the edge of Jericho. The same word names the fortified cities of the land and the walls that fall when Israel shouts. Walls protect, and walls shut people out, and Scripture uses both sides of that truth.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe walls in the Bible show where human safety ends and God's protection begins. The sea stood as a wall because God held it, and Jericho's wall fell because God brought it down. I hold that no wall is stronger than the God who commands it, and no wall is safer than the one He builds.
RelatedEvents: The Exodus and the Red Sea; The Walls of Jericho
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a cove (as a sheltered bay)
BiblicalUsage: The shore is where the land meets the sea, and Jacob blesses Zebulun with a haven for ships on the coast. Moses sends Israel toward the hill country and the shore, and the tribes settle along it. Asher stays by the shore in Deborah's song instead of joining the battle, and the shore becomes a picture of safety chosen over duty.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the shore is a place of decision in Scripture, where comfort and calling pull in different directions. Zebulun's blessing is a shore used well, and Asher's shore is a blessing kept for himself. My position is that God gives good places, but He means them to serve His purposes, not our ease.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a cavity, socket, den
KeyPassages: 1 Samuel 14:11; 2 Kings 12:9; Job 30:6; Song of Solomon 5:4
BiblicalUsage: A hole is a hiding place and a poor man's home: the Philistines watch the Hebrews creep out of their holes, Job's outcasts live in the clefts of the rocks, and a priest bores a hole in a chest for the temple money. The beloved puts her hand through the hole of the door in the Song, and the same small opening becomes a place of longing.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that holes in Scripture mark the low places — fear, poverty, and hiding — and also the small openings through which love and generosity enter. God sees the people in the holes, and He does not leave them there. I believe that is why the chest with a hole in its lid matters: even a small opening can carry the gifts of a whole people.
RelatedBooks: 1 Samuel; 2 Kings; Job; Song of Solomon
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a cavity, socket, den
KeyPassages: 1 Samuel 14:11; 2 Kings 12:9; Job 30:6; Song of Solomon 5:4
BiblicalUsage: A hole is a hiding place and a poor man's home: the Philistines watch the Hebrews creep out of their holes, Job's outcasts live in the clefts of the rocks, and a priest bores a hole in a chest for the temple money. The beloved puts her hand through the hole of the door in the Song, and the same small opening becomes a place of longing.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that holes in Scripture mark the low places — fear, poverty, and hiding — and also the small openings through which love and generosity enter. God sees the people in the holes, and He does not leave them there. I believe that is why the chest with a hole in its lid matters: even a small opening can carry the gifts of a whole people.
RelatedBooks: 1 Samuel; 2 Kings; Job; Song of Solomon
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chotham, the name of two Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Chotham is the name of two Israelites, one a son of Heber in Asher's line and one a father of two of David's mighty men. The name appears only in lists, with no story attached to either man. Both are remembered because their families and their sons were counted among God's people.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe names in the lists matter even when no story survives, because God counts people the world forgets.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a signature-ring
KeyPassages: Genesis 38:18; Exodus 28:11; 1 Kings 21:8; Song of Solomon 8:6
BiblicalUsage: A signet ring is a person's name in wax and stone, and Judah leaves his with Tamar as a pledge. The high priest's stones are engraved like a signet, and Jezebel seals letters with Ahab's ring to have Naboth killed. The Song turns the same image into a prayer: set me as a seal upon your heart.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a seal says two things at once: this belongs to someone, and this person stands behind it. Judah's seal convicts him, Jezebel's seal kills an innocent man, and the Song's seal asks for love that will not let go. My position is that God has sealed His own people the same way — marked as His, and held by Him.
RelatedBooks: Genesis; Exodus; 1 Kings; Song of Solomon
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chozai, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Hozai is named once, as the writer of the record of Manasseh's prayer and repentance. Nothing else is said about him, and his words are not quoted. His name survives because he kept the account of a king who turned back to God.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Hozai matters because someone had to write down that Manasseh prayed. A king's repentance is only known because a recorder kept it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a beholder in vision; also a compact (as looked upon with approval)
BiblicalUsage: A seer is one who sees what God shows, and Gad is called David's seer when the word of the LORD comes to him. The prophets and seers warned Israel again and again to turn from evil, and the history of Solomon's reign is written in the records of the seers. Seeing is not guessing: it is receiving, and then speaking what was received.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God has always spoken through seers, not because He needs a mouthpiece, but because His people need to hear. The seer's job is plain — see truly, speak plainly, and leave the results to God. I hold that every believer is called to something like it: to see what God is doing and to say so.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: power
BiblicalUsage: Strength here is the strong hand that brings Israel out of Egypt, and Moses tells the people to remember it every year. Amos turns the word against those who boast in their own strength, taking a thing of nothing and calling it power. Haggai promises that God will overthrow the strength of kingdoms.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe strength belongs to God first, and every human claim on it is borrowed. The Exodus proves it: Israel did not break its own chains. My position is that boasting in our own strength is the surest way to lose it, because God gives strength to the humble and takes it from the proud.
RelatedEvents: The Exodus and the Red Sea; The Ten Plagues
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: vehemence (usually in a bad sense)
BiblicalUsage: Force is power used hard: Jabin oppresses Israel with it for twenty years, a priest's servant demands his portion by force, and workmen are paid for repairing the temple with strength. Ezekiel charges the shepherds who rule God's flock with force and cruelty, and the word carries the bruise with it.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe force reveals the heart of the one who uses it. The same strength that repairs a temple can crush a flock, and God notices which one it is. I hold that leadership in God's house is never measured by how hard it can press, but by how gently it can carry.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably the same as the base of G5530; to loan:--lend.
BiblicalUsage: Chrao means to lend, and it stands once, in the parable of the friend at midnight: a man knocks on his neighbour’s door and says, Friend, lend me three loaves. The Greek spells it chrēson, and the text behind the King James lemmatizes it as kíchrēmi, the older form of the same verb for lending.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the one place this word stands is a parable about asking: a neighbour who will not be put off, and a God who gives to those who ask.
RelatedEvents: The Parable of the Friend at Midnight
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: middle voice of a primary verb (perhaps rather from G5495, to handle); to furnish what is needed; (give an oracle, "graze" (touch slightly), light upon, etc.), i.e. (by implication) to employ or (by extension) to act towards one in a given manner:--entreat, use. Compare G5531; G5534.
BiblicalUsage: To use a thing is to take it up for its purpose, and Paul uses the word for the law, for marriage, for freedom, and even for a kind word from a centurion. A slave who can gain freedom should use it, and a man who uses the law must use it lawfully. The word covers the whole range of handling what God has put in our hands.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe use is a moral question, not a neutral one, because everything we handle belongs to God. Paul's rule is plain: use the world, but do not abuse it, and use freedom for the good of others. I hold that the test of any use is whether it serves love.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: third person singular of the same as G5530 or G5531 used impersonally; it needs (must or should) be:--ought.
BiblicalUsage: James says blessing and cursing come from the same mouth, and adds that these things ought not to be so. The word is small — it ought not — but it carries the whole weight of the rebuke.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe James is right: a mouth that blesses God cannot rightly curse the people made in His likeness.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from the base of G5530 or G5534; employment, i.e. an affair; also (by implication) occasion, demand, requirement or destitution:--business, lack, necessary(-ity), need(-ful), use, want.
BiblicalUsage: Need is the word for what a person lacks, and John the Baptist says he has need to be baptized by Jesus instead. Jesus says the sick have need of a physician, and John says Jesus has no need to be told what is in a man. The word runs from a felt lack to the One who knows every lack without being told.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe need is where the gospel begins, because only people who know they lack something come to be filled. Jesus does not wait to be told our need; He already knows it, and He meets it. My position is that admitting need is not weakness — it is the door to grace.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G5532; to make (i.e. have) necessity, i.e. be in want of:--(have) need.
BiblicalUsage: To be in need is to lack something and feel it, and Jesus says the Father knows what we need before we ask. The friend at midnight calls for bread because of his persistence, not his politeness, and Paul asks the Romans to assist Phoebe because she is in need. The word covers both the lack and the asking.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God wants us to bring our needs to Him plainly, because He already knows them and still invites the asking. Need is not a failure of faith; it is the reason for prayer. I hold that a church that meets needs is a church that has understood the gospel.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: something useful or needed, i.e. wealth, price:--money, riches.
BiblicalUsage: Money is called needful things in the New Testament, and Jesus warns how hard it is for those who trust in riches to enter the kingdom. Barnabas lays the price of his field at the apostles' feet, and Simon offers money to buy the power of the Spirit. The same word covers honest provision and the attempt to purchase what cannot be bought.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe money is a tool that turns into a master the moment we trust it. Barnabas shows its right use, and Simon shows its wrong one, and the difference is worship. My position is that wealth is never the problem on its own — trusting it is.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G5537; a divine response or revelation:--answer of God.
BiblicalUsage: The answer of God is the reply God gave Elijah when he thought he was the only faithful one left: seven thousand have not bowed to Baal. The word appears once, and it carries the whole weight of God's correction to a lonely prophet.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God always keeps a remnant, even when His servants cannot see them.
RelatedEvents: Elijah at Horeb: The Still Small Voice
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G5536; to utter an oracle (compare the original sense of G5530), i.e. divinely intimate; by implication, (compare the secular sense of G5532) to constitute a firm for business, i.e. (generally) bear as a title:--be called, be admonished (warned) of God, reveal, speak.
BiblicalUsage: To be warned by God is to receive His direction in a dream or a word, and the wise men are warned not to return to Herod. Simeon is told he will not die before he sees the Lord's Christ, and Cornelius is told by an angel to send for Peter. The same word names the woman who is called an adulteress while her husband lives.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God still directs His people, and the warnings in Scripture are always for protection, never for punishment. The wise men obeyed a dream and saved a child's life, and Simeon waited on a promise and saw it kept. I hold that hearing God is less about the method and more about the obedience that follows.
RelatedEvents: The Magi Visit Jesus; The Presentation of Jesus in the Temple
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a derivative of G5531 and G3781; a loan-ower, i.e. indebted person:--debtor.
BiblicalUsage: A debtor is one who owes, and Jesus tells of two debtors, one owing five hundred pence and one fifty, and both are forgiven. The unjust steward calls in his master's debtors one by one and cuts what they owe. The word appears in the Greek text with a spelling that differs by a single letter from the dictionaries' form.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Jesus chose debtors for His picture of forgiveness because every one of us owes more than we can pay.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G5540; serviceable:--profit.
BiblicalUsage: This word never stands in the Greek New Testament; the idea of being useful or profitable is carried by other words, like the verb for using and the adjective for kind. The dictionaries list it so the family can be traced, but no verse can be cited for it.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that usefulness is still the question the word points to: whether a life is serviceable to God and to others.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G5530; employment, i.e. (specially), sexual intercourse (as an occupation of the body):--use.
BiblicalUsage: Use here is the employment of the body, and Paul says men and women exchanged the natural use for what is against nature. The word is plain, and Paul uses it to name a sin that turns God's design upside down.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Paul is plain because the truth is plain: God designed the body with a purpose, and turning from that purpose is sin.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: middle voice from G5543; to show oneself useful, i.e. act benevolently:--be kind.
BiblicalUsage: Love is kind, Paul says, and the word for kind is the verb for showing oneself useful and gentle. It is the only place the verb stands, and it stands in the middle of love's definition.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe kindness is love in action, and a love that is never kind is not love at all.
RelatedTopics: Love; Kindness; Fruit of the Spirit
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a compound of G5543 and G3004; fair speech, i.e. plausibility:--good words.
BiblicalUsage: Good words are smooth, plausible speech, and Paul warns that false teachers use them to deceive the hearts of the simple. The words sound good, and that is exactly the danger.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe smooth speech is no proof of truth, and the church must weigh words by Scripture, not by how pleasant they sound.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G5530; employed, i.e. (by implication) useful (in manner or morals):--better, easy, good(-ness), gracious, kind.
BiblicalUsage: Kind and easy is the word Jesus uses for His yoke, and the word for the old wine that tastes better than the new. Paul says the kindness of God leads to repentance, and then warns that evil company corrupts good character. The word moves from a yoke to a character, and both are about what is good to live with.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God's kindness is not softness; it is the strength that draws sinners home. Jesus says His yoke is easy because He carries it with us, and Paul says that same kindness is what turns a heart. I hold that the church's first argument for the gospel should be its kindness.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G5543; usefulness, i.e. morally, excellence (in character or demeanor):--gentleness, good(-ness), kindness.
BiblicalUsage: Gentleness is listed among the fruit of the Spirit, and Paul names it among the marks of a true minister. Romans says it is the kindness of God that leads to repentance, and Ephesians says God will show the exceeding riches of His grace in His kindness toward us. The word is both God's character and the Christian's calling.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe gentleness is strength under control, and it is one of the clearest proofs that the Spirit is at work. A harsh church cannot show a gentle God, and a gentle church preaches without a word. My position is that kindness is not a garnish on the gospel — it is part of the gospel itself.
RelatedTopics: Kindness; Fruit of the Spirit; Grace
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably akin to G5530 through the idea of contact; to smear or rub with oil, i.e. (by implication) to consecrate to an office or religious service:--anoint.
BiblicalUsage: To anoint is to smear with oil, and Jesus opens His ministry by reading that the Spirit has anointed Him to preach good news to the poor. The early church prays that God anointed His holy child Jesus, and Hebrews says God anointed Him with the oil of gladness above His fellows. Anointing marks the one God has chosen for a work.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe anointing is God's way of saying the work is His, not ours. Jesus was anointed for the poor, the brokenhearted, and the captive, and that is the shape of His ministry still. I hold that every believer shares in that anointing, because the same Spirit who rested on Him rests on His people.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G5548; an unguent or smearing, i.e. (figuratively) the special endowment ("chrism") of the Holy Spirit:--anointing, unction.
BiblicalUsage: The anointing is the gift every believer has received from the Holy One, and John says it teaches them all things. It abides in them, so they do not need a teacher who would lead them away.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the anointing John means is the Spirit Himself, given to ordinary believers, and no believer is left without a teacher.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G5547; a Christian, i.e. follower of Christ:--Christian.
BiblicalUsage: The name Christian is given first at Antioch, by outsiders watching the disciples of Jesus. Agrippa uses it almost mockingly, asking Paul if he would persuade him to become one. Peter tells suffering believers not to be ashamed if they suffer as Christians, but to glorify God in that name.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the name was first a label from the world, and the church took it up as a badge of honour. To be called a Christian is to be named after Christ, and that is a name worth suffering for. My position is that the name still asks the same question Agrippa heard: does your life show whose you are?
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G5550; to take time, i.e. linger:--delay, tarry.
BiblicalUsage: To delay is to take longer than expected, and Jesus warns of the servant who says his master delays his coming. The bridegroom tarries and all the virgins sleep, and the people wonder why Zacharias lingers so long in the temple. Hebrews answers the waiting: He who is coming will come, and will not tarry.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe delay in Scripture is never God's absence; it is God's patience, and the waiting itself is part of the test. The servant who takes delay as permission to strike his fellows has misunderstood the master entirely. I hold that waiting well is one of the hardest and holiest things a believer does.
RelatedTopics: Patience; Waiting on God; Second Coming
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain derivation; a space of time (in general, and thus properly distinguished from G2540, which designates a fixed or special occasion; and from G165, which denotes a particular period) or interval; by extension, an individual opportunity; by implication, delay:--+ years old, season, space, (X often-)time(-s), (a) while.
BiblicalUsage: Time is the space in which life happens, and Herod asks the wise men diligently when the star appeared. Jesus says the friends of the bridegroom cannot fast while He is with them, and Elizabeth's full time comes for her son to be born. The man at the pool has been sick a long time, and Jesus asks him if he will be made whole.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe time is a gift God gives and a trust He will ask about. Herod uses time to hunt a child, and Jesus uses it to heal one, and the difference is everything. My position is that no season is wasted when it is spent with Christ, however long it lasts.
RelatedEvents: The Magi Visit Jesus; The Birth of John the Baptist
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a presumed compound of G5550 and the base of G5147; to be a time-wearer, i.e. to procrastinate (linger):--spend time.
BiblicalUsage: Paul hastens to be at Jerusalem for Pentecost if possible, and the word is the wearing away of time by delay. He will not spend time in Asia, because the days will not wait for him.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Paul shows us urgency without panic: the days are short, and the work is great, so he spends them on purpose.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably akin to the base of G5530 through the idea of handling; the body (properly, its surface or skin):--body.
BiblicalUsage: The body here is the skin itself, and handkerchiefs taken from Paul's body carry healing to the sick. The word is as plain as it gets — the surface of a person — and God works through it.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God is not embarrassed by the body, and He can use the most ordinary things, even cloth that has touched a servant, to heal.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G5557; made of gold:--of gold, golden.
BiblicalUsage: In a great house there are vessels of gold and of silver, and also of wood and of earth. Paul says the gold vessels are for honour, and the point is not the material but the use.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God cares less about what a vessel is made of than about whether it is clean and ready for the Master's use.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: diminutive of G5557; a golden article, i.e. gold plating, ornament, or coin:--gold.
BiblicalUsage: Gold in the New Testament is what people reach for first and what God tests most: Peter has no silver or gold to give the lame man, but he gives him Jesus. Paul tells women not to dress in gold, and Hebrews lists the golden censer and the ark overlaid with gold. Peter says faith is more precious than gold that perishes, though it is tried with fire.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe gold is the Bible's test of what we value, because it shines and it lasts and it still cannot save. The lame man got something better than gold, and so does every believer. I hold that faith tried by fire is the only gold that survives the testing.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G5557 and G1146; gold-ringed, i.e. wearing a golden finger-ring or similar jewelry:--with a gold ring.
BiblicalUsage: A man with a gold ring walks into the assembly in fine clothing, and James says the church must not give him the good seat while the poor man stands. The ring is the whole sermon: wealth worn where everyone can see it.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe James is right that favouritism by wealth is a denial of the gospel, because God chose the poor of this world to be rich in faith.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G5557 and G3037; gold-stone, i.e. a yellow gem ("chrysolite"):--chrysolite.
BiblicalUsage: The chrysolite is one of the foundation stones of the New Jerusalem, the seventh in John's list. It is a yellow gem, named from gold and stone together, and it holds up the wall of the city of God.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the foundations of the holy city are made of precious things because the God who builds it spares nothing for His people.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G5557; to gild, i.e. bespangle with golden ornaments:--deck.
BiblicalUsage: The woman on the beast is decked with gold, and the great city is decked with gold and precious stones and pearls. The gilding is the point: Babylon dresses its sin in splendour so that no one will call it sin.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Babylon's gold is a warning that evil rarely looks poor, and the church must not be dazzled by what is decked.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G5557 and πράσον (a leek); a greenish-yellow gem ("chrysoprase"):--chrysoprase.
BiblicalUsage: The chrysoprase is the tenth foundation stone of the New Jerusalem, a greenish-yellow gem like a leek. John lists it without a sermon, as one stone among twelve, and the city needs every one of them.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe every stone in the city's wall matters, because God builds His city from the particular and the precious, not the generic.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: perhaps from the base of G5530 (through the idea of the utility of the metal); gold; by extension, a golden article, as an ornament or coin:--gold.
BiblicalUsage: Gold is the first gift the wise men lay before the child, and Paul tells the Athenians that God is not like gold or silver shaped by human hands. The builder's work is tried by fire, and gold survives where wood and stubble burn. James says the rich man's gold is cankered, and the rust testifies against him.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe gold in Scripture is always a question, never an answer: will you worship it, or will you offer it? The wise men gave it to Jesus, and that is the only safe place for gold to go. I hold that whatever survives the fire is what was built on Christ.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain derivation; "yesterday"; by extension, in time past or hitherto:--yesterday.
BiblicalUsage: Yesterday is the word for the day before, and the nobleman's servants tell him his son began to amend yesterday at the seventh hour. Hebrews says Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, and today, and forever. The Greek text spells the word with a leading letter that the dictionaries' form does not have.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word matters most in Hebrews: the Christ of yesterday is the Christ of today, and nothing about Him changes.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chuldah, an Israelitess
BiblicalUsage: Huldah is the prophetess the king's men consult when the book of the law is found in the temple. She speaks plainly: the judgment written in the book will come, and Josiah will be gathered to his grave in peace because his heart was tender. Her name appears only in the account of that one errand, and the errand changes a kingdom.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Huldah shows that God speaks through whomever He chooses, and a prophetess's word can turn a king to his knees.
RelatedEvents: Josiah Finds the Book of the Law
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Chumtah, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Humtah is a town in the hill country of Judah, named once in the list of the tribe's inheritance. No story is attached to it, and no person is tied to its name. It stands in the record because the land was divided town by town, and every town counted.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Humtah matters because God gave His people a real land with real towns, and no part of the inheritance was too small to record.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: liberty (from slavery)
