Definition: a hurricane
BiblicalUsage: A whirlwind is a storm that catches and carries away, and the book of the wars of the LORD names the whirlwind in the Red Sea. Job says the wicked are as stubble before the wind, and the psalm asks God to make His enemies as the whirlwind drives. Proverbs says destruction will come as a whirlwind when fear arrives.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the whirlwind is God's picture of judgment that cannot be outrun. It takes the stubble and leaves the root, and the wicked are stubble. I hold that the same storm that destroys the wicked also clears the air for the righteous, and God sends it in His time.
RelatedEvents: The Exodus and the Red Sea
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: turned off, i.e. deteriorated
BiblicalUsage: Turned aside is what Israel has become: God planted a noble vine, wholly a right seed, and it has turned into a degenerate plant. The word appears once, and it names the change from what God planted to what it became.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the degenerate vine is the story of every heart that turns from what God planted, and the grace is that God still calls it His vine.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Sur, a gate of the temple
BiblicalUsage: Sur is a gate of the temple, named once in the ordering of the guards who protect the young king Joash. A third part of the guard keeps the gate of Sur, and the gate is part of the plan that keeps a king alive. The name is a door, and the door is a defence.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the gate of Sur shows that God protects His anointed with ordinary doors and ordinary guards.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: turned off, i.e. deteriorated
BiblicalUsage: Turned aside is what Israel has become: God planted a noble vine, wholly a right seed, and it has turned into a degenerate plant. The word appears once, and it names the change from what God planted to what it became.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the degenerate vine is the story of every heart that turns from what God planted, and the grace is that God still calls it His vine.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: covering, i.e. clothing
BiblicalUsage: A covering is clothing, and Jacob's blessing of Judah says he will wash his garments in wine and his clothes in the blood of grapes. The word appears once, in the blessing of the tribe that will carry the sceptre. The covering is the robe of a king.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Judah's covering shows that the King will come in robes washed in wine, and the blessing points to Him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: covering, i.e. clothing
BiblicalUsage: A covering is clothing, and Jacob's blessing of Judah says he will wash his garments in wine and his clothes in the blood of grapes. The word appears once, in the blessing of the tribe that will carry the sceptre. The covering is the robe of a king.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Judah's covering shows that the King will come in robes washed in wine, and the blessing points to Him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to pine
BiblicalUsage: To pine is to waste away with longing or grief, and Jeremiah says the soul of the weary will be satisfied and will not sorrow any more. The LORD says He will satiate the soul of the priests with fatness, and the psalmist's eye mourns by reason of affliction. The word is the slow wasting of a heart that waits.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe pining is the honest condition of the afflicted, and God does not rebuke it; He satisfies it. Jeremiah promises a day when the soul will sorrow no more, and that promise is the anchor for every pining heart. I hold that God counts the tears of the wasting, and He will repay them with fullness.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: be anxious
BiblicalUsage: To be anxious is to fear what may come, and Saul's father worries that his son has been lost looking for the asses. The psalmist is sorry for his sin and anxious over it, and Isaiah asks whom Israel feared that they lied and forgot God. Jeremiah says the tree planted by the waters will not be anxious in the year of drought.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe anxiety in Scripture is always a question of trust: whom do you fear, and where do you stand? The tree by the water does not fear the drought because its roots are already deep. My position is that the cure for anxiety is not a calmer temper but deeper roots.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: the kite (from its rapid flight)
BiblicalUsage: The kite is a bird of prey, named once in the law of unclean birds. It flies fast and hunts from the air, and Israel may not eat it. The word is a kind of hawk, and the law lists it among the birds that are an abomination.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the kite is listed because God teaches His people to tell clean from unclean, even in the sky.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: the kite (from its rapid flight)
BiblicalUsage: The kite is a bird of prey, named once in the law of unclean birds. It flies fast and hunts from the air, and Israel may not eat it. The word is a kind of hawk, and the law lists it among the birds that are an abomination.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the kite is listed because God teaches His people to tell clean from unclean, even in the sky.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to be extinguished; figuratively, to expire or be dried up
BiblicalUsage: To be quenched is to go out like a fire, and Job says the streams of the brooks vanish when the heat comes. The psalmist says his enemies compassed him like bees and are quenched as the fire of thorns, and Proverbs says the lamp of the wicked will be put out. Isaiah says the chariots and the army are quenched as tow.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the quenching of the wicked is God's promise that evil does not burn forever. The fire of thorns flares and dies, and the lamp of the wicked goes out, but the light of the righteous shines. I hold that God quenches what He did not kindle, and keeps burning what He did.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: knowledge
BiblicalUsage: Knowledge is the fruit of the tree in the garden, the wisdom God fills Bezalel with for the work of the tabernacle, and the knowledge of the Most High that Balaam claims. Hosea says God's people are destroyed for lack of knowledge, and the same word that tempts in the garden also builds in the tabernacle. Knowledge is a gift, and it is a danger, and the difference is the fear of the LORD.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe knowledge without God destroys, and knowledge with God builds. The tree promised to make men like God, and the tabernacle was built by men God filled with His Spirit. My position is that the knowledge that saves is the knowledge of God Himself, and Hosea's warning still stands over every generation that forgets Him.
RelatedTopics: Knowledge of God; Wisdom; The Fall
RelatedEvents: The Fall; The Tabernacle Is Built
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: this
BiblicalUsage: This is the Aramaic word for this, and Daniel uses it to point at the things in front of him: this is the Babylon Nebuchadnezzar built, and this is the handwriting that troubles Belshazzar. The beasts come up from the sea, and this horn has eyes like a man. The word does no more than point, and the pointing is the whole work.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the plainness of this is the point: Daniel does not dress up what he sees, and the visions are terrible enough without adornment. The word points, and the prophet names what is pointed at. I hold that plain speech is the prophet's duty, and Daniel keeps it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to move slowly, i.e. glide
BiblicalUsage: To move gently is to glide, and the Song says the beloved's words are like the best wine that goes down sweetly, causing the lips of those who are asleep to speak. The word appears once, in the praise of love that moves slowly and sweetly.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the Song's gentle movement shows that love does not rush, and the best wine is the one that goes down sweetly.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, to impinge, i.e. cling or adhere; figuratively, to catch by pursuit
BiblicalUsage: To cleave is to stick fast, and a man leaves his father and mother and cleaves to his wife. The inheritance must cleave to its tribe, and Israel is told to cleave to the LORD and to serve Him. Joshua repeats it at his farewell: cleave to the LORD your God, and keep His commandments. The word is the picture of a bond that will not let go.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe cleaving is the Bible's picture of covenant: a man to his wife, a tribe to its land, and a people to their God. The same word holds them all, and the holding is the point. My position is that a faith that does not cleave is not faith at all — it is acquaintance, and acquaintance does not save.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: perhaps properly, to arrange; but used figuratively (of words), to speak; rarely (in a destructive sense) to subdue
BiblicalUsage: To speak is the most common action in the Bible, and God speaks to Noah after the flood, and to Moses from the tabernacle, and to Israel in the wilderness. The midwives fear God and do not do as Pharaoh speaks to them, and the word covers both God's command and man's answer. The verb is the engine of the whole story: God speaks, and things happen.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word of God is the most powerful thing in the Bible, because God speaks and the world obeys. The flood ends with a word, the law begins with a word, and the gospel is a word preached. My position is that a God who speaks is a God who can be known, and the speaking is the grace.
RelatedTopics: Word of God; Scripture; God's Power
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a word
BiblicalUsage: A word here is the saying of Moses, and the blessing says all the saints are in God's hand, and they sit down at His feet and receive His words. The word appears once, in the blessing that closes the law. The saints receive God's words because they sit at His feet.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the saints' place is at God's feet, receiving His words, and that is where every believer still belongs.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Dabbesheth, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Dabbesheth is a town on the border of Zebulun, named once in the list of the tribe's inheritance. The name means a hump, like the hump of a camel, and the town stands on the border of the land. Nothing more is told of it.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Dabbesheth is remembered because the borders of the tribes are drawn town by town, and God gives His people a bounded land.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a sticky mass, i.e. the hump of a camel
BiblicalUsage: The hump is the hump of a camel, and Isaiah pictures the beasts of the south carrying riches on the hump of camels into Egypt. The word appears once, in the judgment on those who go down to Egypt for help. The hump carries the treasure, and the treasure is wasted.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the camel's hump shows how much effort people spend carrying their wealth to the wrong helper.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: adhering
BiblicalUsage: Adhering is the state of sticking fast, and the wings of the cherubim touch each other in the temple, spanning the house. Moses says those who cleave to the LORD are alive today, every one of them. Proverbs says there is a friend who sticks closer than a brother, and the word is the same bond in three places.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe adhering is the picture of a faith that holds on, and a God who holds on tighter. The cherubim touch wingtip to wingtip, the faithful cleave to the LORD and live, and the friend sticks closer than a brother. My position is that the bond is the blessing: to adhere to God is to be alive.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H1732); Dabid (i.e. David), the Israelite king:--David.
BiblicalUsage: Dabid is the Greek spelling of David's name as it stands in the older copies, where the letter is a beta where the common text has an upsilon. Matthew opens his gospel with the book of the generation of Jesus Christ, the son of Dabid, and Paul in Antioch says God raised up David to be their king. The name is David's, and the spelling is the only difference.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the spelling matters because it shows the gospel was copied by real hands in real places, and the same king stands behind every spelling. David is the king after God's own heart, and Jesus is his son.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Daberath, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Daberath is a town on the border of Issachar, given to the Levites as a city of their inheritance. The name appears in the border list and in the list of Levitical towns, and the town stands on the edge of the tribe. It is a boundary town with a priestly household.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Daberath matters because the Levites are given towns among the tribes, and God places His servants in the middle of His people.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to push down
BiblicalUsage: To push down is to thrust away, and the psalm asks that the angel of the LORD chase the enemy and drive them down. The wicked is driven away in his wickedness, and Isaiah says God will gather the outcasts of Israel from the four corners. Jeremiah says the false prophets' way will be slippery, and they will be driven on and fall. The word is the push of judgment, and the gathering of grace.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the pushing down of the wicked and the gathering of the outcasts are two sides of one judgment. God drives away those who will not turn, and He gathers those who will. My position is that the same hand that pushes down the proud lifts up the humble.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to urge, i.e. hasten
BiblicalUsage: To hasten is to press forward in a hurry, and the priests thrust Uzziah out of the temple when leprosy breaks out on his forehead. The posts hurry out with Haman's decree, and Mordecai hurries home in sorrow, and the posts hasten again with the counter-decree that saves the Jews. The word is speed under pressure, and it carries both judgment and deliverance.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe haste in Esther is the picture of a world out of control, and God's hand moving faster still. The decree of death goes out in haste, and the decree of life goes out in haste, and the second one wins. I hold that God is never late, even when the posts are running.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to press, i.e. oppress
BiblicalUsage: To press is to crowd and oppress, and Joel says the locust army will not press upon one another as they march. The LORD raises up judges because He is pressed by the groaning of His people under their oppressors. The word is pressure from without and pressure from within.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God hears the groaning of the pressed, and He raises up deliverance for them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably a musical instrument (as being struck)
BiblicalUsage: A musical instrument is what the king gives up for the night: Darius goes to his palace and fasts, and no instrument of music is brought before him. The word appears once, in the night Daniel spends in the lions' den. The king's music stops because his conscience will not let him sleep.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the silenced music shows that a king's conscience can be louder than his orchestra, and God uses it to keep a man awake.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: the breast (as the seat of love, or from its shape)
BiblicalUsage: The breast is the seat of love and the sign of a mother's care, and Ezekiel uses it in the harsh picture of two sisters who played the harlot in Egypt. Their breasts are pressed in the sin of their youth, and the prophet names the sin plainly. Proverbs turns the same word toward marriage, telling a man to be satisfied with the breasts of his own wife. The word holds both the abuse and the blessing of love.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the breast shows how love can be twisted and how it can be honoured, and Scripture does not hide either one. Ezekiel's picture is a warning, and Proverbs is a blessing, and the difference is faithfulness. My position is that God made love for marriage, and the same gift that blesses there destroys when it is stolen.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to walk gently
BiblicalUsage: Hezekiah uses this word for the slow, careful walk of a man who has faced death and been spared, going softly through the rest of his years in bitterness of soul. The psalmist uses it the same way, remembering how he once went with the multitude up to the house of God.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word pictures repentance as a pace, not a moment: a life that has been humbled walks differently from then on.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a fish (often used collectively)
BiblicalUsage: Fish stand in Scripture as part of the creaturely world God made and gave into human care, from the blessing of the sea creatures to the dominion spoken of in the psalm of creation. They also show up as food and as judgment: the prophet pictures men dragged up like fish in a net, and the fish of the sea are taken away when the land mourns. Jonah's great fish is the best-known of all, the creature God prepared to swallow the runaway prophet and bring him back.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the fish remind us how small our control really is. We fish, we net, we count the catch, yet the sea and everything in it belong to the Lord who made them, and He uses even a fish to carry out His purposes.
RelatedTopics: Creation; Goodness of Creation; God's Sovereignty
RelatedEvents: Jonah and Nineveh; Noah and the Flood
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to spawn, i.e. become numerous
BiblicalUsage: Jacob borrows the picture of fish spawning and multiplying when he blesses Joseph's sons, praying that they would grow into a multitude in the midst of the earth. One word for teeming life carries the whole blessing.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe fruitfulness is God's design for His people, not an accident of history.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to spawn, i.e. become numerous
BiblicalUsage: Jacob borrows the picture of fish spawning and multiplying when he blesses Joseph's sons, praying that they would grow into a multitude in the midst of the earth. One word for teeming life carries the whole blessing.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe fruitfulness is God's design for His people, not an accident of history.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to flaunt, i.e. raise a flag; figuratively, to be conspicuous
KeyPassages: Psalms 20:5; Song of Solomon 5:10; Song of Solomon 6:4; Song of Solomon 6:10
BiblicalUsage: To raise a banner is to make yourself seen, and the word carries both the battle standard and the lover's boast. The psalmist vows to set up banners in the name of God when salvation comes, and the Song pictures the beloved as terrible as an army with banners, beautiful and impossible to ignore. The same word names the one who stands out among ten thousand.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God gives His people a banner worth raising, and it is His name, not our own. When we lift Him up, we are seen for what we are: His, and marching under His standard.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, increase, i.e. grain
BiblicalUsage: Corn, or grain, is the staple the land either gives or withholds, and Scripture ties it to blessing and to judgment in the same breath. God promises corn and wine and oil to a people who keep His covenant, and the prophets withdraw the same gifts when the people turn away. At its best it is the firstfruit offering brought in abundance; at its worst the hungry cry for it in streets where there is none.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that daily bread is a sermon about dependence. The grain in the field is God's increase, not ours, and the tithe of it confesses that the whole harvest came from His hand.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to brood over eggs or young
BiblicalUsage: The word pictures a bird brooding over eggs, sitting patiently until life comes. Isaiah sets the picture in a ruined land where the owl nests and hatches, and Jeremiah turns it into a warning: the partridge that sits on eggs it did not lay ends with nothing, like the man who gathers riches by wrong means.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the image cuts both ways: patient care brings life, but claiming what is not yours leaves you empty in the end.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Dagon, a Philistine deity
BiblicalUsage: Dagon was the god of the Philistines, and his story in Scripture is a story of falling down. The ark of the Lord was set beside him in his own temple, and by morning he lay face down before it, his head and hands broken off on the threshold. The Philistines also feasted before Dagon when they thought their god had delivered Samson into their hands, and Saul's armour was later hung in Dagon's house after his death on the battlefield.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Dagon shows what every false god does in the end: it falls before the true God, and it cannot save the people who trust in it. My position is plain — there is one God, and idols are only wood and stone that break.
RelatedEvents: The Ark Captured and Returned; Samson and Delilah
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a gallop
BiblicalUsage: The word appears once, in Deborah's song, as the gallop of the horses whose hooves break in the charge. It is the sound of a battle already won.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe even a single gallop in Scripture is there to make us hear what God did.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to be dumb, i.e. (figuratively) dumbfounded
BiblicalUsage: Jeremiah uses this word once, asking why God should seem like a man astonished, a mighty man who cannot save. The question is the cry of a people who feel abandoned, even while they confess that the Lord is in their midst.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the verse gives us honest language for the dark days: we may ask God why He seems silent, and still hold that He has not left us.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to curvet or move irregularly
BiblicalUsage: Nahum uses the word once, for the prancing horses and jumping chariots of Nineveh's fall. It is the restless, irregular movement of a warhorse in the noise of battle.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word belongs to judgment: the proud city's horses prance for the last time before it falls.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Dahava, a people colonized in Samaria
BiblicalUsage: The Dehavites appear once, named among the peoples settled in Samaria who wrote to stop the rebuilding of the temple. They are one of the colonist peoples the Assyrians planted in the land after carrying Israel away.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the verse reminds us that opposition to God's work often comes from people who were planted there by someone else's empire.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from δαίω (to distribute fortunes); a dæmon or supernatural spirit (of a bad nature):--devil.
BiblicalUsage: This is the New Testament word for a demon, a spirit of a bad nature, and it appears once in this exact form, when the devils in the Gadarene demoniacs beg Jesus to send them into the swine. The demons know who He is, and they know He can cast them out.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the demons' fear is instructive: even the spirits of darkness confess Christ's authority, and we should not fear what fears Him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1140 and G1142; dæmon-like:--devilish.
BiblicalUsage: James uses this word once to name the wisdom that does not come from above: earthly, sensual, devilish. It is wisdom that looks clever and serves the devil's ends.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the verse gives us a test for every clever idea: if it breeds envy and strife, it is not from God, whatever it calls itself.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: neuter of a derivative of G1142; a dæmonic being; by extension a deity:--devil, god.
BiblicalUsage: Demons fill the Gospels, and this is the ordinary word for them: unclean spirits that possess, torment, and speak, yet always yield to Jesus. He casts them out with a word, gives His disciples authority over them, and the demons themselves confess that He is the Son of God. Paul warns that the things the Gentiles sacrifice are offered to demons, not to God, and Revelation pictures fallen Babylon as a haunt of demons.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the New Testament is sober about demons: they are real, they are hostile, and they are defeated. I hold that no believer needs to fear them, because the One who cast them out lives in us, and the demons know it.
RelatedEvents: Jesus Heals the Gerasene Demoniac; The Healing of the Demon-Possessed Boy
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: middle voice from G1142; to be exercised by a dæmon:--have a (be vexed with, be possessed with) devil(-s).
BiblicalUsage: To be demon-possessed is to be held by a demon, and the Gospels show the condition in all its misery: the man among the tombs, fierce and uncontrollable; the boy thrown down and tormented; the daughter grievously vexed. In every case the person is brought to Jesus, and in every case He frees them. Even the charge against Jesus Himself was that He had a devil, which His works answered.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe these accounts are given so that sufferers and their families know where to turn. Christ's authority over demons is not a theory; it is the freedom of real people, and it still stands.
RelatedEvents: Jesus Heals the Gerasene Demoniac; The Healing of the Demon-Possessed Boy
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: crushed, i.e. (figuratively) injured
BiblicalUsage: The word names the crushed and the oppressed, the people the world steps on. The psalms call the Lord a refuge for the oppressed, and promise that He will judge the fatherless and the oppressed so that the man of the earth may oppress no more. Proverbs warns that a lying tongue hates those it has afflicted, and the oppressed are not to return ashamed.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God has a special care for the crushed. When the world grinds people down, the Lord lifts them up, and that is why the poor and needy can praise His name.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to crumble; transitively, to bruise (literally or figuratively)
BiblicalUsage: To crush is what the world does to the poor and what God does to sin, and the word holds both. The prophets charge the rulers who beat God's people to pieces and grind the faces of the poor, and Job pictures frail men crushed before the moth. But the same word falls on the Servant: He was bruised for our iniquities, and it pleased the Lord to bruise Him. The high and lofty One dwells with the one who is of a contrite and humble spirit, to revive the heart of the contrite.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the cross is where the two meanings meet. The crushing that should have fallen on us fell on Christ, and the God who bruised His own Son now revives the bruised and broken who come to Him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to collapse (phys. or mentally)
BiblicalUsage: The word speaks of collapsing under a weight, whether the body or the heart. David cries that he is feeble and sore broken, roaring by reason of the disquietness of his heart, and the psalms return again and again to bones broken and a spirit broken before God. Yet the same brokenness becomes an offering: the sacrifices of God are a broken spirit, and a broken and contrite heart He will not despise.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God does not waste our breaking. He hears the cry of the crushed, and the heart that collapses before Him is the very sacrifice He accepts.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: crushed (literally powder, or figuratively, contrite)
BiblicalUsage: Contrite is the word for a heart that has been ground to powder by its own sin and is honest about it. The Lord is near to the brokenhearted and saves those of a contrite spirit, and He promises to dwell with the humble to revive them. The same word can mean turned to dust, as man returns to the dust from which he came.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe contrition is the doorway to mercy. God does not despise the heart that knows it is dust, and He revives the very spirit the world calls ruined.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: mutilated
BiblicalUsage: The word appears once, in the law that bars a man who is mutilated from entering the congregation of the Lord. It is a hard verse about wholeness and the assembly.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the law guarded the holiness of the gathered people, and Christ has since opened the assembly to all who come to Him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a prolonged form of a primary root; to bite, i.e. (figuratively) thwart:--bite.
BiblicalUsage: Paul uses the word once, as a warning to a quarrelling church: if you bite and devour one another, take heed that you are not consumed by one another. The bite is the church turning on itself.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the verse is a mirror for every congregation: the teeth we use on each other will eat us too.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: or δάκρυον of uncertain affinity; a tear:--tear.
BiblicalUsage: Tears run through the New Testament as the language of grief and of love. The woman washed Jesus' feet with her tears, Paul served the Lord with many tears under persecution, and the promise at the end is that God will wipe away all tears from our eyes. The word itself survives in the older spelling, the form the manuscripts carry where the word lists give the shorter form.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God keeps every tear, and the day is coming when He will wipe them away Himself.
RelatedTopics: Grief; Comfort; Hope; Love for God
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1144; to shed tears:--weep. Compare G2799.
BiblicalUsage: Jesus wept. Two words, the shortest verse in the Bible, and the whole of the incarnation is in them: the Lord who raises the dead first stands at the grave and weeps with the sisters who mourn.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe those two words are the answer to everyone who wonders whether God cares about our grief.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1147; a finger-ring:--ring.
BiblicalUsage: The ring appears once, on the hand of the returning prodigal. The father orders the best robe, a ring, and shoes: the runaway is not taken back as a servant but restored as a son, with the sign of the family on his finger.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the ring is grace made visible: the Father does not make us earn our way back, He dresses us as His own.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably from G1176; a finger:--finger.
BiblicalUsage: The finger is the smallest part of the hand and the instrument of God's power: Jesus casts out devils by the finger of God, and the law itself was written by it. Thomas demands to put his finger into the print of the nails before he will believe, and the risen Lord invites him to do just that. The rich man in torment begs for one fingertip of water, and the Pharisees will not lift a finger to ease the burdens they lay on others.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the finger of God teaches us that His power is both immense and precise. He writes His law, opens deaf ears, and answers a doubter's demand with His own wounded hands.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, dangling, i.e. (by implication) weak or thin
BiblicalUsage: The poor are everywhere in Scripture, and this word names the thin, the weak, the dangling ones with nothing to hold onto. Hannah sang that the Lord raises the poor out of the dust and lifts the beggar from the dunghill to sit among princes, and the prophets charge Israel to defend the poor and to give them bread. The remnant God leaves in the midst of Jerusalem is an afflicted and poor people, and they trust in the name of the Lord.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God's heart for the poor is not an afterthought in Scripture; it is one of its loudest themes. I hold that how we treat the poor is how we treat Him, because He has put His own name beside theirs, and the one who gives to the poor lends to the Lord.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to roil water
BiblicalUsage: Ezekiel uses the word twice, both times of Pharaoh fouling the waters: he troubles the rivers with his feet and roils what was clear. God answers that the beasts will be destroyed from the great waters, and no foot of man or beast will trouble them any more.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the picture warns the powerful: those who muddy the water for everyone else will answer to the God who made it clear.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to spring
KeyPassages: 2 Samuel 22:30; Isaiah 35:6; Song of Solomon 2:8; Zephaniah 1:9; Psalms 18:29
BiblicalUsage: To leap is the joy of the lame made whole and the strength of the warrior, and the word carries both. David leaps over a wall by his God, the lame man in the desert shall leap as a hart when the wilderness breaks out in streams, and the beloved comes leaping upon the mountains. The same word turns dark when men leap on the threshold to fill their masters' houses with violence.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the leap pictures what God does for the weak: He does not teach us to climb the wall, He carries us over it. That is the joy of salvation, and it makes the lame sing.
RelatedBooks: 2 Samuel; Psalms; Song of Solomon; Isaiah; Zephaniah
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, to dangle, i.e. to let down a bucket (for drawing out water); figuratively, to deliver
BiblicalUsage: The word begins with drawing water and ends with deliverance. Moses' future wife draws water for her father's flock, and the daughters tell their father that an Egyptian delivered them and drew water enough for them. Proverbs pictures counsel as deep water that a man of understanding draws out, and the psalmist praises the Lord who has lifted him up and not let his foes rejoice over him.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe drawing water is a picture of how God delivers: He reaches down into the deep and lifts us out, and what He draws up is life itself. The water we draw in prayer is the counsel God has already given, and the wise man draws it out.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to slacken or be feeble; figuratively, to be oppressed
BiblicalUsage: The word names the thin, slack, brought-low condition of a people under judgment. The glory of Jacob grows thin, the rivers dry up, and the psalmist cries that we are brought very low. Israel was greatly impoverished because of the Midianites, and they cried to the Lord.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe being brought low is often the beginning of prayer. When we are thin and slack in our own strength, we finally cry to the One who can lift us.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to drip; by implication, to weep
BiblicalUsage: The word pictures water dripping through a roof and a heart weeping itself away. The Preacher warns that by slothfulness the building decays and the roof drips, Job's friends weep for him, and the psalmist's soul melts for heaviness. Drip by drip, neglect and sorrow wear a house down.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe small leaks sink great houses, and the verse warns us to mend the roof of our lives before the rain comes through. The drip is slow, but it never stops, and the house that ignores it will one day find the roof gone.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to flame (literally or figuratively)
BiblicalUsage: To flame is to burn hot, whether with fire or with pursuit or with anger. The word describes Israel pursuing the Philistines after the battle, the drunkard rising early to follow strong drink, and the wicked whose eyes flame with malice. Fire is never neutral in Scripture: it purifies or it consumes.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word warns us about what burns in us. A fire for God purifies, but a fire for drink or for revenge only consumes the one who carries it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: something dangling, i.e. a bough
BiblicalUsage: The word names the dangling boughs of a tree, and Ezekiel uses it for the spreading branches of the vine and the cedar. The vine becomes a spreading vine of low stature, and the cedar's boughs shelter the birds of heaven. Jeremiah pictures a green olive tree, fair and of goodly fruit, whose boughs are broken when judgment comes.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the boughs remind us that God grows His people like a tree: spreading, sheltering, and accountable for the fruit. The branches that shelter the birds are the same branches the fire will take if the tree bears no fruit.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, something dangling, i.e. a loose thread or hair; figuratively, indigent
KeyPassages: 2 Kings 24:14; Genesis 41:19; Jeremiah 52:15; Song of Solomon 7:5; Isaiah 38:12
BiblicalUsage: The word is a thread, a loose hair, a thing that dangles, and it gathers two pictures: the thin and poor, and the lock of hair. Pharaoh's lean cattle are thin-favoured, the poor of the land are left behind when the rest are carried away, and the beloved's hair hangs like a flock of goats on the mountain. The psalmist's life is cut off like a weaver's thread.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word shows how Scripture sees the poor and the small: God counts the loose threads, and He does not lose one. The thread is small, but the Weaver does not lose it, and the poor He counts are never forgotten.
RelatedBooks: Genesis; 2 Kings; Song of Solomon; Isaiah; Jeremiah
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a burning fever
BiblicalUsage: The word appears once, naming the burning fever among the curses of the covenant: the Lord will strike a disobedient people with a fever that consumes. It is sickness as judgment, the body burning from within.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the verse is a sober reminder that our bodies are not our own, and obedience is not a small thing.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably of Chaldee origin; Dalmanutha, a place in Palestine:--Dalmanutha.
BiblicalUsage: Dalmanutha is named once, as the place where Jesus landed after feeding the four thousand. The Pharisees came out there to test Him, seeking a sign from heaven, and He sighed deeply and refused them.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the place is a warning: even after a miracle, men can demand one more sign and miss the One standing in front of them.
RelatedEvents: The Feeding of the Four Thousand
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably of foreign derivation; Dalmatia, a region of Europe:--Dalmatia.
BiblicalUsage: Dalmatia is named once, when Paul writes that Titus has gone there. It is a brief line in a lonely letter, a companion sent out while Paul waits for the end.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the verse shows the spread of the gospel in a single name: the message had reached the far coast, carried by faithful men.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Dalphon, a son of Haman
BiblicalUsage: Dalphon was a son of Haman, named once among the ten sons who were hanged with their father after the plot against the Jews failed. His name survives only in the list of the judged.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the list is there to show that God finishes what He starts: the house that plotted murder fell by its own design.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: blood (as that which when shed causes death) of man or an animal; by analogy, the juice of the grape; figuratively (especially in the plural) bloodshed (i.e. drops of blood)
BiblicalUsage: Blood is the life, and Scripture says so plainly: the life of the flesh is in the blood, and it is given on the altar to make atonement for the soul. God forbids eating blood because it carries life, and He commands the blood of the Passover lamb on the doorposts, so that when He sees the blood He will pass over. The whole sacrificial system runs on this one truth: without shedding of blood there is no remission, and the blood points to Christ.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the blood of the lambs was always pointing forward, and I hold that the blood of Christ is the only blood that finally cleanses. That is why the Passover still matters: it taught Israel to trust a substitute, and it teaches us the same.
RelatedEvents: The Passover; The Exodus and the Red Sea
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to weep
BiblicalUsage: Jeremiah uses the word once, for the tears that will not stop: his eyes run down with tears night and day, and will not cease, for the virgin daughter of his people is broken with a great breach. It is weeping as a ministry.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the verse gives the prophet's heart its voice: some sorrows are too deep for words, and tears are the prayer.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to be dumb or silent; hence, to fail or perish; trans. to destroy
BiblicalUsage: The word means to fall silent, to fail, to be destroyed, and it gathers the silences of Scripture into one. Isaiah cries that he is undone before the holy God, Hosea warns that the people will fall, and Lamentations weeps that the tears have no rest. Silence before God is either judgment or worship, and this word knows both.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the verse in Isaiah is the hinge: the man who says he is undone is the man God then cleanses and sends. Silence is where the vision begins.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to be dumb or silent; hence, to fail or perish; trans. to destroy
BiblicalUsage: The word means to fall silent, to fail, to be destroyed, and it gathers the silences of Scripture into one. Isaiah cries that he is undone before the holy God, Hosea warns that the people will fall, and Lamentations weeps that the tears have no rest. Silence before God is either judgment or worship, and this word knows both.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the verse in Isaiah is the hinge: the man who says he is undone is the man God then cleanses and sends. Silence is where the vision begins.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably from the base of G1150; a heifer (as tame):--heifer.
BiblicalUsage: The red heifer appears once by this word, in the law of cleansing: its ashes, mixed with water, cleanse the one defiled by touching the dead. A heifer that had never borne a yoke, burned whole, became the means of purification.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the red heifer points forward to a cleansing that no water could give on its own, and finds its answer in Christ.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to be dumb; by implication, to be astonished, to stop; also to perish
BiblicalUsage: To be silent can be reverence, stillness, or ruin, and this word carries all three. The wicked shall be silent in darkness, the psalmist's soul waits in quiet trust, and the prophet laments a city brought to silence by judgment. In the stillness God is either near or the silence is the sentence.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe silence is the posture of the soul that knows it cannot answer God. I hold that the quiet heart is the one God fills, and the loudest faith is sometimes the one that says nothing at all.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably from the base of G1150; perhaps gentle; Damaris, an Athenian woman:--Damaris.
BiblicalUsage: Damaris is named once, among the few who believed when Paul spoke in Athens. Dionysius the Areopagite and a woman named Damaris are the named fruit of a sermon most of the city mocked.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Damaris matters because she shows that the gospel finds its hearers even in the hardest ground: a few believed, and Luke bothered to name them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1154; a Damascene or inhabitant of Damascus:--Damascene.
BiblicalUsage: The Damascene appears once, in Paul's own retelling of his escape: the governor under Aretas kept the city of the Damascenes with a garrison, desiring to apprehend him, and Paul was let down in a basket through the wall. The citizen of Damascus is the persecutor turned apostle, fleeing the city where he first preached Christ.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the verse shows how quickly the persecutor became the persecuted, and how God keeps His own even in a guarded city.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H1834); Damascus, a city of Syria:--Damascus.
BiblicalUsage: Damascus is the city of Paul's conversion, named fifteen times in the New Testament. He was on the road there, breathing threats, when the light struck him down; Ananias was sent to him there; and he preached Christ in its synagogues at once, so that the Jews took counsel to kill him. It is the city where the persecutor became the preacher.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Damascus is where grace interrupts a life mid-stride. The road to Damascus is my picture of conversion: Christ meets a man going the wrong way and turns him around in a moment.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a variation of an obsolete primary of the same meaning; to tame:--tame.
BiblicalUsage: To tame is what man does to every kind of beast and bird and serpent, and James says the one thing no man can tame is the tongue. The wild horse is broken, the demon-possessed man could not be bound with chains, yet the tongue runs loose in every gathering. The contrast is the point: we have mastered the creatures and failed to master ourselves.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the untamed tongue is the proof of our need for grace. Only the Spirit can bridle what no man can tame, and the tongue is where that work shows first.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Damascus, a city of Syria
BiblicalUsage: Damascus is the ancient Syrian capital that stands at the edge of Israel's story from Abraham to the prophets. David struck down its armies when they came to help Hadadezer, and the prophets pronounced judgment on it for its cruelty in war. It is also the city where the road of Paul's conversion runs, the place where the persecutor was struck down and raised up a preacher.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Damascus shows that no city is outside God's reach, whether for judgment or for mercy. The same streets that heard the prophets' woe later heard the gospel from a man who came there to destroy it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Dan-Jaan, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Dan-Jaan is named once, as a place on the border of David's census, between Gilead and the land of the Hittites. It is a boundary marker in a counting that would bring a plague.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe even a boundary town has its place in the story, marking how far the king's pride reached.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Dan, one of the sons of Jacob; also the tribe descended from him, and its territory; likewise a place in Palestine colonized by them
BiblicalUsage: Dan is the son of Jacob and the tribe that bears his name, and his story runs from the blessing to the border. Jacob prophesied that Dan would judge his people as one of the tribes of Israel, and the tribe settled in the north, where its city gave the land its northern boundary, from Dan to Beersheba. The tribe's allotment, its judge Samson, and its later idolatry all belong to this name.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Dan's story is a warning about the edges: a tribe at the border can guard the land or open the gate, and Dan did both. My position is that blessing carries responsibility, and the tribe that was promised judgment ended up needing it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from δάνος (a gift); probably akin to the base of G1325; a loan:--debt.
BiblicalUsage: The word appears once, in the parable of the unmerciful servant: the lord forgave his servant the debt, and the servant seized his fellow and demanded payment. The loan is the picture of what we owe God, and the forgiveness is the picture of what He gives.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the parable turns on this word: the debt we owe is unpayable, and the mercy we receive must be passed on.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1155; a lender:--creditor.
BiblicalUsage: The creditor appears once, in the parable of the two debtors: a certain creditor had two debtors, one owing five hundred pence and the other fifty, and when they had nothing to pay he frankly forgave them both. The word survives in the manuscripts under the spelling with a single vowel, where the word lists give the fuller form.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the parable is the gospel in miniature: we are the debtors with nothing to pay, and the creditor is the God who forgives frankly.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1156; to loan on interest; reflexively, to borrow:--borrow, lend.
BiblicalUsage: To lend and to borrow is the daily business of neighbours, and Jesus turns it into a test of love: lend, hoping for nothing again, and your reward shall be great. The law already told Israel to lend freely to the poor, and the Sermon on the Mount tells the disciple to give to him that asks and not to turn away the one who would borrow.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe lending without return is one of the plainest marks of a child of God. The world lends to get back; the disciple lends because he has already received.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H1840); Daniel, an Israelite:--Daniel.
BiblicalUsage: Daniel is named once in the Gospels, and it is Jesus who names him: when you shall see the abomination of desolation, spoken of by Daniel the prophet, stand in the holy place, then let them which be in Judaea flee. The prophet's name carries the authority of the prophecy.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the Lord's use of Daniel's name settles the prophet's standing: Jesus treats his words as Scripture, and so do I.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a Danite (often collectively) or descendants (or inhabitants) of Dan
BiblicalUsage: The Danite is the tribesman of Dan, and the word gathers the tribe's fighting men and its most famous son. The Danites march armed and take Laish for themselves, and the angel announces the birth of Samson to a Danite woman whose husband is Manoah. The tribe that judged Israel produced the judge who could not judge himself.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the Danites show that a tribe's calling is not its character: the name is noble, but the men must live up to it. The tribe that was named for judgment must live by judgment, and the name is a charge, not a boast.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Danijel, the Hebrew prophet
BiblicalUsage: Daniel is the prophet of the exile who purposed in his heart not to defile himself, and God gave him favour. His name appears when the king's decree threatens the wise men of Babylon, when Belshazzar clothes him in scarlet for reading the writing on the wall, and when his visions leave him troubled to the end of the book. He is the man who prayed with his windows open toward Jerusalem and was thrown to the lions for it.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Daniel is the pattern for the believer in a foreign land: resolve first, pray openly, and trust God with the lions. My position is that faithfulness in small things, like a meal, is what prepares a man for the den.
RelatedEvents: Daniel in the Lions' Den; Daniel's Resolve in Babylon
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Danijel, the Hebrew prophet
BiblicalUsage: Daniel is the prophet of the exile who purposed in his heart not to defile himself, and God gave him favour. His name appears when the king's decree threatens the wise men of Babylon, when Belshazzar clothes him in scarlet for reading the writing on the wall, and when his visions leave him troubled to the end of the book. He is the man who prayed with his windows open toward Jerusalem and was thrown to the lions for it.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Daniel is the pattern for the believer in a foreign land: resolve first, pray openly, and trust God with the lions. My position is that faithfulness in small things, like a meal, is what prepares a man for the den.
RelatedEvents: Daniel in the Lions' Den; Daniel's Resolve in Babylon
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Dannah, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Dannah is named once, as a town in the hill country of Judah given to the tribe in the allotment. It is one name in the long list of the inheritance.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the list matters because the inheritance was real: every town was counted, and every family had its place.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1160; to expend, i.e. (in a good sense) to incur cost, or (in a bad one) to waste:--be at charges, consume, spend.
BiblicalUsage: To spend is the story of the prodigal, the widow, and the apostle. The prodigal wasted his substance with riotous living until he had spent all; the woman with the issue of blood spent all she had on physicians and was nothing bettered; and Paul was willing to spend and be spent for the souls of the Corinthians. The same word covers waste and sacrifice, and the difference is what it is spent on.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word asks us what our lives are being spent on. Paul's answer is my own: to be spent for others is not waste, it is the offering.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from δάπτω (to devour); expense (as consuming):--cost.
BiblicalUsage: The tower builder's parable turns on this word: which of you, intending to build a tower, does not sit down first and count the cost, whether he has sufficient to finish it? The cost is the whole question of discipleship.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Jesus wants us to count the cost before we build, and to build anyway once we have counted it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to knock; by analogy, to press severely
BiblicalUsage: To knock is the sound of a visitor at the door and of a man pressed hard in flight. The Shunammite's son is dead and the mother knocks at Elisha's door; the men of Gibeah beat at the old man's door demanding the guest; and the Song pictures the beloved knocking, his head wet with the dew of the night. The knock is a demand to be let in.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the knock is also the Lord's own image: He stands at the door and knocks, and the one who opens finds a guest, not an intruder. The knock that is answered is the knock of the one who keeps knocking, and the Lord hears it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: crushed, i.e. (by implication) small or thin
BiblicalUsage: Small and thin is the word's range, from the thin ears of corn in Pharaoh's dream to the small still voice on the mountain. The manna lay small as the hoar frost on the ground, the fine flour of the offering was beaten small, and Elijah heard God not in the wind or the earthquake or the fire, but in the still small voice that followed.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God delights to speak in the small things. The thin ear and the still voice both say the same thing: power is not always loud, and the Lord is often found in the quiet.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to crush (or intransitively) crumble
BiblicalUsage: To crush is the work of the pestle, the millstone, and the reformer: the golden calf is ground to powder and scattered on the water, the high places are broken down and stamped small, and the king crushes the idols of a generation. The word is judgment on what men worship, ground to dust.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the crushing of idols is mercy, not cruelty: what we worship must be broken before it breaks us. The idols we grind to powder are the ones that can no longer grind us down.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to stab; by analogy, to starve; figuratively, to revile
BiblicalUsage: To pierce is the wound of the sword and the thrust of the spear, and the word gathers the battlefield and the prophecy. Saul falls on his own sword, the slain lie pierced in the streets, and the prophet says they shall look on Him whom they have pierced. The wound that kills is also the wound that saves.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the pierced One is the centre of the word: the spear that opened His side opened the way for us. The spear that pierced Him is the proof that He was really dead, and really raised.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an age
BiblicalUsage: The word means an age, a generation's span, and it appears twice in Daniel's praise of the God whose dominion is an everlasting dominion, whose kingdom endures from generation to generation. An age is long to us and a breath to Him.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word steadies us: our ages pass, and His dominion does not.
RelatedTopics: Eternity; God's Sovereignty; Kingdom of God
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, a pearl (from its sheen as rapidly turned); by analogy, pearl-stone, i.e. mother-of-pearl or alabaster
BiblicalUsage: The word appears once, among the white and blue hangings of the palace at Shushan, where the feast of Ahasuerus spread its wealth before the princes. A pearl, or mother-of-pearl, set in the pavement of a king's court.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the verse shows how Scripture notices beauty even in a pagan palace, and how quickly that beauty fades.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Dara, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Dara is named once, among the wise men Solomon surpassed: Ethan the Ezrahite, Heman, Chalcol, and Dara, the sons of Mahol. His name survives because Solomon's wisdom was greater.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the verse humbles every reputation: even the wisest of a generation are remembered as the measure of someone wiser.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to tread; by implication, to walk; also to string a bow (by treading on it in bending)
BiblicalUsage: To tread is the march of armies, the pressing of the winepress, and the walk of the believer. The warrior treads his enemies underfoot, the Lord treads the winepress of His wrath, and the psalmist treads on the lion and the adder under God's protection. The same word strings a bow, treading it to bend it for the shot.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe treading pictures authority: the ground we walk on is either ours by promise or the enemy's by trespass, and the Lord gives His people the high places to tread upon. The high places are the Lord's to give, and the feet that walk them are the feet He has shod.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, to tread or frequent; usually to follow (for pursuit or search); by implication, to seek or ask; specifically to worship
BiblicalUsage: To seek is the great verb of the spiritual life, and it appears over a hundred and fifty times. The prophets cry seek the Lord and live, the kings enquire of Him before battle, and the psalms promise that those who seek Him will not lack any good thing. Seeking is not a single prayer but a way of life: to frequent God's presence until it becomes home.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe seeking is the whole of the Christian life in one word. I hold that God is not hiding from us; He has promised that those who seek Him with all their heart will find Him, and the finding is worth the search.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Darda, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Darda is named once, among the wise men of Solomon's day: Ethan, Heman, Chalcol, and Darda, the sons of Mahol, all surpassed by the king's wisdom. His name is a benchmark, not a biography.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the verse teaches the same humility as his brother's name: human wisdom, however great, is only the measure of the wisdom God gives.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a thorn
BiblicalUsage: Thorns are the curse of the ground and the picture of a wasted life. The Lord promised thorns and thistles after the fall, and Hosea pictures the thorn growing up in the altars of a people who have forgotten God. The thorn chokes the seed and tears the hand that reaches for fruit.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the thorn is honest about sin: it does not look dangerous until it draws blood, and by then the field is already overgrown.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {Darejavesh, a title (rather than name) of several Persian kings}
BiblicalUsage: Darius is the title of the Persian kings under whom the exiles lived, and the name appears for the Darius who received Daniel's accusers and for the Darius under whom the temple was finished. He is the king who signed the decree that threw Daniel to the lions, and the king whose second year saw the house of God rebuilt.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Darius shows how God uses even foreign kings: one signed a death warrant and the other a building permit, and the Lord's purpose stood through both.
RelatedTopics: God's Sovereignty; Exile and Return; Rebuilding
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a 'drachma', or coin
BiblicalUsage: The drachma is the coin of the returned exiles, counted by the thousand when the people gave for the rebuilding. The chief of the fathers gave gold and silver and garments, and the darics were weighed into the treasury. A small coin, faithfully given, built a temple.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the verse honours the small gift: the kingdom is built on drachmas, not only on gold talents. The giving was counted coin by coin, and the Lord who counts the coins counts the givers too.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: the south; poet. the south wind
BiblicalUsage: The south is the direction of the wind and the quarter of the land, and the word gathers the map of Israel into one. The south wind brings heat and the rain, the southern border runs to the desert, and the blessing of Naphtali is to possess the west and the south. The chambers of the temple face south, and the prophet walks the south side of the house of God.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the south reminds us that God's land has directions, and every quarter of it belongs to Him. The south wind comes when God sends it, and the land that waits for rain waits on Him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Darkon, one of 'Solomon's servants'
BiblicalUsage: Darkon is named twice, among the children of Solomon's servants who returned from exile with Zerubbabel. His name is a line in the register of the homecoming.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the register honours the servants: the children of Solomon's servants came home too, and their names were written down.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to sprout
BiblicalUsage: To sprout is the first green of creation, when God said let the earth bring forth grass, and it did. Joel promises that the pastures will spring and the trees will bear their fruit when the locust years are over. Sprouting is the earth's yes to God's word.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the sprout is the picture of resurrection in miniature: life comes up where only dry ground was.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: fat; figuratively, rich, fertile
BiblicalUsage: Fat is the picture of richness and plenty in Scripture: the fat pastures, the fat of the land, and the people who grow fat and flourish like the palm tree. Isaiah promises fat things full of marrow at the feast of the Lord, and the psalmist pictures the righteous flourishing in the courts of God, bearing fruit in old age.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe fatness in Scripture is not excess but abundance: the Lord feeds His people richly, and the flourishing life is the one planted in His house. The fat of the land is the Lord's table, and the people who eat at it are the people He has fed.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {a royal edict or statute}
BiblicalUsage: The word is the royal edict, the law of the Medes and Persians that cannot be changed. Daniel's enemies use the king's own law against him, and the decree stands even when the king regrets it. Ezra carries the law of the king of kings alongside it, and the two laws meet in the exile's life.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the edict shows the limit of human law: a king can sign what he cannot undo, but the law of God stands above every decree of men. The king's law can bind a man, but it cannot bind the God who overrules it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Dathan, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Dathan is the Reubenite who joined Korah's rebellion against Moses and Aaron, and the earth opened its mouth and swallowed him. Moses called him to come, and he refused, saying they had not brought them into a land of milk and honey. The psalm remembers it plainly: the earth opened and swallowed up Dathan, and the fire burned in their company.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Dathan is the picture of rebellion that will not be reasoned with. He would not come when Moses called, and the ground he stood on gave way beneath him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to be sick (as if in menstruation)
BiblicalUsage: The word appears once, in the law of the woman after childbirth: she shall be unclean as in the days of her sickness, and the days of her purifying follow. It is the language of the law's care for the body.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the law's attention to the body's seasons shows that God cares for the whole person, not only the soul.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: sick (especially in menstruation)
BiblicalUsage: Sick is the word for the body in its weakness and the land in its defilement. The law names the sick woman and the sick bed, Isaiah pictures the whole head sick and the whole heart faint, and Lamentations weeps over a soul made sick by grief. The same word names the menstruous cloth, cast away as unclean.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe sickness in Scripture is never only physical: it is the sign of a world out of joint, and the God who heals the sick is the God who heals the land. The sickness of the body is the picture of the sickness of the soul, and the same Physician heals both.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: David, the youngest son of Jesse
BiblicalUsage: David is the youngest son of Jesse, anointed by Samuel while still a shepherd boy, and the man after God's own heart. He slew Goliath with a sling and a stone, fled from Saul, and was made king over all Israel, and the Lord promised him a house and a throne forever. His psalms are the prayer book of the church, and his line is the line of Christ.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe David matters because God chose the least and made him the greatest, and I hold that his life is the pattern of repentance: a great sinner who fell hard and came home harder, and whose throne outlasted his failures.
RelatedEvents: David Anointed by Samuel; David and Goliath; Davidic Covenant
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a fisherman
BiblicalUsage: The fisherman appears twice, in the prophets' pictures of the end: the fishers who will be set over the waters of the Dead Sea, and the fishers who will fish for men among the nations. The net is the picture of judgment and of the gospel both.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the fisherman's trade became the apostles' calling: Christ took men who fished for fish and made them fishers of men.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: sick; figuratively, troubled
BiblicalUsage: Sick and troubled is the word for the heart that cannot rest. Isaiah pictures the whole head sick and the heart faint, Jeremiah cries that his heart is faint within him, and Lamentations weeps for a people whose hearts are sick with sorrow. It is the sickness of a soul under judgment.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the sick heart is the truest diagnosis of sin: the whole person aches, and only the Physician can heal it. The troubled heart is the heart that has not yet learned to rest, and the rest is found in Him alone.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: enough (as noun or adverb), used chiefly with preposition in phrases
BiblicalUsage: Enough is the word that stops the giving and satisfies the heart. The people brought more than enough for the building of the tabernacle, and Moses had to restrain them. The years are enough, the days are enough, and the land is enough for the people who trust Him.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe enough is the hardest word in the language of contentment: we always want more, and God says the portion He gives is sufficient. The portion God gives is enough, and the heart that says so has found contentment.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a fisherman
BiblicalUsage: The fisherman appears twice, casting his net in the waters and angling on the shore. Isaiah pictures the fishers mourning when the waters fail, and Jeremiah sends for many fishers who will fish the people out of every hole and hiding place. The net gathers what the hook cannot reach.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the fishers are the picture of God's own work: He sends for His people where they hide, and He draws them in.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a falcon (from its rapid flight)
BiblicalUsage: The falcon is the swift bird of prey, named among the unclean birds of the law and pictured in the ruined land where the birds of prey gather. It flies fast and strikes without warning, and the law keeps it from the table.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the falcon reminds us that swiftness is not wisdom: the fastest bird in the sky is still unclean.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {a judge or advocate}
BiblicalUsage: The judge appears once, in Ezra's commission: the king tells him to appoint judges and magistrates who know the laws of God, to judge all the people beyond the river. A judge who knows God's law is the foundation of a just land.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the verse ties justice to knowledge: a land is only as just as the law its judges know.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {a judge or advocate}
BiblicalUsage: The judge appears once, in Ezra's commission: the king tells him to appoint judges and magistrates who know the laws of God, to judge all the people beyond the river. A judge who knows God's law is the foundation of a just land.

Definition: a battering-tower
BiblicalUsage: The battering tower is the engine of siege, built against the walls of Jerusalem and set up by the king of Babylon. Ezekiel pictures the ramps and the towers rising against the city, and Jeremiah records the siege that ended it. The tower is the slow, certain work of judgment.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the tower warns the proud city: walls that are trusted instead of God will be battered down. The tower rises slowly and falls quickly, and the city that trusts its walls has trusted the wrong thing.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: threshing-time
