Definition: from G1223 and G906; (figuratively) to traduce:--accuse.
BiblicalUsage: This word means to accuse, to speak against a man through a crowd until the charge sticks. It stands only once, where the unjust steward is accused to his master of wasting his goods, and the accusation is what brings his whole life to a reckoning.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that an accusation is a serious thing, whether it is true or false; the steward's waste was real, and the master had a right to ask for an account, which is why the parable ends by asking me to look at my own stewardship.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: middle voice of a compound of G1223 and G950; to confirm thoroughly (by words), i.e. asseverate:--affirm constantly.
BiblicalUsage: To affirm constantly is to insist on a thing with all the weight you can put behind it. Paul tells Titus to affirm the good works of believers, and he tells Timothy that some who teach the law affirm what they do not understand.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that there is a difference between affirming truth and merely insisting on an opinion; Paul wants Titus to press home what is good and true, and he warns Timothy that loud certainty is no substitute for knowing what you are talking about.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1223 and G991; to look through, i.e. recover full vision:--see clearly.
BiblicalUsage: To see clearly is what the blind man in Bethsaida receives and what the Pharisee in the parable lacks. The blind man looks up and sees every man clearly, while the man with the beam in his own eye is told to cast it out first, so that he can see clearly to help his brother.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe clear sight begins at home. I cannot help my brother with his fault while my own beam blinds me, and the mercy of Christ is that He opens blind eyes — first mine, then through me, others.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1225; a traducer; specially, Satan (compare H7854):--false accuser, devil, slanderer.
BiblicalUsage: The devil is the accuser, the slanderer who speaks against God and against men. He tempts Jesus in the wilderness, he puts betrayal into the heart of Judas, he prowls like a roaring lion, and at the end he is cast into the lake of fire.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the devil is real, defeated, and still dangerous. He is real because Scripture names his work plainly, defeated because Christ bound him at the cross, and dangerous because a cornered accuser still roars — so I resist him, and I do it standing in Christ.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1223 and a derivative of G5495; to handle thoroughly, i.e. lay violent hands upon:--kill, slay.
BiblicalUsage: To lay violent hands on a man is what the rulers did to the apostles and what the Jews tried to do to Paul. Peter charges them with slaying Jesus by wicked hands, and Paul's enemies in the temple seized him and sought to kill him.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that violent hands tell the truth about a heart; the men who laid hands on the apostles and on Paul were not defending the truth; they were defending their own power, and God turned their violence into a witness.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1223 and the middle voice of G5563; to remove (oneself) wholly, i.e. retire:--depart.
BiblicalUsage: This word means to depart or withdraw, and it stands only once, at the moment Moses and Elijah depart from Jesus on the mountain. Peter speaks up as they are leaving, not knowing what he says, because the glory is too much for him.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Peter's words on the mountain are a comfort to me; he spoke in wonder and got it wrong, and Jesus did not rebuke him for it — He simply let the cloud speak instead.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1223 and G1209; to receive in turn, i.e. (figuratively) succeed to:--come after.
BiblicalUsage: To receive in turn is to come after another in the same place. Stephen says the fathers received the tabernacle and brought it in with Joshua, taking up the work the generation before them had carried.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the faith is handed down, not invented; one generation receives what the last one carried, and the tabernacle came into the land because faithful men took their turn.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a compound of G1223 and G1210; a "diadem" (as bound about the head):--crown. Compare G4735.
BiblicalUsage: A diadem is a crown bound about the head, the crown of a king, and Revelation sets three of them before us. The dragon wears seven, the beast wears ten, and the Rider on the white horse wears many — and the difference between them is everything.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the crowns in Revelation are the test of who truly reigns. The dragon and the beast wear borrowed glory that fades, but Christ wears many crowns because the kingdom is His by right, and His victory is the one that lasts.
RelatedTopics: Kingship of Christ; End Times; Victory
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1223 and G1325; to give throughout a crowd, i.e. deal out; also to deliver over (as to a successor):--(make) distribute(-ion), divide, give.
BiblicalUsage: To distribute is to give out through a crowd until everyone has a share. The apostles lay the money at their feet and distribution is made to every man according to need, Jesus takes the loaves and distributes them to the five thousand, and the rich young ruler is told to sell all and give to the poor.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe distribution is the gospel made practical. When the church shares what it has, no one goes without, and the loaves in Jesus' hands are the picture of a God who gives until the baskets overflow.
RelatedEvents: The Feeding of the Five Thousand
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1237; a successor in office:--room.
BiblicalUsage: A successor is the man who comes into another's room, and the word stands once for Porcius Festus, who came into Felix's room as governor of Judea. Paul's case passes from one ruler to the next, and still waits.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the changing of governors is a quiet lesson in patience; men come and go from their rooms of power, but Paul's witness goes on, and the gospel is not hurried by any man's timetable.
RelatedEvents: Paul Before Felix, Festus, and Agrippa
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1223 and G1096; to elapse meanwhile:--X after, be past, be spent.
BiblicalUsage: This word means time passing by, days going on until a moment arrives. The Sabbath passes and the women come to the tomb, some days pass before Agrippa and Bernice arrive, and Paul's voyage drags on until the fast is past.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the passing of days is where faith is tested. Nothing happens quickly in these verses — a Sabbath, some days, a long voyage — and God keeps His people through the waiting as surely as through the wonders.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1223 and G1097; to know thoroughly, i.e. ascertain exactly:--(would) enquire, know the uttermost.
BiblicalUsage: To know thoroughly is to find out exactly, and Felix uses the word when he adjourns Paul's case, saying he will know the uttermost of the matter once Lysias comes down. He wants the full truth before he judges.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Felix's delay is a warning to me; he knew enough to be afraid and never enough to decide, and a man can keep asking for more light while the light he already has is enough to act on.
RelatedEvents: Paul Before Felix, Festus, and Agrippa
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1123 and G1107; to tell abroad:--make known.
BiblicalUsage: This word means to make known abroad, to tell a thing widely, and it stands in the King James text at the verse where the shepherds make known what was told them about the child. It does not appear in the Greek text most modern Bibles follow, where the verse simply says they made it known.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the shepherds' telling is the first evangelism, whether the word carries its full prefix or not; they heard, they saw, and they could not keep it to themselves.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1231; (magisterial) examination ("diagnosis"):--hearing.
BiblicalUsage: A hearing is a formal examination, the sitting where a case is weighed. Paul asks for his case to be kept for the hearing of Augustus, and the word is the courtroom's name for the day the truth will be heard.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Paul's appeal to Caesar was an act of faith; he trusted the Roman court to hear him, and behind the court he trusted the God who had promised he would testify in Rome.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1223 and G71; to pass time or life:--lead life, living.
BiblicalUsage: To lead a life is to spend it day by day, and Paul uses the word twice for the same thing: the quiet and peaceable life believers are to lead, and the life the Cretans led before they knew God, passing their time in malice and envy.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the life I lead is the sermon people hear most; Paul does not ask for a spectacular life, only a quiet one lived in godliness, and that is a harder and holier calling than it sounds.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1223 and G1111; to complain throughout a crowd:--murmur.
BiblicalUsage: To murmur through a crowd is to complain until the whole company is buzzing with it. The Pharisees murmur when Jesus eats with publicans, and again when He goes to be the guest of Zacchaeus, and their complaint is always the same: He welcomes sinners.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that their murmuring is the sound of a heart that has forgotten grace; the Pharisees could not bear a Saviour who ate with sinners, and I must ask whether I ever murmur the same way when His mercy reaches someone I think unworthy.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1223 and G1127; to waken thoroughly:--be awake.
BiblicalUsage: To be fully awake is what the disciples were not, until the glory woke them. On the mountain of transfiguration they were heavy with sleep, but when they were awake they saw His glory and the two men standing with Him.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the disciples' waking is a picture of my own; I sleep through much of God's glory, and His mercy is that He wakes me to see Christ as He is, if only for a moment.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1223 and G138; to separate, i.e. distribute:--divide.
BiblicalUsage: To divide is to part a thing out, and the two places here could not be more different. The father in the parable divides his living between his sons, and the Spirit divides His gifts to every man severally as He wills.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the Spirit's dividing is the opposite of the father's; one division wastes an inheritance on riotous living, and the other gives every believer exactly the gift the body needs, and both are left in God's hands.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1244; a distinction or (concretely) variety:--difference, diversity.
BiblicalUsage: Diversities are the differences the Spirit delights in, and Paul names them three times in a single breath. There are diversities of gifts, diversities of administrations, and diversities of operations, but the same Spirit, the same Lord, the same God.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the church's variety is God's design, not a problem to solve. One Spirit gives many gifts for many works, and the unity of the body is proved by its differences, not by sameness.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: middle voice from G1223 and a compound of G2596 and G1651; to prove downright, i.e. confute:--convince.
BiblicalUsage: To confute thoroughly is to prove a thing downright, leaving no room for argument, and Apollos does it in public, showing from the Scriptures that Jesus is the Christ. The Jews have no answer because the proof is in the text they already own.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Apollos is the pattern for answering honest objections; he did not shout the Jews down; he opened the Scriptures and proved his case, and the truth did the convincing.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1223 and G2511; to cleanse perfectly, i.e. (specially) winnow:--thoroughly purge.
BiblicalUsage: To purge thoroughly is to clean out completely, and John the Baptist uses it for the winnowing fork in Christ's hand. He will thoroughly purge His floor, gathering the wheat into His garner and burning the chaff with unquenchable fire.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Christ's winnowing is both warning and comfort; the chaff is burned, but the wheat is gathered, and the same fork that separates is the proof that nothing good in God's harvest is lost.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1223 and G2967; to hinder altogether, i.e. utterly prohibit:--forbid.
BiblicalUsage: To forbid altogether is to hinder completely, and John the Baptist does it once, when Jesus comes to be baptized. John forbids Him, saying he needs to be baptized by Jesus instead, and Jesus answers that it must be so to fulfil all righteousness.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe John's forbidding shows how strange the gospel looks to a faithful man; the greater comes to the lesser to be baptized, and righteousness turns out to mean Jesus stepping into our place, not the other way around.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1249; to be an attendant, i.e. wait upon (menially or as a host, friend, or (figuratively) teacher); technically, to act as a Christian deacon:--(ad-)minister (unto), serve, use the office of a deacon.
BiblicalUsage: To serve is to wait on others, and the word runs from the table to the cross. The Son of Man came not to be ministered unto but to minister, the apostles say it is not right to leave the word of God and serve tables, and Jesus promises that where He is, there shall His servant be.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe serving is the shape of greatness in the kingdom. Christ did not come to be waited on but to wait on us, and every table I serve, every need I meet, is a share in His own work.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1249; attendance (as a servant, etc.); figuratively (eleemosynary) aid, (official) service (especially of the Christian teacher, or technically of the diaconate):--(ad-)minister(-ing, -tration, -try), office, relief, service(-ing).
BiblicalUsage: Ministry is service with a task attached to it, and the New Testament gives it many names: the ministry of the word, the ministry of reconciliation, the perfecting of the saints, and the gift of ministering itself. One word covers them all because one heart drives them all.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe ministry is never a title before it is a towel. The apostles gave themselves to prayer and to the ministry of the word, and the same word names the collection for the poor, because serving God and serving His people are one work.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably from an obsolete διάκω (to run on errands; compare G1377); an attendant, i.e. (genitive case) a waiter (at table or in other menial duties); specially, a Christian teacher and pastor (technically, a deacon or deaconess):--deacon, minister, servant.
BiblicalUsage: A servant is one who waits at table, and in the New Testament the word grows into deacon, minister, and servant of Christ. Phoebe is called a servant of the church at Cenchrea, Paul greets the deacons at Philippi and sets out how a deacon must live, and Jesus says whoever would be great among His people must be their minister.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the title servant is the highest honour the church gives. Christ took the towel and the basin, and every deacon and minister since stands in that line, serving the table and the people of God.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1364 and G1540; two hundred:--two hundred.
BiblicalUsage: Two hundred is a round number the Gospels use to measure what seems impossible. Two hundred pennyworth of bread would not feed the crowd, the ship holds two hundred and seventy-six souls in all, and the two witnesses prophesy for a thousand two hundred and threescore days.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that two hundred is the number of our insufficiency. The disciples counted the cost and found it short, and that is exactly where Jesus begins, because His provision never starts with what we have.
RelatedEvents: The Feeding of the Five Thousand
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: middle voice from G1223 and G191; to hear throughout, i.e. patiently listen (to a prisoner's plea):--hear.
BiblicalUsage: This word means to hear a man through, to listen patiently to the end of his plea, and it stands once, where Felix promises Paul he will hear him fully when his accusers come. The form in the text is the future of the simpler verb to hear, and it carries the whole weight of a fair hearing.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that a patient hearing is the least justice owes a man; Felix promised it and delayed it, but the promise itself is right: every plea deserves to be heard to the end.
RelatedEvents: Paul Before Felix, Festus, and Agrippa
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1223 and G2919; to separate thoroughly, i.e. (literally and reflexively) to withdraw from, or (by implication) oppose; figuratively, to discriminate (by implication, decide), or (reflexively) hesitate:--contend, make (to) differ(-ence), discern, doubt, judge, be partial, stagger, waver.
BiblicalUsage: To discern is to separate one thing from another, and the word covers both good judgment and doubting faith. James warns the doubter who wavers like a wave, Paul says the man who doubts over his food is condemned, and Jude tells the church to make a difference between the doubting and the hardened.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe discernment is the gift of seeing what is truly there. It separates truth from error and faith from wavering, and it is the gift I need most when my own heart is divided.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1252; judicial estimation:--discern(-ing), disputation.
BiblicalUsage: Discerning is the judgment that tells good from evil, and it belongs to the mature. The gift of discerning of spirits sorts true prophecy from false, the strong meat of the word trains the senses to discern both good and evil, and Paul tells the Romans not to judge one another over doubtful things.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a trained conscience is a gift of the Spirit. It is not suspicion, and it is not cynicism — it is the steady ability to tell what honours God from what only looks like it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1223 and G2980; to talk throughout a company, i.e. converse or (genitive case) publish:--commune, noise abroad.
BiblicalUsage: To talk abroad is to carry news through a whole company until everyone has heard it. The news of John's birth spreads through all the hill country of Judea, and the Pharisees reason among themselves against Jesus after He heals on the Sabbath.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that news travels, whether it is good or bad; the birth of John filled the hills with talk, and the healing on the Sabbath filled the Pharisees with anger, and both crowds were talking about the same God at work.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: middle voice from G1223 and G3004; to say thoroughly, i.e. discuss (in argument or exhortation):--dispute, preach (unto), reason (with), speak.
BiblicalUsage: To reason together is to argue a thing out, and Paul does it everywhere he goes. He reasons in the synagogue at Thessalonica for three Sabbaths, he speaks boldly for three months in the synagogue at Ephesus, he preaches until midnight at Troas, and in the letter to the Hebrews the word is used of God reasoning with us as sons.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe reasoning is part of preaching, not the opposite of it. Paul opened the Scriptures and reasoned from them, and a faith that cannot be argued from the text is not the faith the apostles preached.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1223 and G3007; to leave off in the middle, i.e. intermit:--cease.
BiblicalUsage: This word means to leave off or cease, and it stands once, where the woman who anointed Jesus' feet is praised because she has not ceased to kiss them since He came in. Her devotion never paused.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that a love that does not cease is the best apology for the gospel; the woman's kisses never stopped, and neither should my gratitude.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1256; a (mode of) discourse, i.e. "dialect":--language, tongue.
BiblicalUsage: A tongue is the language a people speaks, and at Pentecost the word does its great work. The crowd hears the apostles speak in their own tongue, Paul addresses the Jerusalem crowd in the Hebrew tongue, and the voice from heaven speaks to him in the same tongue on the Damascus road.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God speaks every tongue because He made them all. At Pentecost the gospel crossed the language barrier in a single morning, and it has been crossing it ever since.
RelatedTopics: Language; Mission; Outpouring of the Spirit
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1223 and G236; to change thoroughly, i.e. (mentally) to conciliate:--reconcile.
BiblicalUsage: This word means to be reconciled, to make peace where there was enmity, and it stands in the Sermon on the Mount. The form in the text is the middle voice of the same verb, and the command is plain: first be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe reconciliation comes before worship; God will not take my gift while my brother and I are at odds, and the altar can wait until the relationship is mended.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1260; discussion, i.e. (internal) consideration (by implication, purpose), or (external) debate:--dispute, doubtful(-ing), imagination, reasoning, thought.
BiblicalUsage: Thoughts are the reasonings of the heart, and the Gospels show them at work in friend and enemy alike. Jesus perceives the thoughts of the Pharisees, evil thoughts proceed from the heart to defile a man, and Paul tells the Philippians to do all things without disputing.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe my thoughts are never private from God. He reads them as plainly as words, and the question is whether they are turned toward Him or curled inward on myself.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1223 and G3049; to reckon thoroughly, i.e. (genitive case) to deliberate (by reflection or discussion):--cast in mind, consider, dispute, muse, reason, think.
BiblicalUsage: To reason within oneself is to argue in the heart, and the Gospels are full of it. The scribes reason that Jesus blasphemes, the disciples reason about bread, and the rich fool reasons with himself about his barns.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe reasoning in the heart is where faith is won or lost. The scribes reasoned themselves away from Jesus, while the disciples who brought their questions to Him found answers, and the difference is whether I reason alone or with Him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1223 and G3089; to dissolve utterly:--scatter.
BiblicalUsage: This word means to be dissolved or come to nothing, and it stands once, where Gamaliel reminds the council that Theudas rose up, boasting himself to be somebody, and was slain, and all his followers were scattered and brought to nothing.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Gamaliel's counsel still stands; movements built on a man come to nothing when the man falls, but the work of God cannot be overthrown, and time itself proves which is which.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1223 and G3164; to fight fiercely (in altercation):--strive.
BiblicalUsage: To strive or fight is what the Pharisees and Sadducees do over Paul in the council, contending so fiercely that the captain fears Paul will be torn apart. The word stands only once, and the fight is over the resurrection.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the council's fight is a picture of religion without grace; men who agreed on nothing could agree on tearing Paul apart, and the resurrection they argued over is the very truth that would have united them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1223 and G3140; to attest or protest earnestly, or (by implication) hortatively:--charge, testify (unto), witness.
BiblicalUsage: To testify solemnly is to charge a thing with the full weight of a witness, and Paul and Peter do it at every turning point. Peter testifies that they should save themselves from this untoward generation, Paul testifies to Jews and Greeks alike of repentance and faith, and Timothy is charged before God to preach the word.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe solemn testimony is the preacher's duty. It is not an opinion offered for discussion but a charge laid down before God, and the gospel deserves to be spoken as though eternity depended on it — because it does.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1223 and G3306; to stay constantly (in being or relation):--continue, remain.
BiblicalUsage: To remain is to stay when everything else passes away, and the word is used of the faithful and the fading alike. The disciples remain with Jesus in His temptations, the gospel remains with the Galatians, the heavens and the earth will pass away while Christ remains, and the scoffers ask where the promise of His coming is.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe remaining is the whole of the Christian life. Temptations come, the world scoffs, and heaven and earth themselves will change, but Christ remains, and those who remain in Him remain forever.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1266; disunion (of opinion and conduct):--division.
BiblicalUsage: Division is what the word names, and Jesus says He came to bring it, not peace as the world counts peace. A household will be divided over Him, father against son and mother against daughter, and the division is the sign that the gospel has arrived.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the division Jesus brings is honest, not cruel; he does not divide families for sport; He divides them because truth demands a choice, and the choice reveals where each heart truly stands.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1223 and G3307; to partition thoroughly (literally in distribution, figuratively in dissension):--cloven, divide, part.
BiblicalUsage: To divide is to part out, and the word stands at the cross and in the church. The soldiers divide Christ's garments among them and cast lots for His coat, and the first believers sell their possessions and divide them to all who have need.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the dividing at the cross and the dividing in the church are two sides of one coin. Men divided His clothes in greed, and His people divided their goods in love, and the difference is the difference the cross makes.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1223 and the base of G3551; to distribute, i.e. (of information) to disseminate:--spread.
BiblicalUsage: To spread abroad is what the rulers feared the gospel would do, and they were right. The apostles are warned to speak no more in the name of Jesus, lest the word spread further among the people, but the warning only proves how far it has already gone.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the gospel spreads because it cannot be contained; the rulers tried to stop it with a threat, and the threat itself is the confession that the name of Jesus was already on every tongue in Jerusalem.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1223 and G3506; to nod (or express by signs) across an intervening space:--beckon.
BiblicalUsage: To beckon is to nod or gesture without words, and Luke uses it once, where Zechariah comes out of the temple unable to speak and beckons to the people. His silence says what his voice cannot.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Zechariah's beckoning is the picture of a man struck silent by wonder; he had asked for a sign and received one, and the gesture is worth more than words because it says he has seen God at work.
RelatedPeople: Zechariah, Father of John the Baptist
RelatedEvents: The Birth of John the Baptist
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1223 and the base of G32; to herald thoroughly:--declare, preach, signify.
BiblicalUsage: To declare abroad is to publish a thing widely, and the word stands in three very different mouths. Paul declares his purification in the temple, Jesus tells the disciples to preach the kingdom, and God declares to Pharaoh that His name will be published through all the earth.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God's name is declared whether men mean it or not. Pharaoh's hardness became the occasion for it, the disciples' preaching carried it, and the same name is still being published wherever the gospel goes.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a compound of G1223 and G3539; something thought through, i.e. a sentiment:--thought.
BiblicalUsage: A thought is the reasoning of the heart, and the word stands once, where Jesus knows the thoughts of the Pharisees and answers them before they speak. Their thought is that He casts out devils by Beelzebub, and His answer exposes the thought for what it is.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Jesus knows my thoughts before I speak them; that is a frightening truth and a comforting one, because the same Lord who sees the worst of my thinking is the one who came to cleanse it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1223 and G3563; deep thought, properly, the faculty (mind or its disposition), by implication, its exercise:-- imagination, mind, understanding.
BiblicalUsage: The mind is the seat of understanding, and Scripture calls it to love God with all of it. The greatest commandment takes the whole mind, the Ephesians are told their minds were darkened before they knew Christ, and John writes that the Son of God has given us understanding to know Him who is true.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the mind is not the enemy of faith but its instrument. God gave me understanding to know Him, and loving Him with all my mind is the first and great commandment, not an afterthought.
RelatedTopics: Knowledge of God; Love for God; Transformation
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1223 and G455; to open thoroughly, literally (as a first-born) or figuratively (to expound):--open.
BiblicalUsage: To open is what God does to eyes, to minds, and to hearts. The disciples' eyes are opened at the breaking of bread, Lydia's heart is opened to attend to Paul's words, their understanding is opened to the Scriptures, and the deaf man's ears are opened at a word.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe opening is God's work, not mine. I cannot open my own eyes or my own heart, but He opens both, and the moment He does, the Christ I had walked beside all day is suddenly known.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1223 and a derivative of G3571; to sit up the whole night:--continue all night.
BiblicalUsage: To spend the whole night is what Jesus does once, and Luke records it simply: He went out into a mountain to pray, and continued all night in prayer to God. The next morning He chooses the twelve.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the night of prayer before the choosing of the twelve is the pattern for every great decision; Jesus did not rush the choosing; He spent the night with His Father first, and so should I.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1223 and ἀνύω (to effect); to accomplish thoroughly:--finish.
BiblicalUsage: To finish a course is to bring a journey to its end, and Paul uses the word once, when the ship from Tyre reaches Ptolemais and the voyage is finished. The course is complete, the anchor is down, and the travellers go ashore.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that finishing is a grace; Paul's course ended in a harbour, and the same God who kept him through the storm brought him safely to land, which is how every faithful course ends.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1223 and the genitive case of G3956; through all time, i.e. (adverbially) constantly:--alway(-s), continually.
BiblicalUsage: This entry is not one word but two standing together, through and all, and the Greek text never joins them into a single word. Luke says the disciples were continually in the temple praising God, and Peter quotes the psalm that the Lord is always before his face, and in both places the two words together mean always.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that always is the right way to read these verses; the disciples did not visit the temple now and then; they lived there in praise, and the Lord was not before David sometimes, but continually.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1223 and a derivative of the base of G4008; to cross entirely:--go over, pass (over), sail over.
BiblicalUsage: To pass over is to cross from one shore to another, and the word is used of boats, of crowds, and of the gulf no man can cross. Jesus passes over the sea to His own city, He comes to the land of Gennesaret, Paul's ship passes over to Phoenicia, and Abraham tells the rich man that none may pass from torment to comfort.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the crossings in the Gospels show who Jesus is. He crosses seas the disciples fear, He crosses into the country of the Gerasenes to free one man, and the gulf He cannot cross is the one sin fixed between the lost and God.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1223 and G5316; appearing through, i.e. "diaphanous":--transparent.
BiblicalUsage: This word means transparent, clear as glass, and it is the word the King James translators used for the street of the new Jerusalem, pure gold as it were transparent glass. It belongs to the Received Text, where the verse reads transparent; the Greek text most modern Bibles follow uses a closely related word for clear instead.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the picture stands even so; the city of God is clear as crystal, and whether the word is transparent or clear, the promise is the same: nothing hidden, nothing clouded, in the city where God dwells.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1223 and a derivative of G5345; to report thoroughly, i.e. divulgate:--blaze abroad, commonly report, spread abroad, fame.
BiblicalUsage: To spread abroad is what happens to news no one can keep quiet. The leper Jesus healed spreads the report everywhere, the fame of the blind men who were healed goes through all the land, and the soldiers spread the lie about the empty tomb for money.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that news always spreads, and the question is which news I spread. The healed could not keep silent about Jesus, and the soldiers were paid to lie about Him, and I must choose whose report I carry.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1223 and G5342; to bear through, i.e. (literally) transport; usually to bear apart, i.e. (objectively) to toss about (figuratively, report); subjectively, to "differ", or (by implication) surpass:--be better, carry, differ from, drive up and down, be (more) excellent, make matter, publish, be of more value.
BiblicalUsage: To be different is to carry more weight than something else, and Jesus uses the word to lift fear off His disciples. The birds of the air are fed by the Father, and you are of more value than many sparrows; the same word tells the Philippians to approve the things that are excellent.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the worth Jesus gives me is not a price I set but a value He declares. I am worth more than sparrows because the Father who feeds them loves me, and that is enough to quiet every fear about tomorrow.
RelatedTopics: God's Provision; Love of God; Fear
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1223 and G5343; to flee through, i.e. escape:--escape.
BiblicalUsage: To escape is to get away, and the word stands once, where the soldiers plan to kill the prisoners lest any of them escape when the ship breaks apart. The centurion stops them because he wants to save Paul.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the soldiers' plan and the centurion's mercy are the whole voyage in miniature; men meant to kill to keep order, and God used one man's regard for Paul to save every soul aboard.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1308; varying; also surpassing:--differing, divers, more excellent.
BiblicalUsage: Different is the word for what is more excellent, and Hebrews uses it of Christ and His covenant. He has obtained a more excellent ministry, a better covenant, and a more excellent name than the angels, and the gifts of the Spirit differ one from another.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the better things in Hebrews are all found in Christ. A better covenant, a better name, a better ministry — the old was good, but the new is more excellent because it rests on His blood, not on ours.
RelatedTopics: Superiority of Christ; Covenant; Spiritual gifts
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1225 and G5351; to rot thoroughly, i.e. (by implication) to ruin (passively, decay utterly, figuratively, pervert):--corrupt, destroy, perish.
BiblicalUsage: To corrupt is to ruin a thing from the inside, and the word covers bodies, minds, and treasures. Paul warns that men of corrupt minds suppose gain is godliness, the outward man perishes while the inward is renewed, the moth corrupts no treasure laid up in heaven, and the destroyers of the earth will themselves be destroyed.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe corruption is the slow work of sin, and the antidote is the daily renewing of the inward man. The body wastes, the mind is pierced by greed, but God renews what the world cannot touch.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1311; decay:--corruption.
BiblicalUsage: Corruption is the decay of the grave, and Peter's sermon turns on it. David saw corruption, but Christ did not, because God would not leave His Holy One to see it, and the promise is that the same God who raised Him will raise us.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the empty tomb is the answer to corruption. Death decays everything it touches, but it could not hold the Holy One, and His rising is the pledge that my own body will not be left to decay forever.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1223 and G5442; to guard thoroughly, i.e. protect:--keep.
BiblicalUsage: To keep safe through danger is what the angels are charged to do, and the word stands once, in the psalm the devil quotes to Jesus. He shall give His angels charge over thee, to keep thee, and the promise is that they will bear Him up in their hands.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the devil's quoting of this verse is the warning to handle Scripture rightly; the promise is true — God does keep His own — but it is not a licence to throw oneself off the pinnacle to prove it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1223 and G4126; to sail through:--sail over.
BiblicalUsage: To sail over is to cross open water, and Luke uses it once on the voyage to Rome, when the ship sails over the sea of Cilicia and Pamphylia. It is a plain travel note from a man who was there.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Luke's sailing notes are the fingerprint of an eyewitness; he writes the sea's name because he crossed it, and the plainness of the detail is what makes the whole voyage ring true.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1223 and a derivative of G4192; to toil through, i.e. (passively) be worried:--be grieved.
BiblicalUsage: This word means to be grieved or worn out by trouble, and the form in the text is the middle voice of the same verb. The apostles are grieved because Peter and John teach the resurrection, and Paul is grieved by the spirit that follows the slave girl, until he turns and commands it out.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe grief at the truth being opposed is a holy thing; the apostles were grieved because men could not bear to hear of the resurrection, and Paul's grief ended in deliverance, which is where all holy grief should lead.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1223 and G639; to be thoroughly nonplussed:--(be in) doubt, be (much) perplexed.
BiblicalUsage: To be perplexed is to be at a loss, standing before something you cannot explain. The crowd is perplexed at Pentecost, Herod is perplexed at the report of Jesus, the rulers doubt what the apostles' escape will come to, and Peter doubts what his vision means.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe perplexity is often the beginning of understanding. The crowd at Pentecost did not know what to make of the sound, and the wondering that followed is what opened their ears to Peter's sermon.
RelatedTopics: Faith; Outpouring of the Spirit; Evangelism
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1223 and G4198; to travel through:--go through, journey in, pass by.
BiblicalUsage: To pass through is to travel across a place on the way to somewhere else. Jesus passes through the cornfields on the Sabbath, He passes through towns and villages teaching on His way to Jerusalem, and Paul passes through the churches confirming them.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that passing through is the picture of the Christian life. We are travellers, not settlers, and every town and field we cross is a place to teach, to heal, and to leave stronger than we found it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1223 and G4231; to thoroughly occupy oneself, i.e. (transitively and by implication) to earn in business:--gain by trading.
BiblicalUsage: To trade is to put money to work, and the word stands once, where the nobleman's servants are asked what they gained by trading. One reports ten pounds made, and the master answers that faithfulness with little earns rule over much.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the trading in this parable is the stewardship of every gift God gives; he does not ask for success I cannot produce, only for faithfulness with what is in my hand, and the reward is more trust, not less.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1223 and the base of G4249; to saw asunder, i.e. (figuratively) to exasperate:--cut (to the heart).
BiblicalUsage: This word means to be cut to the heart, sawn asunder by anger, and the form in the text is the middle voice of the same verb. The council is cut to the heart when the apostles speak, and again when Stephen speaks, and in both places the cutting leads to rage, not repentance.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a heart can be cut in two directions; the same word that describes the council's fury describes a wound that could have led to repentance, and the tragedy is that they chose rage over the sorrow that saves.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1223 and G726; to seize asunder, i.e. plunder:--spoil.
BiblicalUsage: To plunder is to carry off a house's goods, and Jesus uses it once in a parable of binding the strong man. No one can spoil the strong man's house unless he first binds the strong man, and then he may spoil his house.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the strong man in this parable is the devil, and the binding is the cross; Christ bound the strong man, and ever since, His people have been spoiling the house, setting captives free one by one.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1223 and G4486; to tear asunder:--break, rend.
BiblicalUsage: This word means to tear asunder, to rend, and it stands in the forms of a stronger verb for tearing. The net breaks under the catch of fish, and the demoniac tears apart his chains, and the tearing shows a strength no man could master until Christ came.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the tearing in these verses shows what sin and glory both do; sin tears nets and chains and garments, but the tearing of the veil is what the rending of the high priest's clothes could never do — open the way to God.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1223 and σαφής (clear); to clear thoroughly, i.e. (figuratively) declare:--tell unto.
BiblicalUsage: To explain plainly is to make a thing clear, and the word stands twice in Matthew. The disciples ask Jesus to declare the parable of the tares, and the servants come to their lord and declare plainly all that was done to his fellow servant.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that plain explaining is a mercy; Jesus does not leave His disciples guessing at the parable, and the servant who declares the whole matter plainly is the one the master hears.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1223 and G4579; to shake thoroughly, i.e. (figuratively) to intimidate:--do violence to.
BiblicalUsage: To do violence to a man is to shake him down by force, and the word stands once, where John tells the soldiers to do violence to no man and to be content with their wages. It is the only place the soldiers are told how to behave.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that John's charge to the soldiers is the gospel applied to power; men with swords are told to use them justly and to be content, which is the beginning of all honest government.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1223 and G4650; to dissipate, i.e. (genitive case) to rout or separate; specially, to winnow; figuratively, to squander:--disperse, scatter (abroad), strew, waste.
BiblicalUsage: To scatter is what happens when the shepherd is struck and the sheep are driven apart. Jesus quotes it on the night of His arrest, the prodigal scatters his inheritance in riotous living, and the disciples are scattered abroad after Stephen's death, preaching wherever they go.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe scattering is God's strange way of sowing. The sheep scattered at the cross, the money scattered in the far country, the church scattered by persecution — and every scattering spread the seed further than staying home ever would.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1223 and G4982; to save thoroughly, i.e. (by implication or analogy) to cure, preserve, rescue, etc.:--bring safe, escape (safe), heal, make perfectly whole, save.
BiblicalUsage: To save through is to bring safely to the other side, and the form in the text spells the verb with a different vowel than the dictionary entry. The sick are saved by touching the hem of His garment, the sailors are saved through the wreck, and eight souls are saved by water in the days of Noah.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe saving through is the whole story of grace; God does not always keep His people out of the water; He brings them through it, and the ark, the garment, and the broken ship all tell the same tale.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1223 and G4685; to draw apart, i.e. sever or dismember:--pluck asunder, pull in pieces.
BiblicalUsage: To tear apart is what a mob does, and the word stands twice in scenes of violence. The crowd in Jerusalem seizes Paul and tears him apart, and the demoniac in the tombs tears his chains asunder, and no man can tame him.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that tearing is what a crowd does when it has no truth left; the mob tore at Paul and the demon tore at the boy, and in both places Christ stood between the torn and those who tore.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1223 and G4687; to sow throughout, i.e. (figuratively) distribute in foreign lands:--scatter abroad.
BiblicalUsage: To scatter abroad is what persecution did to the church in Jerusalem, and the scattering became sowing. After Stephen's death the disciples are scattered through Judea and Samaria, and those who are scattered preach the word wherever they go.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the scattering after Stephen is the church's first missionary journey. It was meant to destroy them, and instead it planted the gospel in every town they fled to.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1289; dispersion, i.e. (specially and concretely) the (converted) Israelite resident in Gentile countries:--(which are) scattered (abroad).
BiblicalUsage: The dispersion is the scattering itself, the Jews living far from Jerusalem among the nations. Peter writes to the strangers scattered through Pontus and Asia, James writes to the twelve tribes scattered abroad, and the Greeks ask where Jesus will go, to the dispersed among the Gentiles.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the dispersion is the church's address. God's people have always lived scattered among the nations, and the letters to them are letters to us — strangers and pilgrims, waiting for home.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: middle voice from G1223 and G4724; to set (oneself) apart (figuratively, distinguish), i.e. (by implication) to enjoin:--charge, that which was (give) commanded(-ment).
BiblicalUsage: To charge strictly is to command with an order not to be broken, and Jesus does it after every wonder. He charges the healed not to tell, He charges the disciples not to tell any man He is the Christ, and the apostles write that they gave no such commandment to trouble the Gentiles.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the charge to keep silent was for a season, not forever. The wonders were not yet finished, and the time to speak would come when the cross had made the meaning plain.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1339; an interval:--space.
BiblicalUsage: An interval is the space between two things, and the word stands once, for the space of about three hours between Ananias and Sapphira coming before Peter. Three hours is all that separates one lie from the next.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the three hours between the two lies are the measure of a chance refused; Sapphira had three hours to turn back, and she used them to agree with the lie instead.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1291; a variation:--difference, distinction.
BiblicalUsage: A distinction is a difference that matters, and Paul makes it twice in Romans. There is no distinction between Jew and Greek, for all have sinned and all are justified freely, and the same Lord is rich unto all who call upon Him.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe no distinction is the heart of the gospel. The law makes distinctions, the world makes distinctions, but grace makes none, and that is why the gospel is good news for everyone.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1223 and G4762; to distort, i.e. (figuratively) misinterpret, or (morally) corrupt:--perverse(-rt), turn away.
BiblicalUsage: To pervert is to turn a thing from its straight course, and the word is used of the crooked generation and the false teachers. The Jews pervert the way of the Lord, Elymas seeks to turn the deputy from the faith, and Paul warns that grievous wolves will arise speaking perverse things.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe perverting is the devil's favourite work. He does not need to deny the truth outright; he only needs to bend it a little, and a bent road leads a whole generation astray.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1299; arrangement, i.e. institution:--instrumentality.
BiblicalUsage: An ordinance is a thing appointed by authority, and the word stands twice for very different appointments. The law was ordained by angels in the hand of a mediator, and Paul tells the Romans that whoever resists the ordinance of God resists the power God set in place.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that ordinances are God's ordering of the world; the law came by angels, the powers that be are ordained by God, and resisting them is not freedom but rebellion against the hand that set them there.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1299; an arrangement, i.e. (authoritative) edict:--commandment.
BiblicalUsage: A command is the word of a king, and the word stands once, for the commandment of the king of Egypt, whose word was law. Moses' parents hid him by faith, not fearing the king's commandment.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the king's commandment in Hebrews is the test of faith; the parents of Moses feared God more than Pharaoh, and the child they hid became the deliverer of a nation.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1223 and G5015; to disturb wholly, i.e. agitate (with alarm):--trouble.
BiblicalUsage: To trouble greatly is to be thrown into confusion, and the word stands once, where Mary is troubled at the angel's greeting. She casts in her mind what manner of salutation this should be, and the angel answers her fear with a promise.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Mary's troubling is the honest response to grace; she did not pretend to understand the angel's words; she pondered them, and her pondering is the pattern of every believer who hears more than they can take in at once.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1223 and G5021; to arrange thoroughly, i.e. (specially) institute, prescribe, etc.:--appoint, command, give, (set in) order, ordain.
BiblicalUsage: To appoint is to set in order, to arrange a thing as it should be, and Paul uses the word for the ordering of the churches. John tells the publicans to exact no more than is appointed them, the apostles appoint elders in every city, and the collection for the saints is appointed to be gathered on the first day of the week.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe appointing is how the church stays a church. Elders are appointed, collections are ordered, and the work is arranged so that nothing is left to chance and no one is left to carry it alone.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1223 and G5055; to accomplish thoroughly, i.e. (subjectively) to persist:--continue.
BiblicalUsage: To continue is to keep at a thing until it is done, and the word stands once, where Paul and his companions continue fasting until the fourteenth day of the storm. They had eaten nothing for two weeks, and Paul urges them to eat for their health.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that continuing through the storm is the whole voyage in one word; the wind did not stop, the ship did not mend, but the men kept on, and the God who kept them through fourteen days brought them safe to land.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1223 and G5083; to watch thoroughly, i.e. (positively and transitively) to observe strictly, or (negatively and reflexively) to avoid wholly:--keep.
BiblicalUsage: To keep is to hold a thing safe, and the word is used of Mary keeping all these sayings in her heart and of the Gentile believers keeping themselves from idols. One keeps by treasuring, the other by turning away, and both are the keeping of faith.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe keeping is the quiet work of a lifetime; Mary kept the words in her heart until their meaning opened, and the church keeps itself from idols by the same patience, holding fast what is good and letting go of what is not.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1303; properly, a disposition, i.e. (specially) a contract (especially a devisory will):--covenant, testament.
BiblicalUsage: A covenant is a binding promise, and the word carries the whole Bible from Abraham to the cross. God makes a covenant with Abraham, the blood of the new covenant is shed for many, and Christ is the mediator of a better covenant, established on better promises.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the covenant is the spine of Scripture. Every promise God makes is kept in Christ, and the new covenant is not a new idea but the old promise come to its fullness in His blood.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1223 and G5101; through what cause?, i.e. why?:--wherefore, why.
BiblicalUsage: These are two words standing together, through and what, and the Greek text never joins them into a single word. The Pharisees ask why Jesus eats with publicans and sinners, and the same two words ask the question again in Luke, and in both places the question is why.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that why is the question the Pharisees never got past; they asked why Jesus ate with sinners, and the answer is the gospel itself: He came to call sinners, not the righteous, to repentance.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: middle voice from G1223 and G5087; to put apart, i.e. (figuratively) dispose (by assignment, compact, or bequest):--appoint, make, testator.
BiblicalUsage: To make a covenant is to settle it by a promise, and the word is used of God making His covenant with His people. He appoints a kingdom to His disciples, He makes a covenant with the house of Israel, and a testament is of force only after the death of the one who made it.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the covenant is made sure by death. A will means nothing until the testator dies, and the new covenant stands because Christ died to make it stand, which is why it cannot be broken.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1223 and the base of G5147; to wear through (time), i.e. remain:--abide, be, continue, tarry.
BiblicalUsage: To tarry is to stay on in a place, and Acts uses the word for Paul's long stays in the churches. He tarries long with the disciples at Iconium, he stays at Antioch teaching and preaching, he spends seven days at Troas, and Jesus tarries in Judea with His disciples.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that tarrying is the unglamorous half of mission. Paul did not only arrive and preach; he stayed, and the staying is what turned converts into churches.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a compound of G1223 and G5142; nourishment:--food.
BiblicalUsage: Food is the daily provision, and the word stands once, where Paul tells Timothy that having food and raiment we should be content. It is the simplest list of needs in the New Testament, and the contentment it asks for is the hardest.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that food and raiment are enough, and the wanting of more is the snare; Paul does not promise riches to the godly; he promises enough, and enough with contentment is great gain.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1223 and G826; to glimmer through, i.e. break (as day):--dawn.
BiblicalUsage: To shine through is what the day star does in the heart, and Peter uses the word once, for the morning that rises when the prophetic word is heeded. The day dawns and the day star arises in your hearts, and the light that was outside becomes the light within.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the day star in Peter is the promise that the word will not always be a lamp in the dark; the morning is coming when Christ Himself will rise in the heart, and the waiting is worth it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1223 and G2224; to gird tightly:--gird.
BiblicalUsage: To gird oneself is to tie up the loose robe for work, and John uses it three times for Jesus and Peter. Jesus girds Himself with a towel to wash the disciples' feet, and Peter girds his fisher's coat to swim to the risen Lord.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the girding in John is the picture of a servant's love. Jesus tied on the towel before He took the basin, and Peter tied on his coat before he swam to shore, and both were hurrying to the Lord they loved.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: slander
BiblicalUsage: An evil report is a tale carried to harm a man, and it runs through the Bible from Joseph to Jeremiah. Joseph brings his brothers' evil report to their father, the spies bring an evil report of the land, and the psalmist hears the slander of many who take counsel against him.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe an evil report is a weapon, and the Bible shows both its edges. A true report can expose real sin, and a false one can destroy a good name, and the difference is the heart of the one who carries it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Diblah, a place in Syria
BiblicalUsage: Diblah is a place named only once, in the judgment on Israel, where the land is made more desolate than the wilderness toward Diblah. It stands in Ezekiel as a byword for desolation, a place the exiles would have known by name.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that a place named once in judgment is still worth knowing. Diblah is the measure of how far desolation reaches when a nation turns from God, and the warning is for any land that forgets Him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Diblajim, a symbolic name
BiblicalUsage: Diblajim is named only once, as the father of Gomer, the wife Hosea is told to take. The name is a sign in itself, tied to the prophet's marriage that pictures Israel's unfaithfulness and God's redeeming love.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Hosea's marriage is the hardest picture in the Bible, and Diblajim's daughter stands at its centre. God told a prophet to marry unfaithfulness itself, so that Israel would see its own heart and His.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {a reason, suit or style}
BiblicalUsage: This is the Aramaic word for a matter or a cause, the business that brings a thing before the king. Daniel's matter is the dream no wise man can tell, and the cause of the wise men is pleaded before the king who would kill them.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that a matter before the king is the place where God's wisdom shows; the wise men of Babylon had no answer, and Daniel's God had the whole dream, which is why the matter ends in worship, not in death.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {a reason, suit or style}
BiblicalUsage: This is the Aramaic word for a matter or a cause, the business that brings a thing before the king. Daniel's matter is the dream no wise man can tell, and the cause of the wise men is pleaded before the king who would kill them.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that a matter before the king is the place where God's wisdom shows; the wise men of Babylon had no answer, and Daniel's God had the whole dream, which is why the matter ends in worship, not in death.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Dibri, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Dibri is named only once, as the father of Shelomith, the Israelitish woman whose son blasphemed the Name and was stoned. His name survives in the record of a judgment the law made plain.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that even a hard judgment is worth recording truly. Dibri's son is named, his mother is named, and the law is carried out, because God's name is not a thing to be spoken lightly.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably some cheap vegetable, perhaps a bulbous root
BiblicalUsage: This word means dove's dung, and it stands once, in the famine of besieged Samaria, where an ass's head sold for eighty pieces of silver and the fourth part of a cab of dove's dung for five. It is the measure of a city starving.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the price of dove's dung is the measure of what siege does to a people; when a city turns from God, even the refuse becomes food, and the famine is the judgment the prophets warned of.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a derivative of G1364; to make apart, i.e. sunder (figuratively, alienate):--set at variance.
BiblicalUsage: To set at variance is to divide a household against itself, and Jesus uses the word once, for the sword He brings. A man will be set at variance against his father, and a daughter against her mother, and the division is over Him.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the variance Jesus brings is the cost of following Him; he does not divide families for sport; He divides them because truth demands a choice, and the choice is the most serious thing in life.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a derivative of G1364 and G4714; disunion, i.e. (figuratively) dissension:--division, sedition.
BiblicalUsage: Divisions are the splits that tear a church apart, and Paul names them among the works of the flesh. He warns the Romans to mark those who cause divisions contrary to the doctrine learned, and he lists them with hatred, wrath, and strife.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe divisions are a work of the flesh, not of the Spirit; the Spirit makes one body, and those who split it for their own doctrine or pride are working against Him, whatever they claim.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a compound of a derivative of G1364 and a derivative of τέμνω (to cut); to bisect, i.e. (by extension) to flog severely:--cut asunder (in sunder).
BiblicalUsage: To cut asunder is the judgment on the unfaithful servant, and Jesus uses it twice for the same sentence. The lord of that servant will come in a day he looks not for, and will cut him asunder and appoint his portion with the hypocrites.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the cutting asunder is a warning against presuming on delay; the servant thought his lord delayed his coming, and the delay was the very thing that exposed him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1321; instruction (the act or the matter):--doctrine, hath been taught.
BiblicalUsage: Teaching is the doctrine itself, what is taught, and the Gospels measure every teacher by it. The crowds are astonished at Jesus' doctrine, the apostles continue steadfastly in it, and Paul warns that the time will come when men will not endure sound doctrine.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe doctrine is not the enemy of devotion but its backbone. The teaching of Christ astonished the crowds because it had authority, and the church stands or falls by whether it keeps that teaching pure.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1318; instructive ("didactic"):--apt to teach.
BiblicalUsage: Apt to teach is the mark of the overseer, and Paul requires it twice, of the bishop and of the servant of the Lord. He must be able to teach, gentle unto all men, and ready to instruct those who oppose themselves.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe aptness to teach is a gift of patience as much as of knowledge; the overseer must know the truth, but he must also be gentle enough to teach it to those who oppose it, which is the harder half.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1321; (subjectively) instructed, or (objectively) communicated by teaching:--taught, which … teacheth.
BiblicalUsage: Taught of God is the promise for everyone who hears and learns of the Father, and the word stands twice for it. Paul says the words he speaks are taught not by man's wisdom but by the Holy Spirit, and Jesus says all who have heard and learned of the Father come to Him.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe being taught of God is the quiet miracle behind every conversion; no man comes to Christ by argument alone; the Father teaches, and those who hear Him come.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1320; instruction (the function or the information):--doctrine, learning, teaching.
BiblicalUsage: Doctrine is the teaching itself, and the letters are full of commands about it. The teacher is to wait on his teaching, Timothy is to give himself to reading and exhortation and doctrine, all Scripture is profitable for doctrine, and the aged are to speak the things which become sound doctrine.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe doctrine matters because it is the teaching of Christ, not the opinions of men. A church that will not endure sound doctrine will endure every wind of teaching instead, and the difference is the difference between life and death.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1321; an instructor (genitive case or specially):--doctor, master, teacher.
BiblicalUsage: A teacher is one who teaches, and the word is used of Jesus above all, and then of the church's teachers. The disciples call Him Master, the church is given teachers among its gifts, and James warns that teachers will receive the stricter judgment.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the title teacher belongs first to Christ. He is the Master who teaches with authority, and every teacher in the church stands under His judgment, which is why James says we should not be many masters.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a prolonged (causative) form of a primary verb δάω (to learn); to teach (in the same broad application):--teach.
BiblicalUsage: To teach is the work Jesus did everywhere He went, and the word follows Him from the synagogue to the mountain to the temple. He teaches in the synagogues of Galilee, He sits down and teaches the multitudes, and He promises the Spirit will teach His disciples all things.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe teaching is the heart of Jesus' ministry. He did not only heal and feed; He taught, and the teaching is what the church still lives by, because His words are spirit and life.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a prolonged form of a primary verb (which is used as an alternative in most of the tenses); to give (used in a very wide application, properly, or by implication, literally or figuratively; greatly modified by the connection):--adventure, bestow, bring forth, commit, deliver (up), give, grant, hinder, make, minister, number, offer, have power, put, receive, set, shew, smite (+ with the hand), strike (+ with the palm of the hand), suffer, take, utter, yield.
BiblicalUsage: To give is the simplest verb in the Bible and the deepest, and it runs from the Father's gift of His Son to the daily bread we ask for. God gave His only begotten Son, the Father gives the Holy Spirit to them that ask Him, and every good gift comes down from the Father of lights.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe giving is the nature of God. He gives His Son, He gives His Spirit, He gives daily bread, and the whole gospel is the story of a God who gives until there is nothing left to give.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1364 and G1406; a double drachma (didrachm):--tribute.
BiblicalUsage: The didrachmon is the half-shekel, the tribute money, and it stands once, when the collectors ask Peter whether his master pays tribute. The question leads to the coin in the fish's mouth, and to the lesson that the sons are free.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the tribute money is the picture of Christ's freedom; he pays what He does not owe, so as not to offend, and the coin in the fish's mouth is the proof that the King provides for His own.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: prolongation from G1364; double, i.e. twin; Didymus, a Christian:--Didymus.
BiblicalUsage: Didymus is the name the Gospels give Thomas, the Twin, and it stands three times, always beside his name. He speaks up to go and die with Jesus, he doubts until he sees, and he is there at the lake when the risen Lord appears.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Thomas the Twin is the apostle for every doubter. He asked to see, he touched, and he confessed My Lord and my God, and his doubt became the clearest confession in the Gospels.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1223 and G1453; to wake fully; i.e. arouse (literally or figuratively):--arise, awake, raise, stir up.
BiblicalUsage: To wake up is to be stirred from sleep, and the word is used of storms and of souls. Jesus wakes and rebukes the wind on the lake, the disciples wake Him in fear, and Peter writes of stirring up pure minds by way of remembrance.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe waking is the work of Christ in every storm. The disciples woke Him in fear, and He woke the wind into stillness, and the same Lord still wakes drowsy hearts to remember what He has done.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1223 and G2233; to relate fully:--declare, shew, tell.
