BiblicalUsage: To declare is to tell a thing fully, to rehearse it from beginning to end, and the word is used of the works of God. The demoniac declares what Jesus did for him, Peter declares how the Lord brought him out of prison, and Hebrews says time would fail to tell of all the saints.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe declaring is the duty of everyone God has helped. The demoniac could not be silent, the apostles could not stop telling, and the telling itself is the witness that spreads the gospel.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1334; a recital:--declaration.
BiblicalUsage: A declaration is a setting forth in order, a narrative drawn up with care, and Luke uses the word once, for the many who undertook to set forth in order the things most surely believed among us. His own Gospel is the declaration he writes to Theophilus.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Luke's declaration is the pattern for honest history; he did not invent what he wrote; he set it in order from eyewitnesses, and the order itself is part of the proof.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: neuter of a compound of G1223 and a derivative of an alternate of G5342; carried through, i.e. (adverbially with G1519 and G3588 prefixed) perpetually:--+ continually, for ever.
BiblicalUsage: Continually means without ceasing, forever, and Hebrews uses the word four times for what Christ does and what He is. His priesthood continues forever, the sacrifices offered year by year could never make perfect, and by one offering He has perfected forever those who are sanctified.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe continually is the word that separates Christ from every priest before Him. They died and their work ended, but He lives forever, and His one offering keeps working for me without ceasing.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1223 and G2064; to traverse (literally):--come, depart, go (about, abroad, everywhere, over, through, throughout), pass (by, over, through, throughout), pierce through, travel, walk through.
BiblicalUsage: To pass through is to go from place to place, and the word follows Jesus and the apostles across the whole New Testament. The shepherds pass through to Bethlehem, Peter says Jesus went about doing good, death passed upon all men, and all our fathers passed through the sea.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe passing through is the missionary's life. Jesus and Paul never settled in one place when the next town still needed the gospel, and the church is still a people on the move.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1223 and G2059; to explain thoroughly, by implication, to translate:--expound, interpret(-ation).
BiblicalUsage: To interpret is to make plain what is not understood, and the word is used of tongues and of Scripture alike. Jesus interprets the Scriptures to the disciples on the road to Emmaus, Tabitha's name is interpreted as Dorcas, and the gift of tongues needs an interpreter to be understood.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe interpretation is a gift of love. A tongue no one understands helps no one, and the Scriptures no one opens stay shut, so God gives interpreters to make His word plain.
RelatedTopics: Scripture; Spiritual gifts; Knowledge of God
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1329; an explainer:--interpreter.
BiblicalUsage: An interpreter is the one who makes a tongue plain, and Paul names the gift once, in the ordering of the church's worship. If there is no interpreter, the speaker is to keep silence in the church and speak to himself and to God.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the interpreter's silence is as much a gift as his speaking; the church's worship is for edification, not display, and a tongue without an interpreter builds no one up.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1223 and G2065; to question throughout, i.e. ascertain by interrogation:--make enquiry for.
BiblicalUsage: To inquire is to ask after a thing until it is found, and the word stands once, where the men Cornelius sends inquire for Simon's house, asking their way to the gate while Peter wonders within himself what the vision means.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the asking of the men and the wondering of Peter belong together; the men asked their way to the right house, and Peter asked what God meant, and the two questions met at the gate.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1364 and G2094; of two years (in age):--two years old.
BiblicalUsage: Two years old is the age Herod uses for his slaughter, and the word stands once, for the children of Bethlehem from two years old and under. It is the measure of a king's fear and a prophet's sorrow.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the two years in Matthew are the measure of Herod's terror; he could not bear a rival king, and the children who died for a throne they never sought are remembered in the same breath as the child who escaped.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1332; a space of two years (biennium):--two years.
BiblicalUsage: Two years is the time Paul spends in his own hired house in Rome, and the word stands twice for it. He is kept two years under Felix, and he dwells two whole years in Rome receiving all who come to him and preaching the kingdom with all confidence.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the two years in Rome are the quiet triumph of the gospel; Paul is a prisoner, and yet the word is not bound, and the hired house becomes a church where the kingdom is preached without hindrance.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1223 and G1841; an outlet through, i.e. probably an open square (from which roads diverge):--highway.
BiblicalUsage: The highways are the streets and the crossroads, the places where the crowds pass, and the word stands once, in the parable of the wedding feast. The servants are sent into the highways to gather all they find, both bad and good, and the wedding is furnished with guests.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the highways are where the gospel goes; the invited guests refused, so the servants went to the crossroads, and the feast was filled with people no one expected to see there.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1223 and the base of G2425; to reach through, i.e. penetrate:--pierce.
BiblicalUsage: The word of God pierces, and this is the verb for that piercing, going right through and dividing soul and spirit. Hebrews uses it once, of a sword that cuts deeper than any blade we know.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Scripture does not skim the surface of my life; it pierces to the joints and marrow, and that is why I let it search me.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1223 and a derivative of G2478; to stout it through, i.e. asservate:--confidently (constantly) affirm.
BiblicalUsage: To insist strongly, to affirm something with full confidence even when others doubt it. Rhoda insisted Peter really stood at the door, and another bystander insisted Peter was a follower of Jesus.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that some truths are worth insisting on even when the room disagrees, because confidence is not stubbornness when the fact is true.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1223 and G2476; to stand apart, i.e. (reflexively) to remove, intervene:--go further, be parted, after the space of.
BiblicalUsage: This word means to stand apart, to step away or be parted from someone. Luke uses it when Jesus is parted from His disciples at the ascension, and when the ship's crew had gone a little further before sounding again. It also marks the space of about an hour between Peter's denials.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe parting is part of the story, not the end of it. Jesus was parted from His disciples only to be enthroned, and the distance never broke the promise that He would be with them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1342 and G2920; a just sentence:--righteous judgment.
BiblicalUsage: Righteous judgment, God's sentence that is just and not arbitrary, and Paul warns that a hard heart stores up wrath against the day when that judgment is revealed.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God's judgment is righteous through and through, which is exactly why I want mercy to meet me there instead of my own record.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1344; an equitable deed; by implication, a statute or decision:--judgment, justification, ordinance, righteousness.
BiblicalUsage: A dikaioma is a righteous deed or a just decree, sometimes the ordinance itself and sometimes the right act it requires. Zacharias and Elisabeth walked in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord blameless, and Paul sets one man's righteous act against Adam's offence. In Revelation the fine linen of the bride is the righteous acts of the saints.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God's righteous requirements are not a ladder I climb to earn His favour. Christ's one righteous act did what I never could, and now my own righteous deeds are the fruit of His work, not the price of it.
RelatedEvents: The Birth of John the Baptist
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1342; to render (i.e. show or regard as) just or innocent:--free, justify(-ier), be righteous.
BiblicalUsage: To justify is to declare someone righteous, to acquit them as if innocent. Paul insists we are justified freely by God's grace through the redemption in Christ, by faith apart from the works of the law. The result is peace with God, not a probationary pardon.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that justification is the hinge of my whole hope. If God Himself declares me righteous in Christ, no accuser can reopen the case, and my standing rests on His verdict, not my performance.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: adverb from G1342; equitably:--justly, (to) righteously(-ness).
BiblicalUsage: Dikaios as an adverb means justly, righteously, acting the way a righteous person acts. Paul calls the Corinthians to wake up and live righteously, and reminds the Thessalonians how justly he behaved among them. Even the thief on the cross admitted he and his fellow criminal were suffering justly.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe living justly is not a pose but the natural shape of a life that has been made right with God. Christ suffered without threatening, leaving His cause to the righteous Judge, and I follow Him by doing the same.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1349; equitable (in character or act); by implication, innocent, holy (absolutely or relatively):--just, meet, right(-eous).
BiblicalUsage: The righteous person is the one who is right with God and does what is right, like Joseph, who would not expose Mary, and the sheep who inherit eternal life. Paul's great claim is that the just shall live by faith, and John calls Jesus Christ the righteous advocate who pleads for us.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe righteousness is first a gift and then a life. Christ is righteous for me before God, and His Spirit makes me righteous in practice, so that the verdict and the walk belong together.
RelatedTopics: Righteousness; Righteousness of God; Justification by faith
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1344; aquittal (for Christ's sake):--justification.
BiblicalUsage: Justification itself, the acquittal Christ won. He was delivered for our offences and raised again for our justification, and through one righteous act the free gift comes to all men.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe my acquittal was settled at an empty tomb, and because Christ was raised for my justification, I never have to earn the verdict again.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a derivative of G1349; a judger:--judge.
BiblicalUsage: A judge, and in Acts it is Moses, whom Israel rejected with the words about who made him a ruler and a judge, yet God sent him as both ruler and deliverer.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the judge Israel rejected was the deliverer God had chosen, and I take care not to dismiss the one God sends to save me.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably from G1166; right (as self-evident), i.e. justice (the principle, a decision, or its execution):--judgment, punish, vengeance.
BiblicalUsage: Dike is justice itself, the right sentence and the punishment that follows it. The islanders saw the viper fasten on Paul and assumed justice would not let a murderer live, and Jude holds up Sodom as an example of eternal fire. Paul warns that those who do not obey the gospel will be punished with everlasting destruction.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe justice is real and terrible, which is why the cross matters so much. Christ bore the sentence I deserved, so that justice is satisfied and mercy can reach me.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: this
BiblicalUsage: This, the little Aramaic pointer word that Daniel uses again and again to point at the dream and the vision. Nebuchadnezzar saw this great image, and Daniel points to this horn that made war with the saints. It does the plain work of saying which thing is meant.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that God's revelation is specific, not vague. Daniel does not gesture at some general idea; he points at this image, this horn, this kingdom, and I believe God speaks that plainly still.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a register
BiblicalUsage: A register or memorandum, the written record the king's enemies asked to be searched, and the scroll found in the palace at Ecbatana that recorded Cyrus's decree.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God's work is written down and remembered, and no opposition can erase a decree the king has already recorded.
RelatedEvents: Cyrus's Decree and Return from Exile
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably from a primary verb δίκω (to cast); a seine (for fishing):--net.
BiblicalUsage: A fishing net, the working tool of the first disciples, left at once when Jesus called them to follow Him. Peter let down the net at Jesus' word and caught so many fish it began to break, and after the resurrection the net came up full of a hundred and fifty-three great fishes without tearing.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe following Jesus starts with leaving the net behind and ends with a catch I could never haul in alone. The same hands that mended nets were given a new trade, and the net that once fed a family now pictures a kingdom gathering people.
RelatedEvents: The Calling of the First Disciples
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Dilan, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Dilean was one of the cities in the lowlands of Judah, named in the allotment Joshua set out for the tribe. Its site is uncertain today, and the name itself means gourd.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe even a town whose stones are lost still belongs in the record, because God gave His people a real land with real borders.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1364 and G3056; equivocal, i.e. telling a different story:--double-tongued.
BiblicalUsage: Double-tongued, saying one thing to one person and another to another, the opposite of the plain speech a deacon must have.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that a double tongue disqualifies a servant of the church, because God's people must be able to trust what I say in every room.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: weeping
BiblicalUsage: Tears, the word that covers weeping itself, from the psalmist who waters his couch with tears through the night to Hezekiah, whose tears God saw and answered with fifteen more years. Isaiah promises the day God wipes away tears from every face, and Ecclesiastes sees the tears of the oppressed with no one to comfort them.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God keeps every tear, and none of them is wasted. He saw Hezekiah's tears and He sees mine, and the promise that He will wipe them away is what lets me weep honestly now.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Dimnah, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Dimnah was a Levitical city in Zebulun, given to the Levites along with its pasture lands. The name means dunghill, a plain name for a town set apart for God's servants.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God provides a place for those who serve Him, even when the name of the place is nothing to boast about.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: resemblance
BiblicalUsage: Likeness or resemblance, and the psalmist's enemies are like a lion, crouching and watching, the word being the picture of something matching something else.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the enemies of God's people are only ever like a lion, never the Lion Himself, and that likeness is all the power they have.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Dinhabah, an Edomitish town
BiblicalUsage: Dinhabah was the capital city of Bela, the first king of Edom named in Genesis, and it stands at the head of the Edomite king list. The name means give thou judgment.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the kings of Edom are listed because God keeps the record of nations outside Israel too, and no kingdom is beneath His notice.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1223 and G3739; through which thing, i.e. consequently:--for which cause, therefore, wherefore.
BiblicalUsage: Therefore, the small word that turns a truth into a command. Paul argues from what God has done to what we must do, and Peter does the same when he tells us to gird up our minds because Christ is coming. The therefore always points backward before it points forward.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the Christian life runs on therefores. Because God has done this, I do that, and whenever I lose the reason, the obedience loses its strength, so I keep going back to what God has done.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1223 and G3593; to travel through:--go throughout, pass through.
BiblicalUsage: To travel through, as Jesus went throughout every city and village preaching, and Paul passed through Amphipolis and Apollonia on the way to Thessalonica.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the gospel travels, and the preacher must travel with it, because good news kept in one place is not good news at all.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1377; persecution:--persecution.
BiblicalUsage: Persecution, the pressure that fell on the church from the day Stephen was killed, scattering believers out of Jerusalem. Paul lists persecutions among the things he takes pleasure in for Christ's sake, and he reminds Timothy of the persecutions he endured at Antioch, Iconium, and Lystra.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe persecution does not prove God has left us; it proves we belong to a kingdom the world still resists. Paul was delivered out of them all, and that is the pattern I hold to when pressure comes.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a prolonged (and causative) form of a primary verb δίω (to flee; compare the base of G1169 and G1249); to pursue (literally or figuratively); by implication, to persecute:--ensue, follow (after), given to, (suffer) persecute(-ion), press forward.
BiblicalUsage: To pursue, the same word that covers chasing after righteousness and being chased for it. Paul presses toward the mark for the prize, tells the Romans to pursue hospitality, and Jesus blesses those who are persecuted for righteousness' sake.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the Christian life is a pursuit, not a drift. I press on because Christ first pursued me, and the prize is not my effort but the upward call of God in Him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1377; a persecutor:--persecutor.
BiblicalUsage: A persecutor, and Paul names himself one, a blasphemer and injurious man who hunted the church before mercy found him.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that no persecutor is beyond mercy, because the chief of them became an apostle, and that gives me hope for the hardest heart I know.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from Διόνυσος (Bacchus); reveller; Dionysius, an Athenian:--Dionysius.
BiblicalUsage: Dionysius the Areopagite, one of the few in Athens who believed Paul's preaching about the resurrection and joined him.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God keeps a remnant even in the proudest city, and one listener who believes is worth the whole sermon.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1352 and G4007; on which very account:--wherefore.
BiblicalUsage: Wherefore, on which very account, Paul's therefore tying his argument about idols to the command to flee idolatry and to give up meat rather than wound a brother.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that love limits liberty, and the wherefore of the gospel always lands on how I treat my brother.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from the alternate of G2203 and the alternate of G4098; sky-fallen (i.e. an aerolite):--which fell down from Jupiter.
BiblicalUsage: Fallen down from Jupiter, the image of Artemis at Ephesus, which the town clerk claimed had fallen from the sky, and the crowd's excuse for its riot.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe idols always need a story to prop them up, and a god that fell from the sky cannot stand against the God who made it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a compound of G1223 and a derivative of G3717, meaning to straighten thoroughly; rectification, i.e. (specially) the Messianic restauration:--reformation.
BiblicalUsage: Reformation, the setting straight of things, used of the time when the old ordinances of meat and drink and washings give way to the better order Christ brings.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Christ is the reformation the old covenant was waiting for, and nothing in the old order needs patching once He has come.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1223 and G3736; to penetrate burglariously:--break through (up).
BiblicalUsage: To break through, the thief's word, digging through a wall to steal what is inside. Jesus warns that thieves break through and steal treasure laid up on earth, and tells us to watch because we do not know when the thief comes.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe earthly treasure is never safe, and that is why Jesus tells me to lay it up where no thief breaks through. What I store in heaven is the only wealth no one can dig out.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from the alternate of G2203 and a form of the base of G2877; sons of Jupiter, i.e. the twins Dioscuri:--Castor and Pollux.
BiblicalUsage: Castor and Pollux, the twin sons of Jupiter, the figurehead of the Alexandrian ship that carried Paul from Malta toward Rome.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that even a pagan ship's figurehead cannot steer God's purpose, because Paul was headed to Rome on God's errand, not the twins'.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1223 and G3754; on the very account that, or inasmuch as:--because (that), for, therefore.
BiblicalUsage: Because, for, inasmuch as, the word that gives the reason underneath the command. Paul says he is not fit to be called an apostle because he persecuted the church, and Peter quotes the call to be holy because God is holy. David's psalm is quoted because God would not let His Holy One see corruption.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe every command in Scripture stands on a because, and the because is always who God is or what He has done. Holiness is not bare duty; it is the shape of a life that belongs to a holy God.
RelatedPeople: Jesus; Paul; Simon Peter; King David
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from the alternate of G2203 and G5142; Jove-nourished; Diotrephes, an opponent of Christianity:--Diotrephes.
BiblicalUsage: Diotrephes loved to have the preeminence among the church, and John writes that he refused to receive the brethren and cast out those who would. The Greek text behind our Bibles spells his name with the accent on a different syllable, but it is the same man.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe loving the first place is the oldest church trouble there is, and John names it plainly so I can recognize it in myself.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1362; to render two-fold:--double.
BiblicalUsage: To double, as Babylon is to be paid back double for what she did, the judgment measured out in the same cup she filled for others.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that God's justice measures exactly, and Babylon's double portion is the proof that no wrong is forgotten and no cry goes unheard.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1364 and (probably) the base of G4119; two-fold:--double, two-fold more.
BiblicalUsage: Twofold, double, as elders who rule well are counted worthy of double honour, while the scribes and Pharisees make their converts twice as much children of hell as themselves. In Revelation, Babylon's reward is double, the measure of her own deeds returned.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God doubles both honour and judgment, and the difference is the heart underneath. Faithful service is met with double honour; hypocrisy that leads others astray is met with a double reckoning.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a variation of G1373; to thirst for (literally or figuratively):--(be, be a-)thirst(-y).
BiblicalUsage: To thirst, the ache Jesus blesses in those who hunger and thirst after righteousness, and the thirst He promises to satisfy forever. The woman at the well heard that whoever drinks the water He gives will never thirst again, and the Spirit and the bride still call the thirsty to come and drink freely.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe thirst is the honest shape of faith: I come empty and He fills me. The water Jesus gives is not a ration but a spring, and the invitation at the end of the Bible is still open to anyone who thirsts.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain affinity; thirst:--thirst.
BiblicalUsage: Thirst itself, which Paul lists among his sufferings, in fastings often, in cold and nakedness, in hunger and thirst.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the apostle's thirst was part of his apostleship, and comfort is not the measure of faithfulness.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1364 and G5590; two-spirited, i.e. vacillating (in opinion or purpose):--double minded.
BiblicalUsage: Double-minded, a person of two souls, wavering in opinion and purpose, unstable in all his ways and told to purify his heart.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a divided heart cannot stand, and the cure James gives is to draw near to God with a single, undivided loyalty.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Diklah, a region of Arabia
BiblicalUsage: Diklah was a son of Joktan, named in the table of nations, and the name also stands for the Arabian region his people settled. The word means palm grove.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the table of nations matters because God traces every people back to one family, and no nation is an accident.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: adverb from G1417; twice:--again, twice.
BiblicalUsage: Twice, the small adverb that counts, from the Pharisee who fasted twice in the week to the cock that would crow twice before Peter denied Jesus. Paul was hindered once and again from coming to the Thessalonians, and Jude's twice-dead trees bear no fruit at all.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God counts what I repeat, whether it is fasting, failure, or fruitlessness. Twice can be a boast, a warning, or a sorrow, and I want my twice to be the kind that bears fruit.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1364 and G5507; two thousand:--two thousand.
BiblicalUsage: Two thousand, the number of the swine that ran down the steep place into the sea when the demons left the man among the tombs.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that one delivered man was worth two thousand swine, and the people who counted the pigs missed the miracle standing in front of them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1364; properly, to duplicate, i.e. (mentally) to waver (in opinion):--doubt.
BiblicalUsage: To doubt, to waver between two minds, as Peter doubted while he sank, and even some who saw the risen Jesus on the mountain doubted.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe doubt does not disqualify me, because Jesus caught Peter's hand while he was still doubting and welcomed worshippers who doubted too.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1364 and G4750; double-edged:--with two edges, two-edged.
BiblicalUsage: Two-edged, the sharp sword with two mouths, as the Greek puts it, that cuts both ways. The word of God is sharper than any two-edged sword, and the risen Christ carries one in His mouth as He speaks to the churches.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God's word cuts both ways on purpose: it wounds my excuses and heals my conscience in the same stroke. A sword with one edge can only push; His word pierces and discerns.
RelatedEvents: John's Vision of the Risen Christ on Patmos
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1364 and G2281; having two seas, i.e. a sound with a double outlet:--where two seas meet.
BiblicalUsage: Where two seas meet, the place of two seas, the reef where Paul's ship struck and broke apart on the way to Malta.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that God's purpose held even when the ship did not, because every soul aboard came safe to land.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Dizahab, a place in the Desert
BiblicalUsage: Dizahab was a place in the wilderness on the border of Moab, named in the opening verse of Deuteronomy as Moses spoke to all Israel. The name means enough gold.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the wilderness places are named because God met His people there, and the journey mattered as much as the destination.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: that, used as relative conjunction, and especially (with a preposition) in adverbial phrases; also as preposition of
BiblicalUsage: That, who, which, the little Aramaic link word that ties a sentence together, used hundreds of times in Daniel and Ezra. Nebuchadnezzar demands the dream and its meaning, the king's officers write that they are the men of the king, and Jeremiah's single Aramaic verse warns that the gods that did not make heaven and earth shall perish.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that small words carry the weight of the sentence, and the God who speaks Aramaic in exile is the same God who speaks Hebrew at home. Nothing about His people is foreign to Him, not even their language.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Dibon, the name of three places in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Dibon was a town in Moab east of the Jordan, taken by Israel and rebuilt by the children of Gad, and the prophets later pronounced judgment on it. The name means wasting.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Dibon stands as a warning and a witness at once: God gave it to His people, and when Moab trusted in its own strength, the prophets said its glory would come down to the dust. The same God who gives a city can take it away.
RelatedEvents: The Defeat of Sihon and Og
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to fish
BiblicalUsage: To fish, as God says He will send fishers to fish for His people out of every place they have hidden, before He sends the hunters.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God fishes for His own with patience and purpose, and no hiding place is beyond His reach.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1223 and ὑλίζω (to filter); to strain out:--strain at (probably by misprint).
BiblicalUsage: To strain out, as the Pharisees strained at a gnat and swallowed a camel, straining their wine for the smallest speck while missing the great beast.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that straining at gnats while swallowing camels is the oldest religious mistake there is, and I would rather be caught being merciful than being exact.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Dimon, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Dimon was a town in Moab whose waters Isaiah says would be full of blood, a place of judgment in the oracle against Moab. The name means river bed, or silence.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the judgment on Moab was not cruelty but justice, and the waters of Dimon ran red because Moab's pride had run so long unchecked.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Dimonah, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Dimonah was a town in the south of Judah, listed among the cities given to the tribe in the allotment. Its name, like Dimon, means river bed.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe every town in the allotment counted, even the small southern ones, because God's gift to Judah came with borders He drew Himself.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to judge
BiblicalUsage: To judge, as Ezra was told to appoint magistrates and judges who would judge the people beyond the river according to the law of God.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that true judgment starts with knowing God's law, and Ezra's judges were to teach before they sentenced.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to judge
BiblicalUsage: To judge, as Ezra was told to appoint magistrates and judges who would judge the people beyond the river according to the law of God.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that true judgment starts with knowing God's law, and Ezra's judges were to teach before they sentenced.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to judge
BiblicalUsage: To judge, as Ezra was told to appoint magistrates and judges who would judge the people beyond the river according to the law of God.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that true judgment starts with knowing God's law, and Ezra's judges were to teach before they sentenced.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to judge
BiblicalUsage: To judge, as Ezra was told to appoint magistrates and judges who would judge the people beyond the river according to the law of God.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that true judgment starts with knowing God's law, and Ezra's judges were to teach before they sentenced.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Dinah, the daughter of Jacob
BiblicalUsage: Dinah was the daughter of Jacob by Leah, named at her birth in the record of Jacob's family. Genesis tells how she went out to see the daughters of the land, and how Shechem the Hivite took her and spoke kindly to her afterward.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Dinah's story is told without hiding what happened to her, and the Bible does not look away from her pain. Her brothers' revenge and her father's silence are both recorded, and I read them as a warning about what happens when justice is taken into angry hands.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a Dinaite or inhabitant of some unknown Assyria province
BiblicalUsage: The Dinaites were colonists settled in Samaria by the king of Assyria, named among the peoples who wrote to Artaxerxes against the rebuilding of Jerusalem. Their name means judgment.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the opposition to God's work is always a crowd, and the letter they wrote is still in the record as proof that rebuilding was resisted from the start.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Dishan, an Edomite
BiblicalUsage: Dishan was the fifth son of Seir the Horite, named in the genealogy of Edom, and his name means thresher. The same record names a Dishon who was his brother's son, and the two are easy to confuse.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the genealogies keep the Horites straight even when their names sound alike, because God remembers families the world forgets.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: the leaper, i.e. an antelope
BiblicalUsage: The pygarg, a clean animal, a kind of antelope or mountain goat, listed among the beasts Israel was allowed to eat.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the clean and unclean lists taught Israel that God cares about the details of daily life, even what is on the table.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Dishon, the name of two Edomites
BiblicalUsage: Dishon was the name of two Edomites in Seir's family: the fifth son of Seir, and the son of Anah his grandson. The record keeps them apart by their fathers, and the name means thresher.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the Bible's care with two men of one name shows me that God knows each person by more than a label.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Doeg, an Edomite
BiblicalUsage: Doeg the Edomite was Saul's chief herdsman, present at Nob when David ate the showbread, and he reported it to Saul. When Saul ordered the priests killed, his own servants refused, and Doeg himself carried out the slaughter of the priests.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Doeg is the warning about what a tongue can do when it serves a jealous king. He reported what he saw, and then he did what Saul's own servants refused to do, and I take care never to let loyalty to a man overrule loyalty to God.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {the bear (as slow)}
BiblicalUsage: A bear, the second beast in Daniel's vision, raised up on one side with three ribs in its mouth, told to arise and devour much flesh.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the bear in Daniel's night vision is a kingdom God already knew by name, and no empire rises without His permission.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {the bear (as slow)}
BiblicalUsage: A bear, the second beast in Daniel's vision, raised up on one side with three ribs in its mouth, told to arise and devour much flesh.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the bear in Daniel's night vision is a kingdom God already knew by name, and no empire rises without His permission.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: quiet
BiblicalUsage: Strength, or rest, the meaning is obscure, and Moses' blessing says that as your days are, so shall your strength be, the word standing for whatever carries you through them.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God matches my strength to my days, not my days to my strength, and that is enough to walk on.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a pasture (from its arrangement of the flock)
BiblicalUsage: A pasture, the place where the flock is arranged and fed, and Isaiah pictures the lambs feeding in their pasture after judgment has passed. The word also carries the sense of word or speaking, and Jeremiah's false prophets are called wind because their word is not in them. Micah promises to gather the remnant like sheep into a fold.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God is the shepherd who finds pasture for His flock even after judgment, and His word is what feeds them. The false prophet has wind; the true shepherd has a pasture.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a raft
BiblicalUsage: Floats, or rafts, as the timber for Solomon's temple came down from Lebanon by sea on rafts, and Hiram promised to bring it to the place Solomon appointed.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that even the temple's cedar travelled by raft, because God's house was built from the work of many hands and many miles.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: millet
BiblicalUsage: Millet, one of the grains Ezekiel was told to mix into his bread during the siege sign, a poor man's grain for a hard season.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God speaks through a loaf of mixed grain as plainly as through a sermon, and the siege bread preached judgment before a word was said.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1209; a reception, i.e. convivial entertainment:--feast.
BiblicalUsage: A feast, a reception, as Levi made a great feast for Jesus in his house, and Jesus told His host to invite the poor and the lame to the banquet instead of friends who could repay him.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the table is where the gospel is proved, because Jesus ate with tax collectors and told me to feed the ones who cannot pay me back.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Dodanites, or descendants of a son of Javan
BiblicalUsage: The Dodanim, or Rodanim, were the descendants of Javan, named in the table of nations among the sons of Japheth. Their name means leaders.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the sons of Javan are named because the nations that came from them, the peoples of the coasts and islands, were never outside God's sight.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1417 and G1176; two and ten, i.e. a dozen:--twelve.
BiblicalUsage: Twelve, the number of the tribes and the apostles, and the number that keeps turning up when God gathers His people. The risen Christ was seen by the twelve, the apostles called the twelve together to appoint servants, and the baskets left over from the feeding were twelve. James writes to the twelve tribes scattered abroad.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe twelve is God's number for a complete people, and the fragments gathered up after the feeding are the picture of it. Nothing He gives is wasted, and no one He calls is left out of the count.
RelatedEvents: The Feeding of the Five Thousand
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1427 and G5443; the commonwealth of Israel:--twelve tribes.
BiblicalUsage: The twelve tribes, the commonwealth of Israel, whose promise Paul says the twelve tribes earnestly serve God night and day hoping to attain.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the hope of the twelve tribes is my hope too: the promise God made to the fathers, kept for the children.
RelatedEvents: Paul Before Felix, Festus, and Agrippa
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1427; twelfth:--twelfth.
BiblicalUsage: Twelfth, the twelfth foundation of the New Jerusalem is garnished with amethyst, the last stone in the wall of the city.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the city God builds is finished down to the twelfth stone, and the last foundation matters as much as the first.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from the base of G1380; a law (civil, ceremonial or ecclesiastical):--decree, ordinance.
BiblicalUsage: A decree or ordinance, the law as it is handed down, from Caesar's decree that all the world should be taxed to the decrees of the Jerusalem council carried to the churches. Paul says Christ blotted out the handwriting of ordinances that was against us and abolished the law of commandments in ordinances.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the decrees of men pass, but the decree of the cross stands. Caesar taxed the world and the council wrote letters, yet it is Christ who nailed the ordinances against me to His cross, and I live free of them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1378; to prescribe by statute, i.e. (reflexively) to submit to, ceremonially rule:--be subject to ordinances.
BiblicalUsage: To be subject to ordinances, as Paul asks why believers submit to rules like touch not and taste not, as though they still lived in the world. The word stands in the Greek text in its middle voice, as a submitting of oneself to man-made decrees.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Christ's death freed me from man-made ordinances, and I will not let a rulebook take the place of the risen Lord.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a prolonged form of a primary verb, δόκω (used only in an alternate in certain tenses; compare the base of G1166) of the same meaning; to think; by implication, to seem (truthfully or uncertainly):--be accounted, (of own) please(-ure), be of reputation, seem (good), suppose, think, trow.
BiblicalUsage: To think, to seem, what a person supposes, whether it is true or not. Paul warns that if anyone thinks he is wise in this world, he must become a fool to become wise, and Peter did not think the angel's rescue was real. Paul laid his gospel before the leaders at Jerusalem in case he had run in vain.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe thinking and knowing are not the same thing, and my opinions need the same testing Paul gave his own gospel. What seems wise to me may be foolishness to God, and I would rather find that out in His word than at the end of my life.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1384; to test (literally or figuratively); by implication, to approve:--allow, discern, examine, X like, (ap-)prove, try.
BiblicalUsage: To test, to prove, the assaying of metal, applied to faith, teaching, and the will of God. Paul tells us to prove what is the good and acceptable will of God, and to prove all things and hold fast to what is good. John warns not to believe every spirit but to test them, and Peter says the trial of faith is more precious than gold.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God tests what He loves, and the testing is how I learn what is real. Faith that has been tried is not weaker for the fire; it is proved, like gold, and the praise of it belongs to God.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from the same as G1384; test (abstractly or concretely); by implication, trustiness:--experience(-riment), proof, trial.
BiblicalUsage: Proof, experience, the trustworthiness that comes out of testing, the character a person shows when tried. Paul knew the proof of the Corinthians' obedience, and Timothy's proof as a son with his father in the gospel. Patience works experience, and the churches of Macedonia showed the proof of their joy in deep poverty.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe experience is what patience produces, and patience is what suffering produces when I do not quit. The proof of a life is not what I claim in the easy days but what the trial reveals.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: neuter of a presumed derivative of G1382; a testing; by implication, trustworthiness:--trial, trying.
BiblicalUsage: The trying of faith, as James says the trying of your faith works patience, and Peter says it is more precious than gold that perishes.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the trying of my faith is not God doubting me but God proving me, and patience is the proof.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1380; properly, acceptable (current after assayal), i.e. approved:--approved, tried.
BiblicalUsage: Approved, the metal that has passed the assay, the workman who needs not to be ashamed. Paul greets Apelles, approved in Christ, and tells Timothy to study to show himself approved unto God. James blesses the man who endures temptation, for when he is tried he shall receive the crown of life.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe approval from God is the only approval that finally counts, and it comes to the one who endures the trial rather than the one who avoids it. My aim is to stand before Him as a workman who has handled the word rightly.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a dashing of surf
BiblicalUsage: The dashing of surf, the pounding of waves, as the psalm pictures the floods lifting up their pounding against the throne that is established from of old.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the waves may pound, but the throne stands, because the Lord is mightier than the noise of many waters.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1209 (through the idea of holding up); a stick of timber:--beam.
BiblicalUsage: A beam, the great log in my own eye, set against the speck in my brother's. Jesus asks why I look at the mote in his eye and never notice the beam in my own, and tells me to cast the beam out first so I can see clearly.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe judgment starts at home, with the beam, not the mote. When I deal with my own log first, I can finally help my brother instead of condemning him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1386; to be guileful:--use deceit.
BiblicalUsage: To use deceit, as Paul quotes the psalm about throats like open graves and tongues that practise deceit, the picture of speech that baits a trap.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that deceitful speech is a grave with the lid off, and the gospel is what shuts it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1388; guileful:--deceitful.
BiblicalUsage: Deceitful, Paul's word for the false apostles who transform themselves into apostles of Christ, deceitful workers wearing a disguise.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a false apostle is known by his deceit, not his eloquence, and I test every teacher by the truth he handles.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1388; to ensnare, i.e. (figuratively) adulterate:--handle deceitfully.
BiblicalUsage: To handle deceitfully, as Paul says he has renounced the hidden things of dishonesty and does not handle the word of God deceitfully.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the word of God must be handled straight, because a crooked handling of a straight word still leads people crooked.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from an obsolete primary verb, δέλλω (probably meaning to decoy; compare G1185); a trick (bait), i.e. (figuratively) wile:--craft, deceit, guile, subtilty.
BiblicalUsage: Guile, deceit, the baited trap, the fishhook hidden in the offer. Jesus saw Nathanael and said here is an Israelite in whom there is no guile, and Peter tells believers to lay aside all guile along with malice and hypocrisy. Paul insists his exhortation was not in deceit, even when his enemies charged him with catching them by craft.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe guile is the opposite of the gospel, because the gospel has nothing to hide. A life without guile is the proof that Christ has made me new, and I want to be known for it.
RelatedEvents: The Calling of the First Disciples
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from δέμω (to build); properly, an edifice, i.e. (specially) a roof:--housetop.
BiblicalUsage: The housetop, the flat roof where Peter went up to pray at noon, and where the friends of the paralytic let their man down through the tiles. Jesus tells His disciples to shout from the housetops what He whispers in the ear, and warns the one on the housetop not to go back down for his goods.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the housetop is where private prayer becomes public witness. What I hear from Jesus in secret, I am to proclaim in the open, and I must not climb down to gather what the coming day will burn.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from the base of G1325; a present:--gift.
BiblicalUsage: A gift, what a father gives, and what the ascended Christ gives to His church. Jesus asks how much more the heavenly Father will give good gifts, and especially the Holy Spirit, to those who ask Him. Paul calls the Philippians' offering a gift that abounds to their account, and the ascended Lord gave gifts to men.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe every good gift comes down from a Father who knows how to give, and the greatest gift is His own Spirit. I ask boldly because He gives freely, and I give freely because I have first received.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: manure
BiblicalUsage: Dung, the refuse left in the field, the end of those who refuse God. Jezebel's body was to be as dung on the face of the field at Jezreel, and Jeremiah says the slain shall be as dung upon the ground, unburied and unlamented. The psalm names the dead at Endor who became as dung for the earth.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the Bible's blunt word is meant to shock me awake: a life that despises God ends as refuse. The warning is severe because the mercy is real, and I would rather repent now than be left in the field.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a stumbling-block
BiblicalUsage: Slander, as the psalm says thou sittest and speakest against thy brother, thou slanderest thine own mother's son, and this word is the slander the tongue speaks against its own kin.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that a tongue given to slander frames its own deceit, and God hears every stitch of it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Dophkah, a place in the Desert
BiblicalUsage: Dophkah was a camp of Israel in the wilderness, named in the list of the journeys between the Red Sea and the wilderness of Sin. The name is tied to knocking or striking.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe every camp in the journey is recorded because God was with His people at each one, and the wilderness road is His story too.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: something crumbling, i.e. fine (as a thin cloth)
BiblicalUsage: Thinness, a thin veil, as Isaiah says God spreads out the heavens like a curtain, thin and fine, and stretches them out as a tent to dwell in.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the heavens are as thin as a veil in God's hands, and the God who stretches them out can hold my life just as easily.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a goad
BiblicalUsage: A goad, the sharp point the Philistines charged Israel to sharpen, and the Preacher's picture of the words of the wise as goads that prod the ox forward.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe wise words are meant to prod me, not pamper me, and a goad in the right hand moves me toward God.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1435; a gratuity:--gift.
BiblicalUsage: A free gift, the gift of God that Jesus offered the woman at the well, and the gift of the Holy Ghost promised to all who repent and are baptized. Paul sets the free gift against Adam's offence: where sin abounded, the gift abounded much more, and Hebrews warns those who have tasted the heavenly gift.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the gift of God is free because it cost Him everything, and it cannot be earned, only received. The living water, the Holy Spirit, and the grace that covers Adam's offence are all one gift with one price already paid.
RelatedEvents: Jesus and the Samaritan Woman; Pentecost
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: accusative case of G1431 as adverb; gratuitously (literally or figuratively):--without a cause, freely, for naught, in vain.
BiblicalUsage: Freely, without a cause, the adverb of the free gift. Jesus told the disciples to give freely because they had received freely, and He was hated without a cause, exactly as the psalm said. Paul insists we are justified freely by God's grace, and warns that if righteousness came by the law, Christ died in vain.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe freely is the only word that fits what God has done for me. I received without paying, so I give without charging, and I refuse any gospel that puts a price on what Christ gave His life to make free.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1433; a bestowment:--gift.
BiblicalUsage: A gift, a bestowment, as James says every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights, and Paul sets the free gift against the judgment that followed one offence.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that every good gift comes down from above, and the Father of lights does not change His mind about giving.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: middle voice from G1435; to bestow gratuitously:--give.
BiblicalUsage: To give freely, to bestow, the verb of God's giving, used when Pilate gave the body of Jesus to Joseph, and when Peter says God's divine power has given us all things that pertain to life and godliness. The promises by which we partake of the divine nature are given, not earned.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God gives all things for life and godliness before I ask for any of them, and the gift is already in my hands. My part is to add to my faith the virtues that grow from what He has already bestowed.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: gazelle; Dorcas, a Christian woman:--Dorcas.
BiblicalUsage: Dorcas, also called Tabitha, a disciple at Joppa full of good works and almsdeeds, whose death brought the widows to Peter with the coats and garments she had made, and whose raising brought many to believe.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a life of quiet good works is a sermon that outlives the preacher, because the widows showed Peter the coats and the Lord showed Joppa the empty grave.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a present; specially, a sacrifice:--gift, offering.
BiblicalUsage: A gift, an offering, the gift laid on the altar, and the gifts the wise men opened before the child. Jesus says if I remember my brother has something against me, I must leave my gift at the altar and be reconciled first. The leper He cleansed was told to offer the gift Moses commanded, and every high priest is appointed to offer gifts and sacrifices.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God values the heart behind the gift more than the gift itself. The wise men gave gold, frankincense, and myrrh, but the offering He wants most from me is a reconciled heart laid on the altar before the gift.
RelatedEvents: The Magi Visit Jesus; The Sermon on the Mount
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from the base of G1325; a giving; by implication, (concretely) a gift:--gift, giving.
BiblicalUsage: A giving, as James speaks of the giving from above, and Paul thanks the Philippians because no church shared with him in the matter of giving and receiving except them alone.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that giving is a two-way street in the gospel: God gives from above, and His people give to one another below.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from the base of G1325; a giver:--giver.
BiblicalUsage: A giver, Paul's word in the cheerful giver God loves, the one who gives not grudgingly or of necessity but from a willing heart.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God loves a cheerful giver because cheerfulness proves the gift was free, and a free gift is the only kind that looks like Him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Dothan, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Dothan was the place where Joseph's brothers pastured the flock and where Joseph found them, and centuries later the city where Elisha was surrounded by the Syrian army. The Lord opened the servant's eyes to see the mountain full of horses and chariots of fire.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Dothan teaches me that the same ground can hold a betrayal and a deliverance. Joseph was sold there, and Elisha was saved there, and in both stories God was working where His people could not see Him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a presumed compound of G1401 and G71; to be a slave-driver, i.e. to enslave (figuratively, subdue):--bring into subjection.
BiblicalUsage: To bring into subjection, to lead as a slave, as Paul says he keeps his body under and brings it into subjection, lest after preaching to others he himself should be disqualified.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that my body is a servant to be led, not a master to be obeyed, and the preacher must first preach to himself.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: feminine of G1401; a female slave (involuntarily or voluntarily):--handmaid(-en).
BiblicalUsage: A female servant, a handmaid, as Mary called herself the handmaid of the Lord when the angel brought her the news, and she sang that God had regarded the low estate of His handmaiden. Joel's promise, quoted at Pentecost, is that God will pour out His Spirit on His servants and handmaidens.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God chooses handmaidens for His greatest work, and Mary's low estate was no barrier to His favour. The Spirit falls on servants and handmaidens alike, and that is the church I belong to.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1398; slavery (ceremonially or figuratively):--bondage.
BiblicalUsage: Bondage, slavery, the yoke Christ came to break, and the fear of death that held people in bondage all their lives. Paul contrasts the Jerusalem below, which is in bondage with her children, with the freedom of the Jerusalem above, and says we did not receive the spirit of bondage again to fear.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Christ broke the bondage I could not break myself, and freedom is not the absence of a master but the presence of the right one. I stand fast in the liberty He bought, because going back to bondage would make His cross pointless.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1401; to be a slave to (literal or figurative, involuntary or voluntary):--be in bondage, (do) serve(-ice).
BiblicalUsage: To serve as a slave, to be in bondage, the word for Israel's four hundred years in Egypt and for the Thessalonians who turned from idols to serve the living and true God. Paul tells servants to serve their masters well, and the Colossians that the service they give is really service to the Lord Christ.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe serving God is the only slavery that sets me free, because the Master I serve gave Himself for me. Israel was freed from Egypt to serve God, and I was freed from idols for the same purpose.
RelatedEvents: The Exodus and the Red Sea
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: neuter of G1401; subservient:--servant.
BiblicalUsage: Servant, the form of the word for slave that Simeon uses when he asks the Lord to let His servant depart in peace, and the word for the unprofitable servant cast into outer darkness. The Greek text spells it as a form of the word for a bondservant, not as a separate word.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the servant who departs in peace and the servant cast out are separated by one thing: whether they trusted the Master who called them.
RelatedEvents: The Presentation of Jesus in the Temple
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1401; to enslave (literally or figuratively):--bring into (be under) bondage, X given, become (make) servant.
BiblicalUsage: To enslave, to bring into bondage, the verb for what sin does and what false teachers promise to free men from while they are slaves of corruption themselves. Paul says a brother or sister is not under bondage when an unbelieving partner departs, and that being made free from sin we became the servants of righteousness.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe sin enslaves by promising freedom, and the only escape is a new master. Whoever I yield myself to obey becomes my master, so I yield myself to righteousness, whose service is the only freedom there is.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1210; a slave (literal or figurative, involuntary or voluntary; frequently, therefore in a qualified sense of subjection or subserviency):--bond(-man), servant.
BiblicalUsage: A bondservant, a slave, the word Jesus used when He said whoever would be first must be the servant of all, and when He washed the disciples' feet, saying the servant is not greater than his lord. Paul thanks God that the Romans, once servants of sin, obeyed the form of doctrine delivered to them, and that Christ took the form of a servant.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the gospel turns slavery upside down: the Master became a servant, and His servants become sons. I am no longer a slave to sin but a servant of righteousness, and that service is the highest honour I know.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: (figuratively) to love; by implication, a love-token, lover, friend; specifically an uncle
KeyPassages: Song of Solomon 1:2; Song of Solomon 1:4; Song of Solomon 4:10; Song of Solomon 7:12
BiblicalUsage: Beloved, the word for the lover in the Song, whose love is better than wine, and whose name the bride calls out again and again. The beloved's love is sweeter than wine and more fragrant than ointments, and the bride begs him to come away to the fields. The same word names the uncle and the kinsman elsewhere, but here it is love speaking.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the Song gives me a word for Christ that no other book does: He is my beloved, and His love is better than wine. The love that draws the bride to the fields is the same love that drew Christ to the cross, and I answer it by going where He calls.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an aunt
BiblicalUsage: An aunt, the father's sister, the woman the law names when it forbids uncovering her nakedness. Amram took Jochebed his father's sister as his wife, and the law of Leviticus forbids a man to approach his father's brother's wife. The word marks the boundary of the family God drew around His people.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God's laws about family are not arbitrary lines but a fence around what He made holy. The aunt is named in the law because the family is named in His heart, and purity begins at home.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Dodavah, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Dodavah was the father of Eliezer, the prophet who told Jehoshaphat that the Lord had broken his ships because he joined himself with Ahaziah. His name is tied to that one warning.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a father's name is remembered because his son spoke the truth to a king, and the warning about an unholy alliance still stands.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Dodai, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Dodai the Ahohite was the captain of the second month's course, commanding twenty-four thousand men in David's army. His name stands in the list of the monthly captains.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the captains are listed because God's people were organized for service, and every month had its man ready.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Dodo, the name of three Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Dodo was the name of three Israelites: the father of Eleazar, one of David's mighty men; the father of another mighty man; and the father of Tola, the judge who arose after Abimelech. The name means beloved.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the three Dodos are kept apart in the record by their sons, because God knows which man is which. A father is remembered by the son he raised, and the mighty men by the father who named them.
RelatedEvents: David's Mighty Men and the Philistine Giants
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: wax;
BiblicalUsage: To melt, as wax melts before the fire, the picture of mountains melting under the Lord's feet and the heart of the psalmist melting like wax within him. Micah says the mountains shall be molten under Him, and the psalms say the wicked perish as wax melts before the fire.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe everything solid melts before the Lord, whether it is a mountain or my own heart. The fire of His presence is what makes the hard places soft, and I would rather melt before Him than stand against Him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Dor, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Dor was a coastal town in Manasseh's territory, given with its villages to the sons of Joseph, and the district Solomon's officer Ben-Abinadab governed from the heights of Dor. The name shares its spelling with the word for generation, but this Dor is a place, not a time.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the towns of the allotment are named because God gave His people a coastline as well as a hill country, and Dor's heights watched over both.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, a revolution of time, i.e. an age or generation; also a dwelling
BiblicalUsage: A generation, the circle of people alive at one time, and the measure of God's memory: He is the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and this is His name for ever, unto all generations. The Amorites' iniquity would not be full until the fourth generation, and one generation passes away while another comes.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God keeps His promises across generations, because His name is the same to my children's children as it was to Abraham. One generation passes and another comes, but the earth abides and the God of the generations abides with it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1391; to render (or esteem) glorious (in a wide application):--(make) glorify(-ious), full of (have) glory, honour, magnify.
BiblicalUsage: To glorify, to give glory, whether the shepherds returning to glorify God for all they had seen, or the Son asking the Father to glorify Him so He might glorify the Father. Paul calls believers to glorify God with one mind and one mouth, and to glorify God in the body, because they were bought with a price.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe glorifying God is the purpose I was bought for, and it is done with the body as well as the voice. The shepherds went back to their flocks glorifying God, and I go back to my work doing the same.
RelatedEvents: The Shepherds Visit the Newborn Jesus
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1405; a drachma or (silver) coin (as handled):--piece (of silver).
BiblicalUsage: A drachma, the silver coin the woman lost, swept the house to find, and called her friends to rejoice over when it was found.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that one lost coin is worth lighting a lamp and sweeping the house for, because God rejoices over one sinner who repents.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably from an alternate form of δέρκομαι (to look); a fabulous kind of serpent (perhaps as supposed to fascinate):--dragon.
BiblicalUsage: The dragon, the great red dragon of Revelation, the old serpent called the Devil and Satan, who deceives the whole world. He stood before the woman to devour her child, gave his power to the beast from the sea, and at the end is bound for a thousand years and cast into the lake of fire.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the dragon is real, ancient, and already defeated, because the child he tried to devour is enthroned and the angel who binds him needs only a chain. The war is won at the cross, and the binding at the end is the sentence being carried out.
RelatedEvents: The Woman and the Dragon; The Beasts from the Sea and the Land
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: perhaps akin to the base of G1404 (through the idea of capturing); to grasp, i.e. (figuratively) entrap:--take.
BiblicalUsage: To catch, to take hold of, as Paul quotes Job to say God takes the wise in their own craftiness, catching them in the very trap they set.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that God's wisdom catches the crafty in their own craft, and the trap I set for others is the one I fall into myself.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from δρέπω (to pluck); a gathering hook (especially for harvesting):--sickle.
BiblicalUsage: A sickle, the harvest tool, put in at once when the grain is ripe, and the sharp sickle of the angel who reaps the earth. The harvest of the earth is ripe, and the sickle falls on the vine of the earth as well as on the wheat.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the harvest is coming and the sickle is already in the angel's hand, which is why the sowing matters now. Every seed I sow is headed for a harvest, and I want mine to be wheat, not grapes of wrath.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from the alternate of G5143; a race, i.e. (figuratively) career:--course.
