BiblicalUsage: A course, a race, the course Paul was determined to finish with joy, testifying to the gospel of the grace of God. At the end he could say he had fought the good fight and finished his course, and John said the same about his own course when he told the crowds he was not the Christ.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe life is a course to finish, not a sprint to win, and the joy is in finishing it faithfully. Paul counted his life dear only so far as he could finish, and I want to be able to say the same at the end.
RelatedEvents: Paul's Farewell to the Ephesian Elders
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a feminine diminutive of Drusus (a Roman name); Drusilla, a member of the Herodian family:--Drusilla.
BiblicalUsage: Drusilla was the Jewish wife of Felix the governor, who sent for Paul to hear him concerning the faith in Christ, and trembled with her husband at his preaching about righteousness, temperance, and judgment to come.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that hearing the gospel is not the same as obeying it, because Felix and Drusilla listened and then sent Paul away.
RelatedEvents: Paul Before Felix, Festus, and Agrippa
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: desolation; concretely, desolate
BiblicalUsage: Silence, or a lament, the word the sailors lift over Tyre, saying what city is like Tyre, like the destroyed in the midst of the sea.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the lament over Tyre is the end of every pride that trusted in ships and silver, because the sea keeps what it takes.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to thrust away; figuratively, to cleanse
BiblicalUsage: To rinse, to wash, the washing of the sacrifices in the temple, where the lavers stood to rinse the burnt offering, and the chambers where the offering was washed. Isaiah promises the Lord will wash away the filth of the daughters of Zion, and Nebuchadnezzar is charged with devouring Israel like a dragon and rinsing her out.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe washing is God's way of making the unclean clean, and the temple lavers pointed to the washing He would do Himself. The filth of Zion is washed by the spirit of judgment and burning, and I am washed in the same way.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to mope, i.e. (figuratively) pine
BiblicalUsage: To pine away, as God warns that disobedience will bring terror, consumption, and the burning ague that makes the eyes fail and the soul pine away.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that pining away is what disobedience does to a soul, and the cure is to turn back before the wasting begins.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a pot (for boiling); also (by resemblance of shape) a basket
BiblicalUsage: A pot or basket, the vessel of the tabernacle and the kitchen, into which the priest's servant thrust his fleshhook, and in which the Passover lambs were boiled. The king of Israel's men put the heads of Ahab's sons in baskets, and Jeremiah saw two baskets of figs set before the temple.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a pot is only a pot until God fills it with meaning, and the baskets of figs in Jeremiah were a sermon about good and bad alike. What I carry matters less than who carries me.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a boiler or basket; also the mandrake (as an aphrodisiac)
KeyPassages: Genesis 30:14; Jeremiah 24:1; Song of Solomon 7:13; Genesis 30:15
BiblicalUsage: Mandrakes, and baskets, the love-apples Reuben found in the field at wheat harvest, which Rachel begged from Leah, and the Song says the mandrakes give a sweet smell at our gates. The same root names the baskets of figs Jeremiah saw set before the temple, one good and one evil.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the mandrakes tell the truth about grasping for what only God can give: Rachel traded a night for a plant, and the plant could not open her womb. God gives children; the field only gives apples.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, fishery, i.e. a hook for fishing
BiblicalUsage: A hook, the fishhooks by which God says the women of Samaria will be taken away, carried out through the breaches in the wall.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the hook is God's judgment on those who oppressed the poor, and the proud who pushed others down will themselves be hauled away.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to bruise in a mortar
BiblicalUsage: To beat, to pound, as the people ground the manna in mills and beat it in a mortar, then baked it into cakes that tasted like fresh oil.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that God gave bread that needed beating, because daily bread is work as well as gift, and the manna never fell ready-baked.
RelatedEvents: Manna and Quail in the Wilderness
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: the hoopoe or else the grouse
BiblicalUsage: The hoopoe, an unclean bird, named among the birds Israel was not to eat, a crested bird of the field.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the unclean birds taught Israel that not everything that flies is food, and holiness sometimes means leaving alone what others take.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Dumah, a tribe and region of Arabia
BiblicalUsage: Dumah was a son of Ishmael, named among the twelve princes of his line, and the name also stands for the Arabian tribe and region that came from him. Isaiah's oracle cries to the watchman from Dumah, asking what of the night.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Dumah's place in the record is a mercy: Ishmael's sons are named one by one, because God remembered the boy He promised to make a nation. The watchman's cry from Dumah is still the question every night-watchman asks.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: silence; figuratively, death
BiblicalUsage: Silence, the silence of the grave, where the dead cannot praise God, and the psalmist says his soul would have dwelt in silence if the Lord had not helped him. The earth He has given to the children of men, but the dead go down into silence.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that silence is what death offers and praise is what life answers, so I will praise Him while I still have breath.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: still; adverbially, silently
BiblicalUsage: Silently, in silence, the command to be silent before an idol that cannot speak, and the call to sit in silence as the daughter of the Babylonians falls. Jeremiah says it is good that a man both hope and quietly wait for the salvation of the Lord.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe silence before God is not emptiness but waiting, and the idol that cannot answer deserves silence while the Lord deserves my quiet trust. To wait quietly for His salvation is the hardest and best work I do.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: stillness; adverbially, silently; abstractly quiet, trust
BiblicalUsage: Silence, the psalmist's cry by day and by night with no silence, and his resolve to hold his peace before the wicked. Truly my soul waits in silence for God alone, the psalm says, and praise waits in silence for Him in Zion.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the psalms give me permission to be silent and to cry out in the same breath. My soul waits in silence because my salvation is from Him alone, and the silence is not giving up but holding on.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to crumble
BiblicalUsage: To crumble, the Aramaic verb for what happens to the image in Nebuchadnezzar's dream, when the stone strikes and the iron, clay, brass, silver, and gold are broken in pieces together and become like chaff. The word stands in Daniel's Aramaic under the root for crushing, the same verb that breaks the kingdoms of the earth.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that every kingdom of man crumbles before the stone cut without hands, and the God who raises the stone is the God who outlasts them all.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to reside
BiblicalUsage: To dwell, the Aramaic word for where men and beasts live, used when Nebuchadnezzar is told that wherever the children of men dwell, God has given them into his hand. The great tree of his dream had fair leaves and fruit for all, and the beasts of the field dwelt under its shadow.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe dwelling is a gift God gives and a trust He measures, because the tree that sheltered the beasts was cut down when its branches grew proud. Where I dwell, and under whose shadow, is a question God asks of kings and of me.
RelatedEvents: Nebuchadnezzar's Dream of the Image; Nebuchadnezzar's Humbling
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to reside
BiblicalUsage: To dwell, the Aramaic word for where men and beasts live, used when Nebuchadnezzar is told that wherever the children of men dwell, God has given them into his hand. The great tree of his dream had fair leaves and fruit for all, and the beasts of the field dwelt under its shadow.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe dwelling is a gift God gives and a trust He measures, because the tree that sheltered the beasts was cut down when its branches grew proud. Where I dwell, and under whose shadow, is a question God asks of kings and of me.
RelatedEvents: Nebuchadnezzar's Dream of the Image; Nebuchadnezzar's Humbling
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to reside
BiblicalUsage: To dwell, the Aramaic word for where men and beasts live, used when Nebuchadnezzar is told that wherever the children of men dwell, God has given them into his hand. The great tree of his dream had fair leaves and fruit for all, and the beasts of the field dwelt under its shadow.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe dwelling is a gift God gives and a trust He measures, because the tree that sheltered the beasts was cut down when its branches grew proud. Where I dwell, and under whose shadow, is a question God asks of kings and of me.
RelatedEvents: Nebuchadnezzar's Dream of the Image; Nebuchadnezzar's Humbling
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Dura, a place in Babylonia
BiblicalUsage: Dura was the plain in Babylon where Nebuchadnezzar set up the golden image, sixty cubits high and six broad, and commanded all peoples to fall down and worship it. The plain's name is all we know of it, and its story is the furnace.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the plain of Dura is where true worship was tested, because three men would not bow on a plain built for bowing. The furnace was seven times hotter, and the fourth man walked in it with them.
RelatedEvents: Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego in the Fiery Furnace
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to trample
BiblicalUsage: To tread down, as the fourth beast in Daniel's vision devours the whole earth, treads it down, and breaks it in pieces.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the beast that treads down the earth is already measured by God, because the Ancient of Days sits above every kingdom that tramples.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to trample
BiblicalUsage: To tread down, as the fourth beast in Daniel's vision devours the whole earth, treads it down, and breaks it in pieces.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the beast that treads down the earth is already measured by God, because the Ancient of Days sits above every kingdom that tramples.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to leap
BiblicalUsage: To leap for joy, to dance, as strength dwells in the neck of leviathan, and sorrow dances before him, the word for the leaping joy that goes ahead of terror.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that sorrow dancing before leviathan is the picture of a power no man can tame, and only God can look it in the eye.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain affinity; to be able or possible:--be able, can (do, + -not), could, may, might, be possible, be of power.
BiblicalUsage: To be able, to have power, the word for what man can and cannot do. The natural man cannot receive the things of the Spirit, and whoever is born of God cannot sin because His seed remains in him. God is faithful and will not let us be tempted beyond what we are able, and even when we believe not, He abides faithful because He cannot deny Himself.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe my cannots are the measure of my need, and God's cannots are the measure of His faithfulness. I cannot receive the Spirit's things on my own, but He can keep me in the temptation, and He cannot deny Himself, and that is the ground I stand on.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1410; force (literally or figuratively); specially, miraculous power (usually by implication, a miracle itself):--ability, abundance, meaning, might(-ily, -y, -y deed), (worker of) miracle(-s), power, strength, violence, mighty (wonderful) work.
BiblicalUsage: Power, the power of God unto salvation, the power the disciples would receive when the Holy Ghost came upon them, and the power that makes the preaching of the cross foolishness to the perishing and salvation to the saved. Paul prays that God would do exceeding abundantly above all we ask or think, according to the power that works in us.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the power of God is not a force I summon but a Person who fills me, and the gospel is powerful because Christ is in it. The same power that raised Him from the dead works in me, and it is able to do far more than I ask.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1411; to enable:--strengthen.
BiblicalUsage: To make strong, to empower, as Paul prays the Colossians would be strengthened with all might, and Hebrews says faith made the weak strong out of weakness and turned them to flight the armies of the aliens.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that God strengthens the weak out of weakness, and the might I pray for is the might to endure with joy.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1410; a ruler or officer:--of great authority, mighty, potentate.
BiblicalUsage: A ruler, a mighty one, as the Ethiopian eunuch was a man of great authority under Candace, and Mary sang that God has put down the mighty from their seats. Paul calls Christ the only Potentate, the King of kings and Lord of lords, who alone has immortality.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe every potentate on earth is a small shadow of the one Potentate, and the mighty are put down so the lowly can be lifted. Christ alone holds immortality, and I bow to Him, not to them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1415; to be efficient (figuratively):--be mighty.
BiblicalUsage: To be able, to be powerful, as God is able to make all grace abound toward us, and He is able to make a man stand whom others would judge. Paul says Christ is not weak toward the Corinthians but mighty in them, and the power that proves itself is Christ's, not his.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God is able to make all grace abound, and the proof is that He has already made me stand. The Christ who is mighty in me is the same Christ who is able to keep me.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1410; powerful or capable (literally or figuratively); neuter possible:--able, could, (that is) mighty (man), possible, power, strong.
BiblicalUsage: Able, mighty, powerful, as Mary sang that He that is mighty has done great things for her, and Apollos was mighty in the Scriptures. Paul says the strong ought to bear the infirmities of the weak, and the weapons of our warfare are mighty through God to the pulling down of strongholds.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe might belongs to God first and to His people second, and the might He gives is for bearing the weak, not breaking them. The weapons He puts in my hands are mighty because they are His, and the strongholds they pull down are the ones that held me.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: or δῦμι prolonged forms of an obsolete primary δύο (to sink); to go "down":--set.
BiblicalUsage: To set, of the sun, as when the sun was setting, all who had any sick brought them to Jesus, and He laid His hands on every one of them and healed them.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the setting sun was the signal for the healing to begin, because the day's work ended and the Saviour's work went on into the night.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a primary numeral; "two":--both, twain, two.
BiblicalUsage: Two, the number of witnesses the law requires, the two or three gathered in Christ's name, and the two witnesses who prophesy clothed in sackcloth. Two men in white stood by as Jesus was taken up, and the law says the testimony of two men is true.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe two is the smallest company God calls a church, and the smallest witness the law calls true. Where two or three gather in His name, He is there, and I never have to stand alone to be heard.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a primary inseparable particle of uncertain derivation; used only in composition as a prefix; hard, i.e. with difficulty:--+ hard, + grievous, etc.
BiblicalUsage: Hard, ill, difficult, the inseparable prefix that turns a good word bad, as in hard to bear or hard to understand. It never stands on its own in the Greek New Testament; it only ever appears joined to another word, doing its work inside it.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the little prefix preaches its own sermon: some things are hard by nature, and the gospel never pretends otherwise.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1418 and a derivative of G941; oppressive:--grievous to be borne.
BiblicalUsage: Hard to bear, as Jesus charged the lawyers with loading men with burdens grievous to be borne, burdens they would not touch with one of their fingers.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the burdens men load on others are the opposite of Christ's yoke, because His yoke is easy and His burden is light.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1418 and a compound of G1787 (meaning a bowel); a "dysentery":--bloody flux.
BiblicalUsage: Dysentery, the bloody flux, as the father of Publius lay sick with a fever and a bloody flux, and Paul went in, prayed, and laid his hands on him and healed him. The Greek text spells the sickness with a different ending, but it is the same disease Luke the physician names.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Luke the physician recorded the disease and the healing side by side, because the God who made the body can mend it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1418 and a presumed derivative of G2059; difficult of explanation:--hard to be uttered.
BiblicalUsage: Hard to explain, hard to interpret, as the writer of Hebrews says there is much to say about Melchizedek, but it is hard to utter because the hearers are dull of hearing.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe some truth is hard to explain only because my ears are dull, and the cure is to grow up into the solid food of the word.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: adverb from G1422; impracticably:--hardly.
BiblicalUsage: Hardly, with difficulty, as Jesus said it three times, in three Gospels, about the rich entering the kingdom of God. How hardly shall they that have riches enter, He said, looking at the young ruler who went away sorrowful.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Jesus repeated the warning because riches make the narrow gate look unnecessary, and the camel and the needle are His way of saying it is impossible with men. What is impossible with men is possible with God, and that is the only hope the rich man has.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1418 and κόλον (food); properly, fastidious about eating (peevish), i.e. (genitive case) impracticable:--hard.
BiblicalUsage: Hard, as the disciples were astonished at Jesus' words about how hard it is for those who trust in riches to enter the kingdom of God.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that trusting in riches is the hardness Jesus names, not the riches themselves, and the cure is to trust in God instead.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1416; the sun-set, i.e. (by implication) the western region:--west.
BiblicalUsage: The west, where the sun goes down, the quarter from which the cloud rises that brings the shower, and the direction from which many shall come to sit down with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom. The New Jerusalem has three gates on the west, as on every side.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the west is the picture of the wide welcome of the kingdom, because they shall come from the east and the west to sit at the table. The gates stand open on every side, and the sunset quarter is no farther from the feast than the sunrise.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1418 and a derivative of G3539; difficult of perception:--hard to be understood.
BiblicalUsage: Hard to understand, as Peter says there are some things hard to be understood in Paul's epistles, which the unlearned and unstable wrest to their own destruction.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that hard passages are not an excuse to twist them, because Peter counts Paul's letters as Scripture and warns me to handle them straight.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a compound of G1418 and G5345; defamation:--evil report.
BiblicalUsage: Evil report, defamation, as Paul commends himself as a minister of God through honour and dishonour, through evil report and good report, as deceivers and yet true.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a good report and an evil report are both part of the ministry, because the world will call the true deceivers and the deceivers true.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an adverb of confirmation; perhaps intensive of G2228; used only (in the New Testament) before G3303; assuredly:--surely.
BiblicalUsage: Surely, assuredly, the little particle of confirmation that stands before the word for indeed in God's oath to Abraham, saying, surely blessing I will bless thee. The Greek text behind our Bibles carries this particle; the text used by modern editors reads the same oath with a different first word.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that God's oath to Abraham is sure twice over, because He swore by Himself, and the little word surely is the sound of a promise that cannot fail.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a primary particle of distinction between two connected terms; disjunctive, or; comparative, than:--and, but (either), (n-)either, except it be, (n-)or (else), rather, save, than, that, what, yea. Often used in connection with other particles. Compare especially G2235, G2260, G2273.
BiblicalUsage: Or, the word that forces a choice between two masters, two ways, two loyalties. No man can serve two masters, Jesus said, and Paul asks whether Christ is divided, or whether he was crucified for the Corinthians. John reminds us that greater is He that is in us than he that is in the world.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe every or in Scripture is a crossroads, and I cannot walk both roads at once. God or mammon, Christ or the world, the choice is mine to make, and the choosing is the life of faith.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: apparent imperative of G1439; properly, let it be, i.e. (as interjection) aha!:--let alone.
BiblicalUsage: An exclamation, let alone, as the demon's cry in the synagogue at Capernaum, let us alone, what have we to do with thee, thou Jesus of Nazareth.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the demon knew Jesus before the congregation did, and the cry of let us alone is the sound of darkness meeting the light.
RelatedEvents: Jesus Heals a Demoniac in the Capernaum Synagogue
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: i.e. G1437 and G3361; if not, i.e. unless:--X before, but, except, if, no, (if, + whosoever) not.
BiblicalUsage: If not, unless, the two-word phrase that sets the condition, as in except your righteousness exceed the righteousness of the scribes, or except a man be born of water and of the Spirit. The words never stand as one word in the Greek text; they are two words working as one condition.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the unless of Jesus is the narrow door of the kingdom, because except we turn and become as little children, we shall not enter in.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1487 and G302; a conditional particle; in case that, provided, etc.; often used in connection with other particles to denote indefiniteness or uncertainty:--before, but, except, (and) if, (if) so, (what-, whither-)soever, though, when (-soever), whether (or), to whom, (who-)so(-ever). See G3361.
BiblicalUsage: If, the great conditional word of the New Testament, the hinge on which the promises turn. If you forgive men their trespasses, your Father will forgive you, and if you confess with your mouth the Lord Jesus, you shall be saved. If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us, and if I have all faith but have not charity, I am nothing.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the ifs of Scripture are not God's uncertainty but my responsibility, because His promises are sure and my part is to meet the condition. The if does not make God doubtful; it makes me answerable, and I answer by believing.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain affinity; to let be, i.e. permit or leave alone:--commit, leave, let (alone), suffer. See also G1436.
BiblicalUsage: To allow, to permit, to let alone, as God will not suffer you to be tempted above what you are able, and in times past He suffered all nations to walk in their own ways. Jesus did not suffer the devils to speak because they knew Him, and the goodman of the house would not have suffered his house to be broken up if he had known the hour.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God permits what He does not approve, and His permission is never His approval. He suffered the nations to walk their own ways for a season, yet He never left Himself without witness, and He will not suffer my temptation to outrun my strength.
RelatedTopics: Temptation; God's Sovereignty; Faithfulness of God
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {a green plant}
BiblicalUsage: Fruit, the Aramaic word for the fruit of Nebuchadnezzar's great tree, whose leaves were fair and whose fruit was much, with food for all under it. The watcher commanded the tree to be cut down and its fruit scattered, and Daniel told the king the tree was him, great and strong.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the fruit of the tree was the king's greatness, and the scattering of it was God's judgment on pride. A tree that feeds all is a gift, but a tree that forgets who planted it is cut down.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {a green plant}
BiblicalUsage: Fruit, the Aramaic word for the fruit of Nebuchadnezzar's great tree, whose leaves were fair and whose fruit was much, with food for all under it. The watcher commanded the tree to be cut down and its fruit scattered, and Daniel told the king the tree was him, great and strong.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the fruit of the tree was the king's greatness, and the scattering of it was God's judgment on pride. A tree that feeds all is a gift, but a tree that forgets who planted it is cut down.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Ebed, the name of two Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Ebed is the name of two Israelites, and both appear only in passing. The first is the father of Gaal, who stirred up Shechem against Abimelech in the days of the judges, and the second is the son of Jonathan who returned from exile with Ezra.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that even these brief names matter, because God remembers the men history forgets. Their stories sit inside His larger work, whether in rebellion or in return.
RelatedPeople: Ebed, Father of Gaal; Ebed, Son of Jonathan; Gaal, Son of Ebed
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Ebed-Melek, a eunuch of Zedekeah
BiblicalUsage: Ebed-Melek was an Ethiopian eunuch in the court of King Zedekiah, and his name means servant of the king. When Jeremiah was sinking in the cistern, Ebed-Melek spoke up for him and pulled him out with ropes and rags, and God promised him his life as a reward for trusting Him.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Ebed-Melek shows that courage is not about rank or birth, but about doing right when it costs something. A foreign servant trusted God, and God did not forget him.
RelatedPeople: Ebed-Melech; Jeremiah; Zedekiah, King of Judah
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a servant
BiblicalUsage: The word for servant covers a slave, a hired worker, a subject of the king, and a worshipper of God, and the Bible uses the same word for all of them. Samuel answers the Lord's call with the words of a servant ready to hear, and the prophets are called God's servants because they belong to Him and do His bidding. In Isaiah the Servant is the chosen one on whom God puts His Spirit, the figure who carries God's work to the nations.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that serving God is the highest calling a person can have, not the lowest. The Bible never treats God's servants as disposable labour; it treats them as His own household, honoured and kept. That is why I would rather be called His servant than anything else the world offers.
RelatedEvents: The Exodus and the Red Sea
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: the papyrus
BiblicalUsage: Job says his days pass like swift ships, and the word behind those ships is papyrus, the light reed boats that skimmed the water. His life feels that fast, and that fragile.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Job's picture still fits, because our days pass just as swiftly, and only God gives them weight.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: lamentation
BiblicalUsage: Mourning in the Bible is public and physical, with weeping, torn clothes, and days set aside for grief. Esau waits for the days of mourning for his father before he plans his revenge, and all Israel mourns Moses for thirty days. The preacher says the house of mourning is better than the house of feasting, because grief teaches the heart what pleasure never will.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God does not rush us past grief, because He gave it a place and a season in His people's life. Mourning is honest before Him, and He meets us in it rather than asking us to pretend.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {a stone}
BiblicalUsage: In Daniel the Aramaic word for stone does heavy work in two stories. A stone cut out without hands strikes Nebuchadnezzar's great image and grows into a mountain that fills the whole earth, and a stone is laid over the mouth of the lions' den to seal Daniel in. The same plain word carries both judgement on human kingdoms and the sealing of a den.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the stone in Daniel's vision is Christ's kingdom, which no human power builds and no human power stops. God does not need our hands to start His kingdom, and He will finish it Himself.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Eben-ha-Ezer, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Eben-ha-Ezer means stone of help, and it is the place where Israel twice met the Philistines and where Samuel set up a memorial stone. After God gave the victory, Samuel raised the stone and said that hitherto the Lord had helped them, so the name itself became a reminder. The place keeps the memory of a defeat turned into deliverance.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe we all need an Ebenezer, a plain marker that says God helped us here. Remembering His help in the past is what steadies us for the next battle.
RelatedEvents: The Ark Captured and Returned; Samuel Leads Israel at Mizpah
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {a stone}
BiblicalUsage: In Daniel the Aramaic word for stone does heavy work in two stories. A stone cut out without hands strikes Nebuchadnezzar's great image and grows into a mountain that fills the whole earth, and a stone is laid over the mouth of the lions' den to seal Daniel in. The same plain word carries both judgement on human kingdoms and the sealing of a den.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the stone in Daniel's vision is Christ's kingdom, which no human power builds and no human power stops. God does not need our hands to start His kingdom, and He will finish it Himself.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H5677); Eber, a patriarch:--Eber.
BiblicalUsage: Luke names Eber in the genealogy of Jesus, between Serug and Peleg, and the spelling in the Greek text is Eber with a rough breathing, not the form Strong's lists. He is the patriarch whose name the Hebrews carry, and his place in the line keeps the promise moving from Shem toward Abraham.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe every name in that genealogy matters, because God kept His promise through real people in a real line.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, a region across; but used only adverbially (with or without a preposition) on the opposite side (especially of the Jordan; ususally meaning the east)
BiblicalUsage: This word marks the other side, most often the far side of the Jordan, and it draws the map of Israel's story. Moses speaks to Israel beyond Jordan, the tribes settle on both sides of the river, and Solomon's kingdom stretches from beyond the river to the border of Egypt. The word is small, but it tells you where God's people stand and which way they are facing.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that God meets His people on both sides of every river, because no boundary keeps Him out. The far side is still His ground, and the crossing is still His doing.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Eber, the name of two patriarchs and four Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Eber is the son of Salah and the father of Peleg and Joktan, and his name is tied to the word Hebrew itself. Genesis traces the line from Shem through Eber down to Abraham, so he stands at the head of the family God chose. The other men who share his name are a Gadite chief, two Benjamites, and a priest in the days of Joiakim, each named only in the lists.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Eber's place in the genealogy shows how God works through ordinary families over long stretches of time. The promise did not arrive all at once; it travelled through fathers and sons like him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a pinion
BiblicalUsage: A pinion is the strong flight feather of a bird's wing, and the Bible uses it for speed, strength, and escape. Ezekiel's great eagle has great wings and long pinions, Isaiah promises that those who wait on the Lord will mount up with wings as eagles, and the psalmist longs for wings like a dove so he can fly away and be at rest.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God gives wings to the weary, not just to the strong, because waiting on Him is what renews strength. The bird does not earn the wind; it rides it, and so do we.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Ebets, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Abez is a town in the land of Issachar, named once in the list of towns given to that tribe. Its name means something like I will make white, and beyond its place in the boundary list we know nothing more about it. The Bible still records it, because every town in the inheritance mattered.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that no place God gives His people is too small to be named. If He counted Abez, He counts the small corners of our lives too.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an outburst of passion
BiblicalUsage: This is wrath that bursts out, an overflow of fury, and the Bible uses it most often for God's anger against sin and for the arrogance of men. Jacob curses the fierce anger of Simeon and Levi, Isaiah says the land is darkened by the wrath of the Lord of hosts, and Ezekiel says God will pour out His indignation on a people that would not listen. It is not a slow burn; it is a flood breaking its banks.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God's wrath is real and righteous, and that is good news, because a God who never burned against evil would never rescue anyone from it. His anger is the other side of His love for what is right, and it falls hardest where His patience has been refused longest.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {a pinion}
BiblicalUsage: This is the same word for a bird's pinion as the masculine form, and its most tender use is in the song of Moses. As an eagle stirs up her nest and flutters over her young, spreading her wings to carry them, so God carried Israel. The psalms take the picture further, hiding us under His feathers and beneath His wings.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God's strength is a shelter before it is a weapon, because He spreads His wings over His people before He lifts them. I would rather be under those wings than anywhere else.
RelatedEvents: The Exodus and the Red Sea
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Ebron, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Ebron is a town in the territory of Asher, named once in the boundary list of Joshua, and it is not the same place as Hebron in Judah despite the similar name. It sits on the northern coast, and the Bible says nothing more about it than its place in the inheritance. The name means alliance, and it marks one small corner of the land God gave.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that God keeps careful track of the places He gives, down to towns named only once. Nothing in His gift is forgotten, even when the record is short.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Ebronah, place in the Desert
BiblicalUsage: Ebronah was one of the camps of Israel in the wilderness, the stop just before Ezion-geber on the way to the Red Sea. The journey list in Numbers names it twice, once for arriving and once for leaving, and then the people moved on. Its name means passage, which fits a camp that was only a place to pass through.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God led His people one camp at a time, and even the stops we barely remember were part of His route. Ebronah reminds me that the journey matters even when the stay is short.
RelatedEvents: The Exodus and the Red Sea
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a manger or stall
BiblicalUsage: A manger is a feeding trough for animals, a plain wooden box, and the Bible uses it to make a sharp point. Isaiah says the ox knows his owner and the ass his master's crib, yet Israel does not know God. Job asks whether the wild ox will stay by the crib, and Proverbs says where there are no oxen the crib is clean, but much increase comes by the strength of the ox.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God notices the small, dirty work of feeding and tending, because He uses a manger to teach His people about knowing Him. The crib is a test of attention, and Israel failed it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Ebjasaph, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Ebiasaph is a son of Korah, named in the genealogies of the Levites who served at the tabernacle, and his descendants kept the gates of God's house. His name means my father has gathered, and the lists place him in the line of the Korahites who sang and guarded. He is one of the quiet Levites whose work was to keep the house of God in order.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the gatekeepers and singers matter as much as the priests, because God's house needs people who show up and serve faithfully. Ebiasaph's line did that for generations.
RelatedPeople: Abiasaph, Son of Korah; Korah, Son of Izhar
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Ebjathar, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Abiathar was the priest who escaped Saul's slaughter at Nob and carried the ephod to David, staying loyal to him through flight and war. He served as priest beside Zadok, but in David's old age he backed Adonijah's claim to the throne, and Solomon removed him from the priesthood for it. His life runs from faithful service to a final, costly mistake.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Abiathar warns me that a long record of loyalty does not protect the last chapter. Finishing well matters as much as starting well, and I want to finish well.
RelatedPeople: Abiathar, Son of Ahimelech; King David; Adonijah, Son of David
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: destitute
BiblicalUsage: The needy in the Bible are not a problem to manage but people God claims as His own concern. Moses says the poor will never cease out of the land, so Israel must open its hand wide, and Hannah's song says God raises the poor out of the dust and sets them among princes. Amos warns the merchants who swallow up the needy, and the psalmist tells judges to deliver the poor and needy out of the hand of the wicked.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe how a people treats its poor shows what it really believes about God, because He calls the needy His own. Caring for them is not charity on the side; it is part of obeying Him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Esar-chaddon, an Assyrian king
BiblicalUsage: Esarhaddon was king of Assyria after his father Sennacherib, who was killed by his own sons in the temple of his god. His name means Ashur has given a brother, and the Bible names him twice: once in the story of Sennacherib's death, and once when the enemies of Judah claim he settled foreign peoples in Samaria. He rules an empire, but in Scripture he is only a marker on the edge of God's story with His people.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the kings of the earth are footnotes in God's story, not the other way round. Esarhaddon ruled an empire, yet the Bible remembers him only because of what God did with Judah.
RelatedPeople: Sennacherib, King of Assyria; King Hezekiah
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an interdict
BiblicalUsage: This is the Aramaic word for a royal decree that cannot be changed, and it appears only in the story of Daniel and the lions' den. The princes persuade Darius to sign a decree that no one may pray to any god or man for thirty days, and the king seals it with his signet so it stands. The decree is meant to trap Daniel, and it does, but it cannot trap God.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe human decrees look unbreakable until they meet God's law, and then they break. Daniel prayed anyway, and the den could not hold the man the decree was meant to kill.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, united, i.e. one; or (as an ordinal) first
BiblicalUsage: One is the first number and the simplest word, but the Bible loads it with weight. The first day is called one day, a man leaves his father and mother and becomes one flesh with his wife, and Israel confesses that the Lord our God is one Lord. Zechariah looks ahead to a day when the Lord will be one and His name one, the same unity spread over the whole earth.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the oneness of God is the foundation of everything, because one Lord means one truth, one way, and one people gathered under Him. My position is that unity among God's people is not a preference; it flows from who He is.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2279; to make a loud noise, i.e. reverberate:--roar, sound.
BiblicalUsage: Paul uses this word once, for a sounding brass or a tinkling cymbal, the loud empty noise of a gong. Without love, he says, even the most gifted speech is only that, a noise that rings and means nothing.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe love is what turns noise into something real, and without it my words are only a clanging sound.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain origin; an adder or other poisonous snake (literally or figuratively):--viper.
BiblicalUsage: A viper is a poisonous snake, and John the Baptist and Jesus both use it as a name for people whose religion is a cover for poison. John calls the Pharisees a generation of vipers and asks who warned them to flee the wrath to come, and Jesus says the same to the Pharisees whose words are full of evil. In Acts the word turns literal again, when a viper fastens on Paul's hand on Malta and he shakes it off unharmed.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe words reveal the heart the way a snake's bite reveals its venom, and religious language is no antidote. Only a changed heart makes the speech safe, and God is the one who changes it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Echi, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Ehi is a son of Benjamin, named once in the list of Jacob's family that went down into Egypt. His name means my brother, and beyond that single mention we know nothing more about him. He travelled with the family into a foreign land, and his name survives in the genealogy.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that God counts every member of the family, even the ones named only once. Ehi went down to Egypt with the rest, and he was part of the promise all the same.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: , including an alternate form σχέω; (used in certain tenses only) a primary verb; to hold (used in very various applications, literally or figuratively, direct or remote; such as possession; ability, contiuity, relation, or condition):--be (able, X hold, possessed with), accompany, + begin to amend, can(+ -not), X conceive, count, diseased, do + eat, + enjoy, + fear, following, have, hold, keep, + lack, + go to law, lie, + must needs, + of necessity, + need, next, + recover, + reign, + rest, + return, X sick, take for, + tremble, + uncircumcised, use.
BiblicalUsage: To have, in the New Testament, is usually about possession that changes the possessor, not about owning things. John says whoever believes in the Son has everlasting life, and whoever has the Son has life, while whoever has not the Son has not life. Paul says our bodies are the temple of the Holy Spirit, whom we have from God, and Jesus says He came that we might have life more abundantly.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe having Christ is the only possession that cannot be taken, because it is a person, not a thing. Everything else I hold can slip away, but the life He gives stays.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain affinity; a loud or confused noise ("echo"), i.e. roar; figuratively, a rumor:--fame, sound.
BiblicalUsage: A sound can be a rushing wind, a rumour, or a trumpet, and this word covers all three. On Pentecost a sound like a rushing mighty wind fills the house, the fame of Jesus spreads through the country around Galilee, and Hebrews remembers the sound of the trumpet at Sinai that made Israel beg for silence. The word moves from a noise you hear to news that travels.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God speaks in sounds we cannot ignore, whether a wind at Pentecost or a trumpet at the mountain, and His news still travels. I want my life to carry His sound, not just make noise.
RelatedTopics: Outpouring of the Spirit; Word of God; Worship
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: feminine of G2190; hostility; by implication, a reason for opposition:--enmity, hatred.
BiblicalUsage: Enmity is settled hostility, not a passing quarrel, and the New Testament uses it for the deepest divides. Paul says the carnal mind is enmity against God, lists hatreds among the works of the flesh, and says Christ broke down the wall of enmity between Jew and Gentile in His own body. James warns that friendship with the world is enmity with God, so the word always forces a choice of sides.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Christ is the only one who can end real enmity, because He did it by taking the hostility into Himself on the cross. My position is that peace with God is not a truce; it is the end of the war.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a primary ἔχθω (to hate); hateful (passively, odious, or actively, hostile); usually as a noun, an adversary (especially Satan):--enemy, foe.
BiblicalUsage: An enemy is one who hates and opposes, and the Bible names enemies both human and spiritual, with Satan at the head of them. Jesus commands us to love our enemies and pray for those who persecute us, Zechariah's song promises deliverance from the hand of our enemies, and Paul says we were reconciled to God while we were still enemies. The last enemy, Paul says, is death itself, and it will be destroyed.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe loving enemies is the hardest command Jesus gave, and the clearest proof of His life in us. God loved me while I was His enemy, so I have no excuse for hating mine.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Echud, the name of three Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Ehud is the name of three Israelites in the records, and this single verse names one of them, a Benjamite listed among the sons of Ehud's line in the days of the return. The better-known Ehud is the left-handed judge who killed Eglon of Moab, but the man in this verse is only a name in a genealogy. The lists keep him because the family line mattered, even when the story does not.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that God remembers names the story forgets, and every one of them belonged to a real person in a real family. The genealogy is not filler; it is His record.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Ester, the Jewish heroine
BiblicalUsage: Esther is the Jewish orphan raised by her cousin Mordecai who became queen of Persia, and her Hebrew name Hadassah means myrtle while Esther means star. She risked her life to go before the king uninvited, saying that if she perished, she perished, and her courage saved her people from Haman's plot. The book that bears her name never mentions God by name, yet His hand is everywhere in it.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Esther shows that God places His people where they are needed before they know why, and courage is saying yes when the moment comes. Her story is my reminder that I may be here for such a time as this.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {a bond (especially manacles of a prisoner)}
BiblicalUsage: In Aramaic this word is a band or bond, and Daniel uses it for the band of iron and brass put around the stump of Nebuchadnezzar's tree in his dream. Ezra uses it differently, in the king's letter, where the punishments for breaking God's law include imprisonment, the house of bonds. The word holds both meanings at once: a band that binds and a prison that holds.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God can bind a king and loose a prisoner, because no band holds what He means to free. Nebuchadnezzar's tree was bound until God said otherwise, and Daniel walked free.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a bond (especially manacles of a prisoner)
BiblicalUsage: The Hebrew word for a bond is a rope or fetter, and it shows up in hard places. Samson snaps the new ropes that bind him as if they were flax, the preacher says a seductive woman is a snare whose hands are as bands, and Jeremiah is thrown into prison, the house of bonds, for speaking God's word. The same word binds the strong, tempts the foolish, and holds the faithful.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe only God's truth cuts the bands that hold us, because Samson's strength broke ropes but could not break his own desires. I want the bonds I carry to be the ones He ties, not the ones sin ties.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: concretely, a witness; abstractly, testimony; specifically, a recorder, i.e. prince
BiblicalUsage: A witness is someone who saw and can speak, and the law of God rests on that simple fact. The ninth commandment forbids false witness against a neighbour, Deuteronomy requires two or three witnesses before anyone is put to death, and Samuel calls on the Lord and His anointed as witnesses that he took nothing from Israel. The psalmist even calls the moon God's faithful witness in the sky, because creation itself testifies.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe truth needs witnesses, and God gave His people the job of telling what they have seen Him do. My position is that a faithful witness is worth more than a clever argument, because the truth stands on what really happened.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a fog
BiblicalUsage: Before any rain fell, a mist went up from the earth and watered the whole face of the ground, and Job says God draws up the drops of water that distil as rain from His mist. The word is small and quiet, just vapour rising, yet it watered Eden.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God waters His world gently before He ever sends the storm, and His quiet provision comes first.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: testimony
BiblicalUsage: The testimonies are God's laws spoken as witness, the fixed words He gave Israel to keep and teach. Moses calls them testimonies, statutes, and judgements, and commands parents to keep them diligently and answer their children when they ask what they mean. The psalmist calls blessed those who keep His testimonies and seek Him with the whole heart, and says his soul has kept them and loves them exceedingly.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God's testimonies are not opinions to weigh but words to keep, because they come from the One who made us. They tell the truth about Him and about us, and I hold that keeping them is the way to walk blessed.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1475; to raze:--lay even with the ground.
BiblicalUsage: Jesus uses this word once, in His warning over Jerusalem, saying her enemies will lay her even with the ground and not leave one stone upon another. It is a word of total levelling, a city brought down flat because she did not know the time of her visitation.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Jesus wept over Jerusalem because He knew what was coming, and His warning still calls every city and every heart to recognise Him while there is time.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from the base of G1476; a basis (bottom), i.e. the soil:--ground.
BiblicalUsage: Paul uses this word once, telling how he fell to the ground on the road to Damascus and heard the voice of Jesus asking why he persecuted Him. The ground is the lowest place, and that is where Paul's old life ended and his new one began.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God often brings us to the ground before He lifts us up, because pride has to fall before grace can raise us.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: then (of time)
BiblicalUsage: Then is the word that moves the story forward in Daniel and Ezra, marking what happened next after God acted or a king spoke. Daniel goes to his friends after the king's decree, the princes gather when Nebuchadnezzar calls them, and Darius orders a search of the records when the work on the temple is questioned. The word is plain, but it carries the turning points of the story.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that God's story always has a then, a next step after the crisis, and Daniel's life proves it. The decree is not the end; what God does next is.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: apparently from G2228 (or possibly G2229) and G1211; even now:--already, (even) now (already), by this time.
BiblicalUsage: Already means the time has come, and the New Testament uses it for things that are true now, not only later. Paul says it is high time to awake out of sleep, John says the darkness is past and the true light already shines, and Paul, near the end, says he is already being offered up. The word presses the present moment, because the hour is now.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the gospel makes already a word of urgency, because salvation is here now and the night is far spent. I do not want to live as if God's hour were still far off when it is already here.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Eden, a place in Mesopotamia
BiblicalUsage: This Eden is not the garden but a place in Mesopotamia, a land of traders conquered by Assyria. The king of Assyria boasts that his fathers destroyed the people of Eden, and Ezekiel lists Eden among the merchants who traded with Tyre. It is a wealthy place that fell, and the Bible names it only to mark what Assyria did.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that wealthy cities fall like poor ones when God judges, because no trade or treasure protects a people from Him. Eden's end is a warning, not a footnote.
RelatedPeople: Sennacherib, King of Assyria; King Hezekiah
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: pleasure
BiblicalUsage: Delight here is luxury and pleasure, the fine things of life, and the Bible uses it in both directions. Sarah laughs at the thought of pleasure in her old age, David laments Saul and Jonathan who clothed Israel's daughters in scarlet and delights, and the psalmist says God gives His people drink from the river of His pleasures. Jeremiah turns the word against Babylon, who devoured Israel like a dragon and filled her belly with delicacies.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe true delight is found in God Himself, not in the luxuries that pass, because His river of pleasures never runs dry. The world's delights are borrowed; His are the real thing.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Eden, the region of Adam's home
BiblicalUsage: Eden is the garden God planted in the east, where He put the man He had formed to dress it and keep it, and from which Adam and Eve were driven out after they ate of the forbidden tree. The garden held the tree of life and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, and cherubim guarded the way back once the man and woman were sent out. A Levite named Eden also served in Hezekiah's day, but the garden is the Eden the Bible means most often.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Eden shows what we lost and what God promises to restore, because the garden was good and the exile from it was real. I hold that the way back runs through the cross, and the end of the story is a garden again.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a basis (of a building, a column, etc.)
KeyPassages: Exodus 26:19; Exodus 26:32; Numbers 4:31; Song of Solomon 5:15
BiblicalUsage: The sockets are the heavy bases that hold the tabernacle upright, silver feet under wooden boards, and the Bible counts them with care. Exodus lists the sockets under every board and pillar, Numbers charges the sons of Merari with carrying them, and the Song pictures a lover's legs as pillars of marble set on sockets of fine gold. The foundation is not decoration; it is what keeps the whole house standing.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God builds on a firm foundation, and He counts the parts nobody sees. The sockets were buried under the boards, but the tabernacle stood on them, and my life stands on Christ the same way.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Eder, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Eder is a Benjamite, son of Beriah, named once in the genealogy of the tribe of Benjamin. His name means flock, and the list calls him a chief of the inhabitants of Aijalon, but the Bible tells us nothing more about his life. He stands in the record as one of the heads of a family in Israel.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the heads of families matter to God even when their stories are short, because the people of God is built from households like his. Eder's name is kept, and that is enough.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an arrangement, i.e. muster (of animals)
BiblicalUsage: A flock is sheep or goats gathered and kept, and the Bible's shepherds watch them day and night. Jacob waters the flocks at the well in Haran, David tells Saul he killed a lion and a bear to save a lamb from his father's flock, and Isaiah says the Lord will feed His flock like a shepherd and carry the lambs in His arms. The flock is never just animals; it is the picture of God's people under His care.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe I am one of His flock, and that changes how I hear His voice, because sheep know the shepherd and follow him. He carries the lambs, and I am glad to be carried.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Eder, the name of an Israelite and of two places in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Eder is the name of a Merarite Levite in David's day and of two towns, one in the far south of Judah and one named in the lists beside it. The Levite is counted among the sons of Mushi who served in the temple, and the towns sit on the border of Edom, at the edge of the inheritance. The same name covers a man who served and places that marked the boundary.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that serving God and marking His boundaries both matter, because the Levite kept the worship going and the towns kept the land. Eder's name, flock, fits both: a people kept and a place kept.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: amplitude, i.e. (concrete) a mantle; also (figuratively) splendor
BiblicalUsage: This word is a wide mantle or cloak, and by extension the splendour it gives the one who wears it. Micah says the rich strip the robe from those passing by in peace, and Zechariah is told to throw the price of a betrayed shepherd, thirty pieces of silver, to the potter, calling it the goodly price they valued him at. The mantle stands for honour, and both verses show honour being stripped away.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe true splendour is not a cloak men can strip off, because the honour God gives cannot be taken by thieves or traitors.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Edom, the elder twin-brother of Jacob; hence the region (Idumaea) occupied by him
BiblicalUsage: Edom is Esau, the elder twin who sold his birthright for red stew and was called Edom, red, and it is also his descendants and their land south-east of Judah. Genesis traces the kings of Edom before Israel had a king, and Numbers tells how Edom refused Israel passage through their land. The name runs from one man's appetite to a nation's pride.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Esau's story warns me that a single careless choice can shape generations, because Edom's pride grew from his contempt for the birthright. God keeps His promises to Jacob's line, and He judges Edom's line for what it did with its own.
RelatedEvents: Esau Sells His Birthright; Edom Refuses Israel Passage
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an Edomite, or descendants from (or inhabitants of) Edom
BiblicalUsage: An Edomite is a descendant of Esau, and the most famous one in the Bible is Doeg, Saul's chief herdsman. Doeg saw David at Nob and told Saul, and then he killed the priests of the Lord with his own sword when no one else would.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Doeg shows how far a man will go when he serves a king instead of God, because he murdered priests to please Saul. Loyalty to the wrong master is still treachery, and God saw it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an arm, i.e. (figuratively) power
BiblicalUsage: In Aramaic this word is an arm, and by figure it means force or power, and it occurs once in Ezra. When the king's letter arrives, the enemies of Judah go up to Jerusalem in haste and make them stop building by force and power. One word carries the whole threat: the king's arm against God's house.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe no arm of man can stop what God has commanded to be built, because the temple rose again despite the force sent against it.
RelatedEvents: Cyrus's Decree and Return from Exile
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Edrei, the name of two places in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Edrei is a chief city of Bashan, where Og the king ruled, and it is named whenever Israel's victory over him is told. Moses recounts the battle at Edrei, where Og came out with all his people and Israel struck him down and took his land. The city marks the northern edge of the conquest, a strong place that fell to God's people.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Edrei reminds me that no stronghold is too strong for God, because Og's iron bed and high walls could not save him. The giants fall when God fights for His people.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: testimony
BiblicalUsage: The testimony is the stone tablets God gave Moses, kept inside the ark under the mercy seat, and the word means witness in stone. God tells Moses to put the testimony in the ark, and when the work is done He gives him two tables of testimony written with the finger of God. At the crowning of young Joash, the priest puts the crown on him and gives him the testimony, the written law set over the king as over the people.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God's testimony is written, not whispered, because He put His words in stone and set them at the centre of His people's worship. I hold that the same written word still testifies to Him today, and I trust it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: love (concretely), i.e. amative words
BiblicalUsage: This word is love as a feeling, the pleasant sound of lovely words, and Ezekiel uses it twice against a people who hear God's word as entertainment. They come and listen to the prophet as though he sang a lovely song, but their hearts chase after gain, and the words never reach their hands. It is love that enjoys the sound and refuses the substance.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe hearing God's word as a pleasant song is dangerous, because it can feel like love while the heart stays far from Him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably akin to the base of G58 (through the idea of collecting one's faculties); to waken (transitively or intransitively), i.e. rouse (literally, from sleep, from sitting or lying, from disease, from death; or figuratively, from obscurity, inactivity, ruins, nonexistence):--awake, lift (up), raise (again, up), rear up, (a-)rise (again, up), stand, take up.
BiblicalUsage: To raise is to wake from sleep, to stand up from lying down, and to rise from the dead, and the New Testament uses one word for all three. The angel says He is not here, for He is risen, the women find the tomb empty on the first day, and Paul says Christ was buried and rose again the third day according to the Scriptures. The same word that wakes a sleeper raises a Saviour, and it will raise us too.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the resurrection is the hinge of my faith, because if Christ is not raised, my preaching and my hope are empty. He is risen, and that means death is not the end of my story either.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a (male) calf (as frisking round), especially one nearly grown (i.e. a steer)
BiblicalUsage: A calf is a young bull, and in the Bible it is most often an idol, the shape men's hands give to a god they can see. Aaron fashions a golden calf while Moses is on the mountain, Jeroboam sets up two calves at Dan and Bethel and tells Israel these are the gods that brought them out of Egypt, and Hosea says the calf of Samaria will be broken in pieces. The animal is innocent; the worship is the sin.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe idolatry always makes God smaller than He is, because a calf can be carried, melted, and broken, and the true God cannot. I hold that anything I shape to control God is a calf, and I want no part of it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a reservoir
BiblicalUsage: This word is a store or reservoir, a collection held back, and it occurs once, when God asks Job who fathered the rain and the drops of dew. The question is not about a place but about a source: who keeps the store of water that falls on the earth.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the stores of rain belong to God alone, and Job's silence is the right answer when the Creator asks who holds them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1453; a resurgence (from death):--resurrection.
BiblicalUsage: This word is the rising itself, a resurgence from death, and it occurs once, after the death of Jesus. The graves open, the bodies of saints who slept arise, and they go into the holy city and appear to many. One verse holds a whole resurrection, a sign that His death broke death's hold.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the saints rising at His death was a sign of what His rising would finish, because His death opened graves that stayed open.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Eglah, a wife of David
BiblicalUsage: Eglah was a wife of David and the mother of his son Ithream, and her name means a heifer. The lists name her in both the record of David's sons born in Hebron and the genealogy of his house, and beyond those two mentions we know nothing more about her. She is one of the wives whose names survive only because her son did.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that God remembers the mothers as well as the sons, because Eglah's name is kept in the record of the king's house. Her place in the family of David is part of the line that leads to Christ.
RelatedPeople: Eglah, Wife of David; King David; Ithream
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a (female) calf, especially one nearly grown (i.e. a heifer)
BiblicalUsage: A heifer is a young cow, and the Bible uses her in covenant, in atonement, and in daily work. God tells Abram to take a heifer three years old for the covenant, the law commands a heifer to be killed when a slain man is found in a field and no one knows who struck him, and Samuel takes a heifer to Bethlehem so his journey to anoint David looks like a sacrifice. Hosea pictures Israel as a trained heifer that loves to tread out the corn, working in comfort until the yoke comes.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the heifer shows how God meets His people in the ordinary work of the field, because He takes a farm animal and makes it part of His covenant and His law. The God of the threshing floor is the God of the promise too.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Eglajim, a place in Moab
BiblicalUsage: Eglaim is a town in Moab, named once in Isaiah's oracle against that nation, where the cry of its destruction reaches to its borders. Its name means double reservoir, and it sits in the list of Moabite towns whose weeping fills the land. Beyond this one verse we know nothing more about it, except that God saw it and judged it.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that God sees the small towns as well as the great cities, because Eglaim's cry reached Him in the day of Moab's judgement. No place is too small for His notice, whether for blessing or for judgement.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Eglon, the name of a place in Palestine and of a Moabitish king
BiblicalUsage: Eglon is both a royal city in the lowlands of Judah and the fat king of Moab who oppressed Israel for eighteen years. Joshua's army took the city of Eglon in the conquest, and later the king Eglon ruled from his summer parlour until Ehud the left-handed judge came with a message from God and struck him down. The same name covers a city that fell and a king who fell, both before God's people.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Eglon shows that oppression has a set time, because eighteen years felt endless to Israel and ended in a single afternoon. God raises up deliverers, and the fattest king is no match for Him.
RelatedPeople: Eglon, King of Moab; Ehud, Son of Gera; Joshua
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a primary pronoun of the first person I (only expressed when emphatic):--I, me. For the other cases and the plural see G1691, G1698, G1700, G2248, G2249, G2254, G2257, etc.
BiblicalUsage: I is the word a speaker uses when the emphasis falls on himself, and in the New Testament it carries the weight of who is speaking. Jesus says I am before Abraham was, I am the good shepherd, and I am the way, the truth, and the life, and Paul says I am what I am by the grace of God. The little word matters because the person behind it matters.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the I am of Jesus is the claim of God Himself, because no mere man can say before Abraham was, I am, and be telling the truth. My position is that everything stands or falls on who He says He is, and I believe Him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a nut
BiblicalUsage: The word is nuts, and it occurs once, when the lover goes down into the garden of nuts to see the fruits of the valley and whether the vine has budded. It is a small, sweet detail in a love song, a garden full of good things to taste and see.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God made the garden and its fruit to be enjoyed, and the Song's small details are His gift, not an accident.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: the clenched hand
