BiblicalUsage: A fist is a clenched hand, and the Bible uses it for a blow and for oppression. The law deals with a man who strikes his neighbour with a fist, and Isaiah says a fast that ends in striking with the fist of wickedness is no fast God accepts. The same hand that should feed the hungry can close into a weapon.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God watches what my hands do, because a fist and an open hand tell two different stories about the heart.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: where
BiblicalUsage: This little word asks where, and Hosea uses it twice to taunt a kingless people and then to promise God's victory. Where is thy king now, that he may save thee, the prophet asks, and then God answers, O death, where are thy plagues, and O grave, where is thy destruction. The question turns from mockery to triumph in four verses.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God's where is the last word over death, because He asks where its sting is and then takes it away.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Ehud, the name of two or three Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Ehud was the left-handed judge from Benjamin whom God raised up to deliver Israel from Eglon, king of Moab. He made a double-edged dagger, hid it under his clothes, and used a private message to reach the king alone in his summer parlour, and after the deed he blew the trumpet and led Israel to take the fords of Jordan. The land had rest for eighty years after him, and the story is told in full in the third chapter of Judges.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God uses the left-handed, the overlooked, and the unlikely, because Ehud's weakness was the very thing that got him past the guards. I hold that no limitation disqualifies a person God has chosen.
RelatedPeople: Ehud, Son of Gera; Eglon, King of Moab
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1487, G1161, and G3361 (sometimes with G1065 added); but if not:--(or) else, if (not, otherwise), otherwise.
BiblicalUsage: This is a phrase, not a single word, built from if and but and not, and it means otherwise or but if not. Jesus warns that if you do your alms before men to be seen, otherwise you have no reward of your Father, and He tells His disciples that in His Father's house are many mansions, and if it were not so He would have told them. The phrase turns on a condition, and the warning or the comfort follows from it.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Jesus uses otherwise to make the stakes plain, because the condition decides whether the reward stands or falls.
RelatedTopics: Fear of the Lord; Faith; Hope
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: second person singular present of G1510; thou art:--art, be.
BiblicalUsage: This is the word thou art, the second person of the verb to be, and the Greek text never spells it as a separate lemma: it always appears as a form of the verb to be. The tempter says, If thou be the Son of God, and John's messengers ask Jesus, Art thou he that should come. The word is small, but it carries the question of who Jesus is.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the question art thou is still the question, because everything turns on who Jesus is, and I answer that He is the Son of God.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1487 and G2532; if also (or even):--if (that), though.
BiblicalUsage: This is another phrase, if also or even if, made of the little word if and the word and. A friend will rise and give bread because of importunity even if friendship alone would not move him, and Paul says that even if the outward man perishes, the inward man is renewed day by day. The phrase admits the hard case and then answers it.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe even if is a word of faith, because it holds on to God when the outward case looks lost.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1508 and the neuter of G5100; if not somewhat:--except.
BiblicalUsage: This phrase means except or if not somewhat, and in the Greek text it stands as if followed by a single particle that asks whether, written as one word. The disciples say they have no more than five loaves and two fishes except they go and buy food, and Paul says husbands and wives should not deprive one another except by consent for a time. The phrase draws the one exception and holds everything else firm.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the exceptions in God's word are as careful as His commands, because He draws the line exactly where He means it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1487 and G3361; if not:--but, except (that), if not, more than, save (only) that, saving, till.
BiblicalUsage: This phrase means if not, but, or except, and it is one of the commonest turns in the Gospels, always made of if and not standing side by side. Salt is good for nothing except to be cast out, no one knows the Father except the Son, and David ate the showbread, which was not lawful for him to eat except for the priests alone. The phrase marks the one door through which the rule opens.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe except is the word that keeps God's rules from becoming traps, because He always names the way through.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1487 and G4007; if perhaps:--if so be (that), seeing, though.
BiblicalUsage: This phrase means if indeed or if so be, and in the Greek text it is written as a single word, with if and indeed joined together. Paul says you are in the Spirit if indeed the Spirit of God dwells in you, and that we are heirs of God if so be we suffer with Him. The phrase does not doubt; it states the condition on which the promise stands.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe if so be is a promise with a condition attached, and the condition is real, because the Spirit's presence is the proof of the promise.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1487 and G4458; if somehow:--if by any means.
BiblicalUsage: This phrase means if by any means, and Paul uses it for the hopes he holds lightly and prays about. He prays that by any means he might come to Rome, that by any means he might provoke his fellow Jews to jealousy and save some, and that by any means he might attain to the resurrection of the dead. The phrase is the sound of a man who will take any road God opens.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe if by any means is honest praying, because Paul did not demand his road, he asked for any road that led where God wanted him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1487 and G5100; if any:--he that, if a(-ny) man('s thing, from any, ought), whether any, whosoever.
BiblicalUsage: This phrase means if any or if anyone, and it opens the door to whoever will listen. Jesus says, If any man have ears to hear, let him hear, Paul says the commandments are summed up in loving your neighbour, and he warns that if any man defiles the temple of God, God will destroy him. The phrase is wide open, and it includes me.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe if any means the invitation and the warning are both for everyone, because no one is left out of either.
RelatedTopics: Obedience; Fear of the Lord; Faith
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a primary particle of conditionality; if, whether, that, etc.:--forasmuch as, if, that, (al-)though, whether. Often used in connection or composition with other particles, especially as in G1489, G1490, G1499, G1508, G1509, G1512, G1513, G1536, G1537. See also G1437.
BiblicalUsage: If is the hinge of the New Testament, the little word that turns a promise into a condition and a warning into a choice. Paul says if any man's work abides, he shall receive a reward, and if a brother is grieved by what we eat, we are no longer walking in love. Titus must be blameless if he is to serve as an elder, and every if in Scripture asks the reader to decide.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God's ifs are not traps but invitations, because He sets the condition plainly and then waits for our answer. My position is that faith is saying yes to His if before I see the whole road.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a primary verb; used only in certain past tenses, the others being borrowed from the equivalent G3700 and G3708; properly, to see (literally or figuratively); by implication, (in the perfect tense only) to know:--be aware, behold, X can (+ not tell), consider, (have) know(-ledge), look (on), perceive, see, be sure, tell, understand, wish, wot. Compare G3700.
BiblicalUsage: This is the old form of the verb to know or to see, and the Greek text carries it only as a form of the verb to know, spelled I might know. Paul says if he had all knowledge and understood all mysteries but had not love, he would be nothing, and he says that if he does not know the meaning of a voice, he will be a barbarian to the speaker. The word is rare, but the knowing it names is the heart of the passage.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe knowing without love is nothing, because Paul puts knowledge on trial and finds it empty without it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: neuter of a presumed derivative of G1497; an image-fane:--idol's temple.
BiblicalUsage: This word is an idol's temple, the place where meat offered to idols was eaten, and Paul uses it once. He warns that if a weak brother sees a man with knowledge sitting at meat in the idol's temple, his conscience will be emboldened to eat what his faith cannot carry. The building is not the problem; the brother watching is.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe my freedom ends where my brother's faith begins, because love, not knowledge, decides what I do in front of him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1497 and G2999; image-worship (literally or figuratively):--idolatry.
BiblicalUsage: This is the worship of images, and the Greek text spells it with a short vowel in the middle, idololatry, where Strong's lists it with a long one. Paul names idolatry among the works of the flesh, tells the Colossians to put it to death as covetousness, and warns the Corinthians to flee from it. The spelling differs, but the sin is the same.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe idolatry is still the worship of anything in place of God, and Paul's command is still the same: flee from it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1497 and the base of G3000; an image- (servant or) worshipper (literally or figuratively):--idolater.
BiblicalUsage: An idolater is one who serves images, and Paul puts the word in his hardest lists. He tells the Corinthians not to keep company with a brother who is an idolater, says idolaters will not inherit the kingdom of God, and warns the Ephesians that no covetous man, who is an idolater, has any inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God. The word covers both the temple worshipper and the greedy heart, because both bow to something other than God.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe covetousness is idolatry with a respectable name, because it bows the heart to getting instead of to God. My position is that the kingdom has no room for a divided heart, and mine must belong wholly to Him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1491; an image (i.e. for worship); by implication, a heathen god, or (plural) the worship of such:--idol.
BiblicalUsage: An idol is an image made for worship, a god shaped by hands, and Paul says plainly that an idol is nothing in the world and that there is no other God but one. He asks what an idol is, and answers that it is nothing, yet the Corinthians still feared the meat offered to it, and John closes his letter with the warning to keep yourselves from idols. The Thessalonians turned from idols to serve the living and true God, and that turning is the whole story.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe an idol is nothing, and that is exactly why it is dangerous, because it takes the worship owed to the living God and gives it to nothing. I hold that turning from idols is not a one-time act but a daily one.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: neuter of a compound of G1497 and a presumed derivative of G2380; an image-sacrifice, i.e. part of an idolatrous offering:--(meat, thing that is) offered (in sacrifice, sacrificed) to (unto) idols.
BiblicalUsage: This is meat that has been sacrificed to an idol, food that carries a history with it, and the New Testament argues about it more than any other food. Paul says knowledge about idols puffs up, but love builds up, and the council at Jerusalem tells Gentile believers to abstain from things offered to idols. Jesus rebukes the church at Pergamos for eating things sacrificed to idols, because the food had become fellowship with false gods.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the question is never only about the food, because what we eat together says who we belong to. Love decides the table, not knowledge, and I want my table to build up, not to trip up.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1492; a view, i.e. form (literally or figuratively):--appearance, fashion, shape, sight.
BiblicalUsage: This word is a form or appearance, what a thing looks like when you see it, and the New Testament uses it for the deepest sights. At Jesus' baptism the Holy Spirit descends in bodily shape like a dove, on the mountain His face changes and His clothing becomes white and glistering, and the Father says no one has seen His form or heard His voice at any time. Paul closes his letter by telling the Thessalonians to abstain from all appearance of evil, because what a thing looks like matters too.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the form matters because God showed Himself in one, and the Spirit came down where everyone could see. I hold that we should avoid even the appearance of evil, because the look of a thing teaches before its words do.
RelatedTopics: Outpouring of the Spirit; Jesus Christ; Holiness
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: optative (i.e. English subjunctive) present of G1510 (including the other person); might (could, would, or should) be:--mean, + perish, should be, was, were.
BiblicalUsage: This is the optative of the verb to be, the form that says might be or would be, and the first-person form itself never stands in the Greek text. What does stand is the third-person form, the word might be, as when Mary wonders what manner of greeting the angel's words might be, and the people wonder whether John might be the Christ. The form carries a question, not a certainty.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God meets honest wondering, because Mary and the crowds asked might it be and He answered them.
RelatedEvents: The Birth of Jesus; The Birth of John the Baptist
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1487 and G1065; if indeed, seeing that, unless, (with negative) otherwise:--if (so be that, yet).
BiblicalUsage: This phrase means if indeed or seeing that, and it is if joined to the little word indeed. Paul says we shall be clothed upon if indeed we are found not naked, asks the Galatians whether they suffered so many things in vain if indeed it was in vain, and reminds the Ephesians that they heard of his stewardship if indeed they did. The phrase states a fact and builds on it, rather than doubting it.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe if indeed is faith reasoning from what God has already done, because Paul builds his argument on facts his readers already know.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably from G1502 (through the idea of failure); idly, i.e. without reason (or effect):--without a cause, (in) vain(-ly).
BiblicalUsage: This word means idly, without reason, or in vain, and the Greek text spells it with a long vowel at the end, where Strong's lists it with a short one. Paul says the ruler does not bear the sword in vain, tells the Corinthians they are saved by the gospel if they keep it in memory, unless they believed in vain, and asks the Galatians whether they suffered so many things in vain. The word asks whether anything we do has a reason behind it.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe nothing God does is in vain, and my suffering is not wasted when it is His hand that allows it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: apparently a primary verb (perhaps akin to G1502 through the idea of faintness as a copy); to resemble:--be like.
BiblicalUsage: This word means to yield or give place, to step aside, and Paul uses it once. He says that to the false brethren who came to spy out their liberty, he gave place by subjection not even for an hour, so that the truth of the gospel might continue with the Galatians. One refusal to yield kept the gospel free.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe some ground must never be yielded, because the truth of the gospel is worth more than an hour of peace.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: apparently a primary verb (perhaps akin to G1502 through the idea of faintness as a copy); to resemble:--be like.
BiblicalUsage: This word means to yield or give place, to step aside, and Paul uses it once. He says that to the false brethren who came to spy out their liberty, he gave place by subjection not even for an hour, so that the truth of the gospel might continue with the Galatians. One refusal to yield kept the gospel free.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe some ground must never be yielded, because the truth of the gospel is worth more than an hour of peace.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1503; a likeness, i.e. (literally) statue, profile, or (figuratively) representation, resemblance:--image.
BiblicalUsage: An image is a likeness, a representation that shows what the original is like, and the New Testament uses it for Christ and for us. Christ is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of every creature, and believers are being renewed in knowledge after the image of Him who created them. Paul says God predestined us to be conformed to the image of His Son, and that as we have borne the image of the earthy, we shall also bear the image of the heavenly.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe being made in God's image is the dignity of every person, and being remade into Christ's image is the goal of my life. My position is that the image is not something I earn; it is something God restores in me.
RelatedTopics: Image of God; Jesus Christ; Salvation
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain affinity; a score:--twenty.
BiblicalUsage: Twenty is a round number, a score, and the Greek text writes it as a form of the word twenty with the final letter sometimes added. A king with ten thousand men considers whether he can meet an enemy coming with twenty thousand, the disciples row about twenty-five furlongs on the sea before they see Jesus walking on the water, and about a hundred and twenty names gather to choose a replacement for Judas. The number itself is plain; the stories around it are not.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God counts His people exactly, whether twenty thousand enemies or a hundred and twenty disciples, because every number in His story is a real number of real people.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1506; clearness, i.e. (by implication) purity (figuratively):--sincerity.
BiblicalUsage: Sincerity is clearness, purity judged in the sunlight, and Paul uses it for the way Christians should live and speak. He says to keep the feast with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth, boasts that his conduct was in simplicity and godly sincerity, and says he speaks in Christ as of sincerity, as of God. The word pictures something held up to the sun to see whether it is clean all the way through.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe sincerity is the test of everything I say about God, because words spoken in the dark cannot stand in His light. I want my life to be clean all the way through, not only on the surface.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from εἵλη (the sun's ray) and G2919; judged by sunlight, i.e. tested as genuine (figuratively):--pure, sincere.
BiblicalUsage: This word means sincere or pure, tested by sunlight, and it occurs twice. Paul prays that the Philippians may approve the excellent things and be sincere and without offence until the day of Christ, and Peter says he writes to stir up their pure minds by way of remembrance. The picture is the same: a life with nothing hidden from the light.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God wants a pure mind, not just pure actions, because what I think in the dark shapes what I do in the light.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: the first person singular present indicative; a prolonged form of a primary and defective verb; I exist (used only when emphatic):--am, have been, X it is I, was. See also G1488, G1498, G1511, G1526, G2258, G2071, G2070, G2075, G2076, G2771, G2468, G5600.
BiblicalUsage: To be is the commonest verb in the New Testament, and it carries the greatest claim in the Bible. John opens his Gospel by saying the Word was in the beginning and the Word was God, Jesus says before Abraham was, I am, calls Himself the good shepherd, and says, I am the way, the truth, and the life. The verb is ordinary everywhere else, but in His mouth it is the name God gave Moses at the burning bush.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Jesus is the I am, and that changes everything, because the God who spoke to Moses now speaks to me in a man I can follow. My position is that there is no other name under heaven by which I can be saved.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: present infinitive from G1510; to exist:--am, was. come, is, X lust after, X please well, there is, to be, was.
BiblicalUsage: This is the infinitive of the verb to be, the form that says to be, and the Greek text always carries it under the heading of that verb. Jesus asks His disciples who men say that He is, and then who they say He is, and Peter answers on the mountain that it is good for them to be there. The word is the plainest in the language, and it holds the plainest question in the Gospels.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe who do you say that I am is the question every person must answer, and my answer is that He is the Christ, the Son of the living God.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1515; to be (act) peaceful:--be at (have, live in) peace, live peaceably.
BiblicalUsage: This word means to be at peace or to live peaceably, and the New Testament uses it as a command, not a wish. Jesus says to have salt in yourselves and be at peace with one another, Paul says to live peaceably with all men if it is possible, and he tells the Corinthians to be of good comfort, be of one mind, and live in peace. Peace is something to do, not only something to feel.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe peace with others is part of peace with God, because the same gospel that reconciles me to Him reconciles me to my brother. I hold that I should pursue peace as far as it depends on me, and leave the rest to Him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1515; pacific; by implication, salutary:--peaceable.
BiblicalUsage: This word means peaceable, and by extension wholesome, like fruit that does good to the one who eats it. Hebrews says chastening seems grievous at the time, but afterwards it yields the peaceable fruit of righteousness to those who are exercised by it, and James says the wisdom from above is first pure, then peaceable, gentle, and full of mercy. Peace is the fruit, and wisdom is the tree.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God's discipline is peaceable in the end, because He chastens the children He loves to make them fruitful.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1518; to be a peace-maker, i.e. (figuratively) to harmonize:--make peace.
BiblicalUsage: This word means to make peace, to bring warring sides together, and Paul uses it once, for what Christ did on the cross. Having made peace through the blood of His cross, God reconciles all things to Himself, whether things on earth or things in heaven. One act of peacemaking covers the whole creation.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the cross is where peace was made, because God did not wait for us to come to Him; He came to us and paid for the peace Himself.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1515 and G4160; pacificatory, i.e. (subjectively) peaceable:--peacemaker.
BiblicalUsage: A peacemaker is one who makes peace between others, and Jesus uses the word once, in the Beatitudes. Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called the children of God, He says, and the blessing falls on those who carry His peace into other people's wars. The name fits the children because it fits the Father.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe peacemakers look like their Father, because God is the great Peacemaker and His children carry His likeness into every quarrel.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a primary preposition; to or into (indicating the point reached or entered), of place, time, or (figuratively) purpose (result, etc.); also in adverbial phrases:--(abundant-)ly, against, among, as, at, (back-)ward, before, by, concerning, + continual, + far more exceeding, for (intent, purpose), fore, + forth, in (among, at, unto, -so much that, -to), to the intent that, + of one mind, + never, of, (up-)on, + perish, + set at one again, (so) that, therefore(-unto), throughout, til, to (be, the end, -ward), (here-)until(-to), …ward, (where-)fore, with. Often used in composition with the same general import, but only with verbs (etc.) expressing motion (literally or figuratively).
BiblicalUsage: Into is the word of movement and destination, and the New Testament uses it for baptism, belief, and belonging. Jesus sends His disciples to baptise all nations into the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, John says those who receive Him become children of God, and Peter tells the crowd to be baptised for the remission of sins. Paul says we are baptised into Jesus Christ and into His death, so the little word carries us from outside to inside.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe faith moves a person into Christ, not just toward Him, because baptism and belief both speak of entering, not of standing at the door. My position is that being in Christ is the whole of salvation, and this small word says it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1519 and G71; to introduce (literally or figuratively):--bring in(-to), (+ was to) lead into.
BiblicalUsage: To bring in is to carry someone or something inside, and the Gospels use it for the temple and the house. Simeon brings the child Jesus into the temple, the servant brings the poor, the maimed, the halt, and the blind into his master's house, and Stephen says the fathers brought the tabernacle in with Joshua. Hebrews says when God brings His firstborn into the world, all the angels are told to worship Him.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God brings people in, because His house has room for the poor and the broken, and He brought His own Son into the world to open the door. I want to be one who brings others in, not one who keeps them out.
RelatedEvents: The Presentation of Jesus in the Temple
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1519 and G191; to listen to:--hear.
BiblicalUsage: To hear in this word is to listen and answer, not only to catch a sound, and the Bible uses it for God's hearing of prayer. Jesus warns against thinking we will be heard for our much speaking, the angel tells Zacharias his prayer is heard, Cornelius is told his prayers and alms have come up as a memorial before God, and Jesus offered prayers with strong crying and tears and was heard because He feared. The word always means a hearing that answers.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God hears prayer the way a father hears a child, because He does not only catch the sound, He answers it. I hold that no honest prayer is ever lost on Him.
RelatedEvents: The Birth of John the Baptist
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1519 and G1209; to take into one's favor:--receive.
BiblicalUsage: This word means to take into one's favour, to receive with welcome, and Paul uses it once, quoting the prophet. Come out from among them, and be separate, and I will receive you, says the Lord, and the promise that follows is that He will be a Father to us and we shall be His sons and daughters. One word of welcome holds the whole adoption.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God's welcome is the reason to come out from the world, because separation is not His punishment but the way into His arms.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1519 and εἶμι (to go); to enter:--enter (go) into.
BiblicalUsage: To enter is to go in, and the word appears in the temple and the city. The lame man asks Peter and John for alms as they enter the temple, Paul goes in to James and the elders at Jerusalem, and the priests enter the first tabernacle continually to accomplish the service of God. The word is plain, but every entrance in Acts opens a new chapter.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God still opens doors for His people to enter, because the temple, the city, and the council all had doors that led somewhere new. I want to walk through the doors He opens and not force the ones He shuts.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1519 and G2064; to enter (literally or figuratively):--X arise, come (in, into), enter in(-to), go in (through).
BiblicalUsage: To enter is the word of the door, and Jesus uses it for the kingdom itself. No one can enter the kingdom of God unless he is born of water and of the Spirit, and Jesus says He is the door, and whoever enters by Him will be saved and go in and out and find pasture. Paul says sin entered the world by one man and death by sin, and Revelation promises that those who do His commandments may enter through the gates into the city.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Jesus is the door, and there is no other way in, because He said so plainly and His own death opened it. My position is that the gate is narrow and the door is one, and I am glad I found it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: 3rd person plural present indicative of G1510; they are:--agree, are, be, dure, X is, were.
BiblicalUsage: This is the word they are, the third person plural of the verb to be, and in the Greek text it stands as a single form with a grave accent, not the acute accent Strong's lists. It occurs once, when Paul says the witnesses of the resurrection are the men who came up with Jesus from Galilee to Jerusalem, who are now His witnesses to the people. One small form carries the whole testimony of the risen Christ.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the witnesses are still speaking, because the men who saw Him risen could not keep quiet, and their word reaches me today.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1519 and G2564; to invite in:--call in.
BiblicalUsage: This word means to call in or invite in, and the Greek text carries it in the middle voice, as having called in, where Strong's lists the plain active form. Peter calls Cornelius's men in and lodges them, the first step toward a Gentile's house and a Gentile's faith. One invitation opens the door to the nations.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God calls outsiders in, because Peter's invitation to strangers was the beginning of the gospel reaching the Gentiles, and me.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1519 and G3598; an entrance (literally or figuratively):--coming, enter(-ing) in (to).
BiblicalUsage: An entrance is a coming in, and the New Testament uses it for the gospel's arrival and for ours. Paul speaks of John's preaching before Christ's coming, the Thessalonians tell how the gospel's entrance among them turned them from idols, and Hebrews says we have boldness to enter into the holiest by the blood of Jesus. Peter promises an entrance shall be ministered abundantly into the everlasting kingdom for those who make their calling sure.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Christ opened the entrance, and the gospel opens it in every place it arrives, because the same boldness that enters the holiest also enters a new town. I want my life to be an open door, not a shut one.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1519 and πηδάω (to leap); to rush in:--run (spring) in.
BiblicalUsage: This word means to leap or rush in, and it occurs once, in the Philippian jail. The keeper calls for a light, springs in trembling, and falls down before Paul and Silas, asking what he must do to be saved. One rush into a prison cell becomes the beginning of a household's salvation.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God can turn a jailer's terror into faith in a single night, because the earthquake shook the prison and the gospel shook the man.
RelatedEvents: Paul and Silas in the Philippian Prison
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1519 and G5342; to carry inward (literally or figuratively):--bring (in), lead into.
BiblicalUsage: To bring in is to carry inward, and the word appears in the prayer Jesus taught and in the sickbeds of Galilee. Lead us not into temptation, we pray, and the friends of a paralysed man carry him in on his bed to lay him before Jesus. Hebrews says the bodies of the animals whose blood is brought into the sanctuary are burned outside the camp, and the word holds both the prayer and the offering.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the prayer lead us not into temptation is the wisest prayer I can pray, because I know my own heart wanders and only God can keep me from the places I should not go. He brings us in; He also keeps us out.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1519 and G4198; to enter (literally or figuratively):--come (enter) in, go into.
BiblicalUsage: To go in is to enter a place or a heart, and the Gospels use it for both. Jesus enters the synagogue at Capernaum and teaches, the cares of the world enter in and choke the word, and no one lights a candle and puts it in a secret place, but on a candlestick, so that those who come in may see the light. Acts shows the lame man carried daily to the temple gate, asking alms of those entering in.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe what enters my heart decides what grows there, because the cares of the world choke the word just as surely as a stone chokes a seed. I want the light to come in, and the cares to stay out.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1519 and G5143; to hasten inward:--run in.
BiblicalUsage: This word means to run in hastily, and it occurs once, when Rhoda hears Peter's voice at the gate. She is so glad she forgets to open the gate and runs in to tell the praying church that Peter is standing outside, and they tell her she is mad. One girl's joy runs faster than her manners, and the church's prayer is answered while they are still praying.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God answers prayer while we are still praying, because Peter was at the gate before the church had finished asking.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain affinity; a particle of succession (in time or logical enumeration), then, moreover:--after that(-ward), furthermore, then. See also G1899.
BiblicalUsage: Then is the word of what happens next, and the Gospels use it for the quiet steps of the story. Jesus rises from supper and then pours water into a basin to wash His disciples' feet, and from the cross He says to John, Behold thy mother, and from that hour John takes her to his own home. Paul says Christ was seen by Cephas, then by the twelve, and James says lust conceives and brings forth sin, and sin, when it is finished, brings forth death.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the then after Jesus' words is where obedience lives, because He washed feet and then we must, and He spoke from the cross and then John obeyed. My position is that the next step is always the one in front of me.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1487 and G5037; if too:--if, or, whether.
BiblicalUsage: Whether is the word that covers both sides, and Paul uses it to say that the answer is the same either way. Whether you eat or drink, do all to the glory of God, whether we are Jews or Gentiles we are all baptised into one body, and whether there are prophecies, they shall fail, but love never fails. The word holds the choices together and lets love decide them.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe whether is God's way of saying the details do not divide us, because the same Lord covers both sides of every honest choice. Love is the rule that settles what whether leaves open.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: or ἐξ a primary preposition denoting origin (the point whence action or motion proceeds), from, out (of place, time, or cause; literal or figurative; direct or remote):--after, among, X are, at, betwixt(-yond), by (the means of), exceedingly, (+ abundantly above), for(- th), from (among, forth, up), + grudgingly, + heartily, X heavenly, X hereby, + very highly, in, …ly, (because, by reason) of, off (from), on, out among (from, of), over, since, X thenceforth, through, X unto, X vehemently, with(-out). Often used in composition, with the same general import; often of completion.
BiblicalUsage: Out of is the word of origin, the point a thing comes from, and the New Testament uses it for Christ, for the world, and for us. Paul says we are of God in Christ Jesus, and the first man is of the earth, earthy, while the second man is the Lord from heaven. John says those who went out from us were not of us, and that love is of God, because everyone who loves is born of God. The little word always asks where a thing comes from.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe origin decides everything, because what comes from God lasts and what comes from the world passes. My position is that I am of God in Christ, and that is the only origin that matters.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1537 and G906; to eject (literally or figuratively):--bring forth, cast (forth, out), drive (out), expel, leave, pluck (pull, take, thrust) out, put forth (out), send away (forth, out).
BiblicalUsage: To cast out is to throw out with force, and the Gospels use it for demons, for buyers in the temple, and for the lost. Jesus casts out devils by the Spirit of God, preaches in the synagogues and casts out devils, and promises that whoever comes to Him He will in no wise cast out. The same force that drives out evil welcomes in the sinner, and that is the whole gospel in one word.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Jesus casts out demons but never casts out sinners, because His power drives away what harms us and His mercy keeps what comes to Him. I hold that no one who comes to Him will be turned away, and that includes me.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a compound of G1537 and the base of G939 (meaning to go out); an exit (literally or figuratively):--end, way to escape.
BiblicalUsage: This word is an exit, a way out, and by extension the end of a life, and it occurs twice. Paul promises that God will make a way to escape every temptation, so that we may be able to bear it, and Hebrews tells us to consider the end of our leaders' lives and follow their faith. The word holds both the door out of trouble and the end of the road.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God always makes a way out, because He never allows a temptation without also providing the escape.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1544; ejection, i.e. (specially) a throwing overboard of the cargo:--+ lighten the ship.
BiblicalUsage: This word is the throwing of cargo overboard to lighten a ship, and it occurs once, in the storm that carried Paul to Rome. The next day, being exceedingly tossed with a tempest, the sailors lighten the ship, throwing out what they had carried so far. The word is the sound of a crew choosing the ship over its cargo.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe storms show what is worth keeping, because the sailors threw away their goods to save their lives, and God used the wreck to save them all.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: , or (by variation) ἐκχύνω from G1537 and χέω (to pour); to pour forth; figuratively, to bestow:--gush (pour) out, run greedily (out), shed (abroad, forth), spill.
BiblicalUsage: To pour out is to empty a vessel, and the Bible uses it for blood, for the Spirit, and for love. Jesus says His blood is shed for many for the remission of sins, Peter says God will pour out His Spirit on all flesh in the last days, and Paul says the love of God is shed abroad in our hearts by the Holy Ghost. The same word pours out judgement on the earth in Revelation, because God pours out whatever He gives, good or terrible, without holding back.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God pours out, never drips, because His blood, His Spirit, and His love are all given in full measure. I hold that the same fullness is what He asks of me, a life poured out, not measured.
RelatedTopics: Salvation; Outpouring of the Spirit; Love of God
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1537 and G5562; to depart:--depart out.
BiblicalUsage: This word means to depart out, to leave a place, and Jesus uses it once, in His warning about Jerusalem. When you see the city compassed with armies, He says, let those in the midst of it depart out, and let those in the country not enter in. The word is a plain order to leave before the judgement falls.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Jesus warns because He loves, and His order to leave Jerusalem was mercy before the judgement, not cruelty after it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1537 and G1159; to expend (wholly), i.e. (figuratively) exhaust:--spend.
BiblicalUsage: This word means to spend wholly, to exhaust oneself, and the Greek text carries it in the middle voice, as I will be spent, where Strong's lists the plain active form. Paul says he will very gladly spend and be spent for the Corinthians, though the more abundantly he loves them, the less he is loved. The word is the sound of a man pouring himself out for people who do not return it.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe love spends itself without keeping accounts, because Paul spent himself for a church that repaid him with suspicion, and Christ did the same for me.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1537 and G1209; to accept from some source, i.e. (by implication) to await:--expect, look (tarry) for, wait (for).
BiblicalUsage: To wait for is to expect and receive, and the word covers both waiting and welcoming. Paul tells the Corinthians to send Timothy on his way in peace, that he may come to him, for he looks for him with the brethren, and Luke says Paul's spirit was stirred while he waited at Athens. Abraham looked for a city with foundations, and James says the husbandman waits for the precious fruit of the earth with long patience.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe waiting on God is active, not idle, because Abraham looked for a city while he lived in tents, and the farmer waits while he works. I hold that the God who is worth waiting for is worth waiting on.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1537 and G1212; wholly evident:--manifest.
BiblicalUsage: This word means wholly evident, plain to everyone, and Paul uses it once, about the false teachers of the last days. Their folly shall be manifest to all men, as the folly of Jannes and Jambres was, and the exposure is certain even when the deception looks strong. The word promises that the truth will show.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe folly always shows itself in the end, because God does not let deception wear a disguise forever.
RelatedTopics: Truth; Judgment on false teachers; Judgment
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a compound of G1537 and G1218; to emigrate, i.e. (figuratively) vacate or quit:--be absent.
BiblicalUsage: This word means to be away from home, to live abroad, and Paul uses it for the body and the Lord. While we are at home in the body, he says, we are absent from the Lord, and we are willing rather to be absent from the body and present with the Lord. The word makes this life a foreign country and heaven the home we are travelling toward.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe heaven is home and this world is the journey, because Paul calls the body a tent we live in while we are away. I hold that to be absent from the body and present with the Lord is the Christian's hope, and it makes death a homecoming.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1537 and G1325; to give forth, i.e. (specially) to lease:--let forth (out).
BiblicalUsage: To let out is to lease, to hand over a vineyard to tenants, and the Gospels tell the same parable with this word. A householder plants a vineyard, hedges it, and lets it out to husbandmen, and when he sends servants for the fruit, they beat one, kill another, and stone another. The tenants forget the vineyard is not theirs, and the parable ends with the vineyard given to others who will render the fruit.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe everything I have is leased from God, because the vineyard was never the tenants', and neither is my life. I hold that the fruit He asks for is His by right, and I want to render it gladly.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1537 and a compound of G1223 and G2233; to narrate through wholly:--declare.
BiblicalUsage: This word means to narrate through, to tell a story all the way to the end, and Luke uses it twice. Paul quotes the prophet, warning the despisers who will wonder and perish at the work God is doing, and the church at Jerusalem hears Paul and Barnabas declare all the things God has done with the Gentiles. The word is for stories that must be told in full.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God's works must be told all the way through, because a half-told story hides the very part where He acted.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1558; to vindicate, retaliate, punish:--a (re-)venge.
BiblicalUsage: To avenge is to vindicate, to put right what was done wrong, and the Bible gives the job to God, not to us. The widow in the parable cries, Avenge me of mine adversary, and the unjust judge gives in, but Paul says vengeance is God's and He will repay. Revelation says God's judgements are true and righteous because He has avenged the blood of His servants on the great whore. The word belongs to the Judge, and He does not share it.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe leaving vengeance to God is the hardest and freest thing I can do, because my hands want to settle the score and His hands settle it rightly. My position is that I will not take the Judge's seat, because it is not mine.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1556; vindication, retribution:--(a-, re-)venge(-ance), punishment.
BiblicalUsage: Vengeance is the vindication itself, the settling of the account, and the New Testament speaks of it as God's work at the end. Jesus asks whether God will not avenge His own elect who cry day and night to Him, and answers that He will avenge them speedily, while Paul warns us not to avenge ourselves but to give place to wrath. The same word describes the Lord taking vengeance in flaming fire on those who do not obey the gospel.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God's vengeance is His justice, not His temper, because He settles every account exactly and on time. I hold that trusting His timing is part of trusting Him, and I will wait for it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1537 and G1349; carrying justice out, i.e. a punisher:--a (re-)venger.
BiblicalUsage: An avenger is one who carries justice out, a punisher, and Paul uses the word twice, once for the ruler and once for the Lord. The ruler is the minister of God, a revenger to execute wrath on him that does evil, and the Lord is the avenger of all who defraud their brother. The word puts a sword in the hand of authority and a warning in the ear of the oppressor.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God has His avengers, both in government and in Himself, and no wrong goes unanswered forever.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1537 and G1377; to pursue out, i.e. expel or persecute implacably:--persecute.
BiblicalUsage: This word means to pursue out, to chase away and persecute without rest, and Paul uses it once, for the Jews who killed the Lord Jesus and their own prophets and persecuted the apostles. He says they please not God and are contrary to all men, forbidding the gospel to be spoken to the Gentiles. The word is pursuit that never stops, a hatred that follows its victims from town to town.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe persecution is the world's answer to the gospel, because the truth threatens every power that lives by a lie.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1551; expectation:--looking for.
BiblicalUsage: This word is expectation, a looking for, and it occurs once, in the warning of Hebrews. For those who sin wilfully after receiving the knowledge of the truth, there remains a certain fearful looking for of judgement and fiery indignation. The word is dread, the expectation of a judgement that is already certain.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the fearful expectation of judgement is real, because Hebrews says it plainly, and it is meant to drive me back to the sacrifice while there is still time.
RelatedTopics: Judgment; Fear of the Lord; Repentance
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1537 and a derivative of G1325; given out or over, i.e. surrendered:--delivered.
BiblicalUsage: This word means given out or over, surrendered, and Peter uses it once, in his sermon at Pentecost. Jesus, being delivered by the determinate counsel and foreknowledge of God, was taken by wicked hands and crucified and slain. The word holds both truths at once: God gave Him up, and men took Him.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the cross was both God's plan and man's crime, because Peter says God delivered Him and wicked hands slew Him, and both are true.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1537 and the base of G1416; to cause to sink out of, i.e. (specially as of clothing) to divest:--strip, take off from, unclothe.
BiblicalUsage: To strip off is to take clothing away, and the Gospels use it for Jesus and for the man on the Jericho road. The soldiers strip Jesus and put a scarlet robe on Him, then take the robe off and put His own clothes back on Him to lead Him to the cross, and the thieves strip the traveller, wound him, and leave him half dead. The word is shame and robbery in both stories, and one ends in a cross while the other ends in a Samaritan's mercy.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Jesus was stripped so that I could be clothed, because He bore the shame of nakedness that I might be covered in His righteousness. I hold that the good Samaritan's mercy is the picture of what Christ did for me on the road.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a fetter; hence, an anklet
BiblicalUsage: This word is a fetter or an anklet, a chain worn on the ankle, and it occurs twice, once as jewellery and once as a trap. Isaiah says the Lord will take away the finery of the daughters of Zion, including their tinkling ornaments, and Proverbs says a young man follows a seductress as an ox goes to the slaughter, or as a fool to the correction of the stocks. The same chain can be an ornament or a prison.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the chains I choose to wear can become the chains that hold me, because beauty without wisdom is a fetter, not a freedom.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain affinity; there; by extension, thither:--there, thither(-ward), (to) yonder (place).
BiblicalUsage: There is the word of place, and the New Testament uses it to put the reader on the scene. There was a marriage in Cana of Galilee, and there were six waterpots of stone standing there, and Peter finds a man named Aeneas lying on a bed for eight years there in Lydda. James warns against telling a poor man to stand there while the rich man sits in a good place, because there can be a place of honour or a place of shame.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God is there, wherever there is, because the wedding, the sickbed, and the assembly are all places He visits. My position is that no place is too ordinary for Him to show up in.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1563; that one (or (neuter) thing); often intensified by the article prefixed:--he, it, the other (same), selfsame, that (same, very), X their, X them, they, this, those. See also G3778.
BiblicalUsage: That one is the word that points, and John uses it more than anyone to point at Jesus. John the Baptist says, He that sent me to baptise with water, the same said unto me, and, He must increase, but I must decrease, while the letter of John says whoever claims to abide in Him ought to walk as He walked, and everyone who has this hope in Him purifies himself. The word always points away from the speaker and toward Christ.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe pointing at Christ is the whole job of a witness, because John the Baptist did it with one word and I should do it with my whole life. He must increase, and I must decrease.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1563; thither:--there.
BiblicalUsage: This word means thither, to that place, and it occurs twice in Paul's journeys. The ship sails to Cyprus and leaves it on the left hand as they go to Syria, and Paul says he went to Damascus with letters to bring the believers there bound to Jerusalem. The word is the sound of travel, of going where the road leads.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God leads His people thither, to places they did not choose, because Paul's road to Damascus was not his plan but God's.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1563; thence:--from that place, (from) thence, there.
BiblicalUsage: Thence is the word for from that place, and the Gospels use it for the next step of the journey. Jesus departs thence and comes near the Sea of Galilee, goes out from thence to His own country, and after two days departs thence into Galilee, while Paul and Barnabas, sent forth by the Holy Ghost, depart thence to Seleucia and sail to Cyprus. The word is always a leaving that leads to a new place of work.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God always has a thence after every there, because His people never settle where they first arrive. The journey goes on, and so does the work.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a load; by implication, a stroke (others dignity)
BiblicalUsage: This word is a load or a stroke, a weight laid on a person, and it occurs once, when Elihu speaks to Job. My terror shall not make thee afraid, he says, neither shall my hand be heavy upon thee, and the word is the heaviness he promises not to lay on his friend. One verse holds a whole promise of gentleness.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God does not lay His hand heavily on the suffering, because Elihu's promise is His character: He corrects without crushing.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1537 and G1061; the same as 1547:--give in marriage.
BiblicalUsage: This word means to give in marriage, and it stands in the Textus Receptus reading of the days before the flood, when men were marrying and giving in marriage until Noah entered the ark. The Greek text used for this study carries only the plain verb to marry in that verse, so this compound form belongs to the older printed text, not to the manuscripts behind it. The two spellings, with iz and with isk, are the same verb in different dress.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the days of Noah warn me plainly, because life went on as usual, marrying and giving in marriage, until the flood came and took them all away.
RelatedTopics: Judgment; Marriage; Fear of the Lord
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1537 and a form of G1061 (compare G1548); to marry off a daughter:--give in marriage.
BiblicalUsage: This is the same compound verb as the last word, to give a daughter in marriage, and it stands in the Textus Receptus at both of the flood passages. In Matthew the days before the flood are spent marrying and giving in marriage, and in Luke the people of Noah's day ate, drank, married wives, and were given in marriage until the day Noah entered the ark. The Greek text used for this study carries only the plain verb to marry in both verses, so this compound is a reading of the older printed text.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe ordinary life is no shelter from judgement, because the flood came on a day like any other, when people were marrying and giving in marriage.
RelatedTopics: Judgment; Marriage; Fear of the Lord
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: neuter of a derivative of a compound of G1537 and G1096; a descendant, i.e. (specially) grandchild:--nephew.
BiblicalUsage: This word is a descendant, a grandchild, and Paul uses it once, in his instructions for the care of widows. If a widow has children or grandchildren, he says, let them first learn to show piety at home and to repay their parents, for that is good and acceptable before God. The word puts the family's duty before the church's, and the grandchildren first.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe caring for our own parents and grandparents is part of the gospel, because Paul says the family learns piety at home before it shows it anywhere else.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1537 and G2545; to inflame deeply:--burn.
BiblicalUsage: This word means to burn deeply, to be inflamed, and the Greek text carries it in the middle voice, as burned, where Strong's lists the plain active form. Paul says the men, leaving the natural use of the woman, burned in their lust one toward another, men with men working that which is unseemly. The word is a fire that consumes the one who carries it.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe lust burns the one who carries it, because Paul describes a fire that starts in the heart and ends in judgement, and only God can quench it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1537 and G2556; to be (bad or) weak, i.e. (by implication) to fail (in heart):--faint, be weary.
BiblicalUsage: This word means to lose heart, to faint and be weary, and the Greek text spells it with a g sound, to fail, where Strong's lists it with a k. Jesus tells the parable of the unjust judge so that men ought always to pray and not to faint, and Paul says not to be weary in well doing, for in due season we shall reap if we faint not. The spelling differs, but the warning is the same.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe weariness is the enemy of prayer, because Jesus told His parable precisely so that we would pray on and not faint.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1537 and G2508; to cleanse thoroughly:--purge (out).
BiblicalUsage: This word means to cleanse thoroughly, to purge out, and Paul uses it twice, once for the church and once for the man. Purge out the old leaven, he says, that you may be a new lump, and if a man purge himself from dishonourable vessels, he shall be a vessel unto honour, sanctified and fit for the Master's use. The word is housekeeping for the soul.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God purges what He loves, because a clean vessel is the only kind the Master can use.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1537 and the base of G2759; to transfix:--pierce.
BiblicalUsage: This word means to pierce through, to transfix, and it occurs twice, both times for the same wound. John quotes the prophet, They shall look on Him whom they pierced, and Revelation says every eye shall see Him, and they also who pierced Him, and all kindreds of the earth shall wail because of Him. The word is the spear in His side, seen from the cross and from the end of the world.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the pierced One is the coming One, because the same wound that proved His death will prove His return.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1537 and G2806; to exscind:--break off.
BiblicalUsage: To break off is to cut a branch from a tree, and Paul uses it for the branches of Israel broken off from the olive tree. If some of the branches were broken off, and you, a wild olive tree, were grafted in among them, he says, do not boast against the branches, because they were broken off through unbelief, and you stand by faith. The word is a warning to every branch that forgets it did not plant itself.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God can break off and graft in, because the tree is His and the branches are held by faith, not by birth. I hold that I stand only by faith, and if I forget that, I forget everything.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1537 and G2808; to shut out (literally or figuratively):--exclude.
BiblicalUsage: This word means to shut out or exclude, and Paul uses it twice, once for boasting and once for false teachers. Where is boasting then, he asks; it is excluded by the law of faith, and he says the Judaisers zealously affect the Galatians, but not well, because they want to exclude them and make them seek their favour instead. The word shuts the door on boasting and on those who would shut others out.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe faith shuts out boasting, because there is nothing left to boast about when salvation is a gift.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1537 and G2827; to deviate, i.e. (absolutely) to shun (literally or figuratively), or (relatively) to decline (from piety):--avoid, eschew, go out of the way.
BiblicalUsage: To turn aside is to deviate from the road, and the Bible uses it for the whole human race and for the Christian's duty. Paul says they are all gone out of the way, they are together become unprofitable, and he tells the Romans to mark those who cause divisions and avoid them. Peter says to let him eschew evil and do good, to seek peace and ensue it, because the same word that describes the fall also describes the escape from it.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe turning aside is the story of every heart, because we all go out of the way, and turning back is the story of grace. I hold that avoiding evil is not fear but wisdom, and seeking peace is not weakness but strength.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1537 and G2860; to escape by swimming:--swim out.
BiblicalUsage: This word means to escape by swimming out, and it occurs once, in the shipwreck that carried Paul to Malta. The soldiers want to kill the prisoners so none can swim away and escape, but the centurion stops them, and those who can swim cast themselves first into the sea and get to land. The word is the sound of men swimming for their lives in a storm.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God saves through the storm, not only from it, because the ship broke apart and yet every soul reached the shore.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1537 and G2865; to bear forth (to burial):--carry out.
BiblicalUsage: This word means to carry out, to bear a body to burial, and it occurs once, at the gate of Nain. As Jesus comes near the gate, a dead man is carried out, the only son of a widow, and a great crowd follows her, and Jesus touches the bier and says, Young man, I say unto thee, arise. The carrying out becomes a carrying home.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Jesus meets us at the gate of our grief, because He stopped a funeral and gave a son back to his mother.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1537 and G2875; to exscind; figuratively, to frustrate:--cut down (off, out), hew down, hinder.
BiblicalUsage: To cut off is to hew down, and John the Baptist and Jesus use it for the tree that bears no fruit. Every tree that does not bring forth good fruit is hewn down and cast into the fire, Jesus says, and Paul warns the Romans to behold the goodness and severity of God, because the branches that do not continue in His goodness will be cut off. The axe is already laid to the root, and the word leaves no room for a fruitless tree.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe fruit is the proof of the root, because a tree that bears nothing will be cut down, and a life that bears nothing is in the same danger. I hold that God's severity is as real as His goodness, and I want to continue in both.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: middle voice from G1537 and G2910; to hang upon the lips of a speaker, i.e. listen closely:--be very attentive.
BiblicalUsage: This word means to hang upon the lips of a speaker, to listen so closely that you hang on every word, and it occurs once, for the crowds who heard Jesus in the temple. The chief priests and scribes seek to destroy Him and cannot find a way, because all the people are very attentive to hear Him, hanging on His words. One verb holds a whole crowd still.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe hanging on Jesus' words is the right posture, because the crowds who listened could not be moved by the priests who plotted.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1537 and G2980; to divulge:--tell.
BiblicalUsage: This word means to tell out, to divulge, and it occurs once, when the chief captain warns Paul's nephew. He lets the young man go and charges him to tell no man that he has shown him the plot against Paul's life, and the boy's silence keeps the apostle alive. One secret kept is the difference between life and death.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God protects His servants through small obediences, because a boy's silence and a captain's warning were enough to save Paul.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1537 and G2989; to be resplendent:--shine forth.
BiblicalUsage: This word means to shine forth, to be resplendent, and Jesus uses it once, at the end of the parable of the wheat and the tares. Then shall the righteous shine forth as the sun in the kingdom of their Father, He says, and the sentence ends with the call to hear. The word is the brightness of the harvest, when the wheat is finally seen for what it is.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the righteous will shine, because Jesus says so, and the day of harvest will show what the world could not see.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: middle voice from G1537 and G2990; to be utterly oblivious of:--forget.
BiblicalUsage: This word means to be utterly oblivious, to forget completely, and the Greek text carries it as the plain verb to forget, where Strong's lists the longer compound form. Hebrews says, Ye have forgotten the exhortation which speaketh unto you as unto children, My son, despise not thou the chastening of the Lord. The forgetting is not an accident; it is a failure to remember that chastening is a father's love.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe forgetting God's discipline is forgetting His fatherhood, because chastening is the proof that I am His child, not His stranger.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: middle voice from G1537 and G3004 (in its primary sense); to select:--make choice, choose (out), chosen.
BiblicalUsage: To choose is to select, and the New Testament says God does the choosing before we do. Jesus says, Have not I chosen you twelve, and, Ye have not chosen me, but I have chosen you, and Paul says God chose us in Him before the foundation of the world. The apostles pray for God to show which of two men He has chosen to take Judas's place, because the choice is His to make.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe election is the comfort of my faith, because I did not choose God first; He chose me, and His choice does not change. My position is that being chosen makes me secure, not proud, because the choice was grace from the start.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1537 and G3007; to omit, i.e. (by implication) cease (die):--fail.
BiblicalUsage: To fail is to run out, to cease, and the word covers money, faith, and light. Jesus tells His disciples to make friends with the mammon of unrighteousness so that when it fails they will receive us into everlasting habitations, and He tells Peter that He has prayed for him that his faith fail not. The sun is darkened at the cross, and Hebrews says of the Son that His years shall not fail, because He is the same forever.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe my faith can fail, and that is why Jesus prays for it, because Peter's faith was kept by prayer, not by his own strength. I hold that the Son whose years never fail is the one who keeps me from failing.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1586; select; by implication, favorite:--chosen, elect.
BiblicalUsage: Elect means chosen, select, a favourite, and the New Testament uses it for angels, for Christ, and for God's people. Jesus says the angels will gather His elect from the four winds, and asks whether God will not avenge His own elect who cry day and night, while Paul asks who shall lay anything to the charge of God's elect, and tells the Colossians to put on the character of the elect, holy and beloved. The word is always God's choosing, never man's earning.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe I am elect because God chose me, and that choice is my confidence when accusations come. My position is that election is not a puzzle to solve but a promise to rest in, because the One who chose me will keep me.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1586; (divine) selection (abstractly or concretely):--chosen, election.
BiblicalUsage: Election is God's selection, His choosing of a people for Himself, and Paul uses it for Israel and for the church. He says the purpose of God according to election stands, not of works but of Him who calls, and that at this present time there is a remnant according to the election of grace. The Lord tells Ananias that Paul is a chosen vessel to bear His name before Gentiles and kings, and the word holds both the choosing and the sending.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe election means God has a purpose that no failure of mine can undo, because His choosing stands on His call, not on my works. My position is that grace chose me, and grace will finish what it started.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1537 and G3089; to relax (literally or figuratively):--faint.
BiblicalUsage: This word means to relax, to grow faint, and the Greek text carries it in the middle voice, as fainting or being wearied, where Strong's lists the plain active form. Jesus says the multitude has been with Him three days and has nothing to eat, and He will not send them away fasting lest they faint by the way, while Paul warns not to be weary in well doing and Hebrews tells us to consider Him who endured, lest we be wearied and faint in our minds. The word is the body's warning and the soul's.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Jesus cares for fainting bodies as well as fainting hearts, because He fed the multitude before He sent them home, and He feeds me still.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1537 and the base of G3145; to knead out, i.e. (by analogy) to wipe dry:--wipe.
BiblicalUsage: ekmássō means to wipe dry. In Luke 7:38, the text says "and did wipe [them] with the hairs of her head." In Luke 7:44, the text says "and wiped [them] with the hairs of her head."
TheologicalSignificance: What ekmássō teaches me is that serving is not earning; it is answering love with love. That shapes how I read the passages where it appears: not as filler, but as God's own wording for what He is doing.
RelatedEvents: Raising of Lazarus; The Sinful Woman Anoints Jesus; The Anointing at Bethany
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1537 and G3456; to sneer outright at:--deride.
BiblicalUsage: ekmyktērízō is the word for deride. In Luke 16:14, the text says "and they derided him."
TheologicalSignificance: For me, ekmyktērízō means deride, and I leave it at that.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1537 and G3525; (figuratively) to rouse (oneself) out of stupor:--awake.
BiblicalUsage: The word eknḗphō carries the sense of awake. In 1 Corinthians 15:34, the text says "Awake to righteousness."
TheologicalSignificance: For me, eknḗphō means awake, nothing more and nothing less.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1537 and G3506; (by analogy) to slip off, i.e. quietly withdraw:--convey self away.
BiblicalUsage: Scripture uses ekneúō where we would say to slip away quietly. In John 5:13, the text says "for Jesus had conveyed himself away."
TheologicalSignificance: I take ekneúō as it stands: to slip away quietly.
RelatedEvents: The Healing at the Pool of Bethesda
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1537 and G3819; long ago, for a long while:--of a long time, of old.
BiblicalUsage: In the New Testament, ékpalai is the word for of a long time, of old. In 2 Peter 2:3, the text says "whose judgment now of a long time lingereth not."
