Definition: from G1722 and G991; to look on, i.e. (relatively) to observe fixedly, or (absolutely) to discern clearly:--behold, gaze up, look upon, (could) see.
BiblicalUsage: The word emblépō carries the sense of to look intently at. In Matthew 6:26, the text says "Behold the fowls of the air." In Mark 8:25, the text says "After that he put [his] hands again upon his eyes."
TheologicalSignificance: I believe emblépō shows us that faith is not a feeling but a holding-on — trusting what God has said when nothing else makes sense. That shapes how I read the passages where it appears: not as filler, but as God's own wording for what He is doing.
RelatedEvents: The Calling of the First Disciples; The Parable of the Wicked Tenants; Jesus Heals a Blind Man at Bethsaida
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1722 and βριμάομαι (to snort with anger); to have indignation on, i.e. (transitively) to blame, (intransitively) to sigh with chagrin, (specially) to sternly enjoin:--straitly charge, groan, murmur against.
BiblicalUsage: embrimáomai is how Scripture says to be deeply moved, to sternly charge. In Matthew 9:30, the text says "and Jesus straitly charged them." In Mark 1:43, the text says "And he straitly charged him."
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that embrimáomai matters because compassion is not pity from a distance; it is drawing near and doing something. That is why I keep this word in mind when I read those passages — it carries more than its size suggests.
RelatedEvents: Raising of Lazarus; Jesus Heals a Man with Leprosy; The Anointing at Bethany
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a station, i.e. domicile
BiblicalUsage: ʻemdâh means a station, a dwelling place — a settled spot. It appears once, in Micah 1:11, where Beth-ezel's standing is taken away.
TheologicalSignificance: In ʻemdâh I find no hidden theology; it simply means a station, a dwelling place.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a prolonged form of G3165; me:--I, me, my(-self).
BiblicalUsage: In the New Testament, emé is the word for me, myself. It appears in Matthew and John, and each time it carries that same plain sense.
TheologicalSignificance: For me, emé means me, myself, and I leave it at that.
RelatedEvents: Jesus Sends Out the Twelve; Jesus and the Samaritan Woman
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a prolonged form of G2258; I was:--be, was. (Sometimes unexpressed).
BiblicalUsage: This is the first-person singular past of 'to be' — 'I was.' Jesus uses it looking back on His time with His disciples in John 17:12, and Peter uses it telling how he was praying in Joppa in Acts 11:5.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the little word 'was' carries the weight of a life already lived before God, and what we were is never hidden from Him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain affinity; to vomit:--(will) spue.
BiblicalUsage: It is a blunt word: to vomit. Christ turns it on the lukewarm church at Laodicea in Revelation 3:16, saying He will spue them out of His mouth.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the picture is meant to shock us awake — a faith that is neither hot nor cold is not safe, it is sickening to the Lord.
RelatedEvents: The Letter to the Church in Laodicea
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a vale (i.e. broad depression)
BiblicalUsage: A valley is the low ground between hills, where harvests are reaped and battles are fought — the men of Beth-shemesh were reaping in the valley when the ark came back in 1 Samuel 6:13, and Jehoshaphat's people blessed the LORD in the valley of Berachah in 2 Chronicles 20:26. The Syrians claimed the LORD was only God of the hills, but in 1 Kings 20:28 He proves Himself God of the valleys too.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the valley is where most of life is actually lived — not on the mountain tops but down in the low places — and I hold that God meets us there just as surely as on the heights. The valley of Berachah was named for blessing because God's people praised Him there before the battle was even over, and that is the pattern I want for my own low places.
RelatedTopics: Nature and Creation; God's Providence; Worship
RelatedEvents: Jehoshaphat's Victory by Prayer and Praise
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: something said
BiblicalUsage: Emer is simply something said — a word, a saying, a promise, a command. Moses opens his song with it in Deuteronomy 32:1, calling heaven and earth to hear the words of his mouth, and Jacob's blessing gives Naphtali 'goodly words' in Genesis 49:21. But words cut both ways: Hosea says God hewed His people by the words of His mouth in Hosea 6:5, and Isaiah warns of lying words that destroy the poor in Isaiah 32:7.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe words are never just sounds — God's words create and judge, and our words bless or destroy. That is why I want my own words weighed before they are spoken, because Scripture treats a word as a deed with consequences.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: yesterday or last night
BiblicalUsage: Emesh means yesterday, or last night — the very recent past. The LORD tells Jehu He saw yesterday the blood of Naboth in 2 Kings 9:26, and Laban warns Jacob about what God spoke to him yesternight in Genesis 31:29. It also stretches a little: Job's outcasts flee into the wilderness 'in former time' in Job 30:3, a yesterday that has already gone desolate.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe 'yesterday' in Scripture is never far away — God remembers what happened last night as clearly as we remember this morning, and His justice does not forget with time. What was done yesterday still stands before Him today, and that is both a warning and a comfort.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: well-loined (i.e. burly) or mighty
BiblicalUsage: A rare Aramaic word for something dreadful and mighty — Daniel uses it once, for the fourth beast in his night vision in Daniel 7:7, a creature dreadful and terrible and strong exceedingly, with great iron teeth.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Daniel's beast reminds me that earthly power can look terrifying, but it is still only a beast in a vision God gave, and God alone decides where its story ends.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: stability; (figuratively) certainty, truth, trustworthiness
BiblicalUsage: Emeth is firmness — truth you can stand on, faithfulness you can trust. David charges Solomon to walk before the LORD in truth with all his heart in 1 Kings 2:4, Samuel calls Israel to serve Him in truth in 1 Samuel 12:24, and Hezekiah pleads that he has walked before God in truth and with a perfect heart in 2 Kings 20:3. The queen of Sheba finds the same thing from the other side: the report she heard was true in 2 Chronicles 9:5.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe truth is not an idea first, it is a Person who keeps His word — and I hold that a life built on emeth, on what is firm and faithful, will stand when everything shaky falls. God is true, so I can be true, and that steadiness is what I want my own word to carry.
RelatedPeople: King David; King Hezekiah; King Solomon
RelatedEvents: The Queen of Sheba Visits Solomon
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1722 and G3105; to rave on, i.e. rage at:--be mad against.
BiblicalUsage: Paul uses this word against himself, remembering how he was exceedingly mad against the Christians in Acts 26:11, punishing them in every synagogue and chasing them into strange cities.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Paul's honesty here is the point — the man who once raged against the church became its greatest apostle, and no past fury is beyond God's reach.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H6005); God with us; Emmanuel, a name of Christ:--Emmanuel.
BiblicalUsage: Emmanuel is the name the angel gives the child born of the virgin in Matthew 1:23, and Matthew pauses to translate it himself: God with us. It is the only place the name stands in the New Testament, and it stands at the very beginning of the story, before Jesus does a single thing.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this name is the whole gospel in two words — God did not stay far off, He came to be with us. That is the promise I hold onto when God feels distant: Emmanuel means He already came near.
RelatedPeople: Jesus; Mary, Mother of Jesus; Joseph, Husband of Mary
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably of Hebrew origin (compare H3222); Emmaus, a place in Palestine:--Emmaus.
BiblicalUsage: Emmaus is the village two disciples were walking to on the first Easter evening in Luke 24:13, about threescore furlongs from Jerusalem, when the risen Jesus joined them on the road and they did not know Him.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the road to Emmaus is where many of us live — walking away disappointed while Jesus walks beside us unrecognized — and He still opens our eyes over bread and Scripture.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1722 and G3306; to stay in the same place, i.e. (figuratively) persevere:--continue.
BiblicalUsage: Emmeno means to stay put — to continue in something rather than drift from it. Paul and Barnabas urge the new disciples to continue in the faith in Acts 14:22, and Paul warns that the one who does not continue in all the law is cursed in Galatians 3:10. The sad side is in Hebrews 8:9, where Israel continued not in God's covenant, and the quiet side is Paul dwelling two whole years in his own hired house in Acts 28:30.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe continuing is the real test of faith — starting is easy, staying is hard. I hold that God keeps those who keep on with Him, and the promise in Acts is that continuing in the faith is the road into the kingdom, tribulation and all.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H2544); Emmor (i.e. Chamor), a Canaanite:--Emmor.
BiblicalUsage: Emmor is the Greek form of Hamor, the Canaanite whose sons sold Abraham the burial ground at Sychem. Stephen names him once, in Acts 7:16, when the patriarchs were carried over into Sychem and laid in the sepulchre Abraham bought from the sons of Emmor. His life story is told under Hamor.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe even a single name in Stephen's speech matters — Abraham's purchase was real land bought from real men, and God's promises have always been anchored in real ground. Emmor's part is small, but it is part of the deed.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a prolonged form of G3427; to me:--I, me, mine, my.
BiblicalUsage: Emoi is simply 'to me' — the dative of 'I.' Jesus says the one who follows me shall not walk in darkness in John 8:12, and the King says that what was done to the least of His brethren was done unto me in Matthew 25:40.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this little word is where the gospel gets personal — Jesus does not speak about people in general, He speaks to me, and what I do to others I do to Him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an Emorite, one of the Canaanitish tribes
BiblicalUsage: The Amorites were one of the peoples of Canaan, east of the Jordan and beyond, whose land Israel inherited. Their kings Sihon and Og held the country of Gilead in 1 Kings 4:19, their cities were restored to Israel and there was peace between Israel and the Amorites in 1 Samuel 7:14, and the remnant of them were still there as forced labour in Solomon's day in 2 Chronicles 8:7.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the Amorites show both sides of God's dealings with nations — He gave them centuries of patience, and then He gave their land to Israel when their iniquity was full. I hold that no nation stands forever on its own strength, and God's promises to His people outlast every empire that stands in the way.
RelatedEvents: The Defeat of Sihon and Og
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from the oblique cases of G1473 (G1698, G1700, G1691); my:--of me, mine (own), my.
BiblicalUsage: Emos is 'my' or 'mine own' — the possessive that marks something as belonging to the speaker. Paul says he baptized no one in his own name in 1 Corinthians 1:15, calls God as a record upon his soul in 2 Corinthians 1:23, and signs off with the salutation of Paul with mine own hand in 2 Thessalonians 3:17. Peter looks ahead to his own decease in 2 Peter 1:15 and wants the churches to remember these things after he is gone.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe 'mine own' is a word of responsibility — Paul owns his words, his handwriting, and his name, and he will answer for them. I hold that what is truly mine is what I will stand behind before God, and that is why I want my own words to be few and true.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a prolonged form of G3449; of me:--me, mine, my.
BiblicalUsage: Emou is 'of me' — the genitive of 'I.' Jesus blesses those reviled falsely for my sake in Matthew 5:11, and promises that whoever loses his life for my sake shall find it in Matthew 16:25.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe 'for my sake' is the hinge of the whole Christian life — suffering and loss only make sense when they are for Him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1702; derision:--mocking.
BiblicalUsage: One word, one verse: in Hebrews 11:36 the heroes of faith had trial of cruel mockings and scourgings, of bonds and imprisonment — mockery listed among the sufferings that faith endures.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe mockery is a real cost of faith, and the fact that Scripture names it beside scourgings tells me God sees the words that wound, not only the blows.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1702; a derider, i.e. (by implication) a false teacher:--mocker, scoffer.
BiblicalUsage: The mocker is the one who derides what is holy. Peter warns that scoffers will come in the last days, walking after their own lusts, in 2 Peter 3:3, and Jude says the same in Jude 1:18 — mockers in the last time, walking after their own ungodly lusts.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the scoffer's mark is not cleverness but appetite — he mocks because he wants to keep his lusts, and I want no part of that trade.
RelatedPeople: Simon Peter; Jude, Brother of James
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1722 and G3815; to jeer at, i.e. deride:--mock.
BiblicalUsage: To mock is to jeer at someone as if they were nothing. Herod felt mocked by the wise men and answered with slaughter in Matthew 2:16, Jesus says He will be mocked and spitefully entreated in Luke 18:32, and Mark records the same prediction in Mark 10:34. The word also warns ordinary people: the builder who cannot finish is mocked by all who see it in Luke 14:29.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe mockery is the weapon of the proud against the lowly, and the Lord took it on Himself before He asked us to bear it. I hold that when I am mocked for following Him, I am standing where He stood — and He rose on the third day.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1722 and G4043; to perambulate on a place, i.e. (figuratively) to be occupied among persons:--walk in.
BiblicalUsage: A single, beautiful use: in 2 Corinthians 6:16 God says, I will dwell in them, and walk in them — the God who lives among His people also moves among them, as He walked in the garden of old.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God does not visit His people from a distance — He dwells in them and walks in them, and that nearness is what makes us His people.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a compound of G1722 and G5316; apparent in self:--manifest, openly.
BiblicalUsage: Emphanes means openly shown, made manifest. God raised Jesus the third day and showed Him openly in Acts 10:40 — not to everyone, but to chosen witnesses — and Isaiah says God was made manifest to those who did not even ask for Him in Romans 10:20.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God shows Himself openly to those He chooses, and even to those who were not looking, which gives me hope for everyone I love who is not looking yet.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1717; to exhibit (in person) or disclose (by words):--appear, declare (plainly), inform, (will) manifest, shew, signify.
BiblicalUsage: Emphanizo is to show or declare plainly — in person or in words. The conspirators ask the council to signify to the chief captain in Acts 23:15, Christ appears in the presence of God for us in Hebrews 9:24, and Jesus promises to manifest Himself to the one who keeps His commandments in John 14:21. After His resurrection, the saints came out of the graves and appeared unto many in Matthew 27:53.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God is not hidden — He shows Himself, in Christ standing before the Father for us and in the quiet manifestation to a heart that obeys. I hold that the God who appears is the God who keeps His promises in the open, where anyone can see.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1722 and G5401; in fear, i.e. alarmed:--affrighted, afraid, tremble.
BiblicalUsage: Emphobos is fear that takes hold of you — Cornelius was afraid when the angel stood before him in Acts 10:4, the women at the tomb were afraid and bowed their faces to the earth in Luke 24:5, and Felix trembled as Paul reasoned of righteousness and judgment to come in Acts 24:25. Even the remnant in Revelation 11:13 were affrighted by the earthquake and gave glory to God.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe fear is the right first response to meeting God, but it is never meant to be the last — the angel's first word to Cornelius was an answer to prayer, and the women's fear turned to joy at the empty tomb. I hold that godly fear drives us toward God, never away from Him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1722 and φυσάω (to puff) (compare G5453); to blow at or on:--breathe on.
BiblicalUsage: One verse, and a great one: on Easter evening Jesus breathed on His disciples in John 20:22 and said, Receive ye the Holy Ghost — the risen Lord breathing new life into His people, as God once breathed life into Adam.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this breath is no symbol — the same Lord who breathed life into dust now breathes His Spirit into His church, and I live by that breath.
RelatedEvents: Jesus Appears to the Disciples on Easter Evening
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1722 and a derivative of G5453; implanted (figuratively):--engrafted.
BiblicalUsage: James calls the word of God the engrafted word in James 1:21 — planted in us like a cutting grafted into a tree, able to save our souls if we receive it with meekness.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God's word is not meant to sit on my shelf but to take root in me, and a grafted word bears fruit that my own words never could.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: or ἐμπλήθω from G1722 and the base of G4118; to fill in (up), i.e. (by implication) to satisfy (literally or figuratively):--fill.
BiblicalUsage: To fill up, to satisfy. Mary sings that God has filled the hungry with good things in Luke 1:53, and after the feeding of the five thousand the disciples were filled and gathered up the fragments in John 6:12.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God fills the hungry and sends the full away empty — His filling is for the needy, and I would rather come hungry than come full.
RelatedEvents: The Feeding of the Five Thousand
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1722 and G4098; to fall on, i.e. (literally) to be entrapped by, or (figuratively) be overwhelmed with:--fall among (into).
BiblicalUsage: Empipto is to fall into something — a pit, a ditch, a snare. A novice lifted up with pride may fall into the condemnation of the devil in 1 Timothy 3:6, and the blind leading the blind both fall into the ditch in Luke 6:39. But the heaviest use is Hebrews 10:31: it is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe falling into God's hands is fearful only for those who refuse Him — the same hands that judge are the hands that lift the sheep out of the pit on the Sabbath, as Jesus says in Matthew 12:11. I hold that the fear of God is the beginning of wisdom because it teaches me where the pit is and who can pull me out.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1722 and G4120; to entwine, i.e. (figuratively) involve with:--entangle (in, self with).
BiblicalUsage: To entwine, to get tangled up in. Paul says no soldier entangles himself with the affairs of this life in 2 Timothy 2:4, and Peter warns that those who escape the pollutions of the world and are again entangled in them end worse than they began in 2 Peter 2:20.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe entanglement is slow — nobody plans to be trapped, they just get busy with the affairs of this life until the snare closes, and I want to keep my hands free for the one who chose me to be His soldier.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1707; elaborate braiding of the hair:--plaiting.
BiblicalUsage: Peter lists the plaiting of hair among the outward adornings in 1 Peter 3:3 — braided hair, gold, and fine apparel — and says a wife's beauty should not be that outward adorning.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Peter is not banning braids but reordering beauty — the hidden person of the heart outlasts every hairstyle.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1722 and G4154; to inhale, i.e. (figuratively) to be animated by (bent upon):--breathe.
BiblicalUsage: Saul was yet breathing out threatenings and slaughter against the disciples in Acts 9:1 — his very breath was set against the church, and he carried letters to Damascus to hunt them down.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the man who breathed out murder became the man who breathed out the gospel, and no one's breath is too poisoned for God to change.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1722 and G4198; to travel in (a country as a pedlar), i.e. (by implication) to trade:--buy and sell, make merchandise.
BiblicalUsage: The word of the travelling trader — to buy and sell, to make merchandise. James warns those who plan to go to a city and buy and sell and get gain in James 4:13, and Peter says false teachers will make merchandise of you through covetousness in 2 Peter 2:3.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the warning is about what we do with people — trading in them for gain — and I want my plans held loosely, because my life is a vapour, not a business venture.
RelatedPeople: James, Brother of Jesus; Simon Peter
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: feminine from G1713; traffic:--merchandise.
BiblicalUsage: One verse: in the parable of the wedding feast in Matthew 22:5, the invited guests made light of the king's invitation and went their ways, one to his farm, another to his merchandise.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe business is a poor excuse for missing a king's feast, and I never want my work to be the reason I turn down God's invitation.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: neuter from G1713; a mart ("emporium"):--merchandise.
BiblicalUsage: Jesus drives the traders out and says it plainly in John 2:16: make not my Father's house an house of merchandise.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe my Father's house is for prayer, not profit, and anything that turns worship into trade has to go.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1722 and the base of G4198; a (wholesale) tradesman:--merchant.
BiblicalUsage: The merchant is the wholesale trader. In the kingdom parable of Matthew 13:45 he is seeking goodly pearls, and when he finds one of great price he sells all he has for it. In Revelation the merchants of the earth grow rich from Babylon's delicacies in Revelation 18:3, then weep and mourn when no one buys their merchandise any more in Revelation 18:11, standing afar off for the fear of her torment in Revelation 18:15.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe every one of us is a merchant of something — the question is what we are buying. The pearl merchant sold everything for one pearl, and the merchants of Babylon lost everything when their market fell. I hold that the only trade that never fails is selling all for the kingdom.
RelatedEvents: The Hidden Treasure and the Pearl
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1722 and πρήθω (to blow a flame); to enkindle, i.e. set on fire:--burn up.
BiblicalUsage: The king in the parable sends his armies, destroys the murderers, and burns up their city in Matthew 22:7 — a picture of judgment carried out to the end.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God's judgment is not a threat He forgets — the city that refused the invitation and killed the messengers was burned, and I take that warning seriously.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1722 and G4314; in front of (in place (literally or figuratively) or time):--against, at, before, (in presence, sight) of.
BiblicalUsage: Emprosthen means 'in front of' — before someone's face. We assure our hearts before Him in 1 John 3:19, our work of faith stands in the sight of God in 1 Thessalonians 1:3, and we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ in 2 Corinthians 5:10. Even prayer stands before God as a memorial, as Cornelius learned in Acts 10:4.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe everything I do is done before Someone — there is no private corner outside God's sight, and that is both sobering and comforting. I hold that living 'before Him' is the whole of the Christian life: my prayers rise as a memorial, my works will be shown, and my heart can rest because the Judge is also my Saviour.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1722 and G4429; to spit at or on:--spit (upon).
BiblicalUsage: To spit on someone is the lowest contempt, and Jesus took it. He says He will be mocked and spitted on in Luke 18:32, the soldiers spit in His face and buffet Him in Matthew 26:67, and in Mark 14:65 they cover His face and strike Him and say, Prophesy.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe there is no depth of shame Christ did not taste for us — He let men spit in the face of God, and answered with silence. I hold that when I am treated with contempt for His sake, I am sharing the smallest part of what He bore, and He counts it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: established, i.e. (figuratively) trusty; also (abstractly) trustworthiness
BiblicalUsage: Emuwn is faithfulness — being established, trusty, true. Moses says Israel are children in whom is no faith in Deuteronomy 32:20, Isaiah opens the gates for the righteous nation which keeps the truth in Isaiah 26:2, and Proverbs sets the faithful ambassador against the wicked messenger in Proverbs 13:17 and the faithful witness against the false one in Proverbs 14:5.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe faithfulness is proved in small things — a true witness, a trustworthy messenger, a nation that keeps the truth. I hold that God is faithful even when His people are not, and His faithfulness is what makes my faithfulness possible.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: imperfect of G1510; I (thou, etc.) was (wast or were):--+ agree, be, X have (+ charge of), hold, use, was(-t), were.
BiblicalUsage: En is 'was' — the imperfect of 'to be.' In the beginning was the Word in John 1:1, and the birth of Jesus Christ was on this wise in Matthew 1:18.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe 'was' at the start of John's gospel reaches back before time began, and the Word who was with God is the same Word who was born of Mary — eternity stepped into history.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a primary preposition denoting (fixed) position (in place, time or state), and (by implication) instrumentality (medially or constructively), i.e. a relation of rest (intermediate between G1519 and G1537); "in," at, (up-)on, by, etc.:--about, after, against, + almost, X altogether, among, X as, at, before, between, (here-)by (+ all means), for (… sake of), + give self wholly to, (here-)in(-to, -wardly), X mightily, (because) of, (up-)on, (open-)ly, X outwardly, one, X quickly, X shortly, (speedi-)ly, X that, X there(-in, -on), through(-out), (un-)to(-ward), under, when, where(-with), while, with(-in). Often used in compounds, with substantially the same import; rarely with verbs of motion, and then not to indicate direction, except (elliptically) by a separate (and different) preposition.
BiblicalUsage: En is the little word 'in,' and it carries the whole gospel. We are sanctified in Christ Jesus in 1 Corinthians 1:2, in Him is no darkness at all in 1 John 1:5, elect through sanctification of the Spirit in 1 Peter 1:2, and the church stands in God the Father and in the Lord Jesus Christ in 1 Thessalonians 1:1.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe 'in Christ' is where everything happens — I am not saved by standing near Him but by being in Him, the way a branch is in the vine. I hold that the Christian life is not a place I visit but a Person I live in, and that is why Paul can say it two thousand times and never wear it out.
RelatedTopics: Identity in Christ; Jesus Christ; Unity in Christ
RelatedPeople: Paul; Simon Peter; John the Apostle
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a grape
BiblicalUsage: A grape — the fruit of the vine. Joseph's fellow prisoner dreams of a vine whose clusters bring forth ripe grapes in Genesis 40:10, the traveller may eat grapes his fill in his neighbour's vineyard in Deuteronomy 23:24, and Amos promises a day when the mountains drop sweet wine in Amos 9:13. But Hosea warns that Israel loves flagons of wine while looking to other gods in Hosea 3:1.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the grape shows how God turns small fruit into joy — wine for gladness, harvest for hope — and how the same gift can be twisted into idolatry. I hold that every good gift is meant to point me back to the Giver, and the day Amos promises, when the hills melt with sweet wine, is worth waiting for.
RelatedTopics: Nature and Creation; God's Provision; Idolatry
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1722 and G251; in the sea, i.e. marine:--thing in the sea.
BiblicalUsage: James says every kind of beast and bird and serpent and thing in the sea is tamed, and has been tamed of mankind, in James 3:7 — and then he turns to the one thing no man can tame, the tongue.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe James names the creatures of the sea to show how far our mastery reaches, so the failure to master our own tongue will sting all the more.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1722 and a derivative of G43; to take in one's arms, i.e. embrace:--take up in arms.
BiblicalUsage: To take up in one's arms. Jesus takes a child in His arms in Mark 9:36 and sets him in the midst of the disciples, and He takes the little children up in His arms and blesses them in Mark 10:16.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Jesus taking children into His arms is the gospel in miniature — the kingdom belongs to those small enough to be carried, and I want to be carried too.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1722 and G473; in front (i.e. figuratively, presence) of:--before.
BiblicalUsage: Enanti means 'before' — in front of, in the sight of. Peter tells Simon his heart is not right in the sight of God in Acts 8:21, and Zacharias executes the priest's office before God in Luke 1:8.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe every heart stands before God exactly as it is, and no religious office can cover a heart that is not right.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: neuter of G1727; (adverbially) in the presence (view) of:--before, in the presence of.
BiblicalUsage: Enantion is 'before' — in the presence or view of someone. Joseph found favour and wisdom in the sight of Pharaoh in Acts 7:10, Zacharias and Elisabeth were righteous before God in Luke 1:6, and the rulers could not take hold of Jesus' words before the people in Luke 20:26. Isaiah's sheep was dumb before his shearer in Acts 8:32.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe 'before God' is the only audience that finally matters — Joseph's favour came from standing well in Pharaoh's sight, but Zacharias and Elisabeth were righteous in God's sight, and that is the sight I want my life to pass. I hold that a life lived before God needs no other stage.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1725; opposite; figuratively, antagonistic:--(over) against, contrary.
BiblicalUsage: Enantios is what stands opposite — contrary, against. The wind was contrary to the disciples as they rowed in Mark 6:48 and Matthew 14:24, Paul once thought he ought to do many things contrary to the name of Jesus in Acts 26:9, and Paul says the persecutors are contrary to all men in 1 Thessalonians 2:15.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe contrary winds are part of the voyage — the disciples rowed against the wind all night and Jesus still came walking to them on the sea. I hold that opposition does not mean God has left us; often it is the very place where He shows up.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1722 and G756; to commence on:--rule (by mistake for G757).
BiblicalUsage: To begin, to commence. Paul asks the Galatians, having begun in the Spirit, are you now made perfect by the flesh, in Galatians 3:3 — and he is confident that He who began a good work in you will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ in Philippians 1:6.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the God who begins a work finishes it, and the danger is not that He will stop but that I will try to finish in the flesh what He started in the Spirit.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a man
BiblicalUsage: Enash is the Aramaic word for man — a human being, or mankind together. The Chaldeans tell Nebuchadnezzar there is not a man on earth who can show the king's matter in Daniel 2:10, and Daniel tells him that wherever the children of men dwell, God has given him rule in Daniel 2:38. In Ezra the men on this side of the river write their letter to Artaxerxes in Ezra 4:11.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Daniel's 'man' puts us in our place — no man on earth can do what God does, and yet God gives men their kingdoms and their days. I hold that knowing I am only a man is the start of wisdom, because it leaves room for the God who is more.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1722 and G5548; to rub in (oil), i.e. besmear:--anoint.
BiblicalUsage: Jesus counsels the Laodiceans to anoint their eyes with eyesalve that they may see in Revelation 3:18 — the church that thought it was rich and needed nothing could not even see itself.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe I need Christ's eyesalve as much as Laodicea did, because self-deception is the blindness that never feels blind.
RelatedEvents: The Letter to the Church in Laodicea
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: third person singular present of a compound of G1722 and G1209; (impersonally) it is accepted in, i.e. admitted (possible):--can (+ not) be.
BiblicalUsage: Jesus says it cannot be that a prophet perish out of Jerusalem in Luke 13:33 — He must walk today and tomorrow and the day following, because Jerusalem is where prophets die.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Jesus walked toward Jerusalem knowing exactly what waited there, and that steady courage is what I want when my own road turns hard.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a compound of G1722 and G1210 (in the sense of lacking); deficient in:--lacking.
BiblicalUsage: In the early church neither was there any among them that lacked in Acts 4:34 — those with lands and houses sold them and brought the prices, so that need was met from plenty.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a church where no one lacks is not a dream but a pattern, and it starts with open hands, not full storehouses.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1731; an indication (concretely):--manifest token.
BiblicalUsage: Paul calls the Thessalonians' suffering a manifest token of the righteous judgment of God in 2 Thessalonians 1:5 — their endurance under persecution is the visible evidence that they will be counted worthy of the kingdom.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe suffering borne patiently is evidence, not accident — it shows whose kingdom we belong to.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1722 and G1166; to indicate (by word or act):--do, show (forth).
BiblicalUsage: To show, to indicate by word or deed. Christ showed forth all longsuffering in Paul first, for a pattern to believers, in 1 Timothy 1:16, and God will show the exceeding riches of His grace in the ages to come in Ephesians 2:7. Paul also tells the Corinthians to show the proof of their love in 2 Corinthians 8:24 — and Alexander the coppersmith did Paul much evil, as he notes in 2 Timothy 4:14.
TheologicalSignificance: To me, the proof is in people — His longsuffering in Paul, His grace in the ages to come, and our love in the open before the churches. I hold that a faith nobody can see is a faith nobody can follow, so I want my life to show what I say I believe.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1731; indication (abstractly):--declare, evident token, proof.
BiblicalUsage: Endeixis is the proof, the declaration — the evidence shown. Paul asks the Corinthians for the proof of their love in 2 Corinthians 8:24, calls the Philippians' boldness an evident token of salvation in Philippians 1:28, and says God set forth Christ to declare His righteousness in Romans 3:25-26, that He might be just and the justifier of him who believes.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God never asks for blind faith — He declares His righteousness in the open, at the cross, and He gives us proof we can point to. I hold that the gospel is not a guess but a declaration, made in history, in blood, for all to see.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a compound of G1722 and G1218; to be in one's own country, i.e. home (figuratively):--be at home (present).
BiblicalUsage: To be at home — in one's own country. Paul says while we are at home in the body we are absent from the Lord in 2 Corinthians 5:6, but we are willing rather to be absent from the body and present with the Lord in 2 Corinthians 5:8, and so we labour to be accepted of Him whether present or absent in 2 Corinthians 5:9.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe home is not this body — it is with the Lord, and this life is a stay away from home. I hold that knowing where home is changes how I live here: I labour to please Him, whether I am present or absent, because He is the one I am coming home to.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a prolonged form of G1746; to invest (with a garment):--clothe in, wear.
BiblicalUsage: To clothe, to put a garment on someone. The rich man was clothed in purple and fine linen in Luke 16:19, and the soldiers clothed Jesus with purple and crowned Him with thorns in Mark 15:17.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe clothes tell a story — purple on a rich man who ignored Lazarus, purple mocked onto a King who was dying for him — and God sees past both to the heart.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1722 and G1349; in the right, i.e. equitable:--just.
BiblicalUsage: Endikos means just — in the right, equitable. Every transgression under the word spoken by angels received a just recompense in Hebrews 2:2, and Paul says the damnation of those who say 'let us do evil that good may come' is just in Romans 3:8.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God's justice is exactly just — never too little, never too much — and that is why I can trust His judgments even when I cannot trace them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a compound of G1722 and a derivative of the base of G1218; a housing in (residence), i.e. structure:--building.
BiblicalUsage: Paul says we have a building of God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens, in 2 Corinthians 5:1 — a home that waits for us when our earthly tent is taken down. This is the one place the word stands, in the reading carried by the Textus Receptus.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the building God has for me is already standing, and my tent here is only temporary — I can bear its tearing down because something eternal is already built.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1741; to glorify:--glorify.
BiblicalUsage: Christ will come to be glorified in His saints in 2 Thessalonians 1:10, and the name of the Lord Jesus is glorified in us in 2 Thessalonians 1:12 — His glory shown in the very people the world despised.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the day is coming when Jesus will be glorified in ordinary believers like me, and that hope makes today's small faithfulness worth everything.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1722 and G1391; in glory, i.e. splendid, (figuratively) noble:--glorious, gorgeous(-ly), honourable.
BiblicalUsage: Endoxos is what is glorious, splendid, honourable. The apostles were despised while the Corinthians were honourable in 1 Corinthians 4:10, Christ will present His church glorious, without spot or wrinkle, in Ephesians 5:27, and the people rejoiced for all the glorious things Jesus did in Luke 13:17. The word also dresses kings' courts, where men live gorgeously apparelled in Luke 7:25.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe true glory is not the court's gorgeously apparelled life but a church without spot, presented to Christ. I hold that the honour the world gives fades, but the glory Christ gives His people lasts — and I would rather be despised with the apostles than honoured without Him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1746; apparel (especially the outer robe):--clothing, garment, raiment.
BiblicalUsage: Endyma is clothing, the outer robe. John the Baptist's raiment was camel's hair in Matthew 3:4, and Jesus says the body is more than raiment in Matthew 6:25 and Luke 12:23, and asks why we take thought for raiment when the lilies neither toil nor spin in Matthew 6:28.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Jesus puts clothing in its place — the body is more than what covers it, and the Father who dresses the lilies will dress me. I hold that worry about clothes is a small window into a bigger fear, and the cure is to look at what God already provides.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1722 and G1412; to empower:--enable, (increase in) strength(-en), be (make) strong.
BiblicalUsage: To empower, to make strong. Christ enabled Paul and counted him faithful in 1 Timothy 1:12, Paul tells Timothy to be strong in the grace that is in Christ Jesus in 2 Timothy 2:1, and Saul increased the more in strength after his conversion in Acts 9:22. The call to every believer is the same in Ephesians 6:10: be strong in the Lord, and in the power of His might.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe strength is not something I work up but something I am given — Christ enabled Paul, and He enables me. I hold that the Lord's strength is for His work, not my comfort, and it is always enough for the day's battle.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1772 and G1416; to sink (by implication, wrap (compare G1746) on, i.e. (figuratively) sneak:--creep.
BiblicalUsage: Paul warns of men who creep into houses and lead captive silly women laden with sins in 2 Timothy 3:6 — false teachers who do not knock at the front door but slip in quietly.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe error rarely announces itself — it creeps in, and the defence is a household that knows the truth well enough to spot a stranger.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1722 and G1416 (in the sense of sinking into a garment); to invest with clothing (literally or figuratively):--array, clothe (with), endue, have (put) on.
BiblicalUsage: To put on, as a garment. This corruptible must put on incorruption in 1 Corinthians 15:53, we put on the breastplate of faith and love in 1 Thessalonians 5:8, and Paul hopes that being clothed we shall not be found naked in 2 Corinthians 5:3. The word also dresses a king: Herod arrayed in royal apparel sat on his throne in Acts 12:21.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe putting on Christ is the daily work of the Christian — I put on the breastplate in the morning and I will put on incorruption at the last trumpet. I hold that what I wear spiritually matters more than what I wear outwardly, because God sees the clothing of the heart.
RelatedTopics: Identity in Christ; Resurrection; Spiritual Warfare
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1746; investment with clothing:--putting on.
BiblicalUsage: Peter says a wife's adorning should not be the putting on of apparel in 1 Peter 3:3 — the outward dress is not where her beauty is meant to live.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Peter is pointing wives, and all of us, to a beauty that does not come off at night — the hidden person of the heart.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1722 and G2192; to hold in or upon, i.e. ensnare; by implication, to keep a grudge:--entangle with, have a quarrel against, urge.
BiblicalUsage: Enecho is a word with three faces: to be entangled, to hold a grudge, and to press hard. Paul says do not be entangled again with the yoke of bondage in Galatians 5:1, Herodias had a quarrel against John and would have killed him in Mark 6:19, and the scribes began to urge Jesus vehemently in Luke 11:53.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the thread through all three is grip — a yoke that grips, a grudge that grips, a crowd that grips at Jesus with questions. I hold that Christ came to loose every grip but His own, and His yoke is easy because His hands are kind.
RelatedEvents: The Death of John the Baptist
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: feminine from G1722 and the base of G1476; an ambuscade, i.e. (figuratively) murderous purpose:--lay wait. See also G1749.
BiblicalUsage: An ambush — a lying in wait to kill. Paul's nephew heard of the Jews lying in wait for Paul in Acts 23:16 and told him, and the chief priests asked Festus to send Paul to Jerusalem, laying wait in the way to kill him, in Acts 25:3.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the ambush failed because God had a nephew listening at the right moment, and no plot against His servant goes forward without His leave.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1747; to lurk, i.e. (figuratively) plot assassination:--lay wait for.
BiblicalUsage: To lurk, to plot an ambush. Forty men bound themselves with an oath not to eat or drink till they had killed Paul in Acts 23:21, and the scribes lay in wait for Jesus, seeking to catch something from His mouth, in Luke 11:54.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the ambushers' oath shows how far hatred will go, and the fact that both plots failed shows how far God's protection reaches.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: neuter of the same as G1747; an ambush, i.e. (figuratively) murderous design:--lying in wait.
BiblicalUsage: The same ambush as its sister word: in Acts 25:3 the Jews ask Festus to bring Paul to Jerusalem, laying wait in the way to kill him — the ambush laid in the road, and the plot never reaches Paul.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God lets us see the ambush in Scripture so we will not be surprised by our own — the road to Jerusalem is still watched, and the Lord still watches the road.
RelatedEvents: Paul Before Felix, Festus, and Agrippa
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1772 and the base of G1507; to enwrap:--wrap in.
BiblicalUsage: Joseph of Arimathaea bought fine linen, took Jesus down, and wrapped Him in the linen in Mark 15:46, and laid Him in a tomb hewn out of rock.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe there is tenderness in this wrapping — a stranger's hands doing for Jesus what His own disciples had fled from — and love still finds work to do even at the grave.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1772 and G1510; to be within (neuter participle plural):--such things as … have. See also G1762.
BiblicalUsage: Jesus tells the Pharisees to give alms of such things as they have in Luke 11:41 — the things within, the contents of the cup and platter — and then all things will be clean to them.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Jesus goes straight for the inside — clean hands with a greedy heart are still unclean, and generosity from within is what makes a person clean.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1756; efficiency ("energy"):--operation, strong, (effectual) working.
BiblicalUsage: Energeia is working in power — energy at work. There is the working of Satan with all power and lying wonders in 2 Thessalonians 2:9, and there is the working of God's mighty power in us in Ephesians 1:19. Paul labours striving according to His working which works in him mightily in Colossians 1:29, and Christ will change our bodies according to the working by which He subdues all things in Philippians 3:21.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe there are only two energies at work in the world — God's and the enemy's — and they are not equal. I hold that the same power that raised Christ is working in me right now, and that is why I can labour without burning out: it is His working, not mine.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1754; an effect:--operation, working.
BiblicalUsage: Paul lists the diversities of operations in 1 Corinthians 12:6 and the working of miracles in 1 Corinthians 12:10 — different workings, but the same God working all in all.
TheologicalSignificance: To me, God's workings come in many shapes, and the variety in His people is His design, not His accident.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1756; to be active, efficient:--do, (be) effectual (fervent), be mighty in, shew forth self, work (effectually in).
BiblicalUsage: To work, to be active and effectual. The same God works all in all in 1 Corinthians 12:6, His word effectually works in those who believe in 1 Thessalonians 2:13, and the mystery of iniquity already works in 2 Thessalonians 2:7. Paul says affliction itself is effectual in the enduring of suffering in 2 Corinthians 1:6.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God's working is never idle — His word works in believers, His Spirit works through suffering, and even the mystery of evil works only until He removes the restraint. I hold that my job is not to make God work but to get out of the way of the work He is already doing.
RelatedTopics: God's Power; Spiritual gifts; Word of God
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1722 and G2041; active, operative:--effectual, powerful.
BiblicalUsage: Energes is active, operative, powerful. A great door and effectual is opened to Paul in 1 Corinthians 16:9, the word of God is quick and powerful in Hebrews 4:12, and Paul prays that the sharing of Philemon's faith may become effectual in Philemon 1:6.
TheologicalSignificance: The word of God is not a dead letter but a living power, I believe — it pierces, it discerns, it opens doors no man can shut. I hold that when I read Scripture I am handling something alive, and I should expect it to cut.
RelatedTopics: Word of God; God's Power; Prayer
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1722 and G2127; to confer a benefit on:--bless.
BiblicalUsage: To bless — to confer God's benefit. Peter tells the Jews that in Abraham's seed all the kindreds of the earth shall be blessed in Acts 3:25, and Paul says Scripture preached the gospel to Abraham beforehand, saying, In thee shall all nations be blessed, in Galatians 3:8.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the blessing promised to Abraham has reached me, a Gentile, and that is the gospel — God blesses the nations through one Seed.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1451; to make near, i.e. (reflexively) approach:--approach, be at hand, come (draw) near, be (come, draw) nigh.
BiblicalUsage: To come near, to draw nigh. The end of all things is at hand in 1 Peter 4:7, the time of the promise drew nigh in Acts 7:17, and we draw nigh to God through a better hope in Hebrews 7:19. James gives the promise both ways in James 4:8: draw nigh to God, and He will draw nigh to you.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe nearness to God is not a feeling but a direction — I draw near, and He draws near, and the distance closes from both sides. I hold that the end being at hand is not a threat but an invitation to come close while there is still time.
RelatedTopics: Nearness to God; Hope; Second Coming
RelatedPeople: James, Brother of Jesus; Simon Peter
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1722 and G1125; to "engrave", i.e. inscribe:--write (in).
BiblicalUsage: To engrave, to inscribe. Paul tells the Corinthians they are his epistle written in his heart in 2 Corinthians 3:2, and the epistle of Christ written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, not on stone but on the heart, in 2 Corinthians 3:3. Jesus tells His disciples to rejoice because their names are written in heaven in Luke 10:20.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God writes in two places — His Spirit on my heart and my name in heaven — and both writings are permanent. I hold that the heart is the only tablet that matters, because stone breaks and ink fades, but what the Spirit writes stays.
RelatedTopics: New covenant; Assurance; Word of God
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1722 and γυῖον (a limb); pledged (as if articulated by a member), i.e. a bondsman:--surety.
BiblicalUsage: Jesus was made a surety of a better testament in Hebrews 7:22 — He stands as the guarantee of the new covenant, the one who answers for it with His own life.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a surety is only as good as his ability to pay, and Jesus paid in full, which is why the better covenant can never fail.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a primary verb ἄγχω (to squeeze or throttle; akin to the base of G43); near (literally or figuratively, of place or time):--from, at hand, near, nigh (at hand, unto), ready.
BiblicalUsage: Engys is 'near' — of place or of time. The Mount of Olives is a Sabbath day's journey from Jerusalem in Acts 1:12, the Passover was at hand in John 2:13, and those who were far off are made nigh by the blood of Christ in Ephesians 2:13. The warning side is Hebrews 6:8: ground that bears thorns is nigh unto cursing.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe nearness is the gospel's great gift — the far off made nigh by blood, the feast at hand, the mountain a short walk away. I hold that God has closed the distance Himself, and my job is simply to walk the short road He opened.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: neuter of the comparative of G1451; nearer:--nearer.
BiblicalUsage: Paul says our salvation is nearer than when we believed in Romans 13:11 — time has passed, the night is far spent, and it is high time to wake out of sleep.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe every day brings my salvation one day nearer, and that should wake me up, not put me to sleep.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: contraction for the third person singular present indicative of G1751; impersonally, there is in or among:--be, (there) is.
BiblicalUsage: Eni is 'there is' — a small word that carries big claims. Paul asks whether there is not a wise man among the Corinthians in 1 Corinthians 6:5, and then declares where there is neither Greek nor Jew in Colossians 3:11, and neither Jew nor Greek, bond nor free, male nor female, in Galatians 3:28. James says with the Father of lights there is no variableness in James 1:17.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe 'there is' is the most hopeful phrase in the Bible when it is followed by 'neither' — in Christ the divisions that run the world simply are not there any more. I hold that the oneness Paul describes is not a dream for heaven but a fact for the church now, because Christ is all, and in all.
RelatedTopics: Unity in Christ; Identity in Christ; God's Sovereignty
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: prolongation from a primary ἔνος (a year); a year:--year.
BiblicalUsage: A year — the full round of seasons. Paul and Barnabas spent a whole year assembling with the church at Antioch in Acts 11:26, the high priest entered the second tabernacle once every year in Hebrews 9:7, and James warns the planners who say they will spend a year in a city buying and selling in James 4:13. Paul also rebukes the Galatians for observing days and months and years in Galatians 4:10.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a year is long enough to change a church — Antioch did more in one year than most do in ten — and short enough to humble a planner. I hold that my years are not mine to schedule but God's to spend, and the high priest's once-a-year entry reminds me that access to God was once rare and is now open.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1722 and G2480; to invigorate (transitively or reflexively):--strengthen.
BiblicalUsage: To strengthen, to invigorate. Saul received meat and was strengthened in Acts 9:19, and an angel appeared to Jesus in Gethsemane, strengthening Him, in Luke 22:43.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe strength comes in the darkest hours — to a blinded Saul after three days without food, and to Jesus on the night before the cross — and God still sends it by food and by angels.
RelatedEvents: Jesus Prays in Gethsemane; The Conversion of Paul
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1722 and G2476; to place on hand, i.e. (reflexively) impend, (participle) be instant:--come, be at hand, present.
BiblicalUsage: Enistemi is what is present, at hand, pressing in. Things present and things to come are all yours in 1 Corinthians 3:22, Paul warns the Thessalonians not to be troubled as though the day of Christ is at hand in 2 Thessalonians 2:2, and he says perilous times shall come in the last days in 2 Timothy 3:1. Christ gave Himself to deliver us from this present evil world in Galatians 1:4.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the present age is evil but it is not final — Christ has already delivered us from it, even while we still live in it. I hold that the things present are mine to use, not mine to fear, because the One who gave Himself for me is greater than the age I live in.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: neuter plural of a presumed compound from G1722 and G2537; innovatives, i.e. (specially) renewal (of religious services after the Antiochian interruption):--dedication.
BiblicalUsage: The feast of the dedication in John 10:22 — the winter feast at Jerusalem remembering the cleansing of the temple — is the one place this word stands, and it is where Jesus walks in Solomon's porch and the Jews gather around Him.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the feast that remembered a cleansed temple is the right setting for Jesus to say He and the Father are one, because He is the true temple, cleansed and dedicated once for all.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1456; to renew, i.e. inaugurate:--consecrate, dedicate.
BiblicalUsage: To dedicate, to inaugurate. The first testament was not dedicated without blood in Hebrews 9:18, and Christ has consecrated for us a new and living way through the veil, that is, His flesh, in Hebrews 10:20.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe every dedication God accepts is sealed in blood, and the new way is open because Christ's flesh was torn like the veil — I walk through by His body, not my own.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1722 and G2564; to call in (as a debt or demand), i.e. bring to account (charge, criminate, etc.):--accuse, call in question, implead, lay to the charge.
BiblicalUsage: To bring a charge, to call to account. The town clerk tells the Ephesians to implead one another in the open courts in Acts 19:38, and Paul asks who shall lay anything to the charge of God's elect in Romans 8:33. Lysias brought Paul before the council to learn the cause wherefore he was accused in Acts 23:28.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the charge-book against God's elect is empty — God justifies, so no accusation stands. I hold that every charge men bring will be answered the same way: it is God who justifies, and Christ who died.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1722 and G2641; to leave behind in some place, i.e. (in a good sense) let remain over, or (in a bad sense) to desert:--forsake, leave.
BiblicalUsage: To leave behind — in a good sense, to let remain; in a bad sense, to desert. Paul says we are persecuted but not forsaken in 2 Corinthians 4:9, and he names Demas, who forsook him having loved this present world, in 2 Timothy 4:10. David's prophecy says God will not leave Christ's soul in hell in Acts 2:27, and Hebrews warns us not to forsake assembling together in Hebrews 10:25.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe forsaking is the one thing God never does to His own — men forsake, Demas forsook Paul, but God did not forsake Christ in the grave and He will not forsake me. I hold that the gathering of believers is the visible proof of that promise, and I will not give it up.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1722 and a derivative of G2524; subinduced, i.e. surreptitiously suborned as a lier-in-wait:--spy.
BiblicalUsage: The chief priests sent spies in Luke 20:20 — men feigning themselves just, watching Jesus to take hold of His words and deliver Him to the governor.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the spies' question about Caesar was a trap, and Jesus turned the trap into teaching — render to Caesar what is Caesar's, and to God what is God's.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1722 and G2730; to settle down in a place, i.e. reside:--dwell among.
BiblicalUsage: Lot is the righteous man dwelling among the wicked in 2 Peter 2:8 — seeing and hearing their unlawful deeds day by day, vexing his righteous soul.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe dwelling among evil without becoming evil is possible but costly, and Lot's vexed soul is the proof that a righteous heart cannot make peace with what it sees.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1722 and a derivative of G2759; to prick in, i.e. ingraft:--graff in(-to).
BiblicalUsage: To graft in — the gardener's word. Wild olive branches are grafted into the good olive tree in Romans 11:17, and Paul says the natural branches can be grafted in again if they do not abide in unbelief in Romans 11:23. The grafting was contrary to nature in Romans 11:24, which is exactly the point: God's grace does what nature never would.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe I am a wild branch grafted into a tree I did not plant, living off a root I did not grow. I hold that grafting is grace from first to last — God cut me out of the wild and joined me to His people, and He can graft the natural branches back in again whenever they believe.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1458; an accusation, i.e. offence alleged:--crime laid against, laid to charge.
BiblicalUsage: The formal accusation, the crime laid against a man. Lysias found Paul accused of questions of their law but with nothing laid to his charge worthy of death in Acts 23:29, and Festus explains that Rome does not deliver a man to die before he can answer the crime laid against him in Acts 25:16.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Paul's empty charge-sheet is the pattern for every believer — accused, but with nothing worthy of death, because Christ already died.
RelatedEvents: Paul Before Felix, Festus, and Agrippa
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: middle voice from G1722 and κομβόω (to gird); to engirdle oneself (for labor), i.e. figuratively (the apron as being a badge of servitude) to wear (in token of mutual deference):--be clothed with.
BiblicalUsage: Peter tells all of us to be clothed with humility in 1 Peter 5:5 — to gird ourselves with it like a servant's apron — for God resists the proud and gives grace to the humble.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe humility is something I put on, not something I feel — an apron I tie on every morning before I serve anyone.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1465; a hindrance:--X hinder.
BiblicalUsage: Paul says he suffered all things lest he should hinder the gospel of Christ in 1 Corinthians 9:12 — he gave up his right to support so that nothing would stand in the gospel's way.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the gospel is worth any sacrifice of my rights, and the question I should ask of every privilege is whether it helps the gospel or hinders it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1722 and G2875; to cut into, i.e. (figuratively) impede, detain:--hinder, be tedious unto.
BiblicalUsage: To cut into, to hinder, to get in the way. Paul says Satan hindered him from coming to Thessalonica in 1 Thessalonians 2:18, husbands are warned that their prayers may be hindered in 1 Peter 3:7, and the Galatians were running well until someone hindered them from obeying the truth in Galatians 5:7.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe hindrances come from every direction — Satan, sin, and even a careless marriage — and the race is won by those who notice the obstacle and refuse to stop. I hold that the truth is worth running for, and no hinderer gets the last word.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1468; self-control (especially continence):--temperance.
BiblicalUsage: Self-control — temperance. It stands in the ladder of graces in 2 Peter 1:6, beside knowledge and patience and godliness, and Paul reasoned of righteousness, temperance, and judgment to come until Felix trembled in Acts 24:25. It is also a fruit of the Spirit in Galatians 5:23, against which there is no law.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe self-control is not willpower but fruit — the Spirit grows it in me the way He grows love and peace. I hold that the man who cannot govern himself is not free, and the Spirit's temperance is the freedom I actually want.
RelatedTopics: Fruit of the Spirit; Godliness; Temptation
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1722 and G2904; strong in a thing (masterful), i.e. (figuratively and reflexively) self-controlled (in appetite, etc.):--temperate.
BiblicalUsage: An elder must be temperate in Titus 1:8 — sober, just, holy, self-controlled, a lover of hospitality and of good men.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe leadership in the church is proved by self-mastery first, and the temperate man is the one others can safely follow.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: middle voice from G1468; to exercise self-restraint (in diet and chastity):--can(-not) contain, be temperate.
BiblicalUsage: To exercise self-restraint. Paul says if they cannot contain, let them marry, in 1 Corinthians 7:9, and that every man who strives for mastery is temperate in all things in 1 Corinthians 9:25 — training for a corruptible crown, while we run for one incorruptible.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe self-control is training, not punishment — the athlete denies himself for a crown that fades, and I run for one that never will.
RelatedTopics: Fruit of the Spirit; Marriage; Perseverance
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1722 and G2919; to judge in, i.e. count among:--make of the number.
BiblicalUsage: Paul says he dares not make himself of the number of those who commend themselves in 2 Corinthians 10:12 — men measuring themselves by themselves and comparing themselves among themselves, which is not wise.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe self-measurement is a fool's game, and the only comparison that matters is Christ's measure, not my neighbour's.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1722 and G2928; to conceal in, i.e. incorporate with:--hid in.
BiblicalUsage: The kingdom of heaven is like leaven which a woman took and hid in three measures of meal in Matthew 13:33, till the whole was leavened.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the kingdom works like leaven — hidden, small, and quietly spreading until the whole lump is changed.
RelatedTopics: Kingdom of God; Kingdom of heaven
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1722 and the base of G2949; swelling inside, i.e. pregnant:--great with child.
BiblicalUsage: Mary travelled to Bethlehem with Joseph to be taxed, being great with child, in Luke 2:5 — the word holds the whole weight of the incarnation in three words.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God entered the world the way we all do, carried by a young mother on a hard road, and that humbleness is the point.
RelatedPeople: Mary, Mother of Jesus; Joseph, Husband of Mary
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: ordinal from G1767; ninth:--ninth.
BiblicalUsage: The ninth — the ninth hour of prayer, when Peter and John went up to the temple in Acts 3:1, and the ninth foundation stone of the New Jerusalem, a topaz, in Revelation 21:20.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God marks ordinary hours and ordinary stones — the ninth hour became the hour of a lame man's healing, and the ninth stone shines in the city that never needs a temple.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a primary number; nine:--nine.
BiblicalUsage: Nine — the number left behind. The shepherd leaves the ninety and nine to seek the one lost sheep in Luke 15:4 and Matthew 18:12, heaven rejoices over one sinner more than over ninety and nine just persons in Luke 15:7, and Jesus asks where the nine are when only one leper returns to give thanks in Luke 17:17.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the ninety and nine are safe, but the one matters enough to leave them for. I would rather be the one leper who came back than one of the nine who never did.
RelatedEvents: The Lost Sheep; The Healing of the Ten Lepers
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a (tenth) multiple of G1767 and G1767 itself; ninety-nine:--ninety and nine.
BiblicalUsage: Ninety and nine — two words in the Greek, one number in the story. The shepherd leaves the ninety and nine in the wilderness and goes after the one that is lost in Luke 15:4, and the same in Matthew 18:12.
TheologicalSignificance: The ninety and nine are not forgotten, I believe — they are left in the wilderness, safe in the shepherd's care, while he goes after the one who is not.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1770; dumb (as making signs), i.e. silent from astonishment:--speechless.
BiblicalUsage: The men travelling with Saul stood speechless in Acts 9:7 — hearing a voice but seeing no man — struck silent by astonishment on the Damascus road.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe there are moments when God leaves us with nothing to say, and silence is the right answer to glory we cannot explain.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1722 and G3506; to nod at, i.e. beckon or communicate by gesture:--make signs.
BiblicalUsage: When Zacharias could not speak, they made signs to him in Luke 1:62, asking how he would have the child called — and he wrote, His name is John.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God can work through gestures and written words as well as speech, and Zacharias's silence ended in a name that means God is gracious.
RelatedEvents: The Birth of John the Baptist
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a compound of G1722 and G3563; thoughtfulness, i.e. moral understanding:--intent, mind.
BiblicalUsage: Thought, intent — the mind's purpose. Peter says to arm yourselves with the same mind as Christ who suffered in the flesh in 1 Peter 4:1, and Hebrews says the word of God discerns the thoughts and intents of the heart in Hebrews 4:12.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe my intents are not hidden from God, and the word that discerns them is the same word that arms me with Christ's mind.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1722 and G3551; (subjectively) legal, or (objectively) subject to:--lawful, under law.
BiblicalUsage: Lawful, or under law. Paul says he became as one under the law to Christ to gain those without law in 1 Corinthians 9:21, and the town clerk says other matters must be settled in a lawful assembly in Acts 19:39.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Paul's freedom was not lawlessness — he was under law to Christ, and that law set him free to reach anyone.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)
