Definition: neuter of a compound of G1722 and G3571; (adverbially) by night:--before day.
BiblicalUsage: A great while before day, Jesus rose up in Mark 1:35, went out to a solitary place, and prayed — before the crowds, before the demands, before the day began.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the first hours belong to God, and if Jesus needed a solitary place before daybreak, I need one too.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H2585); Enoch (i.e. Chanok), an antediluvian:--Enoch.
BiblicalUsage: Enoch stands in Luke's genealogy as the son of Jared in Luke 3:37, and Hebrews tells the rest in Hebrews 11:5: by faith Enoch was translated that he should not see death, because God had translated him, and before his translation he had this testimony, that he pleased God. Jude adds that Enoch, the seventh from Adam, prophesied of the Lord coming with ten thousands of His saints in Jude 1:14.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Enoch's life is summed up in one phrase — he pleased God — and his exit from this world without dying is the proof that pleasing God is worth everything. His story lives on his People profile.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1722 and G3791; to crowd in, i.e. (figuratively) to annoy:--trouble.
BiblicalUsage: To trouble, to crowd in and annoy. A root of bitterness springing up can trouble many and defile them in Hebrews 12:15, and those vexed with unclean spirits came to Jesus and were healed in Luke 6:18.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe bitterness is a root that troubles a whole church, and the cure is the same as for the vexed — to come to Jesus and be healed.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1758; liable to (a condition, penalty or imputation):--in danger of, guilty of, subject to.
BiblicalUsage: Enochos is to be liable — guilty of, in danger of, subject to. Whoever eats the bread unworthily is guilty of the body and blood of the Lord in 1 Corinthians 11:27, whoever offends in one point is guilty of all in James 2:10, and the blasphemer against the Holy Ghost is in danger of eternal damnation in Mark 3:29. But Christ came to deliver those who through fear of death were all their lifetime subject to bondage in Hebrews 2:15.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe guilt is real and total — one offence makes me guilty of all — and that is exactly why Christ's deliverance has to be total too. I hold that the fear of death held me in bondage until He who died set me free, and now no charge can hold me.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1722 and G3611; to inhabit (figuratively):--dwell in.
BiblicalUsage: To dwell in — God in us, His word in us, faith in us. God says I will dwell in them in 2 Corinthians 6:16, the word of Christ is to dwell in us richly in Colossians 3:16, and the Spirit who raised Jesus dwells in us in Romans 8:11. Timothy's unfeigned faith dwelt first in his grandmother Lois and his mother Eunice in 2 Timothy 1:5.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe dwelling is God's way — He does not visit and leave, He moves in, and His word and His Spirit take up residence in me. I hold that a faith that dwelt in a grandmother and a mother can dwell in a grandson too, and that is how the gospel travels: from one home to the next.
RelatedTopics: Presence of God; Word of God; Outpouring of the Spirit
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: neuter of a compound of G1722 and a derivative of G3700; in the face of (literally or figuratively):--before, in the presence (sight) of, to.
BiblicalUsage: Enopion is 'in the face of' — before, in the sight of. No flesh should glory in His presence in 1 Corinthians 1:29, a meek and quiet spirit is in the sight of God of great price in 1 Peter 3:4, and what we ask we receive because we do what is pleasing in His sight in 1 John 3:22.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe everything is done in God's sight, and that sight is not a threat but a comfort — the meek spirit is of great price to Him, and no flesh can boast there. I hold that living in His sight is the freest way to live, because there is nothing to hide and nothing to prove.
RelatedPeople: Paul; Simon Peter; John the Apostle
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H583); Enos (i.e. Enosh), a patriarch:--Enos.
BiblicalUsage: Enos stands in Luke's genealogy as the son of Seth in Luke 3:38, the grandson of Adam. He carries the line from the first man down through the generations that followed.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a name in a genealogy is never just a name — Enos links Adam to the world that followed, and every generation in between is part of the story God is telling. His story lives on his People profile.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: middle voice from a compound of G1722 and G3775; to take in one's ear, i.e. to listen:--hearken.
BiblicalUsage: Peter stands up with the eleven on the day of Pentecost and says, be this known unto you, and hearken to my words, in Acts 2:14 — the word is an ear opened wide to listen.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Pentecost began with listening, and the gospel still begins the same way — hearken first, and the Spirit does the rest.
RelatedTopics: Outpouring of the Spirit; Listening Well
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Enosh, a son of Seth
BiblicalUsage: Enosh is the son of Seth, named in the first verse of the Chronicler's genealogy in 1 Chronicles 1:1, and in Genesis 4:26 his birth is the moment when men began to call upon the name of the LORD. Seth lived a hundred and five years and begat Enos in Genesis 5:6, carrying the line of promise forward from Adam.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Enosh matters because his name marks a turning point — the generation that began to call on the LORD by name. His story lives on his People profile.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a man in general (singly or collectively)
BiblicalUsage: Enosh is man in general — frail, mortal man, singly or together. Asa prays that man will not prevail against God in 2 Chronicles 14:11, God says He will make the remembrance of men cease in Deuteronomy 32:26, and Isaiah is told to write with a man's pen in Isaiah 8:1. Jeremiah hears the defaming of many and the plots of his familiars in Jeremiah 20:10 — man at his worst, watching for a fall.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe enosh is the Bible's honest word for what we are — weak, short-lived, and prone to plot against each other. I hold that the contrast is the whole point: man is frail, but the LORD who helps Asa is not, and I would rather trust Him than prevail by my own strength.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1781; an injunction, i.e. religious precept:--commandment.
BiblicalUsage: An entalma is a commandment — but in every New Testament use it is the commandments of men. Jesus says they worship in vain, teaching for doctrines the commandments of men, in Mark 7:7 and Matthew 15:9, and Paul says the things that perish with the using are after the commandments and doctrines of men in Colossians 2:22.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the difference between God's commandments and men's is the difference between life and vain worship — one frees, the other only burdens. I hold that any rule that stands on human authority alone, however old or pious, is not binding on my conscience.
RelatedTopics: Tradition; True Worship; Word of God
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1779; preparation for interment:--burying.
BiblicalUsage: The preparation for burial. Jesus says Mary kept her ointment against the day of His burying in John 12:7, and that she came beforehand to anoint His body for the burying in Mark 14:8.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Mary's anointing was understood by Jesus before anyone else did — she prepared Him for burial while He was still alive, and love that sees ahead is never wasted.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a compound of G1722 and G5028; to inswathe with cerements for interment:--bury.
BiblicalUsage: To wrap a body for burial. They wound Jesus' body in linen with spices, as the manner of the Jews is to bury, in John 19:40, and Mary poured ointment on His body for His burial in Matthew 26:12.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the burial matters because the resurrection needed a real grave — He was truly dead, truly buried, and truly raised.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1722 and the base of G5056; to enjoin:--(give) charge, (give) command(-ments), injoin.
BiblicalUsage: To enjoin, to give charge or command. Jesus gave commandments to His apostles through the Holy Ghost before He was taken up in Acts 1:2, Moses sprinkled the blood and said this is the blood of the testament which God has enjoined unto you in Hebrews 9:20, and the devil quotes the promise that God shall give His angels charge over Jesus in Luke 4:10. Jesus answers the devil's misuse with His own obedience: as the Father gave Me commandment, even so I do, in John 14:31.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe commandments are not suggestions — they come with the authority of the one who gives them, and Jesus obeyed His Father's commandment all the way to the cross. I hold that the angels' charge over me is real, but it is God's command, not the devil's quotation, that I live by.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from the same as G1759; hence (literally or figuratively); (repeated) on both sides:--(from) hence, on either side.
BiblicalUsage: Enteuthen is 'from hence' — from this place, or on either side. James asks where wars come from — hence, from our lusts, in James 4:1 — Jesus tells the traders to take these things hence in John 2:16, and the devil tells Him to cast Himself down from hence, from the pinnacle, in Luke 4:9. In Revelation the tree of life stands on either side of the river in Revelation 22:2.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe 'hence' is a word of direction — wars come from hence, from my own lusts, and the cleansing of the temple begins with taking these things hence. I hold that the tree of life standing on either side of the river is the end of the story: what was driven out is brought back, on both sides.
RelatedEvents: The Cleansing of the Temple; The Temptation in the Wilderness
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1793; an interview, i.e. (specially) supplication:--intercession, prayer.
BiblicalUsage: Intercession — prayer made on behalf of another. Paul urges supplications, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgivings for all men in 1 Timothy 2:1, and says food is sanctified by the word of God and prayer in 1 Timothy 4:5.
TheologicalSignificance: To me, intercession is the widest kind of prayer — it reaches people I will never meet, and God counts it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a prolonged form of G1722; properly, within, i.e. (of place) here, hither:--(t-)here, hither.
BiblicalUsage: Enthade is 'here' — this place, hither. The Samaritan woman asks for water so she need not come hither to draw in John 4:15, the risen Jesus asks the disciples if they have here any meat in Luke 24:41, and Paul cries out in the Philippian prison, we are all here, in Acts 16:28. Peter is asked whether Simon is lodged there — here — in Acts 10:18.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe 'here' is where Jesus meets us — at the well, at the table, in the prison at midnight. I hold that He is not far off in some other place; He is here, in this place, with food and forgiveness and freedom.
RelatedTopics: Presence of God; Nearness to God; Evangelism
RelatedEvents: Jesus and the Samaritan Woman; Paul and Silas in the Philippian Prison
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a compound of G1722 and G2372; to be inspirited, i.e. ponder:--think.
BiblicalUsage: To think, to ponder over. While Joseph thought on these things, the angel appeared to him in a dream in Matthew 1:20, and Jesus, knowing their thoughts, asked the scribes why they think evil in their hearts in Matthew 9:4.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God meets us in our thinking — Joseph's pondering was interrupted by an angel, and the scribes' evil thoughts were known before they spoke.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1760; deliberation:--device, thought.
BiblicalUsage: Thought, deliberation, device. Paul tells the Athenians not to think the Godhead is like gold or stone, graven by art and man's device, in Acts 17:29, and Hebrews says the word of God discerns the thoughts and intents of the heart in Hebrews 4:12. Jesus knew the thoughts of the scribes in Matthew 9:4 and of the Pharisees in Matthew 12:25, and answered what they had only thought.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe my thoughts are not private — the Godhead is not a device of my making, and the word that discerns my intents is the same word that can cleanse them. I hold that Jesus knowing my thoughts is a comfort, not a threat, because He answers them with truth.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1722 and G5092; valued (figuratively):--dear, more honourable, precious, in reputation.
BiblicalUsage: Entimos is what is valued — dear, precious, held in honour. Christ is the living stone, chosen of God and precious, in 1 Peter 2:4 and 2:6, the centurion's servant was dear unto him in Luke 7:2, and Paul tells the Philippians to hold such as Epaphroditus in reputation in Philippians 2:29.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe value is decided by the Valuer — men disallowed the Stone, but God chose Him and called Him precious. I hold that what God calls precious is precious, whatever men say, and I want to hold in reputation the people He honours.
RelatedEvents: The Healing of the Centurion's Servant
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1781; injunction, i.e. an authoritative prescription:--commandment, precept.
BiblicalUsage: The commandment — God's authoritative prescription. Keeping the commandments of God is what matters in 1 Corinthians 7:19, we know that we know Him if we keep His commandments in 1 John 2:3, and Timothy is charged to keep the commandment without spot until Christ appears in 1 Timothy 6:14. John rejoiced to find children walking in truth as commanded in 2 John 1:4.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe commandments are how love shows itself — keeping them is not earning God's favour but proving I know Him. I hold that the commandment is not a burden but a boundary, and inside it is where the freedom is.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1722 and G5117; a resident:--of that place.
BiblicalUsage: The people of that place — the residents of Caesarea — joined Paul's companions in begging him not to go up to Jerusalem in Acts 21:12, when they heard what waited for him there.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe love tries to protect us from the road God has set, and Paul's refusal to be persuaded is the measure of a man who knows where he must go.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1722; inside (adverb or noun):--within.
BiblicalUsage: Within — inside. Jesus says the kingdom of God is within you in Luke 17:21, and He tells the Pharisees to cleanse first that which is within the cup, that the outside may be clean also, in Matthew 23:26.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the kingdom is not a place on a map but a reign inside me, and the cleaning God wants starts within, not without.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1722 and G5142; (figuratively) to educate:--nourish up in.
BiblicalUsage: Paul tells Timothy he will be a good minister if he is nourished up in the words of faith and of good doctrine in 1 Timothy 4:6 — fed on them the way a child is fed, until they become his strength.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a minister is made by what he feeds on, and good doctrine is food, not decoration.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1722 and the base of G5157; to invert, i.e. (figuratively and reflexively) in a good sense, to respect; or in a bad one, to confound:--regard, (give) reference, shame.
BiblicalUsage: Entrepo turns two ways: to respect, and to shame. Paul writes not to shame the Corinthians but to warn them as beloved sons in 1 Corinthians 4:14, and the disobedient brother is to be noted that he may be ashamed in 2 Thessalonians 3:14. We gave reverence to our earthly fathers who corrected us in Hebrews 12:9, and the unjust judge in Luke 18:2 feared not God and regarded not man.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe shame and reverence are two sides of the same coin — both come from knowing who stands before us. I hold that a father who corrects earns reverence, a brother who is shamed may be won back, and the Judge who neither fears God nor regards man is the warning of what I must never become.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1722 and G5156; terrified:--X quake, X trembled.
BiblicalUsage: Terrified — trembling with fear. Moses trembled at the burning bush and durst not behold in Acts 7:32, and at Sinai he said, I exceedingly fear and quake, in Hebrews 12:21. The Philippian jailer came trembling and fell down before Paul and Silas in Acts 16:29.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe trembling is the honest response to glory — Moses at the bush, Moses at the mountain, a jailer in the dark. I hold that the fear that falls down before God is the beginning of the freedom that stands up in Him.
RelatedEvents: The Burning Bush; Paul and Silas in the Philippian Prison
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1788; confusion:--shame.
BiblicalUsage: Shame — Paul speaks to the Corinthians' shame twice: there is not a wise man among them to judge between brethren in 1 Corinthians 6:5, and some have not the knowledge of God in 1 Corinthians 15:34.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Paul uses shame as a spur, not a whip — he names what is wrong so the church will wake up and put it right.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1722 and G5171; to revel in:--sporting selves.
BiblicalUsage: Peter describes false teachers counting it pleasure to riot in the daytime and sporting themselves with their own deceivings while they feast with you, in 2 Peter 2:13 — revelling in the very thing that condemns them.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the worst deceit is the one enjoyed in the open, at the table with God's people, and the feast will not cover it forever.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1722 and τυλίσσω (to twist; probably akin to G1507); to entwine, i.e. wind up in:--wrap in (together).
BiblicalUsage: To wrap up, to wind in cloth. Joseph wrapped Jesus' body in a clean linen cloth in Matthew 27:59 and laid it in the tomb in Luke 23:53, and on the morning of the resurrection the napkin that had been about His head lay wrapped together in a place by itself in John 20:7.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the folded napkin is the quietest proof of the resurrection — no thief folds the grave-clothes, and no grave-robber leaves things tidy. I hold that the linen that wrapped a dead body now testifies that the body is gone because He lives.
RelatedEvents: The Burial of Jesus; The Resurrection
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1722 and G5177; to chance upon, i.e. (by implication) confer with; by extension to entreat (in favor or against):--deal with, make intercession.
BiblicalUsage: To meet with, to entreat — and in its highest use, to make intercession. Festus says the Jews dealt with him about Paul in Acts 25:24, but Paul's great use is in Romans: the Spirit makes intercession for the saints in Romans 8:27, and Christ at the right hand of God makes intercession for us in Romans 8:34. Hebrews adds that He ever lives to make intercession for them in Hebrews 7:25.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe intercession is the work of heaven right now — the Spirit praying in me and Christ praying for me, both at once, without ceasing. I hold that I am never without an advocate, because the One at the right hand of God never stops speaking my name.
RelatedTopics: Prayer; Jesus Christ; Outpouring of the Spirit
RelatedEvents: Paul Before Felix, Festus, and Agrippa
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1722 and a derivative of G5179; to enstamp, i.e. engrave:--engrave.
BiblicalUsage: The ministration of death, written and engraven in stones, was glorious in 2 Corinthians 3:7 — so glorious that Israel could not look steadily at Moses' face.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the law engraved in stone was glorious and still could not save, which is why the Spirit writes the same law on hearts instead.
RelatedTopics: Word of God; New covenant; Glory
RelatedEvents: Moses Sees God's Glory and the Second Tablets
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: affliction
BiblicalUsage: One psalm verse: God has not despised nor abhorred the affliction of the afflicted in Psalm 22:24 — He has not hidden His face, but when the afflicted cried, He heard.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this is the promise for every afflicted heart — God does not despise the cry, He hears it, and the psalm that begins in forsakenness ends in hearing.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1722 and G5195; to insult:--do despite unto.
BiblicalUsage: To insult, to do despite unto — Hebrews asks what punishment belongs to the one who has trodden under foot the Son of God and done despite unto the Spirit of grace in Hebrews 10:29.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe insulting the Spirit of grace is the last step of a long road away from God, and the warning is written so I will never take the first step.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: middle voice from G1798; to dream:--dream(-er).
BiblicalUsage: To dream. In the last days old men shall dream dreams, says Joel as Peter quotes him in Acts 2:17 — and Jude warns of filthy dreamers who defile the flesh and despise dominion in Jude 1:8.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe dreams can carry God's Spirit or the flesh's filth, and the difference is whether they lead me to prophesy His word or despise His rule.
RelatedTopics: Dreams; Visions; Outpouring of the Spirit
RelatedPeople: Simon Peter; Jude, Brother of James
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1722 and G5258; something seen in sleep, i.e. a dream (vision in a dream):--dream.
BiblicalUsage: A dream — something seen in sleep. Peter promises on Pentecost that old men shall dream dreams in Acts 2:17, when God pours out His Spirit on all flesh.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God still speaks in dreams when He chooses, and the promise of Pentecost is that His Spirit falls on the old as well as the young.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and G71; to superinduce, i.e. inflict (an evil), charge (a crime):--bring upon.
BiblicalUsage: To bring upon — to inflict. False teachers bring upon themselves swift destruction in 2 Peter 2:1, God brought the flood upon the world of the ungodly in 2 Peter 2:5, and the council accuses the apostles of intending to bring this man's blood upon us in Acts 5:28.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe what we bring upon ourselves is the surest judgment of all — the flood came on a world that would not listen, and destruction comes on teachers who deny the Lord who bought them. I hold that the blood the council feared is the very blood that saves anyone who will own it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and G75; to struggle for:--earnestly contend for.
BiblicalUsage: Jude says it was needful to write and exhort the saints to earnestly contend for the faith once delivered in Jude 1:3 — to struggle for it, as an athlete struggles for the prize.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the faith was delivered once, and my job is not to improve it but to contend for it, earnestly and without apology.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and G134; to applaud:--commend, laud, praise.
BiblicalUsage: To applaud, to commend, to praise. Paul praises the Corinthians for keeping the ordinances in 1 Corinthians 11:2 and then says in the same chapter that he praises them not, because they come together for the worse in 1 Corinthians 11:17. The lord commended the unjust steward because he had done wisely in Luke 16:8, and Paul calls all nations to praise the Lord in Romans 15:11.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe praise should be honest — Paul praises what is right and withholds praise where it is not deserved, and the Lord's commendation of a shrewd steward is about wisdom, not dishonesty. I hold that I should praise God and praise what is praiseworthy, and keep my applause for what is truly good.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1867; praised; Epænetus, a Christian:--Epenetus.
BiblicalUsage: Epaenetus is the wellbeloved of Paul in Romans 16:5 — the firstfruits of Achaia unto Christ, the first convert of the province. He is greeted in the church that met in Priscilla and Aquila's house.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe being first matters to God — the firstfruits belong to Him, and Epaenetus's name is remembered because he was first to believe in a whole province. His story lives on his People profile.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and the base of G134; laudation; concretely, a commendable thing:--praise.
BiblicalUsage: Praise — the commendation itself. Every man shall have praise of God when the Lord comes in 1 Corinthians 4:5, the trial of faith will be found unto praise and honour and glory in 1 Peter 1:7, and all God's grace works to the praise of the glory of His grace in Ephesians 1:6. The brother sent with Titus had praise in the gospel throughout all the churches in 2 Corinthians 8:18.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the praise that matters is the praise of God, not of men — it waits until the Lord comes and brings hidden things to light. I hold that a faith tried by fire and found true will be praised by God Himself, and no human applause can compare.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and G142; to raise up (literally or figuratively):--exalt self, poise (lift, take) up.
BiblicalUsage: To lift up, to raise. Men are to pray everywhere lifting up holy hands in 1 Timothy 2:8, Jesus tells the disciples to lift up their eyes on the fields white for harvest in John 4:35, and He was taken up before their eyes in Acts 1:9. But the word also warns: every high thing that exalts itself against the knowledge of God must be cast down in 2 Corinthians 10:5.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe lifting up is the posture of the Christian life — hands lifted in prayer, eyes lifted to the harvest, and every proud thought brought low. I hold that what I lift up to God, He lifts up in blessing, and what exalts itself against Him will fall.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and G153; to feel shame for something:--be ashamed.
BiblicalUsage: To feel shame for something. Paul tells Timothy not to be ashamed of the testimony of the Lord or of him His prisoner in 2 Timothy 1:8, and Hebrews says Christ is not ashamed to call us brethren in Hebrews 2:11. Jesus warns that whoever is ashamed of Him and His words will be met with the same shame when He comes in glory in Luke 9:26 and Mark 8:38.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe shame runs both ways — I can be ashamed of Him, or He can be unashamed of me, and the difference is everything. I hold that He who is not ashamed to call me His brother deserves a witness who is not ashamed to call Him Lord.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and G154; to ask for:--beg.
BiblicalUsage: To beg. The unjust steward says, I cannot dig, to beg I am ashamed, in Luke 16:3, and the blind man sat by the wayside begging as Jesus passed near Jericho in Luke 18:35.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe begging is the honest posture of us all before God — the steward was too proud for it, and the blind man was not, and only one of them went home seeing.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and G190; to accompany:--follow (after).
BiblicalUsage: To follow after, to accompany. Christ suffered for us, leaving an example that we should follow His steps in 1 Peter 2:21, and the widow is well reported if she has diligently followed every good work in 1 Timothy 5:10. Signs followed the preaching of the word in Mark 16:20, and some men's sins follow after them to judgment in 1 Timothy 5:24.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe following is not a feeling but a path — Christ's steps are marked, and I walk in them or I do not. I hold that good works follow a faithful life and sins follow an unfaithful one, and both arrive at the judgment together.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and G191; to hearken (favorably) to:--hear.
BiblicalUsage: Paul quotes Isaiah: I have heard thee in a time accepted, and in the day of salvation have I succoured thee, in 2 Corinthians 6:2 — God heard, and God helped, and now is the accepted time.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God hears in the accepted time, and the accepted time is now — I do not have to wait for a better day to be heard.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and the base of G202; to listen (intently) to:--hear.
BiblicalUsage: At midnight Paul and Silas prayed and sang praises to God in Acts 16:25, and the prisoners heard them — listening intently in the dark to men in chains singing.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe praise in prison is the loudest sermon there is, and the prisoners heard it because no one can sing like that without a reason.
RelatedEvents: Paul and Silas in the Philippian Prison
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and G302; a particle of indefinite contemporaneousness; whenever, as soon as:--when.
BiblicalUsage: Epan is 'when' — whenever, as soon as. When a stronger than he comes upon the strong man, he takes his armour in Luke 11:22, Herod says when you have found the child bring me word in Matthew 2:8, and when your eye is single your whole body is full of light in Luke 11:34.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe 'when' is the word of readiness — the stronger comes, the child is found, the eye is single, and the moment matters. I hold that God's 'when' is never late, and my job is to be ready for it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and G321; to lead up on, i.e. (technical) to put out (to sea); (intransitively) to return:--launch (thrust) out, return.
BiblicalUsage: To put out to sea, or to return. Jesus tells Simon to launch out into the deep in Luke 5:4, after teaching from his boat a little way from land in Luke 5:3, and in the morning He returned into the city and hungered in Matthew 21:18.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe 'launch out' is still the Lord's word to me — the deep is where the draught is, and the shallow water never caught anything. I hold that the same Lord who went back into the city hungry is the Lord who fills the nets when I obey Him.
RelatedEvents: The Calling of the First Disciples
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and G363; to remind of:--put in mind.
BiblicalUsage: Paul says he wrote boldly to the Romans as putting them in mind in Romans 15:15 — reminding them of what they already knew, because of the grace given to him.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe reminding is a ministry — most of what I need I already know, and I forget it anyway, so God sends men like Paul to put me in mind again.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: neuter of a presumed compound of G1909 and G318; (adverbially) on necessity, i.e. necessarily:--necessary.
BiblicalUsage: The council at Jerusalem writes that it seemed good to the Holy Ghost and to us to lay upon you no greater burden than these necessary things in Acts 15:28 — the few things that truly had to be kept.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the church does its best work when it lays down only what is necessary, and leaves the rest to conscience and grace.
RelatedPeople: James, Brother of Jesus; Simon Peter; Paul
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: middle voice from G1909 and G373; to settle on; literally (remain) or figuratively (rely):--rest in (upon).
BiblicalUsage: To settle on, to rest upon. If the son of peace is there, your peace shall rest upon it, in Luke 10:6 — and Paul says the Jew rests in the law and makes his boast of God in Romans 2:17.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe peace rests where it is welcome and returns where it is not, and the only safe resting place is not the law but the Lord who gave it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and G424; to come up on, i.e. return:--come again, return.
BiblicalUsage: To come again, to return. The good Samaritan tells the host that when he comes again he will repay whatever more is spent in Luke 10:35, and the nobleman returns having received the kingdom in Luke 19:15 to call his servants to account.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the Lord who went away will come again, and the account will be settled then — what I spent on the wounded traveller will be repaid.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1861; an announcement (for information, assent or pledge; especially a divine assurance of good):--message, promise.
BiblicalUsage: The promise — God's announced assurance of good. The promise He has promised us is eternal life in 1 John 2:25, godliness has promise of the life that now is and of that which is to come in 1 Timothy 4:8, and all the promises of God in Christ are yea and Amen in 2 Corinthians 1:20. The scoffers ask where the promise of His coming is in 2 Peter 3:4.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe every promise of God is yea in Christ — not maybe, not one day perhaps, but yes and Amen. I hold that the promise of His coming is the one the scoffers mock and the saints wait for, and I would rather wait with the saints than laugh with the scoffers.
RelatedPeople: John the Apostle; Paul; Simon Peter
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and the base of G32; to announce upon (reflexively), i.e. (by implication) to engage to do something, to assert something respecting oneself:--profess, (make) promise.
BiblicalUsage: To promise — to announce and engage to do it. Abraham was fully persuaded that what God had promised He was able also to perform in Romans 4:21, God who cannot lie promised eternal life before the world began in Titus 1:2, and we hold fast because He who promised is faithful in Hebrews 10:23. The crown of life is promised to those who love Him in James 1:12.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God's promises are only as good as His power and His truth, and He has both — He cannot lie, and He is able to perform. I hold that Abraham's persuasion is the pattern for my faith: fully persuaded, not half-hoping, that what He promised He will do.
RelatedTopics: God's promises; Faith; Faithfulness of God
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1861; a self-committal (by assurance of conferring some good):--promise.
BiblicalUsage: Peter calls them exceeding great and precious promises in 2 Peter 1:4 — promises by which we become partakers of the divine nature — and says we look for new heavens and a new earth according to His promise in 2 Peter 3:13.
TheologicalSignificance: The promises are the means by which He makes me a partaker of His nature, I believe, and the new heavens are not a dream but a promise I can look for.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: middle voice from G1909 and G450; to stand up on, i.e. (figuratively) to attack:--rise up against.
BiblicalUsage: To rise up against — children against parents, brother against brother. Jesus says children shall rise up against their parents and cause them to be put to death in Mark 13:12 and Matthew 10:21, when brother betrays brother for His name's sake.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the gospel divides even families, and the rising up Jesus foretold is the cost of following Him when those nearest to us will not.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and G507; up above, i.e. over or on (of place, amount, rank, etc.):--above, more than, (up-)on, over.
BiblicalUsage: Epano means up above, over, on top of — a small word that sets the height of things. A city set on a hill cannot be hid, the charge against Jesus was set up over his head, and the one who comes from above is above all. It marks rank as much as place: who stands over whom, and what sits above what.
TheologicalSignificance: What comes from above carries authority over what comes from below, and that is why John's words about Christ land with such weight. He is above all because He is from above, and I believe that settles where my trust should rest.
RelatedEvents: The Crucifixion; Jesus Calms the Storm
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a compound of G1909 and G461; a straightening up again, i.e. (figuratively) rectification (reformation):-- correction.
BiblicalUsage: Epanorthosis is correction — a straightening up again — and it appears once, in Paul's claim that Scripture is profitable for it. The word pictures something bent being set straight, not punished for being bent.
TheologicalSignificance: Correction is one of Scripture's kindest gifts, I believe: God does not leave us crooked, He straightens us by His word.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: contracted from G1891; Epaphras, a Christian:--Epaphras.
BiblicalUsage: Epaphras was Paul's fellow worker from Colossae, the man who taught the Colossians the gospel and then laboured for them in prayer, always wrestling that they might stand complete in the will of God. Paul calls him a faithful minister of Christ and, in Philemon, his fellow prisoner. His name reaches us through prayer more than preaching: he is remembered on his knees.
TheologicalSignificance: Prayer is real work, done for people you love before the God who hears, and Epaphras did it faithfully. I believe his example rebukes my hurry: the man remembered on his knees accomplished more than the man remembered on a platform.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and G875; to foam upon, i.e. (figuratively) to exhibit (a vile passion):--foam out.
BiblicalUsage: Epaphrizo means to foam out, and Jude uses it once, of false teachers foaming out their own shame like wild waves of the sea. The picture is ugly on purpose: what is inside them spills out for everyone to see.
TheologicalSignificance: What a person foams out reveals what is really inside them, and Jude warns us to look at the fruit, not the fine words.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 (in the sense of devoted to) and Ἀφροδίτη (Venus); Epaphroditus, a Christian:--Epaphroditus. Compare G1889.
BiblicalUsage: Epaphroditus carried the Philippians' gift to Paul in prison, and Paul calls him his brother, companion in labour, and fellow soldier. He was sent home with honour, and Paul tells the church to hold such men in reputation.
TheologicalSignificance: Paul calls him brother, companion in labour, and fellow soldier, and tells the church to hold such men in reputation. I believe that is how the church should treat its faithful servants: with honour, not silence.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a compound of G1909 and G757 (meaning a governor of a district, "eparch"); a special region of government, i.e. a Roman præfecture:--province.
BiblicalUsage: Eparchia is a province, a Roman district under a governor — the word appears when the governor asks Paul what province he is from, and when Festus arrives in his province. It is the language of empire, of borders and rulers and who answers to whom.
TheologicalSignificance: Paul's trial moves through Roman provinces while a higher court is really in session, and I believe God works through the empire's machinery rather than being stopped by it.
RelatedEvents: Paul Before Felix, Festus, and Agrippa
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and G714; to avail for, i.e. help:--relieve.
BiblicalUsage: Eparkeo means to relieve, to help in a way that actually meets the need. Paul uses it of the church relieving widows: a widow who has relieved the afflicted is herself to be relieved, and believers should relieve their own widows so the church is not burdened.
TheologicalSignificance: Real relief is practical, not sentimental — it is help that arrives, and the church is meant to carry it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and ἀθροίζω (to assemble); to accumulate:--gather thick together.
BiblicalUsage: Epathroizo means to gather thick together, to crowd in. Luke uses it once, when the people were gathered thick together to hear Jesus, and He began to speak about this evil generation seeking a sign.
TheologicalSignificance: The crowd's pressing in shows how hungry people were to hear Jesus, and how He refused to give them a sign on demand.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and an equivalent of G833; a hut over the head, i.e. a dwelling:--habitation.
BiblicalUsage: Epaulis is a habitation, a dwelling place. Peter quotes the psalm over Judas: let his habitation be desolate, and let no man dwell therein — the empty house of a man who betrayed his Master and left his place vacant.
TheologicalSignificance: An empty habitation is a sober picture of what betrayal costs, I hold: a place prepared, then left desolate.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and G839; occurring on the succeeding day, i.e. (G2250 being implied) to-morrow:--day following, morrow, next day (after).
BiblicalUsage: Epaurion simply means the next day, the morrow — and the Gospels and Acts are full of it. The next day John sees Jesus coming and says, Behold the Lamb of God; the next day Peter goes with Cornelius's men; the next day the disciples break bread at Troas. Ordinary days, carrying extraordinary things.
TheologicalSignificance: God works on plain tomorrows, not only on feast days, and the next day is often when the promise arrives. I hold that the Gospels' habit of saying 'the next day' is itself a sermon: keep walking, because tomorrow may be the day you meet the Lamb of God.
RelatedPeople: John the Baptist; Simon Peter; Paul
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and G846 and (the dative case singular of) a derivative of φώρ (a thief); in theft itself, i.e. (by analogy) in actual crime:--in the very act.
BiblicalUsage: Epautophoroi means in the very act — caught in theft itself, in the middle of the crime. The scribes and Pharisees bring the woman to Jesus with this word on their lips: she was taken in adultery, in the very act. The phrase is their charge, not the whole story.
TheologicalSignificance: The accusers wanted the act, not the woman, but Jesus saw the woman and answered the accusers instead of condemning her.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and G2192; to hold upon, i.e. (by implication) to retain; (by extension) to detain; (with implication, of G3563) to pay attention to:--give (take) heed unto, hold forth, mark, stay.
BiblicalUsage: Epecho means to hold upon — to hold forth, to pay attention, to stay with something. Jesus marks how guests choose the chief rooms; the lame man gives heed to Peter and John, expecting to receive; Paul tells the Philippians to hold forth the word of life, and Timothy to take heed to himself and the doctrine.
TheologicalSignificance: Attention is faithfulness, and what we keep our eyes on shapes what we become. I hold that holding forth the word and holding fast to it are the same posture, and Timothy's charge is mine too: take heed to yourself and to the doctrine.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and G1453; to rouse upon, i.e. (figuratively) to excite against:--raise, stir up.
BiblicalUsage: Epegeiro means to stir up, to rouse against. In Acts it is what the Jews do to the crowds: they stir up persecution against Paul and Barnabas at Antioch, and stir up the Gentiles against the brethren at Iconium.
TheologicalSignificance: Opposition to the gospel is rarely an accident, I believe — somebody stirs it up, and the stirring itself is part of the story.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and G1487; thereupon, i.e. since (of time or cause):--because, else, for that (then, -asmuch as), otherwise, seeing that, since, when.
BiblicalUsage: Epei is a hinge word — since, because, seeing that, for then. Paul leans on it when he reasons: since God is judge, since grace is grace, since Christ has appeared once to put away sin. It is the word that carries an argument from what is true to what must follow.
TheologicalSignificance: The gospel is not a feeling but a case that holds together, and this little word carries the argument from what is true to what must follow. I believe Paul's reasoning is worth imitating: start from what God has done, and reason forward from there.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1893 and G1211; since now, i.e. (of time) when, or (of cause) whereas:--after that, because, for (that, -asmuch as), seeing, since.
BiblicalUsage: Epeide means since now, whereas, because — a word for giving the reason things stand as they do. Luke uses it to open a new scene, Paul uses it to explain why God chose foolish preaching to save believers, and why the word went to the Gentiles when it was spoken against.
TheologicalSignificance: Reasons matter to God, and when Scripture says because, I should stop and listen to the reason it gives. I hold that He does not act without cause, and the reasons He gives — foolish preaching, a door opened to the Gentiles — are worth more than my own explanations.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1894 and G4007; since indeed (of cause):--forasmuch.
BiblicalUsage: Epeideper means forasmuch, since indeed — Luke's opening word for why he wrote at all. Forasmuch as many have taken in hand to set forth the things most surely believed among us, he will write them in order, that Theophilus may know the certainty.
TheologicalSignificance: Luke's careful opening is a gift, I hold: the gospel was investigated, ordered, and written down so faith could rest on certainty, not rumour.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: and other moods and persons of the same tense; from G1909 and G1492; to regard (favorably or otherwise):--behold, look upon.
BiblicalUsage: Epeidon is the aorist form of looking upon with favour — God regarding His people. Elizabeth says the Lord looked on her to take away her reproach, and the church prays, Lord, behold their threatenings, and grant boldness to speak.
TheologicalSignificance: The comfort of this word is that God sees, I believe: He looked on Elizabeth, and He looks on His threatened people still.
RelatedEvents: The Birth of John the Baptist
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1893 and G4007; since indeed (of cause):--seeing.
BiblicalUsage: Epeiper means seeing that, since indeed — Paul's word in Romans for the oneness of God: seeing it is one God, who shall justify the circumcision by faith and the uncircumcision through faith. One God, one way of being made right.
TheologicalSignificance: One God means one door, and faith is how both Jew and Gentile walk through it, and I hold that this single verse holds the whole gospel together.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a compound of G1909 and G1521; a superintroduction:--bringing in.
BiblicalUsage: Epeisagoge is a bringing in, a superintroduction — the bringing in of a better hope, by which we draw nigh unto God. The law made nothing perfect, but this bringing in does what the law could not.
TheologicalSignificance: The better hope is not a better rule but a nearer God, and that is the whole difference between the law and Christ.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and G1534; thereafter:--after that(-ward), then.
BiblicalUsage: Epeita means then, after that — the word that keeps events in their order. Then Paul went up to Jerusalem; then Christ was seen by above five hundred brethren at once; then they that are Christ's at his coming; then we which are alive shall be caught up together with them.
TheologicalSignificance: The order matters: Christ first, then those who are His, and my hope rests on that order holding firm. I believe the gospel's sequence is a comfort, not a timetable to argue over — the dead in Christ rise, and then we who are alive are caught up with them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and (the accusative case plural neuter of) G1565; upon those parts of, i.e. on the further side of:--beyond.
BiblicalUsage: Epekeina means beyond, on the further side. Stephen quotes Amos against Israel: you took up the tabernacle of Moloch, and I will carry you away beyond Babylon. Beyond is where judgment sends them — further than they ever meant to go.
TheologicalSignificance: Idolatry always carries you further from home than you planned, and beyond Babylon is the proof of it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: middle voice from G1909 and G1614; to stretch (oneself) forward upon:--reach forth.
BiblicalUsage: Epekteinomai means to stretch oneself forward, reaching forth. Paul says he forgets what is behind and reaches forth to what is before, pressing toward the mark for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus.
TheologicalSignificance: Not leaning back on yesterday but stretched forward toward Christ, who is ahead of me — that is the Christian posture, I believe.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: middle voice from G1909 and G1746; to invest upon oneself:--be clothed upon.
BiblicalUsage: Ependyomai means to be clothed upon — put on over what is already there. Paul groans, earnestly desiring to be clothed upon with our house which is from heaven, that mortality might be swallowed up of life.
TheologicalSignificance: The groaning is honest and the longing is right, I hold: we are not meant to be unclothed, but clothed upon with something better.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1902; a wrapper, i.e. outer garment:--fisher's coat.
BiblicalUsage: Ependytes is an outer garment, a fisher's coat. When John tells Peter it is the Lord, Peter girds his fisher's coat about him — he was naked — and casts himself into the sea to reach Jesus.
TheologicalSignificance: Peter's rush, coat and all, says more than words could, I believe: he would rather swim to Jesus than wait for the boat.
RelatedTopics: Jesus Christ; Love for God; Discipleship
RelatedEvents: Jesus Appears to Seven Disciples by the Sea of Galilee
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2228 and G4007; than at all (or than perhaps, than indeed):--than.
BiblicalUsage: Eper means than — a word of comparison, and John uses it once to expose a sad trade: men loved the praise of men more than the praise of God. Than is where the choice shows.
TheologicalSignificance: We choose the praise we can hear over the praise we cannot see, and this one comparison explains so much compromise.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and G2064; to supervene, i.e. arrive, occur, impend, attack, (figuratively) influence:--come (in, upon).
BiblicalUsage: Eperchomai means to come upon — to arrive, to overtake, to fall upon. The Holy Ghost shall come upon Mary; power shall come upon the disciples; in the ages to come God will show the riches of His grace; and miseries shall come upon the rich who heaped treasure in the last days.
TheologicalSignificance: What comes upon us reveals who we are, and both arrivals are certain: the Spirit comes upon the willing, and judgment comes upon the careless. I hold that I should pray for the first coming daily and live ready for the second.
RelatedTopics: Outpouring of the Spirit; Grace; Judgment
RelatedPeople: Mary, Mother of Jesus; Simon Peter; Paul
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a compound of G1909 and (probably) ἀρειά (threats); to insult, slander:--use despitefully, falsely accuse.
BiblicalUsage: Epereazo means to use despitefully, to insult and falsely accuse. Jesus says bless them that curse you, and pray for them which despitefully use you; Peter says keep a good conscience, that those who falsely accuse your good conversation in Christ may be ashamed.
TheologicalSignificance: The answer to spite is not spite but blessing, I hold — and a clear conscience is the quietest reply of all.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and G2065; to ask for, i.e. inquire, seek:--ask (after, questions), demand, desire, question.
BiblicalUsage: Eperotao means to ask, to inquire, to demand an answer — and the Gospels are full of it. The boy Jesus is found in the temple asking questions; the rich young ruler runs up asking what he must do; the Pharisees ask to trap Him; and Paul says God was found by those who asked not for Him.
TheologicalSignificance: Questions brought to Jesus honestly are never wasted, even when the answer costs everything. I believe the asking matters more than I used to think: the boy in the temple, the ruler on the road, and the Pharisees with their traps all found that Jesus answers questions with truth, not flattery.
RelatedEvents: The Boy Jesus in the Temple; The Rich Young Ruler
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1905; an inquiry:--answer.
BiblicalUsage: Eperotema is an inquiry, an answer — and Peter uses it once, in the verse about baptism: not the putting away of the filth of the flesh, but the answer of a good conscience toward God, by the resurrection of Jesus Christ.
TheologicalSignificance: Baptism is an answer, not a bath, I believe: a conscience speaking to God, grounded in a risen Christ.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an asp or other venomous serpent
BiblicalUsage: Eph'eh is an asp, a venomous serpent — the kind of word that bites. The wicked shall suck the poison of asps; the viper's tongue shall slay him; they hatch cockatrice eggs, and he that eateth of their eggs dieth. It is always a picture of evil that looks harmless until it strikes.
TheologicalSignificance: Sin poisons quietly: it does not announce itself, it hatches, and then it bites. I believe the asp is Scripture's warning that evil looks harmless until it strikes, and the wicked man's end shows where the poison leads.
RelatedEvents: Job's Losses in a Single Day
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, a breath, i.e. nothing
BiblicalUsage: Epha means nothing, worthless, a breath. God taunts the idols with it: behold, ye are of nothing, and your work of nought — an abomination is he that chooseth you. The word is God's verdict on every rival.
TheologicalSignificance: Every idol, weighed honestly, comes to nothing, and only God remains when the scales settle.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and G242; to spring upon:--leap on.
BiblicalUsage: Ephallomai means to leap upon, to spring on. The man with the evil spirit leaps on the seven sons of Sceva, overcomes them, and prevails against them, so that they flee out of the house naked and wounded.
TheologicalSignificance: Borrowed authority is no authority at all, and the evil one knows the difference — that is the warning of the sons of Sceva.
RelatedEvents: The Sons of Sceva at Ephesus
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and G530; upon one occasion (only):--(at) once (for all).
BiblicalUsage: Ephapax means once, once for all — and it carries the weight of the gospel. Christ died unto sin once; He was seen by above five hundred brethren at once; He offered Himself once, entered the holy place once, and by one offering we are sanctified.
TheologicalSignificance: Once for all is the sweetest phrase in the Bible, and I rest on it. The work is done, it does not need doing again, and I believe a finished sacrifice is the only ground for a settled conscience.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Ephes-Dammim, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Ephes-Dammim — the edge of blood — is the place where the Philistines camped when they gathered to fight Israel, between Socoh and Azekah. It is the ground where David and Goliath would meet, and the name fits the blood that would be shed there.
TheologicalSignificance: Where armies gather, blood follows, and it was on that edge that a shepherd boy trusted God instead of armour. I believe the place name is no accident: the edge of blood became the field where faith beat the sword.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: cessation, i.e. an end (especially of the earth); often used adverb, no further; also the ankle (in the dual), as being the extremity of the leg or foot
BiblicalUsage: Ephes means an end, a ceasing — no further, the uttermost part. Look unto me, and be ye saved, all the ends of the earth; the Lord will judge His people when He sees their power is gone; is there not yet any of the house of Saul, that I may show the kindness of God unto him?
TheologicalSignificance: The ends of the earth are not too far for God's salvation, and the end of our strength is not the end of His mercy. I hold that both are where He begins, and that is why the call goes out to every end of the earth without exception.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2184; diurnality, i.e. (specially) the quotidian rotation or class of the Jewish priests' service at the Temple, as distributed by families:--course.
BiblicalUsage: Ephemeria is a course, a turn of service — the daily rotation of the priests at the temple. Zacharias was of the course of Abia, and it was his turn to burn incense when the angel came with the news of John.
TheologicalSignificance: The ordinary turn of duty is where God often meets us, I believe: Zacharias was simply doing his course when heaven broke in.
RelatedPeople: Zechariah, Father of John the Baptist
RelatedEvents: The Birth of John the Baptist
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and G2250; for a day ("ephemeral"), i.e. diurnal:--daily.
BiblicalUsage: Ephemeros means daily, for a day — and James uses it of the brother or sister who is naked and destitute of daily food. The word makes the need urgent: not a plan for next month, but bread for today.
TheologicalSignificance: Daily needs test whether our faith is real, I hold: a blessing without bread is no blessing at all.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Epher, the name of an Arabian and of two Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Epher — a calf — is the name of three men in Scripture: the second son of Midian, a son of Ezra among the descendants of Judah, and a head of a family of Manasseh east of the Jordan. The name is shared; the men are not, and each stands in his own genealogy.
TheologicalSignificance: God keeps the record, and no one in His story is only a name on a list. I believe even a name carried by three men matters, because each man stood in his own place in the genealogy that leads to David.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: ashes
BiblicalUsage: Epher is ashes — dust and ashes, the sign of mourning and of humility. Abraham says, I am but dust and ashes; Job repents in dust and ashes; Daniel seeks God with fasting and sackcloth and ashes; Mordecai puts on sackcloth with ashes when his people are threatened.
TheologicalSignificance: I am dust, and the moment I know it, I am ready to hear God. Ashes teach me the right posture, I believe: Abraham, Job, Daniel, and Mordecai all came to God the same way, low and honest.
RelatedEvents: Job's Restoration; Esther Saves Her People
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2181; Ephesine, or situated at Ephesus:--of Ephesus.
BiblicalUsage: Ephesinos means of Ephesus — an Ephesian, situated at Ephesus. It stands in the older text of the letter to the church of Ephesus, addressed to the angel of the church in that city, the first of the seven letters.
TheologicalSignificance: The word marks a people by their city, and the church of Ephesus is the one the risen Christ addresses first among the seven.
RelatedEvents: The Letter to the Church in Ephesus
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2181; an Ephesian or inhabitant of Ephesus:--Ephesian, of Ephesus.
BiblicalUsage: Ephesios is an Ephesian, a person of Ephesus. The word rings through the riot: Great is Diana of the Ephesians, the crowd cries for two hours, and Trophimus the Ephesian is the man Paul is accused of bringing into the temple.
TheologicalSignificance: A whole city can be stirred by a threatened idol, and one Ephesian's name could put Paul's life at risk — that is the power of a riot, I believe.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably of foreign origin; Ephesus, a city of Asia Minor:--Ephesus.
BiblicalUsage: Ephesus was the great city of Asia Minor, home of the temple of Artemis, where Paul arrived and preached. It was the city where he called the elders to his farewell, and where the risen Christ later sent a letter to the church.
TheologicalSignificance: A city where Paul arrived and preached, and where the risen Christ later sent a letter: Ephesus carries both the gospel's advance and the Lord's own address to His church. I believe the letter's place in the canon is the warning and the honour at once, because Christ writes to His churches, and He writes to this one first.
RelatedEvents: The Riot at Ephesus; Paul's Farewell to the Ephesian Elders; The Letter to the Church in Ephesus
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a compound of G1909 and G2147; a discoverer, i.e. contriver:--inventor.
BiblicalUsage: Epheuretes is an inventor — of evil things. Paul lists it among the sins of those who knew God and refused Him: inventors of evil things, disobedient to parents, without understanding.
TheologicalSignificance: Evil is not only committed, it is invented, and a heart that invents evil has turned its creativity against God.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and a cognate of G2240; to arrive upon, i.e. extend to:--reach.
BiblicalUsage: Ephikneomai means to reach, to extend to. Paul says he will not boast beyond his measure, but according to the measure God distributed to him — a measure to reach even unto the Corinthians.
TheologicalSignificance: God gives each of us a measure to reach, and faithfulness is reaching as far as He measured, no further and no less.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and G2476; to stand upon, i.e. be present (in various applications, friendly or otherwise, usually literal); --assault, come (in, to, unto, upon), be at hand (instant), present, stand (before, by, over).
BiblicalUsage: Ephistemi means to stand upon, to be present, to come suddenly. The angel of the Lord came upon the shepherds; Martha was cumbered about much serving and came to Jesus; the angel stood by Peter in prison; the Lord stood by Paul in the night; and Timothy is told to be instant in season and out of season.
TheologicalSignificance: God stands by His people suddenly, and His people are to stand by their calling constantly. I believe the two truths belong together: the angel in the prison, the Lord in the night, and Timothy told to be instant in season and out of season.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Ephlal, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Ephlal — intercessor — is a descendant of Pharez named once in the genealogy of Judah, the son of Zabad. One verse is all he gets, and it is enough: his name is kept in the line that leads to David.
TheologicalSignificance: A single verse in a genealogy is still a place in God's story. I believe Ephlal is remembered because the line was remembered, and the line was remembered because it led to David.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Ephod, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Ephod is the father of Hanniel, a chief of the tribe of Manasseh named when the land was divided. He appears once, at the dividing of the inheritance, as the man whose son helped apportion the promise.
TheologicalSignificance: The work of dividing God's gift took real men with real names, and God recorded them. I believe Ephod's one mention is enough to show that no part in the apportioning of the promise was beneath God's notice.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: strictly a demonstrative particle, here; but used of time, now or then
BiblicalUsage: Ephow is a small word for then, now, so — the word that turns a sentence into a question or a plea. Isaac trembles and asks, who then is he that hath taken venison; Moses asks, wherein shall it be known then that I have found grace; Job cries, Oh that my words were now written.
TheologicalSignificance: Then is when the truth lands, and now is when the cry goes up, and this little word carries the weight of the moment.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a girdle; specifically the ephod or highpriest's shoulder-piece; also generally, an image
BiblicalUsage: Ephowd is the ephod, the priestly garment of gold, blue, purple, scarlet, and fine linen, with shoulder pieces and a breastplate of judgment. Samuel ministered before the Lord as a child, girded with a linen ephod; Gideon made an ephod of gold that became a snare; and Hosea says Israel shall abide many days without ephod or teraphim.
TheologicalSignificance: A holy thing can be worn rightly or wrongly, and the garment was never the problem — the heart was. I hold that the ephod proves it: on Aaron it pointed to God, and in Gideon's house it became an idol.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Chaldee origin (H6606); be opened!:--Ephphatha.
BiblicalUsage: Ephphatha is the Aramaic word Jesus spoke to the deaf man: Be opened. He looked up to heaven, sighed, and said it — and straightway his ears were opened, and the string of his tongue was loosed, and he spake plain.
TheologicalSignificance: Jesus opens what is shut — ears, tongues, and hearts — and He does it with a sigh and a command.
RelatedEvents: Jesus Heals a Deaf and Mute Man in the Decapolis
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H669 or better H6085); Ephraim, a place in Palestine:--Ephraim.
BiblicalUsage: Ephraim is the city where Jesus went when the chief priests plotted to kill Him — a city near the wilderness, where He continued with His disciples until the Passover drew near. The place bears the patriarch's name, and for a little while it sheltered the Lord.
TheologicalSignificance: When the plot closed in, Jesus withdrew to a small city, and even the withdrawal was part of the road to the cross. I believe Ephraim's quiet role matters because it shows the Lord choosing the unnoticed place to wait for the appointed hour.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Ephrath, another name for Bethlehem;
BiblicalUsage: Ephrath is another name for Bethlehem, the place where Rachel died and was buried on the way, where Ruth was blessed by the elders, and where the prophet says the ruler of Israel shall come forth. Ash-heap and fruitfulness, grief and promise, in one name.
TheologicalSignificance: Rachel's grave and the Messiah's birthplace share one field, and the name holds sorrow and hope together. I believe Ephrath is the whole story in miniature: grief where Rachel died, and promise where the ruler of Israel would come forth.
RelatedPeople: Ephrath, Wife of Caleb; Rachel; Ruth
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an Ephrathite or an Ephraimite
BiblicalUsage: Ephrathiy means an Ephrathite or an Ephraimite — a person of Ephrath or Ephraim. At the fords of Jordan the Gileadites challenge the men who would pass, and the Ephraimites are known by their speech; Elkanah is an Ephrathite of Ramathaim; David is the son of Jesse the Ephrathite of Bethlehem.
TheologicalSignificance: A man's people were known by where he came from and how he spoke, and David the Ephrathite was chosen from that small place. I hold that God delights to raise His chosen from overlooked towns, and Bethlehem proves it twice over.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Ephrajim, a son of Joseph; also the tribe descended from him, and its territory
BiblicalUsage: Ephraim — I shall be doubly fruitful — is Joseph's second son, blessed by Jacob with his right hand over the younger. His name became the tribe's, and then the name of the whole northern kingdom in the prophets.
TheologicalSignificance: The blessing crossed hands, and the second son became the greater, because God gives as He wills and not as men expect. I believe Ephraim is the picture of God's freedom to choose the younger, and Joseph's joy at his fruitfulness was only the beginning.
RelatedPeople: Ephraim; Joseph, Son of Jacob; Jacob
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: the brood of a bird
BiblicalUsage: Ephroach is the young of birds — the brood in the nest. The law says if you take the young, let the mother go, that it may be well with you; the eagle's young suck up blood where the slain are; and the sparrow finds a house and the swallow a nest for her young, even at God's altars.
TheologicalSignificance: God's care reaches the smallest nest, and His law protects even the mother bird. I believe the young birds preach tenderness written into the commandments: the God who feeds the eagle's young has not forgotten mine.
RelatedTopics: Nature and Creation; God's Provision; Compassion
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Ephron, the name of a Canaanite and of two places in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Ephron the Hittite owned the field and the cave of Machpelah. Abraham bought them from him for four hundred shekels of silver — the first piece of the promised land owned outright, where Sarah was buried and where Abraham himself would lie.
TheologicalSignificance: A grave bought in faith is the beginning of the promise taking ground, held for a people who did not yet own the land. I believe Ephron's field matters because Abraham paid full price for it: faith does not take shortcuts, even with a grave.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a girding on (of the ephod); hence, generally, a plating (of metal)
BiblicalUsage: Ephuddah is the girding on of the ephod — the curious girdle of the priestly garment, woven of gold, blue, purple, scarlet, and fine linen, and also the plating of metal over an idol. The same word covers the girdle of the high priest and the silver overlay of a graven image.
TheologicalSignificance: What is woven for worship and what is plated for idols can look alike, and the difference is whom it serves. I hold that the word warns me to ask the question about every fine thing in my life: is this girded for God, or plated for an idol?
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a primary preposition; properly, meaning superimposition (of time, place, order, etc.), as a relation of distribution (with the genitive case), i.e. over, upon, etc.; of rest (with the dative case) at, on, etc.; of direction (with the accusative case) towards, upon, etc.:--about (the times), above, after, against, among, as long as (touching), at, beside, X have charge of, (be-, (where-))fore, in (a place, as much as, the time of, -to), (because) of, (up-)on (behalf of), over, (by, for) the space of, through(-out), (un-)to(-ward), with. In compounds it retains essentially the same import, at, upon, etc. (literally or figuratively).
BiblicalUsage: Epi is the most common preposition in the New Testament — on, upon, over, against, at, by — and it carries the weight of where things rest. Thy kingdom come on earth; upon this rock I will build my church; the Holy Ghost shall come upon thee; we have access by faith into this grace wherein we stand.
TheologicalSignificance: Christ's kingdom comes upon earth, His church stands upon a rock, and His Spirit comes upon His people. I believe this small word holds the gospel's posture: God does not hover at a distance, He rests upon us.
RelatedTopics: Kingdom of God; Church; Outpouring of the Spirit
RelatedEvents: The Sermon on the Mount; Pentecost
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and the base of G939; to walk upon, i.e. mount, ascend, embark, arrive:--come (into), enter into, go abroad, sit upon, take ship.
