BiblicalUsage: Epibaino means to mount, to embark, to go aboard — to step up onto something that will carry you. Tell the daughter of Sion, thy King cometh unto thee, meek, and sitting upon an ass; Paul finds a ship sailing to Phenice and goes aboard; and the prisoners embark for Italy.
TheologicalSignificance: The King rides a borrowed ass and Paul boards a ship he does not command, and both are carried exactly where God intends. I hold that mounting up is an act of trust, and the mount — ass or ship — is God's provision, not mine.
RelatedEvents: Triumphal Entry; Paul Shipwrecked on Malta
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and G906; to throw upon (literal or figurative, transitive or reflexive; usually with more or less force); specially (with G1438 implied) to reflect; impersonally, to belong to:--beat into, cast (up-)on, fall, lay (on), put (unto), stretch forth, think on.
BiblicalUsage: Epiballo means to throw upon, to lay on, to cast — hands laid on Jesus in the garden, hands laid on the apostles, a patch laid on an old garment, a thought laid on the heart. It is the word for what is put onto something else, whether violence or repair.
TheologicalSignificance: Hands that seize and hands that heal are not the same, though the word is the same. I believe the gospel is the story of the second kind winning: the hands laid on Jesus in violence became, in His own hands, the laying on of life.
RelatedEvents: The Arrest of Jesus in Gethsemane
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and G916; to be heavy upon, i.e. (pecuniarily) to be expensive to; figuratively, to be severe towards:--be chargeable to, overcharge.
BiblicalUsage: Epibareo means to be heavy upon, to be chargeable, to burden. Paul says he would not overcharge the Corinthians with grief over one man's sin, and that he worked night and day so as not to be chargeable to the Thessalonians.
TheologicalSignificance: The gospel is free, and the messenger should not make it costly. I hold that Paul's care not to burden the church is a model for every minister, and I should watch my own weight on the people I serve.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and a reduplicated derivative of the base of G939 (compare G307); to cause to mount (an animal):--set on.
BiblicalUsage: Epibibazo means to set upon — to set a man on a beast. The Samaritan sets the wounded man on his own beast and brings him to an inn; the disciples set Jesus on the colt; the soldiers are ordered to provide beasts to set Paul on, to bring him safe to Felix.
TheologicalSignificance: Somebody else's beast, somebody else's trouble, carried at somebody else's cost — that is the gospel in miniature. I believe the Samaritan, the disciples, and the soldiers each set a man on a beast, and each time the carrying pictures Christ carrying me.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1911; a patch:--piece.
BiblicalUsage: Epiblema is a patch, a piece of cloth laid on a garment. No man putteth a piece of new cloth unto an old garment, Jesus says, for that which is put in to fill it up taketh from the garment, and the rent is made worse.
TheologicalSignificance: You cannot mend the old life with a piece of the new, and the whole garment must be made new. I hold that the patch teaches what the new covenant is not: a repair job on a life that needs replacing.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and G991; to gaze at (with favor, pity or partiality):--look upon, regard, have respect to.
BiblicalUsage: Epiblepo means to look upon with favour, pity, or partiality. Mary sings that God hath regarded the low estate of His handmaiden; a father cries, look upon my son, for he is mine only child; and James warns against looking with respect to the man in fine clothing while the poor man stands.
TheologicalSignificance: God looks on the lowly with favour, and I must not look on the rich with favour. I believe the word convicts me twice, and His gaze and mine should point the same way: toward the low estate, not the fine clothing.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and G994; to exclaim against:--cry.
BiblicalUsage: Epiboao means to cry out against — and Festus says it of Paul's accusers: the whole multitude of the Jews cried out that he ought not to live any longer. The cry is a demand for death, dressed as justice.
TheologicalSignificance: A crowd's cry can become a demand to kill, spoken before a governor, and Paul stood in it without flinching.
RelatedEvents: Paul Before Felix, Festus, and Agrippa
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a presumed compound of G1909 and G1014; a plan against someone, i.e. a plot:--laying (lying) in wait.
BiblicalUsage: Epiboule is a plot, a laying in wait — a plan made against someone in secret. The Jews lay in wait to kill Paul at Damascus, and again in Greece, and again on the road; and Paul serves the Lord with all humility of mind, and with many tears, and temptations, which befell him by the lying in wait of the Jews.
TheologicalSignificance: Every lying in wait became another road by which the gospel travelled further. I hold that the plots never once stopped the work, and Paul's tears and temptations are the proof that opposition is part of the calling, not a sign it failed.
RelatedEvents: The Plot against Paul Foiled; Paul's Farewell to the Ephesian Elders
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and G5495; to put the hand upon, i.e. undertake:--go about, take in hand (upon).
BiblicalUsage: Epicheireo means to take in hand, to undertake — to put the hand to a work. Many have taken in hand to set forth the gospel in order; Paul disputes with the Grecians, who go about to slay him; and the vagabond Jews take upon them to call over the name of the Lord Jesus.
TheologicalSignificance: Luke's careful history, Paul's bold dispute, and the exorcists' empty imitation all took something in hand, but the authority was not the same. I believe the word separates the three undertakings: the hand is the same, and only the Name makes the difference.
RelatedEvents: The Sons of Sceva at Ephesus
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and χέω (to pour); --to pour upon:--pour in.
BiblicalUsage: Epicheo means to pour upon — and the Samaritan pours oil and wine into the wounded man's wounds, binding them up, setting him on his beast, and taking care of him.
TheologicalSignificance: What heals is poured out by a stranger who stops, at his own cost, and the oil and wine are the gospel in a picture.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and G5524; to furnish besides, i.e. fully supply, (figuratively) aid or contribute:--add, minister (nourishment, unto).
BiblicalUsage: Epichoregeo means to furnish besides, to supply fully — to add, to minister nourishment. God ministers the Spirit and works miracles among you; He that ministers seed to the sower will minister bread for food; the body grows by the supply of the Head; and we are to add to our faith virtue.
TheologicalSignificance: God supplies and we add: He furnishes the seed and the growth, and our part is to add diligence to what He has already given. I hold that this is the right order — His supply first, my adding second — and reversing it is how I grow weary.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2023; contribution:--supply.
BiblicalUsage: Epichoregia is supply, contribution — the supply of every joint in the body, by which it grows in love; and the supply of the Spirit of Jesus Christ, by which Paul's bonds turn to salvation.
TheologicalSignificance: The church grows by supply, not by strain, I believe: every joint furnishing its part, and the Spirit furnishing His.
RelatedTopics: Church; Unity; Outpouring of the Spirit
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and G5548; to smear over:--anoint.
BiblicalUsage: Epichrio means to smear over, to anoint — and Jesus anoints the blind man's eyes with clay made of spittle, then sends him to wash in Siloam. The man says, He put clay upon mine eyes, and I washed, and do see.
TheologicalSignificance: Jesus heals in His own way, I hold: strange means, simple obedience, and sight that no one can explain away.
RelatedEvents: The Healing of the Man Born Blind
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and G1209; to admit (as a guest or (figuratively) teacher):--receive.
BiblicalUsage: Epidechomai means to receive, to admit — and Diotrephes, who loves the preeminence, receives not the brethren, and forbids those who would receive them, casting them out of the church.
TheologicalSignificance: Refusing to receive the brethren is refusing Christ's own welcome, and John names it plainly so the church can see it for what it is.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and G1166; to exhibit (physically or mentally):--shew.
BiblicalUsage: Epideiknymi means to show, to exhibit, to prove by showing. Show me the tribute money, Jesus says; go show yourselves unto the priests, He tells the lepers; Apollos mightily convinced the Jews, showing by the Scriptures that Jesus was Christ; and God, willing to show the immutability of His counsel, confirmed it by an oath.
TheologicalSignificance: God shows rather than merely says, and each proof is evidence you can look at: the coin, the cleansed skin, the Scriptures, the oath. I believe showing is His way with doubters, and I should answer questions the same way — with something to see, not only something to hear.
RelatedEvents: The Healing of the Ten Lepers; Apollos Taught at Ephesus
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a compound of G1909 and G1218; to make oneself at home, i.e. (by extension) to reside (in a foreign country):--(be) dwelling (which were) there, stranger.
BiblicalUsage: Epidemeo means to reside as a stranger, to make oneself at home in a foreign place. Dwellers in Mesopotamia and strangers of Rome were at Pentecost; and the Athenians spent their time in nothing else but to tell or to hear some new thing.
TheologicalSignificance: The Christian's position is at home nowhere on earth for long, and always listening — the question is what we are listening for.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: middle voice from G1909 and G1299; to appoint besides, i.e. supplement (as a codicil):--add to.
BiblicalUsage: Epidiatassomai means to add to a covenant, to appoint besides — and Paul says no man disannulleth or addeth thereto once a covenant is confirmed. God's promise to Abraham cannot be edited by the law that came four hundred years later.
TheologicalSignificance: The covenant stands as God made it, I hold: no codicil, no addition, no fine print added later — the promise is the promise.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and G1325; to give over (by hand or surrender):--deliver unto, give, let (+ (her drive)), offer.
BiblicalUsage: Epididomi means to give over, to hand to — a book delivered to Jesus in the synagogue, a piece of broiled fish given to Him after the resurrection, a letter delivered to the church at Antioch. It is the word for what is placed into someone's hands.
TheologicalSignificance: The book, the fish, the letter — each one is given, and the giving is what moves the story forward. I believe the handing over is the heart of it: God places things into hands, and hands that receive become hands that carry.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and a derivative of G3717; to straighten further, i.e. (figuratively) arrange additionally:--set in order.
BiblicalUsage: Epidiorthoo means to set in order what remains — to straighten further. Paul left Titus in Crete to set in order the things that are wanting, and ordain elders in every city, as he had appointed him.
TheologicalSignificance: Paul did not leave Crete half-ordered, and the church still needs men who will set in order what remains.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and G1416; to set fully (as the sun):--go down.
BiblicalUsage: Epidyo means to go down, of the sun — and Paul uses it once, in the command not to let the sun go down upon your wrath. The day has an end, and anger is not to outlast it.
TheologicalSignificance: The sunset is God's deadline for anger, I believe: settle it before the day ends, or it will settle in you.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1933; suitableness, i.e. (by implication) equity, mildness:--clemency, gentleness.
BiblicalUsage: Epieikeia is gentleness, equity, clemency — the reasonableness that does not press a case to the letter. Paul asks Felix to hear him of his clemency a few words, and beseeches the Corinthians by the meekness and gentleness of Christ.
TheologicalSignificance: Gentleness is not weakness but equity, I hold: the strength that knows when to press and when to forbear, after the pattern of Christ.
RelatedEvents: Paul Before Felix, Festus, and Agrippa
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and G1503; appropriate, i.e. (by implication) mild:--gentle, moderation, patient.
BiblicalUsage: Epieikes means gentle, moderate, patient — the word for a spirit that is not harsh or grasping. Let your moderation be known unto all men; a bishop must be no striker, but gentle; we are to speak evil of no man, to be gentle, showing all meekness; and the wisdom from above is first pure, then peaceable, gentle, and easy to be intreated.
TheologicalSignificance: Gentleness is what heaven looks like when it wears a human face, and the church needs it more than it needs sharpness. I hold that the wisdom from above proves itself by being peaceable and easy to be intreated, and I want that wisdom, not the other kind.
RelatedPeople: Paul; Timothy; James, Brother of Jesus; Simon Peter
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and a derivative of G1062; to form affinity with, i.e. (specially) in a levirate way:--marry.
BiblicalUsage: Epigambreuo means to marry the widow of a brother, the levirate marriage — to raise up seed unto a brother. The Sadducees quote Moses to Jesus: if a man die having no children, his brother shall marry his wife and raise up seed unto his brother.
TheologicalSignificance: A brother's line was not to die out for want of someone to stand in, and the law shows how seriously God takes a name continuing.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and G1093; worldly (physically or morally):--earthly, in earth, terrestrial.
BiblicalUsage: Epigeios means earthly, of the earth — the things of this world set against the things above. If I have told you earthly things and ye believe not, how shall ye believe heavenly things; there are celestial bodies and bodies terrestrial; our earthly house of this tabernacle shall be dissolved; and the wisdom that is earthly is sensual, devilish.
TheologicalSignificance: Earthly wisdom and earthly houses pass, and only what is heavenly endures. I believe the word draws the line I live on every day, and I must not build my hope on what dissolves.
RelatedPeople: Jesus; Paul; James, Brother of Jesus
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and G1096; to arrive upon, i.e. spring up (as a wind):--blow.
BiblicalUsage: Epiginomai means to come upon, to spring up — and Luke uses it of a wind: the south wind blew, and the ship came the next day to Puteoli, near the end of Paul's long voyage to Rome.
TheologicalSignificance: After storm and shipwreck, a fair wind is God's quiet kindness carrying Paul home, and even a south wind is worth recording.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and G1097; to know upon some mark, i.e. recognize; by implication, to become fully acquainted with, to acknowledge:--(ac-, have, take)know(-ledge, well), perceive.
BiblicalUsage: Epiginosko means to know fully, to recognise — to know upon some mark. Ye shall know them by their fruits; the disciples' eyes were opened and they knew Him; the council perceived that Peter and John had been with Jesus; and now we see through a glass darkly, but then face to face, and I shall know even as also I am known.
TheologicalSignificance: To know God is to be changed by Him, and the day is coming when I shall know Him as fully as He knows me. I believe this is the knowledge that saves: not knowing about Christ, but recognising Him — by His fruits, by His voice, by His presence.
RelatedPeople: Jesus; Simon Peter; John the Apostle; Paul
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1921; recognition, i.e. (by implication) full discernment, acknowledgement:--(ac-)knowledge(-ing, - ment).
BiblicalUsage: Epignosis is full knowledge, recognition, acknowledgement — the knowledge that changes a person. By the law is the knowledge of sin; Paul prays for the spirit of wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of Him; he prays the Colossians be filled with the knowledge of His will; and grace and peace are multiplied through the knowledge of God and of Jesus our Lord.
TheologicalSignificance: Grace multiplies exactly as the knowledge of God grows, and that knowledge is acquaintance, not information. I hold that to know God is to be changed by Him, and Paul's prayers for full knowledge are prayers I should pray daily.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1924; an inscription:--superscription.
BiblicalUsage: Epigraphe is an inscription, a superscription — the words written on a thing. Whose is this image and superscription, Jesus asks of the penny: Caesar's. And over His own head on the cross the superscription read, This is the King of the Jews.
TheologicalSignificance: Caesar's image is on the coin, and Christ's kingship is over the cross, and I must decide which claim owns me. I believe the two inscriptions frame the whole story, and the superscription over Jesus is the truer one.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and G1125; to inscribe (physically or mentally):--inscription, write in (over, thereon).
BiblicalUsage: Epigrapho means to write upon, to inscribe. Paul finds an altar with the inscription, To the unknown God; and God promises, I will put my laws into their mind, and write them in their hearts; and the names of the twelve tribes are written on the twelve gates of the New Jerusalem.
TheologicalSignificance: God writes where it matters: not on stone that breaks, but on hearts that live. I hold that the altar to the unknown God shows how hungry men are for the God who writes there, and Paul's sermon is the answer to that hunger.
RelatedTopics: Word of God; New covenant; Evangelism
RelatedEvents: Paul at Athens; The New Jerusalem
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: middle voice from G1909 and G2564; to entitle; by implication, to invoke (for aid, worship, testimony, decision, etc.):--appeal (unto), call (on, upon), surname.
BiblicalUsage: Epikaleomai means to call upon, to invoke — to call on the name of the Lord. Whosoever shall call on the name of the Lord shall be saved; and Paul is sent to open eyes, that men may call on Him in whom they have believed.
TheologicalSignificance: Calling on His name is the simplest and greatest act of faith, I believe: a cry for help that God has promised to answer.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1943; a covering, i.e. (figuratively) pretext:--cloke.
BiblicalUsage: Epikalyma is a covering, a cloak — and Peter warns against using liberty as a cloke of maliciousness. Freedom is not a cover for wrongdoing; it is the dress of servants of God.
TheologicalSignificance: The same freedom that serves God can be pulled over evil, and Peter tells us not to wear it that way.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and G2572; to conceal, i.e. (figuratively) forgive:--cover.
BiblicalUsage: Epikalypto means to cover — and Paul quotes the psalm: Blessed are they whose iniquities are forgiven, and whose sins are covered. The covering is not hiding; it is forgiveness.
TheologicalSignificance: Covered sins are the only blessed ones, I hold: not sins denied, but sins forgiven and covered by God Himself.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and a derivative of G2672; imprecated, i.e. execrable:--accursed.
BiblicalUsage: Epikataratos means accursed, under a curse. Cursed is every one that continueth not in all things written in the book of the law to do them — and Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us.
TheologicalSignificance: The curse is real and the rescue is real, I believe: Christ took the curse so the blessing of Abraham might come on the Gentiles through Him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and G2523; to seat upon:--set on.
BiblicalUsage: Epikathizo means to set upon — and the disciples bring the ass and the colt, put their clothes on them, and set Jesus thereon, as He rides into Jerusalem.
TheologicalSignificance: No throne, no crown, only a borrowed colt and cloaks — and the King rides in anyway, and that is the coronation in miniature.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and G2749; to rest upon (literally or figuratively):--impose, be instant, (be) laid (there-, up-)on, (when) lay (on), lie (on), press upon.
BiblicalUsage: Epikeimai means to lie upon, to rest upon, to press — a weight that sits on something. The people pressed upon Jesus to hear the word; a stone lay upon the tomb of Lazarus; a tempest lay upon the ship for many days; necessity is laid upon Paul to preach; and divers washings were imposed until the time of reformation.
TheologicalSignificance: The crowd's pressure, the stone's weight, the storm's burden — and the necessity laid on Paul, which he called a woe if he did not preach. I believe what lies upon us shows what carries us, and I want the necessity of the gospel to lie on me the way it lay on him.
RelatedEvents: Raising of Lazarus; Paul Shipwrecked on Malta
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from Ἐπίκουρος (compare G1947) (a noted philosopher); an Epicurean or follower of Epicurus:--Epicurean.
BiblicalUsage: Epikoureios is an Epicurean, a follower of Epicurus — and certain philosophers of the Epicureans and of the Stoicks encountered Paul at Athens, saying, What will this babbler say?
TheologicalSignificance: Men who sought pleasure and peace met a man who preached Jesus and the resurrection, and the babbler had the better news.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a compound of G1909 and a (prolonged) form of the base of G2877 (in the sense of servant); assistance:--help.
BiblicalUsage: Epikouria is help, aid — and Paul says, Having therefore obtained help of God, I continue unto this day, witnessing both to small and great, saying none other things than those which the prophets and Moses did say should come.
TheologicalSignificance: Paul's whole defence rests on two words, I hold: help of God — without it he would not have continued a day, and with it he stood before kings.
RelatedEvents: Paul Before Felix, Festus, and Agrippa
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and G2919; to adjudge:--give sentence.
BiblicalUsage: Epikrino means to give sentence, to adjudge — and Pilate gave sentence that it should be as they required, and delivered Jesus to their will.
TheologicalSignificance: A judge who knew Jesus was innocent, giving sentence to please a crowd, is the darkest verdict in history.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: middle voice from G1909 and G2983; to seize (for help, injury, attainment, or any other purpose; literally or figuratively):--catch, lay hold (up-)on, take (by, hold of, on).
BiblicalUsage: Epilambanomai means to take hold of, to seize — for help, for rescue, for attainment. Jesus immediately stretched forth His hand and caught Peter sinking; He took a child and set him by Him; Barnabas took Paul and brought him to the apostles; He took on Him the seed of Abraham; and we are told to lay hold on eternal life.
TheologicalSignificance: Christ takes hold of the sinking, the child, and the seed of Abraham, and then tells us to take hold of eternal life the same way. I hold that the gospel is a taking hold, and the hand that caught Peter is the hand that holds me.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: middle voice from G1909 and G2990; to lose out of mind; by implication, to neglect:--(be) forget(-ful of).
BiblicalUsage: Epilanthanomai means to forget, to lose out of mind, to neglect. The disciples forgot to take bread; not one sparrow is forgotten before God; God is not unrighteous to forget your work and labour of love; be not forgetful to entertain strangers; and the hearer who forgets is like a man who looks in a glass and goes away.
TheologicalSignificance: God never forgets a sparrow or a labour of love, and I must not forget the stranger or the word I heard. I believe the word cuts both ways and comforts both ways, and remembering is a duty I owe in both directions.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: middle voice from G1909 and G3004; to surname, select:--call, choose.
BiblicalUsage: Epilegomai means to surname, to choose, to call by an added name. There is at Jerusalem a pool called in the Hebrew tongue Bethesda; and Paul chose Silas, and departed, being recommended by the brethren unto the grace of God.
TheologicalSignificance: Names given and choices made both mark a person, I believe: the pool is known by its name, and Paul by the companion he chose.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and G3007; to leave upon, i.e. (figuratively) to be insufficient for:--fail.
BiblicalUsage: Epileipo means to fail, to be insufficient — and the writer of Hebrews says, what shall I more say, for the time would fail me to tell of Gideon, and Barak, and Samson, and Jephthae, of David also, and Samuel, and of the prophets.
TheologicalSignificance: The failing of time is the highest praise, I hold: the stories of faith are too many to tell, and the list runs out before the faith does.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a derivative of G1950; negligence:--X forgetful.
BiblicalUsage: Epilesmone is forgetfulness — and James contrasts the forgetful hearer with the man who looks into the perfect law of liberty and continues therein, not being a forgetful hearer but a doer of the work.
TheologicalSignificance: Forgetfulness is the quiet enemy of faith, I believe: the word heard and forgotten is the word never obeyed.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and G3062; left over, i.e. remaining:--rest.
BiblicalUsage: Epiloipos means the rest, what remains — and Peter says we should no longer live the rest of our time in the flesh to the lusts of men, but to the will of God.
TheologicalSignificance: The past is past, and what remains is to be lived to the will of God — that is the real question of the rest of my time.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and G3089; to solve further, i.e. (figuratively) to explain, decide:--determine, expound.
BiblicalUsage: Epilyo means to explain, to decide, to solve further. Jesus expounded all things to His disciples when they were alone; and the townclerk says if ye enquire anything concerning other matters, it shall be determined in a lawful assembly.
TheologicalSignificance: Jesus explains to His own in private, and the city decides its business in lawful assembly, and both are order, not confusion.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1956; explanation, i.e. application:--interpretation.
BiblicalUsage: Epilysis is interpretation, explanation — and Peter says no prophecy of the Scripture is of any private interpretation. The prophets did not speak their own meaning into the words; holy men spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost.
TheologicalSignificance: Scripture interprets Scripture, and no one man's reading owns it — that is how this verse guards the Bible from private invention.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and G3140; to attest further, i.e. corroborate:--testify.
BiblicalUsage: Epimartyreo means to testify further, to corroborate — and Peter writes by Silvanus, exhorting and testifying that this is the true grace of God wherein ye stand.
TheologicalSignificance: Not new doctrine, but a witness that the grace they stand in is the true grace of God: that is Peter's parting gift, I believe.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1959; carefulness, i.e. kind attention (hospitality):--+ refresh self.
BiblicalUsage: Epimeleia is care, kind attention — and Julius, the centurion, courteously entreated Paul and gave him liberty to go unto his friends to refresh himself, on the voyage to Rome.
TheologicalSignificance: One courteous centurion, one visit to friends, and Paul is refreshed for the road ahead — the kindness of a stranger matters.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: middle voice from G1909 and the same as G3199; to care for (physically or otherwise):--take care of.
BiblicalUsage: Epimeleomai means to take care of — and the Samaritan takes care of the wounded man, leaving two pence with the host and saying, take care of him, and whatsoever thou spendest more, I will repay. Paul asks the same of a bishop: if a man know not how to rule his own house, how shall he take care of the church of God?
TheologicalSignificance: The Samaritan's care and the bishop's care are the same word, and the church is the inn where the wounded are left. I hold that taking care is the test of leadership and of love alike, and the two pence left with the host are still the measure.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: adverb from a derivative of G1959; carefully:--diligently.
BiblicalUsage: Epimelos means diligently, carefully — and the woman who loses one piece of silver lights a candle, sweeps the house, and seeks diligently till she finds it.
TheologicalSignificance: Candle lit, house swept, nothing left unturned until the lost is found: that is how God searches for us, I believe.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and G3306; to stay over, i.e. remain (figuratively, persevere):--abide (in), continue (in), tarry.
BiblicalUsage: Epimeno means to remain, to continue, to abide — to stay over and not leave. Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound? God forbid. Peter tarries certain days with Cornelius; Paul tells the Colossians to continue in the faith grounded and settled; and Timothy is told to continue in the doctrine, for in doing this thou shalt save thyself and them that hear thee.
TheologicalSignificance: Continuing is the whole of the Christian life: not starting well, but staying — grounded, settled, and not moved away from the hope of the gospel. I believe the staying is the proof, and Timothy's charge is mine too: continue in the doctrine, and save both yourself and your hearers.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and G3506; to nod at, i.e. (by implication) to assent:--consent.
BiblicalUsage: Epineuo means to nod assent, to consent — and the Jews at Ephesus desire Paul to tarry longer with them, but he consented not, and bade them farewell.
TheologicalSignificance: Paul's no is as instructive as his yes, I hold: he would not stay where God had not sent him, even when the invitation was warm.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and G3563; attention of the mind, i.e. (by implication) purpose:--thought.
BiblicalUsage: Epinoia is a thought, a purpose of the mind — and Peter tells Simon the sorcerer to repent and pray, if perhaps the thought of thine heart may be forgiven thee, for thou art in the gall of bitterness and the bond of iniquity.
TheologicalSignificance: God sees the thought before the act, I believe: Simon's heart was already in bonds, and repentance had to reach the thought, not only the deed.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1965; to commit perjury:--forswear self.
BiblicalUsage: Epiorkeo means to swear falsely, to forswear oneself — and Jesus quotes the old word: Thou shalt not forswear thyself, but shalt perform unto the Lord thine oaths. Then He raises the standard higher: swear not at all.
TheologicalSignificance: Jesus is after a heart that needs no oath to be believed, I hold: let your yes be yes, and your no be no.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and G3727; on oath, i.e. (falsely) a forswearer:--perjured person.
BiblicalUsage: Epiorkos is a perjured person, one who swears falsely — listed by Paul among those for whom the law is made: lawless, disobedient, ungodly, murderers, whoremongers, menstealers, liars, and perjured persons.
TheologicalSignificance: The law names the perjurer because a false oath breaks trust at its root, and trust is what a people runs on.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably from G2031; properly, affable, i.e. mild or kind:--gentle.
BiblicalUsage: Epios means gentle, mild, kind — affable. Paul says, we were gentle among you, even as a nurse cherisheth her children; and the servant of the Lord must not strive, but be gentle unto all men, apt to teach, patient.
TheologicalSignificance: A nurse's care and a teacher's patience — gentleness is strength under control, and the Lord's servant cannot afford to lose it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: feminine singular participle of a compound of G1909 and εἶμι (to go); supervening, i.e. (G2250 or G3571 being expressed or implied) the ensuing day or night:--following, next.
BiblicalUsage: Epiousa is the coming day, the next day — the day that follows. Stephen says the next day Moses showed himself to two Israelites striving; Paul's company sails, and the next day comes to Neapolis; and the next day they arrive over against Chios.
TheologicalSignificance: Moses returns, Paul sails on, and God's work does not wait for a convenient morning: the next day is where the story keeps moving.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: perhaps from the same as G1966; tomorrow's; but more probably from G1909 and a derivative of the present participle feminine of G1510; for subsistence, i.e. needful:--daily.
BiblicalUsage: Epiousios is the word for daily bread — tomorrow's bread, or bread for the coming day, in the prayer Jesus taught. Give us this day our daily bread.
TheologicalSignificance: Enough for today, asked for today, from the Father who gives today: daily bread is the whole of trust in one phrase.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and G5316; to shine upon, i.e. become (literally) visible or (figuratively) known:--appear, give light.
BiblicalUsage: Epiphaino means to shine upon, to appear, to become visible. To give light to them that sit in darkness and in the shadow of death, to guide our feet into the way of peace; the grace of God that bringeth salvation hath appeared to all men; and after the kindness and love of God our Saviour toward man appeared.
TheologicalSignificance: Light shining on people who sat in darkness is the gospel itself, and once it has appeared, no one can honestly say they never saw it. I believe the appearing is both past and present: grace appeared to all men, and it still gives light to whoever sits in darkness today.
RelatedPeople: Paul; Zechariah, Father of John the Baptist
RelatedEvents: The Birth of John the Baptist
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2016; a manifestation, i.e. (specially) the advent of Christ (past or future):--appearing, brightness.
BiblicalUsage: Epiphaneia is an appearing, a manifestation — the advent of Christ, past and future. He hath abolished death and brought life and immortality to light through the gospel by His appearing; we look for the blessed hope and the glorious appearing of our great God and Saviour; and there is a crown of righteousness for all them that love His appearing.
TheologicalSignificance: He appeared once to abolish death, and He will appear again to crown those who love Him, and my life is lived between the two. I hold that the appearing has two faces, and loving His appearing is the surest sign I am ready for it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2014; conspicuous, i.e. (figuratively) memorable:--notable.
BiblicalUsage: Epiphanes means notable, conspicuous, memorable — and Peter quotes Joel: the sun shall be turned into darkness and the moon into blood, before that great and notable day of the Lord come.
TheologicalSignificance: A day so great it darkens the sun is worth the warning, and the only safe place on it is calling on the name of the Lord.
RelatedTopics: Day of the Lord; Judgment; Prophecy
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a form of G2014; to illuminate (figuratively):--give light.
BiblicalUsage: Epiphauo means to give light, to shine upon — and Paul quotes the call: Awake thou that sleepest, and arise from the dead, and Christ shall give thee light.
TheologicalSignificance: He does not only show the way, He shines on the sleeper until the sleeper wakes: the light is Christ Himself.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and G5342; to bear upon (or further), i.e. adduce (personally or judicially (accuse, inflict)), superinduce:--add, bring (against), take.
BiblicalUsage: Epiphero means to bring upon, to bring against — to adduce a charge. Paul asks, is God unrighteous who taketh vengeance, if our unrighteousness commend the righteousness of God? And Michael the archangel, when disputing with the devil, durst not bring against him a railing accusation.
TheologicalSignificance: If an archangel would not rail, I should not either, and the restraint of Michael rebukes my readiness to accuse.
RelatedEvents: Michael Disputes over the Body of Moses
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and G5455; to call at something, i.e. exclaim:--cry (against), give a shout.
BiblicalUsage: Epiphoneo means to cry out against, to shout at — and in every case the subject is a crowd. They cried, saying, Crucify him, crucify him; the people gave a shout, It is the voice of a god, and not of a man; some cried one thing, some another; and they cried against Paul until the chief captain could not learn the certainty.
TheologicalSignificance: A crowd's shout crucified Jesus, crowned Herod, and nearly killed Paul, and I must beware of joining a shout I have not examined. I believe the crowd's voice is the most dangerous sound in the Gospels, because it feels like agreement and acts like judgment.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a form of G2017; to begin to grow light:--begin to dawn, X draw on.
BiblicalUsage: Epiphosko means to begin to dawn, to draw on — and Matthew says, as it began to dawn toward the first day of the week, Mary Magdalene and the other Mary came to see the sepulchre; and Luke says the sabbath drew on as they laid Jesus in the tomb.
TheologicalSignificance: The sabbath drawing on over a sealed tomb, and the first day dawning on an empty one: the dawning holds the hinge of history.
RelatedEvents: The Resurrection; The Burial of Jesus
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and G4098; to embrace (with affection) or seize (with more or less violence; literally or figuratively):--fall into (on, upon) lie on, press upon.
BiblicalUsage: Epipipto means to fall upon — to embrace, to seize, to come over. The father ran and fell on the prodigal's neck and kissed him; the Holy Ghost fell on all them which heard the word at Cornelius's house; fear fell on all at Ephesus; and the reproaches of them that reproached thee fell on me.
TheologicalSignificance: A father's embrace, the Spirit's coming, and Christ bearing reproaches that were not His own — that is what falls upon us. I hold that what falls reveals the heart of God, and the prodigal's welcome is the picture I should carry into every return.
RelatedTopics: Grace; Outpouring of the Spirit; Repentance
RelatedEvents: The Prodigal Son; Peter and Cornelius
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and G4141; to chastise, i.e. (with words) to upbraid:--rebuke.
BiblicalUsage: Epiplesso means to rebuke, to upbraid — and Paul tells Timothy, rebuke not an elder, but intreat him as a father, and the younger men as brethren.
TheologicalSignificance: The manner of correction matters as much as the correction, I believe: an elder is entreated as a father, not scolded as a servant.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and G4155; to throttle upon, i.e. (figuratively) overgrow:--choke.
BiblicalUsage: Epipnigo means to choke, to throttle upon — and the seed that fell among thorns was choked by them as they sprung up, and it yielded no fruit.
TheologicalSignificance: Cares and riches grow up around the word until it cannot breathe, and the thorns are the picture of a crowded heart.
RelatedTopics: Jesus Christ; Temptation; Fruit of the Spirit
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and G4198; to journey further, i.e. travel on (reach):--come.
BiblicalUsage: Epiporeuomai means to journey on, to come together from every side — and when much people were gathered together, and were come to Him out of every city, Jesus spake by a parable.
TheologicalSignificance: People came from every city to hear Him, and He answered with a story about seed — that is the hunger the gathering shows.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and potheo (to yearn); to dote upon, i.e. intensely crave possession (lawfully or wrongfully):--(earnestly) desire (greatly), (greatly) long (after), lust.
BiblicalUsage: Epipotheo means to long for, to yearn intensely — to dote upon with lawful desire. Paul longs to see the Romans that he may impart a spiritual gift; we groan, earnestly desiring to be clothed upon with our house from heaven; God is my record, how greatly I long after you all in the bowels of Jesus Christ; and as newborn babes, desire the sincere milk of the word, that ye may grow thereby.
TheologicalSignificance: A heart that longs for nothing is a heart that is not alive, and the newborn, the apostle, and the saint all prove it. I believe longing is the mark of life: milk for the newborn, brethren for the apostle, heaven for the saint.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1971; a longing for:--earnest (vehement) desire.
BiblicalUsage: Epipothesis is earnest longing, vehement desire — and Paul tells of Titus's earnest desire toward the Corinthians, his mourning and fervent mind; and of the Corinthians' own vehement desire, their zeal and revenge against the sin that had grieved him.
TheologicalSignificance: Longing that leads to repentance is the proof of love, I believe: Titus longed to see them, and they longed to make it right.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and a derivative of the latter part of G1971; yearned upon, i.e. greatly loved:--longed for.
BiblicalUsage: Epipothetos means longed for, greatly loved — and Paul calls the Philippians his brethren dearly beloved and longed for, my joy and crown, so stand fast in the Lord, my dearly beloved.
TheologicalSignificance: Not as a task, but as a joy and a crown: that is how Paul loved his people, longed for and not merely managed.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1971; intense longing:--great desire.
BiblicalUsage: Epipothia is great desire, intense longing — and Paul says, having a great desire these many years to come unto you, whensoever I take my journey into Spain, I will come to you.
TheologicalSignificance: Years of desire, carried patiently until the road opens: Paul's longing to visit Rome shows the apostle's heart.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and the base of G4476; to stitch upon, i.e. fasten with the needle:--sew on.
BiblicalUsage: Epirrhapto means to sew on, to stitch upon — and no man seweth a piece of new cloth on an old garment, else the new piece that filled it up taketh away from the old, and the rent is made worse.
TheologicalSignificance: The new covenant is not sewn onto the old life, I hold: it is a new garment altogether, and the stitching proves it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and G4496; to throw upon (literally or figuratively):--cast upon.
BiblicalUsage: Epirrhipto means to cast upon — to throw a burden onto another. The disciples cast their garments upon the colt and set Jesus thereon; and Peter says, casting all your care upon Him, for He careth for you.
TheologicalSignificance: Garments cast on the colt for the King, and cares cast on the King for us: both are acts of trust, and the two castings belong together.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and G2480; to avail further, i.e. (figuratively) insist stoutly:--be the more fierce.
BiblicalUsage: Epischyo means to grow stronger, to insist more fiercely — and the chief priests were the more fierce, saying, He stirreth up the people, teaching throughout all Jewry, beginning from Galilee to this place.
TheologicalSignificance: Louder, not truer: that is what accusation becomes when it has no case, and Pilate heard the volume, not the evidence.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and some form of the base of G4591; remarkable, i.e. (figuratively) eminent:--notable, of note.
BiblicalUsage: Episemos means notable, of note, remarkable — and the word cuts both ways. Barabbas was a notable prisoner, chosen over Jesus; and Andronicus and Junia are of note among the apostles, fellow prisoners with Paul.
TheologicalSignificance: Barabbas was notable and guilty, Andronicus and Junia were notable and faithful, and being notable is no measure of being right.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a compound of G1909 and a derivative of G4621; a provisioning, i.e. (concretely) food:--victuals.
BiblicalUsage: Episitismos is a provisioning, food for the journey — and the twelve say to Jesus, send the multitude away, that they may go into the towns and country round about, and lodge, and get victuals, for we are here in a desert place.
TheologicalSignificance: They saw a desert and no victuals, and Jesus saw five thousand people He intended to feed: the disciples' practical worry sets up the miracle.
RelatedEvents: The Feeding of the Five Thousand
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and G4637; to tent upon, i.e. (figuratively) abide with:--rest upon.
BiblicalUsage: Episkenoo means to rest upon, to tent upon — and Christ says to Paul, My grace is sufficient for thee, for my strength is made perfect in weakness, that the power of Christ may rest upon me.
TheologicalSignificance: Not removal, but presence: the resting is the answer to the thorn, and Christ's power pitches its tent over my weakness.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: middle voice from G1909 and the base of G4649; to inspect, i.e. (by implication) to select; by extension, to go to see, relieve:--look out, visit.
BiblicalUsage: Episkeptomai means to visit, to look upon, to inspect with care. Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, for He hath visited and redeemed His people; God hath visited His people, the crowd says at Nain; I was sick, and ye visited me; let us go again and visit our brethren; and pure religion is to visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction.
TheologicalSignificance: He visited us in Christ, and pure religion is visiting those He loves — the sick, the fatherless, the widow — in theirs. I believe visiting is God's own pattern, and the visit is where the gospel stops being words.
RelatedPeople: Jesus; James, Brother of Jesus; Paul; Barnabas
RelatedEvents: The Raising of the Widow's Son at Nain
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and a derivative of G4639; to cast a shade upon, i.e. (by analogy) to envelop in a haze of brilliancy; figuratively, to invest with preternatural influence:--overshadow.
BiblicalUsage: Episkiazo means to overshadow, to cast a shade upon. The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee; a bright cloud overshadowed them on the mountain, and a voice said, This is my beloved Son; and the sick were laid in the streets, that the shadow of Peter passing by might overshadow some of them.
TheologicalSignificance: A cloud on the mountain, the Spirit on Mary, a shadow on the street — and in each case, power follows the shade. I hold that the overshadowing is God's nearness made visible, and I should expect His presence to bring His power with it.
RelatedTopics: Presence of God; Outpouring of the Spirit; Jesus Christ
RelatedPeople: Jesus; Simon Peter; Mary, Mother of Jesus
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1980; inspection (for relief); by implication, superintendence; specially, the Christian "episcopate":--the office of a "bishop", bishoprick, visitation.
BiblicalUsage: Episkope is visitation, oversight, inspection — the office of a bishop. Jerusalem knew not the time of her visitation; let his habitation be desolate, and his bishoprick let another take; if a man desire the office of a bishop, he desireth a good work; and the Gentiles shall glorify God in the day of visitation.
TheologicalSignificance: God visits to redeem and to reckon, and the bishop's office is to watch in the meantime, as one who will give account. I believe visitation is both mercy and judgment, and Jerusalem's failure to know the time of hers is the warning.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and G4648; to oversee; by implication, to beware:--look diligently, take the oversight.
BiblicalUsage: Episkopeo means to oversee, to look diligently — to take the oversight. Looking diligently lest any man fail of the grace of God, lest any root of bitterness springing up trouble you; and feed the flock of God which is among you, taking the oversight thereof, not by constraint, but willingly.
TheologicalSignificance: Bitterness springs up quietly, and the overseer's eye must catch it early, because oversight is watching for roots, not only for wolves.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and G4649 (in the sense of G1983); a superintendent, i.e. Christian officer in genitive case charge of a (or the) church (literally or figuratively):--bishop, overseer.
BiblicalUsage: Episkopos is an overseer, a bishop — a superintendent of the flock. Take heed to the flock over which the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers, to feed the church of God; a bishop must be blameless, the husband of one wife, vigilant, sober; and ye are now returned unto the Shepherd and Bishop of your souls.
TheologicalSignificance: Christ is the Bishop of our souls first, and the overseers serve under Him. I believe the bishop's office only makes sense that way: He oversees us, and those who oversee the flock answer to the Shepherd.
RelatedEvents: Paul's Farewell to the Ephesian Elders
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and G4987; to accumulate further, i.e. (figuratively) seek additionally:--heap.
BiblicalUsage: Episoreuo means to heap up, to accumulate teachers — and Paul warns that the time will come when men will not endure sound doctrine, but after their own lusts shall they heap to themselves teachers, having itching ears.
TheologicalSignificance: Not one teacher too many, but teachers chosen to say what we already want to hear: heaping teachers is the mark of itching ears.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and G4685; to draw over, i.e. (with G203 implied) efface the mark of circumcision (by recovering with the foreskin):--become uncircumcised.
BiblicalUsage: Epispaomai means to draw over, to efface the mark of circumcision — and Paul says, Is any man called being circumcised? Let him not become uncircumcised, and let the uncircumcised man not seek circumcision.
TheologicalSignificance: The outward mark is not the matter, I believe: keeping the commandments of God is.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a compound of G1909 and σφάλλω (to trip); figuratively, insecure:--dangerous.
BiblicalUsage: Episphales means dangerous, insecure — and Paul warns that sailing was now dangerous, because the fast was already past, and Paul admonished them.
TheologicalSignificance: Paul saw the danger before the storm did, and the ship sailed anyway — to its cost, and the warning was wisdom, not fear.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: apparently a middle voice of G2186 (with G3563 implied); to put the mind upon, i.e. comprehend, or be acquainted with:--know, understand.
BiblicalUsage: Epistamai means to know, to understand, to put the mind upon — the knowledge that comes from attention. Ye know how it is an unlawful thing for a man that is a Jew to keep company with one of another nation; the king knoweth of these things, before whom I speak freely; ye know not what shall be on the morrow; and they speak evil of the things they know not.
TheologicalSignificance: I should know before I speak, and hold lightly what I cannot know. I hold that knowing is a duty: James says we do not know tomorrow, and Jude says men speak evil of what they do not know.
RelatedPeople: Paul; Simon Peter; James, Brother of Jesus
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and a presumed derivative of G2476; an appointee over, i.e. commander (teacher):--master.
BiblicalUsage: Epistates is Master — the title the disciples use for Jesus in Luke alone. Master, we have toiled all the night and have taken nothing; Master, Master, we perish; Master, it is good for us to be here; Master, we saw one casting out devils in thy name; and the lepers lift up their voices, Jesus, Master, have mercy on us.
TheologicalSignificance: He is the one in charge of the boat, the mountain, and the mercy, and Master is the right name for Him. I believe the title says what the disciples knew, and what I am still learning: the boat is His, and so is the storm.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and G4724; to enjoin (by writing), i.e. (genitive case) to communicate by letter (for any purpose):--write (a letter, unto).
BiblicalUsage: Epistello means to enjoin by letter, to write with authority — and the council writes to the Gentiles that they abstain from pollutions of idols, and from fornication, and from things strangled, and from blood; and the writer of Hebrews says, I beseech you, suffer the word of exhortation, for I have written a letter unto you in few words.
TheologicalSignificance: What is written and sent binds the churches together across the miles, and a letter can carry the authority of a council.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1987; intelligent:--endued with knowledge.
BiblicalUsage: Epistemon means understanding, endued with knowledge — and James asks, Who is a wise man and endued with knowledge among you? Let him shew out of a good conversation his works with meekness of wisdom.
TheologicalSignificance: The wise man proves it by his works, not by his words, and true knowledge shows itself in meekness.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and G4741; to support further, i.e. reestablish:--confirm, strengthen.
BiblicalUsage: Episterizo means to strengthen, to confirm, to establish again — to put support under what is already standing. Paul and Barnabas confirm the souls of the disciples, exhorting them to continue in the faith, and that we must through much tribulation enter into the kingdom of God; Judas and Silas exhort and confirm the brethren with many words.
TheologicalSignificance: The gospel plants, and then someone must return to strengthen — and tribulation is part of the strengthening, not a sign it failed. I hold that confirmation is the apostles' second visit, and the church still needs it: souls confirmed, not merely converted.
RelatedPeople: Paul; Barnabas; Silas; Judas, Son of James
RelatedEvents: Paul and Barnabas at Iconium; Jerusalem Council
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1989; a written message:--"epistle," letter.
BiblicalUsage: Epistole is a letter, an epistle — a written message that travels where the writer cannot. Saul desires letters to Damascus to bind the disciples; Paul says, ye are our epistle written in our hearts, known and read of all men; and Peter warns that in Paul's epistles are some things hard to be understood, which the unlearned wrestle to their destruction.
TheologicalSignificance: A page carries the writer's heart across the miles, and a church becomes a letter others can read. I believe the letter is God's chosen way to speak across distance, and my life is the epistle my neighbours are reading.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and G4750; to put something over the mouth, i.e. (figuratively) to silence:--stop mouths.
BiblicalUsage: Epistomizo means to stop the mouth, to silence — and Paul says of false teachers, whose mouths must be stopped, who subvert whole houses, teaching things which they ought not, for filthy lucre's sake.
TheologicalSignificance: When teaching subverts whole houses for money, silence is mercy to the house, and some mouths must be stopped, not answered.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and G4762; to revert (literally, figuratively or morally):--come (go) again, convert, (re-)turn (about, again).
BiblicalUsage: Epistrepho means to turn, to return, to be converted — to come back to where you belong. He shall turn many of the children of Israel to the Lord their God; repent ye therefore, and be converted, that your sins may be blotted out; to open their eyes, and to turn them from darkness to light; and ye were as sheep going astray, but are now returned unto the Shepherd and Bishop of your souls.
TheologicalSignificance: From darkness to light, from straying to the Shepherd — the turning is both God's work and mine. I believe turning is the whole of conversion, and the blotting out of sins follows the turning, not the other way round.
RelatedPeople: Jesus; Simon Peter; Paul; James, Brother of Jesus
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1994; reversion, i.e. morally, revolution:--conversion.
BiblicalUsage: Epistrophe is conversion — a turning — and Paul and Barnabas, passing through Phenice and Samaria, declare the conversion of the Gentiles, and cause great joy unto all the brethren.
TheologicalSignificance: When Gentiles turn to God, the whole church rejoices, and conversion is never a private event.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and G4863; to collect upon the same place:--gather (together).
BiblicalUsage: Episynago means to gather together — to collect upon the same place. O Jerusalem, how often would I have gathered thy children together, even as a hen gathereth her chickens under her wings, and ye would not; and He shall send His angels, and they shall gather together His elect from the four winds.
TheologicalSignificance: The hen who would gather and was refused, and the angels who will gather and cannot be refused — the gathering shows the heart of Christ twice. I believe His longing to gather Jerusalem is the measure of His love for me, and His final gathering is the measure of His power.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1996; a complete collection; especially a Christian meeting (for worship):--assembling (gathering) together.
BiblicalUsage: Episynagoge is a gathering together, an assembling — our gathering together unto Him at His coming, and the assembling of ourselves together, which we are not to forsake, as the manner of some is, but exhorting one another, and so much the more, as ye see the day approaching.
TheologicalSignificance: We gather now because we shall be gathered then, and neither gathering should be forsaken.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and G4936; to hasten together upon one place (or a particular occasion):--come running together.
BiblicalUsage: Episyntrecho means to run together, to hasten to one place — and when Jesus saw that the people came running together, He rebuked the foul spirit, saying, Thou dumb and deaf spirit, I charge thee, come out of him.
TheologicalSignificance: People hastening together, and Jesus acting before the crowd can settle: the running crowd is the scene of so many miracles.
RelatedEvents: The Healing of the Demon-Possessed Boy
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from the middle voice of a compound of G1909 and G4921; a conspiracy, i.e. concourse (riotous or friendly):--that which cometh upon, + raising up.
BiblicalUsage: Episystasis is a coming upon, a conspiracy, a pressure that crowds in. Paul says, beside those things that are without, that which cometh upon me daily, the care of all the churches; and he answers his accusers that they neither found him in the temple disputing, nor raising up the people.
TheologicalSignificance: Not one crisis, but the care of all the churches, coming upon him every day: that is the apostle's real burden.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2004; an injunction or decree; by implication, authoritativeness:--authority, commandment.
BiblicalUsage: Epitage is a command, an injunction, an authoritative charge. Paul speaks by permission and not of commandment; he gives his judgment as one that hath obtained mercy; he proves the sincerity of love not by commandment; and he is an apostle by the commandment of God our Saviour.
TheologicalSignificance: Not every wise word is a command, and not every command may be softened into advice. I hold that Paul's careful line between permission and commandment teaches me to do the same, and the church is healthier when the two are not confused.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and G5021; to arrange upon, i.e. order:--charge, command, injoin.
BiblicalUsage: Epitasso means to command, to charge, to arrange upon. The people are amazed: with authority He commands even the unclean spirits, and they obey Him; He commands the winds and water, and they cease — yet Paul, who might boldly enjoin Philemon, chooses for love's sake to beseech instead.
TheologicalSignificance: Demons obey, winds obey — and the apostle who could command chooses to beseech, because love outranks command. I believe the authority is the point, and the restraint is the greater point: power that could compel, choosing to persuade.
RelatedEvents: Jesus Heals a Demoniac in the Capernaum Synagogue
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from ἐπιτηδές (enough); serviceable, i.e. (by implication) requisite:--things which are needful.
BiblicalUsage: Epitedeios means needful, serviceable — the things which are needful. James asks, if a brother or sister be naked, and destitute of daily food, and one of you say, Depart in peace, be ye warmed and filled, notwithstanding ye give them not those things which are needful to the body, what doth it profit?
TheologicalSignificance: A blessing that gives nothing needful profits nothing, and needful things are the test of words.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and G5055; to fulfill further (or completely), i.e. execute; by implication, to terminate, undergo:--accomplish, do, finish, (make) (perfect), perform(X -ance).
BiblicalUsage: Epiteleo means to finish, to complete, to perform — to bring a work to its end. He which hath begun a good work in you will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ; having begun in the Spirit, are ye now made perfect by the flesh? and the priests accomplish the service of God continually.
TheologicalSignificance: God does not start a good work in me and leave it half done. I hold that the Finisher is the same as the Beginner, and He will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ — that is my assurance, not my achievement.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and G2288; doomed to death:--appointed to death.
BiblicalUsage: Epithanatios means appointed to death, doomed to die — and Paul says, I think God hath set forth us the apostles last, as it were appointed to death, for we are made a spectacle unto the world, and to angels, and to men.
TheologicalSignificance: Last, exposed, appointed to death — and yet the gospel advanced on men the world counted as dying, and that is Paul's spectacle.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2007; an imposition (of hands officially):--laying (putting) on.
BiblicalUsage: Epithesis is the laying on of hands — the imposition by which gifts are given and ministries confirmed. Simon sees that through laying on of the apostles' hands the Holy Ghost is given; Timothy is told to neglect not the gift given him by prophecy, with the laying on of the hands of the presbytery; and Paul tells him to stir up the gift of God which is in thee by the putting on of my hands.
TheologicalSignificance: Hands, prayer, and a gift that must be stirred up, not left to cool — that is what the laying on of hands means. I believe the gift is real and the church stands behind it, and Timothy's charge is mine: stir up what God has given.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and G2372; to set the heart upon, i.e. long for (rightfully or otherwise):--covet, desire, would fain, lust (after).
BiblicalUsage: Epithymeo means to set the heart upon, to long for — rightly or wrongly. Whosoever looketh on a woman to lust after her hath committed adultery already in his heart; with desire I have desired to eat this passover with you; I had not known lust, except the law had said, Thou shalt not covet; and the flesh lusteth against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh.
TheologicalSignificance: Set on Christ, desire is devotion; set on what is forbidden, it is adultery before the act. I believe desire is the hinge of the heart, and the law's job is to name it so I can fight it — before it becomes the deed.
RelatedPeople: Jesus; Paul; James, Brother of Jesus
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1937; a craver:--+ lust after.
BiblicalUsage: In Scripture, epithymētḗs means a craver. It occurs just once, in 1 Corinthians.
TheologicalSignificance: I take epithymētḗs as it stands — craver — and read the passage with that plain sense in mind.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1937; a longing (especially for what is forbidden):--concupiscence, desire, lust (after).
BiblicalUsage: Epithymía is desire — a longing, especially for what is forbidden. The lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life are all of this world, John says, and they do not come from the Father. Paul traces sin's work through it: where there is no law, desire has no handle, but the commandment wakes it up.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe epithymía is the word for the wanting that rules us before Christ rules us. I hold that the answer is not to pretend the wanting is gone, but to walk in the Spirit, so the desire no longer gets its way.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and G5091; to tax upon, i.e. censure or admonish; by implication, forbid:--(straitly) charge, rebuke.
BiblicalUsage: Epitimáō means to rebuke — to speak sharply against, to charge with authority. Jesus rebukes the winds and the sea, rebukes unclean spirits, and rebukes Peter; Paul charges Timothy to reprove, rebuke, and exhort. It is correction with authority behind it, not mere scolding.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe epitimáō shows that rebuke belongs to love: Jesus rebukes what harms His people, and He commands His servants to do the same. I hold that a rebuke spoken in season is a mercy, not an insult.
RelatedEvents: Jesus Calms the Storm; Jesus Heals a Demoniac in the Capernaum Synagogue
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a compound of G1909 and G5092; properly, esteem, i.e. citizenship; used (in the sense of G2008) of a penalty:--punishment.
BiblicalUsage: Epitimía means punishment — the penalty the church imposes, in the sense of a rebuke carried through. It occurs just once, where Paul says the punishment inflicted by many is enough for the man who sinned. The word is discipline with a limit: enough is enough.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe epitimía is the measure of church discipline: the punishment is enough when it brings the man back, not when it breaks him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and G5087; to impose (in a friendly or hostile sense):--add unto, lade, lay upon, put (up) on, set on (up), + surname, X wound.
BiblicalUsage: Epitíthēmi means to lay upon — to put a hand, a name, or a burden on something. The apostles lay hands on the seven, and on new believers who receive the Spirit; Jesus lays His hands on children and blesses them. The laying on of hands is the visible sign of blessing and commissioning.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe epitíthēmi is a word for how blessing passes from person to person: by touch, in the open, before witnesses. I hold that the laying on of hands still matters, because God still works through His people's hands.
RelatedEvents: Martyrdom of Stephen; Philip Preaches in Samaria
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and the base of G5157; to turn over (transfer), i.e. allow:--give leave (liberty, license), let, permit, suffer.
BiblicalUsage: Epitrépō means to allow — to turn a matter over to someone and let them do it. Jesus allows the demons to enter the swine; Paul will not allow a woman to teach or to usurp authority over a man; Agrippa allows Paul to speak for himself. Permission is never casual in Scripture — it is a judgment about what may go ahead.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe epitrépo reminds me that permission is a form of authority: what I allow, I answer for. I hold that the church should give permission slowly and withhold it plainly, the way Paul does.
RelatedEvents: Paul's Missionary Journeys; Jesus Heals the Gerasene Demoniac
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2010; permission, i.e. (by implication) full power:--commission.
BiblicalUsage: epitropḗ means permission, that is full power. It occurs just once, in Acts.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold epitropḗ to its plain sense and let the passage speak for itself.
RelatedEvents: Paul Before Felix, Festus, and Agrippa
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and G5158 (in the sense of G2011); a commissioner, i.e. domestic manager, guardian:--steward, tutor.
BiblicalUsage: The word epítropos covers a commissioner. Across Matthew, Luke, and Galatians it keeps the same plain meaning. It is a small word, and its few uses are each worth the look.
TheologicalSignificance: I am convinced epítropos is worth knowing, because the passages above lean on it. It is a small word with a steady job, and I trust it to do that job.
RelatedEvents: The Parable of the Workers in the Vineyard
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and G5177; to chance upon, i.e. (by implication) to attain:--obtain.
BiblicalUsage: Epitynchánō means to chance upon — to attain, to obtain what you sought. Abraham obtained the promise; the elders obtained a good report through faith; and Israel did not obtain what it sought, because it sought it by works. It is the word for getting hold of what God promised.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe epitynchánō is the word for faith's reward: those who seek God by faith obtain what they seek. I hold that the difference is the way — by faith, not by works — and the promise is sure to those who come that way.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and G2212; to search (inquire) for; intensively, to demand, to crave:--desire, enquire, seek (after, for).
BiblicalUsage: Epizētéō means to seek after — to search for, to demand, to inquire earnestly. The Gentiles seek after these things, Jesus says; the scribes seek a sign; and the Hebrews seek a country of their own, a heavenly one. It is the word for what a heart is set on finding.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe epizētéō is the word for the direction of my life: what I seek after is what I worship. I hold that seeking first the kingdom is the only seeking that ends in finding.
RelatedEvents: The Sermon on the Mount; Peter's Escape from Prison
