Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a primary verb (used only in the definite past tense, the others being borrowed from G2046, G4483, and G5346); to speak or say (by word or writing):--answer, bid, bring word, call, command, grant, say (on), speak, tell. Compare G3004.
BiblicalUsage: Épō is the aorist stem of the verb for saying — the 'he said' and 'they said' of the Gospels. It is the form the narrative uses when someone speaks and the story moves on it. You meet it everywhere the Gospels report speech.
TheologicalSignificance: I take épō as it stands — the plain past tense of saying — and let the reported words carry the weight, not the verb itself.
RelatedEvents: The Temptation in the Wilderness; Raising of Lazarus
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and G3618; to build upon, i.e. (figuratively) to rear up:--build thereon (thereupon, on, upon).
BiblicalUsage: Epoikodoméō means to build upon — to rear up on a foundation already laid. Paul lays the foundation and another builds on it; the church is built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets; and believers are built up together into a holy temple. It is the word for the church's construction.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe epoikodoméō is the word for the church: one foundation, many builders, and Christ the cornerstone. I hold that I am both a builder and a stone, and I should take care how I build.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and ὀκέλλω (to urge); to drive upon the shore, i.e. to beach a vessel:--run aground.
BiblicalUsage: Epokéllō means to drive a ship upon the shore — to run aground. It occurs just once, when Paul's ship strikes the sandbar and the prow sticks fast. The word is the moment the voyage ends and the wreck begins.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that epokéllō is worth knowing because it marks the exact turn in Paul's journey: the ship is lost, and the men are saved anyway.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and G3687; to name further, i.e. denominate:--call.
BiblicalUsage: Eponomázō means to be called by a name — to bear a name as your own. It occurs just once, where Paul says the Jew who relies on the law is called a Jew. The name is a claim, and Paul tests whether the life matches it.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe eponomázō cuts straight to the point: a name you carry is a claim you have to live up to.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and a presumed derivative of G3700; a looker-on:--eye-witness.
BiblicalUsage: epóptēs means a looker-on. It occurs just once, in 2 Peter.
TheologicalSignificance: My position is to take epóptēs at face value and move on to the passage itself.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and a derivative of G3700; to inspect, i.e. watch:--behold.
BiblicalUsage: epopteúō is the word for to inspect. It occurs twice, in 1 Peter.
TheologicalSignificance: I take epopteúō as it stands — to inspect — and read the passage with that plain sense in mind.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2036; a word:--X say.
BiblicalUsage: In Scripture, épos means a word. It occurs just once, in Hebrews.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold épos to its plain sense and let the passage speak for itself.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1909 and G3772; above the sky:--celestial, (in) heaven(-ly), high.
BiblicalUsage: Epouránios means heavenly — of the heaven above, not of the earth below. Paul blesses God for every spiritual blessing in heavenly places in Christ, and Hebrews calls believers partakers of the heavenly calling. It is the word for the life that already belongs to heaven while it is still lived on earth.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe epouránios is the word for where my life is seated: with Christ in heavenly places, even while my feet are on the ground. I hold that this is not escape from the world — it is the power to live in it as heaven's citizen.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: burning, i.e. a carbuncle or other fiery gem
BiblicalUsage: ʼEqdâch means a carbuncle — a burning, fiery gem. It occurs just once, where God promises to make Jerusalem's windows of agates and her gates of carbuncles. The word is fire made into stone.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe ʼeqdâch is a word for the city God builds: burning stones and bright gates, and a glory no enemy can dim.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a heel, i.e. (figuratively) the last of anything (used adverbially, for ever); also result, i.e. compensation; and so (adverb with preposition or relatively) on account of
BiblicalUsage: ʻÊqeb is the heel — and from the heel, the end, the consequence, the reward. God blesses Abraham's seed because Abraham obeyed His voice; the psalmist keeps God's statutes to the end, for the reward. It is the word for what follows obedience, step by step.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe ʻêqeb is the word for the long view: obedience has a consequence, and the consequence is blessing. I hold that keeping God's word to the end is worth it, because the reward is at the end, not the beginning.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Eker, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Êqer — Eker — was an Israelite of the tribe of Judah, a son of Ram. He appears once, in the genealogy of Judah in Chronicles. His fuller story is on his People profile.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Eker matters because the genealogy matters: God kept the record of Judah's sons, and He kept Eker's name in it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: figuratively, a transplanted person, i.e. naturalized citizen
BiblicalUsage: ʻÊqer means a transplanted person — one taken up and set down elsewhere, a naturalized citizen. It occurs just once, in the law about a poor Israelite who sells himself to the stock of a stranger's family. The word is about belonging somewhere you were not born.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that êqer is a word for the stranger's place in Israel: the law made room for the one who had been transplanted.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Ekron, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: ʻEqrôwn was a city of the Philistines, on the coastal plain. The name occurs 20 times, most often in 1 Samuel. There is no People profile for it, because it is a place, not a person.
TheologicalSignificance: I take ʻEqrôwn as it stands: a place named in the record, a small mark on the map. That is enough reason to slow down and notice the name rather than skip it.
RelatedEvents: The Ark Captured and Returned; Elijah and Ahaziah's Messengers
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an Ekronite or inhabitant of Ekron
BiblicalUsage: ʻEqrôwnîy is the word for an Ekronite or inhabitant of Ekron. It occurs twice, in 1 Samuel and Joshua.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe ʻEqrôwnîy is best left as Scripture leaves it: Ekronite or inhabitant of Ekron.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a hero (collectively)
BiblicalUsage: In Scripture, ʼerʼêl means a hero. It occurs just once, in Isaiah.
TheologicalSignificance: My position is to take ʼerʼêl at face value and move on to the passage itself.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H6147); Er, an Israelite:--Er.
BiblicalUsage: The word Ḗr covers Er, an Israelite. It occurs just once, in Luke.
TheologicalSignificance: I take Ḗr as it stands — Er, an Israelite — and read the passage with that plain sense in mind.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Er, the name of two Israelites
BiblicalUsage: ʻÊr — Er — was the name of two Israelites: Judah's firstborn son, who died young in Canaan, and a later Er of Judah's line, the father of Lecah. Both appear in the genealogies, and neither gets more than a few verses.
TheologicalSignificance: I take Er as he stands: two men, one name, both remembered only in the record. That is enough — God kept their names when the story moved on.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Eran, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: ʻÊrân was an Ephraimite, a son of Shuthelah. The name occurs once, in Numbers. The fuller story lives on the People profile.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe ʻÊrân is worth noticing precisely because so little is said — the record kept the name anyway. That is enough reason to slow down and notice the name rather than skip it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an Eranite or descendant (collectively) of Eran
BiblicalUsage: In Scripture, ʻÊrânîy means an Eranite or descendant of Eran. It occurs just once, in Numbers.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe ʻÊrânîy is best left as Scripture leaves it: Eranite or descendant of Eran.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from ἐράω (to love); beloved; Erastus, a Christian:--Erastus.
BiblicalUsage: Érastos — Erastus — was a companion of Paul, sent with Timothy into Macedonia, and later the chamberlain of Corinth. He is named in Acts and in Romans, and again in Timothy, where Paul says Erastus stayed at Corinth. His fuller story is on his People profile.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Erastus matters because he is the faithful helper, not the headline name: sent, stayed, and named by Paul with honour. I hold that the church runs on men like him.
RelatedEvents: Paul's Missionary Journeys; The Riot at Ephesus
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: middle voice of a primary verb (used only in the present and imperfect tenses, the others being supplied by a kindred (middle voice) ἐλεύθομαι, or (active) ἔλθω, which do not otherwise occur); to come or go (in a great variety of applications, literally and figuratively):--accompany, appear, bring, come, enter, fall out, go, grow, X light, X next, pass, resort, be set.
BiblicalUsage: Érchomai is the word for coming — the common verb for arriving, appearing, and approaching. John the Baptist came; Jesus came; the kingdom comes; and the last word of the Bible is a promise that He will come quickly. It is the verb of the whole story, from the first coming to the second.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe érchomai is the heartbeat of the gospel: God comes to us, and we are to watch for His coming again. I hold that every 'come' in Scripture is either a promise kept or a promise still to be kept.
RelatedEvents: The Baptism of Jesus; John the Baptist Asks from Prison
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: dusk
BiblicalUsage: ʻEreb is evening — the dusk that closes the day. There was evening and there was morning, the first day; the Passover lamb was killed in the evening; and the evening sacrifice went up as the day ended. It is the word for the day's close, when work stops and worship rises.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe ʻereb teaches me that God measures days from evening to morning — rest comes before the work, not after it. I hold that the evening sacrifice is the picture of my day: it ends with worship, not with worry.
RelatedEvents: Creation; The Exodus and the Red Sea
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: the web (or transverse threads of cloth); also a mixture, (or mongrel race)
BiblicalUsage: ʻÊreb is the web — the transverse threads of cloth — and by extension a mixture, a mingled crowd. The law speaks of the web in a garment; a mixed multitude went up with Israel out of Egypt, and Nehemiah separated the mixed multitude from Israel; and the prophets name the mingled peoples among the nations. It is the word for what is woven together, and for who is mixed in.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe ʻêreb is a word for the mixture in the midst of God's people: the web in the cloth, and the crowd in the camp. I hold that the mixed multitude is a warning — not everyone who comes out of Egypt belongs to Israel.
RelatedEvents: The Exodus and the Red Sea; The Passover
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: ambuscade
BiblicalUsage: The word ʼereb covers ambuscade. It occurs twice, in Job.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe ʼereb is best left as Scripture leaves it: ambuscade.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a weaving; a braid; also a shuttle
BiblicalUsage: ʼereg means a weaving. It occurs twice, in Judges and Job.
TheologicalSignificance: My position is to take ʼereg at face value and move on to the passage itself.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of obscure affinity; to prop, i.e. (reflexively) get fast:--stick fast.
BiblicalUsage: ereídō is the word for to prop. It occurs just once, in Acts.
TheologicalSignificance: I take ereídō as it stands — to prop — and read the passage with that plain sense in mind.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a pile, equipment, estimate
BiblicalUsage: ʻÊrek is an arrangement — a pile, an order, a valuation, the setting of things in their place. The showbread is set in order on the table; the wood is arranged on the altar; and the priest values a vow at its price. It is the word for things put in order before God.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe ʻêrek is a word for worship: God is a God of order, and His house is set in order. I hold that arranging things rightly — bread, wood, vow — is part of honouring Him.
RelatedEvents: The Tabernacle Is Built; Joash Repairs the Temple
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Erek, a place in Babylon
BiblicalUsage: ʼErek was a city in the land of Shinar, in Nimrod's kingdom. The name occurs once, in Genesis. There is no People profile for it, because it is a place, not a person.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe ʼErek matters because Scripture bothered to record the name. That is enough reason to slow down and notice the name rather than skip it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2048; solitude (concretely):--desert, wilderness.
BiblicalUsage: Erēmía is solitude — the lonely place, the wilderness where no one lives. Jesus feeds the multitude in a desert place; Paul is in perils in the wilderness; and Hebrews says the world was not worthy of those who wandered in deserts. It is the word for being alone with God — or alone without Him.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe erēmía is the word for the lonely places God uses: the wilderness where Jesus feeds, and the desert where His people wander. I hold that solitude with God is never truly alone.
RelatedEvents: The Feeding of the Four Thousand
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2048; to lay waste (literally or figuratively):--(bring to, make) desolate(-ion), come to nought.
BiblicalUsage: Erēmóō means to lay waste — to leave a place desolate and stripped. Jesus uses it for a kingdom divided against itself, brought to desolation (Matthew 12:25; Luke 11:17), and it returns in Revelation, where the great city is laid waste in a single hour and the merchants weep over her. The word is never gentle; it is the language of judgment falling all at once.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe erēmóō shows what judgment looks like when it arrives: sudden, total, and impossible to argue with. That is why the merchants' weeping matters — the city they trusted is gone in an hour.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: perhaps by transposition from G2048 (through the idea of stillness); tranquil:--quiet.
BiblicalUsage: Ḗremos means quiet — at rest, still, peaceable. It occurs just once, where Paul tells Timothy to pray for kings and all in authority, that we may lead a quiet and peaceable life. The word is the goal of the praying: a life at rest.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that ḗremos is the picture of the life prayer aims at: quiet, peaceable, and godly, not anxious and loud.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain affinity; lonesome, i.e. (by implication) waste (usually as a noun, G5561 being implied):--desert, desolate, solitary, wilderness.
BiblicalUsage: Érēmos is the wilderness — the lonely, waste place, and also the desert itself. Jesus is driven into the wilderness to be tempted; Israel wanders in the wilderness for forty years; and John cries in the wilderness, 'Prepare ye the way of the Lord'. It is the place where God meets His people alone.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe érēmos is the place of testing and of meeting: God leads His people into the wilderness to speak to them there. I hold that my own wilderness seasons are not abandonment — they are where He does His clearest work.
RelatedEvents: The Baptism of Jesus; The Burning Bush
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2049; despoliation:--desolation.
BiblicalUsage: Erḗmōsis is desolation — the laying waste itself, the ruined state after the destroying. Jesus warns of the abomination of desolation standing in the holy place, and of Jerusalem's desolation drawing near. It is the word for what is left when judgment has done its work.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe erḗmōsis is a word to heed, not to argue over: Jesus warns, and the warning is meant to move feet. I hold that the sign is given so that God's people will flee, not so that scholars will debate.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably a fuller form of G4483; an alternate for G2036 in certain tenses; to utter, i.e. speak or say:--call, say, speak (of), tell.
BiblicalUsage: Eréō is the future of the verb for saying — 'I will say', 'he will say'. It is the form Jesus uses when He tells what will happen, and Paul uses when he asks what we shall say then. The future tense is the point: the words are promised before they are spoken.
TheologicalSignificance: I take eréō as it stands — saying, still to come — and read the promises attached to it as promises, not guesses.
RelatedEvents: The Parable of the Wheat and the Weeds; The Sheep and the Goats
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a couch (properly, with a canopy)
BiblicalUsage: ʻEres is a couch — a bed, a resting place, sometimes with a canopy. There are beds of ivory in Zion; the psalmist waters his couch with tears; and the harlot spreads her couch with coverings. It is the word for where a person lies down, in rest or in sorrow or in sin.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe ʻeres is a word for the private place: what I do on my couch — weep, rest, or sin — God sees. I hold that the psalmist's tear-wet couch is the honest picture of sorrow brought to God.
RelatedEvents: The Defeat of Sihon and Og
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a presumed prolonged form of G2054; to stimulate (especially to anger):--provoke.
BiblicalUsage: The word erethízō covers to stimulate. It occurs twice, in 2 Corinthians and Colossians.
TheologicalSignificance: I take erethízō as it stands — to stimulate — and read the passage with that plain sense in mind.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: the earth (at large, or partitively a land)
BiblicalUsage: ʼErets is the earth — the whole world God made, and also the land He gave to Israel. In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth, and the earth is the LORD's and the fullness thereof. It is the ground under every story in the Bible, from Eden to the new earth.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe ʼerets keeps me grounded: the earth is God's, not ours, and He gave it to us as stewards. I hold that caring for the land and longing for the new earth belong together, because both honour the Maker.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain affinity; to belch, i.e. (figuratively) to speak out:--utter.
BiblicalUsage: Ereúgomai means to utter — to speak out, as a spring bubbles up. It occurs just once, where Jesus says He will utter things kept secret from the foundation of the world. The word is speech pouring out of a full heart.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe ereúgomai is a word for how Jesus speaks: what has been hidden pours out, like water from a spring.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: apparently from G2046 (through the idea of inquiry); to seek, i.e. (figuratively) to investigate:--search.
BiblicalUsage: Ereunáō means to search out — to examine carefully, the way you would search the Scriptures or search a heart. Jesus tells the Jews to search the Scriptures, and Paul says the Spirit searches the deep things of God. It is diligent looking, not a glance.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe ereunáō is a word for how I should read the Bible: search it, the way Jesus said, because it testifies of Him. And I hold that the Spirit who searches all things is the same Spirit who searches me.
RelatedEvents: The Letter to the Church in Thyatira
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a cedar tree (from the tenacity of its roots)
BiblicalUsage: ʼErez is the cedar — the great tree of Lebanon, the timber of kings. Solomon builds the temple with cedars; the righteous flourish like the cedar; and the cedars of Lebanon are the LORD's planting. It is the word for strength that grows slowly and stands for centuries.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe ʼerez is the picture of the righteous life: planted by God, growing slowly, and standing when storms come. I hold that the cedar's strength is borrowed strength — it stands because He planted it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2040; occupation; by implication, profit, pains:--craft, diligence, gain, work.
BiblicalUsage: Ergasía is work — the occupation, the business, the doing. The masters of the damsel made much gain by her divination; Demetrius the silversmith made silver shrines; and Paul says the Gentiles gave themselves over to work all uncleanness with greediness. It is the word for what a person does for a living — and for what it does to them.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe ergasía shows that work is never neutral: the same word covers honest trade and the gain of soothsayers. I hold that what I do for a living must be work God can bless, not work that profits from sin.
RelatedEvents: Paul's Missionary Journeys; Paul Frees the Enslaved Girl at Philippi
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2041; a toiler; figuratively, a teacher:--labourer, worker(-men).
BiblicalUsage: Ergátēs is a worker — a labourer, one who toils at the job. The harvest is plenteous and the labourers are few, Jesus says, so pray the Lord of the harvest to send out labourers; and the workman is worthy of his hire. It is the word for the people God sends into His field.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe ergátēs is a word for me: the harvest is still plenteous, and the labourers are still few. I hold that praying for labourers starts with being willing to be one.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: middle voice from G2041; to toil (as a task, occupation, etc.), (by implication) effect, be engaged in or with, etc.:--commit, do, labor for, minister about, trade (by), work.
BiblicalUsage: Ergázomai means to work — to toil at a task, to labour with your hands. Paul works with his own hands so as not to burden the churches, and he tells the Thessalonians to work quietly and eat their own bread. It is honest labour, and Scripture treats it as a duty, not a curse.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe ergázomai dignifies ordinary work: God gave it before the Fall, and He still blesses the hands that do it. I hold that working with my own hands is part of my witness, not a distraction from it.
RelatedEvents: The Feeding of the Five Thousand
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a primary (but obsolete) ἔργω (to work); toil (as an effort or occupation); by implication, an act:--deed, doing, labour, work.
BiblicalUsage: Érgon is work — the deed, the task, the thing done. Paul says we are God's workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works; James says faith without works is dead; and Jesus says the work of God is to believe in Him whom He sent. The word holds the whole question of what faith does.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe érgon settles the argument about faith and works: faith that does nothing is not faith, and works that do not come from faith are not God's work. I hold that the works God prepared for me are the ones I should be walking in today.
RelatedEvents: The Feeding of the Five Thousand; The Resurrection
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of obscure affinity; wool:--wool.
BiblicalUsage: érion means wool. It occurs twice, in Hebrews and Revelation.
TheologicalSignificance: My position is to take érion at face value and move on to the passage itself.
RelatedEvents: John's Vision of the Risen Christ on Patmos
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2056; a kidling, i.e. (genitive case) goat (symbolically, wicked person):--goat.
BiblicalUsage: eríphion is the word for a kidling. It occurs just once, in Matthew.
TheologicalSignificance: I take eríphion as it stands — kidling — and read the passage with that plain sense in mind.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: perhaps from the same as G2053 (through the idea of hairiness); a kid or (genitive case) goat:--goat, kid.
BiblicalUsage: In Scripture, ériphos means a kid or goat. It occurs twice, in Matthew and Luke.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold ériphos to its plain sense and let the passage speak for itself.
RelatedEvents: The Prodigal Son; The Sheep and the Goats
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain affinity; a quarrel, i.e. (by implication) wrangling:--contention, debate, strife, variance.
BiblicalUsage: Éris is strife — quarrelling, wrangling, the contention that splits a church. Paul lists it among the works of the flesh, and he writes to Corinth because there is strife among them. It is the word for the fighting that proves the flesh is still in charge.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe éris is the test of a church: where there is strife, the Spirit is being quenched. I hold that the answer is not to win the argument, but to put the flesh to death.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: perhaps as the same as G2042; properly, intrigue, i.e. (by implication) faction:--contention(-ious), strife.
BiblicalUsage: Eritheía is selfish ambition — the party spirit, the intrigue that builds a faction. Paul names it among the works of the flesh, and James says where envying and strife are, there is confusion and every evil work. It is the word for ambition that serves itself.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe eritheía is the most respectable sin in the church: ambition dressed up as zeal. I hold that the cure is the mind of Christ, who made Himself of no reputation.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a Erite (collectively) or descendants of Eri
BiblicalUsage: ʻÊrîy is the word for a Erite or descendants of Eri. It occurs just once, in Numbers.
TheologicalSignificance: My position is to take ʻÊrîy at face value and move on to the passage itself.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a Erite (collectively) or descendants of Eri
BiblicalUsage: ʻÊrîy is the word for a Erite or descendants of Eri. It occurs just once, in Numbers.
TheologicalSignificance: My position is to take ʻÊrîy at face value and move on to the passage itself.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2054; to wrangle:--strive.
BiblicalUsage: The word erízō covers to wrangle. It occurs just once, in Matthew.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold erízō to its plain sense and let the passage speak for itself.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: apparently from G2046 (compare G2045); to interrogate; by implication, to request:--ask, beseech, desire, intreat, pray. Compare G4441.
BiblicalUsage: Erōtáō means to ask — to interrogate, to request, to beseech. The disciples ask Jesus when He will restore the kingdom; Jesus asks the Father for His own; and He tells His disciples to ask the Father in His name. It is the word for asking that expects an answer.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe erōtáō is the word for prayer as asking: Jesus asks the Father, and He tells us to ask too. I hold that asking is not begging — it is the way children speak to a Father who hears.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: nudity, literally (especially the pudenda) or figuratively (disgrace, blemish)
BiblicalUsage: ʻErvâh is nakedness — the shame of being uncovered, the disgrace of exposure. Ham sees his father's nakedness, and the law guards the nakedness of kin; the prophets use it for a nation's disgrace laid bare. It is the word for shame made visible.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe ʻervâh shows why clothing matters in Scripture: nakedness is shame, and covering is mercy. I hold that the coats of skins God made for Adam and Eve are the first picture of covering — and of the covering Christ provides.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: nudity
BiblicalUsage: ʻeryâh means nudity. Most of its 6 occurrences are in Ezekiel. It is a plain word, and that plainness is the point: Scripture does not dress it up.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe ʻeryâh matters because it names something Scripture keeps returning to. It shapes how I hear those verses, and I think it should shape how you hear them too.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain affinity; red, i.e. (with G2281) the Red Sea:--red.
BiblicalUsage: The word erythrós covers red, that is the Red Sea. It occurs just once, in Hebrews.
TheologicalSignificance: I take erythrós as it stands — red, that is the Red Sea — and read the passage with that plain sense in mind.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H6215); Esau, an Edomite:--Esau.
BiblicalUsage: Esaû is Esau, the elder twin of Isaac and Rebekah, who sold his birthright for a meal. The New Testament holds him up twice: as the one God loved less than Jacob, and as the profane man who found no place of repentance. His fuller story is on his People profile.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Esau in the New Testament is the same warning as in Genesis: do not trade what is eternal for what is immediate. I hold that his story is meant to make me tremble, not to make me argue.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Esav, a son of Isaac, including his posterity
BiblicalUsage: ʻÊsâv — Esau — was the elder twin of Isaac and Rebekah, a man of the field who sold his birthright for a meal of lentils. He comes back into the story when Jacob meets him again on the way home, and his descendants become the Edomites. His fuller story is on his People profile.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Esau matters because he is the warning in the family: a birthright thrown away for one meal. I hold that his tears afterward, when no repentance could undo it, are the soberest verses in Genesis.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: adverb from G2078; finally, i.e. (with G2192) at the extremity of life:--point of death.
BiblicalUsage: In Scripture, eschátōs means finally, that is at the extremity of life. It occurs just once, in Mark.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe eschátōs is best left as Scripture leaves it: finally, that is at the extremity of life.
RelatedEvents: Jairus' Daughter and the Bleeding Woman
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a superlative probably from G2192 (in the sense of contiguity); farthest, final (of place or time):--ends of, last, latter end, lowest, uttermost.
BiblicalUsage: Éschatos means last — the farthest, the final, the end of the line. The last shall be first, Jesus says; the last enemy to be destroyed is death; and these are the last days, John says. It is the word for the end of things, and for what comes after the end.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe éschatos keeps me honest about the end: death is the last enemy, and it has already been defeated. I hold that living in the last days means living as if the end were near — because it is.
RelatedEvents: The Resurrection; The Rich Young Ruler
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: grass (or any tender shoot)
BiblicalUsage: ʻeseb means grass. It turns up in Exodus, Deuteronomy, and Psalms, and the sense holds steady from place to place. It is a plain word, and that plainness is the point: Scripture does not dress it up.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe ʻeseb matters because it names something Scripture keeps returning to. So I hold the meaning steady and let the context do the rest.
RelatedEvents: The Ten Plagues; The Plague of Hail
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: strife
BiblicalUsage: ʻêseq is the word for strife. It occurs just once, in Genesis.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold ʻêseq to its plain sense and let the passage speak for itself.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: ten (as an accumulation to the extent of the digits)
BiblicalUsage: ʻEser is ten — the number of the commandments God spoke from Sinai, and the number of the plagues that fell on Egypt. Israel counted ten as the shape of the covenant, and the ten words as the whole law in miniature.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe ʻeser matters because the ten words are the covenant in miniature: ten commands that hold the whole relationship between God and His people. I hold that they are still the measure of a life lived toward God and neighbour.

Definition: Ethnan, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: ʼEthnan was an Israelite of the house of Ashhur, named among the sons of Helah in Judah's genealogy. He appears once, in Chronicles. His fuller story is on his People profile.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Ethnan matters the way every name in the genealogy matters: God kept the record, and He kept this name in it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a gift (as the price of harlotry or idolatry)
BiblicalUsage: ʼEthnan is the hire of a harlot — the price paid for prostitution, named as a gift that must never be brought into God's house. Moses forbids bringing the hire of a whore into the house of the LORD, and the prophets use the word for Israel's payment to her lovers. It is money earned by unfaithfulness, and God will not take it as an offering.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe ʼethnan shows how seriously God takes the source of what we offer Him: a gift bought with unfaithfulness is no gift at all. I hold that the warning still stands — what I bring to God must come from a faithful life, not merely a full hand.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1484 and G746; the governor (not king) of a district:--ethnarch.
BiblicalUsage: ethnárchēs means the governor of a district. It occurs just once, in 2 Corinthians.
TheologicalSignificance: I take ethnárchēs as it stands — governor of a district — and read the passage with that plain sense in mind.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: adverb from G1482; as a Gentile:--after the manner of Gentiles.
BiblicalUsage: ethnikōs is the word for as a Gentile. It occurs just once, in Galatians.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold ethnikōs to its plain sense and let the passage speak for itself.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1484; national ("ethnic"), i.e. (specially) a Gentile:--heathen (man).
BiblicalUsage: In Scripture, ethnikós means national, that is a Gentile. Most of its 4 occurrences are in Matthew. The word does quiet work, and the passages below show it in its ordinary setting.
TheologicalSignificance: My position is simple: ethnikós means what it says, and what it says matters. It is a small word with a steady job, and I trust it to do that job.
RelatedEvents: The Sermon on the Mount; Diotrephes Refuses the Brethren
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Ethni, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: ʼEthnîy was a Levite, a son of Zerah. The name occurs once, in 1 Chronicles. The fuller story lives on the People profile.
TheologicalSignificance: For me, ʼEthnîy is a reminder that God works through ordinary people whose names we barely know. That is enough reason to slow down and notice the name rather than skip it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably from G1486; a race (as of the same habit), i.e. a tribe; specially, a foreign (non-Jewish) one (usually, by implication, pagan):--Gentile, heathen, nation, people.
BiblicalUsage: Éthnos is a nation — a people, a tribe, and in the New Testament most often the Gentiles, the nations outside Israel. God promised Abraham that in him all nations would be blessed, and Jesus sends His disciples to make disciples of all nations. It is the word for the whole world God intends to reach.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe éthnos is the word for the scope of the gospel: it was never meant for one nation alone. I hold that every nation, including mine, is called into the blessing promised to Abraham.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a primary verb; to be used (by habit or conventionality); neuter perfect participle usage:--be custom (manner, wont).
BiblicalUsage: Éthō means to be accustomed — to do a thing as a matter of custom, the way you always have. Jesus went into the synagogue on the Sabbath 'as his custom was', and Paul reasoned in the synagogue three Sabbaths 'as his manner was'. The word is habit made visible.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe éthō shows me the shape of a faithful life: it is built out of customs kept week after week. Jesus and Paul both had a 'as his custom was', and I want one too.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a strengthened form of G1485; usage, i.e. (plural) moral habits:--manners.
BiblicalUsage: In Scripture, ēthos means usage, that is moral habits. It occurs just once, in 1 Corinthians.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold ēthos to its plain sense and let the passage speak for itself.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1486; a usage (prescribed by habit or law):--custom, manner, be wont.
BiblicalUsage: Éthos is custom — the usage, the way things are done, the practice handed down. The Jews accuse Paul of teaching customs against Moses, and Paul keeps the customs of the law where he can. It is the word for the habits that hold a people together.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe éthos is a word for the weight of habit: customs shape a people more than speeches do. I hold that the customs worth keeping are the ones that point to Christ, and the ones that do not should be let go.
RelatedEvents: The Birth of Jesus; The Crucifixion
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: perhaps akin to G2094; "yet," still (of time or degree):--after that, also, ever, (any) further, (t-)henceforth (more), hereafter, (any) longer, (any) more(-one), now, still, yet.
BiblicalUsage: Éti means yet — still, more, after that, the word that keeps a sentence going. He was yet in Galilee, the angel says; the Corinthians are yet carnal, Paul says; and Hebrews says there is yet need of another priest. It is the word for what is still true, and still to come.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe éti is a word of patience: God is not finished, and neither am I. I hold that 'yet' is the space where grace works — what is not yet true can still become true.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: third person singular imperative of G1510; let him (or it) be:--let … be.
BiblicalUsage: Ḗtō is the word for 'let him be' — the third-person imperative of the verb to be. It occurs twice: 'let him be Anathema' and 'let your yea be yea, and your nay, nay'. The form hands the matter over to what must be.
TheologicalSignificance: I take ḗtō as it stands — let it be — and I hear in it both a curse and a command to plain speech.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2228 and G5104; either indeed:--whether.
BiblicalUsage: In Scripture, ḗtoi means either indeed. It occurs just once, in Romans.
TheologicalSignificance: I take ḗtoi as it stands — either indeed — and read the passage with that plain sense in mind.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: apparently a primary word; a year:--year.
BiblicalUsage: Étos is a year — the measure of a life, counted one year at a time. Anna the prophetess was a widow of eighty-four years; Abraham's seed would be strangers four hundred years; and with the Lord one day is as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day. It is the word for time given and time spent.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe étos teaches me to number my days: the years are God's gift, and He asks me to spend them wisely. I hold that a thousand years in His sight is a reminder, not an excuse — my years are short, and they matter.
RelatedEvents: The Birth of Jesus; Martyrdom of Stephen
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, a step-chain; by analogy, a bracelet
BiblicalUsage: ʼetsʻâdâh means properly, a step-chain. It occurs twice, in Numbers and 2 Samuel.
TheologicalSignificance: For me, ʼetsʻâdâh is a reminder to read plainly rather than to force a meaning.
RelatedEvents: Saul's Death at Gilboa; War against Midian
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a tree (from its firmness); hence, wood (plural sticks)
BiblicalUsage: ʻÊts is a tree — and by extension, wood, the stuff trees are made of. The tree of life stood in the garden, the tree of knowledge brought the Fall, and the psalmist's righteous man is like a tree planted by rivers of water. It is the word for rooted, growing, fruitful life.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe ʻêts is the Bible's picture of the blessed life: planted, watered, and bearing fruit in season. I hold that the tree planted by the rivers of water is the end of the story too — rooted, growing, and bearing fruit.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: advice; by implication, plan; also prudence
BiblicalUsage: ʻÊtsâh is counsel — advice, a plan, the guidance of the wise. The counsel of the LORD stands forever, the psalmist says, while the counsel of the nations comes to nothing; and a man's friends and counsellors shape his way. It is the word for the advice you live by.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe ʻêtsâh is a word for choosing whose counsel I take: the LORD's counsel stands, and man's counsel fails. I hold that the blessed man of the first psalm is blessed because he walks in no counsel but God's.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: advice; by implication, plan; also prudence
BiblicalUsage: ʻÊtsâh is counsel — advice, a plan, the guidance of the wise. The counsel of the LORD stands forever, the psalmist says, while the counsel of the nations comes to nothing; and a man's friends and counsellors shape his way. It is the word for the advice you live by.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe ʻêtsâh is a word for choosing whose counsel I take: the LORD's counsel stands, and man's counsel fails. I hold that the blessed man of the first psalm is blessed because he walks in no counsel but God's.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {something to sieze with, i.e. a finger; by analogy, a toe}
BiblicalUsage: ʼEtsbaʻ is a finger — or a toe, the thing you seize with. It turns up in Daniel: the toes of the king's image, part iron and part clay, and the fingers of a man's hand writing on the wall at Belshazzar's feast. It is the word for the small, decisive thing.
TheologicalSignificance: What I take from ʼetsbaʻ is straightforward: God writes with a finger, and the empires it touches fall. I hold that the small, decisive thing is the one to watch — the finger on the wall, the toe of iron and clay.
RelatedEvents: Nebuchadnezzar's Dream of the Image; Belshazzar's Handwriting on the Wall
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {something to sieze with, i.e. a finger; by analogy, a toe}
BiblicalUsage: ʼEtsbaʻ is a finger — or a toe, the thing you seize with. It turns up in Daniel: the toes of the king's image, part iron and part clay, and the fingers of a man's hand writing on the wall at Belshazzar's feast. It is the word for the small, decisive thing.
TheologicalSignificance: What I take from ʼetsbaʻ is straightforward: God writes with a finger, and the empires it touches fall. I hold that the small, decisive thing is the one to watch — the finger on the wall, the toe of iron and clay.
RelatedEvents: Nebuchadnezzar's Dream of the Image; Belshazzar's Handwriting on the Wall
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Etsbon, the name of two Israelites
BiblicalUsage: ʼEtsbôwn was the name of two Israelites, one of Gad and one of Benjamin. The name occurs in Genesis and 1 Chronicles. There is no People profile for this name, so this study covers the name's use only.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe ʼEtsbôwn matters because Scripture bothered to record the name. That is enough reason to slow down and notice the name rather than skip it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an earthen vessel; usually (painful) toil; also a pang (whether of body or mind)
BiblicalUsage: ʻEtseb is sorrow — painful toil, the pang of body or mind — and once, an earthen vessel. In sorrow shalt thou bring forth children, God says after the Fall; the blessing of the LORD adds no sorrow with it; and in all labour there is profit. It is the word for the ache that came with the curse, and for the vessel that holds it.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe ʻetseb names the sorrow I know by heart: work that wearies, pain that stays, and the ache of a world under the curse. I hold that the blessing of the LORD is the other side — riches without the sorrow.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a side; (as a preposition) near
BiblicalUsage: ʼÊtsel means beside — at the side of, near, close by. Joseph's garment is left beside her; the child is taken from beside its mother; and the man of God is slain by the lion beside the way. It is the word for nearness, for being at someone's side.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe ʼêtsel is a word for the nearness God gives: He is beside me, not far off. I hold that the side of the road, the side of the bed, the side of the throne — Scripture keeps putting people beside each other, and God beside them.
RelatedEvents: Solomon's Wise Judgment; The Man of God from Judah
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Etsem, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: ʻEtsem was a town in the south of Judah, named among the cities of the tribe. It appears in the lists of Joshua and Chronicles, on the border country toward the Negev. There is no People profile for it, because it is a place, not a person.
TheologicalSignificance: I take Etsem as it stands: a town named in the record, a small mark on the map of Judah's inheritance.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a bone (as strong); by extension, the body; figuratively, the substance, i.e. (as pron.) selfsame
BiblicalUsage: ʻEtsem means a bone — and by extension the body itself, the substance of a person. God made the woman from the bone of the man's side, and Joseph made Israel swear to carry his bones out of Egypt. The prophets see dry bones rise, and the psalmist says He keeps all his bones, and not one of them is broken. It is the word for what holds a person together.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe ʻetsem carries the whole story of the body: God formed us from bone and breath, and He can raise what is dry and scattered. I hold that the dry bones of Ezekiel are the proof — what is dead in me is not beyond His making alive.
RelatedEvents: Creation; The Exodus and the Red Sea
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a spear
BiblicalUsage: The word ʻêtsen covers a spear. It occurs just once, in 2 Samuel.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe ʻêtsen is best left as Scripture leaves it: spear.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: restraint
BiblicalUsage: ʻetser means restraint. It occurs just once, in Judges.
TheologicalSignificance: My position is to take ʻetser at face value and move on to the passage itself.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Etser, an Idumaean
BiblicalUsage: ʼEtser was an Idumaean, a son of Seir. The name occurs 5 times, most often in Genesis. There is no People profile for this name, so this study covers the name's use only.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that ʼEtser is there on purpose, like every name in Scripture. That is enough reason to slow down and notice the name rather than skip it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Etsjon-Geber, a place on the Red Sea
BiblicalUsage: ʻEtsyôwn Geber was a port on the Red Sea, where Solomon built ships. The name occurs 7 times, most often in 1 Kings. There is no People profile for it, because it is a place, not a person.
TheologicalSignificance: What strikes me about ʻEtsyôwn Geber is that the name survives in a record most readers skim. That is enough reason to slow down and notice the name rather than skip it.
RelatedEvents: Jehoshaphat's Victory by Prayer and Praise
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, twisted (yarn), i.e. tapestry
BiblicalUsage: The word ʼêṭûwn covers properly, twisted, that is tapestry. It occurs just once, in Proverbs.
TheologicalSignificance: For me, ʼêṭûwn is a reminder to read plainly rather than to force a meaning.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: neuter of a primary εὖς (good); (adverbially) well:--good, well (done).
BiblicalUsage: Eû means well — good, well done. The servant hears 'well done, thou good and faithful servant', and Paul says it shall be well with those who honour their parents. It is the word for God's approval, spoken plainly.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe eû is the word I want to hear one day: well done. I hold that living well now is the way to hear it then.
RelatedEvents: The Anointing at Bethany; The Parable of the Talents
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H2332); Eua (or Eva, i.e. Chavvah), the first woman:--Eve.
BiblicalUsage: Eûa is Eve, the first woman, the mother of all living. Paul points back to her when he warns the Corinthians not to be led astray as the serpent beguiled Eve, and again when he writes that Adam was formed first, then Eve. Her fuller story is on her People profile.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Eve matters because the whole story starts with her: the first woman, the first deception, and the first promise that her seed would bruise the serpent's head.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2097; a preacher of the gospel:--evangelist.
BiblicalUsage: Euangelistḗs is an evangelist — a preacher of the gospel. Philip is called the evangelist in Acts; Paul lists evangelists among the gifts Christ gave His church; and Timothy is told to do the work of an evangelist. It is the office of telling the good news.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe euangelistḗs matters because the church needs tellers, not just hearers: someone has to carry the good news out. I hold that doing the work of an evangelist is every believer's call, whether or not it is his title.
RelatedEvents: Paul's Missionary Journeys; Agabus Foretells Paul's Bonds
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2095 and G32; to announce good news ("evangelize") especially the gospel:--declare, bring (declare, show) glad (good) tidings, preach (the gospel).
BiblicalUsage: Euangelízō means to announce good news — to evangelize, to preach the gospel. The angel brings good tidings of great joy to the shepherds; Philip preaches Christ to the Ethiopian; Paul says woe is unto him if he preaches not the gospel. It is the verb of the whole mission.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe euangelízō is the church's first job: to announce the good news, not to keep it. I hold that Paul's 'woe is me' is the measure — if I am not telling it, something is wrong.
RelatedEvents: The Birth of Jesus; The Resurrection
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2101; to gratify entirely:--please (well).
BiblicalUsage: Euarestéō means to please — to gratify entirely, to be well-pleasing. Enoch pleased God, and by faith he was translated; and the sacrifices of doing good and sharing are well-pleasing to God. It is the word for a life God is glad of.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe euarestéō is the measure of a life: not whether I am busy, but whether God is pleased. I hold that Enoch's walk — pleasing God — is the life I want.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: adverb from G2101; quite agreeably:--acceptably, + please well.
BiblicalUsage: euaréstōs is the word for quite agreeably. It occurs just once, in Hebrews.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe euaréstōs is best left as Scripture leaves it: quite agreeably.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2095 and G701; fully agreeable:--acceptable(-ted), wellpleasing.
BiblicalUsage: Euárestos means well-pleasing — fully agreeable to God. Paul says to present our bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable unto God; and to prove what is acceptable unto the Lord; and children who obey their parents are well pleasing unto the Lord. It is the word for what God receives with gladness.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe euárestos is the test of my offering: not whether it is impressive, but whether it pleases Him. I hold that a life offered to God is acceptable because He says so, not because I feel so.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2095 and G1014; good-willer; Eubulus, a Christian:--Eubulus.
BiblicalUsage: Eúboulos — Eubulus — was a Christian in Rome who sends greetings to Timothy in Paul's last letter. He is named once, among the few who stood with Paul at the end. His fuller story is on his People profile.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Eubulus matters because he stayed: in Paul's last letter, when many had left, Eubulus sends his greeting. I hold that standing with someone at the end is worth being named for.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2170; to be grateful, i.e. (actively) to express gratitude (towards); specially, to say grace at a meal:--(give) thank(-ful, -s).
BiblicalUsage: Eucharistéō means to give thanks — to express gratitude to God, actively and out loud. Jesus gives thanks before He breaks the bread; Paul gives thanks for every church he writes to; and we are told to give thanks in everything. It is the word for gratitude turned into speech.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe eucharistéō is a discipline, not a feeling: thanks given, not merely felt, is what changes a heart. I hold that giving thanks in everything is the way to see God's hand in everything.
RelatedEvents: The Last Supper; The Feeding of the Four Thousand
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2170; gratitude; actively, grateful language (to God, as an act of worship):--thankfulness, (giving of) thanks(-giving).
BiblicalUsage: Eucharistía is thanksgiving — gratitude, and the words of thanks themselves. Paul prays that thanksgiving would abound, and he tells the Colossians to abound in it with thanksgiving. It is the sound of a people who know they have been given everything.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe eucharistía is the mark of a healthy church: where thanksgiving abounds, complaining starves. I hold that the more I thank God, the more I notice what He has done.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2095 and a derivative of G5483; well favored, i.e. (by implication) grateful:--thankful.
BiblicalUsage: In Scripture, eucháristos means well favored, that is grateful. It occurs just once, in Colossians.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe eucháristos is best left as Scripture leaves it: well favored, that is grateful.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2172; properly, a wish, expressed as a petition to God, or in votive obligation:--prayer, vow.
BiblicalUsage: Euchḗ is prayer — a wish expressed as a petition to God, or a vow made to Him. Paul takes a vow in Acts, and James says the prayer of faith shall save the sick. It is the word for asking God, and for the promise made when He answers.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe euchḗ is the word for prayer as a promise: the wish I lay before God, and the vow I keep when He answers. I hold that prayer is not only asking — it is the promise I make back to Him.
RelatedEvents: Paul's Missionary Journeys; Paul Purifies Himself at the Temple
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: middle voice of a primary verb; to wish; by implication, to pray to God:--pray, will, wish.
BiblicalUsage: Eúchomai means to wish — and by extension, to pray, to ask God for what you wish. Paul wishes the Corinthians would be perfect, and James says to pray one for another, that ye may be healed. It is the word for the heart's wish turned toward God in prayer.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe eúchomai shows that prayer starts with wishing — with wanting something enough to ask God for it. I hold that praying for one another is not fancy words, but a plain wish laid before God.
RelatedEvents: Paul Before Felix, Festus, and Agrippa
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2095 and G5543; easily used, i.e. useful:--profitable, meet for use.
BiblicalUsage: eúchrēstos is the word for profitable, meet for use. In 2 Timothy 2:21, the text says "and meet for the master's use." In 2 Timothy 4:11, the text says "for he is profitable to me for the ministry."
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that eúchrēstos matters because serving is not earning; it is answering love with love. That is why I keep this word in mind when I read those passages — it carries more than its size suggests.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: feminine from G2095 and the alternate of G2203 (as the god of the weather); a clear sky, i.e. fine weather:--fair weather.
BiblicalUsage: The word eudía carries the sense of fair weather. In Matthew 16:2, the text says "It will be] fair weather."
TheologicalSignificance: In eudía I find no hidden theology; it simply means fair weather.
RelatedTopics: Nature and Creation; Goodness of Creation; Provision
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2095 and G1380; to think well of, i.e. approve (an act); specially, to approbate (a person or thing):--think good, (be well) please(-d), be the good (have, take) pleasure, be willing.
BiblicalUsage: eudokéō is a plain word for think good, (be well) please(-d), be the good (have, take) pleasure, be willing. In Matthew 3:17, the text says "in whom I am well pleased." In Mark 1:11, the text says "in whom I am well pleased."
TheologicalSignificance: eudokéō convinces me that grace is God giving what we could never earn, and never taking it back. That is why I keep this word in mind when I read those passages — it carries more than its size suggests.
RelatedTopics: God's Will; Grace; Love of God
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a presumed compound of G2095 and the base of G1380; satisfaction, i.e. (subjectively) delight, or (objectively) kindness, wish, purpose:--desire, good pleasure (will), X seem good.
BiblicalUsage: In the New Testament, eudokía is the word for desire, good pleasure (will), X seem good. In Matthew 11:26, the text says "for so it seemed good in thy sight." In Luke 2:14, the text says "good will toward men."
TheologicalSignificance: For me, eudokía is a reminder that grace is God giving what we could never earn, and never taking it back. That shapes how I read the passages where it appears: not as filler, but as God's own wording for what He is doing.
RelatedEvents: The Birth of Jesus; The Shepherds Visit the Newborn Jesus
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2110; beneficence (genitive case or specially):--benefit, good deed done.
BiblicalUsage: euergesía means benefit, good deed done. In Acts 4:9, the text says "If we this day be examined of the good deed done to the impotent man."
TheologicalSignificance: I take euergesía as it stands: benefit, good deed done.
RelatedEvents: Peter and John Before the Sanhedrin
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2110; to be philanthropic:--do good.
BiblicalUsage: euergetéō is the word for do good. In Acts 10:38, the text says "who went about doing good."

BiblicalUsage: ʻêyrôm means nudity. It appears in Genesis, Deuteronomy, and Ezekiel, and each time it carries that same plain sense. The word keeps that same sense wherever it appears.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe ʻêyrôm shows us that sin is not a mistake; it is rebellion, and it needs a Saviour, not an excuse. That shapes how I read the passages where it appears: not as filler, but as God's own wording for what He is doing.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Etam, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Etam is a place in Palestine. In Judges 15:8, the text says "and he went down and dwelt in the top of the rock Etam." It is a place, not a person, so there is no People profile for it.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Etam matters because God's story happened in real places, and Etam is one of them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Ethan, the name of four Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Ethan is the name of four Israelites. In 1 Kings 4:31, the text says "than Ethan the Ezrahite." The life behind the name is told on the Ethan People profile.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Ethan matters because God knows His people by name, and Ethan is one of them. That is why I want the name, and the person behind it, kept straight.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: permanence; hence (concrete) permanent; specifically a chieftain
BiblicalUsage: ʼêythân is a plain word for permanence, enduring. It appears in Genesis, Exodus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy, and each time it carries that same plain sense. The word keeps that same sense wherever it appears.
TheologicalSignificance: ʼêythân convinces me that strength is not something we muster; it is something God gives to the weak. That is why I keep this word in mind when I read those passages — it carries more than its size suggests.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Ethanim, the name of a month
BiblicalUsage: Ethanim is the name of a month. In 1 Kings 8:2, the text says "And all the men of Israel assembled themselves unto king Solomon at the feast in the month Ethanim."
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Ethanim matters because God knows His people by name — even the ones Scripture mentions only once.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {a she-goat (as strong), but masculine in plural (which also is used elliptically for goat's hair)}
BiblicalUsage: ʻêz means a she-goat. In Ezra 6:17, the text says "twelve he goats."
TheologicalSignificance: I take ʻêz as it stands: a she-goat.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {a she-goat (as strong), but masculine in plural (which also is used elliptically for goat's hair)}
BiblicalUsage: ʻêz means a she-goat. In Ezra 6:17, the text says "twelve he goats."
TheologicalSignificance: I take ʻêz as it stands: a she-goat.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Ezbai, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Ezbai is named only once, as the father of Naarai, one of David's mighty men in 1 Chronicles 11:37. The verse gives us nothing else about him — no deed, no speech, no story of his own. His name survives because his son stood among the men who fought beside David.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God keeps the names of the faithful even when their stories are lost to us. Ezbai matters because his son is counted among David's men, and that is enough for Scripture to remember him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H2396); Ezekias (i.e. Hezekeiah), an Israelite:--Ezekias.
BiblicalUsage: Ezekias is the Greek form of Hezekiah, and it appears in Matthew's genealogy: Achaz begat Ezekias in Matthew 1:9, and Ezekias begat Manasses in Matthew 1:10. The name stands in the line of kings that leads to Jesus, between Ahaz and Manasseh. Matthew spells it the Greek way because he is writing the family line for a Greek-speaking world.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Matthew put Hezekiah in this list on purpose, not as filler. A reforming king who trusted God against Assyria belongs in the ancestry of the Messiah, and his name reminds me that God works through real kings with real failures around them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Ezel, a memorial stone in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Ezel is a stone, not a man — a landmark in the field where David hid from Saul, named in 1 Samuel 20:19. Jonathan told David to stay by the stone Ezel for three days while he tested his father's mood. The place is remembered because it marks the spot where a friendship was tested and proved true.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God marks the places where loyalty is proved, even a bare stone in a field. Ezel has no beauty and no building, yet it stands in Scripture as the witness of Jonathan's faithfulness to David.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: aid
BiblicalUsage: Ezer is the plain word for help, and it runs through Scripture from the first chapters to the last. Moses named his son Eliezer because God was his help against Pharaoh's sword in Exodus 18:4, and Moses blesses God as Israel's help in Deuteronomy 33:26. The psalmist looks to the hills and says his help comes from the LORD in Psalms 121:2, and Daniel sees God's people helped with a little help in trouble in Daniel 11:34.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe help is one of the truest names for what God is to us. He does not only command and judge; He helps, and the Bible says so in the plainest word it has. When I have no strength left, my help comes from the LORD, not from myself.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Ezer, the name of four Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Ezer is a name carried by four different men, and two of them are named in the verses here. In 1 Chronicles 4:4 he is Ezer the father of Hushah, among the sons of Hur, and in Nehemiah 12:42 he is one of the singers who sang loud at the dedication of the wall. The name means help, and each of these men carries it in a different generation.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a name can be a small sermon. Every Ezer in the record carries the word for help, and I take that as a reminder that God raises up helpers in every generation, whether they are fathers, singers, or men whose names we nearly pass over.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Ezer, the name of two Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Ezer son of Ephraim is named once, in 1 Chronicles 7:21, and the verse that names him is a sad one. He and his brother Elead went down to take cattle from the men of Gath, and the men of Gath killed them. His father Ephraim mourned for them many days.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Scripture does not hide the losses of God's people. Ezer's name is kept in a genealogy that remembers a raid gone wrong, and I hold that even a short, sorrowful life is worth recording.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: hyssop
BiblicalUsage: Hyssop is a small, common plant, but it does holy work in Scripture. At the first Passover the Israelites dipped hyssop in blood and struck the doorposts in Exodus 12:22, and the same plant appears in the cleansing of the leper in Leviticus 14:4 and in the water of purification in Numbers 19:18. Solomon could speak of trees from the cedar in Lebanon down to the hyssop that springs out of the wall in 1 Kings 4:33.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God delights to use the lowliest things for the greatest work. Hyssop is no cedar, yet it carried the blood that saved the firstborn and the water that cleansed the unclean. That tells me no one is too small for God to use.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: something girt; a belt, also a band
BiblicalUsage: A girdle is the belt a man wore around his waist, and Scripture uses it for readiness, strength, and identity. Elijah is recognised by his girdle of leather about his loins in 2 Kings 1:8, and Jeremiah is told to get a linen girdle and put it upon his loins in Jeremiah 13:1. The prophets also use it as a picture: righteousness shall be the girdle of the Messiah's loins in Isaiah 11:5.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the girdle is a picture of being ready. A man girded his loins to run, to fight, or to work, and I hold that the Christian life is a girded life — truth and righteousness bound close, ready for whatever the day brings.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Ezra, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Ezra the scribe appears in this form in the Aramaic of King Artaxerxes' letter, where the king addresses him as Ezra the priest, a scribe of the law of the God of heaven, in Ezra 7:12. The same letter gives him authority over the treasurers beyond the river in Ezra 7:21, so that whatever he requires for the house of God is done speedily. The name stands in a foreign king's decree because the king recognised the God Ezra served.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Ezra's standing came from the law he carried, not from any office he held. A pagan king honoured him because he was a scribe of the law of the God of heaven, and I hold that devotion to God's word still commands respect in places we would not expect.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Ezra, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Ezra the scribe appears in this form in the Aramaic of King Artaxerxes' letter, where the king addresses him as Ezra the priest, a scribe of the law of the God of heaven, in Ezra 7:12. The same letter gives him authority over the treasurers beyond the river in Ezra 7:21, so that whatever he requires for the house of God is done speedily. The name stands in a foreign king's decree because the king recognised the God Ezra served.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Ezra's standing came from the law he carried, not from any office he held. A pagan king honoured him because he was a scribe of the law of the God of heaven, and I hold that devotion to God's word still commands respect in places we would not expect.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a spontaneous growth, i.e. native (tree or persons)
BiblicalUsage: Ezrach means one born in the land, a native, set against the stranger who sojourns among Israel. The Passover law makes the rule plain in Exodus 12:19, where leaven is forbidden whether the eater is a stranger or born in the land, and the Day of Atonement binds the native and the stranger alike in Leviticus 16:29. When Israel stands to bless the people in Joshua 8:33, the stranger and he that was born among them stand together before the ark.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the native-born and the stranger standing together before God is a picture of His welcome. The law drew a line between them in some things, yet in worship and in atonement they stood side by side, and I hold that the gospel has now made that welcome full.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an Ezrachite or descendant of Zerach
BiblicalUsage: Ezrachite is a title, not a name on its own — it marks a man as a descendant of Zerach. Solomon's wisdom is measured against Ethan the Ezrahite in 1 Kings 4:31, and Solomon was wiser than them all. The same title stands in the headings of two psalms, over the songs of Heman and Ethan, though those headings carry no verse number of their own.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe it matters that wisdom had a measuring stick before Solomon; Ethan the Ezrahite was the wise man of his day, and Solomon surpassed him — which tells me God's wisdom is greater than the best wisdom of men.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Ezrah, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Ezrah is a Judahite, named in the genealogy of 1 Chronicles 4:17 as the father of Jether, Mered, Epher, and Jalon.
