The King James spells his name Ezra in that verse, but he is not Ezra the scribe — he belongs to an older generation of Judah, and his sons are listed among the families of the tribe. His name survives in a single verse of a long genealogy.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God keeps the fathers of families even when they never stand on a stage. Ezrah did nothing famous, yet his four sons are named, and I hold that faithfulness inside a family is worth recording.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: aid
BiblicalUsage: Ezrah is the word for help, and it most often describes help that fails or help that is sought too late. Ahaz took treasure from the house of the LORD and gave it to Assyria, but he helped him not, in 2 Chronicles 28:21. Pharaoh's army came forth to help Judah in Jeremiah 37:7, only to return to Egypt, and Job asks where his help stands in Job 31:21. The word also carries the cry of a man looking for help and finding none in Isaiah 10:3.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this word warns me where not to look for help. Assyria did not help Ahaz and Egypt did not help Judah, and I hold that help from men always fails in the end. The help that holds is the help of God alone.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Ezri, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Ezri is named once, in 1 Chronicles 27:26, as the son of Chelub who was over the work of the field for the tillage of the ground under David. He is one of the stewards who kept the king's lands and made the kingdom run. No deed of his is told, only his charge.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe kingdoms run on faithful stewards whose names are nearly forgotten. Ezri tilled the ground so that David's house could stand, and I hold that quiet, unseen work is the backbone of God's people.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: the arm
BiblicalUsage: Ezroa is the arm, and Scripture uses it for the strength that acts. God brought Israel out of Egypt with a strong hand and a stretched out arm in Jeremiah 32:21, and Job, swearing his innocence, says let his arm fall from his shoulder blade if he has wronged the fatherless in Job 31:22. The arm is the picture of power put to work.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the arm of God is the strongest thing in the Bible; it brought a nation out of slavery, and I hold that the same arm still reaches for His people today.
RelatedEvents: The Exodus and the Red Sea
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: forcibleness
BiblicalUsage: Ezuz is force, might, the strength that overpowers. Isaiah shows it turned against Israel in judgment in Isaiah 42:25, where the fury of God's anger is poured out and the strength of battle sets them on fire. But the psalms turn the same word toward praise: men shall speak of the might of God's terrible acts in Psalms 145:6, and fathers tell their children of His strength and wonderful works in Psalms 78:4.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe strength is fearful when it stands against us and wonderful when it stands for us. The same might that judged Israel is the might that saves, and I hold that God's power is never wasted — it either corrects or delivers.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to bellow (as cattle)
BiblicalUsage: Gaah is the lowing of cattle, the plain sound of an animal calling for what it wants. The kine that carried the ark went along the highway lowing as they went in 1 Samuel 6:12, and Job asks whether the ox lows over his fodder in Job 6:5. The word is small and ordinary, and Scripture uses it for a simple, honest need.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that God hears the cry of every creature, even the lowing of cattle; if the kine could find their way to Beth-shemesh while lowing for their calves, then I believe God guides even the simplest longings toward home.
RelatedTopics: Nature and Creation; God's Providence; Guidance
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to mount up; hence, in general, to rise, (figuratively) be majestic
BiblicalUsage: Gaah means to rise up, to mount up, and it carries the sense of triumph. Moses sings it at the Red Sea in Exodus 15:1 — the LORD has triumphed gloriously — and Miriam answers with the same song in Exodus 15:21. Ezekiel uses it for waters that rise until a man cannot pass in Ezekiel 47:5, and Job feels his troubles increasing like a lion rising against him in Job 10:16.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe rising belongs to God first. He rises in triumph over Pharaoh and His river rises until no man can cross it, and I hold that the same God who rose against Egypt rises for His people still.
RelatedEvents: The Exodus and the Red Sea
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to detest; by implication, to reject
BiblicalUsage: Ga'al means to loathe, to detest, and then to reject what is loathed. David sings of Saul's shield vilely cast away in 2 Samuel 1:21, as though it had not been anointed, and Jerusalem is called her mother's daughter because she loathed her husband and children in Ezekiel 16:45. The deepest use is Jeremiah's question in Jeremiah 14:19: hast thou utterly rejected Judah, and has thy soul loathed Zion?
TheologicalSignificance: I believe rejection is the terrible end of despising what God loves. When a people loathes God's ways, God may loathe them in return, and I hold that the only safe answer is to turn back before rejection becomes final.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Gaal, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Gaal son of Ebed came to Shechem with his brethren in Judges 9:26, and the men of Shechem put their confidence in him. He boasted against Abimelech in Judges 9:28, asking who Abimelech was that they should serve him, and urging the men to serve the men of Hamor instead. His rising ended in battle at the gate, and Abimelech drove him out.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Gaal is a warning about confidence placed in the wrong man. Shechem trusted a loud stranger over their own king, and the city paid for it; I hold that loud promises are no substitute for a leader God has set in place.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to soil or (figuratively) desecrate
BiblicalUsage: Ga'al means to soil or defile, and it touches food, blood, and the priesthood itself. Daniel purposed in his heart that he would not defile himself with the king's meat in Daniel 1:8, and the priests who could not prove their genealogy were put from the priesthood as polluted in Ezra 2:62. Isaiah says the people's hands are defiled with blood in Isaiah 59:3, and Lamentations sees priests who have polluted themselves with blood in Lamentations 4:14.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe defilement is not a small matter, because it touches what is holy. Daniel would not eat what would soil him, and I hold that the same refusal is asked of us: to keep ourselves unspotted from the world.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to chide
BiblicalUsage: Ga'ar is a sharp rebuke, a word that stops something in its tracks. Jacob rebuked Joseph for his dream in Genesis 37:10, asking whether his whole family would bow down to him. God rebukes the rushing nations in Isaiah 17:13 until they flee like chaff before the wind, and the LORD rebukes the seed of corrupt priests in Malachi 2:3. Jeremiah is even asked why no one has reproved the false prophet in Jeremiah 29:27.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a rebuke from God is mercy wearing a hard face. It stops the nations, it stops the proud, and it stopped Joseph's family from missing what God was doing. I would rather be rebuked by God now than left alone in my error.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Gaash, a hill in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Gaash is a hill in the land, named as a landmark in the lists of David's mighty men. Hurai is called a man of the brooks of Gaash in 1 Chronicles 11:32, and Hiddai is named the same way in 2 Samuel 23:30. The hill gives its name to the brooks that ran by it, and the men who lived there carried its name into the king's army.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God marks the small places that send Him faithful men. Gaash is only a hill with brooks, yet two of David's mighty men are known by it, and I hold that the place you come from matters less than the King you serve.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to agitate violently
BiblicalUsage: Ga'ash means to shake violently, to tremble and quake. The earth shook and trembled when God was angry in 2 Samuel 22:8, and the foundations of the hills moved and were shaken in Psalms 18:7. The nations shall drink and be moved and be mad because of the sword in Jeremiah 25:16, and even the mighty are troubled at midnight and pass away in Job 34:20.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the shaking of the earth is God's signature on judgment. Mountains and men alike tremble before Him, and I hold that the only ground that never shakes is the ground of His mercy.
RelatedTopics: God's Power; Judgment; Fear of God
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: arrogance or majesty; by implication, (concretely) ornament
BiblicalUsage: Ga'avah is pride, and it swings both ways in Scripture: God's majesty and man's arrogance. Moses calls God's excellency Israel's help in Deuteronomy 33:26, but Isaiah says God will cause the arrogancy of the proud to cease in Isaiah 13:11. Jeremiah has heard the pride of Moab, exceeding proud, in Jeremiah 48:29, and Proverbs warns that in the mouth of the foolish is a rod of pride in Proverbs 14:3.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe pride is a word with two faces, and I must know which one I am wearing. God's excellency is His rightful majesty; mine is a rod in my own mouth. I hold that the cure for my pride is to look up until His greatness makes mine look small.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: haughty
BiblicalUsage: Ga'ayon is the haughty one, the proud man at ease. The psalmist complains in Psalms 123:4 that his soul is filled with the scorning of those at ease and the contempt of the proud. The word appears only here, in a prayer of a people worn down by the scorn of the comfortable.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God hears the prayer of the scorned; the proud at ease may fill our souls with contempt, but the psalm turns straight to the LORD, and I hold that He lifts His eyes to the afflicted.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {arrogance or majesty; by implication, (concretely) ornament}
BiblicalUsage: Ga'on is majesty and pride together — God's excellency on one side, man's arrogance on the other. The LORD overthrew Pharaoh in the greatness of His excellency in Exodus 15:7, but He swears He abhors the excellency of Jacob in Amos 6:8, and the pride of Israel testifies to his face in Hosea 5:5. Sodom's pride, fullness of bread, and idleness are named as her iniquity in Ezekiel 16:49.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe excellency belongs to God alone, and when men claim it, it turns to pride. Pharaoh's army drowned in the greatness of God's excellency, and Sodom fell to the pride of hers. I hold that the difference between worship and ruin is knowing whose glory it is.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Gatam, an Edomite
BiblicalUsage: Gatam is a son of Eliphaz, named among the dukes of Edom in Genesis 36:11 and again in 1 Chronicles 1:36. He is Esau's grandson, one of the chiefs of the Edomite tribes. His name survives in two genealogies that trace the family of Esau.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the family lines of Esau matter because they show how God kept His promises to Abraham's line even outside the chosen line. Gatam is a duke of Edom, and I hold that God's hand is on the nations as well as on Israel.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {the back (as rounded); by analogy, the top or rim, a boss, a vault, arch of eye, bulwarks, etc.}
BiblicalUsage: Gab is the Aramaic word for the back, the rounded top of a thing. It appears once, in Daniel 7:6, where the leopard of the vision has four wings of a fowl upon its back. The word does the plain work of describing the beast's shape.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe even a single Aramaic word in a vision is placed there on purpose; the back of the beast carries its wings, and I hold that the smallest details of Daniel's visions are worth reading closely.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {the back (as rounded); by analogy, the top or rim, a boss, a vault, arch of eye, bulwarks, etc.}
BiblicalUsage: Gab is the Aramaic word for the back, the rounded top of a thing. It appears once, in Daniel 7:6, where the leopard of the vision has four wings of a fowl upon its back. The word does the plain work of describing the beast's shape.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe even a single Aramaic word in a vision is placed there on purpose; the back of the beast carries its wings, and I hold that the smallest details of Daniel's visions are worth reading closely.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: lofty (literally or figuratively)
BiblicalUsage: Gabahh means lofty, high — and it is almost always a warning. The patient in spirit is better than the proud in spirit in Ecclesiastes 7:8, and everyone that is proud in heart is an abomination to the LORD in Proverbs 16:5. The psalmist says God will not suffer a high look and a proud heart in Psalms 101:5, and the Assyrian's high stature in Ezekiel 31:3 is the picture of an empire about to fall.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe height is a good gift until it becomes a high look. The cedar's top among the thick boughs is beautiful, but God cuts down what lifts itself above Him. I hold that the only safe height is the low place at His feet.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to soar, i.e. be lofty; figuratively, to be haughty
BiblicalUsage: Gabahh means to soar, to be high — and the Bible watches carefully whether the height is God's or man's. Saul stood higher than any of the people from his shoulders upward in 1 Samuel 10:23, and Jehoshaphat's heart was lifted up in the ways of the LORD in 2 Chronicles 17:6. But the daughters of Zion are haughty in Isaiah 3:16, and Sodom's daughters were haughty and committed abomination in Ezekiel 16:50.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe there is a height that pleases God and a height that provokes Him, and the difference is the direction of the heart. Jehoshaphat's heart was lifted up in the ways of the LORD, and I hold that this is the only lifting up that ends well.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, to twist as a rope; to bound (as by a line)
BiblicalUsage: Gabal means to set a bound, to draw the line that must not be crossed. God told Moses to set bounds around Mount Sinai in Exodus 19:12, and the law forbids removing a neighbour's landmark in Deuteronomy 19:14. The Jordan was the border of Benjamin's inheritance in Joshua 18:20, and Hamath also shall border on Tyre and Zidon in Zechariah 9:2.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God's bounds are a kindness, not a cage. The line around Sinai kept the people alive, and the landmark kept a neighbour's field his own. I hold that the boundaries God sets are the fences of a good Father.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to be strong; by implication, to prevail, act insolently
BiblicalUsage: Gabar means to be strong, to prevail, and it decides battles and covenants alike. Judah prevailed above his brethren in 1 Chronicles 5:2, and Hannah sang that by strength shall no man prevail in 1 Samuel 2:9. The messenger told David the men prevailed against Israel in 2 Samuel 11:23, and Daniel sees a prince who shall confirm the covenant with many in Daniel 9:27.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe prevailing is never a matter of strength alone. Hannah knew it when she sang that no man prevails by strength, and I hold that the victories that last are the ones God wins for His people.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: baldness in the forehead; by analogy, a bare spot on the right side of cloth
BiblicalUsage: Gabbachath is baldness in the forehead, and it belongs to the laws of leprosy. If a white reddish sore appears in the bald head or bald forehead, the priest must look upon it in Leviticus 13:42 and Leviticus 13:43, and after washing, if the plague has not changed its colour, the garment must be burned in Leviticus 13:55. The word is a piece of the careful law that kept Israel clean.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the careful laws about skin and cloth show how seriously God takes uncleanness. Nothing was too small to examine, and I hold that the same God still looks closely at the hidden places of our lives.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Chaldee origin (compare H1355); the knoll; gabbatha, a vernacular term for the Roman tribunal in Jerusalem:-- Gabbatha.
BiblicalUsage: Gabbatha is the Hebrew name for the Pavement, the place of Pilate's judgment seat in John 19:13. When Pilate heard the Jews' words, he brought Jesus forth and sat down in the judgment seat, in a place called the Pavement, but in the Hebrew, Gabbatha. The name means a raised place, a knoll, and it is the last public spot where Jesus stood before the cross.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the name of the place matters because the judgment seat of a Roman governor became the stage of the world's greatest injustice — and its greatest mercy. Pilate sat down to judge Jesus, and I hold that the Judge of all the earth was standing before him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Gabbai, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Gabbai is named once, in Nehemiah 11:8, among the men who came to live in Jerusalem after the wall was rebuilt. After him Gabbai, Sallai, nine hundred twenty and eight. He is one of the residents who filled the holy city again.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the rebuilding of Jerusalem needed residents as much as it needed a wall. Gabbai came and lived there, and I hold that the quiet choice to dwell in the city of God is itself an act of faith.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: pride
BiblicalUsage: Gabhuth is pride, the loftiness of men that God promises to bow down. The lofty looks of man shall be humbled in Isaiah 2:11, and the loftiness of men shall be made low in Isaiah 2:17, and the LORD alone shall be exalted in that day. The word appears only in these two verses, and both carry the same sentence.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the day is coming when every high look falls; Isaiah says it twice because it needs saying twice: the LORD alone shall be exalted in that day, and I hold that to bow now is better than to be bowed then.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: crystal (from its resemblance to ice)
BiblicalUsage: Gabish is crystal, a clear, shining stone, though the King James renders it pearls in Job 28:18. No mention shall be made of coral or of pearls, says Job, for the price of wisdom is above rubies. The word names something precious and clear, and Job sets it beside the treasures men chase.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Job is right: wisdom outshines crystal and pearls alike; men dig for stones and dive for pearls, but the price of wisdom is above them all, and I hold that knowing God is the only treasure that never loses its value.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a twisted chain or lace
BiblicalUsage: Gabluth is a twisted chain or lace, the wreathen work of pure gold on the high priest's breastplate. Moses is told to make chains at the ends of wreathen work in Exodus 28:22, and the workmen made them exactly so in Exodus 39:15. The word is a craftsman's word, describing gold twisted into a pattern.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God cares about the details of worship, down to the twist of a gold chain; the breastplate carried the names of Israel over Aaron's heart, and I hold that the God who orders gold chains also orders our lives with care.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a hump or peak of hills
BiblicalUsage: Gabnon is the hump or peak of a hill, the high places that rise above the plain. The hill of God is as the hill of Bashan, an high hill, in Psalms 68:15, and the psalm asks why the high hills leap in Psalms 68:16. This is the hill God desires to dwell in, and the LORD will dwell in it for ever.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God chooses high places for His dwelling, and the hills themselves seem to leap at the thought; the hill of Bashan is high, but God's hill is higher, and I hold that He dwells with His people for ever.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: elevated (or elated), powerful, arrogant
BiblicalUsage: Gaboahh means high, elevated — and it covers hills, horns, and men's hearts. They built high places on every high hill in 1 Kings 14:23, and the LORD warned Samuel not to look on the height of Eliab's stature in 1 Samuel 16:7. The ram in Daniel's vision had two horns that were high in Daniel 8:3, and Israel set up images on every high hill in 2 Kings 17:10.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe height is a test of the heart. God looks past the height of a man's stature to his heart, and I hold that the high places men build for themselves always fall, while the height of God stands for ever.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H1403); Gabriel, an archangel:--Gabriel.
BiblicalUsage: Gabriel is the angel who stands in the presence of God, and Luke names him twice. He tells Zechariah in Luke 1:19 that he is Gabriel, sent to speak glad tidings, and in Luke 1:26 he is sent from God to Nazareth, to a virgin named Mary. The name means God is my strength, and he carries the greatest announcements in the Gospel.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Gabriel matters because he brings God's own words to men; he stood in the presence of God and was sent to speak, and I hold that the announcements he carried — a son to Zechariah, a Son to Mary — changed the world.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Gabriel, an archangel
BiblicalUsage: Gabriel is the angel who explains Daniel's visions. A man's voice between the banks of Ulai calls in Daniel 8:16, Gabriel, make this man to understand the vision, and in Daniel 9:21 the man Gabriel, whom Daniel had seen in the vision at the beginning, touches him about the time of the evening oblation. He is the messenger who makes the mysteries plain.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God sends His messengers to make hard things clear. Daniel could not understand the vision alone, so Gabriel was sent, and I hold that God still gives understanding to those who ask Him for it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Gacham, a son of Nahor
BiblicalUsage: Gacham is a son of Nahor, named once in Genesis 22:24, where Reumah the concubine bore Tebah, and Gaham, and Thahash, and Maachah. The King James spells his name Gaham. He belongs to the family of Abraham's brother, the line that stayed in Haran.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the families around Abraham matter because they show how wide God's story runs. Gacham never leaves Haran, yet his name is kept, and I hold that no family is too far from Abraham for God to remember it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Gachar, one of the Nethinim
BiblicalUsage: Gachar is one of the Nethinim, the temple servants who returned from exile. The children of Gahar are listed among the returnees in Ezra 2:47 and again in Nehemiah 7:49. The King James spells the name Gahar; his family came home to serve in the house of God.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the Nethinim are the quiet heroes of the return. They were servants, not priests, yet they came home to serve, and I hold that the lowest service in God's house is honour enough.
RelatedEvents: Cyrus's Decree and Return from Exile
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: the external abdomen, belly (as the source of the faetus)
BiblicalUsage: Gachon is the belly, the part of the body that crawls on the ground. The serpent is cursed to go upon his belly and eat dust all the days of his life in Genesis 3:14, and the law forbids eating whatever goes upon the belly in Leviticus 11:42. The word marks the lowest way of moving, close to the dust.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the serpent's belly is a picture of the fall itself; he was made to crawl in the dust because he brought dust and death to man, and I hold that the seed of the woman would one day bruise his head.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H1410); Gad, a tribe of Israelites:--Gad.
BiblicalUsage: Gad is the tribe, named among the twelve sealed in Revelation 7:5. Of the tribe of Gad were sealed twelve thousand, standing between Reuben and Asher in John's vision. The name reaches the end of the Bible because the tribe that bore it is not forgotten.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the sealing of Gad is a promise that God keeps His own. Twelve thousand from a tribe that once settled east of Jordan are counted among the sealed, and I hold that no tribe and no believer is left out of God's number.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Fortune, a Babylonian deity
BiblicalUsage: Gad is Fortune, a Babylonian god, named once in Isaiah 65:11. The prophet accuses those who forsake the LORD, forget His holy mountain, prepare a table for that troop, and furnish the drink offering unto that number. The King James hides the god's name behind the word troop, but the Hebrew names Gad, the god of fortune, and Meni, the god of destiny.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe men still set a table for Fortune today, trusting luck instead of the LORD. Isaiah calls it forsaking God, and I hold that trusting chance is just idolatry with a modern name.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: fortune
BiblicalUsage: Gad means fortune, and Leah used the word when she named her son. A troop cometh, she said in Genesis 30:11, and she called his name Gad. The King James renders it as a troop, but the word carries the sense of good fortune — a troop of blessing arriving at once.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Leah's naming of Gad shows how mothers read God's hand in their children; she saw a troop coming and called it fortune, and I hold that every child is a troop of blessing from God.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Gad, a son of Jacob, including his tribe and its territory; also a prophet
BiblicalUsage: Gad is the seventh son of Jacob, the first by Zilpah, and Leah named him for the troop that came in Genesis 30:11. His sons are listed in Genesis 46:16 — Ziphion, Haggi, Shuni, Ezbon, Eri, Arodi, and Areli — when the family went down into Egypt. The tribe that grew from him took the east side of Jordan and fought for its brothers.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Gad's name is a promise kept. A troop came to Leah, and a tribe of warriors grew from her son, and I hold that God turns a mother's word of hope into a nation of fighters.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: coriander seed (from its furrows)
BiblicalUsage: Gad is coriander seed, the small round seed the manna resembled. The house of Israel called the bread manna, and it was like coriander seed, white, in Exodus 16:31, and the manna was as coriander seed in colour as bdellium in Numbers 11:7. The word gives us the size and shape of the daily bread God sent.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the manna's likeness to coriander seed shows how ordinary God's provision looks; it was small and round and came every morning, and I hold that God still feeds His people with daily bread that looks like nothing much.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to fell a tree; generally, to destroy anything
BiblicalUsage: Gada means to cut off, to fell, to destroy — and it is used for arms, altars, and idols alike. The LORD says He will cut off the arm of Eli's house in 1 Samuel 2:31, and He commands Israel to hew down the graven images of the nations in Deuteronomy 12:3. The horns of the altar at Bethel shall be cut off in Amos 3:14, and the people cut down the groves and threw down the high places in 2 Chronicles 31:1.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe cutting off is God's surgery on what corrupts His people. Altars, groves, and proud arms must all fall, and I hold that the God who cuts away idols is the same God who saves the remnant.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to crowd; also to gash (as if by pressing into)
BiblicalUsage: Gadad means to crowd together, and then to cut or gash as a crowd presses in. The prophets of Baal cut themselves with knives and lancets on Carmel in 1 Kings 18:28, and the law forbids Israel to cut themselves for the dead in Deuteronomy 14:1 and again in Jeremiah 16:6. But the word also gathers: the wicked gather themselves together against the soul of the righteous in Psalms 94:21.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this word shows how false worship turns on the body and how true trouble gathers against the righteous. The Baal prophets cut themselves and got no answer, and I hold that the God who answers by fire needs no blood from us.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a border of a river (as cut into by the stream)
BiblicalUsage: Gadah is the bank of a river, the edge where the water cuts into the land. The river of Assyria shall come up over all his channels and go over all his banks in Isaiah 8:7, and the Jordan overflowed all his banks all the time of harvest when the priests' feet touched the water in Joshua 3:15. The waters returned to their place and flowed over all his banks when the ark came up in Joshua 4:18, and the men who crossed in the first month put to flight all the valleys in 1 Chronicles 12:15.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the overflowing banks are a picture of God's power breaking its bounds. The Jordan was full, yet the priests walked through on dry ground, and I hold that no flood is too full for God to part.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to be (causatively make) large (in various senses, as in body, mind, estate or honor, also in pride)
BiblicalUsage: Gadal means to be great, and to make great — and it is used for God, for kings, and for ordinary men. David prays that God's name may be magnified for ever in 1 Chronicles 17:24, and Solomon exceeded all the kings of the earth for riches and wisdom in 1 Kings 10:23. Samuel tells Israel to consider how great things the LORD has done for them in 1 Samuel 12:24, and Rehoboam's young men boast that his little finger shall be thicker than his father's loins in 2 Chronicles 10:10.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe greatness is measured by whose name grows. David wanted God's name magnified, and Rehoboam's friends wanted his own finger thicker. I hold that the greatness that lasts is the greatness that points away from ourselves and toward God.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to hack (with words), i.e. revile
BiblicalUsage: Gadaph means to reproach, to hack at a man with words — and its worst use is against God Himself. Sennacherib's messenger asks whom Hezekiah has reproached and blasphemed in 2 Kings 19:22, and the same words stand in Isaiah 37:23, where the prophet answers him. The fathers blasphemed God by trespass in Ezekiel 20:27, and the soul that sins presumptuously reproaches the LORD in Numbers 15:30.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe words can wound God, and that is a fearful thing. To reproach the Holy One of Israel is not a small sin, and I hold that the tongue that blasphemes will answer for it, while the tongue that repents will be forgiven.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to wall in or around
BiblicalUsage: Gadar means to wall in, to build the wall that guards a place. Masons were hired to repair the house of the LORD in 2 Kings 22:6, and God promises to raise up the tabernacle of David and close up its breaches in Amos 9:11. The false prophets did not go up into the gaps or make up the hedge for Israel in Ezekiel 13:5, but the faithful shall be called the repairer of the breach in Isaiah 58:12.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God is the great repairer of breaches, and He calls His people to the same work. The wall that guards the vineyard and the hedge that stands in the battle are worth building, and I hold that mending what is broken is holy work.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from Γαδαρά (a town east of the Jordan); a Gadarene or inhabitant of Gadara:--Gadarene.
BiblicalUsage: Gadarene is the word for a man of Gadara, east of the Jordan, and it stands in Matthew 8:28, where Jesus met two men possessed with devils coming out of the tombs. The King James says the country of the Gergesenes there, following a different manuscript reading, while the Greek text behind most modern Bibles reads Gadarenes. Either way, the place is the far side of the lake, Gentile country, where Jesus cast out demons.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe it matters that Jesus crossed the lake to Gentile country for two tormented men; the name of the town is disputed in the manuscripts, but the mercy is not: He came to them, and I hold that no one is too far across the water for Him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Gaddiel, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Gaddiel son of Sodi is one of the twelve spies, named in Numbers 13:10 as the spy of the tribe of Zebulun. He went up with the others to search the land, and he came back with the report that turned the people's hearts. His name is kept in the list of the twelve.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the spies' list is a warning as much as a record. Ten of the twelve brought back fear, and Gaddiel's name stands among them; I hold that the report we believe shapes the future we get.
RelatedEvents: The Twelve Spies and Israel's Unbelief
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Gaddi, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Gaddi son of Susi is one of the twelve spies, named in Numbers 13:11 as the spy of the tribe of Manasseh. He searched the land with the others and stood in the company that brought back the evil report. His name is kept in the list of the twelve.
TheologicalSignificance: Ten men came back with fear and two with faith, and Gaddi's name is on the fearful side. I hold that the report we believe shapes the future we get, and the majority is not always right.
RelatedEvents: The Twelve Spies and Israel's Unbelief
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: large (literally or figuratively)
BiblicalUsage: Gadel means large, and it describes growth in body and in standing. The child Samuel grew on in 1 Samuel 2:26, in favour with the LORD and with men, and the man Isaac waxed great until he became very great in Genesis 26:13. Jehoshaphat waxed great exceedingly in 2 Chronicles 17:12, and the same word can turn sour: Jerusalem's neighbours are called great of flesh in Ezekiel 16:26.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe growth is good when it grows toward God. Samuel grew in favour, Isaac grew in blessing, and Jehoshaphat grew in strength — but greatness of flesh alone is no blessing. I hold that the size that matters is the size of a life before God.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a circumvallation; by implication, an inclosure
BiblicalUsage: Gader is a hedge or a wall, the barrier that guards a vineyard or a city. He that breaks an hedge shall be bitten by a serpent in Ecclesiastes 10:8, and God says He will take away the hedge of His vineyard in Isaiah 5:5. The prophets failed to make up the hedge for Israel in Ezekiel 13:5, but Ezra thanked God for a wall in Judah and Jerusalem in Ezra 9:9.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the hedge is God's protection and the wall is His mercy. When the hedge is taken away, the vineyard is eaten, and when the wall is given, the city stands. I hold that God still builds walls around His people, and breaks them down only to bring them back.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a Gadite (collectively) or descendants of Gad
BiblicalUsage: Gadite means a man of Gad, the tribe that settled east of Jordan. David made rulers over the Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half tribe of Manasseh in 1 Chronicles 26:32, and the land of the Gadites is named as the far east of Israel in 2 Kings 10:33. The word marks a people by their father's name.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the Gadites show that faithfulness is not about where you settle; they lived east of Jordan, across the river from the rest, yet they served the king and the LORD, and I hold that distance from the centre is no distance from God.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a Gadite (collectively) or descendants of Gad
BiblicalUsage: Gadite means a man of Gad, the tribe that settled east of Jordan. David made rulers over the Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half tribe of Manasseh in 1 Chronicles 26:32, and the land of the Gadites is named as the far east of Israel in 2 Kings 10:33. The word marks a people by their father's name.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the Gadites show that faithfulness is not about where you settle; they lived east of Jordan, across the river from the rest, yet they served the king and the LORD, and I hold that distance from the centre is no distance from God.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a stack of sheaves; by analogy, a tomb
BiblicalUsage: Gadish is a shock or stack of sheaves, and by the same picture, a tomb. Samson burned the shocks of the Philistines in Judges 15:5, and the law makes the man who kindles a fire pay for the stacks of corn in Exodus 22:6. But Job uses the same word for the grave: he shall be brought to the grave and remain in the tomb in Job 21:32, and a man shall come to his grave in full age, like a shock of corn in his season, in Job 5:26.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the shock of corn is a gentle picture of death. A sheaf is gathered in its season, not torn up green, and Job's hope is to come to his grave the same way. I hold that God gathers His people in their season, as a farmer gathers his harvest.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: great (in any sense); hence, older; also insolent
BiblicalUsage: Gadol means great, and it is one of the largest words in the Bible, used nearly five hundred times. The LORD saved Israel by a great deliverance in 1 Chronicles 11:14, and Solomon made a great throne of ivory in 1 Kings 10:18. Samuel tells Israel to stand and see the great thing the LORD will do in 1 Samuel 12:16, and the covenant binds small and great alike in 2 Chronicles 15:13.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe great is a word that belongs to God first and to men second. The great deliverance, the great thing, the great throne — all of them point up to a greatness beyond our own. I hold that when we call anything great, we should ask whether it makes God look great.
RelatedTopics: God's glory; Majesty of God; Victory
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a roof; by analogy, the top of an altar
BiblicalUsage: Gag is the roof, the flat top of a house where men walked, talked, and looked out. Samuel communed with Saul upon the top of the house in 1 Samuel 9:25, and David arose from his bed and walked upon the roof of the king's house in 2 Samuel 11:2, where he saw Bathsheba. The law commands a battlement for the roof in Deuteronomy 22:8, so no one falls from it, and the grass on the housetops withers in 2 Kings 19:26.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the roof is where a man's heart is tested. David walked on his roof in the evening and fell, and Samuel spoke with Saul on a roof before he was king. I hold that high places are dangerous when the heart is idle.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to remove (a bandage from a wound, i.e. heal it)
BiblicalUsage: Gahah means to take off a bandage, to heal a wound by uncovering it. It appears once, in Hosea 5:13, where Ephraim saw his sickness and Judah saw his wound, and went to Assyria for healing — yet the Assyrian king could not heal them, nor cure them of their wound.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Assyria could not heal because the wound was God's doing; men run to kings and physicians for cures only God can give, and I hold that the healing we need most is the one that comes from the hand that wounded us.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to prostrate oneself
BiblicalUsage: Gahar means to bow down low, to stretch oneself out flat. Elijah cast himself down upon the earth on Carmel and put his face between his knees in 1 Kings 18:42, waiting for rain. Elisha went up and stretched himself upon the dead child in 2 Kings 4:34, mouth to mouth and hands to hands, until the flesh waxed warm, and in 2 Kings 4:35 he stretched himself upon him again, and the child sneezed seven times and opened his eyes.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe bowing low is the posture of power in God's kingdom. Elijah bowed on Carmel and the rain came; Elisha stretched himself over a dead boy and life returned. I hold that God works through those willing to get low.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Latin origin; Gaius (i.e. Caius), a Christian:--Gaius.
BiblicalUsage: Gaius is a name carried by four different men in the New Testament, and three of them are named here. Gaius of Macedonia was seized by the Ephesian mob with Paul in Acts 19:29, Gaius of Corinth was Paul's host and host of the whole church in Romans 16:23, and the wellbeloved Gaius received John's third letter in 3 John 1:1. One name, four men, each known for standing close to an apostle.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the four men named Gaius show how the gospel makes strangers into hosts and friends. A Macedonian seized in a riot, a Corinthian who opened his house, and a beloved brother who walked in the truth — I hold that hospitality and truth are the marks of the name.
RelatedPeople: Gaius of Macedonia; Gaius of Corinth; Gaius (3 John)
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Galed, a memorial cairn East of the Jordan
BiblicalUsage: Galeed is the heap of witness, the pile of stones Jacob and Laban raised between them. Jacob called it Galeed in Genesis 31:47, and Laban said in Genesis 31:48 that this heap is a witness between me and thee this day. The name means heap of witness, and the stones stood as a boundary neither man would cross to harm the other.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God sets stones as witnesses between men who cannot trust each other. Jacob and Laban parted with a heap between them, and I hold that a boundary kept in peace is better than a quarrel won.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: something rolled, i.e. a heap of stone or dung (plural ruins), by analogy, a spring of water (plural waves)
BiblicalUsage: Gal is a heap, a wave, a pile of stones — anything rolled together. Jacob's men gathered stones and made a heap at Galeed in Genesis 31:46, and Absalom's body was covered with a very great heap of stones in 2 Samuel 18:17. The sea causes its waves to come up against Tyre in Ezekiel 26:3, and the fenced cities of Judah were laid waste into ruinous heaps in 2 Kings 19:25.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe heaps tell the story of a life. Jacob's heap was a witness of peace, and Absalom's heap was a monument of rebellion. I hold that what we pile up in life — stones of witness or stones of ruin — is the choice we make every day.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain affinity; milk (figuratively):--milk.
BiblicalUsage: Gala is milk, and the apostles use it for the first food of faith. Paul fed the Corinthians with milk and not with meat, because they were not able to bear it, in 1 Corinthians 3:2, and he says the same to the Hebrews in Hebrews 5:12: they have need of milk, and not of strong meat. Peter tells newborn babes to desire the sincere milk of the word, that they may grow thereby, in 1 Peter 2:2.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe milk is the right food for the newborn, and the wrong food for the grown. The apostles never despised milk — they fed it gladly — but they expected growth, and I hold that a Christian who still needs only milk has stopped growing.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to be obstinate
BiblicalUsage: Gala means to be obstinate, to meddle where a man has no business. The beginning of strife is as when one lets out water, says Proverbs 17:14, so leave off contention before it is meddled with. A man who separates himself seeks and intermeddles with all wisdom in Proverbs 18:1, and it is an honour for a man to cease from strife, but every fool will be meddling, in Proverbs 20:3.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe meddling is the fool's work and ceasing from strife is the honourable work. The wise man leaves off contention before it floods, and I hold that the quarrels we refuse to start are the victories we never have to win.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, to be bald, i.e. (causatively) to shave; figuratively to lay waste
BiblicalUsage: Galach means to shave, and it is used for shame, for cleansing, and for priests. Hanun shaved David's servants and cut their garments in half in 2 Samuel 10:4, and the same shame is told again in 1 Chronicles 19:4. A captive woman must shave her head before she joins Israel in Deuteronomy 21:12, and the priests must neither shave their heads nor let their locks grow long in Ezekiel 44:20.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe shaving shows how much hair and honour meant in that world. To shave a man's beard was to shame him, and to shave a priest's head was to break his order. I hold that God cares about the outward signs of honour because the heart follows the head.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to denude (especially in a disgraceful sense); by implication, to exile (captives being usually stripped); figuratively, to reveal
BiblicalUsage: Galah is a wide word: to uncover, to reveal, and to carry away into exile. God told His servant David what He would do in 1 Chronicles 17:25, and Jonathan and Saul discovered themselves to the Philistines in 1 Samuel 14:11. But the same word carries Israel away: Nebuchadnezzar carried them to Babylon in 2 Chronicles 36:20, and Tiglath-pileser carried Galilee captive to Assyria in 2 Kings 15:29.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe uncovering and exile are two sides of the same word because sin uncovers what should be hidden and exile carries away what should stay home. God reveals His plans to His servants and His judgments to the nations, and I hold that both revelations are mercy: one to build faith, the other to call us home.
RelatedEvents: Fall of Jerusalem and the Exile
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: dung (as in balls)
BiblicalUsage: Galal is dung, and it appears once, in the judgment on Jeroboam's house in 1 Kings 14:10. God says He will take away the remnant of the house of Jeroboam, as a man takes away dung, till it is all gone. The word is as blunt as the judgment it carries.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God speaks bluntly about the house that leads His people into sin; Jeroboam's line is taken away like dung, and I hold that a house built on idolatry ends in the same place as refuse.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: dung (as in balls)
BiblicalUsage: Galal is dung, and it appears once, in the judgment on Jeroboam's house in 1 Kings 14:10. God says He will take away the remnant of the house of Jeroboam, as a man takes away dung, till it is all gone. The word is as blunt as the judgment it carries.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God speaks bluntly about the house that leads His people into sin; Jeroboam's line is taken away like dung, and I hold that a house built on idolatry ends in the same place as refuse.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Galal, the name of two Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Galal is a Levite, named twice among the families who served in the temple. He stands in the list of Levites in 1 Chronicles 9:15, and in Nehemiah 11:17 his grandson Mattaniah leads the thanksgiving in prayer, as the son of Micha, the son of Zabdi, the son of Asaph — with Abda the son of Shammua, the son of Galal, the son of Jeduthun. His name survives because his family sang.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the Levites who sang are the backbone of Israel's worship. Galal's name is kept because his sons led the thanksgiving, and I hold that a family that sings God's praise leaves a longer mark than a family that builds an empire.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to roll (literally or figuratively)
BiblicalUsage: Galal means to roll, and it rolls stones, bodies, and judgment alike. Jacob rolled the stone from the well's mouth in Genesis 29:10, and Saul told the people to roll a great stone to him in 1 Samuel 14:33. Amasa wallowed in blood in the highway in 2 Samuel 20:12, and Amos cries that judgment should run down as waters in Amos 5:24.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe rolling is the motion of God's work in the world. Stones roll away from wells so flocks can drink, and judgment rolls down like water so the land can be cleansed. I hold that the God who rolls stones away is the God who rolls our burdens away too.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to fold
BiblicalUsage: Galam means to fold or wrap together, and it appears once, in 2 Kings 2:8, when Elijah took his mantle and wrapped it together and smote the waters, and they were divided so that he and Elisha went over on dry ground. The prophet folds his cloak before he parts the river.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the folded mantle is a picture of power held in a prophet's hand; Elijah wrapped it together and the Jordan parted, and I hold that the God who divided the sea for Moses still divides rivers for His prophets.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably to caper (as a goat)
KeyPassages: Song of Solomon 4:1; Song of Solomon 6:5
BiblicalUsage: Galash means to caper or leap, and it describes the hair of the beloved in the Song of Solomon. Her hair is as a flock of goats that appear from Mount Gilead in Song of Solomon 4:1, and the same picture returns in Song of Solomon 6:5. The goats come down the mountain in a moving, leaping line, and the poet sees her hair the same way.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the Song's picture of goats on a hillside is a lover's eye, not a scholar's; the hair moves like a flock coming down from Gilead, and I hold that God gave us poetry to say what plain words cannot.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1053; a Galatian or inhabitant of Galatia:--Galatian.
BiblicalUsage: Galatian is the word for a man of Galatia, and Paul uses it once, in Galatians 3:1, when he calls his readers foolish Galatians. Who has bewitched you, he asks, that you should not obey the truth, before whose eyes Jesus Christ has been evidently set forth, crucified among you? The name carries Paul's frustration with a church turning back to the law.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Paul's rebuke is love wearing a hard face; he calls them foolish because they were turning from grace to law, and I hold that the gospel is too precious to trade for rules.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of foreign origin; Galatia, a region of Asia:--Galatia.
BiblicalUsage: Galatia is the region of Asia Minor where Paul planted churches. He writes to all the brethren with him, unto the churches of Galatia, in Galatians 1:2, and he gives the Corinthians the same order he gave the churches of Galatia about the collection for the saints in 1 Corinthians 16:1. The region is known for its churches and its troubles.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Galatia shows how quickly a church can drift. Paul planted it, wrote to it twice, and still had to plead with it not to leave the gospel; I hold that every church needs the letter to the Galatians read aloud again.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1053; Galatic or relating to Galatia:--of Galatia.
BiblicalUsage: Galatic means of Galatia, belonging to that region. Paul and his company went throughout Phrygia and the region of Galatia in Acts 16:6, forbidden by the Holy Ghost to preach in Asia, and later he went over all the country of Galatia and Phrygia in order, strengthening all the disciples, in Acts 18:23. The word marks the ground Paul walked to strengthen the churches.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the strengthening of disciples is the quiet work of the apostle; Paul went over the country in order, church by church, and I hold that the gospel spreads not only by preaching but by returning to strengthen those already won.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain derivation; tranquillity:--calm.
BiblicalUsage: Galene is a calm, the stillness after the storm. Jesus rebuked the wind and the raging of the water in Luke 8:24, and there was a calm. He said to the sea, Peace, be still, in Mark 4:39, and there was a great calm, and Matthew tells it the same way in Matthew 8:26: He arose and rebuked the winds and the sea, and there was a great calm.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the calm after the storm is the proof of who Jesus is. The wind and the sea obey Him, and the disciples' fear turns to wonder. I hold that the same voice that said Peace, be still still speaks over the storms in my life.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a wheel
BiblicalUsage: Galgal is the Aramaic word for a wheel, and it appears once, in Daniel 7:9, where the Ancient of Days sits on a throne like fiery flame, and His wheels are as burning fire. The word gives the throne its motion and its terror.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the burning wheels of God's throne show that He is not still or far away; his throne moves, His fire burns, and I hold that the Ancient of Days is coming to judge the earth in righteousness.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a wheel
BiblicalUsage: Galgal is the Aramaic word for a wheel, and it appears once, in Daniel 7:9, where the Ancient of Days sits on a throne like fiery flame, and His wheels are as burning fire. The word gives the throne its motion and its terror.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the burning wheels of God's throne show that He is not still or far away; his throne moves, His fire burns, and I hold that the Ancient of Days is coming to judge the earth in righteousness.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H1551); Galilæa (i.e. the heathen circle), a region of Palestine:--Galilee.
BiblicalUsage: Galilee is the northern region where Jesus grew up and did most of His ministry. Matthew calls it Galilee of the Gentiles in Matthew 4:15, quoting the prophet, and Luke says the angel Gabriel was sent to a city of Galilee named Nazareth in Luke 1:26. The region the prophets called the land of darkness became the land where the great light shone.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God chose a despised region for His Son's home. Galilee of the Gentiles was far from Jerusalem's glory, yet the light dawned there first; I hold that God still begins His greatest works in the places men overlook.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1056; Galilean or belonging to Galilea:--Galilean, of Galilee.
BiblicalUsage: Galilean means a man of Galilee, and it was a word that marked a man out. A damsel said to Peter in Matthew 26:69, Thou also wast with Jesus of Galilee, and on the day of Pentecost the crowd marvelled, saying, Are not all these which speak Galilaeans, in Acts 2:7. The accent and the home gave them away.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe being a Galilean was both a shame and a glory; men despised the region, yet Jesus chose Galileans for His apostles, and I hold that God still chooses the unregarded to carry His word.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Galil (as a special circuit) in the North of Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Galil is the Hebrew name for Galilee, the northern circuit of cities. Solomon gave Hiram twenty cities in the land of Galilee in 1 Kings 9:11, and Tiglath-pileser took Galilee captive to Assyria in 2 Kings 15:29. The region passed from a king's gift to a conqueror's spoil.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the gift of Galilee and the loss of Galilee are the story of Israel in miniature. Solomon gave it away and Assyria took it away, yet the prophets said light would dawn there; I hold that no land is lost to God.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a valve of a folding door (as turning); also a ring (as round)
BiblicalUsage: Galil means a folding leaf, a valve of a door that turns, and also a ring. The two doors of the temple were of fir tree, and the two leaves of the one door were folding, in 1 Kings 6:34. The same word is a ring: the hangings were fastened to silver rings in Esther 1:6, and the beloved's hands are as gold rings set with the beryl in Song of Solomon 5:14.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the folding door and the gold ring show how one word can hold two beauties. A door that turns and a ring that shines both belong to God's house, and I hold that He makes the useful beautiful and the beautiful useful.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a barber
BiblicalUsage: Gallab is a barber, and the word appears once, in Ezekiel 5:1, where the prophet is told to take a barber's razor and cause it to pass upon his head and his beard, then weigh and divide the hair. The barber's work becomes a sign of judgment on Jerusalem.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God uses the commonest trades for His signs; a barber's razor in a prophet's hand becomes the picture of a city weighed and divided, and I hold that no work is too ordinary for God to speak through.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Latin origin; Gallion (i.e. Gallio), a Roman officer:--Gallio.
BiblicalUsage: Gallio was the deputy of Achaia, the Roman proconsul before whom the Jews brought Paul in Acts 18:12. They accused Paul of persuading men to worship God contrary to the law, and when Paul was about to speak, Gallio said in Acts 18:14 that if it were a matter of wrong or wicked lewdness, he would bear with them — but this was a matter of words and names, and he drove them from the judgment seat.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Gallio's refusal is a small mercy in the book of Acts. A Roman governor would not judge the gospel, and Paul went on his way unharmed; I hold that God can use even a careless judge to protect His servants.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Gallim, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Gallim is a place in the hill country, named twice as a landmark of sorrow. Saul gave Michal, David's wife, to Phalti the son of Laish, which was of Gallim, in 1 Samuel 25:44, and Isaiah cries to the daughter of Gallim to lift up her voice in Isaiah 10:30. The town is remembered for a marriage broken and a city threatened.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Gallim is a place where vows were broken and voices were raised in fear. Michal was given away and a city was warned, and I hold that God remembers the towns where His people suffered.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: sterile (as wrapped up too hard); figuratively, desolate
BiblicalUsage: Galmud means sterile, wrapped up too hard to bear fruit, and then desolate. Zion asks who has begotten her children, seeing she has lost them and is desolate in Isaiah 49:21, and the congregation of hypocrites shall be desolate in Job 15:34. Job's friends were solitary, fleeing into the wilderness in former time desolate and waste, in Job 30:3, and Job curses the night to be solitary in Job 3:7.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe desolation is the fruit of hypocrisy and the cry of the afflicted alike. The hypocrite's house is desolate and Job's night is solitary, yet God answers both. I hold that the desolate are not forgotten, for God promises to comfort Zion.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {captivity; concretely, exiles (collectively)}
BiblicalUsage: Galuth is the captivity, and concretely the exiles themselves. Daniel is called a man of the captives of Judah in Daniel 2:25, and the king asks whether he is that Daniel, which is of the children of the captivity of Judah, in Daniel 5:13. The same Daniel is accused as one of the children of the captivity in Daniel 6:13, and after the return the children of the captivity kept the dedication of the house of God with joy in Ezra 6:16.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the captivity is the long shadow over Daniel's whole life, and the joy of the return is its sunrise. Daniel stayed faithful in exile, and the exiles came home to dedicate the house. I hold that God keeps His people in captivity and brings them home in joy.
RelatedEvents: Fall of Jerusalem and the Exile
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {captivity; concretely, exiles (collectively)}
BiblicalUsage: Galuth is the captivity, and concretely the exiles themselves. Daniel is called a man of the captives of Judah in Daniel 2:25, and the king asks whether he is that Daniel, which is of the children of the captivity of Judah, in Daniel 5:13. The same Daniel is accused as one of the children of the captivity in Daniel 6:13, and after the return the children of the captivity kept the dedication of the house of God with joy in Ezra 6:16.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the captivity is the long shadow over Daniel's whole life, and the joy of the return is its sunrise. Daniel stayed faithful in exile, and the exiles came home to dedicate the house. I hold that God keeps His people in captivity and brings them home in joy.
RelatedEvents: Fall of Jerusalem and the Exile
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, assemblage; used only adverbially also, even, yea, though; often repeated as correl. both... and
BiblicalUsage: Gam is the little word also, even, yea, though — the word that adds one thing to another. Saul died for his transgression, even against the word of the LORD, and also for asking counsel of a familiar spirit, in 1 Chronicles 10:13. The navy also of Hiram brought gold from Ophir in 1 Kings 10:11; the word is small, but it carries the weight of one more thing.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the smallest words in Scripture carry the heaviest loads; also and even can turn a list into a judgment, and I hold that God notices every also in our lives.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to absorb
BiblicalUsage: Gama means to swallow or drink down, to take in eagerly. Abraham's servant ran to meet Rebekah and said, Let me, I pray thee, drink a little water of thy pitcher, in Genesis 24:17. Job uses the same word for the war horse, which swallows the ground with fierceness and rage in Job 39:24.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the servant's request and the horse's charge show the two sides of thirst; one drinks humbly from a pitcher, the other swallows the ground in war, and I hold that God gives water to the humble and restrains the violent.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a camel
BiblicalUsage: Gamal is the camel, the ship of the desert that carries kings and queens. The Queen of Sheba came to Jerusalem with camels that bore spices and gold in 1 Kings 10:2, and the same visit is told again in 2 Chronicles 9:1. Obil the Ishmaelite was over the camels in David's household in 1 Chronicles 27:30, and Saul was told to smite Amalek and spare not camel or ass in 1 Samuel 15:3.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the camel carries the wealth of the world to the feet of wisdom. Sheba's camels bore spices to Solomon, and I hold that the riches of the nations still come to the King who is greater than Solomon.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to treat a person (well or ill), i.e. benefit or requite; by implication (of toil), to ripen, i.e. (specifically) to wean
BiblicalUsage: Gamal means to deal with a person, to benefit or to requite — and it covers both weaning a child and rewarding a man. Hannah would not go up until the child was weaned in 1 Samuel 1:22, and Tahpenes weaned Genubath in Pharaoh's house in 1 Kings 11:20. David sings that the LORD rewarded him according to his righteousness in 2 Samuel 22:21, and the enemies of Judah say, Behold, how they reward us, in 2 Chronicles 20:11.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God deals with us as a mother weans a child and as a judge rewards the righteous. He brings us from milk to meat and repays us according to our ways, and I hold that His dealing is always just and always kind.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H1583); Gamaliel (i.e. Gamliel), an Israelite:--Gamaliel.
BiblicalUsage: Gamaliel was a Pharisee, a doctor of the law, had in reputation among all the people. He stood up in the council in Acts 5:34 and commanded the apostles to be put forth a little space, then counselled restraint: if their work were of men it would fail, but if of God it could not be overthrown. Paul later said he was brought up at the feet of Gamaliel in Acts 22:3, taught according to the perfect manner of the law.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Gamaliel is the wise voice in a room full of anger. He counselled patience, and he taught Paul, and I hold that God uses a wise teacher's restraint to protect His church in its most dangerous hour.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to end (in the sense of completion or failure)
BiblicalUsage: Gamar means to end, to complete, or to fail. The LORD will perfect that which concerns me, says the psalmist in Psalms 138:8, and God performs all things for me in Psalms 57:2. But the word also fails: the godly man ceases and the faithful fail in Psalms 12:1, and the psalmist asks whether God's promise fails for evermore in Psalms 77:8.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the two ends of this word meet in God alone. Men fail and promises seem to end, but the LORD perfects what concerns me, and I hold that His mercy endures for ever while ours runs out.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1062; to wed (of either sex):--marry (a wife).
BiblicalUsage: Gameo means to marry, and the New Testament uses it for the bonds and the breaking of marriage. Paul commands the married not to depart in 1 Corinthians 7:10, and he warns of those forbidding to marry in 1 Timothy 4:3. A man says he has married a wife and cannot come to the supper in Luke 14:20, and Jesus says whoever puts away his wife and marries another commits adultery in Mark 10:11.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe marriage is a covenant God guards with His own words. Paul commands it, Jesus defines it, and the man who pleads his new wife as an excuse for missing the supper shows how easily even a good gift becomes a reason to stay away. I hold that marriage is honourable, and the wedding feast greater still.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1062; to espouse (a daughter to a husband):--give in marriage.
BiblicalUsage: Gamisko means to give in marriage, to espouse a daughter to a husband. It appears once, in Luke 20:34, where Jesus says the children of this world marry and are given in marriage. The word belongs to this age, and Jesus sets it against the age to come, where they neither marry nor are given in marriage.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Jesus draws a clear line between this world and the next; marriage belongs to this age, and the resurrection belongs to the age where death is no more; I hold that the love we know now is a shadow of the love that waits.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Gamliel, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Gamliel son of Pedahzur was the prince of the tribe of Manasseh in the wilderness. He is named among the princes in Numbers 1:10, and he was over the host of Manasseh when the tribes set out in Numbers 10:23. His name means my reward is God, and he led his tribe through the desert.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the princes of the wilderness matter because they carried the tribes. Gamliel led Manasseh by God's order, and I hold that faithful leadership in a desert is as great as leadership in a palace.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a warrior (as grasping weapons)
BiblicalUsage: Gammadim is a people named once, in Ezekiel 27:11, among the defenders of Tyre. The men of Arvad with the army were upon the walls round about, and the Gammadims were in the towers, hanging their shields upon the walls. Their name may mean brave men or men of Gammad, a place unknown to us now.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Tyre's towers needed brave men, and the Gammadims stood in them; their shields made the city's beauty perfect, yet the city fell, and I hold that no wall is stronger than the God who judges it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain affinity; nuptials:--marriage, wedding.
BiblicalUsage: Gamos is marriage and the wedding feast, and it runs from Cana to the kingdom. There was a marriage in Cana of Galilee in John 2:1, and Jesus turned the water into wine there. Marriage is honourable in all, says Hebrews 13:4, and the servants are to wait like men who wait for their lord when he returns from the wedding in Luke 12:36. The king's wedding was furnished with guests, both bad and good, in Matthew 22:10.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe marriage is God's picture of His joy, and the wedding feast is His picture of the kingdom. Cana's wine and the king's feast both point to a day when the Bridegroom comes, and I hold that the marriage supper of the Lamb is the end of every wedding.
RelatedTopics: Marriage; Jesus Christ; Kingdom of God
RelatedEvents: Jesus Turns Water into Wine at Cana
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Gamul, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Gamul is a priest, named once in 1 Chronicles 24:17, where the lots of the priestly courses are drawn. The one and twentieth lot fell to Jachin, and the two and twentieth to Gamul. His course served in the house of the LORD in its turn.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the lot that fell to Gamul shows that God's house runs on order, not chance. Twenty-two courses, each in its turn, and I hold that the smallest course is as much God's appointment as the first.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a garden (as fenced)
BiblicalUsage: Gan is a garden, a fenced place of growing things. Ahab wanted Naboth's vineyard for a garden of herbs in 1 Kings 21:2, and Manasseh was buried in the garden of his own house, in the garden of Uzza, in 2 Kings 21:18. The land of promise is not like Egypt, where a man watered his seed with his foot, as a garden of herbs, in Deuteronomy 11:10 — and the king of Tyre is told he was in Eden, the garden of God, in Ezekiel 28:13.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the garden runs from Eden to the grave, and God is in both. Eden was His garden, and a king's garden became his burial place. I hold that the garden God plants is the one that never fades.
RelatedTopics: Creation; Nature and Creation; God's Provision
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to thieve (literally or figuratively); by implication, to deceive
BiblicalUsage: Ganab means to steal, and it steals things, hearts, and people alike. Rachel stole her father's images in Genesis 31:19, and Absalom stole the hearts of the men of Israel in 2 Samuel 15:6. The law commands that a man found stealing a brother shall die in Deuteronomy 24:7, and Jehosheba stole the child Joash from among the king's sons that were slain in 2 Chronicles 22:11, and hid him from Athaliah.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe stealing is the same sin whether it takes an idol, a heart, or a child. Rachel stole what was not hers and Absalom stole what was not his, yet Jehosheba stole a child to save his life. I hold that the command against stealing stands, and the mercy that hides the innocent stands beside it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to hedge about, i.e. (generally) protect
BiblicalUsage: Ganan means to hedge about, to guard and defend — and it is God's own promise to Jerusalem. The LORD says He will defend this city in 2 Kings 19:34, for His own sake and for His servant David's sake, and the same promise stands in 2 Kings 20:6, when He adds fifteen years to Hezekiah's days. Isaiah pictures Him as birds flying over the nest in Isaiah 31:5, defending and delivering, and Zechariah says the LORD shall defend the inhabitants of Jerusalem in Zechariah 12:8.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the hedge around Jerusalem is the hedge around every believer. God defends His city for His own sake and for David's, and I hold that He defends us the same way — not because we are strong, but because we are His.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from γραίνω (to gnaw); an ulcer ("gangrene"):--canker.
BiblicalUsage: Gangraina is gangrene, an eating ulcer, and Paul uses it once for false teaching in 2 Timothy 2:17. Their word will eat as a canker does, he says, of whom is Hymenaeus and Philetus. The word paints error as a wound that spreads through the body.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe false teaching spreads like gangrene because it eats what is healthy; Paul names the men and the disease together, and I hold that the cure is the truth that cuts out the rot before it takes the limb.
