Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a stealer
BiblicalUsage: Gannab is the thief, the stealer, and the prophets use him as the picture of a guilty nation. If a man is found stealing a brother, the thief shall die, says Deuteronomy 24:7. The thief comes in by night in Hosea 7:1, the princes are companions of thieves in Isaiah 1:23, and the house of Israel is ashamed as the thief is ashamed when he is found in Jeremiah 2:26.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the thief is ashamed when he is found, and so are we. The law, the prophets, and the shame all point the same way: what is taken in secret will be found out. I hold that the only thief who goes free is the one who confesses and restores.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a garden
BiblicalUsage: Gannah is a garden, and it is the place where men plant and God judges. Solomon made gardens and orchards in Ecclesiastes 2:5, and the exiles are told to plant gardens and eat the fruit of them in Jeremiah 29:28. But the gardens Israel chose for idols bring shame in Isaiah 1:29, and the palmerworm devoured their gardens and vineyards in Amos 4:9.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a garden shows what a man worships. Solomon's garden was pleasure, the exiles' garden was patience, and the idolaters' garden was shame. I hold that the garden God plants is the one that bears fruit in the right season.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a wing
BiblicalUsage: Gap is the Aramaic word for a wing, and it belongs to Daniel's beasts. The first beast was like a lion and had eagle's wings in Daniel 7:4, and the leopard had four wings of a fowl upon its back in Daniel 7:6. The word gives the empires their speed and their terror.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the wings on Daniel's beasts show how fast earthly power moves; a lion with eagle's wings and a leopard with four wings — yet the Ancient of Days sits unmoved above them; I hold that no empire flies faster than God's judgment.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a wing
BiblicalUsage: Gap is the Aramaic word for a wing, and it belongs to Daniel's beasts. The first beast was like a lion and had eagle's wings in Daniel 7:4, and the leopard had four wings of a fowl upon its back in Daniel 7:6. The word gives the empires their speed and their terror.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the wings on Daniel's beasts show how fast earthly power moves; a lion with eagle's wings and a leopard with four wings — yet the Ancient of Days sits unmoved above them; I hold that no empire flies faster than God's judgment.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a primary particle; properly, assigning a reason (used in argument, explanation or intensification; often with other particles):--and, as, because (that), but, even, for, indeed, no doubt, seeing, then, therefore, verily, what, why, yet.
BiblicalUsage: Gar is the little word for, the hinge on which an argument turns. Paul says in 1 Corinthians 10:1 that he would not have the brethren ignorant how all our fathers were under the cloud, and John says in 1 John 2:19 that they went out from us because they were not of us. The word gives the reason, and the reason carries the teaching.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the smallest words do the heaviest work in Scripture; for can turn a story into a doctrine, and I hold that the reasons God gives are always worth hearing.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to scrape off; by implication, to shave, remove, lessen, withhold
BiblicalUsage: Gara means to scrape off, to lessen, to take away — and the law forbids it where God's word is concerned. Ye shall not add to the word, neither shall ye diminish from it, says Deuteronomy 4:2. Nothing can be put to what God does, nor anything taken from it, says Ecclesiastes 3:14. The same word covers a husband's duty, which shall not be diminished in Exodus 21:10, and a nation's food, diminished in judgment in Ezekiel 16:27.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God's word is a measure that must not be tampered with. To add to it or to take from it is the same sin, and I hold that the safest way to handle Scripture is to leave it exactly as God gave it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: scurf (from itching)
BiblicalUsage: Garab is scurf, scab, the itching sore that marks a man or a beast unclean. The LORD will smite with the botch of Egypt and the scab and the itch in Deuteronomy 28:27, and a priest with a blemish, scurvy or scabbed, cannot serve in Leviticus 21:20. An animal that is scurvy or scabbed cannot be offered in Leviticus 22:22.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the scab is a small sign of a great truth: God requires wholeness in what is offered to Him. The sore that cannot be healed keeps a man from the altar, and I hold that the healing we need is the one only Christ can give.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to crush; also (intransitively and figuratively) to dissolve
BiblicalUsage: Garas means to crush, to break, and in its figurative use, to dissolve with longing. Jeremiah says his teeth are broken with gravel stones in Lamentations 3:16, and the psalmist says his soul breaks for the longing it has for God's judgments in Psalms 119:20. The word crushes stone and soul alike.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe longing can break a soul the way gravel breaks teeth; Jeremiah's sorrow and the psalmist's desire are the same crushing, and I hold that God hears the broken soul that longs for His judgments.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to abrade
BiblicalUsage: Garad means to scrape, and it appears once, in Job 2:8, where Job took a potsherd to scrape himself withal, and sat down among the ashes. The word is the sound of a broken man trying to ease his sores with a piece of pottery.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Job's potsherd is one of the saddest pictures in the Bible; he scraped his wounds with broken clay because he had nothing else, and I hold that God saw him there in the ashes and did not look away.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, to grate, i.e. (figuratively) to anger
BiblicalUsage: Garah means to grate, to stir up, to meddle — and it is the word for picking a fight. Amaziah is warned not to meddle to his hurt in 2 Kings 14:10, and the same warning stands in 2 Chronicles 25:19. The sons of the king of the north shall be stirred up in Daniel 11:10, and Israel is told not to meddle with the children of Ammon in Deuteronomy 2:19.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe meddling is the road to a fall. Amaziah was told to stay home, and he went out and fell, and I hold that the fights God tells us not to pick are the ones that would destroy us.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: (causative) to bone, i.e. denude (by extensive, craunch) the bones
BiblicalUsage: Garam means to strip the bones, to gnaw them bare. God says Israel shall eat up the nations, break their bones, and pierce them with arrows, in Numbers 24:8. The princes of Jerusalem are evening wolves who gnaw not the bones till the morrow in Zephaniah 3:3, and the unfaithful woman must break the sherds and pluck off her own breasts in Ezekiel 23:34.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the stripped bone is the picture of judgment without mercy. The wolves gnaw all night and leave nothing, and I hold that the God who breaks bones can also set them, if we turn to Him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to bear off violently
BiblicalUsage: Garaph means to bear off violently, to sweep away, and it appears once, in the song of Deborah in Judges 5:21. The river of Kishon swept them away, that ancient river, the river Kishon. The flood carried Sisera's army off as a torrent carries driftwood.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the Kishon is God's broom, sweeping the proud army away; sisera's chariots were no match for a river in flood, and I hold that the God who drowned Pharaoh's host still sweeps away the enemies of His people.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to drag off roughly; by implication, to bring up the cud (i.e. ruminate); by analogy, to saw
BiblicalUsage: Garar means to drag off roughly, and by the same motion, to chew the cud and to saw. The costly stones of the temple were sawed with saws in 1 Kings 7:9, and the fishermen drag their catch in the net in Habakkuk 1:15. The swine chews not the cud in Leviticus 11:7, and the robbery of the wicked shall destroy them in Proverbs 21:7, because they drag away what is not theirs.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe dragging is the motion of both work and wickedness. The saw drags through stone to build God's house, and the wicked drag away their neighbour's goods. I hold that the difference is not the motion but the master.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to drive out from a possession; especially to expatriate or divorce
BiblicalUsage: Garash means to drive out from a possession, to expel — and it is used for nations, priests, and men alike. God drove out nations before His people in 1 Chronicles 17:21, and Solomon thrust out Abiathar from the priesthood in 1 Kings 2:27. David says the children of men have driven him out from abiding in the inheritance of the LORD in 1 Samuel 26:19, and the enemies of Judah would cast them out of their possession in 2 Chronicles 20:11.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe driving out is God's judgment and man's cruelty in the same word. God drives out nations to give His people a home, and men drive out David to take his home away. I hold that the inheritance God gives cannot be taken by men.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to cut off
BiblicalUsage: Garaz means to cut off, and it appears once, in Psalms 31:22, where the psalmist says in his haste, I am cut off from before thine eyes. He thought God had cut him off, yet the same verse says God heard the voice of his supplications when he cried.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the feeling of being cut off is the haste of fear, not the truth of God; the psalmist said it in haste, and God heard him anyway; I hold that even when I feel cut off, He hears my cry.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Gareb, the name of an Israelite, also of a hill near Jerusalem
BiblicalUsage: Gareb is the name of an Ithrite, one of David's mighty men, named in 1 Chronicles 11:40 and again in 2 Samuel 23:38. Ira the Ithrite, Gareb the Ithrite — the two stand together in the lists. The same name belongs to a hill near Jerusalem, but the man is the one the lists remember.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the lists of David's mighty men are a roll of honour, and Gareb's name is on it. He fought beside the king, and I hold that standing beside God's anointed is the highest place a man can stand.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a berry (as if a pellet of rumination)
BiblicalUsage: Gargar is a berry, the few olives left after the shaking. Yet gleaning grapes shall be left in it, says Isaiah 17:6, as the shaking of an olive tree — two or three berries in the top of the uppermost bough, four or five in the outmost fruitful branches. The word is the small remnant after the harvest.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the two or three berries are the remnant God always keeps; the tree is shaken and the harvest is taken, yet a few remain in the topmost bough; I hold that God never leaves Himself without a remnant.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: the throat (as used in rumination)
BiblicalUsage: Gargeroth is the throat or the neck, and Proverbs uses it for the place where wisdom hangs. Instruction shall be an ornament of grace unto thy head and chains about thy neck in Proverbs 1:9, and mercy and truth shall be life unto thy soul and grace to thy neck in Proverbs 3:22. Let not mercy and truth forsake thee, says Proverbs 3:3, bind them about thy neck, and bind them continually upon thine heart in Proverbs 6:21.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the neck is where wisdom is worn, close to the voice and the heart. Mercy and truth bound about the neck go everywhere we go, and I hold that the words we carry there shape the life we live.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: bony, i.e. strong
BiblicalUsage: Garmi is a name that appears once, in 1 Chronicles 4:19, where the sons of Hodiah are listed: the father of Keilah the Garmite, and Eshtemoa the Maachathite. The word means bony, that is, strong, and it marks Keilah as a man of Garm.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the Garmite is remembered because his town and his strength were known; Keilah's father is named for his place, and I hold that God knows the small towns and the strong men in them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: harsh
BiblicalUsage: Garol means harsh, and it appears once, in Proverbs 19:19, where a man of great wrath shall suffer punishment. If you deliver him, you must do it again — the harsh man does not learn from rescue.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the harsh man is his own punishment; his wrath brings the penalty, and rescuing him only sets him up to do it again; I hold that anger must be repented of, not merely rescued from.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: the throat (as roughened by swallowing)
BiblicalUsage: Garon is the throat, the passage of breath and voice. God put a chain on Jerusalem's neck in Ezekiel 16:11, and the daughters of Zion walk with stretched forth necks in Isaiah 3:16. Jeremiah is told to withhold his throat from thirst in Jeremiah 2:25, and the idols have mouths but speak not through their throat in Psalms 115:7.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the throat shows what a man loves. The proud stretch their necks, the thirsty run after strangers, and the idols cannot speak at all. I hold that the throat God made for praise should not be spent on pride.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an axe
BiblicalUsage: Garzen is the axe, the tool that fells trees and builds houses. When the temple was built, the stone was made ready before it was brought, so that neither hammer nor axe nor any tool of iron was heard in the house in 1 Kings 6:7. A man's hand fetches a stroke with the axe to cut down a tree in Deuteronomy 19:5, and Isaiah asks whether the axe shall boast itself against him that hews with it in Isaiah 10:15.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the axe is a servant, and it must never boast against the hand that wields it. The temple rose in silence because the stones were cut elsewhere, and I hold that God's house is built by quiet preparation, not by noise.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to shower violently
BiblicalUsage: Gasham means to shower violently, to pour down rain. It appears once, in Jeremiah 14:22, where the prophet asks whether any of the vanities of the Gentiles can cause rain, or whether the heavens can give showers. The answer is no — only the LORD our God makes all these things.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the showers belong to God alone; the idols of the nations cannot make it rain, and I hold that the God who sends the showers is the only God worth waiting on.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to feel about
BiblicalUsage: Gashash means to feel about, to grope, and it appears once, in Isaiah 59:10, where the people grope for the wall like the blind, and grope as if they had no eyes. They stumble at noonday as in the night, in desolate places as dead men.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe groping in the dark is the picture of sin's blindness; men feel along the wall at noonday because their eyes are shut, and I hold that only the light of God can open them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain derivation; the stomach; by analogy, the matrix; figuratively, a gourmand:--belly, + with child, womb.
BiblicalUsage: Gaster is the womb, the belly, and the place where life is carried. The angel tells Mary she shall conceive in her womb in Luke 1:31, and Matthew says she was found with child of the Holy Ghost in Matthew 1:18. Jesus warns of woe to them that are with child in those days in Mark 13:17, and Paul says sudden destruction comes as travail upon a woman with child in 1 Thessalonians 5:3.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the womb is where God hid His greatest secret. The Son was carried in a woman's womb, and I hold that the incarnation began in the most hidden and ordinary place of all.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Gath, a Philistine city
BiblicalUsage: Gath is a Philistine city, the home of Goliath and the refuge of David. Goliath of Gath stood six cubits and a span in 1 Samuel 17:4, and David smote the Philistines and took Gath and her towns in 1 Chronicles 18:1. Shimei's servants ran away to Achish, king of Gath, in 1 Kings 2:39; the city is the stronghold of Israel's enemies and the shelter of its fugitives.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Gath is the city where God's strength is proved. Goliath fell before a shepherd boy, and David took the city that once sheltered him; I hold that no stronghold is too strong for the LORD.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Gath-Chepher, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Gath-hepher is a town in Zebulun, known as the home of the prophet Jonah. Jeroboam restored Israel's coast according to the word the LORD spoke by Jonah, the son of Amittai, the prophet, which was of Gath-hepher, in 2 Kings 14:25. The border of Zebulun passes by Gittah-hepher in Joshua 19:13, the same town under a slightly different spelling.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a prophet's hometown matters, because God calls men from small places. Jonah came from Gath-hepher and was sent to Nineveh, and I hold that the God who sent a man from a small town to a great city still sends small people on great errands.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Gath-Rimmon, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Gath-rimmon is a Levitical city, named in the lists of the tribe of Dan in Joshua 19:45 and among the cities given to the Kohathites in 1 Chronicles 6:69. It was a city set apart for the priests' families to live in.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the Levitical cities show that God provides for those who serve Him. Gath-rimmon was a home for the priests' families, and I hold that the Lord still provides a dwelling for His servants.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a wine-press (or vat for holding the grapes in pressing them)
BiblicalUsage: Gath is the winepress, the vat where grapes are trodden. Gideon threshed wheat by the winepress to hide it from the Midianites in Judges 6:11, and Nehemiah saw men treading wine presses on the Sabbath in Nehemiah 13:15. The prophets use it for judgment: the LORD treads the virgin daughter of Judah as in a winepress in Lamentations 1:15, and He asks why His garments are red like one who treads in the winefat in Isaiah 63:2.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the winepress is both a place of work and a picture of wrath. Grapes are trodden to make wine, and the wicked are trodden in judgment. I hold that the winepress of God's wrath fell on Christ, so that we might drink the wine of His mercy.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: the middle
BiblicalUsage: Gav is the Aramaic word for the midst, the middle of a thing. The men who refuse the king's image shall be cast into the midst of a burning fiery furnace in Daniel 3:11, and the king warns them again in Daniel 3:15 that they shall be cast the same hour into the midst of the furnace. They were bound and cast into the midst of the burning fiery furnace in Daniel 3:21, and the city of Jerusalem is accused of moving sedition within the same of old time in Ezra 4:15.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the midst of the furnace is where God's presence is proved. The three men were cast into the middle of the fire, and the fourth stood with them there. I hold that God does not always keep us out of the fire — sometimes He stands in it with us.
RelatedEvents: Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego in the Fiery Furnace
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: the middle
BiblicalUsage: Gav is the Aramaic word for the midst, the middle of a thing. The men who refuse the king's image shall be cast into the midst of a burning fiery furnace in Daniel 3:11, and the king warns them again in Daniel 3:15 that they shall be cast the same hour into the midst of the furnace. They were bound and cast into the midst of the burning fiery furnace in Daniel 3:21, and the city of Jerusalem is accused of moving sedition within the same of old time in Ezra 4:15.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the midst of the furnace is where God's presence is proved. The three men were cast into the middle of the fire, and the fourth stood with them there. I hold that God does not always keep us out of the fire — sometimes He stands in it with us.
RelatedEvents: Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego in the Fiery Furnace
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to breathe out, i.e. (by implication) expire
BiblicalUsage: Gava means to breathe out, to expire — to give up the ghost. Ishmael gave up the ghost and died and was gathered to his people in Genesis 25:17, and Job wishes he had given up the ghost before any eye saw him in Job 10:18. Achan perished not alone in his iniquity in Joshua 22:20, and the priests and elders gave up the ghost in the city in Lamentations 1:19.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe giving up the ghost is the last breath of every life, and the Bible does not hide it. Ishmael and Job and the priests of Jerusalem all breathed their last, and I hold that the breath God gave returns to God who gave it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a gorge (from its lofty sides; hence, narrow, but not a gully or winter-torrent)
BiblicalUsage: Gay is a valley, a gorge between high sides. The valley of salt is where Abishai slew eighteen thousand Edomites in 1 Chronicles 18:12, and Amaziah led his people to the valley of salt and smote ten thousand in 2 Chronicles 25:11. Joash slew ten thousand Edomites there in 2 Kings 14:7, and another company turned to the valley of Zeboim in 1 Samuel 13:18.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the valley of salt is a place of battle and of burial. Armies met there and kings were made there, and I hold that the valleys of our lives are where God wins His victories.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H5804); Gazah (i.e. Azzah), a place in Palestine:--Gaza.
BiblicalUsage: Gaza is the Philistine city on the way south from Jerusalem, named once in the New Testament in Acts 8:26. The angel of the Lord spoke to Philip, saying, Arise, and go toward the south unto the way that goes down from Jerusalem unto Gaza, which is desert. Philip went, and on that desert road he met the Ethiopian and preached Christ to him.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the road to Gaza is the road of obedience. Philip left a revival in Samaria for a desert road because an angel told him to, and I hold that the greatest fruit often grows on the road we would not have chosen.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of foreign origin; a treasure:--treasure.
BiblicalUsage: Gaza means a treasure, the wealth of a king kept in store. It appears once, in Acts 8:27, where the Ethiopian eunuch of great authority under Candace, queen of the Ethiopians, had the charge of all her treasure. He had come to Jerusalem to worship, and he carried the queen's riches with him.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the treasurer of Ethiopia shows that the gospel reaches the keepers of wealth as well as the poor; he had charge of all her treasure, yet he came to Jerusalem to worship, and I hold that the true treasure is the Christ he found on the road.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to cut off, i.e. portion out
BiblicalUsage: Gazah means to cut off, to portion out — and in its one use it is God who does the cutting. The psalmist says in Psalms 71:6, By thee have I been holden up from the womb: thou art he that took me out of my mother's bowels. The word for took me out is the word for cutting the cord, the portioning of a child from its mother.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the psalmist's picture is tender and true: God cut the cord that held me, and He has held me up ever since; I hold that the God who brought me out of the womb will not let me go now.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to pluck off; specifically to flay, strip or rob
BiblicalUsage: Gazal means to pluck off, to strip, to rob — and it takes a spear, a land, and a poor man's goods. Benaiah went down to the Egyptian with a staff and plucked the spear out of his hand in 2 Samuel 23:21. The oppressor shall be only oppressed and spoiled evermore in Deuteronomy 28:29, and the wicked spoil by violence and do not restore the pledge in Ezekiel 18:12. But the psalmist cries that God delivers the poor from him that is too strong for him in Psalms 35:10.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe robbery is the sin of the strong against the weak, and God takes the side of the robbed. The spear is plucked from the Egyptian's hand, and the poor are delivered from the spoiler. I hold that the God who hates robbery loves the poor.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a kind of locust
BiblicalUsage: Gazam is the palmerworm, the first of the four locusts that eat the land bare. That which the palmerworm has left the locust has eaten, says Joel 1:4, and the palmerworm devoured the gardens and vineyards in Amos 4:9. But God promises to restore the years that the locust has eaten, the cankerworm and the caterpillar and the palmerworm, in Joel 2:25.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the palmerworm is the first bite of judgment, and the promise of Joel is the last word. The years the locust ate are not lost to God, and I hold that He restores what the devourer has taken.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to cut down or off; (figuratively) to destroy, divide, exclude, or decide
BiblicalUsage: Gazar means to cut down or off, to divide, and to decree. Solomon said to divide the living child in two in 1 Kings 3:25, and the axe men cut down wood at Jordan in 2 Kings 6:4. Uzziah the leper was cut off from the house of the LORD in 2 Chronicles 26:21, and Ahasuerus remembered Vashti and what was decreed against her in Esther 2:1.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe cutting is the work of kings and of God alike. Solomon cut to find the truth, and God cuts off the leper from His house. I hold that the cut that divides is also the cut that heals, when the hand that holds the knife is just.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to cut off; specifically to shear a flock or shave the hair; figuratively to destroy an enemy
BiblicalUsage: Gazaz means to shear, to cut off the wool of a flock. Laban went to shear his sheep in Genesis 31:19, and Rachel stole his images while he was away. Nabal's shearers ate and drank at the feast in 1 Samuel 25:11, and Absalom had sheepshearers in Baal-hazor in 2 Samuel 13:23. The law forbids shearing the firstling of the sheep in Deuteronomy 15:19.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe shearing is the season when a man's heart shows. Laban sheared and lost his gods, Nabal feasted and refused a kindness, and Absalom's shearing feast ended in murder. I hold that the harvest feast tests what we truly love.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: robbery, or (concretely) plunder
BiblicalUsage: Gazal is robbery, the taking of what belongs to another by force. The people of the land have used oppression and exercised robbery in Ezekiel 22:29, and the LORD says He hates robbery for burnt offering in Isaiah 61:8. A soul that takes a thing away by violence has committed a trespass in Leviticus 6:2, and the psalmist warns not to become vain in robbery in Psalms 62:10.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God hates robbery most when it is dressed up as worship. A burnt offering bought with stolen goods is an abomination, and I hold that the only offering God accepts is the one that comes from honest hands.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Gazez, the name of two Israelites

Definition: probably akin to G142; to take for oneself, i.e. to prefer:--choose. Some of the forms are borrowed from a cognate ἕλλομαι; which is otherwise obsolete.
BiblicalUsage: Scripture uses hairéomai where we would say to choose. In Philippians 1:22, the text says "yet what I shall choose I wot not." The word keeps that same sense wherever it appears.
TheologicalSignificance: I take hairéomai to mean that faith is not a feeling but a holding-on — trusting what God has said when nothing else makes sense. That is why I keep this word in mind when I read those passages — it carries more than its size suggests.
RelatedEvents: Moses' Birth and Flight to Midian
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G138; properly, a choice, i.e. (specially) a party or (abstractly) disunion:--heresy (which is the Greek word itself), sect.
BiblicalUsage: In the New Testament, haíresis is the word for heresy (which is the Greek word itself), sect. In Acts 5:17, the text says "which is the sect of the Sadducees." In 1 Corinthians 11:19, the text says "that they which are approved may be made manifest among you."
TheologicalSignificance: My position is simple: haíresis tells me that false teaching sounds close to true, and that is what makes it dangerous. That shapes how I read the passages where it appears: not as filler, but as God's own wording for what He is doing.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from the same as G140; a schismatic:--heretic (the Greek word itself).
BiblicalUsage: hairetikós means heretic (the Greek word itself). In Titus 3:10, the text says "A man that is an heretick after the first and second admonition reject."
TheologicalSignificance: Out of hairetikós I do not force more than it gives: heretic.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a derivative of G138; to make a choice:--choose.
BiblicalUsage: The word hairetízō carries the sense of to choose, chosen. In Matthew 12:18, the text says "whom I have chosen."
TheologicalSignificance: I read hairetízō plainly — it means to choose, chosen, and I do not build a doctrine on it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to injure
BiblicalUsage: hâkar is how Scripture says to make strange, to injure. In Job 19:3, the text says "ye are not ashamed [that] ye make yourselves strange to me."
TheologicalSignificance: This one, hâkar, I take at face value: to make strange, to injure.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: respect, i.e. partiality
BiblicalUsage: hakkârâh is a plain word for a shew, a look, partiality. In Isaiah 3:9, the text says "The shew of their countenance doth witness against them."
TheologicalSignificance: In hakkârâh I find no hidden theology; it simply means a shew, a look, partiality.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to remove or be remote
BiblicalUsage: hâlâʼ turns up where the Bible says to cast far off, to remove. In Micah 4:7, the text says "and her that was cast far off a strong nation."
TheologicalSignificance: For me, hâlâʼ means to cast far off, to remove, and I leave it at that.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to walk
BiblicalUsage: hălak means to walk. In Daniel 3:25, the text says "walking in the midst of the fire." In Daniel 4:29, the text says "At the end of twelve months he walked in the palace of the kingdom of Babylon."
TheologicalSignificance: For me, hălak is a reminder that obedience is not drudgery; it is trusting that God's way is the good way. That shapes how I read the passages where it appears: not as filler, but as God's own wording for what He is doing.
RelatedEvents: Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego in the Fiery Furnace; Nebuchadnezzar's Humbling
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, a journey, i.e. (by implication) toll on goods at a road
BiblicalUsage: hălâk is the word for properly, a journey, i.e. (by implication) toll on goods at a road. In Ezra 4:13, the text says "then] will they not pay toll." In Ezra 4:20, the text says "and toll."
TheologicalSignificance: I take hălâk to mean that obedience is not drudgery; it is trusting that God's way is the good way. That is why I keep this word in mind when I read those passages — it carries more than its size suggests.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to walk (in a great variety of applications, literally and figuratively)
BiblicalUsage: hâlak is how Scripture says to walk (in a great variety of applications, literally and figuratively). In Exodus 2:5, the text says "and her maidens walked along by the river's side." The word keeps that same sense wherever it appears.
TheologicalSignificance: My position is simple: hâlak tells me that obedience is not drudgery; it is trusting that God's way is the good way. That shapes how I read the passages where it appears: not as filler, but as God's own wording for what He is doing.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to be clear (orig. of sound, but usually of color); to shine; hence, to make a show, to boast; and thus to be (clamorously) foolish; to rave; causatively, to celebrate; also to stultify
BiblicalUsage: Scripture uses hâlal where we would say to praise, to boast, to shine. In Genesis 12:15, the text says "The princes also of Pharaoh saw her." In Judges 16:24, the text says "they praised their god."
TheologicalSignificance: Reading hâlal this way, I believe worship is not a performance but a response — we answer what God has done with what we are. That is why I keep this word in mind when I read those passages — it carries more than its size suggests.
RelatedEvents: Abram in Egypt; Absalom Returns to Jerusalem
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to strike down; by implication, to hammer, stamp, conquer, disband
BiblicalUsage: hâlam turns up where the Bible says to strike down, to hammer. In 1 Samuel 14:16, the text says "and they went on beating down [one another]." In Psalm 74:6, the text says "But now they break down the carved work thereof at once with axes and hammers."
TheologicalSignificance: I believe hâlam shows us that God's judgment is just, and it falls where it should — no one escapes it, and no one suffers it unjustly. That shapes how I read the passages where it appears: not as filler, but as God's own wording for what He is doing.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G251; salt; figuratively, prudence:--salt.
BiblicalUsage: hálas means salt. In Matthew 5:13, the text says "Ye are the salt of the earth." In Mark 9:50, the text says "Salt [is] good."
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that hálas matters because purity is not prudishness; it is keeping ourselves for the God who made us. That is why I keep this word in mind when I read those passages — it carries more than its size suggests.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to the distance, i.e. far away; also (of time) thus far
BiblicalUsage: hâlᵉʼâh is the word for far away, far off. In Leviticus 22:27, the text says "and from the eighth day and thenceforth it shall be accepted for an offering made by fire unto the LORD." The word keeps that same sense wherever it appears.
TheologicalSignificance: What hâlᵉʼâh teaches me is that fear is honest, but it is not the last word — God is bigger than what frightens us. That shapes how I read the passages where it appears: not as filler, but as God's own wording for what He is doing.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G231; to be a fisher, i.e. (by implication) to fish:--go a-fishing.
BiblicalUsage: The word halieúō carries the sense of go a-fishing. In John 21:3, the text says "I go a fishing. They say unto him."
TheologicalSignificance: For me, halieúō means go a-fishing, and I leave it at that.
RelatedEvents: Jesus Appears to Seven Disciples by the Sea of Galilee
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G251; a sailor (as engaged on the salt water), i.e. (by implication) a fisher:--fisher(-man).
BiblicalUsage: halieús is a plain word for fisher(-man). In Matthew 4:18, the text says "for they were fishers." In Matthew 4:19, the text says "and I will make you fishers of men."
TheologicalSignificance: For me, halieús is a reminder that the gospel was never meant to stay where it started — it goes out, because God sends it out. That shapes how I read the passages where it appears: not as filler, but as God's own wording for what He is doing.
RelatedEvents: The Calling of the First Disciples
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a walk, i.e. (by implication) a step
BiblicalUsage: In the Old Testament, hâlîyk is the word for a walk, i.e. (by implication) a step. In Job 29:6, the text says "When I washed my steps with butter."
TheologicalSignificance: I take hâlîyk as it stands: a walk,  a step.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a walking; by implication, a procession or march, a caravan
BiblicalUsage: hălîykâh means a going, a troop, a procession. In Job 6:19, the text says "The troops of Tema looked." In Psalm 68:24, the text says "They have seen thy goings."
TheologicalSignificance: My position is simple: hălîykâh tells me that the journey matters as much as the destination, because God walks it with His people. That shapes how I read the passages where it appears: not as filler, but as God's own wording for what He is doing.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G251; to salt:--salt.
BiblicalUsage: halízō is the word for salt. In Matthew 5:13, the text says "Ye are the salt of the earth."
TheologicalSignificance: Out of halízō I do not force more than it gives: salt.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: this or that
BiblicalUsage: The word hallâz carries the sense of this or that, on this side or that. In 1 Samuel 14:1, the text says "that [is] on the other side. But he told not his father." The word keeps that same sense wherever it appears.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe hallâz shows us that hope is not wishing; it is trusting God for what He has promised, even before we see it. That shapes how I read the passages where it appears: not as filler, but as God's own wording for what He is doing.
RelatedEvents: Gideon's Victory over Midian; Elisha and the Shunammite's Son; Jonathan's Victory at Michmash
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: this very
BiblicalUsage: hallâzeh is a plain word for this dreamer, this one. In Genesis 37:19, the text says "And they said one to another."
TheologicalSignificance: This one, hallâzeh, I take at face value: this dreamer, this one.
RelatedEvents: Joseph and His Brothers; Isaac and Rebekah
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: that
BiblicalUsage: In the Old Testament, hallêzûw is the word for that. It appears in Ezekiel, and each time it carries that same plain sense.
TheologicalSignificance: In hallêzûw I find no hidden theology; it simply means that.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: middle voice of apparently a primary verb; to jump; figuratively, to gush:--leap, spring up.
BiblicalUsage: hállomai means leap, spring up. In John 4:14, the text says "but the water that I shall give him shall be in him a well of water springing up into everlasting life." In Acts 3:8, the text says "And he leaping up stood."
TheologicalSignificance: hállomai convinces me that hope is not wishing; it is trusting God for what He has promised, even before we see it. That is why I keep this word in mind when I read those passages — it carries more than its size suggests.
RelatedEvents: Jesus and the Samaritan Woman; Peter Heals the Lame Man; Paul Stoned at Lystra
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a hammer (or mallet)
BiblicalUsage: halmûwth is the word for a hammer (or mallet). In Judges 5:26, the text says "and her right hand to the workmen's hammer."
TheologicalSignificance: For me, halmûwth means a hammer, nothing more and nothing less.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: hither
BiblicalUsage: Hither is a word that points somewhere close by, and the Bible uses it at moments when someone is being called to come nearer. Moses hears it at the burning bush in Exodus 3:5, Ruth hears it when Boaz invites her to eat in Ruth 2:14, and Samuel hears it when the people ask whether Saul has come in 1 Samuel 10:22.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God still speaks this way, calling me to come nearer rather than shouting from a distance.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably from the base of G1507; a threshing-floor (as rolled hard), i.e. (figuratively) the grain (and chaff, as just threshed):--floor.
BiblicalUsage: A threshing floor was where the wheat was separated from the chaff, and John the Baptist uses that picture for the coming judgment. In Matthew 3:12 and Luke 3:17 he says the Lord will purge his floor, gathering the wheat into the garner and burning the chaff with unquenchable fire.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the threshing floor is a warning and a comfort together: God knows how to tell the wheat from the chaff, and I want to be found among the wheat.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a collateral form of G138; capture:--be taken.
BiblicalUsage: Halosis means being taken, caught like an animal in a trap, and Peter uses it once, for false teachers who speak evil of things they do not understand. In 2 Peter 2:12 he calls them brute beasts made to be taken and destroyed, and says they will perish in their own corruption.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the warning is plain: a mind that mocks what it refuses to understand is already caught.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a primary word; "salt":--salt.
BiblicalUsage: Salt keeps food from rotting and gives it flavour, and Jesus tells his disciples that is what they are meant to be. In Matthew 5:13 he calls them the salt of the earth, in Mark 9:50 he tells them to have salt in themselves and be at peace with one another, and in Luke 14:34 he warns that salt without its savour is fit for nothing.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that a disciple who has lost the saltiness has lost the very thing that made them useful, and Jesus does not soften that warning.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G251; briny:--salt.
BiblicalUsage: James asks a question with only one honest answer: can a fountain give both salt water and fresh at the same spring. In James 3:12 he uses this word for the salt water, and the point is that a mouth cannot bless God and curse men from the same source.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe my words show which spring I am drawing from, and I want the fresh water to be the one that runs.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain derivation; a fetter or manacle:--bonds, chain.
BiblicalUsage: Chains are what hold a prisoner fast, and the New Testament shows them holding Peter in Acts 12:6 until an angel strikes them off his hands in Acts 12:7. Paul wears them as an ambassador in Ephesians 6:20, and Revelation 20:1 turns the picture around, showing an angel with a great chain to bind the dragon himself.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe no chain is stronger than the God who breaks them, and no chain is too strong for the God who binds the enemy with one. What held Peter could not hold him when God sent his angel, and what binds Satan is the same power.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Ham, a region of Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Ham is a place name that appears only once, in the account of the kings who swept through Canaan before Abraham rescued Lot. In Genesis 14:5 Chedorlaomer and the kings with him smote the Zuzims in Ham, on their way to the battle that would draw Abraham out to fight.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the verse matters because it sets the scene for Abraham's rescue: the invaders were already deep in the land, and God still gave Abraham the victory.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a primary particle; properly, at the "same" time, but freely used as a preposition or adverb denoting close association:--also, and, together, with(-al).
BiblicalUsage: Hama means together, at the same time, and it quietly shapes the verses it stands in. In Matthew 13:29 the wheat and the tares grow together until the harvest, in Romans 3:12 the whole world has gone together out of the way, and in 1 Thessalonians 4:17 the living are caught up together with the risen dead to meet the Lord.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe together is the word that holds the church fast: we grow together, we fall together, and one day we rise together.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a dry twig or brushwood
BiblicalUsage: Hamac is dry brushwood, the kindling that catches in a moment, and Isaiah uses it once, in his cry for God to come down. In Isaiah 64:1 he pictures God's coming like fire catching on dry brushwood, so sudden and so fierce that the mountains flow down at his presence.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a prayer like that one still burns: come down, Lord, and let the dry places catch fire.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to make a loud sound (like English 'hum'); by implication, to be in great commotion or tumult, to rage, war, moan, clamor
BiblicalUsage: Hamah is the sound of roaring, moaning and murmuring, and it runs through the whole Bible like a low noise underneath the words. The psalmist's soul roars within him in Psalms 42:5, the waters roar in Psalms 46:3, the people mourn like doves in Isaiah 59:11, and Jeremiah cries that his heart makes a noise within him in Jeremiah 4:19.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God hears the roar before he hears the words, and he is not put off by the noise of a troubled heart. The groaning is itself a prayer, and the psalmist shows me I can bring it to God as it is.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, to put in commotion; by implication, to disturb, drive, destroy
BiblicalUsage: To put an army in commotion is to throw it into confusion, and that is what God does to his enemies. He troubled the Egyptians in Exodus 14:24, he discomfited the Amorites before Joshua in Joshua 10:10, and David sings in Psalms 18:14 and 2 Samuel 22:15 that God shot out his arrows and scattered them.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the confusion of the enemy is God's own work, not mine to arrange. When the battle is the Lord's, the other side falls apart before it ever reaches me.
RelatedEvents: The Exodus and the Red Sea
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Haman, a Persian vizier
BiblicalUsage: Haman rose to be the king's favourite, and the promotion went straight to his head. In Esther 3:1 the king sets his seat above all the princes, in Esther 3:5 his rage catches fire because Mordecai will not bow, and in Esther 7:10 the gallows he built for Mordecai takes Haman himself.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Haman is the warning against pride that cannot bear to be ignored: the trap he set for another man was the one he fell into himself.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: perhaps from G1 (as a negative particle) and the base of G3313; properly, to miss the mark (and so not share in the prize), i.e. (figuratively) to err, especially (morally) to sin:--for your faults, offend, sin, trespass.
BiblicalUsage: To sin is to miss the mark, and Paul states the case plainly in Romans 3:23: all have sinned and come short of the glory of God. Romans 5:12 traces it back to one man, and 1 John 2:1 gives the remedy, an advocate with the Father, while the prodigal in Luke 15:18 shows the way home, saying, I have sinned against heaven and before thee.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the doctrine only helps when it is personal: I have missed the mark, and I have an advocate. That is the whole gospel in one sentence, and it is the reason I can come back.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G264; a sin (properly concrete):--sin.
BiblicalUsage: A hamartema is a sin as a deed, the thing done, and Jesus speaks of it with startling generosity in Mark 3:28, where all sins shall be forgiven unto the sons of men, and then with startling gravity in Mark 3:29, where blasphemy against the Holy Ghost has never forgiveness. Paul sets the deed against the blood in Romans 3:25, and warns in 1 Corinthians 6:18 that the sin against the body is its own kind of wound.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the two verses in Mark belong together and must not be pulled apart: forgiveness is wide, and the one sin that cannot be forgiven is the one that refuses the Spirit who brings it. I hold that as both comfort and warning.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G264; sinful, i.e. a sinner:--sinful, sinner.
BiblicalUsage: A sinner is not a label for other people; it is the word the Bible uses for the ones Jesus came to find. In Luke 15:1 the publicans and sinners draw near to hear him, and in Luke 15:7 he says there is joy in heaven over one sinner that repenteth. Paul says in Romans 5:8 that Christ died for us while we were yet sinners, and in 1 Timothy 1:15 he calls himself the chief of them.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word loses its sting only when I take it for myself first. If Paul could call himself chief of sinners and still preach grace, then grace is wide enough for me too.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a necklace
BiblicalUsage: A necklace was a king's reward, and Belshazzar offered one to anyone who could read the writing on the wall. In Daniel 5:7 he promises a chain of gold about the neck, in Daniel 5:16 he repeats the offer to Daniel, and in Daniel 5:29 the king keeps his word and clothes Daniel in scarlet with the chain, on the very night his kingdom falls.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the chain shows how cheap a king's honours are: Daniel wore it for a few hours, and Babylon was gone by morning.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: the multitude of Gog; the fanciful name of an emblematic place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Hamon-Gog is the name God gives to the valley where Gog's armies will be buried, the multitude of Gog laid out in the land of Israel. In Ezekiel 39:11 God says he will give Gog a place of graves there, and in Ezekiel 39:15 the travellers who find a bone set up a sign until the buriers have buried it.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the valley is God's answer to every army that rises against his people: the multitude ends in graves, and the land is cleansed.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a noise, tumult, crowd; also disquietude, wealth
BiblicalUsage: Hamon is a crowd, a noise, a multitude, and it can be the sound of rain or the sound of trouble. Elijah hears the sound of abundance of rain in 1 Kings 18:41, Jehoshaphat cries that a great multitude has come against him in 2 Chronicles 20:12, Amos hears the noise of songs God will not hear in Amos 5:23, and Ezekiel warns that violence has risen up in Ezekiel 7:11.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word teaches me to listen to what a crowd really is: a multitude can be God's rain coming, or it can be the noise of a people God has stopped listening to. The difference is whether the crowd is turned toward him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Hamonah
BiblicalUsage: Hamonah is the name of a city that will stand beside the valley of Hamon-Gog, named for the multitude buried there. In Ezekiel 39:16 God says the name of the city shall be Hamonah, and so shall they cleanse the land.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the city is a marker set down by God himself: the place where the enemy's multitude fell will carry the memory, and the land will be clean again.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a sound
BiblicalUsage: Hamullah is a sound, the noise of something moving with power, and it appears twice. In Ezekiel 1:24 it is the sound of the living creatures' wings, like the noise of great waters, and in Jeremiah 11:16 it is the sound of a great tumult when the olive tree is set on fire.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the sound tells me what is coming before I see it: wings like rushing water, or fire in the branches.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: permission of rest, i.e. quiet
BiblicalUsage: Hanachah is a release, a rest from burdens, and it appears once, in the feast the king makes for Esther. In Esther 2:18 Ahasuerus makes a release to the provinces and gives gifts with royal bounty, lifting the load off his people for the day.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a true king knows how to give his people rest, and this small release points to the greater one Esther will win for them all.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1 (as a particle of union) and G3956; absolutely all or (singular) every one:--all (things), every (one), whole.
BiblicalUsage: Hapas means all, absolutely all, with nothing left out, and Luke loves the word. In Acts 2:44 all that believed were together and had all things common, in Acts 4:31 they were all filled with the Holy Ghost, in Luke 19:37 the whole multitude began to praise God, and in Matthew 6:32 Jesus says the Father knows we have need of all these things.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word leaves me nowhere to hide: all believed, all were filled, all praised. The gospel is not a partial thing, and neither is the Father's care.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably from G537; one (or a single) time (numerically or conclusively):--once.
BiblicalUsage: Hapax means once, one time only, and Hebrews builds the whole argument of the cross on it. In Hebrews 9:26 Christ appeared once to put away sin, in Hebrews 9:27 it is appointed unto men once to die, and in Hebrews 9:28 Christ was once offered to bear the sins of many. Peter adds in 1 Peter 3:18 that Christ suffered once for sins, the just for the unjust.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe once is the most comforting word in the Bible, because it means the sacrifice does not need repeating. He did it once, and it was enough.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to turn about or over; by implication, to change, overturn, return, pervert
BiblicalUsage: Haphak means to turn over, to overturn, and it can destroy or it can heal. God overthrew Sodom in Genesis 19:25, Jonah warned that Nineveh would be overthrown in Jonah 3:4, and yet the same word turns the other way in Psalms 30:11, where God turned mourning into dancing, and in Deuteronomy 23:5, where he turned the curse into a blessing.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the God who overturns cities is the same God who overturns my mourning, and I would rather have him turn my sorrow than have him turn against my sin. The word cuts both ways, and I want to be on the side where he turns things for good.
RelatedEvents: Destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah; Jonah and Nineveh
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: very perverse
BiblicalUsage: Haphakpak is a word for someone thoroughly twisted, very perverse, and it appears once. In Proverbs 21:8 the way of man is froward and strange, and the verse sets that crooked path against the pure work of the upright man.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the proverb is a mirror, not a weapon: the crooked way is the one I must check in myself before I point at it in anyone else.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G680; probably a ligament (as fastening):--joint.
BiblicalUsage: A joint is where the parts of a body fasten together, and Paul uses the picture for the church. In Ephesians 4:16 the whole body is fitly joined together by every joint that supplies strength, and in Colossians 2:19 the body grows from the Head through the joints and bands.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the joints are the ordinary believers holding the body together, and the body only grows when they do their quiet work.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: destruction
BiblicalUsage: Haphekah is destruction, the overthrow itself, and it appears once, in the sentence that sums up Sodom. In Genesis 19:29 God remembered Abraham and sent Lot out of the midst of the overthrow when he overthrew the cities where Lot dwelt.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the verse holds judgment and mercy in the same breath: the cities fell, and Lot was sent out alive because God remembered Abraham.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: relaxation
BiblicalUsage: Haphugah is a pause, a letting up, and Jeremiah says there was none. In Lamentations 3:49 his eye trickles down and ceases not, without any intermission, and the grief runs on because the ruin is still in front of him.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe some sorrows have no pause built in, and the Bible does not pretend otherwise: the tears keep coming, and God is still there in the middle of them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: adverb from G573 (in the objective sense of G572); bountifully; --liberally.
BiblicalUsage: Haplos means simply, generously, with a single undivided heart, and it appears once. In James 1:5 God gives wisdom to all men liberally, without reproach, and the word for liberally is this one: he gives plainly, freely, and without holding back.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God is not stingy with wisdom, and the only thing standing between me and it is whether I will ask.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G573; singleness, i.e. (subjectively) sincerity (without dissimulation or self-seeking), or (objectively) generosity (copious bestowal):--bountifulness, liberal(-ity), simplicity, singleness.
BiblicalUsage: Haplotes is singleness of heart, a life without a second face, and Paul ties it to giving. In 2 Corinthians 8:2 the churches of Macedonia gave out of deep poverty with the riches of their liberality, in 2 Corinthians 9:11 that liberality works thanksgiving to God, in Romans 12:8 the giver is to give with simplicity, and in Colossians 3:22 servants are to obey with singleness of heart.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe singleness is the opposite of the divided life: one heart, one motive, no performance. The Macedonians gave from poverty because their hearts were not split, and that is the giving God loves.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably from G1 (as a particle of union) and the base of G4120; properly, folded together, i.e. single (figuratively, clear):--single.
BiblicalUsage: Haplous means single, sound, healthy, and Jesus uses it for the eye. In Matthew 6:22 he says if the eye is single the whole body is full of light, and in Luke 11:34 he repeats it: the light of the body is the eye, and a sound eye fills the body with light.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a single eye is a life that looks at one thing, and the light that follows is the proof that I am looking in the right direction.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a primary verb; properly, to fasten to, i.e. (specially) to set on fire:--kindle, light.
BiblicalUsage: Hapto means to fasten to, to touch, and in its active voice the New Testament uses it for lighting a fire. In Luke 8:16 and Luke 11:33 no man lights a candle and hides it, in Luke 15:8 the woman lights a candle to search for her lost coin, and in Acts 28:2 the islanders kindled a fire for Paul and his companions in the cold rain.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the picture is simple and searching: a lit candle is meant to be seen, and a fire is meant to warm strangers. The touching sense of this verb belongs to its middle voice, and I want the light it kindles to be the thing people remember.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: reflexive of G681; properly, to attach oneself to, i.e. to touch (in many implied relations):--touch.
BiblicalUsage: Haptomai is the middle voice of the verb to touch, the form the Gospels use when someone reaches out and takes hold. In Matthew 8:3 Jesus puts forth his hand and touches the leper, in Matthew 9:20 the woman touches the hem of his garment, and in John 20:17 the risen Jesus tells Mary, touch me not.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the touch is the point: Jesus did not heal from a distance, and the woman did not wait for permission to reach for him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: mount of God; figuratively, the altar of burnt-offering
BiblicalUsage: Har'el means the mount of God, and it is the name for the altar hearth itself, the raised place where the offerings burned. In Ezekiel 43:15 the altar shall be four cubits, and from the altar upward shall be four horns, and the word marks the hearth as God's own mountain in miniature.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the altar was a mountain a man could approach, and the fire on it was the sign that God had come down to meet him there.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a mountain or range of hills (sometimes used figuratively)
BiblicalUsage: A mountain is where God comes down and where his people look up. The Lord came down upon Mount Sinai in Exodus 19:20, the psalmist lifts his eyes to the hills in Psalms 121:1, Isaiah sees the mountain of the Lord's house established above the hills in Isaiah 2:2, and Moses is told to climb up and view the land in Deuteronomy 32:49.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the mountains in the Bible are never just scenery: they are where God speaks, where help comes from, and where the future is seen from. When I lift my eyes to the hills, I am looking toward the place God has always met his people.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Hara, a region of Media
BiblicalUsage: Hara is a region of Media, named once as one of the places to which the exiles were carried. In 1 Chronicles 5:26 the God of Israel stirred up the king of Assyria, and he carried the Reubenites and Gadites and the half tribe of Manasseh away to Halah and Habor and Hara and the river Gozan.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the verse is a sober reminder that exile has an address: real people were carried to real places, and God kept count of every one of them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to pull down or in pieces, break, destroy
BiblicalUsage: Haras means to pull down, to break to pieces, and it is used for enemies, for cities, and for foolish choices alike. In Exodus 15:7 God overthrows them that rise up against him, in Jeremiah 1:10 the prophet is set to root out and to pull down, in Proverbs 14:1 the foolish woman plucks down her house with her hands, and in Psalms 28:5 the wicked shall be destroyed and not built up.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe pulling down is God's work and mine to fear in equal measure: he pulls down what rises against him, and my own hands can pull down what I was meant to build. The wise woman builds; the foolish one breaks, and I want to know which one I am being.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to smite with deadly intent
BiblicalUsage: Harag means to smite with deadly intent, to kill, and its first appearance is the worst of all. In Genesis 4:8 Cain rose up against Abel and slew him, in Exodus 2:14 Moses is accused of slaying the Egyptian, in 1 Samuel 24:10 David refuses to slay Saul when he has him in his power, and in 2 Samuel 12:9 Nathan charges David with slaying Uriah by the sword.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word is blunt on purpose: the Bible does not dress killing up. Cain did it in anger, Moses did it in fear, David refused it once and did it once, and the difference between those choices is the whole story of a life.
RelatedEvents: Cain Murders Abel; David Spares Saul at En Gedi
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to be (or become) pregnant, conceive (literally or figuratively)
BiblicalUsage: Harah means to conceive, and it carries the whole story of the promised seed from the first family to the first king's mother. In Genesis 4:1 Eve conceives Cain, in Genesis 16:4 Hagar conceives and despises her mistress, in Genesis 21:2 Sarah conceives Isaac in her old age, and in 1 Samuel 1:20 Hannah conceives Samuel after years of barrenness.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word is full of hope and full of trouble at once: conception brings the child of promise and the child of strife, and God works through both. Sarah laughed, Hannah wept, and God kept his word to each of them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Haran, the name of two men
BiblicalUsage: Haran is the name of two men, and the first is the one the story remembers. In Genesis 11:26 Terah begat Abram, Nahor and Haran, in Genesis 11:27 Haran is named as the father of Lot, and in 1 Chronicles 23:9 a later Haran appears among the sons of Shimei the Levite.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Haran matters because of who came from him: Lot, whose rescue would shape Abraham's whole story, and a family line that runs straight into the promise.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a mountain
BiblicalUsage: Harar is a mountain, the high ground itself, and the poets use it for strength that does not move. In Deuteronomy 33:15 Moses blesses Joseph with the chief things of the ancient mountains, in Psalms 36:6 God's righteousness is like the great mountains, in Psalms 30:7 God made the psalmist's mountain stand strong, and in Habakkuk 3:6 the everlasting mountains are scattered before him.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the mountains in these verses are a picture of God himself: high, old, and unmoved. My mountain stands only because he made it stand, and when he moves, even the everlasting hills give way.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {Hararite}
BiblicalUsage: Hararite means a man from the hill country, and the name marks three of David's mighty men. In 1 Chronicles 11:34 Jonathan the son of Shage is called a Hararite, in 2 Samuel 23:11 Shammah the son of Agee defends a field of lentils alone, and in 2 Samuel 23:33 another Hararite stands in the same honoured list.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the list is the point: God keeps the names of men who stood their ground, even when all we know about them is where they came from.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: slaughter
BiblicalUsage: Haregah is slaughter, the killing floor itself, and the prophets use it for the places where judgment falls. In Jeremiah 7:32 the valley of Tophet shall be called the valley of slaughter, in Jeremiah 12:3 the wicked are pulled out like sheep for the slaughter, in Jeremiah 19:6 the same valley is named again, and in Zechariah 11:4 the flock is called the flock of slaughter.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the prophets name the place plainly because the people needed to hear it plainly: a valley of slaughter is what a nation becomes when it burns its children to idols. The name is the warning.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: pregnant
BiblicalUsage: Hareh means pregnant, with child, and the word carries some of the greatest promises in the Bible. In Genesis 16:11 the angel tells Hagar she is with child and shall bear Ishmael, in Isaiah 7:14 a virgin shall conceive and bear a son called Immanuel, in Judges 13:5 the wife of Manoah is told she shall bear Samson, and in Genesis 38:24 Tamar is found to be with child.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word is a reminder that God writes his promises into women's lives before anyone else can see them. Hagar in the wilderness, the virgin in Isaiah, the barren wife of Manoah: each one carried a future she did not choose and could not have imagined.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a mental conception
BiblicalUsage: Harhor is an Aramaic word for a thought, a mental conception, and it appears once, in the king's troubled night. In Daniel 4:5 Nebuchadnezzar says he saw a dream that made him afraid, and the thoughts upon his bed and the visions of his head troubled him.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the verse shows how God reaches a proud king: not with an army first, but with a thought in the night that will not let him sleep.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: something demolished
BiblicalUsage: Harisah is a ruin, something demolished, and it appears once, in the promise that the ruin will be rebuilt. In Amos 9:11 God says he will raise up the tabernacle of David that is fallen, and close up the breaches thereof, and raise up his ruins.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the promise is aimed straight at the ruins: God does not clear them away and start elsewhere, he raises up the very thing that fell.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: demolition
BiblicalUsage: Harisuth is demolition, the wreckage itself, and it appears once, in a verse that turns the wreckage into a crowd. In Isaiah 49:19 the waste places and the desolate places and the land of destruction shall even now be too narrow for the inhabitants, because the children are coming home.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the verse is one of the most hopeful in Isaiah: the ruined land will be too small for the people God brings back to it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably from G142 (perhaps with G1 (as a particle of union) prefixed); a chariot (as raised or fitted together (compare G719)):--chariot.
BiblicalUsage: A chariot was the fastest seat in the ancient world, and the New Testament puts two very different riders in one. In Acts 8:28 the Ethiopian eunuch sits in his chariot reading Isaiah, in Acts 8:29 the Spirit tells Philip to go near it, and in Acts 8:38 they stop the chariot and Philip baptizes him. Revelation 9:9 turns the picture dark, with locusts whose wings sound like many chariots running to battle.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the chariot shows me both ends of the gospel: a seeking man reading the prophet on the road, and the judgment that comes for those who will not listen. Philip ran to the one, and the other is still coming.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from the same as G716; an articulation (of the body):--joint.
BiblicalUsage: Harmos is a joint, the place where bone meets bone, and it appears once, in the sharpest verse in the Bible. In Hebrews 4:12 the word of God is sharper than any two-edged sword, piercing even to the dividing asunder of soul and spirit, and of the joints and marrow.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the verse means the word gets into places I cannot reach myself: it finds the joint and the marrow, and it tells the truth about what is hiding there.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a castle (from its height)
BiblicalUsage: Harmon is a name that appears once, in a verse about judgment on Samaria, and even the scholars are not sure whether it is a place or a palace. In Amos 4:3 the women of Samaria shall go out at the breaches and cast themselves into the palace, or into Harmon, and the uncertainty is part of the verse: the end of the proud is confusion.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the obscurity is honest to the text: Amos does not name a place I can find on a map, he names a fall, and the fall is the point.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G719; to joint, i.e. (figuratively) to woo (reflexively, to betroth):--espouse.
BiblicalUsage: Harmozo means to join together, to betroth, and Paul uses it once, for the church itself. In 2 Corinthians 11:2 he says he has espoused the Corinthians to one husband, that he may present them as a chaste virgin to Christ.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the marriage picture is the tenderest one Paul ever uses for the church: we are not hired hands, we are a bride, and he is jealous for us with a godly jealousy.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a Harorite or mountaineer
BiblicalUsage: Haroriy means a Harorite, a man from the hill country, and it appears once. In 1 Chronicles 11:27 Shammoth the Harorite stands in the list of David's mighty men, named and counted among the warriors who fought beside the king.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the list is worth reading slowly: a man whose only story is his name and his place still has a place in Scripture.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G726; pillage (properly abstract):--extortion, ravening, spoiling.
