BiblicalUsage: Harpage is plunder, extortion, the thing seized by force, and the New Testament uses it for both suffering and sin. In Hebrews 10:34 the believers took joyfully the spoiling of their goods, knowing they had a better substance in heaven, while in Luke 11:39 and Matthew 23:25 Jesus charges the Pharisees that their cups are full of ravening and wickedness.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the contrast is the whole sermon: one group loses its goods and rejoices, the other fills its cup by taking, and only one of them has anything that lasts. I want to be the one who can be plundered and still be rich.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G726; plunder (properly concrete):--robbery.
BiblicalUsage: Harpagmos is a prize seized and clung to, and it appears once, in the verse that defines humility. In Philippians 2:6 Christ, being in the form of God, thought it not robbery to be equal with God, which means he did not treat equality with God as something to grab and hold.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the verse turns every ambition I have upside down: the one who had everything to cling to let it go, and that is what makes him Lord.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G726; rapacious:--extortion, ravening.
BiblicalUsage: Harpax means rapacious, a person who grabs, and the New Testament puts the extortioner on every list of those who will not inherit the kingdom. In 1 Corinthians 5:10 and 5:11 Paul tells the church not to keep company with one, in 1 Corinthians 6:10 he says extortioners shall not inherit the kingdom of God, in Luke 18:11 the Pharisee thanks God he is not one, and in Matthew 7:15 false prophets come as ravening wolves.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the Pharisee in Luke is the warning for me: he was right that he was not an extortioner, and wrong about everything else. The list is not for sorting other people, it is for examining my own hands.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a derivative of G138; to seize (in various applications):--catch (away, up), pluck, pull, take (by force).
BiblicalUsage: Harpazo means to seize, to snatch away, and it is used for the Spirit's work and the enemy's alike. In 1 Thessalonians 4:17 the living are caught up together to meet the Lord, in Acts 8:39 the Spirit catches Philip away, in John 10:28 no man can pluck the sheep out of Jesus' hand, and in Matthew 11:12 the violent take the kingdom by force.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word holds both the danger and the comfort: the enemy snatches, but the Shepherd's grip is stronger, and the catching up at the end is his hand, not mine. No one can pluck me out of it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Harum, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Harum is a name that appears once, in the middle of a genealogy. In 1 Chronicles 4:8 Coz begat Anub and Zobebah and the families of Aharhel the son of Harum, and the verse gives us nothing more about him than his son and his grandsons.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the genealogy is doing what it always does: keeping the name of a man whose story is lost, so that his family is not lost with it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Hashem, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Hashem is a name that appears once, as the father of two of David's mighty men. In 1 Chronicles 11:34 the sons of Hashem the Gizonite stand in the list, and the verse gives us nothing else about the father himself.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the verse is a reminder that the mighty men had fathers, and the fathers had names, and God kept them all.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: announcement
BiblicalUsage: Hashma'uth is an announcement, a report brought to the ear, and it appears once. In Ezekiel 24:26 God tells Ezekiel that the day the city falls, a fugitive shall come to cause him to hear the news with his own ears.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the verse is about how bad news travels: it does not come as a rumour, it comes as a man standing in front of you, telling you what your own eyes cannot yet see.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Hathak, a Persian eunuch
BiblicalUsage: Hathak was one of the king's chamberlains, and he becomes the go-between in the most urgent conversation in the book of Esther. In Esther 4:5 Esther sends him to Mordecai, in Esther 4:6 he carries her message to the square, and in Esther 4:9 he brings Mordecai's answer back.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Hathak matters because the whole rescue turns on messages carried faithfully: a servant who runs between a queen and a Jew in sackcloth, and does not add or take away a word.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to deride; by implication, to cheat
BiblicalUsage: Hathal means to mock, to cheat, to make a fool of someone, and it runs through the stories of deceivers and the deceived. In Genesis 31:7 Laban changed Jacob's wages ten times, in Judges 16:10 and 16:13 Delilah says Samson has mocked her and told her lies, and in 1 Kings 18:27 Elijah mocks the prophets of Baal when their god does not answer.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word cuts both ways, and I need to know which side I am on: Laban's mockery was theft, Delilah's was a trap, and Elijah's was the truth told with a sharp edge. Mockery is only righteous when the lie is the thing being mocked.
RelatedEvents: Samson and Delilah; Elijah on Mount Carmel
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, to break in upon, i.e. to assail
BiblicalUsage: Hathath means to break in upon, to assail, and it appears once, in a psalm about men rushing at one man. In Psalms 62:3 David asks how long they will imagine mischief against a man, when they mean to push him down like a bowing wall and a tottering fence.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the picture is the point: the attackers do not come with swords first, they come leaning, pushing, waiting for the wall to give way.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a derision
BiblicalUsage: Hathul is derision, open mockery, and it appears once, in Job's complaint. In Job 17:2 he says there are mockers with him, and his eye continues in their provocation, watching them laugh while he suffers.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Job names the worst part of suffering plainly: the pain is bad enough, and the mockery of the people watching is worse.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: rescue
BiblicalUsage: Hatstsalath is deliverance, a rescue that breaks through, and it appears once, in the most famous sentence in Esther. In Esther 4:14 Mordecai tells her that enlargement and deliverance shall arise to the Jews from another place, and asks who knows whether she has come to the kingdom for such a time as this.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the verse is the hinge of the whole book: deliverance will come, with Esther or without her, and the question is whether she will be part of it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: contracted for G1438; self (in some oblique case or reflexive relation):--her (own), (of) him(-self), his (own), of it, thee, their (own), them(-selves), they.
BiblicalUsage: Hautou is the shortened form of the word for self, himself or itself, and it appears wherever the New Testament speaks of what someone does by himself. In Hebrews 1:3 Christ by himself purged our sins, in John 2:24 Jesus did not commit himself unto men, and in Ephesians 2:15 he made in himself one new man out of two.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the little word carries the gospel: he did it by himself, because no one else could, and the one new man is made in himself, not in me.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to exist; used in a great variety of applications (especially in connection with other words)
BiblicalUsage: Hava' is the Aramaic word for to be, to exist, and it is the word the court of Babylon uses for everything that stands. In Daniel 2:28 there is a God in heaven that revealeth secrets, in Daniel 2:31 the king saw a great image that stood before him, in Daniel 4:25 the king shall know that the most High ruleth, and in Ezra 5:11 the builders say they are the servants of the God of heaven and earth.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the Aramaic is the point: the God of Israel is not only the God of Hebrew, he is the God who is, in the language of the empire itself. The king's own tongue confesses that he exists.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to exist; used in a great variety of applications (especially in connection with other words)
BiblicalUsage: Hava' is the Aramaic word for to be, to exist, and it is the word the court of Babylon uses for everything that stands. In Daniel 2:28 there is a God in heaven that revealeth secrets, in Daniel 2:31 the king saw a great image that stood before him, in Daniel 4:25 the king shall know that the most High ruleth, and in Ezra 5:11 the builders say they are the servants of the God of heaven and earth.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the Aramaic is the point: the God of Israel is not only the God of Hebrew, he is the God who is, in the language of the empire itself. The king's own tongue confesses that he exists.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: by implication, of falling); desire; also ruin
BiblicalUsage: Havvah is desire that has curdled into ruin, craving that destroys, and the Bible uses it for both. In Job 6:2 it is Job's calamity, in Proverbs 10:3 it is the craving of the wicked that God casts away, in Psalms 5:9 it is the destruction in the mouth of liars, and in Micah 7:3 the great man utters his mischievous desire.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word is a warning about what desire becomes when it is left to itself: it starts as wanting and ends as wreckage. The psalmist shows me the same mouth can carry ruin, and I want mine to carry something else.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: ruin
BiblicalUsage: Hayah is ruin, calamity, the thing that falls on a man, and it appears once, in the same verse where Job weighs his grief. In Job 6:2 he wishes his grief were weighed and his calamity laid in the balances together, as if sorrow itself could be put on a scale.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Job is asking for something honest: let the weight be measured, and let God see how heavy it really is.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to exist, i.e. be or become, come to pass (always emphatic, and not a mere copula or auxiliary)
BiblicalUsage: Hayah is the verb to be, to become, to come to pass, and it is the most used word in the whole Bible. In Genesis 1:3 God says let there be light, and there was light, in Genesis 2:7 man became a living soul, in Exodus 3:14 God names himself I AM THAT I AM, and in Exodus 3:12 he promises Moses, Certainly I will be with thee.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this is the word the whole Bible stands on: God is, and because he is, everything else can become. He does not merely exist, he is with me, and that is the promise I hold when I am afraid.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to dream
BiblicalUsage: Hazah means to dream, and it appears once, in Isaiah's charge against blind watchmen. In Isaiah 56:10 the watchmen are dumb dogs that cannot bark, sleeping, lying down, loving to slumber, and the dreaming is part of the indictment: they are asleep on duty.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the verse is aimed at every shepherd who would rather dream than watch, and I want to be the one who stays awake.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: aha!
BiblicalUsage: He'ach is a cry, aha, the sound of someone gloating or exulting, and it is never a kind word in the Bible. In Ezekiel 25:3 Ammon says aha against the sanctuary, in Ezekiel 26:2 Tyre says aha against Jerusalem, and in Job 39:25 the horse says ha, ha, at the sound of the trumpet.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the cry gives the enemy away: aha is what you say when someone else falls, and the horse is the only one of the three with an excuse.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {lo!}
BiblicalUsage: He' is an Aramaic word for lo, behold, a finger pointing at something, and Daniel uses it twice. In Daniel 2:43 it points at the kingdoms that will mingle but not hold together, and in Daniel 3:25 it points at the fourth man walking in the fire, loose and unhurt.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the two verses show both sides of the word: lo, the kingdoms fall apart, and lo, the Son of God walks in the fire with his people.
RelatedEvents: Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego in the Fiery Furnace
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {lo!}
BiblicalUsage: He' is an Aramaic word for lo, behold, a finger pointing at something, and Daniel uses it twice. In Daniel 2:43 it points at the kingdoms that will mingle but not hold together, and in Daniel 3:25 it points at the fourth man walking in the fire, loose and unhurt.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the two verses show both sides of the word: lo, the kingdoms fall apart, and lo, the Son of God walks in the fire with his people.
RelatedEvents: Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego in the Fiery Furnace
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a reflexive pronoun otherwise obsolete and the genitive case (dative case or accusative case) of G846; him- (her-, it-, them-, also (in conjunction with the personal pronoun of the other persons) my-, thy-, our-, your-) self (selves), etc.:--alone, her (own, -self), (he) himself, his (own), itself, one (to) another, our (thine) own(-selves), + that she had, their (own, own selves), (of) them(-selves), they, thyself, you, your (own, own conceits, own selves, -selves).
BiblicalUsage: Heautou is the word for self, himself, herself, itself, and it is everywhere in the New Testament because the gospel is always personal. In Matthew 16:24 a man must deny himself and take up his cross, in 1 Corinthians 11:28 a man must examine himself before he eats, and in 2 Corinthians 13:5 Paul says examine yourselves whether ye be in the faith.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word keeps the faith honest: denying self, examining self, proving self; the gospel is not about other people's sins, it starts with my own.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1442 and a modified form of G1176; seventy:--seventy, three score and ten.
BiblicalUsage: Seventy is a number with a history: seventy elders, seventy souls, and in the New Testament, seventy messengers. In Luke 10:1 the Lord appoints seventy others and sends them two by two, in Luke 10:17 the seventy return with joy because the devils are subject to them, and in Acts 27:37 there are two hundred and seventy-six souls on the ship with Paul.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the seventy show me that the mission was never meant for twelve men only: Jesus sent seventy, and he still sends ordinary people two by two. The number seventy is the number of the nations in Genesis 10, and I take that as no accident: the mission was always meant for the whole world.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: multiple adverb from G1440; seventy times:--seventy times.
BiblicalUsage: Hebdomekontakis means seventy times, and it appears once, in Jesus' answer to Peter's question about forgiveness. In Matthew 18:22 Peter asks whether seven times is enough, and Jesus says not seven times, but seventy times seven.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the number is meant to end the counting: if I am still counting how many times I have forgiven, I have not yet understood forgiveness.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: ordinal from G2033; seventh:--seventh.
BiblicalUsage: Hebdomos means seventh, and the Bible counts to seven with purpose. In Hebrews 4:4 God rested on the seventh day, in John 4:52 the fever left the nobleman's son at the seventh hour, in Revelation 11:15 the seventh angel sounds and the kingdoms become the Lord's, and in Jude 1:14 Enoch, the seventh from Adam, prophesies.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe seven is the number of completion, and each of these sevens is a promise that God finishes what he starts: the rest, the healing, the kingdom, and the prophecy all arrive on time. I hold that God counts in sevens because he finishes in sevens, and the seventh day, the seventh hour and the seventh angel all say the same thing.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Hebel, the son of Adam
BiblicalUsage: Abel is the second son of Adam and Eve, a keeper of sheep, and his story is the first murder in the Bible. In Genesis 4:2 he keeps the flock while Cain tills the ground, in Genesis 4:4 the Lord has respect unto Abel and his offering, and in Genesis 4:8 Cain rises up against him in the field and slays him.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Abel matters because God accepted the offering and remembered the blood: his name means breath, and his life was short, but his faith still speaks.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: emptiness or vanity; figuratively, something transitory and unsatisfactory; often used as an adverb
BiblicalUsage: Hebel means breath, vapour, vanity, and it is the word Ecclesiastes cannot stop saying. In Ecclesiastes 1:2 all is vanity, in Ecclesiastes 1:14 all is vanity and vexation of spirit, in Psalms 39:5 every man at his best state is altogether vanity, and in Job 7:16 Job says he would not live alway, for his days are vanity.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word is not despair but honesty: life without God is a breath that passes, and the Teacher says it so that I will stop building on breath. The answer is not to pretend the vapour is solid, but to fear God and keep his commandments.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1443; Hebraic or the Jewish language:--Hebrew.
BiblicalUsage: Hebraikos means Hebrew, of the Jewish language, and it appears once, in the inscription over the cross. In Luke 23:38 the title was written in Greek and Latin and Hebrew, and this is the word for the Hebrew part of it. The older Greek text behind the King James carries the three languages here, while the shorter text used by modern editions leaves the list out.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the three languages on that board matter: the King of the Jews was announced to the whole world, in the tongue of the empire, the tongue of the law, and the tongue of the people.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1443; a Hebræan (i.e. Hebrew) or Jew:--Hebrew.
BiblicalUsage: A Hebrew was an Israelite by birth and by tongue, and Paul claims the name with pride. In 2 Corinthians 11:22 he asks, are they Hebrews, so am I, in Philippians 3:5 he calls himself a Hebrew of the Hebrews, and in Acts 6:1 the Grecian widows are neglected in the daily ministration while the Hebrews are served.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the name is about belonging: Paul never stopped being a Hebrew when he became an apostle to the Gentiles, and the church had to learn that belonging to Christ does not erase where you came from. I hold that the church is wider than any one tongue or tribe, and the Hebrew of the Hebrews proves it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1443; the Hebraistic (Hebrew) or Jewish (Chaldee) language:--Hebrew.
BiblicalUsage: Hebraïs is the Hebrew tongue itself, the language Paul speaks when he wants to be heard. In Acts 21:40 he stands on the stairs and speaks to the crowd in the Hebrew tongue, in Acts 22:2 the crowd keeps silence when they hear it, and in Acts 26:14 the voice from heaven speaks to him in the Hebrew tongue on the road to Damascus.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God speaks to a man in his own language at the turning point of his life, and the crowd goes quiet because the familiar tongue carries an unfamiliar message. I hold that the voice on the Damascus road chose Hebrew because Paul was a Hebrew, and grace always comes in the language the hearer knows best.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: adverb from G1446; Hebraistically or in the Jewish (Chaldee) language:--in (the) Hebrew (tongue).
BiblicalUsage: Hebraisti means in the Hebrew tongue, and John uses it to name the places and words of Jerusalem. In John 5:2 there is a pool called in the Hebrew tongue Bethesda, in John 19:13 Pilate sits in the place called in the Hebrew tongue Gabbatha, and in John 19:20 the title on the cross was written in Hebrew and Greek and Latin.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe John names the Hebrew words because the story happened in a real place with a real language, and the cross stood at the meeting point of three worlds.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a shout
BiblicalUsage: Hed is a shout, a cry of alarm, and it appears once, in the morning Ezekiel warns about. In Ezekiel 7:7 the morning has come upon the land, the time is come, the day of trouble is near, and it is not the shouting of the mountains but the sound of judgment arriving.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the verse is a shout that comes too late for those who would not listen: the morning is come, and there is no more time to get ready.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: adverb from a derivative of the base of G2237; sweetly, i.e. (figuratively) with pleasure:--gladly.
BiblicalUsage: Hedeos means gladly, with pleasure, and it shows up in three very different moods. In 2 Corinthians 11:19 Paul says the Corinthians gladly suffer fools, in Mark 6:20 Herod hears John gladly and does many things, and in Mark 12:37 the common people hear Jesus gladly.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word asks me what I enjoy hearing: Herod liked John's preaching and still killed him, and the crowd liked Jesus and still left him; glad hearing is not the same as obeying.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: honour; used (figuratively) for the capital city (Jerusalem)
BiblicalUsage: Heder means honour, glory, the splendour of a kingdom, and it appears once, in Daniel's portrait of a king who taxes his people to keep it. In Daniel 11:20 a raiser of taxes stands up in the glory of the kingdom, and within a few days he is destroyed, neither in anger nor in battle.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the verse is a small, cold biography of power: glory bought with taxes, and gone in a few days.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: neuter plural of the superlative of the same as G2234; with great pleasure:--most (very) gladly.
BiblicalUsage: Hedista means most gladly, with the greatest pleasure, and Paul uses it twice, both times about weakness. In 2 Corinthians 12:9 he says he will most gladly glory in his infirmities, that the power of Christ may rest upon him, and in 2 Corinthians 12:15 he will very gladly spend and be spent for the Corinthians.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe most gladly is the hardest gladly in the Bible: to boast in weakness and to be spent for people who do not thank you for it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from ἁνδάνω (to please); sensual delight; by implication, desire:--lust, pleasure.
BiblicalUsage: Hedone is pleasure, lust, the craving for what feels good, and James names it as the root of war. In James 4:1 wars come from the lusts that war in the members, in James 4:3 men ask and do not receive because they ask to spend it on their lusts, in Luke 8:14 the seed is choked by the pleasures of this life, and in Titus 3:3 Paul says we were once serving divers lusts and pleasures.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe James is right about where fights start: not in the other person, but in the pleasure I want and cannot have. The seed that falls among pleasures does not die loudly, it is simply choked, and that quiet death is the one I should fear most.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a derivative of G1476; a support, i.e. (figuratively) basis:--ground.
BiblicalUsage: Hedraioma is a support, a stay, the ground a thing stands on, and it appears once, for the church itself. In 1 Timothy 3:15 Paul writes so that Timothy may know how to behave in the house of God, which is the church of the living God, the pillar and ground of the truth.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the church is not the truth itself, it is the pillar that holds the truth up where people can see it, and a pillar that leans is no use to anyone.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a derivative of ἕζομαι (to sit); sedentary, i.e. (by implication) immovable:--settled, stedfast.
BiblicalUsage: Hedraios means settled, steadfast, sitting firm, and Paul uses it for the believer who will not be moved. In 1 Corinthians 7:37 the man who stands steadfast in his heart does well, in 1 Corinthians 15:58 the church is to be steadfast, unmoveable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, and in Colossians 1:23 they are to continue in the faith, grounded and settled.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe steadfast is not stubbornness, it is staying where you were planted. The resurrection is the reason Paul gives for it: because the work is not in vain, the worker can stand still.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: neuter of the compound of the same as G2234 and G3744; a sweet-scented plant, i.e. mint:--mint.
BiblicalUsage: Hedyosmon is mint, the sweet-smelling herb, and it appears twice, both times in Jesus' charge against the Pharisees. In Matthew 23:23 and Luke 11:42 they tithe mint and anise and cummin and have omitted the weightier matters of the law, judgment, mercy and faith.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the mint is the indictment in miniature: they counted the leaves and missed the law; I can be exact about the small things and still fail the weighty ones.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Hege or Hegai, a eunuch of Xerxes
BiblicalUsage: Hege was the keeper of the women in the king's house, the eunuch in charge of preparing Esther for the king. In Esther 2:3 the king's servants put the maidens in his hand, in Esther 2:8 Esther is brought to his house, and in Esther 2:15 she asks him for nothing more than what he appoints, and obtains favour in the sight of all who look upon her.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Hege is the quiet helper in the story: he gives Esther what she needs and nothing extra, and her favour with him is the first step toward her favour with the king.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a muttering (in sighing, thought, or as thunder)
BiblicalUsage: Hegeh is a muttering, a sighing, a sound under the breath, and it can be a lament, a thunder, or a lifetime. In Ezekiel 2:10 the scroll is written with lamentations and mourning and woe, in Job 37:2 Elihu says hear the noise of his voice and the sound that goes out of his mouth, and in Psalms 90:9 we spend our years as a tale that is told, like a sigh.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word gathers up everything I cannot say loudly: the groan of the scroll, the mutter of the thunder, and the sigh of a life passing. God hears the muttering too, and he counts the sighs as prayer.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2233; a leader, i.e. chief person (or figuratively, place) of a province:--governor, prince, ruler.
BiblicalUsage: A hegemon is a ruler, a governor, the one in charge, and the Gospels put the word on both the child and his judge. In Matthew 2:6 a governor shall come out of Bethlehem to rule Israel, in Matthew 27:11 Jesus stands before the governor and is asked, art thou the King of the Jews, in Luke 20:20 the spies hope to deliver him to the governor, and in Acts 23:24 Paul is sent to Felix the governor.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the contrast is deliberate: the true Governor is the child of Bethlehem, and the men who hold the title are the ones who condemn him. Earthly rulers come and go, and the child rules them all.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2232; to act as ruler:--be governor.
BiblicalUsage: Hegemoneuo means to be governor, to rule as governor, and Luke uses it to date the gospel itself. In Luke 2:2 Cyrenius is governor of Syria when the census is taken, and in Luke 3:1 Tiberius Caesar is in the fifteenth year of his reign when John begins to preach.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Luke dates the story on purpose: the gospel did not happen in a timeless somewhere, it happened under named rulers in named years.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2232; government, i.e. (in time) official term:--reign.
BiblicalUsage: Hegemonia is a government, a term of office, and it appears once, in Luke's dating of John's ministry. In Luke 3:1 it is the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, Pontius Pilate being governor of Judaea, and the verse fixes the preaching of John to a year the whole world could check.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the reign is named so that no one can call the gospel a legend: it began in a dated year, under a dated ruler, in a real province.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: middle voice of a (presumed) strengthened form of G71; to lead, i.e. command (with official authority); figuratively, to deem, i.e. consider:--account, (be) chief, count, esteem, governor, judge, have the rule over, suppose, think.
BiblicalUsage: Hegeomai means to lead, to count, to esteem, and it covers both ruling and reckoning. In Hebrews 13:7 the church is to remember them which have the rule over them, in Hebrews 13:17 they are to obey them that have the rule, in Philippians 2:3 each is to esteem others better than themselves, and in James 1:2 trials are to be counted all joy.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word joins two things I would rather keep apart: leading and counting. The leaders are to be remembered and obeyed, the brother is to be esteemed above me, and the trial is to be counted joy. All three are the same verb, and all three ask me to reckon differently than I want to.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a prolonged form of a primary but defective verb εἵλω (of the same meaning); to coil or wrap:--roll together. See also G1667.
BiblicalUsage: Heilisso means to roll together, to coil up like a scroll, and it appears once, at the end of the world as John sees it. In Revelation 6:14 the heaven departed as a scroll when it is rolled together, and every mountain and island is moved out of its place.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the picture is meant to frighten and to comfort at once: the sky itself is rolled up like a finished letter, and the God who wrote it is the one who closes it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1520 repeated with G2596 inserted; severally:--one by one.
BiblicalUsage: Heis kath' heis means one by one, each in turn, and it appears once, at the table on the night of the betrayal. In Mark 14:19 the disciples begin every one to say to Jesus, is it I, one by one, each asking in turn whether he is the traitor.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the phrase is the saddest in the supper: not one of them points at another, each one asks about himself, and each one is right to be afraid.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: (including the neuter (etc.) ἕν); a primary numeral; one:--a(-n, -ny, certain), + abundantly, man, one (another), only, other, some. See also G1527, G3367, G3391, G3762.
BiblicalUsage: Heis means one, and it is the number the whole faith stands on. In Mark 12:29 the Lord our God is one Lord, in John 10:30 Jesus says I and my Father are one, in Ephesians 4:5 there is one Lord, one faith, one baptism, and in Galatians 3:28 all are one in Christ Jesus.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe one is the word that holds the gospel together: one God, one Lord, one faith, one people. The divisions I make are mine, not his, and the oneness he made is the one I am called to keep.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: as if a superlative of ἕκας (afar); each or every:--any, both, each (one), every (man, one, woman), particularly.
BiblicalUsage: Hekastos means each, every one, and it makes the Bible personal in a way no crowd word can. In Matthew 16:27 the Son of man shall reward every man according to his works, in Romans 2:6 God will render to every man according to his deeds, in Galatians 6:5 every man shall bear his own burden, and in Ephesians 4:7 grace is given to every one of us according to the measure of Christ.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe each is the word that will not let me hide in the crowd: every man bears his own burden, every man is rewarded according to his works, and every one of us is given grace. The judgment is personal, and so is the gift.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: as if from G1538 and G5119; at every time:--always.
BiblicalUsage: Hekastote means at every time, always, and Peter uses it once, for the memory he wants to leave behind. In 2 Peter 1:15 he says he will endeavour that after his decease the church may be able to have these things always in remembrance.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Peter knew he was writing his last letter, and his one wish was that the truth would outlive him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain affinity; a hundred:--hundred.
BiblicalUsage: Hekaton means a hundred, and Jesus uses the round number for the harvest and the flock alike. In Matthew 13:8 the good ground brings forth a hundredfold, in Matthew 18:12 and Luke 15:4 the shepherd leaves the ninety and nine to find the one lost sheep of a hundred, and in John 21:11 the net holds a hundred and fifty-three great fishes and does not break.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the hundred is a number of plenty: a hundredfold harvest, a hundred sheep with one that matters enough to chase, and a net so full it should have broken. God does not deal in small numbers.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1540 and G2094; centenarian:--hundred years old.
BiblicalUsage: Hekatontaetes means a hundred years old, and it appears once, for Abraham. In Romans 4:19 Abraham considered his own body now dead, being about a hundred years old, and the deadness of Sarah's womb, and he was not weak in faith.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the verse is the definition of faith: a body a hundred years old, a womb dead, and a man who still believed God could do what he promised.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1540 and a presumed derivative of G4111; a hundred times:--hundredfold.
BiblicalUsage: Hekatontaplasion means a hundred times as much, and Jesus promises it to those who leave everything. In Luke 8:8 the good ground bears fruit a hundredfold, in Mark 10:30 the one who leaves houses and lands for the gospel receives a hundredfold now in this time, and in Matthew 19:29 he shall inherit everlasting life.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the hundredfold is not a bargain but a promise: what is left for him is not lost, it is multiplied, and the everlasting life at the end is the part that makes the arithmetic true. I hold that the promise covers both the present and the age to come, and the one who leaves everything finds he has lost nothing.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: or ἑκατόνταρχος from G1540 and G757; the captain of one hundred men:--centurion.
BiblicalUsage: A centurion was a captain of a hundred soldiers, and the New Testament gives the rank to some of its finest believers. In Matthew 8:13 the centurion's servant is healed by a word, in Luke 7:2 the same captain's servant lies sick, in Acts 10:1 Cornelius the centurion sends for Peter, and in Acts 27:1 Julius the centurion takes charge of Paul.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the centurions are there to show that faith wears a uniform too: the man who commands a hundred soldiers says, speak the word only, and he is the one Jesus calls a man of great faith. I hold that their faith shames mine sometimes: they understood authority because they lived under it, and they trusted the word of Jesus the way a soldier trusts an order.
RelatedEvents: Peter and Cornelius; The Healing of the Centurion's Servant
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a primary verb; to arrive, i.e. be present (literally or figuratively):--come.
BiblicalUsage: Heko means to come, to arrive, to be present, and it is the word for both comings of the Lord. In John 6:37 all that the Father gives me shall come to me, in Matthew 24:14 the gospel shall be preached in all the world and then shall the end come, in Revelation 3:3 Jesus says he will come on thee as a thief, and in Hebrews 10:37 he that shall come will come and will not tarry.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the two comings frame everything: he came to receive all who come to him, and he is coming again, and the waiting is not empty because the one who promised is the one who comes. I hold that the coming is certain because the one who came once has never broken a promise yet.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain affinity; voluntary:--willingly.
BiblicalUsage: Hekon means willingly, of one's own accord, and Paul uses it twice, once for himself and once for the whole creation. In 1 Corinthians 9:17 he says if I do this thing willingly I have a reward, and in Romans 8:20 the creature was made subject to vanity, not willingly, but by reason of him who subjected it in hope.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the contrast is the whole story of the fall and the gospel: creation did not choose its bondage, and Paul chose his service, and the hope is that the willing service undoes the unwilling bondage.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: neuter of a derivative from G1635; voluntariness:--willingly.
BiblicalUsage: Hekousion means willingly, of free will, and it appears once, in Paul's letter about Onesimus. In Philemon 1:14 Paul says he would do nothing without Philemon's mind, that the benefit should not be as it were of necessity, but willingly.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Paul is showing what love does with authority: he could command, and instead he asks, because a good deed done under pressure is not the same as one done willingly.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: adverb from the same as G1595; voluntarily:--wilfully, willingly.
BiblicalUsage: Hekousios means willingly, and it appears twice, once as a command and once as a warning. In 1 Peter 5:2 the elders are to feed the flock willingly and not by constraint, and in Hebrews 10:26 the one who sins wilfully after receiving the knowledge of the truth has no more sacrifice for sins.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the two verses belong together: willingness is the mark of a true shepherd, and wilfulness is the mark of a heart that has stopped listening; the same word, turned toward God or away from him, is either obedience or rebellion.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: ordinal from G1803; sixth:--sixth.
BiblicalUsage: Hektos means sixth, and the sixth hour and the sixth month mark two of the greatest days in the Bible. In Luke 1:26 the angel Gabriel is sent in the sixth month to Mary, in John 19:14 it is the sixth hour when Pilate brings Jesus out, in Matthew 27:45 darkness covers the land from the sixth hour, and in Revelation 6:12 the sixth seal is opened and the sun becomes black.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the sixth hour is the hour God chose for both the beginning and the end: the announcement to Mary and the darkness on the cross, and the seal that will open at the last. The same number carries the birth announcement and the death darkness, and both belong to the same story.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, a journey, i.e. (by implication) a wayfarer; also a flowing
BiblicalUsage: Helek is a traveller, a wayfarer, and by extension a flowing stream, and it appears twice in two very different scenes. In 1 Samuel 14:26 the honey flows down in the wood as the men go through it, and in 2 Samuel 12:4 a traveller comes to the rich man, and the rich man takes the poor man's lamb to feed him.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the two verses show the word from both sides: the honey flowing freely for the hungry, and the traveller who becomes the excuse for theft; Nathan's parable hangs on that traveller, and David condemns himself with his own answer.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Helem, the name of two Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Helem is a name that appears once, in the genealogy of Asher. In 1 Chronicles 7:35 the sons of Helem his brother are listed, and the verse gives us nothing more about him than his sons and his place in the family.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the genealogy keeps him because families matter to God, even the branches with no story attached.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H5941); Heli (i.e. Eli), an Israelite:--Heli.
BiblicalUsage: Heli is a name that appears in the genealogy of Jesus, as the father of Joseph. In Luke 3:23 Jesus begins his ministry at about thirty years of age, being the son of Joseph, which was the son of Heli, and the line runs back through David to Adam and to God.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the genealogy is the proof that Jesus belongs to a real family with real fathers: Heli's name stands in the line, and the line ends in the Son of God.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H452); Helias (i.e. Elijah), an Israelite:--Elias.
BiblicalUsage: Elias is the Greek name for Elijah, the prophet who never died, and the New Testament cannot stop talking about him. In Matthew 11:14 Jesus says John the Baptist is Elias which was for to come, in Matthew 17:3 Elias appears with Moses on the mount of transfiguration, and in James 5:17 Elias is a man of like passions who prayed that it would not rain.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the three verses together are the whole of Elijah: the forerunner, the glorified saint, and the ordinary man who prayed. If a man of like passions could shut the heavens with prayer, then prayer is not a small thing.
RelatedPeople: Elijah; Jesus; James, Brother of Jesus
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from the same as G2245; maturity (in years or size):--age, stature.
BiblicalUsage: Helikia means age, stature, the measure of a life, and Jesus uses it for both growing and worrying. In Luke 2:52 Jesus increases in wisdom and stature, in Luke 12:25 and Matthew 6:27 no man can add one cubit to his stature by taking thought, and in Ephesians 4:13 the church grows to the measure of the stature of the fulness of Christ.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word teaches me what I can grow and what I cannot: I can grow in wisdom as Jesus did, and I can grow into the stature of Christ, but worry adds nothing to my height. The growing that matters is the one God does.
RelatedEvents: The Boy Jesus in the Temple
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from ἧλιξ (a comrade, i.e. one of the same age); as big as, i.e. (interjectively) how much:--how (what) great.
BiblicalUsage: Helikos means how great, how large, and it appears twice, both times to measure something unseen. In Colossians 2:1 Paul says he has a great conflict for the churches, how great a conflict, and in James 3:5 the tongue is a little member that boasts great things, and a little fire kindles how great a forest.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word is a measuring stick for the invisible: a conflict I cannot see, and a fire I cannot put out once the tongue has lit it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from ἕλη (a ray; perhaps akin to the alternate of G138); the sun; by implication, light:--+ east, sun.
BiblicalUsage: Helios is the sun, and the Bible uses it for God's common grace, his glory, and the end of days. In Matthew 5:45 God makes his sun rise on the evil and on the good, in Matthew 17:2 the face of Jesus shines as the sun on the mountain, in Revelation 21:23 the city has no need of the sun because the glory of God lightens it, and in Acts 2:20 the sun shall be turned into darkness before the great day of the Lord.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the sun is the most honest picture in the Bible of how God works: it rises on everyone, it shines from the face of Christ, and one day it will not be needed because the light it borrowed will be there in person. I hold that the day the sun goes dark is not the end of light, it is the beginning of the light that needs no sun.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a form of G1507; to coil or wrap:--fold up.
BiblicalUsage: Helisso means to coil up, to fold like a garment, and it appears twice, both times for the heavens themselves. In Hebrews 1:12 the Lord will fold the heavens up as a vesture and they shall be changed, and in Revelation 6:14 the heaven departs as a scroll when it is rolled together.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the picture is meant to steady me: the heavens are not eternal, they are a garment God can fold, and the one who folds them is the same yesterday, today and for ever.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1668; to cause to ulcerate, i.e. (passively) be ulcerous:--full of sores.
BiblicalUsage: Helkoo means to be ulcerated, covered with sores, and it appears once, for the beggar at the rich man's gate. In Luke 16:20 Lazarus is laid at the gate full of sores, and the dogs come and lick them, while the rich man feasts inside.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the sores are the whole point of the parable: the man nobody would touch is the one God carries to Abraham's bosom, and the rich man who never saw him is the one left outside.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably from G1670; an ulcer (as if drawn together):--sore.
BiblicalUsage: Helkos is a sore, an ulcer, and it appears three times, once in a parable and twice in judgment. In Luke 16:21 the dogs lick the sores of Lazarus at the rich man's gate, in Revelation 16:2 a grievous sore falls on the men who worship the beast, and in Revelation 16:11 they gnaw their tongues for pain and blaspheme God because of their sores.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the same word carries both pictures on purpose: the sores of the poor man God honours, and the sores of the rebels God judges; the difference is never the wound, it is who the sufferer belongs to.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: or ἕλκω; probably akin to G138; to drag (literally or figuratively):--draw. Compare G1667.
BiblicalUsage: Helkyo means to drag, to draw, and Jesus uses it for the hardest doctrine in the gospel. In John 6:44 no man can come to me except the Father which hath sent me draw him, in John 12:32 Jesus says if I be lifted up I will draw all men unto me, and in Acts 16:19 the masters of the slave girl drag Paul and Silas into the marketplace.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the drawing is the reason anyone comes at all: the Father draws, the Son draws, and the ones who are dragged into court for preaching are the ones who know the drawing is real.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain affinity; Hellas (or Greece), a country of Europe:--Greece.
BiblicalUsage: Hellas is Greece, the land itself, and it appears once, on Paul's third journey. In Acts 20:2 he goes over those parts and gives them much exhortation, and then he comes into Greece, where he stays three months before the Jews lay wait for him.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the single mention is enough to fix Paul's route on the map: the gospel had reached Greece, and the churches there were worth the danger of staying.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1671; a Hellen (Grecian) or inhabitant of Hellas; by extension a Greek-speaking person, especially a non-Jew:-- Gentile, Greek.
BiblicalUsage: Hellen means a Greek, and in the New Testament it comes to mean the whole Gentile world. In Romans 1:16 the gospel is the power of God unto salvation, to the Jew first and also to the Greek, in Romans 10:12 there is no difference between the Jew and the Greek, in Galatians 3:28 there is neither Jew nor Greek in Christ, and in 1 Corinthians 1:22 the Greeks seek after wisdom.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word is the door the gospel walked through: the Greek who sought wisdom found a crucified Christ, and the Jew who kept the law found the same Lord. There is no difference now, and that is the miracle.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1672; Hellenic, i.e. Grecian (in language):--Greek.
BiblicalUsage: Hellenikos means Greek, in the Greek tongue, and it appears once, for the name of the destroyer. In Revelation 9:11 the angel of the bottomless pit has a name in Hebrew, Abaddon, and in the Greek tongue his name is Apollyon.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the two names are the same warning in two languages: the destroyer answers in Hebrew and in Greek, and no nation can say it does not understand him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: feminine of G1672; a Grecian (i.e. non-Jewish) woman:--Greek.
BiblicalUsage: Hellenis is a Greek woman, a Gentile woman, and it appears twice, both times for women who believe. In Acts 17:12 honourable women which were Greeks believe at Berea, and in Mark 7:26 the woman who begs Jesus for her daughter is a Greek, a Syrophoenician by nation.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the two women belong together in the story: one believes the preaching at Berea, the other will not stop asking until her daughter is healed, and neither of them was supposed to be in the story at all.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a derivative of G1672; a Hellenist or Greek-speaking Jew:--Grecian.
BiblicalUsage: A Hellenist was a Greek-speaking Jew, and the early church had to learn how to hold them together with the Hebrews. In Acts 6:1 the Grecians murmur because their widows are neglected, in Acts 9:29 Paul disputes against the Grecians and they go about to slay him, and in Acts 11:20 men of Cyprus and Cyrene preach to the Grecians at Antioch.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the murmuring in Acts 6 is the first church fight, and the answer is the first deacons: the church did not argue the widows away, it appointed men to feed them. That is how a divided church becomes one church.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: adverb from the same as G1675; Hellenistically, i.e. in the Grecian language:--Greek.
BiblicalUsage: Hellenisti means in the Greek tongue, and it appears twice, both times when Greek is the language of the moment. In Acts 21:37 Paul asks the chief captain, canst thou speak Greek, and in John 19:20 the title on the cross is written in Hebrew and Greek and Latin.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the two verses show why Greek mattered: it was the language a Roman officer and a Jewish crowd and a dying Saviour all shared, and the gospel would ride on it to the ends of the earth.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain affinity; a stud, i.e. spike:--nail.
BiblicalUsage: Helos is a nail, the spike itself, and it appears once, in Thomas's condition for believing. In John 20:25 he says except I shall see in his hands the print of the nails, and put my finger into the print, I will not believe.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Thomas asked for the one proof that could not be faked: the marks where the nails went in; the risen Lord still carries them, and that is why Thomas can believe.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: they (only used when emphatic)
BiblicalUsage: Hem is the word for they, used when the people themselves are the point, and it is everywhere in the Old Testament. In 1 Samuel 3:1 the word of the Lord is precious and there is no open vision, in 1 Kings 1:41 Adonijah and his guests hear the sound of the city, and in 1 Chronicles 12:1 the men come to David at Ziklag.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the pronoun does quiet work: it gathers the people into one word, and the story is about what they do together.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: they (only used when emphatic)
BiblicalUsage: Hem is the word for they, used when the people themselves are the point, and it is everywhere in the Old Testament. In 1 Samuel 3:1 the word of the Lord is precious and there is no open vision, in 1 Kings 1:41 Adonijah and his guests hear the sound of the city, and in 1 Chronicles 12:1 the men come to David at Ziklag.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the pronoun does quiet work: it gathers the people into one word, and the story is about what they do together.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: accusative case plural of G1473; us:--our, us, we.
BiblicalUsage: Hemas is us in the accusative, the us that things are done to, and the prayers of the Bible are full of it. In Matthew 6:13 Jesus teaches us to pray, deliver us from evil, in Matthew 8:29 the devils cry, art thou come hither to torment us, and in Matthew 9:27 two blind men cry, have mercy on us.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the prayer is the pattern: deliver us, have mercy on us; the us is the church praying together, and the deliverance is the answer.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: nominative plural of G1473; we (only used when emphatic):--us, we (ourselves).
BiblicalUsage: Hemeis is we, the emphatic we, used when the speakers put themselves forward. In Matthew 19:27 Peter says, behold, we have forsaken all, and followed thee, in Mark 10:28 he says the same, and in 1 John 3:14 John writes, we know that we have passed from death unto life.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the we is the confession of the whole church: we forsook all, and we know we have passed from death to life, because we love the brethren.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: feminine (with G5610 implied) of a derivative of ἧμαι (to sit; akin to the base of G1476) meaning tame, i.e. gentle; day, i.e. (literally) the time space between dawn and dark, or the whole 24 hours (but several days were usually reckoned by the Jews as inclusive of the parts of both extremes); figuratively, a period (always defined more or less clearly by the context):--age, + alway, (mid-)day (by day, (-ly)), + for ever, judgment, (day) time, while, years.
BiblicalUsage: Hemera is a day, and the Bible counts days from the first day to the last. In Matthew 6:34 Jesus says sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof, in John 8:56 Abraham rejoiced to see my day, in 2 Peter 3:8 one day is with the Lord as a thousand years, and in Revelation 1:10 John is in the Spirit on the Lord's day.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the day is the measure God gives me: enough evil for today and no more, a day Abraham saw from far off, a day that is a thousand years to God and a single morning to me. I live one day at a time because he counts them all.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2349; our:--our, your (by a different reading).
BiblicalUsage: Hemeteros means our, belonging to us, and it appears where the apostles share what is theirs. In 1 John 1:3 John declares what he has seen so that the fellowship may be ours with the Father, in Acts 2:11 the crowd hears the wonderful works of God in their own tongues, and in Romans 15:4 the things written aforetime were written for our learning.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the our is the gift: the fellowship is ours, the learning is ours, and the Scriptures were written for us.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: dative case plural of G1473; to (or for, with, by) us:--our, (for) us, we.
BiblicalUsage: Hemin is us in the dative, the us that things are given to, and the Lord's Prayer is built on it. In Matthew 6:11 Jesus teaches us to pray, give us this day our daily bread, in Matthew 6:12 forgive us our debts, and in Luke 11:4 forgive us our sins.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the prayer is daily because the need is daily: bread for today, forgiveness for today, and the us means I do not pray it alone.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from the base of G2255 and G5610; a half-hour:--half an hour.
BiblicalUsage: Hemiorion is half an hour, and it appears once, in the silence before the trumpets. In Revelation 8:1 there is silence in heaven about the space of half an hour when the seventh seal is opened.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the half hour is the most solemn silence in the Bible: heaven itself stops to listen before the judgment begins.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: neuter of a derivative from an inseparable prefix akin to G260 (through the idea of partition involved in connection) and meaning semi-; (as noun) half:--half.
BiblicalUsage: Hemisy means half, and it appears where half is the measure of a promise or a repentance. In Luke 19:8 Zacchaeus says, behold, Lord, the half of my goods I give to the poor, in Mark 6:23 Herod offers the dancer whatsoever she asks, even to the half of my kingdom, and in Revelation 11:9 the dead bodies lie in the street for three days and a half.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the half shows the heart: Zacchaeus gives half his goods gladly, Herod offers half his kingdom rashly, and the dead lie half a week before they rise; half measures reveal whole men.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a presumed compound of the base of G2255 and G2348; half dead, i.e. entirely exhausted:--half dead.
BiblicalUsage: Hemithanes means half dead, and it appears once, in the parable of the good Samaritan. In Luke 10:30 a man going down from Jerusalem to Jericho falls among thieves, who strip him and wound him and depart, leaving him half dead.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe half dead is the exact condition of the man: alive enough to be saved, too hurt to save himself, and lying where the priest and the Levite can walk past him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: genitive case plural of G1473; of (or from) us:--our (company), us, we.
BiblicalUsage: Hemon is our in the genitive, of us, from us, and it carries the two greatest phrases in the Bible. In Matthew 6:9 Jesus teaches us to pray, Our Father which art in heaven, in Matthew 1:23 the child is called Emmanuel, God with us, and in Romans 5:8 Christ died for us while we were yet sinners.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the three verses are one gospel: our Father, God with us, Christ for us; the our is the whole of it, and I am in it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: sound
BiblicalUsage: Hemyah is a sound, a noise, and it appears once, in the fall of the king of Babylon. In Isaiah 14:11 the pomp is brought down to the grave, and the noise of the viols with it, and the worms are spread under him.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the verse is the end of every proud song: the music goes down to the grave with the singer, and the worms keep the beat.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: lo!; also (as expressing surprise) if
BiblicalUsage: Hen means behold, lo, here I am, and it is the word of a servant answering the call. In 1 Samuel 3:4 the child Samuel says, here am I, in 1 Samuel 3:5 he says it again to Eli, here am I, for thou calledst me, and in Isaiah 6:8 the prophet says, here am I, send me.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the three answers are one answer: here I am; Samuel did not know who was calling, Isaiah did not know where he would be sent, and each one answered before he knew.
RelatedEvents: Calling of Samuel; Isaiah's Vision and Call
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

BiblicalUsage: Hen means behold, lo, here I am, and it is the word of a servant answering the call. In 1 Samuel 3:4 the child Samuel says, here am I, in 1 Samuel 3:5 he says it again to Eli, here am I, for thou calledst me, and in Isaiah 6:8 the prophet says, here am I, send me.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the three answers are one answer: here I am; Samuel did not know who was calling, Isaiah did not know where he would be sent, and each one answered before he knew.

RelatedEvents: Calling of Samuel; Isaiah's Vision and Call
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Hena, a place apparently in Mesopotamia
BiblicalUsage: Hena is a place whose gods failed, and the Assyrians use it as a taunt. In 2 Kings 18:34 the Rabshakeh asks where the gods of Hamath and Arpad are, and where the gods of Sepharvaim, Hena and Ivah, in 2 Kings 19:13 Hezekiah's messengers repeat the taunt, and in Isaiah 37:13 the prophet answers it.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the taunt is the warning: the gods of Hena could not save Hena, and the God of Jerusalem is not one more god on the list. Hezekiah knew the difference, and so did Isaiah.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from (the neuter of) G1520 and G1176; one and ten, i.e. eleven:--eleven.
BiblicalUsage: Hendeka means eleven, and after the resurrection there are eleven apostles, not twelve. In Matthew 28:16 the eleven disciples go to the mountain, in Luke 24:9 they tell the women what they have seen, in Acts 1:26 Matthias is numbered with the eleven, and in Acts 2:14 Peter stands up with the eleven on the day of Pentecost.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the eleven are the proof that the church is built on men who failed and came back: one betrayed, one denied, and eleven stood up on Pentecost to preach the risen Lord. I hold that the empty twelfth place is itself a sermon: the betrayal was real, the restoration was real, and the eleven were enough for Pentecost.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: ordinal from G1733; eleventh:--eleventh.
BiblicalUsage: Hendekatos means eleventh, and Jesus uses it for the workers hired last. In Matthew 20:6 the master finds men standing idle at the eleventh hour, in Matthew 20:9 they receive a penny like the rest, and in Revelation 21:20 the eleventh foundation of the city is jacinth.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the eleventh hour is the gospel for latecomers: the men hired last are paid first, and the stone laid eleventh is still a foundation. God does not keep office hours, and his grace is not a wage.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: or ἕνεκεν or εἵνεκεν of uncertain affinity; on account of:--because, for (cause, sake), (where-)fore, by reason of, that.
BiblicalUsage: Heneka means because of, for the sake of, on account of, and it marks the reason behind the deed. In Matthew 19:5 a man leaves father and mother for this cause, in Luke 6:22 men hate the disciples and cast out their name for the Son of man's sake, and in Acts 26:21 Paul says for these causes the Jews caught him in the temple.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word asks me what my sake is: the man leaves home for his wife's sake, the disciple is hated for the Son of man's sake, and Paul is seized for the gospel's sake; the sake is the whole reason.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain affinity; at which time:--when.
BiblicalUsage: Henika means when, at the time when, and Paul uses it twice for the veil over the heart. In 2 Corinthians 3:15 even unto this day, when Moses is read, the vail is upon their heart, and in 2 Corinthians 3:16 when it shall turn to the Lord, the vail shall be taken away.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the when is the promise: the veil stays until the turning, and the turning takes it away in a moment.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: hither or thither (but used both of place and time)
BiblicalUsage: Hennah means hither, to this place, and it is the word of summons and of return. In Genesis 15:16 God tells Abram the fourth generation shall come hither again, in Joshua 3:9 Joshua says come hither and hear the words of the Lord, and in Genesis 42:15 Joseph says hereby ye shall be proved.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word is a call to come closer: the generation comes back, the people come to hear, and the brothers are proved by what they do when they come hither.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: hither or thither (but used both of place and time)

In Genesis 15:16 God tells Abram the fourth generation shall come hither again, in Joshua 3:9 Joshua says come hither and hear the words of the Lord, and in Genesis 42:15 Joseph says hereby ye shall be proved.

Definition: from G1520; oneness, i.e. (figuratively) unanimity:--unity.
BiblicalUsage: Henotes means oneness, unity, and Paul uses it twice, both times for the church. In Ephesians 4:3 the church is to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace, and in Ephesians 4:13 we are to come to the unity of the faith and of the knowledge of the Son of God.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe unity is not something I make, it is something I keep: the Spirit made it, and my job is to guard it in peace until we all arrive at it together.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1859; to observe a festival:--keep the feast.
BiblicalUsage: In Scripture, heortázō means keep the feast. It occurs just once, in 1 Corinthians.
TheologicalSignificance: My position is simple here: heortázō means keep the feast, and I do not stretch it further.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain affinity; a festival:--feast, holyday.
BiblicalUsage: When Scripture says heortḗ, it means feast, holyday. The word appears 23 times, and in Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John it carries that same straightforward meaning. Nothing hidden sits behind it; the sense is the one you would expect from the word itself.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that heortḗ matters because God gave His people feasts so they would remember what He had done. My position is simple: I take God at His word here, and I build on that.
RelatedEvents: The Last Supper; The Boy Jesus in the Temple
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain affinity; a conjunction, preposition and adverb of continuance, until (of time and place):--even (until, unto), (as) far (as), how long, (un-)til(-l), (hither-, un-, up) to, while(-s).
BiblicalUsage: The word héōs is until, as long as — a small word, used 136 times; Matthew and Mark show it in use.
TheologicalSignificance: I take héōs as it stands — until, as long as — and read the passage with that plain sense in mind.
RelatedEvents: The Birth of Jesus; Jesus Sends Out the Twelve
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a turn, i.e. the reverse
BiblicalUsage: In Scripture, hephek means the reverse, the opposite. It occurs just once, in Ezekiel.
TheologicalSignificance: I read hephek plainly: the reverse, the opposite, and I leave it there.

BiblicalUsage: hypostéllō turns up where the Bible says to draw back, to shrink, to withhold. In Acts 20:20, the text says "[And] how I kept back nothing that was profitable [unto you]." In Hebrews 10:38, the text says "but if [any man] draw back."
TheologicalSignificance: I believe hypostéllō shows us that faithfulness is staying when staying is costly — the way God stays with us. That shapes how I read the passages where it appears: not as filler, but as God's own wording for what He is doing.
RelatedEvents: Paul's Farewell to the Ephesian Elders; Paul Confronts Peter at Antioch
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G5288; shrinkage (timidity), i.e. (by implication) apostasy:--draw back.
BiblicalUsage: hypostolḗ means shrinking back, timidity. In Hebrews 10:39, the text says "But we are not of them who draw back unto perdition."
TheologicalSignificance: This one, hypostolḗ, I take at face value: shrinking back, timidity.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G5259 and G4762; to turn under (behind), i.e. to return (literally or figuratively):--come again, return (again, back again), turn back (again).
BiblicalUsage: The word hypostréphō carries the sense of to return, to turn back. In Luke 1:56, the text says "and returned to her own house." In Acts 1:12, the text says "Then returned they unto Jerusalem from the mount called Olivet."
TheologicalSignificance: What hypostréphō teaches me is that repentance is not grovelling; it is turning around and walking the other way. That shapes how I read the passages where it appears: not as filler, but as God's own wording for what He is doing.
RelatedEvents: The Conversion of Paul; Mary Visits Elizabeth
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G5259 and G4766; to strew underneath (the feet as a carpet):--spread.
BiblicalUsage: hypostrṓnnymi is how Scripture says to spread underneath, to strew. In Luke 19:36, the text says "they spread their clothes in the way."
TheologicalSignificance: For me, hypostrṓnnymi means to spread underneath, to strew, and I leave it at that.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G5293; subordination:--subjection.
BiblicalUsage: hypotagḗ is a plain word for subjection, subordination. In Galatians 2:5, the text says "To whom we gave place by subjection." In 1 Timothy 2:11, the text says "Let the woman learn in silence with all subjection."
TheologicalSignificance: For me, hypotagḗ is a reminder that obedience is not drudgery; it is trusting that God's way is the good way. That shapes how I read the passages where it appears: not as filler, but as God's own wording for what He is doing.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G5259 and G5021; to subordinate; reflexively, to obey:--be under obedience (obedient), put under, subdue unto, (be, make) subject (to, unto), be (put) in subjection (to, under), submit self unto.
BiblicalUsage: hypotássō turns up where the Bible says to put under, to be subject, to obey. In Luke 2:51, the text says "and was subject unto them." In Romans 8:7, the text says "for it is not subject to the law of God."
TheologicalSignificance: I take hypotássō to mean that obedience is not drudgery; it is trusting that God's way is the good way. That is why I keep this word in mind when I read those passages — it carries more than its size suggests.

Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G5259 and G5087; to place underneath, i.e. (figuratively) to hazard, (reflexively) to suggest:--lay down, put in remembrance.
BiblicalUsage: hypotíthēmi means to lay down, to put in remembrance. In Romans 16:4, the text says "Who have for my life laid down their own necks."
TheologicalSignificance: This word, hypotíthēmi, does its job quietly — to lay down, to put in remembrance — and I leave it at that.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G5259 and G5143 (including its alternate); to run under, i.e. (specially), to sail past:--run under.
BiblicalUsage: The word hypotréchō carries the sense of to run under, to sail close under. In Acts 27:16, the text says "And running under a certain island which is called Clauda."
TheologicalSignificance: Out of hypotréchō I do not force more than it gives: to run under, to sail close under.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a compound of G5259 and a derivative of G5179; typification under (after), i.e. (concretely) a sketch (figuratively) for imitation:--form, pattern.
BiblicalUsage: The word hypotýpōsis carries the sense of a pattern, an outline, a model. In 1 Timothy 1:16, the text says "for a pattern to them which should hereafter believe on him to life everlasting."
TheologicalSignificance: I read hypotýpōsis plainly — it means a pattern, an outline, a model, and I do not build a doctrine on it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G5259 and G2224; to gird under, i.e. frap (a vessel with cables across the keel, sides and deck):--undergirt.
BiblicalUsage: Scripture uses hypozṓnnymi where we would say to undergird, to frap with cables. In Acts 27:17, the text says "undergirding the ship."
TheologicalSignificance: This one, hypozṓnnymi, I take at face value: to undergird, to frap with cables.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: neuter of a compound of G5259 and G2218; an animal under the yoke (draught-beast), i.e. (specially), a donkey:--ass.
BiblicalUsage: In the New Testament, hypozýgion is the word for a beast under the yoke, an ass. In Matthew 21:5, the text says "and sitting upon an ass."
TheologicalSignificance: In hypozýgion I find no hidden theology; it simply means a beast under the yoke, an ass.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a compound of G5308 and G5424; to be lofty in mind, i.e. arrogant:--be highminded.
BiblicalUsage: hypsēlophronéō means to be high-minded, to be arrogant. In 1 Timothy 6:17, the text says "that they be not highminded."
TheologicalSignificance: For me, hypsēlophronéō means to be high-minded, to be arrogant, and I leave it at that.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)
