Definition: from G5311; lofty (in place or character):--high(-er, -ly) (esteemed).
BiblicalUsage: hypsēlós is the word for high, lofty, exalted. In Matthew 4:8, the text says "the devil taketh him up into an exceeding high mountain." In Mark 9:2, the text says "and leadeth them up into an high mountain apart by themselves."
TheologicalSignificance: For me, hypsēlós is a reminder that glory is the weight of who God is, and it is the end of everything He does. That shapes how I read the passages where it appears: not as filler, but as God's own wording for what He is doing.
RelatedEvents: The Temptation in the Wilderness; Paul's Missionary Journeys; Transfiguration
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: superlative from the base of G5311; highest, i.e. (masculine singular) the Supreme (God), or (neuter plural) the heavens:--most high, highest.
BiblicalUsage: The word hýpsistos carries the sense of highest, most high. In Matthew 21:9, the text says "Hosanna in the highest." In Luke 1:32, the text says "and shall be called the Son of the Highest."
TheologicalSignificance: I take hýpsistos to mean that God is majestic, and the right response to majesty is worship, not familiarity. That is why I keep this word in mind when I read those passages — it carries more than its size suggests.
RelatedEvents: Triumphal Entry; The Annunciation to Mary; Jesus Heals the Gerasene Demoniac
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G5312; an elevated place or thing, i.e. (abstractly) altitude, or (by implication) a barrier (figuratively):-- height, high thing.
BiblicalUsage: hýpsōma is a plain word for height, a high place. In Romans 8:39, the text says "Nor height."
TheologicalSignificance: This word, hýpsōma, does its job quietly — height, a high place — and I leave it at that.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G5311; to elevate (literally or figuratively):--exalt, lift up.
BiblicalUsage: hypsóō turns up where the Bible says to exalt, to lift up. In Matthew 11:23, the text says "which art exalted unto heaven." In Luke 1:52, the text says "and exalted them of low degree."
TheologicalSignificance: Reading hypsóō this way, I believe glory is the weight of who God is, and it is the end of everything He does. That is why I keep this word in mind when I read those passages — it carries more than its size suggests.
RelatedEvents: Pentecost; The Bronze Serpent; Mary Visits Elizabeth
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a derivative of G5228; elevation, i.e. (abstractly) altitude, (specially), the sky, or (figuratively) dignity:--be exalted, height, (on) high.
BiblicalUsage: hýpsos means height, exaltation, what is high. In Luke 1:78, the text says "whereby the dayspring from on high hath visited us." In Ephesians 3:18, the text says "and height."
TheologicalSignificance: I believe hýpsos shows us that glory is the weight of who God is, and it is the end of everything He does. That shapes how I read the passages where it appears: not as filler, but as God's own wording for what He is doing.
RelatedEvents: The Birth of John the Baptist
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: apparently a primary word; a hog ("swine"):--sow.
BiblicalUsage: hŷs is the word for a sow, a hog. In 2 Peter 2:22, the text says "and the sow that was washed to her wallowing in the mire."
TheologicalSignificance: This one, hŷs, I take at face value: a sow, a hog.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of foreign origin (H231); "hyssop":--hyssop.
BiblicalUsage: The word hýssōpos carries the sense of hyssop. In John 19:29, the text says "and put [it] upon hyssop."
TheologicalSignificance: In hýssōpos I find no hidden theology; it simply means hyssop.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G5302; a deficit; specially, poverty:--that which is behind, (that which was) lack(-ing), penury, want.
BiblicalUsage: hystérēma is a plain word for lack, need, poverty. In Luke 21:4, the text says "but she of her penury hath cast in all the living that she had." In 1 Corinthians 16:17, the text says "for that which was lacking on your part they have supplied."
TheologicalSignificance: hystérēma convinces me that God provides, and His provision is enough — even when it does not look like we expected. That is why I keep this word in mind when I read those passages — it carries more than its size suggests.
RelatedEvents: The Widow's Offering; Epaphroditus' Sickness and Recovery
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G5306; to be later, i.e. (by implication) to be inferior; generally, to fall short (be deficient):--come behind (short), be destitute, fail, lack, suffer need, (be in) want, be the worse.
BiblicalUsage: hysteréō turns up where the Bible says to come short, to lack, to be in need. In Matthew 19:20, the text says "what lack I yet?" In Mark 10:21, the text says "One thing thou lackest."
TheologicalSignificance: For me, hysteréō is a reminder that God provides, and His provision is enough — even when it does not look like we expected. That shapes how I read the passages where it appears: not as filler, but as God's own wording for what He is doing.
RelatedEvents: The Prodigal Son; Jesus Turns Water into Wine at Cana; The Rich Young Ruler
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G5302; a falling short, i.e. (specially), penury:--want.
BiblicalUsage: hystérēsis means want, penury, need. In Mark 12:44, the text says "but she of her want did cast in all that she had."
TheologicalSignificance: I take hystérēsis as it stands: want, penury, need.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: neuter of G5306 as adverb; more lately, i.e. eventually:--afterward, (at the) last (of all).
BiblicalUsage: Afterward is a small word that carries a whole change of mind. Hebrews 12:11 says no chastening seems joyful at the time, but afterward it yields the peaceable fruit of righteousness, John 13:36 has Jesus telling Peter he will follow afterward, and Mark 16:14 shows the Lord appearing afterward to the eleven as they sat at meat.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe afterward is where God does some of his best work, in the fruit that only shows up later.
RelatedEvents: The Last Supper; The Resurrection; Jesus Appears to the Disciples on Easter Evening
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: comparative from G5259 (in the sense of behind); later:--latter.
BiblicalUsage: The latter one is the one who comes last, and Jesus uses that order to turn expectations upside down. In Matthew 21:29 the son who first refused afterward repented and went, in Matthew 21:32 the publicans and harlots believed John before the chief priests did, in Matthew 21:37 the householder sends his own son last of all, and in Matthew 25:11 the foolish virgins come afterward saying, Lord, Lord, open to us.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that being last is no small thing in the kingdom: the son who repented late still went, and the door that shut late stayed shut. I want to be among those who answer while the door is still open.
RelatedEvents: The Two Sons; The Wise and Foolish Virgins; The Parable of the Wicked Tenants
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H2971); Jairus (i.e. Jair), an Israelite:--Jairus.
BiblicalUsage: Jairus was a ruler of the synagogue, a man with standing, and he threw it all aside to fall at Jesus' feet for his dying daughter. In Mark 5:22 he comes and falls at his feet and begs him greatly, and in Luke 8:41 the same scene is told again, a father pleading for his only daughter, about twelve years old.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Jairus shows what real faith looks like when it has run out of options: a respected man on his knees, asking Jesus for the one thing nobody else could give.
RelatedEvents: Jairus' Daughter and the Bleeding Woman
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H3290); Jacob (i.e. Ja`akob), the progenitor of the Israelites:--also an Israelite:--Jacob.
BiblicalUsage: Jacob is the patriarch whose name became a nation. Matthew 1:2 places him in the line of Christ, Acts 7:8 tells how God gave him the covenant of circumcision and he begat the twelve patriarchs, and Hebrews 11:9 names him among the heirs of the same promise, dwelling in tabernacles with Abraham and Isaac by faith.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Jacob's life is proof God keeps his promises to unlikely people: the younger son who grabbed at the blessing became the father of Israel.
RelatedEvents: The Birth of Jesus; The Call of Abraham; Martyrdom of Stephen
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: the same as G2384 Græcized; Jacobus, the name of three Israelites:--James.
BiblicalUsage: James is the name of three men in the New Testament, and the Bible does not blur them together. Matthew 4:21 shows James the son of Zebedee mending nets with his father when Jesus calls him, Acts 12:2 tells how Herod killed that same James with the sword, and Galatians 1:19 names a different James, the Lord's brother, whom Paul met in Jerusalem.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the three men who share this name remind me that God calls ordinary working men, and that faithfulness can end in a sword as well as in a letter.
RelatedPeople: James, Son of Zebedee; James, Brother of Jesus
RelatedEvents: The Conversion of Paul; The Calling of the First Disciples; Peter's Escape from Prison
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2390; a cure (the effect):--healing.
BiblicalUsage: A healing is the finished work, the cure itself, and Paul lists it among the gifts the Spirit gives to the church. In 1 Corinthians 12:9 he names the gifts of healing by the same Spirit, in 1 Corinthians 12:28 he sets healings among the ministries God placed in the church, and in 1 Corinthians 12:30 he asks, have all the gifts of healing, expecting the answer no.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe healing is a gift, not a right I can claim or a test of my faith. The Spirit gives it as he wills, and my part is to ask and to trust the Giver.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Egyptian origin; Jambres, an Egyptian:--Jambres.
BiblicalUsage: Jambres is named once, beside Jannes, as one of the men who stood against Moses. In 2 Timothy 3:8 Paul says that as Jannes and Jambres withstood Moses, so do these false teachers resist the truth, men of corrupt minds, reprobate concerning the faith.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Jambres is a warning I should not miss: a man can oppose God's servant with real power behind him and still be on the losing side.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably of Hebrew origin (compare H3238); Janna, an Israelite:--Janna.
BiblicalUsage: Janna is one name in the long line Luke traces back from Jesus to Adam. In Luke 3:24 he stands between Melchi and Joseph in the genealogy, one link in a chain that runs through ordinary men nobody else remembers.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a name like Janna matters because the genealogy is the proof: Jesus came through real people, in a real line, and even the forgotten links count.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Egyptian origin; Jannes, an Egyptian:--Jannes.
BiblicalUsage: Jannes is named once, with Jambres, as one of the magicians who opposed Moses in Egypt. In 2 Timothy 3:8 Paul holds them up as the pattern for the false teachers of the last days, men who resist the truth with corrupt minds.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Jannes shows me that opposition to the truth is nothing new: Pharaoh's court had its own wise men, and they lost.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: middle voice of apparently a primary verb; to cure (literally or figuratively):--heal, make whole.
BiblicalUsage: To heal is what Jesus does with a word, and the Gospels show it happening again and again. In Matthew 8:8 the centurion says, speak the word only, and my servant shall be healed, in Matthew 15:28 Jesus tells the Canaanite woman her daughter is made whole, in Luke 5:17 the power of the Lord is present to heal, and in James 5:16 the prayer of faith is told to heal the sick.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that healing belongs to Jesus first and to my prayers second: he healed with a word then, and James still tells the church to pray for the sick now. I believe the power has not gone anywhere.
RelatedEvents: The Healing of the Paralytic; The Healing of the Centurion's Servant; The Canaanite Woman's Daughter
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H3382); Jared (i.e. Jered), an antediluvian:--Jared.
BiblicalUsage: Jared is one of the long-lived fathers before the flood, and Luke names him in the genealogy of Jesus. In Luke 3:37 he stands between Enoch and Mahalaleel, a link in the line that runs from Adam to Christ.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Jared's place in the list is the point: the promise ran through men who lived and died long before it was kept, and God did not forget a single link.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2390; curing (the act):--cure, heal(-ing).
BiblicalUsage: The act of healing is the work itself, the curing as it happens, and Luke uses it where the healing proves the message. In Acts 4:22 the lame man healed was above forty years old, in Acts 4:30 the church prays for signs and wonders to be done by the name of Jesus, and in Luke 13:32 Jesus says he does cures today and tomorrow before he finishes his course.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the healing was never the show: it was the proof that the kingdom had come. The church still prays the same prayer the first believers prayed.
RelatedEvents: Peter and John Before the Sanhedrin; The Believers Pray for Boldness
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: future active participle masculine of G2390; about to cure; Jason, a Christian:--Jason.
BiblicalUsage: Jason opened his house to Paul in Thessalonica and paid for it. In Acts 17:5 the Jews who believed not set the city in an uproar and assaulted the house of Jason, in Acts 17:6 they dragged him before the rulers crying that these men have turned the world upside down, and in Romans 16:21 Paul greets him as a kinsman and fellow worker.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Jason is the picture of what hospitality costs: he took Paul in, and the mob came to his door. Paul still counted him among his own.
RelatedEvents: Paul's Missionary Journeys; Paul at Thessalonica
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably of foreign origin (see H3471); "jasper", a gem:--jasper.
BiblicalUsage: Jasper is the stone John reaches for when he tries to describe the glory he saw. In Revelation 4:3 the One on the throne is to look upon like a jasper and a sardine stone, in Revelation 21:11 the New Jerusalem shines with a light like a jasper stone, clear as crystal, and in Revelation 21:18 the wall of the city is built of jasper.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe John chose a stone, not a speech, because some glory can only be pointed at. The city God builds will shine like a jewel, and the foundation is his own.
RelatedEvents: The Throne Room and the Lamb; The New Jerusalem
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2390; a physician:--physician.
BiblicalUsage: A physician is the one you call when you know you are sick, and Jesus takes that name for himself. In Matthew 9:12 he says they that be whole need not a physician, but they that are sick, in Mark 2:17 and Luke 5:31 he says it again to the Pharisees who murmured, and in Colossians 4:14 Paul greets Luke, the beloved physician, his companion on the road.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Jesus called himself a physician on purpose: the sick are the ones he came for, and I am sicker than I like to admit. That is good news, not bad, because the Physician is here.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: brandishing of a sword
BiblicalUsage: The brandishing of a sword is the flash of it before it falls, and Ezekiel uses this word once, in the song of the sword. In Ezekiel 21:15 the sword is sharpened to make a sore slaughter, furbished that it may glitter, and the prophet cries that it is pointed against their gates.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the glitter of the sword is meant to frighten before it cuts: God warned Jerusalem first, and the warning itself was mercy.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Ibri, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Ibri was a Merarite Levite of the family of Jaaziah in the time of David. In 1 Chronicles 24:27 he is named among the sons of Jaaziah in the divisions of the Levites, one man in the long list of those set apart to serve the house of God.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a name like Ibri is worth pausing over: the Levites' service ran on men whose names we barely know, and God knew every one of them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Ibri, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Ibri was a Merarite Levite of the family of Jaaziah in the time of David. In 1 Chronicles 24:27 he is named among the sons of Jaaziah in the divisions of the Levites, one man in the long list of those set apart to serve the house of God.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a name like Ibri is worth pausing over: the Levites' service ran on men whose names we barely know, and God knew every one of them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Ibtsan, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Ibzan was a judge of Israel from Bethlehem, and the Bible gives him two verses. In Judges 12:8 he judged Israel seven years, and in Judges 12:10 he died and was buried at Bethlehem, after thirty sons and thirty daughters married out of his house.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Ibzan's short record is a quiet one: seven years of judging, a great family, and a burial at home. Not every faithful life gets a long story.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from ἰκνέομαι (to arrive; compare G2240); a track (figuratively):--step.
BiblicalUsage: A track is the mark a foot leaves behind, and the New Testament tells believers to walk in the tracks left by the faithful. In Romans 4:12 Abraham's children walk in the steps of his faith, in 2 Corinthians 12:18 Paul asks whether he and Titus walked in the same steps, and in 1 Peter 2:21 Christ left us an example that we should follow his steps.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the tracks matter more than the talk: faith leaves footprints. The ones I follow are Abraham's, Paul's, and Christ's own.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: diminutive from G2486; a petty fish:--little (small) fish.
BiblicalUsage: Little fishes are what the disciples had when the crowds were hungry, and Jesus took them anyway. In Matthew 15:34 the disciples count seven loaves and a few little fishes, and in Mark 8:7 they had a few small fishes, and Jesus blessed them and commanded them to be set before the people.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the little fishes are the whole point of the story: what we have is never enough until Jesus takes it, and then it always is.
RelatedEvents: The Feeding of the Four Thousand
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain affinity; a fish:--fish.
BiblicalUsage: A fish is ordinary food in the Gospels, and Jesus makes it the sign of his provision. In Matthew 14:17 the disciples bring five loaves and two fishes, in Matthew 14:19 he blesses them and feeds five thousand, in Luke 5:6 the nets break with the catch at his word, and in John 21:11 Peter drags in a net full of great fishes after the resurrection.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the fish in these stories is never just dinner: it is Jesus providing out of nothing. He calls fishermen, and he feeds a crowd with a boy's lunch.
RelatedEvents: The Feeding of the Five Thousand; The Resurrection; The Calling of the First Disciples; Jesus Appears to Seven Disciples by the Sea of Galilee
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a set time; technically, a year
BiblicalUsage: A set time is God's time, and Daniel uses this Aramaic word for the seasons God appoints. In Daniel 2:21 God changes the times and the seasons, in Daniel 3:5 the music sounds at what time the people must fall down and worship, in Daniel 4:16 seven times pass over Nebuchadnezzar, and in Daniel 4:25 the same seven times teach the king that the Most High rules.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the times are not mine to set: God changes them, measures them, and lets them run their course. The proud learn who rules only when the times have done their work.
RelatedEvents: Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego in the Fiery Furnace; Nebuchadnezzar's Dream of the Image; Nebuchadnezzar's Humbling
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: ample, i.e. a threshing-floor
BiblicalUsage: A threshing floor is where the grain is separated from the chaff, and Daniel uses it once, in the dream of the statue. In Daniel 2:35 the stone cut without hands smites the image, and the iron, clay, brass, silver and gold become like the chaff of the summer threshingfloors, carried away by the wind.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the picture is final: the kingdoms of men end up like chaff on a threshing floor, and the stone becomes a mountain that fills the earth.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Iddo (or Iddi), the name of five Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Iddo is a name carried by several men, and the Bible keeps them distinct by their sons and their times. In Ezra 5:1 Zechariah the son of Iddo prophesies to the Jews, in Ezra 6:14 the elders build by the prophesying of Haggai and Zechariah the son of Iddo, and in Nehemiah 12:16 Zechariah stands among the priests as the son of Iddo.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the name matters because the prophet came through it: Zechariah the son of Iddo spoke God's word to the builders, and the temple rose on it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Iddo, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Iddo was a chief man at Casiphia, the place where Ezra sent for help on the journey home. In Ezra 8:17 Ezra sends men to Iddo the chief at the place Casiphia, to bring ministers for the house of God, and Iddo sends them the Levites and temple servants they needed.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Iddo is one of those quiet helpers the story turns on: Ezra asked, Iddo answered, and the house of God had its servants.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: second person singular imperative active of G1492; used as an interjection to denote surprise; lo!:--behold, lo, see.
BiblicalUsage: Behold is a word that stops you and points, and John the Baptist uses it at the moment that matters most. In John 1:29 he sees Jesus coming and says, Behold the Lamb of God, in John 1:36 he says it again the next day, and in John 11:3 the sisters send word to Jesus, saying, Lord, behold, he whom thou lovest is sick.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe behold is the right word for those moments: stop, look, and see who is standing in front of you.
RelatedEvents: The Baptism of Jesus; Raising of Lazarus; The Calling of the First Disciples
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G1492; a sight (compare figuratively "idea"), i.e. aspect:--countenance.
BiblicalUsage: Countenance is the look of a face, and this word appears once, for the angel at the empty tomb. In Matthew 28:3 his countenance was like lightning, and his raiment white as snow, and the keepers shook for fear of him.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that one verse is enough: the angel's face shone like lightning because he came from the presence of God, and the guards fell like dead men before him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain affinity; pertaining to self, i.e. one's own; by implication, private or separate:--X his acquaintance, when they were alone, apart, aside, due, his (own, proper, several), home, (her, our, thine, your) own (business), private(-ly), proper, severally, their (own).
BiblicalUsage: His own is a small phrase that draws a line around what belongs to a person. In 1 Corinthians 3:8 every man shall receive his own reward according to his own labour, in 1 Corinthians 7:2 every man should have his own wife, and in 1 Corinthians 7:7 Paul wishes all men were even as himself, but every man hath his proper gift of God.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word keeps me honest: my reward follows my labour, my gift is my own, and I answer for what God gave me, not for what he gave someone else.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2398; a private person, i.e. (by implication) an ignoramus (compare "idiot"):--ignorant, rude, unlearned.
BiblicalUsage: An unlearned man is one without schooling, and the New Testament turns that label inside out. In Acts 4:13 the rulers see that Peter and John are unlearned and ignorant men, and marvel that they had been with Jesus, in 1 Corinthians 14:16 Paul asks how the unlearned will say Amen to a prayer they cannot understand, and in 2 Corinthians 11:6 he admits he is rude in speech, yet not in knowledge.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that being unlearned never stopped God: the rulers could tell Peter and John had been with Jesus. That was the only schooling that mattered.
RelatedPeople: Simon Peter; John the Apostle; Paul
RelatedEvents: Peter and John Before the Sanhedrin
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: second person singular imperative middle voice of G1492; used as imperative lo!; --behold, lo, see.
BiblicalUsage: Behold is the word that opens the door to something new. In 2 Corinthians 5:17 Paul writes that if any man be in Christ he is a new creature, behold, all things are become new, in 2 Corinthians 6:2 he cries, behold, now is the accepted time, behold, now is the day of salvation, and in Acts 1:10 two men in white apparel stand by as the disciples behold Jesus taken up.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe behold is a call to look now, not later: new in Christ, salvation today, and a risen Lord going up before their eyes.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H123); Idumæa (i.e. Edom), a region East (and South) of Palestine:--Idumæa.
BiblicalUsage: Idumea is the Greek name for Edom, the land east and south of Palestine, and it appears once in the Gospels. In Mark 3:8 a great multitude came to Jesus from Idumea, and from beyond Jordan, drawn by what they heard he was doing.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that even Edom came: the people of the old enemy's land walked to hear Jesus, and the crowd around him kept growing.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H3204); Jechonias (i.e. Jekonjah), an Israelite:--Jechonias.
BiblicalUsage: Jechonias is the Greek form of Jeconiah, the king carried away to Babylon, and Matthew names him at the hinge of the genealogy. In Matthew 1:11 Josias begat Jechonias and his brethren, about the time they were carried away to Babylon, and in Matthew 1:12 after the carrying away, Jechonias begat Salathiel.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Jechonias stands at the darkest turn in the line: the king in chains, the nation in exile, and the promise still moving through him to Christ.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H3316); Jephthaë (i.e. Jiphtach), an Israelite:--Jephthah.
BiblicalUsage: Jephthah was a judge of Israel, and Hebrews names him once, in the hall of faith. In Hebrews 11:32 the writer says time would fail him to tell of Gedeon, and of Barak, and of Samson, and of Jephthae, and of David, and of Samuel, and of the prophets.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Jephthah's place in that list is grace itself: a flawed man with a rash vow, named among the faithful because he believed God in the battle.
RelatedPeople: Jephthah, Judge of Israel; Gideon; Samson; King David; Samuel
RelatedEvents: Samson and Delilah; Gideon's Victory over Midian
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H3091); Jesus (i.e. Jehoshua), the name of our Lord and two (three) other Israelites:--Jesus.
BiblicalUsage: Jesus is the name above every name, given before he was born. In Matthew 1:21 the angel tells Joseph to call his name Jesus, for he shall save his people from their sins, in Luke 2:21 the child is circumcised and his name is called Jesus, as the angel named him, and in John 14:6 Jesus himself says, I am the way, the truth, and the life.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the name says the whole gospel in one word: Jesus means the Lord saves, and he is the only way to the Father.
RelatedEvents: The Birth of Jesus; The Angel Appears to Joseph
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H3448); Jessæ (i.e. Jishai), an Israelite:--Jesse.
BiblicalUsage: Jesse was the father of David, a farmer of Bethlehem whose name carries the whole promise. In Matthew 1:5 Salmon begat Booz of Rachab, and Booz begat Obed of Ruth, and Obed begat Jesse, in Romans 15:12 Isaiah's word is quoted, there shall be a root of Jesse, and in Acts 13:22 God says he found David the son of Jesse, a man after mine own heart.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Jesse's obscurity is the point: God raised a king from a Bethlehem farmer's house, and the root of Jesse became the hope of the Gentiles.
RelatedEvents: The Birth of Jesus; Paul's Missionary Journeys; Paul Preaches at Pisidian Antioch
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H348); Jezabel (i.e. Jezebel), a Tyrian woman (used as a synonym of a termagant or false teacher):--Jezabel.
BiblicalUsage: Jezebel is the name John gives to the false teacher at Thyatira, borrowing the name of Ahab's queen. In Revelation 2:20 the Lord says, thou sufferest that woman Jezebel, which calleth herself a prophetess, to teach and to seduce my servants to commit fornication, and to eat things sacrificed unto idols.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the borrowed name is the warning: the old Jezebel led Israel into idolatry, and the new one does the same work inside the church.
RelatedEvents: The Letter to the Church in Thyatira
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an epistle (as carried by a state courier or postman)
BiblicalUsage: A letter in Aramaic is how the enemies of the Jews tried to stop the temple. In Ezra 4:8 Rehum and Shimshai write a letter against Jerusalem, in Ezra 4:11 the copy of the letter is set out, and in Ezra 5:6 Tattenai writes another letter to Darius, asking whether the building should go on.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the letters tell the story plainly: men wrote to a king to stop God's house. God answered through a king's search of the records.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an epistle
BiblicalUsage: A letter carries the king's word where the king cannot go, and the Bible shows it doing both good and harm. In 2 Chronicles 30:6 the posts go out with letters from Hezekiah calling Israel to the passover, in Esther 9:26 letters go out to establish Purim, in Nehemiah 6:5 Sanballat sends an open letter to frighten Nehemiah, and in Nehemiah 2:7 Nehemiah asks the king for letters to the governors beyond the river.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a letter is a small thing with a long reach: Hezekiah's letters called a nation to worship. Sanballat's letters tried to call a builder off the wall.
RelatedPeople: King Hezekiah; Nehemiah; Queen Esther; Mordecai
RelatedEvents: Esther Saves Her People; Nehemiah Rebuilds the Wall; Hezekiah Restores Worship and Keeps Passover; Nehemiah's Request to the King
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a farmer
BiblicalUsage: A farmer works land he may not own, and the prophets use his labour as the picture of a people's life. In Amos 5:16 the husbandman is called to mourning, in Isaiah 61:5 strangers shall stand and feed your flocks, and the sons of the alien shall be your plowmen, in Jeremiah 14:4 the ground is chapt because there is no rain, and the plowmen are ashamed, and in Joel 1:11 the husbandmen howl because the harvest of the field is perished.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the farmer's grief in these verses is the grief of a people who forgot the Lord of the harvest. When the rain stops, the field tells the truth about the nation.
RelatedEvents: The Locust Plague in Joel's Day
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: perhaps from G1504; image-like; Iconium, a place in Asia Minor:--Iconium.
BiblicalUsage: Iconium was a city in Asia Minor where Paul preached and was nearly stoned. In Acts 13:51 Paul and Barnabas shake off the dust of their feet and come to Iconium, in Acts 14:1 they go into the synagogue and speak so that a great multitude believed, and in Acts 14:19 Jews from Antioch and Iconium come and stone Paul and drag him out of the city.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Iconium shows both sides of the mission at once: a great multitude believed there, and the same city sent men to stone the preacher.
RelatedEvents: Paul's Missionary Journeys; Paul Preaches at Pisidian Antioch; Paul and Barnabas at Iconium; Paul Stoned at Lystra
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a pretext (as arising artificially)
BiblicalUsage: A pretext is an excuse dressed up as a reason, and Daniel's enemies go looking for one. In Daniel 6:4 the presidents and princes seek to find occasion against Daniel concerning the kingdom, but they can find none, and in Daniel 6:5 they say, we shall not find any occasion against this Daniel, except we find it against him concerning the law of his God.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the pretext they found was really a confession: Daniel's life was so clean that only his faithfulness to God could be used against him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: supreme (i.e. God)
BiblicalUsage: The Most High is the Aramaic name for God enthroned above every king, and Daniel's book rings with it. In Daniel 3:26 Nebuchadnezzar calls the three men servants of the most high God, in Daniel 4:2 he tells the signs the high God has wrought toward him, in Daniel 4:17 the decree stands so the living may know that the most High ruleth in the kingdom of men, and in Daniel 5:18 Daniel tells Belshazzar that the most high God gave his father the kingdom.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the Most High is the name that humbles every throne: kings rise and fall. The One above them gives and takes away as he wills.
RelatedEvents: Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego in the Fiery Furnace; Nebuchadnezzar's Humbling; Belshazzar's Handwriting on the Wall
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: stuttering
BiblicalUsage: Stammering speech is slow and broken, and Isaiah promises it will be healed. In Isaiah 32:4 the heart of the rash shall understand knowledge, and the tongue of the stammerers shall be ready to speak plainly.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the promise is for more than speech: God opens the mouth that could not speak, and the stammerer speaks plainly at last.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: these
BiblicalUsage: These is a word that points at men standing right there, and Daniel's story uses it at the moment of accusation. In Daniel 3:12 the Chaldeans say, there are certain Jews whom thou hast set over the affairs of Babylon, these men have not regarded thee, in Daniel 3:13 Nebuchadnezzar in rage commands them to bring these men, and in Daniel 6:11 the men assemble and find Daniel praying before his God.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the pointing finger is the heart of the story: these men would not bow, and the king could not make them.
RelatedEvents: Daniel in the Lions' Den; Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego in the Fiery Furnace
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: speechless
BiblicalUsage: The mute are those who cannot speak, and the Bible says God is the one who made the mouth. In Exodus 4:11 the Lord asks Moses, who maketh the dumb, or the deaf, or the seeing, or the blind, have not I the LORD, in Isaiah 35:6 the tongue of the dumb shall sing when the desert blossoms, and in Psalms 38:13 David says, I was as a dumb man that openeth not his mouth.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the mute are not forgotten by the God who made the mouth: he opens it in his time. The song that comes out is his own doing.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: these
BiblicalUsage: These is the word Daniel uses to point at the kingdoms in his visions. In Daniel 2:40 the fourth kingdom shall be strong as iron, and in Daniel 6:6 the presidents and princes assemble together to the king, and in Daniel 7:17 the angel explains, these great beasts, which are four, are four kings which shall arise out of the earth.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the pointing word keeps the visions honest: these kingdoms rise, and these kingdoms fall, and the kingdom of God stands after them.
RelatedEvents: Daniel in the Lions' Den; Nebuchadnezzar's Dream of the Image
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: high; i.e. comparative
BiblicalUsage: The upper springs are the ones on the high ground, and Achsah asks her father for them. In Joshua 15:19 she says, thou hast given me a south land, give me also springs of water, and he gives her the upper springs and the nether springs, and in Judges 1:15 the same request is told again, and Caleb gives her both.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Achsah asked well: she wanted water from the high ground as well as the low, and her father gave her both.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: nay, i.e. (softened) if
BiblicalUsage: If is the word that opens a door that never was, and the Bible uses it to weigh what might have been. In Ecclesiastes 6:6 the Preacher asks, yea, though a man live a thousand years twice told, yet hath he seen no good, and in Esther 7:4 Esther says, if we had been sold for bondmen and bondwomen, I had held my tongue.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word is a mercy in Esther's mouth and a warning in the Preacher's: one life held its tongue too long, and the other had nothing to show for a thousand years.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: neuter of an adjective from a name of uncertain derivation; (the) Illyrican (shore), i.e. (as a name itself) Illyricum, a region of Europe:--Illyricum.
BiblicalUsage: Illyricum was the far edge of Paul's preaching, the region along the Adriatic coast. In Romans 15:19 Paul says he has fully preached the gospel of Christ from Jerusalem, and round about unto Illyricum.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that one verse maps the whole mission: from Jerusalem to Illyricum, Paul carried the gospel until there was no more road to run.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: adverb or preposition, with (i.e. in conjunction with), in varied applications; specifically, equally with; often with prepositional prefix (and then usually unrepresented in English)
BiblicalUsage: With is the smallest word for the greatest promise in the Bible. In Genesis 28:15 God tells Jacob, I am with thee, and will keep thee in all places whither thou goest, in Exodus 3:12 he tells Moses, certainly I will be with thee, and in Hosea 11:12 he says Judah yet ruleth with God, and is faithful with the saints.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe with is the whole of the covenant in one word: God with us, God with Jacob, God with Moses, and God with his faithful ones still.
RelatedEvents: The Burning Bush; Jacob's Dream at Bethel
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: adverb or preposition, with (i.e. in conjunction with), in varied applications; specifically, equally with; often with prepositional prefix (and then usually unrepresented in English)
BiblicalUsage: With is the smallest word for the greatest promise in the Bible. In Genesis 28:15 God tells Jacob, I am with thee, and will keep thee in all places whither thou goest, in Exodus 3:12 he tells Moses, certainly I will be with thee, and in Hosea 11:12 he says Judah yet ruleth with God, and is faithful with the saints.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe with is the whole of the covenant in one word: God with us, God with Jacob, God with Moses, and God with his faithful ones still.
RelatedEvents: The Burning Bush; Jacob's Dream at Bethel
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: used very widely as demonstrative, lo!; interrogative, whether?; or conditional, if, although; also Oh that!, when; hence, as a negative, not
BiblicalUsage: If is the hinge the covenant turns on, and the Bible swings it both ways. In Genesis 4:7 God tells Cain, if thou doest well, shalt thou not be accepted, in Exodus 19:5 he tells Israel, if ye will obey my voice indeed, ye shall be a peculiar treasure unto me, and in Deuteronomy 28:1 he promises, if thou shalt hearken diligently unto the voice of the LORD thy God, he will set thee on high above all nations.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the if is not a threat but an open door: God puts the choice in our hands, and the blessing waits on the other side of it.
RelatedEvents: The Ten Commandments; Cain Murders Abel
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: along with
BiblicalUsage: With is the word for standing beside someone, and the Bible uses it for loyalty that stays. In 1 Samuel 10:2 Samuel tells Saul his father has left the asses and sorrows for you, in Deuteronomy 5:31 God tells Moses, stand thou here by me, and I will speak unto thee, and in 2 Samuel 19:33 the king says to Barzillai, come thou over with me, and I will feed thee with me in Jerusalem.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word is about presence: God asked Moses to stand with him, and David asked Barzillai to come with him, and I want to be the one who stays beside.
RelatedEvents: The Ten Commandments; Anointing of Saul as King
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Immanuel, a type name of Isaiah's son
BiblicalUsage: Immanuel means God with us, and Isaiah gives it as the sign of the child to come. In Isaiah 7:14 a virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel, and in Isaiah 8:8 the flood of Assyria stretches out its wings and fills the breadth of thy land, O Immanuel.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the name is the promise itself: God did not stay far off, he came to be with us, and Matthew says the child of the virgin is the one Isaiah meant.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a lamb
BiblicalUsage: A lamb is the offering the returning exiles brought to the house of God. In Ezra 6:9 the king commands that lambs be given to the priests day by day, in Ezra 6:17 they offer a hundred bullocks, two hundred rams, and four hundred lambs at the dedication, and in Ezra 7:17 Ezra is told to buy bullocks, rams and lambs with the king's silver.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the lambs at the dedication say what the whole book is about: the exiles came home to worship. The altar was the first thing they rebuilt.
RelatedEvents: Ezra Reads the Law; Rebuilding of the Temple
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Immer, the name of five Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Immer is the name of a priestly house, and of the priest who struck Jeremiah. In 1 Chronicles 24:14 the sixteenth lot falls to Immer, in Ezra 2:37 the children of Immer come up from Babylon, a thousand and fifty-two, and in Jeremiah 20:1 Pashur the son of Immer, chief governor in the house of the LORD, hears Jeremiah prophesy and smites him.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the name carries both sides of the priesthood: a house set apart to serve, and a son of that house who used his office to strike the prophet.
RelatedPeople: Immer; Jeremiah; Pashur, Son of Immer
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {something said}
BiblicalUsage: A word, a saying, is what God speaks and what men answer with, and this word follows God's speech through the Bible. In Deuteronomy 32:2 Moses says, my doctrine shall drop as the rain, my speech shall distil as the dew, in 2 Samuel 22:31 David sings that the word of the LORD is tried, in Isaiah 5:24 the people cast away the law and despised the word of the Holy One, and in Genesis 4:23 Lamech says to his wives, hear my speech.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God's word is like rain in Moses' song: it falls where it will, and it is tried and true in David's. It is despised only by those who cast it away.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Imri, the name of two Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Imri is the name of two men, a man of Judah and the father of a builder. In 1 Chronicles 9:4 Uthai the son of Ammihud, the son of Omri, the son of Imri, dwells in Jerusalem after the return, and in Nehemiah 3:2 the men of Jericho build beside Zaccur the son of Imri.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Imri's name is carried by his sons: one dwells in Jerusalem, and one builds the wall, and the father's name lives in the work they did.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: they
BiblicalUsage: They is a small word that points at the powers in Daniel's visions. In Daniel 2:44 the God of heaven shall set up a kingdom which shall never be destroyed, and it shall break in pieces all these kingdoms, in Daniel 7:17 the angel says, these great beasts are four kings which shall arise out of the earth, and in Ezra 5:4 the governor asks, what are the names of the men that make this building.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word keeps the visions straight: they are the kings who rise, and the kingdom God sets up outlasts them all.
RelatedEvents: Rebuilding of the Temple; Nebuchadnezzar's Dream of the Image
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: ado, i.e. (generally) employment or (specifically) an affair
BiblicalUsage: A task is the work God gives a man to do, and the Preacher weighs it and finds it heavy. In Ecclesiastes 1:13 he gives his heart to seek out the sore travail God has given to the sons of men, in Ecclesiastes 2:23 all his days are sorrows and his travail grief, in Ecclesiastes 3:10 he sees the travail God has given to be exercised in it, and in Ecclesiastes 5:14 those riches perish by evil travail.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the Preacher is honest about work in a way I need: the task God gives is real and heavy. Only God can make it light.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: feminine of the same as G2491; Joanna, a Christian:--Joanna.
BiblicalUsage: Joanna was one of the women who followed Jesus and served him with what they had. In Luke 8:3 she is named among the women who ministered unto him of their substance, the wife of Chuza, Herod's steward, and in Luke 24:10 she is among the women who tell the apostles the tomb is empty.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Joanna's story is the quiet backbone of the Gospels: she gave her money to the ministry, and she was one of the first to carry the news of the resurrection.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a form of G2491; Joannas, an Israelite:--Joannas.
BiblicalUsage: Joannas is one name in the genealogy Luke traces from Jesus back to Adam. In Luke 3:27 he stands between Rhesa and Zerubbabel, a link in the line that runs through the kings after the exile.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a name like Joannas is there to be counted, not skipped: the line to Christ runs through men history forgot, and Luke wrote every one of them down.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H3110); Joannes (i.e. Jochanan), the name of four Israelites:--John.
BiblicalUsage: John is the name of the Baptist who prepared the way and the apostle who leaned on Jesus' breast. In Matthew 3:1 John the Baptist comes preaching in the wilderness of Judea, in John 1:6 there is a man sent from God, whose name is John, and in Acts 3:1 Peter and John go up together to the temple at the hour of prayer.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the two Johns show two kinds of faithfulness: one cried in the wilderness and lost his head, and the other stayed beside Jesus to the end and wrote it all down.
RelatedPeople: John the Baptist; John the Apostle; Simon Peter
RelatedEvents: The Baptism of Jesus; Peter Heals the Lame Man
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H3147); Joatham (i.e. Jotham), an Israelite:--Joatham.
BiblicalUsage: Joatham is the Greek form of Jotham, the king of Judah, and Matthew names him twice in one verse. In Matthew 1:9 Ozias begat Joatham, and Joatham begat Achaz, and Achaz begat Ezekias, in the line that runs from Abraham to Christ.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Joatham's two mentions in a single verse are the point: a king who did right, named once as a son and once as a father, in the line God kept.
RelatedPeople: Jotham, King of Judah; Ahaz, Son of Jotham
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H347); Job (i.e. Ijob), a patriarch:--Job.
BiblicalUsage: Job is named once in the New Testament, and James names him for his patience. In James 5:11 he writes, ye have heard of the patience of Job, and have seen the end of the Lord, that the Lord is very pitiful, and of tender mercy.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that one verse is the whole book in a sentence: Job suffered, Job waited, and the end of the Lord was mercy.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H3100); Joel, an Israelite:--Joel.
BiblicalUsage: Joel is the prophet Peter quotes on the day of Pentecost. In Acts 2:16 Peter stands up and says, this is that which was spoken by the prophet Joel, and pours out the promise that God will pour out his Spirit upon all flesh.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Joel's name is tied to Pentecost forever: the prophet who saw the Spirit poured out, and the apostle who saw it happen.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably for G2491 or G2495; Jonan, an Israelite:--Jonan.
BiblicalUsage: Jonan is one name in Luke's genealogy, standing between Joseph and Eliakim. In Luke 3:30 he is named in the line that runs from Jesus back through David to Adam, one of the links the world forgot.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the forgotten links are the proof of the promise: God kept the line through men whose names we would never know if Luke had not written them down.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H3124); Jonas (i.e. Jonah), the name of two Israelites:--Jonas.
BiblicalUsage: Jonas is the Greek form of Jonah, and Jesus makes him the sign of his own death and rising. In Matthew 12:39 he says an evil generation seeks a sign, and no sign shall be given but the sign of the prophet Jonas, in Matthew 12:40 as Jonas was three days and three nights in the whale's belly, so shall the Son of man be in the heart of the earth, and in Luke 11:30 as Jonas was a sign unto the Ninevites, so shall the Son of man be to this generation.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the sign of Jonah is the gospel in miniature: three days in the dark, and then the prophet walks out alive to preach repentance.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H3305); Joppe (i.e. Japho), a place in Palestine:--Joppa.
BiblicalUsage: Joppa was the seaport where Peter raised Tabitha and learned the gospel was for the Gentiles. In Acts 9:36 Tabitha, full of good works, dies at Joppa, in Acts 10:5 the angel tells Cornelius to send to Joppa and call for Simon Peter, and in Acts 9:43 Peter tarries many days in Joppa with Simon the tanner.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Joppa is where the church turned a corner: a disciple raised from the dead, and a vision on a rooftop that opened the door to the nations.
RelatedPeople: Simon Peter; Tabitha; Simon the Tanner; Cornelius
RelatedEvents: Peter and Cornelius; Peter Raises Tabitha
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H3141); Joram, an Israelite:--Joram.
BiblicalUsage: Joram is the king of Judah in Matthew's genealogy, the son of Jehoshaphat. In Matthew 1:8 Josaphat begat Joram, and Joram begat Ozias, in the line that runs from Abraham to Christ through the kings.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Joram's place in the list is a warning and a comfort together: a king who married into Ahab's house and still could not break the line God was keeping.
RelatedPeople: Joram, Son of Jehoshaphat; King Jehoshaphat
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H3383); the Jordanes (i.e. Jarden), a river of Palestine:--Jordan.
BiblicalUsage: The Jordan is the river where Israel crossed in and John baptized. In Matthew 3:6 the people are baptized of John in Jordan, confessing their sins, in Mark 1:5 all the land of Judea goes out to him and is baptized in the river, and in John 1:28 these things were done in Bethabara beyond Jordan, where John was baptizing.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the Jordan is the river of new beginnings: Israel entered the land through it, and the crowds went down into it to be washed clean.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: perhaps for G2496; Jorim, an Israelite:--Jorim.
BiblicalUsage: Jorim is one name in Luke's genealogy, standing between Eliezer and Matthat. In Luke 3:29 he is named in the line that runs from Jesus back to Adam, a link between two men the world has forgotten.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Jorim's name is there for the same reason every link is there: the promise did not skip a generation, and God kept count of them all.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: perhaps from εἶμι (to go) or ἵημι (to send); rust (as if emitted by metals); also venom (as emitted by serpents):--poison, rust.
BiblicalUsage: Poison and rust are the two faces of this word, and both eat away at what they touch. In James 3:8 the tongue is an unruly evil, full of deadly poison, in James 5:3 the rust of the rich men's gold shall witness against them and eat their flesh as fire, and in Romans 3:13 the poison of asps is under the lips of men whose mouths are full of cursing.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word is a warning about what corrodes: a tongue full of poison and gold eaten with rust are the same decay. Both testify against their owners.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H3092); Josaphat (i.e. Jehoshaphat), an Israelite:--Josaphat.
BiblicalUsage: Josaphat is the Greek form of Jehoshaphat, the king who sought the Lord, and Matthew names him in the genealogy. In Matthew 1:8 Asa begat Josaphat, and Josaphat begat Joram, and Joram begat Ozias, in the line of the kings from Abraham to Christ.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Josaphat's name in the list is a bright spot among the kings: a man who set his heart to seek God, and whose son's line God kept.
RelatedPeople: King Jehoshaphat; Joram, Son of Jehoshaphat
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: genitive case of G2500; Jose, an Israelite:--Jose.
BiblicalUsage: Jose is the name Luke gives to one ancestor of Jesus, in the genealogy that runs back to Adam. In Luke 3:29 the line runs through Jose, the son of Eliezer, the son of Jorim, and the Greek text writes his name with the same letters as the name Jesus, which is why the old copies spell it Jose here and Jesus elsewhere.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Jose is a reminder that the genealogy is made of real men with shared names: this Jose is not the Lord, he is one more link in the Lord's line.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H3130); Joseph, the name of seven Israelites:--Joseph.
BiblicalUsage: Joseph is the name of the patriarch, the husband of Mary, and the rich man of Arimathea, and the New Testament holds them apart by their deeds. In Matthew 1:20 the angel tells Joseph, thou son of David, fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife, in Matthew 27:59 Joseph of Arimathea takes the body of Jesus and wraps it in clean linen, and in Acts 7:9 the patriarchs, moved with envy, sold Joseph into Egypt.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the three Josephs show three kinds of faithfulness: one believed a dream, one gave his tomb, and one forgave the brothers who sold him.
RelatedPeople: Joseph, Son of Jacob; Joseph, Husband of Mary; Joseph of Arimathea
RelatedEvents: The Birth of Jesus; The Crucifixion; Martyrdom of Stephen; The Angel Appears to Joseph; The Burial of Jesus
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: perhaps for G2501; Joses, the name of two Israelites:--Joses. Compare G2499.
BiblicalUsage: Joses is the brother of James, one of the sons of Mary who watched the cross. In Mark 6:3 the people of Nazareth ask, is not this the carpenter, the son of Mary, the brother of James, and Joses, and of Juda, and Simon, in Mark 15:40 Mary the mother of James the less and of Joses looks on from afar, and in Mark 15:47 Mary the mother of Joses watches where the body is laid.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Joses is the quiet brother: named at the cross, named at the tomb, and never given a speech of his own.
RelatedPeople: Joses, Brother of Jesus; James, Brother of Jesus; Jesus
RelatedEvents: The Crucifixion; Jesus Rejected at Nazareth; The Burial of Jesus
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H2977); Josias (i.e. Joshiah), an Israelite:--Josias.
BiblicalUsage: Josias is the Greek form of Josiah, the boy king who found the book of the law. In Matthew 1:10 Ezekias begat Manasses, and Manasses begat Amon, and Amon begat Josias, and in Matthew 1:11 Josias begat Jechonias and his brethren, about the time they were carried away to Babylon.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Josias is the brightest king in the list: eight years old when he took the throne, and the man who tore down the idols and read the book to the people.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (the tenth letter of the Hebrew alphabet); "iota", the name of the eighth letter of the Greek alphabet, put (figuratively) for a very small part of anything:--jot.
BiblicalUsage: An iota is the smallest letter of the alphabet, and Jesus stakes everything on it. In Matthew 5:18 he says, till heaven and earth pass, one jot or one tittle shall in no wise pass from the law, till all be fulfilled.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the smallest letter is the surest thing in the Bible: not one stroke of God's word will fail.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H3063 or perhaps H3194); Judah (i.e. Jehudah or Juttah), a part of (or place in) Palestine:--Judah.
BiblicalUsage: Juda is the name of the land and the tribe, the country of the promise, and the Gospels use it where the place matters. In Matthew 2:6 Bethlehem stands in the land of Juda, in Luke 1:39 Mary goes into a city of Juda to greet Elisabeth, and in Hebrews 7:14 it is evident that our Lord sprang out of Juda, a tribe of which Moses spake nothing concerning priesthood.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the land and the tribe are one promise: the Christ came out of Juda, from Bethlehem in the land of Juda, and no other tribe could have given him.
RelatedPeople: Judah; Jesus; Mary, Mother of Jesus
RelatedEvents: The Birth of Jesus; Mary Visits Elizabeth; The Magi Visit Jesus
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: feminine of G2453 (with G1093 implied); the Judæan land (i.e. Judæa), a region of Palestine:--Judæa.
BiblicalUsage: Judea is the land where the story happens, from Bethlehem to Jerusalem. In Matthew 2:1 Jesus is born in Bethlehem of Judea in the days of Herod, in Acts 1:8 the disciples are told they will be witnesses in Jerusalem, and in all Judea, and in Samaria, and in Acts 9:31 the churches have rest throughout all Judea and Galilee and Samaria.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Judea is the ground the gospel walked on first: born there, preached there, and then sent out from there to the ends of the earth.
RelatedEvents: The Birth of Jesus; The Conversion of Paul; The Ascension; The Great Commission; The Magi Visit Jesus; Saul Received in Jerusalem and Sent to Tarsus
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: adverb from G2451; Judaïcally or in a manner resembling a Judæan:--as do the Jews.
BiblicalUsage: As do the Jews is the phrase Paul throws at Peter in Antioch, and it stings because it is true. In Galatians 2:14 Paul says to Peter before them all, if thou, being a Jew, livest after the manner of Gentiles, why compellest thou the Gentiles to live as do the Jews.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the rebuke is the gospel itself: Peter was living like a Gentile until the men from James came, and Paul would not let him put the yoke back on.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2453; Judaïc, i.e. resembling a Judæan:--Jewish.
BiblicalUsage: Jewish is the word Paul uses for the fables the Cretans were chasing. In Titus 1:14 he tells Titus not to give heed to Jewish fables, and commandments of men, that turn from the truth.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the warning still stands: fables dressed as religion turn men from the truth, and the truth is a Person, not a story.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2448 (in the sense of G2455 as a country); Judæan, i.e. belonging to Jehudah:--Jew(-ess), of Judæa.
BiblicalUsage: A Jew is one of the people of Judah, and Paul uses the name for the people he came from and the people he preached to. In 1 Corinthians 1:22 the Jews require a sign, and the Greeks seek after wisdom, in 1 Corinthians 9:20 Paul says, unto the Jews I became as a Jew, that I might gain the Jews, and in 1 Corinthians 10:32 he says, give none offence, neither to the Jews, nor to the Gentiles, nor to the church of God.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Paul's heart for his own people runs through these verses: he became as a Jew to win Jews, and he would not offend them, or anyone, on the way.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2450; "Judaism", i.e. the Jewish faith and usages:--Jews' religion.
BiblicalUsage: Judaism is the religion Paul left, and he names it when he tells his own story. In Galatians 1:13 he says, ye have heard of my conversation in time past in the Jews' religion, how that beyond measure I persecuted the church of God, and in Galatians 1:14 he profited in the Jews' religion above many of his equals, being more exceedingly zealous of the traditions of his fathers.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Paul's past is the proof of grace: the most zealous defender of the old religion became its greatest preacher of the new one.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2453; to become a Judæan, i.e. "Judaize":--live as the Jews.
BiblicalUsage: To live as the Jews is the charge Paul lays on Peter at Antioch. In Galatians 2:14 he asks Peter before them all, why compellest thou the Gentiles to live as do the Jews, when thou thyself livest after the manner of Gentiles.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the question cuts to the heart of the gospel: if Peter lived free of the law, he had no right to lay it on the Gentiles.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H3063); Judas (i.e. Jehudah), the name of ten Israelites; also of the posterity of one of them and its region:--Juda(-h, -s); Jude.
BiblicalUsage: Judas is the name of the traitor, and of other men who bore it faithfully. In Matthew 10:4 Simon the Canaanite and Judas Iscariot, who also betrayed him, are named among the twelve, in Acts 1:16 Peter says the scripture must needs have been fulfilled concerning Judas, which was guide to them that took Jesus, and in Acts 15:22 the church sends Judas Barsabbas with Paul and Barnabas to Antioch.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the name carries both stories at once: one Judas sold the Lord for silver, and another Judas carried the letter of freedom to the Gentiles.
RelatedEvents: Jerusalem Council; Paul's Missionary Journeys; Jesus Sends Out the Twelve; The Choice of Matthias
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: feminine of the same as G2457; Julia, a Christian woman:--Julia.
BiblicalUsage: Julia is one of the believers Paul greets at the end of his letter to Rome. In Romans 16:15 he says, salute Philologus, and Julia, and Nereus, and his sister, and Olympas, and all the saints which are with them.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Julia's name in the greeting is the whole church in miniature: ordinary believers, named one by one, and called saints.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Latin origin; Julius, a centurion:--Julius.
BiblicalUsage: Julius was the centurion who took Paul to Rome, and he treated his prisoner kindly. In Acts 27:1 Paul is delivered to Julius, a centurion of Augustus' band, and in Acts 27:3 Julius courteously entreated Paul, and gave him liberty to go unto his friends to refresh himself.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Julius is a small kindness in a hard voyage: a Roman soldier who saw something in his prisoner worth respecting.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Latin origin; Junias, a Christian:--Junias.
BiblicalUsage: Junias is the name Paul greets in Rome, among the apostles before him. In Romans 16:7 he says, salute Andronicus and Junias, my kinsmen, and my fellowprisoners, who are of note among the apostles, who also were in Christ before me.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the greeting is worth reading slowly: a fellow prisoner, of note among the apostles, and in Christ before Paul himself.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Latin origin ("just"); Justus, the name of three Christian:--Justus.
BiblicalUsage: Justus is the name of three men in the New Testament, and each one is named for a different reason. In Acts 1:23 Joseph called Barsabas, who was surnamed Justus, stands as a candidate to take Judas' place, in Acts 18:7 Paul enters the house of Justus, one that worshipped God, whose house joined hard to the synagogue, and in Colossians 4:11 Jesus, which is called Justus, sends his greeting as a fellow worker.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the three men who share the name show how common faithfulness is: a candidate, a host, and a fellow worker, all called Justus.
RelatedPeople: Jesus Justus; Justus of Corinth; Paul
RelatedEvents: Paul's Missionary Journeys; The Choice of Matthias; Paul at Corinth
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a stock
BiblicalUsage: A stump is what is left when the tree is cut down, and Daniel's dream leaves one standing on purpose. In Daniel 4:15 the watcher commands, leave the stump of his roots in the earth, in Daniel 4:23 the stump means the kingdom shall be sure unto thee, and in Daniel 4:26 the stump is the promise that the kingdom will be restored after the king learns that heaven rules.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the stump is the mercy in the judgment: the tree falls, but the roots stay, and the kingdom grows back when the king bows.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Ikkesh, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Ikkesh was the father of Ira, one of David's mighty men, and the Bible names him by his son. In 1 Chronicles 11:28 Ira the son of Ikkesh the Tekoite stands among the mighty men, in 2 Samuel 23:26 the same Ira is listed again, and in 1 Chronicles 27:9 Ira the son of Ikkesh commands the sixth course for the sixth month.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Ikkesh is remembered the way fathers often are: by the son who served the king, and by the course that bore his son's name.
RelatedPeople: Ikkesh; Ira, Son of Ikkesh; King David
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: distorted; hence, false
BiblicalUsage: Crooked is the word for a path that will not run straight, and the Bible uses it for men who will not walk straight either. In Deuteronomy 32:5 Moses calls Israel a perverse and crooked generation, in Proverbs 2:15 the wicked walk in crooked paths, in Proverbs 8:8 wisdom says all her words are plain and there is nothing froward or perverse in them, and in Proverbs 11:20 the froward in heart are an abomination to the LORD.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the crooked path is always a choice: wisdom walks straight and plain. The heart that turns aside knows exactly what it is doing.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: perversity
BiblicalUsage: Perversity is crookedness in the mouth and in the walk, and Proverbs warns against both. In Proverbs 4:24 the father says, put away from thee a froward mouth, and perverse lips put far from thee, and in Proverbs 6:12 a naughty person walketh with a froward mouth.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that perversity starts small, in the lips, and ends in the walk: guard the mouth and the feet will follow.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: perhaps from G2046 (as a symbol of the female messenger of the pagan deities); a rainbow ("iris"):--rainbow.
BiblicalUsage: A rainbow is the bow around the throne, and John sees it twice. In Revelation 4:3 there is a rainbow round about the throne, in sight like unto an emerald, and in Revelation 10:1 a mighty angel comes down from heaven, clothed with a cloud, and a rainbow is upon his head.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the rainbow around the throne is the same sign as the rainbow after the flood: judgment is real, and mercy rings it round.
RelatedEvents: The Throne Room and the Lamb; The Little Scroll
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H3327); Isaac (i.e. Jitschak), the son of Abraham:--Isaac.
BiblicalUsage: Isaac is the son of the promise, the child Abraham waited for, and the New Testament holds him up as the pattern of faith. In Matthew 1:2 Abraham begat Isaac, and Isaac begat Jacob, in Hebrews 11:17 Abraham offered up Isaac when he was tried, and in Galatians 4:28 Paul says, we, brethren, as Isaac was, are the children of promise.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Isaac is the proof that God's promises are born, not earned: the child of old age became the father of the nation, and we are his children by promise too.
RelatedEvents: The Binding of Isaac; The Birth of Jesus
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H3485); Isachar (i.e. Jissaskar), a son of Jacob (figuratively, his descendant):--Issachar.
BiblicalUsage: Issachar is one of the twelve tribes sealed in John's vision. In Revelation 7:7 twelve thousand are sealed of the tribe of Issachar, standing in the list between Simeon and Levi.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the sealing of Issachar is the promise kept to the last tribe: God counts his people by name, and not one tribe is left out.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2470 and G32; like an angel, i.e. angelic:--equal unto the angels.
BiblicalUsage: Equal unto the angels is the promise Jesus gives for the resurrection. In Luke 20:36 he says the children of the resurrection neither marry nor are given in marriage, for they cannot die any more, for they are equal unto the angels, and are the children of God, being the children of the resurrection.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the promise is bigger than marriage: death ends, and the children of God rise to a life like the angels' own.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2479; to have (or exercise) force (literally or figuratively):--be able, avail, can do(-not), could, be good, might, prevail, be of strength, be whole, + much work.
BiblicalUsage: To be able is to have the strength to do it, and the New Testament measures that strength by God, not by us. In Acts 19:20 the word of God grew mightily and prevailed, in Galatians 5:6 neither circumcision availeth any thing, nor uncircumcision, but faith which worketh by love, and in Philippians 4:13 Paul says, I can do all things through Christ which strengtheneth me.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the strength Paul claims is not his own: Christ strengthens him. The word prevails because God is the one doing the prevailing.
RelatedEvents: Paul's Missionary Journeys; The Sons of Sceva at Ephesus
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2479; forcible (literally or figuratively):--boisterous, mighty(-ier), powerful, strong(-er, man), valiant.
BiblicalUsage: Strong is the word for power that cannot be moved, and the Bible gives it to God and to his people in turn. In 1 Corinthians 1:25 the weakness of God is stronger than men, in 1 John 2:14 the young men are strong because the word of God abides in them, in Hebrews 5:7 Jesus offers prayers with strong crying and tears, and in Hebrews 6:18 God gives strong consolation to those who flee for refuge.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe true strength is the kind that cries out and holds on: Jesus prayed with strong crying. God answers with strong consolation.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)
