Definition: from a derivative of ἰς (force; compare ἔσχον, a form of G2192); forcefulness (literally or figuratively):--ability, might(-ily), power, strength.
BiblicalUsage: Strength is what God gives and what he is owed, and the Bible holds both together. In Ephesians 6:10 Paul says, be strong in the Lord, and in the power of his might, in Mark 12:30 Jesus says to love the Lord with all thy strength, in 1 Peter 4:11 the speaker speaks as the oracles of God, that God in all things may be glorified, and in Revelation 5:12 the Lamb is worthy to receive power, and riches, and wisdom, and strength.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that strength flows one way first: God gives it, and I spend it loving him. Heaven gives it back to the Lamb who was slain.
RelatedEvents: The Greatest Commandment; The Throne Room and the Lamb
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: assumed by some as the base of certain irregular forms of G1492; to know:--know.
BiblicalUsage: To know is what the old scholars guessed this word meant, but the word itself never appears in the Greek New Testament as it stands. It was assumed to be the base of certain forms of the verb to know, yet no verse in the Greek text carries this form, so no passage can be cited for it.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the honest thing is to say so plainly: a word that never occurs cannot teach me anything, and I will not invent a verse for it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: entity, used only adverbially, there is or are
BiblicalUsage: There is, there are, is the word that says something exists when it should not. In 2 Samuel 14:19 the woman of Tekoah tells the king, is there any that can turn to the right hand or to the left from what my lord the king has spoken, and in Micah 6:10 the prophet asks, are there yet the treasures of wickedness in the house of the wicked.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the little word carries a heavy question: is there any way round what the king has said, and are the treasures of wickedness still in the house.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a woman
BiblicalUsage: A woman is the word for wife and for woman alike, and the Bible honours her from the first page to the last. In Genesis 2:22 the LORD builds the rib into a woman and brings her to the man, in Genesis 2:24 a man leaves his father and mother and cleaves to his wife, in Deuteronomy 22:30 the law guards a father's wife from his son, and in Proverbs 31:10 the question is asked, who can find a virtuous woman, for her price is far above rubies.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the Bible's first word about the woman is that she is built by God himself and brought to the man. Its last word is that her worth is beyond rubies.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a woman
BiblicalUsage: A woman is the word for wife and for woman alike, and the Bible honours her from the first page to the last. In Genesis 2:22 the LORD builds the rib into a woman and brings her to the man, in Genesis 2:24 a man leaves his father and mother and cleaves to his wife, in Deuteronomy 22:30 the law guards a father's wife from his son, and in Proverbs 31:10 the question is asked, who can find a virtuous woman, for her price is far above rubies.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the Bible's first word about the woman is that she is built by God himself and brought to the man. Its last word is that her worth is beyond rubies.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (probably H377 and H7149); inhabitant of Kerioth; Iscariotes (i.e. Keriothite), an epithet of Judas the traitor:--Iscariot.
BiblicalUsage: Iscariot is the name that follows Judas wherever he goes, the man from Kerioth. In Matthew 10:4 he is named last among the twelve, Judas Iscariot, who also betrayed him, in John 13:26 Jesus dips the sop and gives it to Judas Iscariot, and in Luke 22:3 Satan enters into Judas surnamed Iscariot, and he goes to the chief priests.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the name is a warning written into the list of the twelve: he sat at the table, he took the sop, and he still went out to betray him.
RelatedEvents: The Last Supper; Jesus Sends Out the Twelve; Judas Agrees to Betray Jesus
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2470 and G5590; of similar spirit:--likeminded.
BiblicalUsage: Likeminded is the word Paul uses for Timothy, and he says he has no one else like him. In Philippians 2:20 he writes, I have no man likeminded, who will naturally care for your state.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe likemindedness is the rarest gift in ministry: a man who cares for the flock the way I would, without being asked.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: adverb from G2470; likely, i.e. perhaps:--it may be.
BiblicalUsage: Perhaps is the word of a father's hope in the parable of the vineyard. In Luke 20:13 the lord of the vineyard says, I will send my beloved son, it may be they will reverence him when they see him.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the perhaps is the tragedy of the parable: the father hoped, and the husbandmen killed the son anyway.
RelatedEvents: The Parable of the Wicked Tenants
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably from G1492 (through the idea of seeming); similar (in amount and kind):--+ agree, as much, equal, like.
BiblicalUsage: Equal is the word that measures sameness, and the Bible uses it for wages, for Christ, and for the city of God. In Matthew 20:12 the labourers complain, thou hast made them equal unto us, in Philippians 2:6 Christ thought it not robbery to be equal with God, in Revelation 21:16 the city lies foursquare, its length and breadth and height equal, and in John 5:18 the Jews seek to kill Jesus because he made himself equal with God.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word holds the gospel together: Christ was equal with God and did not cling to it. The labourers who came last are made equal with the first.
RelatedEvents: The Parable of the Workers in the Vineyard; The New Jerusalem
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: likeness (in condition or proportion); by implication, equity:--equal(-ity).
BiblicalUsage: Equality is the fairness Paul asks the churches to practise. In 2 Corinthians 8:13 he says, I mean not that other men be eased, and ye burdened, but by an equality, in 2 Corinthians 8:14 your abundance may be a supply for their want, that there may be equality, and in Colossians 4:1 masters are told to give unto their servants that which is just and equal.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that equality in Paul's mouth is not sameness of purse but fairness of heart: abundance supplies want. The master treats the servant as the Lord treats him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2470 and G5092; of equal value or honor:--like precious.
BiblicalUsage: Like precious is the faith Peter says we share. In 2 Peter 1:1 he writes to them that have obtained like precious faith with us through the righteousness of God and our Saviour Jesus Christ.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the phrase is the whole of the letter in two words: the faith I hold is the same precious faith the apostles held, and it came through the same righteousness.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H3478); Israel (i.e. Jisrael), the adopted name of Jacob, including his descendants (literally or figuratively):--Israel.
BiblicalUsage: Israel is the name God gave to Jacob, and the name of the people who came from him. In Matthew 2:20 the angel tells Joseph to take the child into the land of Israel, in John 1:49 Nathanael confesses, thou art the King of Israel, and in Romans 11:26 Paul writes that all Israel shall be saved.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the name carries the whole story: a man who wrestled with God, a people God chose, and a promise God has not forgotten.
RelatedEvents: The Birth of Jesus; The Calling of the First Disciples; The Flight into Egypt
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2474; an "Israelite", i.e. descendant of Israel (literally or figuratively):--Israelite.
BiblicalUsage: Israelites are the descendants of Israel, and the apostles address them as their own people. In Acts 2:22 Peter cries, ye men of Israel, hear these words, in Romans 9:4 Paul says the adoption and the glory belong to the Israelites, and in 2 Corinthians 11:22 he asks, are they Israelites, so am I.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the name is a claim of belonging: Peter and Paul stood up and said, these are my people, and I am one of them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: (fractional) a tenth part
BiblicalUsage: A tenth part is the measure for the offerings, the flour that goes with the lamb. In Exodus 29:40 a tenth deal of flour mingled with oil is offered with the lamb, in Leviticus 23:13 the meat offering is two tenth deals of fine flour, and in Numbers 15:4 the offering is a tenth deal of flour mingled with oil.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the tenth part is the picture of proportion: God does not ask for the whole harvest in the offering. He asks for a measured part, given willingly.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: second person imperative present of G1510; be thou:--+ agree, be, X give thyself wholly to.
BiblicalUsage: Be thou is the command Jesus gives, and it lands like a word spoken straight to one person. In Matthew 5:25 he says, agree with thine adversary quickly, whiles thou art in the way with him, in Mark 5:34 he tells the woman, daughter, thy faith hath made thee whole, go in peace, and be whole of thy plague, and in Luke 19:17 the nobleman says to his servant, well, thou good servant, because thou hast been faithful in a very little, have thou authority over ten cities.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the little command carries the whole gospel: agree, be whole, and have authority, all because he spoke it.
RelatedEvents: The Sermon on the Mount; Jairus' Daughter and the Bleeding Woman; The Parable of the Talents
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably of foreign origin; Italia, a region of Europe:--Italy.
BiblicalUsage: Italy is the land Paul sails to as a prisoner and writes back to as a friend. In Acts 18:2 Aquila and Priscilla come from Italy because Claudius commanded all Jews to depart from Rome, in Acts 27:1 Paul is delivered to sail into Italy, and in Hebrews 13:24 the writer sends greeting from they of Italy.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Italy is where the gospel arrived by ship and by prison: Paul came in chains, and the saints there sent their love back.
RelatedEvents: Paul's Missionary Journeys; Paul at Corinth
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2482; Italic, i.e. belonging to Italia:--Italian.
BiblicalUsage: Italian is the word for the band Cornelius commanded, the cohort from Italy. In Acts 10:1 there is a man in Caesarea called Cornelius, a centurion of the band called the Italian band, a devout man who feared God with all his house.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the Italian band is the door the gospel walked through: a Roman soldier who prayed, and an angel who answered.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H3195); Ituræa (i.e. Jetur), a region of Palestine:--Ituræa.
BiblicalUsage: Iturea is the region Philip the tetrarch ruled when John began to preach. In Luke 3:1, in the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar, Philip is tetrarch of Iturea and of the region of Trachonitis, and John the son of Zacharias comes preaching in the wilderness.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Luke names the rulers to pin the gospel to real time: while Philip ruled Iturea, the word of God came to John.
RelatedPeople: John the Baptist; Philip the Tetrarch
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: worrisomeness, i.e. labor or pain
BiblicalUsage: Sorrow in labour is the curse God speaks over the ground and over childbirth. In Genesis 3:16 he tells the woman, I will greatly multiply thy sorrow and thy conception, in Genesis 3:17 he tells the man, in sorrow shalt thou eat of the ground all the days of thy life, and in Genesis 5:29 Lamech names his son Noah, saying, this same shall comfort us concerning our work and toil of our hands.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the sorrow is real and the comfort is real too: the ground is cursed. A son named Rest is promised in the middle of it.
RelatedPeople: Adam; Eve; Noah; Lamech, Father of Noah
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Ittai or Ithai, the name of a Gittite and of an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Ittai the Gittite was the foreigner who would not leave David when Absalom rose against him. In 2 Samuel 15:19 the king tells him to return, but in 2 Samuel 15:21 Ittai answers, as the LORD liveth, where my lord the king shall be, there will thy servant be, and in 2 Samuel 18:2 David sets him over a third part of the army.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Ittai is the loyal stranger the story turns on: a Gittite who swore to stay, and a king who trusted him with a third of the army.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: shut up, i.e. impeded (as to the use of the right hand)
BiblicalUsage: Shut up in the right hand is the phrase for a man who cannot use it, a left-handed man. In Judges 3:15 Ehud is a Benjamite, a man lefthanded, and the LORD raises him up to deliver Israel, and in Judges 20:16 there are seven hundred chosen men lefthanded, every one of whom can sling stones at an hair breadth and not miss.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the left hand is the point: God raises a deliverer from the hand nobody would choose, and seven hundred men who cannot miss with the other one.
RelatedEvents: Ehud and Eglon; The Levite's Concubine and the War against Benjamin
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: timely
BiblicalUsage: In due season is the word for the goat sent away at the right time. In Leviticus 16:21 Aaron lays both his hands on the head of the live goat, confesses over him all the iniquities of Israel, and sends him away by the hand of a fit man into the wilderness.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the fit man matters: the sins are carried away on time, by the hand appointed for it, into a land not inhabited.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Ivvah or Avva, a region of Assyria
BiblicalUsage: Ivvah was a region of Assyria whose gods could not save it, and the Bible names it three times in the taunts of the Assyrians. In 2 Kings 17:24 the king of Assyria brings men from Ivvah to settle Samaria, in 2 Kings 18:34 Rabshakeh asks, where are the gods of Hamath, and of Arpad, and of Sepharvaim, of Hena, and of Ivah, and in Isaiah 37:13 the same question is asked again.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the taunt is the warning: the gods of Ivvah could not save Ivvah, and the God of Israel is not one god among many.
RelatedEvents: Fall of Samaria; Hezekiah and Sennacherib's Invasion
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: blindness
BiblicalUsage: Blindness is the curse on a people who will not see, and the promise on the horses of their enemies. In Deuteronomy 28:28 the LORD shall smite thee with madness, and blindness, and astonishment of heart, in Zechariah 12:4 God says he will smite every horse with astonishment, and his rider with madness, and in Leviticus 22:22 the blind animal is not to be offered to the LORD.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that blindness in these verses is never only about eyes: a people who will not see are struck with not seeing. God opens the eyes of those who ask.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: silliness
BiblicalUsage: Folly is the opposite of wisdom, and Proverbs holds it up in every chapter. In Proverbs 12:23 a prudent man concealeth knowledge, but the heart of fools proclaimeth foolishness, in Proverbs 14:1 every wise woman buildeth her house, but the foolish plucketh it down with her hands, in Proverbs 14:8 the wisdom of the prudent is to understand his way, but the folly of fools is deceit, and in Proverbs 5:23 the fool dies for want of instruction.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe folly is not a lack of brains but a refusal to listen: the fool proclaims it and plucks down the house with it. He dies for want of the instruction he would not take.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: blind (literally or figuratively)
BiblicalUsage: Blind is the word for eyes that cannot see, and the Bible says God is the one who opens them. In Exodus 4:11 the LORD asks, who maketh the dumb, or the deaf, or the seeing, or the blind, have not I the LORD, in Isaiah 29:18 the eyes of the blind shall see out of obscurity, and out of darkness, in Isaiah 35:5 the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and in Deuteronomy 27:18 cursed be he that maketh the blind to wander out of the way.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the blind in these verses are the promise and the warning together: God opens the eyes of the blind. Cursed is the man who leads them astray.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: perverseness
BiblicalUsage: Perverseness is the crookedness Daniel tells Nebuchadnezzar to break off. In Daniel 4:27 Daniel says, break off thy sins by righteousness, and thine iniquities by shewing mercy to the poor, if it may be a lengthening of thy tranquillity.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Daniel's counsel is the only way out of perverseness: break it off, do right, and show mercy, and the king's peace may last a little longer.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Iezer, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Iezer was a son of Gilead, and the father of the family of the Iezrites. In Numbers 26:30 the sons of Gilead are numbered, of Jeezer, the family of the Jeezerites, in the census of Israel in the wilderness.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Iezer's name lives in the census: one man, one family, counted among the tribes on the way to the land.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an Iezrite or descendant of Iezer
BiblicalUsage: An Iezrite is a descendant of Iezer, one of the families of Manasseh. In Numbers 26:30 the census names the family of the Jeezerites among the sons of Gilead, in the numbering of Israel in the plains of Moab.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the family name is the point: Iezer's sons are counted as a family, and the family is counted as part of Israel.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: alas!
BiblicalUsage: Alas is the cry of the Preacher over a man alone and a land badly ruled. In Ecclesiastes 4:10 he says, woe to him that is alone when he falleth, for he hath not another to help him up, and in Ecclesiastes 10:16 he says, woe to thee, O land, when thy king is a child, and thy princes eat in the morning.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the alas is practical wisdom: do not walk alone, and do not trust a land whose rulers feast while the people hunger.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: alas!
BiblicalUsage: Alas is the cry of the Preacher over a man alone and a land badly ruled. In Ecclesiastes 4:10 he says, woe to him that is alone when he falleth, for he hath not another to help him up, and in Ecclesiastes 10:16 he says, woe to thee, O land, when thy king is a child, and thy princes eat in the morning.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the alas is practical wisdom: do not walk alone, and do not trust a land whose rulers feast while the people hunger.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

BiblicalUsage: Alas is the cry of the Preacher over a man alone and a land badly ruled. In Ecclesiastes 4:10 he says, woe to him that is alone when he falleth, for he hath not another to help him up, and in Ecclesiastes 10:16 he says, woe to thee, O land, when thy king is a child, and thy princes eat in the morning.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the alas is practical wisdom: do not walk alone, and do not trust a land whose rulers feast while the people hunger.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a ruin (as if overturned)
BiblicalUsage: A ruin is what is left when the city falls, and the prophets say Jerusalem will become one. In Jeremiah 26:18 Micah's word is quoted, Zion shall be plowed like a field, and Jerusalem shall become heaps, in Micah 3:12 the same word is spoken, and in Psalms 79:1 the psalmist cries, O God, the heathen are come into thine inheritance, thy holy temple have they defiled, and laid Jerusalem on heaps.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the ruin is the warning the prophets would not stop giving: the city God loved became heaps. It became heaps because the people would not hear.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Ikabod, a son of Phineas
BiblicalUsage: Ichabod is the name a dying mother gave her son when the ark was taken. In 1 Samuel 4:21 she names the child Ichabod, saying, the glory is departed from Israel, because the ark of God was taken, and in 1 Samuel 14:3 Ahiah, the son of Ahitub, Ichabod's brother, wears the ephod before the people.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the name is the saddest in the Bible: a child named for the glory that left, on the day the ark was taken and his father and grandfather died.
RelatedEvents: The Ark Captured and Returned; Jonathan's Victory at Michmash
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: alas!
BiblicalUsage: Alas is the cry of the Preacher over a man alone and a land badly ruled. In Ecclesiastes 4:10 he says, woe to him that is alone when he falleth, for he hath not another to help him up, and in Ecclesiastes 10:16 he says, woe to thee, O land, when thy king is a child, and thy princes eat in the morning.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the alas is practical wisdom: do not walk alone, and do not trust a land whose rulers feast while the people hunger.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Ije-ha-Abarim, a place near Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Ije-abarim is a place on the journey, the ruins of Abarim in the wilderness. In Numbers 21:11 Israel pitches in Ije-abarim, in the wilderness which is before Moab, toward the sunrising, and in Numbers 33:44 the same camp is listed in the stages of the journey from Egypt.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the place name is a marker on the road: Israel camped there on the way to the land, and the journey is remembered stage by stage.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Ijim, a place in the Desert.
BiblicalUsage: Ijim is a place in the desert, and a town in the south of Judah. In Numbers 33:45 Israel departs from Iim and pitches in Dibon-gad, and in Joshua 15:29 Iim is named among the cities of the tribe of Judah toward the coast.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the two mentions are two places with one name: a camp in the wilderness and a town in Judah, both remembered because Israel passed through them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a tree
BiblicalUsage: A tree is what Nebuchadnezzar sees in his dream, and Daniel tells him the tree is the king himself. In Daniel 4:10 a tree grows in the midst of the earth, in Daniel 4:11 it grows and is strong and its height reaches unto heaven, in Daniel 4:20 the tree that thou sawest is thou, O king, and in Daniel 4:23 the watcher commands to cut it down but leave the stump.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the tree is the proudest image in the Bible: a king grown tall as heaven, cut down in a night. He is left with his stump until he learns that heaven rules.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Ilai, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Ilai was one of David's mighty men, an Ahohite. In 1 Chronicles 11:29 Ilai the Ahohite stands in the list of the valiant men who served David, named among the thirty.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a place in that list is honour enough: Ilai the Ahohite is remembered because he stood with David when it counted.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: is it not?
BiblicalUsage: Is it not is the question David asks when he needs a weapon in a hurry. In 1 Samuel 21:8 David says to Ahimelech, is there not here under thine hand spear or sword, for I have neither brought my sword nor my weapons with me, because the king's business required haste.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the hurried question tells the whole story: David is running, unarmed, and the priest gives him the sword of Goliath.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Ijob, the patriarch famous for his patience
BiblicalUsage: Job is the man whose patience James holds up, and the book that bears his name tells his story. In Job 1:1 there is a man in the land of Uz, whose name is Job, and that man is perfect and upright, and one that feareth God, and escheweth evil, in Job 1:8 the LORD asks Satan, hast thou considered my servant Job, that there is none like him in the earth, and in Ezekiel 14:14 God names Noah, Daniel, and Job as the three righteous men who could only deliver their own souls.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Job's story is the hardest in the Bible and the most honest: a righteous man who loses everything, and a God who answers him out of the whirlwind.
RelatedEvents: Job's Suffering and Restoration; Job's Losses in a Single Day
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Ijon, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Ijon was a city of Naphtali that two kings smote in turn. In 1 Kings 15:20 Benhadad smites Ijon, and Dan, and Abel-beth-maachah, in 2 Kings 15:29 Tiglath-pileser takes Ijon, and Abel-beth-maachah, and Janoah, and carries them captive to Assyria, and in 2 Chronicles 16:4 Benhadad's captains smite Ijon again.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Ijon is the picture of a border town caught between empires: smitten by Syria, taken by Assyria, and named in the record every time.
RelatedPeople: Ben-hadad, King of Syria; Tiglath-Pileser, King of Assyria
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Ir, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Ir was a son of Benjamin, named in the genealogy of the tribes. In 1 Chronicles 7:12 Shuppim and Huppim are named, and the sons of Ir, in the families of Benjamin that came out of Egypt.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Ir's one verse is the whole of his record: a son of Benjamin, named among the families, and counted in the tribe.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a watcher, i.e. an angel (as guardian)
BiblicalUsage: A watcher is an angel who keeps guard, and Daniel's dream is full of them. In Daniel 4:13 a watcher and an holy one comes down from heaven, in Daniel 4:17 the sentence is by the decree of the watchers, and the demand by the word of the holy ones, and in Daniel 4:23 the watcher commands to cut the tree down but leave the stump.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the watchers are the proof that heaven is awake: the decree against the proud king is not made on earth. It is made by the holy ones who watch.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Irham-Melach, a place near Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Irham-Melach is the city of salt, named among the cities of Judah in the wilderness. In Joshua 15:62 it stands in the list with Nibshan and Engedi, in the wilderness toward the Salt Sea.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the city of salt is remembered for where it stood: in the wilderness of Judah, near the sea that nothing lives in.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Ir-hat-Temarim, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Ir-hat-Temarim is the city of palm trees, another name for Jericho, and the Bible calls it that in two places. In Judges 1:16 the children of the Kenite go up out of the city of palm trees with the children of Judah, and in 2 Chronicles 28:15 the captives are brought to Jericho, the city of palm trees, to their brethren.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the name is the picture of Jericho itself: a city of palms in the desert, where the Kenites dwelt and the captives were brought home.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Ir-Nachash, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Ir-Nachash is a place in Judah, named once in the genealogies. In 1 Chronicles 4:12 Ir-nahash stands among the sons of Eshton, in the families of the tribe of Judah.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the one mention is enough: a place in Judah, named in the family list, and remembered because the family was.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Ir-Shemesh, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Ir-Shemesh is the city of the sun, a town of the tribe of Dan. In Joshua 19:41 it stands in the border list with Zorah and Eshtaol, in the inheritance of Dan toward the hill country.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the city of the sun is named for what it was: a town on the border of Dan, listed among the cities the tribe was given.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a watcher, i.e. an angel (as guardian)
BiblicalUsage: A watcher is an angel who keeps guard, and Daniel's dream is full of them. In Daniel 4:13 a watcher and an holy one comes down from heaven, in Daniel 4:17 the sentence is by the decree of the watchers, and the demand by the word of the holy ones, and in Daniel 4:23 the watcher commands to cut the tree down but leave the stump.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the watchers are the proof that heaven is awake: the decree against the proud king is not made on earth. It is made by the holy ones who watch.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Ira, the name of three Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Ira is the name of three men who served David, and the Bible keeps them apart by their fathers and their towns. In 2 Samuel 20:26 Ira the Jairite is chief ruler about David, in 2 Samuel 23:26 Ira the son of Ikkesh the Tekoite stands among the mighty men, and in 1 Chronicles 11:28 the same Ira the son of Ikkesh is listed again.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the three Iras show how the kingdom ran: a ruler, a mighty man, and a captain of the course, all serving the same king.
RelatedPeople: Ira the Jairite; Ira, Son of Ikkesh; King David
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Irad, an antediluvian
BiblicalUsage: Irad is a son of Enoch in the line of Cain, named in the first genealogy. In Genesis 4:18 unto Enoch is born Irad, and Irad begat Mehujael, and Mehujael begat Methusael, and Methusael begat Lamech.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Irad's name is there to trace the line of Cain: four generations from Enoch to Lamech, and the line runs to murder.
RelatedPeople: Enoch; Lamech, Son of Methusael; Cain
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Iram, an Idumaean
BiblicalUsage: Iram was a chief of Edom, named in the list of the dukes who ruled before Israel had a king. In Genesis 36:43 Iram stands among the dukes of Edom, and in 1 Chronicles 1:54 the same list is given again, duke Iram among the dukes of Edom.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the dukes of Edom are remembered because Esau's line mattered too: a brother's people, with chiefs of their own, before Israel had a king.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Iri, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Iri was a son of Bela, named in the genealogy of Benjamin. In 1 Chronicles 7:7 the sons of Bela are listed, Ezbon, and Uzzi, and Uzziel, and Jerimoth, and Iri, five heads of the house of their fathers, mighty men of valour.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Iri's name is carried by his brothers: five sons of Bela, five heads of houses, and all mighty men of valour.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Iru, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Iru was a son of Caleb, named in the families of Judah. In 1 Chronicles 4:15 the sons of Caleb the son of Jephunneh are listed, Iru, Elah, and Naam, and the sons of Elah, even Kenaz.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Iru's name lives in his father's line: a son of Caleb, counted among the families of Judah.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Ish-Bosheth, a son of King Saul
BiblicalUsage: Ish-bosheth was the son of Saul whom Abner made king over Israel, and his reign was short and bloody. In 2 Samuel 2:8 Abner takes Ish-bosheth and makes him king over Gilead, in 2 Samuel 3:8 Abner is wroth because Ish-bosheth accuses him of going in to Rizpah, and in 2 Samuel 4:5 two captains come to his house at noon and slay him on his bed.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Ish-bosheth is the warning against a throne held by another man's strength: Abner made him king, Abner left him, and two murderers finished him at noon.
RelatedPeople: Ish-bosheth, Son of Saul; Abner, Son of Ner; King David
RelatedEvents: David Becomes King; David's War with the House of Saul
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Ishchail (or Ish-chai), an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Ish-chail is a name Strong's lists for an Israelite, but no verse in the Hebrew text names such a man. The two words that make it up occur together only as the ordinary phrase for a valiant man, never as the name of a person, so no passage can be cited for it.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that silence is the honest answer here: a name with no verse behind it cannot be given a story, and I will not invent one.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to be a man, i.e. act in a manly way
BiblicalUsage: To act like a man is the call God gives to the rebels in Isaiah. In Isaiah 46:8 he says, remember this, and shew yourselves men, bring it again to mind, O ye transgressors.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the call is still God's word to me: remember, show yourself a man, and bring to mind what you have forgotten.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Ish-Tob, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Ish-tob is the land of Tob, whose men the Ammonites hire against David. In 2 Samuel 10:6 the children of Ammon hire twelve thousand men of Ish-tob, and in 2 Samuel 10:8 the men of Ish-tob stand by themselves in the field against Israel.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Ish-tob is a hired sword in the story: twelve thousand men paid to fight David, and David's captains beat them in the field.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to be a man, i.e. act in a manly way
BiblicalUsage: To act like a man is the call God gives to the rebels in Isaiah. In Isaiah 46:8 he says, remember this, and shew yourselves men, bring it again to mind, O ye transgressors.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the call is still God's word to me: remember, show yourself a man, and bring to mind what you have forgotten.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Ishod, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Ishod was a son of Hammoleketh, named in the families of Manasseh. In 1 Chronicles 7:18 his sister Hammoleketh bare Ishod, and Abiezer, and Mahalah.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Ishod's one verse is the family record: a son of Manasseh, named with his brother and sister, in the tribe's genealogy.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: the little man of the eye; the pupil or ball; hence, the middle (of night)
BiblicalUsage: The apple of the eye is the pupil, the tenderest part, and God uses it for his people. In Deuteronomy 32:10 he keeps Jacob as the apple of his eye, in Psalms 17:8 David prays, keep me as the apple of the eye, hide me under the shadow of thy wings, and in Proverbs 7:2 the father says, keep my law as the apple of thine eye.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the picture is the tenderest in the Bible: God guards his people the way an eye guards its pupil. He is quick to close and quick to keep.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to swoop down upon (literally or figuratively)
BiblicalUsage: To swoop down is what hungry men and greedy hands do, and the Bible uses it for sin done in haste. In 1 Samuel 14:32 the people fly upon the spoil and eat flesh with the blood, in 1 Samuel 15:19 Samuel asks Saul, wherefore then didst thou not obey the voice of the LORD, but didst fly upon the spoil, and in 1 Samuel 25:14 Abigail's servant tells her that David's men swooped down on Nabal's shepherds with railing.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the swoop is the picture of disobedience in a hurry: the spoil is taken before the command is heard. The sin follows the speed.
RelatedEvents: David and Abigail; Jonathan's Victory at Michmash
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Ithamar, a son of Aaron
BiblicalUsage: Ithamar was the youngest son of Aaron, and his name runs through the priestly records from Exodus to Numbers. When Nadab and Abihu died for offering strange fire, Ithamar and his brother Eleazar carried the priesthood on, and Moses charged him with the care of the Gershonites and Merarites and their service of the tabernacle.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Ithamar shows that God's work goes on even after terrible loss. The priesthood did not end with Nadab and Abihu; God kept a line of servants, and ordinary faithfulness — carrying the tabernacle, tending the service — is how His worship stood.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, entity; used only as a particle of affirmation, there is
BiblicalUsage: ʼIythay is the Aramaic word for 'there is' or 'there are,' the plain way of saying that something exists. Daniel uses it to tell Nebuchadnezzar there is a God in heaven who reveals secrets, and the three friends use it to say there is a God able to deliver them from the furnace.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that this little word matters because the whole question of the exile was whether there is a God in heaven who rules kings and rescues His people — and Daniel answers yes.
RelatedEvents: Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego in the Fiery Furnace
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Ithiel, the name of an Israelite, also of a symbolical person
BiblicalUsage: Two men share this name, and Scripture keeps them apart. One Ithiel is a Benjamite who settled in Jerusalem after the return from exile, and the other is the man to whom Agur speaks the words of Proverbs 30 — the man spake unto Ithiel, even unto Ithiel and Ucal.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the name reminds me that God knows His people by name, whether they are listed among the returned exiles or named once as the hearer of a proverb.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Izebel, the wife of king Ahab
BiblicalUsage: Jezebel was the Sidonian princess Ahab married, and she turned Israel toward Baal with a persistence no king before her had matched. She fed the prophets of Baal, hunted Elijah after Carmel, and threatened his life — and in the end she was thrown from her window at Jezreel, just as Elijah had said.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Jezebel stands as Scripture's clearest warning that idolatry is never only a private belief: it builds altars, kills prophets, and bends a whole nation, and God answers it in His own time.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a signet-ring (as engraved)
BiblicalUsage: ʼIzqa is the signet-ring, the king's own seal. When Daniel was thrown to the lions, the king sealed the mouth of the den with his signet and the signets of his lords, so that no one could change what had been done to Daniel.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the sealed stone is part of the point: men shut Daniel in, but the seal could not shut God out.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: trade, i.e. the place (mart) or the payment (revenue)
BiblicalUsage: ʼIzzabown is trade itself — the goods carried, the market where they were sold, and the payment that came back. Ezekiel 27 names it again and again in the lament over Tyre: Tarshish traded silver and iron for it, Syria brought emeralds and fine linen, and the merchants of Sheba and Raamah came with spices and gold.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Tyre's trade shows how wealth can look like strength and still be nothing in God's hands. The ships were full and the markets were busy, and then the whole city sank — and that is why I hold wealth lightly and put my trust somewhere it cannot sink.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: forcible; collectively and concretely, an army
BiblicalUsage: ʼIzzuwz is force — an army in its strength, the power that marches out to war. Isaiah pictures God bringing out the chariot and horse, the army and the power together, and then quenching them like a wick; and the psalm asks who the King of glory is and answers, the LORD strong and mighty, the LORD mighty in battle.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word puts human armies in their place: the strongest force on earth goes out at God's word and goes out like a candle, and the only might that stands is His.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, to feel pain; by implication, to grieve; figuratively, to spoil
BiblicalUsage: Ka-ab is the pain that sits in the body and the heart together — the ache of grief, the soreness of a wound. Job says the flesh upon him shall have pain and his soul within him shall mourn; the proverb says even in laughter the heart is sorrowful; and the psalmist cries out that he is poor and sorrowful, asking God to set him on high.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God does not dismiss this pain or tell us to get over it. Scripture names it plainly and then sets it before the God who heals — and that is why I take my own grief to Him instead of hiding it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: vexation
BiblicalUsage: Ka-ac is vexation — the sharp irritation that provokes and grieves, whether it comes from a rival or from our own folly. Peninnah provoked Hannah sore to make her fret; the Preacher warns that anger rests in the bosom of fools; and Moses says God saw the provoking of His sons and daughters and abhorred them.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe vexation is a warning light, not a virtue. It shows me where I am provoking others or being provoked into sin — and the wise answer is not to nurse it but to bring it to the God who is slow to anger.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to despond; causatively, to deject
BiblicalUsage: Ka-ah is the sinking of the spirit — to despond, to grow faint, to be cast down. The king of the north is grieved and turns back; the false prophets make the heart of the righteous sad with lies; and the psalmist describes the wicked crouching low to catch the poor and the broken in heart.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God sees the despondent heart and does not despise it. The same Scriptures that name this sinking also show Him lifting the broken — and that is where I look when my own spirit sinks.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to trample; hence, to wash (properly, by stamping with the feet), whether literal (including the fulling process) or figurative
BiblicalUsage: Kabac is washing by trampling — the fuller's work of treading cloth clean, and by extension any thorough washing. Judah's blessing pictures him washing his garments in wine; Moses has the people wash their clothes before Sinai; the law makes the unclean wash after touching a carcass; and David begs God to wash him thoroughly from his iniquity.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this word shows that cleansing is God's work and it goes deep. We cannot rinse ourselves clean with a quick pass — He washes thoroughly, and the washing that matters most is the one He does in the heart.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to be heavy, i.e. in a bad sense (burdensome, severe, dull) or in a good sense (numerous, rich, honorable; causatively, to make weighty (in the same two senses)
BiblicalUsage: Kabad means to be heavy, and from that weight come two opposite pictures: honour and dullness. The command is to honour father and mother; God promises to honour those who honour Him; the proverb tells us to honour the LORD with our substance — and the same word describes a heart grown heavy and dull, unable to hear.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe honour is weight given where it belongs. God is not honoured by light words but by a life that treats Him as weighty — and a heart that will not honour Him grows heavy the other way, deaf to His voice.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to expire or (causatively) to extinguish (fire, light, anger)
BiblicalUsage: Kabah is a fire or a lamp going out — to expire, to be quenched, to be put out. The law says the fire on the altar shall never go out; Isaiah promises that the Servant will not quench the smoking flax; the proverb says where there is no wood the fire goes out; and in the tabernacle the lamp of God went out before Samuel was called.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this word holds both a warning and a comfort. The fire God kindles is not ours to let die — yet the bruised and smouldering, the smoking flax of a weak faith, He will not quench. He tends the flame; our part is to keep coming to Him for oil.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, to plait together, i.e. (figuratively) to augment (especially in number or quantity, to accumulate)
BiblicalUsage: Kabar means to plait together, and so to add to or multiply — Elihu's charge is that Job multiplies words without knowledge, plaiting speech upon speech.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that more words are not more wisdom, and God is not impressed by a long argument that says nothing.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to tread down; hence, negatively, to disregard; positively, to conquer, subjugate, violate
BiblicalUsage: Kabash is treading down — to subdue, to conquer, to bring under foot. God gives it as the first charge to mankind, to subdue the earth; Joshua's generation sees the land subdued before them; and Micah promises that God will subdue our iniquities and cast our sins into the depths of the sea.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe dominion begins with God and ends with God. He gave us the earth to rule under Him, and He Himself subdues the one enemy we cannot — our own sin — and that is why the gospel, not our effort, is the ground of our freedom.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: vast, whether in extent (figuratively, of power, mighty; of time, aged), or in number, many
BiblicalUsage: Kabbiyr is vastness — mighty in power, great in extent, aged in years. Bildad asks how long Job's words will be a strong wind; Elihu says God is mighty and does not despise any; and Isaiah pictures the Lord's strong and mighty one sweeping down like a storm of hail.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this word is a reminder of scale. Our words feel vast to us and our troubles feel vast to us — but God is vaster, and His might is not against us but for us when we come to Him humbly.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Cabon, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Cabon is a town in the lowlands of Judah, named once among the cities given to the tribe. It appears in the long list of Judah's inheritance, a small place kept in the record because every town of the promised land mattered to the God who gave it.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe no place is too small for God's record. Cabon is named once and never again, and that is enough to tell me He sees the small towns and the forgotten names.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: the liver (as the heaviest of the viscera)
BiblicalUsage: Kabed is the liver — the heaviest of the inner organs, and the one the law names again and again in the sacrifices. The fat upon the liver was burned on the altar with the peace offering and the sin offering, and the proverb pictures a young man following temptation like an arrow striking the liver.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the liver matters because God claimed the inward parts for Himself. The sacrifices were not only outward show; the fat and the inward parts went up to Him, and that is how I understand worship — God wants the inside, not only the outside.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

The fat upon the liver was burned on the altar with the peace offering and the sin offering, and the proverb pictures a young man following temptation like an arrow striking the liver.

Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Cabul, the name of two places in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Cabul is two places at once: a town on the border of Asher, and the district of twenty towns Solomon gave to Hiram of Tyre. Hiram looked at them and was not pleased, and he named the land Cabul — and the name stuck, a reminder that even a gift from a king can disappoint when it is not what was hoped for.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Cabul is a small warning about judging God's gifts by first appearances. Hiram saw twenty towns and called them good-for-nothing — and I wonder how often I have done the same with what God has given me.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to estimate
BiblicalUsage: Kacac means to count or reckon — here, to count the household for the Passover lamb, so that each family takes according to what it can eat.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that God counts His people household by household, and no one at His table is an afterthought.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to cut off
BiblicalUsage: Kacach means to cut off. Isaiah pictures the peoples burned as thorns cut down, and the psalm cries over the vine that the boar has wasted and the fire has cut off.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word is a sober one: what God plants He can also cut off, and that is why I want to abide in the vine rather than be cut from it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, to plump, i.e. fill up hollows; by implication, to cover (for clothing or secrecy)
BiblicalUsage: Kacah is covering — to fill up the hollows and hide what lies beneath. The waters returned and covered Pharaoh's chariots; Shem and Japheth walked backward to cover their father's nakedness; and God Himself says to Jerusalem, I spread my skirt over thee and covered thee.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this is the word behind atonement itself: to cover is what God does with sin. He does not pretend it is not there — He covers it, and in Christ the covering is complete.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, to be fat, i.e. (figuratively) silly
BiblicalUsage: Kacal means to be fat, and so to be dull or silly. Jeremiah's charge against the idols is blunt: those who teach vanities are altogether brutish and foolish, fattened on what cannot save.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe folly fattens quietly: feed on idols long enough and the heart grows dull, which is why I keep my appetite on the living God.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to shear
BiblicalUsage: Kacam means to shear — the priests of the new temple were not to shave their heads or let their locks grow long, but to shear them, keeping a plain and ordered appearance before the LORD.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that God cares about how His servants carry themselves, not for show but because order and restraint honour Him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, to become pale, i.e. (by implication) to pine after; also to fear
BiblicalUsage: Kacaph is longing that pales the face — to pine after, to yearn for what is absent. Laban says Jacob stole away because he sore longed after his father's house; Job says God will have a desire to the work of His hands; and the psalmist cries that his soul longeth, yea, even fainteth for the courts of the LORD.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe longing is one of the truest things about us. We pine after home and after God because we were made for both — and the ache itself is a signpost pointing me home to Him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {a Kasdite, or descendant of Kesed; by implication, a Chaldaean (as if so descended); also an astrologer (as if proverbial of that people}
BiblicalUsage: Kacday is a Chaldaean — the people of the land Nebuchadnezzar ruled. Ezra's enemies remind the king that the God of heaven gave Israel into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar the Chaldaean, who destroyed the house and carried the people away.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that empires rise and fall at God's word, and the Chaldaeans who carried Judah away were themselves only instruments in His hand.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to secrete, by act or word; hence (intensively) to destroy
BiblicalUsage: Kachad is hiding — to keep a thing back by act or by word, and sometimes to destroy it by hiding it away. The Egyptians tell Joseph they cannot hide their poverty from him; God promises to cut off the nations before Israel; and David says he has not hid God's righteousness within his heart but has declared it.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe hiding is the first instinct of sin and the last thing faith does. Adam hid, David declared — and I have learned that what I hide grows in the dark, while what I confess to God loses its power.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to paint (with stibium)
BiblicalUsage: Kachal means to paint — here, to paint the eyes, the cosmetic art of a faithless woman decking herself out for her lovers in Ezekiel's parable of Oholah and Oholibah.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that painted beauty cannot cover an unfaithful heart, and God sees through every cosmetic we put on sin.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: literally a failure of flesh, i.e. emaciation; figuratively, hypocrisy
BiblicalUsage: Kachash is the lying of the flesh — leanness and hypocrisy, the body failing and the tongue denying. Hosea says Israel ate the fruit of lies; Job says his leanness bears witness against him; and the psalmist asks God to catch the wicked in the cursing and lying that they speak.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this word ties the body to the tongue: lies make a people lean, and hypocrisy wastes us from the inside. Truth is not only right — it is nourishing, and that is why I want to live on it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to be untrue, in word (to lie, feign, disown) or deed (to disappoint, fail, cringe)
BiblicalUsage: Kachash is to be untrue — to lie, to feign, to deny, to disappoint. Sarah denied that she laughed; the law forbids lying to one another; the proverb prays not to be fed with lies; and Joshua sets up a stone that will witness against Israel if they deny their God.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe lying is never small, because it strikes at the God who is truth itself. Every denial, every feigned word, is a little rehearsal of unbelief — and I would rather be caught telling an uncomfortable truth than a comfortable lie.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Casiphja, a place in Babylon
BiblicalUsage: Casiphia is a place in Babylon where Ezra sent for Levites and temple servants to join the return to Jerusalem. It is named once, at the moment when Ezra would not go up to the house of God without the men appointed to serve there.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Casiphia matters because Ezra would rather wait than go without God's servants. The work of the house needs the people of the house — and that is still true.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Casluchim, a people cognate to the Egyptians
BiblicalUsage: The Casluchim are a people of the table of nations, sons of Mizraim, from whom the Philistines came. They appear only in the genealogies, a branch of Egypt's line whose descendants would become Israel's long enemies.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that even a two-verse people has a place in God's record, because the nations all come from somewhere and His story runs through every one of them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, covered, i.e. (as noun) a covering
BiblicalUsage: Kacuwy is a covering — the cloth spread over the holy things when the camp moved. The Kohathites spread a covering of badgers' skins over the ark, and another over the altar, so that the holy things travelled hidden and untouched.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the coverings teach reverence: God's holy things were not handled casually, and I should not handle holy things casually either.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, a pail; but generally of earthenware; a jar for domestic purposes
BiblicalUsage: Kad is the household jar — the earthen pitcher for water, meal, and oil. Rebekah carries her pitcher to the well; Gideon gives each man a pitcher with a torch hidden inside; the widow of Zarephath has only a handful of meal in a barrel and a little oil in a cruse; and Elijah has the altar drenched with four barrels of water.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God loves to work through jars. The pitcher at the well, the broken pitcher at Midian, the widow's barrel that never ran dry — He fills the ordinary vessels, and that is why I do not wait to be impressive before I offer Him what I have.
RelatedEvents: Elijah and the Widow of Zarephath
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a sparkling gem, probably the ruby
BiblicalUsage: Kadkod is a sparkling gem, probably the ruby — named among the jewels Tyre traded for and among the stones God promises for the walls of the restored Jerusalem.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the same jewel Tyre sold for profit, God sets in the walls of His city, and what the world trades, He builds with.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2532 and G1473; so also the dative case κἀμοί, and accusative case κἀμέ and (or also, even, etc.) I, (to) me:--(and, even, even so, so) I (also, in like wise), both me, me also.
BiblicalUsage: Kago is 'and I' — Paul's way of putting himself beside what he has just said. 'And I, brethren, when I came to you'; 'Be ye followers of me'; 'and last of all he was seen of me also.'
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that this little word shows how Paul preached: not above his hearers but beside them, a fellow witness saying 'and I' before he says anything else.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {properly, like this, i.e. by implication, (of manner) thus (or so); also (of place) here (or hither); or (of time) now}
BiblicalUsage: Kah means 'like this' — 'thus,' 'so,' 'in this manner.' Daniel closes his vision with it: hitherto is the end of the matter, thus far and no further.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that even a word like 'thus' has its place: God's revelations end where He ends them, and I am not meant to add a word beyond.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to be weak, i.e. (figuratively) to despond (causatively, rebuke), or (of light, the eye) to grow dull
BiblicalUsage: Kahah is growing dim — eyes that fail, strength that fades, a spirit that sinks. Isaac's eyes were dim so that he could not see; Moses died with his eye not dim and his natural force unabated; and Isaiah promises that the Servant shall not fail nor be discouraged till He has set judgment in the earth.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this word draws the line between age and despair. Eyes dim with years, but the Servant does not grow dim — and that is why I look to Him when my own strength fades, because His does not.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to officiate as a priest; figuratively, to put on regalia
BiblicalUsage: Kahan is doing the priest's work — to minister, to officiate, to stand before God on behalf of the people. God takes Aaron and his sons to minister unto Him in the priest's office; He sanctifies the tabernacle and the altar and Aaron and his sons to minister; and the chronicler notes the priest who executed the office in Solomon's temple.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the priesthood was never a job men took up for themselves. God called Aaron, God sanctified him, and God set the pattern — and that is why I hold that ministry still begins with God's call, not with our ambition.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {one officiating, a priest; also (by courtesy) an acting priest (although a layman)}
BiblicalUsage: Kahen is the Aramaic word for priest, the word the Persian court and the returned exiles used for the men who served at the altar. Darius orders provision for the priests at Jerusalem; Artaxerxes writes to Ezra the priest; and the king's decree gives Ezra authority over the priests of the house of God.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word shows that God's priests kept their standing even under a foreign king. The empire changed, the language changed, and the priesthood went on — because it was God's appointment, not Persia's.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: apparently, a primary particle, having a copulative and sometimes also a cumulative force; and, also, even, so then, too, etc.; often used in connection (or composition) with other particles or small words:--and, also, both, but, even, for, if, or, so, that, then, therefore, when, yet.
BiblicalUsage: Kai is the little word that holds the New Testament together — 'and,' 'also,' 'even.' It joins clause to clause thousands of times, and sometimes it carries the weight itself: believe also in me; seek first the kingdom and all these things shall be added; how shall He not with Him also freely give us all things.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this smallest of words teaches me that nothing in the gospel stands alone, for faith and obedience, promise and command, Christ and His people are joined by the 'and', and a gospel without its 'ands' would fall apart in my hands.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Chaldee origin; the dell; Caiaphas (i.e. Cajepha), an Israelite:--Caiaphas.
BiblicalUsage: Caiaphas was the high priest who judged Jesus, and his name is tied to the night of the trial. It was he who said it was expedient that one man should die for the people, and it was to his house that Jesus was led bound after Gethsemane.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Caiaphas shows how a true word can be spoken by a false heart. He prophesied that one man would die for the people, and he meant it as politics — but God meant it as the gospel, and the cross turned his sentence into salvation.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2532 and G1065; and at least (or even, indeed):--and, at least.
BiblicalUsage: Kaige is 'and at least' or 'and even' — the compound of 'and' and the little particle 'indeed.' It stands at the head of the promise that God will pour out His Spirit upon His servants and handmaidens, and in Paul's word that men might feel after God, though He be not far from every one of us.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that this small word carries a large mercy: God is not far, His Spirit falls even on servants, and the 'even' is the gospel reaching further than we expect.
RelatedTopics: Presence of God; Outpouring of the Spirit
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H7014); Cain, (i.e. Cajin), the son of Adam:--Cain.
BiblicalUsage: Cain is the first murderer, the son of Adam who killed his brother Abel and then went out from the presence of the LORD. Hebrews remembers Abel's better sacrifice, John says Cain was of that wicked one and slew his brother because his own works were evil, and Jude warns of those who have gone in the way of Cain.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Cain is the first picture of what sin does when it is not mastered: it starts with a rejected offering and ends with a brother's blood. The way of Cain is still open, and the only way out of it is the better sacrifice Abel offered by faith.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H7018); Cainan (i.e. Kenan), the name of two patriarchs:--Cainan.
BiblicalUsage: Cainan is the name of two men in the genealogy of Jesus, one the son of Arphaxad and the other the son of Enos. Luke names them both as he traces the line back from Jesus through the patriarchs to Adam.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the two Cainans show how carefully Luke traced the line of the Saviour: no generation is skipped, and every name in the chain matters because the promise ran through every one of them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain affinity; new (especially in freshness; while G3501 is properly so with respect to age:--new.
BiblicalUsage: Kainos is new in the sense of fresh — not new in time but new in kind. If any man be in Christ, he is a new creature; Jesus gives a new commandment, that we love one another; God promises a new covenant; and Peter says we look for new heavens and a new earth wherein dwelleth righteousness.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this word is the gospel in one syllable. God does not patch the old; He makes new — a new heart, a new covenant, a new creation — and that is my position: what Christ does in a life is not a repair, it is a new beginning.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2537; renewal (figuratively):--newness.
BiblicalUsage: Kainotes is newness itself — the fresh state that belongs to those raised with Christ. We are buried with Him by baptism into death, that like as Christ was raised up from the dead, we also should walk in newness of life; and we serve in newness of spirit, not in the oldness of the letter.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that newness is not a feeling but a walk: the risen life shows itself in how we live, and the Spirit writes the law on the heart where the letter could only condemn.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: apparently a primary verb; to set on fire, i.e. kindle or (by implication) consume:--burn, light.
BiblicalUsage: Kaio is to kindle, to set on fire. Men do not light a candle and put it under a bushel; Jesus tells His disciples to let their loins be girded and their lights burning; the branches that do not abide are cast into the fire and burned; and Hebrews says we have not come to the mount that burned with fire.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe fire in Scripture is both warning and welcome. The lamp is lit to shine, the branch is burned because it bore nothing, and the mountain burned because God is holy — and I want to be the lamp, not the branch.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2532 and G4007; and indeed, i.e. nevertheless or notwithstanding:--and yet, although.
BiblicalUsage: Kaiper is 'and indeed' or 'though' — the word that concedes a point and then presses past it. Though He were a Son, yet learned He obedience by the things which He suffered; Esau found no place of repentance, though he sought it carefully with tears; and Peter will put the saints always in remembrance, though they know the truth already.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that this word teaches me to hold two truths at once: Christ learned obedience though He was the Son, and I must be reminded though I already know.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Latin origin; Cæsar, a title of the Roman emperor:--Cæsar.
BiblicalUsage: Kaisar is Caesar, the title of the Roman emperor, and the name that stood behind every tax, every census, and every appeal in the New Testament. The Pharisees ask whether it is lawful to give tribute unto Caesar; Jesus answers, render unto Caesar the things that are Caesar's and unto God the things that are God's; and Paul, a prisoner, appeals unto Caesar.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Jesus drew the line that every believer still walks: Caesar gets his coin, but God gets the heart. The emperor can stamp his image on money, but the image of God is stamped on us — and that is why my first loyalty is never to an empire.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2541; Cæsaria, the name of two places in Palestine:--Cæsarea.
BiblicalUsage: Caesarea is the seaport city where the gospel crossed its great divide. Cornelius the centurion lived there, and Peter came to his house and saw the Holy Spirit fall on Gentiles; and years later Paul was kept prisoner there before he sailed for Rome.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Caesarea matters because it is where the door opened. The gospel did not stay in Jerusalem; it went to a Roman soldier's house by the sea, and the Spirit fell there just as He had fallen at Pentecost.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2532 and G5104; and yet, i.e. nevertheless:--although.
BiblicalUsage: Kaitoi is 'and yet' — the word that holds a concession and a contradiction together. God left not Himself without witness, and yet He gave rain and fruitful seasons; and the works were finished from the foundation of the world, and yet some did not enter into rest.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that 'and yet' is the shape of faith: God has spoken and God has provided, and yet men still refuse — and the fault is never His.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2543 and G1065; and yet indeed, i.e. although really:--nevertheless, though.
BiblicalUsage: Kaitoige is 'and yet indeed' — a single use, in the note that Jesus Himself baptized not, but His disciples did, though the crowds were coming to Him.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the verse quietly honours the disciples' share in the work: the Lord received the crowds, and His servants did the baptizing.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: just so, referring to the previous or following context
BiblicalUsage: Kakah means 'just so' — in this manner, after this fashion. Thus shall ye eat the Passover, with loins girded and staff in hand; thus shall the LORD do to all your enemies; thus shall it be done unto the man whom the king delighteth to honour.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that 'thus' is a word of pattern: God gives the manner as well as the matter, and doing it His way is part of doing it at all.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2532 and G1563; likewise in that place:--and there, there (thither) also.
BiblicalUsage: Kakei is 'and there' — the word that moves the scene along. If thou bring thy gift to the altar, and there rememberest that thy brother hath ought against thee; into whatsoever city ye shall enter, and there abide till ye go thence; and Jesus walked no more openly among the Jews, but went thence into a country near the wilderness, and there continued with His disciples.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that 'and there' reminds me God meets us in places: at the altar, in the city, in the wilderness near Ephraim — and the place matters because He is there.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2532 and G1565; likewise that (or those):--and him (other, them), even he, him also, them (also), (and) they.
BiblicalUsage: Kakeinos is 'that one also' — the same person or thing, and yet more. The works that I do shall he do also; Father, I will that they also, whom Thou hast given me, be with me where I am; and they also, if they abide not still in unbelief, shall be grafted in.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that this word is the gospel's 'also': the same works, the same presence, the same grafting — what Christ has, His people share, and what Israel lost, the grafted branch can still receive.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2532 and G1564; likewise from that place (or time):--and afterward (from) (thence), thence also.
BiblicalUsage: Kakeithen is 'and from there' — the travelling word of Acts. From there God gave Israel a king; from there Paul and Barnabas sailed back to Antioch; from there they came the next day to Miletus, on the road to Jerusalem.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Luke's 'from there' shows the gospel moving: it never stayed where it started, and neither should I.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2556; badness, i.e. (subjectively) depravity, or (actively) malignity, or (passively) trouble:--evil, malice(-iousness), naughtiness, wickedness.
BiblicalUsage: Kakia is badness itself — depravity in the heart, malice in the hand. Jesus says sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof; Paul says let all bitterness and wrath and clamour and evil speaking be put away from you, with all malice; Peter says lay aside all malice and all guile; and James says receive with meekness the engrafted word.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe malice is not a mood but a weight to be laid aside. Scripture never tells me to manage it or excuse it — it tells me to put it off, and the engrafted word is what takes its place.
