Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a compound of G2556 and G2239; bad character, i.e. (specially) mischievousness:--malignity.
BiblicalUsage: Kakoetheia is bad character at its worst — malignity, the settled habit of thinking the worst of others, named in Paul's list of what fills a mind that has turned from God.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that malignity is what a godless mind grows into when it stops trusting God, and the cure is not better thoughts about people but a renewed mind.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a compound of G2556 and G3056; to revile:--curse, speak evil of.
BiblicalUsage: Kakologeo is to speak evil of — to revile, to curse. The law says he that curseth father or mother, let him die the death, and Jesus throws it back at the Pharisees who set aside the commandment; and the silversmiths at Ephesus spoke evil of the Way before the multitude.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe cursing a parent or reviling the gospel are the same sin wearing different clothes: contempt spoken aloud. The tongue that curses is the heart showing itself, and that is why I watch mine.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2556; to injure; figuratively, to exasperate:--make evil affected, entreat evil, harm, hurt, vex.
BiblicalUsage: Kakoo is to injure, to make evil-affected — to turn minds against the good. Pharaoh dealt subtly with Israel and afflicted their fathers; the unbelieving Jews stirred up the Gentiles and made their minds evil affected against the brethren; and Peter asks, who is he that will harm you, if ye be followers of that which is good.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this word names a real danger: minds can be poisoned against the truth by a word in the ear. The answer is not fear but doing good — no one can truly harm the one who follows what is good.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a compound of G2556 and G3806; hardship:--suffering affliction.
BiblicalUsage: Kakopatheia is hardship itself — suffering affliction, the lot of the prophets. James holds them up as the example: take the prophets, who have spoken in the name of the Lord, for an example of suffering affliction, and of patience.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that affliction is not a sign God has left us; the prophets suffered it and are called blessed, and patience in it is the proof of faith.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from the same as G2552; to undergo hardship:--be afflicted, endure afflictions (hardness), suffer trouble.
BiblicalUsage: Kakopatheo is to undergo hardship — to endure affliction for the gospel's sake. Paul says the word of God is not bound though he suffers trouble as an evildoer, and he charges Timothy to endure afflictions and do the work of an evangelist; and James says, is any among you afflicted, let him pray.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe hardship is part of the calling, not an accident in it. Paul suffered it, Timothy was charged to endure it, and James turns the afflicted to prayer — and that is the pattern I follow when trouble comes.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2555; to be a bad-doer, i.e. (objectively) to injure, or (genitive) to sin:--do(ing) evil.
BiblicalUsage: Kakopoieo is to do evil — to be a bad-doer. Jesus asks in the synagogue whether it is lawful on the Sabbath to do good or to do evil; and Peter says it is better, if the will of God be so, that ye suffer for well doing than for evil doing; and John warns, he that doeth evil hath not seen God.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the choice is put to us every day, and the Sabbath question is the daily question: to do good or to do evil. Suffering for doing good is better than suffering for doing evil — and doing evil is the surest proof a man has not seen God.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2556 and G4160; a bad-doer; (specially), a criminal:--evil-doer, malefactor.
BiblicalUsage: Kakopoios is the evil-doer — the one whose deeds are bad, and in Peter's letters the name the world gives to Christians it wants to accuse. Let your conversation be honest among the Gentiles, that whereas they speak against you as evildoers, they may by your good works glorify God; and let none of you suffer as a murderer, or as a thief, or as an evildoer.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the Christian's answer to a false charge is not a loud defence but a good life. If they call us evildoers, let the works prove them wrong — and let us never give them a true charge to bring.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2556; badly (physically or morally):--amiss, diseased, evil, grievously, miserably, sick, sore.
BiblicalUsage: Kakos is the adverb 'badly' — to be ill, to fare badly, to be in evil case. They that be whole need not a physician, but they that are sick; and Jesus says, if I have spoken evil, bear witness of the evil.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this word puts sickness and sin side by side on purpose: both are a bad state, and both need the same Physician — and that is why Jesus came, for the sick and not for the whole. That is the gospel in one line: the Physician came for the sick, and I am glad He did.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: apparently a primary word; worthless (intrinsically, such; whereas G4190 properly refers to effects), i.e. (subjectively) depraved, or (objectively) injurious:--bad, evil, harm, ill, noisome, wicked.
BiblicalUsage: Kakos is evil in its plainest form — worthless, bad, harmful. Paul says Israel's story was written so we should not lust after evil things; love thinketh no evil; evil communications corrupt good manners; Peter says not to render evil for evil; and the love of money is the root of all evil.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe evil is not a mystery to be solved but a master to be refused. It corrupts, it returns evil for evil, and it roots itself in love of money — and the only answer is the love that thinketh no evil and the life that renders good for evil.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2559; maltreatment:--affliction.
BiblicalUsage: Kakosis is affliction — maltreatment, the oppression of a people. God says to Moses, I have seen the affliction of my people which is in Egypt, and I am come down to deliver them.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that God sees affliction and comes down: the cry of the oppressed is never unheard, and deliverance begins with His seeing.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a presumed compound of G2556 and G2192; to maltreat:--which suffer adversity, torment.
BiblicalUsage: Kakoucheo is to maltreat — to suffer hardship with those who suffer. The heroes of faith were destitute, afflicted, tormented; and the Hebrews are told to remember them that are in bonds, as bound with them, and them which suffer adversity, as being yourselves also in the body.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this word makes suffering a shared thing: I am to remember the afflicted as if I were bound with them, because in the body of Christ their bonds are mine too.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2556 and the base of G2041; a wrong-doer, i.e. criminal:--evil-doer, malefactor.
BiblicalUsage: Kakourgos is the criminal, the wrong-doer — the name given to the two men crucified beside Jesus. Two malefactors were led with Him to be put to death, and one of them railed on Him; and Paul says he suffers trouble as an evildoer, even unto bonds, but the word of God is not bound.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the malefactors are the gospel in miniature: one railed and one repented, and the dying thief who asked to be remembered went to Paradise that day. No one is too far gone to ask, and no one is so far gone that asking is too late.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to restrict, by act (hold back or in) or word (prohibit)
BiblicalUsage: Kala is to hold back — to restrain by act or by word. The rain from heaven was restrained after the flood; Moses had to restrain the people from bringing more for the tabernacle; and David says he has not refrained his lips from declaring God's righteousness, and has refrained his feet from every evil way.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe restraint cuts both ways: God restrains the rain and the offering, and I must restrain my feet from evil while refusing to restrain my lips from His praise. The same hand that holds back the rain opens the mouth of praise, and I want both restraints in my life.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a completion; adverb, completely; also destruction
BiblicalUsage: Kalah is completion — the end, the finishing, and by extension utter destruction. Daniel speaks of the consummation poured out upon the desolate; Isaiah says the Lord will make a consumption, even determined, in the midst of the land; and Jeremiah promises that God will make a full end of the nations but will not make a full end of Israel.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this word holds judgment and mercy in one breath. God finishes what He determines — the desolation is complete, and so is the deliverance — and that is why I trust His endings as much as His beginnings.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a completion; adverb, completely; also destruction
BiblicalUsage: Kalah is completion — the end, the finishing, and by extension utter destruction. Daniel speaks of the consummation poured out upon the desolate; Isaiah says the Lord will make a consumption, even determined, in the midst of the land; and Jeremiah promises that God will make a full end of the nations but will not make a full end of Israel.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this word holds judgment and mercy in one breath. God finishes what He determines — the desolation is complete, and so is the deliverance — and that is why I trust His endings as much as His beginnings.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to complete
BiblicalUsage: Kalal means to complete or perfect — here, the builders of Tyre perfecting her beauty. Her borders were in the midst of the seas, and her builders made her beauty perfect, a ship fitted out like a city.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Tyre's perfected beauty is a warning: men can finish a thing beautifully and still see it sink, because no beauty survives that is built without God.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, to wound; but only figuratively, to taunt or insult
BiblicalUsage: Kalam is the wound of words — to taunt, to insult, to put to shame. David's men tell Nabal's shepherds they were not hurt by them; the servants of Saul say the men were very good unto us and we were not hurt; and Ezra says he is ashamed and blushes to lift up his face to God.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this word shows that shame is a wound too, and words can inflict it. David's men did not hurt Nabal's shepherds, and Ezra felt the hurt of his people's sin — and that is why I want my words to heal rather than wound.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: feminine of G2563; a stalk of grain, i.e. (collectively) stubble:--stubble.
BiblicalUsage: Kalame is stubble — the stalk of grain left after the harvest, the lightest and least of building materials. Paul says if any man build on the foundation with gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, stubble, the fire shall try every man's work of what sort it is.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that stubble is the test of my building: what is light and dry will burn, and only what is precious survives the fire.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain affinity; a reed (the plant or its stem, or that of a similar plant); by implication, a pen:--pen, reed.
BiblicalUsage: Kalamos is a reed — the stalk by the water, the measuring rod, the mock sceptre. Jesus asks what the crowds went out to see, a reed shaken with the wind; He says the bruised reed He will not break; the soldiers put a reed in His right hand and mocked Him; and John is given a reed like unto a rod to measure the temple.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the reed is the whole gospel in one picture: the weakest thing, shaken by the wind, is the thing Christ will not break — and the same reed that mocked Him becomes the rod that measures His temple. A bruised reed is still a reed, and He does not break it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Caleb-Ephrathah, a place in Egypt (if the text is correct)
BiblicalUsage: Caleb-Ephrathah is named once, in the genealogy of Judah: after Hezron was dead in Caleb-Ephrathah, his wife Abiah bore him Ashur the father of Tekoa. The text itself is uncertain — the name may join Caleb and Ephrathah, and the place may be in Egypt, if the text is correct.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the honest uncertainty is part of the record: Scripture does not hide where the text is hard, and I would rather say plainly what I do not know than invent a certainty.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Caleb, the name of three Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Caleb is the spy who believed. He and Joshua alone brought back a good report, and when the people refused, Caleb waited forty years and then asked for the mountain. Moses swore that Caleb would enter the land because he wholly followed the LORD, and Joshua gave him Hebron for an inheritance.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Caleb is the pattern of a faith that outlasts delay. He wholly followed the LORD at forty and at eighty-five, and the mountain he asked for was the one the giants held — and that is the faith I want, that still asks for the hard ground.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: pining
BiblicalUsage: Kaleh is pining — the failing of the eyes with longing. In the curses of the covenant, Moses warns that a father's sons and daughters shall be given to another people, and his eyes shall look and fail with longing for them all the day long.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that this verse is the saddest picture of exile: eyes that look and look and cannot bring back what was taken, and the longing itself becomes the punishment.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: akin to the base of G2753; to "call" (properly, aloud, but used in a variety of applications, directly or otherwise):--bid, call (forth), (whose, whose sur-)name (was (called)).
BiblicalUsage: Kaleo is to call — to summon aloud, to name, to invite. God is faithful, by whom ye were called unto the fellowship of His Son; He has called us out of darkness into His marvellous light; and John marvels that we should be called the sons of God — and that is what we are.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe calling is the beginning of everything. God calls, and the called answer; He names us His sons, and the name is not a title but a fact — and that is why I hold that no one who is called is ever called by accident.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a Calebite or descendant of Caleb
BiblicalUsage: Kalibbow is a Calebite — a descendant of Caleb. Nabal, the churlish rich man of Carmel who refused David bread, was a Calebite, of the house of Caleb.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the word is a quiet irony: the descendant of the man who wholly followed the LORD would not follow Him at all, and a good name does not make a good man.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: complete; as noun, the whole (specifically, a sacrifice entirely consumed); as adverb, fully
BiblicalUsage: Kaliyl is the whole — complete, entire, and as a noun the whole burnt offering, the sacrifice consumed entirely on the altar. Every meat offering for the priest shall be wholly burnt; Moses says Levi shall put whole burnt sacrifice upon God's altar; and Samuel offered a sucking lamb for a burnt offering wholly unto the LORD.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the whole burnt offering is the picture of a whole life given. Nothing was kept back, nothing eaten, nothing sold — it all went up to God, and that is what I hold consecration to mean.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Calcol, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Calcol is an Israelite remembered for wisdom — named with Ethan and Heman and Darda as the men Solomon's wisdom surpassed, and listed among the sons of Zerah in the genealogy of Judah. His name survives because Solomon surpassed him, and that is how the wise are remembered.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Calcol shows that wisdom has a history: Solomon was wiser than the wise men before him, and the wisdom of God in Christ surpasses them all.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a bride (as if perfect); hence, a son's wife
BiblicalUsage: Kallah is the bride — the son's wife, the woman made perfect for her husband. Tamar waits as a widow in her father's house for the son promised to her; Isaiah says the bridegroom decketh himself with ornaments and the bride with her jewels; and God says, as the bridegroom rejoiceth over the bride, so shall thy God rejoice over thee.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the bride is the picture God chose for His love. He does not love us coldly; He rejoices over us as a bridegroom over a bride, and the marriage of the Lamb is the end toward which the whole story runs.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from the base of G2566 and G1636; a cultivated olive tree, i.e. a domesticated or improved one:--good olive tree.
BiblicalUsage: Kallielaios is the cultivated olive tree — the tame, tended tree into which the wild branch is grafted. Paul says if thou wert cut out of the olive tree which is wild by nature, and wert grafted contrary to nature into a good olive tree, how much more shall the natural branches be grafted into their own olive tree.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the good olive tree is Israel's root, and Gentiles are grafted in by grace, not by nature — and the graft stands only by faith.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: neuter of the (irregular) comparative of G2570; (adverbially) better than many:--very well.
BiblicalUsage: Kallion is 'better' — the comparative of good, used here as an adverb. Paul tells Festus he has done the Jews no wrong, as thou very well knowest.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Paul's 'very well' is the quiet confidence of a clear conscience: the truth is known, and it needs no embellishment.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Calneh or Calno, a place in the Assyrian empire
BiblicalUsage: Calneh is a city of the ancient empires — named among the cities of Nimrod's kingdom, and held up by the prophets as a warning to complacent Israel. Go to Calneh and see, says Amos, whether your kingdom is better than theirs; and Isaiah asks whether Calneh is not as Carchemish, and whether its gods saved it.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Calneh is a warning to any nation that trusts its walls: the cities of Nimrod fell, and the cities of Israel fell too, and only the city God builds stands.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2570 and G1320; a teacher of the right:--teacher of good things.
BiblicalUsage: Kalodidaskalos is a teacher of good things — the charge given to the aged women, that they be in behaviour as becometh holiness, not false accusers, not given to much wine, teachers of good things.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that teaching good things is a calling for the older women of the church, and the home is the first classroom where the faith is taught.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: plural of G2570 and G3040; Good Harbors, i.e. Fairhaven, a bay of Crete:--fair havens.
BiblicalUsage: Fair Havens is the bay on the south coast of Crete where Paul's ship put in on the voyage to Rome. The name promised more than the harbour gave: the crew wanted to winter somewhere better, sailed on, and met the storm.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Fair Havens warns me that a fair name is not a safe harbour. The sailors left a good anchorage for a better one and lost the ship — and I have learned to be thankful for the shelter God gives rather than always sailing on.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2570 and G4160; to do well, i.e. live virtuously:--well doing.
BiblicalUsage: Kalopoieo is to do well — to live virtuously, to keep doing good. Paul says to the Thessalonians, be not weary in well doing.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that weariness in well doing is the commonest temptation of all, and the answer is not to stop but to keep going, because the harvest comes in its season.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: adverb from G2570; well (usually morally):--(in a) good (place), honestly, + recover, (full) well.
BiblicalUsage: Kalos is 'well' — rightly, honourably, in a good way. Ye did run well, says Paul, who did hinder you; Peter says ye do well that ye take heed to the word as unto a light that shineth in a dark place; and the elders that rule well are counted worthy of double honour.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe 'well' is the word of a life well run. The race is run well when the word is heeded, the elders rule well, and the brethren are sent forward after a godly sort — and that is the standard I measure my own running by.
RelatedTopics: Good works; Leadership; Word of God
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain affinity; properly, beautiful, but chiefly (figuratively) good (literally or morally), i.e. valuable or virtuous (for appearance or use, and thus distinguished from G18, which is properly intrinsic):--X better, fair, good(-ly), honest, meet, well, worthy.
BiblicalUsage: Kalos is good — beautiful to look on and good in its use, the word the New Testament reaches for when it means what is right and sound. The law is good if a man use it lawfully; to desire the office of a bishop is to desire a good work; and Paul says, prove all things, hold fast that which is good.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe goodness is not a feeling but a test: prove all things, and hold fast what is good. The law is good when it is used lawfully, the work is good when it is done faithfully, and the good is what survives the proving.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2572; a cover, i.e. veil:--vail.
BiblicalUsage: Kalyma is a veil — the cover Moses put over his face when he came down from the mountain, because the children of Israel could not look at the glory. Paul says the same veil lies on the heart whenever Moses is read, but when it shall turn to the Lord, the veil shall be taken away.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the veil is still the difference between reading and seeing, for Moses is read with a veil until the heart turns to the Lord, and when it turns, the veil comes off and we see the glory with open face.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: akin to G2813 and G2928; to cover up (literally or figuratively):--cover, hide.
BiblicalUsage: Kalypto is to cover up — to hide a thing from sight, whether a lamp under a vessel or a multitude of sins under love. Jesus says there is nothing covered that shall not be revealed; no man lights a candle and covers it; and Peter says charity shall cover the multitude of sins.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe covering cuts two ways, and I must know which one I am doing. To cover a lamp is to hide the light, and that is wrong — but to cover a brother's sins with love is to do what Christ did for me, and that is right.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to store away, i.e. (figuratively) in the memory
BiblicalUsage: Kamac means to store away — to lay up in the memory, to keep in reserve. Moses says of God's judgment, is not this laid up in store with me, and sealed up among my treasures?
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that God forgets nothing: vengeance is stored up with Him, sealed among His treasures, and the day of reckoning comes in His time, not mine.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to pine after
BiblicalUsage: Kamahh is to pine after — to long for with the whole body. David cries in the wilderness of Judah, O God, Thou art my God; early will I seek Thee: my soul thirsteth for Thee, my flesh longeth for Thee in a dry and thirsty land, where no water is.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that this is the truest thirst there is: the flesh itself longing for God, and no water but Him will satisfy it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, an ascetic (as if shrunk with self-maceration), i.e. an idolatrous priest (only in plural)
BiblicalUsage: Kamar is the idolatrous priest — the Chemarim, the black-robed priests of Baal whom Josiah put down, whose name the prophets use for the priests of the calf at Bethel and the remnant of Baal God promises to cut off. The name itself became a byword for a priesthood God rejected.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the Chemarim show that false worship always finds its priests. Baal had his, the calf had his, and God cut them off — and that is why I hold that true worship needs no priest but Christ.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, to intertwine or contract, i.e. (by implication) to shrivel (as with heat); figuratively, to be deeply affected with passion (love or pity)
BiblicalUsage: Kamar is the inward burning — bowels yearning, a heart turned within, skin blackened like an oven. Joseph's bowels yearned upon his brother; the true mother's bowels yearned upon her son; God says His heart is turned within Him toward Ephraim; and Jerusalem says her skin was black like an oven because of famine.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this word shows that God's compassion is not cool and distant. His bowels yearn, His heart turns within Him — the same inward fire that marks a mother's love marks His, and that is why I trust Him with my own yearnings.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H1581); a "camel":--camel.
BiblicalUsage: Kamelos is the camel — the beast of the desert, the garment of the Baptist, and the measure of the impossible. John wore raiment of camel's hair; and Jesus says it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter into the kingdom of God.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the camel is there to make the impossible plain: no man can thread himself through the needle's eye, and that is exactly why the rich man — and I — need God to do what is impossible with men. With men it is impossible, but with God all things are possible.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably from G2545; a furnace:--furnace.
BiblicalUsage: Kaminos is the furnace — the place of burning, whether the furnace of fire where the wicked are cast at the end of the age, or the furnace in which the feet of the risen Christ glow like fine brass. The same fire that judges the wicked refines the righteous.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the furnace is the end of two roads: the fire that refines the feet of Christ is the same fire that consumes what is false, and I want to be refined by it, not consumed. Refined, not consumed — that is my prayer.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: 'cummin' (from its use as a condiment)
BiblicalUsage: Kammon is cummin — the small spice seed the farmer sows and threshes gently, not with the cart wheel but with the staff. Isaiah uses it to show that God threshes His people wisely, not crushing the small seed with the heavy wheel.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that God knows how to thresh cummin: He does not crush the small and the weak with the same force as the strong, and His judgments are measured to what we can bear.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a compound of G2596 and the base of G3466; to shut down, i.e. close the eyes:--close.
BiblicalUsage: Kammyo is to shut the eyes — to close them down so they cannot see. Jesus quotes Isaiah: this people's heart is waxed gross, and their ears are dull of hearing, and their eyes they have closed; lest at any time they should see with their eyes, and hear with their ears, and should understand with their heart, and should be converted.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that closed eyes are a choice, not an accident: the people shut their own eyes lest they should see, and that is why I pray God to keep mine open.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: apparently a primary verb; properly, to toil, i.e. (by implication) to tire (figuratively, faint, sicken):--faint, sick, be wearied.
BiblicalUsage: Kamno is to toil, and so to grow weary or to be sick. Hebrews warns us not to be wearied and faint in our minds when we consider Him who endured such contradiction of sinners; and James says the prayer of faith shall save the sick.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that weariness and sickness are both carried to the same place: to Him who endured, and to prayer, which saves the sick.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: apparently a primary verb; to bend:--bow.
BiblicalUsage: Kampto is to bend — to bow the knee. God tells Elijah He has reserved seven thousand men who have not bowed the knee to Baal; the prophet says every knee shall bow to Him; Paul says, for this cause I bow my knees unto the Father; and at the name of Jesus every knee should bow.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe every knee bows somewhere — to Baal, to Caesar, to self — and the only knee that will not be forced is the one bowed willingly now. I bow mine to the Father, because one day every knee will bow to the Son.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2532 and G1437; and (or even) if:--and (also) if (so much as), if but, at the least, though, yet.
BiblicalUsage: Kan is 'and if' — the word that hangs a promise on a condition. If I may touch but His clothes, I shall be whole; though he were dead, yet shall he live; and if it bear fruit, well.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that this little word carries the gospel's 'if': if I touch, if I believe, if it bears fruit — and the promise stands behind every one of them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (compare H7071); Cana, a place in Palestine:--Cana.
BiblicalUsage: Cana is the village of Galilee where Jesus turned water into wine, the first of His signs. The wedding at Cana, the nobleman's son healed from Cana, and the disciple Nathanael of Cana all bind the place to the beginning of His ministry.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Cana shows that Jesus begins in ordinary places: a village wedding, a jar of water, and the glory revealed where no one was looking for it.
RelatedEvents: Jesus Turns Water into Wine at Cana
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, to bend the knee; hence, to humiliate, vanquish
BiblicalUsage: Kana is to bend the knee — to humble oneself, to be brought low, and so to be subdued. God promises that if His people shall humble themselves and pray and seek His face, He will hear from heaven and heal their land; the princes of Judah humbled themselves and the wrath was turned away; and Ahab humbled himself before the LORD and the evil was stayed.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe humbling is the one road to healing. God does not heal the proud land or the proud heart — He heals the one that bows, and that is why I bow mine before I ask Him for anything.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to collect; hence, to enfold
BiblicalUsage: Kanac is to gather — to collect, to enfold, to bring together. The Preacher gathered silver and gold and singers; there is a time to cast away stones and a time to gather stones together; the LORD builds up Jerusalem and gathers together the outcasts of Israel; and Esther says, go, gather together all the Jews that are present in Shushan.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe gathering is God's work as much as scattering is His judgment. He gathers the outcasts, He gathers His people to fast and pray, and one day He will gather them all home.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to address by an additional name; hence, to eulogize
BiblicalUsage: Kanah is to give a name — to address a man by an added name, to surname him, and so to honour or to flatter. Isaiah says one shall call himself by the name of Jacob and another shall subscribe with his hand unto the LORD and surname himself by the name of Israel; and Elihu says he will not give flattering titles unto man.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe names are not flattery: God surnames His people Israel, and that is honour, but Elihu will not flatter a man with titles, because flattery is a lie dressed as honour. A name from God is honour; a title from man is only flattery.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to set out, i.e. plant
BiblicalUsage: Kanan is a word Strong's lists for setting out or planting, but it never actually occurs in the Hebrew text — no verse uses it, and no form of the root stands anywhere in the Scriptures.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that honesty matters more than filling a gap: where the text is silent, I say so, and I will not invent a verse for a word God never used.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Chaldee origin (compare H7067); zealous; Cananites, an epithet:--Canaanite (by mistake for a derivative from G5477).
BiblicalUsage: The Cananites is the name the King James gives to Simon, one of the twelve — Simon the Canaanite, the Zealot. The Greek text behind it reads Cananaean, the Aramaic word for zealous, and the two names are the same man: the apostle whose zeal once burned for Israel and then burned for Christ. The form itself stands only in the Received Text; the older manuscripts read Cananaean.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Simon's nickname is a small picture of conversion: the zeal that once guarded the law was turned to follow the Lord, and Christ takes zealots and makes them apostles.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an edge or extremity; specifically (of a bird or army) a wing, (of a garment or bedclothing) a flap, (of the earth) a quarter, (of a building) a pinnacle
BiblicalUsage: Kanaph is the wing — the edge or extremity of a garment, a bird, or an army. Ruth asks Boaz to spread his skirt over her; the psalm says He shall cover thee with His feathers, and under His wings shalt thou trust; Malachi promises the Sun of righteousness with healing in His wings; and David cuts off the skirt of Saul's robe in the cave.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the wing is where God's protection and man's appeal meet. Ruth asks for the covering, the psalmist trusts under it, and the Sun rises with healing in His wings — and that is where I hide too.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, to project laterally, i.e. probably (reflexive) to withdraw
BiblicalUsage: Kanaph is to withdraw to the side — here, the teachers who will no longer hide in a corner. Though the LORD give you the bread of adversity and the water of affliction, yet shall not thy teachers be removed into a corner any more, but thine eyes shall see thy teachers.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the promise is plain: after affliction, the teachers come out of the corner, and the eyes of the people see them again.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to assemble
BiblicalUsage: Kanash is to assemble — to gather together, here the gathering of the whole empire before Nebuchadnezzar's image. The princes, the governors, the captains, the judges, the treasurers, the counsellors, the sheriffs, and all the rulers of the provinces were gathered together unto the dedication of the image; and after the furnace, the same princes gathered together and saw that the fire had no power upon the bodies of the three.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the two gatherings frame the story: the empire assembles to worship an image, and then assembles again to see that the fire could not touch the faithful. God gathers His witnesses too, and His gathering is the one that lasts.
RelatedEvents: Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego in the Fiery Furnace
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of foreign origin; Candacè, an Egyptian queen:--Candace.
BiblicalUsage: Candace is the title of the queen of Ethiopia, and the name by which Luke calls her — the queen under whom the Ethiopian eunuch served as treasurer. He had come to Jerusalem to worship and was reading Isaiah on the road home when Philip met him.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Candace matters because her servant's conversion opened the gospel to a new continent. The queen never met Philip, but her treasurer carried the gospel home to Ethiopia, and the church there traces its faith to that chariot.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a plant (as set)
BiblicalUsage: Kannah is a plant — something set out and planted. The psalm cries over the vineyard which God's right hand has planted, and the branch that He made strong for Himself, asking Him to visit it and save it.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the planted thing belongs to the Planter: the vineyard is His, the branch is His, and the prayer is that He would visit what His own hand set in the ground.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Canneh, a place in Assyria
BiblicalUsage: Canneh is a place in Assyria, named once among the merchants of Tyre — Haran and Canneh and Eden, the merchants of Sheba, Asshur, and Chilmad, were thy merchants. It is named once and never again, a single line in the lament over Tyre.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Canneh shows how far Tyre's trade reached, and how far its fall reached too: the merchants of Assyria traded with her, and the lament over her names them all.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from κάνη (a straight reed, i.e. rod); a rule ("canon"), i.e. (figuratively) a standard (of faith and practice); by implication, a boundary, i.e. (figuratively) a sphere (of activity):--line, rule.
BiblicalUsage: Kanon is a rule — a straight reed, a measuring rod, and so the measure of a man's work and the rule of his walk. Paul says we will not boast of things without our measure, but according to the measure of the rule which God hath distributed to us; and he blesses all who walk according to this rule, with peace and mercy upon them.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the rule is God's measure, not mine. Paul would not boast beyond the line God drew for him, and I should not measure my work by another man's rule — only by the one God has given me.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from κάπηλος (a huckster); to retail, i.e. (by implication) to adulterate (figuratively):--corrupt.
BiblicalUsage: Kapeleuo is to retail — to huckster, to peddle, to adulterate the goods for profit. Paul says, we are not as many, which corrupt the word of God, but as of sincerity, as of God, in the sight of God speak we in Christ.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the word of God is not a market stall: it is not to be watered down, repackaged, or sold for gain, and sincerity is the only honest way to speak it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (probably H3723 and H5151); Capernaum (i.e. Caphanachum), a place in Palestine:--Capernaum.
BiblicalUsage: Capernaum is the town by the Sea of Galilee that became Jesus' own city. He came and dwelt there after leaving Nazareth, taught in its synagogue, healed the centurion's servant there, and pronounced woe upon it because it was exalted to heaven and would be brought down to hell.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Capernaum is the sobering side of privilege: the town that heard the most and saw the most was judged the hardest, and nearness to the truth is no substitute for receiving it.
RelatedEvents: Jesus Heals a Demoniac in the Capernaum Synagogue
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: the hollow hand or palm (so of the paw of an animal, of the sole, and even of the bowl of a dish or sling, the handle of a bolt, the leaves of a palm-tree); figuratively, power
BiblicalUsage: Kaph is the hollow hand — the palm, the sole of the foot, the paw. Abigail tells David his soul shall be bound in the bundle of life; Solomon spreads forth his hands toward heaven in prayer; Elijah's servant sees a little cloud like a man's hand rising out of the sea; and Jonathan took his life in his hand to deliver Israel.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the hand is the Bible's picture of power and of prayer: the hand that takes its life in its palm, the hands spread toward heaven, the little cloud like a hand that brings the rain — and the hand of God that holds us is stronger than any of them. My hands are weak, but His are not, and I am held by them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, to bend, i.e. (figuratively) to tame or subdue
BiblicalUsage: Kaphah means to bend or subdue — here, to tame anger with a secret gift. A gift in secret pacifieth anger, and a reward in the bosom strong wrath.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that a quiet gift can do what a loud argument cannot: it bends anger without breaking the man.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to fold together; figuratively, to repeat
BiblicalUsage: Kaphal is to fold together — to double, to repeat. The curtains of the tabernacle were coupled together, five and five, and the sixth curtain doubled over at the forefront; the breastplate was foursquare, doubled, a span long and a span broad; and the sword of the king of Babylon is doubled the third time.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the doubling is God's way of making things strong and sure: the curtain doubled, the breastplate doubled, and the judgment doubled — what God repeats, He means. What He doubles, He confirms.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: hunger (as making to stoop with emptiness and pain)
BiblicalUsage: Kaphan is hunger that makes a man stoop — the emptiness that bends the body with pain. Eliphaz says at destruction and famine thou shalt laugh, and Job describes the solitary ones, fleeing into the wilderness, for want and famine, who were solitary.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that famine stoops a man, but it does not have the last word: the God who feeds ravens and clothes lilies is the same God who lifts the hungry.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to bend
BiblicalUsage: Kaphan is to bend — here, the vine bending its roots toward a second eagle. There was also another great eagle with great wings and many feathers, and behold, this vine did bend her roots toward him, seeking water from the furrows where she was planted.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the bending vine is a picture of a faithless people: planted by one eagle, it bent toward another, and God saw the bending and judged it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to curve
BiblicalUsage: Kaphaph is to curve — to bow down, to bend the head or the knee. Isaiah asks whether a fast is to bow down the head as a bulrush; Micah asks whether he shall come before the LORD and bow himself before the high God; and the psalm says the LORD raiseth them that are bowed down.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the bowed head is the posture of the fast and of the prayer, and the God who sees the bowed head is the God who raises it again. He lifts the head that bows to Him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a village (as protected by walls)
BiblicalUsage: Kaphar is a village — a small unwalled settlement, as distinct from the fenced city. The storehouses of the villages held the king's substance, and the lover in the Song says, come, my beloved, let us go forth into the field, let us lodge in the villages.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the villages matter to God as much as the cities: the king's storehouses stood in them, and love itself chose to lodge in them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to cover (specifically with bitumen); figuratively, to expiate or condone, to placate or cancel
BiblicalUsage: Kaphar is to cover — with pitch, with a gift, with blood — and so to expiate, to make atonement. Jacob says, I will appease Esau with the present that goeth before me; the priest lays his hand on the burnt offering and it is accepted to make atonement; the coal touches Isaiah's lips and his sin is purged; and Daniel hears that seventy weeks are determined to make reconciliation for iniquity.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this is the heart of the whole Bible: sin is covered, not by pretending it is not there, but by a gift, a sacrifice, and a Saviour — and the covering God provides is the one that stands. The blood covers what the gift and the sacrifice point to, and the Saviour finishes it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to tread down; figuratively, to humiliate
BiblicalUsage: Kaphash means to tread down — to humiliate, to grind into the dust. Jeremiah says, He hath also broken my teeth with gravel stones, He hath covered me with ashes.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the verse is the bottom of the lament: teeth broken on gravel, a man trodden into ashes — and even there, the prophet goes on to say that His compassions fail not.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a girder
BiblicalUsage: Kaphiyc is a girder — the beam or rafter of a house. Habakkuk says the stone shall cry out of the wall, and the beam out of the timber shall answer it, against the man who builds his house with blood and iniquity.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that even the beams bear witness: a house built on blood cries out against its builder, and no timber is silent before God.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Caphtor (i.e. a wreath-shaped island), the original seat of the Philistines
BiblicalUsage: Caphtor is the original home of the Philistines, the island or coastland from which they came to the shores of Canaan. Amos says the Philistines came from Caphtor as Israel came from Egypt; Deuteronomy says the Caphtorims destroyed the Avims and dwelt in their stead; and Jeremiah says the LORD will spoil the Philistines, the remnant of the country of Caphtor.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Caphtor reminds me that God moves nations as He moved Israel: the Philistines had their own exodus, and the God who brought Israel out of Egypt also brought them out of Caphtor.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a chaplet; but used only in an architectonic sense, i.e. the capital of a column, or a wreath-like button or disk on the candelabrum
BiblicalUsage: Kaphtor is the chaplet — the knob or capital worked into the golden lampstand, a bud and a flower of beaten gold. The lampstand was made with its shaft and branches, its bowls and its knops and its flowers, all of one beaten work; and Amos sees the Lord standing upon the altar, commanding, smite the lintel of the door, that the posts may shake.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the knop on the lampstand and the lintel of the temple both say the same thing: God's house is made beautiful down to the smallest knob, and the same ornament that adorned the lampstand stood above the door where judgment fell. Beauty and judgment stood in the same house, and both were His.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a Caphtorite (collectively) or native of Caphtor
BiblicalUsage: The Caphtorim are the people of Caphtor, named in the table of nations and in the story of the Avims, whom the Caphtorims destroyed and replaced.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the Caphtorim, named only in genealogies and histories, show that God keeps the record of peoples who never knew Him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain affinity; smoke:--smoke.
BiblicalUsage: Kapnos is smoke — the sign of fire, whether the wonders in heaven above and signs in the earth beneath, blood and fire and vapour of smoke, or the smoke of the incense which came up with the prayers of the saints before God, or the smoke of torment ascending for ever and ever. Smoke rises from every fire, and the question is always which fire it comes from.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe smoke goes up from two altars: the incense of the prayers of the saints, and the torment of those who worshipped the beast. The same smoke that carries prayer to God carries judgment away from Him — and I want my prayers on the first altar.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of foreign origin; Cappadocia, a region of Asia Minor:--Cappadocia.
BiblicalUsage: Cappadocia is a region of Asia Minor, named among the dwellers at Pentecost and among the scattered strangers Peter writes to. The men of Cappadocia heard the wonderful works of God in their own tongue, and the exiles of the dispersion in Cappadocia received Peter's letter of hope.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Cappadocia shows the gospel travelling: heard at Pentecost in one tongue, written to exiles in another land, and the same hope reaching both.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a lid (used only of the cover of the sacred Ark)
BiblicalUsage: Kapporeth is the mercy seat — the lid of gold over the ark, where the cherubim spread their wings and God met with Moses. Thou shalt make a mercy seat of pure gold; thou shalt put the mercy seat above upon the ark; and there I will meet with thee, and I will commune with thee from above the mercy seat.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the mercy seat is the most hopeful piece of furniture in the Bible. The law was inside the ark, the blood was sprinkled above it, and God met His people there — mercy above the law, and the meeting place is still open.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a ram (as full-grown and fat), including a battering-ram (as butting); hence, a meadow (as for sheep); also a pad or camel's saddle (as puffed out)
BiblicalUsage: Kar is the ram — full-grown and fat, the pride of the flock and the measure of wealth, and by extension the battering-ram that breaks a wall. Saul spared the best of the sheep and the fatlings; Mesha of Moab rendered a hundred thousand rams to the king of Israel; Amos rebukes those who eat the lambs out of the flock; and Ezekiel is told to set battering rams against the city.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the ram holds both pictures at once: the fat of the flock that men spare for themselves, and the ram that breaks the wall. What we keep back for ourselves becomes the thing that breaks us — and that is why Saul's sparing was his undoing.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to bend the knee; by implication, to sink, to prostrate
BiblicalUsage: Kara is to bend the knee — to sink down, to prostrate oneself, whether in prayer or in worship or in fear. Solomon arose from before the altar, from kneeling on his knees with his hands spread up to heaven; God tells Elijah He has reserved seven thousand who have not bowed the knee to Baal; and Isaiah hears the LORD swear that unto Him every knee shall bow.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the knee is the body's confession. Solomon knelt to pray, the seven thousand refused to kneel to Baal, and one day every knee will bow to the Lord — and I have decided to bow mine now, willingly.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: the leg (from the knee to the ankle) of men or locusts (only in the dual)
BiblicalUsage: Kara is the leg — from the knee to the ankle, of men and of locusts, named in the law of the sacrifices. The Passover lamb was not to be eaten raw or sodden, but roast with fire, his head with his legs; and the legs of the burnt offering were washed with water and burned on the altar.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the leg matters because the sacrifice was whole: head and legs and inwards, washed and burned together, and nothing left unexamined — and that is how I understand consecration, the whole of me offered, not a part. He asks for the whole of me, and I will not offer Him a part.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to grieve
BiblicalUsage: Kara means to grieve — here, the grief that seizes the spirit. Daniel says, I Daniel was grieved in my spirit in the midst of my body, and the visions of my head troubled me.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that visions can grieve as well as gladden: Daniel was troubled by what he saw, and the grief itself was part of hearing God.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to purchase
BiblicalUsage: Karah is to purchase — to buy food and drink in the wilderness, to provide for an enemy and send him home, to buy a wife back with silver and barley. Moses tells Israel to buy meat and water from the Edomites for money; Elisha makes a great provision for the Syrian raiders and sends them to their master; and Hosea buys back his wife for fifteen pieces of silver.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this word runs straight to the cross: Hosea bought back a faithless wife, and God bought back a faithless people — and the price was not silver and barley but the blood of His Son. Fifteen pieces of silver bought a wife; the blood of Christ bought a people.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to purchase
BiblicalUsage: Karah is to purchase — to buy food and drink in the wilderness, to provide for an enemy and send him home, to buy a wife back with silver and barley. Moses tells Israel to buy meat and water from the Edomites for money; Elisha makes a great provision for the Syrian raiders and sends them to their master; and Hosea buys back his wife for fifteen pieces of silver.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this word runs straight to the cross: Hosea bought back a faithless wife, and God bought back a faithless people — and the price was not silver and barley but the blood of His Son. Fifteen pieces of silver bought a wife; the blood of Christ bought a people.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to purchase
BiblicalUsage: Karah is to purchase — to buy food and drink in the wilderness, to provide for an enemy and send him home, to buy a wife back with silver and barley. Moses tells Israel to buy meat and water from the Edomites for money; Elisha makes a great provision for the Syrian raiders and sends them to their master; and Hosea buys back his wife for fifteen pieces of silver.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this word runs straight to the cross: Hosea bought back a faithless wife, and God bought back a faithless people — and the price was not silver and barley but the blood of His Son. Fifteen pieces of silver bought a wife; the blood of Christ bought a people.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to dance (i.e. whirl)
BiblicalUsage: Karar is to dance — to whirl, to spin round. David danced before the LORD with all his might, wearing a linen ephod, while Michal watched from a window and despised him in her heart.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that David's dancing is worship without self-consciousness: he whirled before the ark and did not care who watched, and the one who despised him was the one left barren.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to cut (off, down or asunder); by implication, to destroy or consume; specifically, to covenant (i.e. make an alliance or bargain, originally by cutting flesh and passing between the pieces)
BiblicalUsage: Karath is to cut — to cut off, to cut down, and so to cut a covenant. God cut a covenant with Abram when the smoking furnace and burning lamp passed between the pieces; Moses sprinkled the blood and said, behold the blood of the covenant; and the psalm says, I have made a covenant with my chosen, I have sworn unto David my servant.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the cutting is the point: a covenant is not a handshake but a sacrifice, sealed with blood and bound by an oath. God cut His covenant with Abram and with David, and in Christ He cut the new covenant in His own blood — and that is why it cannot be broken.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to gird or clothe
BiblicalUsage: Karbel means to gird or clothe — here, the robe David wore when the ark came up to Jerusalem, clothed with a robe of fine linen, and all the Levites that bare the ark, and the singers, and David with them.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the robe matters: the king who danced before the ark was clothed in linen like a priest, and worship dresses itself for the Lord.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a mantle
BiblicalUsage: Karbela is a mantle — the outer garment, named among the clothes the three friends wore into the furnace: bound in their coats, their hosen, and their hats, and their other garments, and cast into the midst of the burning fiery furnace.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the mantle is part of the miracle: they went in fully clothed, and came out with not even the smell of fire on their garments.
RelatedEvents: Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego in the Fiery Furnace
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: prolonged from a primary κάρ (Latin cor, "heart"); the heart, i.e. (figuratively) the thoughts or feelings (mind); also (by analogy) the middle:--(+ broken-)heart(-ed).
BiblicalUsage: Kardia is the heart — not only the muscle but the seat of thought, will, and love. The end of the commandment is charity out of a pure heart; sanctify the Lord God in your hearts; if our heart condemn us, God is greater than our heart; and eye hath not seen, nor ear heard, neither have entered into the heart of man, the things which God hath prepared for them that love Him.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the heart is where everything is decided. God looks on the heart, the heart condemns or acquits, and the things He has prepared are beyond what the heart can even imagine — and that is why I ask Him to make mine pure and keep it His.
RelatedTopics: Human Nature; Purity; Love of God
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2588 and G1097; a heart-knower:--which knowest the hearts.
BiblicalUsage: Kardiognostes is the heart-knower — God, who knows the hearts of all men. The apostles prayed, Thou, Lord, which knowest the hearts of all men, shew whether of these two Thou hast chosen; and Peter says God, which knoweth the hearts, bare them witness, giving them the Holy Ghost, even as He did unto us.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that this name is my comfort and my warning: God knows my heart better than I do, and no prayer needs to explain me to Him — but no hiding works either.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a life-guardsman
BiblicalUsage: Kariy is the life-guardsman — the Carites, the king's bodyguard, the men Jehoiada called to guard the child Joash in the temple, and who brought the young king out and set him on the throne of Judah. They kept the king safe while the usurper ruled, and they set him on the throne when the time came.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the Carites show that God guards His anointed: while Athaliah ruled the land, the guard kept the child king safe in the temple, and the throne was kept for the line of David. The throne was kept, and the king was kept, and both were God's doing.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Karkas, a eunuch of Xerxes
BiblicalUsage: Karkas is a eunuch of Xerxes, one of the seven chamberlains who served in the king's presence. When the heart of the king was merry with wine, he commanded his chamberlains to bring Queen Vashti before him — and the refusal that followed set the whole story of Esther in motion.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Karkas shows how small a hinge a great story can turn on: a chamberlain's errand, a queen's refusal, and the way opened for Esther to save her people.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a dromedary (from its rapid motion as if dancing)
BiblicalUsage: Karkarah is a dromedary — the swift camel, named among the beasts that will bring the exiles home. They shall bring all your brethren for an offering unto the LORD out of all nations, upon horses, and in chariots, and in litters, and upon mules, and upon swift beasts, to My holy mountain Jerusalem.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the swift beast is the picture of the gathering: the exiles come home by every road and every mount, and God provides the swiftest beast for the longest journey.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Karkemish, a place in Syria
BiblicalUsage: Karkemish is a city on the Euphrates, the place where empires met and broke. Necho of Egypt went up to fight against Carchemish, and Josiah went out against him and fell; Isaiah asks whether Calno is as Carchemish; and Jeremiah prophesies against the army of Pharaoh at Carchemish, which Nebuchadnezzar smote.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Carchemish is where the pride of empires was judged: Egypt met Babylon there and lost, and Josiah died there for meddling in a war that was not his — and God was sovereign over them all.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a rim or top margin
BiblicalUsage: Karkob is the rim or top margin — the network of brass set like a compass upon the altar of burnt offering, halfway up, to hold the fire and carry the rings.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that even the rim of the altar was made to God's pattern: nothing in His worship was left to guesswork, and the smallest margin had its place.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: the crocus
BiblicalUsage: Karkom is the crocus — saffron, named among the spices of the garden: spikenard and saffron, calamus and cinnamon, with all trees of frankincense, myrrh and aloes, with all the chief spices.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the garden's spices are the language of love: the bride's garden is fragrant with the best of things, and love itself is the chief spice.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Karmel, the name of a hill and of a town in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Karmel is the hill and the town — the green mountain by the sea where Elijah faced the prophets of Baal, and the town in Judah where Nabal kept his flocks. Ahab gathered all Israel and the prophets to Mount Carmel; Elijah bowed himself to the earth and put his face between his knees; and Nabal of Carmel refused David bread and paid for it with his life.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Carmel holds two stories at once: the mountain where fire fell and the town where a churl refused bread — and God answered the first with fire and the second with judgment, because He is Lord of both.
RelatedEvents: Elijah on Mount Carmel; David and Abigail
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a planted field (garden, orchard, vineyard or park); by implication, garden produce
BiblicalUsage: Karmel is a planted field — a garden, an orchard, a fruitful vineyard, and by extension the fruitful land itself. Isaiah says Lebanon shall be turned into a fruitful field, and the fruitful field shall be esteemed as a forest; Jeremiah says God brought Israel into a plentiful country to eat the fruit thereof; and the law forbids eating the new grain until the offering is brought.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the fruitful field is the picture of what God does with a wilderness: He plants it, He waters it, and the desert becomes a garden — and that is what He does with a barren heart too. The wilderness I bring Him is the garden He makes.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a Karmelite or inhabitant of Karmel (the town)
BiblicalUsage: Karmeliy is a Carmelite — a man of Carmel the town. Nabal was a Carmelite, and his wife Abigail became David's wife; and David's son Chileab was born to Abigail the Carmelitess.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the Carmelite's story is Abigail's story: a wise woman of Carmel who saved her household by her words, and a churlish husband who would not listen — and wisdom, not wealth, is what God honours.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a Karmelitess or female inhabitant of Karmel
BiblicalUsage: Karmeliyth is a Carmelitess — a woman of Carmel the town. Abigail the Carmelitess lived with David at Gath, and her son Chileab is listed among the sons born to David in Hebron.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Abigail's title is her honour: the woman of Carmel who spoke wisely and saved her house is remembered by her town and by her son.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a Karmite or descendant of Karmi
BiblicalUsage: Karmiy is a Karmite — a descendant of Karmi, of the sons of Reuben. The census of the second generation names the family of the Carmites, one of the families counted in the wilderness before the entry into the land.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the census kept every family: the Karmites are named once, and the God who counts His people counts them all.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a Karmite or descendant of Karmi
BiblicalUsage: Karmiy is a Karmite — a descendant of Karmi, of the sons of Reuben. The census of the second generation names the family of the Carmites, one of the families counted in the wilderness before the entry into the land.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the census kept every family: the Karmites are named once, and the God who counts His people counts them all.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: carmine, a deep red
BiblicalUsage: Karmiyl is carmine — a deep red, the crimson of the temple. Solomon asks Hiram for a man cunning to work in gold and silver and brass, in purple and crimson and blue; and the veil of the temple was made of blue and purple and crimson and fine linen, with cherubim wrought upon it.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the crimson in the veil is no accident: the colour of blood hangs between the holy and the most holy, and the way in is through the blood — and that is why the veil tore when the blood was shed. The way in was always through the blood, and the torn veil proves it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a herald
BiblicalUsage: Karowz is a herald — the crier who proclaims the king's command aloud. Then an herald cried aloud: to you it is commanded, O people, nations, and languages, that at what time ye hear the sound of the cornet, flute, harp, sackbut, psaltery, dulcimer, and all kinds of musick, ye fall down and worship the golden image.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the herald's cry is the test of the hour: bow to the image or burn in the furnace — and the three friends chose the furnace, because they served a greater King.
RelatedEvents: Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego in the Fiery Furnace
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: byssus or fine vegetable wool
BiblicalUsage: Karpac is byssus — fine white linen, the hangings of the king's court. White, green, and blue hangings, fastened with cords of fine linen and purple to silver rings and pillars of marble, dressed the court where Ahasuerus feasted his princes.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the fine linen is the show of the empire: white hangings and silver rings, and behind them a king who could not rule his own household — and God used that household to save His people.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from κάρφω (to wither); a dry twig or straw:--mote.
BiblicalUsage: Karphos is the mote — the dry twig, the speck of straw in a brother's eye. Why beholdest thou the mote that is in thy brother's eye, but considerest not the beam that is in thine own eye? Thou hypocrite, first cast out the beam out of thine own eye, and then shalt thou see clearly to cast out the mote out of thy brother's eye.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the mote is the test of my sight: if I can see the speck in my brother's eye but not the beam in my own, I am blind — and the first surgery is always on myself. Clear sight begins at home.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2593; to be fertile (literally or figuratively):--be (bear, bring forth) fruit(-ful).
BiblicalUsage: Karpophoreo is to bear fruit — to be fertile, in the field and in the life. The seed sown in good ground brings forth fruit, some an hundredfold, some sixty, some thirty; and the gospel, Paul says, bringeth forth fruit in all the world, as it doth also in you.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe fruit is the proof of the seed: the good ground bears it, the gospel bears it in all the world, and a life that bears none has not yet received the seed. The seed proves itself by the fruit, and the fruit proves the ground.
RelatedTopics: Fruit of the Spirit; Growth; Evangelism
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2590 and G5342; fruitbearing (figuratively):--fruitful.
BiblicalUsage: Karpophoros is fruit-bearing — fruitful, the word Paul uses for the seasons themselves. God left not Himself without witness, in that He did good, and gave us rain from heaven, and fruitful seasons, filling our hearts with food and gladness.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that fruitful seasons are God's witness to the nations: rain from heaven and food and gladness, given even to those who never thanked Him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: perhaps for G2590; Carpus, probably a Christian:--Carpus.
BiblicalUsage: Carpus is a Christian of Troas, named once, in Paul's last letter: the cloak that I left at Troas with Carpus, when thou comest, bring with thee, and the books, but especially the parchments. He kept the cloak and the books for a prisoner he may never have met again.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Carpus shows that the gospel runs on small kindnesses: a cloak left in a friend's keeping, books and parchments carried on a journey, and a prisoner who still wanted to read.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably from the base of G726; fruit (as plucked), literally or figuratively:--fruit.
BiblicalUsage: Karpos is fruit — what is plucked from the tree, whether the fruit of the vine or the fruit of the Spirit. I am the vine, ye are the branches: he that abideth in Me, and I in him, the same bringeth forth much fruit; herein is My Father glorified, that ye bear much fruit; and the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe fruit is the whole test of the Christian life: not the leaves, not the talk, but the fruit — and the fruit grows only by abiding in the Vine, because a branch cut off can do nothing. I would rather bear a little fruit abiding than make a great show cut off.
RelatedTopics: Fruit of the Spirit; Vine and Branches; Growth
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Karshena, a courtier of Xerxes
BiblicalUsage: Karshena is a courtier of Xerxes, one of the seven princes of Persia and Media who saw the king's face and sat first in the kingdom. When the king asked what should be done to Vashti, Karshena was among those who answered.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Karshena shows how God uses even a king's council: the princes gave their counsel, the queen was set aside, and the way opened for Esther — and none of them knew what they were doing.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a derivative of G2904 (transposed); to be strong, i.e. (figuratively) steadfast (patient):--endure.
BiblicalUsage: Moses left Egypt behind and kept going because he was looking at the One no eye can see, and that steady looking carried him through fear of the king.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe endurance is not gritting my teeth but keeping my eyes on the God I cannot see.
RelatedEvents: The Exodus and the Red Sea
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: something cut, i.e. a hewn timber
BiblicalUsage: These were the hewn beams set into the courts and the house Solomon built, cut timber laid in careful rows as part of the temple work.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that even the beams mattered because the house was built for the Lord, and no part of work done for Him is wasted.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to grow fat (i.e. be covered with flesh)
BiblicalUsage: Jeshurun grew fat and kicked, full and comfortable and then turning away from the God who made him.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe plenty is a test of its own, because a full belly can forget the hand that filled it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a Chaldaean or inhabitant of Chaldaea; by implication, a Magian or professional astrologer
