BiblicalUsage: The Chaldeans were the wise men of Babylon, the ones the kings called on to read dreams and signs, and they stood before Nebuchadnezzar and Belshazzar with all their learning and could not answer what only God could reveal. Daniel stood among them yet apart from them, and the king himself said the spirit of the holy gods was in him. Their wisdom was real as far as it went, but it stopped where God's wisdom begins.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this is the difference between man's wisdom and God's: the Chaldeans could describe the dream only if the king told it first, while God both knows and reveals. I hold that no amount of learning replaces a God who speaks, and that is why Daniel's God, not Babylon's wise men, gets the last word.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a Kasdite, or descendant of Kesed; by implication, a Chaldaean (as if so descended); also an astrologer (as if proverbial of that people
BiblicalUsage: The Chaldeans were the people of the land where Abram's family lived, and centuries later they were the army that broke into Jerusalem and carried Judah away. Their name runs through the story from Ur to Babylon, and Daniel was carried off to live and serve among them. The fuller story of that people and their kings belongs with the people they touched.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the Chaldeans show how God works through the rise and fall of whole peoples, and I hold that their place in the story is best read beside the kings and prophets who lived under their power.
RelatedEvents: Fall of Jerusalem and the Exile
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to totter or waver (through weakness of the legs, especially the ankle); by implication, to falter, stumble, faint or fall
BiblicalUsage: To stumble is what weak legs do, and Scripture uses it for the righteous man who falls seven times and gets up again, for young men who faint and grow weary, and for the proud who trip over their own sin. The word covers a tottering step and a full collapse, and it falls on the wicked and the weary alike. Yet the same word carries the promise that the just shall walk in the ways of the Lord, and the transgressors shall fall in them.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe stumbling is not the end of the story for God's people, because the same God who watches the fall also steadies the step. I hold that the difference is never whether we stumble but whether we get up and walk on, and that is grace, not strength of our own.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, to whisper a spell, i.e. to inchant or practise magic
BiblicalUsage: This is the word for whispering spells and practising sorcery, the craft God flatly forbade His people and said must not live among them. Pharaoh's magicians used it, Manasseh used it in the valley of Hinnom, and God names sorcerers among those He will judge. It is never treated as a curiosity or a harmless skill, but as a rival trust set against the Lord.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God bans sorcery because it seeks power apart from Him, and I hold that any path to hidden knowledge that goes around the Lord is a snare, not a shortcut. My position is plain: the God who speaks is enough, and I will not trade His voice for a whisper.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: by implication, to be acceptable; also to succeed or prosper
BiblicalUsage: The word means to succeed, to please, to be right and proper, and it shows up where a dull axe needs sharpening, where a man sows his seed morning and evening not knowing which will prosper, and where Esther asks the king if it pleases him to undo Haman's letters. It ties success to doing the fitting thing at the fitting time rather than to luck.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe success in Scripture is not grabbing what I want but doing what is right and leaving the outcome with God. I hold that Esther's question is the model: if it pleases the king, and if I have found favour, then let the good be done.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a magician
BiblicalUsage: Jeremiah warned the people not to listen to their sorcerers, the ones who promised peace and told the kings what they wanted to hear.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a prophet who tells me what I want to hear is the most dangerous voice in the room.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, a feller, i.e. an axe
BiblicalUsage: The psalm remembers the enemy breaking down the carved work of the sanctuary with axes, smashing what was made beautiful for God's house.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that what men build for God can be broken by men, but the God it was built for is never broken.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a primary particle; (prepositionally) down (in place or time), in varied relations (according to the case (genitive, dative or accusative) with which it is joined):--about, according as (to), after, against, (when they were) X alone, among, and, X apart, (even, like) as (concerning, pertaining to touching), X aside, at, before, beyond, by, to the charge of, (charita-)bly, concerning, + covered, (dai-)ly, down, every, (+ far more) exceeding, X more excellent, for, from … to, godly, in(-asmuch, divers, every, -to, respect of), … by, after the manner of, + by any means, beyond (out of) measure, X mightily, more, X natural, of (up-)on (X part), out (of every), over against, (+ your) X own, + particularly, so, through(-oughout, -oughout every), thus, (un-)to(-gether, -ward), X uttermost, where(-by), with. In composition it retains many of these applications, and frequently denotes opposition, distribution, or intensity.
BiblicalUsage: This little word does heavy work, and almost every time it appears it is setting the measure of something: according to God's purpose, according to the counsel of His will, according to the Scriptures, and even greeting friends by name, each one on his own account. It tells me whose standard counts and whose story I am living inside. Read it slowly and the sentence changes, because who sets the measure decides what the words mean.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this word is the hinge of the gospel, because everything hangs on whether things happen according to God or according to me. I hold that Romans 8:28 is only good news if the purpose is His, and the counsel is His, and the Scriptures are His, and my part is to trust the measure He has set.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and the base of G939; to descend (literally or figuratively):--come (get, go, step) down, fall (down).
BiblicalUsage: To come down is what the Son of Man did from heaven, what the Spirit did like a dove at the Jordan, and what Philip did into the water with the Ethiopian. The word carries the whole movement of God toward us and of His people toward one another, down from the heights to where the need is. No one ascends into heaven but He who first descended, and that descent is the shape of the gospel.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the gospel moves downward before it moves upward, because God came down to us before He asks us to rise to Him. I hold that every baptism and every act of coming alongside someone is a small copy of that first great descent.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and G906; to throw down:--cast down, lay.
BiblicalUsage: Paul says we are cast down but not destroyed, and Hebrews urges us to leave the first principles behind and go on, laying down the foundation once and for all.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe being thrown down is not the same as being finished, because God picks up what men cast down.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and G916; to impose upon:--burden.
BiblicalUsage: Paul tells the Corinthians he would not burden them, refusing to use his place among them to weigh them down.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that a true servant never makes himself a burden on the people he was sent to serve.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2597; a declivity:--descent.
BiblicalUsage: The crowd came down the descent of the Mount of Olives, praising God with a loud voice for the mighty works they had seen.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe praise is the right answer when you have just watched God do what only God can do.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and a derivative of the base of G939; to cause to go down, i.e. precipitate:--bring (thrust) down.
BiblicalUsage: Capernaum, lifted up to heaven in its privilege, would be thrust down to hell for refusing the light it had been given.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe privilege without repentance only raises the fall.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2598; a deposition, i.e. founding; figuratively, conception:--conceive, foundation.
BiblicalUsage: The foundation of the world is where the Bible starts the story before the story starts, chosen in Him before it was laid, hidden in parables since it was laid, and written in the Lamb's book since it was laid. It is the fixed point behind everything, the moment when God had already decided what He would do. Whatever I face now was already inside His plan before the first day ever dawned.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe my salvation does not start with me, because God chose before the foundation of the world and the Lamb was slain before it too. I hold that this is the deepest comfort there is: nothing about my life caught God by surprise, and nothing can undo what He settled before the beginning.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and G1018 (in its original sense); to award the price against, i.e. (figuratively) to defraud (of salvation):--beguile of reward.
BiblicalUsage: Paul warns against anyone who would beguile you of your reward, judging you by visions and humility he does not have.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a teacher who adds rules to Christ is not protecting me, he is robbing me.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and cheo (to pour); to pour down (out):--pour.
BiblicalUsage: A woman poured the ointment down over Jesus, breaking the box and anointing His head while He sat at meat.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe her pouring was worship, and the waste the others saw was the point.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and G5530; to overuse, i.e. misuse:--abuse.
BiblicalUsage: Paul says to use the world without abusing it, and he himself refused to use his right to be paid for the gospel so nothing would hinder it.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the gospel is not a thing to be used up for my own advantage.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and χθών (the ground); subterranean, i.e. infernal (belonging to the world of departed spirits):--under the earth.
BiblicalUsage: At the name of Jesus every knee shall bow, of things in heaven and things in earth and things under the earth.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the day is coming when even the dead below will bend the knee they refused above.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 intensive and G1212; manifest:--far more evident.
BiblicalUsage: It is far more evident that another priest arises after the likeness of Melchisedec, not after Aaron.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the new priesthood is not a small repair but a far clearer proof that Christ is the priest we need.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and G1210; to tie down, i.e. bandage (a wound):--bind up.
BiblicalUsage: The Samaritan bound up the wounded man's wounds, pouring in oil and wine before he set him on his own beast.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe mercy does not walk past, it stops and binds up.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and a derivative of G1349; to adjudge against, i.e. pronounce guilty:--condemn.
BiblicalUsage: To condemn is to pass the sentence, and Jesus puts the power of it in our own mouths: by your words you shall be justified, and by your words you shall be condemned. He also takes it out of our hands, telling us not to condemn if we do not want to be condemned, and reminding us that the guiltless were condemned by men who knew the law and missed mercy. The word is a warning in every direction it points.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe my words will be weighed one day, and that is why I want to speak mercy now. I hold that the judge who condemned no one wrongly is the only safe judge, and I am glad the sentence is His to pass, not mine.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and G1377; to hunt down, i.e. search for:--follow after.
BiblicalUsage: Simon and those with him followed after Jesus, hunting Him down in the early morning to tell Him everyone was looking for Him.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the disciples had the right instinct, even when they had the wrong idea of what He should do next.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and G1402; to enslave utterly:--bring into bondage.
BiblicalUsage: Paul names the men who bring the church into bondage, false brethren who slip in to spy out our liberty and enslave the free.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe freedom in Christ is worth guarding, because bondage always comes back dressed as religion.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and a derivative of G1413; to exercise dominion against, i.e. oppress:--oppress.
BiblicalUsage: God anointed Jesus to heal all who were oppressed of the devil, while James asks the rich who oppress the poor and drag them before the judgment seats.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe oppression is the devil's work, and healing is God's answer to it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to laugh down, i.e. deride:--laugh to scorn.
BiblicalUsage: They laughed Jesus to scorn when He said the damsel was not dead but sleeping, and the same laughter met Him in every house where grief had already decided how the story ended. The mourners knew death when they saw it, and they were sure He was wrong. Then He took her by the hand, and the laughter stopped.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the world's scorn is often just grief that has given up, and Jesus walks into that room anyway. I hold that the One they laughed at is the One who gets the last word over death, and the scoffers always go quiet when He speaks.
RelatedEvents: Jairus' Daughter and the Bleeding Woman
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and G1097; to note against, i.e. find fault with:--blame, condemn.
BiblicalUsage: To find fault is to note the charge and hold it up, and Paul did it to Peter at Antioch because Peter stood blamed for pulling back from the Gentiles. John turns the same word inward: if our heart condemns us, God is greater than our heart, and if our heart condemns us not, then we have confidence toward God. The word works both ways, against others and against ourselves.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a condemning heart is not the final judge, because God is greater than my heart and knows all things. I hold that honest blame can be a gift when it turns us back, but my confidence rests on Him, not on whether my heart feels clear.
RelatedPeople: Paul; Simon Peter; John the Apostle
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and the base of G4486; to rend in pieces, i.e. crack apart:--break.
BiblicalUsage: The soldiers broke the legs of the two thieves to hasten their death, but when they came to Jesus they found Him dead already and did not break His. Matthew had already said He would not break the bruised reed, and the same verb holds both pictures: legs broken in cruelty, and a bruised reed left unbroken in mercy. The law said no bone of the Passover lamb should be broken, and He kept it to the letter.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Jesus was not broken by men because He was already the Lamb, given, not taken. I hold that the bruised reed is safe with Him, and the same hands that refused to break Him will not break me either.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and G71; to lead down; specially, to moor a vessel:--bring (down, forth), (bring to) land, touch.
BiblicalUsage: To bring down a ship is to make land, and Luke uses the word for Paul's voyage to Rome, for the landing at Syracuse, and for the fishermen who brought their ships to land and left everything to follow Jesus. Paul borrows it too, asking who shall descend into the deep to bring Christ up again. The word moves from harbours to heaven and back.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe following Jesus always costs a landing, because the fishermen had to bring the boats in before they could walk away. I hold that Christ has already made the only descent that matters, and I do not need to fetch Him down again.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and G75; to struggle against, i.e. (by implication) to overcome:--subdue.
BiblicalUsage: By faith they subdued kingdoms, wrought righteousness, and obtained promises.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe faith does not sit still, it subdues what stands against God's promises.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and G153; to shame down, i.e. disgrace or (by implication) put to the blush:--confound, dishonour, (be a-, make a-)shame(-d).
BiblicalUsage: Hope does not make ashamed, and whoever believes on Him shall not be ashamed, and yet the word also falls the other way: the rulers were ashamed when Jesus healed the bent woman on the Sabbath, and the Corinthians were told they would not be put to shame. Shame is the weapon of the world against God's people, and God turns it back on those who wield it.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe hope is the answer to shame, because the God who raised Jesus will not let those who trust Him be put to confusion. I hold that the shame I fear most is already answered at the cross, and I will not live under a sentence God has overturned.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and G2545; to burn down (to the ground), i.e. consume wholly:--burn (up, utterly).
BiblicalUsage: To burn up is to consume wholly, and John the Baptist says the chaff will be burned with unquenchable fire while the wheat is gathered in. Paul says a man's work may be burned and he himself saved, yet so as by fire, and Babylon is burned in a single day. The fire tests everything, and what is not built on Christ does not survive it.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God's fire is both judgment and mercy, because it burns away what cannot last and leaves what is real. I hold that I want my work to survive that fire, and the only way is to build it on Christ.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and G2572; to cover wholly, i.e. veil:--cover, hide.
BiblicalUsage: Paul says a woman who will not cover her head should be shorn, and a man should not cover his, since he is the image and glory of God.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the covering was about honour in worship, and the honour still matters even when the customs change.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and G2744; to exult against (i.e. over):--boast (against), glory, rejoice against.
BiblicalUsage: To boast against is to exult over someone, and Paul tells the Gentiles not to boast against the branches, while James says mercy rejoices against judgment and bitter envying should not glory against the truth. The word always picks a side: pride against the other branch, or mercy against the sentence. One is forbidden and the other is the gospel.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe boasting against my brother forgets that I am a branch grafted in by grace, not a root holding myself up. I hold that mercy is the only boasting that is safe, because it rejoices against judgment and leaves the last word to God.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and G2749; to lie down, i.e. (by implication) be sick; specially, to recline at a meal:--keep, lie, sit at meat (down).
BiblicalUsage: To lie down is to be sick in bed, to be laid out where others must carry you, and the Gospels are full of it: the paralytic let down through the roof, the man at the pool who had lain there thirty-eight years, the father of Publius lying sick of a fever, and Levi rising from his table to make Jesus a great feast. The word holds the sickbed and the table together, because Jesus meets people in both places.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Jesus still comes to the sickbed first, because He saw the man lying there and knew how long it had been. I hold that the same Lord who lifts the sick also sits at the table with sinners, and I am glad He does both.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and G2806; to break down, i.e. divide:--break.
BiblicalUsage: Jesus took the loaves, looked up to heaven, blessed, and broke them, and the disciples set the broken bread before the crowd.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the breaking is where the multiplying happens, because He feeds thousands with what is broken in His hands.
RelatedEvents: The Feeding of the Five Thousand
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and G2808; to shut down (in a dungeon), i.e. incarcerate:--shut up.
BiblicalUsage: Paul shut up the saints in prison, and Herod added John to his other evils by shutting him up too.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the prison door is the world's answer to a voice it cannot silence.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and a derivative of a compound of G2819 and G1325; to be a giver of lots to each, i.e. (by implication) to apportion an estate:--divide by lot.
BiblicalUsage: God destroyed seven nations in Canaan and divided their land to His people by lot.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the land was gift, not conquest, because God gave what Israel could never have taken alone.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and G2827; to recline down, i.e. (specially) to take a place at table:--(make) sit down (at meat).
BiblicalUsage: To recline is to take your place at the table, and Jesus is always doing it: making the five thousand sit down in companies, teaching the guest not to take the highest room, reclining at Emmaus to break the bread, and lying at meat in a Pharisee's house while a sinful woman wept at His feet. The table is where He teaches, where He feeds, and where He is recognised.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the table is one of the holiest places in the Gospels, because Jesus chose it again and again to show us the kingdom. I hold that the lowest place is the safest seat, since the Host Himself promises to come and serve those who take it.
RelatedEvents: The Feeding of the Five Thousand; The Road to Emmaus
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2626; an inundation:--flood.
BiblicalUsage: The flood is the word for the deluge, and Jesus uses it twice as the picture of His coming: in the days of Noah they were eating and drinking and marrying until the flood came and took them all away. Peter adds that God spared not the old world but saved Noah, a preacher of righteousness. The flood is the warning that normal life is no shelter from judgment.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the flood still preaches, because people go on eating and drinking right up to the day the door shuts. I hold that Noah's ark is the picture of Christ: the only shelter is the one God provides, and the time to enter it is now.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and the base of G2830; to dash (wash) down, i.e. (by implication) to deluge:--overflow.
BiblicalUsage: The world that then was, being overflowed with water, perished.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the first world drowned so the second would know that God judges, and the next judgment will be by fire.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and G190; to accompany closely:--follow (after).
BiblicalUsage: The women followed after Joseph to see where the body was laid, and the damsel with the spirit of divination followed Paul crying out that these men were the servants of the most high God.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe following closely is how the truth is learned, whether by friends at the tomb or by a voice that will not be quiet.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and G2875; to chop down, i.e. mangle:--cut.
BiblicalUsage: Night and day the man was in the mountains and in the tombs, crying and cutting himself with stones.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe that is what the devil does to a man, and only Jesus could make him sit clothed and in his right mind.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and a derivative of G2911; to precipitate down:--cast down headlong.
BiblicalUsage: They rose up and thrust Jesus out of the city and led Him to the brow of the hill, to cast Him down headlong.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a town that tries to throw Jesus off a cliff has already decided it will not hear Him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2632; an adverse sentence (the verdict):--condemnation.
BiblicalUsage: Condemnation is the sentence hanging over us, and Paul sets it against the free gift: the judgment was by one offence to condemnation, but the free gift is of many offences unto justification. By one man's offence judgment came upon all men, and by one man's obedience the free gift came upon all men. Then comes the word that undoes it all: there is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe there is no condemnation for me because the sentence fell on Christ instead. I hold that this is the whole gospel in one verse, and I will stand on it when the accuser comes.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and G2919; to judge against, i.e. sentence:--condemn, damn.
BiblicalUsage: To condemn is to pass the guilty sentence, and the men of Nineveh will rise and condemn this generation because they repented at Jonah's preaching, and the queen of the south will do the same. God condemned sin in the flesh by sending His own Son, and now Christ is at the right hand of God making intercession, so who is he that condemneth. The sentence has been passed, and it fell on Him.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the only condemnation that matters has already been carried out at the cross, and no other court can reopen the case. I hold that the risen Judge is also my intercessor, and that is why I am not afraid of the verdict.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2632; sentencing adversely (the act):--condemn(-ation).
BiblicalUsage: If the ministration of condemnation was glorious, how much more does the ministration of righteousness exceed in glory, and Paul says he speaks not to condemn the Corinthians, for they are in his heart to die and live with.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the ministry that condemns was glorious, but the ministry that justifies is more glorious still.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and G2961; to lord against, i.e. control, subjugate:--exercise dominion over (lordship), be lord over, overcome.
BiblicalUsage: The princes of the Gentiles exercise dominion over their people, and Jesus says it shall not be so among you, because whoever will be great must be a minister. Peter tells the elders not to be lords over God's heritage but examples to the flock, and the possessed man in Ephesus overcame the seven sons of Sceva by the same power turned evil. Dominion is either service or tyranny, and the difference is the heart.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the kingdom turns dominion upside down, because the greatest is the servant of all. I hold that any leader who lords it over God's people has forgotten whose they are, and I want no part of that kind of power.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2637; to be a traducer, i.e. to slander:--speak against (evil of).
BiblicalUsage: To speak against is to slander a brother, and James says whoever speaks evil of his brother speaks evil of the law and judges the law. Peter turns it around: keep your conversation honest among the Gentiles, so that where they speak against you as evildoers, they may glorify God when they see your good works, and those who falsely accuse your good conversation in Christ may be ashamed. The tongue is judged by the life behind it.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe speaking against my brother is really speaking against the law that commands me to love him. I hold that the best answer to slander is a life that shames it, because good works outlast evil words.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2637; defamation:--backbiting, evil speaking.
BiblicalUsage: Paul fears he will find backbitings and whisperings among the Corinthians, and Peter tells the believers to lay aside all malice and all guile and all evil speaking.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe backbiting is a small sin with a long reach, and the church is told to lay it aside like an old garment.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and the base of G2980; talkative against, i.e. a slanderer:--backbiter.
BiblicalUsage: Backbiters are named among those who hate God, who invent evil things and disobey their parents.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God puts the backbiter in hard company, and that should make me guard my tongue.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and G2983; to take eagerly, i.e. seize, possess, etc. (literally or figuratively):--apprehend, attain, come upon, comprehend, find, obtain, perceive, (over-)take.
BiblicalUsage: To take hold is to seize and to understand at once, and John says the light shines in darkness and the darkness comprehended it not. Paul says he presses on to apprehend that for which he was apprehended, and he prays we may comprehend the breadth and length and depth and height of Christ's love. The word is both a grip and a grasp of the mind, and the race is run to lay hold of the prize.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Christ took hold of me first, and that is why I press on to take hold of Him. I hold that the love of Christ is wider than I can measure and still worth measuring, and the race is worth running because the prize is Him.
RelatedTopics: Light and Darkness; Perseverance; Love of God
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and G3004 (in its original meaning); to lay down, i.e. (figuratively) to enrol:--take into the number.
BiblicalUsage: A widow is to be taken into the number only if she is not under sixty years old, having been the wife of one man.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the church's care was ordered, not careless, and honour was given where a life had earned it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2641; a remainder, i.e. (by implication) a few:--remnant.
BiblicalUsage: Even so at this present time there is a remnant according to the election of grace.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the remnant is God's proof that He has never left Himself without a people, even when the numbers look small.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and G3007; to leave down, i.e. behind; by implication, to abandon, have remaining:--forsake, leave, reserve.
BiblicalUsage: To leave behind is what a man does to father and mother when he cleaves to his wife, what Moses did when he forsook Egypt not fearing the wrath of the king, and what God did not do when He reserved seven thousand men who had not bowed to Baal. The word holds both the leaving and the keeping: some things are left so better things can be kept, and some are kept because God never leaves them.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe leaving is the price of cleaving, whether to a wife or to the God who calls me out. I hold that God always keeps a remnant for Himself, and I want to be among those He keeps.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and G3034; to stone down, i.e. to death:--stone.
BiblicalUsage: The chief priests feared the people would stone them, because all were persuaded that John was a prophet.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the fear of the crowd kept them from saying what they really thought, and that is the fear of man at work.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2644; exchange (figuratively, adjustment), i.e. restoration to (the divine) favor:--atonement, reconciliation(-ing).
BiblicalUsage: Reconciliation is the exchange that restores us to God's favour, and Paul says we have now received the atonement, and that the casting away of Israel was the reconciling of the world. God was in Christ reconciling the world unto Himself, not imputing their trespasses, and He has given us the ministry of reconciliation. The word is the whole story of the cross in one breath: enemies made friends by the blood of Christ.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe reconciliation is the heart of the gospel, because I was God's enemy and He made peace at His own cost. I hold that I am now trusted with that same ministry, and I will carry the word of peace to everyone I meet.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and G236; to change mutually, i.e. (figuratively) to compound a difference:--reconcile.
BiblicalUsage: To be reconciled is to have the difference compounded, and Paul says while we were enemies we were reconciled to God by the death of His Son, and now we are ambassadors begging men to be reconciled to God. The same word is used for a wife returning to her husband, because reconciliation always means coming back to the one you left. It is never God who moves first in anger, but God who moves first in grace.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe I was reconciled while I was still an enemy, and that is the measure of His love. I hold that the ambassador's plea is the most urgent work in the world, because men are still at war with the God who has already made peace.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and G3062; left down (behind), i.e remaining (plural the rest):--residue.
BiblicalUsage: The residue of men shall seek after the Lord, and all the Gentiles upon whom His name is called.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the remnant was never only Israel, because God always meant the nations to seek Him too.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2647; properly, a dissolution (breaking up of a journey), i.e. (by implication) a lodging-place:-- guestchamber, inn.
BiblicalUsage: The guestchamber is the lodging place where a journey breaks up, and there was no room for them in the inn when Jesus was born, so Mary laid Him in a manger. Years later the same word names the upper room where the Passover was kept and the Lord's Supper was given. The word runs from the manger to the table, from the night He had no room to the night He made room for us.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the inn that had no room and the upper room that did are the two answers men give to Jesus. I hold that the table He prepared is still open, and I will take my place at it while there is room.
RelatedEvents: The Birth of Jesus; The Last Supper
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and G3089; to loosen down (disintegrate), i.e. (by implication) to demolish (literally or figuratively); specially (compare G2646) to halt for the night:--destroy, dissolve, be guest, lodge, come to nought, overthrow, throw down.
BiblicalUsage: To loosen down is to demolish, and Jesus says He came not to destroy the law but to fulfil it, and then says of the temple that not one stone shall be left upon another. Paul says if our earthly house is dissolved we have a building of God, and the false witnesses said Jesus would destroy the temple made with hands. The word breaks what men build and frees what God has built.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Jesus fulfils what He does not destroy, and that is why the law stands and the temple fell. I hold that my earthly house will be dissolved one day, and I am glad the building God has for me is eternal.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and G3129; to learn thoroughly, i.e. (by implication) to note carefully:--consider.
BiblicalUsage: Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow, for they toil not, neither do they spin.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a flower that never worries is a better teacher than a sermon on anxiety.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and G3140; to testify against:--witness against.
BiblicalUsage: To witness against is to testify against, and at the trial the high priest stood and demanded what these witnesses testified against Jesus, and Pilate asked if He heard how many things they witnessed against Him. The witnesses came forward and the charges piled up, yet Jesus answered nothing, and the silence was louder than the testimony. The word belongs to the courtroom where the innocent was condemned.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the false witnesses prove the trial was already decided before it began, because truth needs no hired voices. I hold that Jesus' silence was His strength, and the day is coming when every false witness will answer for what he said.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and G3306; to stay fully, i.e. reside:--abide.
BiblicalUsage: They went up into an upper room and abode there, the apostles waiting together after the ascension.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe waiting together in prayer is the first work of the church, and it came before any preaching.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and accusative case plural feminine of G3441 (with G5561 implied); according to sole places, i.e. (adverbially) separately:--alone.
BiblicalUsage: When Jesus was alone, those around Him with the twelve asked Him about the parables, and again He was alone praying when the disciples joined Him and He asked who men said He was.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the alone times with Jesus are where the parables open and the real questions get asked.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and G355; to consume utterly:--consume.
BiblicalUsage: Our God is a consuming fire.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the fire that consumes is the same God who saves, and I will come to Him with reverence, not carelessness.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and ναρκάω (to be numb); to grow utterly torpid, i.e. (by implication) slothful (figuratively, expensive):--be burdensome (chargeable).
BiblicalUsage: Paul was determined not to be burdensome to the Corinthians, and he asks what they were made inferior in, except that he himself was not burdensome to them. He says the third time he is ready to come and will not be burdensome, for he seeks not theirs but them. The word is Paul's pride in reverse: he boasts that he cost them nothing.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a minister who refuses to be a burden is showing the gospel, not just preaching it. I hold that the church is not a purse to be emptied, and the best gift a teacher can give is himself.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 (intensive) and G331; an imprecation:--curse.
BiblicalUsage: There shall be no more curse, but the throne of God and of the Lamb shall be in it, and His servants shall serve Him.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the last page of the Bible undoes the first curse, and that is the end God had in mind all along.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 (intensive) and G332; to imprecate:--curse.
BiblicalUsage: Peter began to curse and to swear that he knew not the man, and the Jews bound themselves under a curse that they would neither eat nor drink till they had killed Paul.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a curse is a terrible vow to make, and both passages show men using it to seal a wrong choice.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and G3506; to nod down (towards), i.e. (by analogy) to make signs to:--beckon.
BiblicalUsage: They beckoned to their partners in the other ship to come and help them, and both ships began to sink with the catch.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the beckon is the moment a good catch becomes too much for one boat, and the call for help is part of the miracle.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2605; a proclaimer:--setter forth.
BiblicalUsage: The philosophers called Paul a setter forth of strange gods, because he preached Jesus and the resurrection.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the world will always call the gospel strange before it calls it true.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and the base of G32; to proclaim, promulgate:--declare, preach, shew, speak of, teach.
BiblicalUsage: To proclaim is to declare openly, and Paul proclaimed the forgiveness of sins through Christ at Antioch, opened the Scriptures at Thessalonica to show Christ must suffer and rise, and warned every man in all wisdom to present every man perfect in Christ. The word is the apostles' work in one verb: they declared what God had done and would not keep it quiet. Your faith is spoken of throughout the whole world because it was first proclaimed.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe proclaiming is not an option for the church, because the forgiveness of sins is news too good to whisper. I hold that the message is the same everywhere Paul went, Christ crucified and risen, and I will not change it to suit the room.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and G3539; to observe fully:--behold, consider, discover, perceive.
BiblicalUsage: To consider is to observe fully, and we are told to consider the Apostle and High Priest of our confession, to consider one another to provoke unto love and good works, to consider the lilies and the ravens, and to see the man who beholds his face in a glass and goes away forgetting what he looked like. The word asks for a long look, not a glance, and what you look at longest shapes what you become.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe consideration is the discipline behind devotion, because you become like what you keep looking at. I hold that if I consider Christ first, everything else falls into its right place.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and a derivative of G473; to meet against, i.e. arrive at (literally or figuratively):--attain, come.
BiblicalUsage: To arrive is to meet against and come to the end of the journey, and Paul arrived at Rhegium on the way to Rome, and the church is to come to the unity of the faith and the knowledge of the Son of God. Paul pressed on to attain the resurrection of the dead, and the Corinthians are asked whether the word of God came only to them. The word holds the harbour and the goal together: arrival is the point of the voyage.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the Christian life is a voyage with a harbour, and the unity of the faith is the shore we are sailing for. I hold that I have not arrived yet, but I know where the journey ends, and that keeps me rowing.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and G3572; to pierce thoroughly, i.e. (figuratively) to agitate violently ("sting to the quick"):--prick.
BiblicalUsage: When they heard this, they were pricked in their heart, and said to Peter and the rest of the apostles, Men and brethren, what shall we do.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the prick of the heart is the beginning of repentance, and it is the Spirit's work, not the preacher's.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2660; a prickling (sensation, as of the limbs asleep), i.e. (by implication, (perhaps by some confusion with G3506 or even with G3571)) stupor (lethargy):--slumber.
BiblicalUsage: God gave them the spirit of slumber, eyes that they should not see and ears that they should not hear.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a slumbering spirit is the saddest judgment of all, because the truth is preached and the ears are closed.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and G3961; to trample down; figuratively, to reject with disdain:--trample, tread (down, underfoot).
BiblicalUsage: To trample down is to walk over what is precious, and Jesus says salt that has lost its savour is trodden under foot, pearls are not to be cast before swine lest they trample them, and the seed fell by the wayside and was trodden down. Hebrews warns of the one who has trodden under foot the Son of God and counted His blood unholy. The word is a picture of contempt made visible.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe trampling is what contempt looks like when it puts on boots, and the Son of God will not be walked over forever. I hold that the blood they count common is the blood that saves, and the day is coming when the tramplers will wish they had knelt instead.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and G3973; to settle down, i.e. (literally) to colonize, or (figuratively) to (cause to) desist:--cease, (give) rest(-rain).
BiblicalUsage: To settle down into rest is what God did on the seventh day, and what Joshua could not give, because if he had, God would not have spoken of another day. The one who has entered His rest has ceased from his own works as God did from His, and the crowd at Lystra could scarcely be restrained from sacrificing to Paul and Barnabas. Rest is the gift that stops the striving and the sacrifice both.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God's rest is still open, because Joshua's rest was only a shadow of it. I hold that ceasing from my own works is the hardest work I will ever do, and the only rest worth having.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2664; reposing down, i.e. (by Hebraism) abode:--rest.
BiblicalUsage: Rest is the abode God promises and the place He will not give to the unbelieving, and we who have believed do enter into rest, so we must labour to enter it. Heaven is His throne and earth is His footstool, and God asks what house men will build Him when He made them all. The rest is both a promise to take and a warning to heed, and the same chapter holds both.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the rest of God is entered by faith and missed by unbelief, and the line between them is the hearing of His voice today. I hold that labouring to enter rest is no contradiction, because the labour is believing, and the rest is His.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a compound of G2596 and a congener of G4072; something spread thoroughly, i.e. (specially) the door screen (to the Most Holy Place) in the Jewish Temple:--vail.
BiblicalUsage: The veil was the curtain spread across the holy place, and when Jesus died it was torn in two from top to bottom, the sun was darkened, and the way into the holiest was opened. Hebrews says we now have boldness to enter by the blood of Jesus, through the veil, that is to say, His flesh. The tear was from the top, because God did it, not man.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the torn veil is the loudest sermon the temple ever preached, because it says the way is open and the price is paid. I hold that I do not need a priest to go in for me anymore, because my Priest has gone in and left the door open.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and G5342 (including its alternate); to bear down, i.e. (figuratively) overcome (with drowsiness); specially, to cast a vote:--fall, give, sink down.
BiblicalUsage: To bear down is to sink under the weight, and Eutychus sank into a deep sleep and fell from the third loft, and the Jews laid many grievous complaints against Paul which they could not prove, and Paul himself had once cast the saints into prison with authority. The word carries the weight of sleep, of accusation, and of persecution, and all three press down hard.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the weight that bore Eutychus down was lifted by Paul's prayer, and the weight of false charges falls the same way. I hold that no accusation can stand against a man God has cleared, and no sleep is too deep for the Lord to wake.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and G5343; to flee down (away):--flee.
BiblicalUsage: Paul and Barnabas fled to Lystra and Derbe when they knew the plot against them, and we are told to flee for refuge to lay hold on the hope set before us.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe fleeing is not cowardice when the refuge is God Himself.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from 2596 and 5368; to kiss earnestly:--kiss.
BiblicalUsage: To kiss earnestly is to kiss again and again, and the sinful woman kissed the feet of Jesus and the father fell on the neck of his returning son and kissed him, while Judas came and kissed the Master to betray Him. The same act carries worship, welcome, and treachery, and the difference is the heart behind the lips. One kiss says I love you, another says I have sold you.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the kiss is the test of the heart, because lips can lie and still be warm. I hold that the father's kiss is the picture of my welcome home, and the traitor's kiss is the warning that closeness without love is the worst betrayal of all.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and G5426; to think against, i.e. disesteem:--despise.
BiblicalUsage: To think against is to despise, and Jesus says no man can serve two masters, for he will hate the one and despise the other, and warns us not to despise one of these little ones. Paul asks whether we despise the riches of God's goodness, and tells Timothy to let no man despise his youth. The word names the quiet contempt that chooses the wrong master and scorns the small and the young.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe despising is the sin I commit without noticing, because it hides inside a preference for money or a shrug at a child. I hold that God's goodness is not to be despised but to lead me to repentance, and I will not despise the young when God has given them the word.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2706; a contemner:--despiser.
BiblicalUsage: Behold, ye despisers, and wonder, and perish, for I work a work in your days which ye will not believe though a man declare it.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God warns the despisers first, because the work He is doing is too great to be laughed away.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and G5351; to spoil entirely, i.e. (literally) to destroy; or (figuratively) to deprave; --corrupt, utterly perish.
BiblicalUsage: As Jannes and Jambres withstood Moses, so do these resist the truth, men of corrupt minds, reprobate concerning the faith.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe truth has always had its counterfeits, and the test is whether the mind is sound or corrupt.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and G4095; to drink down, i.e. gulp entire (literally or figuratively):--devour, drown, swallow (up).
BiblicalUsage: To drink down is to swallow whole, and death is swallowed up in victory, and our mortality is swallowed up of life, while the blind guides strain at a gnat and swallow a camel. Peter warns that the devil walks about as a roaring lion seeking whom he may devour. The word holds both the victory and the danger: what swallows what decides everything.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe death has been swallowed by life, and that is the victory I stand in. I hold that the lion is still looking for someone to swallow, so I will stay sober and watchful, and I will not be the one he finds asleep.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and G4098; to fall down:--fall (down).
BiblicalUsage: To fall down is what Paul did on the road to Damascus when the light shone and the voice said it was hard to kick against the pricks, what the people of Malta expected of him when the viper fastened on his hand, and what the seed did on the rock and withered for lack of moisture. The word holds a conversion, a false expectation, and a warning, and all three end on the ground.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe falling down before the Lord is the beginning of standing up for Him, because Paul rose a different man than the one who fell. I hold that the seed on the rock warns me to go deep, and the viper warns me that falling is not always fatal when God is in it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and G4126; to sail down upon a place, i.e. to land at:--arrive.
BiblicalUsage: They arrived at the country of the Gadarenes, which is over against Galilee.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the landing matters, because the man in the tombs was waiting on the other side.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and a derivative of G4192; to labor down, i.e. wear with toil (figuratively, harass):--oppress, vex.
BiblicalUsage: Moses saw one of his brethren suffer wrong and defended him, and Lot was vexed with the filthy conversation of the wicked.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a righteous soul feels the weight of the wickedness around it, and that vexing is a sign the heart is still alive.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and a derivative of the same as G4195; to plunge down, i.e. submerge:--drown, sink.
BiblicalUsage: Peter saw the wind and was afraid, and beginning to sink he cried, Lord, save me, and Jesus warns that whoever offends one of these little ones should be sunk in the depth of the sea with a millstone about his neck.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Peter's sinking is my story too, because fear takes my eyes off Jesus, and His hand is still there to catch me.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and G5594; to cool down (off), i.e. refresh:--cool.
BiblicalUsage: Send Lazarus, that he may dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue, for I am tormented in this flame.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the rich man asked for a drop and could not have it, because the time for mercy was past.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 (intensive) and G685; imprecation, execration:--curse(-d, ing).
BiblicalUsage: The curse is the sentence hanging over everyone who does not continue in all things written in the law, and Christ redeemed us from it by being made a curse for us, hanging on a tree. The ground that bears thorns is near to cursing, and James says out of the same mouth come blessing and cursing, which ought not so to be. The curse is real, and so is the redemption from it.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Christ took the curse I earned so that I could receive the blessing I did not, and that exchange is the whole gospel. I hold that my mouth should bless more than it curses, because the One who bore the curse has given me a new tongue.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: middle voice from G2671; to execrate; by analogy, to doom:--curse.
BiblicalUsage: To curse is to execrate, and the King will say to those on His left, Depart from me, ye cursed, into everlasting fire, while Peter remembered the fig tree Jesus had cursed and saw it withered. Yet the same Lord says to bless them that curse you and pray for them that despitefully use you, and Paul says the same. The word is both a judgment to fear and a command to reverse.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the curse on the last day is real, and that is why I bless now instead of cursing. I hold that blessing my enemies is the proof that Christ has changed my heart, because the world curses back and I am called to do the opposite.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and G691; to be (render) entirely idle (useless), literally or figuratively:--abolish, cease, cumber, deliver, destroy, do away, become (make) of no (none, without) effect, fail, loose, bring (come) to nought, put away (down), vanish away, make void.
BiblicalUsage: To render idle is to abolish and make useless, and Paul says our old man is crucified that the body of sin might be destroyed, and charity never faileth, and the last enemy that shall be destroyed is death, and whoever seeks to be justified by the law is fallen from grace. The word undoes what stands against God: sin, death, and the law's claim on us.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Christ has abolished the power of sin and will abolish death itself, and that is the victory I live in. I hold that love never fails because it is the one thing death cannot destroy, and I will build my life on what lasts.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and G705; to reckon among:--number with.
BiblicalUsage: Judas was numbered with us and had obtained part of this ministry.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe being counted among the twelve did not save Judas, because a place at the table is not a place in the heart.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2675; thorough equipment (subjectively):--perfection.
BiblicalUsage: We are glad when we are weak and ye are strong, and this also we wish, even your perfection.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Paul's wish for the church was its perfection, and his own weakness was the price he gladly paid.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2675; complete furnishing (objectively):--perfecting.
BiblicalUsage: The gifts were given for the perfecting of the saints, for the work of the ministry, for the edifying of the body of Christ.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the church is built by gifts given for that very purpose, and every saint has a part in it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and a derivative of G739; to complete thoroughly, i.e. repair (literally or figuratively) or adjust:--fit, frame, mend, (make) perfect(-ly join together), prepare, restore.
BiblicalUsage: To complete thoroughly is to mend and restore, and Jesus saw James and John mending their nets, and Paul tells the spiritual to restore the fallen in meekness, and Hebrews prays that God would make us perfect in every good work. Peter says the God of all grace will make us perfect, stablish, strengthen, and settle us after we have suffered. The word holds the net, the brother, and the saint together: all are mended by the same hands.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God mends what is broken, whether it is a net, a brother, or my own heart. I hold that restoration is His work and His promise, and suffering is not the end of it but the way through it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2722; a holding down, i.e. occupancy:--possession.
BiblicalUsage: God gave Abraham no inheritance in the land, not so much as to set his foot on, yet promised it to him and his seed, and the fathers brought the tabernacle in with Joshua into the possession of the Gentiles.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a promise held by faith is as sure as land held by foot, because God keeps what He promises.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and G4579; to sway downward, i.e. make a signal:--beckon.
BiblicalUsage: To beckon is to sway the hand downward, and Peter beckoned to the house of Mary to hold their peace, and Paul beckoned with his hand in the synagogue and began to preach, and Alexander beckoned to make his defence, and Paul stood on the stairs and beckoned to the people. The word is the gesture before the speech, the hand that asks for silence so the voice can be heard.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the beckon matters, because the preacher asks for quiet before he speaks of Christ. I hold that Peter's beckon from prison's door and Paul's beckon in the synagogue are the same gesture: listen, because what comes next is the gospel.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and G4626; to undermine, i.e. (by implication) destroy:--dig down, ruin.
BiblicalUsage: After this I will return and build again the tabernacle of David which is fallen down, and Elijah said they have digged down Thine altars and killed Thy prophets.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God rebuilds what men dig down, and the fallen tabernacle is not the end of the story.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and G4637; to camp down, i.e. haunt; figuratively, to remain:--lodge, rest.
BiblicalUsage: To camp down is what the birds do in the branches of the mustard tree, lodging there when the smallest seed has grown greater than the herbs, and David says his flesh shall rest in hope because God will not leave his soul in hell. The word holds the bird in the branch and the body in the grave together: both are resting in a place they did not build, waiting for what comes next.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the kingdom is the tree the birds lodge in, and my flesh rests in hope for the same reason David's did. I hold that God will not leave His Holy One in the grave, and He will not leave me there either.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2681; an encamping, i.e. (figuratively) a perch:--nest.
BiblicalUsage: The foxes have holes and the birds of the air have nests, but the Son of man hath not where to lay His head.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the birds have more home than the Lord of heaven did on earth, and that is the price of His coming to us.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and a derivative of G4632; to prepare thoroughly (properly, by external equipment; whereas G2090 refers rather to internal fitness); by implication, to construct, create:--build, make, ordain, prepare.
BiblicalUsage: To prepare thoroughly is what Noah did when he built the ark, what God does as the builder of every house, what was written for the messenger to prepare the way before the Lord, and what John the Baptist came to do for a people prepared for the Lord. The word holds the ark, the house, and the way together: God prepares, and His people prepare, and the preparation is the point.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God prepares the way before He walks it, and He asks me to prepare my heart the same way. I hold that Noah's ark is the picture of a prepared faith, and John's preaching is the picture of a prepared people.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and a derivative of G4639; to overshade, i.e. cover:--shadow.
BiblicalUsage: Over the ark were the cherubims of glory shadowing the mercyseat, of which we cannot now speak particularly.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the overshadowing cherubim guarded a mercy too deep for words, and the silence is part of the reverence.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2685; to be a sentinel, i.e. to inspect insidiously:--spy out.
BiblicalUsage: False brethren came in privily to spy out our liberty in Christ Jesus, that they might bring us into bondage.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe liberty is spied on before it is stolen, and the church must watch for the spies.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 (intensive) and G4649 (in the sense of a watcher); a reconnoiterer:--spy.
BiblicalUsage: By faith the harlot Rahab perished not with them that believed not, when she had received the spies with peace.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Rahab's faith saved her, and the spies she sheltered were the proof of it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: middle voice from G2596 and G4679; to be crafty against, i.e. circumvent:--deal subtilly with.
BiblicalUsage: Pharaoh dealt subtly with our kindred, and evil entreated our fathers, so that they cast out their young children to the end they might not live.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the subtlety of Pharaoh is the devil's craft, and God saw it and answered it with deliverance.
RelatedEvents: The Exodus and the Red Sea
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and G4969; to kill down, i.e. slaughter:--slay.
BiblicalUsage: Those mine enemies, which would not that I should reign over them, bring hither, and slay them before me.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the King's judgment is terrible to those who refuse His reign, and the parable ends where refusal ends.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and G4972; to seal closely:--seal.
BiblicalUsage: I saw in the right hand of Him that sat on the throne a book written within and on the backside, sealed with seven seals.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the sealed book is God's plan held shut until the Lamb is found worthy to open it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and G4724; to put down, i.e. quell:--appease, quiet.
BiblicalUsage: The townclerk appeased the people and said these things cannot be spoken against, so ye ought to be quiet and do nothing rashly.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the townclerk's calm saved the church that day, and God can use a steady voice in a loud crowd.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2525; properly, a position or condition, i.e. (subjectively) demeanor:--behaviour.
BiblicalUsage: The aged women are to be in behaviour as becometh holiness, not false accusers, not given to much wine, teachers of good things.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe godly older women are the church's teachers, and their behaviour is the lesson.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2687; a deposit, i.e. (specially) costume:--apparel.
BiblicalUsage: Women are to adorn themselves in modest apparel, with shamefacedness and sobriety, not with broided hair or gold or pearls or costly array.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe modesty is not about hiding beauty but about wearing the kind that lasts.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and G4763; to become voluptuous against:--begin to wax wanton against.
BiblicalUsage: The younger widows are to be refused, for when they have begun to wax wanton against Christ, they will marry.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Paul's plain counsel protects both the widow and the church from a promise made too soon.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and G4762; to turn upside down, i.e. upset:--overthrow.
BiblicalUsage: Jesus overthrew the tables of the moneychangers and the seats of them that sold doves.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the overturned tables are the sign that the temple is for prayer, not for profit.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and G4766; to strew down, i.e. (by implication) to prostrate (slay):--overthrow.
BiblicalUsage: With many of them God was not well pleased, for they were overthrown in the wilderness.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the wilderness is full of the overthrown, and the warning is written for me.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2690; an overturn ("catastrophe"), i.e. demolition; figuratively, apostasy:--overthrow, subverting.
BiblicalUsage: Strive not about words to no profit, and remember that God turned the cities of Sodom and Gomorrha into ashes, making them an example.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe words that subvert the hearers are as dangerous as the fire that fell on Sodom.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and G4951; to drag down, i.e. arrest judicially:--hale.
BiblicalUsage: When thou goest with thine adversary to the magistrate, as thou art in the way, give diligence that thou mayest be delivered from him, lest he hale thee to the judge.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe it is better to agree with the adversary on the way than to be dragged before the judge at the end.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and G5087; to place down, i.e. deposit (literally or figuratively):--do, lay, shew.
BiblicalUsage: Felix left Paul bound, willing to shew the Jews a pleasure, and Festus asked if Paul would go up to Jerusalem to be judged there.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Paul was left in chains by men who wanted favour, and the chains were the price of his innocence.
RelatedEvents: Paul Before Felix, Festus, and Agrippa
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a compound of G2596 and τέμνω (to cut); a cutting down (off), i.e. mutilation (ironically):--concision. Compare G609.
BiblicalUsage: Beware of dogs, beware of evil workers, beware of the concision.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Paul's warning is blunt because the danger is real, and the true circumcision is the heart.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and a derivative of G5115; to shoot down with an arrow or other missile:--thrust through.
BiblicalUsage: This word has no occurrence anywhere in the Greek New Testament, and no verse in the New Testament carries it.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a word with no verse to stand on should be said so plainly, and I will not invent a passage to fill the gap.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and G5143; to run down, i.e. hasten from a tower:--run down.
BiblicalUsage: The chief captain ran down to them with soldiers and centurions, and when they saw him they left beating Paul.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the running down of the soldiers was God's rescue arriving on time.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and G515; to deem entirely deserving:--(ac-)count worthy.
BiblicalUsage: To be counted worthy is to be deemed deserving, and those who attain the resurrection are counted worthy, and the apostles rejoiced that they were counted worthy to suffer shame for His name, and Paul prays the Thessalonians may be counted worthy of the kingdom of God. The word holds the honour and the suffering together: worthiness is given by God and proved in the bearing of shame.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe worthiness is not earned but given, and the proof of it is joy in suffering for His name. I hold that the kingdom is worth the shame, and the One who counts me worthy will keep me to the end.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and G2279; to sound down into the ears, i.e. (by implication) to indoctrinate ("catechize") or (genitive case) to apprise of:--inform, instruct, teach.
BiblicalUsage: To sound down into the ears is to instruct by word of mouth, and Luke writes so Theophilus may know the certainty of the things he was instructed in, and Apollos was instructed in the way of the Lord, and Paul says let him that is taught in the word share with him that teaches. The word is the passing of truth from mouth to ear, and the church lives on it.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe instruction is how certainty is passed on, because Luke wrote so that we may know, not guess. I hold that the taught should share with the teacher, because the word that feeds me should also feed the one who brought it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and G2192; to hold down (fast), in various applications (literally or figuratively):--have, hold (fast), keep (in memory), let, X make toward, possess, retain, seize on, stay, take, withhold.
BiblicalUsage: To hold down fast is to keep a firm grip, and we are told to hold fast the profession of our faith without wavering, to hold fast the confidence and the rejoicing of hope firm to the end, to prove all things and hold fast that which is good, and warned of those who hold the truth in unrighteousness. The same grip can hold the faith or hold the truth down, and the difference is the heart.
