TheologicalSignificance: I believe holding fast is the whole work of the Christian life, because the faith is worth the grip and the hope is worth the holding. I hold that I will prove all things and keep what is good, and I will not let go of the confession He gave me.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2725; to be a plaintiff, i.e. to charge with some offence:--accuse, object.
BiblicalUsage: To accuse is to bring the charge, and Jesus says Moses is the one who accuses them, and the accuser of the brethren is cast down, and the chief priests accused Him before Pilate and He answered nothing, and Tertullus accused Paul before Felix with flattery. The word runs from the courtroom to the throne of God, and the accuser is always busy, but the Advocate is busier still.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the accuser's voice is loud, but the Advocate's blood speaks better things. I hold that Moses accuses those who trust in Moses and miss Christ, and I will trust in Christ instead.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2725; a complaint ("category"), i.e. criminal charge:--accusation (X -ed).
BiblicalUsage: The accusation is the complaint brought against a man, and Pilate asked what accusation the Jews brought against Jesus, and Paul says no accusation against an elder is to be received without two or three witnesses, and an elder must be blameless with faithful children and no accusation of riot. The word guards the accused as much as it charges him, because a charge without witnesses is no charge at all.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God guards His servants with the witness rule, because a single voice should never ruin a man. I hold that the accusation against Jesus was the one charge that could not stand, and the court that heard it condemned an innocent man anyway.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and G58; against one in the assembly, i.e. a complainant at law; specially, Satan:--accuser.
BiblicalUsage: The accuser is the plaintiff who stands against a man in the assembly, and Paul's accusers were told to come to Caesarea and say what they had against him, and Festus said it was not the Roman manner to deliver any man to die before the accused had his accusers face to face. The word is the courtroom word for the one who brings the charge, and Paul met his accusers again and again.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the Roman rule was just, because a man should face his accusers and answer them. I hold that Paul's courage before his accusers is the pattern for mine, because the truth does not fear a hearing.
RelatedEvents: Paul Before Felix, Festus, and Agrippa
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 (intensively) and G1497; utterly idolatrous:--wholly given to idolatry.
BiblicalUsage: Paul's spirit was stirred within him when he saw the city wholly given to idolatry.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a city full of idols should stir the spirit, not dull it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and G1725; directly opposite:--before, over against.
BiblicalUsage: To be directly opposite is to stand before, and Abraham believed God who quickens the dead and calls things that are not as though they were, and Paul says we speak before God in Christ, and again he writes that they speak before God in Christ for the Corinthians' edifying. The word is the place of standing before God, where nothing is hidden and everything is weighed.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe standing before God is the most serious place in the world, and the most comforting, because the God before whom I stand is the God who quickens the dead. I hold that I will speak as before God or not speak at all, because His presence is the only audience that matters.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and G1799; directly in front of:--before (the presence of), in the sight of.
BiblicalUsage: To be directly in front of is to stand before the presence of, and God chose us in Him before the foundation of the world that we should be holy and without blame before Him in love, and Christ will present us holy and unblameable and unreproveable in His sight, and Jude says He is able to present us faultless before the presence of His glory with exceeding joy. The word is the place we will stand, and the state we will stand in.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe I will stand before Him holy and without blame, not because I am blameless but because Christ presents me. I hold that this is the end of the gospel: faultless before glory, with exceeding joy, and I will live toward that day.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a compound of G2596 and perhaps a derivative of the base of G5316 (meaning downcast in look); demureness, i.e. (by implication) sadness:--heaviness.
BiblicalUsage: Be afflicted, and mourn, and weep, for let your laughter be turned to mourning and your joy to heaviness.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe godly sorrow is the door to repentance, and laughter that will not mourn is the sign of a hard heart.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and G2186; to stand over against, i.e. rush upon (assault):--make insurrection against.
BiblicalUsage: The Jews made insurrection with one accord against Paul and brought him to the judgment seat.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the judgment seat was where Paul's accusers thought they had him, and it became his pulpit instead.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and G2064 (including its alternate); to come (or go) down (literally or figuratively):--come (down), depart, descend, go down, land.
BiblicalUsage: To come down is what Philip did to Samaria to preach Christ, and what the prophets did from Jerusalem to Antioch, and what Jesus did to Capernaum to teach on the Sabbath, while James says the wisdom that descends not from above is earthly, sensual, and devilish. The word moves people down from one place to another, and it also names where wisdom comes from, above or below.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the gospel always comes down to where people are, because Philip went down to Samaria and Jesus went down to Capernaum. I hold that wisdom from above is pure and peaceable, and I will test every wisdom by where it came down from.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and G2038; to work fully, i.e. accomplish; by implication, to finish, fashion:--cause, to (deed), perform, work (out).
BiblicalUsage: To work fully is to accomplish, and Paul says sin wrought in him all manner of concupiscence by the commandment, and asks whether the good became death to him, and then says to work out your own salvation with fear and trembling, and godly sorrow worketh repentance to salvation. The word holds both the working of sin and the working of salvation, and the difference is who is doing the work and to what end.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe sin works death in me and God works salvation in me, and the two workings are at war in the same heart. I hold that I work out what God works in, because my salvation is His work first and my obedience second.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and G2068 (including its alternate); to eat down, i.e. devour (literally or figuratively):--devour.
BiblicalUsage: To eat down is to devour, and the disciples remembered that the zeal of God's house had eaten Him up, and the fowls came and devoured the seed by the wayside, and the scribes devour widows' houses, and John ate the little book and it was sweet in his mouth and bitter in his belly. The word holds zeal, theft, and prophecy together: what devours us decides what we become.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe zeal for God's house should eat me up the way it ate Him up, because a cold heart is no heart at all. I hold that the book is sweet to taste and bitter to carry, and the prophet's life is the proof of it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and G2116; to straighten fully, i.e. (figuratively) direct:--guide, direct.
BiblicalUsage: To straighten fully is to direct, and Zechariah says the dayspring shall guide our feet into the way of peace, and Paul prays that God would direct our way unto the Thessalonians, and that the Lord would direct our hearts into the love of God and the patient waiting for Christ. The word is the prayer of a traveller who knows the road is crooked and asks God to make it straight.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God directs the feet that ask to be directed, because Zechariah's prayer is still answered today. I hold that the way of peace and the love of God are the two directions my heart needs, and I will ask Him to point me straight every morning.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and G1850; to have (wield) full privilege over:--exercise authority.
BiblicalUsage: The princes of the Gentiles exercise authority upon them, and they that are accounted to rule over the Gentiles exercise authority upon them.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the world's authority presses down, and Christ's authority lifts up.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and the neuter plural of G3739; according to which things, i.e. just as:--as.
BiblicalUsage: They gave the thirty pieces of silver for the potter's field, as the Lord appointed me.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe even the blood money was counted in prophecy, and nothing about the betrayal surprised God.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: something written, i.e. a writing, record or book
BiblicalUsage: A writing is a record or a book, and the king's letters were written in his name and sealed with his ring, and the book of truth holds the names of those who stand in the battle, and the priests sought their register among the writings and were put from the priesthood when they were not found. David received the pattern of the temple in writing from the hand of the Lord. The word holds the decree, the record, and the pattern together, and all three are written down so they will not be lost.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God writes things down because He wants us to remember, and the book of truth is still open. I hold that my name is written where it matters, and the writings of men will fade while His remain.
RelatedPeople: Queen Esther; Daniel; Ezra; King David
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to grave, by implication, to write (describe, inscribe, prescribe, subscribe)
BiblicalUsage: To write is to grave and inscribe, and God wrote the tables with His own finger, and commanded the words to be written on the doorposts of the house, and promised to write His law in their hearts, and told the prophet to write the vision plainly on tables so that he who reads it may run. The word runs from stone to doorpost to heart, and each writing goes deeper than the last.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God's writing goes deeper than stone, because the law on the heart outlasts the law on the tablet. I hold that the vision written plainly is still running its course, and I will write down what God shows me so I do not forget it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and G138 (including its alternate); to lower (or with violence) demolish (literally or figuratively):--cast (pull, put, take) down, destroy.
BiblicalUsage: To pull down is to lower with force, and Mary sang that God has put down the mighty from their seats and exalted them of low degree, and God destroyed seven nations and gave their land to Israel, and Paul says the weapons of our warfare are mighty to the pulling down of strong holds, and Joseph took the body of Jesus down from the cross. The word holds the throne, the nation, the stronghold, and the cross together, and God pulls down what stands against Him.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God pulls down the mighty and lifts up the lowly, and the cross is where both happened at once. I hold that my weapons are not carnal but mighty through God, and the strongholds in my own heart are the first ones to fall.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2507; demolition; figuratively, extinction:--destruction, pulling down.
BiblicalUsage: Destruction is the pulling down, and Paul says our weapons are mighty to the pulling down of strong holds, and his authority was given for edification and not for destruction, and he writes sharply so he will not have to use sharpness when he comes. The word is the power to tear down, and Paul insists it was given to build up instead. Authority that destroys is authority misused.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe authority is given to build, not to destroy, and the apostle who could tear down chose to build up. I hold that the sharpest letter is the kind one, because it warns before it wounds, and I want my words to do the same.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2513; to cleanse, i.e. (specially) to prune; figuratively, to expiate:--purge.
BiblicalUsage: Every branch in Me that beareth not fruit He taketh away, and every branch that beareth fruit He purgeth it, that it may bring forth more fruit.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the pruning hurts, but the branch that is pruned bears more, and the Gardener knows what He is doing.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, to carve or engrave, i.e. (by implication) to inscribe indelibly
BiblicalUsage: Though thou wash thee with nitre and take thee much soap, yet thine iniquity is marked before Me, saith the Lord God.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe no washing of my own can clean what only God can forgive.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2505 and G4007; exactly as:--(even, as well) as.
BiblicalUsage: As we have many members in one body, and all members have not the same office, so the body is one and hath many members, and all the members of that one body are one.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the body works because the members are different, and no member is the whole body alone.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and G680; to seize upon:--fasten on.
BiblicalUsage: Paul gathered a bundle of sticks and laid them on the fire, and a viper came out of the heat and fastened on his hand.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the viper fastened on the wrong man, because the fire that should have killed Paul only proved God was with him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to enclose; hence (in a friendly sense) to crown, (in a hostile one) to besiege; also to wait (as restraining oneself)
BiblicalUsage: To enclose is to crown and surround, and strong bulls of Bashan compassed the sufferer round, and the psalmist asks to be brought out of prison, and Habakkuk says the wicked compass about the righteous so that wrong judgment goes forth, and Elihu says God has yet to speak on His behalf. The word holds the surrounding enemy and the surrounding God together: one encloses to crush, the other encloses to keep.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the bulls of Bashan are real, because the righteous are still compassed about by the wicked. I hold that the same word says God compasses His people too, and the enclosure of His presence is the safer one.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2511; a washing off, i.e. (ceremonially) ablution, (morally) expiation:--cleansing, + purge, purification(-fying).
BiblicalUsage: Purification is the washing off, and the Son purged our sins by Himself and sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high, and the days of Mary's purification were accomplished, and there arose a question between John's disciples and the Jews about purifying, and Peter warns of the one who has forgotten that he was purged from his old sins. The word holds the cleansing of the sinner and the ceremony of the law together, and both point to the same blood.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe my purification was finished by the Son Himself, and that is why He sat down. I hold that forgetting I was purged is the first step back into the old sins, and I will remember what the blood has done.
RelatedEvents: The Presentation of Jesus in the Temple
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2513; to cleanse (literally or figuratively):--(make) clean(-se), purge, purify.
BiblicalUsage: To cleanse is what Jesus did when He touched the leper and said I will, be thou clean, and the leprosy departed, and the ten lepers were cleansed as they went, and John says if we confess our sins He is faithful and just to forgive us and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness. The word holds the touch on the skin and the washing of the soul together, and the same Lord does both.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the leper's prayer is mine too, Lord, if Thou wilt, Thou canst make me clean. I hold that confession is the way the cleansing comes, because He is faithful and just to do what He promised.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain affinity; clean (literally or figuratively):--clean, clear, pure.
BiblicalUsage: Clean is the word for the pure in heart who shall see God, and for the branches made clean through the word He has spoken, and for the love that comes out of a pure heart and a good conscience and faith unfeigned, and for the religion that is pure before God. The word holds the heart, the branch, the conscience, and the religion together, and all of them are clean the same way: washed by the word and kept by grace.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the pure in heart shall see God, and that promise is worth every washing. I hold that purity is not a performance but a cleansing, and the clean heart is the one He has made clean.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2513; cleanness (ceremonially):--purification.
BiblicalUsage: The blood of bulls and goats and the ashes of an heifer sprinkling the unclean sanctifieth to the purifying of the flesh.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the old purifying reached only the flesh, and the blood of Christ reaches the conscience.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to butt or pound
BiblicalUsage: Though thou shouldest bray a fool in a mortar among wheat with a pestle, yet will not his foolishness depart from him.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe some foolishness will not be pounded out, because the heart has to change, not just the habits.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to bruise or violently strike
BiblicalUsage: To bruise and strike is what the nations will do to their swords when they beat them into plowshares, and what Joel reverses when he says beat your plowshares into swords, and what Hezekiah did when he brake in pieces the brasen serpent Moses had made. The word holds the beating of swords into ploughs and the breaking of idols together: one is the promise of peace, the other is the price of it.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the swords will become plowshares when the Lord judges, and the idols must be broken before that day comes. I hold that Hezekiah's hammer is the picture of repentance, because what was once lifted up for healing had become an idol, and it had to come down.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and the same as G1476; a bench (literally or figuratively):--seat.
BiblicalUsage: The seat is the bench of authority, and the scribes and Pharisees sit in Moses' seat, and Jesus overthrew the tables of the moneychangers and the seats of them that sold doves. The word holds the teaching seat and the merchant's seat together, and Jesus honours the one and overturns the other. The seat of Moses is for teaching the law, and the seat of the seller is for making the temple a den of thieves.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe authority is judged by what it does with its seat, because Moses' seat is for teaching and the moneychanger's seat is for profit. I hold that Jesus still overturns the tables that turn His house into a market, and I want my seat to be the low one.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a compound of G2596 and G2233; a guide, i.e. (figuratively) a teacher:--master.
BiblicalUsage: Neither be ye called masters, for one is your Master, even Christ.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe there is one Master in the church, and every other title is borrowed.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and G2240; to reach to, i.e. (neuter of present active participle, figuratively as adjective) becoming:-- convenient, fit.
BiblicalUsage: They gave him audience unto this word and then lifted up their voices, away with such a fellow from the earth, and God gave them over to a reprobate mind, to do those things which are not convenient.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the crowd that stops listening is the same heart that God gives over, and both end in the same place.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596; and ἧμαι (to sit; akin to the base of G1476); to sit down; figuratively, to remain, reside:--dwell, sit (by, down).
BiblicalUsage: To sit down is what the Son of man will do at the right hand of power, and the high priest heard it from His own mouth, and Paul says to seek those things which are above, where Christ sitteth on the right hand of God. The word holds the trial and the throne together: the One they condemned is the One who sits, and the sitting is the verdict on the trial.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the seated Christ is the proof that the trial was wrong and the cross was right. I hold that my life is hid with Him where He sits, and I will set my mind on the things above, not on the things of the earth.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and G2250; quotidian:--daily.
BiblicalUsage: There arose a murmuring of the Grecians against the Hebrews, because their widows were neglected in the daily ministration.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the daily bread of widows is the church's first test, and the murmuring was the sign it was failing.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: the shoulder (proper, i.e. upper end of the arm; as being the spot where the garments hang); figuratively, side-piece or lateral projection of anything
BiblicalUsage: The shoulder is where the burden is carried and the strength is shown, and Aaron bore the names of the sons of Israel on the stones of the ephod on his shoulders, and Benjamin dwells safely because the Lord shall cover him and dwell between his shoulders, and the idol is carried on the shoulder because it cannot walk, and Goliath wore a coat of mail between his shoulders. The word holds the priest, the tribe, the idol, and the giant together, and only one of them carries what it claims.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the shoulder is where God puts the burden and where He gives the strength to carry it. I hold that the idol on the shoulder is the picture of every false god, carried by its worshippers because it cannot carry them, while my God carries me.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and εὕδω (to sleep); to lie down to rest, i.e. (by implication) to fall asleep (literally or figuratively):--(be a-)sleep.
BiblicalUsage: To sleep is to lie down to rest, and Jesus found the disciples sleeping in Gethsemane and asked whether they could not watch one hour, and Paul says let us not sleep as do others, but let us watch and be sober, and the word says awake thou that sleepest, and arise from the dead. The word holds the garden, the night, and the resurrection together: sleep is the picture of death, and waking is the picture of life.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe sleep in the garden is the warning for every disciple, because the hour of prayer is the hour I am most likely to close my eyes. I hold that the call to awake is still sounding, and the One who slept in the boat and woke to calm the storm is the One who wakes me.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and G1836; thereafter, i.e. consecutively; as a noun (by ellipsis of noun) a subsequent person or time:--after(-ward), by (in) order.
BiblicalUsage: Thereafter is the word for in order, and Luke writes in order to Theophilus so he may know the certainty, and Peter rehearsed the matter from the beginning and expounded it by order, and Paul went over the country in order strengthening the disciples, and Samuel and the prophets after him foretold these days. The word is the order of the story told straight, from the beginning to the end, and the certainty is in the order.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the gospel is told in order because God works in order, and Luke's careful account is the proof of it. I hold that the prophets spoke in order too, each one adding to the last, and the story they told is the one I am living in.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and the base of G1476; to sit down:--sit.
BiblicalUsage: To sit down is what Jesus did at the well, wearied with His journey, and what the boy Jesus did in the temple among the doctors, and what He did daily in the temple teaching, and what the two angels did in the sepulchre, one at the head and one at the feet where the body had lain. The word holds the well, the temple, and the tomb together, and the same Lord sat in all three places.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the seated Jesus is the weary Jesus, the teaching Jesus, and the risen Jesus, and He is the same in all three. I hold that the angels sitting in the tomb are the proof that the sitting is finished, because the body is gone and the grave is empty.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596; and ἵημι (to send); to lower:--let down.
BiblicalUsage: To let down is what the disciples did when they lowered Paul in a basket by the wall, and what Peter saw when the sheet was let down from heaven, and what the friends did when they let the paralytic down through the tiling into the midst before Jesus. The word holds the basket, the sheet, and the bed together: all three are lowered by hands that believe the Lord is on the other end.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the lowered basket is the picture of the church at its best, because friends who let a man down by a wall are the same friends who let a man down through a roof. I hold that the sheet from heaven and the bed through the roof are the same message: God lets His gifts down to us, and we let one another down to Him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and G2476; to place down (permanently), i.e. (figuratively) to designate, constitute, convoy:--appoint, be, conduct, make, ordain, set.
BiblicalUsage: Kathistemi means to place down permanently, to appoint, to set someone in a place that holds. Romans 5:19 says by one man's disobedience many were made sinners, and by the obedience of one shall many be made righteous. Titus 1:5 has Paul telling Titus to ordain elders in every city, as I had appointed thee. James 3:6 says the tongue is set among our members, and is set on fire of hell, and 2 Peter 1:8 says if these things be in you, they make you neither barren nor unfruitful.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God is the one who sets things in place: Adam's fall made us sinners, and Christ's obedience makes us righteous. I hold that the same word that appoints elders is the word that decides what we become. My position is simple: I want to be set by God, not by hell.
RelatedPeople: Paul; Simon Peter; James, Brother of Jesus
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: beaten, i.e. pure (oil)
BiblicalUsage: Kathiyth means beaten, pure oil, olive oil pounded fine until it is clear. Exodus 27:20 commands the children of Israel to bring pure oil olive beaten for the light, to cause the lamp to burn always, and Leviticus 24:2 repeats the command, to cause the lamps to burn continually. Numbers 28:5 mixes the daily meat offering with beaten oil, and 1 Kings 5:11 says Solomon gave Hiram twenty measures of pure oil year by year.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe beaten oil is the picture of a life pressed until it is pure: God does not light his lamp with cloudy oil. I hold that the beating is not punishment, it is preparation, and the light that burns always is worth the pressing.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: another (active) form for G2516; to seat down, i.e. set (figuratively, appoint); intransitively, to sit (down); figuratively, to settle (hover, dwell):--continue, set, sit (down), tarry.
BiblicalUsage: Kathizo means to sit down, to take a seat, and so to settle and rule. Matthew 25:31 says when the Son of man shall come in his glory, then shall he sit upon the throne of his glory. Luke 14:28 asks which of you, intending to build a tower, sitteth not down first, and counteth the cost. 1 Corinthians 6:4 tells the church to set the least esteemed to judge, and Revelation 20:4 says I saw thrones, and they sat upon them, and judgment was given unto them.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe sitting is the posture of authority: Christ sits to judge, and his people sit with him. I hold that counting the cost is sitting down first, not rushing to build. My position is that the throne belongs to the Son of man, and I want to be found on his side when he sits.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and G3739; according to which thing, i.e. precisely as, in proportion as:--according to that, (inasmuch) as.
BiblicalUsage: Katho means according as, precisely as, the word that measures one thing against another. Romans 8:26 uses it when Paul says we know not what we should pray for as we ought, and 1 Peter 4:13 uses it when Peter says to rejoice inasmuch as ye are partakers of Christ's sufferings.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the little word as matters most when it joins our weakness to Christ's sufferings and our prayers to the Spirit's help.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and G3650; on the whole, i.e. entirely:--at all.
BiblicalUsage: Katholou means on the whole, entirely, and here it means at all. Acts 4:18 shows the council commanding Peter and John not to speak at all nor teach in the name of Jesus.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the world's at all is no match for the name they were told never to speak.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596; and G3695; to equip fully with armor:--arm.
BiblicalUsage: Kathoplizo means to arm fully, to equip with armour from head to foot. Luke 11:21 pictures a strong man armed keeping his palace, his goods in peace, until a stronger than he comes.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe no armour we put on ourselves can stand against the stronger man, Christ, who takes the spoil.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and G3708; to behold fully, i.e. (figuratively) distinctly apprehend:--clearly see.
BiblicalUsage: Kathorao means to see clearly, to take something in fully. Romans 1:20 says the invisible things of God from the creation of the world are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe creation leaves no one an excuse, because God made himself plain to see in what he made.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and G5613; just (or inasmuch) as, that:--according to, (according, even) as, how, when.
BiblicalUsage: Kathos means just as, even as, the little word that ties one thing to another. Romans 15:21 quotes it as it is written, to whom he was not spoken of, they shall see, and 1 Corinthians 1:6 says even as the testimony of Christ was confirmed in you.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that as is the hinge of the gospel: what God promised, he did, and what Christ did, he confirms in us.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596; and G3739 and G5100; according to which certain thing, i.e. as far (or inasmuch) as:--(according, forasmuch) as, because (that).
BiblicalUsage: Kathoti means inasmuch as, because, the word that gives the reason. Luke 19:9 has Jesus saying salvation is come to this house, forsomuch as Zacchaeus also is a son of Abraham, and Acts 2:24 says God raised Jesus up because it was not possible that death should hold him.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the reason always runs back to God: salvation came because Zacchaeus belonged, and death lost because it could not hold Christ.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and a derivative of G2447; to rust down, i.e. corrode:--canker.
BiblicalUsage: Katioo means to rust down, to corrode. James 5:3 warns the rich that their gold and silver is cankered, and the rust of them shall be a witness against them.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe rust is God's quiet verdict on treasure kept for ourselves: it eats what we refused to give.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and G2480; to overpower:--prevail (against).
BiblicalUsage: Katischyo means to overpower, to prevail against. Matthew 16:18 says the gates of hell shall not prevail against the church Christ builds. Luke 21:36 tells us to watch and pray always, that ye may be accounted worthy to escape all these things, and to stand before the Son of man. Luke 23:23 shows the other side: the voices of the chief priests prevailed, and Jesus was crucified.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe prevailing is the promise and the warning both: hell will not prevail against the church, but loud voices can prevail against one man for an hour. I hold that the church stands because Christ builds it, not because the world stops shouting.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: ; also (compare) κατωτέρω (compare G2737); adverb from G2596; downwards:--beneath, bottom, down, under.
BiblicalUsage: Kato means down, beneath, to the bottom. Matthew 27:51 says the veil of the temple was rent in twain from the top to the bottom, and Acts 2:19 promises signs in the earth beneath.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe down is where God meets us: the veil tore from top to bottom so the way in was open.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2596 and G3611; to house permanently, i.e. reside (literally or figuratively):--dwell(-er), inhabitant(-ter).
BiblicalUsage: Katoikeo means to dwell permanently, to make a home and stay: Acts 22:12 speaks of the Jews which dwelt in Damascus, where Ananias lived. Ephesians 3:17 prays that Christ may dwell in your hearts by faith. 2 Peter 3:13 says we look for new heavens and a new earth, wherein dwelleth righteousness. Revelation 17:8 says they that dwell on the earth shall wonder at the beast.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe dwelling is the question of every life: Christ dwells in hearts by faith, righteousness dwells in the new earth, and the beast only impresses those who dwell on this earth. I hold that where I dwell decides what I worship, and I want Christ at home in me.
RelatedPeople: Paul; Simon Peter; John the Apostle
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2730; residence (properly, the act; but by implication, concretely, the mansion):--dwelling.
BiblicalUsage: Katoikesis means a dwelling, a residence. Mark 5:3 says the man with the unclean spirit had his dwelling among the tombs, and no man could bind him.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe where a man dwells shows who rules him, and only Jesus could enter that graveyard and set him free.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a derivative of G2730; a dwelling-place:--habitation.
BiblicalUsage: Katoiketerion means a dwelling-place, a habitation. Ephesians 2:22 says believers are builded together for an habitation of God through the Spirit, while Revelation 18:2 says fallen Babylon is become the habitation of devils.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe every heart is a habitation for somebody, and mine is built to be God's house, not the devil's.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: residence (properly, the condition; but by implication, the abode itself):--habitation.
BiblicalUsage: Katoikia means a habitation, the place where people dwell. Acts 17:26 says God made all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth, and determined the bounds of their habitation.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God set every nation's borders himself, so no people is an accident and none is outside his reach.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: middle voice from a compound of G2596 and a derivative of G3700 (compare G2072); to mirror oneself, i.e. to see reflected (figuratively):--behold as in a glass.
BiblicalUsage: Katoptrizomai means to behold as in a glass, to see yourself mirrored. 2 Corinthians 3:18 says we all, with open face beholding as in a glass the glory of the Lord, are changed into the same image from glory to glory.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe looking at Christ is what changes us: we become like what we behold.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a compound of G2596 and a derivative of G3717 (compare G1357); something made fully upright, i.e. (figuratively) rectification (specially, good public administration):--very worthy deed.
BiblicalUsage: Katorthoma means a very worthy deed, a public good done well. Acts 24:2 has Tertullus flattering Felix, saying that very worthy deeds are done unto this nation by thy providence.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe flattery calls any deed worthy, but God weighs what was actually done.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: comparative from G2736; inferior (locally, of Hades):--lower.
BiblicalUsage: Katoteros means lower, the parts beneath. Ephesians 4:9 says Christ descended first into the lower parts of the earth before he ascended.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Christ went down before he went up, so there is no depth he has not already been.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from some (obsolete) base akin to that of αὐχέω (to boast) and G2172; to vaunt (in a good or a bad sense):--(make) boast, glory, joy, rejoice.
BiblicalUsage: Kauchaomai means to boast, to glory, to rejoice in something. Romans 5:11 says we also joy in God through our Lord Jesus Christ, by whom we have now received the atonement. 1 Corinthians 1:29 says no flesh should glory in his presence, and 1 Corinthians 1:31 says, he that glorieth, let him glory in the Lord. Galatians 6:14 says, God forbid that I should glory, save in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe boasting is only safe when the boast is the cross: everything else is flesh glorying in God's presence. I hold that joy in God is the right kind of glorying, because it gives him what he gave us. My position is Paul's: if I boast, let it be the cross.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2744; a boast (properly, the object; by implication, the act) in a good or a bad sense:--boasting, (whereof) to glory (of), glorying, rejoice(-ing).
BiblicalUsage: Kauchema means the boast itself, the thing you glory in. Romans 4:2 says if Abraham were justified by works, he hath whereof to glory, but not before God. 1 Corinthians 5:6 warns, your glorying is not good, for a little leaven leaveneth the whole lump. 2 Corinthians 1:14 calls the Corinthians Paul's rejoicing in the day of the Lord Jesus, and Hebrews 3:6 says we are Christ's house, if we hold fast the confidence and the rejoicing of the hope firm unto the end.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the boast tells you what you trust: Abraham had nothing to boast of before God, and neither do I. I hold that the only boast that holds to the end is the hope firm in Christ's house.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2744; boasting (properly, the act; by implication, the object), in a good or a bad sense:--boasting, whereof I may glory, glorying, rejoicing.
BiblicalUsage: Kauchesis means boasting, the act of glorying: Romans 15:17 says, I have therefore whereof I may glory through Jesus Christ in those things which pertain to God. 1 Corinthians 15:31 has Paul protesting by his rejoicing in Christ Jesus, I die daily. 2 Corinthians 7:4 says great is my glorying of you, and 1 Thessalonians 2:19 asks, what is our hope, or joy, or crown of rejoicing? Are not even ye in the presence of our Lord Jesus Christ at his coming?
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Paul's boasting was never about Paul: it was about the people God gave him and the Christ who died daily in him. I hold that the best crown of rejoicing is not a thing, but people standing before the Lord at his coming.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2545; properly, a burn (concretely), but used (abstractly) of a glow:--heat.
BiblicalUsage: Kauma means heat, a burning glow. Revelation 7:16 promises the redeemed shall hunger no more, neither shall the sun light on them, nor any heat, while Revelation 16:9 says men were scorched with great heat and blasphemed God.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the same heat that scorches the unrepentant will never touch those sheltered in Christ.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2738; to burn:--scorch.
BiblicalUsage: Kaumatizo means to scorch, to burn with the sun's heat. Matthew 13:6 says the seed on stony ground was scorched when the sun was up, because it had no root, and Mark 4:6 tells the same parable. Revelation 16:8 says power was given to the sun to scorch men with fire, and Revelation 16:9 says men were scorched with great heat, and blasphemed the name of God.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the sun tests every plant: rootless seed withers, and scorched men curse God instead of repenting. I hold that the same heat that withers the shallow only hardens the deep-rooted.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2545; burning (the act):--be burned.
BiblicalUsage: Kausis means burning, the act of being burned. Hebrews 6:8 warns that ground bearing thorns and briers is rejected, and whose end is to be burned.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe fruit is the test: ground that bears only thorns ends in fire.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2741; a glare:--(burning) heat.
BiblicalUsage: Kauson means burning heat, the glare of the midday sun. Matthew 20:12 has the labourers complaining they have borne the burden and heat of the day. Luke 12:55 says when ye see the south wind blow, ye say, there will be heat, and it cometh to pass. James 1:11 says the sun is no sooner risen with a burning heat, but it withereth the grass, and the flower thereof falleth.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the heat of the day is the test of the labourer and the rich man alike: it withers the flower and shows what the work was worth. I hold that God counts the burden borne in the heat, not the hour hired.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2740; to set on fire:--fervent heat.
BiblicalUsage: Kausoo means to burn with fervent heat, to set on fire. 2 Peter 3:10 says the elements shall melt with fervent heat on the day of the Lord, and 2 Peter 3:12 says the heavens being on fire shall be dissolved.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this world is not forever: it will melt, and only what God remakes will stand.
RelatedTopics: Day of the Lord; Second Coming
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a derivative of G2545; to brand ("cauterize"), i.e. (by implication) to render unsensitive (figuratively):--sear with a hot iron.
BiblicalUsage: Kauteriazo means to sear with a hot iron, to brand until feeling is gone. 1 Timothy 4:2 warns of men speaking lies in hypocrisy, having their conscience seared with a hot iron.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a conscience can be burned until it stops feeling, and that is why I want mine kept tender before God.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a window (as a perforation)
BiblicalUsage: Kav is the Aramaic word for a window. Daniel 6:10 says Daniel went into his house, and his windows being open in his chamber toward Jerusalem, he kneeled upon his knees three times a day, and prayed.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Daniel's open window is the picture of prayer that will not hide, even when the law says to shut it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, to prick or penetrate; hence, to blister (as smarting or eating into)
BiblicalUsage: Kavah means to burn, to scorch, to be branded by fire. Proverbs 6:28 asks, can one go upon hot coals, and his feet not be burned, and Isaiah 43:2 promises that when thou walkest through the fire, thou shalt not be burned.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe fire tests everyone, but God's promise is that his people walk through it unburned.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: something prepared, i.e. a sacrificial wafer
BiblicalUsage: Kavvan means a cake, a sacrificial wafer. Jeremiah 7:18 says the women knead their dough, to make cakes to the queen of heaven, and Jeremiah 44:19 has the people admitting they made her cakes to worship her.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a cake baked for a false god is still idolatry, even when the whole family helps make it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: falsehood; literally (untruth) or figuratively (idol)
BiblicalUsage: Kazab means falsehood, a lie, an untruth: Proverbs 14:5 says a faithful witness will not lie, but a false witness will utter lies. Proverbs 19:5 warns a false witness shall not be unpunished, and he that speaketh lies shall not escape. Amos 2:4 says Judah's lies caused them to err, after the which their fathers have walked. Zephaniah 3:13 promises the remnant of Israel shall not speak lies, neither shall a deceitful tongue be found in their mouth.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe lies are not small sins: they caused Judah to err and they follow fathers into sons. I hold that the remnant God keeps is marked by a clean mouth, and I want mine to be one of them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to lie (i.e. deceive), literally or figuratively
BiblicalUsage: Kazab means to lie, to deceive, to tell a lie: 2 Kings 4:16 has the Shunammite begging Elisha, do not lie unto thine handmaid, when he promises her a son. Job 24:25 challenges, who will make me a liar, and make my speech nothing worth? Psalms 116:11 says, I said in my haste, all men are liars. Micah 2:11 warns of a man walking in falsehood who says, I will prophesy unto thee of wine and of strong drink.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the lie wears many coats: a prophet's promise of wine, a hasty word about all men, a fear that God's promise is too good. I hold that God calls the liar what he is, and his own promises are the one place a lie cannot live.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: now
BiblicalUsage: Ke-an is the Aramaic word for now, at this time. Ezra 6:6 opens the king's order with now therefore, and Daniel 2:23 has Daniel thanking God who hast made known unto me now what we desired.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe now is God's favourite word: he answers in this time, not only in some later one.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: suffering (physical or mental), adversity
BiblicalUsage: Ke-eb means pain, sorrow, suffering of body or mind: Job 2:13 says his friends sat with him seven days and seven nights, and none spake a word, for they saw that his grief was very great. Psalms 39:2 says, I was dumb with silence, I held my peace, even from good, and my sorrow was stirred. Isaiah 17:11 says the harvest shall be a heap in the day of grief and of desperate sorrow. Jeremiah 15:18 cries, why is my pain perpetual, and my wound incurable, which refuseth to be healed?
TheologicalSignificance: I believe sorrow is the one language every sufferer speaks: Job's friends knew to sit silent, David knew to hold his peace, and Jeremiah asked God why the pain would not end. I hold that God hears the question even when the wound refuses to heal.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: thus (only in the formula 'and so forth')
BiblicalUsage: Ke-eneth means thus, and so forth, the clerk's way of closing a list. Ezra 4:10 ends the roll of nations with and at such a time, and Ezra 4:11 opens the copy of the letter the same way.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe even the driest clerk's phrase matters, because it sits in a letter God used to test his people's resolve.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Kebar, a river of Mesopotamia
BiblicalUsage: Kebar is the river in Babylon where the exiles settled, and where Ezekiel saw the heavens open. Ezekiel 1:1 says, as I was among the captives by the river of Chebar, the heavens were opened, and I saw visions of God. Ezekiel 1:3 says the word of the LORD came expressly unto Ezekiel by the river Chebar, and Ezekiel 3:15 says he came to them of the captivity at Tel-abib, that dwelt by the river of Chebar, and sat where they sat.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God meets his people in exile, by a foreign river, and the heavens open there as surely as in the temple.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, extent of time, i.e. a great while; hence, long ago, formerly, hitherto
BiblicalUsage: Kebar means already, long ago, a great while. Ecclesiastes 1:10 asks, is there anything whereof it may be said, see, this is new? it hath been already of old time, and Ecclesiastes 2:12 says the man that cometh after the king can only do that which hath been already done.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Solomon is right: nothing under the sun is really new, and that is why I look above the sun for hope.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a sieve (as netted)
BiblicalUsage: Kebarah means a sieve, a sifter. Amos 9:9 says God will sift the house of Israel among all nations, like as corn is sifted in a sieve, yet shall not the least grain fall upon the earth.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God's sieve keeps every grain: he shakes his people hard, but he loses none of them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: difficulty
BiblicalUsage: Kebeduth means heaviness, difficulty. Exodus 14:25 says God took off the Egyptians' chariot wheels, that they drave them heavily, and the Egyptians said, let us flee from the face of Israel.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God can make the enemy's road heavy while he makes his people's way through the sea.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a fetter
BiblicalUsage: Kebel means a fetter, a bond. Psalms 105:18 says Joseph's feet they hurt with fetters, and Psalms 149:8 says God's people bind their kings with chains, and their nobles with fetters of iron.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe fetters change hands in God's story: the bound become the binders, and the prisoner becomes the ruler.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a ram (just old enough to butt)
BiblicalUsage: Kebes means a lamb, a young ram: Leviticus 23:12 says ye shall offer an he lamb without blemish for a burnt offering unto the LORD. Numbers 15:11 sets the rule for one bullock, or one ram, or for a lamb, or a kid. 1 Chronicles 29:21 says they offered a thousand lambs with their drink offerings for all Israel. Proverbs 27:26 says the lambs are for thy clothing, and the goats are the price of the field.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the lamb runs through the whole Bible: offered without blemish, counted by the thousand, and worn as clothing. I hold that every lamb on those altars was pointing to the one Lamb who would take away the sin of the world.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a footstool (as trodden upon)
BiblicalUsage: Kebesh means a footstool, something trodden upon. 2 Chronicles 9:18 describes Solomon's throne, with a footstool of gold, fastened to the throne.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe even a king's footstool is gold in God's house, because the throne it serves belongs to him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a matrass (of intertwined materials)
BiblicalUsage: Kebiyr means a pillow, a quilt, something netted and soft. 1 Samuel 19:13 says Michal put a pillow of goats' hair for David's bolster to fool Saul's messengers, and 1 Samuel 19:16 says the messengers found the image in the bed, with the pillow for his bolster.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Michal's pillow is a small picture of how God hides his anointed until the danger passes.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: weightiness, i.e. magnificence, wealth
BiblicalUsage: Kebuwddah means weightiness, magnificence, wealth, gloriousness. Judges 18:21 says the Danites put the little ones and the cattle and the carriage before them as they marched. Psalms 45:13 says the king's daughter is all glorious within, her clothing is of wrought gold. Ezekiel 23:41 says she sat upon a stately bed, and a table prepared before it.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe weightiness shows what a people values: Dan counted his goods first, the king's daughter wore glory within, and Jerusalem set her table for idols. I hold that true magnificence is glory within, not goods marched in front.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {a flag; also a sail; by implication, a flagstaff; generally a signal; figuratively, a token}
BiblicalUsage: Kec means a throne, a seat of honour. Exodus 17:16 says, because the LORD hath sworn that the LORD will have war with Amalek, the hand upon the throne of the LORD.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Amalek's war was against the throne itself, and that is why the LORD swore it would last from generation to generation.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Kesalon, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Kesalon is a town on the northern border of Judah, named in the allotment. Joshua 15:10 says the border passed along unto the side of mount Jearim, which is Chesalon, on the north side, and went down to Beth-shemesh.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe every border town in the allotment matters, because God drew the lines of his people's inheritance himself.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {silver (from its pale color); by implication, money}
BiblicalUsage: Kecaph is the Aramaic word for silver, and so for money. Ezra 7:15 sends the silver and gold freely offered unto the God of Israel, whose habitation is in Jerusalem. Daniel 2:32 says the image's breast and arms were of silver, and Daniel 2:35 says the silver and the gold were broken to pieces together. Daniel 2:45 says the stone cut out without hands brake the silver and the gold in pieces.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe silver is the metal of empires: offered freely to God in Ezra, and smashed by the stone in Daniel. I hold that every kingdom built on silver ends the same way, broken to pieces by the kingdom God cuts out himself.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, fulness or the full moon, i.e. its festival
BiblicalUsage: Kece means the full moon, the time appointed. Psalms 81:3 says blow up the trumpet in the new moon, in the time appointed, on our solemn feast day, and Proverbs 7:20 says the goodman will come home at the day appointed.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God's calendar runs on appointed times, and he is never late to his own feast.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, fatness, i.e. by implication (literally) the loin (as the seat of the leaf fat) or (generally) the viscera; also (figuratively) silliness or (in a good sense) trust
BiblicalUsage: Kecel means the loins, the flank, and so by figure both folly and trust: Leviticus 3:4 takes the fat that is by the flanks for the offering. Job 8:14 says the hypocrite's trust shall be a spider's web. Psalms 78:7 says they might set their hope in God, and not forget his works. Ecclesiastes 7:25 says Solomon applied his heart to know the wickedness of folly, even of foolishness and madness.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe one word can hold both folly and trust because both live in the same place: the gut where a man leans. I hold that the difference is what you lean on: a spider's web, or God.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: silver (from its pale color); by implication, money
BiblicalUsage: Keceph means silver, and so money: 1 Chronicles 18:10 says Tou sent vessels of gold and silver and brass to David. Ezra 1:10 counts thirty basons of gold, silver basons of a second sort four hundred and ten. Psalms 12:6 says the words of the LORD are pure words, as silver tried in a furnace of earth, purified seven times. Zephaniah 1:18 says neither their silver nor their gold shall be able to deliver them in the day of the LORD's wrath.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe silver is the test of every age: counted in basons, sent as tribute, tried seven times in the furnace. I hold that God's words are the only silver that comes out of the fire pure, and no man's silver can buy him out of the day of wrath.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a cushion or pillow (as covering a seat or bed)
BiblicalUsage: Keceth means a cushion or band, the false prophetesses' magic pillows. Ezekiel 13:18 cries woe to the women that sew pillows to all armholes to hunt souls, and Ezekiel 13:20 says God is against those pillows and will tear them from their arms.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God hates religion that hunts souls, and he tears the pillows away to set the hunted free.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: faithless
BiblicalUsage: Kechash means deceitful, false, lying. Isaiah 30:9 says this is a rebellious people, lying children, children that will not hear the law of the LORD.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe lying and rebellion walk together: a people that will not hear the law soon cannot tell the truth.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: any notable constellation; specifically Orion (as if a burly one)
BiblicalUsage: Keciyl means Orion, the great constellation, the burly one in the sky: Job 9:9 says God maketh Arcturus, Orion, and Pleiades, and the chambers of the south. Job 38:31 asks, canst thou loose the bands of Orion? Isaiah 13:10 says the stars of heaven and the constellations thereof shall not give their light. Amos 5:8 says seek him that maketh the seven stars and Orion, and turneth the shadow of death into the morning.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Orion is God's handwriting in the night sky: he made it, he binds it, and he can darken it when he judges. I hold that the one who made the stars is the one to seek, because he turns death's shadow into morning.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: any notable constellation; specifically Orion (as if a burly one)
BiblicalUsage: Keciyl means Orion, the great constellation, the burly one in the sky: Job 9:9 says God maketh Arcturus, Orion, and Pleiades, and the chambers of the south. Job 38:31 asks, canst thou loose the bands of Orion? Isaiah 13:10 says the stars of heaven and the constellations thereof shall not give their light. Amos 5:8 says seek him that maketh the seven stars and Orion, and turneth the shadow of death into the morning.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Orion is God's handwriting in the night sky: he made it, he binds it, and he can darken it when he judges. I hold that the one who made the stars is the one to seek, because he turns death's shadow into morning.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, fat, i.e. (figuratively) stupid or silly
BiblicalUsage: Keciyl means the fool, the stupid fellow, the dullard: Psalms 94:8 says, understand, ye brutish among the people, and ye fools, when will ye be wise? Proverbs 15:14 says the mouth of fools feedeth on foolishness. Ecclesiastes 2:14 says the fool walketh in darkness, and one event happeneth to them all. Ecclesiastes 5:1 warns to be more ready to hear, than to give the sacrifice of fools, for they consider not that they do evil.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the fool is not the man who lacks wit, but the man who feeds on foolishness and walks in darkness. I hold that the wise man's eyes are in his head, and the fool's sacrifice is refused because he never stopped to hear.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: silliness
BiblicalUsage: Keciyluwth means silliness, foolishness. Proverbs 9:13 says a foolish woman is clamorous: she is simple, and knoweth nothing.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe folly is loud because it has nothing to say, and wisdom is quiet because she has already set her table.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Kesulloth, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Kesulloth is a town in Issachar, near Jezreel, named in the tribal allotment. Joshua 19:18 says their border was toward Jezreel, and Chesulloth, and Shunem.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the small towns of the allotment are as much God's doing as the great cities, and he named them one by one.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a cover (garment); figuratively, a veiling
BiblicalUsage: Kecuwth means a covering, clothing, a veil: Genesis 20:16 has Abimelech giving Sarah a thousand pieces of silver, saying, he is to thee a covering of the eyes. Exodus 22:27 says the poor man's covering is his raiment for his skin, wherein shall he sleep? Deuteronomy 22:12 says thou shalt make thee fringes upon the four quarters of thy vesture, wherewith thou coverest thyself. Job 24:7 says the oppressors cause the naked to lodge without clothing, that they have no covering in the cold.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a covering is a mercy: it hides shame, it keeps a man warm, and God hears the cry of the one who has none. I hold that the law's fringes and the poor man's cloak both say the same thing, that God covers his people.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: false
BiblicalUsage: Kedab is the Aramaic word for false, lying. Daniel 2:9 has Nebuchadnezzar telling the wise men they have prepared lying and corrupt words to speak before him.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a king can smell a lie even when he cannot remember his dream, and God can do far more.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Kedorlaomer, an early Persian king
BiblicalUsage: Kedorlaomer was the king of Elam who ruled the cities of the plain: Genesis 14:1 names him with Amraphel and Arioch and Tidal, the kings of the east. Genesis 14:4 says twelve years they served Chedorlaomer, and in the thirteenth year they rebelled. Genesis 14:5 says in the fourteenth year came Chedorlaomer, and the kings that were with him, and smote the Rephaims.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Chedorlaomer is the picture of every power that taxes God's people until Abraham rises to take them back.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H6939); Cedron (i.e. Kidron), a brook near Jerusalem:--Cedron.
BiblicalUsage: Cedron, the Kidron, is the brook between Jerusalem and the Mount of Olives. John 18:1 says Jesus went forth with his disciples over the brook Cedron, where was a garden, into the which he entered.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the brook is the last water before the garden: Jesus crossed it knowing what waited on the other side.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, a weakening; figuratively, alleviation, i.e. cure
BiblicalUsage: Kehah means a weakening, an alleviation, a cure. Nahum 3:19 says of Nineveh, there is no healing of thy bruise; thy wound is grievous.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe some wounds have no healing because the sin behind them never repented, and Nineveh is the warning.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to be able
BiblicalUsage: Kehal is the Aramaic word to be able. Daniel 2:26 has the king asking, art thou able to make known unto me the dream? Daniel 4:18 says all the wise men of my kingdom are not able to make known the interpretation, but thou art able. Daniel 5:8 says the wise men could not read the writing, and Daniel 5:15 says they could not shew the interpretation of the thing.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe able is the word that separates God's servants from the king's wise men: they could not, and Daniel could, because the spirit of the holy gods was in him. I hold that my own ability is nothing until God gives the interpretation.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: feeble, obscure
BiblicalUsage: Keheh means dim, dull, feeble, colourless: Leviticus 13:6 says if the plague be somewhat dark, and spread not, the priest shall pronounce him clean. 1 Samuel 3:2 says Eli's eyes began to wax dim, that he could not see. Isaiah 42:3 says a bruised reed shall he not break, and the smoking flax shall he not quench. Isaiah 61:3 promises the garment of praise for the spirit of heaviness.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God is gentle with the dim: the dark spot is pronounced clean, the bruised reed is not broken, the smoking flax is not quenched. I hold that the spirit of heaviness gets a garment of praise, because God restores what has gone dull.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: priesthood
BiblicalUsage: Kehunnah means the priesthood, the priest's office: Exodus 29:9 says the priest's office shall be Aaron's and his sons' for a perpetual statute. Numbers 25:13 gives Phinehas the covenant of an everlasting priesthood, because he was zealous for his God. 1 Samuel 2:36 says the fallen house of Eli will beg, put me into one of the priests' offices, that I may eat a piece of bread. Nehemiah 13:29 prays, remember them, because they have defiled the priesthood.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the priesthood is a gift God gives and a trust men can defile: Phinehas won it by zeal, Eli's house begged for it as bread, and Nehemiah prayed against those who stained it. I hold that the true priesthood is kept by zeal for God, not by birth alone.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: middle voice of a primary verb; to lie outstretched (literally or figuratively):--be (appointed, laid up, made, set), lay, lie. Compare G5087.
BiblicalUsage: Keimai means to lie, to be laid, to be set: Luke 2:34 has Simeon saying, behold, this child is set for the fall and rising again of many in Israel. John 21:9 says the disciples saw fish laid thereon, and bread. 1 Corinthians 3:11 says other foundation can no man lay than that is laid, which is Jesus Christ. Revelation 21:16 says the city lieth foursquare, and the length is as large as the breadth.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe everything is laid somewhere: the child is set for fall and rising, the foundation is laid once, and the city lies foursquare. I hold that the only foundation that holds is the one already laid, Jesus Christ.
RelatedPeople: Jesus; Paul; John the Apostle; Simeon
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain affinity; a swathe, i.e. winding-sheet:--graveclothes.
BiblicalUsage: Keiria means graveclothes, the winding-sheet of the dead. John 11:44 says he that was dead came forth, bound hand and foot with graveclothes, and Jesus said, loose him, and let him go.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Jesus does not leave his people bound: he calls them out and then he looses them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a primary verb; to shear:--shear(-er).
BiblicalUsage: Keiro means to shear, to cut the hair or the fleece. Acts 8:32 quotes the scripture, he was led as a sheep to the slaughter, and like a lamb dumb before his shearer, so opened he not his mouth. Acts 18:18 says Paul, having shorn his head in Cenchrea, for he had a vow. 1 Corinthians 11:6 says if the woman be not covered, let her also be shorn.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the shearer is the picture of the whole gospel: the Lamb dumb before his shearer opened not his mouth, and so we were saved. I hold that Paul's shorn head and the church's covering both say the same thing, that a vow is kept in the open.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Kelach, a place in Assyria
BiblicalUsage: Kelach, Calah, is one of the most ancient cities of Assyria, built by Asshur. Genesis 10:11 says out of that land went forth Asshur, and builded Nineveh, and the city Rehoboth, and Calah. Genesis 10:12 says Resen between Nineveh and Calah, the same is a great city.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Calah is the reminder that the great cities of men were built early, and God watched every one of them rise.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: maturity
BiblicalUsage: Kelach means maturity, full strength, vigour. Job 5:26 promises thou shalt come to thy grave in a full age, like as a shock of corn cometh in in his season, and Job 30:2 asks what the strength of old men's hands could profit, in whom old age was perished.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a full age is a harvest, not a waste: God gathers the ripe corn in its season.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Kelal, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Kelal, Chelal, is an Israelite named among those who had taken foreign wives in Ezra's day. Ezra 10:30 lists him with the sons of Pahath-moab: Adna, and Chelal, Benaiah, Maaseiah, Mattaniah, Bezaleel, and Binnui, and Manasseh.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Chelal's name is kept because the reckoning was real: every man who had married outside the covenant was named, and the people put the wives away.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to complete
BiblicalUsage: Kelal is the Aramaic word to complete, to finish: Ezra 4:12 accuses the Jews of building the rebellious city and joining the foundations. Ezra 4:13 warns that if the city be builded, they will not pay toll, tribute, and custom. Ezra 4:16 certifies that if the city be builded again, the king shall have no portion on this side the river. Ezra 5:3 has Tatnai asking, who hath commanded you to build this house, and to make up this wall?
TheologicalSignificance: I believe finishing is the word the enemies feared: a finished wall meant a finished people, and a finished city meant lost revenue. I hold that God finishes what he starts, even when letters from the king say to stop.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a prison
BiblicalUsage: Kele means a prison, confinement: 1 Kings 22:27 has Ahab saying, put this fellow in the prison, and feed him with bread of affliction. 2 Kings 25:27 says Evil-merodach lifted up the head of Jehoiachin out of prison. Isaiah 42:22 says God's people are hid in prison houses, and none delivereth. Jeremiah 52:33 says Jehoiachin changed his prison garments, and did eat bread before the king all the days of his life.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe prison is where God does some of his deepest work: the prophet fed on affliction, the people hid with none to deliver, and the king changed his garments and ate at the table. I hold that no prison holds forever when God lifts up the head.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a dog; hence (by euphemism) a male prostitute
BiblicalUsage: Keleb means a dog: 1 Kings 14:11 says him that dieth of Jeroboam in the city shall the dogs eat. 2 Kings 9:36 says in the portion of Jezreel shall dogs eat the flesh of Jezebel. Psalms 68:23 says thy foot may be dipped in the blood of thine enemies, and the tongue of thy dogs in the same. Isaiah 66:3 says he that sacrificeth a lamb, as if he cut off a dog's neck.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the dog is the Bible's picture of contempt: the unclean eater, the shame of the unburied, the insult to a sacrifice. I hold that the same word that shames the wicked also shows how far God will go to cleanse the unclean.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2753; a cry of incitement:--shout.
BiblicalUsage: Keleuma means a shout, a cry of command. 1 Thessalonians 4:16 says the Lord himself shall descend from heaven with a shout, with the voice of the archangel, and with the trump of God.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the Lord's return will not be quiet: a shout, a voice, and a trumpet will wake the dead in Christ first.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a primary κέλλω (to urge on); "hail"; to incite by word, i.e. order:--bid, (at, give) command(-ment).
BiblicalUsage: Keleuo means to command, to order, to bid. Matthew 27:64 has the chief priests saying, command therefore that the sepulchre be made sure until the third day. Luke 18:40 says Jesus stood, and commanded the blind man to be brought unto him. Acts 4:15 says the council commanded Peter and John to go aside, and Acts 5:34 says Gamaliel commanded to put the apostles forth a little space.
