TheologicalSignificance: I believe every command in these verses is answered by a greater one: the priests command the tomb shut, and Jesus commands the blind to come. I hold that the council's commands fade, but the Lord's command brings the blind near.
RelatedPeople: Jesus; Simon Peter; John the Apostle
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: disgrace
BiblicalUsage: Kelimmah means disgrace, shame, confusion: Job 20:3 says, I have heard the check of my reproach, and the spirit of my understanding causeth me to answer. Psalms 109:29 says let mine adversaries be clothed with shame, and cover themselves with their own confusion, as with a mantle. Isaiah 30:3 says the strength of Pharaoh shall be your shame. Ezekiel 16:52 says, bear thine own shame for thy sins, in that thou hast justified thy sisters.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe shame is a garment God can make the proud wear: adversaries clothed in it, Pharaoh's strength turned to it, Jerusalem told to bear her own. I hold that the only way out of shame is to bear it honestly before God.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: disgrace
BiblicalUsage: Kelimmuth means disgrace, reproach. Jeremiah 23:40 says God will bring an everlasting reproach upon you, and a perpetual shame, which shall not be forgotten.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe shame that God lays on is not forgotten, because the prophets he mocked were his own messengers.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a prison
BiblicalUsage: Keliy means a prison, a place of confinement. Jeremiah 37:4 says Jeremiah came in and went out among the people, for they had not put him into prison, and Jeremiah 52:31 says Evil-merodach brought Jehoiachin forth out of prison.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe prison could not hold the prophet's word or the king's freedom, because God opens doors men shut.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: something prepared, i.e. any apparatus (as an implement, utensil, dress, vessel or weapon)
BiblicalUsage: Keliy means a vessel, an implement, anything prepared for use: Exodus 25:9 says, according to all that I shew thee, after the pattern of all the instruments thereof, even so shall ye make it. Exodus 40:10 says thou shalt anoint the altar and all his vessels, and sanctify the altar. 1 Chronicles 9:28 says certain Levites had the charge of the ministering vessels, that they should bring them in and out by tale. Zechariah 11:15 says, take unto thee yet the instruments of a foolish shepherd.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a vessel is only as good as its use: the tabernacle's vessels were anointed, the Levites counted them in and out, and the foolish shepherd's instruments were a warning. I hold that God makes vessels for honour, and I want to be one he can use.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Kelub, the name of two Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Kelub is the name of two Israelites. 1 Chronicles 4:11 says Chelub the brother of Shuah begat Mehir, which was the father of Eshton. 1 Chronicles 27:26 says over them that did the work of the field was Ezri the son of Chelub.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe both Kelubs are kept for the same reason: one fathered a family, and the other raised a son who tilled David's fields.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a bird-trap (as furnished with a clap-stick or treadle to spring it); hence, a basket (as resembling a wicker cage)
BiblicalUsage: Keluwb means a bird-trap, a cage, and also a basket. Jeremiah 5:27 says as a cage is full of birds, so are their houses full of deceit. Amos 8:1 shows the Lord a basket of summer fruit, and Amos 8:2 says, the end is come upon my people of Israel, I will not again pass by them any more.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the cage and the basket are the same warning: houses full of deceit are traps, and summer fruit ripens for the end. I hold that God shows the prophet what is coming, and then he does not pass by any more.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Kelubai, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Kelubai, Chelubai, is a son of Hezron, named in the genealogy of Judah. 1 Chronicles 2:9 says the sons also of Hezron, that were born unto him, Jerahmeel, and Ram, and Chelubai.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Chelubai's one verse is enough: he is counted among the sons of Judah, in the line that leads to David and to Christ.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Keluhai, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Keluhai, Chelluh, is an Israelite named among those who had taken foreign wives. Ezra 10:35 lists him plainly: Benaiah, Bedeiah, Chelluh.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Chelluh's name stands in the list because Ezra's reckoning left no one out, and the people answered it together.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: bridehood (only in the plural)
BiblicalUsage: Keluwlah means bridehood, the love of the espousals. Jeremiah 2:2 says God remembers the kindness of thy youth, the love of thine espousals, when thou wentest after me in the wilderness.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God remembers our first love for him, and he calls us back to the wilderness road where we once followed close.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a form of the prefix 'k-', but used separately as, thus, so
BiblicalUsage: Kemow means as, like, thus, the word that draws the comparison. 1 Chronicles 17:20 says, O LORD, there is none like thee, neither is there any God beside thee, and Zechariah 10:8 says they shall increase as they have increased.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that like is the word that keeps God incomparable: nothing is like him, and his people grow like nothing else grows.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Kemosh, the god of the Moabites
BiblicalUsage: Kemosh, Chemosh, is the god of the Moabites: Numbers 21:29 cries, woe to thee, Moab, thou art undone, O people of Chemosh. Judges 11:24 asks, wilt not thou possess that which Chemosh thy god giveth thee to possess? 1 Kings 11:7 says Solomon built an high place for Chemosh, the abomination of Moab, in the hill before Jerusalem.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Chemosh is the god who could not save his people, and Solomon's high place for him is the saddest verse in his story.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: so
BiblicalUsage: Ken is the Aramaic word for so, thus. Ezra 6:2 says a roll was found, and therein was a record thus written, and Daniel 2:24 has Daniel saying thus unto Arioch, destroy not the wise men of Babylon.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe thus is the word of the record: what is written stands, and Daniel spoke by it to save lives.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: so
BiblicalUsage: Ken is the Aramaic word for so, thus. Ezra 6:2 says a roll was found, and therein was a record thus written, and Daniel 2:24 has Daniel saying thus unto Arioch, destroy not the wise men of Babylon.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe thus is the word of the record: what is written stands, and Daniel spoke by it to save lives.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: so
BiblicalUsage: Ken is the Aramaic word for so, thus. Ezra 6:2 says a roll was found, and therein was a record thus written, and Daniel 2:24 has Daniel saying thus unto Arioch, destroy not the wise men of Babylon.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe thus is the word of the record: what is written stands, and Daniel spoke by it to save lives.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

BiblicalUsage: Ken is the Aramaic word for so, thus. Ezra 6:2 says a roll was found, and therein was a record thus written, and Daniel 2:24 has Daniel saying thus unto Arioch, destroy not the wise men of Babylon.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe thus is the word of the record: what is written stands, and Daniel spoke by it to save lives.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Kenaan, a son a Ham; also the country inhabited by him
BiblicalUsage: Kenaan is both a man, the son of Ham, and the land his children inhabited: Genesis 12:5 says Abram went forth to go into the land of Canaan, and into the land of Canaan they came. 1 Chronicles 1:8 lists the sons of Ham: Cush, and Mizraim, Put, and Canaan. Zephaniah 2:5 cries woe to Canaan, the land of the Philistines, for the word of the LORD is against you.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Canaan holds both the promise and the judgment: the land God gave, and the land God judged when its sins were full.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Kenaanah, the name of two Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Kenaanah is the name of two Israelites: 1 Kings 22:24 says Zedekiah the son of Chenaanah went near, and smote Micaiah on the cheek. 1 Chronicles 7:10 lists another Chenaanah among the sons of Bilhan. 2 Chronicles 18:23 tells the same smiting again, when Zedekiah asked which way went the Spirit of the LORD from me.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the two Chenaanahs show both sides of the name: one raised a son who struck a prophet, and the other is only a name in a list, remembered by God.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a Kenaanite or inhabitant of Kenaan; by implication, a pedlar (the Canaanites standing for their neighbors the Ishmaelites, who conducted mercantile caravans)
BiblicalUsage: Kena-aniy means a Canaanite, an inhabitant of Canaan, and so a trader: Exodus 3:8 promises a land flowing with milk and honey, unto the place of the Canaanites. Joshua 12:8 lists the Canaanites among the peoples of the land. 1 Chronicles 2:3 says Judah's three sons were born of the daughter of Shua the Canaanitess. Zechariah 14:21 says in that day there shall be no more the Canaanite in the house of the LORD of hosts.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the Canaanite runs through the story as the neighbour, the wife, the trader, and the one who must go: God promised the land, judged its people, and ends with a house where no Canaanite remains. I hold that the promise is bigger than the peoples who stood in its way.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Kenani, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Kenani, Chenani, is a Levite who stood on the stairs and cried to God. Nehemiah 9:4 says Chenani stood up upon the stairs, of the Levites, and cried with a loud voice unto the LORD their God.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Chenani's loud cry is the right answer to a rebuilt wall: the people prayed before they built, and they prayed when the building was done.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Kenanjah, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Kenanyah, Chenaniah, is a Levite chief over the song and over the outward business of Israel: 1 Chronicles 15:22 says Chenaniah, chief of the Levites, was for song: he instructed about the song, because he was skilful. 1 Chronicles 15:27 says he was the master of the song with the singers when David brought up the ark. 1 Chronicles 26:29 says Chenaniah and his sons were for the outward business over Israel, for officers and judges.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Chenaniah is the Levite who did both: he led the song when the ark came up, and he judged the outward business when the singing was done.
RelatedEvents: David Brings the Ark to Jerusalem
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {a colleague (as having the same title)}
BiblicalUsage: Kenath means a colleague, a companion, one who shares the same title: Ezra 4:9 lists Rehum and Shimshai and the rest of their companions, the nations settled in Samaria. Ezra 4:17 has the king answering Rehum and the rest of their companions that dwell in Samaria. Ezra 4:23 says the companions went up in haste to Jerusalem and made the Jews cease by force and power. Ezra 5:3 has Tatnai and Shethar-boznai and their companions asking who commanded the building.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe companionship cuts both ways: these companions joined to stop God's house, and the builders' companions joined to raise it. I hold that the company you keep decides the wall you build.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {a colleague (as having the same title)}
BiblicalUsage: Kenath means a colleague, a companion, one who shares the same title: Ezra 4:9 lists Rehum and Shimshai and the rest of their companions, the nations settled in Samaria. Ezra 4:17 has the king answering Rehum and the rest of their companions that dwell in Samaria. Ezra 4:23 says the companions went up in haste to Jerusalem and made the Jews cease by force and power. Ezra 5:3 has Tatnai and Shethar-boznai and their companions asking who commanded the building.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe companionship cuts both ways: these companions joined to stop God's house, and the builders' companions joined to raise it. I hold that the company you keep decides the wall you build.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably from κέγχρος (millet); Cenchreæ, a port of Corinth:--Cencrea.
BiblicalUsage: Kenchreai, Cenchrea, is the port of Corinth, where Paul shaved his head for a vow and where Phoebe served the church. Acts 18:18 says Paul sailed thence into Syria, having shorn his head in Cenchrea, for he had a vow. Romans 16:1 says, I commend unto you Phebe our sister, which is a servant of the church which is at Cenchrea.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Cenchrea is the small port with a big story: a vow kept, a sister commended, and a church that sent its servants out into the world.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: so or thus
BiblicalUsage: Kenema means so, thus, after this manner. Ezra 4:8 says Rehum and Shimshai wrote a letter against Jerusalem in this sort, and Ezra 5:4 says they asked after this manner, what are the names of the men that make this building?
TheologicalSignificance: I believe even the enemies' letters are part of the record, and God kept the builders' names in it anyway.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2755; empty glorying, i.e. self-conceit:--vain-glory.
BiblicalUsage: Kenodoxia means vainglory, empty glorying. Philippians 2:3 says let nothing be done through strife or vainglory, but in lowliness of mind let each esteem other better than themselves.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe vainglory is glory with nothing inside, and lowliness is the only cure for it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2756 and G1391; vainly glorifying, i.e. self-conceited:--desirous of vain-glory.
BiblicalUsage: Kenodoxos means desirous of vainglory, self-conceited. Galatians 5:26 says let us not be desirous of vain glory, provoking one another, envying one another.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe wanting to be admired is the root of provoking and envying, and Paul cuts it off at the root.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2756; to make empty, i.e. (figuratively) to abase, neutralize, falsify:--make (of none effect, of no reputation, void), be in vain.
BiblicalUsage: Kenoo means to make empty, to make void, to make of none effect: Romans 4:14 says if they which are of the law be heirs, faith is made void, and the promise made of none effect. 1 Corinthians 1:17 says Christ sent me to preach the gospel, not with wisdom of words, lest the cross of Christ should be made of none effect. 2 Corinthians 9:3 says Paul sent the brethren, lest our boasting of you should be in vain. Philippians 2:7 says Christ made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe emptiness is the word of the gospel two ways: men empty the cross when they trust the law or wisdom of words, and Christ emptied himself when he took the servant's form. I hold that his emptying is what fills us, and their emptying is what leaves men with nothing.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a presumed compound of G2756 and G5456; empty sounding, i.e. fruitless discussion:--vain.
BiblicalUsage: Kenophonia means empty sounding, vain babbling, fruitless talk. 1 Timothy 6:20 tells Timothy to avoid profane and vain babblings, and 2 Timothy 2:16 says shun them, for they will increase unto more ungodliness.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe empty talk is never harmless: it grows, and what it grows into is more ungodliness.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: adverb from G2756; vainly, i.e. to no purpose:--in vain.
BiblicalUsage: Kenos means in vain, to no purpose. James 4:5 asks, do ye think that the scripture saith in vain, the spirit that dwelleth in us lusteth to envy?
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Scripture never speaks in vain, so when it warns about envy, I had better listen.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: apparently a primary word; empty (literally or figuratively):--empty, (in) vain.
BiblicalUsage: Kenos means empty, vain, to no purpose: 1 Corinthians 15:10 says his grace which was bestowed upon me was not in vain. 1 Corinthians 15:14 says if Christ be not risen, then is our preaching vain, and your faith is also vain. Ephesians 5:6 says let no man deceive you with vain words. Philippians 2:16 says hold forth the word of life, that I have not run in vain, neither laboured in vain.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe empty is the word that decides everything: if Christ is not risen, our preaching is vain, and if he is, no labour in him is vain. I hold that grace was not bestowed on Paul in vain, and it is not bestowed on me in vain either.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Latin origin; properly, an enrollment ("census"), i.e. (by implication) a tax:--tribute.
BiblicalUsage: Kensos means the census tax, the tribute paid to Caesar: Matthew 17:25 has Jesus asking Peter, of whom do the kings of the earth take custom or tribute? Matthew 22:17 asks, is it lawful to give tribute unto Caesar, or not? Matthew 22:19 says, shew me the tribute money, and they brought him a penny. Mark 12:14 asks the same, is it lawful to give tribute to Caesar, or not?
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the tribute question is the trap that caught the trappers: they brought the penny, and the penny bore Caesar's image. I hold that what bears Caesar's image goes to Caesar, and what bears God's image goes to God.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from κεντέω (to prick); a point ("centre"), i.e. a sting (figuratively, poison) or goad (figuratively, divine impulse):--prick, sting.
BiblicalUsage: Kentron means a sting, a prick, a goad: Acts 26:14 has the Lord saying to Saul, it is hard for thee to kick against the pricks: 1 Corinthians 15:55 cries, O death, where is thy sting? O grave, where is thy victory? 1 Corinthians 15:56 says the sting of death is sin, and the strength of sin is the law. Revelation 9:10 says the locusts had stings in their tails, and their power was to hurt men five months.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the sting is sin, and the goad is God: Saul kicked against the pricks until the Lord stopped him, and death's sting is pulled out at the resurrection. I hold that the victory song is already written, and the grave has no answer to it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Latin origin; a centurion, i.e. captain of one hundred soldiers:--centurion.
BiblicalUsage: Kentyrion means a centurion, a captain of a hundred soldiers. Mark 15:39 says when the centurion saw that Jesus so cried out, and gave up the ghost, he said, truly this man was the Son of God. Mark 15:44 says Pilate called the centurion, and asked him whether Jesus had been any while dead. Mark 15:45 says when Pilate knew it of the centurion, he gave the body to Joseph.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the centurion saw what the priests missed: the way Jesus died proved who he was. I hold that the soldier's confession stands at the foot of the cross, and Pilate's question only confirmed it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a hollow rock
BiblicalUsage: Keph means a hollow rock, a cliff. Job 30:6 says the outcasts dwell in the cliffs of the valleys, in caves of the earth, and in the rocks, and Jeremiah 4:29 says the people climb up upon the rocks when the horsemen come.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe rocks are a poor hiding place from God, but a good picture of how the poor live when the world casts them out.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: neuter of a derivative of G2776; a principal thing, i.e. main point; specially, an amount (of money):--sum.
BiblicalUsage: Kephalaion means the main point, the sum, or the sum of money. Acts 22:28 has the chief captain saying, with a great sum obtained I this freedom, and Hebrews 8:1 says, now of the things which we have spoken this is the sum: we have such an high priest.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the sum of it all is the priest: everything else adds up to him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from the same as G2774; (specially) to strike on the head:--wound in the head.
BiblicalUsage: Kephalaioo means to wound in the head. Mark 12:4 says the husbandmen cast stones at the servant, and wounded him in the head, and sent him away shamefully handled.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the wounded servant is every prophet before him, and the son they would kill next.
RelatedEvents: The Parable of the Wicked Tenants
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from the primary κάπτω (in the sense of seizing); the head (as the part most readily taken hold of), literally or figuratively:--head.
BiblicalUsage: Kephale means the head, the part that leads and rules: Romans 12:20 says if thine enemy hunger, feed him, for in so doing thou shalt heap coals of fire on his head. 1 Corinthians 11:3 says the head of every man is Christ, and the head of the woman is the man, and the head of Christ is God. 1 Corinthians 11:4 says every man praying or prophesying, having his head covered, dishonoureth his head. Ephesians 1:22 says God gave Christ to be the head over all things to the church.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe headship is a chain, not a ladder: God is the head of Christ, Christ is the head of every man, and Christ is the head over all things to the church. I hold that the head serves by ruling, and rules by serving, and that is why coals of fire on an enemy's head means kindness, not revenge.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2776; properly, a knob, i.e. (by implication) a roll (by extension from the end of a stick on which the manuscript was rolled):--volume.
BiblicalUsage: Kephalis means a roll, the volume of a book. Hebrews 10:7 says, lo, I come, in the volume of the book it is written of me, to do thy will, O God.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the whole book is about him: the volume was written so he could come and do the Father's will.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Kefar-ha-Ammoni, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Kephar-ha-Ammoni is a town in the allotment of Benjamin. Joshua 18:24 lists it among the twelve cities with their villages: Chephar-haammonai, and Ophni, and Gaba.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the town's name, village of the Ammonites, is a reminder that Benjamin's border ran right up against the nations around them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Chaldee origin (compare H3710); the Rock; Cephas (i.e. Kepha), a surname of Peter:--Cephas.
BiblicalUsage: Kephas, Cephas, is the Aramaic name Jesus gave to Simon, the Rock: John 1:42 says, thou art Simon the son of Jona: thou shalt be called Cephas, which is by interpretation, A stone. 1 Corinthians 1:12 shows the church dividing into parties: I am of Paul, and I of Apollos, and I of Cephas, and I of Christ. 1 Corinthians 15:5 says the risen Lord was seen of Cephas, then of the twelve.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Cephas is the name that holds Peter's whole story: the stone Jesus named, the party men divided over, and the first witness who saw the risen Lord.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to fetter
BiblicalUsage: Kephath means to fetter, to bind: Daniel 3:20 says Nebuchadnezzar commanded the most mighty men to bind Shadrach, Meshach, and Abed-nego, and cast them into the burning fiery furnace. Daniel 3:21 says these men were bound in their coats, their hosen, and their hats. Daniel 3:23 says they fell down bound into the midst of the fire. Daniel 3:24 says the king was astonied, and asked, did not we cast three men bound into the midst of the fire?
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the binding is the point: they went in bound, and the king saw four men walking loose. I hold that the fire burns the ropes, not the righteous, and the fourth man in the furnace is the one who was never bound at all.
RelatedPeople: Daniel; Shadrach; Meshach; Abednego; King Nebuchadnezzar
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a duplicate
BiblicalUsage: Kephel means a duplicate, double. Job 41:13 asks who can come to Leviathan with his double bridle, and Isaiah 40:2 says Jerusalem hath received of the LORD's hand double for all her sins.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe double cuts both ways: double judgment for sin, and double comfort when the warfare is accomplished.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a village (as covered in by walls); also a young lion (perhaps as covered with a mane)
BiblicalUsage: Kephiyr means a village, and also a young lion: Nehemiah 6:2 says Sanballat sent, come, let us meet together in some one of the villages in the plain of Ono, but they thought to do me mischief. Isaiah 11:6 says the calf and the young lion and the fatling together, and a little child shall lead them. Amos 3:4 asks, will a young lion cry out of his den, if he have taken nothing? Zechariah 11:3 says there is a voice of the roaring of young lions, for the pride of Jordan is spoiled.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the young lion is two pictures at once: the predator that roars when it has prey, and the cub that lies down with the lamb when the child leads. I hold that the villages of Ono were a trap, and the peace of Isaiah is the promise that the trap is not the end.
RelatedPeople: Nehemiah; Isaiah; Amos; Zechariah the Prophet
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Kephirah, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Kephirah is a town in Benjamin, named in the allotment and in the return from exile: Joshua 18:26 lists Mizpeh, and Chephirah, and Mozah. Ezra 2:25 counts the children of Kirjath-arim, Chephirah, and Beeroth, seven hundred and forty and three. Nehemiah 7:29 counts the same men of Kirjath-jearim, Chephirah, and Beeroth.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Chephirah's story is the return itself: a town named in the allotment, emptied by exile, and counted again when the exiles came home.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, a cover, i.e. (by implication) a tankard (or covered goblet); also white frost (as covering the ground)
BiblicalUsage: Kephowr means a bowl or covered cup, and also the hoarfrost: Exodus 16:14 says upon the face of the wilderness there lay a small round thing, as small as the hoar frost on the ground. 1 Chronicles 28:17 gives pure gold for the bowls and the cups of the temple. Ezra 1:10 counts thirty basons of gold, silver basons of a second sort four hundred and ten. Psalms 147:16 says he scattereth the hoarfrost like ashes.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the same word holds manna and gold: the frost that fed Israel in the wilderness, and the bowls that served his house. I hold that God provides both the daily bread and the holy vessels, and both are his.
RelatedEvents: Manna and Quail in the Wilderness
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain affinity; a garden:--garden.
BiblicalUsage: Kepos means a garden: Luke 13:19 says the mustard seed grew into a great tree in a man's garden, and the fowls lodged in its branches. John 18:1 says Jesus went over the brook Cedron, where was a garden, into the which he entered. John 18:26 asks, did not I see thee in the garden with him? John 19:41 says in the place where he was crucified there was a garden, and in the garden a new sepulchre.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the garden holds the whole story: the seed that grows, the garden where he was betrayed, and the garden where he was buried. I hold that the new tomb in the garden is where death ended, because the gardener himself rose there.
RelatedEvents: Jesus Prays in Gethsemane; The Resurrection
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2779 and οὖρος (a warden); a garden-keeper, i.e. gardener:--gardener.
BiblicalUsage: Kepouros means a gardener, the keeper of a garden. John 20:15 says Mary, supposing him to be the gardener, asked Jesus where he had laid the Lord's body.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Mary mistook the risen Lord for the gardener because he was the gardener, the one tending the new garden.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a purchase
BiblicalUsage: Kerah means a purchase, a provision bought for the table. 2 Kings 6:23 says Elisha prepared great provision for the Syrian raiders, and when they had eaten and drunk, he sent them away.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe feeding your enemies is stronger than fighting them: the bands of Syria came no more into the land of Israel.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: feminine of a presumed derivative of the base of G2768; something horn-like, i.e. (specially) the apex of a Hebrew letter (figuratively, the least particle):--tittle.
BiblicalUsage: Keraia means a tittle, the smallest stroke of a letter. Matthew 5:18 says one jot or one tittle shall in no wise pass from the law, till all be fulfilled, and Luke 16:17 says it is easier for heaven and earth to pass than one tittle of the law to fail.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God dots every letter of his law, and heaven and earth will pass before one of them does.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2766; a potter:--potter.
BiblicalUsage: Kerameus means a potter, one who shapes clay. Matthew 27:7 says they bought with the thirty pieces the potter's field, to bury strangers in. Matthew 27:10 says, and gave them for the potter's field, as the Lord appointed me. Romans 9:21 asks, hath not the potter power over the clay, of the same lump to make one vessel unto honour, and another unto dishonour?
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the potter's field is the price of betrayal turned into a burial ground for strangers, and the potter's power is the answer to every question about God's justice. I hold that I am the clay, not the potter, and the lump belongs to him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2766; made of clay, i.e. earthen:--of a potter.
BiblicalUsage: Keramikos means of a potter, made of clay. Revelation 2:27 says the overcomer shall rule the nations with a rod of iron, as the vessels of a potter shall they be broken to shivers.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe clay vessels break easily, and that is why I would rather be held by the potter than rule against him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: neuter of a presumed derivative of G2766; an earthenware vessel, i.e. jar:--pitcher.
BiblicalUsage: Keramion means a pitcher, an earthen jar for water. Mark 14:13 says the disciples will meet a man bearing a pitcher of water, and Luke 22:10 says the same: follow him into the house where he entereth in.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the man with the pitcher is the quiet signpost to the upper room, where the Lord had already prepared everything.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably from the base of G2767 (through the idea of mixing clay and water); earthenware, i.e. a tile (by analogy, a thin roof or awning):--tiling.
BiblicalUsage: Keramos means earthenware, tiling. Luke 5:19 says the friends let the paralysed man down through the tiling with his couch into the midst before Jesus.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the roof was no barrier to faith: they broke through the tiling because they knew Jesus could heal.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Keran, an aboriginal Idumaean
BiblicalUsage: Keran, Cheran, is a son of Dishon, named in the genealogy of Edom. Genesis 36:26 lists the children of Dishon: Hemdan, and Eshban, and Ithran, and Cheran. 1 Chronicles 1:41 repeats the line: the sons of Dishon, Amram, and Eshban, and Ithran, and Cheran.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Cheran is kept in the record because God counts the families of Edom as carefully as he counts the families of Israel.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: prolonged form of a more primary κεράω (which is used in certain tenses); to mingle, i.e. (by implication) to pour out (for drinking):--fill, pour out. Compare G3396.
BiblicalUsage: Kerannymi means to mingle, to pour out mixed. Revelation 14:10 says the wine of the wrath of God is poured out without mixture into the cup of his indignation, and Revelation 18:6 says in the cup which she hath filled fill to her double.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God's wrath is unmixed and full measure, and that is why I want my cup filled with his mercy instead.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a primary κάρ (the hair of the head); a horn (literally or figuratively):--horn.
BiblicalUsage: Keras means a horn, the sign of strength and power: Luke 1:69 says God hath raised up an horn of salvation for us in the house of his servant David. Revelation 5:6 shows the Lamb as it had been slain, having seven horns and seven eyes. Revelation 9:13 hears a voice from the four horns of the golden altar. Revelation 12:3 shows a great red dragon, having seven heads and ten horns.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the horn is strength with a direction: the dragon's horns are power for evil, and the Lamb's seven horns are power for salvation. I hold that the horn raised up in David's house is the one that saves, because it belongs to the Lamb who was slain.
RelatedPeople: Jesus; King David; John the Apostle
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: neuter of a presumed derivative of G2768; something horned, i.e. (specially) the pod of the carob-tree:--husk.
BiblicalUsage: Keration means a husk, the pod of the carob tree. Luke 15:16 says the prodigal would fain have filled his belly with the husks that the swine did eat, and no man gave unto him.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe husks are what sin leaves you hungry for, and no man can give you what only the Father's house has.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to proclaim
BiblicalUsage: Keraz is the Aramaic word to proclaim, to cry out. Daniel 5:29 says Belshazzar made a proclamation concerning Daniel, that he should be the third ruler in the kingdom.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the king's proclamation came too late to save him, but Daniel's God had already written the true verdict on the wall.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2771; to gain (literally or figuratively):--(get) gain, win.
BiblicalUsage: Kerdaino means to gain, to win: Matthew 16:26 asks, what is a man profited, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul? Luke 9:25 asks the same, for what is a man advantaged, if he gain the whole world, and lose himself? 1 Corinthians 9:19 says Paul made himself servant unto all, that I might gain the more. Philippians 3:8 says Paul counts all things but loss, that I may win Christ.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe gain is the question every life answers: the world gained and the soul lost, or all things lost and Christ won. I hold that Paul's arithmetic is the only one that adds up, because Christ is worth more than the whole world.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain affinity; gain (pecuniary or genitive case):--gain, lucre.
BiblicalUsage: Kerdos means gain, profit, lucre. Philippians 1:21 says, for to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain. Philippians 3:7 says, what things were gain to me, those I counted loss for Christ. Titus 1:11 warns of men subverting whole houses, teaching things which they ought not, for filthy lucre's sake.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe gain is holy when it is Christ and filthy when it is money: Paul counted death gain because living was Christ. I hold that the teachers who sell the gospel for lucre have their gain and their judgment both.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a garden or vineyard
BiblicalUsage: Kerem means a vineyard, a garden of vines: 1 Chronicles 27:27 names Shimei over the vineyards, and Zabdi over the increase of the vineyards for the wine cellars. Isaiah 5:1 sings to the wellbeloved a song touching his vineyard, in a very fruitful hill. Isaiah 36:17 promises a land of corn and wine, a land of bread and vineyards. Zephaniah 1:13 says they shall plant vineyards, but not drink the wine thereof.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the vineyard is Israel in miniature: planted in a fruitful hill, tended by stewards, and judged when it bears wild grapes. I hold that the land of vineyards is the promise, and the vineyard planted but never drunk from is the judgment.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: the paunch or belly (as swelling out)
BiblicalUsage: Keres means the belly, the paunch. Jeremiah 51:34 says Nebuchadrezzar hath swallowed me up like a dragon, he hath filled his belly with my delicates.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Babylon's belly is never full, and God will make her give back what she swallowed.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a Kerethite or life-guardsman
BiblicalUsage: Kerethiy means a Cherethite, one of David's life-guardsmen: 1 Samuel 30:14 says the Amalekites made an invasion upon the south of the Cherethites, and burned Ziklag with fire. 2 Samuel 20:7 says Joab's men, and the Cherethites, and the Pelethites went out to pursue Sheba. 1 Chronicles 18:17 says Benaiah was over the Cherethites and the Pelethites. Zephaniah 2:5 cries woe to the nation of the Cherethites, for the word of the LORD is against you.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the Cherethites show how a people can be both guard and judged: they kept David's life, and their own coast fell under the word of the LORD. I hold that nearness to the king is no shelter when the king's God speaks against you.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: diminutive from κηός (wax); a cell for honey, i.e. (collectively) the comb:--(honey-)comb.
BiblicalUsage: Kerion means a honeycomb, the comb of the hive. Luke 24:42 says they gave the risen Jesus a piece of a broiled fish, and of an honeycomb.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the risen Lord ate fish and honey to prove he was no ghost: he has a body, and it is hungry.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Kerith, a brook of Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Kerith is the brook where God hid Elijah from Ahab. 1 Kings 17:3 says, hide thyself by the brook Cherith, that is before Jordan. 1 Kings 17:5 says Elijah went and did according unto the word of the LORD, and dwelt by the brook Cherith.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the brook is God's hiding place: the ravens brought bread there, and the prophet learned that God feeds his own in the wilderness.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a cutting (of the matrimonial bond), i.e. divorce
BiblicalUsage: Keriythuwth means a cutting, a bill of divorcement: Deuteronomy 24:1 says if a man find some uncleanness in his wife, let him write her a bill of divorcement, and send her out of his house. Deuteronomy 24:3 covers the latter husband who does the same. Isaiah 50:1 asks, where is the bill of your mother's divorcement, whom I have put away? Jeremiah 3:8 says God gave backsliding Israel a bill of divorce, yet her treacherous sister Judah feared not.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe divorce is a cutting, and God uses the word for his own people: he put Israel away for adultery, and still asked where the bill was. I hold that the law's bill was God's mercy to the wife, and the prophets' bill was God's grief over the bride.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2751; a clipping (bit), i.e. (specially) a coin:--money.
BiblicalUsage: Kerma means a small coin, a clipping. John 2:15 says Jesus poured out the changers' money, and overthrew the tables.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe small coins in God's house can still be a big offence when the house becomes a market.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a derivative of G2772; a handler of coins, i.e. money-broker:--changer of money.
BiblicalUsage: Kermatistes means a money-changer, a handler of coins. John 2:14 says Jesus found in the temple those that sold oxen and sheep and doves, and the changers of money sitting.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the changers sat comfortably in God's house until Jesus stood up, and I want no seat where he would overturn the table.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Kerub, a place in Babylon
BiblicalUsage: Kerub is a place in Babylon, named among the towns the exiles came up from. Ezra 2:59 says these were they which went up from Tel-melah, Tel-harsa, Cherub, Addan, and Immer, but they could not shew their father's house. Nehemiah 7:61 says the same, from Tel-melah, Tel-haresha, Cherub, Addon, and Immer.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Cherub is remembered for a hard reason: the men who came from it could not prove their house, and the record says so honestly.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a cherub or imaginary figure
BiblicalUsage: Keruwb means a cherub, the winged figure of God's presence: Genesis 3:24 says God placed Cherubims at the east of the garden of Eden, and a flaming sword, to keep the way of the tree of life. Exodus 25:18 says thou shalt make two cherubims of gold, in the two ends of the mercy seat. 1 Chronicles 13:6 says the ark of God dwelleth between the cherubims. Psalms 99:1 says he sitteth between the cherubims, let the earth be moved.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the cherubim guard the way back to life and overshadow the mercy seat: the same wings that shut Eden open the way to atonement. I hold that the God who sits between the cherubim is not far off, and the earth should tremble because he reigns.
RelatedEvents: Creation; David Brings the Ark to Jerusalem
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2784; a proclamation (especially of the gospel; by implication, the gospel itself):--preaching.
BiblicalUsage: Kerygma means a proclamation, the preaching itself: Matthew 12:41 says the men of Nineveh repented at the preaching of Jonas. 1 Corinthians 1:21 says it pleased God by the foolishness of preaching to save them that believe. 2 Timothy 4:17 says the Lord stood with Paul, that by me the preaching might be fully known, and all the Gentiles might hear. Titus 1:3 says God manifested his word through preaching, committed unto me.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the proclamation is the power: Nineveh repented at it, the Gentiles heard it, and God saves by its foolishness. I hold that preaching is not man's idea, it is God's chosen way to save, and I will not be ashamed of it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain affinity; to herald (as a public crier), especially divine truth (the gospel):--preacher(-er), proclaim, publish.
BiblicalUsage: Kerysso means to herald, to preach as a public crier: Matthew 4:17 says from that time Jesus began to preach, and to say, repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand. Luke 12:3 says what ye have spoken in the ear in closets shall be proclaimed upon the housetops. Romans 10:15 asks, how shall they preach, except they be sent? 1 Corinthians 1:23 says, but we preach Christ crucified, unto the Jews a stumblingblock, and unto the Greeks foolishness.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe preaching is a herald's work: Jesus began with repent, the closets will be shouted from the rooftops, and the message is Christ crucified. I hold that no one preaches unless sent, and the sent ones carry the same word Paul did.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2784; a herald, i.e. of divine truth (especially of the gospel):--preacher.
BiblicalUsage: Keryx means a herald, a preacher of divine truth. 1 Timothy 2:7 says, whereunto I am ordained a preacher, and an apostle, a teacher of the Gentiles in faith and verity. 2 Timothy 1:11 says the same, I am appointed a preacher, and an apostle, and a teacher. 2 Peter 2:5 says God saved Noah the eighth person, a preacher of righteousness, bringing in the flood upon the world of the ungodly.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the herald is appointed, not self-made: Paul was ordained and appointed, and Noah preached righteousness while the world drowned. I hold that the preacher's job is the same in every age, to speak the truth in Christ and not lie.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a young sheep
BiblicalUsage: Keseb means a young sheep, a lamb: Genesis 30:40 says Jacob did separate the lambs, and set the faces of the flocks toward the ringstraked. Leviticus 7:23 says ye shall eat no manner of fat, of ox, or of sheep, or of goat. Numbers 18:17 says the firstling of a sheep thou shalt not redeem, for they are holy. Deuteronomy 14:4 lists the beasts which ye shall eat: the ox, the sheep, and the goat.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the lamb is the quiet centre of the whole law: separated by Jacob, kept holy as firstling, and eaten only as God commanded. I hold that every young sheep in these verses was a rehearsal for the Lamb who would be offered once.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Kesed, a relative of Abraham
BiblicalUsage: Kesed, Chesed, is a son of Nahor, Abraham's brother, named in the genealogy after the binding of Isaac. Genesis 22:22 lists him with his brothers: Chesed, and Hazo, and Pildash, and Jidlaph, and Bethuel.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Chesed's one verse is the quiet after the mountain: the family goes on, and from Bethuel his brother will come Rebekah, the wife of Isaac.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: magic
BiblicalUsage: Kesheph means magic, sorcery, witchcraft: 2 Kings 9:22 has Jehu asking, what peace, so long as the whoredoms of thy mother Jezebel and her witchcrafts are so many? Isaiah 47:9 says loss of children and widowhood shall come upon Babylon for the multitude of thy sorceries. Micah 5:12 promises, I will cut off witchcrafts out of thine hand. Nahum 3:4 calls Nineveh the mistress of witchcrafts, that selleth nations through her whoredoms.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe sorcery is never a small thing: it sells nations, it crowns harlots, and it brings the loss of children in one day. I hold that God cuts it off with his own hand, and I want no part of what he cuts off.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {something written, i.e. a writing, record or book}
BiblicalUsage: Kethab means something written, a writing, a record, a book: Ezra 7:22 gives salt without prescribing how much, the king's order written down. Daniel 5:7 has the king crying, whosoever shall read this writing, and shew me the interpretation, shall be clothed with scarlet. Daniel 5:8 says the wise men could not read the writing. Daniel 5:15 says they could not shew the interpretation of the thing.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe writing is the test of every kingdom: the king's order is written and obeyed, but God's writing on the wall no wise man can read. I hold that the only writing that matters in the end is the one God's finger writes.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {to grave, by implication, to write (describe, inscribe, prescribe, subscribe)}
BiblicalUsage: Kethab means to write, to grave, to inscribe: Ezra 5:7 says they sent a letter unto Darius, wherein was written thus, unto Darius the king, all peace. Daniel 5:5 says fingers of a man's hand wrote over against the candlestick upon the plaister of the wall. Daniel 6:25 says king Darius wrote unto all people, nations, and languages, Peace be multiplied unto you. Daniel 7:1 says Daniel wrote the dream, and told the sum of the matters.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe writing fixes what men say: a letter to a king, a decree to all nations, a dream told in full, and a hand writing on a wall. I hold that God writes too, and his writing outlasts every king's.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {a wall (as gathering inmates)}
BiblicalUsage: Kethal means a wall, the wall of a house. Ezra 5:8 says the house of the great God is builded with great stones, and timber is laid in the walls, and Daniel 5:5 says fingers wrote upon the plaister of the wall of the king's palace.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe walls tell the story either way: one wall rose for God's house, and on the other his finger wrote a kingdom's end.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, something carved out, i.e. ore; hence, gold (pure as originally mined)
KeyPassages: Job 28:16; Song of Solomon 5:11; Lamentations 4:1; Daniel 10:5
BiblicalUsage: Kethem means fine gold, ore carved out pure as it was mined: Job 28:16 says wisdom cannot be valued with the gold of Ophir, with the precious onyx, or the sapphire: Song of Solomon 5:11 says his head is as the most fine gold, his locks are bushy, and black as a raven. Lamentations 4:1 cries, how is the gold become dim! how is the most fine gold changed! Daniel 10:5 shows a man clothed in linen, whose loins were girded with fine gold of Uphaz.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe fine gold is the measure of everything: wisdom is worth more than it, love's bridegroom is crowned with it, and Jerusalem's gold went dim when she sinned. I hold that the gold that never dims is the man in linen, girded with the gold of Uphaz.
RelatedBooks: Job; Song of Solomon; Lamentations; Daniel
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, a circlet, i.e. a diadem
BiblicalUsage: Kether means a crown, a diadem, a circlet. Esther 1:11 says bring Vashti the queen before the king with the crown royal, to shew the people her beauty. Esther 2:17 says the king set the royal crown upon Esther's head, and made her queen instead of Vashti. Esther 6:8 says let the royal apparel be brought, and the crown royal which is set upon his head.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the crown passes in this book from the disobedient to the chosen: Vashti wore it and refused, Esther wore it and risked her life. I hold that a crown is only safe on the head God puts it on.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a letter or other mark branded on the skin
BiblicalUsage: Kethobeth means a mark branded on the skin, a tattoo. Leviticus 19:28 says ye shall not make any cuttings in your flesh for the dead, nor print any marks upon you.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God marks his people by his Spirit, not by cuts in the flesh, and this law kept Israel from copying the mourning rites of the dead.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a shirt
KeyPassages: Genesis 3:21; Genesis 37:3; 2 Samuel 13:18; Song of Solomon 5:3
BiblicalUsage: Kethoneth means a coat, a shirt, a tunic: Genesis 3:21 says unto Adam also and to his wife did the LORD God make coats of skins, and clothed them. Genesis 37:3 says Israel made Joseph a coat of many colours. 2 Samuel 13:18 says Tamar had a garment of divers colours upon her, for with such robes were the king's daughters apparelled. Song of Solomon 5:3 says, I have put off my coat, how shall I put it on?
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the coat tells the story of the Bible: God sewed the first one to cover shame, Jacob sewed one that bred envy, and a king's daughter wore one that was torn away. I hold that the only coat that never tears is the one God sews himself.
RelatedPeople: Adam; Eve; Joseph, Son of Jacob; Jacob
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably from the base of G5490; a huge fish (as gaping for prey):--whale.
BiblicalUsage: Kētos is the huge fish, the great sea creature that gapes for its prey. Matthew 12:40 puts it at the centre of Jesus' own sign: as Jonas was three days and three nights in the whale's belly, so the Son of man would be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Jesus chose this sign on purpose, because the fish that swallowed Jonah and gave him back is the picture of a death that does not keep its dead.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a branding
BiblicalUsage: Keviyah is a branding, a burn-mark left by fire. Exodus 21:25 sets it in the law of like for like: burning for burning, wound for wound, stripe for stripe.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the brand matters because God measures out justice exactly, never more than the hurt and never less.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a club or sledge-hammer
BiblicalUsage: Keylaph is a club or sledge-hammer, a heavy tool for breaking. Psalms 74:6 shows the enemy using axes and hammers to break down the carved work of the sanctuary all at once.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the hammer in this psalm is a warning that what took generations of craftsmen to carve can be smashed in a day when God lets the enemy in.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Kezib, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Chezib is a place in Palestine, named once, in Genesis 38:5, where Judah's wife bore Shelah while the family story was turning dark. The verse gives no description of the town, only the fact that Shelah was born there.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe even a one-verse place belongs on the map, because God records where His promises travel, not only where they arrive.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain derivation; a box, i.e. the sacred ark and that of Noah:--ark.
KeyPassages: Matthew 24:38; Luke 17:27; Hebrews 9:4; Hebrews 11:7; 1 Peter 3:20; Revelation 11:19
BiblicalUsage: Kibōtos is the ark, and the New Testament uses the one word for both arks. Matthew 24:38 and Luke 17:27 tell of Noah entering the ark before the flood destroyed all, Hebrews 11:7 says he prepared it by faith to the saving of his house, and 1 Peter 3:20 counts the eight souls saved by water. Hebrews 9:4 turns to the other ark, the ark of the covenant overlaid with gold, holding the manna, Aaron's rod and the tables; Revelation 11:19 sees that ark again in the temple of God in heaven.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the two arks are one story: God saves His people through a wooden box, and He meets them above the mercy seat. I hold that Noah's ark points to Christ, who carries His people through the judgment instead of leaving them in it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, length, i.e. a measure (of uncertain dimension)
BiblicalUsage: Kibrah is a little way, a short measure of distance. Genesis 35:16 says there was but a little way to come to Ephrath when Rachel travailed and died, and Genesis 48:7 has Jacob remembering the same road and the same loss. 2 Kings 5:19 uses it once more, when Naaman departs from Elisha a little way.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a little way can hold a whole life: Rachel died a little way from Ephrath, and Jacob never forgot the road.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a ewe
KeyPassages: Genesis 21:28; Genesis 21:29; Genesis 21:30; Leviticus 14:10; Numbers 6:14; 2 Samuel 12:3
BiblicalUsage: Kibsah is a ewe, a female sheep. Genesis 21:28 has Abraham setting seven ewe lambs apart, and Genesis 21:29 and Genesis 21:30 carry Abimelech's question and Abraham's answer, that they are a witness, Leviticus 14:10 calls for one ewe lamb without blemish in the cleansing of the leper, and Numbers 6:14 brings one for the Nazirite's sin offering. 2 Samuel 12:3 makes the word unforgettable: the poor man's one little ewe lamb, which ate of his meat and lay in his bosom like a daughter, is the lamb the rich man takes for his traveller.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the ewe lamb is where the Bible teaches the heart what the law teaches the head: a sacrifice is not a thing, it is something loved. I hold that Nathan's parable works because the lamb had a name in the poor man's house, and that is why David's anger was right and his guilt was plain.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a smelting furnace (as reducing metals)
BiblicalUsage: Kibshan is a smelting furnace, the place where metal is reduced by fire. Genesis 19:28 shows the smoke of Sodom and Gomorrah going up as the smoke of a furnace, Exodus 19:18 has Sinai itself smoking as a furnace when the LORD descends upon it in fire, and Exodus 9:8 and Exodus 9:10 take handfuls of ashes from the furnace, which Moses sprinkles toward heaven until boils break out on man and beast.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the furnace is God's picture of judgment as refining fire: what goes into it comes out changed, and the smoke of Sodom rises like a warning to every city that forgets Him. I hold that the ashes of the furnace in Egypt became boils on Pharaoh's people, because the fire God lights against the proud always falls on the proud.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, covered, i.e. a throne (as canopied)
KeyPassages: Genesis 41:40; 2 Samuel 3:10; 1 Kings 10:18; Isaiah 6:1; Jeremiah 17:12; Psalms 103:19
BiblicalUsage: Kisse is the throne, the covered seat of a king. Genesis 41:40 has Pharaoh telling Joseph that only in the throne will he be greater than him, 2 Samuel 3:10 promises the throne of David over Israel and Judah, and 1 Kings 10:18 describes Solomon's great throne of ivory overlaid with gold. Isaiah 6:1 lifts the word past every earthly king: in the year king Uzziah died, Isaiah saw the Lord sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up. Jeremiah 17:12 calls it a glorious high throne from the beginning, the place of God's sanctuary, and Psalms 103:19 says the LORD hath prepared his throne in the heavens, and his kingdom ruleth over all.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe every throne in the Bible is measured against the one in heaven. I hold that Pharaoh's throne and Solomon's throne and David's throne all pass away, and the throne that stands is the one Isaiah saw, high and lifted up, where the Lord still sits.
RelatedBooks: Genesis; 2 Samuel; 1 Kings; Isaiah; Jeremiah; Psalms
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: in a good sense, trust; in a bad one, silliness
BiblicalUsage: Kislah holds two meanings at once: in a good sense, trust; in a bad one, silliness. Job 4:6 asks, is not this thy fear, thy confidence, thy hope, and the uprightness of thy ways, while Psalms 85:8 warns God's saints not to turn again to folly.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the one word carries its own warning: confidence in God and folly look alike from the outside, and only the direction of the trust tells them apart.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Kisleu, the 9th Hebrew month
BiblicalUsage: Chisleu is the ninth Hebrew month. Nehemiah 1:1 dates Nehemiah's grief for Jerusalem to the month Chisleu, in the twentieth year, as he stood in Shushan the palace, and Zechariah 7:1 dates the word of the LORD to Zechariah to the fourth day of the ninth month, even in Chisleu.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the month matters because God dates His work: Nehemiah's prayer and Zechariah's word both arrived in Chisleu, and the calendar of His people is a record of when He spoke.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Kisloth-Tabor, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Chisloth-tabor is a place in Palestine, named once as a border mark. Joshua 19:12 draws the border of Issachar from Sarid eastward to the border of Chisloth-tabor, then out to Daberath.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe border towns belong in the record too: the inheritance was measured out town by town, and God gave His people land with edges they could walk.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Kislon, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Chislon is an Israelite, named once as a father. Numbers 34:21 names Elidad the son of Chislon, of the tribe of Benjamin, among the princes appointed to divide the land.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Chislon is remembered the way most faithful men are: not for what he did, but for the son he raised to stand in the work of dividing God's land.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a circle, i.e. (by implication) a circumjacent tract or region, especially the Ghor or valley of the Jordan; also a (round) loaf; also a talent (or large [round] coin)
KeyPassages: Genesis 13:10; Exodus 25:39; Deuteronomy 34:3; Judges 8:5; 1 Samuel 2:36; 2 Samuel 12:30
BiblicalUsage: Kikkar is a circle, and the word stretches to cover a plain, a loaf, and a talent. Genesis 13:10 shows Lot beholding all the plain of Jordan, well watered like the garden of the LORD, and Deuteronomy 34:3 calls it the plain of the valley of Jericho. Exodus 25:39 measures the lampstand's gold by a talent of pure gold, and 2 Samuel 12:30 weighs a king's crown at a talent of gold with precious stones. Judges 8:5 asks for loaves of bread for Gideon's faint men, and 1 Samuel 2:36 has the fallen house of Eli begging for a morsel of bread.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the round word teaches a round truth: the plain that tempted Lot, the talent that crowned a king, and the loaf that fed a faint man are all measured by God. I hold that what is round in Scripture comes back to where it began, and the plain of Jordan ends in judgment while the bread of God ends in life.
RelatedBooks: Genesis; Exodus; Deuteronomy; Judges; 1 Samuel; 2 Samuel
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a talent
BiblicalUsage: Kikker is the Aramaic word for a talent. Ezra 7:22 sets the king's limit at an hundred talents of silver for the house of God, with measures of wheat and baths of wine and oil beside it, and salt without prescribing how much.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the open-handed measure at the end is the point: silver and wheat are counted, but the salt for God's house is given without a limit.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Kilab, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Chileab is David's second son, named once in the list of his sons born in Hebron. 2 Samuel 3:3 calls him the son of Abigail the wife of Nabal the Carmelite, between Amnon and Absalom.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Chileab's single verse is enough: he is the son of the wise woman who kept David from bloodguilt, and his name stands in the line that led to the throne.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: two heterogeneities
BiblicalUsage: Kilayim means two heterogeneities, two kinds that must not be mixed. Leviticus 19:19 forbids letting cattle gender with a diverse kind, sowing a field with mingled seed, or wearing a garment mingled of linen and woollen, and Deuteronomy 22:9 repeats the ban on divers seeds in the vineyard, lest the fruit be defiled.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the mixtures are forbidden because God loves clean lines: His people were to look separate, sow separate, and keep separate what He made separate.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably of foreign origin; Cilicia, a region of Asia Minor:--Cilicia.
BiblicalUsage: Cilicia is a region of Asia Minor, and it sits at the edge of the gospel's first journeys. Acts 6:9 has men of Cilicia disputing with Stephen, Acts 15:23 sends the apostles' letter to the Gentile brethren in Antioch and Syria and Cilicia, and Galatians 1:21 has Paul himself coming into the regions of Syria and Cilicia.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Cilicia matters because it is where the persecutor came from and where the preacher went back to: Paul's home ground became the gospel's ground.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: pining, destruction
BiblicalUsage: Killayon is pining, a wasting away, and in its second use, destruction. Deuteronomy 28:65 promises the disobedient a trembling heart, and failing of eyes, and sorrow of mind, and Isaiah 10:22 says the consumption decreed shall overflow with righteousness.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the pining of Deuteronomy and the consumption of Isaiah are the same word from two sides: what wastes the rebel is what God has decreed, and it overflows with righteousness.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Kilmad, a place apparently in the Assyrian empire
BiblicalUsage: Chilmad is a place apparently in the Assyrian empire, named once among the merchants of Tyre. Ezekiel 27:23 lists Haran, and Canneh, and Eden, the merchants of Sheba, Asshur, and Chilmad, as traders with Tyre.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Chilmad stands in the list to show how wide Tyre's trade ran, and how far the fall of a proud city reaches.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a kidney (as an essential organ); figuratively, the mind (as the interior self)
KeyPassages: Exodus 29:13; Leviticus 3:4; Deuteronomy 32:14; Job 16:13; Psalms 7:9; Proverbs 23:16
BiblicalUsage: Kilyah is a kidney, and in the Bible the kidneys are the seat of the inner self. Exodus 29:13 and Leviticus 3:4 take the two kidneys with their fat for the altar, and Deuteronomy 32:14 praises the fat of kidneys of wheat. Job 16:13 cries that God cleaveth my reins asunder, and Psalms 7:9 says the righteous God trieth the hearts and reins, while Proverbs 23:16 promises, my reins shall rejoice, when thy lips speak right things.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God reads the reins the way men read the face: the kidneys are where motives live, and He tries them. I hold that the same inward parts offered on the altar are the ones that rejoice when truth is spoken, because God made the inside to answer to Him.
RelatedBooks: Exodus; Leviticus; Deuteronomy; Job; Psalms; Proverbs
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Kiljon, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Chilion is one of the two sons of Elimelech and Naomi. Ruth 1:2 names Mahlon and Chilion, Ephrathites of Bethlehem-judah, who came into the country of Moab, and Ruth 1:5 says both sons died there, leaving Naomi a widow of her two sons and her husband.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Chilion's short life is the hinge of Ruth: his death in Moab leaves Naomi empty, and her emptiness is what brings Ruth to Bethlehem and to Boaz.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Kimham, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Chimham is an Israelite who crosses the Jordan in David's place. 2 Samuel 19:37 has Barzillai asking David to let his servant Chimham go over with the king instead of him, and 2 Samuel 19:38 has David answering, Chimham shall go over with me, and I will do to him that which shall seem good unto thee. Jeremiah 41:17 remembers him still, in the habitation of Chimham by Bethlehem, where the fugitives stopped on their way to Egypt.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Chimham is the picture of a faithful servant carried by another man's loyalty: Barzillai's gift became David's companion, and his name outlived them both beside Bethlehem.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: obscuration (as if from shrinkage of light, i.e. an eclipse (only in plural)
BiblicalUsage: Kimrir is obscuration, a darkening of the light as if the sun were shrinking. Job 3:5 calls on darkness and the shadow of death to stain the day of his birth, and on the blackness of the day to terrify it.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Job's eclipse is honest grief: he does not ask God to explain the darkness, he asks the darkness to cover the day he was born.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a package
BiblicalUsage: Kinah is a package, a bundle of wares. Jeremiah 10:17 tells the inhabitant of the fortress to gather up her wares out of the land, because the siege is coming.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the single verse is a whole sermon: when judgment comes, all you can carry is what you can bundle, and the rest stays behind.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of foreign origin (compare H7076); cinnamon:--cinnamon.
BiblicalUsage: Kinamomon is cinnamon, the sweet spice of the merchants. Revelation 18:13 lists it among the cargoes of fallen Babylon: cinnamon, and odours, and ointments, and frankincense, and wine, and oil, and fine flour, and wheat, and beasts, and sheep, and horses, and chariots, and slaves, and souls of men.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe cinnamon belongs in that list on purpose: the luxury that perfumed Babylon's trade ends in the same sentence as the souls of men she bought and sold.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2794; to undergo peril:--be in danger, be (stand) in jeopardy.
BiblicalUsage: Kindyneuo means to be in danger, to stand in jeopardy. Luke 8:23 has the disciples in jeopardy on the lake when the storm fills the boat, Acts 19:27 and Acts 19:40 have Demetrius and the town clerk warning that the silversmiths' craft and the city itself are in danger, and 1 Corinthians 15:30 has Paul asking, why stand we in jeopardy every hour?
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Paul's question answers the storm: the disciples were in jeopardy for an hour, and Paul stood in it every hour, because the gospel is worth the danger. I hold that jeopardy is the normal weather of the Christian life, not the exception.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain derivation; danger:--peril.
BiblicalUsage: Kindynos is danger, peril itself. Romans 8:35 asks whether peril shall separate us from the love of Christ, and 2 Corinthians 11:26 counts Paul's perils one by one: perils of waters, of robbers, of his own countrymen, of the heathen, in the city, in the wilderness, in the sea, among false brethren.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Romans 8:35 is the answer to 2 Corinthians 11:26: Paul survived every peril on the list because none of them could separate him from the love of Christ.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from κίω (poetic for εἶμι, to go); to stir (transitively), literally or figuratively:--(re-)move(-r), way.
KeyPassages: Matthew 23:4; Matthew 27:39; Mark 15:29; Acts 17:28; Acts 21:30; Revelation 2:5
BiblicalUsage: Kineo means to stir, to move. Matthew 23:4 says the Pharisees will not move heavy burdens with one of their fingers, Matthew 27:39 and Mark 15:29 have the passers-by wagging their heads at the crucified Jesus, and Acts 21:30 says all the city was moved when Paul was seized in the temple. Acts 17:28 turns the word toward God: in him we live, and move, and have our being. Revelation 2:5 warns the church at Ephesus that Christ will remove its candlestick unless it repents.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe kineo runs both ways: men move their heads in mockery and cities move in rage, but we live and move in God. I hold that the only moving that matters is the one in Acts 17:28, because a candlestick can be removed and a city can be stirred, but in Him we have our being.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2795; a stirring:--moving.
BiblicalUsage: Kinesis is a stirring, the moving of the water. John 5:3 pictures the multitude of impotent folk, of blind, halt, withered, waiting for the moving of the water at Bethesda. The word stands only here, in the Received Text's account of the pool.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the waiting is the picture: a crowd of sick people hoping the water will stir, and the Healer standing among them unrecognized.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Kinneroth or Kinnereth, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Chinnereth is a place in Palestine, the sea and the plain beside it. Numbers 34:11 sets the border of the land at the side of the sea of Chinnereth, Deuteronomy 3:17 names Chinnereth as the northern edge of the plain down to the salt sea, and Joshua 11:2 places kings south of Chinneroth among those Joshua fought.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the sea of Chinnereth is the same water Jesus would walk and preach beside: the border of the old land became the shore of the new teaching.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a harp
KeyPassages: Genesis 4:21; 1 Samuel 10:5; 2 Samuel 6:5; 1 Kings 10:12; 1 Chronicles 13:8; 2 Chronicles 5:12
BiblicalUsage: Kinnor is the harp. Genesis 4:21 names Jubal as the father of all such as handle the harp and organ, 1 Samuel 10:5 has prophets coming down with harp before them, and 2 Samuel 6:5 and 1 Chronicles 13:8 have David and all Israel playing before the LORD on harps. 1 Kings 10:12 says Solomon made harps of almug trees for the house of the LORD, and 2 Chronicles 5:12 sets the Levite singers with harps at the east end of the altar.
