TheologicalSignificance: I believe the harp runs from Jubal to the temple because music was never decoration in Israel: it was how the people played before the LORD. I hold that David's harp and the Levites' harps say the same thing, that worship is something you do with your hands, not only with your mouth.
RelatedBooks: Genesis; 1 Samuel; 2 Samuel; 1 Kings; 1 Chronicles; 2 Chronicles
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a leaf of a palmtree
BiblicalUsage: Kippah is the branch of a palm tree, the top of the tree. Job 15:32 says the wicked man's branch shall not be green, and Isaiah 9:14 and Isaiah 19:15 both use it with head and tail: the LORD will cut off from Israel head and tail, branch and rush, in one day, and no work shall remain for Egypt which the head or tail, branch or rush, may do.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe branch and rush are the whole nation from top to bottom: when God cuts them off, nothing is left to do the work.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: expiation (only in plural)
KeyPassages: Exodus 29:36; Exodus 30:10; Leviticus 23:27; Leviticus 23:28; Leviticus 25:9; Numbers 5:8
BiblicalUsage: Kippur is expiation, the atonement, and it is always plural in this form. Exodus 29:36 commands the daily bullock for a sin offering for atonement, Exodus 30:10 has Aaron making atonement on the horns of the altar once a year with the blood of the sin offering of atonements, and Leviticus 23:27 and Leviticus 23:28 name the tenth day of the seventh month a day of atonement, when Israel shall afflict their souls and do no work. Numbers 5:8 provides the ram of the atonement for a trespass with no kinsman, and Leviticus 25:9 sounds the trumpet of the jubile on the day of atonement.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the day of atonement is the hinge of the whole year: one day when the blood is carried in and the people wait outside. I hold that every kippur pointed forward to the one atonement that does not need repeating, because the blood offered once is enough.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to lay waste
BiblicalUsage: Kirsem means to lay waste, to gnaw a thing down. Psalms 80:13 pictures it plainly: the boar out of the wood doth waste the vine, and the wild beast of the field doth devour it.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the boar is the enemy at the wall: Israel is the vine God planted, and the wild beast eats what God planted when the hedge is down.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H7027); Cis (i.e. Kish), an Israelite:--Cis.
BiblicalUsage: Cis is Kish, the father of Saul. Acts 13:21 says that when Israel desired a king, God gave unto them Saul the son of Cis, a man of the tribe of Benjamin, by the space of forty years.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Kish is named because Saul's kingship is a family story before it is a national one: the son of Cis was the king Israel asked for, and the king they had to learn from.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a young ewe
BiblicalUsage: Kisbah is a young ewe, a female lamb of the flock. Leviticus 5:6 brings her as the trespass offering for a sin: a female from the flock, a lamb or a kid of the goats, for a sin offering, and the priest shall make an atonement for him concerning his sin.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the young ewe is the quiet side of sacrifice: not the great bullock of the feast, but the small female lamb a single sinner could bring, and God accepted it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: success, advantage
BiblicalUsage: Kishron is success, advantage, the profit of a man's work. Ecclesiastes 2:21 sees a man whose labour is in wisdom and knowledge and equity, yet leaves it to a man that hath not laboured therein, and Ecclesiastes 4:4 sees every right work envied by a neighbour. Ecclesiastes 5:11 adds that when goods increase, they are increased that eat them, and what good is there to the owners thereof, saving the beholding of them with their eyes?
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that success is the Preacher's hardest word: the profit of wisdom is handed to a stranger, the profit of work is eaten by the envious, and the profit of wealth is only the sight of it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, a tottering, i.e. ruin
BiblicalUsage: Kishshalon is a tottering, a ruin waiting to happen. Proverbs 16:18 sets it beside the most quoted warning in the book: pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the totter comes before the fall: pride does not drop a man all at once, it sets him swaying first.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain affinity; a lyre:--harp.
BiblicalUsage: Kithara is the lyre, the harp. 1 Corinthians 14:7 asks how a harp is known unless it gives a distinction in the sounds, Revelation 5:8 gives every elder a harp before the Lamb, and Revelation 14:2 and Revelation 15:2 hear harpers harping with their harps and the victors standing on the sea of glass, having the harps of God.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe heaven's harp is the answer to the harp on earth: what was tuned for worship here is tuned for victory there. I hold that the elders' harps and the victors' harps are the same instrument in the same hands, and the song does not stop.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2788; to play on a lyre:--harp.
BiblicalUsage: Kitharizo means to play on the lyre, to harp. 1 Corinthians 14:7 uses the harp to teach about clear speech in the church, and Revelation 14:2 hears the voice of harpers harping with their harps in heaven.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the harp's two uses belong together: a harp that gives no distinction in its sounds is no use in church, and the harps of heaven give a sound no one mistakes.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2788 and a derivative of the same as G5603; a lyre-singer(-player), i.e. harpist:--harper.
BiblicalUsage: Kitharoidos is the harper, the lyre-singer. Revelation 14:2 hears the voice of harpers harping with their harps, and Revelation 18:22 says the voice of harpers shall be heard no more at all in fallen Babylon.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the harper's voice marks the difference between the two cities: in heaven it sounds forever, and in Babylon it falls silent.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Kithlish, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Kithlish is a place in Palestine, named once in the town list. Joshua 15:40 names it among the cities of Judah, beside Cabbon and Lahmam.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the town lists are the Bible's way of saying the inheritance was real: every name was a place where people lived, and God counted them all.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a Kittite or Cypriote; hence, an islander in general, i.e. the Greeks or Romans on the shores opposite Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Kittiy is a Kittite or Cypriote, an islander of the western sea. Genesis 10:4 and 1 Chronicles 1:7 both list Kittim among the sons of Javan, and Numbers 24:24 says ships shall come from the coast of Chittim, and shall afflict Asshur, and shall afflict Eber, and he also shall perish for ever.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Chittim is the far edge of the map, where ships from the west bring affliction to empires, and no nation is too far for God's word to reach.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: (by implication) very widely used as a relative conjunction or adverb (as below); often largely modified by other particles annexed
BiblicalUsage: Kiy is the little word for, because, that, and it holds half the Bible together. Genesis 1:4 says God saw the light, that it was good, Exodus 1:10 has Pharaoh scheming lest Israel multiply, and Leviticus 1:2 opens the law of offerings with if any man bring an offering unto the LORD.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the small words carry the big reasons: God saw the light, that it was good, and everything since has been God giving the reason for what He does.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: (by implication) very widely used as a relative conjunction or adverb (as below); often largely modified by other particles annexed
BiblicalUsage: Kiy is the little word for, because, that, and it holds half the Bible together. Genesis 1:4 says God saw the light, that it was good, Exodus 1:10 has Pharaoh scheming lest Israel multiply, and Leviticus 1:2 opens the law of offerings with if any man bring an offering unto the LORD.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the small words carry the big reasons: God saw the light, that it was good, and everything since has been God giving the reason for what He does.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a cup; also a bag for money or weights
KeyPassages: Deuteronomy 25:13; Proverbs 1:14; Proverbs 16:11; Proverbs 23:31; Isaiah 46:6; Micah 6:11
BiblicalUsage: Kis is a cup, and also a bag for money or weights. Deuteronomy 25:13 forbids divers weights in the bag, a great and a small, Proverbs 16:11 says a just weight and balance are the LORD's and all the weights of the bag are his work, and Micah 6:11 asks whether God shall count pure the man with the bag of deceitful weights. Proverbs 1:14 has the sinners saying, let us all have one purse, Isaiah 46:6 shows idol-makers lavishing gold out of the bag to hire a goldsmith, and Proverbs 23:31 warns against the wine when it giveth his colour in the cup.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the bag is where honesty is weighed: the same bag holds the merchant's weights and the idolater's gold, and God owns the scales. I hold that a just weight is worship, because the LORD's balance does not lie.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a crushing; figuratively, calamity
BiblicalUsage: Kid is a crushing, and by figure, calamity. Job 21:20 says of the wicked, his eyes shall see his destruction, and he shall drink of the wrath of the Almighty.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Job's word is blunt on purpose: calamity is not an accident that finds the wicked, it is a cup they drink.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, something struck off, i.e. a spark (as struck)
BiblicalUsage: Kidod is a spark struck off, as from flint. Job 41:19 pictures Leviathan: out of his mouth go burning lamps, and sparks of fire leap out.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the spark shows what Leviathan is: a creature whose very breath is fire, and no man can stand before him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Kidon, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Chidon is a place in Palestine, the threshingfloor where the ark stopped. 1 Chronicles 13:9 says that when they came unto the threshingfloor of Chidon, Uzza put forth his hand to hold the ark, for the oxen stumbled.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Chidon is remembered for one terrible moment: the place where a good intention touched what God said not to touch, and the ark went on without Uzza.
RelatedEvents: David Brings the Ark to Jerusalem
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, something to strike with, i.e. a dart
KeyPassages: Joshua 8:18; Joshua 8:26; 1 Samuel 17:6; 1 Samuel 17:45; Job 39:23; Jeremiah 6:23
BiblicalUsage: Kidown is a dart, something to strike with. Joshua 8:18 has the LORD telling Joshua to stretch out the spear toward Ai, for I will give it into thine hand, and Joshua 8:26 says he drew not his hand back until he had utterly destroyed all the inhabitants of Ai. 1 Samuel 17:6 arms Goliath with a target of brass between his shoulders, and 1 Samuel 17:45 has David answering, thou comest to me with a sword, and with a spear, and with a shield, but I come to thee in the name of the LORD of hosts. Job 39:23 hears the quiver rattle against the war horse, the glittering spear and the shield, and Jeremiah 6:23 arms the invader with bow and spear, cruel, and with no mercy.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the spear in these verses is always a signal, not just a weapon: Joshua's stretched spear is God's promise, and David's answer is God's name. I hold that the dart never decides the battle; the hand that stretches it, and the name it is stretched in, decide it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: perhaps tumult
BiblicalUsage: Kidor is perhaps tumult, a word that stands only once. Job 15:24 says trouble and anguish shall make the wicked afraid, and prevail against him, as a king ready to the battle.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the tumult is the sound of conscience: trouble and anguish march on the wicked like a king ready for battle, and there is nowhere to hide from them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: niggardly
BiblicalUsage: Kilay is niggardly, the churl, the stingy man. Isaiah 32:5 promises the vile person shall be no more called liberal, nor the churl said to be bountiful, and Isaiah 32:7 says the instruments of the churl are evil: he deviseth wicked devices to destroy the poor with lying words, even when the needy speaketh right.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Isaiah names the churl twice because stinginess is not a small fault: it devises wicked devices against the poor, and the day is coming when no one will call it generous.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a cluster of stars, i.e. the Pleiades
BiblicalUsage: Kimah is the Pleiades, the cluster of stars. Job 9:9 says God maketh Arcturus, Orion, and Pleiades, and the chambers of the south, Job 38:31 asks, canst thou bind the sweet influences of Pleiades, or loose the bands of Orion, and Amos 5:8 says to seek him that maketh the seven stars and Orion, and turneth the shadow of death into the morning.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the Pleiades are God's signature in the sky: He made them, He binds them, and the only right response is to seek Him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, something round (as excavated or bored), i.e. a chafing-dish for coals or a caldron for cooking; hence (from similarity of form) a washbowl; also (for the same reason) a pulpit or platform
KeyPassages: Exodus 30:18; Leviticus 8:11; 1 Samuel 2:14; 1 Kings 7:30; 2 Kings 16:17; 2 Chronicles 4:6
BiblicalUsage: Kiyor is a laver, a great round vessel for washing, and also the caldron and the platform of the same round shape. Exodus 30:18 commands a laver of brass to wash withal, set between the tabernacle and the altar, Leviticus 8:11 anoints the laver and his foot to sanctify them, and 2 Chronicles 4:6 makes ten lavers to wash the burnt offerings in. 1 Samuel 2:14 shows the other sense, the caldron into which the fleshhook strikes for the priest's portion, and 1 Kings 7:30 and 2 Kings 16:17 describe the lavers on their bases in Solomon's temple, until Ahaz cuts off their borders.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the laver stands between the altar and the tent for a reason: no priest comes to God without washing first. I hold that the water in the laver is the Old Testament's picture of the washing the New Testament promises, and Ahaz cutting it down is what happens when kings stop valuing it.
RelatedBooks: Exodus; Leviticus; 1 Samuel; 1 Kings; 2 Kings; 2 Chronicles
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a cooking range (consisting of two parallel stones, across which the boiler is set)
BiblicalUsage: Kir is a cooking range, two parallel stones with the boiler set across them. Leviticus 11:35 says that where a carcase falls, whether it be oven or ranges for pots, they shall be broken down, for they are unclean.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the range is broken, not washed, because some uncleanness goes too deep for scrubbing: what death has touched must come down.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: literally a director, i.e. the spindle or shank of a distaff, by which it is twirled
BiblicalUsage: Kishor is the spindle, the shank of the distaff by which it is twirled. Proverbs 31:19 pictures the virtuous woman at her work: she layeth her hands to the spindle, and her hands hold the distaff.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the spindle is the whole portrait in one verse: her hands are busy, her work is skilled, and her diligence is done at home where no one applauds it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, a statue, i.e. idol; but used (by euphemism) for some heathen deity (perhaps corresponding to Priapus or Baal-peor)
BiblicalUsage: Chiun is an idol, a statue carried in procession, named as a heathen god. Amos 5:26 charges Israel: ye have borne the tabernacle of your Moloch and Chiun your images, the star of your god, which ye made to yourselves.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Chiun is the saddest god in the Bible: a star-god Israel made with their own hands and then carried on their own shoulders, worshipping what they had built.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2806; a twig or bough (as if broken off):--branch.
KeyPassages: Matthew 13:32; Matthew 21:8; Matthew 24:32; Mark 4:32; Luke 13:19; Romans 11:16
BiblicalUsage: Klados is a branch, a twig broken off. Matthew 13:32 and Mark 4:32 and Luke 13:19 all tell the mustard seed growing into a tree, so that the birds lodge in the branches, Matthew 21:8 has the multitude cutting down branches to straw in the way before Jesus, Matthew 24:32 teaches the parable of the fig tree, when his branch is yet tender and putteth forth leaves, and Romans 11:16 says, if the root be holy, so are the branches.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a branch lives only because it is joined to the root, and it bears only what the root supplies. I hold that the branches cut for the road and the branches of the mustard tree are the same picture, that the kingdom grows where no one expects and shelters whom no one expects.
RelatedTopics: Kingdom of God; Faith; Vine and Branches
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain affinity; to sob, i.e. wail aloud (whereas 1145 is rather to cry silently):--bewail, weep.
KeyPassages: Matthew 2:18; Mark 5:38; Luke 6:21; John 11:31; Acts 9:39; Romans 12:15
BiblicalUsage: Klaio means to weep aloud, to sob and wail. Matthew 2:18 hears Rachel weeping for her children and refusing to be comforted, Mark 5:38 shows the house in tumult with them that wept and wailed greatly, and John 11:31 follows Mary to the grave to weep there. Luke 6:21 promises, blessed are ye that weep now, for ye shall laugh, Acts 9:39 has the widows standing by Peter weeping and showing the coats Dorcas made, and Romans 12:15 commands, weep with them that weep.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the Bible never tells the weeping to stop: Rachel weeps, Mary weeps, the widows weep, and the promise is not that tears are wrong but that they will turn to laughter. I hold that Romans 12:15 is the whole ministry of tears in one line, that we weep with them that weep because Christ wept with us first.
RelatedBooks: Matthew; Mark; Luke; John; Acts; Romans
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a primary verb; to break (specially, of bread):--break.
KeyPassages: Matthew 14:19; Matthew 15:36; Mark 8:6; Luke 22:19; Acts 2:46; 1 Corinthians 10:16
BiblicalUsage: Klao means to break, specially of bread. Matthew 14:19 and Matthew 15:36 and Mark 8:6 have Jesus taking the loaves, blessing, and breaking them for the multitudes, Luke 22:19 has Him taking bread at the supper, giving thanks, and breaking it, saying, this is my body which is given for you, Acts 2:46 has the church breaking bread from house to house with gladness, and 1 Corinthians 10:16 asks, the bread which we break, is it not the communion of the body of Christ?
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the broken bread is the gospel in the hands: Jesus broke it for the hungry, broke it for His disciples the night He died, and the church has been breaking it ever since. I hold that nothing is lost in the breaking, because the hands that break the bread are the hands that feed the five thousand.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2806; fracture (the act):--breaking.
BiblicalUsage: Klasis is the breaking, the act itself. Luke 24:35 says the risen Jesus was known to the Emmaus disciples in breaking of bread, and Acts 2:42 says the first church continued stedfastly in breaking of bread, and in prayers.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the breaking is where He is known: not in the argument on the road, but in the bread broken at the table.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2806; a piece (bit):--broken, fragment.
KeyPassages: Matthew 14:20; Matthew 15:37; Mark 6:43; Mark 8:8; Luke 9:17; John 6:12
BiblicalUsage: Klasma is the fragment, the broken piece left over. Matthew 14:20 and Mark 6:43 and Luke 9:17 all count twelve baskets full of fragments after the five thousand ate and were filled, Matthew 15:37 and Mark 8:8 count seven baskets after the four thousand, and John 6:12 has Jesus saying, gather up the fragments that remain, that nothing be lost.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the fragments are the proof of abundance: twelve baskets after five thousand and seven after four thousand, because with Jesus there is always more left than there was to begin with. I hold that gather up the fragments is a command for every church, because nothing the Lord multiplies is meant to be wasted.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain derivation; Claude, an island near Crete:--Clauda.
BiblicalUsage: Clauda is an island near Crete, called Cauda in the Greek text. Acts 27:16 says that running under a certain island which is called Clauda, Paul's ship had much work to come by the boat in the storm.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Clauda is the small shelter in a great storm: the ship runs under it for a moment, and the moment is all the crew gets before the wind takes them again.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: feminine of G2804; Claudia, a Christian woman:--Claudia.
BiblicalUsage: Claudia is a Christian woman, named once in Paul's last greetings. 2 Timothy 4:21 has Paul writing, do thy diligence to come before winter, and then, Eubulus greeteth thee, and Pudens, and Linus, and Claudia, and all the brethren.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Claudia's single greeting is a whole commendation: she stood with Paul at the end, when coming before winter mattered, and her name is written with the brethren.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Latin origin; Claudius, the name of two Romans:--Claudius.
BiblicalUsage: Claudius is the name of two Romans. Acts 11:28 dates the great dearth to the days of Claudius Caesar, Acts 18:2 says Claudius had commanded all Jews to depart from Rome, and Acts 23:26 opens the letter of Claudius Lysias to the most excellent governor Felix.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the pair of Claudiuses frames the story: an emperor whose edict scattered the Jews, and a tribune whose letter carried Paul toward Rome.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2799; lamentation:--wailing, weeping, X wept.
KeyPassages: Matthew 2:18; Matthew 8:12; Matthew 13:42; Matthew 13:50; Luke 13:28; Acts 20:37
BiblicalUsage: Klauthmos is wailing, weeping aloud. Matthew 2:18 hears lamentation and weeping and great mourning, Rachel weeping for her children, Matthew 8:12 and Matthew 13:42 and Matthew 13:50 and Luke 13:28 all warn of outer darkness where there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth, and Acts 20:37 shows the other side: the elders of Ephesus wept sore, and fell on Paul's neck, and kissed him.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe klauthmos holds two wailings that must never be confused: the wailing of those cast out, and the weeping of those who love Paul and will not see his face again. I hold that the first is judgment and the second is love, and the Bible lets both sound at full volume.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a primary verb; to close (literally or figuratively):--shut (up).
KeyPassages: Matthew 6:6; Luke 4:25; John 20:19; Acts 5:23; 1 John 3:17; Revelation 3:7
BiblicalUsage: Kleio means to shut, to close. Matthew 6:6 says when thou prayest, shut thy door and pray to thy Father in secret, Luke 4:25 recalls the heaven shut up three years and six months in the days of Elias, and John 20:19 has Jesus standing in the midst though the doors were shut for fear of the Jews. Acts 5:23 finds the prison shut with all safety and the keepers standing without, yet no man within, 1 John 3:17 warns the man who shutteth up his bowels of compassion from his brother, and Revelation 3:7 praises Him that openeth, and no man shutteth, and shutteth, and no man openeth.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe shutting is the test of the heart: the door shut for prayer is holy, the heart shut against a brother is not. I hold that the doors shut against Jesus in John 20:19 could not keep Him out, and the prison shut in Acts 5:23 could not keep His apostles in.
RelatedBooks: Matthew; Luke; John; Acts; 1 John; Revelation
RelatedPeople: Jesus; John the Apostle; Simon Peter
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2808; a key (as shutting a lock), literally or figuratively:--key.
KeyPassages: Matthew 16:19; Luke 11:52; Revelation 1:18; Revelation 3:7; Revelation 9:1; Revelation 20:1
BiblicalUsage: Kleis is a key, the thing that shuts and opens. Matthew 16:19 gives Peter the keys of the kingdom of heaven, Luke 11:52 rebukes the lawyers who have taken away the key of knowledge, Revelation 1:18 has the risen Christ holding the keys of hell and of death, Revelation 3:7 gives the key of David to Him that openeth and no man shutteth, and Revelation 9:1 and Revelation 20:1 give the key of the bottomless pit to the angel who binds the dragon.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the keys all belong to one hand in the end: Peter holds them by gift, the lawyers lose them by theft, and Christ holds the keys of hell and of death because He died and lives again. I hold that the key of David is the key of the whole Bible, that the door Christ opens no man shuts.
RelatedPeople: Jesus; Simon Peter; John the Apostle
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2806; a limb or shoot (as if broken off):--branch.
BiblicalUsage: Klema is a branch, a limb or shoot broken off the vine. John 15:2 says every branch in me that beareth not fruit he taketh away, and every branch that beareth fruit he purgeth, John 15:4 says the branch cannot bear fruit of itself except it abide in the vine, John 15:5 says, I am the vine, ye are the branches, and John 15:6 warns that the branch that abides not is cast forth, and withered, and cast into the fire.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe no branch has life of its own: it bears only while it abides, and it withers the hour it leaves the vine. I hold that John 15:5 is the whole Christian life in one sentence, and without me ye can do nothing is not a warning, it is a fact.
RelatedTopics: Vine and Branches; Faith; Fruit of the Spirit
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Latin origin; merciful; Clemes (i.e. Clemens), a Christian:--Clement.
BiblicalUsage: Clement is a Christian, Paul's fellowlabourer. Philippians 4:3 has Paul asking his true yokefellow to help the women who laboured with him in the gospel, with Clement also, and with other fellowlabourers, whose names are in the book of life.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Clement is remembered exactly as a fellowlabourer should be: not for a speech or a miracle, but for a name written in the book of life.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2813; stealing (properly, the thing stolen, but used of the act):--theft.
BiblicalUsage: Klemma is theft, the thing stolen and the act of stealing. Revelation 9:21 says that even after the plagues, men repented not of their thefts, nor of their murders, nor of their sorceries, nor of their fornications.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the unrepented theft in Revelation is the mark of a hard heart: the plagues could not make them sorry for what their hands had taken.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably contracted from Κλεόπατρος (compound of G2811 and G3962); Cleopas, a Christian:--Cleopas.
BiblicalUsage: Cleopas is a Christian, one of the two on the road to Emmaus. Luke 24:18 has him answering the stranger: art thou only a stranger in Jerusalem, and hast not known the things which are come to pass there in these days?
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Cleopas asks the great question of Easter without knowing it: he asks the stranger if he knows what happened, and the stranger is the one it happened to.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a shorter form of G2564; renown (as if being called):--glory.
BiblicalUsage: Kleos is renown, glory as if from being called by name. 1 Peter 2:20 asks, for what glory is it, if, when ye be buffeted for your faults, ye shall take it patiently? but if, when ye do well, and suffer for it, ye take it patiently, this is acceptable with God.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Peter turns glory upside down: the renown God counts is not applause for success, but patience under a blow you did not deserve.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2813; a stealer (literally or figuratively):--thief. Compare G3027.
KeyPassages: Matthew 6:19; Luke 12:33; John 10:1; 1 Corinthians 6:10; 1 Thessalonians 5:2; 1 Peter 4:15
BiblicalUsage: Kleptes is a thief. Matthew 6:19 warns against treasures where thieves break through and steal, Luke 12:33 promises a treasure in the heavens where no thief approacheth, and John 10:1 calls the man who climbeth up some other way into the sheepfold a thief and a robber. 1 Corinthians 6:10 says thieves shall not inherit the kingdom of God, 1 Thessalonians 5:2 says the day of the Lord so cometh as a thief in the night, and 1 Peter 4:15 warns, let none of you suffer as a thief.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the thief is the Bible's picture of the wrong way in: he breaks through, he climbs over, he takes what is not his. I hold that the day of the Lord comes as a thief because no one is watching for it, and the only safe treasure is the one no thief can approach.
RelatedBooks: Matthew; Luke; John; 1 Corinthians; 1 Thessalonians; 1 Peter
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a primary verb; to filch:--steal.
KeyPassages: Matthew 6:19; Mark 10:19; Luke 18:20; John 10:10; Romans 2:21; Ephesians 4:28
BiblicalUsage: Klepto means to steal, to filch. Matthew 6:19 has thieves breaking through to steal, Mark 10:19 and Luke 18:20 both carry the commandment, do not steal, John 10:10 says the thief cometh not, but for to steal, and to kill, and to destroy, Romans 2:21 asks the teacher who preaches a man should not steal, dost thou steal, and Ephesians 4:28 turns the thief around: let him that stole steal no more, but rather let him labour, working with his hands the thing which is good, that he may have to give to him that needeth.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Ephesians 4:28 is the gospel of the thief in one verse: the hands that took are to work, and the work is to give. I hold that stealing is never only about the thing taken, because the thief in John 10:10 comes to steal and to kill and to destroy, and only the Good Shepherd gives life.
RelatedBooks: Matthew; Mark; Luke; John; Romans; Ephesians
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2818; to be an heir to (literally or figuratively):--be heir, (obtain by) inherit(-ance).
KeyPassages: Matthew 5:5; Mark 10:17; Luke 10:25; 1 Corinthians 6:9; Galatians 4:30; Hebrews 1:4
BiblicalUsage: Kleronomeo means to be an heir, to inherit. Matthew 5:5 promises the meek shall inherit the earth, Mark 10:17 and Luke 10:25 both ask, what shall I do that I may inherit eternal life, 1 Corinthians 6:9 warns the unrighteous shall not inherit the kingdom of God, Galatians 4:30 says the son of the bondwoman shall not be heir with the son of the freewoman, and Hebrews 1:4 says Christ hath by inheritance obtained a more excellent name than the angels.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe inheritance in the Bible is always by promise, never by wages: the meek inherit the earth because God gives it, and the unrighteous do not inherit because God withholds it. I hold that the question in Mark 10:17 and Luke 10:25 is the question every man must answer, and the answer is the Son who inherited the excellent name.
RelatedBooks: Matthew; Mark; Luke; 1 Corinthians; Galatians; Hebrews
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2818; heirship, i.e. (concretely) a patrimony or (genitive case) a possession:--inheritance.
KeyPassages: Matthew 21:38; Mark 12:7; Luke 12:13; Acts 7:5; Galatians 3:18; Ephesians 1:14
BiblicalUsage: Kleronomia is the inheritance itself, the heirship. Matthew 21:38 and Mark 12:7 have the husbandmen saying, this is the heir, come, let us kill him, and let us seize on his inheritance, Luke 12:13 has a man asking Jesus to divide the inheritance with his brother, Acts 7:5 says God gave Abraham none inheritance in the land, yet promised it to his seed, Galatians 3:18 says if the inheritance be of the law, it is no more of promise, but God gave it to Abraham by promise, and Ephesians 1:14 calls the Spirit the earnest of our inheritance until the redemption of the purchased possession.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the inheritance is the whole gospel in one word: promised to Abraham, refused by the husbandmen, divided by brothers, and sealed by the Spirit. I hold that Galatians 3:18 settles it forever, because what comes by promise cannot come by law.
RelatedBooks: Matthew; Mark; Luke; Acts; Galatians; Ephesians
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2819 and the base of G3551 (in its original sense of partitioning, i.e. (reflexively) getting by apportionment); a sharer by lot, i.e. inheritor (literally or figuratively); by implication, a possessor:--heir.
KeyPassages: Matthew 21:38; Mark 12:7; Luke 20:14; Romans 4:13; Galatians 3:29; Titus 3:7
BiblicalUsage: Kleronomos is the heir. Matthew 21:38 and Mark 12:7 and Luke 20:14 all show the husbandmen plotting against the heir, Romans 4:13 says the promise that Abraham should be the heir of the world was not through the law but through the righteousness of faith, Galatians 3:29 says, if ye be Christ's, then are ye Abraham's seed, and heirs according to the promise, and Titus 3:7 says we should be made heirs according to the hope of eternal life.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the heir is whoever belongs to Christ: the husbandmen tried to kill the heir and seize the inheritance, but the promise went to Abraham's seed by faith. I hold that Galatians 3:29 is the open door, because if I am Christ's, I am an heir.
RelatedBooks: Matthew; Mark; Luke; Romans; Galatians; Titus
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2819; to allot, i.e. (figuratively) to assign (a privilege):--obtain an inheritance.
BiblicalUsage: Kleroo means to allot, to assign a portion by lot. Ephesians 1:11 says, in whom also we have obtained an inheritance, being predestinated according to the purpose of him who worketh all things after the counsel of his own will.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Ephesians 1:11 means the lot is not chance: it is the counsel of God's own will, and the inheritance is assigned before we ever ask for it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably from G2806 (through the idea of using bits of wood, etc., for the purpose; a die (for drawing chances); by implication, a portion (as if so secured); by extension, an acquisition (especially a patrimony, figuratively):--heritage, inheritance, lot, part.
KeyPassages: Matthew 27:35; Mark 15:24; Luke 23:34; John 19:24; Acts 1:17; Colossians 1:12
BiblicalUsage: Kleros is the lot, the portion secured by casting lots, and so the heritage itself. Matthew 27:35 and Mark 15:24 and Luke 23:34 and John 19:24 all tell how the soldiers parted Jesus' garments, casting lots, that the scripture might be fulfilled, Acts 1:17 says Judas had obtained part of this ministry, and Colossians 1:12 thanks the Father which hath made us meet to be partakers of the inheritance of the saints in light.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the lots at the cross and in Acts 1:17 are the same word with opposite ends: the soldiers cast lots for His clothes, and the apostles cast lots for His ministry. I hold that the inheritance of Colossians 1:12 is the portion God assigns, not the portion men gamble for.
RelatedBooks: Matthew; Mark; Luke; John; Acts; Colossians
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a shorter form of G2564; an invitation (figuratively):--calling.
KeyPassages: Romans 11:29; 1 Corinthians 1:26; Ephesians 1:18; Philippians 3:14; 2 Thessalonians 1:11; 2 Timothy 1:9
BiblicalUsage: Klesis is the calling, the invitation of God. Romans 11:29 says the gifts and calling of God are without repentance, 1 Corinthians 1:26 says, ye see your calling, brethren, how that not many wise men after the flesh are called, Ephesians 1:18 prays that we may know the hope of his calling, Philippians 3:14 presses toward the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus, 2 Thessalonians 1:11 prays that God would count us worthy of this calling, and 2 Timothy 1:9 says He called us with an holy calling, not according to our works, but according to his own purpose and grace.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the calling is without repentance because God does not take back His invitations: He calls the foolish, He calls the weak, and He calls them holy. I hold that the high calling of Philippians 3:14 is the prize itself, and the race is worth running because the caller is God.
RelatedBooks: Romans; 1 Corinthians; Ephesians; Philippians; 2 Thessalonians; 2 Timothy
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from the same as G2821; invited, i.e. appointed, or (specially), a saint:--called.
KeyPassages: Matthew 22:14; Romans 1:1; Romans 1:6; 1 Corinthians 1:1; Jude 1:1; Revelation 17:14
BiblicalUsage: Kletos means called, invited, appointed. Matthew 22:14 says, for many are called, but few are chosen, Romans 1:1 has Paul called to be an apostle, Romans 1:6 says the Romans are the called of Jesus Christ, 1 Corinthians 1:1 repeats the apostle's calling, Jude 1:1 writes to them that are called, and Revelation 17:14 says they that are with the Lamb are called, and chosen, and faithful.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe called is the Christian's first name: before apostle, before saint, before faithful, we are the called. I hold that many are called and few are chosen, and the difference is not in the call but in the answer.
RelatedPeople: Paul; Jesus; James, Brother of Jesus
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain derivation; an earthen pot used for baking in:--oven.
BiblicalUsage: Klibanos is an oven, an earthen pot for baking. Matthew 6:30 and Luke 12:28 both say the grass of the field is today, and tomorrow is cast into the oven, and ask, shall God not much more clothe you, O ye of little faith?
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the oven is the measure of God's care: if He clothes grass that is burned tomorrow, He will clothe His children who live forever.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2827; a slope, i.e. (specially) a "clime" or tract of country:--part, region.
BiblicalUsage: Klima is a region, a tract of country. Romans 15:23 says Paul has no more place in these parts, 2 Corinthians 11:10 locates his boasting in the regions of Achaia, and Galatians 1:21 says afterwards he came into the regions of Syria and Cilicia.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the regions are the map of Paul's obedience: he went where there was no more place, and he boasted only where Christ was true.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2827; a couch (for sleep, sickness, sitting or eating):--bed, table.
KeyPassages: Matthew 9:2; Matthew 9:6; Mark 4:21; Mark 7:4; Luke 5:18; Revelation 2:22
BiblicalUsage: Kline is a bed, a couch for sleep, sickness, or eating. Matthew 9:2 has the palsied man lying on a bed, and Matthew 9:6 has Jesus telling him to arise, take up his bed, and go to his house, Mark 4:21 asks whether a candle is brought to be put under a bed, Mark 7:4 counts the washing of tables among the traditions, Luke 5:18 has men bringing a palsied man in a bed to lay before Jesus, and Revelation 2:22 warns that Jezebel shall be cast into a bed of tribulation.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a sickbed is where faith is proved: the palsied man was carried to Jesus on one, and told to carry it home on his own legs. I hold that the bed of sickness and the bed of tribulation are not the same bed, because the first is where Jesus heals and the second is where He judges.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: neuter of a presumed derivative of G2825; a pallet or little couch:--bed.
BiblicalUsage: Klinidion is a little couch, a pallet. Luke 5:19 has the friends letting the palsied man down through the tiling with his couch into the midst before Jesus, and Luke 5:24 has Jesus telling him to arise, and take up his couch, and go into his house.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the little couch carries the whole story: it lowered a man who could not walk, and it was carried home by a man who could.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a primary verb; to slant or slope, i.e. incline or recline (literally or figuratively):--bow (down), be far spent, lay, turn to flight, wear away.
KeyPassages: Matthew 8:20; Luke 9:12; Luke 9:58; Luke 24:5; John 19:30; Hebrews 11:34
BiblicalUsage: Klino means to bow down, to incline, to lay the head. Matthew 8:20 and Luke 9:58 both say the Son of man hath not where to lay his head, Luke 9:12 says the day began to wear away, Luke 24:5 has the women bowing down their faces to the earth at the empty tomb, John 19:30 says Jesus bowed his head and gave up the ghost, and Hebrews 11:34 says the faithful turned to flight the armies of the aliens.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the bowed head in John 19:30 is the centre of the word: the Son who had nowhere to lay His head laid it down on the cross, and finished it. I hold that the women bowing at the tomb and the armies turning to flight are the two ends of the same story, because the One who bowed His head rose again.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a derivative of G2827; properly, reclination, i.e. (concretely and specially), a party at a meal:--company.
BiblicalUsage: Klisia is a company at a meal, a party seated together. Luke 9:14 says the five thousand were made to sit down by fifties in a company, before the loaves were broken.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the companies are the order before the miracle: five thousand men seated in fifties, because God feeds His people in order, not in a crowd.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Chaldee origin (corresponding to H256); Clopas, an Israelite:--Cleophas.
BiblicalUsage: Clopas is an Israelite, the husband of Mary who stood by the cross. John 19:25 says there stood by the cross of Jesus his mother, and his mother's sister, Mary the wife of Cleophas, and Mary Magdalene.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Clopas is remembered by his wife's place at the cross: Mary stood there when the disciples had fled, and her husband's name stands with her.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2813; stealing:--theft.
BiblicalUsage: Klope is theft. Matthew 15:19 says thefts proceed out of the heart, and Mark 7:21 says the same: from within, out of the heart of men, proceed evil thoughts, adulteries, fornications, murders, thefts.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Jesus puts theft in the heart before it reaches the hand: the hand only takes what the heart has already claimed.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from κλύζω (to billow or dash over); a surge of the sea (literally or figuratively):--raging, wave.
BiblicalUsage: Klydon is a wave, a surge of the sea. Luke 8:24 has Jesus rebuking the wind and the raging of the water until there was a calm, and James 1:6 says the doubter is like a wave of the sea driven with the wind and tossed.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the wave is the picture of doubt itself: driven and tossed, with no shore of its own, until the voice that calmed the sea speaks to it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: middle voice from G2830; to surge, i.e. (figuratively) to fluctuate:--toss to and fro.
BiblicalUsage: Klydonizomai means to be tossed to and fro like a wave. Ephesians 4:14 warns that we be no more children, tossed to and fro, and carried about with every wind of doctrine, by the sleight of men, and cunning craftiness, whereby they lie in wait to deceive.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the tossing is the danger of childhood in the faith: the wind of doctrine carries the child, and only the truth in love holds him steady.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a primary κνάω (to scrape); to scratch, i.e. (by implication) to tickle:--X itching.
BiblicalUsage: Knetho means to scratch, to tickle, and so to have itching ears. 2 Timothy 4:3 warns that the time will come when men will not endure sound doctrine, but after their own lusts shall heap to themselves teachers, having itching ears.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the itching ear is the mark of a hard heart: it does not want truth, it wants to be scratched, and it will heap up teachers until it finds one who scratches.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably of foreign origin; Cnidus, a place in Asia Minor:--Cnidus.
BiblicalUsage: Cnidus is a place in Asia Minor, a port on Paul's voyage to Rome. Acts 27:7 says the ship sailed slowly many days, and scarce was come over against Cnidus, the wind not suffering them to sail on.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Cnidus is the place where the voyage nearly stopped: the wind would not suffer them, and the long road to Rome began with slow sailing.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: vigor, literally (force, in a good or a bad sense) or figuratively (capacity, means, produce); also (from its hardiness) a large lizard
KeyPassages: Genesis 4:12; Exodus 9:16; Leviticus 11:30; Numbers 14:13; Deuteronomy 4:37; Joshua 14:11
BiblicalUsage: Koach is strength, power, vigour, in body and in means. Genesis 4:12 says the ground shall not yield her strength to Cain, Exodus 9:16 says God raised Pharaoh up to show His power, Numbers 14:13 and Deuteronomy 4:37 remember the might that brought Israel out of Egypt, Joshua 14:11 has Caleb saying, as my strength was then, even so is my strength now, for war. Leviticus 11:30 carries the odd second sense, naming a large lizard among the creeping things.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe strength in the Bible is always borrowed: the ground keeps hers from Cain, Pharaoh's is raised up to show God's, and Caleb's at eighty-five is the same as at forty because God gave it. I hold that the lizard in Leviticus 11:30 is the joke and the warning both, that the same word names the power of empires and a creature in the dust.
RelatedBooks: Genesis; Exodus; Leviticus; Numbers; Deuteronomy; Joshua
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: weight, multitude, vehemence
BiblicalUsage: Kobed is weight, multitude, vehemence. Proverbs 27:3 says a stone is heavy, and the sand weighty, but a fool's wrath is heavier than them both, Isaiah 21:15 flees from the grievousness of war, Isaiah 30:27 says the name of the LORD cometh burning with anger, and the burden thereof is heavy, and Nahum 3:3 counts a multitude of slain and a great number of carcases.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe weight is the Bible's measure of what matters: a fool's wrath outweighs stone and sand, and the name of the LORD comes heavy with fire. I hold that the multitude of slain in Nahum is the end of every weight God does not carry, because only His burden is light.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Latin origin; a quadrans, i.e. the fourth part of an as:--farthing.
BiblicalUsage: Kodrantes is a quadrans, a farthing, the smallest Roman coin. Matthew 5:26 warns the debtor shall not come out till he has paid the uttermost farthing, and Mark 12:42 shows the poor widow throwing in two mites, which make a farthing.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the farthing is the measure of two opposite things: the debt that must be paid to the last coin, and the gift that is worth more than all the rich men's offerings.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, like this, i.e. by implication, (of manner) thus (or so); also (of place) here (or hither); or (of time) now
BiblicalUsage: Koh is the little word thus, so, here, now. Genesis 15:5 has God saying, so shall thy seed be, as the stars, Exodus 2:12 has Moses looking this way and that way before he slew the Egyptian, and Numbers 6:23 has God telling Aaron, on this wise ye shall bless the children of Israel.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe thus is the word God uses when He gives the pattern: so shall thy seed be, on this wise ye shall bless, and the blessing has been spoken the same way ever since.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: literally one officiating, a priest; also (by courtesy) an acting priest (although a layman)
KeyPassages: Genesis 14:18; Exodus 2:16; Leviticus 1:5; Numbers 3:3; Deuteronomy 17:9; Joshua 3:3
BiblicalUsage: Kohen is a priest, one who officiates. Genesis 14:18 introduces Melchizedek, priest of the most high God, bringing bread and wine, Exodus 2:16 names the priest of Midian with his seven daughters, Leviticus 1:5 has Aaron's sons bringing the blood to sprinkle on the altar, Numbers 3:3 names the priests anointed to minister, Deuteronomy 17:9 sends the hard case to the priests the Levites, and Joshua 3:3 has the priests bearing the ark of the covenant before the people.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the priest is the man who stands between: Melchizedek brings bread and wine, Aaron's sons bring blood, and the Levites carry the ark ahead of the people. I hold that every priest in these verses is a shadow of the one Priest who does not stand between by office but by His own blood.
RelatedBooks: Genesis; Exodus; Leviticus; Numbers; Deuteronomy; Joshua
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from κοῖλος ("hollow"); a cavity, i.e. (especially) the abdomen; by implication, the matrix; figuratively, the heart:--belly, womb.
KeyPassages: Matthew 12:40; Mark 7:19; Luke 1:15; John 3:4; Acts 3:2; Romans 16:18
BiblicalUsage: Koilia is the belly, the womb, the hollow within. Matthew 12:40 has Jonas in the whale's belly, Mark 7:19 says food entereth not into the heart but into the belly, Luke 1:15 says John shall be filled with the Holy Ghost even from his mother's womb, John 3:4 has Nicodemus asking, can a man enter the second time into his mother's womb, Acts 3:2 carries the man lame from his mother's womb to the Beautiful gate, and Romans 16:18 warns of men who serve not Christ but their own belly.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the belly and the womb are the Bible's two pictures of the inside: one is fed and the other is formed. I hold that John was filled from his mother's womb and the false teachers serve their own belly, and the difference is what fills the hollow.
RelatedBooks: Matthew; Mark; Luke; John; Acts; Romans
RelatedPeople: Jesus; John the Baptist; Nicodemus; Simon Peter
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2749; to put to sleep, i.e. (passively or reflexively) to slumber; figuratively, to decease:--(be a-, fall a-, fall on) sleep, be dead.
BiblicalUsage: Koimao means to fall asleep, and in the New Testament it is the gentle word for dying. John 11:11 has Jesus saying, our friend Lazarus sleepeth, but I go, that I may awake him out of sleep, 1 Thessalonians 4:13 comforts the brethren concerning them which are asleep, that ye sorrow not, even as others which have no hope, and 1 Corinthians 15:20 calls Christ the firstfruits of them that slept.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe sleep is the Christian's word for death because the sleeper wakes: Lazarus woke, the brethren will wake, and Christ is the firstfruits of all who slept.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2837; sleeping, i.e. (by implication) repose:--taking of rest.
BiblicalUsage: Koimesis is taking of rest in sleep. John 11:13 explains that Jesus spake of Lazarus's death, but the disciples thought He had spoken of taking of rest in sleep.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the misunderstanding is the point: the disciples heard rest, and Jesus meant death, because for His friend the two were the same.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2844; to share with others (objectively or subjectively):--communicate, distribute, be partaker.
KeyPassages: Romans 12:13; Galatians 6:6; Philippians 4:15; 1 Timothy 5:22; Hebrews 2:14; 1 Peter 4:13
BiblicalUsage: Koinoneo means to share, to communicate, to take part with others. Romans 12:13 commands distributing to the necessity of saints and being given to hospitality, Galatians 6:6 says let him that is taught communicate unto him that teacheth in all good things, Philippians 4:15 remembers the church that communicated with Paul in giving and receiving, 1 Timothy 5:22 warns not to be partaker of other men's sins, Hebrews 2:14 says Christ Himself took part of flesh and blood, and 1 Peter 4:13 calls us partakers of Christ's sufferings.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe sharing is the shape of the whole gospel: Christ took part in our flesh and blood so that we might take part in His sufferings and His glory. I hold that the church that communicates in giving and receiving is the church that understands the sharing, and the warning of 1 Timothy 5:22 is its guard.
RelatedBooks: Romans; Galatians; Philippians; 1 Timothy; Hebrews; 1 Peter
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2844; communicative, i.e. (pecuniarily) liberal:--willing to communicate.
BiblicalUsage: Koinonikos means willing to communicate, ready to share. 1 Timothy 6:18 tells the rich to do good, to be rich in good works, ready to distribute, willing to communicate.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the rich man's duty is one word: willing, because God does not ask for a grudging gift but for a ready hand.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2839; a sharer, i.e. associate:--companion, X fellowship, partaker, partner.
KeyPassages: Matthew 23:30; Luke 5:10; 1 Corinthians 10:18; 2 Corinthians 1:7; Philemon 1:17; Hebrews 10:33
BiblicalUsage: Koinonos is a sharer, a companion, a partner. Matthew 23:30 has the Pharisees claiming they would not have been partakers with their fathers in the blood of the prophets, Luke 5:10 names James and John as partners with Simon, 1 Corinthians 10:18 asks, are not they which eat of the sacrifices partakers of the altar, 2 Corinthians 1:7 says, as ye are partakers of the sufferings, so shall ye be also of the consolation, Philemon 1:17 has Paul asking Philemon to receive Onesimus as a partner, and Hebrews 10:33 remembers those who became companions of them that were afflicted.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a partner is known by what he shares: the altar, the suffering, the consolation, and the afflicted. I hold that Paul's ask in Philemon 1:17 is the boldest use of the word, because he asks Philemon to receive a runaway slave as he would receive Paul himself.
RelatedBooks: Matthew; Luke; 1 Corinthians; 2 Corinthians; Philemon; Hebrews
RelatedPeople: Jesus; Paul; Simon Peter; Philemon; Onesimus
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2839; to make (or consider) profane (ceremonially):--call common, defile, pollute, unclean.
KeyPassages: Matthew 15:11; Matthew 15:18; Matthew 15:20; Mark 7:15; Acts 10:15; Hebrews 9:13
BiblicalUsage: Koinoo means to make common, to defile, to call unclean. Matthew 15:11 says not that which goeth into the mouth defileth a man, but that which cometh out of the mouth, Matthew 15:18 and Matthew 15:20 press the point, that the things which proceed out of the mouth come forth from the heart, and they defile the man, Mark 7:15 says nothing from without can defile him, but the things which come out of him, Acts 10:15 has the voice saying, what God hath cleansed, that call not thou common, and Hebrews 9:13 remembers the blood of bulls and of goats sanctifying to the purifying of the flesh.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Jesus moved defilement from the hands to the heart: the mouth does not defile, the heart behind the mouth does. I hold that Acts 10:15 is the turning point, because what God has cleansed no man may call common, and the church has lived by that voice ever since.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably from G4862; common, i.e. (literally) shared by all or several, or (ceremonially) profane:--common, defiled, unclean, unholy.
KeyPassages: Mark 7:2; Acts 2:44; Romans 14:14; Titus 1:4; Hebrews 10:29; Jude 1:3
BiblicalUsage: Koinos means common, shared by all, and so, in the ceremonial sense, profane. Mark 7:2 faults the disciples for eating with defiled, unwashen hands, Acts 2:44 says all that believed were together and had all things common, Romans 14:14 says there is nothing unclean of itself, but to him that esteemeth any thing to be unclean, to him it is unclean, Titus 1:4 greets Titus in the common faith, Hebrews 10:29 warns of counting the blood of the covenant an unholy thing, and Jude 1:3 writes of the common salvation.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe koinos holds the whole argument of the church: what is common is shared, and what is shared is holy. I hold that the common faith and the common salvation are the same gift, and the blood no one may call common is the blood that makes all things common.
RelatedBooks: Mark; Acts; Romans; Titus; Hebrews; Jude
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2749; a couch; by extension, cohabitation; by implication, the male sperm:--bed, chambering, X conceive.
BiblicalUsage: Koite is a bed, and by extension, the marriage bed and what happens in it. Luke 11:7 has the man saying his children are with him in bed and he cannot rise, Romans 9:10 speaks of Rebecca conceiving by Isaac, Romans 13:13 forbids chambering and wantonness, and Hebrews 13:4 says marriage is honourable in all, and the bed undefiled, but whoremongers and adulterers God will judge.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the marriage bed is honoured when it is kept and judged when it is defiled: Hebrews 13:4 draws the line plainly, and the line is God's. I hold that the same word that names the children's bed in Luke 11:7 names the marriage bed in Hebrews 13:4, because God made the home before He made the law about it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2845; a bedroom:--+ chamberlain.
BiblicalUsage: Koiton is a bedroom, and so the chamberlain who guards it. Acts 12:20 says the men of Tyre and Sidon made Blastus the king's chamberlain their friend, and desired peace, because their country was nourished by the king's country.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Blastus is a small lesson in access: the chamberlain guarded the king's door, and the cities that needed bread made the doorkeeper their friend.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2848 (from the kernel-shape of the insect); crimson-colored:--scarlet (colour, coloured).
KeyPassages: Matthew 27:28; Hebrews 9:19; Revelation 17:3; Revelation 17:4; Revelation 18:12; Revelation 18:16
BiblicalUsage: Kokkinos is scarlet, crimson, the colour of the worm. Matthew 27:28 puts a scarlet robe on Jesus in mockery, Hebrews 9:19 sprinkles the book and the people with scarlet wool, Revelation 17:3 and Revelation 17:4 dress the harlot's beast and the woman in scarlet, and Revelation 18:12 and Revelation 18:16 list scarlet among the merchandise and the clothing of fallen Babylon.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe scarlet is the colour of both the mockery and the atonement: the robe they put on Jesus and the wool that sprinkled the covenant are the same red. I hold that Babylon wears scarlet as a boast, and the Lamb wore it as a robe, and only one of them is clothed in the end.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: apparently a primary word; a kernel of seed:--corn, grain.
KeyPassages: Matthew 13:31; Matthew 17:20; Mark 4:31; Luke 13:19; John 12:24; 1 Corinthians 15:37
BiblicalUsage: Kokkos is a grain, a kernel of seed. Matthew 13:31 and Mark 4:31 and Luke 13:19 all compare the kingdom of heaven to a grain of mustard seed, the least of all seeds that grows into a tree, Matthew 17:20 says faith as a grain of mustard seed shall move a mountain, John 12:24 says except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abideth alone, but if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit, and 1 Corinthians 15:37 says that which thou sowest is bare grain, not the body that shall be.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the grain is the kingdom's whole method: the smallest seed, the dying wheat, the bare grain in the ground. I hold that nothing in the kingdom grows without dying first, and the mountain moves only for faith as small as a mustard seed.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Col-Chozeh, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Col-hozeh is an Israelite, the father of Shallun and the ancestor of Maaseiah. Nehemiah 3:15 says Shallun the son of Col-hozeh repaired the gate of the fountain, and Nehemiah 11:5 names Maaseiah the son of Baruch, the son of Col-hozeh, among those who dwelt in Jerusalem.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Col-hozeh is remembered by his sons' work: one repaired the gate of the fountain, and the other lived in the rebuilt city.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {properly, the whole; hence, all, any or every (in the singular only, but often in a plural sense)}
BiblicalUsage: Kol is the Aramaic word for all, the whole, every. Daniel 2:35 says the stone cut out without hands became a great mountain and filled the whole earth, Daniel 2:44 says the God of heaven shall set up a kingdom which shall break in pieces and consume all these kingdoms, and Daniel 7:14 says all people, nations, and languages shall serve the Son of man.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe all is the word Daniel's visions turn on: the stone fills the whole earth, the kingdom consumes all kingdoms, and all peoples serve the One like the Son of man.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {properly, the whole; hence, all, any or every (in the singular only, but often in a plural sense)}
BiblicalUsage: Kol is the Aramaic word for all, the whole, every. Daniel 2:35 says the stone cut out without hands became a great mountain and filled the whole earth, Daniel 2:44 says the God of heaven shall set up a kingdom which shall break in pieces and consume all these kingdoms, and Daniel 7:14 says all people, nations, and languages shall serve the Son of man.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe all is the word Daniel's visions turn on: the stone fills the whole earth, the kingdom consumes all kingdoms, and all peoples serve the One like the Son of man.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a derivative of κόλαξ (a fawner); flattery:-- X flattering.
BiblicalUsage: Kolakeia is flattery, fawning words. 1 Thessalonians 2:5 has Paul saying, neither at any time used we flattering words, as ye know, nor a cloke of covetousness, God is witness.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Paul pairs flattery with covetousness on purpose: the flattering word is the cloak the greedy man wears, and God sees under it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a derivative of the base of G2849; to rap with the fist:--buffet.
BiblicalUsage: Kolaphizo means to buffet, to strike with the fist. Matthew 26:67 has the council buffeting Jesus and smiting Him with their palms, Mark 14:65 has the servants buffeting Him and saying, prophesy, 1 Corinthians 4:11 has Paul saying, we are buffeted, and have no certain dwellingplace, 2 Corinthians 12:7 calls the thorn in the flesh a messenger of Satan to buffet Paul, and 1 Peter 2:20 asks what glory it is to take patiently a buffeting for your faults.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the buffet is the suffering that has no dignity in it: spat on, struck with palms, buffeted by servants. I hold that Paul's thorn and Peter's question belong together, because the buffet for Christ's sake is taken patiently, and the buffet for our faults is taken quietly.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2849; penal infliction:--punishment, torment.
BiblicalUsage: Kolasis is punishment, penal infliction. Matthew 25:46 says the goats shall go away into everlasting punishment, but the righteous into life eternal, and 1 John 4:18 says fear hath torment, because perfect love casteth out fear.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Matthew 25:46 and 1 John 4:18 are the two ends of the word: everlasting punishment for those who go away, and torment cast out by perfect love for those who stay.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from κόλος (dwarf); properly, to curtail, i.e. (figuratively) to chastise (or reserve for infliction):--punish.
BiblicalUsage: Kolazo means to punish, to chastise, to reserve for infliction. Acts 4:21 says the council let Peter and John go, finding nothing how they might punish them, because the people glorified God, and 2 Peter 2:9 says the Lord knoweth how to deliver the godly out of temptations, and to reserve the unjust unto the day of judgment to be punished.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Acts 4:21 and 2 Peter 2:9 show both hands of God: He delivers the godly and reserves the unjust, and the council that could not punish the apostles learned that the Lord can.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from κόλλα ("glue"); to glue, i.e. (passively or reflexively) to stick (figuratively):--cleave, join (self), keep company.
BiblicalUsage: Kollao means to glue, to cleave, to join oneself. Matthew 19:5 says a man shall leave father and mother, and shall cleave to his wife, and they twain shall be one flesh, Luke 15:15 has the prodigal joining himself to a citizen of that country, and being sent to feed swine, and 1 Corinthians 6:17 says, he that is joined unto the Lord is one spirit.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe three joinings make the whole moral map: cleave to a wife, join yourself to a citizen and feed swine, or be joined to the Lord and be one spirit.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: neuter of a presumed derivative of κολλύρα (a cake; prob akin to the base of G2853); properly, a poultice (as made of or in the form of crackers), i.e. (by analogy) a plaster:-- eyesalve.
BiblicalUsage: Kollyrion is eyesalve, a plaster for the eyes. Revelation 3:18 has Christ counselling Laodicea to anoint thine eyes with eyesalve, that thou mayest see, because they thought themselves rich and knew not they were blind.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the eyesalve is Christ's own prescription: the blind church is told to buy sight from Him, and the price is admitting it cannot see.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a presumed derivative of κόλλυβος (a small coin; probably akin to G2854); a coin-dealer:--(money-)changer.
BiblicalUsage: Kollybistes is a money-changer, a dealer in coins. Matthew 21:12 and Mark 11:15 both have Jesus overthrowing the tables of the moneychangers in the temple, and John 2:15 has Him pouring out the changers' money and overthrowing the tables.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the overthrown tables are the sign of a cleansing: the house of prayer had become a market, and Jesus drove the market out. I hold that the moneychangers are still with us whenever the church sells what God gives freely, and the tables still need turning.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a derivative of the base of G2849; to dock, i.e. (figuratively) abridge:--shorten.
BiblicalUsage: Koloboo means to shorten, to dock, to cut short. Matthew 24:22 says except those days should be shortened, there should no flesh be saved, but for the elect's sake those days shall be shortened, and Mark 13:20 says the same: for the elect's sake, whom he hath chosen, he hath shortened the days.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the shortened days are mercy measured in time: God cuts the tribulation short because His elect are in it, and no flesh would survive if He did not.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from the base of G2849; a limb of the body (as if lopped):--carcase.
BiblicalUsage: Kolon is a carcase, a limb lopped off. Hebrews 3:17 asks, was it not with them that had sinned, whose carcases fell in the wilderness, after God was grieved forty years?
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the carcases in the wilderness are the end of unbelief: a whole generation that saw the miracles and would not enter, and fell where they wandered.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Latin origin; a Roman "colony" for veterans:--colony.
BiblicalUsage: Kolonia is a colony, a Roman settlement for veterans. Acts 16:12 calls Philippi the chief city of that part of Macedonia, and a colony, where Paul abode certain days.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the colony matters because Paul preached the gospel of a heavenly citizenship in a city proud of its Roman one.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2857; a Colossæan, (i.e. inhabitant of Colossæ:--Colossian.
BiblicalUsage: Kolossaeus is a Colossian, an inhabitant of Colosse, but the word never actually occurs in the Greek text: no verse uses it, and no form of it stands anywhere in the Scriptures.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that honesty matters more than filling a gap: where the text is silent, I say so, and I will not invent a verse for a word the apostles never wrote.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: apparently feminine plural of κολοσσός ("colossal"); Colossæ, a place in Asia Minor:--Colosse.
BiblicalUsage: Colosse is a place in Asia Minor, the city of the saints Paul wrote to. Colossians 1:2 addresses the saints and faithful brethren in Christ which are at Colosse, with grace and peace from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Colosse is remembered for one letter: a small city that received a great epistle, because Christ in you, the hope of glory, was preached there.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: apparently a primary word; the bosom; by analogy, a bay:--bosom, creek.
KeyPassages: Luke 6:38; Luke 16:22; Luke 16:23; John 1:18; John 13:23; Acts 27:39
BiblicalUsage: Kolpos is the bosom, the fold of the garment where things are carried close. Luke 6:38 promises good measure, pressed down and running over, shall men give into your bosom, Luke 16:22 and Luke 16:23 carry Lazarus into Abraham's bosom, John 1:18 says the only begotten Son is in the bosom of the Father, John 13:23 has the disciple whom Jesus loved leaning on Jesus' bosom, and Acts 27:39 finds a certain creek with a shore for the ship.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the bosom is the Bible's picture of nearness: the Son in the Father's bosom, the disciple on Jesus' bosom, and Lazarus in Abraham's bosom. I hold that the measure given into the bosom in Luke 6:38 is the same nearness, because God gives back pressed down and running over to those who give.
RelatedPeople: Jesus; Abraham; Lazarus; John the Apostle; Paul
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from κόλυμβος (a diver); to plunge into water:--swim.
BiblicalUsage: Kolymbao means to swim, to plunge into the water. Acts 27:43 says the centurion commanded that they which could swim should cast themselves first into the sea, and get to land.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the swimmers are the picture of deliverance by effort: the ship is lost, but those who can swim are told to cast themselves in and get to land.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2860; a diving-place, i.e. pond for bathing (or swimming):--pool.
BiblicalUsage: Kolymbethra is a pool, a place for bathing and swimming. John 5:2 names the pool of Bethesda at Jerusalem, with five porches, John 5:7 has the impotent man saying he has no man to put him into the pool when the water is troubled, and John 9:7 sends the blind man to wash in the pool of Siloam, and he came seeing.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the pools are where Jesus meets the helpless: the man with no one to put him in, and the blind man sent to wash. I hold that Bethesda and Siloam are the same lesson, that the water does nothing until the word of Jesus sends a man to it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from the base of G2849; to estop, i.e. prevent (by word or act):--forbid, hinder, keep from, let, not suffer, withstand.
KeyPassages: Matthew 19:14; Mark 9:38; Luke 6:29; Acts 8:36; Romans 1:13; 1 Corinthians 14:39
BiblicalUsage: Kolyo means to hinder, to forbid, to keep from. Matthew 19:14 has Jesus saying, suffer little children, and forbid them not, to come unto me, Mark 9:38 has John forbidding a man who cast out devils because he followeth not us, Luke 6:29 says him that taketh away thy cloke forbid not to take thy coat also, Acts 8:36 has the eunuch asking, what doth hinder me to be baptized, Romans 1:13 says Paul was let hitherto from coming to Rome, and 1 Corinthians 14:39 says, forbid not to speak with tongues.
