TheologicalSignificance: I believe kolyo is a warning against hindering: John hindered a man casting out devils, and the disciples hindered the children, and Jesus corrected them both. I hold that the eunuch's question is the right one to ask of every hindrance, because if water is there and faith is there, nothing may stand between.
RelatedBooks: Matthew; Mark; Luke; Acts; Romans; 1 Corinthians
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2864; to wear tresses of hair:--have long hair.
BiblicalUsage: Komao means to have long hair, to wear tresses. 1 Corinthians 11:14 asks, doth not even nature itself teach you, that, if a man have long hair, it is a shame unto him, and 1 Corinthians 11:15 says, if a woman have long hair, it is a glory to her, for her hair is given her for a covering.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Paul's point is nature's order: the same hair that is a shame on the man is a glory on the woman, because God gave it for a covering.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2749; a hamlet (as if laid down):--town, village.
KeyPassages: Matthew 9:35; Matthew 10:11; Mark 6:6; Luke 5:17; John 7:42; Acts 8:25
BiblicalUsage: Kome is a village, a hamlet. Matthew 9:35 has Jesus going about all the cities and villages, teaching and preaching and healing, Matthew 10:11 tells the disciples to enquire who is worthy in whatever town they enter, Mark 6:6 has Jesus going round about the villages, teaching, Luke 5:17 has Pharisees come out of every town of Galilee and Judaea, John 7:42 says Christ cometh out of the town of Bethlehem, where David was, and Acts 8:25 has the apostles preaching the gospel in many villages of the Samaritans.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the villages are where the gospel did its ordinary work: not only in Jerusalem, but in every town of Galilee and in the villages of the Samaritans. I hold that Bethlehem the village is the centre of the word, because Christ came out of it, and the villages He walked are the measure of His ministry.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: apparently from the same as G2865; the hair of the head (locks, as ornamental, and thus differing from G2359; which properly denotes merely the scalp):--hair.
BiblicalUsage: Kome is the hair of the head, the locks worn as ornament. 1 Corinthians 11:15 says, if a woman have long hair, it is a glory to her, for her hair is given her for a covering.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the glory is in the giving: the hair is not the woman's achievement, it is God's gift, given for a covering.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a primary κομέω (to tend, i.e. take care of); properly, to provide for, i.e. (by implication) to carry off (as if from harm; genitive case obtain):--bring, receive.
KeyPassages: Matthew 25:27; Luke 7:37; 2 Corinthians 5:10; Ephesians 6:8; Colossians 3:25; Hebrews 10:36
BiblicalUsage: Komizo means to carry off, to receive, to bring back. Matthew 25:27 has the master saying the servant should have put the money to the exchangers, that at his coming he should have received his own with usury, Luke 7:37 has the woman bringing an alabaster box of ointment to Jesus, 2 Corinthians 5:10 says we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ, that every one may receive the things done in his body, Ephesians 6:8 says whatsoever good thing any man doeth, the same shall he receive of the Lord, Colossians 3:25 says he that doeth wrong shall receive for the wrong he hath done, and Hebrews 10:36 says after doing the will of God, ye might receive the promise.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe receiving is the end of every road in these verses: the servant receives with usury, the worker receives of the Lord, and the patient receive the promise. I hold that the judgment seat of 2 Corinthians 5:10 is where all the receiving is settled, because every man receives according to what he has done.
RelatedBooks: Matthew; Luke; 2 Corinthians; Ephesians; Colossians; Hebrews
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2968 and G4172; an unwalled city:--town.
BiblicalUsage: Komopolis is a town, an unwalled city. Mark 1:38 has Jesus saying, let us go into the next towns, that I may preach there also, for therefore came I forth.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the next towns are the whole mission: Jesus came forth to preach, and He would not stay where the crowd wanted Him to stay.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2749; a carousal (as if letting loose):--revelling, rioting.
BiblicalUsage: Komos is a carousal, revelling, rioting. Romans 13:13 says, let us walk honestly, as in the day, not in rioting and drunkenness, not in chambering and wantonness, not in strife and envying, Galatians 5:21 lists revellings among the works of the flesh that shall not inherit the kingdom of God, and 1 Peter 4:3 says the time past of our life may suffice us to have wrought the will of the Gentiles, when we walked in revellings, banquetings, and abominable idolatries.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Peter's word is the key to the other two: the time past may suffice us, because the revels are behind us, not before us. I hold that the works of the flesh are named so plainly because God wants us to recognize them, not to argue about them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: neuter comparative of a derivative of the base of 2865 (meaning, properly, well dressed, i.e. nice); figuratively, convalescent:--+ began to amend.
BiblicalUsage: Kompsoteron means better, more nicely, and here it means convalescent, beginning to amend. John 4:52 has the nobleman asking the hour when his son began to amend, and the servants answering, yesterday at the seventh hour the fever left him.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the hour is the proof: the fever left at the seventh hour, the very hour Jesus said, thy son liveth, and the father's faith began when the fever ended.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from κονία (dust; by analogy, lime); to whitewash:--whiten.
BiblicalUsage: Koniao means to whitewash, to whiten a wall. Matthew 23:27 calls the scribes and Pharisees whited sepulchres, beautiful outward but within full of dead men's bones, and Acts 23:3 has Paul calling the high priest a whited wall, who sits to judge after the law and commands him to be smitten contrary to the law.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the whitewash is the Bible's picture of hypocrisy: a coat of lime over dead bones, and a wall that looks clean while it breaks the law it sits to judge.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from the base of G2867 and ὄρνυμι (to "rouse"); pulverulence (as blown about):--dust.
BiblicalUsage: Koniortos is dust, the fine powder blown about. Matthew 10:14 and Luke 9:5 command the disciples to shake off the dust of their feet against the house or city that will not receive them, Luke 10:11 has them wiping off even the dust of the city that cleaveth to them, Acts 13:51 shows Paul and Barnabas shaking off the dust of their feet against Iconium, and Acts 22:23 has the crowd casting off their clothes and throwing dust into the air.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the shaken dust is a testimony, not a tantrum: the disciples leave the dust of the rejecting city behind, and the city keeps its dust. I hold that the crowd throwing dust in Acts 22:23 is the same dust turned to rage, because men who will not hear the word throw what they have at the man who speaks it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: apparently a derivative of the base of G2759 and a derivative of G3700; a mosquito (from its stinging proboscis):--gnat.
BiblicalUsage: Konops is a gnat, a mosquito. Matthew 23:24 has Jesus saying, ye blind guides, which strain at a gnat, and swallow a camel.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the gnat and the camel are the Pharisees in one picture: careful about the smallest impurity, and swallowing the largest one whole.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Conjah, an Israelite king
BiblicalUsage: Coniah is a king of Judah, the son of Jehoiakim, also called Jeconiah. Jeremiah 22:24 says though Coniah were the signet upon God's right hand, He would pluck him thence, Jeremiah 22:28 asks, is this man Coniah a despised broken idol, a vessel wherein is no pleasure, and Jeremiah 37:1 says king Zedekiah reigned instead of Coniah, whom Nebuchadrezzar made king.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Coniah is the king God plucked from His own hand: the signet ring cast off, the vessel with no pleasure in it, and the throne given to another.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2873; to tire, i.e. (figuratively) to relax:--cease.
BiblicalUsage: Kopazo means to tire, to relax, and so to cease. Matthew 14:32 says when Jesus and Peter came into the ship, the wind ceased, Mark 4:39 has Him rebuking the wind, and the wind ceased, and there was a great calm, and Mark 6:51 has Him going up into the ship, and the wind ceased, and they were sore amazed.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the wind ceases when He comes aboard: the storm that tired the rowers relaxes at His word, and the great calm follows the great fear. I hold that the amazement in Mark 6:51 is the right response, because the wind obeys the voice that made it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2875; cutting, i.e. carnage:--slaughter.
BiblicalUsage: Kope is a cutting, a slaughter. Hebrews 7:1 tells how Melchisedec, king of Salem, priest of the most high God, met Abraham returning from the slaughter of the kings, and blessed him.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the slaughter is the setting of the blessing: Abraham comes back from the battle, and the priest of the most high God meets him with bread and wine.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2875; mourning (properly, by beating the breast):--lamentation.
BiblicalUsage: Kopetos is lamentation, mourning by beating the breast. Acts 8:2 says devout men carried Stephen to his burial, and made great lamentation over him.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the great lamentation is the church's first funeral: the deacon stoned for preaching, and the devout men beating their breasts over him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, a cover, i.e. (literally) a village (as covered in); (specifically) bitumen (as used for coating), and the henna plant (as used for dyeing); figuratively, a redemption-price
KeyPassages: Genesis 6:14; Exodus 21:30; Numbers 35:31; 1 Samuel 6:18; Job 33:24; Psalms 49:7
BiblicalUsage: Kopher is a cover, and the word carries three senses: pitch, a village, and a ransom. Genesis 6:14 tells Noah to pitch the ark within and without with pitch, 1 Samuel 6:18 counts the country villages of the Philistines, Exodus 21:30 lays a sum of money for the ransom of a man's life, Numbers 35:31 forbids taking any satisfaction for the life of a murderer, Job 33:24 says, deliver him from going down to the pit, I have found a ransom, and Psalms 49:7 says none can give to God a ransom for his brother.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe pitch, village, and ransom are one truth: the pitch covers the ark, the ransom covers the life, and the price no man can pay for his brother is the price God paid Himself. I hold that Psalms 49:7 is the question and Job 33:24 is the answer, because the ransom is found, not bought.
RelatedBooks: Genesis; Exodus; Numbers; 1 Samuel; Job; Psalms
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain derivation; a (small) basket:--basket.
KeyPassages: Matthew 14:20; Matthew 16:9; Mark 6:43; Mark 8:19; Luke 9:17; John 6:13
BiblicalUsage: Kophinos is a basket, a small basket for carrying. Matthew 14:20 and Mark 6:43 and Luke 9:17 and John 6:13 all count twelve baskets full of fragments after the five thousand were fed, Mark 8:19 has Jesus asking how many baskets full they took up, and Matthew 16:9 repeats the question.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the twelve baskets are the signature of the miracle: one basket for each tribe, one for each apostle, and nothing lost. I hold that Jesus asking how many baskets they took up is a test of memory, because the disciples who counted the baskets should have remembered who filled them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2875; blunted, i.e. (figuratively) of hearing (deaf) or speech (dumb):--deaf, dumb, speechless.
KeyPassages: Matthew 9:32; Matthew 9:33; Matthew 11:5; Matthew 12:22; Mark 7:32; Luke 1:22
BiblicalUsage: Kophos means blunted, and so deaf or dumb. Matthew 9:32 brings a dumb man possessed with a devil, and Matthew 9:33 has the dumb speaking when the devil is cast out, Matthew 11:5 lists the deaf hearing among the signs of the Messiah, Matthew 12:22 heals a man blind and dumb, both speaking and seeing, Mark 7:32 brings one deaf with an impediment in his speech, and Luke 1:22 leaves Zacharias speechless after his vision in the temple.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the deaf and dumb are the Messiah's own signs: the blind see, the deaf hear, and the dumb speak, because the kingdom has come. I hold that Zacharias was made speechless for not believing, and the dumb man was made to speak for believing, and the difference is faith.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a derivative of G2873; to feel fatigue; by implication, to work hard:--(bestow) labour, toil, be wearied.
KeyPassages: Matthew 6:28; Luke 5:5; John 4:6; Acts 20:35; Romans 16:6; 1 Corinthians 4:12
BiblicalUsage: Kopiao means to labour, to toil until weary. Matthew 6:28 says the lilies toil not, neither do they spin, Luke 5:5 has Simon saying, we have toiled all the night, and have taken nothing, John 4:6 has Jesus being wearied with His journey and sitting on Jacob's well, Acts 20:35 says so labouring ye ought to support the weak, Romans 16:6 greets Mary who bestowed much labour on us, and 1 Corinthians 4:12 has Paul labouring, working with his own hands.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the toil in these verses is the whole working life of the church: Simon toiling all night for nothing, Paul toiling with his hands, and Mary bestowing much labour. I hold that Jesus wearied with His journey is the centre of it, because the Lord of the harvest grew tired on the road to the well, and still stopped to save a woman.
RelatedBooks: Matthew; Luke; John; Acts; Romans; 1 Corinthians
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2875; a cut, i.e. (by analogy) toil (as reducing the strength), literally or figuratively; by implication, pains:--labour, + trouble, weariness.
KeyPassages: Matthew 26:10; Mark 14:6; Luke 11:7; John 4:38; 1 Corinthians 3:8; 2 Corinthians 6:5
BiblicalUsage: Kopos is labour, toil, weariness, and by extension trouble. Matthew 26:10 and Mark 14:6 have Jesus saying, why trouble ye the woman, for she hath wrought a good work upon me, Luke 11:7 has the man in bed saying, trouble me not, John 4:38 says other men laboured, and ye are entered into their labours, 1 Corinthians 3:8 says every man shall receive his own reward according to his own labour, and 2 Corinthians 6:5 lists labours among Paul's stripes and imprisonments and fastings.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the labour is honoured in every verse: the woman's good work, the planters' and waterers' reward, and Paul's labours in stripes. I hold that the trouble in Matthew 26:10 and the labour in 1 Corinthians 3:8 are the same word, because the work that troubles the critics is the work God rewards.
RelatedBooks: Matthew; Mark; Luke; John; 1 Corinthians; 2 Corinthians
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from κόπρος (ordure; perhaps akin to G2875); manure:--dung(-hill).
BiblicalUsage: Kopria is dung, manure, the dunghill. Luke 14:35 says salt that has lost its savour is neither fit for the land, nor yet for the dunghill, but men cast it out.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the dunghill is the end of useless salt: it cannot season the land and it cannot even enrich the dunghill, so it is cast out.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a primary verb; to "chop"; specially, to beat the breast in grief:--cut down, lament, mourn, (be-)wail. Compare the base of G5114.
KeyPassages: Matthew 11:17; Matthew 21:8; Matthew 24:30; Mark 11:8; Luke 8:52; Revelation 1:7
BiblicalUsage: Kopto means to cut down, and specially to beat the breast in grief, to lament. Matthew 11:17 says, we have mourned unto you, and ye have not lamented, Matthew 21:8 and Mark 11:8 have the multitude cutting down branches and strawing them in the way, Matthew 24:30 says all the tribes of the earth shall mourn when they see the Son of man coming, Luke 8:52 has all weeping and bewailing the dead girl, and Revelation 1:7 says all kindreds of the earth shall wail because of Him.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the cutting and the mourning are one word because they are one act: branches cut for the King, and breasts beaten for the dead. I hold that the tribes mourning in Matthew 24:30 and the kindreds wailing in Revelation 1:7 are the last lamentation, because they mourn the One they pierced.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, a deep round vessel, i.e. (specifically) a cor or measure for things dry
KeyPassages: 1 Kings 4:22; 1 Kings 5:11; 2 Chronicles 2:10; 2 Chronicles 27:5; Ezra 7:22; Ezekiel 45:14
BiblicalUsage: Kor is a cor, a deep round measure for dry things. 1 Kings 4:22 counts Solomon's daily provision at thirty measures of fine flour and threescore of meal, 1 Kings 5:11 has Solomon giving Hiram twenty thousand measures of wheat year by year, 2 Chronicles 2:10 promises the hewers twenty thousand measures of beaten wheat and barley, 2 Chronicles 27:5 takes ten thousand measures of wheat and barley as tribute from Ammon, Ezra 7:22 allows an hundred measures of wheat for the house of God, and Ezekiel 45:14 sets the ordinance of oil at the tenth part of a bath out of the cor.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the cor is the measure of a kingdom's daily bread: Solomon's table, Hiram's wages, the temple's store, and the tribute of Ammon are all counted in cors. I hold that the measure in Ezekiel 45:14 is the same measure in 1 Kings 4:22, because God's house and the king's house are both fed by measure, and the measure is God's.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: neuter of a presumed derivative of κόρη (a maiden); a (little) girl:--damsel, maid.
KeyPassages: Matthew 9:24; Matthew 9:25; Matthew 14:11; Mark 5:41; Mark 5:42; Mark 6:22
BiblicalUsage: Korasian is a little girl, a damsel, a maid. Matthew 9:24 has Jesus saying, the maid is not dead, but sleepeth, and Matthew 9:25 has Him taking her by the hand, and the maid arose, Matthew 14:11 has the damsel carrying John's head in a charger to her mother, Mark 5:41 has Him saying, Talitha cumi, damsel, I say unto thee, arise, Mark 5:42 has the damsel arising and walking, for she was of the age of twelve years, and Mark 6:22 has the daughter of Herodias dancing before Herod.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the damsel is the Bible's picture of resurrection in miniature: twelve years old, dead, and raised by a hand and a word. I hold that the two damsels are the contrast of the gospel, because one arose at His word and the other carried a prophet's head on a charger.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: perhaps from G2880; a crow (from its voracity):--raven.
BiblicalUsage: Korax is a raven, a crow. Luke 12:24 says, consider the ravens, for they neither sow nor reap, which neither have storehouse nor barn, and God feedeth them: how much more are ye better than the fowls?
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the raven is the argument for trust: the bird that neither sows nor reaps is fed by God, and His children are worth more than the fowls.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: and κορβανᾶς of Hebrew and Chaldee origin respectively (H7133); a votive offering and the offering; a consecrated present (to the Temple fund); by extension (the latter term) the Treasury itself, i.e. the room where the contribution boxes stood:--Corban, treasury.
BiblicalUsage: Korban is a votive offering, a consecrated gift to the Temple. Mark 7:11 has Jesus exposing the trick: a man says to his father or mother, it is Corban, that is to say, a gift, by whatsoever thou mightest be profited by me, and so he is free from helping them.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Corban is the gift that steals: a vow to God used as an excuse to starve a parent, and Jesus calls it what it is.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a throne
BiblicalUsage: Korse is the Aramaic word for a throne. Daniel 5:20 says Belshazzar's father was deposed from his kingly throne when his heart was lifted up and his mind hardened in pride, and Daniel 7:9 sees the thrones cast down, and the Ancient of days sitting, whose throne was like the fiery flame.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Daniel's two thrones are the whole book of Daniel: the king deposed from his, and the Ancient of days sitting on His.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H7141); Core (i.e. Korach), an Israelite:--Core.
BiblicalUsage: Core is Korah, the Israelite who rose against Moses and Aaron. Jude 1:11 pronounces woe on those who have perished in the gainsaying of Core, beside the way of Cain and the error of Balaam.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Korah's name stands in Jude as the third warning: Cain's way, Balaam's error, and Korah's gainsaying, and all three end in perishing.
RelatedPeople: Korah, Son of Izhar; Moses; Aaron
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a vinedresser
BiblicalUsage: Korem is a vinedresser, a keeper of vines. 2 Kings 25:12 and Jeremiah 52:16 leave the poor of the land to be vinedressers and husbandmen when Jerusalem falls, 2 Chronicles 26:10 has Uzziah's husbandmen and vinedressers in the mountains and in Carmel, Isaiah 61:5 says the sons of the alien shall be your plowmen and your vinedressers, and Joel 1:11 cries, howl, O ye vinedressers, for the wheat and the barley, because the harvest of the field is perished.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the vinedresser is the man left behind: the poor of the land kept to tend the vines when the city fell, and the strangers shall tend them when it rises. I hold that Joel's howling vinedresser is the honest one, because he mourns the harvest instead of pretending it did not perish.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a primary verb; to cram, i.e. glut or sate:--eat enough, full.
BiblicalUsage: Korennymi means to be glutted, to eat enough, to be full. Acts 27:38 says the ship's company, when they had eaten enough, lightened the ship and cast the wheat into the sea, and 1 Corinthians 4:8 has Paul saying, now ye are full, now ye are rich, ye have reigned as kings without us.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the fullness in both verses is a warning: the sailors ate enough and threw the wheat away, and the Corinthians thought themselves full and rich while Paul went hungry.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2882; a Corinthian, i.e. inhabitant of Corinth:--Corinthian.
BiblicalUsage: Korinthios is a Corinthian, an inhabitant of Corinth. Acts 18:8 says many of the Corinthians hearing believed, and were baptized, and 2 Corinthians 6:11 has Paul saying, O ye Corinthians, our mouth is open unto you, our heart is enlarged.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the Corinthians are the church Paul loved and rebuked in the same breath: many believed and were baptized, and his heart was enlarged toward them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain derivation; Corinthus, a city of Greece:--Corinth.
BiblicalUsage: Corinth is a city of Greece, the church Paul wrote to twice. Acts 18:1 says Paul departed from Athens and came to Corinth, 1 Corinthians 1:2 addresses the church of God which is at Corinth, to them that are sanctified in Christ Jesus, and 2 Corinthians 1:1 writes again to the church of God which is at Corinth, with all the saints in all Achaia.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Corinth is the church of second chances: a city of sinners sanctified in Christ Jesus, written to twice because once was not enough.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Latin origin; Cornelius, a Roman:--Cornelius.
BiblicalUsage: Cornelius is a Roman centurion, the first Gentile convert. Acts 10:1 names him a centurion of the band called the Italian band, Acts 10:3 shows him seeing an angel of God in a vision, and Acts 10:17 has the men sent from Cornelius standing at Simon's gate while Peter doubted what his vision meant.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Cornelius is the door of the Gentiles: a Roman soldier who prayed and gave alms, and whose vision sent for Peter. I hold that the angel coming to a centurion is the sign that the gospel was never only for Israel, because God heard a Gentile's prayers.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H3734); a cor, i.e. a specific measure:--measure.
BiblicalUsage: Koros is a cor, a measure for wheat. Luke 16:7 has the steward asking the debtor, how much owest thou, and the man answering, an hundred measures of wheat, and the steward saying, take thy bill, and write fourscore.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the hundred measures are the whole parable in one number: a debt too big to pay, cut down by a steward too clever to be honest.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain origin; Cos, an island in the Mediterranean:--Cos.
BiblicalUsage: Cos is an island in the Mediterranean, a stop on Paul's voyage to Jerusalem. Acts 21:1 says the ship came with a straight course unto Coos, and the day following unto Rhodes, and from thence unto Patara.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Cos is one more island on the road to Jerusalem: the voyage runs straight, and Paul does not turn back.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (compare H7081); Cosam (i.e. Kosam) an Israelite:--Cosam.
BiblicalUsage: Cosam is an Israelite, a name in the genealogy of Jesus. Luke 3:28 names him the son of Melchi, the son of Addi, the son of Cosam, the son of Elmodam, the son of Er, in the line that runs back to Adam.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Cosam's single verse is enough: his name stands in the line of the Messiah, and the genealogy is the proof that Jesus came in the flesh.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2889; to put in proper order, i.e. decorate (literally or figuratively); specially, to snuff (a wick):--adorn, garnish, trim.
KeyPassages: Matthew 12:44; Luke 11:25; 1 Timothy 2:9; Titus 2:10; 1 Peter 3:5; Revelation 21:2
BiblicalUsage: Kosmeo means to adorn, to put in proper order, to garnish. Matthew 12:44 and Luke 11:25 have the unclean spirit finding his house empty, swept, and garnished, 1 Timothy 2:9 says women should adorn themselves in modest apparel, Titus 2:10 says servants should adorn the doctrine of God our Saviour in all things, 1 Peter 3:5 says the holy women of old adorned themselves, trusting in God, and Revelation 21:2 sees the holy city, new Jerusalem, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe adorning is the question of every life: the swept and garnished house is empty and the devil returns, but the bride adorned for her husband is full of glory. I hold that Titus 2:10 is the true adornment, because a servant's fidelity adorns the doctrine of God better than gold or pearls.
RelatedBooks: Matthew; Luke; 1 Timothy; Titus; 1 Peter; Revelation
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2889 (in its secondary sense); terrene ("cosmic"), literally (mundane) or figuratively (corrupt):--worldly.
BiblicalUsage: Kosmikos means worldly, of this world, terrene. Titus 2:12 teaches us to deny ungodliness and worldly lusts, and to live soberly, righteously, and godly in this present world, and Hebrews 9:1 says the first covenant had ordinances of divine service, and a worldly sanctuary.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the worldly sanctuary and the worldly lusts are the two things the new covenant leaves behind: a sanctuary made with hands, and a life ruled by lusts.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2889 (in its primary sense); orderly, i.e. decorous:--of good behaviour, modest.
BiblicalUsage: Kosmios means orderly, decorous, of good behaviour. 1 Timothy 2:9 says women should adorn themselves in modest apparel, and 1 Timothy 3:2 says a bishop must be blameless, vigilant, sober, of good behaviour, given to hospitality, apt to teach.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe good behaviour is the bishop's first credential after blamelessness: orderly in life, because the church is ordered by God.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2889 and G2902; a world-ruler, an epithet of Satan:--ruler.
BiblicalUsage: Ephesians 6:12 is the word's only appearance, and it lands in the middle of Paul's picture of spiritual war. The "rulers of the darkness of this world" are not human officials but the spiritual powers ranged against God's people.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this one verse keeps me honest about where the real fight is: not against people, but against the dark powers behind the evil I see.
RelatedTopics: Spiritual Warfare; Satan; Evil and Suffering
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably from the base of G2865; orderly arrangement, i.e. decoration; by implication, the world (in a wide or narrow sense, including its inhabitants, literally or figuratively (morally)):--adorning, world.
BiblicalUsage: Kosmos starts with the idea of order and arrangement, and in the New Testament it most often means the world as a whole: the created order, the people in it, and the system of life that runs apart from God. John 3:16 says God loved this world enough to give His Son, while 1 John 2:15 warns, "Love not the world", so the same word carries both God's love for people and the world's rebellion against Him. In 1 John 2:2 Christ is the propitiation for the sins of the whole world, and in 1 Corinthians 1:20 God makes foolish the wisdom of this world.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that this world is both loved and lost: loved, because God gave His Son for it, and lost, because it has chosen its own way over His. My position is that a Christian lives in the world without belonging to its values, loving its people while refusing its rebellion.
RelatedTopics: Creation; Love of God; Salvation; Worldviews
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a wall (as gathering inmates)
BiblicalUsage: Song of Solomon 2:9 is the word's only appearance, a single quiet picture: the beloved stands behind the wall of the house, looking in through the windows and the lattice. The wall is simply the wall of a home, doing what walls do, standing between the lover outside and the one he longs to see.
TheologicalSignificance: My position is simply that even a passing detail like this matters, because the Song treats ordinary things — a wall, a window — as part of a love story, and God gave us that picture on purpose.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: the capital of a column
BiblicalUsage: The chapiter is the carved crown on top of a pillar, and nearly every appearance of this word belongs to Solomon's temple. In 1 Kings 7:16 the two chapiters of the great pillars were five cubits high, worked in brass with nets, chains, and rows of pomegranates, and 2 Chronicles 4:12 describes the same work from the other account.
TheologicalSignificance: I am convinced the temple's beauty was not decoration for its own sake; it was craftsmanship offered to God, and I believe the care poured into those capitals still says something true about worship that costs us our best work.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Latin origin (fourth); Quartus, a Christian:--Quartus.
BiblicalUsage: Quartus appears once, in the greetings at the end of Romans, where Paul calls him simply "a brother" alongside Gaius and Erastus in Romans 16:23. He is not given a title or a task in the letter, only a place among the saints who send their greeting.
TheologicalSignificance: For me, Quartus matters because the gospel made room for ordinary brothers whose names we would never know if Paul had not written them down.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Chaldee origin (H6966); cumi (i.e. rise!):--cumi.
BiblicalUsage: Cumi is the Aramaic word for "arise," and it survives in the New Testament only inside Jesus' own words to the dead girl in Mark 5:41: "Talitha cumi," damsel, arise. The Greek text keeps the Aramaic just as Jesus spoke it, then translates it for the reader.
TheologicalSignificance: What I take from it is that the word is precious because it is Jesus' voice, untranslated: a command spoken to death itself, and death obeyed.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from κοῦφος (light in weight); to unload:--lighten.
BiblicalUsage: Acts 27:38 is the word's only appearance, in the middle of the storm: after eating, the sailors lightened the ship by throwing the wheat into the sea. It is a plain, practical word for unloading weight to save the vessel.
TheologicalSignificance: I take it as given that there is a small lesson here I keep coming back to: sometimes survival means letting go of the cargo, and the cargo is not always worth the ship.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Latin origin; "custody", i.e. a Roman sentry:--watch.
BiblicalUsage: The word is a Latin loanword, custodia, a Roman guard, and all three appearances belong to the guard at Jesus' tomb. Pilate grants the watch in Matthew 27:65, the chief priests set it in Matthew 27:66, and in Matthew 28:11 some of the watch report to the chief priests what happened at the resurrection.
TheologicalSignificance: I am sure this guard is the proof of the resurrection's enemies: they did everything they could to keep the tomb shut, and it did not hold.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a helmet (as arched)
BiblicalUsage: The helmet is the soldier's headpiece, and it shows up on Goliath in 1 Samuel 17:5 and on the armies Jeremiah summons in Jeremiah 46:4. But the verse that stays with me is Isaiah 59:17, where the Lord Himself puts on righteousness as a breastplate and a helmet of salvation upon His head.
TheologicalSignificance: What convinces me here is that the helmet matters most where Isaiah puts it: salvation is not only something God gives, it is something He wears into battle for His people.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a cup (as a container), often figuratively, a lot (as if a potion); also some unclean bird, probably an owl (perhaps from the cup-like cavity of its eye)
BiblicalUsage: The cup is first an ordinary vessel — Pharaoh's cup in the butler's hand in Genesis 40:11, the great sea's brim wrought like the brim of a cup in 1 Kings 7:26 — and then it becomes a picture of what God gives a person to drink, for good or for ill. David says "my cup runneth over" in Psalms 23:5, the psalmist lifts "the cup of salvation" in Psalms 116:13, and Ezekiel 23:31 warns Jerusalem she will drink her sister's cup of judgment.
TheologicalSignificance: In my reading, the cup is one of Scripture's plainest pictures of a lot in life: what God pours for us, whether blessing or judgment, is the portion we must drink, and Christ drank the bitter cup so that mine could run over. That is why I lift the cup of salvation and call on the name of the Lord.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a star (as round or as shining); figuratively, a prince
BiblicalUsage: Stars are the lights God set in the heavens, and Scripture uses them three ways: as the countless multitude of Abraham's seed in Deuteronomy 1:10, as the rulers and powers of the age, and as the shining of the righteous. Balaam's prophecy in Numbers 24:17 says "there shall come a Star out of Jacob," Daniel 12:3 promises those who turn many to righteousness will shine "as the stars for ever and ever," and Amos 5:26 warns Israel for worshipping "the star of your god."
TheologicalSignificance: To my mind, the stars preach both ways: they declare God's power and His promises, and they expose the folly of worshipping the creation instead of the Creator who hung them there. I look up at the stars and remember that the God who hung them there also promised to multiply His people like them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Conanjah, the name of two Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Cononiah — spelled Conaniah in 2 Chronicles 35:9 — was a Levite ruler under Hezekiah, set over the offerings and tithes brought into the temple in 2 Chronicles 31:12, with overseers working under his hand in 2 Chronicles 31:13. In Josiah's day another Conaniah, chief of the Levites, gave five thousand passover offerings in 2 Chronicles 35:9.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe men like Cononiah are the quiet backbone of the story: no speeches, no miracles, just faithful oversight of what God's people brought, so the work of the house could go on.
RelatedPeople: Cononiah, Chief of the Levites; Cononiah, the Levite; King Hezekiah
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Cor-Ashan, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Chor-ashan appears once, in the list of towns to which David sent spoil after recovering Ziklag in 1 Samuel 30:30. It was a town in Judah, and its name means furnace of smoke.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the town's one mention still counts: David shared the spoil with the towns that had stood with him, and God remembers faithfulness in places the map barely notes.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {Koresh (or Cyrus), the Persian king}
BiblicalUsage: Cyrus was the Persian king who conquered Babylon and then did what no conqueror before him had done: he sent God's people home. In the first year of his reign he made a decree to rebuild the house of God at Jerusalem, as the record found in Ezra 6:3 sets out, he returned the gold and silver vessels Nebuchadnezzar had taken in Ezra 5:13, and Daniel prospered in his reign in Daniel 6:28.
TheologicalSignificance: My position is simply that Cyrus is the proof that God rules over kings who do not know Him: He named Cyrus long before he was born, and used a pagan emperor to open the way home.
RelatedTopics: Exile and Return; God's Sovereignty; Prophecy
RelatedEvents: Cyrus's Decree and Return from Exile
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {Koresh (or Cyrus), the Persian king}
BiblicalUsage: Cyrus was the Persian king who conquered Babylon and then did what no conqueror before him had done: he sent God's people home. In the first year of his reign he made a decree to rebuild the house of God at Jerusalem, as the record found in Ezra 6:3 sets out, he returned the gold and silver vessels Nebuchadnezzar had taken in Ezra 5:13, and Daniel prospered in his reign in Daniel 6:28.
TheologicalSignificance: My position is simply that Cyrus is the proof that God rules over kings who do not know Him: He named Cyrus long before he was born, and used a pagan emperor to open the way home.
RelatedTopics: Exile and Return; God's Sovereignty; Prophecy
RelatedEvents: Cyrus's Decree and Return from Exile
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: prosperity; in plural freedom
BiblicalUsage: Psalms 68:6 is the word's only appearance, and the King James Version renders it "chains": God "bringeth out those which are bound with chains." The Hebrew word itself speaks of prosperity and freedom, so the verse pictures God leading His bound people out into a broad, free place.
TheologicalSignificance: I am convinced the verse says what the word means: God does not only release His people, He brings them out into prosperity, and the chains are left behind.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Cozeba, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Chozeba appears once, in the genealogy of Judah in 1 Chronicles 4:22, among the men of Chozeba and the ancient things of that family line. It was a city in Judah, and its name means falsehood.
TheologicalSignificance: For me, even a one-line town in a genealogy has its place: the record keeps the names, and God keeps the people.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Cozbi, a Midianitess
BiblicalUsage: Cozbi was the daughter of Zur, a chief of the Midianites, and her name is tied to the sin at Peor. Numbers 25:15 names her as the Midianite woman Phinehas slew, and Numbers 25:18 says the Midianites beguiled Israel "in the matter of Cozbi."
TheologicalSignificance: What I take from it is that Cozbi stands as a warning written into the record: a single act of seduction drew Israel into idolatry, and the plague that followed cost twenty-four thousand lives.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably of foreign origin; a mattress:--bed.
BiblicalUsage: The mattress or pallet is the bed the sick lay on, and it shows up in the healing stories: the paralytic carried on his bed in Mark 2:4, the man at Bethesda told to take up his bed and walk in John 5:8, and Aeneas, who had kept his bed eight years, healed in Acts 9:33. The Greek text spells the word with double tau, κράβαττος, where the King James tradition has double beta.
TheologicalSignificance: I take it as given that this bed matters because Jesus kept telling people to pick it up: the thing that carried them became the proof they were healed.
RelatedEvents: The Healing at the Pool of Bethesda
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably from the same as G726; properly, a headache (as a seizure of pain) from drunkenness, i.e. (by implication) a debauch (by analogy, a glut):--surfeiting.
BiblicalUsage: Surfeiting is the heavy, sick feeling after too much drink and too much food, and it appears once, in Jesus' warning in Luke 21:34: take heed lest your hearts be overcharged with surfeiting and drunkenness and the cares of this life, so that the day comes upon you unawares.
TheologicalSignificance: I am sure Jesus put surfeiting beside drunkenness and daily worry for a reason: a dulled heart is as dangerous as a drunk one, and both miss the day when it comes.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: diminutive of a derivative of the base of G2768; a skull ("cranium"):--Calvary, skull.
BiblicalUsage: Kranion is simply the word for a skull, and it names the place where Jesus died. Matthew 27:33, Mark 15:22, and John 19:17 all call it Golgotha, the place of a skull, and Luke 23:33 uses the Latin form the English Bible keeps as Calvary.
TheologicalSignificance: What convinces me here is that the name fits the deed: at the place of the skull, the head of the serpent was crushed, and death itself was put to death. The place of the skull became the place where death died.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain derivation; a margin, i.e. (specially), a fringe or tassel:--border, hem.
BiblicalUsage: The hem or fringe is the border of a garment, and it carries the whole story of the woman who touched it. In Matthew 9:20 and Luke 8:44 she touches the hem of Jesus' garment and is healed at once, in Mark 6:56 and Matthew 14:36 whole crowds beg only to touch it, and in Matthew 23:5 Jesus rebukes the Pharisees for enlarging the borders of their garments to be seen of men.
TheologicalSignificance: In my reading, the hem teaches me that faith does not need a grand gesture: one touch of the edge of His garment was enough, and it still is. One touch was enough then, and one touch is enough now.
RelatedEvents: Jairus' Daughter and the Bleeding Woman
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2900; to empower, i.e. (passively) increase in vigor:--be strengthened, be (wax) strong.
BiblicalUsage: To be strengthened is what happened to Jesus as a child and to the church as it grew. Luke 1:80 says the child John "waxed strong in spirit," Luke 2:40 says the child Jesus "waxed strong in spirit, filled with wisdom," and Paul tells the Corinthians in 1 Corinthians 16:13 to "be strong." The Greek text carries this word in the middle voice, κραταιόομαι.
TheologicalSignificance: To my mind, strength in Scripture is something God grows in a person, not something a person manufactures: John and Jesus both waxed strong because God was at work in them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2904; powerful:--mighty.
BiblicalUsage: Mighty appears once, and it is attached to the hand of God: "Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time" in 1 Peter 5:6. The word is the adjective behind power and strength, used here of God's hand alone.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the verse pairs the two things exactly right: God's hand is mighty, and mine is not, so humility under that hand is the only safe place to stand.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2904; to use strength, i.e. seize or retain (literally or figuratively):--hold (by, fast), keep, lay hand (hold) on, obtain, retain, take (by).
BiblicalUsage: Krateo is the word for holding on with strength, and it covers everything from taking someone by the hand to holding fast to the truth. In Hebrews 4:14 we are told to "hold fast our profession," in 2 Thessalonians 2:15 to "hold the traditions" taught by the apostles, in John 20:23 the apostles are given power to retain sins, and in Revelation 2:13 the church at Pergamos is praised because it held fast Christ's name.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the Christian life is largely a holding: holding fast the confession, holding the traditions once delivered, and holding on to Christ Himself when the world pulls the other way. What I hold fast to holds me, and that is why I will not let go.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: superlative of a derivative of G2904; strongest, i.e. (in dignity) very honorable:--most excellent (noble).
BiblicalUsage: Most excellent is the courteous title Luke uses for men of rank. He addresses his gospel to "most excellent Theophilus" in Luke 1:3, and the same title is given to the governors Felix in Acts 23:26 and Festus in Acts 26:25, where Paul speaks to Festus as "most noble."
TheologicalSignificance: My position is simply that the title is worth noting because Luke and Paul used the language of respect for rulers even while answering to a higher King, and that is a pattern for how I speak to authority.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: perhaps a primary word; vigor ("great") (literally or figuratively):--dominion, might(-ily), power, strength.
KeyPassages: 1 Peter 4:11; 1 Timothy 6:16; Acts 19:20; Colossians 1:11; Ephesians 1:19; Jude 1:25
BiblicalUsage: Kratos is might, dominion, and power, and it belongs first to God. Paul prays in Ephesians 1:19 that believers would know "the exceeding greatness of his power," Colossians 1:11 speaks of being strengthened with all might, and the doxologies give God "honour and power everlasting" in 1 Timothy 6:16 and dominion forever in Jude 1:25.
TheologicalSignificance: I am convinced might is not a thing God has; it is what He is, and every doxology that hands it back to Him is simply telling the truth about who holds it. That is the truth the doxologies sing, and I sing it with them.
RelatedBooks: 1 Peter; 1 Timothy; Acts; Colossians; Ephesians; Jude
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2906; to clamor:--cry out.
KeyPassages: Acts 22:23; John 11:43; Luke 4:41; Matthew 12:19; John 12:13; John 19:6
BiblicalUsage: To cry out is the loud, public shout, and John's Gospel uses it for the crowds at the cross. In John 12:13 they cry "Hosanna," in John 19:6 they cry "Crucify him," in John 11:43 Jesus cries with a loud voice, "Lazarus, come forth," and in Luke 4:41 the demons cry out that He is Christ the Son of God.
TheologicalSignificance: For me, the same loud voice can bless or curse, and the crowds prove it: one week they cried Hosanna, the next they cried Crucify, and only Christ's own cry raised the dead. I need to watch my own voice, because it can turn that fast.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2896; an outcry (in notification, tumult or grief):--clamour, cry(-ing).
BiblicalUsage: Krauge is the outcry itself, the noise of a crowd or the sound of grief. It rises in Acts 23:9 when the Pharisees raise a great cry for Paul, it is the "clamour" Paul tells believers to put away in Ephesians 4:31, it is the "strong crying and tears" of Christ in Hebrews 5:7, and it is the cry at midnight in Matthew 25:6, "Behold, the bridegroom cometh."
TheologicalSignificance: What I take from it is that the word draws a line between two kinds of crying: the clamour we are told to put away, and the cry of prayer that God hears, and I want mine to be the second. I want my cry to be prayer, not clamour, and God knows the difference.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a primary verb; properly, to "croak" (as a raven) or scream, i.e. (genitive case) to call aloud (shriek, exclaim, intreat):--cry (out).
KeyPassages: Acts 7:57; Acts 7:60; Galatians 4:6; James 5:4; John 1:15; Luke 9:39
BiblicalUsage: Krazo is to cry aloud, to shriek or call out, and it runs through the whole New Testament as the sound of people in extremity. Stephen cries with a loud voice in Acts 7:57 and again in Acts 7:60, "Lord, lay not this sin to their charge"; the Galatians passage says the Spirit cries "Abba, Father" in our hearts in Galatians 4:6; the cries of the reapers enter the ears of the Lord in James 5:4.
TheologicalSignificance: I take it as given that God hears every cry, whether it is Stephen's dying prayer, a child's Abba, or the wages of the oppressed: none of it is lost on Him, and that is both comfort and warning. Stephen's cry, a child's Abba, and the reapers' cry all reached the same ears.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: perhaps a primary word; (butcher's) meat:--flesh.
BiblicalUsage: Meat here is butcher's meat, flesh as food, and both appearances are about the conscience of a brother. Paul says in 1 Corinthians 8:13 that if meat makes his brother offend, he will eat no flesh while the world stands, and in Romans 14:21 it is good neither to eat flesh nor drink wine where a brother stumbles.
TheologicalSignificance: I am sure Paul's rule still stands: my freedom at the table ends where my brother's faith begins, and love gives up the meat.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: neuter of an alternate form of G2909; (as noun) better, i.e. greater advantage:--better.
BiblicalUsage: Kreisson is the neuter form of the comparative "better," and it appears three times, each time weighing one thing against another. In 1 Corinthians 7:38 the man who gives his virgin in marriage does well, but he who gives her not does better; in 1 Corinthians 11:17 the Corinthians come together "not for the better, but for the worse"; and in Philippians 1:23 Paul says to depart and be with Christ is far better. The form κρεῖσσον sits under the lemma κρείττων, which is the companion word G2909.
TheologicalSignificance: What convinces me here is that Paul's use in Philippians 1:23 settles the question for me: to be with Christ is not merely better, it is far better, and that is the measure for every other comparison.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: comparative of a derivative of G2904; stronger, i.e. (figuratively) better, i.e. nobler:--best, better.
KeyPassages: 1 Corinthians 7:9; 1 Peter 3:17; 2 Peter 2:21; Hebrews 1:4; Hebrews 7:19; Hebrews 7:22
BiblicalUsage: Better is the comparative that runs through Hebrews like a spine. Christ is "made so much better than the angels" in Hebrews 1:4, He is the surety of "a better testament" in Hebrews 7:22, the law made nothing perfect but "the bringing in of a better hope" did in Hebrews 7:19, and Peter says it is better to suffer for well doing than for evil doing in 1 Peter 3:17.
TheologicalSignificance: In my reading, Hebrews answers the whole Old Testament with one word: better — a better hope, a better covenant, a better priest, and the reason is always the same, because Christ is better. A better hope, a better covenant, a better priest, and the reason is always the same.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a prolonged form of a primary verb; to hang:--hang.
KeyPassages: Acts 5:30; Galatians 3:13; Luke 23:39; Matthew 18:6; Acts 10:39; Matthew 22:40
BiblicalUsage: To hang is the word for the cross in the apostles' preaching: "whom ye slew and hanged on a tree" in Acts 5:30 and again in Acts 10:39, and "Cursed is every one that hangeth on a tree" in Galatians 3:13. It also carries the two great commandments, on which "hang all the law and the prophets" in Matthew 22:40, and the warning in Matthew 18:6 about the millstone hanged about the neck of whoever offends a little one.
TheologicalSignificance: To my mind, the word holds the gospel together: Christ hung on a tree to bear the curse, and everything else in the law hangs on love of God and love of neighbour. The curse He bore is the reason I am free.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2910; overhanging, i.e. a precipice:--steep place.
BiblicalUsage: The steep place is the cliff the swine ran down, and all three Gospels tell it the same way: in Matthew 8:32, Mark 5:13, and Luke 8:33 the herd runs violently down a steep place into the sea and perishes.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this steep place shows what a legion of demons does to whatever it gets hold of: it drives it headlong to destruction, and only Jesus stands between a man and that cliff.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2914; a Cretan, i.e. inhabitant of Crete:--Crete, Cretian.
BiblicalUsage: Cretes are the people of Crete, and they appear at Pentecost in Acts 2:11, hearing the wonderful works of God in their own tongues, and again in Titus 1:12, where Paul quotes a Cretan prophet saying "The Cretians are alway liars, evil beasts, slow bellies."
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the two verses belong together: the gospel reached even a people with that reputation, and Paul still left Titus there to set the churches in order.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Latin origin; growing; Cresces (i.e. Crescens), a Christian:--Crescens.
BiblicalUsage: Crescens appears once, in Paul's last letter, in the list of those who had left him: "Demas hath forsaken me... Crescens to Galatia, Titus unto Dalmatia" in 2 Timothy 4:10. Unlike Demas, no reason is given for his going, and nothing in the text blames him for it.
TheologicalSignificance: My position is simply that Crescens is a reminder that not every departure is a desertion: Paul names him plainly, without a word against him, and I take that silence as respect.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain derivation; Crete, an island in the Mediterranean:--Crete.
BiblicalUsage: Crete is the great island in the Mediterranean where Paul's ship was driven in the storm and where Titus was left to finish the work. In Acts 27:7, Acts 27:12, and Acts 27:13 the ship sails under Crete and along its coast, in Acts 27:21 Paul reminds the crew they should not have loosed from Crete, and in Titus 1:5 he tells Titus he left him there to ordain elders in every city.
TheologicalSignificance: I am convinced Crete matters because the gospel took root in hard soil: a people known for lying heard the truth, and elders were ordained in every city anyway. The gospel took root in hard soil, and it can take root in mine.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2919; a decision (the function or the effect, for or against ("crime")):--avenge, condemned, condemnation, damnation, + go to law, judgment.
KeyPassages: Romans 11:33; 1 Peter 4:17; 1 Corinthians 11:29; 2 Peter 2:3; Hebrews 6:2; 1 Timothy 3:6
BiblicalUsage: Krima is the judgment or sentence itself, the decision handed down. Paul warns in 1 Corinthians 11:29 that eating unworthily brings damnation on oneself, Peter says judgment must begin at the house of God in 1 Peter 4:17, Paul tells Timothy a novice may fall into "the condemnation of the devil" in 1 Timothy 3:6, and Hebrews 6:2 lists "eternal judgment" among the foundations of the doctrine of Christ.
TheologicalSignificance: For me, judgment is not a threat God waves at the world; it begins with His own house, and that is why I take the Lord's table and the church's order seriously. That is why I come to the table with fear and to the judgment with hope.
RelatedBooks: Romans; 1 Peter; 1 Corinthians; 2 Peter; Hebrews; 1 Timothy
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, to distinguish, i.e. decide (mentally or judicially); by implication, to try, condemn, punish:--avenge, conclude, condemn, damn, decree, determine, esteem, judge, go to (sue at the) law, ordain, call in question, sentence to, think.
BiblicalUsage: Krino is the great word for judging, and it refuses to be simple. Jesus says "Judge not, that ye be not judged" in Matthew 7:1, then says judge righteous judgment; Paul says in 1 Corinthians 4:5 to judge nothing before the time, until the Lord comes; Peter says God judges every man according to his work in 1 Peter 1:17; and Paul says in 2 Timothy 4:1 that Christ shall judge the quick and the dead.
TheologicalSignificance: What I take from it is that the word holds two truths together that I must not pull apart: I am not the judge of my brother, and there is a Judge before whom we will all stand, and the second truth is what keeps the first one honest. The Judge is coming, and that is what makes my mercy toward others a duty, not a favour.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: perhaps a prim word; a lily:--lily.
BiblicalUsage: The lily is the flower Jesus points to in the Sermon on the Mount. "Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow; they toil not, neither do they spin" in Matthew 6:28, and in Luke 12:27 He adds that Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these.
TheologicalSignificance: I take it as given that the lily is the whole sermon on worry in one flower: God clothes what cannot work for itself, and He will clothe me too.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: decision (subjectively or objectively, for or against); by extension, a tribunal; by implication, justice (especially, divine law):--accusation, condemnation, damnation, judgment.
BiblicalUsage: Krisis is judgment in its full weight: the decision, the tribunal, and the justice itself. Jesus says in John 5:24 that whoever hears His word and believes "shall not come into condemnation, but is passed from death unto life," Hebrews 9:27 says it is appointed unto men once to die, "but after this the judgment," and John writes in 1 John 4:17 that perfect love gives boldness "in the day of judgment."
TheologicalSignificance: I am sure the day of judgment is the reason the gospel is urgent and the reason the believer need not fear it: Christ has already passed through the judgment for those who believe, and love casts out the fear of the day. The day is certain, and so is the escape Christ has made.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Latin origin; "crisp"; Crispus, a Corinthian:--Crispus.
BiblicalUsage: Crispus was the chief ruler of the synagogue at Corinth, and he believed on the Lord with all his house in Acts 18:8. Paul adds in 1 Corinthians 1:14 that he baptized Crispus himself, one of the very few he baptized at Corinth.
TheologicalSignificance: What convinces me here is that Crispus is the proof that no position is too high or too opposed for the gospel: the ruler of the synagogue believed, and his whole house with him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: neuter of a presumed derivative of G2923; a rule of judging ("criterion"), i.e. (by implication) a tribunal:--to judge, judgment (seat).
BiblicalUsage: The judgment seat here is the court, the place where disputes are settled. Paul asks the Corinthians in 1 Corinthians 6:2 whether they are unworthy "to judge the smallest matters," and James says in James 2:6 that the rich "draw you before the judgment seats."
TheologicalSignificance: In my reading, the word warns me twice: the church should be able to settle its own small matters, and the world will drag the poor before its courts, and both are reasons to keep the church honest.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2919; a judge (genitive case or specially):--judge.
BiblicalUsage: Krites is the judge, and the New Testament gives the title to Christ above all. Paul calls Him "the righteous judge" in 2 Timothy 4:8, Peter preaches in Acts 10:42 that He is ordained of God "to be the Judge of quick and dead," and Hebrews 12:23 speaks of "God the Judge of all."
TheologicalSignificance: To my mind, there is comfort in the title: the Judge is righteous, He is the one who died for the judged, and that is the only reason I can look forward to His judgment instead of dreading it. He is the righteous Judge, and He is also my advocate.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain derivation; barley:--barley.
BiblicalUsage: Barley appears once, in the famine measure of Revelation 6:6: "A measure of wheat for a penny, and three measures of barley for a penny." Barley was the poor man's grain, and the measure shows the price of bread in the days of scarcity.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the verse is a small, hard picture of judgment: food is measured out by the penny, and even the cheap grain costs a day's wage.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2915; consisting of barley:--barley.
BiblicalUsage: Barley loaves are the food of the miracle. In John 6:9 a lad has five barley loaves and two small fishes, and in John 6:13 the disciples gather twelve baskets of fragments from those same barley loaves after five thousand have eaten.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the barley matters because God chose the poor man's bread for the greatest feast: five loaves were enough when they were in Jesus' hands, and there was more left over than they started with.
RelatedEvents: The Feeding of the Five Thousand
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2923; decisive ("critical"), i.e. discriminative:--discerner.
BiblicalUsage: The discerner appears once, in Hebrews 4:12: the word of God is "a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart." The word is critical in the old sense — it judges, sifts, and separates what is true in a person from what is not.
TheologicalSignificance: My position is simply that this is why I cannot read Scripture casually: it reads me, and it tells the truth about what is in my heart whether I want to hear it or not.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: apparently a primary verb; to rap:--knock.
BiblicalUsage: To knock is the word of Jesus' promise about prayer: "Ask, and it shall be given you; seek, and ye shall find; knock, and it shall be opened unto you" in Matthew 7:7 and again in Luke 11:9. It is also the knock of Peter at the gate in Acts 12:13 and Acts 12:16, and the knock of Christ Himself in Revelation 3:20: "Behold, I stand at the door, and knock."
TheologicalSignificance: I am convinced the knock is both directions at once: I knock and the door opens, and Christ knocks and waits for me to open, and both promises are true at the same time. Both promises stand, and I answer both knocks.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: adverb from G2928; privately:--in secret.
BiblicalUsage: In secret appears once, in Ephesians 5:12: "For it is a shame even to speak of those things which are done of them in secret." The word is the adverb form, the Greek text carrying the dative κρυφῇ, where the King James tradition has κρυφῆ.
TheologicalSignificance: For me, Paul's point is plain: some sins are so shameful they should not even be named, and the Christian's business is to expose them by light, not to repeat them in the dark.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: feminine of G2927; a hidden place, i.e. cellar ("crypt"):--secret.
BiblicalUsage: The secret place is the cellar or hidden room, and it appears once, in Luke 11:33: no man lights a candle and puts it "in a secret place," but on a candlestick, that they which come in may see the light.
TheologicalSignificance: What I take from it is that the verse is a warning against hiding what God gave to shine: light belongs on the stand, not in the cellar, and so does the truth.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a primary verb; to conceal (properly, by covering):--hide (self), keep secret, secret(-ly).
BiblicalUsage: To hide is to conceal by covering, and it runs from the hidden treasure to the hidden life. In Matthew 13:44 the kingdom is like treasure hid in a field, in Colossians 3:3 "your life is hid with Christ in God," in Hebrews 11:23 Moses was hid three months by his parents, and in Luke 13:21 the kingdom is like leaven hid in meal until the whole is leavened.
TheologicalSignificance: I take it as given that hiding cuts both ways in Scripture: God hides His people and His treasure for safety, and the kingdom hides like leaven until it works through the whole lump, and both are His doing. What God hides, He keeps; what He plants in secret, He grows.
RelatedTopics: Kingdom of God; Salvation; God's Protection
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2928; concealed, i.e. private:--hid(-den), inward(-ly), secret.
BiblicalUsage: Hidden is the adjective for what is concealed, and it is the word of the heart's secrets. Jesus says in Matthew 6:4 that the Father "which seeth in secret" shall reward openly, Paul says in 1 Corinthians 4:5 the Lord "will bring to light the hidden things of darkness," and Peter speaks in 1 Peter 3:4 of "the hidden man of the heart."
TheologicalSignificance: I am sure the hidden things are the real things: God sees in secret, He will bring the hidden to light, and the hidden man of the heart is the person He is forming. The hidden man of the heart is the person God is forming, and He sees him clearly.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2930; to make (i.e. intransitively, resemble) ice ("crystallize"):--be clear as crystal.
BiblicalUsage: Clear as crystal appears once, in the description of the New Jerusalem in Revelation 21:11: her light was like a stone most precious, "clear as crystal." The word is the verb for what crystal does — it shines through, with nothing hidden or clouded.
TheologicalSignificance: What convinces me here is that this city is described that way for a reason: in the end, everything will be clear, and the light will pass through without a shadow.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a derivative of κρύος (frost); ice, i.e. (by analogy) rock "crystal":--crystal.
BiblicalUsage: Crystal is the clear stone of the visions: the sea of glass "like unto crystal" before the throne in Revelation 4:6, and the river of water of life, "clear as crystal," proceeding out of the throne in Revelation 22:1.
TheologicalSignificance: In my reading, crystal is the picture of heaven's purity: nothing murky, nothing stained, the water of life running clear straight from the throne of God.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a primary verb; to get, i.e. acquire (by any means; own):--obtain, possess, provide, purchase.
BiblicalUsage: To obtain or acquire is the word for getting hold of something, and it covers fields, wives, and truth itself. In Acts 1:18 Judas "purchased a field with the reward of iniquity," in 1 Thessalonians 4:4 a man is to possess his vessel in sanctification and honour, in Acts 8:20 Simon thinks the gift of God "may be purchased with money," and in Luke 18:12 the Pharisee boasts of tithes "of all that I possess."
TheologicalSignificance: To my mind, this word draws the line between buying and receiving: Judas bought a field and lost everything, Simon tried to buy the Spirit and was rebuked, and the things that matter are possessed, not purchased. I hold what I have as a steward, not an owner.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2932; an acquirement, i.e. estate:--possession.
BiblicalUsage: Possessions are what a person owns, and both appearances are about what people did with them. In Acts 2:45 the believers "sold their possessions and goods, and parted them to all men, as every man had need," and in Mark 10:22 the rich young ruler went away grieved, "for he had great possessions."
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the two verses are the same test with opposite answers: the believers sold their possessions and found the church, and the young ruler kept his and walked away from Christ.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2932; property, i.e. (specially) a domestic animal:--beast.
BiblicalUsage: The beast here is the domestic animal, the creature a man owns and rides. In Acts 23:24 the chief captain orders them to "provide them beasts, that they may set Paul on," and in 1 Corinthians 15:39 Paul says "all flesh is not the same flesh," but there is one kind of flesh of men, another of beasts.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the word keeps the distinction plain: man and beast are both flesh, but they are not the same flesh, and God made them different on purpose.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2932; an owner:--possessor.
BiblicalUsage: The possessor appears once, in Acts 4:34: "as many as were possessors of lands or houses sold them, and brought the prices of the things that were sold." The early church's owners became its givers, and no one among them lacked.
TheologicalSignificance: My position is that this verse shows what ownership looks like when the gospel takes hold: what I possess becomes what the church needs, and nobody goes without.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2936; original formation (properly, the act; by implication, the thing, literally or figuratively):--building, creation, creature, ordinance.
BiblicalUsage: Ktisis is creation itself — the act of creating and everything created. Paul says in Romans 8:19 that "the earnest expectation of the creature waiteth for the manifestation of the sons of God," in 2 Corinthians 5:17 anyone in Christ is "a new creature," in Colossians 1:15 Christ is "the firstborn of every creature," and in Mark 16:15 the gospel is to be preached "to every creature."
TheologicalSignificance: I am convinced creation is both the world God made and the new world He is making in Christ: the old creation groans and waits, and the new creature in Christ is the first sign of what is coming. The old creation groans, the new creature hopes, and both wait for the sons of God.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2936; an original formation (concretely), i.e. product (created thing):--creature.
BiblicalUsage: The creature is the thing created, and the word gathers up everything God made. In James 1:18 God begat us "that we should be a kind of firstfruits of his creatures," in 1 Timothy 4:4 "every creature of God is good, and nothing to be refused, if it be received with thanksgiving," and in Revelation 5:13 "every creature which is in heaven, and on the earth" gives blessing and honour to the Lamb.
TheologicalSignificance: For me, the word keeps me from despising what God made: every creature is good, the new birth makes us firstfruits of His creatures, and one day every creature will join the song. Every creature is good, and every creature will one day sing.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2936; a founder, i.e. God (as author of all things):--Creator.
BiblicalUsage: The Creator appears once, and it is the name given to God at the end of suffering: "let them that suffer according to the will of God commit the keeping of their souls to him in well doing, as unto a faithful Creator" in 1 Peter 4:19.
TheologicalSignificance: What I take from this is that the title is the anchor of the verse: the One who made me is faithful, so I can commit my soul to Him even when I am suffering and cannot see the way through.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably akin to G2932 (through the idea of proprietorship of the manufacturer); to fabricate, i.e. found (form originally):--create, Creator, make.
BiblicalUsage: To create is God's work alone, and the word is used of Him from the beginning to the end. In Colossians 1:16 "by him were all things created," in Ephesians 2:10 we are "created in Christ Jesus unto good works," in 1 Timothy 4:3 the foods are things "which God hath created to be received with thanksgiving," and in Revelation 10:6 the angel swears by Him "who created heaven, and the things that therein are."
TheologicalSignificance: I take it that creation is the ground of everything else I believe: if God made all things, then He owns all things, and if He made me new in Christ, then my life belongs to His purpose. He made all things, and He made me new; both are His work.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: spelt (from its bristliness as if just shorn)
