BiblicalUsage: Spelt is a hardy, wheat-like grain, and it shows up in the farming and judgment passages. In Exodus 9:32 the wheat and the spelt were not smitten by the hail because they were not grown up, and in Ezekiel 4:9 it is one of the grains Ezekiel is told to mix into his bread.
TheologicalSignificance: I am sure the spelt's survival in Exodus 9:32 is a small mercy worth noticing: the hail took the barley and the flax, but the late crop was spared, and God knew the season of each grain.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Kub, a country near Egypt
BiblicalUsage: Chub appears once, in Ezekiel 30:5, among the nations that will fall with Egypt by the sword. It was a people allied with Egypt, probably in North Africa.
TheologicalSignificance: What convinces me is that the one-line mention still preaches: nations that league themselves with Egypt's pride fall with Egypt, and no alliance saves a people God has judged.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, to keep in; hence, to measure; figuratively, to maintain (in various senses)
BiblicalUsage: Kuwl is the word for holding in, and it stretches from containing to sustaining. Solomon's officers "provided victuals" for the king in 1 Kings 4:7, and Barzillai sustained the king in 2 Samuel 19:32. But the same word says in 2 Chronicles 2:6 that the heaven of heavens "cannot contain" God, in Amos 7:10 the land "is not able to bear" Amos's words, and in Ezekiel 23:32 the cup of judgment "containeth much."
TheologicalSignificance: In my reading, this word's two directions tell one truth: God sustains His people and no vessel contains Him, and the cup He gives the unrepentant is a cup no one can hold. He sustains me, and no vessel can contain Him, and I would not have it any other way.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a jewel (probably gold beads)
BiblicalUsage: The kumaz is a gold ornament, and both appearances are offerings. In Exodus 35:22 willing-hearted men and women brought bracelets, earrings, rings, and tablets of gold for the tabernacle, and in Numbers 31:50 the captains brought jewels of gold, chains and bracelets and tablets, as an oblation to make atonement for their souls.
TheologicalSignificance: To my mind, the gold in both verses says the same thing: what was once worn for beauty was laid down for God, and the offering became the atonement.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Kun, a place in Syria
BiblicalUsage: Chun was a city of Hadarezer in Syria, and it appears once, in the record of David's spoil in 1 Chronicles 18:8. From Tibhath and from Chun David brought very much brass, with which Solomon made the brasen sea, and the pillars, and the vessels of brass.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Chun's one verse reaches further than it looks: brass taken from a Syrian city became the sea and the pillars of God's house, and God turns the spoil of war into the vessels of worship.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, to be erect (i.e. stand perpendicular); hence (causatively) to set up, in a great variety of applications, whether literal (establish, fix, prepare, apply), or figurative (appoint, render sure, proper or prosperous)
BiblicalUsage: Kuwn is one of the great establishing words of the Old Testament, used more than two hundred times for making firm, setting up, and preparing. David's throne was established in 1 Kings 2:12, Samuel told Israel to prepare their hearts unto the Lord in 1 Samuel 7:3, David perceived that the Lord had established him king in 2 Samuel 5:12, and the Kohathites were set over the shewbread "to prepare it every sabbath" in 1 Chronicles 9:32.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the word's whole range is one promise: what God establishes stands, whether it is a throne, a heart turned to Him, or the bread set before Him every Sabbath. What God establishes stands, and I am standing on it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a pot or furnace (as if excavated)
BiblicalUsage: The furnace is the smelting pot, and Scripture makes it the picture of Egypt and of affliction. In Deuteronomy 4:20 and 1 Kings 8:51 Egypt is "the iron furnace" God brought Israel out of, in Ezekiel 22:18 Israel has become dross in the midst of the furnace, and in Isaiah 48:10 God says, "I have chosen thee in the furnace of affliction."
TheologicalSignificance: My position is that the furnace is the proof that affliction is not abandonment: God calls Egypt a furnace and still brings His people out of it, and He chooses His people in the furnace, not after it. The furnace did not destroy Israel, and it will not destroy me.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Cush (or Ethiopia), the name of a son of Ham, and of his territory; also of an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Cush is the son of Ham and the father of peoples, and the name covers a man, a people, and a land. Genesis 10:6 lists Cush among the sons of Ham, the title of Psalms 7 names "Cush the Benjamite" — a different Cush, an Israelite whose words against David drew the psalm — and Isaiah 18:1 speaks of the land beyond the rivers of Ethiopia.
TheologicalSignificance: I am convinced this name's range is the point: from Ham's son to a Benjamite accuser to the far land of Ethiopia, the Bible keeps Cush in the story, and God keeps every nation in His sight.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Cushan-Rishathajim, a Mesopotamian king
BiblicalUsage: Chushan-rishathaim was the king of Mesopotamia who held Israel eight years. Judges 3:8 says the Lord "sold them into the hand of Chushan-rishathaim king of Mesopotamia," and Judges 3:10 says the Spirit of the Lord came upon Othniel, who went out to war, and the Lord delivered the king into his hand.
TheologicalSignificance: For me, the eight years and the one deliverance belong together: God sold Israel into the hand of their enemy for their sin, and God raised up the judge who broke that hand.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Cushan, a region of Arabia
BiblicalUsage: Cushan appears once, in Habakkuk's vision in Habakkuk 3:7, where the prophet saw the tents of Cushan in affliction. The curtains of the land of Midian trembled beside them, for Cushan was a region in Arabia or Mesopotamia, and the prophet sees its tents shaking at God's coming.
TheologicalSignificance: What I take from this is that the trembling tents are the whole prophecy in one line: when God marches, even far-off peoples feel it, and no tent is too distant to shake.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Cushi, the name of two Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Cushi is the name of two Israelites, and both appear in the record by their sons. In Jeremiah 36:14 Cushi is the ancestor of Jehudi, who is sent to fetch Baruch and the roll; in Zephaniah 1:1 Cushi is the father of the prophet Zephaniah, named at the head of his book.
TheologicalSignificance: I take it that the two Cushis show how God keeps a family line: one man's son is sent to fetch the roll, another man's son carries the word of the Lord, and both are remembered by their father's name.
RelatedPeople: Cushi, Father of Zephaniah; Jehudi; Zephaniah
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Cushi, the name of two Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Cushi is the name of two Israelites, and both appear in the record by their sons. In Jeremiah 36:14 Cushi is the ancestor of Jehudi, who is sent to fetch Baruch and the roll; in Zephaniah 1:1 Cushi is the father of the prophet Zephaniah, named at the head of his book.
TheologicalSignificance: I take it that the two Cushis show how God keeps a family line: one man's son is sent to fetch the roll, another man's son carries the word of the Lord, and both are remembered by their father's name.
RelatedPeople: Cushi, Father of Zephaniah; Jehudi; Zephaniah
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a Cushite woman
BiblicalUsage: The Cushite woman appears once, and she is the cause of the quarrel in Numbers 12:1: "Miriam and Aaron spake against Moses because of the Ethiopian woman whom he had married." The text gives her no name and no words of her own, only the fact of the marriage and the complaint it drew.
TheologicalSignificance: I am sure her silence in the text is itself the rebuke: Miriam and Aaron judged a marriage God had not condemned, and the leprosy fell on the accuser, not on the wife.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Cuth or Cuthah, a province of Assyria
BiblicalUsage: Cuthah was one of the provinces of Assyria whose people were settled in Samaria after Israel was carried away. In 2 Kings 17:24 the king of Assyria brought men from Cuthah and placed them in the cities of Samaria, and in 2 Kings 17:30 the men of Cuth made Nergal, their own god, in the land.
TheologicalSignificance: What convinces me is that Cuthah is the warning of the whole chapter: a people moved into God's land brought their gods with them, and the land was filled with a mixture that was neither Israel nor Assyria.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from κύβος (a "cube", i.e. die for playing); gambling, i.e. (figuratively) artifice or fraud:--sleight.
BiblicalUsage: Sleight is the dice-player's trick, and Paul uses it for false teaching in Ephesians 4:14: believers are not to be children "tossed to and fro, and carried about with every wind of doctrine, by the sleight of men, and cunning craftiness, whereby they lie in wait to deceive."
TheologicalSignificance: In my reading, Paul chose a gambler's word on purpose: false doctrine is a loaded die, and the only defence against it is growing up into Christ, the head.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from κυβερνάω (of Latin origin, to steer); pilotage, i.e. (figuratively) directorship (in the church):--government.
BiblicalUsage: Governments here is the gift of steering, and it appears once, in the list of gifts God set in the church in 1 Corinthians 12:28: apostles, prophets, teachers, miracles, healings, helps, "governments," diversities of tongues.
TheologicalSignificance: To my mind, the word is a quiet correction to how I think about leadership: governing the church is a gift of the Spirit, like healing and teaching, and it is given to serve, not to rule.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from the same as G2941; helmsman, i.e. (by implication) captain:--(ship) master.
BiblicalUsage: The shipmaster is the captain, the man who steers, and he appears in two storms. In Acts 27:11 the centurion believed the master and the owner of the ship more than Paul's warning, and in Revelation 18:17 every shipmaster stands afar off weeping when Babylon's riches come to nothing in one hour.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the two shipmasters preach one sermon: the man who trusted the captain over the apostle lost the ship, and the captains who trusted their cargo lost everything in an hour.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: as if dative case of κύκλος (a ring, "cycle"; akin to G2947); i.e. in a circle (by implication, of G1722), i.e. (adverbially) all around:--round about.
BiblicalUsage: Round about is the plain adverb for what surrounds, and it does its work in two kinds of scenes. In Mark 3:34 Jesus looks round about on those sitting around Him and says, "Behold my mother and my brethren," and in Luke 9:12 the disciples ask Him to send the multitude into the towns and country round about.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the word is a small reminder of where Jesus stood: in the middle of the circle, with His people around Him, and that is still where He is.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from the same as G2945; to encircle, i.e. surround:--compass (about), come (stand) round about.
BiblicalUsage: To compass about is to surround, and it happens to Paul, to Jericho, to Jesus, and to Jerusalem. In Acts 14:20 the disciples stood round about Paul after he was stoned, and he rose up; in Hebrews 11:30 the walls of Jericho fell after they were compassed about seven days; in John 10:24 the Jews came round about Jesus demanding a plain answer; and in Luke 21:20 Jerusalem compassed with armies is the sign its desolation is near.
TheologicalSignificance: My position is that the word's four scenes are the whole story of surrounding: the church gathers round the fallen, faith circles the walls until they fall, and enemies circle the city until it falls. Enemies circle, the church gathers, and God decides which circle holds.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: adverb from the same as G2945; from the circle, i.e. all around:--(round) about.
BiblicalUsage: This adverb belongs to the throne room, and all three appearances are in Revelation 4. In Revelation 4:3 a rainbow is round about the throne, and in Revelation 4:4 round about the throne are four and twenty seats with the elders sitting on them.
TheologicalSignificance: I am convinced the word's place is the point: everything in heaven is arranged round about the throne, and the throne is the centre of it all.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from the base of G2949 (through the idea of circularity; compare G2945, G1507); to roll about:--wallow.
BiblicalUsage: To wallow appears once, in the possessed boy's torment in Mark 9:20: the spirit threw him down, "and he fell on the ground, and wallowed, foaming." The Greek text carries the word in the middle voice, κυλίομαι, where the King James tradition has κυλιόω.
TheologicalSignificance: For me, the verse is hard to read on purpose: the demons' work is to throw a child down and roll him in the dirt, and Jesus' work is to lift him up.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2947; a wallow (the effect of rolling), i.e. filth:--wallowing.
BiblicalUsage: Wallowing is the filth a creature rolls in, and it appears once, in the proverb Peter quotes in 2 Peter 2:22: the sow that was washed returns "to her wallowing in the mire." The Greek text carries the word as κυλισμός, where the King James tradition has κύλισμα.
TheologicalSignificance: What I take from this is that Peter's picture is blunt because the sin is blunt: a person washed clean who goes back to the mire proves the washing never reached the heart.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from the same as G2947; rocking about, i.e. crippled (maimed, in feet or hands):--maimed.
BiblicalUsage: Maimed is the word for a body broken in hand or foot, and Jesus uses it both ways. In Matthew 15:30 the maimed are brought to Him and healed, and the multitude wonders in Matthew 15:31 when they see "the maimed to be whole"; but in Mark 9:43 and Matthew 18:8 He says it is better to enter into life maimed than with two hands to go into hell.
TheologicalSignificance: I take it that Jesus means both sayings at once: He heals the maimed here, and He warns that a hand is not worth hell, and the mercy and the warning come from the same mouth. He heals the maimed, and He warns the whole: both are mercy.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from κύω (to swell (with young), i.e. bend, curve); a billow (as bursting or toppling):--wave.
BiblicalUsage: The wave is the billow that rises and breaks, and it is the picture of trouble in all four appearances. In Matthew 8:24 the ship is covered with the waves while Jesus sleeps, in Mark 4:37 the waves beat into the ship, in Matthew 14:24 the ship is tossed with waves, and in Jude 1:13 false teachers are "raging waves of the sea, foaming out their own shame."
TheologicalSignificance: I am sure the waves teach me what the sea always teaches in Scripture: the storm is real, the ship is small, and the Lord who sleeps in the boat is the Lord who stills it. The waves rose against the ship, and the ship held because He was in it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a derivative of the base of G2949; a "cymbal" (as hollow):--cymbal.
BiblicalUsage: The cymbal appears once, in the chapter on love: "Though I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, and have not charity, I am become as sounding brass, or a tinkling cymbal" in 1 Corinthians 13:1. A cymbal makes noise without a tune, and that is Paul's picture of speech without love.
TheologicalSignificance: What convinces me is that Paul's image convicts me every time I hear it: I can say the right words in the right language and still be nothing but noise if love is missing.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of foreign origin (compare H3646); dill or fennel ("cummin"):--cummin.
BiblicalUsage: Cummin is the small seed the Pharisees tithed, and it appears once, in Jesus' woe in Matthew 23:23: they pay tithe of mint and anise and cummin, "and have omitted the weightier matters of the law, judgment, mercy, and faith."
TheologicalSignificance: In my reading, this cummin seed is the whole rebuke in miniature: they measured the smallest herb to the last grain and missed the justice and mercy the law was about.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: neuter of a presumed derivative of G2965; a puppy:--dog.
BiblicalUsage: The little dog is the diminutive Jesus uses with the Syrophenician woman, and her answer turns the word into faith. In Mark 7:27 and Matthew 15:26 Jesus says it is not meet to take the children's bread and cast it to the dogs, and in Mark 7:28 and Matthew 15:27 she answers, "yet the dogs under the table eat of the children's crumbs."
TheologicalSignificance: To my mind, her answer is one of the greatest in the Bible: she did not argue the name, she took the crumbs, and Jesus praised her faith and healed her daughter. She took the crumbs, and the crumbs were enough.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a primary word; a dog ("hound") (literally or figuratively):--dog.
BiblicalUsage: The dog is the unclean scavenger of the ancient world, and Scripture uses it for those outside the covenant and for those who return to sin. Jesus says in Matthew 7:6 not to give what is holy unto the dogs, Paul warns in Philippians 3:2, "Beware of dogs, beware of evil workers," and Peter quotes the proverb in 2 Peter 2:22: "The dog is turned to his own vomit again."
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word is a warning I need to hear straight: the dog returns to what it left, and so does the heart that has been washed but not changed. The washed dog returns to the mire only if the washing never reached the heart.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2954; a Cyprian (Cypriot), i.e. inhabitant of Cyprus:--of Cyprus.
BiblicalUsage: Men of Cyprus are the believers who carried the gospel out of Jerusalem. In Acts 4:36 Barnabas is introduced as a Levite of the country of Cyprus, and in Acts 11:20 men of Cyprus and Cyrene came to Antioch and preached the Lord Jesus to the Grecians.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the Cypriots matter because they crossed the line first: the gospel had gone to Jews only, and it was men of Cyprus who spoke it to Greeks at Antioch, and the church there was born.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain origin; Cyprus, an island in the Mediterranean:--Cyprus.
BiblicalUsage: Cyprus is the island where the gospel first sailed west. In Acts 11:19 believers scattered by the persecution about Stephen travelled as far as Cyprus, in Acts 13:4 Paul and Barnabas sailed to Cyprus on the first missionary journey, and in Acts 15:39 Barnabas took Mark and sailed to Cyprus after parting from Paul.
TheologicalSignificance: My position is that Cyprus is where the church learned to go: persecution scattered the believers, the Spirit sent the apostles, and the island became a sending ground, not just a refuge. The church learned to go because it was first driven out.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably from the base of G2949; to bend forward:--stoop (down).
BiblicalUsage: To stoop down appears once, and it is John the Baptist's picture of his own unworthiness in Mark 1:7: "There cometh one mightier than I after me, the latchet of whose shoes I am not worthy to stoop down and unloose."
TheologicalSignificance: I am convinced the stoop is the whole ministry of John in one gesture: the greatest of the prophets bends low before the shoes of the One who comes after him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2957; i.e. Cyrenæan, i.e. inhabitant of Cyrene:--of Cyrene, Cyrenian.
BiblicalUsage: Men of Cyrene are the believers from North Africa, and the most famous of them carried the cross. In Matthew 27:32, Mark 15:21, and Luke 23:26 Simon a Cyrenian is compelled to bear Jesus' cross, in Acts 6:9 Cyrenians dispute with Stephen, and in Acts 11:20 men of Cyprus and Cyrene preach the Lord Jesus at Antioch.
TheologicalSignificance: For me, Simon of Cyrene is the picture of the disciple: a man pulled from the crowd and made to carry the cross after Jesus, and his sons Alexander and Rufus are named because the church knew them. A man pulled from the crowd became the picture of the disciple.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain derivation; Cyrene, a region of Africa:--Cyrene.
BiblicalUsage: Cyrene appears once, in the list of the peoples at Pentecost in Acts 2:10: Jews and proselytes from "the parts of Libya about Cyrene" heard the apostles speak in their own tongues.
TheologicalSignificance: What I take from this is that the one mention is enough: the gospel was preached to Libya on the day the church was born, and the ends of the earth were in the room from the start.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Latin origin; Cyrenius (i.e. Quirinus), a Roman:--Cyrenius.
BiblicalUsage: Quirinius, called Cyrenius in the King James Version, appears once, in the verse that dates the birth of Christ in Luke 2:2. The taxing was first made when he was governor of Syria, and his census brought Joseph and Mary to Bethlehem.
TheologicalSignificance: I take it that the verse is there to anchor the story in history: the Saviour was born under a named governor, in a counted census, in a real year, and the gospel is not a myth.
RelatedPeople: Quirinius; Jesus; Joseph, Husband of Mary
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: feminine of G2962; Cyria, a Christian woman:--lady.
BiblicalUsage: The elect lady is the one John addresses in his second letter, and her name is the word itself: Kyria, lady. In 2 John 1:1 John writes "unto the elect lady and her children, whom I love in the truth," and in 2 John 1:5 he begs her to love one another. The Greek text carries the word as κυρία, where the King James tradition has Κυρία.
TheologicalSignificance: I am sure the letter's tenderness is the point: the apostle writes to a lady and her children as a father in the faith, and the whole letter is a plea to walk in truth and love.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2962; belonging to the Lord (Jehovah or Jesus):--Lord's.
BiblicalUsage: Belonging to the Lord is the adjective that names two things every believer knows: the Lord's supper in 1 Corinthians 11:20 and the Lord's day in Revelation 1:10. One is the meal, the other is the day, and both belong to Him.
TheologicalSignificance: What convinces me is that the two uses say it all: the supper remembers His death, the day remembers His resurrection, and both are His, not ours.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2962; to rule:--have dominion over, lord, be lord of, exercise lordship over.
BiblicalUsage: To have dominion is to rule as a lord, and the word draws the line between God's rule and man's. Paul says in Romans 6:14 that "sin shall not have dominion over you," and in Romans 6:9 that death "hath no more dominion" over the risen Christ; but in Luke 22:25 the kings of the Gentiles "exercise lordship over them," and in 2 Corinthians 1:24 Paul refuses to have dominion over the Corinthians' faith.
TheologicalSignificance: In my reading, the word's contrast is the gospel in one verb: sin and death have lost their dominion, Christ alone is Lord, and no man is to lord it over another's faith. Sin has lost its rule, death has lost its rule, and Christ alone is Lord.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2962; mastery, i.e. (concretely and collectively) rulers:--dominion, government.
BiblicalUsage: Dominion here is the order of rulers itself, the ranks of authority in heaven and on earth. Paul says in Ephesians 1:21 that Christ is far above "all principality, and power, and might, and dominion," in Colossians 1:16 thrones and dominions were created by Him and for Him, and in Jude 1:8 and 2 Peter 2:10 the false teachers "despise dominion" and speak evil of dignities.
TheologicalSignificance: To my mind, the ranks exist and Christ is above them all: every dominion was made by Him, and the men who despise authority prove they do not know the One who holds it. Every dominion was made by Him, and every dominion answers to Him.
RelatedPeople: Jesus; Paul; Jude, Brother of James; Simon Peter
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from the same as G2962; to make authoritative, i.e. ratify:--confirm.
BiblicalUsage: To confirm is to ratify, to make a thing stand firm, and both appearances are about love and covenant. In 2 Corinthians 2:8 Paul begs the church to "confirm your love" toward the repentant brother, and in Galatians 3:15 he argues that a man's covenant, "if it be confirmed, no man disannulleth, or addeth thereto."
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the two verses belong together: a covenant confirmed cannot be undone, and love confirmed restores a brother, and both are acts of making firm what God has joined.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to deride
BiblicalUsage: To mock appears once, and it is the last straw before the exile in 2 Chronicles 36:16: the people "mocked the messengers of God, and despised his words, and misused his prophets, until the wrath of the LORD arose against his people, till there was no remedy."
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the verse is the saddest in the history: they did not only refuse the word, they mocked the men who brought it, and when there was no remedy left, the judgment came.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: derision, scoffing
BiblicalUsage: Derision is the noun for being laughed to scorn, and it is mostly what God's people suffer at the hands of their enemies. In Psalms 44:13 God has made Israel "a scorn and a derision to them that are round about us," in Job 34:7 Job is accused of drinking up scorning like water, and in Ezekiel 23:32 Jerusalem will drink her sister's cup and be "laughed to scorn and had in derision."
TheologicalSignificance: My position is that derision is the lot of God's people in a mocking world, and the psalms give me the words for it: they laughed at Israel, they laughed at Job, and God heard every laugh. The laughter of the proud is the lot of the righteous, and God will answer it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to deride; by implication (as if imitating a foreigner) to speak unintelligibly
BiblicalUsage: To mock is the verb of scorn, and it runs through the prophets and the wisdom books. Hezekiah's messengers were laughed to scorn in 2 Chronicles 30:10, Sennacherib was laughed to scorn by the daughter of Zion in 2 Kings 19:21, Jeremiah says in Jeremiah 20:7, "I am in derision daily, every one mocketh me," and Job's friends are told in Job 9:23 that God "will laugh at the trial of the innocent."
TheologicalSignificance: I am convinced mockery is the weapon of the proud and the lot of the prophet: the messengers were mocked, Jeremiah was mocked daily, and God Himself laughs last at those who laugh at His people. Jeremiah was mocked daily, and the mockers did not have the last word.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to tire; (figuratively) to be (or make) disgusted
BiblicalUsage: To be weary is to tire, and in this word the weariness is often God's own. The Egyptians "loathe" to drink the river in Exodus 7:18, the men of Sodom "wearied themselves to find the door" in Genesis 19:11, Jerusalem has "wearied herself with lies" in Ezekiel 24:12, and God says in Isaiah 1:14, "I am weary to bear" their feasts.
TheologicalSignificance: For me, the word's sharpest edge is God's weariness: He is not tired the way I am tired, but He is weary of empty religion, and that weariness is a warning to me. God is weary of empty religion, and I do not want to be the cause of His weariness.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: wormwood (regarded as poisonous, and therefore accursed)
BiblicalUsage: Wormwood is the bitter, poisonous herb, and Scripture makes it the taste of sin and judgment. In Deuteronomy 29:18 it is "a root that beareth gall and wormwood" in the heart that turns to other gods, in Jeremiah 9:15 God will feed His people "with wormwood, and give them water of gall to drink," in Amos 5:7 the unjust "turn judgment to wormwood," and in Proverbs 5:4 the strange woman's end "is bitter as wormwood."
TheologicalSignificance: What I take from this is that wormwood is the flavour of every sin that promised sweetness: it turns judgment bitter, it turns the heart bitter, and the end of it is always bitterness. Sin promises sweetness and ends in bitterness, and the wormwood proves it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to swallow greedily; causatively, to feed
BiblicalUsage: To swallow greedily appears once, and it is Esau's hunger in Genesis 25:30: "Feed me, I pray thee, with that same red pottage; for I am faint." The word is the gulp of a starving man, and it cost Esau his birthright.
TheologicalSignificance: I take it that the verse is the whole story of appetite in one gulp: Esau swallowed the pottage and lost the blessing, and I have done the same with cheaper things.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to muffle
BiblicalUsage: To muffle or cover appears once, and it is David's grief in 2 Samuel 19:4: "the king covered his face, and the king cried with a loud voice, O my son Absalom, O Absalom, my son, my son!" The covering is the veil of mourning, drawn over the face of a father who has lost his son.
TheologicalSignificance: I am sure this covered face says what words cannot: David won the battle and lost the son, and no victory covers that grief.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to speak in a foreign tongue
BiblicalUsage: To speak a strange language appears once, in the exodus psalm in Psalms 114:1: "When Israel went out of Egypt, the house of Jacob from a people of strange language." The word marks the Egyptians as foreigners in speech, and Israel's going out as a going out from among strangers.
TheologicalSignificance: What convinces me is that this verse sets the exodus in one line: God's people left a land whose language was not theirs, and went out to hear the voice of their own God.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Ladah, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Laadah, spelled Ladah in the King James Version, appears once, in the genealogy of Judah in 1 Chronicles 4:21. He was the father of Mareshah, of the families that wrought fine linen, and a son of Shelah of the house of Judah.
TheologicalSignificance: In my reading, the linen-makers of Mareshah are worth remembering: the genealogy keeps the craftsmen beside the kings, and God keeps the workers in the record.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Ladan, the name of two Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Ladan — Laadan in the King James Version — is the name of two Israelites, both Levites of the Gershonites. In 1 Chronicles 7:26 he is in the line of Ephraim, and in 1 Chronicles 23:7 and 1 Chronicles 23:8 he is the Gershonite whose sons Jehiel, Zetham, and Joel were chiefs of their fathers' houses.
TheologicalSignificance: To my mind, the two Ladans show how the Levites kept their lines: the same name in two families, both serving the house of the Lord, and both written down.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a buffoon; also a foreigner
BiblicalUsage: The mocker or stammerer is the foreigner whose speech sounds like mockery, and the word appears twice. In Isaiah 28:11 God says, "with stammering lips and another tongue will he speak to this people," and in Psalms 35:16 David complains of "hypocritical mockers in feasts" who gnashed upon him with their teeth.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the two verses show both sides of the same word: God's judgment speaks in a tongue Israel cannot understand, and David's enemies mock him at the table, and in both cases the mocking is the judgment.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Lael an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Lael appears once, as the father of a chief of the Levites in Numbers 3:24. His son Eliasaph was set over the Gershonites in the wilderness, and his name means of God.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Lael's one verse is enough: a father whose son was set over the service of the tabernacle, and a name that says he belonged to God.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, muffled, i.e. silently
BiblicalUsage: Softly or silently appears once, and it is Jael's quiet step in Judges 4:21: she "went softly unto him, and smote the nail into his temples, and fastened it into the ground." The word is the silence of the approach, the muffled footfall before the blow that killed Sisera.
TheologicalSignificance: My position is that the silence is the point of the verse: the deed was done without a sound, and the enemy of God's people died in his sleep.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {not (the simple or abs. negation); by implication, no;}
BiblicalUsage: La is the Aramaic word for "not" and "no," the simple negation of Daniel and Ezra. In Daniel 2:5 the king says, "if ye will not make known unto me the dream, ye shall be cut in pieces," and in Ezra 4:13 the adversaries warn that if Jerusalem is built, the king will have "no" tribute, custom, or toll.
TheologicalSignificance: I am convinced a small word like "not" carries the whole weight of the story: the king's threat, the enemies' accusation, and Daniel's answer all turn on what is not and what cannot be.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: (in a good sense) transport (with love), or (in a bad sense) stultify; to make cakes
BiblicalUsage: Labab is a small word with two very different uses, and both are in the story. In 2 Samuel 13:6 Amnon asks Tamar to come and make him a couple of cakes — but the cakes were a trap, and the request was a lie. The same word is the heart ravished with love in Song of Solomon 4:9, and the empty man in Job 11:12.
TheologicalSignificance: For me, what strikes me is the word's two faces are a warning and a promise: a heart can be ravished by love or emptied by deceit, and the same Hebrew root holds both.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: white
BiblicalUsage: White is the colour of manna, of clean garments, of leprosy, and of heaven's horses. In Exodus 16:31 the manna was white like coriander seed, in Ecclesiastes 9:8 the counsel is "let thy garments be always white," in Leviticus 13:3 the priest looks for hair turned white in the plague of leprosy, in Genesis 30:35 Jacob separates the sheep with white in them, and in Zechariah 1:8 the horses of the vision are white.
TheologicalSignificance: What I take from this is that white carries both meanings at once in Scripture: it is the colour of cleanness and of festivity, and also the mark the priest must read aright, because not every white is clean. The priest had to look twice, and so do I.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Laban, a Mesopotamian; also a place in the Desert
BiblicalUsage: Laban is Jacob's uncle and father-in-law, the Syrian of Padan-aram who gave Jacob his wives and cheated him of his wages. In Genesis 24:29 he runs out to meet Abraham's servant at the well, in Genesis 24:50 he and Bethuel agree the marriage "proceedeth from the LORD," and in Deuteronomy 1:1 the same name marks a place in the wilderness, a different Laban from the man.
TheologicalSignificance: I take it that Laban is the picture of the man who bargains with God and loses: he served the Lord's purpose for Jacob and Rebekah, and he could not keep Jacob from the blessing.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to be (or become) white; to make bricks
BiblicalUsage: To be white is the verb behind the adjective, and it does two kinds of work. In Genesis 11:3 the builders of Babel say "let us make brick," in Exodus 5:7 Pharaoh stops giving straw "to make brick," and in Isaiah 1:18 God promises, "though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow"; in Daniel 11:35 the wise are purged "and to make them white," and in Joel 1:7 the enemy has barked the fig tree and "made it clean bare."
TheologicalSignificance: I am sure the verb's two senses meet in Isaiah 1:18: men make brick to build their own tower, and God makes sinners white, and only one of those makings lasts. Men build towers of brick, and God makes sinners white as snow.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, wrap around, i.e. (by implication) to put on a garment or clothe (oneself, or another), literally or figuratively
BiblicalUsage: To be clothed is to be wrapped in a garment, and the word dresses kings, priests, and the first sinners. In Genesis 3:21 God Himself made coats of skins and clothed Adam and Eve, in 1 Kings 22:10 the kings sat "having put on their robes," in 2 Chronicles 5:12 the singers were "arrayed in white linen," and in 2 Samuel 1:24 David remembers Saul, who "clothed you in scarlet, with other delights."
TheologicalSignificance: What convinces me is that clothing in Scripture is always a covering with a meaning: God clothed the fallen pair, kings clothed themselves for battle and for judgment, and the singers clothed themselves in white for worship. God clothed the fallen pair, and He still covers His people.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to overthrow; intransposed, to fall
BiblicalUsage: To fall is the word's work in all three appearances, and it is always the fall of the fool. In Proverbs 10:8 "a prating fool shall fall," and in Hosea 4:14 "the people that doth not understand shall fall."
TheologicalSignificance: In my reading, the proverb is plain enough to live by: the wise in heart receive commandments, and the fool who keeps talking falls, and the fall is the consequence of the talking.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: flame
BiblicalUsage: The flame appears once, and it is the flame of the burning bush in Exodus 3:2: "the angel of the LORD appeared unto him in a flame of fire out of the midst of a bush: and he looked, and, behold, the bush burned with fire, and the bush was not consumed."
TheologicalSignificance: To my mind, this flame is the whole call of Moses in one sight: fire that burns without consuming, and a God who speaks from the middle of it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to roar; a lion (properly, a lioness as the fiercer (although not a roarer;))
BiblicalUsage: The lion is the king of beasts in Scripture, and this word is the lioness and the old lion together. Judah "is a lion's whelp" in Genesis 49:9, Gad "dwelleth as a lion" in Deuteronomy 33:20, the lioness nourishes her whelps among young lions in Ezekiel 19:2, and the enemy's roaring is "like a lion" in Isaiah 5:29.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the lion is the picture of strength that can bless or destroy: Judah's lion is the king who saves, and the roaring lion of the enemy is the one who devours, and I need to know which lion I am following. I follow the lion who saves, not the one who devours.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a cake (either as fried or turned)
BiblicalUsage: The cake is Tamar's cake, and all three appearances belong to her story. In 2 Samuel 13:6 Amnon asks for "a couple of cakes" made in his sight, in 2 Samuel 13:8 Tamar kneads and bakes them, and in 2 Samuel 13:10 she brings them into the chamber, where Amnon seizes her.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the cakes are the saddest detail in the story: a sister's cooking, made with her own hands, used as the trap for her ruin, and the Bible does not look away from it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: fresh, i.e. unused or undried
BiblicalUsage: Fresh or green is the word for what is still moist and undried. In Genesis 30:37 Jacob takes "rods of green poplar" and peels white strakes in them, and in Ezekiel 17:24 God says He has "dried up the green tree, and have made the dry tree to flourish."
TheologicalSignificance: My position is that the green tree is the promise in one adjective: God dries up the green and makes the dry flourish, and He alone decides which tree stands and which falls.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to lick
BiblicalUsage: To lick is the word for the tongue's work, and it is used for fire, for armies, and for humbled enemies. In 1 Kings 18:38 the fire of the Lord "licked up the water that was in the trench," in Numbers 22:4 Moab fears this company will "lick up all that are round about us, as the ox licketh up the grass," and in Isaiah 49:23 kings "shall lick up the dust of thy feet."
TheologicalSignificance: I am convinced the word's picture is total: fire licks the trench dry, an army licks a land bare, and one day kings will lick the dust before the people they once oppressed. What the fire did to the trench, God will do to the proud.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to feed on; figuratively, to consume; by implication, to battle (as destruction)
BiblicalUsage: To fight is one of the great verbs of the Old Testament, used a hundred and seventy-one times for war in every sense. In Exodus 14:14 Moses tells Israel, "The LORD shall fight for you, and ye shall hold your peace," in Joshua 10:25 Joshua tells the captains not to fear, for the Lord has done this to all their enemies, and in 1 Samuel 4:9 the Philistines urge one another to "quit yourselves like men, and fight."
TheologicalSignificance: For me, this word's first use is the one that matters most: the Lord fights for His people, and my part is to hold my peace and watch Him do it. I hold my peace, and He fights.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from λαχαίνω (to dig); a vegetable:--herb.
BiblicalUsage: Herbs are the garden plants, and the word appears in the parable and in the rebuke. In Mark 4:32 the mustard seed "becometh greater than all herbs," and in Luke 11:42 Jesus rebukes the Pharisees, who "tithe mint and rue and all manner of herbs, and pass over judgment and the love of God."
TheologicalSignificance: What I take from this is that this herbs preach the same sermon twice: the kingdom grows from the smallest seed to the greatest of herbs, and the Pharisees measured the smallest herb and missed the love of God.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, a whisper, i.e. by implication, (in a good sense) a private prayer, (in a bad one) an incantation; concretely, an amulet
BiblicalUsage: The whisper is the word for what is said low, and it covers a charm, an amulet, and a prayer. In Ecclesiastes 10:11 the serpent bites "without enchantment," in Jeremiah 8:17 God sends serpents "which will not be charmed," in Isaiah 3:3 the "eloquent orator" is literally the skilful whisperer, and in Isaiah 26:16 the afflicted "poured out a prayer" — a whispered prayer — when God's chastening was upon them.
TheologicalSignificance: I take it that the word's range is a warning about power: whispered charms cannot stop the serpent, but a whispered prayer in trouble reaches the God who chastens and heals. The charmer's whisper fails, and the sufferer's whisper is heard.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to whisper; by implication, to mumble a spell (as a magician)
BiblicalUsage: To whisper is what servants and enemies do behind a person's back. In 2 Samuel 12:19 David's servants whispered together, and David knew from the whisper that his child was dead; in Psalms 41:7 David says, "All that hate me whisper together against me: against me do they devise my hurt."
TheologicalSignificance: I am sure the whisper is the sound of conspiracy: David heard it in his own house and in the mouths of his enemies, and the psalm gives me the prayer for it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: distress
BiblicalUsage: Oppression is the noun for the crushing weight of a hard master, and it is the word of the exodus. In Exodus 3:9 God says, "I have also seen the oppression wherewith the Egyptians oppress them," in Deuteronomy 26:7 Israel remembers that the Lord "looked on our affliction, and our labour, and our oppression," and in 2 Kings 13:4 He saw "the oppression of Israel" under Syria and hearkened.
TheologicalSignificance: What convinces me is that oppression is never unseen: God saw it in Egypt, He saw it under Syria, and He hears the cry of the oppressed still. No oppression is unseen, and no cry is unheard.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, to press, i.e. (figuratively) to distress
BiblicalUsage: To oppress is the verb of the same weight, and it is laid at the door of Egypt, of Syria, and of every unjust power. In Exodus 3:9 God has seen "the oppression wherewith the Egyptians oppress" Israel, in 1 Samuel 10:18 He reminds Israel He delivered them "out of the hand of all kingdoms, and of them that oppressed you," and in Isaiah 19:20 Egypt's oppressed will cry to the Lord and He will send them a saviour.
TheologicalSignificance: In my reading, the verb is the promise and the warning together: The promise stands for Egypt, for Syria, and for every unjust power since. The promise stands for Egypt, for Syria, and for every unjust power since.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: battle
BiblicalUsage: War appears once, in the song of Deborah in Judges 5:8: "They chose new gods; then was war in the gates: was there a shield or spear seen among forty thousand in Israel?" The word is the battle itself, and Deborah says it came because Israel chose new gods.
TheologicalSignificance: To my mind, the verse is the history of Israel in one line: new gods, then war in the gates, and no shield or spear among forty thousand, because the idols could not defend them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Lachmam or Lachmas, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Lahmam appears once, in the list of the cities of Judah in Joshua 15:40. It was a town in the lowland of Judah, given to the tribe in the division of the land.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the one-line town still belongs in the record: the land was divided town by town, and God kept the list.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Lachmi, an Israelite; or rather probably a brief form
BiblicalUsage: Lahmi appears once, and he is named by the man who killed him in 1 Chronicles 20:5. Elhanan the son of Jair slew Lahmi the brother of Goliath the Gittite, whose spear staff was like a weaver's beam.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Lahmi's one verse closes a circle: the brother of Goliath, with a spear like a weaver's beam, fell to a man whose name the record keeps.
RelatedEvents: David's Mighty Men and the Philistine Giants
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, eaten, i.e. food; also flesh, i.e. body
BiblicalUsage: Flesh or food is the word for what is eaten and for the body itself, and both appearances are judgments. In Job 20:23 God will rain His wrath on the wicked "while he is eating," and in Zephaniah 1:17 the sinners' "flesh" shall be poured out as dung in the day of the Lord.
TheologicalSignificance: My position is that the word's two uses are one warning: the food in the mouth and the flesh on the body are both under God's hand, and neither is safe in the day of His anger.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a flash; figuratively, a sharply polished blade or point of a weapon
BiblicalUsage: The flame or the blade is the bright, sharp point, and it flashes in war and in worship. In Judges 13:20 the angel of the Lord ascends "in the flame of the altar" before Manoah and his wife, in Joel 2:5 the enemy comes "like the noise of a flame of fire that devoureth the stubble," in Job 39:23 the quiver rattles and the glittering spear flashes, and in Isaiah 13:8 the faces of the terrified "shall be as flames."
TheologicalSignificance: I am convinced the flame is both the glory and the terror of God: it carries His angel up to heaven, and it devours the stubble, and the same fire that receives the sacrifice will judge the proud. The same fire carries the angel up and devours the stubble.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Lahad, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Lahad appears once, in the genealogy of Judah in 1 Chronicles 4:2. Jahath begat Ahumai and Lahad, and these are the families of the Zorathites.
TheologicalSignificance: For me, the Zorathites' names are kept for a reason: the families of the craftsmen and the clans are written down beside the kings, and God forgets none of them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: intense mental application
BiblicalUsage: Study is the word for hard thinking, and it appears once, in the Preacher's warning in Ecclesiastes 12:12: "of making many books there is no end; and much study is a weariness of the flesh."
TheologicalSignificance: What I take from this is that the verse is not against learning but against endless learning: books without end weary the flesh, and the fear of God is the end of the matter.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to be rabid (figuratively, insane); also (from the exhaustion of frenzy) to languish
BiblicalUsage: To faint or to be mad is the word for a mind unstrung, and its two appearances are a famine and a madman. In Genesis 47:13 the land of Egypt and Canaan "fainted by reason of the famine," and in Proverbs 26:18 the madman "casteth firebrands, arrows, and death."
TheologicalSignificance: I take it that the word's two pictures belong together: famine faints a whole land, and madness throws firebrands at its neighbours, and both are what happens when life comes apart.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, to burn in, i.e. (figuratively) to rankle
BiblicalUsage: The talebearer's words are wounds, and the proverb says it twice, word for word. In Proverbs 18:8 and again in Proverbs 26:22, "The words of a talebearer are as wounds, and they go down into the innermost parts of the belly."
TheologicalSignificance: I am sure this repetition is the warning: gossip is not idle talk, it is a wound that goes deep, and it stays in the belly long after the words are gone.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an assembly
BiblicalUsage: The company is the assembly of the prophets, and it appears once, in the day Saul's messengers were overcome in 1 Samuel 19:20: they saw "the company of the prophets prophesying, and Samuel standing as appointed over them," and the Spirit of God fell on the messengers too, and they prophesied.
TheologicalSignificance: What convinces me is that the company of prophets is the proof that the Spirit cannot be arrested: Saul sent men to take David, and the Spirit took the men instead.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a blaze; also (from the idea of enwrapping) magic (as covert)
BiblicalUsage: The blaze is the word for both the flaming sword and the magicians' art. In Genesis 3:24 the cherubim guard the garden with "a flaming sword which turned every way," and in Exodus 7:11 Pharaoh's magicians "did in like manner with their enchantments."
TheologicalSignificance: In my reading, this two blazes are the two kinds of fire in the Bible: the sword that guards the way to life, and the enchantment that copies God's wonders, and I need to know them apart.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, to lick, i.e. (by implication) to blaze
BiblicalUsage: To burn or blaze is the word for God's fire, and it devours from Deuteronomy to Malachi. In Deuteronomy 32:22 a fire is kindled in God's anger and burns to the lowest hell, in Joel 1:19 the fire has "devoured the pastures of the wilderness," in Job 41:21 a flame goes out of Leviathan's mouth, and in Malachi 4:1 the day comes that "shall burn as an oven."
TheologicalSignificance: To my mind, the fire in this word is always God's fire: it kindles in His anger, it devours the wilderness, and it will burn the proud as stubble on the day that is coming. The day is coming, and the fire is already kindled.
RelatedTopics: Judgment; God's wrath and refuge; Day of the Lord
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: therefore; also except
BiblicalUsage: Lahen is the Aramaic hinge word, "therefore" or "except," and it turns the sentence on what follows. In Daniel 2:11 the Chaldeans say there is none other who can show the dream, "except the gods, whose dwelling is not with flesh," and in Ezra 5:12 the history turns on it: "But after that our fathers had provoked the God of heaven unto wrath, he gave them into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar."
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the small word carries the whole turn of the story: except the gods, no one could answer, and after their fathers provoked God, the house fell, and both turn on one hinge.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: therefore; also except
BiblicalUsage: Lahen is the Aramaic hinge word, "therefore" or "except," and it turns the sentence on what follows. In Daniel 2:11 the Chaldeans say there is none other who can show the dream, "except the gods, whose dwelling is not with flesh," and in Ezra 5:12 the history turns on it: "But after that our fathers had provoked the God of heaven unto wrath, he gave them into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar."
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the small word carries the whole turn of the story: except the gods, no one could answer, and after their fathers provoked God, the house fell, and both turn on one hinge.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain derivation; a whirlwind (squall):--storm, tempest.
BiblicalUsage: The whirlwind is the sudden storm, and it appears in the storm on the lake and in Peter's warning. In Luke 8:23 "there came down a storm of wind on the lake" while Jesus slept, and in 2 Peter 2:17 false teachers are "clouds that are carried with a tempest," wells without water.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that this whirlwind is the picture of a faith with no anchor: the storm comes down on the lake, the clouds are carried with the tempest, and only the word of Christ holds fast.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to catch (in a net, trap or pit); generally, to capture or occupy; also to choose (by lot); figuratively, to cohere
BiblicalUsage: To take or capture is the verb of conquest, used a hundred and twelve times for taking cities, taking men by lot, and taking a kingdom. In 1 Chronicles 11:5 David "took the castle of Zion, which is the city of David," in 1 Samuel 10:20 the tribe of Benjamin "was taken" by lot, and in 2 Chronicles 12:4 Shishak "took the fenced cities which pertained to Judah."
TheologicalSignificance: My position is that the word's whole history is in those three takings: David took Zion by war, Saul was taken by lot, and Judah's cities were taken in judgment, and God is behind each taking. War, lot, and judgment all took, and God held the taking in His hand.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Lakish, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Lachish was a fenced city of Judah, and its name runs through the wars of the kings. In 2 Chronicles 11:9 Rehoboam fortified it, in 2 Kings 14:19 Amaziah fled to Lachish and was slain there, and in Isaiah 36:2 Sennacherib sent Rabshakeh "from Lachish to Jerusalem" to demand Hezekiah's surrender.
TheologicalSignificance: I am convinced Lachish is the strong city that could not save: it was fortified, it was besieged, and kings fled to it and died in it, because no wall stands when God has given the city up.
RelatedPeople: King Hezekiah; Sennacherib, King of Assyria
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from adverb λάξ (heelwise); to recalcitrate:--kick.
BiblicalUsage: To kick appears once, and it is the voice of Christ to Saul on the Damascus road in Acts 26:14: "Saul, Saul, why persecutest thou me? it is hard for thee to kick against the pricks." The pricks are the goad, and the kicking is the ox fighting the hand that drives it.
TheologicalSignificance: For me, the goad is the mercy in the verse: Saul was kicking against Christ and hurting only himself, and the voice that stopped him was the voice that saved him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a prolonged form of an otherwise obsolete verb; to talk, i.e. utter words:--preach, say, speak (after), talk, tell, utter. Compare G3004.
BiblicalUsage: To speak is the ordinary word for uttering words, used two hundred and seventy-three times, and it carries the whole weight of what is said. In John 3:11 Jesus says, "We speak that we do know, and testify that we have seen," in 1 Corinthians 2:6 Paul says, "we speak wisdom among them that are perfect," and in 1 Peter 3:10 the man who would love life must refrain his tongue from evil.
TheologicalSignificance: What I take from this is that this word's lesson is in John 3:11: we speak what we know, and what we know is what we have seen, and the gospel is not opinion but testimony. Testimony, not opinion: that is what the word demands of my mouth.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2980; talk:--saying, speech.
BiblicalUsage: Speech or talk is the word for what a person says, and it gives people away. In Mark 14:70 the bystanders tell Peter, "thy speech agreeth thereto," and in John 4:42 the Samaritans tell the woman, "Now we believe, not because of thy saying: for we have heard him ourselves."
TheologicalSignificance: I take it that speech is the test of the heart: Peter's accent betrayed him in the courtyard, and the woman's saying brought a city to hear Jesus for themselves.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: or λαμμᾶ; of Hebrew origin (H4100 with prepositional prefix); lama (i.e. why):--lama.
BiblicalUsage: Lama is the Aramaic word for "why," and it survives only in the cry from the cross. In Matthew 27:46 Jesus cries, "Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani?" and in Mark 15:34, "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?" The Greek text carries the word as λεμά, where the King James tradition has λαμά.
TheologicalSignificance: I am sure the word is the deepest question ever asked: the Son crying "why" to the Father, and the answer is the cross itself, borne for me.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, to goad, i.e. (by implication) to teach (the rod being an Oriental incentive)
BiblicalUsage: To teach or to learn is the verb of the rod and the classroom, used eighty times for instructing in war, in song, and in the law. In Deuteronomy 4:1 Moses says, "hearken, O Israel, unto the statutes and unto the judgments, which I teach you," in Psalms 25:4 David prays, "Teach me thy paths," and the title of Psalms 60 says the psalm was written "to teach."
TheologicalSignificance: What convinces me is that teaching in Scripture is never only information: Moses teaches statutes to be done, David asks to be taught the paths to walk, and the psalm itself was written to teach, because the truth must be learned to be lived. I want to be taught that way: statutes to do, and paths to walk.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a prolonged form of a primary verb, which is use only as an alternate in certain tenses; to take (in very many applications, literally and figuratively (properly objective or active, to get hold of; whereas G1209 is rather subjective or passive, to have offered to one; while G138 is more violent, to seize or remove)):--accept, + be amazed, assay, attain, bring, X when I call, catch, come on (X unto), + forget, have, hold, obtain, receive (X after), take (away, up).
BiblicalUsage: To take or receive is the great verb of getting, used two hundred and forty-three times for taking bread, taking a wife, and receiving the Spirit. In John 1:12 "as many as received him, to them gave he power to become the sons of God," in 1 Corinthians 2:12 "we have received, not the spirit of the world, but the spirit which is of God," and in 1 Peter 4:10 every man is to minister "the gift" he has received.
TheologicalSignificance: In my reading, the whole Christian life is in the verb: we receive Him, we receive His Spirit, and we receive gifts to give away, and nothing I have was not first received. I received Him, I received His Spirit, and I received gifts to give away.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H3929); Lamech (i.e. Lemek), a patriarch:--Lamech.
BiblicalUsage: Lamech appears once, in the genealogy of Jesus in Luke 3:36: Noah "was the son of Lamech," and Lamech was the son of Methuselah. He is the Lamech who lived seven hundred and seventy-seven years and died five years before the flood, the father of Noah, whose name means rest.
TheologicalSignificance: To my mind, Lamech's one verse holds the whole hope of the genealogy: the father of Noah, whose son would bring rest from the curse, and whose name stands in the line that leads to Christ.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2989; a "lamp" or flambeau:--lamp, light, torch.
BiblicalUsage: The lamp or torch is the light carried in the night, and it burns in the parable and in the arrest. In Matthew 25:1 the ten virgins "took their lamps, and went forth to meet the bridegroom," in John 18:3 Judas comes to the garden "with lanterns and torches and weapons," and in Revelation 4:5 "seven lamps of fire" burn before the throne.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the lamp is the test of readiness: the wise carried oil with their lamps and the foolish did not, and the difference showed at midnight. Readiness is oil in the vessel, not just a lamp in the hand.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a primary verb; to beam, i.e. radiate brilliancy (literally or figuratively):--give light, shine.
BiblicalUsage: To shine is the verb of light breaking out, and it is used of Christ, of the believer, and of the lightning. In Matthew 5:16 Jesus says, "Let your light so shine before men," in 2 Corinthians 4:6 God "hath shined in our hearts, to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ," and in Acts 12:7 a light shined in Peter's prison.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the shining is always God's doing first: He shined in our hearts, and only then does our light shine before men, and the order matters. His light in me comes first; my light before men comes second.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: adverb from G2986; brilliantly, i.e. figuratively, luxuriously:--sumptuously.
BiblicalUsage: Sumptuously is the adverb for living in luxury, and it appears once, in the parable of the rich man in Luke 16:19: he "was clothed in purple and fine linen, and fared sumptuously every day."
TheologicalSignificance: My position is that the one adverb carries the whole parable: he fared sumptuously every day, and Lazarus lay at his gate, and the luxury is the indictment.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from the same as G2985; radiant; by analogy, limpid; figuratively, magnificent or sumptuous (in appearance):--bright, clear, gay, goodly, gorgeous, white.
BiblicalUsage: Bright or splendid is the adjective for clothing and for glory. In Luke 23:11 Herod arrays Jesus "in a gorgeous robe," in James 2:2 a man comes into the assembly "in goodly apparel," in Acts 10:30 a man stands before Cornelius "in bright clothing," and in Revelation 15:6 the angels are clothed in pure and white linen.
TheologicalSignificance: I am convinced the word's contrast is the sermon: Herod's gorgeous robe mocked the King, and the angels' bright linen is the clothing of those who serve Him, and I want to know which brightness I am wearing. Herod's robe mocked the King, and the angels' linen serves Him.
RelatedPeople: Jesus; Cornelius; James, Brother of Jesus
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2986; brilliancy:--brightness.
BiblicalUsage: Brightness appears once, in Paul's telling of the Damascus light in Acts 26:13: "At midday, O king, I saw in the way a light from heaven, above the brightness of the sun, shining round about me and them which journeyed with me."
TheologicalSignificance: For me, the brightness is the proof of the vision: a light brighter than the noonday sun, and a voice with it, and a persecutor made an apostle in one moment.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a prolonged form of a primary verb, which is only used as an alternate in certain tenses; to lot, i.e. determine (by implication, receive) especially by lot:--his lot be, cast lots, obtain.
BiblicalUsage: To obtain by lot is the word for what falls to a person by God's allotment. In Luke 1:9 Zechariah's "lot was to burn incense" in the temple, in Acts 1:17 Judas "had obtained part of this ministry," and in 2 Peter 1:1 believers "have obtained like precious faith with us."
TheologicalSignificance: What I take from this is that what strikes me is the word's three lots are the whole story of providence: a priest's lot, an apostle's lot, and a faith obtained, and each one fell where God put it.
RelatedPeople: Simon Peter; Zechariah, Father of John the Baptist
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a prolonged form of a primary verb, which is used only as an alternate in certain tenses; to lie hid (literally or figuratively); often used adverbially, unwittingly:--be hid, be ignorant of, unawares.
BiblicalUsage: To escape notice is to lie hidden, and the word is used for ignorance both wilful and unknowing. In 2 Peter 3:5 the scoffers "willingly are ignorant" of the creation and the flood, in Hebrews 13:2 some "have entertained angels unawares," and in Luke 8:47 the woman who touched Jesus saw "she was not hid" and came trembling to tell all.
TheologicalSignificance: I take it that the word draws the line between the two hidings: the scoffer hides the truth from himself on purpose, and the believer hides nothing, because nothing is hid from Him. One hiding is wilful blindness, and the other is no hiding at all.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a compound of G2992 and G1349; Laodicia, a place in Asia Minor:--Laodicea.
BiblicalUsage: Laodicea was one of the seven churches, and Paul's care for it runs through Colossians. In Colossians 2:1 he speaks of his "great conflict" for those at Laodicea, in Colossians 4:13 Epaphras has "a great zeal" for them, in Colossians 4:15 Paul greets the brethren and the church in Nymphas's house, and in Revelation 1:11 Laodicea is one of the seven churches to receive the book.
TheologicalSignificance: I am sure Laodicea is the church I must watch in myself: loved by Paul, prayed for by Epaphras, and still warned by the Lord that lukewarm is the worst state of all. I must watch in myself the very thing the Lord warned them about.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2993; a Laodicean, i.e. inhabitant of Laodicia:--Laodicean.
BiblicalUsage: The Laodiceans are the church at Laodicea, and the word appears once, in the closing of Colossians in Colossians 4:16: when the epistle is read among the Colossians, "cause that it be read also in the church of the Laodiceans."
TheologicalSignificance: What convinces me is that the one verse shows how the churches shared the word: Paul's letter was not for one church only, and the Laodiceans were to hear what Colosse heard.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: apparently a primary word; a people (in general; thus differing from G1218, which denotes one's own populace):--people.
BiblicalUsage: Laos is the people, the nation as a whole, and it is the word of the covenant people from one end of the New Testament to the other. In Luke 2:10 the angel brings "good tidings of great joy, which shall be to all people," in 1 Peter 2:9 believers are "a peculiar people," chosen and holy, in 2 Corinthians 6:16 God says, "I will be their God, and they shall be my people," and in Acts 2:47 the Lord added to the church daily.
TheologicalSignificance: In my reading, the word is the gospel's great transfer: a people who were not a people are now the people of God, and the good tidings are to all people, not to one nation only. The good tidings are to all people, and the people of God are those He has called out of darkness.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, to bend, i.e. (by implication) to clasp; also (reflexively) to turn around or aside
BiblicalUsage: To turn aside or to take hold is the word's work in two very different scenes. In Job 6:18 the paths of the desert caravans "are turned aside; they go to nothing, and perish," and in Judges 16:29 Samson "took hold of the two middle pillars" of the house and brought it down.
TheologicalSignificance: To my mind, the word's two senses are the two ways a life goes: paths that turn aside and come to nothing, and hands that take hold and bring the house down.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a flambeau, lamp or flame
BiblicalUsage: The torch or lamp is the flame carried in the hand, and it burns in the covenant, in the battle, and in the visions. In Genesis 15:17 "a burning lamp" passed between the pieces of the covenant, in Judges 7:16 Gideon put lamps in the pitchers of his three hundred men, in Exodus 20:18 the people saw "the lightnings" on the mountain, and in Isaiah 62:1 Jerusalem's salvation goes forth "as a lamp that burneth."
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this lamp is the light God carries into the dark: it sealed the covenant with Abraham, it won Gideon's battle, and it is the picture of the salvation that will not rest until it shines. From Abraham's covenant to Gideon's battle, the lamp is the light God carries into the dark.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Lappidoth, the husband of Deborah
BiblicalUsage: Lapidoth appears once, as the husband of Deborah in Judges 4:4. Deborah, a prophetess, judged Israel at that time, and nothing more is said of him, only that he was her husband.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the one verse is enough for a husband: he is named beside his wife, and the wife God raised up to judge Israel was his, and the record honours him by naming him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to take (in the widest variety of applications)
BiblicalUsage: lâqach means to take, and Scripture puts it to work in every part of life. In Genesis 2:22, "which the LORD God had taken from man"; and in Genesis 12:5, "And Abram took Sarai his wife". In Exodus 16:33, "Take a pot"; and in Isaiah 53:8, "He was taken from prison and from judgment: and who shall declare his generation?".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe taking is never neutral in Scripture — God takes us to Himself, and we take what He gives or what He forbids. I hold that the hand that takes is the hand that chooses, and every taking answers the question of who we trust. My position is simple: I want to take only what God puts in my hand, and leave the rest alone.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to lick or lap
BiblicalUsage: lâqaq means to lick or lap — an ordinary word that carries real weight in the Bible. In Judges 7:5, "Every one that lappeth of the water with his tongue"; and in Judges 7:7, "By the three hundred men that lapped will I save you". In 1 Kings 21:19, "In the place where dogs licked the blood of Naboth shall dogs lick thy blood"; and in 1 Kings 22:38, "and the dogs licked up his blood".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God sees what lapping dogs and licking tongues reveal — the small, unguarded habits that show a person's heart. I hold that the same lapping that chose Gideon's three hundred also pronounced judgment on Ahab's house. Nothing about us is too small for God to notice, and nothing He notices is without meaning.
RelatedTopics: Judgment; God's Sovereignty; Sin and repentance
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to gather the after crop
BiblicalUsage: lâqash means to gather the after crop, and its few appearances are all worth reading. In Job 24:6, "They reap [every one] his corn in the field: and they gather the vintage of the wicked.".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God sees the poor gathering what the fields leave behind, and He counts how the powerful treat them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, to pick up, i.e. (generally) to gather; specifically, to glean
BiblicalUsage: lâqaṭ means to pick up, and the contexts could hardly be more different.
