In Exodus 16:16, "Gather of it every man according to his eating"; and in Ruth 2:3, "and gleaned in the field after the reapers: and her hap was to light on a part of the field [belonging] unto Boaz". In Leviticus 19:9, "neither shalt thou gather the gleanings of thy harvest."; and in 2 Kings 4:39, "and gathered thereof wild gourds his lap full".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe gleaning is God's welfare system — the field is never stripped bare because the poor still have a right to eat. I hold that the God who rained manna for a day also left grain in the corners for Ruth. My position is that provision is not charity added on afterwards; it is built into the harvest from the start.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Lakkum, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Laqqûwm is the name of Lakkum, a place in Palestine. In Joshua 19:33, "and the outgoings thereof were at Jordan:".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe even a border town named once in a list matters — God measured the land for His people down to the last village. I hold that no place in His promise is too small to be named.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain derivation; the throat ("larynx"):--throat.
BiblicalUsage: lárynx means the throat, and once is enough to see what it is doing. In Romans 3:13, "Their throat [is] an open sepulchre".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Paul is right that sin reaches all the way down the throat — what comes out of us shows what is rotting inside.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain origin; Lasæa, a place in Crete:--Lasea.
BiblicalUsage: Lasaía means Lasea, a place in Crete. In Acts 27:8, "came unto a place which is called The fair havens".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe even a passing mention of a Cretan harbour reminds me that Paul's voyage to Rome was real — real seas, real ports, real danger.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a strengthened form of a primary verb, which only occurs in this and another prolonged form as alternate in certain tenses; to crack open (from a fall):--burst asunder.
BiblicalUsage: láschō means to burst asunder — a small word with a sharp edge. In Acts 1:18, "he burst asunder in the midst".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the burst body of the betrayer is Scripture's blunt verdict on treachery — sin does not end neatly, and Judas's end warns me more than any sermon: the price of betraying Christ is paid in full.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to wag the tongue, i.e. to calumniate
BiblicalUsage: lâshan means to wag the tongue, and its few appearances are all worth reading. In Proverbs 30:10, "Accuse not a servant unto his master"; and in Psalms 101:5, "Whoso privily slandereth his neighbour".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe slander is a small sin with a large ruin — a whispered accusation can curse a servant and cut off a neighbour.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: the tongue (of man or animals), used literally (as the instrument of licking, eating, or speech), and figuratively (speech, an ingot, a fork of flame, a cove of water)
BiblicalUsage: lâshôwn means the tongue — and its range, from the ordinary to the holy, is the point. In Proverbs 18:21, "Death and life [are] in the power of the tongue: and they that love it shall eat the fruit thereof."; and in Psalms 12:4, "With our tongue will we prevail". In Isaiah 50:4, "The Lord GOD hath given me the tongue of the learned"; and in Proverbs 15:4, "A wholesome tongue [is] a tree of life: but perverseness therein [is] a breach in the spirit.".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the tongue is the smallest member with the largest reach — death and life hang on it, and no one tames it alone. I hold that God gave Isaiah a tongue that could speak a word in season to the weary, and that is what I want mine to do. My position is that every word I speak is either a gift or a wound, and I answer to God for which one it was.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, covered, i.e. secret; by implication, incantation; also secrecy or (adverb) covertly
BiblicalUsage: lâṭ means secret arts, enchantment, and no one who reads the Bible can walk past it. In Exodus 7:22, "And the magicians of Egypt did so with their enchantments: and Pharaoh's heart was hardened"; and in Exodus 8:18, "And the magicians did so with their enchantments to bring forth lice". In Ruth 3:7, "he went to lie down at the end of the heap of corn: and she came softly"; and in 1 Samuel 18:22, "Commune with David secretly".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe secret arts are real enough to fool a king, and weak enough to fail at lice. I hold that Pharaoh's magicians could copy the first signs but not the third, because God's power is not a trick to be learned. My position is plain: what is done in secret against God always runs out of power in the open.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, to hammer out (an edge), i.e. to sharpen
BiblicalUsage: lâṭash means to sharpen, and once is enough to see what it is doing. In 1 Samuel 13:20, "to sharpen every man his share"; and in Genesis 4:22, "an instructer of every artificer in brass and iron: and the sister of Tubal-cain [was] Naamah.". In Psalms 7:12, "he will whet his sword".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe sharpening is honest work with a sharp edge — the same skill that keeps a ploughshare cutting can whet a sword, and God notices which one I choose.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: adverb from G2990; privately:--privily, secretly.
BiblicalUsage: láthra means privately, in secret. In Matthew 1:19, "was minded to put her away privily."; and in John 11:28, "and called Mary her sister secretly". In Acts 16:37, "and now do they thrust us out privily?".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe what is done privately still counts — Joseph's quiet mercy, Mary's whispered summons, and Paul's private release all happened out of the public eye, and God saw every one of them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from the same as the first part of G2991 and the base of G5114; to quarry:--hew.
BiblicalUsage: latoméō means hew — a small word with a sharp edge. In Matthew 27:60, "which he had hewn out in the rock: and he rolled a great stone to the door of the sepulchre"; and in Mark 15:46, "and laid him in a sepulchre which was hewn out of a rock".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the hewn tomb matters because it was new, unused, and real — the grave that held Christ for three days was cut out of solid rock by human hands.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3000; ministration of God, i.e. worship:--(divine) service.
BiblicalUsage: latreía means (divine) service, and it shows up wherever God is dealing with His people. In Romans 12:1, "[which is] your reasonable service."; and in Hebrews 9:1, "Then verily the first [covenant] had also ordinances of divine service". In John 16:2, "that whosoever killeth you will think that he doeth God service."; and in Romans 9:4, "and the service [of God]".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe worship is not a song but a service — Paul calls our bodies a living sacrifice, and that is our reasonable worship. I hold that the old tabernacle's service pointed forward to this: God does not want our performance, He wants us. My position is that if my life is not offered, my singing is noise.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from λάτρις (a hired menial); to minister (to God), i.e. render religious homage:--serve, do the service, worship(-per).
BiblicalUsage: latreúō means to serve God, to worship, and the contexts could hardly be more different. In Acts 24:14, "so worship I the God of my fathers"; and in Philippians 3:3, "which worship God in the spirit". In Hebrews 12:28, "whereby we may serve God acceptably with reverence and godly fear:"; and in 2 Timothy 1:3, "whom I serve from [my] forefathers with pure conscience".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe serving God is the work of a free person, not a hireling — Paul served with a pure conscience from his forefathers, and I want that same clean conscience. I hold that true worship is not what I do on Sunday only; it is whose I am every day. My position is that I belong to God, and serving Him is not my burden but my freedom.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to deride
BiblicalUsage: lâtsats means to deride — rare in the text, and exact where it appears. In Hosea 7:5, "he stretched out his hand with scorners.".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe derision is the sin of people who have stopped fearing God — princes drunk with wine, stretching out their hands with scorners.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: derision
BiblicalUsage: lâtsôwn means derision, and the word keeps turning up at decisive moments. In Isaiah 28:14, "ye scornful men"; and in Proverbs 1:22, "and the scorners delight in their scorning". In Proverbs 29:8, "Scornful men bring a city into a snare: but wise [men] turn away wrath.".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe scorn is the one attitude God will not argue with — the scorner delights in scorning, and the city pays for it. I hold that wisdom begins where scorn ends: the moment I stop mocking long enough to listen. My position is that I would rather be corrected by the wise than applauded by the scornful.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, to twine, i.e. (by implication) to unite, to remain; also to borrow (as a form of obligation) or (caus.) to lend
BiblicalUsage: lâvâh means to twine, and it is one of those words that quietly holds a whole theme together. In Deuteronomy 28:44, "and thou shalt not lend to him: he shall be the head"; and in Exodus 22:25, "If thou lend money to [any of] my people [that is] poor by thee". In Esther 9:27, "and upon all such as joined themselves unto them"; in Daniel 11:34, "they shall be holpen with a little help: but many shall cleave to them with flatteries."; and in Zechariah 2:11, "And many nations shall be joined to the LORD in that day".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe joining is a word with two edges — Ruth joined herself to Israel, and a borrower joins himself to a lender. I hold that God warned Israel about both: join the right people, and never let debt make you a servant. My position is that I want to be joined to God's people and free of every other master.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a compound of λᾶς (a stone) and the base of G3584 (in its original sense of scraping); rock-quarried:--hewn in stone.
BiblicalUsage: laxeutós means hewn in stone — a small word with a sharp edge. In Luke 23:53, "and laid it in a sepulchre that was hewn in stone".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the hewn stone of the tomb is part of the proof — Christ was laid in a real sepulchre, cut by hand, and He left it empty.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, a twist (away of the light), i.e. night; figuratively, adversity
BiblicalUsage: layil means night, and it does large work in the story. In Genesis 1:5, "and the darkness he called Night."; and in Psalms 19:2, "and night unto night sheweth knowledge.". In Psalms 91:5, "Thou shalt not be afraid for the terror by night"; in Isaiah 21:11, "what of the night?"; and in Jeremiah 9:1, "that I might weep day and night for the slain of the daughter of my people!".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe night belongs to God as much as day — He made the darkness, He speaks in it, and He watches through it. I hold that the terrors of the night lose their power when I remember who is awake: the same God who divided light from darkness never sleeps. My position is that I do not have to fear the dark, because the One who made it walks in it with me.
RelatedTopics: Darkness; Light and Darkness; God's Protection
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Laish, the name of two places in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Laish the place is a different word from layish the lion, though they share the same letters — this one is a town, and a man's name, in the north. In Judges 18:7, "and came to Laish"; and in Judges 18:27, "and came unto Laish". In 1 Samuel 25:44, "to Phalti the son of Laish".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Laish shows both sides of a name — a careless city taken by Dan, and a father whose son lost his wife to a king. I hold that names in Scripture carry whole histories, and God remembers every one of them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a lion (from his destructive blows)
BiblicalUsage: Layish the lion is a different word from Laish the place, though they share the same letters — this one is the beast, the old lion of the proverbs. In Isaiah 30:6, "from whence [come] the young and old lion"; and in Job 4:11, "and the stout lion's whelps are scattered abroad.". In Proverbs 30:30, "A lion [which is] strongest among beasts".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the old lion teaches me what strength looks like when it is gone — the strongest beast perishes for lack of prey, and turns not away for any. I hold that human strength is the same: fearsome for a season, and then scattered. My position is that I will not put my trust in the lion's strength, but in the God who made the lion.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably of Hebrew origin (H499); Lazarus (i.e. Elazar), the name of two Israelites (one imaginary):--Lazarus.
BiblicalUsage: Lázaros names Lazarus, and its appearances in Scripture are few but pointed. In John 11:1, "[named] Lazarus"; and in John 11:43, "he cried with a loud voice". In Luke 16:20, "And there was a certain beggar named Lazarus".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Lazarus is the proof I hold onto when death looks final — Jesus wept at the grave, then called a dead man out of it by name. My position is that the same voice that said Lazarus should come forth will one day call me too.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Leah, a wife of Jacob
BiblicalUsage: Lêʼâh is the name of Leah, a wife of Jacob. In Genesis 29:16, "And Laban had two daughters: the name of the elder [was] Leah"; and in Genesis 29:25, "it [was] Leah: and he said to Laban". In Genesis 29:31, "And when the LORD saw that Leah [was] hated".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Leah is the Bible's proof that God sees the unloved — Jacob loved Rachel more, but the Lord opened Leah's womb and gave her sons. I hold that her story is for everyone who has felt second-best: God does not overlook the tender-eyed and the passed-over.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a community
BiblicalUsage: lᵉʼôm means a community — an ordinary word that carries real weight in the Bible. In Genesis 25:23, "and two manner of people shall be separated from thy bowels"; and in Genesis 27:29, "and nations bow down to thee: be lord over thy brethren". In Isaiah 34:1, "ye nations"; and in Psalms 2:1, "and the people imagine a vain thing?".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God is the God of peoples, not just persons — two nations struggled in Rebekah's womb, and every nation answers to Him. I hold that no people is too many or too far for His rule: He summons the nations to hear, and He rebukes the ones that rage. My position is that my people is small in His sight, and that is good news, because He holds it all.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Leum mim, an Arabian
BiblicalUsage: Lᵉʼummîym means Leum mim, an Arabian, and its few appearances are all worth reading. In Genesis 25:3, "and Leummim.".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe even a single name in a genealogy counts — Leummim is named once, and God kept the record.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: freshness, i.e. vigor
BiblicalUsage: lêach means freshness, and the verse where it stands does the talking. In Deuteronomy 34:7, "nor his natural force abated.".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Moses' undimmed eye at a hundred and twenty is God's quiet witness — a life spent with Him does not have to end in weakness.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {the heart; also used (figuratively) very widely for the feelings, the will and even the intellect; likewise for the centre of anything}
BiblicalUsage: lêb means the heart — rare in the text, and exact where it appears. In Daniel 7:28, "my cogitations much troubled me".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Daniel's troubled heart shows me that true visions shake the seer — God's revelations are not entertainment, they are weight.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {the heart; also used (figuratively) very widely for the feelings, the will and even the intellect; likewise for the centre of anything}
BiblicalUsage: lêb means the heart — rare in the text, and exact where it appears. In Daniel 7:28, "my cogitations much troubled me".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Daniel's troubled heart shows me that true visions shake the seer — God's revelations are not entertainment, they are weight.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Lebaoth, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Lᵉbâʼôwth is the name Scripture gives to Lebaoth, a place in Palestine. In Joshua 15:32, "And Lebaoth".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Lebaoth earns its one mention honestly — a town in Judah's inheritance, counted among the cities God gave His people.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {the heart (as the most interior organ);}
BiblicalUsage: lᵉbab means the heart, and it is one of those words that quietly holds a whole theme together. In Daniel 5:20, "But when his heart was lifted up"; and in Daniel 5:22, "hast not humbled thine heart". In Daniel 7:4, "and a man's heart was given to it."; and in Daniel 4:16, "and let a beast's heart be given unto him".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the heart is the throne God deposes — Nebuchadnezzar's heart was lifted up in pride, and his heart was made like a beast's. I hold that Daniel's warning to Belshazzar still stands: a heart that will not humble itself will be humbled. My position is that I want God to change my heart before pride changes it for me.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: the heart (as the most interior organ);
BiblicalUsage: Heart is what lêbâb means — the inward place where love and loyalty live, and where God looks first. In Deuteronomy 6:5, "And thou shalt love the LORD thy God with all thine heart"; and in Deuteronomy 30:6, "to love the LORD thy God with all thine heart". In 1 Kings 8:48, "And [so] return unto thee with all their heart"; and in Jeremiah 29:13, "when ye shall search for me with all your heart.".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the heart is where everything is decided — love God with all of it, seek Him with all of it, and let Him circumcise it. I hold that no law can do what Moses promised: only God cuts away the hardness so we can love Him with all our heart. My position is that my heart is His work to do, and my work is to give it to Him without holding any of it back.
RelatedTopics: New heart; Love for God; Repentance
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Lebana or Lebanah, one of the Nethinim
BiblicalUsage: Lᵉbânâʼ is the name of Lebana or Lebanah, one of the Nethinim. In Ezra 2:45, "The children of Lebanah"; and in Nehemiah 7:48, "The children of Lebana".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the Nethinim matter — Lebana's children came back from exile to serve in the house of God, and their names are written down. I hold that God remembers the servants, not only the kings.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, (the) white, i.e. the moon
BiblicalUsage: lᵉbânâh means the moon — and its range, from the ordinary to the holy, is the point. In Isaiah 24:23, "Then the moon shall be confounded"; and in Isaiah 30:26, "Moreover the light of the moon shall be as the light of the sun". In Song of Solomon 6:10, "fair as the moon".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the moon will be confounded on the day the Lord reigns — the lesser light steps back when the true Light comes. I hold that even the moon's brightness is borrowed, and one day it will shine sevenfold because God heals His people. My position is that I worship the Maker of the moon, never the moon itself.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Lebanon, a mountain range in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Lᵉbânôwn belongs to Lebanon, a mountain range in Palestine, and the Bible does not let it pass unnamed. In 1 Kings 5:6, "Now therefore command thou that they hew me cedar trees out of Lebanon"; and in 1 Kings 5:9, "My servants shall bring [them] down from Lebanon unto the sea: and I will convey them by sea in floats unto the place that thou shalt appoint me". In Psalms 92:12, "The righteous shall flourish like the palm tree: he shall grow like a cedar in Lebanon.".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Lebanon is God's lumber yard and His picture of strength — its cedars built the temple, and the righteous flourish like them. I hold that what God plants in high places, He uses for holy work.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {properly, wrap around, i.e. (by implication) to put on a garment or clothe (oneself, or another), literally or figuratively}
BiblicalUsage: lᵉbash means to clothe, and the Bible uses it the way ordinary people use ordinary words — for everything. In Daniel 5:7, "shall be clothed with scarlet"; and in Daniel 5:16, "thou shalt be clothed with scarlet". In Daniel 5:29, "and they clothed Daniel with scarlet".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe clothing tells the story of Daniel's night — Belshazzar promised scarlet to any man who could read the writing, and Daniel wore it for an hour before the kingdom fell. I hold that robes and chains cannot save a king who has weighed himself against God. My position is that I would rather be clothed in humility than in scarlet.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain origin; Lebbæus, a Christian:--Lebbæus.
BiblicalUsage: Lebbaîos is the name of Lebbæus, the apostle also called Thaddaeus. In Matthew 10:3, "and Lebbaeus".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Lebbaeus matters because he is the apostle with two names — Matthew's list calls him Lebbaeus, and the same man is Thaddaeus elsewhere. I hold that God knows His servants by every name they carry.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a brick (from the whiteness of the clay)
BiblicalUsage: lᵉbênâh means a brick — an ordinary word that carries real weight in the Bible. In Exodus 1:14, "and in brick"; and in Exodus 5:7, "Ye shall no more give the people straw to make brick". In Genesis 11:3, "let us make brick"; and in Isaiah 65:3, "and burneth incense upon altars of brick".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe bricks tell two stories — Babel's builders burned them to make a name for themselves, and Pharaoh's slaves made them until their lives were bitter. I hold that God judges both towers and taskmasters: no human work built on pride or cruelty stands. My position is that I will not build my name out of other people's suffering.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Lebonah, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Lebonah the place is a landmark on the road to Shiloh — not the frankincense, which shares its name. In Judges 21:19, "and on the south of Lebonah.".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Lebonah earns its mention as a landmark — the yearly feast at Shiloh had a road, and Lebonah stood beside it. I hold that God marks His people's journeys with real places.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: frankincense (from its whiteness or perhaps that of its smoke)
BiblicalUsage: Frankincense is the spice the Bible calls lebownah — white and costly, burned for God alone, and not to be confused with Lebonah the place, which shares its name. In Exodus 30:34, "[these] sweet spices with pure frankincense: of each shall there be a like [weight]:"; and in Leviticus 2:1, "and put frankincense thereon:". In Isaiah 60:6, "The multitude of camels shall cover thee"; and in Jeremiah 6:20, "To what purpose cometh there to me incense from Sheba".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe frankincense is the smell of prayer that God accepts — white, costly, and burned for Him alone. I hold that when the smoke rises without a heart behind it, God says the offerings are not acceptable. My position is that my worship must be pure frankincense, not a show.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {a garment (literally or figuratively); by implication (euphemistically) a wife}
BiblicalUsage: lᵉbûwsh means a garment — rare in the text, and exact where it appears. In Daniel 3:21, "and their [other] garments"; and in Daniel 7:9, "whose garment [was] white as snow".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe garments mark the two scenes — the three men bound in their coats walked out of the fire, and the Ancient of Days sat in a garment white as snow.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {a garment (literally or figuratively); by implication (euphemistically) a wife}
BiblicalUsage: lᵉbûwsh means a garment — rare in the text, and exact where it appears. In Daniel 3:21, "and their [other] garments"; and in Daniel 7:9, "whose garment [was] white as snow".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe garments mark the two scenes — the three men bound in their coats walked out of the fire, and the Ancient of Days sat in a garment white as snow.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {(for man or beast), especially bread, or grain (for making it)}
BiblicalUsage: lᵉchem means bread, and once is enough to see what it is doing. In Daniel 5:1, "Belshazzar the king made a great feast to a thousand of his lords".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Belshazzar's feast is the warning — a thousand lords eating and drinking while the writing was on the wall.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: food (for man or beast), especially bread, or grain (for making it)
BiblicalUsage: lechem means bread, food, and it is one of those words that quietly holds a whole theme together. In Genesis 3:19, "In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread"; and in Deuteronomy 8:3, "that he might make thee know that man doth not live by bread only". In Psalms 104:15, "and bread [which] strengtheneth man's heart."; and in Exodus 16:15, "This [is] the bread which the LORD hath given you to eat.".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe bread is God's daily sermon — by the sweat of your face you eat it, and yet man does not live by bread alone. I hold that the God who rained manna and gave the psalmist bread to strengthen the heart still feeds His people by His word. My position is that I will ask Him for daily bread, and trust Him for the rest.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a concubine
BiblicalUsage: A concubine is what lᵉchênâh means — a secondary wife in the old household, named without praise or excuse where she appears. In Daniel 5:2, "and his concubines"; and in Daniel 5:3, "and his concubines". In Daniel 5:23, "and thy concubines".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the concubines drinking from the temple vessels is the picture of defiance — holy things used for a drunken feast. I hold that Belshazzar lifted himself against the Lord of heaven, and that night the kingdom was taken. My position is that nothing holy is mine to spend on pleasure.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Lechi, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Lehi the place is where Samson fought with the jawbone — not the cheek itself, which shares its name. In Judges 15:19, "But God clave an hollow place that [was] in the jaw"; and in Judges 15:9, "and spread themselves in Lehi.". In Judges 15:14, "[And] when he came unto Lehi".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Lehi is where God turned a jawbone into a weapon and a hollow place into a spring — Samson drank and revived there. I hold that God gives strength and water in the same place, when His servant is spent.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: the cheek (from its fleshiness); hence, the jaw-bone
BiblicalUsage: Lechi the word is the cheek, and the jawbone — the part of the face that takes the blow, and the bone Samson fought with. In Judges 15:15, "And he found a new jawbone of an ass"; and in 1 Kings 22:24, "and smote Micaiah on the cheek". In Hosea 11:4, "with bands of love: and I was to them as they that take off the yoke on their jaws"; and in Lamentations 3:30, "He giveth [his] cheek to him that smiteth him: he is filled full with reproach.".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the cheek is where humility is tested — the prophet is smitten for speaking truth, and the Lord says to turn the other cheek. I hold that Samson's jawbone won a battle, but God's yoke lifted from the jaws is the greater mercy. My position is that I would rather be smitten for truth than strike back in anger.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Latin origin; a "legion", i.e. Roman regiment (figuratively):--legion.
BiblicalUsage: legeṓn means a legion — rare in the text, and exact where it appears. In Mark 5:9, "My name [is] Legion: for we are many."; and in Luke 8:30, "Legion: because many devils were entered into him.". In Matthew 26:53, "and he shall presently give me more than twelve legions of angels?".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a legion of demons is still only one word from Jesus away from the pigs and the deep — their number is their boast, and it means nothing to Him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a primary verb; properly, to "lay" forth, i.e. (figuratively) relate (in words (usually of systematic or set discourse; whereas G2036 and G5346 generally refer to an individual expression or speech respectively; while G4483 is properly to break silence merely, and G2980 means an extended or random harangue)); by implication, to mean:--ask, bid, boast, call, describe, give out, name, put forth, say(-ing, on), shew, speak, tell, utter.
BiblicalUsage: légō means to say, to speak, and the Bible uses it the way ordinary people use ordinary words — for everything. In Matthew 5:18, "For verily I say unto you"; and in John 8:12, "I am the light of the world: he that followeth me shall not walk in darkness". In Romans 3:19, "Now we know that what things soever the law saith"; and in 1 Corinthians 1:10, "that ye all speak the same thing".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe every word of Christ carries the weight of the One who speaks — His words do not suggest, they settle. I hold that when Scripture says God says, the discussion is over and the obeying begins. My position is that I will build my life on what He has said, not on what I feel about it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {a flash; figuratively, a sharply polished blade or point of a weapon}
BiblicalUsage: lehâbâh means a flash, and Scripture puts it to work in every part of life. In Isaiah 5:24, "and the flame consumeth the chaff"; and in Ezekiel 20:47, "and every dry tree: the flaming flame shall not be quenched". In Hosea 7:6, "in the morning it burneth as a flaming fire."; and in Daniel 11:33, "yet they shall fall by the sword, and by flame".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the flame is God's honest picture of judgment — it devours stubble, it burns in the forest, and it falls on the wise who instruct many. I hold that the same fire that destroys the chaff also lights the assemblies of Zion. My position is that I want to be the one the flame refines, not the one it consumes.
RelatedTopics: Judgment; God's wrath and refuge; Suffering
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Lehabim, a son of Mizraim, and his descendants
BiblicalUsage: Lᵉhâbîym means Lehabim, a son of Mizraim, and his descendants — a small word with a sharp edge. In Genesis 10:13, "and Lehabim"; and in 1 Chronicles 1:11, "and Lehabim".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Lehabim stands in the table of nations as proof that God traces every people back to one family.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3007; a remainder:--remnant.
BiblicalUsage: leîmma means remnant, and its few appearances are all worth reading. In Romans 11:5, "Even so then at this present time also there is a remnant according to the election of grace.".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the remnant is God's answer to despair — even now, at this present time, there is a remnant according to the election of grace.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: apparently a primary word; smooth, i.e. "level":--smooth.
BiblicalUsage: leîos means smooth, and the verse where it stands does the talking. In Luke 3:5, "and the rough ways [shall be] made smooth".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the rough ways made smooth are a promise — the crooked road is straightened before the Lord comes.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a primary verb; to leave, i.e. (intransitively or passively) to fail or be absent:--be destitute (wanting), lack.
BiblicalUsage: leípō means to lack, to be wanting — plain enough to miss, and too important to pass over. In James 1:5, "If any of you lack wisdom"; and in Luke 18:22, "Yet lackest thou one thing: sell all that thou hast". In James 1:4, "wanting nothing."; and in Titus 1:5, "that thou shouldest set in order the things that are wanting".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe lack is the doorway to prayer — if any of you lack wisdom, let him ask of God, who gives liberally. I hold that the rich young ruler lacked one thing, and it was the one thing he would not give up. My position is that I would rather lack everything and have Christ than lack Him and have everything.
RelatedPeople: James, Brother of Jesus; Paul; Jesus
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from ληΐζομαι (to plunder); a brigand:--robber, thief.
BiblicalUsage: lēistḗs means robber, thief, and the word keeps turning up at decisive moments. In Luke 10:30, "and fell among thieves"; and in John 10:1, "the same is a thief and a robber.". In John 18:40, "Now Barabbas was a robber."; and in 2 Corinthians 11:26, "[in] perils of robbers".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the robber is the test of every heart — the thieves on the Jericho road strip and wound, and the crowd chose Barabbas the robber over Christ. I hold that Jesus is the door the robber refuses and the neighbour the wounded man needs. My position is that I will not climb in some other way; I will enter by the door.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3011; to be a public servant, i.e. (by analogy) to perform religious or charitable functions (worship, obey, relieve):--minister.
BiblicalUsage: leitourgéō means minister, and it is one of those words that quietly holds a whole theme together. In Acts 13:2, "As they ministered to the Lord"; and in Hebrews 10:11, "And every priest standeth daily ministering and offering oftentimes the same sacrifices". In Romans 15:27, "their duty is also to minister unto them in carnal things.".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe ministering to the Lord is the highest public service — fasting, praying, and waiting until the Holy Ghost speaks. I hold that the priests who stood daily offering sacrifices that could never take away sins show me what my service is not, and Paul's gift to Jerusalem shows me what it is. My position is that my service must cost me something and carry Christ to someone.
RelatedEvents: Barnabas and Saul Sent Out from Antioch
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3008; public function (as priest ("liturgy") or almsgiver):--ministration(-try), service.
BiblicalUsage: Ministry is what leitourgía means — public service done for God and for His people, and the word carries the weight of both. In Hebrews 8:6, "But now hath he obtained a more excellent ministry"; and in 2 Corinthians 9:12, "For the administration of this service not only supplieth the want of the saints". In Philippians 2:17, "and if I be offered upon the sacrifice and service of your faith"; and in Luke 1:23, "as soon as the days of his ministration were accomplished".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Christ's ministry is more excellent because it rests on a better covenant — the old service was a shadow, and His is the substance. I hold that the gift of the Gentile churches and Paul's poured-out life are the same service: supplying want, and offering faith. My position is that my ministry is measured by what it gives, not by what it gets.
RelatedPeople: Paul; Zechariah, Father of John the Baptist
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from the same as G3008; functional publicly ("liturgic"); i.e. beneficient:--ministering.
BiblicalUsage: leitourgikós means ministering, and its few appearances are all worth reading. In Hebrews 1:14, "sent forth to minister for them who shall be heirs of salvation?".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe angels are ministering spirits sent to serve the heirs of salvation — unseen, unfailing, and on God's errand for me.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a derivative of G2992 and G2041; a public servant, i.e. a functionary in the Temple or Gospel, or (genitive case) a worshipper (of God) or benefactor (of man):--minister(-ed).
BiblicalUsage: leitourgós means minister(-ed) — and its range, from the ordinary to the holy, is the point. In Hebrews 8:2, "A minister of the sanctuary"; and in Romans 15:16, "That I should be the minister of Jesus Christ to the Gentiles". In Philippians 2:25, "and he that ministered to my wants."; and in Romans 13:6, "For for this cause pay ye tribute also: for they are God's ministers".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a minister is a public servant of God, not a master of men — Christ is the minister of the true tabernacle, and Paul was His minister to the Gentiles. I hold that the same word covers the priest, the apostle, and even the tax collector, because all of them serve God's purpose. My position is that I am a servant first, and any honour I receive is borrowed from the Master.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Lekah, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: lêkâh belongs to Lekah, a place in Palestine, and the Bible does not let it pass unnamed. In 1 Chronicles 4:21, "Er the father of Lecah".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Lekah is named once as the father of a line — a place held by the sons of Shelah, counted in Judah's inheritance.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: something to capture with, i.e. a noose
BiblicalUsage: leked means something to capture with, and once is enough to see what it is doing. In Proverbs 3:26, "and shall keep thy foot from being taken.".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God keeps my foot from the snare — the noose is set, but the Lord is my confidence, and He does not let it close.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Lemek, the name of two antediluvian patriarchs
BiblicalUsage: Lemek is the name of Lemek, the name of two antediluvian patriarchs. In Genesis 4:19, "Lamech took unto him two wives"; and in Genesis 5:26, "And Methuselah lived after he begat Lamech seven hundred eighty and two years". In Genesis 5:28, "And Lamech lived an hundred eighty and two years".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Lamech is the warning of what sin becomes when it grows up — Cain's descendant boasted of killing and multiplied vengeance seventy-sevenfold, while the other Lamech, Noah's father, is the quieter proof that God kept a line through the same dark world. My position is that I will not boast in my sin like the first Lamech; I will trust the God who preserved the second.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to or for
BiblicalUsage: lᵉmôw means to, for — a small word with a sharp edge. In Job 27:14, "If his children be multiplied"; and in Job 29:21, "Unto me [men] gave ear". In Job 38:40, "[and] abide in the covert to lie in wait?".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe even a small word like this carries weight in Job — unto me, for the sword, what shall I answer thee — every direction in the book points to God.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2983; receipt (the act):--receiving.
BiblicalUsage: lēmpsis means receiving, and its few appearances are all worth reading. In Philippians 4:15, "no church communicated with me as concerning giving and receiving".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe giving and receiving belong together — the Philippians were the one church that shared with Paul in giving and receiving, and God counts both.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Lemuel or Lemoel, a symbolic name of Solomon
BiblicalUsage: Lᵉmûwʼêl names Lemuel or Lemoel, a symbolic name of Solomon, and its appearances in Scripture are few but pointed. In Proverbs 31:1, "The words of king Lemuel"; and in Proverbs 31:4, "nor for princes strong drink:".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Lemuel's mother's teaching is the Bible's plain wisdom for kings — wine is not for kings, and strength is not for princes who drink. I hold that the words of a mother, taught to her son, are still shaping kingdoms.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: apparently a primary word; a trough, i.e. wine-vat:--winepress.
BiblicalUsage: lēnós means winepress — plain enough to miss, and too important to pass over. In Matthew 21:33, "and digged a winepress in it"; and in Revelation 14:19, "and cast [it] into the great winepress of the wrath of God.". In Revelation 19:15, "that with it he should smite the nations: and he shall rule them with a rod of iron: and he treadeth the winepress of the fierceness and wrath of Almighty God."; and in Revelation 14:20, "And the winepress was trodden without the city".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the winepress is God's last picture of harvest — the householder digs one for his vineyard, and the angel casts the vine of the earth into the great winepress of His wrath. I hold that Christ treads it alone, with a sword from His mouth and a rod of iron. My position is that I want to be gathered into His barn, not trodden in His press.
RelatedTopics: Judgment; God's wrath and refuge; Kingdom of God
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Latin origin; a "linen" cloth, i.e. apron:--towel.
BiblicalUsage: léntion means a linen towel, and once is enough to see what it is doing. In John 13:4, "and took a towel"; and in John 13:5, "and to wipe [them] with the towel wherewith he was girded.".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the towel is the whole gospel in one gesture — the Lord laid aside His garments, girded Himself, and washed feet.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a primary word; a "lion":--lion.
BiblicalUsage: léōn means lion, and it is one of those words that quietly holds a whole theme together. In 1 Peter 5:8, "as a roaring lion"; and in Revelation 5:5, "the Lion of the tribe of Juda". In Hebrews 11:33, "stopped the mouths of lions"; and in 2 Timothy 4:17, "and [that] all the Gentiles might hear: and I was delivered out of the mouth of the lion.".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the lion is both the enemy and the King — the devil walks about as a roaring lion, and the Lion of Judah has prevailed to open the book. I hold that faith stops the mouths of lions, and the Lord delivers from the lion's mouth. My position is that I will be sober and watchful, because the real Lion is on my side.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from λέπω (to peel); a flake:--scale.
BiblicalUsage: lepís means scale — a small word with a sharp edge. In Acts 9:18, "And immediately there fell from his eyes as it had been scales: and he received sight forthwith".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the scales falling from Saul's eyes is the picture of conversion — one moment blind, the next seeing, and everything changed.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from the same as G3013; scaliness, i.e. "leprosy":--leprosy.
BiblicalUsage: lépra means leprosy, and it does large work in the story. In Matthew 8:3, "And immediately his leprosy was cleansed."; and in Mark 1:42, "immediately the leprosy departed from him". In Luke 5:12, "behold a man full of leprosy: who seeing Jesus fell on [his] face"; and in Luke 5:13, "And immediately the leprosy departed from him.".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe leprosy is sin made visible — the man full of leprosy fell on his face, and Jesus touched him and said He would make him clean. I hold that no disease is too defiling for that touch, and no sinner too far gone for that word. My position is that I come to Him as the leper came: Lord, if thou wilt, thou canst make me clean.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from the same as G3014; scaly, i.e. leprous (a leper):--leper.
BiblicalUsage: leprós means leper — and its range, from the ordinary to the holy, is the point. In Matthew 8:2, "there came a leper and worshipped him"; and in Mark 1:40, "And there came a leper to him". In Luke 17:12, "there met him ten men that were lepers"; and in Luke 4:27, "And many lepers were in Israel in the time of Eliseus the prophet".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the leper's prayer is the model for mine — Lord, if thou wilt, thou canst make me clean — and the ten who stood afar off teach me to come near. I hold that Jesus cleansed the outsider Naaman and the ten and the one, because His mercy is not bound by Israel's borders. My position is that I will not stand afar off; I will come to Him and be cleansed.
RelatedEvents: The Healing of the Ten Lepers
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: neuter of a derivative of the same as G3013; something scaled (light), i.e. a small coin:--mite.
BiblicalUsage: leptón means a mite, a small coin, and no one who reads the Bible can walk past it. In Mark 12:42, "and she threw in two mites"; and in Luke 21:2, "And he saw also a certain poor widow casting in thither two mites.". In Luke 12:59, "till thou hast paid the very last mite.".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the widow's two mites are the largest gift in the treasury — she gave all her living, and Jesus watched her do it. I hold that God does not count the size of the coin but the size of the sacrifice. My position is that I would rather give my last mite in faith than my abundance for show.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, something received, i.e. (mentally) instruction (whether on the part of the teacher or hearer); also (in an active and sinister sense) inveiglement
BiblicalUsage: leqach means something received, and the Bible uses it the way ordinary people use ordinary words — for everything. In Deuteronomy 32:2, "My doctrine shall drop as the rain"; and in Proverbs 4:2, "For I give you good doctrine". In Proverbs 1:5, "and will increase learning"; and in Isaiah 29:24, "and they that murmured shall learn doctrine.".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe true doctrine falls like rain — it does not argue, it soaks in and makes things grow. I hold that a wise man hears and increases learning, and that the erring in spirit come to understanding. My position is that I will take God's teaching the way dry ground takes rain: open, and glad for it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: the after crop
BiblicalUsage: leqesh means the after crop. In Amos 7:1, "he formed grasshoppers in the beginning of the shooting up of the latter growth".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the latter growth is God's timing in a vision — the grasshoppers formed just as the king's mowings were done, and Amos saw judgment coming.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: the gleaning
BiblicalUsage: leqeṭ means the gleaning — a small word with a sharp edge. In Leviticus 19:9, "neither shalt thou gather the gleanings of thy harvest."; and in Leviticus 23:22, "neither shalt thou gather any gleaning of thy harvest: thou shalt leave them unto the poor".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the gleanings belong to the poor by law — God told Israel not to reap the corners, so the stranger and the fatherless could eat.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: apparently a primary word; twaddle, i.e. an incredible story:--idle tale.
BiblicalUsage: lēros means idle tale, and its few appearances are all worth reading. In Luke 24:11, "And their words seemed to them as idle tales".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the women's words seemed like idle tales because resurrection always sounds impossible until you see the empty tomb.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Lesha, a place probably East of the Jordan
BiblicalUsage: Leshaʻ names Lesha, a place probably East of the Jordan, and its appearances in Scripture are few but pointed. In Genesis 10:19, "even unto Lasha".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Lesha marks the edge of the Canaanites' border — one more place on the map God drew for His people.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: (figuratively) vigor; also a sweet or fat cake
BiblicalUsage: lᵉshad means vigor, a sweet cake — rare in the text, and exact where it appears. In Numbers 11:8, "and made cakes of it: and the taste of it was as the taste of fresh oil."; and in Psalms 32:4, "For day and night thy hand was heavy upon me: my moisture is turned into the drought of summer.".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe vigor is God's gift and His to take — the manna tasted like fresh oil, and David's moisture dried up under God's heavy hand.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Leshem, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Leshem the town is the city Dan took for itself — not the gem on the breastplate, which shares its name. In Joshua 19:47, "and called Leshem".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Leshem is Dan's second chance — their coast went out too little, so they took Leshem and called it by their father's name.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a gem, perhaps the jacinth
BiblicalUsage: The ligure is the gem the Bible calls leshem — a stone on the high priest's breastplate, not Leshem the town, which shares its name. In Exodus 28:19, "And the third row a ligure"; and in Exodus 39:12, "a ligure, an agate, and an amethyst".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the ligure on the high priest's breastplate shows me that God's people are carried over His heart, stone by stone.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a kind of lizard (from its covert habits)
BiblicalUsage: lᵉṭâʼâh means a kind of lizard — a small word with a sharp edge. In Leviticus 11:30, "and the lizard".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the lizard on the unclean list reminds me that God drew lines His people were meant to keep — even over the small creeping things.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G2990; forgetfulness:--+ forget.
BiblicalUsage: lḗthē means forgetfulness, and its few appearances are all worth reading. In 2 Peter 1:9, "and hath forgotten that he was purged from his old sins.".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe forgetting what Christ purged is the blindness Peter warns about — the man who forgets he was cleansed cannot see afar off.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a measure for things dry
BiblicalUsage: lethek means a measure for things dry, and the verse where it stands does the talking. In Hosea 3:2, "and an half homer of barley:".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the half homer of barley is the price of a bought-back wife — Hosea paid silver and grain to take Gomer home again.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Letushim, an Arabian tribe
BiblicalUsage: Lᵉṭûwshim means Letushim, an Arabian tribe — rare in the text, and exact where it appears. In Genesis 25:3, "and Letushim".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Letushim is named once beside his brothers, and that is enough — God kept the sons of Dedan in the record.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H3878); Levi, the name of three Israelites:--Levi. Compare G3018.
BiblicalUsage: Leuḯ names Levi, and its appearances in Scripture are few but pointed. In Mark 2:14, "he saw Levi the [son] of Alphaeus sitting at the receipt of custom"; and in Luke 3:24, "which was [the son] of Levi". In Hebrews 7:5, "And verily they that are of the sons of Levi".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Levi is three men in one name — the patriarch whose sons became priests, the ancestor in Jesus' line, and the tax collector who left his booth to follow Him. I hold that the same name runs from the tribe to the table of Matthew, and God used every one of them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a form of G3017; Lewis (i.e. Levi), a Christian:--Levi.
BiblicalUsage: Leuḯs means Levi. In Luke 5:29, "And Levi made him a great feast in his own house: and there was a great company of publicans and of others that sat down with them.".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Levi's great feast is the picture of a changed life — the tax collector who followed Jesus threw open his house the same day.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3017; a Levite, i.e. descendant of Levi:--Levite.
BiblicalUsage: Leuḯtēs means a Levite — a small word with a sharp edge. In Luke 10:32, "And likewise a Levite"; and in John 1:19, "when the Jews sent priests and Levites from Jerusalem to ask him". In Acts 4:36, "a Levite, [and] of the country of Cyprus".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the Levite in the parable is the warning — he passed by on the other side, while the priesthood he belonged to was meant to serve, and Barnabas, a Levite, shows the other side by selling his field and laying the money at the apostles' feet.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3019; Levitic, i.e. relating to the Levites:--Levitical.
BiblicalUsage: Leuïtikós means Levitical, and its few appearances are all worth reading. In Hebrews 7:11, "If therefore perfection were by the Levitical priesthood".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the Levitical priesthood was never the end — if perfection had come by it, there would be no need of a priest after Melchizedek.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3022; to whiten:--make white, whiten.
BiblicalUsage: leukaínō means make white, whiten, and the verse where it stands does the talking. In Mark 9:3, "so as no fuller on earth can white them."; and in Revelation 7:14, "and made them white in the blood of the Lamb.".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe whiteness is God's work — no fuller on earth can white a garment like the blood of the Lamb.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from λύκη ("light"); white:--white.
BiblicalUsage: leukós means white — plain enough to miss, and too important to pass over. In Matthew 17:2, "and his raiment was white as the light."; and in Mark 9:3, "so as no fuller on earth can white them.". In Revelation 7:9, "clothed with white robes"; and in Revelation 3:5, "the same shall be clothed in white raiment".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe white is the colour of heaven — Christ's raiment shone white as the light, and the multitude stands before the throne in white robes. I hold that the whiteness is not mine but His: robes washed in the blood of the Lamb. My position is that I will be clothed in white, not because I kept myself clean, but because He washed me.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, adhesion, i.e. (as preposition) with
BiblicalUsage: lᵉvâth means with, and once is enough to see what it is doing. In Ezra 4:12, "building the rebellious and the bad city".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the little word with carries the whole accusation — the Jews came up from the king to Jerusalem, and their enemies counted every step.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {something attached, i.e. a wreath}
BiblicalUsage: Lêvîy means the Levites, and it is one of those words that quietly holds a whole theme together. In Ezra 6:16, "and the Levites"; and in Ezra 6:18, "and the Levites in their courses". In Ezra 7:13, "and [of] his priests and Levites"; and in Ezra 7:24, "that touching any of the priests and Levites".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the Levites in Ezra are the proof that God restores His servants — they kept the dedication, they were set in their courses, and they went up to Jerusalem of their own free will. I hold that the men named here are the Levites, set apart for the service of God's house, and their return is the pattern of every restoration. My position is that serving in God's house is the honour they chose, and I choose it too.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {something attached, i.e. a wreath}
BiblicalUsage: Lêvîy means the Levites, and it is one of those words that quietly holds a whole theme together. In Ezra 6:16, "and the Levites"; and in Ezra 6:18, "and the Levites in their courses". In Ezra 7:13, "and [of] his priests and Levites"; and in Ezra 7:24, "that touching any of the priests and Levites".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the Levites in Ezra are the proof that God restores His servants — they kept the dedication, they were set in their courses, and they went up to Jerusalem of their own free will. I hold that the men named here are the Levites, set apart for the service of God's house, and their return is the pattern of every restoration. My position is that serving in God's house is the honour they chose, and I choose it too.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a Levite or descendant of Levi
BiblicalUsage: Levites are what Lêvîyîy means — descendants of Levi, set apart for the work of the tabernacle and the temple. In Numbers 3:12, "I have taken the Levites from among the children of Israel instead of all the firstborn that openeth the matrix among the children of Israel: therefore the Levites shall be mine"; and in Deuteronomy 18:1, "The priests the Levites". In 1 Chronicles 6:48, "Their brethren also the Levites [were] appointed unto all manner of service of the tabernacle of the house of God."; and in Ezra 2:40, "The Levites: the children of Jeshua and Kadmiel".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the Levites are God's chosen servants — taken instead of the firstborn, set apart to bear the ark, and given the tithes for their work. I hold that their service is the pattern of mine: appointed by God, sustained by God's people, and offered back to God. My position is that I do not choose my service; the Lord takes me for it, as He took Levi.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {Lael an Israelite}
BiblicalUsage: lêylᵉyâʼ means night, and it does large work in the story. In Daniel 2:19, "Then was the secret revealed unto Daniel in a night vision."; and in Daniel 5:30, "In that night was Belshazzar the king of the Chaldeans slain.". In Daniel 7:2, "I saw in my vision by night"; and in Daniel 7:13, "I saw in the night visions".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe night is when God speaks in Daniel — the secret revealed in a night vision, the king slain in that night, and the Son of man coming with the clouds. I hold that the darkest hours in Babylon were the clearest hours of revelation. My position is that I will not fear the night visions; the God who gives them is the God who explains them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: perverseness
BiblicalUsage: lᵉzûwth means perverseness, and the verse where it stands does the talking. In Proverbs 4:24, "and perverse lips put far from thee.".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe perverse lips are a small crookedness with a long reach — put them far from me, and my mouth will stop betraying my heart.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain affinity; much (adverbially):--exceeding, great(-ly), sore, very (+ chiefest).
BiblicalUsage: lían means greatly, very much — rare in the text, and exact where it appears. In Mark 16:2, "And very early in the morning the first [day] of the week"; and in Matthew 27:14, "insomuch that the governor marvelled greatly.". In 2 John 1:4, "I rejoiced greatly that I found of thy children walking in truth".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe greatly is the word for joy that cannot be measured — John rejoiced greatly to find children walking in truth, and that is still the best news a teacher can hear.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of foreign origin (H3828); the incense-tree, i.e. (by implication) incense itself:--frankincense.
BiblicalUsage: líbanos means frankincense, and once is enough to see what it is doing. In Matthew 2:11, "and frankincense"; and in Revelation 18:13, "and frankincense".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe frankincense belongs at the manger and at the altar — the wise men laid it before the child, and Babylon traded in it to the end.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3030; frankincense, i.e. (by extension) a censer for burning it:--censer.
BiblicalUsage: libanōtós means censer. In Revelation 8:3, "having a golden censer"; and in Revelation 8:5, "And the angel took the censer".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the golden censer is the picture of prayer — incense rises with the prayers of the saints, and fire from the same altar falls on the earth.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: the heart
BiblicalUsage: libbâh means the heart — an ordinary word that carries real weight in the Bible. In Proverbs 17:3, "and the furnace for gold: but the LORD trieth the hearts."; and in Psalms 7:9, "but establish the just: for the righteous God trieth the hearts and reins.". In Proverbs 21:2, "Every way of a man [is] right in his own eyes: but the LORD pondereth the hearts."; and in Ezekiel 16:30, "How weak is thine heart".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the heart is the furnace God tests — the fining pot is for silver, but the Lord trieth the hearts. I hold that every way of a man is right in his own eyes, yet the Lord pondereth the hearts and is not fooled. My position is that a weak heart, honestly given to God, is stronger than a proud one He must break.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Latin origin; a Roman freedman:--Libertine.
BiblicalUsage: Libertînos means a Roman freedman, and its few appearances are all worth reading. In Acts 6:9, "which is called [the synagogue] of the Libertines".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the Libertines show how freedom can turn to bondage — freedmen arguing against Stephen, and losing the argument to the Spirit.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Libnah, a place in the Desert and one in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Libnah the city is a priestly town in Judah that revolted and was besieged — not the word for whiteness, which shares its name. In Isaiah 37:8, "and found the king of Assyria warring against Libnah: for he had heard that he was departed from Lachish."; and in Jeremiah 52:1, "And his mother's name [was] Hamutal the daughter of Jeremiah of Libnah.". In 2 Kings 8:22, "Then Libnah revolted at the same time.".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Libnah is the city that revolted and the city where the Assyrian camped — a priestly city that chose its own way, and a battlefield in Hezekiah's day. I hold that God records both its rebellion and its siege, because places have histories too.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, whiteness, i.e. (by implication) transparency
BiblicalUsage: Whiteness is what libnah means — a clearness like sapphire under God's feet, not Libnah the city, which shares its name. In Exodus 24:10, "and as it were the body of heaven in [his] clearness.".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the whiteness under God's feet is the closest Moses came to describing Him — a paved work of sapphire, clear as the body of heaven.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: some sort of whitish tree, perhaps the storax
BiblicalUsage: libneh means some sort of whitish tree, perhaps the storax, and once is enough to see what it is doing. In Genesis 30:37, "and pilled white strakes in them"; and in Hosea 4:13, "under oaks and poplars and elms".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the poplar's white streaks are Jacob's cunning and Israel's idolatry in one tree — rods pilled for breeding, and shade used for sacrifice.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a Libnite or descendants of Libni (collectively)
BiblicalUsage: Libnîy means a Libnite or descendants of Libni. In Numbers 3:21, "Of Gershon [was] the family of the Libnites"; and in Numbers 26:58, "These [are] the families of the Levites: the family of the Libnites".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the Libnites are named in their families because God counts His servants by name — the sons of Gershon, the families of the Levites.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a Libnite or descendants of Libni (collectively)
BiblicalUsage: Libnîy means a Libnite or descendants of Libni. In Numbers 3:21, "Of Gershon [was] the family of the Libnites"; and in Numbers 26:58, "These [are] the families of the Levites: the family of the Libnites".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the Libnites are named in their families because God counts His servants by name — the sons of Gershon, the families of the Levites.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably from G3047; Libye, a region of Africa:--Libya.
BiblicalUsage: Libýē means Libya, a region of Africa — a small word with a sharp edge. In Acts 2:10, "and in the parts of Libya about Cyrene".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Libya on the Pentecost list is the promise — Jews and proselytes from Africa heard the gospel in their own tongue on the first day.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from λικμός, the equivalent of λίκνον (a winnowing fan or basket); to winnow, i.e. (by analogy), to triturate:--grind to powder.
BiblicalUsage: likmáō means grind to powder, and its few appearances are all worth reading. In Luke 20:18, "it will grind him to powder."; and in Matthew 21:44, "it will grind him to powder.".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the stone grinds to powder whoever it falls on — fall on it and be broken, or let it fall on you and be ground.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: apparently a primary word; a harbor:--haven. Compare G2568.
BiblicalUsage: limḗn means a haven, a harbour, and the verse where it stands does the talking. In Acts 27:12, "And because the haven was not commodious to winter in".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the haven at Fair Havens is the sailor's wisdom — a harbour not fit to winter in is a warning not to stay.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: instructed
BiblicalUsage: limmûwd means instructed, and no one who reads the Bible can walk past it. In Isaiah 50:4, "he wakeneth mine ear to hear as the learned."; and in Isaiah 54:13, "And all thy children [shall be] taught of the LORD". In Isaiah 8:16, "seal the law among my disciples."; and in Jeremiah 13:23, "or the leopard his spots?".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the instructed are the ones God teaches Himself — the tongue of the learned that speaks a word in season, and the children taught of the Lord. I hold that the same word marks those accustomed to do evil: we become what we are taught. My position is that I want to be taught of the Lord, morning by morning, until His word is the first thing on my tongue.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably from G3040 (through the idea of nearness of shore); a pond (large or small):--lake.
BiblicalUsage: límnē means a lake, and the Bible uses it the way ordinary people use ordinary words — for everything. In Luke 5:1, "he stood by the lake of Gennesaret"; and in Luke 8:23, "But as they sailed he fell asleep: and there came down a storm of wind on the lake". In Luke 8:33, "and entered into the swine: and the herd ran violently down a steep place into the lake"; and in Revelation 19:20, "These both were cast alive into a lake of fire burning with brimstone.".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the lake is where Jesus shows His power over wind and water and demons — the storm rises, the swine run down, and the beast is cast into the lake of fire. I hold that the same water that filled the disciples' boat is the picture of the final judgment. My position is that I will not fear the lake, because the One who walks on it is in my boat.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably from G3007 (through the idea of destitution); a scarcity of food:--dearth, famine, hunger.
BiblicalUsage: limós means famine, hunger, and Scripture puts it to work in every part of life. In Acts 11:28, "and signified by the Spirit that there should be great dearth throughout all the world: which came to pass in the days of Claudius Caesar."; and in Luke 4:25, "when great famine was throughout all the land". In Luke 15:14, "there arose a mighty famine in that land"; and in 2 Corinthians 11:27, "in hunger and thirst".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe famine is God's loudest sermon on dependence — the widows of Elijah's day, the prodigal perishing with hunger, and Paul cold and naked. I hold that hunger drives men home: the prodigal remembered his father's bread, and that was the beginning of his return. My position is that when the famine comes, I will remember whose house has bread enough and to spare.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably a primary word; flax, i.e. (by implication) "linen":--linen.
BiblicalUsage: línon means flax, linen — a small word with a sharp edge. In Matthew 12:20, "and smoking flax shall he not quench"; and in Revelation 15:6, "clothed in pure and white linen".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the smoking flax is the bruised reed's twin — Christ will not quench the faintest spark of faith.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: perhaps from G3043; Linus, a Christian:--Linus.
BiblicalUsage: Línos belongs to Linus, a Christian, and the Bible does not let it pass unnamed. In 2 Timothy 4:21, "Eubulus greeteth thee, and Pudens, and Linus, and Claudia".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Linus is named in Paul's last letter because faithful friends are worth naming — he greets the church with Eubulus and Pudens and Claudia, and the brethren.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from λίπος (grease); fat, i.e. (figuratively) sumptuous:--dainty.
BiblicalUsage: liparós means dainty, and the verse where it stands does the talking. In Revelation 18:14, "and all things which were dainty and goodly are departed from thee".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Babylon's dainty fruits are the picture of luxury that does not last — all things dainty and goodly departed, and they shall be found no more.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: anterior
BiblicalUsage: liphnay means before, in front — rare in the text, and exact where it appears. In 1 Kings 6:17, "the temple before it".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the temple before the temple — the house before it, forty cubits long — shows me that God's house had rooms for every part of His service.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably from λείβω (to pour a "libation"); the south(- west) wind (as bringing rain, i.e. (by extension) the south quarter):--southwest.
BiblicalUsage: líps means the south-west wind, and once is enough to see what it is doing. In Acts 27:12, "and lieth toward the south west and north west.".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the south-west wind is the sailor's gamble — a fair wind to Phenice, and a storm waiting beyond it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Likchi, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Liqchîy belongs to Likchi, an Israelite, and the Bible does not let it pass unnamed. In 1 Chronicles 7:19, "Ahian, and Shechem, and Likhi, and Aniam".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Likhi is named once among the sons of Shemidah, and that is enough — God keeps the families of Manasseh in the record.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a room in a building (whether for storage, eating, or lodging)
BiblicalUsage: Chambers are what lishkâh means — rooms in the house of God, for storing, eating, or lodging, and the Bible keeps track of who uses them. In 1 Chronicles 9:26, "and were over the chambers and treasuries of the house of God."; and in 2 Chronicles 31:11, "Then Hezekiah commanded to prepare chambers in the house of the LORD". In 1 Samuel 9:22, "and made them sit in the chiefest place among them that were bidden"; and in Nehemiah 13:5, "And he had prepared for him a great chamber".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the chambers are where God's house is kept — the porters over the treasuries, the singers in their rooms, the offerings stored by Hezekiah's command.
