I hold that a temple with no chambers is a temple with no order, and God is a God of order. My position is that my service, like the porters', is to keep what God has given, faithfully and out of sight.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: speech, i.e. a nation
BiblicalUsage: lishshân means speech, a language, and it does large work in the story. In Daniel 3:4, "and languages"; and in Daniel 3:29, "and language". In Daniel 4:1, "and languages"; and in Daniel 6:25, "and languages".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the languages of Babylon are God's audience — every people, nation, and language heard the king's decree, and then heard Daniel's God praised. I hold that no tongue is outside His reach: Nebuchadnezzar wrote to all languages, and Darius did the same. My position is that my language is one of many, and God speaks them all.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3037; to lapidate:--stone.
BiblicalUsage: litházō means to stone — and its range, from the ordinary to the holy, is the point. In Acts 14:19, "having stoned Paul"; and in John 10:31, "Then the Jews took up stones again to stone him.". In 2 Corinthians 11:25, "once was I stoned"; and in Hebrews 11:37, "They were stoned".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe stoning is the price of telling the truth — Paul was stoned and left for dead, and the Jews took up stones against Jesus for His good works. I hold that the heroes of faith were stoned, sawn asunder, and slain, and still they did not turn back. My position is that I will speak the truth even if stones are the answer.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3037; stony, i.e. made of stone:--of stone.
BiblicalUsage: líthinos means of stone, and no one who reads the Bible can walk past it. In 2 Corinthians 3:3, "not in tables of stone"; and in John 2:6, "And there were set there six waterpots of stone". In Revelation 9:20, "and idols of gold, and silver, and brass, and stone".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe stone is the Bible's picture of a heart that will not bend — tables of stone, hearts of stone, and idols of stone. I hold that the new covenant writes on hearts of flesh, not stone, and the waterpots of stone at Cana were waiting to be filled with better wine. My position is that I want my heart written on by the Spirit, not carved by my own hand.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a compound of G3037 and G906; to throw stones, i.e. lapidate:--stone, cast stones.
BiblicalUsage: lithoboléō means to stone, to cast stones, and the Bible uses it the way ordinary people use ordinary words — for everything. In Acts 7:59, "And they stoned Stephen"; and in Matthew 21:35, "and stoned another.". In Luke 13:34, "and stonest them that are sent unto thee"; and in Hebrews 12:20, "it shall be stoned".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the stones thrown at Stephen are the Church's first blood — he called on the Lord Jesus and received His spirit, and Saul watched the coats. I hold that Jerusalem kills the prophets and stones them that are sent, and still the Lord would have gathered her children. My position is that I will stand with Stephen, not with the throwers.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: apparently a primary word; a stone (literally or figuratively):--(mill-, stumbling-)stone.
BiblicalUsage: líthos means a stone, and Scripture puts it to work in every part of life. In Matthew 21:42, "The stone which the builders rejected"; and in 1 Peter 2:4, "[as unto] a living stone". In 1 Peter 2:6, "I lay in Sion a chief corner stone"; and in 1 Corinthians 3:12, "precious stones".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Christ is the stone the builders refused and God made the head of the corner — the living stone, chosen and precious. I hold that we are lively stones built into a spiritual house, and that the same stone is a stumbling stone to the disobedient. My position is that I will build on Him and Him only, because every other foundation is wood, hay, and stubble.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3037 and a derivative of G4766; stone-strewed, i.e. a tessellated mosaic on which the Roman tribunal was placed:--Pavement.
BiblicalUsage: lithóstrōtos means Pavement — a small word with a sharp edge. In John 19:13, "and sat down in the judgment seat in a place that is called the Pavement".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the Pavement is where the judgment seat sat — Pilate brought Jesus out, sat down, and handed Him over on a mosaic floor.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Latin origin (libra); a pound in weight:--pound.
BiblicalUsage: lítra means a pound in weight, and its few appearances are all worth reading. In John 19:39, "about an hundred pound [weight]."; and in John 12:3, "Then took Mary a pound of ointment of spikenard".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a pound of spikenard is the measure of love — Mary poured it on Jesus' feet, and Nicodemus brought a hundred pound to His burial.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: something attached, i.e. a wreath
BiblicalUsage: livyâh means a wreath, an ornament, and the verse where it stands does the talking. In Proverbs 1:9, "For they [shall be] an ornament of grace unto thy head"; and in Proverbs 4:9, "She shall give to thine head an ornament of grace: a crown of glory shall she deliver to thee.".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe wisdom is an ornament of grace — a wreath for the head and a crown of glory, given to the one who listens.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a wreathed animal, i.e. a serpent (especially the crocodile or some other large sea-monster); figuratively, the constellation of the dragon; also as a symbol of Babylon
BiblicalUsage: livyâthân means Leviathan, the sea serpent — plain enough to miss, and too important to pass over. In Isaiah 27:1, "even leviathan that crooked serpent"; and in Job 41:1, "Canst thou draw out leviathan with an hook?". In Psalms 74:14, "Thou brakest the heads of leviathan in pieces"; and in Psalms 104:26, "There go the ships: [there is] that leviathan".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Leviathan is God's answer to every proud power — the piercing serpent punished by His sword, the sea monster broken and given for meat, the great beast made to play in the sea. I hold that no creature is too large for God to handle, and no chaos too deep for Him to rule. My position is that the monster I fear is God's plaything, and the God I worship is its Master.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a night spectre
BiblicalUsage: lîylîyth means a night spectre, and once is enough to see what it is doing. In Isaiah 34:14, "the screech owl also shall rest there".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the night spectre haunts only the ruins — Isaiah sets it in Edom's desolation, where the wild beasts meet and the screech owl rests.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Lo-Ammi, the symbolic name of a son of Hosea
BiblicalUsage: Lo-ammi means 'not my people' — the symbolic name God gave to Hosea's son. In Hosea 1:9, "Call his name Lo-ammi: for ye [are] not my people".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Lo-ammi is the hardest name in the Bible — ye are not my people — and it is also the promise, because the God who named him so will one day say thou art my people again.
RelatedEvents: Hosea Marries Gomer and Names the Children
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Lo-Debar, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Lôʼ Dᵉbar names Lo-Debar, a place in Palestine, and its appearances in Scripture are few but pointed. In 2 Samuel 9:4, "in Lo-debar."; and in 2 Samuel 9:5, "from Lo-debar.". In 2 Samuel 17:27, "and Machir the son of Ammiel of Lo-debar".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Lo-debar is the place of the forgotten — Mephibosheth lived there lame and out of sight, until the king sent and fetched him to his own table. I hold that God fetches His people out of Lo-debar too: no place is too far for His kindness to reach.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Lo-Ruchamah, the symbolic name of a daughter of Hosea
BiblicalUsage: Lo-ruhamah means 'no mercy' — the symbolic name God gave to Hosea's daughter. In Hosea 1:6, "Call her name Lo-ruhamah: for I will no more have mercy upon the house of Israel"; and in Hosea 1:8, "and bare a son.".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Lo-ruhamah is the name of a mercy withheld — I will no more have mercy upon the house of Israel — and the mercy that returns, because Hosea's God does not leave His people in that name forever.
RelatedEvents: Hosea Marries Gomer and Names the Children
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: not (the simple or abs. negation); by implication, no; often used with other particles
BiblicalUsage: lôʼ means not, no, and the verse where it stands does the talking. In Genesis 2:17, "thou shalt not eat of it: for in the day that thou eatest thereof thou shalt surely die."; and in Exodus 20:13, "Thou shalt not kill.". In Psalms 23:4, "I will fear no evil".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God's not is a fence, not a prison — thou shalt not eat, thou shalt not kill, I will fear no evil — every no of His is a yes to life.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: the gullet
BiblicalUsage: lôaʻ means the gullet — rare in the text, and exact where it appears. In Proverbs 23:2, "And put a knife to thy throat".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the knife at the throat is wisdom's picture of appetite — if I am given to it, I had better fear it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Lod, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Lôd names Lod, a place in Palestine, and its appearances in Scripture are few but pointed. In 1 Chronicles 8:12, "who built Ono, and Lod, with the towns thereof"; and in Ezra 2:33, "The children of Lod". In Nehemiah 7:37, "The children of Lod".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Lod is the town that came home — its children returned from exile, seven hundred and twenty-five of them, and rebuilt among the craftsmen.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a log or measure for liquids
BiblicalUsage: lôg means a log, a measure of oil. In Leviticus 14:10, "and one log of oil."; and in Leviticus 14:12, "and the log of oil". In Leviticus 14:15, "And the priest shall take [some] of the log of oil".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the log of oil is the measure of cleansing — poured on the leper's head, waved before the Lord, and enough to make the unclean clean.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3056 (in the commercial sense); a contribution:--collection, gathering.
BiblicalUsage: logía means a collection — a small word with a sharp edge. In 1 Corinthians 16:1, "Now concerning the collection for the saints"; and in 1 Corinthians 16:2, "that there be no gatherings when I come.".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the collection is worship with an order to it — every man laying by on the first day, so that when Paul comes there are no gatherings to be made in a hurry.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3056; rational ("logical"):--reasonable, of the word.
BiblicalUsage: logikós means reasonable, of the word, and its few appearances are all worth reading. In Romans 12:1, "[which is] your reasonable service."; and in 1 Peter 2:2, "desire the sincere milk of the word".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe reasonable service is the milk of the word — newborn babes desiring it, and living sacrifices offering it.
RelatedTopics: Growth; True Worship; Word of God
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: neuter of G3052; an utterance (of God):--oracle.
BiblicalUsage: lógion means oracle, and the contexts could hardly be more different. In Romans 3:2, "because that unto them were committed the oracles of God."; and in Acts 7:38, "and [with] our fathers: who received the lively oracles to give unto us:". In Hebrews 5:12, "ye have need that one teach you again which [be] the first principles of the oracles of God"; and in 1 Peter 4:11, "[let him speak] as the oracles of God".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the oracles of God are a trust, not a trophy — committed to Israel, received in the wilderness, and spoken now by any man who speaks. I hold that the first principles of those oracles are milk for babes and the measure of teachers. My position is that if I speak, I will speak as the oracles of God, and let God be the judge of my words.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3056; fluent, i.e. an orator:--eloquent.
BiblicalUsage: lógios means eloquent — rare in the text, and exact where it appears. In Acts 18:24, "an eloquent man".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Apollos is the pattern of the eloquent believer — mighty in the Scriptures, and still willing to be taught the way of God more perfectly.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3049; computation, i.e. (figuratively) reasoning (conscience, conceit):--imagination, thought.
BiblicalUsage: logismós means imagination, thought, and once is enough to see what it is doing. In Romans 2:15, "and [their] thoughts the mean while accusing or else excusing one another"; and in 2 Corinthians 10:4, "but mighty through God to the pulling down of strong holds".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe thoughts are strongholds — the weapons of our warfare pull them down, and the conscience bears witness whether they accuse or excuse.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: middle voice from G3056; to take an inventory, i.e. estimate (literally or figuratively):--conclude, (ac-)count (of), + despise, esteem, impute, lay, number, reason, reckon, suppose, think (on).
BiblicalUsage: logízomai means to reckon, to count, to think, and it is one of those words that quietly holds a whole theme together. In Romans 4:3, "and it was counted unto him for righteousness."; and in 2 Corinthians 5:19, "not imputing their trespasses unto them". In 1 Corinthians 13:5, "thinketh no evil"; and in Romans 8:18, "For I reckon that the sufferings of this present time [are] not worthy [to be compared] with the glory which shall be revealed in us.".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe reckoning is the arithmetic of grace — Abraham believed, and it was counted to him for righteousness, and God does not impute our trespasses to us in Christ. I hold that love thinketh no evil, and the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory to come. My position is that I will let God do the counting: my sins reckoned to Christ, and His righteousness reckoned to me.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a compound of G3056 and G3164; to be disputatious (on trifles):--strive about words.
BiblicalUsage: logomachéō means strive about words — a small word with a sharp edge. In 2 Timothy 2:14, "charging [them] before the Lord that they strive not about words to no profit".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe striving about words subverts the hearers — Paul charges Timothy before the Lord not to do it, and I take the charge for myself.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from the same as G3054; disputation about trifles ("logomachy"):--strife of words.
BiblicalUsage: logomachía means strife of words, and its few appearances are all worth reading. In 1 Timothy 6:4, "but doting about questions and strifes of words".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe strife of words is the fruit of pride — the man who knows nothing dotes about questions, and envy and railings follow.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3060; to reproach, i.e. vilify:--revile.
BiblicalUsage: loidoréō means revile — and its range, from the ordinary to the holy, is the point. In 1 Peter 2:23, "reviled not again"; and in 1 Corinthians 4:12, "working with our own hands: being reviled". In John 9:28, "Then they reviled him"; and in Acts 23:4, "Revilest thou God's high priest?".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe reviling answered with blessing is the Christian's mark — Paul was reviled and blessed, and Christ when He was reviled reviled not again. I hold that the high priest's name is not mine to curse, and the blind man's healing is not theirs to mock. My position is that I will commit myself to Him that judgeth righteously, and leave the reviling unanswered.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3060; slander or vituperation:--railing, reproach(-fully).
BiblicalUsage: loidoría means railing, reproach — rare in the text, and exact where it appears. In 1 Timothy 5:14, "give none occasion to the adversary to speak reproachfully."; and in 1 Peter 3:9, "or railing for railing: but contrariwise blessing".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe railing for railing is the trade of the world, and blessing is the trade of the called — we are called to inherit a blessing, not to return one.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from λοιδός (mischief); abusive, i.e. a blackguard:--railer, reviler.
BiblicalUsage: loídoros means railer, reviler, and once is enough to see what it is doing. In 1 Corinthians 6:10, "nor revilers"; and in 1 Corinthians 5:11, "or a railer".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the reviler is named among those who shall not inherit the kingdom — not to shame the struggling, but to warn the church whom it must not keep company with.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain affinity; a plague (literally, the disease, or figuratively, a pest):--pestilence(-t).
BiblicalUsage: loimós means pestilence. In Luke 21:11, "and pestilences"; and in Acts 24:5, "For we have found this man [a] pestilent [fellow]".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe pestilence is both a sign and a slander — Jesus said famines and pestilences would come, and Paul's enemies called him a pestilent fellow for preaching.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: masculine plural of a derivative of G3007; remaining ones:--other, which remain, remnant, residue, rest.
BiblicalUsage: loipoí means the remaining ones — a small word with a sharp edge. In Matthew 22:6, "And the remnant took his servants"; and in Romans 11:7, "and the rest were blinded". In Revelation 20:5, "But the rest of the dead lived not again until the thousand years were finished.".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the rest are the ones God keeps His eye on — the remnant that did not bow, and the dead that lived not again until the thousand years were finished.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: neuter singular of the same as G3062; something remaining (adverbially):--besides, finally, furthermore, (from) henceforth, moreover, now, + it remaineth, then.
BiblicalUsage: loipón means finally, what remains, and its few appearances are all worth reading. In Philippians 3:1, "Finally, my brethren, rejoice in the Lord"; and in 1 Thessalonians 4:1, "Furthermore then we beseech you". In 2 Timothy 4:8, "Henceforth there is laid up for me a crown of righteousness".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe finally is Paul's favourite word for the end of a letter and the start of the Christian life — finally, brethren, rejoice, walk, and receive the crown.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: genitive case singular of the same as G3062; remaining time:--from henceforth.
BiblicalUsage: loipoû means from henceforth, and the verse where it stands does the talking. In Galatians 6:17, "From henceforth let no man trouble me: for I bear in my body the marks of the Lord Jesus."; and in Ephesians 6:10, "Finally, my brethren, be strong in the Lord".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe from henceforth is the line Paul draws — let no man trouble me, for I bear the marks of the Lord Jesus, and henceforth I am strong in Him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain origin; Lois, a Christian woman:--Lois.
BiblicalUsage: Lōḯs is the name of Lois. In 2 Timothy 1:5, "which dwelt first in thy grandmother Lois".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Lois is the grandmother every family needs — the unfeigned faith that dwelt first in her, then in Eunice, then in Timothy. I hold that faith passed down is the truest inheritance.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: perhaps a primary word; a "lance":--spear.
BiblicalUsage: lónchē means a spear, and once is enough to see what it is doing. In John 19:34, "But one of the soldiers with a spear pierced his side".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the spear is the proof of His death and the fountain of our life — blood and water came out, and the soldier's thrust settled it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H3876); Lot, a patriarch:--Lot.
BiblicalUsage: Lṓt belongs to Lot, the patriarch, and the Bible does not let it pass unnamed. In Luke 17:28, "Likewise also as it was in the days of Lot"; and in Luke 17:29, "But the same day that Lot went out of Sodom it rained fire and brimstone from heaven". In 2 Peter 2:7, "And delivered just Lot".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Lot is the righteous man vexed by the filthy — delivered, but only just, and his wife remembered as a warning, and the days of Lot will come again, with fire falling the same day he went out. My position is that I will not linger in Sodom; I will go out when God says go.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a gum (from its sticky nature), probably ladanum
BiblicalUsage: lôṭ means a gum — a small word with a sharp edge. In Genesis 37:25, "a company of Ishmeelites came from Gilead with their camels bearing spicery and balm and myrrh"; and in Genesis 43:11, "a little balm".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the ladanum on the Ishmaelites' camels is the smell of the journey — the spice that carried Joseph down to Egypt, and the gift Jacob sent back.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: contracted from Latin Lucanus; Lucas, a Christian:--Lucas, Luke.
BiblicalUsage: Loukâs is the name of Luke, the beloved physician. In Colossians 4:14, "the beloved physician"; and in 2 Timothy 4:11, "Only Luke is with me.". In Philemon 1:24, "Marcus, Aristarchus, Demas, Lucas, my fellowlabourers.".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Luke is the beloved physician who stayed — when everyone else left, only Luke was with Paul. I hold that the man who wrote two books of the Bible did it as a fellow labourer, not a bystander.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Latin origin; illuminative; Lucius, a Christian:--Lucius.
BiblicalUsage: Loúkios means Lucius, a Christian, and the verse where it stands does the talking. In Romans 16:21, "and Lucius"; and in Acts 13:1, "and Lucius of Cyrene".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Lucius of Cyrene is the proof the church was never one nation's — a prophet at Antioch and a kinsman greeted in Rome.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a primary verb; to bathe (the whole person; whereas G3538 means to wet a part only, and G4150 to wash, cleanse garments exclusively):--wash.
BiblicalUsage: loúō means wash, and no one who reads the Bible can walk past it. In John 13:10, "He that is washed needeth not save to wash [his] feet"; and in Hebrews 10:22, "and our bodies washed with pure water.". In Acts 16:33, "and washed [their] stripes"; and in Acts 9:37, "and died: whom when they had washed".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe washing is the picture of a clean conscience — he that is washed need not save to wash his feet, and our bodies are washed with pure water. I hold that the jailer washed the apostles' stripes the same hour he believed, and the dead were washed before they were laid out. My position is that I am washed, and I will live like a washed person.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3068; a bath, i.e. (figuratively), baptism:--washing.
BiblicalUsage: loutrón means washing, and once is enough to see what it is doing. In Ephesians 5:26, "That he might sanctify and cleanse it with the washing of water by the word"; and in Titus 3:5, "by the washing of regeneration".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the washing of water by the word is how Christ sanctifies His church — not by our works, but by His mercy and the renewing of the Holy Ghost.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Lochesh, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Lôwchêsh is the name of Lochesh, an Israelite. In Nehemiah 3:12, "And next unto him repaired Shallum the son of Halohesh"; and in Nehemiah 10:24, "Hallohesh, Pileha, Shobek,".
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Hallohesh is the father whose children built — Shallum repaired the wall with his daughters, and the name stands among the sealers of the covenant.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Lot, Abraham's nephew
BiblicalUsage: Lot was Abraham's nephew, and the two men travelled together until their herdsmen quarrelled and they parted ways. Lot chose the well-watered plain of the Jordan and settled near Sodom, where two angels came to his house at evening. When God destroyed the cities of the plain, He remembered Abraham and sent Lot out of the overthrow.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Lot shows how close a man can live to judgment and still be pulled out by grace. His rescue was not earned by his choices; it was God's mercy answering Abraham's faith.
RelatedEvents: Abram and Lot Part Ways; Destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a veil
BiblicalUsage: The word names a veil or covering, and Isaiah uses it for the covering cast over all people and spread over all nations. God promises to destroy that covering on His mountain.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the veil Isaiah names is the blindness and sorrow that hangs over every nation, and God Himself will lift it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Lotan, an Idumaean
BiblicalUsage: Lotan was one of the sons of Seir the Horite, who lived in the land of Edom before any king reigned in Israel. His children were Hori and Hemam, and his sister was Timna. The genealogies list him twice, in Genesis and again in Chronicles, as part of the Horite line.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe even a bare name in a genealogy matters, because God keeps the record of peoples the world forgets.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a wreath
BiblicalUsage: The word names the wreath-shaped ornaments worked into the bronze bases Solomon had made for the temple. Lions, oxen and cherubim stood on the borders between the ledges, with the wreaths set beneath them and around them.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that even the decoration of God's house was made with care, because nothing offered to Him is too small to be done well.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a loop
BiblicalUsage: The word names the loops of blue fastened along the edges of the tabernacle curtains, fifty on one curtain and fifty on the next, so the two could be coupled together. The loops held the covering of God's dwelling in place.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the smallest fastening in the tabernacle mattered, because God gave the pattern and His people followed it exactly.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a conditional particle; if; by implication (interj. as a wish) would that!
BiblicalUsage: This little word carries a wish: Abraham cries out that Ishmael might live before God, Moses wishes Israel were wise enough to consider their latter end, and Isaiah wishes they had hearkened to God's commandments. In each place it is the sound of a heart longing for what might have been.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God lets His people speak their longings plainly, and the wishes of Scripture show us what He Himself desires for us.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to gulp; figuratively, to be rash
BiblicalUsage: The word means to gulp or swallow down, and Job uses it for his own words, saying they are swallowed up by grief heavier than the sand of the sea. Obadiah turns it against the nations, who shall drink and swallow down until they are as though they had not been.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that what men swallow in pride, God will make them swallow in judgment, while the sufferer who speaks honestly is heard.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably meaning to glisten; a tablet (as polished), of stone, wood or metal
BiblicalUsage: The word names the tablets of stone on which God wrote His covenant, and Moses went up the mountain and stayed there forty days and forty nights to receive them. Scripture calls them the tablets of the covenant, written with the finger of God, and when Moses came down his face shone from speaking with the LORD. The tablets were not man's idea of right and wrong; they were God's own words cut in stone.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the tablets matter because God wrote them Himself, and no one may edit what He has written. I hold that the same God who carved His law in stone writes it now on the hearts of His people, so His commands are not a burden to escape but a covenant to keep.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a Libyan or inhabitant of interior Africa (only in plural)
BiblicalUsage: The Libyans were a people of North Africa who appear in Scripture as soldiers and allies in the armies of other nations. They marched with Shishak against Jerusalem, and Asa remembered them as part of the huge host God delivered into his hand when he relied on the LORD. Prophets name them again among the nations drawn into the wars of the last days and among the helpers of fallen Nineveh.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the Libyans remind us that no nation's strength stands on its own, and armies without number are nothing against the LORD. I hold that God rules over every people, whether they serve Him or march against His people, and history bends to His purposes.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Luchith, a place East of the Jordan
BiblicalUsage: Luhith was a place east of the Jordan, on the road up from Moab, where fugitives fled weeping when judgment fell. Isaiah cries out for Moab as its people go up to Luhith with weeping, and Jeremiah repeats the same going up in his oracle against Moab.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Luhith stands in Scripture as a road of tears, and the prophets name it so we feel what judgment costs real people.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Lud, the name of two nations
BiblicalUsage: Lud was a son of Shem, named among the peoples spread out after the flood, and his name stands for a nation of bowmen. Isaiah says God will send those who escape to Lud and the far nations, so they declare His glory among the Gentiles. Ezekiel pictures the men of Lud as warriors in the army of Tyre, hanging shield and helmet in her ranks.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Lud shows God's reach: a people named in a genealogy becomes a people who hear His glory, and no nation is beyond His sending.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a Ludite or inhabitants of Lud (only in plural)
BiblicalUsage: The Ludites were the people of Lud, named among the sons of Mizraim in the table of nations, and Jeremiah calls them to come forth with shield and bow among the mighty men of Egypt's army. They are a people known to Scripture mainly as warriors for hire, standing with the powers of their day.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the Ludites warn us that skill with a bow is no substitute for standing with God. I hold that nations are known by whom they serve, and those who sell their strength to the highest bidder end up on the losing side.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a spiral step
BiblicalUsage: The word names the winding stairs that led up through the temple Solomon built, from the middle chamber to the third. It appears only once, in the description of how the house of God was put together.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Scripture's care over a staircase shows God notices the way up into His presence, and no step toward Him is wasted.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: if not
BiblicalUsage: The word means if not, or except, and it marks the turning point of a story: Jacob says except the God of his father had been with him, Laban would have sent him away empty. Abigail's haste kept David from bloodshed, and Joab says unless Abner had spoken, the fighting would have gone on till morning.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this small word carries some of the Bible's greatest mercies, because except God had stepped in, the story would have ended in ruin.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to stop (usually over night); by implication, to stay permanently; hence (in a bad sense) to be obstinate (especially in words, to complain)
BiblicalUsage: The word means to lodge or spend the night, and it covers both the welcome of a guest and the stubbornness of a complaint. Lot begged the angels to turn in and tarry all night in his house, Ruth promised Naomi that where she lodged, she would lodge, and the psalm promises that whoever dwells in the secret place of the Most High shall abide under His shadow. Israel also lodged in the wilderness on the way to the promised land, and the stones from the Jordan were left in the lodging place.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe lodging is a picture of belonging: we stay where we are welcome, and God makes His presence our lodging place. I hold that the one who abides under His shadow is not a visitor passing through, but a child at home, and that is the rest every weary heart is looking for.
RelatedEvents: Destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah; Ruth's Loyalty
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Lush, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: The name stands once in Scripture, joined to Laish, the father of Phaltiel, from whom Michal was taken and brought back to David. Ish-bosheth sent and took her from her husband, and the single mention fixes the name in the middle of the struggle over David's house.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe even one mention is enough to show how costly the quarrels of kings were for ordinary people caught between them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to knead
BiblicalUsage: The word means to knead, the ordinary work of hands in dough, and it appears at both holy and shameful tables. Sarah kneaded cakes for the three visitors at Abraham's tent, and Tamar kneaded cakes in her brother Amnon's sight before he seized her. Jeremiah shows whole families kneading dough for cakes to the queen of heaven, and Hosea pictures adulterers as an oven heated by the baker after he has kneaded the dough.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe kneading shows how the same hands can serve God or serve idols, and the difference is not the work but the worship. I hold that God sees the quiet work of the kitchen as clearly as the work of the temple, and He calls His people to knead for Him alone.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to wrap up
BiblicalUsage: The word means to wrap up, and it is used for a prophet hiding his face, a sword kept in cloth, and a covering over the nations. Elijah wrapped his face in his mantle when he heard the still small voice at Horeb, and David took Goliath's sword, wrapped in a cloth behind the ephod, when he fled from Saul. Isaiah says God will destroy the covering cast over all people.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe wrapping marks both reverence and hiding: Elijah covered his face before a holy God, and men wrap what they fear to show. I hold that God Himself will unwrap the covering over the nations, so what was hidden will be seen plainly at last.
RelatedEvents: Elijah at Horeb: The Still Small Voice
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, to make mouths at, i.e. to scoff; hence (from the effort to pronounce a foreign language) to interpret, or (generally) intercede
BiblicalUsage: The word carries two faces: it names the interpreter who stands between speakers, and the scorner who mocks what is true. Joseph's brothers did not know he understood them, because he spoke to them by an interpreter, and the same root names the scoffers Proverbs warns against. Isaiah tells the mockers not to mock, lest their bands be made strong, and Proverbs says the scorner delights in his scorning while the wise man loves rebuke.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the difference between an interpreter and a scorner is the heart: one stands between people to help them understand, the other stands above them to laugh. I hold that God gives understanding to the humble, but the mocker closes his own ears and calls it wisdom.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: some kind of nuttree, perhaps the almond
BiblicalUsage: The word names a kind of nut tree, probably the almond or hazel, and it appears once, when Jacob took rods of green poplar, hazel and chestnut and peeled white streaks in them. The rods were part of his bargain with Laban over the flocks.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that God worked through Jacob's ordinary tools, and the rods remind me He blesses the work of our hands without needing our schemes.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Luz, the name of two places in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Luz was the old name of Bethel, the city where Jacob dreamed of the ladder reaching to heaven and called the place the house of God. Jacob renamed it Bethel, but Scripture keeps the old name so we know it is the same city. Long after, the house of Joseph sent men to spy out Bethel, and the text notes again that the name of the city before was Luz.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Luz matters because God met Jacob there before the place had a holy name, and He still meets people in ordinary places and renames their lives.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: some kind of nuttree, perhaps the almond
BiblicalUsage: The word names a kind of nut tree, probably the almond or hazel, and it appears once, when Jacob took rods of green poplar, hazel and chestnut and peeled white streaks in them. The rods were part of his bargain with Laban over the flocks.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that God worked through Jacob's ordinary tools, and the rods remind me He blesses the work of our hands without needing our schemes.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3088; a lamp-stand (literally or figuratively):--candlestick.
BiblicalUsage: The word names the lampstand, the stand that lifts a lamp high enough to light the room, and Jesus says no one lights a lamp and puts it under a basket, but on a lampstand, so it gives light to all in the house. The tabernacle held a golden lampstand before the LORD, and John saw seven golden lampstands in his vision, which are the seven churches.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the lampstand teaches us that light is meant to be lifted up, not hidden, and the church exists to hold Christ's light where all can see it. I hold that a lampstand does not make its own light; it only holds the flame, and so the church's job is to hold up Jesus and get out of the way.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from the base of G3022; a portable lamp or other illuminator (literally or figuratively):--candle, light.
BiblicalUsage: The word names a portable lamp, the small oil lamp carried in the hand, and Jesus uses it for the light of the body, the eye, and for the lamp a woman lights to search her house for a lost coin. John the Baptist was a burning and shining lamp, and Peter calls the prophetic word a lamp shining in a dark place until the day dawns.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a lamp is the right picture for God's word, because it does not light the whole road at once, only the next step. I hold that John was a lamp and not the light itself, and every faithful witness is the same: a small flame pointing to the true Light.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H3850); Lydda (i.e. Lod), a place in Palestine:--Lydda.
BiblicalUsage: Lydda was a town in Palestine where Peter came down to the saints who lived there. When Peter healed Aeneas, all who lived at Lydda and Sharon saw it and turned to the Lord, and the town sent for Peter again when Tabitha died at nearby Joppa.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Lydda shows how one healing in one town can turn a whole district to the Lord, because God works through ordinary places.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, feminine of Ludios (of foreign origin) (a Lydian, in Asia Minor); Lydia, a Christian woman:--Lydia.
BiblicalUsage: Lydia was a seller of purple from Thyatira who worshipped God, and when Paul preached at Philippi, the Lord opened her heart to attend to the things he spoke. She was baptised with her household and pressed Paul and his companions to stay in her house, and after their release from prison they went again to her house to encourage the brethren.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Lydia shows that God opens hearts before anyone preaches a word, and the first convert in Europe was a businesswoman whose home became the church.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: perhaps remotely from G3074; Lycaonia, a region of Asia Minor:--Lycaonia.
BiblicalUsage: Lycaonia was a region of Asia Minor where Paul and Barnabas fled when a plot formed against them at Iconium. They came to Lystra and Derbe, cities of Lycaonia, and preached the gospel there, and the region's name marks the border of their escape.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Lycaonia reminds me that flight from danger is sometimes faithfulness, and the gospel went where the apostles' feet carried it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: adverb from a derivative of G3071; Lycaonistically, i.e. in the language of the Lycaonians:--in the speech of Lycaonia.
BiblicalUsage: The word is an adverb meaning in the language of Lycaonia, and it appears once, when the crowds at Lystra saw Paul heal the lame man and lifted up their voices in the speech of Lycaonia, saying the gods had come down to them in the likeness of men.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the crowd's own tongue betrayed them: they cried out in Lycaonian because the miracle had struck them where they lived, and yet they still missed who had done it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably remotely from G3074; Lycia, a province of Asia Minor:--Lycia.
BiblicalUsage: Lycia was a province on the southern coast of Asia Minor. Paul's ship sailed past it on the voyage to Rome, coming to Myra, a city of Lycia, after crossing the sea of Cilicia and Pamphylia.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe even a passing mention of Lycia matters, because Luke the historian kept the route, and God's purposes rode on a real ship through real seas.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: perhaps akin to the base of G3022 (from the whitish hair); a wolf:--wolf.
BiblicalUsage: The word means a wolf, and Jesus uses it for the false prophets who come in sheep's clothing but inwardly are ravening wolves, and for the danger His disciples face, sent as lambs among wolves. The hireling sees the wolf coming and flees, because the sheep are not his own, and Paul warns the Ephesian elders that after his departing grievous wolves will enter in among them, not sparing the flock.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the wolf is Scripture's plainest picture of false teaching: it looks like a sheep until it is close enough to kill. I hold that the true Shepherd does not flee when the wolf comes, and the test of any shepherd is whether he stays with the flock when it costs him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: middle voice from a probably derivative of G3089 (meaning filth); properly, to soil, i.e. (figuratively) insult (maltreat):--make havock of.
BiblicalUsage: The word means to ravage or make havoc, and it appears once, for Saul as he tore at the church after Stephen's death, entering into every house and dragging men and women off to prison.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Saul's havoc is the darkest picture of what religion without Christ does, and the same man became the gospel's greatest preacher.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a primary verb; to "loosen" (literally or figuratively):--break (up), destroy, dissolve, (un-)loose, melt, put off. Compare G4486.
BiblicalUsage: The word means to loosen, and it stretches from untying a sandal to undoing the works of the devil. Jesus gives the keys of the kingdom with power to bind and loose, and He cries loose him at the tomb of Lazarus. Peter says God loosed the pains of death because it was not possible for death to hold Christ, and John says the Son of God appeared to destroy the works of the devil.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe loosening is the work of Christ from first to last: He unties what sin has bound, and death itself could not hold Him. I hold that what He looses on earth is loosed in heaven, so His people need not stay tied to anything He has already undone.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: apparently a primary word; sadness:--grief, grievous, + grudgingly, heaviness, sorrow.
BiblicalUsage: The word names sorrow, grief and heaviness, and Scripture is honest about how much of it God's people carry. The disciples' hearts were filled with sorrow at Jesus' farewell words, and Paul says godly sorrow works repentance to salvation, while the sorrow of the world works death. Even chastening seems grievous for the present, yet afterward it yields the peaceable fruit of righteousness.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe sorrow is not wasted in God's hands, because He tells the two sorrows apart and uses the godly one to bring us home. I hold that the grief that drives us to repentance is a gift, and the grief that only hardens us is the world's sorrow, which ends in death.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3077; to distress; reflexively or passively, to be sad:--cause grief, grieve, be in heaviness, (be) sorrow(-ful), be (make) sorry.
BiblicalUsage: The word means to cause grief or to be made sorrowful, and it runs through the letters as the cost of honest love. Paul wrote to the Corinthians so that they would not be made sorry, and then rejoiced that their sorrow led to repentance, and he tells the Thessalonians not to sorrow over the dead as others who have no hope. He also warns us not to grieve the Holy Spirit of God, and Peter was grieved when Jesus asked him the third time whether he loved Him.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe grief is not a sign that faith has failed, because even the apostles grieved and the Spirit Himself can be grieved. I hold that the sorrow of God's people has hope woven through it, and the Spirit who can be grieved is the same Spirit who comforts us in it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3080 and ἀνία (trouble); grief-dispelling; Lysanias, a governor of Abilene:--Lysanias.
BiblicalUsage: Lysanias was tetrarch of Abilene, and Luke names him among the rulers of the day when John the Baptist began his ministry, in the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar. His name fixes the gospel in real history, under real governors.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Lysanias matters because Luke dated the gospel by rulers like him, and the good news entered history, not a fairy tale.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain affinity; Lysias, a Roman:--Lysias.
BiblicalUsage: Lysias, whose full name was Claudius Lysias, was the chief captain in Jerusalem who rescued Paul from the mob and wrote to Governor Felix on his behalf. Felix deferred Paul's case, saying he would decide it when Lysias the chief captain came down, and the letter shows a Roman officer caught between a riot and the law.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Lysias shows how God can use even an unbelieving officer to protect His servant, and the law became a shield for the gospel that day.
RelatedEvents: Paul Before Felix, Festus, and Agrippa
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3089; a loosening, i.e. (specially), divorce:--to be loosed.
BiblicalUsage: The word names a loosening, and Paul uses it for the bond of marriage: if a man is loosed from a wife, he is not to seek one. It is the one place the word stands, and it speaks of release from a bond.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that loosening is never light in Scripture, because bonds are made before God and only God unties what He has joined.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: third person singular present indicative active of a derivative of a compound of G3080 and G5056; impersonally, it answers the purpose, i.e. is advantageous:--it is better.
BiblicalUsage: The word means it were better, or it is profitable, and Jesus uses it once, for the man who offends one of His little ones: it were better for him that a millstone were hanged about his neck and he were cast into the sea.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Jesus' hard word shows how fiercely He guards His little ones, and no one should trifle with a child's faith.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain origin; Lystra, a place in Asia Minor:--Lystra.
BiblicalUsage: Lystra was a city of Lycaonia where Paul healed a man crippled from his mother's womb, and where the crowd first hailed him as a god and then stoned him and dragged him out of the city. Paul returned there on his second journey and found Timothy, a disciple whose mother was a Jewess and whose father was a Greek, and Timothy became his fellow worker from that day.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Lystra holds both the best and worst of ministry in one place: a miracle, a stoning, and a young man called to carry the gospel on.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3089; something to loosen with, i.e. a redemption price (figuratively, atonement):--ransom.
BiblicalUsage: The word names a ransom, the price paid to set someone free, and Jesus uses it for His own life: the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give His life a ransom for many. Matthew and Mark both keep the saying, and it stands at the heart of the gospel.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that ransom is the word that makes the cross personal: Jesus did not pay a price in the abstract, He gave His life for many, and I am one of them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3083; to ransom (literally or figuratively):--redeem.
BiblicalUsage: The word means to redeem, to buy back by paying a price, and the New Testament uses it for what Christ did for His people. On the road to Emmaus the two disciples said they had trusted He was the one who would redeem Israel, and Paul says Christ gave Himself to redeem us from all iniquity, while Peter says we were not redeemed with silver and gold but by His blood.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that redemption is not a figure of speech: we were bought, and the price was Christ Himself, so my life is no longer my own.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3084; a ransoming (figuratively):--+ redeemed, redemption.
BiblicalUsage: The word names redemption, the ransoming itself, and it appears where Scripture celebrates the rescue God has already worked. Zechariah blesses the Lord God of Israel because He has visited and redeemed His people, and Anna spoke of the child to all who looked for redemption in Jerusalem. Hebrews says Christ entered the holy place by His own blood, having obtained eternal redemption for us.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe redemption is eternal because the blood that bought it is Christ's own, and no one can undo what He has finished. I hold that Anna and Zechariah were right to rejoice, because the redemption they had waited for was standing in front of them.
RelatedPeople: Zechariah, Father of John the Baptist
RelatedEvents: The Birth of John the Baptist
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3084; a redeemer (figuratively):--deliverer.
BiblicalUsage: The word names a deliverer, and Stephen uses it once, for Moses: the same Moses the people refused, saying who made you a ruler and a judge, God sent to be a ruler and a deliverer, by the hand of the angel who appeared to him in the bush.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that God delights to send the very man a people rejected, and Moses the deliverer points to the greater Deliverer they would reject too.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to stain; a blemish (physically or morally)
KeyPassages: Leviticus 21:17; Deuteronomy 17:1; Song of Solomon 4:7; 2 Samuel 14:25
BiblicalUsage: The word names a blemish, a stain or defect, and the law would not accept an offering with one: no animal with a blemish could be offered, and no priest with a blemish could come near to offer bread. The same word reaches beyond the body to the heart, for Deuteronomy calls a crooked generation a blemish upon themselves, yet the Song says of the beloved that there is no spot in her, and Absalom is praised as having no blemish from head to foot.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the blemish laws teach us that God is holy and His worship is not careless, yet the same word shows His grace, because He calls His beloved spotless. I hold that only Christ is truly without blemish, and He is the offering God accepts on our behalf.
RelatedBooks: Leviticus; Deuteronomy; Song of Solomon; 2 Samuel
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a crossing-place (of a river, a ford; of a mountain, a pass); abstractly, a transit, i.e. (figuratively) overwhelming
BiblicalUsage: The word names a crossing place, a ford where a river can be passed or a pass through the mountains, and it marks the places where journeys turn. Jacob passed over the ford of Jabbok on the night he wrestled with God, the men of Gilead held the passages of Jordan against Ephraim, and the spies' pursuers went out after them to the fords.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the crossing places of Scripture are where God meets His people between one life and the next, and no one crosses alone. I hold that the ford is a picture of every hard passage in life: God goes before us through the water, and what waits on the other side is His promise.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, compact (part of soil), i.e. loam
BiblicalUsage: The word names the compact clay ground, the loam of the Jordan plain, where Solomon had the bronze vessels of the temple cast, between Succoth and Zarthan. It appears only once, in the account of the casting.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that God chose ordinary clay ground for the making of holy vessels, and He still shapes His work in plain places.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a granary
BiblicalUsage: The word names a granary or storehouse, and Jeremiah uses it once, in the oracle against Babylon: open her storehouses, cast her up as heaps, and destroy her utterly. The storehouse that once held plenty becomes the spoil of judgment.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the storehouse warns us that plenty hoarded against God becomes plunder, and no granary is safer than the hand of the LORD.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to spurn; also (intransitively) to disappear
BiblicalUsage: The word means to spurn or reject, and it is one of Scripture's saddest words, because it is used of God being rejected and of His people rejecting Him. When Israel asked for a king, God told Samuel they had not rejected him but had rejected God from reigning over them, and Samuel told Saul that because he had rejected the word of the LORD, the LORD had rejected him from being king. Hosea says God's people rejected knowledge, and the psalm says the stone the builders refused has become the head stone of the corner.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe rejection is the heart of sin: we do not only break God's law, we refuse God Himself. I hold that the stone the builders rejected became the cornerstone, so God's answer to our rejection is not to give up on us but to build His house on the One we threw away.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to waver
BiblicalUsage: The word means to waver or slip, and the psalms use it for feet that hold firm and feet that would fall. David says God enlarged his steps under him so his feet did not slip, and he prays that his steps would hold fast in God's paths. Job says the wavering foot is despised by those at ease, and the psalm of the man who trusts God says the law of God is in his heart and none of his steps shall slide.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the wavering foot is the picture of every believer's weakness, and God does not ask us to stand on our own strength. I hold that He enlarges our steps beneath us, so the one who walks with Him does not slip, even on ground that would make others fall.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a delicacy or (abstractly) pleasure (adverbially, cheerfully)
BiblicalUsage: The word names delicacies, the rich food and pleasures that mark a life of ease, and it appears in blessing and in warning alike. Asher's bread shall be fat and he shall yield royal dainties, the daughters of Zion who lived delicately are brought down in Lamentations, and the proverb says a son who is corrected will give delight to his soul. Agag came delicately before Samuel, thinking the bitterness of death was past.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe delicacies are a gift of God to enjoy, but a dangerous master when they become the goal of life. I hold that the delight God gives is meant to point us back to the Giver, and the one who corrects a child in love gives a deeper delight than any feast.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a bond, i.e. group
BiblicalUsage: The word names a bond or binding, and it appears once, when God asks Job whether he can bind the sweet influences of the Pleiades or loose the bands of Orion. The stars themselves are held in bonds only God can fasten or loose.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the bands of the stars remind me how small my power is and how great God's, because He ties what no man can untie.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Maadai, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Maadai was an Israelite of the sons of Bani, named among those who had taken foreign wives and put them away at Ezra's command. His name stands in the list of those who repented and set their households right.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Maadai's single mention matters, because repentance is recorded by name, and God remembers those who turn back to Him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Maadjah, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Maadiah was a priest who returned with Zerubbabel, named among the heads of the priestly courses in the days of Nehemiah. His name stands in the record of the priests who served when the wall was dedicated and the worship of the temple was set in order.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the priests are named because God keeps the record of those who serve Him, even when the world has forgotten their faces.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to press, i.e. to pierce, emasculate, handle
BiblicalUsage: The word means to press or crush, and its three uses show how one word can serve worship, lust and war. The law forbids offering an animal that is bruised or crushed or broken, Ezekiel says the breasts of Oholah and Oholibah were pressed in the sins of their youth, and Saul's spear was stuck in the ground at his bolster when David crept into the camp by night.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word warns us that what is crushed cannot be offered to God, and what is pressed in secret will be named in the open. I hold that God alone can take what is broken and make it whole, and He does not accept a bruised offering in place of a whole heart.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Maakah (or Maakath), the name of a place in Syria, also of a Mesopotamian, of three Israelites, and of four Israelitesses and one Syrian woman
BiblicalUsage: Maakah is a name worn by many, and Scripture keeps them apart by their stories. One Maacah was the concubine of Nahor, Abraham's brother, and another was the daughter of Talmai, king of Geshur, who became David's wife and the mother of Absalom. A later Maachah was the mother of King Abijam, and the Chronicles call her the mother of Asa as well.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the many Maakahs remind us that a name is not a person, and God knows each one by her own story.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an eatable (includ. provender, flesh and fruit)
BiblicalUsage: The word names food, what is eaten, and it runs from the garden to the exile. God made every tree pleasant to the sight and good for food, and the woman saw the tree was good for food and took of its fruit. The queen of Sheba saw the meat of Solomon's table and there was no more spirit in her, and Daniel asked that his food not defile him with the king's meat.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe food is the first gift and the first temptation, because the same tree that fed us became the tree we stole from. I hold that God still provides our daily bread, and the table is holy when we receive it from His hand and refuse what would defile us.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a Maakathite, or inhabitant of Maakah
BiblicalUsage: The Maakathites were the people of Maakah, a small kingdom east of Jordan, and they held their land when Israel took the country around them. Moses gave their territory to the half tribe of Manasseh, Joshua lists their border among the unconquered lands, and a Maakathite named Eliphelet stood among David's mighty men.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the Maakathites show that God keeps peoples the conquerors pass by, and a small kingdom can outlast an empire. I hold that the one Maakathite among David's mighty men is proof that God draws His servants from every nation, not only from Israel.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: something to eat with,i.e. a knife
BiblicalUsage: The word names the knife used for eating and for sacrifice, and it appears at the sharpest moments of the Bible. Abraham took the knife in his hand to slay his son on Mount Moriah, and again he stretched out his hand and took the knife before the angel called. The Levite took a knife and divided his concubine into twelve pieces, and the proverb says the teeth of the wicked are as knives, devouring the poor from off the earth.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the knife in Abraham's hand is the Bible's sharpest picture of faith, because he trusted God would provide even as he raised it. I hold that the same knife in wicked hands shows what happens when men use holy things for violence, and only God can turn the blade aside.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: something eaten (by fire), i.e. fuel
BiblicalUsage: The word names fuel, what is eaten by fire, and Isaiah uses it twice for the burning of war: every battle of the warrior is with confused noise and garments rolled in blood, but this shall be with burning and fuel of fire, and the people shall be as the fuel of the fire.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Isaiah's fuel is a warning: what men feed with pride, God will feed to the fire, and only His peace ends the burning.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: treachery, i.e. sin
BiblicalUsage: The word names treachery, unfaithfulness against God, and it is the charge laid against Israel again and again. Achan committed a trespass in the accursed thing and the anger of the LORD was kindled against Israel, the princes of the people trespassed in the holy things, and Ezra confessed that the people had joined themselves to the abominations of the land. Daniel confesses that shame belongs to Israel because of the trespass they trespassed against God.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe treachery is worse than ordinary sin, because it breaks a covenant made in love, and Israel's history is the story of a faithless wife and a faithful Husband. I hold that confession is the only answer to treachery, and God hears the one who names his sin plainly and turns back to Him.
RelatedEvents: The Defeat at Ai and Achan's Sin
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: treachery, i.e. sin
BiblicalUsage: The word names treachery, unfaithfulness against God, and it is the charge laid against Israel again and again. Achan committed a trespass in the accursed thing and the anger of the LORD was kindled against Israel, the princes of the people trespassed in the holy things, and Ezra confessed that the people had joined themselves to the abominations of the land. Daniel confesses that shame belongs to Israel because of the trespass they trespassed against God.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe treachery is worse than ordinary sin, because it breaks a covenant made in love, and Israel's history is the story of a faithless wife and a faithful Husband. I hold that confession is the only answer to treachery, and God hears the one who names his sin plainly and turns back to Him.
RelatedEvents: The Defeat at Ai and Achan's Sin
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, to cover up; used only figuratively, to act covertly, i.e. treacherously
BiblicalUsage: The word means to act treacherously, to cover up and deal falsely, and it is used of kings, priests and whole generations. Moses says Israel trespassed against God at the waters of Meribah, Achan's trespass brought defeat at Ai, and Uzziah trespassed against the LORD when he entered the temple to burn incense. Ezra confesses that the people had trespassed by taking foreign wives, and the prophets name the trespass again and again.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe acting treacherously is the sin of the heart that hides, because it covers what it does even from itself. I hold that no cover holds before God, and the only safe place is to uncover the sin and let Him cleanse it.
RelatedEvents: The Defeat at Ai and Achan's Sin
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: elevation, i.e. the act (literally, a journey to a higher place, figuratively, a thought arising), or (concretely) the condition (literally, a step or grademark, figuratively, a superiority of station); specifically a climactic progression (in certain Psalms)
BiblicalUsage: The word names a going up, a flight of steps, and it marks the way into God's presence and the signs He gives in time. Solomon's throne had six steps with lions standing on either side, and the steps of the temple gates rose toward the house of the LORD. Hezekiah asked for a sign, and the shadow went back ten degrees on the dial of Ahaz, and Ezra's company went up from Babylon to Jerusalem in the first month.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the steps of Scripture teach us that the way to God is a going up, and He meets us on the climb. I hold that the shadow going backward on the dial is God's own sign that He can turn time itself for the sake of a praying king.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an act (good or bad)
BiblicalUsage: The word names deeds, the acts men do whether good or bad, and the prophets weigh them in God's balance. God warns Israel that their doings will not allow them to turn to Him, and He repays every man according to his doings. Jeremiah says God tries the heart and gives to every man according to his ways and according to the fruit of his doings, and Hosea says Ephraim's doings are before God's face.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe our doings are never hidden from God, because He reads the heart behind every act. I hold that the same God who repays deeds also forgives them, and the one who turns to Him finds his doings covered by grace.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Steep of Scorpions, a place in the Desert
BiblicalUsage: Maaleh-acrabbim, the ascent of scorpions, was a pass on the southern border of the promised land, named for the scorpions that haunted its rocks. The border of Judah went up by it, and the coast of the Amorites ran from the same ascent.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the scorpion pass reminds us that the border of God's promise was not an easy road, and His people entered it anyway.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an elevation, i.e. (concretely) acclivity or platform; abstractly (the relation or state) a rise or (figuratively) priority
BiblicalUsage: The word names an ascent, a going up, and it is used for the steep ways of the land and for the going up to God's house. David went up the ascent of the Mount of Olives weeping, with his head covered, when he fled from Absalom, and Saul met young women going up to the city to draw water, who told him the seer was just ahead. Isaiah pictures the fugitives of Moab going up to Luhith with weeping, and Nehemiah's procession went up the stairs of the city of David.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the ascents of Scripture are climbed weeping as often as singing, and God walks the steep road with His people. I hold that David's weeping ascent and the singers' going up are the same road, and both end in the house of the LORD.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: burdensomeness
BiblicalUsage: The word names burdensomeness, a heavy weight, and Zechariah uses it once, for Jerusalem: God will make Jerusalem a burdensome stone for all people, and all that burden themselves with it shall be cut in pieces.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Jerusalem is a stone no nation can lift, because God has set it in place, and those who try to move it will be cut by it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: (figuratively) a position
BiblicalUsage: The word names a station or standing place, the post where a man stands to serve, and it is used for the queen of Sheba's wonder and for the priests of the temple. She saw the attendance of Solomon's ministers and their apparel and the cupbearers and their ascent, and there was no more spirit in her. Isaiah says God will drive Shebna from his station, and the Levites stood in their station to serve in the house of the LORD.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a station is the place God gives a man to stand, and faithfulness is standing there until He moves us. I hold that Shebna lost his station by pride and the Levites kept theirs by service, and the difference is everything.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a deep
BiblicalUsage: The word names the depths, the deep waters where a man sinks and cannot stand, and the psalms cry out from them. David says he is come into deep waters where the floods overflow him, and again he cries that the floods would not overflow him nor the deep swallow him up. The psalmist cries out of the depths to the LORD, and Isaiah says God made the depths of the sea a way for the ransomed to pass over.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the depths are where prayer begins, because a man who cannot stand learns to cry out. I hold that God made the depths themselves a road for His ransomed, so the very waters that would drown us become the way home.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: something (authoritatively) said, i.e. an edict
BiblicalUsage: The word names something said with authority, an edict or command, and it appears in the book of Esther for the laws of the king and the words of Mordecai. The king's commandment went out that Vashti should come no more before him, Esther kept the commandment of Mordecai as she had done when she was brought up with him, and the decree of Esther confirmed the matters of Purim and was written in the book.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe an edict shows where true authority lies, because the king's word could banish a queen and Mordecai's word could save a people. I hold that Esther kept Mordecai's commandment because she trusted the man who had raised her, and obedience to godly authority is the mark of wisdom.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: strength, i.e. (plural) resources
BiblicalUsage: The word names strength or resources, and Elihu uses it once, asking Job whether God will esteem his riches, or gold, or all the forces of strength. No amount of wealth or power can buy a man out of the distress God has appointed.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that riches and strength are no ransom before God, and the man who trusts in them will find them empty when he needs them most.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, heed, i.e. purpose; used only adverbially, on account of (as a motive or an aim), teleologically, in order that
BiblicalUsage: The word means on account of, or for the sake of, and it is the hinge on which God's promises turn.
