Abram says it may be well with him for Sarai's sake, God gives His commandments that it may be well with His people, and He honours His father and mother commandment that their days may be long in the land. The word always points to the reason behind the blessing.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this small word carries the heart of the gospel: God blesses for His own name's sake, not because we have earned it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a furrow
BiblicalUsage: The word names a furrow, the trench a plough cuts in the ground, and it appears in war and in suffering alike. Jonathan's first slaughter of the Philistines fell within half an acre of land, as it were a furrow a yoke of oxen might plough, and the psalm says the plowers plowed upon the sufferer's back and made long their furrows.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the furrow is a picture of what suffering does to a man, and God can plough even a wounded back into good ground.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a reply (favorable or contradictory)
BiblicalUsage: The word names an answer, a reply, and Proverbs returns to it again and again. A soft answer turns away wrath, a man has joy by the answer of his mouth, and a word spoken in due season is good. The preparations of the heart are man's, but the answer of the tongue is from the LORD, and when the prophets have no answer from God, the seers are ashamed and cover their lips.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the right answer is a gift from God, not a trick of the tongue, and the soft answer is stronger than the loud one. I hold that silence from God is the most terrible judgment on a prophet, because a man with no answer has nothing left to say.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: something baked, i.e. a batch
BiblicalUsage: The word names something baked, a batch from the oven, and it appears once, in the law of the meat offering: if a man brings an oblation baken in the oven, it shall be unleavened cakes of fine flour mingled with oil.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that God receives the ordinary work of the oven, and unleavened bread offered in obedience is as holy as any sacrifice.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: something opaque
BiblicalUsage: The word names thick darkness, opaqueness, and it appears once, when Joshua reminds Israel how God put darkness between them and the Egyptians and brought the sea upon their pursuers. The darkness that blinded Egypt was the same darkness that sheltered Israel.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that God's darkness is never empty: it hides His people from their enemies and opens the sea before them.
RelatedEvents: The Exodus and the Red Sea
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a crook (in a road)
BiblicalUsage: The word names a crook in a road, and Isaiah uses it once, for God's promise to the blind: He will lead them in paths they have not known, and make crooked things straight. The crooked road is made straight by the hand that leads.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that God does not wait for us to straighten our own road; He takes the blind by the hand and makes the crooked places straight Himself.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a parapet
BiblicalUsage: The word names a parapet, the battlement around a roof, and the law commands it for a new house: when a man builds a new house, he shall make a battlement for his roof, so he does not bring blood upon his house if any man fall from it.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that God's law cares about the roof as much as the altar, because loving your neighbour means keeping him from falling.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a nude place, i.e. (literally) the pudenda, or (figuratively) a vacant space
BiblicalUsage: The word names a bare or open place, and its two uses could hardly be further apart. On the bronze bases of the temple it marks the open space around the carved cherubim and lions, measured out in proportion, while Nahum turns it against Nineveh, saying God will show the nations her nakedness and the kingdoms her shame.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that what is bare before God is either beautiful or shameful, and the difference is whether He has covered it or we have uncovered it ourselves.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to be bitter or (causatively) to embitter, i.e. be painful
BiblicalUsage: The word means to be bitter or painful, and the law uses it for a plague that eats away at cloth or a house, a fretting leprosy that spreads and cannot be cleansed. Ezekiel uses it for the pricking brier and the grieving thorn that shall trouble Israel no more when God restores her.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the fretting plague is a picture of sin: it spreads quietly and eats what it touches, and only the priest's cleansing can name it clean. I hold that God's promise to remove the grieving thorn is the promise of the gospel, that what has eaten at us will not eat at us forever.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: traffic; by implication, mercantile goods
BiblicalUsage: The word names traffic, the merchandise of Tyre's markets, and Ezekiel's lament over the city is full of it. The ancients of Gebal caulked her ships, Javan and Tubal traded the persons of men and vessels of brass in her market, and when her wares went forth out of the seas, she filled many people and enriched the kings of the earth with her riches.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Tyre's merchandise shows how trade can become an idol, because a city that sells everything ends up selling men. I hold that wealth which fills the world and empties the soul is no wealth at all, and God sinks the ships that carry it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: traffic; by implication, mercantile goods
BiblicalUsage: The word names traffic, the merchandise of Tyre's markets, and Ezekiel's lament over the city is full of it. The ancients of Gebal caulked her ships, Javan and Tubal traded the persons of men and vessels of brass in her market, and when her wares went forth out of the seas, she filled many people and enriched the kings of the earth with her riches.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Tyre's merchandise shows how trade can become an idol, because a city that sells everything ends up selling men. I hold that wealth which fills the world and empties the soul is no wealth at all, and God sinks the ships that carry it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an ambuscade
BiblicalUsage: The word names an ambush, men lying in wait to strike, and it appears in the wars of Israel and in the psalm of the wicked. Joshua sent men to lie in ambush between Bethel and Ai, and Jeroboam set an ambush behind Judah so the battle was before and behind them. The psalm says the wicked sits in the lurking places of the villages and murders the innocent in secret.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the ambush is the picture of sin's way of working: it waits in secret and strikes where we are not looking. I hold that God sees the lurking places as clearly as the open field, and no ambush laid against His people escapes His eye.
RelatedEvents: The Defeat at Ai and Achan's Sin
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an open spot
BiblicalUsage: The word names an open place or rank, and it appears once, when Goliath came up out of the ranks of the Philistines and spoke the same defiant words, and David heard them. The champion stood in the open ground between the armies, and the word marks the place where he stood.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the open ground between the armies is where faith is tested, and David stepped into it while an army watched from the hill.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an arrangement, i.e. (figuratively) mental disposition
BiblicalUsage: The word names an arrangement, the disposition of the heart, and it appears once, in the proverb that says the preparations of the heart in man, and the answer of the tongue, is from the LORD. The heart arranges its plans, but God orders the words.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that God is sovereign over the heart's arrangements, and the plans we lay are only as good as the tongue He gives us to speak them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an arrangement; concretely, a pile; specifically a military array
BiblicalUsage: The word names a battle array, the lines of an army drawn up for war, and it is the word of David's fight. The Philistines put themselves in array against Israel and slew four thousand men, Goliath cried to the armies of Israel to choose a man to come down to him, and David came to the trench as the host was going forth to the fight and shouted for the battle.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the battle array is where Israel learned that numbers do not win wars, because the Philistines' array broke before a boy with a sling. I hold that the armies of the living God are not counted by heads but by faith, and one man who trusts the LORD is an army by himself.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Maarath, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Maarath was a city in the hill country of Judah, named in the list of the cities given to the tribe, alongside Beth-anoth and Eltekon. It stands in the record as one of the six cities with their villages in that district.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Maarath matters because God gave His people towns by name, and every city in the inheritance was counted and kept.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: violence
BiblicalUsage: The word names violence, and Isaiah uses it once, for the lopping of the bough: the Lord of hosts shall lop the bough with terror, and the high ones of stature shall be hewn down, and the haughty shall be humbled.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that God's violence against pride is mercy to the lowly, because the high bough must fall before the humble can grow.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a nude place, i.e. a common
BiblicalUsage: The word names an open place, a common or meadow, and it appears once, when the liers in wait of Israel came forth out of their places, even out of the meadows of Gibeah, in the war against Benjamin. The meadow hid the ambush until the moment it sprang.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the meadow of Gibeah warns us how quickly a quiet field can turn into a battlefield, and how one sin can draw a whole tribe into war.
RelatedEvents: The Levite's Concubine and the War against Benjamin
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an arrangement, i.e. (concretely) a pile (of loaves)
BiblicalUsage: The word names the rows of the showbread, the twelve loaves set in two rows of six upon the pure table before the LORD, with pure frankincense upon each row. The Levites set the bread in order every Sabbath, and the priests of Abijah's day said they set the shewbread in order upon the pure table and kept the charge of the LORD their God.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the rows of bread teach us that God provides for His people continually, and the table before Him is never empty. I hold that the bread set in order every Sabbath is a picture of Christ, the Bread of Life, who is always before the Father on our behalf.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: bare
BiblicalUsage: The word means bare or naked, and it appears once, when the men of Judah clothed the captives of Israel who were naked among them, and arrayed them and shod them and gave them to eat and to drink, and carried the feeble upon asses to Jericho. The bare were covered by the hands of their enemies' brothers.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that clothing the naked captive is one of the tenderest acts in Scripture, because mercy clothed those whom war had stripped bare.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Maasai, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Maasai was a priest, the son of Adiel, named in the genealogy of those who dwelt in Jerusalem after the return from exile. His line runs back through Jahzerah and Meshullam to Immer, and his name stands in the record of the priests who served in the restored city.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Maasai's name is kept because God counts His priests, and the men who served in the restored temple were not forgotten.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an action (good or bad); generally, a transaction; abstractly, activity; by implication, a product (specifically, a poem) or (generally) property
BiblicalUsage: The word names a work or deed, what hands make and what men do, and it is one of the Bible's biggest words. God blessed the works of men's hands and warned that their hands would make idols, the heavens declare the glory of God and the firmament shows His handywork, and the Preacher says God has made everything beautiful in its time, though no man can find out the work God makes from beginning to end.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe every work is weighed by the hands that made it, and the works of God are beautiful while the works of men turn to idols. I hold that our work is holy when it is done before God, because He blesses the work of our hands and the heavens themselves declare the work of His.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a tenth; especially a tithe
BiblicalUsage: The word names a tenth, the tithe, and it runs from Abram to Malachi. Abram gave tithes of all to Melchizedek, priest of the most high God, and the law says all the tithe of the land is holy unto the LORD. Israel was to eat the tithe before the LORD in the place He chose, that they might learn to fear Him always, and Malachi says to bring all the tithes into the storehouse, that there may be meat in God's house.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the tithe teaches us that the first tenth belongs to God, and giving it is how we learn to fear Him and trust Him. I hold that God opens the windows of heaven to the cheerful giver, and the tithe is not a tax but a confession that everything we have is His.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Maasejah, the name of sixteen Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Maaseiah is a name worn by many men, and Scripture names them by their work. One was a porter among the brethren of the second degree when the ark was brought to Jerusalem, another was a priest among the sons of Jeshua who had taken foreign wives, and another stood beside Ezra on the pulpit of wood when he read the law to the people.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the many Maaseiahs show that God calls ordinary men to stand beside His word, whether they carry the ark, confess a sin, or hold up the reader.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: oppression
BiblicalUsage: The word names oppression, the gain squeezed out of the weak, and it appears in the portrait of the righteous man and the warning to princes. The man who walks righteously despises the gain of oppressions and shakes his hands from holding bribes, while the prince who lacks understanding is a great oppressor, and the one who hates covetousness shall prolong his days.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that oppression is the sin of power without mercy, and the righteous man is known by the bribes he refuses and the gains he despises.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, to pare off, i.e. lessen; in transitively, to be (or causatively, to make) small or few (or figuratively, ineffective)
BiblicalUsage: The word means to make less, to diminish, and it is the word of God's equal provision in the wilderness. When Israel gathered manna, some gathered more and some less, yet he that gathered much had nothing over and he that gathered little had no lack. The rich were not to give more than half a shekel for the atonement, and the poor were not to give less, and Elisha told the widow to borrow vessels, but not a few.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe less is God's word against our fear of not having enough, because He measures out exactly what each household needs. I hold that the manna teaches contentment: the one who gathered little had no lack, and the one who gathered much had nothing over, so our sufficiency is in God and not in the heap.
RelatedEvents: Manna and Quail in the Wilderness
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a cloak
BiblicalUsage: The word names a cloak or mantle, and it appears once, in Isaiah's oracle against the proud daughters of Zion, among the changeable suits of apparel and the mantles that God will strip away in judgment.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the cloak in Isaiah's list is a warning: the garments we wear to be seen will be taken when God judges pride.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a vestment
BiblicalUsage: The word names a vestment or garment, and Isaiah uses it once, in the promise to those who mourn in Zion: God will give them the garment of praise for the spirit of heaviness, that they might be called trees of righteousness.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the garment of praise is God's own exchange: He takes the heaviness we wear and dresses us in praise instead.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Maats, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Maats was a son of Ram, the firstborn of Jerahmeel, named in the genealogy of Judah. His brothers were Jamin and Eker, and his name stands in the record of the family of Hezron.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Maats is kept in the record because God counts the families of Judah by name, and no branch of the line is forgotten.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an axe
BiblicalUsage: The word names an axe, and it appears where men make idols with their own hands. Isaiah sets it in the smith's hands as he works the iron with tongs and hammers, and Jeremiah says the customs of the people are vain, for one cuts a tree out of the forest, the work of the hands of the workman, with the axe.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the axe is the tool of idolatry's folly: men cut down a tree, shape it with their hands, and then bow to what their own axe made.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: anguish
BiblicalUsage: The word names anguish, and Isaiah uses it once, for those who kindle their own fire and compass themselves about with sparks: walk in the light of your fire, he says, and in the sparks you have kindled, and this shall you have of my hand, that you shall lie down in sorrow.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the anguish Isaiah names is the end of lighting our own fires: the sparks we kindle ourselves leave us lying down in sorrow.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a desire
BiblicalUsage: The word names a desire, and the psalm uses it once, in a prayer that God would not grant it: grant not, O LORD, the desires of the wicked, and further not his wicked device, lest they exalt themselves.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that not every desire should be granted, and the psalm teaches us to pray that the wicked man's plans would fail.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Maai, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Maai was a priest and musician who walked in the procession at the dedication of Jerusalem's wall, with the musical instruments of David the man of God, and Ezra the scribe before them. His name stands among the brethren who sang as the wall was given back to God.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Maai's place in the procession matters, because God is praised by named musicians, and the dedication was sung, not only built.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Maazjah, the name of two Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Maaziah was a priest whose name stands in two records of the restored worship. His course was the four and twentieth in David's order of the priests, and his name appears again among the priests who sealed the covenant in Nehemiah's day.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Maaziah's course is remembered because God orders His worship by name, and the twenty-fourth course was as holy as the first.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an act
BiblicalUsage: The word is the Aramaic word for an act or deed, and it appears once, in Nebuchadnezzar's praise after his humbling: now I praise and extol and honour the King of heaven, all whose works are truth, and His ways judgment, and those that walk in pride He is able to abase.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the proudest king on earth learned what this word means: God's acts are truth, and He abases those who walk in pride.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an act
BiblicalUsage: The word is the Aramaic word for an act or deed, and it appears once, in Nebuchadnezzar's praise after his humbling: now I praise and extol and honour the King of heaven, all whose works are truth, and His ways judgment, and those that walk in pride He is able to abase.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the proudest king on earth learned what this word means: God's acts are truth, and He abases those who walk in pride.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a (weeding) hoe
BiblicalUsage: The word names a weeding hoe, a mattock, and Isaiah uses it once, for the hills that shall be dug with the mattock, where the fear of briers and thorns shall not come, but the land shall be for the sending forth of oxen and the treading of lesser cattle.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the hoe in Isaiah's picture is the sign of a land returned to ordinary work, and God's judgment ends in pasture, not ruin.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: unwilling
BiblicalUsage: The word means to refuse, to be unwilling, and it is the word of Pharaoh's stubbornness. If you refuse to let my people go, God says, I will smite your borders with frogs, and if you refuse and hold them still, the plagues will follow, and if you refuse again, the locusts will come tomorrow. Jeremiah hears the same word when he tells Zedekiah that if he refuses to go forth to the king of Babylon, the city will fall.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe refusal is the sin that hardens with every warning, because each no makes the next one easier. I hold that Pharaoh's refusals built his own ruin, and the same word still stands before every heart that will not let God's people go.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: unwilling
BiblicalUsage: The word means to refuse, to be unwilling, and it is the word of Pharaoh's stubbornness. If you refuse to let my people go, God says, I will smite your borders with frogs, and if you refuse and hold them still, the plagues will follow, and if you refuse again, the locusts will come tomorrow. Jeremiah hears the same word when he tells Zedekiah that if he refuses to go forth to the king of Babylon, the city will fall.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe refusal is the sin that hardens with every warning, because each no makes the next one easier. I hold that Pharaoh's refusals built his own ruin, and the same word still stands before every heart that will not let God's people go.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a track (literally or figuratively); also a rampart (as circular)
BiblicalUsage: The word names a track or path, a rut worn by feet, and Proverbs and Isaiah both weigh it. Wisdom says the path of the just is uprightness, and the LORD weighs the path of the just, while the ways of the wicked are crooked and they are froward in their paths. David came to the trench as the host went forth to the fight, and the psalm says God leads His people in the paths of righteousness for His name's sake.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the track is the picture of a life: every step wears the path deeper, and the only safe ruts are the ones God has weighed. I hold that He does not only point to the right path, He walks it with us, and the paths of righteousness are His own leading.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a utensil
BiblicalUsage: The word is the Aramaic word for a vessel, and it is the word of the temple's stolen gold. Belshazzar commanded the golden and silver vessels his father had taken out of the temple in Jerusalem to be brought, so the king and his princes and wives and concubines might drink from them, and that same night the writing appeared on the wall. Cyrus took the vessels out of the temple of Babylon and delivered them to Sheshbazzar, and Darius decreed they should be restored to the temple at Jerusalem, every one to his place.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the vessels teach us that holy things are not safe in profane hands, and God writes judgment on the wall the night they are misused. I hold that the same vessels came home again, because what men steal from God's house, God restores to His house in His own time.
RelatedEvents: Belshazzar's Handwriting on the Wall; Rebuilding of the Temple
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: thinned (as to the edge), i.e. sharp
BiblicalUsage: The word means thinned to the edge, sharp, and Ezekiel uses it once, for the sword God has set against the gates: it is made bright, it is wrapped up for the slaughter, that hearts may faint and ruins be multiplied.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the sharpened sword is God's warning made bright, and a bright edge means judgment is no longer far off.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: refuse
BiblicalUsage: The word names refuse, the offscouring swept away, and Jeremiah uses it once, in the lament over Jerusalem: God has made us as the offscouring and refuse in the midst of the people. The holy city has become the sweepings of the nations.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the refuse in Lamentations is the lowest place a people can fall, and yet the prophet keeps praying, because even the offscouring is not beyond God's mercy.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a cake of bread; parasite
BiblicalUsage: The word names a cake of bread, and it appears at two tables. The widow of Zarephath tells Elijah she has not a cake, only a handful of meal and a little oil, enough for one last meal for her and her son before they die, and the psalm turns the word against hypocritical mockers at feasts, who gnash upon the sufferer with their teeth.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the widow's cake is the measure of faith: she had almost nothing, and God made it enough, while the mockers at the feast had plenty and used it to bite.
RelatedEvents: Elijah and the Widow of Zarephath
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Maok, a Philistine
BiblicalUsage: Maok, also spelled Maoch, was the father of Achish, king of Gath, and his name stands once, when David passed over with his six hundred men to Achish, the son of Maoch. The Philistine king who sheltered David was the son of a man whose name Scripture keeps.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Maok's single mention matters, because even the father of a Philistine king is named when David's story passes through his house.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Maon, the name of an Israelite and of a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Maon was a town in the hill country of Judah, listed among the cities of the tribe, and the wilderness of Maon was where David hid from Saul. Nabal lived at Maon, a very great man with three thousand sheep, and his shearing feast there brought David and Abigail together. The name also belongs to a man, Maon the son of Shammai, father of Beth-zur.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Maon shows how one name can hold a town, a wilderness and a man, and God met David in all three while he was running for his life.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an abode, of God (the Tabernacle or the Temple), men (their home) or animals (their lair); hence, a retreat (asylum)
BiblicalUsage: The word names a dwelling place, an abode, and it is used for the homes of men, the dens of beasts, and the habitation of God Himself. Moses asks God to look down from His holy habitation, from heaven, and bless His people Israel, and the psalm says the LORD has been our dwelling place in all generations. The psalmist calls God his strong habitation where he may continually resort, and Jeremiah hears the LORD roar from on high and utter His voice from His holy habitation.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a dwelling is more than a house: it is where a person belongs, and God has made Himself our dwelling place. I hold that the one who lives in God is never homeless, because the holy habitation is not a building but the LORD Himself.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: nakedness, i.e. (in plural) the pudenda
BiblicalUsage: The word names nakedness, and Habakkuk uses it once, in a woe against the man who gives his neighbour drink and makes him drunken, so he may look on his nakedness. The drink is given to uncover what should stay covered.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the woe falls on the man who uncovers his neighbour for sport, because shame is not a spectacle, and God sees the hand that pours the drink.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, a luminous body or luminary, i.e. (abstractly) light (as an element); figuratively, brightness, i.e. cheerfulness; specifically, a chandelier
BiblicalUsage: The word names a light, a luminous body, and it is the word of the first day's lights. God said let there be lights in the firmament of heaven to divide the day from the night, and to be for signs and for seasons and for days and years, and He made two great lights, the greater to rule the day and the lesser to rule the night. The same word names the oil for the light of the tabernacle, beaten olive oil to cause the lamp to burn always, and the psalm says God made the light and the sun His own.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the lights of heaven were made to rule and to mark time, and the lamp of the tabernacle was made to burn always, so God's people never sit in the dark. I hold that the God who set the sun in the sky also keeps a lamp burning before Him, and His light does not go out.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a fortified place; figuratively, a defence
BiblicalUsage: The word names a fortress, a stronghold, and it is the refuge of the psalms. David says God is his strength and power and makes his way perfect, and the psalm says the LORD is his light and his salvation, and the strength of his life, of whom shall he be afraid. He asks God to be his strong rock, a house of defence to save him, and Isaiah says the LORD is a strength to the poor and a refuge from the storm.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the fortress is not a place but a Person, because David's strength was God Himself and not the walls around him. I hold that the poor and the needy find their stronghold in the same LORD, and no storm can take the house whose rock is God.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: opaqueness
BiblicalUsage: The word names opaqueness, thick darkness, and Jeremiah uses it once, when God asks His people whether He has been a wilderness to Israel, a land of darkness, that they should say they are lords and will come no more to Him.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the land of darkness is the place God's people imagine when they leave Him, and it is a land He never made for them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: subjectively, control
BiblicalUsage: The word names control, the rule a man has over his own spirit, and Proverbs uses it once, for the man who has none: he that has no rule over his own spirit is like a city broken down and without walls.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that a man without rule over his spirit is a city without walls, and every enemy walks in through the breach.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: objectively, a hindrance
BiblicalUsage: The word names a hindrance, what holds a thing back, and Jonathan uses it once, when he tells his armourbearer there is no restraint to the LORD to save by many or by few. Nothing hinders God from saving, whether the army is great or small.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that no hindrance stands before God, and Jonathan's faith is the proof: the LORD saves by many or by few, and the odds do not bind Him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: darkness
BiblicalUsage: The word names darkness, gloom, and Isaiah uses it once, for the people who look to the earth and see only trouble and darkness, dimness of anguish, and are driven to darkness. The land itself goes dark for those who will not look up.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the darkness Isaiah names is what happens when men look down instead of up, and the earth gives back only what they brought to it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a fountain (also collectively), figuratively, a source (of satisfaction)
BiblicalUsage: The word names a fountain, a spring of water, and it runs from the flood to the gospel. In the days of Noah all the fountains of the great deep were broken up, and after the flood the fountains of the deep were stopped and the rain was restrained. Isaiah says with joy shall you draw water out of the wells of salvation, and Hosea warns that the east wind will dry up Ephraim's spring and his fountain shall be dried up.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the fountain is the Bible's picture of God's supply: He breaks it open in judgment and stops it in mercy, and He opens it again for joy. I hold that the wells of salvation never run dry, because the Fountain is God Himself, and those who draw from Him draw with joy.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: (as indefinitely) that
BiblicalUsage: The word is the Aramaic word for that, and it appears in two royal scenes. A spirit came forth and stood before the LORD in the vision of Ahab's lying prophets, and Darius made a decree for the building of the house of God, that expenses should be given to the elders of the Jews so the work would not be hindered.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that even a small word like that carries weight in a king's decree, because God's house was built on the strength of it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably of Hebrew origin; Maath, an Israelite:--Maath.
BiblicalUsage: Maath stands in the genealogy Luke gives for Jesus, named among the ancestors between Mattathias and the Joseph of that generation, and his name is the only place the word appears in Scripture. The Greek text spells the name with the accent on its first syllable, while Strong's lexicon spells it with the accent on the second.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Maath matters because Luke's genealogy names every link in the chain, and the Saviour's line runs through men the world never heard of.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: something expected, i.e. (abstractly) expectation
BiblicalUsage: The word names expectation, what a man waits for, and the prophets use it for hopes that fail. Isaiah says Ethiopia and Egypt were the expectation of those who fled to them for help, and they shall be afraid and ashamed, and Zechariah says the expectation of Ekron shall be ashamed when the king perishes from Gaza.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe expectation is the test of where our hope lies, because the hopes we set on men and nations will be ashamed. I hold that only the expectation set on God stands, and every other hope ends in fear.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a fountain
BiblicalUsage: The word names a fountain or spring, and it appears at the end of life and in the promise of restoration. The Preacher says the pitcher is broken at the fountain and the wheel broken at the cistern, and Isaiah says the parched ground shall become a pool and the thirsty land springs of water, and the Shepherd shall lead His people by the springs of water.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the fountain is broken at death and opened again in the promise, because God gives water to the thirsty land. I hold that He who leads His people by springs of water will not let them thirst forever.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a deluge
BiblicalUsage: The word names the deluge, the flood of waters, and it is the word of Noah's day. God said He would bring a flood of waters upon the earth to destroy all flesh, and Noah was six hundred years old when the flood of waters was upon the earth. Afterward God made a covenant that the waters should no more become a flood to destroy all flesh, and the psalm says the LORD sits upon the flood, King forever.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the flood shows that God judges the world He made, and yet He sets His bow in the cloud and promises never again. I hold that the LORD sits upon the flood as King, so the waters that drown the wicked are the same waters that carry His people to dry land.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: desistance (or rather desolation)
BiblicalUsage: The word names desistance or desolation, and Jeremiah uses it once, when he would comfort himself against sorrow and his heart is faint within him. The comfort he reaches for will not come, and the word carries the weight of a grief that will not lift.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Jeremiah's faint heart is the honest prayer of a prophet who cannot comfort himself, and God hears it anyway.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an entrance (the place or the act); specifically sunset or the west; also (adverb with preposition) towards
BiblicalUsage: The word names an entrance, the place of going in, and it is used for the going down of the sun, the west. The blessings and curses were set on the far side of Jordan, by the way where the sun goes down, and Joshua's border ran to the great sea toward the going down of the sun. Malachi says God's name shall be great from the rising of the sun even unto the going down of the same, and the psalm says the sun knows his going down.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the going down of the sun marks the edge of the day God made, and His name is great from its rising to its setting. I hold that the sun's faithful going down is a picture of God's own faithfulness, and the whole earth from east to west belongs to Him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: instructing
BiblicalUsage: The word never actually occurs in the Hebrew text: no verse uses it, and no form of it stands anywhere in the Scriptures. Strong's lexicon lists it as a word meaning instructing, but the concordance finds no token for it, so there is no passage to cite.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that honesty matters more than filling a gap: where the text is silent, I say so, and I will not invent a verse for a word the writers never used.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: (plural) the (male) pudenda
BiblicalUsage: The word names the male pudenda, and it appears once, in the law of a fight between men: if a wife draws near to deliver her husband and takes the other man by the secrets, her hand shall be cut off. The law guards the body even in the heat of a quarrel.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the law's severity here shows how seriously God guards the body, and even in a fight there are lines no one may cross.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: fainting, i.e. (figuratively) disconsolate
BiblicalUsage: The word names fainting, being disconsolate, and Job uses it once, for the afflicted man who needs pity from his friend. To him that is afflicted pity should be shown, Job says, even though he has forsaken the fear of the Almighty.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the fainting man deserves pity before he deserves a lecture, and Job's friends failed him the moment they chose argument over compassion.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, a burden (as causing to faint), i.e. a tax in the form of forced lab or
BiblicalUsage: The word names forced labour, a tax paid in work, and it is the word of Solomon's building and Pharaoh's bondage alike. Pharaoh set taskmasters over Israel to afflict them with their burdens, and Solomon raised a levy of forced labour out of all Israel to build the house of the LORD. Joshua put the Canaanites to tribute and made them serve, and the proverb says the hand of the diligent shall bear rule, but the slothful shall be under tribute.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe forced labour is the mark of a kingdom built on backs instead of blessing, whether the king is Pharaoh or Solomon. I hold that God hears the cry of those under tribute, and the diligent hand He blesses is not the hand that drives others, but the hand that works.
RelatedEvents: The Exodus and the Red Sea
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to liquefy; figuratively, to waste (with disease), to faint (with fatigue, fear or grief)
BiblicalUsage: The word means to melt away, to liquefy, and it is used for hearts that fail and for bodies that waste. Moses says the hearts of the people melted when they heard of the giants, and the spies' report made the heart of Israel melt before Jericho. Samson's bonds melted like flax in the fire, and the psalm says the sufferer's heart is like wax, melted in the midst of his bowels.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a melting heart is the honest picture of fear, and God does not despise the heart that melts, because He melts it to remake it. I hold that the same word that melts the fearful also melts the bonds of the strong, and God can dissolve what holds us and what frightens us alike.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to dissolve
BiblicalUsage: The word means to dissolve or melt, and it is used for tears, beauty and snow alike. The psalmist says he waters his couch with tears all the night, and God makes man's beauty consume away like a moth, and the psalm of the thaw says God sends out His word and melts the ice, and the winds blow and the waters flow. Caleb says his brethren made the heart of the people melt, but he wholly followed the LORD.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe melting is what sorrow does to us and what God's word does to the ice, and the difference is who does the melting. I hold that tears dissolve the strong and God's word dissolves the winter, and the heart that melts before Him will not melt before men.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a cover, i.e. veil
BiblicalUsage: The word names a covering, a veil, and it is the word of the tabernacle's doors. God commanded a hanging for the door of the tent, blue and purple and scarlet, and a covering for the gate of the court, and the veil was spread over the ark when the camp moved. The same word covers the well at Bahurim where Jonathan and Ahimaaz hid from Absalom's men.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the veil is the sign of holiness and of hiding both: it covers the holy place from common eyes, and it covered two men from their enemies. I hold that God veils what is holy until He is ready to show it, and the veil He tore at the cross is the veil that kept us out.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to mix, especially wine (with spices)
BiblicalUsage: The word means to mix, especially wine with spices, and it is used for Wisdom's feast and for the drunkard's boast alike. Wisdom has mingled her wine and calls the simple to come and eat of her bread, while Isaiah says the mighty men of Israel are strong to mingle strong drink. The psalmist says he has mingled his drink with weeping, because his tears fall into the cup.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the mingled cup shows what we put into our lives: Wisdom mingles wine for a feast, and the drunkard mingles it for ruin. I hold that the tears mingled with drink are the truest cup of all, because God counts the tears we cannot swallow.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to sunder, i.e. (transitively) set apart, or (reflex.) apostatize
BiblicalUsage: The word means to set apart or sunder, and it appears twice in the war against Midian. Twelve thousand were set apart from the thousands of Israel, a thousand of every tribe, armed for war, and the same chapter says the women of Midian, through the counsel of Balaam, caused Israel to commit trespass against the LORD in the matter of Peor.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that being set apart cuts both ways: Israel was set apart for war, and the women who caused Israel to sin were set apart for judgment.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a missile (spear or arrow); also a quarry (whence stones are, as it were, ejected)
BiblicalUsage: The word names a missile, a spear or arrow, and also a quarry from which stones are cut, and its two uses show both meanings. The temple was built of stone made ready in the quarry before it was brought to the house, so no hammer or axe was heard in it, and Job says of Leviathan that the sword of him that lays at him cannot hold, nor the spear, the dart, nor the habergeon.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the silent temple and the unpierced Leviathan teach the same lesson: God's house is built without the noise of iron, and God's creatures cannot be wounded by man's weapons.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a departure (from striking the tents), i.e. march (not necessarily a single day's travel); by implication, a station (or point of departure)
BiblicalUsage: The word names a journey, a departure, the breaking of camp, and it is the word of Israel's wanderings. Abram went on his journeys from the south to Bethel, where his tent had been at the beginning, and all the congregation journeyed from the wilderness of Sin after their journeys, according to the commandment of the LORD. When the cloud was taken up from over the tabernacle, the children of Israel went onward in all their journeys, and they took their journeys out of the wilderness of Sinai.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe every journey in Scripture is a picture of the Christian life, because we do not settle, we follow the cloud. I hold that the God who ordered every departure also ordered every rest, and the journey ends where He pitches the tent, not where we choose to stop.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a cordon, (adverbially) or (as a) military barrier
BiblicalUsage: The word names a cordon, a military barrier or guard, and it appears once, in the guarding of the young king Joash: a third part of the guard stood at the gate behind the guard, so they would keep the watch of the house and the king would not be broken in upon.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the guard around Joash is the picture of God's own watch over His anointed, and no usurper breaks through it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a foundation
BiblicalUsage: The word names a foundation, and it appears once, in the building of Solomon's house: all the stones were costly stones, hewed and sawed within and without, from the foundation to the coping, and on the outside toward the great court.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that a house is only as true as its foundation, and Solomon's costly stones ran from the foundation to the coping without a break.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Massah, a place in the Desert
BiblicalUsage: Massah was the place in the wilderness where Israel tempted the LORD, asking whether He was among them or not, and Moses called its name Massah, testing, and Meribah, chiding, because of the chiding of the children of Israel. Moses warns the people never to tempt the LORD their God as they tempted Him in Massah, and Levi's blessing remembers that God proved His holy one at Massah.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Massah is the name of every place we demand proof from God instead of trusting Him, and the rock that gave water there still cries against us.
RelatedEvents: Water from the Rock at Meribah
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a testing, of men (judicial) or of God (querulous)
BiblicalUsage: The word names a testing, a trial, and Moses uses it for the wonders God worked to take a nation from the midst of another nation. By temptations, by signs and wonders, by war and a mighty hand, God brought Israel out of Egypt, and the psalm warns us not to harden our hearts as in the provocation, in the day of temptation in the wilderness. Job says if the scourge slays suddenly, God will laugh at the trial of the innocent.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe testing is how God shows a people who He is, because Egypt's plagues were His signs, not accidents. I hold that the same God who tested Israel in the wilderness tests us now, and the hardening of the heart is the one answer He will not accept.
RelatedEvents: The Exodus and the Red Sea
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, a pouring over, i.e. fusion of metal (especially a cast image); by implication, a libation, i.e. league; concretely a coverlet (as if poured out)
BiblicalUsage: The word names a molten image, a god poured in metal, and it is the sin of Israel from Sinai to Samaria. While Moses was on the mountain, the people made a molten calf and said these are your gods, and God told Moses they had quickly turned aside and made a molten image. Jeroboam made two calves and Israel worshipped the host of heaven, and the law curses the man who makes any graven or molten image and puts it in a secret place.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the molten image is the oldest idolatry and the newest, because we still pour our gods out of what we own. I hold that the calf was made while Moses was still on the mountain, and that is how fast a people forgets: the gold in their ears became the god in their hands.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: something expanded, i.e. the warp in a loom (as stretched out to receive the woof)
BiblicalUsage: The word names the web in a loom, the warp stretched out to receive the woof, and it appears once, in the story of Samson and Delilah. Samson told her that if she wove the seven locks of his head with the web, he would be weak, and she fastened it with the pin and cried that the Philistines were upon him.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the web is the picture of Delilah's whole trade: she wove Samson's strength into her loom, and he woke with his hair pinned to the beam.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a fastener, i.e. (of a person) a smith, (of a thing) a prison
BiblicalUsage: The word names a fastener, and it is used for the smith who works metal and for the prison that holds men. Nebuchadnezzar carried away the craftsmen and smiths of Jerusalem, and Jeremiah lists the carpenters and smiths among those who went into exile. Isaiah says God will bring the prisoners out of the prison, and the psalm cries to bring my soul out of prison, that I may praise God's name.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the same word holds the smith and the prisoner, because the hands that forge chains are the hands God looses. I hold that He opens the prison house for those who sit in darkness, and the soul He brings out will praise His name.
RelatedEvents: Fall of Jerusalem and the Exile
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to rub or strike the hands together (in exultation)
BiblicalUsage: The word means to clap the hands together, and it is used for joy and for spite alike. The mountains and hills shall break forth into singing and the trees of the field shall clap their hands when God's people go out with joy, and the floods clap their hands with them. But Ammon clapped his hands and stamped his feet and rejoiced with all his despite against the land of Israel, and God heard that clapping too.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe clapping is the body's praise, and the trees themselves will do it when God's people come home. I hold that the same hands can clap in joy or in spite, and God tells the two apart.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a pan for baking in
BiblicalUsage: The word names a pan for baking, and it is the word of the meat offering and of Ezekiel's sign. The offering baken in a pan was fine flour mingled with oil, and the priest took his portion from it, and Ezekiel took an iron pan and set it for a wall of iron between himself and the city, and laid siege against it as a sign to the house of Israel.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the pan is holy because God said what goes in it is His, and the same pan became a wall of iron when the prophet acted out the siege. I hold that the ordinary tools of the kitchen become holy in God's service, and the sign of judgment is cooked in the same pan as the offering.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a refuge
BiblicalUsage: The word names a refuge, a hiding place, and it appears in Saul's hunt for David and in Isaiah's promise of shelter. Saul asks the Ziphites to find all the lurking places where David hides himself, and Isaiah says a man shall be as a hiding place from the wind and a covert from the tempest, as rivers of water in a dry place.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the hiding place Saul sought to find is the same hiding place Isaiah promises, and the difference is who is looking for it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a shelter (literally or figuratively)
BiblicalUsage: The word names a shelter, a refuge, and it is one of the Bible's great promises. Isaiah says there shall be a tabernacle for a shadow in the daytime from the heat and a place of refuge from storm and rain, and God has been a strength to the poor and a refuge from the storm. Jeremiah calls God his hope in the day of evil, and the proverb says in the fear of the LORD is strong confidence, and His children shall have a place of refuge.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a refuge is not a hiding hole but a strong place, and God is the shadow from the heat and the covert from the storm. I hold that the fear of the LORD is itself the refuge, because the child who fears God need fear nothing else.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a girdle
BiblicalUsage: The word names a girdle, and Isaiah uses it once, in the stripping of the proud daughters of Zion: instead of sweet smell there shall be stink, and instead of a girdle a rent, and instead of well set hair baldness, and instead of a stomacher a girding of sackcloth.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the girdle torn away is the sign of a beauty that was worn for show, and God strips what pride has dressed.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, to stroke or rub; by implication, to erase; also to smooth (as if with oil), i.e. grease or make fat; also to touch, i.e. reach to
BiblicalUsage: The word means to blot out, to erase, and it is used for names, sins and whole nations. God tells Moses to let Him alone that He may blot out the name of the idolaters from under heaven, and Moses begs God to blot him out of His book rather than destroy Israel. The law says to blot out the remembrance of Amalek, and David prays that God would blot out his transgressions according to His tender mercies.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe blotting out is God's terrible mercy: He erases the names of the unrepentant and the sins of the penitent, and the difference is everything. I hold that Moses offering to be blotted out for Israel is the picture of Christ, who was blotted out in our place so our names would stay in the book.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably feminine of a presumed derivative of G3163; a knife, i.e. dirk; figuratively, war, judicial punishment:--sword.
BiblicalUsage: The word names a sword, a knife or dirk, and it is the weapon of the New Testament. Peter drew his sword and cut off the ear of the high priest's servant, and Jesus told him to put up his sword, for all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword. Paul calls the word of God the sword of the Spirit, and Hebrews says it is sharper than any twoedged sword, piercing to the dividing of soul and spirit.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the sword shows us both kinds of warfare: Peter's sword cut a man's ear and was rebuked, while the sword of the Spirit cuts the heart and saves. I hold that the only sword Christians are told to take up is the word of God, and it is sharper than any blade men forge.
RelatedEvents: The Arrest of Jesus in Gethsemane
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a (sacrificial) knife (as gliding through the flesh)
BiblicalUsage: The word names a sacrificial knife, a blade that glides through flesh, and it appears once, in the count of the vessels Cyrus returned to the temple: thirty chargers of gold, a thousand chargers of silver, and nine and twenty knives.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that even the knives were counted when the vessels came home, because God keeps track of the smallest tools of His house.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Machalath, the name of an Ishmaelitess and of an Israelitess
BiblicalUsage: Machalath is a name worn by two women, and Scripture keeps them apart by their fathers. Esau took Mahalath, the daughter of Ishmael, Abraham's son, to be his wife, and Rehoboam took Mahalath, the daughter of Jerimoth the son of David, to wife, with Abihail the daughter of Eliab.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the two Mahalaths remind us that a name is not a person, and God knows each woman by her own father and her own house.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: 'Machalath', probably the title (initial word) of a popular song
BiblicalUsage: The word appears only in the titles of two psalms, Psalms 53 and 88, where it stands as the name of a song or tune, upon Mahalath. No verse of the psalms themselves uses the word, and its meaning lives only in those headings.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that even a word found only in a title is worth naming honestly, because the headings of the psalms are part of Scripture too.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a mantle (as easily drawn off)
BiblicalUsage: The word names a mantle, a garment easily drawn off, and it appears in judgment and in cleansing alike. Isaiah lists it among the fine clothing God will strip from the proud daughters of Zion, and Zechariah sees the filthy garments taken from Joshua the high priest, and he is clothed with a change of raiment.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the mantle is taken from the proud and given to the cleansed, and the same garment means judgment in one place and grace in the other.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: sickness
BiblicalUsage: The word names sickness, and it is used for the diseases of Egypt and the prayers of kings. God promises Israel that if they hearken to His voice He will put none of the diseases of Egypt upon them, for He is the LORD that heals them, and He will take sickness away from their midst. Solomon prays that whatever plague or sickness comes upon the land, God would hear from heaven, and the proverb says the spirit of a man will sustain his infirmity, but a wounded spirit who can bear.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe sickness is in God's hands, because He sends it and He heals it, and the prayer of a king is heard from heaven. I hold that the body can bear much when the spirit is whole, and the wounded spirit is the sickness no physician can reach.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a section (of Levites, people or soldiers)
BiblicalUsage: The word names a division, a section of men ordered for service, and it is the word of David's organisation of the kingdom. The sons of Aaron were divided into courses, the children of Israel were ordered by their courses month by month throughout the year, and the priests and Levites kept their divisions in the house of the LORD in Hezekiah's day.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the divisions show that God's worship is ordered, not random, and every course has its month and its men. I hold that the God who numbers the courses also numbers His people, and no one serves in His house by accident.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: something buttery (i.e. unctuous and pleasant), as (figuratively) flattery
BiblicalUsage: The word names something buttery, smooth and unctuous, and the psalm uses it once, for flattery: the words of his mouth were smoother than butter, but war was in his heart, and his words were softer than oil, yet they were drawn swords.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that smooth words with war in the heart are the most dangerous weapon, because butter hides the blade until it is drawn.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: choking
BiblicalUsage: The word names choking, strangling, and Job uses it once, when his soul chooses strangling and death rather than his life. The suffering has pressed him until breath itself feels like the enemy.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Job's terrible choice shows how far suffering can press a man, and God still heard the man who said it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Machanajim, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Mahanaim was the place where Jacob saw the angels of God and said this is God's host, and he called the name of that place Mahanaim, two hosts. The name stayed on the map: Abner brought Ish-bosheth there and made him king over Israel, David fled there when Absalom rebelled, and the men of Mahanaim brought him bread and beds and basins in his need.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Mahanaim is the place where two hosts meet, the angels of God and the armies of men, and God camps with His people in their worst hour.
RelatedEvents: Jacob Wrestles with God; Absalom's Rebellion
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Machaneh-Dan, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Mahaneh-dan, the camp of Dan, was the place where the Danites pitched on their way north to Laish, at Kirjath-jearim in Judah, and the name stayed on that ground. It marks the camp where a tribe stopped on its journey to a new home.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the camp of Dan is a warning in a name, because a tribe on the move stopped to take what was not theirs, and the camp is remembered for it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an encampment (of travellers or troops); hence, an army, whether literal (of soldiers) or figurative (of dancers, angels, cattle, locusts, stars; or even the sacred courts)
BiblicalUsage: The word names a camp, an encampment of travellers or troops, and it is one of the Bible's great words. Jacob saw the host of God and called the place Mahanaim, the angel of God went before the camp of Israel at the Red Sea, and the tribes pitched their camps around the tabernacle in order. Gideon crept down to the camp of Midian by night, and the camp of the Syrians was struck by the angel of the LORD.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the camp is the picture of God's people on the move, because Israel never built a city in the wilderness, only a camp. I hold that the God who camps with His people in the desert is the same God who pitches His tent among us now, and the camp is holy because He is in it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to crush
BiblicalUsage: The word means to crush, and it appears once, in the song of Deborah: Jael put her hand to the nail and her right hand to the workman's hammer, and with the hammer she smote Sisera, she smote off his head, when she had pierced and stricken through his temples.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Jael's hammer is the hardest verse in the song, and God used a woman's hand to crush the captain who had oppressed Israel for twenty years.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, deferred, i.e. the morrow; usually (adverbially) tomorrow; indefinitely, hereafter
BiblicalUsage: The word means tomorrow, the morrow, and it is the word of God's appointments. Pharaoh said tomorrow for the frogs to be removed, and Moses said tomorrow the LORD would bring the locusts, and the manna was kept until the morning. Saul was told that tomorrow about this time God would send the man to be captain over Israel, and Joshua told the people to sanctify themselves, for tomorrow the LORD would do wonders among them.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe tomorrow is God's word, not ours, because every tomorrow in Scripture arrives on His appointment and not a moment sooner. I hold that the manna teaches us to wait for tomorrow's bread, and the wonders God promises for tomorrow are worth sanctifying ourselves for today.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a sink
BiblicalUsage: The word names a sink, a draught house, and it appears once, when Jehu broke down the house of Baal and made it a draught house unto this day. The temple of the idol became a latrine, and the place of false worship was turned to shame.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the draught house is God's final word on Baal: the idol's temple ends as a sewer, and no one worships there again.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably a pick-axe
BiblicalUsage: Machareshah is the mattock, the farmer's pick-axe, and it shows up in the days when Israel had no smith of their own and had to go down to the Philistines to sharpen every tool. The list in 1 Samuel 13:20 names the share, the coulter, the axe, and the mattock, and 1 Samuel 13:21 adds the file they used to keep those edges keen.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe even a sharpening file in this story preaches: when God's people lose the means to work and to fight, they end up dependent on their enemies.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably a hoe
BiblicalUsage: Macharesheth is the hoe, named once, in the same list of farm tools the Israelites carried down to the Philistines for sharpening in 1 Samuel 13:20.
TheologicalSignificance: I take it as a small, honest detail: the Bible names ordinary tools, because ordinary work mattered to the people God was shaping.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a contrivance, i.e. (concretely) a texture, machine, or (abstractly) intention, plan (whether bad, a plot; or good, advice)
BiblicalUsage: Machashabah is the thought, the plan, the device of the heart, and it runs both ways in Scripture. Genesis 6:5 says every imagination of the thoughts of man's heart was only evil continually, while Jeremiah 29:11 says God's thoughts toward His people are thoughts of peace and not of evil. Isaiah 55:8 draws the line between the two: God's thoughts are not our thoughts, and Proverbs 16:3 tells us to commit our works to the LORD so that our thoughts shall be established.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this word is a mirror: it shows me that thoughts are never neutral, they are either devices I hatch against God or plans He plants in me. My position is that the only safe thoughts are the ones handed over to Him first, because Jeremiah 29:11 promises His thoughts toward us are peace, and Proverbs 16:3 shows the way to share in them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Machath, the name of two Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Machath is the name of two Levites, and the verses keep them distinct. 1 Chronicles 6:35 names a Mahath son of Amasai in the line of the singers, and 2 Chronicles 29:12 names Mahath the son of Amasai among the Levites who rose to cleanse the house of the LORD under Hezekiah, while 2 Chronicles 31:13 names a Mahath among the overseers of the offerings.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that names like this one matter because God keeps the record of servants nobody else would remember.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a contusion
BiblicalUsage: Machats is a bruise, a contusion, and it appears once, in Isaiah 30:26, in the day the LORD binds up the breach of His people and heals the stroke of their wound.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the wound and the healing belong together in this verse: the same God who struck is the God who binds up.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to dash asunder; by implication, to crush, smash or violently plunge; figuratively, to subdue or destroy
BiblicalUsage: Machats means to crush, to smash, to wound with a shattering blow. Deuteronomy 32:39 puts it in God's own mouth: I wound, and I heal, and no one delivers out of His hand. Job 5:18 says the same thing from the sufferer's side: He maketh sore, and bindeth up. Judges 5:26 shows the human side, Jael smiting Sisera through the temples, and Psalms 110:5 looks to the end, when the Lord at God's right hand shall strike through kings in the day of His wrath.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this word holds judgment and mercy in one hand: the God who wounds is the God who heals, and no wound He gives is ever without a purpose. My position is that I would rather be wounded by Him than struck by anyone else, because His wounds are the ones that make whole.
RelatedTopics: Judgment; Healing; God's wrath and refuge
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a halving or the middle
BiblicalUsage: Machatsith is the half, and it does steady work all through the law: the half shekel every numbered man gave in Exodus 30:13, rich and poor alike in Exodus 30:15, and the half of the spoil set apart for the priest in Numbers 31:29.
TheologicalSignificance: I take it that God counts halves as carefully as wholes: nobody's share is too small to matter to Him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a Machavite or inhabitant of some place named Machaveh
BiblicalUsage: Eliel the Mahavite is named once, in 1 Chronicles 11:46, in the roll of David's mighty men.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that a single-line name in David's army still counts: loyalty that shows up gets written down.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a vision
BiblicalUsage: Machazeh is a vision, a seeing, and it belongs to the prophets and to Abram. Genesis 15:1 says the word of the LORD came to Abram in a vision, and Numbers 24:4 and Numbers 24:16 both say Balaam saw the vision of the Almighty with his eyes open. Ezekiel 13:7 turns the word against the false prophets who claim a vain vision the LORD never gave.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a true vision is never a man's own idea dressed up in God's name: it comes from the LORD, and it is tested by whether He actually spoke. My position is that Ezekiel 13:7 is the warning label on every claim to have seen something from God.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Machazioth, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Machazioth was a son of Heman, one of the singers set apart for the service of song in 1 Chronicles 25:4, and 1 Chronicles 25:30 says the three and twentieth course fell to Mahazioth, he, his sons, and his brethren, twelve in all. His course was the three and twentieth, and he served with his sons and his brethren, twelve in all.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God orders worship down to the rota: every singer had his course, and none of them was left out of the count.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a junction, i.e. seam or sewed piece
BiblicalUsage: Machbereth is the coupling, the seam where the curtains of the tabernacle joined. Exodus 26:4 commands the loops of blue on the edge of the curtain in the coupling, and Exodus 36:12 says the loops held one curtain to another when it was made.
TheologicalSignificance: I take it that God cares about the joins: the holy place held together because every loop caught its fellow.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Machsejah, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Machsejah, also spelled Maaseiah, is named as a father rather than for himself. Jeremiah 32:12 calls Baruch the son of Neriah, the son of Maaseiah, the man who received the evidence of the purchase, and Jeremiah 51:59 names Seraiah the son of Neriah, the son of Maaseiah, who carried Jeremiah's word to Babylon.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that a father's name in these verses is a thread: it ties Baruch and Seraiah to one family that kept showing up where God's word was being carried.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a muzzle
BiblicalUsage: Machsom is a muzzle, a bridle for the mouth, and it appears once, in Psalms 39:1, where the psalmist says he will keep his mouth with a bridle while the wicked is before him.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the bridle is the right picture for my tongue: some words are better kept behind it than let loose.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: deficiency; hence, impoverishment
BiblicalUsage: Machsor is want, lack, the empty place where something is missing. Deuteronomy 15:8 commands an open hand to lend a brother sufficient for his need, and Psalms 34:9 promises there is no want to them that fear the LORD.
