Proverbs 6:11 warns the sluggard that poverty comes as one that travelleth and want as an armed man, while Proverbs 28:27 says he that giveth unto the poor shall not lack.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe want is both a warning and a promise in this word: laziness and a shut hand bring it on, and generosity and the fear of the LORD keep it away. My position is that the open hand in Deuteronomy 15:8 is the cure Proverbs keeps pointing to.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3164; a battle, i.e. (figuratively) controversy:--fighting, strive, striving.
BiblicalUsage: Mache is fighting, contention, strife, and the New Testament treats it as something to flee rather than to win. 2 Corinthians 7:5 says Paul had fightings without and fears within, and James 4:1 asks where wars and fightings come from and answers: from lusts that war in our members. 2 Timothy 2:23 and Titus 3:9 both say to avoid the foolish questions that gender strifes.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe James 4:1 names the root of every quarrel I have ever been in: the fight outside starts as a war inside. My position is that the apostles are right to tell me to avoid the argument rather than win it, because a strife I refuse to enter cannot master me.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Machlah, the name apparently of two Israelitesses
BiblicalUsage: Mahlah was one of the five daughters of Zelophehad, named in Numbers 27:1 when the sisters came to ask for their father's inheritance, and again in Joshua 17:3 when the land was divided. Numbers 36:11 says Mahlah and her sisters married their father's brothers' sons, keeping the inheritance inside the tribe.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Mahlah's story shows that God hears a plain request for what is fair, and that He answers it without taking anything from anyone else.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a ringlet of hair (as gliding over each other)
BiblicalUsage: Machlaphah is a lock of hair, and both of its appearances belong to Samson. Judges 16:13 has him telling Delilah to weave the seven locks of his head with the web, and Judges 16:19 has her shaving off the seven locks of his head while he slept, and his strength went from him.
TheologicalSignificance: I take it that the locks were never the strength itself, but the sign of the vow Samson had already been breaking piece by piece.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a section (of the Levites)
BiblicalUsage: Machleqah is the Aramaic word for a division or course, and it appears once, in Ezra 6:18, where the priests were set in their divisions and the Levites in their courses for the service of God at Jerusalem.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that ordered service is still service: God set the courses so that worship would go on without confusion.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a Machlite or (collectively) descendants of Machli
BiblicalUsage: Machli is the name behind the Mahlites, the family of Merari named in Numbers 3:33, and the family is listed again among the Levites in Numbers 26:58.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a family name in a census list still says something: the Mahlites had their place, and God kept count of them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a Machlite or (collectively) descendants of Machli
BiblicalUsage: Machli is the name behind the Mahlites, the family of Merari named in Numbers 3:33, and the family is listed again among the Levites in Numbers 26:58.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a family name in a census list still says something: the Mahlites had their place, and God kept count of them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Machlon, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Mahlon was the son of Elimelech and Naomi, named in Ruth 1:2 when the family came into the country of Moab, and Ruth 1:5 says Mahlon and Chilion died there, leaving Naomi a widow. Ruth 4:10 names him again when Boaz buys all that was Mahlon's and takes Ruth, the wife of Mahlon, to raise up the name of the dead upon his inheritance.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Mahlon's short life is the hinge of the whole book: his death empties Naomi's house, and his name is the one Boaz raises back up.
RelatedPeople: Mahlon, Son of Elimelech; Ruth; Naomi
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a disease
BiblicalUsage: Machluy is a disease, and it appears once, in 2 Chronicles 24:25, where Joash's servants left him in great diseases and then conspired against him and slew him on his bed.
TheologicalSignificance: I take it as a grim end to a king who turned away: sickness left him helpless, and the men around him finished what the disease began.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: delightful; hence, a delight, i.e. object of affection or desire
KeyPassages: Ezekiel 24:16; Ezekiel 24:21; Song of Solomon 5:16; Lamentations 1:10
BiblicalUsage: Machmad is the delight, the thing the eyes desire, and it is always the thing that can be taken away. Ezekiel 24:16 has God telling the prophet He will take away the desire of his eyes with a stroke, and Ezekiel 24:21 says He will profane the sanctuary, the desire of their eyes. Lamentations 1:10 says the adversary spread out his hand upon all her pleasant things, while Song of Solomon 5:16 turns the word toward the beloved, who is altogether lovely.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this word warns me about what I call my delight: if it is a place or a person I hold tighter than God, it can be taken, and I will feel the loss. My position is that the only delight that cannot be taken is the one Song of Solomon 5:16 names, a beloved who is altogether lovely.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, sympathy;
BiblicalUsage: Machmal is pity, sympathy, the thing the soul feels for what it loves, and its one appearance is in Ezekiel 24:21, inside the phrase that which your soul pitieth, spoken of the sanctuary God is about to profane.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the pity here is the point: God's people loved the temple with their souls, and that love is exactly what the judgment strikes.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: desired; hence, a valuable
BiblicalUsage: Machmud is the desired thing, the valuable, and both of its appearances are in Lamentations 1, where Jerusalem remembers all her pleasant things in Lamentations 1:7 and then gives her pleasant things for meat to relieve the soul in Lamentations 1:11.
TheologicalSignificance: I take it that Lamentations 1:11 is the lowest point of this word: the city's treasures end up traded for bread.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: middle voice of an apparently primary verb; to war, i.e. (figuratively) to quarrel, dispute:--fight, strive.
BiblicalUsage: Machomai means to fight, to quarrel, to strive, and it covers both fists and words. Acts 7:26 shows Moses stepping between two Hebrews as they strove, and John 6:52 has the Jews striving among themselves over Christ's words. James 4:2 says men fight and war because they lust and have not, and 2 Timothy 2:24 commands the servant of the Lord not to strive but to be gentle unto all men.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the command in 2 Timothy 2:24 is the harder half of this word: not fighting back is itself a kind of fighting, against my own temper. My position is that Moses in Acts 7:26 shows the better use of the word, stepping between fighters instead of joining them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Machol, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Machol was the father of Ethan, Heman, Chalcol, and Darda, the wise men Solomon is measured against in 1 Kings 4:31, where Solomon was wiser than all men, than Ethan the Ezrahite, and Heman, and Chalcol, and Darda, the sons of Mahol. His sons were the wise men of their day, and Solomon was counted wiser than all of them.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Machol is remembered only as a father, and that is enough: his sons' wisdom is the record of his house.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a (round) dance
BiblicalUsage: Machol is the dance, the round dance of rejoicing, and it turns up where mourning turns to joy. Psalms 30:11 says God turned mourning into dancing, and Jeremiah 31:13 says the virgin shall rejoice in the dance, young men and old together, because God will turn their mourning into joy. Psalms 149:3 puts the dance in worship itself: let them praise His name in the dance, with timbrel and harp.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the dance in these verses is not entertainment but testimony: a body that was bowed in grief standing up to praise. My position is that Psalms 30:11 is the pattern of the Christian life, mourning turned into dancing by the God who does the turning.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a harbor (as shut in by the shore)
BiblicalUsage: Machoz is the haven, the harbour, and it appears once, in Psalms 107:30, where the sailors are glad because the sea is quiet, and God brings them unto their desired haven.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the haven here is the whole point of the psalm: God does not only calm the storm, He brings His people safely in.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: darkness; concretely, a dark place
BiblicalUsage: Machshak is darkness, the dark place, and it is where people hide and where God finds them. Isaiah 42:16 promises God will make darkness light before the blind, and Lamentations 3:6 has the sufferer set in dark places, as they that be dead of old. Psalms 74:20 says the dark places of the earth are full of the habitations of cruelty.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this word is honest about darkness: it is real, it is where cruelty lives, and it is not beyond God's reach. My position is that Isaiah 42:16 is the promise that holds the other two verses together, because the God who leads the blind out of darkness does not leave His people in it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a peeling
BiblicalUsage: Machsoph is the peeling, the stripping back, and it appears once, in Genesis 30:37, where Jacob pilled white strakes in the rods and made the white appear which was in them.
TheologicalSignificance: I take it as one of Jacob's shrewdest moments: he peeled the rods to make the white show, and the white was there all along.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a pan for live coals
BiblicalUsage: Machtah is the censer, the pan for live coals, and it stands at the centre of both true worship and rebellion. Leviticus 10:1 has Nadab and Abihu taking their censers and offering strange fire, and Numbers 16:38 has the censers of the rebels beaten into broad plates for the altar, while Numbers 16:46 has Aaron taking a censer to make atonement when the plague had begun.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the same pan tells both stories: fire offered wrongly kills, and fire carried rightly makes atonement.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a burglary; figuratively, unexpected examination
BiblicalUsage: Machtereth is a breaking in, a burglary, and it appears twice: in Exodus 22:2, where a thief found breaking up by night may be struck down without bloodguilt, and in Jeremiah 2:34, where the blood of the poor innocents is found in Judah's skirts, not by secret search but in the open.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the law in Exodus 22:2 and the charge in Jeremiah 2:34 belong together: God protects the householder and exposes the violent.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, a hewing; concretely, a quarry
BiblicalUsage: Machtseb is the quarry, the hewing, and both of its appearances are about buying hewn stone to repair the house of the LORD, in 2 Kings 12:12 and again in 2 Kings 22:6.
TheologicalSignificance: I take it that God counts the quarry work as holy work: the stone had to be hewn before the temple could stand.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a thoroughfare (as turnpiked)
BiblicalUsage: Maslul is the raised highway, the thoroughfare, and it appears once, in Isaiah 35:8, where a highway shall be there, called The way of holiness, and the unclean shall not pass over it.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the highway here is grace made passable: even wayfaring men, though fools, shall not err therein.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a peg (as bristling from the surface)
BiblicalUsage: Masmer is the nail, the peg, and it fastens things that should not move. 1 Chronicles 22:3 has David preparing iron in abundance for the nails for the doors of the gates, while Jeremiah 10:4 turns the word against idols, decked with silver and gold and fastened with nails and hammers, that they move not.
TheologicalSignificance: I take it that the nail in Jeremiah 10:4 is the giveaway: a god that has to be nailed down is no god at all.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a band
BiblicalUsage: Masoreth is the bond, the band that binds, and it appears once, in Ezekiel 20:37, where God says He will bring His people into the bond of the covenant.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the bond here is not a chain but a covenant: God binds His people to Himself so they will not wander off.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, a hider, i.e. (abstractly) a hiding, i.e. aversion
BiblicalUsage: Master is the hiding, the turning away of the face, and it appears once, in Isaiah 53:3, where the suffering servant was despised and we hid as it were our faces from him.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this one verse convicts me: I hid my face from Him, and He still bore my griefs.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a veil
BiblicalUsage: Masveh is the veil Moses put on his face, and all three of its appearances are in Exodus 34. Exodus 34:33 says Moses put a veil on his face when he had done speaking, Exodus 34:34 says he took the veil off when he went in before the LORD, and Exodus 34:35 says the children of Israel saw his face shine and he put the veil upon his face again.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the veil on Moses' face marked a glory too bright for the people to bear: Moses hid it so they could look at him at all. My position is that the veil also points forward, because the glory on Moses' face was fading, while the glory we see in Christ does not fade.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, extent, i.e. height; also a measure; by implication, a vesture (as measured); also a carpet
BiblicalUsage: Mad is a measure, and by extension the garment measured out, and it wears both senses in Scripture. 1 Samuel 17:38 has Saul arming David with his armour, a coat of mail, and Leviticus 6:10 has the priest putting on his linen garment, while Psalms 109:18 turns the word dark: the wicked clothed himself with cursing like as with his garment.
TheologicalSignificance: I take it that a garment in these verses is always a covering that tells the truth about the wearer, whether armour, linen, or cursing.
RelatedTopics: Priesthood; Judgment; God's wrath and refuge
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, to stretch; by implication, to measure (as if by stretching a line); figuratively, to be extended
BiblicalUsage: Madad means to measure, to stretch the line, and it belongs to God before it belongs to men. Isaiah 40:12 asks who hath measured the waters in the hollow of His hand, and Jeremiah 31:37 says if heaven above can be measured, then God will cast off Israel, which is to say He never will. Exodus 16:18 has the manna meted with an omer so that none had too much or too little, and Ezekiel 47:3 has the man measuring a thousand cubits and bringing the prophet through waters that rise to the ankles.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this word puts me in my place: God measures the seas in His hand, and I measure out my little lines and call them great. My position is that the manna in Exodus 16:18 is the comfort of it, because the God who measures all things measures out exactly enough for me.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a Madian or native of Madai
BiblicalUsage: Maday is a Mede, a native of Madai, and it appears once, in Daniel 11:1, where the speaker stood to confirm and strengthen Darius the Mede in his first year.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that even a one-word demonym like this one anchors Daniel's visions in real kings and real years.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a sacrificial altar
BiblicalUsage: Madbach is the Aramaic word for the altar, and it appears once, in Ezra 7:17, where the king's money buys bullocks, rams, and lambs to offer upon the altar of the house of God in Jerusalem.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the altar here is the point of the whole letter: the king's silver ends up as sacrifice, not as treasure.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: intelligence or consciousness
BiblicalUsage: Madda is knowledge, intelligence, the knowing that comes from God and is meant to be used. 2 Chronicles 1:10 has Solomon asking for wisdom and knowledge to judge God's people, and Daniel 1:17 says God gave the four children knowledge and skill in all learning and wisdom. Ecclesiastes 10:20 warns the other side of the gift: do not curse the king even in thy thought, for a bird of the air shall carry the voice.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe knowledge in these verses is never just information: it is a gift to be asked for, as Solomon did, and a trust to be guarded, as Ecclesiastes 10:20 warns. My position is that Daniel 1:17 shows where real knowledge comes from, because God gave it, and the giving is the point.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: what (is) enough, i.e. sufficiently
BiblicalUsage: Madday means sufficiently, what is enough, and its one appearance is in 2 Chronicles 30:3, where the priests had not sanctified themselves sufficiently, so the passover could not be kept at that time. In the Hebrew text the word stands as two pieces, the question-word for what joined to the word for enough, which is why the indexes list it under its parts.
TheologicalSignificance: I take it as a sober warning: a passover delayed because the priests were not ready is a picture of worship put off for want of preparation.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: what (is) known?; i.e. (by implication) (adverbially) why?
BiblicalUsage: Maddua is the question why, wherefore, and it is the most honest word in the Bible, asked seventy-one times. Exodus 3:3 has Moses turning aside to see why the bush is not burnt, and Job 21:7 asks wherefore do the wicked live and become old, while Jeremiah 12:1 puts the same question to God Himself: wherefore doth the way of the wicked prosper?
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God leaves the why in His book on purpose, because a faith that cannot ask it is not faith at all.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: seduction
BiblicalUsage: Madduach is seduction, the false burden, and it appears once, in Lamentations 2:14, where the prophets saw vain and foolish things and false burdens and causes of banishment, and never showed the people their iniquity.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that a prophet who will not name sin is worse than silent: his soft words are the seduction itself.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: goldmaking, i.e. exactness
BiblicalUsage: Madhebah is the golden city, the exacting oppressor, and it appears once, in Isaiah 14:4, in the proverb against the king of Babylon: how hath the oppressor ceased, the golden city ceased!
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the taunt song here is God's answer to every golden city: they cease, and the people they crushed get to sing about it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H4080); Madian (i.e. Midian), a region of Arabia:--Madian.
BiblicalUsage: Madian is Midian, the land where Moses fled, and its one New Testament appearance is in Acts 7:29, where Moses fled at this saying and was a stranger in the land of Madian, where he fathered two sons. The Greek text spells the name with a different ending from the form Strong's lists, which is why the indexes carry it under that spelling.
TheologicalSignificance: I take it that Madian is where a prince became a stranger, and where God began the forty years that made him a deliverer.
RelatedEvents: Moses' Birth and Flight to Midian
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Madmannah, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Madmannah was a place in Judah, named twice. 1 Chronicles 2:49 says Shaaph was the father of Madmannah, and Joshua 15:31 lists Madmannah among the cities of Judah, between Ziklag and Sansannah.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that a town in a boundary list still matters: it was somebody's home, inside the inheritance God gave Judah.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Madmen, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Madmen was a place in Moab, named once, in Jeremiah 48:2, where the prophet says there shall be no more praise of Moab, and thou shalt be cut down, O Madmen, and the sword shall pursue thee. The sword pursuing Madmen is the judgment Jeremiah pronounces on the whole of Moab.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Madmen's single verse is a whole sermon on Moab: a city named for its dunghill ends cut down by the sword.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Madmenah, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Madmenah was a place in Benjamin, named once, in Isaiah 10:31, where Madmenah is removed and the inhabitants of Gebim gather themselves to flee before the Assyrian advance. Gebim gathers itself to flee in the same verse, and Madmenah is one of the towns emptied by the advance.
TheologicalSignificance: I take it that Isaiah 10:31 is a snapshot of panic: one town after another empties as the enemy comes down the road.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a dunghill
BiblicalUsage: Madmenah is the dunghill, the heap where straw is trodden down, and it appears once, in Isaiah 25:10, where Moab shall be trodden down under the LORD's hand, even as straw is trodden down for the dunghill.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the picture is deliberate: proud Moab ends up underfoot, like straw on a dungheap.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: extensiveness, i.e. height
BiblicalUsage: Madon is great stature, height, and it appears once, in 2 Samuel 21:20, describing the man of great stature in the battle at Gath, six fingers on every hand and six toes on every foot, born to the giant.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the six fingers are the point of the verse: this was no ordinary fighter, and he still fell.
RelatedEvents: David's Mighty Men and the Philistine Giants
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Madon, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Madon was a Canaanite city with its own king, named twice. Joshua 11:1 has Jabin king of Hazor sending to Jobab king of Madon, and Joshua 12:19 lists the king of Madon among the kings Joshua struck down.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Madon's two verses tell the whole conquest in miniature: a king who joined the alliance, and a king who fell.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: extensiveness, i.e. height

Definition: a wound
BiblicalUsage: Madqarah is a piercing wound, and it appears once, in Proverbs 12:18, where there is one that speaketh like the piercings of a sword, but the tongue of the wise is health.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this proverb is the reason to weigh my words before I speak them: a careless sentence can cut like a sword.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, a step; by implication, a steep or inaccessible place
BiblicalUsage: Madregah is a step, a steep place, a stair, and it appears twice. Ezekiel 38:20 has the steep places falling when the mountains are thrown down, and Song of Solomon 2:14 calls the beloved to come out of the clefts of the rock, in the secret places of the stairs.
TheologicalSignificance: I take it that the same word holds both judgments: steep places fall, and a hidden love is called out of them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: sickness
BiblicalUsage: Madveh is sickness, disease, and both of its appearances are about the diseases of Egypt. Deuteronomy 7:15 promises the LORD will take away all sickness and put none of the evil diseases of Egypt upon His people, while Deuteronomy 28:60 warns He will bring upon them all the diseases of Egypt if they turn away.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the two verses are one promise with two edges: obedience keeps the diseases off, and disobedience brings them back.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, to shield; encompass with; figuratively, to rescue, to hand safely over (i.e. surrender)
BiblicalUsage: Magen means to hand over, to deliver up, and it carries both rescue and surrender in the same breath. Genesis 14:20 blesses the most high God, which hath delivered thine enemies into thy hand, and Proverbs 4:9 says wisdom shall deliver to thine head a crown of glory. Hosea 11:8 turns the word toward God's own heart: how shall I give thee up, Ephraim, how shall I deliver thee, Israel?
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Hosea 11:8 is the tenderest use of this word: the God who delivers enemies into our hands cannot bear to deliver us into theirs. My position is that the handing over in Genesis 14:20 and the refusal to hand over in Hosea 11:8 are the same love, working both ways.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to yield up; intensively, to precipitate
BiblicalUsage: Magar means to cast down, to throw to the ground, and it appears twice. Ezekiel 21:12 has terrors by reason of the sword falling on the princes of Israel, and Psalms 89:44 says God made the king's glory to cease and cast his throne down to the ground.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Psalms 89:44 is the harder half: when God casts a throne down, even the anointed king feels the fall.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Magbish, an Israelite, or a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Magbish is named once, in Ezra 2:30, where the children of Magbish, an hundred fifty and six, are counted among those who came back from the exile. Their hundred and fifty-six came home with the rest of the exiles, and their name is on the list.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a one-line headcount like this one still says the return was real: a hundred and fifty-six people came home.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Chaldee origin (compare H4026); the tower; Magdala (i.e. Migdala), a place in Palestine:--Magdala.
BiblicalUsage: Magdala was a place on the shore of Galilee, and it appears once, in Matthew 15:39, where Jesus sent the multitudes away and came into the coasts of Magdala after feeding the four thousand. The Greek text spells the place with a different ending from the form Strong's lists, which is why the indexes carry it under that spelling.
TheologicalSignificance: I take it that Magdala matters because of who came from there: the town gave its name to Mary Magdalene.
RelatedEvents: The Feeding of the Four Thousand
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: feminine of a derivative of G3093; a female Magdalene, i.e. inhabitant of Magdala:--Magdalene.
BiblicalUsage: Mary Magdalene is the woman from Magdala out of whom Jesus cast seven devils, and she stayed when others left. John 20:1 has her coming early to the sepulchre while it was yet dark, and John 20:18 has her telling the disciples she had seen the Lord, while Mark 16:9 says the risen Jesus appeared first to Mary Magdalene.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Mary Magdalene is the first witness because she was the last one at the cross and the first one at the tomb: love that stays gets to see the risen Lord first.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Magdiel, an Idumaean
BiblicalUsage: Magdiel was a duke of Edom, named twice in the same list: Genesis 36:43 names Duke Magdiel, duke Iram, among the dukes of Edom, and 1 Chronicles 1:54 repeats the list. The same roll is repeated in 1 Chronicles 1:54, and the dukes are named there in the same order.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the dukes of Edom are in the book because Esau's line mattered to God too, even outside the promise.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3096; "magic":--sorcery.
BiblicalUsage: Mageia is sorcery, magic, and it appears once, in Acts 8:11, where the Samaritans had regard to Simon because of long time he had bewitched them with sorceries.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word is a warning about wonder without truth: Simon's sorceries held a whole city until the gospel came.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a shield (i.e. the small one or buckler); figuratively, a protector; also the scaly hide of the crocodile
BiblicalUsage: Magen is the shield, the buckler, and it is one of the Bible's pictures of God Himself. Genesis 15:1 has God telling Abram, I am thy shield, and thy exceeding great reward, and Psalms 3:3 says thou, O LORD, art a shield for me, my glory, and the lifter up of mine head. Proverbs 30:5 says God is a shield unto them that put their trust in Him, and Psalms 84:11 says the LORD God is a sun and shield who will withhold no good thing from them that walk uprightly.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the shield in these verses is not a thing but a Person: God does not only give protection, He is the protection. My position is that Psalms 84:11 says it best, because a sun and a shield together mean light to walk by and cover to hide under, and both come from the same LORD.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3097; to practice magic:--use sorcery.
BiblicalUsage: Mageuo means to use sorcery, to practise magic, and it appears once, in Acts 8:9, where Simon beforetime in Samaria used sorcery and bewitched the people, giving out that himself was some great one.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Simon's sin was not the tricks but the claim: he wanted to be thought some great one, and the gospel exposes that hunger.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a sickle
BiblicalUsage: Maggal is the sickle, and both of its appearances are at harvest, and both are judgments. Jeremiah 50:16 says cut off the sower from Babylon and him that handleth the sickle in the time of harvest, and Joel 3:13 says put ye in the sickle, for the harvest is ripe, for their wickedness is great.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the sickle here is the sharp end of God's patience: when the harvest is ripe, the cutting begins.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a pestilence; by analogy, defeat
BiblicalUsage: Maggephah is the plague, the pestilence, and it falls where sin has broken out and is stayed where atonement is made. Numbers 16:48 has Aaron standing between the dead and the living, and the plague was stayed, and Numbers 25:9 counts twenty and four thousand dead in the plague. 2 Samuel 24:25 has David building an altar and the plague stayed from Israel, and Psalms 106:30 remembers Phinehas standing up and executing judgment, and so the plague was stayed.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the plague in these verses is never random: it follows sin, and it stops at intercession. My position is that Aaron in Numbers 16:48 and Phinehas in Psalms 106:30 show me what to do when judgment is spreading, which is to stand in the gap, not to run from it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H4031); Magog, a foreign nation, i.e. (figuratively) an Antichristian party:--Magog.
BiblicalUsage: Magog is the far northern nation of the last battle, named once in the New Testament, in Revelation 20:8, where Satan goes out to deceive Gog and Magog and gather them together to battle.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Revelation 20:8 is the end of every proud alliance against God: gathered in number as the sand of the sea, and still doomed.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of foreign origin (H7248); a Magian, i.e. Oriental scientist; by implication, a magician:--sorcerer, wise man.
BiblicalUsage: Magos is the Magian, the wise man of the east, and the same word names both the worshippers and the sorcerer. Matthew 2:1 has wise men coming from the east to Jerusalem, and Matthew 2:7 and Matthew 2:16 have Herod calling them privily and then raging when they mock him. Acts 13:6 turns the word dark: Elymas the sorcerer withstands Paul, seeking to turn the deputy from the faith.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the two uses of this word are the test of all wisdom: the wise men of Matthew 2:1 followed the star to Christ, while Elymas in Acts 13:6 used his knowledge to turn men away from Him. My position is that true wisdom always ends in worship, and false wisdom always ends in opposition.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Magog, a son of Japheth; also a barbarous northern region
BiblicalUsage: Magog was a son of Japheth, named in the table of nations in 1 Chronicles 1:5, and the name later stands for the northern land itself: Ezekiel 38:2 tells the prophet to set his face against Gog, the land of Magog, and Ezekiel 39:6 says God will send a fire on Magog. He is named in the table of nations as a son of Japheth, and his name later covers a whole northern land.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Magog's arc runs from a name in a genealogy to a nation under judgment, and that God keeps both ends of the story in His hand.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Magor-mis-Sabib, a symbolic name of Pashur
BiblicalUsage: Magor-missabib means terror on every side, and it is the new name Jeremiah gives Pashur in Jeremiah 20:3, after Pashur smote the prophet and put him in the stocks: the LORD hath not called thy name Pashur, but Magor-missabib. Pashur is told his name is changed, and the terror he made for others becomes his own.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a name like this one is a sentence: Pashur made himself a terror to the prophet, and God made him a terror to himself.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a fright (objective or subjective)
BiblicalUsage: Magor is fear, terror, the dread that stands on every side. Jeremiah 6:25 says fear is on every side, and Jeremiah 20:10 says the same of the prophet's own familiars, who watched for his halting. Psalms 31:13 has the psalmist hearing the slander of many, fear on every side, while they devise to take away his life, and Lamentations 2:22 says God called terrors round about as in a solemn day.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this word names the exact feeling of being surrounded: enemies without, false friends within, and no way out but God. My position is that Psalms 31:13 shows the way through it, because the psalmist who names the fear goes on to trust the LORD who is bigger than it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Magpiash, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Magpiash is named once, in Nehemiah 10:20, in the list of those who sealed the covenant after the return, between Meshullam and Hezir. He sealed the covenant with the rest of the returned exiles, and his name stands between Meshullam and Hezir.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that a signature on a covenant is a small thing and a great one: Magpiash put his name where his people put theirs.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a temporary abode; by extension, a permanent residence
BiblicalUsage: Magur is the sojourning, the pilgrimage, the land where a man lives as a stranger. Genesis 17:8 gives Abraham the land wherein thou art a stranger for an everlasting possession, and Exodus 6:4 calls Canaan the land of their pilgrimage. Genesis 47:9 has Jacob telling Pharaoh the days of the years of my pilgrimage are an hundred and thirty years, and Psalms 119:54 says God's statutes have been my songs in the house of my pilgrimage.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this word is the believer's address: a stranger in a land that is not yet home, singing God's statutes along the way. My position is that Jacob in Genesis 47:9 and the psalmist in Psalms 119:54 agree, because the pilgrimage is hard and the songs are what carry you through it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a cutting implement, i.e. a blade
BiblicalUsage: Magzerah is a cutting implement, a blade, and it appears once, in 2 Samuel 12:31, among the saws and harrows and axes of iron David put the Ammonites under.
TheologicalSignificance: I take it as a hard verse about a hard king: David's judgment on Ammon was thorough, and the tools are listed to prove it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {properly, interrogative what? (including how? why? when?); but also exclamation, what! (including how!), or indefinitely what}
BiblicalUsage: Mah is the Aramaic question word, what, how, why, and it asks the biggest questions in Daniel and Ezra. Daniel 2:22 says God knoweth what is in the darkness, and Daniel 4:35 says none can stay His hand or say unto Him, what doest thou? Ezra 7:23 commands whatsoever is commanded by the God of heaven to be diligently done.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the what in Daniel 2:22 is the comfort: God knows what is in the darkness, even when I do not.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {properly, interrogative what? (including how? why? when?); but also exclamation, what! (including how!), or indefinitely what}
BiblicalUsage: Mah is the Aramaic question word, what, how, why, and it asks the biggest questions in Daniel and Ezra. Daniel 2:22 says God knoweth what is in the darkness, and Daniel 4:35 says none can stay His hand or say unto Him, what doest thou? Ezra 7:23 commands whatsoever is commanded by the God of heaven to be diligently done.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the what in Daniel 2:22 is the comfort: God knows what is in the darkness, even when I do not.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, to question or hesitate, i.e. (by implication) to be reluctant
BiblicalUsage: Mahahh means to linger, to tarry, to hesitate, and it is always a delay that matters. Genesis 19:16 has Lot lingering while the angels lay hold on his hand to bring him out of Sodom, and Exodus 12:39 says Israel could not tarry when they were thrust out of Egypt. Habakkuk 2:3 says of the vision, though it tarry, wait for it, because it will surely come, and Psalms 119:60 says the psalmist made haste and delayed not to keep God's commandments.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this word draws a line between two kinds of delay: Lot's lingering in Genesis 19:16 nearly cost him everything, while the tarrying in Habakkuk 2:3 is God's timing, which is never late. My position is that Psalms 119:60 is the answer to both, because haste to obey is the only delay that is safe.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, to cut down or reduce, i.e. by implication, to adulterate
BiblicalUsage: Mahal is to cut down, to water down, to adulterate, and it appears once, in Isaiah 1:22, where Jerusalem's silver is become dross and her wine mixed with water.
TheologicalSignificance: I take it as a picture of a city that kept the look of wealth and lost the worth of it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a walk, i.e. a passage or a distance
BiblicalUsage: Mahalak is a walk, a passage, a day's journey, and its best-known appearances measure Nineveh: Jonah 3:3 says the city was of three days' journey, and Jonah 3:4 says he began to enter into the city a day's journey, crying, yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the measuring here is God's mercy in disguise: a city that big gets forty days, and a prophet who walked one day into it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Mahalalel, the name of an antediluvian patriarch and of an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Mahalalel was the antediluvian patriarch, son of Cainan and father of Jared, named in Genesis 5:12 and Genesis 5:15, where he lived sixty and five years and begat Jared and lived eight hundred and ninety and five years in all. A later Mahalaleel, of the children of Perez, is named in the Jerusalem list in Nehemiah 11:4.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the long lives in Genesis 5 are not filler: each name is a link in the chain from Adam to Noah, and Mahalalel holds his place in it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: fame
BiblicalUsage: Mahalal is fame, praise, the report of a man, and it appears once, in Proverbs 27:21, where a man is to his praise as silver is to the fining pot and gold to the furnace.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Proverbs 27:21 is the true test of praise: it does not tell you what a man claims, it tells you what he is.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a blow
BiblicalUsage: Mahalummah is a blow, a stroke, and both of its appearances are in Proverbs, where a fool's lips call for strokes in Proverbs 18:6 and stripes are prepared for the back of fools in Proverbs 19:29.
TheologicalSignificance: I take it that Proverbs is blunt on purpose: the mouth that calls for strokes will get them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: perhaps an abyss
BiblicalUsage: Mahamorah is the deep pit, the abyss, and it appears once, in Psalms 140:10, where the psalmist prays that burning coals fall on the wicked and they be cast into deep pits, that they rise not up again.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the pit here is the end of every plot against the righteous: those who dig it fall into it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to bargain (for a wife), i.e. to wed
BiblicalUsage: Mahar is to endow, to bargain for a wife, and it appears once, in Exodus 22:16, where a man who entices a maid that is not betrothed shall surely endow her to be his wife.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the law here protects the woman: desire without responsibility is not love, and the endowment makes it answerable.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to bargain (for a wife), i.e. to wed
BiblicalUsage: Mahar is to endow, to bargain for a wife, and it appears once, in Exodus 22:16, where a man who entices a maid that is not betrothed shall surely endow her to be his wife.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the law here protects the woman: desire without responsibility is not love, and the endowment makes it answerable.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Maharai, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Maharai the Netophathite was one of David's mighty men, named in 1 Chronicles 11:30 and 2 Samuel 23:28, and 1 Chronicles 27:13 says he was the tenth captain for the tenth month, of the Zarhites, with twenty and four thousand in his course. He served as the tenth captain for the tenth month, and his course numbered twenty and four thousand.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Maharai's place on two lists tells his story: a mighty man in battle and a captain in his month, faithful in both.
RelatedEvents: David's Mighty Men and the Philistine Giants
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a delusion
BiblicalUsage: Mahathallah is a delusion, a deceit, and it appears once, in Isaiah 30:10, where the people tell the seers to see not and the prophets to prophesy deceits and smooth things.
TheologicalSignificance: I take it as the saddest request in the Bible: a people asking their prophets to lie to them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Maher-Shalal-Chash-Baz; the symbolical name of the son of Isaiah
BiblicalUsage: Maher-shalal-hash-baz was the symbolic name of Isaiah's son, written first on a great roll in Isaiah 8:1 and then given to the child in Isaiah 8:3, when the prophetess bare a son and the LORD said, call his name Maher-shalal-hash-baz. The name was written on a great roll before the child was born, and it meant Assyria was already on its way.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the boy's name was a sermon in itself: haste to the spoil, speed to the prey, and Assyria coming soon.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, hurrying; hence (adverbially) in a hurry
BiblicalUsage: Maher means hurrying, quickly, soon, and it is the word for how fast Israel turned aside: Deuteronomy 9:12 says they are quickly turned aside out of the way, and Exodus 32:8 says the same at the calf, while Psalms 143:7 turns the speed the other way, hear me speedily, O LORD.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this word convicts me twice: I turn aside quickly, and I want God to answer speedily, and both speeds say something about my heart.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: quick; hence, skilful
BiblicalUsage: Mahir means quick, ready, skilful, and it marks the man whose gift is ready to hand. Ezra 7:6 calls Ezra a ready scribe in the law of Moses, and Proverbs 22:29 says a man diligent in his business shall stand before kings. Psalms 45:1 says the psalmist's tongue is the pen of a ready writer.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this word ties skill to standing: the diligent man in Proverbs 22:29 stands before kings because his gift was ready when the king needed it. My position is that Ezra in Ezra 7:6 shows where readiness comes from, because the hand of the LORD his God was upon him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a walking (plural collectively), i.e. access
BiblicalUsage: Mahlek is a walking, an access, a place to walk, and it appears once, in Zechariah 3:7, where God promises Joshua the high priest places to walk among those that stand by, if he will walk in God's ways and keep His charge.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the promise here is astonishing: a man who walks God's ways gets to walk among the angels.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a destruction
BiblicalUsage: Mahpekah is the overthrow, the destruction, and it always points back to Sodom. Amos 4:11 says God overthrew some of Israel as He overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah, and Deuteronomy 29:23 says the whole land shall be like the overthrow of Sodom and Gomorrah, Admah and Zeboim, while Isaiah 13:19 says Babylon shall be as when God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Sodom is the measure God keeps returning to, because an overthrow that complete is the clearest picture of what sin earns. My position is that Amos 4:11 is the mercy inside the warning, because Israel was plucked out as a firebrand from the burning, and the overthrow was not the end of them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a wrench, i.e. the stocks
BiblicalUsage: Mahpeketh is the stocks, the wrench that held a man fast, and its sharpest appearances belong to Jeremiah: Jeremiah 20:2 has Pashur putting the prophet in the stocks in the high gate of Benjamin, and Jeremiah 20:3 has him brought out of the stocks the next morning.
TheologicalSignificance: I take it that the stocks could hold Jeremiah's body for a night but not his word, which came out the next morning hotter than before.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably of Hebrew origin; Mainan, an Israelite:--Mainan.
BiblicalUsage: Mainan is a name in the genealogy of Jesus, in Luke 3:31, where he stands between Mattatha and Nathan, the son of David. The Greek text spells the name Menna, which is why the indexes carry it under that spelling.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a name in the genealogy is never filler: Mainan is one of the links that ties Jesus to David.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: middle voice from a primary μάω (to long for; through the idea of insensate craving); to rave as a "maniac":--be beside self (mad).
BiblicalUsage: Mainomai means to be mad, beside oneself, raving, and it is the charge thrown at believers and at Christ Himself. 1 Corinthians 14:23 asks whether unbelievers coming into a church where all speak with tongues will say ye are mad, and Acts 12:15 has the household telling Rhoda she is mad when she says Peter is at the door. Acts 26:24 has Festus crying to Paul, thou art beside thyself, much learning doth make thee mad, and John 10:20 has the crowd saying of Jesus, He hath a devil, and is mad.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this word is the world's verdict on a faith it cannot explain: mad, beside oneself, possessed. My position is that Paul's answer in Acts 26:25 is the only answer worth giving, because he does not argue about his sanity, he speaks forth the words of truth and soberness.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: anguish or (figuratively) affliction
BiblicalUsage: Makob is sorrow, grief, pain, the ache that will not leave. Exodus 3:7 has God saying He knows the sorrows of His people in Egypt, and Isaiah 53:3 calls the servant a man of sorrows and acquainted with grief, while Isaiah 53:4 says surely He hath borne our griefs and carried our sorrows. Psalms 32:10 says many sorrows shall be to the wicked, but he that trusteth in the LORD, mercy shall compass him about.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Isaiah 53:4 is the heart of this word: the sorrows I carry were carried first by Him, and that is why they do not have the last word. My position is that Exodus 3:7 and Psalms 32:10 together say everything, because God knows my sorrows and His mercy still compasses me in them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to tumble (in ruins); figuratively, to perish
BiblicalUsage: Makak means to tumble down, to decay, to be brought low, and its three appearances all show the same fall. Ecclesiastes 10:18 says by much slothfulness the building decayeth and the house droppeth through, and Job 24:24 says the wicked are exalted for a little while but are gone and brought low. Psalms 106:43 says Israel was brought low for their iniquity, though God delivered them many times.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this word is a warning against both laziness and pride: the slothful house in Ecclesiastes 10:18 and the exalted wicked in Job 24:24 fall the same way. My position is that Psalms 106:43 is the hope inside it, because the people brought low were delivered many times, and God still delivers.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to sell, literally (as merchandise, a daughter in marriage, into slavery), or figuratively (to surrender)
BiblicalUsage: Makar means to sell, and it sells everything: a birthright, a brother, a people, and the truth itself. Genesis 25:31 has Jacob saying sell me this day thy birthright, and Genesis 37:28 has Joseph's brothers selling him to the Ishmeelites for twenty pieces of silver. Isaiah 52:3 says ye have sold yourselves for nought, and ye shall be redeemed without money, while Proverbs 23:23 commands, buy the truth, and sell it not.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this word is about what a man will trade away when the price looks right: Esau's birthright, Joseph's freedom, a whole people's future. My position is that Isaiah 52:3 is the gospel in one verse, because we sold ourselves for nothing and God redeems us without money.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a prolonged form of the poetical μάκαρ (meaning the same); supremely blest; by extension, fortunate, well off:-- blessed, happy(X -ier).
BiblicalUsage: Makarios means blessed, happy, supremely blest, and it opens the Sermon on the Mount. Matthew 5:3 says blessed are the poor in spirit, and Matthew 5:6 says blessed are they which hunger and thirst after righteousness. Luke 6:20 says blessed be ye poor, for yours is the kingdom of God, and James 1:12 says blessed is the man that endureth temptation, for he shall receive the crown of life.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this word turns the world's idea of blessing upside down: the poor, the mourning, the hungry, and the tempted are the blessed ones. My position is that James 1:12 is the promise that makes the Beatitudes livable, because the blessing is not just a feeling now but a crown of life then.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3106; beatification, i.e. attribution of good fortune:--blessedness.
BiblicalUsage: Makarismos is blessedness, the state of being counted blessed, and Paul uses it to ask who the blessing belongs to. Romans 4:6 says David describeth the blessedness of the man unto whom God imputeth righteousness without works, and Romans 4:9 asks whether this blessedness comes upon the circumcision only or upon the uncircumcision also. Galatians 4:15 asks the Galatians where their blessedness has gone, the joy they once had when they would have plucked out their own eyes for Paul.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Romans 4:9 is the whole argument in one question: if blessedness is for the uncircumcised too, then it is by faith and not by the rite. My position is that Galatians 4:15 is the warning that goes with it, because blessedness can be lost when a church trades faith for rules.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3107; to beatify, i.e. pronounce (or esteem) fortunate:--call blessed, count happy.
BiblicalUsage: Makarizo means to call blessed, to count happy, and its two appearances are a promise and a song. James 5:11 says we count them happy which endure, and Luke 1:48 has Mary saying all generations shall call me blessed.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe both verses bless the same people: the lowly who endure and the lowly whom God lifts up.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a Macbannite or native of Macbena
BiblicalUsage: Machbanai was one of the Gadites who came to David at Ziklag, named once, in 1 Chronicles 12:13, where Jeremiah the tenth and Machbanai the eleventh are listed among the mighty men. He came to David at Ziklag with the rest of the Gadites, and his name is the eleventh on their roll.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the eleventh man on the list mattered as much as the first: David's army was built one faithful name at a time.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a cloth (as netted)
BiblicalUsage: Makbar is a thick cloth, a netted covering, and it appears once, in 2 Kings 8:15, where Hazael took a thick cloth, dipped it in water, and spread it on the king's face, so that he died, and Hazael reigned in his stead.
TheologicalSignificance: I take it as one of the coldest murders in the Bible: a wet cloth, a smothered king, and a usurper on the throne by morning.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Macbena, a place in Palestine settled by him
BiblicalUsage: Macbena was a place in Judah, named once, in 1 Chronicles 2:49, where Sheva is called the father of Machbenah, in the same verse that names Madmannah. Sheva is called the father of Machbenah in the same verse that names Madmannah, and the two places stand side by side in the genealogy.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a place in a genealogy is a home with a name: somebody's father built it, and somebody's children lived in it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a grate
BiblicalUsage: Makber is the grate, the network of brass under the altar, and all of its appearances are in Exodus. Exodus 27:4 commands a grate of network of brass with four brasen rings, and Exodus 38:4 says it was made and set under the compass of the altar.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the grate did unseen work: it held the fire up so the sacrifice could burn, and nobody praised it for it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: plenty
BiblicalUsage: Makbir is plenty, abundance, and it appears once, in Job 36:31, where Elihu says God judgeth the people by the clouds and giveth meat in abundance.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the abundance here is the point: the God who judges by the storm is the same God who feeds by the rain.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain derivation; a Macedon (Macedonian), i.e. inhabitant of Macedonia:--of Macedonia, Macedonian.
BiblicalUsage: Makedon is a Macedonian, a man of Macedonia, and it appears where the gospel meets the province. Acts 16:9 has the man of Macedonia standing and praying, come over into Macedonia and help us, and Acts 19:29 has Gaius and Aristarchus, men of Macedonia, caught with Paul in the riot at Ephesus.
TheologicalSignificance: I take it that the Macedonian's prayer in Acts 16:9 is the call that turned the gospel westward toward Europe.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3110; Macedonia, a region of Greece:--Macedonia.
BiblicalUsage: Macedonia was the province north of Greece where the gospel first took root in Europe. Acts 16:9 has the man of Macedonia pleading, come over and help us, and 2 Corinthians 8:1 tells of the grace of God bestowed on the churches of Macedonia, while Philippians 4:15 says no church shared with Paul in giving and receiving when he departed from Macedonia but the Philippians only.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Macedonia is the pattern of a giving church: poor, generous, and first in line to share. My position is that 2 Corinthians 8:1 and Philippians 4:15 belong together, because the grace that was bestowed on those churches came straight back out as giving.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Latin origin (macellum); a butcher's stall, meat market or provision-shop:--shambles.
BiblicalUsage: Makellon is the shambles, the meat market, and it appears once, in 1 Corinthians 10:25, where Paul says whatsoever is sold in the shambles, that eat, asking no question for conscience sake.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the shambles is where conscience meets the dinner table: eat freely, and let love, not fear, set the limit.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Maki, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Machi was the father of Geuel, named once, in Numbers 13:15, where Geuel the son of Machi is listed among the spies sent from the tribe of Gad. His son Geuel was one of the twelve spies sent from the tribe of Gad, and Machi's name goes with him into the record.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Machi is remembered for his son's mission: Geuel went into the land, and his father's name went with him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Makir, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Machir is two men in one name, and the verses keep them apart. The first is Machir the son of Manasseh, the father of Gilead, named in 1 Chronicles 7:14 and Joshua 17:1, where he is called the firstborn of Manasseh and a man of war. The second is Machir the son of Ammiel of Lo-debar, named in 2 Samuel 9:4, in whose house Mephibosheth was sheltering when David sent for him.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the two Machirs show both sides of the name: one took land by war, and the other kept a crippled prince alive in his house.
RelatedPeople: King David; Joseph, Son of Jacob
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a Makirite or descendant of Makir
BiblicalUsage: Machiri is a Machirite, a descendant of Machir, and it appears once, in Numbers 26:29, where the family of the Machirites is listed among the sons of Manasseh.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that a family name in a census is a promise kept: the Machirites were counted because they belonged.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a wound; figuratively, carnage, also pestilence
BiblicalUsage: Makkah is the wound, the blow, the plague, and it is the word for what sin does to a people and what God heals. Isaiah 1:6 says from the sole of the foot even to the head there is no soundness, but wounds and bruises and putrifying sores, and Jeremiah 30:17 answers, I will restore health unto thee, and I will heal thee of thy wounds. Isaiah 30:26 says the LORD will heal the stroke of their wound, and Zechariah 13:6 asks, what are these wounds in thine hands, and the answer comes, those with which I was wounded in the house of my friends.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this word runs straight to the cross: the wounds in Isaiah 1:6 are mine, and the wounds in Zechariah 13:6 are His. My position is that Jeremiah 30:17 is the promise that holds them together, because the God who wounds is the God who heals.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an acquaintance
BiblicalUsage: Makkar is an acquaintance, a friend, a man you know, and both of its appearances are about the temple repair under Jehoash. 2 Kings 12:5 has the priests taking money every man of his acquaintance to repair the breaches of the house, and 2 Kings 12:7 has the king telling them to take no more money of their acquaintance but to deliver it for the breaches.
TheologicalSignificance: I take it that the acquaintances here are the point: the temple was repaired out of the pockets of men the priests actually knew.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: nourishment
BiblicalUsage: Makkoleth is nourishment, food for a household, and it appears once, in 1 Kings 5:11, where Solomon gave Hiram twenty thousand measures of wheat for food to his household, and twenty measures of pure oil, year by year.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the yearly wheat here is the price of wisdom's peace: Solomon fed the king who cut his timber.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a (hunter's) net (as dark from concealment)
BiblicalUsage: Makmar is the hunter's net, and both of its appearances are about being caught in one. Isaiah 51:20 has Jerusalem's sons lying at the head of the streets as a wild bull in a net, and Psalms 141:10 prays, let the wicked fall into their own nets, whilst that I withal escape.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the net in Psalms 141:10 is justice itself: the trap set for the righteous catches the trapper.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Maknadbai, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Maknadbai is named once, in Ezra 10:40, in the list of those who had taken strange wives and were called to put them away. He is named among those who had taken strange wives, and his name is on the list of those called to put them away.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a name in a repentance list is a hard kind of honesty: Maknadbai's sin was written down, and so was his turning.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, a fixture, i.e. a basis; generally a place, especially as an abode
BiblicalUsage: Makon is the dwelling place, the settled place, the foundation where God abides. Exodus 15:17 calls it the place, O LORD, which Thou hast made for Thee to dwell in, and 1 Kings 8:39 asks God to hear in heaven His dwelling place and forgive. Psalms 89:14 says justice and judgment are the habitation of His throne, and mercy and truth shall go before His face.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this word tells me where God lives: not only in a house of stone, but where justice and judgment hold up His throne. My position is that 1 Kings 8:39 is the prayer that goes with it, because the God whose dwelling is heaven still hears from there and forgives.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Makpelah, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Machpelah was the cave Abraham bought for a burying place, named in Genesis 23:9, where he asks for the cave of Machpelah for as much money as it is worth, and in Genesis 23:19, where he buried Sarah his wife in the cave of the field of Machpelah. Genesis 25:9 says Isaac and Ishmael buried Abraham himself in the same cave.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Machpelah is the first piece of the promised land Abraham ever owned: a grave, bought with silver, holding the promise of more to come.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: feminine accusative case singular of G3117 (G3598 being implied); at a distance (literally or figuratively):--(a-)far (off), good (great) way off.
BiblicalUsage: Makran means far off, a great way off, and it measures the distance between a sinner and home. Luke 15:20 has the prodigal yet a great way off when his father saw him and ran, and Mark 12:34 has Jesus telling the scribe, thou art not far from the kingdom of God.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the two distances here are the whole gospel: a great way off, and not far, and the Father running the gap between them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3117 and G5550; long-timed, i.e. long-lived:--live long.
BiblicalUsage: Makrochronios means long-lived, long-timed, and it appears once, in Ephesians 6:3, in the promise to children who honour their parents, that thou mayest live long on the earth.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the long life here is not a bargain but a blessing: honour opens the door to it, and God gives it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3372; long (in place (distant) or time (neuter plural)):--far, long.
BiblicalUsage: Makros means long, far, distant, and it is the word for how far away we were. Ephesians 2:13 says ye who sometimes were far off are made nigh by the blood of Christ, and Ephesians 2:17 says He preached peace to you which were afar off and to them that were nigh. Acts 2:39 says the promise is unto you and to all that are afar off, as many as the Lord our God shall call, while Luke 20:47 turns the word against the scribes who devour widows' houses and for a shew make long prayers.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this word is the measure of grace: the distance in Ephesians 2:13 was real, and the blood of Christ closed it. My position is that Luke 20:47 is the warning on the other side, because long prayers do not make up for a long way from God.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: adverb from G3117; from a distance or afar:--afar off, from far.
BiblicalUsage: Makrothen means from afar, afar off, and it is the word for standing at a distance. Luke 18:13 has the publican standing afar off, unwilling to lift his eyes to heaven, and Luke 22:54 has Peter following afar off into the high priest's house, while Mark 15:40 has the women looking on afar off at the cross.
TheologicalSignificance: I take it that the distance in all three verses is the same one: close enough to see, too far to stand beside, and honest about it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from the same as G3116; to be long-spirited, i.e. (objectively) forbearing or (subjectively) patient:--bear (suffer) long, be longsuffering, have (long) patience, be patient, patiently endure.
BiblicalUsage: Makrothumeo means to be long-spirited, to bear long, to be patient, and it is both God's character and the believer's command. 1 Corinthians 13:4 says charity suffereth long, and is kind, and 2 Peter 3:9 says the Lord is longsuffering to us-ward, not willing that any should perish. James 5:7 tells the brethren, be patient unto the coming of the Lord, as the husbandman waiteth for the precious fruit of the earth.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this word is the patience of God made visible: He bears long with us, and then He asks us to bear long with each other. My position is that 2 Peter 3:9 is the reason for all of it, because His longsuffering is not slowness but mercy, waiting for sinners to come home.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from the same as G3116; longanimity, i.e. (objectively) forbearance or (subjectively) fortitude:--longsuffering, patience.
BiblicalUsage: Makrothumia is longsuffering, patience, the long temper that does not flare, and it is both a fruit and a divine attribute. Galatians 5:22 lists longsuffering among the fruit of the Spirit, and Romans 2:4 says the riches of God's goodness and forbearance and longsuffering lead men to repentance. 2 Peter 3:15 says to account that the longsuffering of our Lord is salvation.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this word is the clearest proof that God's patience is not weakness: Romans 2:4 says it leads to repentance, and 2 Peter 3:15 says it is salvation itself. My position is that the fruit in Galatians 5:22 grows only where His longsuffering has already grown in me.
RelatedTopics: Patience; Fruit of the Spirit; Repentance
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: adverb of a compound of G3117 and G2372; with long (enduring) temper, i.e. leniently:--patiently.
BiblicalUsage: Makrothumos is the adverb patiently, with a long temper, and it appears once, in Acts 26:3, where Paul asks Agrippa to hear him patiently, because the king is expert in all the customs and questions of the Jews. The Greek text spells the word with a different accent from the form Strong's lists, which is why the indexes carry it under that spelling.
TheologicalSignificance: I take it that Paul's one word of patience is a model for my own defence: ask to be heard, and then speak the truth plainly.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a stumbling-block, but only figuratively (fall, enticement (idol))
BiblicalUsage: Makshelah is the stumbling-block, the ruin, the thing that trips a nation, and it appears twice. Isaiah 3:6 has a man begging his brother to rule, with this ruin under his hand, and Zephaniah 1:3 has God consuming the stumblingblocks with the wicked.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the stumbling-block in Zephaniah 1:3 is the idol itself: the thing men trusted to hold them up is the thing that brings them down.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: dell; the Maktesh, a place in Jerusalem
BiblicalUsage: Maktesh was the hollow, the merchant quarter of Jerusalem, named once, in Zephaniah 1:11, where the prophet cries, howl, ye inhabitants of Maktesh, for all the merchant people are cut down and all they that bear silver are cut off. The merchant people are cut down in the same verse, and the silver they trusted in does not save them.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the merchants of Maktesh are a warning to every market that trusts in silver: the silver stays, and the people are cut off.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a mortar; by analogy, a socket (of a tooth)
BiblicalUsage: Maktesh is the mortar, the hollow place, the socket, and it appears twice. Judges 15:19 has God cleaving a hollow place in the jaw at Lehi, where water came out and Samson's spirit revived, and Proverbs 27:22 says though thou shouldest bray a fool in a mortar among wheat with a pestle, yet will not his foolishness depart from him.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the two hollows could not be more different: one gave a dying man water, and the other cannot pound the folly out of a fool.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an angel
BiblicalUsage: Malak is the Aramaic word for an angel, a messenger, and both of its appearances are rescues. Daniel 3:28 has Nebuchadnezzar blessing the God who sent His angel to deliver Shadrach, Meshach, and Abed-nego from the furnace, and Daniel 6:22 has Daniel saying, my God hath sent His angel, and hath shut the lions' mouths.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the angel in both verses is the same promise: God sends His messenger when His people cannot save themselves.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a messenger; specifically, of God, i.e. an angel (also a prophet, priest or teacher)
BiblicalUsage: Malak is the messenger, the angel, and it is the most frequent heavenly word in the Old Testament. Genesis 16:7 has the angel of the LORD finding Hagar by the fountain in the wilderness, and Exodus 3:2 has the angel of the LORD appearing to Moses in a flame of fire out of the midst of a bush. Judges 6:11 has the angel of the LORD sitting under an oak in Ophrah when Gideon was threshing wheat, and Psalms 91:11 says He shall give His angels charge over thee, to keep thee in all thy ways, while Malachi 3:1 promises the messenger of the covenant, whom ye delight in.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this word is the proof that God does not send His messages by accident: an angel finds Hagar, calls Moses, and sits down with Gideon, each one on purpose. My position is that Psalms 91:11 is the promise that makes the others personal, because the charge given to the angels is over me too, to keep me in all my ways.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Malaki, a prophet
BiblicalUsage: Malachi is the prophet whose name stands at the head of the last book of the Old Testament, in Malachi 1:1, where the burden of the word of the LORD to Israel comes by Malachi. His name means my messenger, and he is the last voice of the Old Testament before the silence.
