TheologicalSignificance: I believe Malachi's place at the end is no accident: his is the last voice before four hundred years of silence, and then the voice in the wilderness.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a message
BiblicalUsage: Malakuth is the message, the word sent, and it appears once, in Haggai 1:13, where Haggai the LORD's messenger speaks in the LORD's message unto the people, saying, I am with you, saith the LORD.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the message here is the whole of Haggai's preaching in five words: I am with you.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a rag or old garment
BiblicalUsage: Malach is a rag, an old cast clout, a rotten garment, and both of its appearances are in the dungeon where Jeremiah lay in the mire. Jeremiah 38:11 has Ebed-melech taking old cast clouts and rotten rags down by cords into the dungeon, and Jeremiah 38:12 has him telling the prophet to put them under his armholes under the cords, so he could be lifted out without the ropes cutting him.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the rags here are the tenderness inside a cruel story: a stranger thought about the prophet's armpits before he pulled him out of the mud.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, to rub to pieces or pulverize; intransitively, to disappear as dust; to salt whether internally (to season with salt) or externally (to rub with salt)
BiblicalUsage: Malach means to salt, to season, to rub with salt, and it also means to vanish away like dust. Leviticus 2:13 commands every meat offering to be seasoned with salt, the salt of the covenant of God, and Exodus 30:35 has the holy perfume tempered together, pure and holy. Ezekiel 16:4 says Jerusalem at her birth was not salted at all, and Isaiah 51:6 says the heavens shall vanish away like smoke and the earth wax old like a garment.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this word holds covenant and judgment together: salt preserves what God keeps, and the unsalted thing vanishes. My position is that the salt of the covenant in Leviticus 2:13 is the promise behind it all, because what God salts, He keeps.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to reign; inceptively, to ascend the throne; causatively, to induct into royalty; hence (by implication) to take counsel
BiblicalUsage: Malak means to reign, to be king, and it is the verb of every throne in the Bible. 1 Samuel 8:7 has God telling Samuel the people have not rejected him but have rejected Me, that I should not reign over them, and 1 Chronicles 16:31 says let men say among the nations, the LORD reigneth. Psalms 97:1 says the LORD reigneth, let the earth rejoice, and Jeremiah 23:5 promises a King who shall reign and prosper and execute judgment and justice in the earth.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this word is the argument of the whole Bible: men keep asking for a king, and God keeps telling them He is the King. My position is that Jeremiah 23:5 is the end of the argument, because the King who reigns in righteousness is the one Israel asked for all along.
RelatedTopics: Kingship of Christ; Kingdom of God; God's Sovereignty
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3120; softness, i.e. enervation (debility):--disease.
BiblicalUsage: Malakia is disease, debility, the sickness that wears a body down, and it appears only where Jesus is healing it. Matthew 4:23 says He went about all Galilee healing all manner of sickness and all manner of disease, and Matthew 9:35 says the same of all the cities and villages, while Matthew 10:1 gives the twelve power to heal all manner of sickness and all manner of disease.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the point of this word is who holds the power over it: disease is real, and Jesus heals it wherever He goes. My position is that Matthew 10:1 is the commission that follows, because the healing Jesus did, His disciples were sent to do.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain affinity; soft, i.e. fine (clothing); figuratively, a catamite:--effeminate, soft.
BiblicalUsage: Malakos means soft, fine, delicate, and it covers both clothing and character. Matthew 11:8 and Luke 7:25 both ask, what went ye out to see, a man clothed in soft raiment, and answer that they who wear soft clothing are in kings' houses. 1 Corinthians 6:9 turns the word toward conduct: neither fornicators, nor idolaters, nor adulterers, nor effeminate shall inherit the kingdom of God.
TheologicalSignificance: I take the two uses of this word as one warning: soft living in Matthew 11:8 and soft morals in 1 Corinthians 6:9 are the same drift, from comfort to compromise. My position is that John the Baptist in Matthew 11:8 is the contrast God holds up, because he wore camel's hair and told the truth.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to speak (mostly poetical) or say
BiblicalUsage: Malal means to speak, to say, to utter, and it is the poet's word for speaking. Genesis 21:7 has Sarah saying, who would have said unto Abraham that Sarah should have given children suck, and Job 33:3 has Elihu saying his lips shall utter knowledge clearly. Psalms 106:2 asks, who can utter the mighty acts of the LORD, who can shew forth all His praise?
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this word is about speech that cannot hold itself back: Sarah's laughter in Genesis 21:7 and the psalmist's question in Psalms 106:2 both come from a wonder too big for silence. My position is that the question in Psalms 106:2 is the right one, because no one can utter all His mighty acts, and that is why we keep trying.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to crack a joint; by implication, to wring the neck of a fowl (without separating it)
BiblicalUsage: Malaq means to wring off, to crack the neck, and both of its appearances are in the bird offerings: Leviticus 1:15 has the priest wringing off the head of the turtledove and burning it on the altar, and Leviticus 5:8 has the same for the sin offering, wringing off the head from the neck but not dividing it asunder.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the wringing here is the cost of atonement in miniature: a small bird, a quick death, and blood at the side of the altar.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, to be smooth, i.e. (by implication) to escape (as if by slipperiness); causatively, to release or rescue; specifically, to bring forth young, emit sparks
BiblicalUsage: Malat means to escape, to slip away, to be delivered, and it is the word for getting out alive. Genesis 19:17 has the angel telling Lot, escape for thy life, look not behind thee, and Psalms 124:7 says our soul is escaped as a bird out of the snare of the fowlers. Daniel 12:1 promises thy people shall be delivered, every one found written in the book, and Joel 2:32 says whosoever shall call on the name of the LORD shall be delivered.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this word is the whole gospel in a verb: escape is not something I manage, it is something God gives. My position is that Joel 2:32 is the open door in all four verses, because calling on the name of the LORD is the one escape that never fails.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to be smooth, i.e. (figuratively) pleasant
BiblicalUsage: Malats means to be smooth, pleasant, sweet, and it appears once, in Psalms 119:103, where the psalmist says, how sweet are Thy words unto my taste, yea, sweeter than honey to my mouth!
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this one verse is the whole reason to read the Bible: His words are sweet because they are true.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a brickkiln
BiblicalUsage: Malben is the brickkiln, and both of its appearances are about hard work in hard places: 2 Samuel 12:31 has David putting the Ammonites to pass through the brickkiln, and Jeremiah 43:9 has the prophet hiding great stones in the clay in the brickkiln at the entry of Pharaoh's house in Tahpanhes.
TheologicalSignificance: I take it that the brickkiln in Jeremiah 43:9 is a signpost: the stones hidden in its clay say Babylon is coming to Egypt.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a garment, or (collectively) clothing
BiblicalUsage: Malbush is clothing, raiment, apparel, and it dresses both the glorious and the guilty. 1 Kings 10:5 has the queen of Sheba breathless at the apparel of Solomon's servants, and Isaiah 63:3 has the LORD's garments sprinkled with blood from treading the winepress, while Zephaniah 1:8 says God will punish all such as are clothed with strange apparel.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe clothing in these verses always tells the truth about the wearer: glory, judgment, or a borrowed strangeness that God will punish.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H4429); Malchus, an Israelite:--Malchus.
BiblicalUsage: Malchus was the high priest's servant whose right ear Peter cut off in the garden, named once, in John 18:10, where Simon Peter drew his sword and smote the servant, and the servant's name was Malchus. He was a servant of the high priest, and his name is given only in John's account.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Malchus is remembered for the worst night of his life and the best: the ear Peter cut off is the ear Jesus healed.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: full (literally or figuratively) or filling (literally); also (concretely) fulness; adverbially, fully
BiblicalUsage: Male is full, filled, fulness, and it is full of everything from houses to hearts. Deuteronomy 6:11 promises houses full of all good things which Israel did not fill, and Deuteronomy 33:23 says Naphtali is full with the blessing of the LORD, while Deuteronomy 34:9 says Joshua the son of Nun was full of the spirit of wisdom. Ruth 1:21 turns the word over: Naomi says, I went out full, and the LORD hath brought me home again empty.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that this word measures a life: full of blessing in Deuteronomy 33:23, full of wisdom in Deuteronomy 34:9, and empty in Ruth 1:21 until God fills it again. My position is that Naomi's emptiness is the honest half of the word, because she names it plainly, and God fills it by the end of the book.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: full (literally or figuratively) or filling (literally); also (concretely) fulness; adverbially, fully
BiblicalUsage: Male is full, filled, fulness, and it is full of everything from houses to hearts. Deuteronomy 6:11 promises houses full of all good things which Israel did not fill, and Deuteronomy 33:23 says Naphtali is full with the blessing of the LORD, while Deuteronomy 34:9 says Joshua the son of Nun was full of the spirit of wisdom. Ruth 1:21 turns the word over: Naomi says, I went out full, and the LORD hath brought me home again empty.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that this word measures a life: full of blessing in Deuteronomy 33:23, full of wisdom in Deuteronomy 34:9, and empty in Ruth 1:21 until God fills it again. My position is that Naomi's emptiness is the honest half of the word, because she names it plainly, and God fills it by the end of the book.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H4111); Maleleel (i.e. Mahalalel), an antediluvian:--Maleleel.
BiblicalUsage: Maleleel is the Greek form of Mahalalel, the antediluvian patriarch, named once in the New Testament, in Luke 3:37, in the genealogy of Jesus, where he stands as the son of Cainan and the father of Jared. His name is Mahalalel in the Hebrew, and he is counted among the patriarchs who lived before the flood.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Maleleel's one verse ties the old world to the new: the patriarch who lived eight hundred and ninety-five years is an ancestor of Jesus.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: neuter plural of the superlative of an apparently primary adverb μάλα (very); (adverbially) most (in the greatest degree) or particularly:--chiefly, most of all, (e-)specially.
BiblicalUsage: Malista means especially, chiefly, most of all, and it is Paul's word for where the duty lands first. Galatians 6:10 says do good unto all men, especially unto them who are of the household of faith, and 1 Timothy 5:8 says a man must provide for his own, and specially for those of his own house, while 1 Timothy 4:10 calls God the Saviour of all men, specially of those that believe.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the especially here is the shape of Christian love: for all, and first for the household of faith.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a queen
BiblicalUsage: Malka is the Aramaic word for a queen, and it appears once, in Daniel 5:10, where the queen came into the banquet house and told the frightened king to let not his thoughts trouble him.
TheologicalSignificance: I take it that the queen's calm in Daniel 5:10 is the one steady voice in Belshazzar's hall: she remembered Daniel when the king had forgotten him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a queen
BiblicalUsage: Malkah is the queen, and the Bible's queens are women who change the story. 1 Kings 10:1 has the queen of Sheba coming to prove Solomon with hard questions, and Esther 5:3 has the king asking queen Esther what her request is, even to the half of the kingdom, while Esther 7:3 has her answering, let my life be given me at my petition, and my people at my request.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the two queens in these verses show the two ways power meets God: Sheba came to test Solomon's wisdom, and Esther risked her life for her people. My position is that Esther 7:3 is the braver of the two, because she asked for her life and her people's in the same breath, before a king who could have refused both.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Malcam or Milcom, the national idol of the Ammonites
BiblicalUsage: Malcam, also called Milcom, was the abomination of the Ammonites, their national god. 1 Kings 11:5 says Solomon went after Milcom the abomination of the Ammonites, and 1 Kings 11:33 says the people worshipped him and forsook God's ways, while 2 Kings 23:13 says Josiah defiled the high places Solomon had built for Milcom.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Milcom is the warning in Solomon's story: the wisest king built a high place for a foreign god, and it took a reforming king to tear it down.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Malkiel, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Malkiel was a son of Beriah, of the tribe of Asher, named in Genesis 46:17 among those who went down into Egypt, and in 1 Chronicles 7:31, where he is called the father of Birzavith, while Numbers 26:45 names the family of the Malchielites after him. He went down into Egypt with Jacob's household, and his family is counted again in the wilderness census.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Malkiel's three verses trace one family's whole story: into Egypt, through the wilderness, and into the census of the new generation.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a Malkielite or descendant of Malkiel
BiblicalUsage: Malkieli is a Malkielite, a descendant of Malkiel, and it appears once, in Numbers 26:45, where the family of the Malchielites is counted among the sons of Beriah.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that being counted by family is a promise kept: the Malkielites belonged, and the census says so.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Malki-Tsedek, an early king in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Melchizedek, king of Salem, was the priest of the most high God who met Abraham with bread and wine in Genesis 14:18, and Psalms 110:4 swears the Messiah shall be a priest for ever after the order of Melchizedek. His name means king of righteousness, and he stands alone in the record, with no father and no mother named.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Melchizedek is the hinge between the testaments: a king and priest with no genealogy, whose order outlasts Aaron's.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Malkijah, the name of ten Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Malkijah is the name of ten Israelites, and the verses show three of them. Jeremiah 38:6 names the dungeon of Malchiah the son of Hammelech, where the prophet was let down into the mire, and Nehemiah 3:11 and Nehemiah 3:14 name two wall-builders, Malchijah the son of Harim and Malchiah the son of Rechab, who repaired the wall after the return.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the name covers both a dungeon and a wall: one Malchiah's pit held a prophet, and two others' hands rebuilt a city.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Malkiram, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Malkiram was a son of Jeconiah, named once, in 1 Chronicles 3:18, in the royal line carried into Babylon. He is one of the sons of Jeconiah listed in the genealogy of the exiled kings.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a name in the exile's genealogy is a thread of hope: the line of David went on, even in Babylon.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Malkishua, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Malkishua was a son of Saul, named in 1 Samuel 14:49 among Saul's sons, and in 1 Chronicles 8:33 in the genealogy of the house of Saul, while 1 Samuel 31:2 says the Philistines slew Jonathan, and Abinadab, and Malchi-shua, the sons of Saul, on Gilboa. He fell with Jonathan and Abinadab on Gilboa, and his death is told in the same verse that ends Saul's house.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Malkishua's death on Gilboa is the end of Saul's house in one verse: three sons fallen, and the kingdom passing to David.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a snare
BiblicalUsage: Malkodeth is a snare, a trap, and it appears once, in Job 18:10, where Bildad says the snare is laid for the wicked in the ground, and a trap for him in the way.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the snare here is the shape of the wicked man's own path: he walks into the trap he set for others.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: dominion (abstractly or concretely)
BiblicalUsage: Malku is dominion, kingdom, the rule of God and of men, and Daniel is its book. Daniel 2:44 says the God of heaven shall set up a kingdom which shall never be destroyed, and Daniel 4:34 says His dominion is an everlasting dominion, and His kingdom is from generation to generation. Daniel 7:14 gives the Son of man a dominion that shall not pass away, and Daniel 7:27 says the kingdom and dominion shall be given to the people of the saints of the most High.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this word is Daniel's whole message: the kingdoms of men rise and fall, and the kingdom of God stands for ever. My position is that Daniel 7:27 is the end of the story, because the kingdom is not only God's, it is given to His people.
RelatedTopics: Kingdom of God; God's Sovereignty; Prophecy
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a rule; concretely, a dominion
BiblicalUsage: Malkuth is the kingdom, the rule, the dominion, and it is the word for God's reign over all. 1 Chronicles 17:14 promises David's son shall be settled in God's house and in His kingdom for ever, and Psalms 103:19 says the LORD hath prepared His throne in the heavens, and His kingdom ruleth over all. Psalms 145:13 says Thy kingdom is an everlasting kingdom, and Thy dominion endureth throughout all generations.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this word is the anchor of every other promise: a kingdom that rules over all cannot be shaken by any king under it. My position is that 1 Chronicles 17:14 is the thread from David to Christ, because the kingdom settled for ever is the one His Son inherits.
RelatedTopics: Kingdom of God; God's Sovereignty; Promise
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a sailor (as following 'the salt')
BiblicalUsage: Mallach is the sailor, the mariner, and all of its appearances belong to Tyre. Ezekiel 27:9 has the ships of the sea with their mariners in Tyre to occupy her merchandise, and Ezekiel 27:27 has the mariners falling into the midst of the seas in the day of Tyre's ruin.
TheologicalSignificance: I take it that Tyre's mariners are the measure of her pride: the men who carried her wealth sank with it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: neuter of the comparative of the same as G3122; (adverbially) more (in a greater degree) or rather:--+ better, X far, (the) more (and more), (so) much (the more), rather.
BiblicalUsage: Mallon means more, rather, much more, and it is the word for choosing the better thing. Romans 5:9 says much more then, being now justified by His blood, we shall be saved from wrath through Him, and Hebrews 11:25 says Moses chose rather to suffer affliction with the people of God than to enjoy the pleasures of sin for a season, while Matthew 6:26 asks, are ye not much better than the fowls of the air?
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the much more in Romans 5:9 is the logic of grace: if God did the hard part while I was His enemy, He will surely finish it now that I am His.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Mallothi, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Mallothi was a son of Heman, one of the singers set apart for the service of song in 1 Chronicles 25:4, and 1 Chronicles 25:26 says the nineteenth course fell to Mallothi, he, his sons, and his brethren, twelve in all. He was one of the fourteen sons of Heman set apart for the song of the LORD.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that God orders worship down to the rota: every singer had his course, and Mallothi's was the nineteenth.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: sea-purslain (from its saltness)
BiblicalUsage: Malluach is the mallow, the sea-purslain, and it appears once, in Job 30:4, where the outcasts cut up mallows by the bushes, and juniper roots for their meat.
TheologicalSignificance: I take it as a picture of how low a man can fall: eating weeds by the bushes, and calling it meat.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Malluk, the name of five Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Malluk is the name of five Israelites, and the verses show three of them: a Levite ancestor in 1 Chronicles 6:44, a man who put away his strange wife in Ezra 10:29, and a priest who sealed the covenant in Nehemiah 12:2. The five men who share the name are counted separately in the lists, and each one is named for his own part in the story.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that five men sharing one name is no confusion to God: each Malluk is counted separately, and each one mattered.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a goad for oxen
BiblicalUsage: Malmad is the ox goad, and it appears once, in Judges 3:31, where Shamgar the son of Anath slew six hundred Philistines with an ox goad, and he also delivered Israel.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the goad is the whole lesson of Shamgar: God does not need a sword, He needs a man willing to use what is in his hand.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a lodgment, i.e. caravanserai or encampment
BiblicalUsage: Malon is the lodging, the inn, the place where travellers stop for the night, and it is where some of the Bible's strangest meetings happen. Exodus 4:24 says it came to pass by the way in the inn that the LORD met Moses and sought to kill him, and Genesis 42:27 has Joseph's brothers opening their sacks in the inn and finding their money returned. Joshua 4:3 has the twelve stones carried to the lodging place where Israel lodged that night, and Jeremiah 9:2 wishes for a lodging place of wayfaring men in the wilderness, to leave a treacherous people behind.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the inn in Exodus 4:24 is the warning in this word: a traveller can be met by God at any stop, and the meeting is not always gentle. My position is that Jeremiah 9:2 is the other side of it, because sometimes the lodging place is not a danger but a refuge, the only place to get away from a faithless people.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: transitively (in dual) the jaws (as taking food); in transitively, spoil (and captives) (as taken)
BiblicalUsage: malqôwach names both the jaws that take food and the spoil taken in war. In Numbers 31:11 the word stands where Israel takes all the spoil and prey after battle, and in Isaiah 49:24 it asks whether the prey can be taken from the mighty. The same word turns up in the psalmist's suffering in Psalms 22:15, where his tongue cleaves to his jaws. Taking and being taken run through the whole word.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe malqôwach shows me that what is taken is never finally lost to God. He promises in Isaiah 49:25 to take the captives of the mighty away, and I hold that His rescue reaches even the prey already carried off. No loss of mine is beyond His taking back.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: the spring rain; figuratively, eloquence
BiblicalUsage: malqôwsh is the latter rain, the spring rain that ripens the crop before harvest. In Deuteronomy 11:14 God promises the first rain and the latter rain in their season, and in Hosea 6:3 His coming is compared to the latter and former rain on the earth. Joel 2:23 and Zechariah 10:1 both bid God's people ask for it and rejoice in it. It is the rain that finishes what the early rain began.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe malqôwsh teaches me that God finishes what He starts. The latter rain comes late, after long waiting, and I hold that His blessing often arrives the same way, near the end of the season. I will keep asking for rain in its time.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a grinder, i.e. back tooth
BiblicalUsage: maltâʻâh is a grinder, a back tooth, and it occurs once, in the psalmist's prayer in Psalms 58:6. There he asks God to break the teeth of the wicked in their mouth and to break out the great teeth of the young lions. The word is the tooth that crushes, and the prayer asks God to take its power away.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe maltâʻâh reminds me that God can break the strength of those who tear others apart, and that prayer is the right place to ask Him to do it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: mixture, i.e. (specifically) wine mixed (with water or spices)
BiblicalUsage: mamçâk is wine mixed with water or spices, the kind of drink people linger over. In Proverbs 23:30 it marks those who tarry long at the wine and go to seek mixed wine, and in Isaiah 65:11 it stands on the table of those who forsake the LORD and furnish a drink offering to a false god. The same mixed cup can be a pleasure or an idol's offering.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe mamçâk warns me that what I linger over shapes what I worship, and I hold that a drink shared at an idol's table is no small thing.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: dominion, i.e. (abstractly) the estate (rule) or (concretely) the country (realm)
BiblicalUsage: mamlâkâh is a kingdom, both the rule itself and the land ruled. In Exodus 19:6 Israel is promised as a kingdom of priests, and in 2 Samuel 7:16 David is told his house and his kingdom shall be established for ever. In 1 Samuel 24:20 Saul himself admits the kingdom of Israel will be established in David's hand, and Isaiah 9:7 looks to a kingdom with no end. The word stretches from earthly thrones to God's own rule.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe mamlâkâh puts every earthly kingdom in its place beneath God's. Kings rise and fall, and I hold that only the kingdom promised to David's line, fulfilled in Christ, stands for ever. That is the kingdom I want to belong to.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {dominion, i.e. (abstractly) the estate (rule) or (concretely) the country (realm)}
BiblicalUsage: mamlâkûwth is the same kingdom word in its Aramaic-tinged form, the realm as a possession that can be given and taken away. In 1 Samuel 15:28 Samuel tells Saul the LORD has rent the kingdom of Israel from him and given it to a neighbour better than he. In Hosea 1:4 God says He will cause the kingdom of the house of Israel to cease, and in 2 Samuel 16:3 Ziba claims the kingdom will be restored to him. In Joshua 13:12 it names the kingdom of Og in Bashan, a kingdom held in the hand that God can open.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe mamlâkûwth shows me that no kingdom is owned outright, only held on loan from God. He gives it and He takes it, and I hold that the only safe trust is in the King who gives.
RelatedTopics: Kingdom of God; God's Sovereignty; Judgment
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of natural origin ("mammy"); a grandmother:--grandmother.
BiblicalUsage: mámmē is a grandmother, and it occurs once, in 2 Timothy 1:5. Paul remembers the unfeigned faith that dwelt first in Timothy's grandmother Lois, and then in his mother Eunice, and he is persuaded it lives in Timothy also. One word carries three generations of faith.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe mámmē honours the faith passed down at home, and I hold that a grandmother's belief can outlive her and take root in her grandchildren.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a granary
BiblicalUsage: mammᵉgurâh is a granary, a storehouse for grain, and it occurs once, in Joel 1:17. There the garners are laid desolate and the barns broken down, because the corn is withered. The word stands in a scene of empty stores and ruined harvest.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe mammᵉgurâh shows me how quickly plenty can turn to emptiness when God withholds the harvest, and that my stores are never my security.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Chaldee origin (confidence, i.e. wealth, personified); mammonas, i.e. avarice (deified):--mammon.
BiblicalUsage: mammōnâs is mammon, wealth treated as a master. In Matthew 6:24 Jesus says no man can serve two masters, and that we cannot serve God and mammon, and Luke 16:13 repeats the warning. In Luke 16:9 He tells His hearers to make friends of the mammon of unrighteousness, using wealth for others before it fails, so the word is not money itself but money enthroned.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe mammōnâs exposes the choice I make every day about who my master is, since wealth used for others is a tool and wealth served is a god, and I want no god but the LORD.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a mortal disease; concretely, a corpse
BiblicalUsage: mâmôwth names a deadly disease and, by extension, the dead themselves. In Jeremiah 16:4 the people shall die of grievous deaths, unlamented and unburied, and in Ezekiel 28:8 the prince of Tyre shall die the deaths of those slain in the midst of the seas. In 2 Kings 11:2 Jehosheba steals the child Joash from among the king's sons who were slain. The word hangs over scenes of death without honour.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe mâmôwth shows me that death without God is a grievous thing, and I hold that the worst death is not the sword but dying unlamented and unremembered. My hope is in the God who raises the slain.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Mamre, an Amorite
BiblicalUsage: Mamrêʼ is Mamre, the Amorite whose oaks gave their name to the plain near Hebron where Abram lived. In Genesis 13:18 Abram dwells in the plain of Mamre and builds an altar to the LORD there, and in Genesis 18:1 the LORD appears to him in the plains of Mamre. In Genesis 23:19 Abraham buries Sarah in the cave of Machpelah before Mamre., and the name marks the ground where God met Abraham again and again.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Mamre matters because it is ordinary ground made holy by God's appearing, and I hold that He still meets His people where they pitch their tents.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a bitterness, i.e. (figuratively) calamity
BiblicalUsage: mamrôr is bitterness, and it occurs once, in Job 9:18. Job says God will not suffer him to take his breath, but fills him with bitterness. The word is the taste of a life that cannot catch its breath.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe mamrôr tells the truth about suffering, that bitterness is real and God hears the man who names it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: something sweet (literally or figuratively)
BiblicalUsage: mamtaq is something sweet, literally or figuratively. In Nehemiah 8:10 the people are told to eat the fat and drink the sweet on a holy day, and to send portions to those with nothing prepared. In Song of Solomon 5:16 the beloved's mouth is most sweet, and he is altogether lovely., and sweetness here is both a feast and a person.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe mamtaq shows me that God gives sweetness to be shared, not hoarded, and I hold that the sweetest thing I know is the LORD's own goodness.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a mongrel, i.e. born of a Jewish father and a heathen mother
BiblicalUsage: mamzêr is a child of mixed and forbidden parentage, rendered bastard, and it occurs twice. In Deuteronomy 23:2 such a one shall not enter into the congregation of the LORD, even to his tenth generation, and in Zechariah 9:6 a bastard shall dwell in Ashdod as God cuts off the pride of the Philistines. The word draws a hard line around the congregation.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe mamzêr shows me how seriously God guards His people, and I hold that the line He drew in the old covenant is answered in Christ, who opens the congregation to all who come.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a delicacy
BiblicalUsage: manʻam is a delicacy, a dainty, and it occurs once, in Psalms 141:4. There the psalmist prays that his heart not be inclined to any evil thing, to practise wicked works with men that work iniquity, and that he not eat of their dainties. The word is the rich food of wicked company, and the prayer refuses it.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe manʻam warns me that the table I sit at shapes the heart I keep, and I will not trade my integrity for a dainty.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: who or what (properly, interrogatively, hence, also indefinitely and relatively)
BiblicalUsage: mân is the Aramaic word for who or what, a question word that can also mean whomsoever. In Ezra 5:3 the governor asks, Who has commanded you to build this house, and in Daniel 4:17 the Most High gives the kingdom to whomsoever He will. The same small word can challenge a work or confess God's freedom.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe mân puts me in my place, since God gives rule to whomsoever He will and no governor's question can undo it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a bolt
BiblicalUsage: manʻûwl is a bolt or lock, the fastening on a door. In Nehemiah 3:3 the builders set up the doors of the fish gate with their locks and bars, and in Song of Solomon 5:5 the beloved's hands drop with myrrh upon the handles of the lock as she rises to open to him. A bolt can shut a city out or keep a lover waiting.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe manʻûwl reminds me that doors matter, and that the heart has its own bolts that only love opens.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: who or what (properly, interrogatively, hence, also indefinitely and relatively)
BiblicalUsage: mân is the Aramaic word for who or what, a question word that can also mean whomsoever. In Ezra 5:3 the governor asks, Who has commanded you to build this house, and in Daniel 4:17 the Most High gives the kingdom to whomsoever He will. The same small word can challenge a work or confess God's freedom.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe mân puts me in my place, since God gives rule to whomsoever He will and no governor's question can undo it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to debar (negatively or positively) from benefit or injury
BiblicalUsage: mânaʻ means to withhold or hold back, for good or for ill. In Proverbs 3:27 the command is to withhold not good from those to whom it is due, and in 1 Samuel 25:26 Abigail tells David the LORD has withholden him from shedding blood. In Jeremiah 31:16 God tells His people to refrain their voice from weeping, and in Psalms 84:11 He promises no good thing will He withhold from those who walk uprightly. The same withholding can be sin, mercy, or promise.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe mânaʻ teaches me that God withholds only what would harm me and never what I truly need. I hold that His withholding is love, and my withholding of good from others is sin.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Manachath, the name of an Edomite and of a place in Moab
BiblicalUsage: Mânachath is the name of a son of Shobal in the Edomite genealogy and of a place in Moab. In Genesis 36:23 Manahath is listed among the children of Shobal, and 1 Chronicles 1:40 repeats the line. In 1 Chronicles 8:6 the sons of Ehud are removed to Manahath., and the name survives in lists, not in a story.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Mânachath shows me that God keeps names in His book even when no story survives, and that no family is forgotten by Him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain origin; Manaën, a Christian:--Manaen.
BiblicalUsage: Manaḗn is Manaen, a prophet and teacher in the church at Antioch, named once in Acts 13:1. He had been brought up with Herod the tetrarch, yet he stands in the list beside Barnabas, Simeon, Lucius, and Saul. A man raised beside a king ends up serving the King.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Manaḗn shows me that no upbringing decides a man's end, and I hold that God can take a companion of Herod and make him a teacher of the church.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, something weighed out, i.e. (generally) a division; specifically (of food) a ration; also a lot
BiblicalUsage: mânâh is a portion, something weighed out and given. In 1 Samuel 1:5 Elkanah gives Hannah a worthy portion because he loves her, and in Esther 9:19 the Jews send portions to one another on the feast day. In Leviticus 7:33 the priest's part of the peace offering is named, and in Psalms 16:5 the LORD Himself is the portion of the psalmist's inheritance and cup. A portion can be food, a share, or God Himself.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe mânâh tells me that God does not deal in scraps. He gives worthy portions to His people, and I hold that the best portion of all is the LORD Himself.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, something weighed out, i.e. (generally) a division; specifically (of food) a ration; also a lot
BiblicalUsage: mânâh is a portion, something weighed out and given. In 1 Samuel 1:5 Elkanah gives Hannah a worthy portion because he loves her, and in Esther 9:19 the Jews send portions to one another on the feast day. In Leviticus 7:33 the priest's part of the peace offering is named, and in Psalms 16:5 the LORD Himself is the portion of the psalmist's inheritance and cup. A portion can be food, a share, or God Himself.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe mânâh tells me that God does not deal in scraps. He gives worthy portions to His people, and I hold that the best portion of all is the LORD Himself.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H4519); Mannasses (i.e. Menashsheh), an Israelite:--Manasses.
BiblicalUsage: Manassēs is Manasseh, the king in Matthew's genealogy and the tribe sealed in Revelation. In Matthew 1:10 Ezekias begets Manasses, and Manasses begets Amon, and in Revelation 7:6 twelve thousand of the tribe of Manasses are sealed. The name runs from a wicked king to a sealed tribe.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Manassēs shows me that God keeps a place for a tribe whose king did great evil, and I hold that His sealing grace reaches further than any family history.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: wisdom or intelligence
BiblicalUsage: mandaʻ is wisdom and understanding in Aramaic, the gift Daniel's world kept noticing. In Daniel 2:21 God gives wisdom to the wise and knowledge to those who know understanding, and in Daniel 5:12 excellent spirit and knowledge and understanding are found in Daniel himself. In Daniel 4:34 and Daniel 4:36 Nebuchadnezzar's understanding returns to him, and with it his kingdom. Wisdom here is not learned but given, and it can be taken and restored.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe mandaʻ teaches me that true understanding comes from God, not from study alone. I hold that He gives it to the wise and restores it to the humbled, and I want to ask Him for it daily.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, a fixed weight or measured amount, i.e. (techn.) a maneh or mina
BiblicalUsage: mâneh is the maneh or mina, a fixed weight of silver. In Ezekiel 45:12 the maneh is defined by shekels, twenty and five and twenty and fifteen, and in 1 Kings 10:17 three pounds of gold go to one shield in Solomon's house. The word is a measure, and Scripture uses it to weigh value exactly.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe mâneh reminds me that God weighs things exactly, and that my measures should be as honest as His.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a satire
BiblicalUsage: mangîynâh is a satire, a song of mockery, and it occurs once, in Lamentations 3:63. Jeremiah says he is his enemies' music, their song as they sit down and rise up. The prophet has become the tune his mockers sing.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe mangîynâh shows me that God's servant may be mocked in song, and that scorn does not make the message false.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3105; craziness:--(+ make) X mad.
BiblicalUsage: manía is madness, and it occurs once, in Acts 26:24. As Paul speaks for himself, Festus cries out with a loud voice, Paul, you are beside yourself, much learning makes you mad. The word is the world's verdict on a man speaking the truth.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe manía warns me that the world will call faithful speech madness, and I hold that Paul's so-called madness was the sanest speech in the room.
RelatedEvents: Paul Before Felix, Festus, and Agrippa
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H4478); manna (i.e. man), an edible gum:--manna.
BiblicalUsage: mánna is manna, the bread from heaven. In John 6:31 the crowd recalls that their fathers ate manna in the desert, and in John 6:49 Jesus answers that those fathers ate manna and are dead. In Hebrews 9:4 a golden pot of manna lies in the ark, and in Revelation 2:17 the overcomer is promised hidden manna. The word runs from daily bread to a hidden promise.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe mánna teaches me that God feeds His people day by day, and I hold that the bread that kept Israel alive points to the living bread who keeps me alive. I will not live on yesterday's manna.
RelatedEvents: Manna and Quail in the Wilderness
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Manoach, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Mânôwach is Manoah, the Danite of Zorah whose wife was barren until the angel came. In Judges 13:2 Manoah is named, and in Judges 13:8 he prays for the man of God to come again and teach them what to do with the child to be born. In Judges 16:31 Samson is buried in the burying place of Manoah his father., and his name belongs to a father who prayed before his son was born.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Mânôwach shows me a father who prayed first and acted second, and I hold that Manoah's prayer is a pattern for every parent waiting on God.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: quiet, i.e. (concretely) a settled spot, or (figuratively) a home
BiblicalUsage: mânôwach is rest, a settled spot, a home where the foot can find a place. In Genesis 8:9 the dove finds no rest for the sole of her foot and returns to the ark, and in Ruth 3:1 Naomi seeks rest for Ruth, that it may be well with her. In Deuteronomy 28:65 the disobedient shall find no ease and no rest for the sole of the foot, and in Isaiah 34:14 the screech owl finds a place of rest. Rest here is a place, not only a feeling.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe mânôwach points me to the rest God gives His people, a real home and not only a pause. I hold that the dove's return to the ark pictures my own return to Him, and that true rest is found only there.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a retreat (literally or figuratively); abstractly, a fleeing
BiblicalUsage: mânôwç is a refuge, a place to flee to, and sometimes the flight itself. In 2 Samuel 22:3 David calls God his refuge and his saviour, and in Jeremiah 16:19 the LORD is the refuge in the day of affliction. In Psalms 142:4 the psalmist says refuge failed him and no man cared for his soul, and in Job 11:20 the wicked shall not escape. The word holds both the shelter and the failure to find one.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe mânôwç names the God I run to when there is nowhere else. I hold that every other refuge fails, as the psalmist found, and that the LORD alone stands when all else gives way.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a nodding or toss (of the head in derision)
BiblicalUsage: mânôwd is a nodding or tossing of the head in derision, and it occurs once, in Psalms 44:14. There God has made His people a byword among the heathen, a shaking of the head among the peoples. The word is the gesture of contempt, the head shaken at a defeated people.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe mânôwd shows me that God's people have borne contempt before, and that the shaking head of the world is not the last word.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a continuator, i.e. heir
BiblicalUsage: mânôwn is a continuator, an heir, and it occurs once, in Proverbs 29:21. There a servant delicately brought up from a child shall at length become a son. The word is the one who carries the house on after the master.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe mânôwn reminds me that how a household is raised decides who inherits it, and that grace can turn a servant into a son.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a yoke (properly, for plowing), i.e. the frame of a loom
BiblicalUsage: mânôwr is a weaver's beam, the heavy frame of a loom, and it is also the yoke for ploughing. In 1 Samuel 17:7 the staff of Goliath's spear is like a weaver's beam, and in 2 Samuel 21:19 the brother of Goliath carries a spear of the same size. The word measures a giant by the loom he would dwarf.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe mânôwr shows me that even giants are measured against ordinary work, and that God delights in bringing down what looks too big to fall.
RelatedTopics: Victory; God's Power; Strength in weakness
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a derivative of G3105 (meaning a prophet, as supposed to rave through inspiration); to divine, i.e. utter spells (under pretense of foretelling:--by soothsaying.
BiblicalUsage: manteúomai is to divine, to utter spells, and it occurs once, in Acts 16:16. A slave girl possessed with a spirit of divination meets Paul and Silas on the way to prayer, and her soothsaying brings her masters much gain. The word is fortune-telling as a business.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe manteúomai exposes divination for what it is, a spirit that profits masters and enslaves the girl, and I hold that God's people have no business buying what it sells.
RelatedEvents: Paul Frees the Enslaved Girl at Philippi
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: prolongation from a primary verb, another form of which, μαθέω, is used as an alternate in certain tenses; to learn (in any way):--learn, understand.
BiblicalUsage: manthánō is to learn, and it runs through the New Testament as a disciple's word. In Matthew 11:29 Jesus says, learn of me, for I am meek and lowly in heart, and in John 6:45 everyone who has heard and learned of the Father comes to Christ. In Hebrews 5:8 the Son Himself learned obedience by the things He suffered, and in Philippians 4:11 Paul says he has learned to be content in whatever state he is in. Learning here is not information but formation.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe manthánō teaches me that discipleship is learning by following, not only by study. I hold that Christ learned obedience through suffering, so I should not expect to learn contentment without cost.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an opener, i.e. a key
BiblicalUsage: maphtêach is a key, an opener. In Isaiah 22:22 the key of the house of David is laid on Eliakim's shoulder, so he shall open and none shall shut, and shut and none shall open. In Judges 3:25 the servants take a key and open the doors of the parlour to find their lord fallen dead., and a key in Scripture is authority, not only iron.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe maphtêach shows me that the right key belongs to the house of David, and I hold that Christ holds it now, opening doors no man can shut.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a breathing out (of life), i.e. expiring
BiblicalUsage: mappâch is the breathing out of life, expiring, and it occurs once, in Job 11:20. There the hope of the wicked shall be as the giving up of the ghost, their last breath. The word is the end of hope itself.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe mappâch warns me that a hope set on anything but God expires with the breath, and that my hope must be fixed where breath does not fail.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a falling off, i.e. chaff; also something pendulous, i.e. a flap
BiblicalUsage: mappâl carries two pictures, the chaff that falls off in winnowing and the flakes that hang loose. In Amos 8:6 the greedy sell the refuse of the wheat to the poor, and in Job 41:23 the flakes of Leviathan's flesh are joined together and cannot be moved. The word is what falls away and what hangs on.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe mappâl shows me the difference between refuse and strength, and I hold that God separates the chaff from the wheat in His own time.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: something fallen, i.e. a ruin
BiblicalUsage: mappâlâh is a ruin, something fallen that stays fallen. In Isaiah 17:1 Damascus shall be taken away from being a city and become a ruinous heap, and in Isaiah 25:2 a defenced city is made a ruin that shall never be built. In Isaiah 23:13 the Assyrian brings Tyre's palaces to ruin. The word is the end of proud cities.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe mappâlâh shows me that no city stands for ever against God. I hold that the ruins of Damascus and Tyre preach what pride refuses to hear, and that only God's city endures.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a smiting to pieces
BiblicalUsage: mappâts is a smiting to pieces, a weapon of slaughter, and it occurs once, in Ezekiel 9:2. There six men come from the higher gate, every man with a slaughter weapon in his hand, to carry out judgment on Jerusalem. The word is the instrument of a judgment already decided.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe mappâts reminds me that God's judgment is not a threat without an instrument, and that the city that refuses Him will meet the weapon.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: fall, i.e. decadence; concretely, a ruin; specifically a carcase
BiblicalUsage: mappeleth is a fall, a ruin, and sometimes a carcase. In Ezekiel 27:27 Tyre's riches and mariners fall into the midst of the seas in the day of her ruin, and in Ezekiel 31:16 the nations shake at the sound of Assyria's fall. In Judges 14:8 Samson turns aside to see the carcase of the lion, and in Proverbs 29:16 the righteous shall see the fall of the wicked. The word is the crash after the pride.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe mappeleth teaches me that every fall has a sound, and the righteous will see it. I hold that the fall of the proud is God's doing, not man's revenge, and I will leave the crashing to Him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a smiter, i.e. a war club
BiblicalUsage: mappêts is a smiter, a war club or battle axe, and it occurs once, in Jeremiah 51:20. There God calls His servant His battle axe and weapons of war, and says with him He will break in pieces the nations and destroy kingdoms. The word is a person used as God's weapon.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe mappêts shows me that God can make a man His battle axe, and I hold that being His weapon is better than being His target.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: the bellows (i.e. blower) of a forge
BiblicalUsage: mappuach is the bellows of a forge, and it occurs once, in Jeremiah 6:29. There the bellows are burned, the lead is consumed of the fire, and the founder melts in vain, for the wicked are not plucked away. The word is the tool of refining worn out on dross that will not purify.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe mappuach shows me that refining can fail when the heart will not melt, and that God's fire is not wasted, only His patience tested.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, a melting, i.e. putridity
BiblicalUsage: maq is rottenness, a melting into putridity. In Isaiah 5:24 the root of the faithless shall be as rottenness and their blossom as dust, because they cast away the law of the LORD, and in Isaiah 3:24 sweet smell gives way to stink and beauty to burning. The word is decay as judgment.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe maq shows me that sin rots from the root, and I hold that a life that despises God's word will not hold its beauty long.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to melt; figuratively, to flow, dwindle, vanish
BiblicalUsage: mâqaq is to melt away, to pine and dwindle. In Leviticus 26:39 those left in their enemies' lands shall pine away in their iniquity, and in Ezekiel 33:10 the house of Israel asks how they shall live if they pine away in their sins. In Psalms 38:5 the psalmist's wounds stink and are corrupt, and in Zechariah 14:12 the flesh of Jerusalem's enemies shall consume away while they stand. The word is the slow wasting of sin and judgment alike.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe mâqaq tells the truth about sin, that it wastes a person away from the inside. I hold that the only answer to pining away is the repentance Ezekiel's hearers were offered, and I will take it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Makats, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Mâqats is Makaz, a place in Solomon's kingdom named once, in 1 Kings 4:9. The son of Dekar is set over Makaz and Shaalbim and Beth-shemesh and Elon-beth-hanan, as one of the officers who provisioned the king's table. The name survives as a line in Solomon's administration.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Mâqats shows me that God records even the small towns that fed a king, and that no place is too small for His book.
RelatedTopics: Kingdom of God; History; God's Provision
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an assembly
BiblicalUsage: maqhêl is an assembly or congregation, and it occurs twice, both times in the Psalms. In Psalms 26:12 the psalmist says in the congregations he will bless the LORD, and in Psalms 68:26 the call is to bless God in the congregations, from the fountain of Israel. The word is God's people gathered to bless Him.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe maqhêl shows me that blessing God is a congregational act, and I hold that my praise is fullest when it joins the assembly.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Makheloth, a place in the Desert
BiblicalUsage: Maqhêlôth is Makheloth, a camp in the wilderness journey, named in Numbers 33:25 and Numbers 33:26. Israel removes from Haradah and pitches in Makheloth, then removes from Makheloth and encamps at Tahath. The name is one night's stop on the long road.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Maqhêlôth reminds me that the wilderness road was walked one camp at a time, and that God led His people through places whose names we barely remember.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, a standing, i.e. a spot; but used widely of a locality (general or specific); also (figuratively) of a condition (of body or mind)
BiblicalUsage: mâqôwm is a place, a standing spot, and it is one of the commonest words in the Bible. In Genesis 31:55 Laban returns to his place, and in Exodus 3:5 the place where Moses stands is holy ground. In Deuteronomy 12:5 the place God chooses to put His name is the place of worship, and in Genesis 28:17 Jacob calls Bethel the house of God and the gate of heaven. A place in Scripture is never only ground.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe mâqôwm teaches me that God hallows places. I hold that the ground where He meets me becomes holy, whether it is a bush, a dream, or a chosen mountain.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, something dug, i.e. a (general) source (of water, even when naturally flowing; also of tears, blood (by euphemism, of the female pudenda); figuratively, of happiness, wisdom, progeny)
BiblicalUsage: mâqôwr is a fountain, a source of water and of life. In Jeremiah 2:13 God calls Himself the fountain of living waters, forsaken for broken cisterns, and in Jeremiah 17:13 those who forsake the fountain of living waters shall be ashamed. In Proverbs 5:18 a man's fountain is blessed, and in Zechariah 13:1 a fountain is opened to the house of David for sin and uncleanness. The word is the source itself, not the stream.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe mâqôwr names the God who is the source of all living water. I hold that every broken cistern I dig will run dry, and that the fountain opened for sin is the only water that cleanses.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, a perforatrix, i.e. a hammer (as piercing)
BiblicalUsage: maqqâbâh is a hammer, the tool that pierces and shapes. In 1 Kings 6:7 the temple is built of stone made ready beforehand, so that neither hammer nor axe nor any tool of iron is heard in the house while it is building. In Isaiah 44:12 the smith fashions an idol with hammers and works with the strength of his arms until he faints., and the same hammer can build God's house in silence or make an idol.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe maqqâbâh shows me that tools take their meaning from the hand that holds them, and I hold that quiet obedience builds better than loud idolatry.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: something received, i.e. merchandise (purchased)
BiblicalUsage: maqqâchâh is merchandise, something received in trade, and it occurs once, in Nehemiah 10:31. There the people promise that if traders bring ware or victuals on the Sabbath to sell, they will not buy it of them on the Sabbath or the holy day. The word is the market held outside the Sabbath.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe maqqâchâh shows me that even honest trade must wait for the Sabbath, and that rest is worth more than a bargain.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, a perforator, i.e. a hammer (as piercing); also (intransitively) a perforation, i.e. a quarry
BiblicalUsage: maqqebeth is a hammer, and also the hole it makes, a quarry. In Judges 4:21 Jael takes a hammer in her hand and smites the nail into Sisera's temples, and in Isaiah 51:1 God's people are told to look to the rock from which they are hewn and the hole of the pit from which they are dug. The word is both the blow and the hollow it leaves.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe maqqebeth reminds me that God hews His people out of hard rock, and that the same blow that kills a tyrant can dig a people out of the pit.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Makkedah, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Maqqêdâh is Makkedah, a Canaanite city Joshua took on the day of the great slaughter. In Joshua 10:10 Israel chases the enemy to Makkedah, and in Joshua 10:28 Joshua takes Makkedah and utterly destroys it and its king. In Joshua 15:41 it stands in the list of Judah's cities., and the name marks a victory and a possession.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Maqqêdâh shows me that God gives His people real victories in real places, and that the ground of those victories is worth remembering.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a shoot, i.e. stick (with leaves on, or for walking, striking, guiding, divining)
BiblicalUsage: maqqêl is a rod or staff, a shoot cut for walking, striking, or guiding. In Exodus 12:11 Israel eats the passover with a staff in hand, ready to travel, and in 1 Samuel 17:40 David takes his staff in his hand to meet Goliath. In Genesis 30:37 Jacob takes rods of green poplar and piles white streaks in them, and in Zechariah 11:7 the prophet takes two staves, Beauty and Bands, to feed the flock. A staff here is a tool, a weapon, and a sign of care.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe maqqêl teaches me that a staff can be a shepherd's tool, a pilgrim's companion, or a prophet's burden. I hold that what I carry in my hand should serve God's purpose.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an angle or recess
BiblicalUsage: maqtsôwaʻ is a corner or angle, the join where walls meet. In Exodus 26:24 the boards of the tabernacle are coupled together for the two corners, and in Nehemiah 3:19 Ezer repairs another piece over against the going up to the armoury at the turning of the wall. The word is the corner that holds the building together.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe maqtsôwaʻ shows me that even the corners of God's house are joined with care, and that no part of His work is careless.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a scraper, i.e. a carving chisel
BiblicalUsage: maqtsuʻâh is a carving chisel, a scraper, and it occurs once, in Isaiah 44:13. There the carpenter stretches out his rule and marks the wood with a line and fits it with planes, and marks it out with the compass, and makes it after the figure of a man, to remain in the house. The word is the tool that turns a tree into an idol.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe maqtsuʻâh warns me that tools in the wrong hands carve idols, and that the same skill can serve God or make a god.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a vision; also (causatively) a mirror
BiblicalUsage: marʼâh is a vision, the sight God gives, and it is also a mirror. In Numbers 12:6 God says He will make Himself known to a prophet in a vision and speak to him in a dream, and in Ezekiel 1:1 the heavens are opened and Ezekiel sees visions of God. In Daniel 10:7 Daniel alone sees the vision while the men with him flee in fear, and in Genesis 46:2 God speaks to Israel in the visions of the night. The word is God showing, not man imagining.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe marʼâh shows me that God speaks in visions to those He has chosen. I hold that a true vision always agrees with His written word.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Maralah, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Marʻălâh is Maralah, a town on the border of Zebulun named once, in Joshua 19:11. There the border goes up toward the sea, and Maralah, and reaches to Dabbasheth and to the river before Jokneam. The name is a mark on the edge of an inheritance.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Marʻălâh shows me that God bounded His people's land with care, and that even a border town is part of the inheritance.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, headship, i.e. (plural for collective) dominion
BiblicalUsage: marʼâshâh is headship, dominion, a principality, and it occurs once, in Jeremiah 13:18. There the king and queen are told to humble themselves and sit down, for their principalities shall come down, even the crown of their glory. The word is the rule that is about to fall.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe marʼâshâh warns me that crowns and principalities come down when God humbles them, and that my pride should sit down before He makes it sit.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a view (the act of seeing); also an appearance (the thing seen), whether (real) a shape (especially if handsome, comeliness; often plural the looks), or (mental) a vision
BiblicalUsage: marʼeh is appearance, the look of a thing and the act of seeing it. In 1 Samuel 16:7 the LORD tells Samuel that man looks on the outward appearance but the LORD looks on the heart, and in 1 Samuel 17:42 Goliath disdains David because he is a youth, ruddy, and of fair countenance. In 2 Samuel 11:2 David sees a woman washing herself, very beautiful to look upon, and in 2 Samuel 14:27 Absalom's daughter Tamar is a woman of fair countenance. The word is the face that deceives and the face that is judged.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe marʼeh teaches me that God judges by the heart and not by the face. I hold that the beauty I chase should be the beauty of a heart seen by Him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Mareshah, the name of two Israelites and of a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Marʼêshâh is the name of two Israelites and of a town in Judah. In 1 Chronicles 2:42 Mareshah is the son of Caleb's brother Jerahmeel and the father of Hebron, and in 2 Chronicles 11:8 Mareshah stands among the fenced cities of Judah. In 2 Chronicles 14:9 Zerah the Ethiopian comes out against Judah as far as Mareshah., and the name is a family line and a fortified place.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Marʼêshâh shows me that one name can belong to a man and a town, and that God keeps both in His record.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a drop
BiblicalUsage: mar is a drop, and it occurs once, in Isaiah 40:15. There the nations are as a drop of a bucket, and are counted as the small dust of the balance, and God takes up the isles as a very little thing. The word makes the whole world a drop in His hand.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe mar shows me how small the nations look beside God, and I hold that my own smallness is no threat to a God who holds the isles like a little thing.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a drop
BiblicalUsage: mar is a drop, and it occurs once, in Isaiah 40:15. There the nations are as a drop of a bucket, and are counted as the small dust of the balance, and God takes up the isles as a very little thing. The word makes the whole world a drop in His hand.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe mar shows me how small the nations look beside God, and I hold that my own smallness is no threat to a God who holds the isles like a little thing.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Mara, a symbolic name of Naomi
BiblicalUsage: Mârâʼ is Mara, the name Naomi takes for herself in her bitterness. In Ruth 1:20 she says, call me not Naomi, call me Mara, for the Almighty has dealt very bitterly with me. The name is not a new person but a sorrowful renaming, and her story lives on her People profile.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Mârâʼ tells me that bitterness can be named honestly before God, and I hold that Naomi's bitter name is not the end of her story.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to rebel; hence (through the idea of maltreating) to whip, i.e. lash (self with wings, as the ostrich in running)
BiblicalUsage: mârâʼ is to rebel, and by a second picture to lash oneself, as the ostrich does with her wings in running. In Zephaniah 3:1 woe is pronounced on the filthy and polluted oppressing city, and in Job 39:18 the ostrich lifts herself up on high and scorns the horse and his rider. The word joins rebellion to a creature showing off its speed.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe mârâʼ warns me that rebellion can look like strength, like an ostrich lifting herself high, and I hold that the city that will not be cleansed will be judged.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, to soften by rubbing or pressure; hence (medicinally) to apply as an emollient
BiblicalUsage: mârach is to soften by rubbing, to apply as an emollient, and it occurs once, in Isaiah 38:21. There Isaiah says to take a lump of figs and lay it for a plaster upon Hezekiah's boil, and he shall recover. The word is the poultice that heals a king.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe mârach shows me that God heals with ordinary means, a lump of figs on a boil, and that I should not despise the simple remedy He gives.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: rebellious
BiblicalUsage: mârâd is rebellious in Aramaic, and it occurs twice, both times in the mouths of Jerusalem's enemies. In Ezra 4:12 the adversaries tell the king the Jews are building the rebellious and the bad city, and in Ezra 4:15 they say search the records and you will find this city is a rebellious city, hurtful to kings. The word is the charge laid against a people rebuilding.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe mârâd shows me how quickly a rebuilding people can be called rebels, and that the accusation does not make it true.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to rebel
BiblicalUsage: mârad is to rebel, and it runs through the history of Israel's kings. In 2 Chronicles 13:6 Jeroboam rebels against his lord Solomon's son, and in 2 Chronicles 36:13 Zedekiah rebels against Nebuchadnezzar, stiffening his neck and hardening his heart from turning to the LORD. In 2 Kings 18:7 Hezekiah rebels against the king of Assyria and prospers, and in 2 Kings 18:20 the Assyrian asks on whom Hezekiah trusts that he rebels. The word is the same act, blessed or cursed by whom it is against.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe mârad shows me that rebellion is never a small thing. I hold that the stiff neck and the hardened heart are the same sin, whether against a king or against God.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Marah, a place in the Desert
BiblicalUsage: Mârâh is Marah, the place of bitter water on the road from the Red Sea. In Exodus 15:23 Israel comes to Marah and cannot drink the waters, for they are bitter, and the place is called Marah. In Numbers 33:8 and Numbers 33:9 Israel pitches in Marah and then removes to Elim, where there are twelve fountains and seventy palm trees., and the name is one stop between bitterness and plenty.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Mârâh shows me that God turns bitter water sweet for His people, and I hold that the places of my bitterness are where He proves Himself.
RelatedEvents: The Exodus and the Red Sea
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to be (causatively, make) bitter (or unpleasant); (figuratively) to rebel (or resist; causatively, to provoke)
BiblicalUsage: mârâh is to be bitter, and figuratively to rebel and resist. In 1 Samuel 12:14 Samuel says that if Israel will not rebel against the commandment of the LORD, they and their king shall continue following Him, and in 1 Kings 13:21 the man of God is judged because he disobeyed the mouth of the LORD. In Hosea 13:16 Samaria shall become desolate because she has rebelled against her God. The word is bitterness that turns into disobedience.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe mârâh shows me that bitterness and rebellion are the same root in the heart. I hold that the cure for both is to obey the voice I have been resisting.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain affinity; to extinguish (as fire), i.e. (figuratively and passively) to pass away:--fade away.
BiblicalUsage: maraínō is to fade away, like a flower scorched by the sun, and it occurs once, in James 1:11. There the sun rises with burning heat and withers the grass, and the flower falls, and the grace of its fashion perishes, and so shall the rich man fade away in his ways. The word is glory wilting in the heat.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe maraínō shows me that the rich man's glory withers like a flower in the heat, and I will not build my life on what fades.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Chaldee origin (meaning our Lord has come); maranatha, i.e. an exclamation of the approaching divine judgment:--Maran-atha.
BiblicalUsage: maràn athá is Maranatha, our Lord has come, and it occurs once, in 1 Corinthians 16:22. There Paul writes that if any man love not the Lord Jesus Christ, let him be Anathema Maranatha. The phrase is a cry of longing and a warning at once.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe maràn athá is my cry as well as Paul's, that the Lord has come and is coming again, and I will not love Him coldly.
RelatedTopics: Second Coming; Love for God; Hope
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: soup (as if a rinsing)
BiblicalUsage: mârâq is broth, soup, the liquid of cooked meat. In Judges 6:19 Gideon puts the broth in a pot and brings it out to the angel under the oak, and in Isaiah 65:4 the faithless eat swine's flesh, and broth of abominable things is in their vessels. The word is the broth of an offering and the broth of an abomination.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe mârâq shows me that a simple broth can be an offering, and that what is abominable in the pot is an abomination before God.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)
