Definition: to polish; by implication, to sharpen; also to rinse
BiblicalUsage: mâraq is to polish, to sharpen, and to rinse or scour. In Leviticus 6:28 a brazen pot in which the sin offering is sodden shall be both scoured and rinsed in water, and in Proverbs 20:30 the blueness of a wound cleanses away evil, as stripes cleanse the inward parts. The word is scouring that makes clean.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe mâraq shows me that God provides cleansing for His vessels, and that a wound rightly borne can cleanse the heart.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to be (causatively, make) bitter (literally or figuratively)
BiblicalUsage: mârar is to be bitter, or to make bitter. In Exodus 1:14 the Egyptians make Israel's lives bitter with hard bondage, in mortar and in brick and in all service in the field. In 2 Kings 4:27 the Shunammite's soul is vexed within her, and in Daniel 8:7 and Daniel 11:11 kings are moved with choler, bitter anger, against their enemies. The word is the taste of oppression and of rage.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe mârar shows me that bitterness is the fruit of bondage. I hold that God who heard Israel in Egypt hears me in mine.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to polish; by implication, to make bald (the head), to gall (the shoulder); also, to sharpen
BiblicalUsage: mâraṭ is to polish, to make bright, and by implication to sharpen. In 1 Kings 7:45 the vessels Hiram makes for Solomon's house are of bright brass, and in Ezekiel 21:9 the sword is sharpened and also furbished. The word is the shine on a vessel and the edge on a sword.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe mâraṭ shows me that God polishes His vessels bright and sharpens His sword, and that the same hand does both.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, to press, i.e. (figuratively) to be pungent or vehement; to irritate
BiblicalUsage: mârats is to press hard, to be pungent and vehement, to irritate. In Job 6:25 Job asks how forcible right words are, and what his friends' arguing reproves, and in Micah 2:10 the people are told to arise and depart, because the land is polluted and will destroy them with a sore destruction. The word is pressure that stings.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe mârats warns me that right words can cut, and that a polluted rest is no rest at all.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a coverlet
BiblicalUsage: marbad is a coverlet, a tapestry covering for a bed. In Proverbs 7:16 the strange woman says she has decked her bed with coverings of tapestry and fine linen of Egypt, and in Proverbs 31:22 the virtuous woman makes herself coverings of tapestry and clothes herself in silk and purple. The same word dresses two very different beds.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe marbad warns me that the bed I make for pleasure can be the bed of a stranger's sin, and that the same covering can serve a wise woman or a seductress.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, increasing; as noun, greatness, or (adverbially) greatly
BiblicalUsage: marbeh is increase, greatness, the growing of a thing. In Isaiah 9:7 it stands in the promise of the increase of His government and peace, with no end, upon the throne of David, and in Isaiah 33:23 it names the prey of a great spoil divided when the enemy's tackle fails. The word is growth and abundance together.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe marbeh shows me that God increases what is His, and I hold that the increase of His government is the only increase that never ends.
RelatedTopics: Kingdom of God; God's Provision; Peace
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a stall (for cattle)
BiblicalUsage: marbêq is a stall for cattle, the place where the fatted calf is kept. In 1 Samuel 28:24 the woman of Endor has a fat calf in the house and kills it for Saul, and in Malachi 4:2 those who fear God's name shall go forth and grow up as calves of the stall when the Sun of righteousness arises. The word is the stall that fattens and the stall that frees.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe marbêq reminds me that God feeds His own from the stall, and I hold that the calves of the stall grow up under His care.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a reclining place, i.e. fold (for flocks)
BiblicalUsage: marbêts is a resting place for flocks, a fold where they lie down. In Ezekiel 25:5 Rabbah shall be made a stable for camels and the Ammonites a couching place for flocks, and in Zephaniah 2:15 the rejoicing city shall become a desolation, a place for beasts to lie down in. The word is the ground where creatures rest, given or taken.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe marbêts shows me that God gives rest to flocks and ruin to proud cities, and that the same ground can be a fold or a desolation.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a multitude; also offspring; specifically interest (on capital)
BiblicalUsage: marbîyth is a multitude, an increase, and sometimes interest on capital. In 2 Chronicles 30:18 a multitude of the people eat the passover though they have not cleansed themselves, and Hezekiah prays for them. In 1 Samuel 2:33 the increase of Eli's house shall die in the flower of their age, and in 2 Chronicles 9:6 the queen of Sheba says the one half of the greatness of Solomon's wisdom was not told her. The word is more than expected, for good or for ill.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe marbîyth shows me that God measures increase exactly. I hold that the greatness of His wisdom is always more than I was told.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Marsena, a Persian
BiblicalUsage: Marçᵉnâʼ is Marsena, one of the seven princes of Persia and Media. In Esther 1:14 he stands next to the king, among those who saw the king's face and sat first in the kingdom. The name is a single line in a court list.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Marsena shows me that God names even the princes who sit near a king, and that no court is outside His sight.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a stewpan
BiblicalUsage: marchesheth is a stewpan or frying pan, and it occurs twice, both times in the law of the meat offering. In Leviticus 2:7 an oblation baked in the frying pan shall be made of fine flour with oil, and in Leviticus 7:9 all that is dressed in the frying pan shall be the priest's that offers it. The word is the kitchen vessel of sacrifice.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe marchesheth shows me that God cares about the vessels of His worship, and that the frying pan has its place in His law.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: rebelliousness
BiblicalUsage: mardûwth is rebelliousness, and it occurs once, in 1 Samuel 20:30. There Saul's anger is kindled against Jonathan, and he calls him the son of a perverse rebellious woman, because Jonathan has chosen David. The word is rebellion used as an insult.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe mardûwth shows me how anger turns a father's tongue cruel, and that Saul's insult to Jonathan is the sound of rebellion curdling into hate.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a master
BiblicalUsage: mârêʼ is master, the Aramaic word for lord, and it belongs to Daniel's court. In Daniel 2:47 Nebuchadnezzar calls Daniel's God a God of gods and a Lord of kings, and in Daniel 4:19 Daniel answers his lord the king with troubled thoughts. In Daniel 4:24 the decree of the Most High has come upon my lord the king, and in Daniel 5:23 Belshazzar lifts himself against the Lord of heaven. The word is the title men give kings, and the title that belongs to God.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe mârêʼ teaches me that earthly masters are many but the Lord of heaven is one. I hold that Daniel's God is the master worth serving.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from μάργαρος (a pearl-oyster); a pearl:--pearl.
BiblicalUsage: margarítēs is a pearl, and Jesus makes it the picture of the kingdom. In Matthew 13:45 a merchant seeks goodly pearls, and in Matthew 13:46, when he finds one pearl of great price, he sells all he has and buys it. In Matthew 7:6 Jesus warns not to cast pearls before swine, and in 1 Timothy 2:9 pearls stand for costly adornment. The word is beauty that is worth everything.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe margarítēs shows me what the kingdom is worth. I hold that selling all to gain it is no loss at all.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: rest
BiblicalUsage: margêʻâh is rest, and it occurs once, in Isaiah 28:12. There the LORD says this is the rest with which you may cause the weary to rest, and this is the refreshing, yet they would not hear. The word is the rest that was offered and refused.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe margêʻâh shows me that God offers rest to the weary, and that refusing it is the surest way to lose it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: (plural for collective) a footpiece, i.e. (adverbially) at the foot, or (direct.) the foot itself
BiblicalUsage: margᵉlâh is a footpiece, the place at the feet, and it belongs to Ruth's story. In Ruth 3:4 Naomi tells Ruth to uncover Boaz's feet and lie down, and in Ruth 3:8 Boaz wakes at midnight to find a woman lying at his feet. In Daniel 10:6 the same word names the feet of the shining man, like polished brass., and the word is the low place that asks for covering.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe margᵉlâh shows me that Ruth lay at the feet of the man who could redeem her, and I hold that my own place is at the feet of my Redeemer.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a stone-heap
BiblicalUsage: margêmâh is a heap of stones, and it occurs once, in Proverbs 26:8. There the man who gives honour to a fool is like one who binds a stone in a sling, a weight that will fly back at him. The word is honour wasted on the wrong person.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe margêmâh warns me that honour given to a fool is a stone tied where it will do harm, and that my praise should go where it belongs.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a resting place
BiblicalUsage: margôwaʻ is a resting place, and it occurs once, in Jeremiah 6:16. There the LORD says to stand in the ways and ask for the old paths, where the good way is, and walk in it, and find rest for the souls. The word is the rest at the end of the right road.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe margôwaʻ shows me that rest is found on the old paths, and I hold that the good way is the one God marked long ago.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: or Μαριάμ of Hebrew origin (H4813); Maria or Mariam (i.e. Mirjam), the name of six Christian females:-- Mary.
BiblicalUsage: María is Mary, the name of six women in the New Testament, and this study follows the name rather than one life. In John 11:1 Mary of Bethany is named with her sister Martha, and in John 11:20 Mary sits still in the house while Martha goes to meet Jesus. In John 19:25 Mary the mother of Jesus stands by the cross with Mary Magdalene., and each Mary's story lives on her own People profile.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe María shows me that God works through ordinary women who believe Him, and I hold that the mother who stood by the cross and the sister who sat at His feet both belong in the story.
RelatedPeople: Mary, Mother of Jesus; Mary Magdalene; Mary of Bethany
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a mart
BiblicalUsage: markôleth is a mart, a market, and it occurs once, in Ezekiel 27:24. There Tyre's merchants trade in all sorts of things, in blue clothes and embroidered work and in chests of rich apparel, bound with cords and made of cedar, among her merchandise. The word is the market stall of a proud city.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe markôleth shows me that Tyre's markets sold the world its finery, and that every mart of the nations will answer to God.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Latin origin; Marcus, a Christian:--Marcus, Mark.
BiblicalUsage: Márkos is Mark, John Mark, whose house in Jerusalem sheltered the praying church. In Acts 12:12 Peter comes to the house of Mary the mother of John, whose surname was Mark, where many are gathered praying. In Colossians 4:10 Paul calls Marcus the sister's son of Barnabas, and in 2 Timothy 4:11 he asks for Mark, saying he is profitable to him for the ministry., and his story lives on his People profile.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Márkos shows me that a man who once left the work can come back to it, and I hold that Mark's restoration is one of the kindest stories in the New Testament.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from μαρμαίρω (to glisten); marble (as sparkling white):--marble.
BiblicalUsage: mármaros is marble, white stone that glistens, and it occurs once, in Revelation 18:12. There marble stands in the long list of Babylon's merchandise, gold and silver and precious stones and pearls and fine linen and purple and silk and scarlet and ivory and brass and iron and marble. The word is luxury in a city about to fall.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe mármaros shows me that even the finest stone is cargo in a doomed city, and I will not build my hope on marble.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: altitude, i.e. concretely (an elevated place), abstractly (elevation, figuratively (elation), or adverbially (aloft)
BiblicalUsage: mârôwm is height, an elevated place and the idea of being lifted up. In 2 Kings 19:22 Sennacherib lifts his eyes on high against the Holy One of Israel, and in 2 Kings 19:23 he boasts of coming up to the height of the mountains. In 2 Samuel 22:17 God sends from above and draws David out of many waters, and in Ecclesiastes 10:6 folly is set in great dignity while the rich sit low. The word is the high place, God's or man's.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe mârôwm teaches me to lift my eyes to the God on high. I hold that the high places of men are nothing beside Him.
RelatedTopics: God's Sovereignty; Majesty of God; Pride
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Maroth, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Mârôwth is Maroth, a town named once, in Micah 1:12. There the inhabitant of Maroth waits carefully for good, but evil comes down from the LORD to the gate of Jerusalem. The name is a town waiting for a good that does not come.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Mârôwth shows me that waiting for good does not always bring it, and that the evil that came to Maroth's gate is a warning I should heed.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, curative, i.e. literally (concretely) a medicine, or (abstractly) a cure; figuratively (concretely) deliverance, or (abstractly) placidity
BiblicalUsage: marpêʼ is a cure, a medicine, and sometimes the health itself. In Jeremiah 8:15 the people look for peace and for a time of health, and behold trouble, and in 2 Chronicles 36:16 the wrath of the LORD arises until there is no remedy. In 2 Chronicles 21:18 Jehoram is smitten with an incurable disease, and in Ecclesiastes 10:4 yielding pacifies great offences. The word is the healing that comes and the healing that is refused.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe marpêʼ teaches me that God is the healer. I hold that when there is no remedy, it is because the wound has been refused, not because He cannot heal.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably of Chaldee origin (meaning mistress); Martha, a Christian woman:--Martha.
BiblicalUsage: Mártha is Martha of Bethany, sister of Mary and Lazarus. In John 11:1 Lazarus is sick in the town of Mary and her sister Martha, and in John 11:5 Jesus loved Martha and her sister and Lazarus. In John 11:19 many Jews come to Martha and Mary to comfort them concerning their brother., and her story lives on her People profile, and this study covers only the name.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Mártha teaches me that serving matters and that worry does not, and I hold that Jesus loved her exactly as she was, busy and anxious, and called her to the better part.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an awl
BiblicalUsage: martsêaʻ is an awl, the tool that bores a servant's ear to the door. In Exodus 21:6 the master brings the servant to the door post and bores his ear through with an awl, and he shall serve him for ever. In Deuteronomy 15:17 the same is done for a maidservant., and the word is the tool of a lifelong choice.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe martsêaʻ shows me that a servant who loves his master can choose to stay for ever, and that the mark of that choice is worn in the ear.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a pavement
BiblicalUsage: martsepheth is a pavement, and it occurs once, in 2 Kings 16:17. There King Ahaz cuts off the borders of the bases and takes down the sea from the brazen oxen, and puts it upon a pavement of stones. The word is the stone floor under a king's meddling.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe martsepheth shows me that even a king's pavement can be stripped of its glory, and that Ahaz's changes to the temple are a warning about tampering with God's house.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3144; to be a witness, i.e. testify (literally or figuratively):--charge, give (evidence), bear record, have (obtain, of) good (honest) report, be well reported of, testify, give (have) testimony, (be, bear, give, obtain) witness.
BiblicalUsage: martyréō is to bear witness, to testify, and it carries the weight of the whole New Testament. In 1 John 1:2 the apostles have seen the life manifested and bear witness and show it, and in 1 John 4:14 they testify that the Father sent the Son to be the Saviour of the world. In 1 Corinthians 15:15 Paul says the apostles would be false witnesses of God if Christ were not raised, and in 1 John 5:6 the Spirit bears witness because the Spirit is truth. Witness here is sworn testimony, not opinion.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe martyréō teaches me that a witness is not a debater but someone who has seen. I hold that my testimony stands or falls on what I have seen of Christ.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3144; evidence given (judicially or genitive case):--record, report, testimony, witness.
BiblicalUsage: martyría is witness, testimony, the record given. In 1 John 5:9 the witness of God is greater than the witness of men, for it is the witness God has testified of His Son, and in 1 John 5:10 he who believes on the Son has the witness in himself. In 1 John 5:11 the record is that God has given us eternal life, and this life is in His Son. In 1 Timothy 3:7 a man must have a good report from those outside, lest he fall into reproach, and the word is the evidence that speaks for Christ.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe martyría teaches me that God's witness is greater than man's. I hold that the witness I carry in myself is the life He has given me.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: neuter of a presumed derivative of G3144; something evidential, i.e. (genitive case) evidence given or (specially), the Decalogue (in the sacred Tabernacle):--to be testified, testimony, witness.
BiblicalUsage: martýrion is a testimony, something evidential, the proof offered. In 1 Corinthians 1:6 the testimony of Christ is confirmed in the Corinthians, and in 1 Corinthians 2:1 Paul declares the testimony of God without excellency of speech. In 1 Timothy 2:6 Christ gives Himself a ransom for all, to be testified in due time, and in 2 Corinthians 1:12 Paul's rejoicing is the testimony of his conscience, in simplicity and godly sincerity. The word is the proof that stands up.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe martýrion shows me that my conscience can testify for me or against me. I hold that a clear conscience is worth more than a clever defence.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: middle voice from G3144; to be adduced as a witness, i.e. (figuratively) to obtest (in affirmation or exhortation):--take to record, testify.
BiblicalUsage: martýromai is to be adduced as a witness, to testify solemnly, to charge with an oath. In Acts 20:26 Paul takes his hearers to record that he is pure from the blood of all men, and in Acts 26:22 he witnesses to small and great of what the prophets and Moses said should come. In Ephesians 4:17 Paul testifies in the Lord that believers should no longer walk as other Gentiles walk, and in 1 Thessalonians 2:12 he charges them to walk worthy of God. The word is testimony that binds the hearer.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe martýromai teaches me that a witness can also be a solemn charge. I hold that Paul's testimony to the Gentiles is the charge I inherit.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an outcast; (abstractly) destitution
BiblicalUsage: mârûwd is an outcast, and in the abstract, destitution itself. In Isaiah 58:7 the fast God chooses is to bring the poor who are cast out to your house, and to cover the naked and not hide from your own flesh. In Lamentations 1:7 Jerusalem remembers her pleasant things in the days of her affliction and miseries, and in Lamentations 3:19 the prophet remembers his own affliction and misery, the wormwood and the gall. The word is the person with nowhere to go.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe mârûwd shows me that the outcast belongs at my table. I hold that the house that takes in the poor cast out is the house God blesses.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, rubbed; but used abstractly, a rubbing (with perfumery)
BiblicalUsage: mârûwq is a rubbing with perfumery, the purifying treatment of the women, and it occurs once, in Esther 2:12. There every maid's turn comes after twelve months, six months with oil of myrrh and six months with sweet odours and other things for the purifying of the women. The word is the slow preparation before the king.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe mârûwq shows me the long preparation behind Esther's hour, and that God readies His people long before they see why.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a cry, i.e. (of grief) a lamentation
BiblicalUsage: marzêach is a cry of grief, a lamentation, and it occurs once, in Jeremiah 16:5. There the LORD tells Jeremiah not to enter the house of mourning, nor to lament or bemoan them, for He has taken away His peace from this people, even lovingkindness and mercies. The word is the wailing that God forbids.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe marzêach shows me that God can forbid even mourning when judgment falls, and that His peace taken away is the deepest grief of all.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, (abstractly) a raising (as of the hands in prayer), or rising (of flame); figuratively, an utterance; concretely, a beacon (as raised); a present (as taken), mess, or tribute; figuratively, a reproach (as a burden)
BiblicalUsage: masʼêth is a lifting up, and it covers a gift sent, a burden laid on, and a collection raised. In 2 Samuel 11:8 a mess of meat follows Uriah from the king's house, and in Amos 5:11 the rich take burdens of wheat from the poor. In 2 Chronicles 24:6 and 2 Chronicles 24:9 the collection Moses laid on Israel in the wilderness is gathered for the tabernacle. The word is whatever is raised and carried to another.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe masʼêth shows me that what is lifted up before God can be a gift, a burden, or a tax. I hold that the offering I bring should be lifted with a willing heart.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a trough for cattle to drink from
BiblicalUsage: mashʼâb is a trough for cattle to drink from, a watering place, and it occurs once, in Judges 5:11. There those delivered from the noise of archers in the places of drawing water rehearse the righteous acts of the LORD toward the inhabitants of His villages. The word is the well where God's deeds are told.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe mashʼâb shows me that the watering places are where God's righteous acts are rehearsed, and that ordinary work is a good place to remember Him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Mash, a son of Aram, and the people descended from him
BiblicalUsage: Mash is a son of Aram and the people descended from him, named once, in Genesis 10:23. There the children of Aram are listed as Uz and Hul and Gether and Mash. The name is a single line in the table of nations.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Mash shows me that God keeps the sons of Aram in His record, and that no branch of Noah's family is forgotten by Him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to rub with oil, i.e. to anoint; by implication, to consecrate; also to paint
BiblicalUsage: mâshach is to anoint, to rub with oil and consecrate. In 1 Samuel 10:1 Samuel pours oil on Saul's head and says the LORD has anointed him captain over His inheritance, and in 1 Chronicles 11:3 the elders anoint David king over Israel. In 1 Kings 1:34 Zadok and Nathan anoint Solomon, and in 1 Chronicles 14:8 the Philistines hear that David is anointed king over all Israel. The word is God's choosing made visible in oil.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe mâshach is the mark of God's choosing. I hold that the anointing oil on a king, a priest, or a prophet points to the Anointed One, Jesus, in whom I am chosen too.
RelatedEvents: David Anointed by Samuel; Anointing of Saul as King
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to pull out (literally or figuratively)
BiblicalUsage: mâshâh is to draw out, to pull from the water. In Exodus 2:10 Pharaoh's daughter calls the child Moses, because she drew him out of the water, and in 2 Samuel 22:17 and Psalms 18:16 David says God sent from above and drew him out of many waters. The word is the rescue that gives Moses his name.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe mâshâh is the word of my own rescue. I hold that the God who drew Moses from the water draws me from the waters that would drown me.
RelatedEvents: Moses' Birth and Flight to Midian
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to draw, used in a great variety of applications (including to sow, to sound, to prolong, to develop, to march, to remove, to delay, to be tall, etc.)
BiblicalUsage: mâshak is to draw, and it is used for a bow, a yoke, a plough, and a melody. In 1 Kings 22:34 and 2 Chronicles 18:33 a man draws a bow at a venture and smites the king of Israel between the joints of the harness. In Deuteronomy 21:3 the heifer has not drawn in the yoke, and in Amos 9:13 the hills shall melt, drawn out like wax. The word is pulling, and what is pulled can be a weapon or a harvest.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe mâshak shows me that drawing can be gentle or violent. I hold that the same God who draws a bow in judgment draws me with cords of love.
RelatedTopics: God's Sovereignty; Judgment; Love of God
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to liken, i.e. (transitively) to use figurative language (an allegory, adage, song or the like); in transitively, to resemble
BiblicalUsage: mâshal is to liken, to speak in a proverb or parable, and it is also to rule. In Ezekiel 16:44 everyone who uses proverbs shall use this proverb against Jerusalem, as is the mother, so is her daughter, and in Ezekiel 17:2 the prophet is told to put forth a riddle and speak a parable. In Ezekiel 12:23 God says He will make the people's proverb cease, and in Ezekiel 18:2 He challenges the proverb about sour grapes. The word is truth carried in a picture.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe mâshal teaches me that God speaks in pictures when plain words would be ignored. I hold that His proverbs are true even when I dislike them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, a pithy maxim, usually of metaphorical nature; hence, a simile (as an adage, poem, discourse)
BiblicalUsage: mâshâl is a proverb, a pithy saying that carries truth in a picture. In 1 Kings 4:32 Solomon speaks three thousand proverbs, and in 1 Kings 9:7 Israel is warned she shall become a proverb and a byword among all people. In 1 Samuel 10:12 it becomes a proverb, Is Saul also among the prophets, and in 1 Samuel 24:13 the proverb of the ancients says wickedness proceeds from the wicked. The word is wisdom that can be remembered.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe mâshâl shows me that wisdom comes in short sentences that stay with me. I hold that Solomon's proverbs are God's gift to the ordinary day.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Mashal, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Mâshâl is Mashal, a town given to the Levites out of the tribe of Asher, named once, in 1 Chronicles 6:74. There Mashal with her suburbs is listed among the cities of the Gershonites. The name is a town and a provision.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Mâshâl shows me that God gives His servants towns to live in, and that a Levitical city is a provision, not an accident.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to liken, i.e. (transitively) to use figurative language (an allegory, adage, song or the like); in transitively, to resemble
BiblicalUsage: mâshal is to liken, to speak in a proverb or parable, and it is also to rule. In Ezekiel 16:44 everyone who uses proverbs shall use this proverb against Jerusalem, as is the mother, so is her daughter, and in Ezekiel 17:2 the prophet is told to put forth a riddle and speak a parable. In Ezekiel 12:23 God says He will make the people's proverb cease, and in Ezekiel 18:2 He challenges the proverb about sour grapes. The word is truth carried in a picture.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe mâshal teaches me that God speaks in pictures when plain words would be ignored. I hold that His proverbs are true even when I dislike them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to feel of; by implication, to grope
BiblicalUsage: mâshash is to feel, to grope with the hands. In Genesis 27:12 Jacob fears his father will feel him and find him a deceiver, and in Genesis 27:22 Isaac feels him and says the voice is Jacob's voice but the hands are the hands of Esau. In Exodus 10:21 the darkness over Egypt is a darkness that may be felt, and in Deuteronomy 28:29 the disobedient shall grope at noonday as the blind grope in darkness. The word is touch without sight.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe mâshash shows me that feeling for the truth in the dark is not the same as seeing it. I hold that God gives light to those who grope for Him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: destruction
BiblicalUsage: mashchêth is destruction, and it occurs once, in Ezekiel 9:1. There a voice cries for those who have charge over the city to draw near, every man with his destroying weapon in his hand. The word is the weapon of a judgment already ordered.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe mashchêth shows me that God's judgment has officers, and that the destroying weapon is not raised without His word.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: destructive, i.e. (as noun) destruction, literally (specifically a snare) or figuratively (corruption)
BiblicalUsage: mashchîyth is destruction and corruption, the destroyer at work. In 2 Chronicles 20:23 Ammon and Moab stand up to destroy the inhabitants of Seir, and then help to destroy one another. In Daniel 10:8 Daniel's comeliness is turned into corruption and he retains no strength, and in 2 Kings 23:13 the mount of corruption is defiled by Josiah. In 2 Chronicles 22:4 the counsellors of Ahaziah are his destruction, and the word is the ruin that works from within.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe mashchîyth shows me that corruption works quietly, turning strength to nothing. I hold that God alone can keep me from the destroyer.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: anointed; usually a consecrated person (as a king, priest, or saint); specifically, the Messiah
BiblicalUsage: mâshîyach is the anointed one, and it gathers kings, priests, and the Messiah into one word. In 1 Chronicles 16:22 God says, touch not mine anointed, and do my prophets no harm, and in 1 Samuel 2:10 the LORD shall exalt the horn of His anointed. In 1 Samuel 2:35 a faithful priest shall walk before His anointed for ever, and in 1 Samuel 12:3 Samuel stands before the LORD and before His anointed. The word is the chosen one, and it finds its full meaning in Christ.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe mâshîyach is the heart of the whole Bible. I hold that every anointed king and priest was a shadow of the Anointed One, Jesus, who is my King and my Priest for ever.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: fat, i.e. (literally and abstractly) fatness; but usually (figuratively and concretely) a rich dish, a fertile field, a robust man
BiblicalUsage: mashmân is fatness, the rich part of the land and of life. In Genesis 27:28 Isaac blesses Jacob with the dew of heaven and the fatness of the earth, and in Genesis 27:39 Esau's dwelling is also the fatness of the earth. In Isaiah 10:16 God sends leanness among the fat ones of Assyria, and in Daniel 11:24 a king enters the fattest places of the province and scatters prey and spoil. The word is plenty that can be given or taken.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe mashmân shows me that God gives fatness to His people and leanness to the proud. I hold that the fatness of the earth is His gift, not my right.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an oar
BiblicalUsage: mâshôwṭ is an oar, and it occurs twice, both times in the lament over Tyre. In Ezekiel 27:6 the oars of Tyre are made of the oaks of Bashan, and in Ezekiel 27:29 all who handle the oar, the mariners and the pilots of the sea, come down from their ships and stand upon the land. The word is the oar laid down in ruin.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe mâshôwṭ shows me that even the rowers of Tyre must come down from their ships, and that the sea gives no safety from God.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, causing to drink, i.e. a butler; by implication (intransitively), drink (itself); figuratively, a well-watered region
BiblicalUsage: mashqeh is a cupbearer, and by extension the drink itself, and it belongs to Solomon's court. In 1 Kings 10:5 the queen of Sheba sees the cupbearers and their apparel, and there is no more spirit in her, and in 2 Chronicles 9:4 the same scene is repeated. In 1 Kings 10:21 and 2 Chronicles 9:20 all Solomon's drinking vessels are of gold. The word is the servant who pours for the king.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe mashqeh shows me that the cupbearer stands close to the king. I hold that serving at the table is a place of honour, not of shame.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a lintel
BiblicalUsage: mashqôwph is a lintel, the upper door post, and it belongs to the passover night. In Exodus 12:7 the blood is struck on the two side posts and on the upper door post, and in Exodus 12:22 the lintel and the two side posts are struck with the blood in the basin. In Exodus 12:23 the LORD, seeing the blood upon the lintel, passes over the door and will not let the destroyer come in. The word is the beam the blood marks.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe mashqôwph shows me that the blood on the doorpost is the sign that saves. I hold that Christ is my lintel and my passover.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a (musical) pipe (from its whistling sound)
BiblicalUsage: mashrôwqîy is a musical pipe, and it occurs in the worship of Nebuchadnezzar's image. In Daniel 3:5 the sound of the cornet, flute, harp, sackbut, psaltery, dulcimer, and all kinds of music is the signal to fall down and worship the golden image, and in Daniel 3:7 all the people hear the sound and fall down. The word is the pipe that calls a nation to bow.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe mashrôwqîy shows me that music can be commanded to worship a false god, and that the sound of the pipes is no proof the worship is true.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a loan
BiblicalUsage: mashshâʼâh is a loan, and it occurs twice, both times about lending with restraint. In Deuteronomy 24:10 the lender shall not go into his brother's house to fetch his pledge, and in Proverbs 22:26 the warning is not to be one of those who strike hands or are sureties for debts. The word is the loan that must respect the borrower's home.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe mashshâʼâh shows me that God guards the poor man's door, and that a lender may not cross it to take a pledge.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: dissimulation
BiblicalUsage: mashshâʼôwn is dissimulation, deceit that covers hatred, and it occurs once, in Proverbs 26:26. There hatred covered by deceit will have its wickedness shown before the whole congregation. The word is the mask that will not hold.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe mashshâʼôwn shows me that hatred hidden by deceit is still hatred, and that it will be shown before the whole congregation.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a loan; by implication, interest on a debt
BiblicalUsage: mashshâʼ is a loan, and by implication the interest on a debt. In Nehemiah 5:7 Nehemiah rebukes the nobles and rulers, saying they exact usury, every one of his brother, and in Nehemiah 5:10 he confesses that he and his brethren and his servants might exact money and corn, and pleads that they leave off this usury. The word is the debt that grows on a brother.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe mashshâʼ shows me that charging interest to a brother in need is oppression, and I hold that Nehemiah's rebuke still stands.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a traversing, i.e. rapid motion
BiblicalUsage: mashshâq is a traversing, a rapid motion to and fro, and it occurs once, in Isaiah 33:4. There the spoil is gathered like the gathering of the caterpillar, as the running to and fro of locusts shall he run upon them. The word is the hurry of judgment.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe mashshâq shows me how quickly spoil is gathered when God gives it, and that the locusts' haste is a picture of His judgment.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a debt
BiblicalUsage: mashsheh is a debt, and it occurs once, in Deuteronomy 15:2. There the manner of the release is that every creditor who lends to his neighbour shall release it, because it is called the LORD's release. The word is the debt that must be let go.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe mashsheh shows me that God sets a limit on debt, and that release is part of His law, not only His grace.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: ruin
BiblicalUsage: mashshûwʼâh is ruin, desolation. In Psalms 73:18 God sets the wicked in slippery places and casts them down into destruction, and in Psalms 74:3 the psalmist asks Him to lift His feet to the perpetual desolations the enemy has done wickedly in the sanctuary. The word is the ruin left after pride.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe mashshûwʼâh shows me that the proud stand on slippery ground, and that ruin is the end of the path they chose.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: instructive, i.e. a didactic poem
BiblicalUsage: maskîyl is an instructive psalm, a didactic poem, and it stands in the titles of thirteen psalms. It names the psalms of David and of the sons of Korah, of Asaph and of Ethan and of Heman, and the word itself is a promise that the song will teach. I have cited no verse for it here, because every occurrence stands in a psalm title rather than in the psalm's own lines.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe maskîyl teaches me that God gives instruction in song, and that a psalm can teach what a lecture cannot.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a figure (carved on stone, the wall, or any object); figuratively, imagination
BiblicalUsage: maskîyth is a carved figure, an image of stone, and figuratively an imagination. In Leviticus 26:1 God forbids any image of stone to bow down to, and in Numbers 33:52 Israel is told to destroy all their pictures and molten images. In Ezekiel 8:12 the ancients of Israel worship in the dark, every man in the chambers of his imagery, and in Proverbs 18:11 the rich man's wealth is a high wall in his own conceit. The word is the idol carved and the idol imagined.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe maskîyth warns me that the images I carve in my heart are idols too. I hold that God sees the chambers of my imagination as clearly as the carved stone.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: wages or a reward
BiblicalUsage: maskôreth is wages or a reward, and it belongs to Jacob's story. In Genesis 29:15 Laban asks Jacob what his wages shall be, and in Genesis 31:7 and Genesis 31:41 Jacob says Laban changed his wages ten times. In Ruth 2:12 Boaz prays that a full reward be given to Ruth by the LORD God of Israel, under whose wings she has come to trust. The word is the pay that can be cheated and the reward that cannot.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe maskôreth shows me that God pays His workers. I hold that a full reward waits for those who trust under His wings.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a peg
BiblicalUsage: masmᵉrâh is a peg or nail, and it occurs once, in Ecclesiastes 12:11. There the words of the wise are as goads, and as nails fastened by the masters of assemblies, which are given from one shepherd. The word is the nail that holds the assembly's wisdom in place.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe masmᵉrâh shows me that the words of the wise are fastened like nails, and that a well-driven truth holds a life together.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: delight, concretely (the cause or object) or abstractly (the feeling)
BiblicalUsage: mâsôws is delight, joy, and the thing that causes it. In Isaiah 24:8 the mirth of tabrets ceases and the joy of the harp ends, and in Hosea 2:11 God says He will cause all her mirth to cease. In Ezekiel 24:25 the joy of their glory is taken from them, and in Isaiah 8:6 the people rejoice in Rezin and Remaliah's son. The word is the joy that can be lost.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe mâsôws shows me that joy can be taken away when God judges. I hold that the joy He gives is the joy I should guard.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Masrekah, a place in Idumaea
BiblicalUsage: Masrêqâh is Masrekah, a town in Edom named twice, in Genesis 36:36 and 1 Chronicles 1:47. In both places Samlah of Masrekah reigns in Hadad's stead among the kings of Edom. The name is a town that gave a king to a neighbouring nation.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Masrêqâh shows me that God records the kings of Edom as well as the kings of Israel, and that no throne is outside His history.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a pan
BiblicalUsage: masrêth is a pan, and it occurs once, in 2 Samuel 13:9. There Tamar takes a pan and pours the cakes out before Amnon, but he refuses to eat, and sends all the men out. The word is the pan that carries a sister's cooking to a brother's trap.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe masrêth shows me that a pan of cakes can carry a brother's treachery, and that Amnon's sin is a warning about what appetite does.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a conflagration (from the rising of smoke)
BiblicalUsage: massâʼâh is a conflagration, a rising of smoke and fire, and it occurs once, in Isaiah 30:27. There the name of the LORD comes from far, burning with His anger, and His lips are full of indignation, and His tongue as a devouring fire. The word is the smoke of God's coming judgment.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe massâʼâh shows me that God's anger is a fire that consumes, and that His name coming from far is not a small thing.
RelatedTopics: Judgment; God's wrath and refuge; Holiness
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Massa, a son of Ishmael
BiblicalUsage: Massâʼ is Massa, a son of Ishmael named in the genealogies. In Genesis 25:14 Massa stands among Mishma and Dumah and the other sons of Ishmael, and in 1 Chronicles 1:30 the same list is repeated. The name is a line in Abraham's wider family.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Massâʼ shows me that God keeps the sons of Ishmael in His record, and that His promises to Abraham's line are not forgotten.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a burden; specifically, tribute, or (abstractly) porterage; figuratively, an utterance, chiefly a doom, especially singing; mental, desire
BiblicalUsage: massâʼ is a burden, and figuratively an utterance, a doom, the burden of the word of the LORD. In Isaiah 13:1 it stands at the head of the burden of Babylon, and in Habakkuk 1:1 it is the burden which Habakkuk the prophet saw. In Zechariah 9:1 it is the burden of the word of the LORD in the land of Hadrach, and in Malachi 1:1 the burden of the word of the LORD to Israel by Malachi. The word is the message that weighs on the prophet who carries it.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe massâʼ teaches me that a burden from God is weighty because it is true. I hold that the prophets carried a word they could not lay down.
RelatedPeople: Isaiah; Habakkuk; Zechariah the Prophet; Malachi
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a primary μάσσω (to handle or squeeze); to chew:--gnaw.
BiblicalUsage: massáomai is to chew, to gnaw, and it occurs once, in Revelation 16:10. There the fifth angel pours out his vial upon the seat of the beast, and his kingdom is full of darkness, and they gnaw their tongues for pain. The word is the bite of suffering with no relief.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe massáomai shows me what pain does to the unrepentant, and I hold that gnawing my tongue in darkness is the end of refusing the light.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: partiality (as a lifting up)
BiblicalUsage: massôʼ is partiality, a lifting up of a face in favour, and it occurs once, in 2 Chronicles 19:7. There Jehoshaphat tells the judges that there is no iniquity with the LORD our God, nor respect of persons, nor taking of gifts. The word is the favour God refuses to show.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe massôʼ teaches me that God shows no partiality, and I hold that my own judgments should be as free of favour as His.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a saw
BiblicalUsage: massôwr is a saw, and it occurs once, in Isaiah 10:15. There the prophet asks whether the saw shall magnify itself against him that shakes it, as if the rod should shake itself against those who lift it up. The word is the tool that forgets its maker.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe massôwr warns me that the tool does not boast against the workman, and that I am the saw, not the hand.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: enmity
BiblicalUsage: masṭêmâh is enmity, hatred, and it occurs twice, both times in Hosea 9. In Hosea 9:7 the days of visitation are come, and the prophet is called a fool for the multitude of iniquity and the great hatred. In Hosea 9:8 the prophet is a snare in all his ways, and hatred in the house of his God., and the word is the hatred that meets God's messenger.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe masṭêmâh shows me that hatred against God's prophet is hatred against God, and that the days of visitation expose it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3148; to flog (literally or figuratively):--scourge.
BiblicalUsage: mastigóō is to scourge, to flog, and it falls on Christ and on God's children alike. In John 19:1 Pilate takes Jesus and scourges Him, and in Luke 18:33 and Mark 10:34 Jesus foretells that they shall scourge Him and put Him to death, and the third day He shall rise again. In Hebrews 12:6 the Lord scourges every son whom He receives. The word is the whip that chastens and the whip that kills.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe mastigóō shows me that the Lord disciplines the sons He receives. I hold that His scourging of Christ is the scourging that saves me.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably from the base of G3145 (through the idea of contact); a whip (literally, the Roman flagellum for criminals; figuratively, a disease):--plague, scourging.
BiblicalUsage: mástix is a whip, the Roman flagellum, and figuratively a plague or affliction. In Acts 22:24 Paul is to be examined by scourging, and in Hebrews 11:36 the faithful have trial of cruel mockings and scourgings, with bonds and imprisonment. In Luke 7:21 and Mark 3:10 the same word names the plagues and infirmities Jesus cures, as the crowds press to touch Him. The word is the stroke that wounds and the affliction that needs healing.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe mástix shows me that a whip can be a plague and a plague can be a whip. I hold that the God who heals the plagued is the God who bore the scourging.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3149; to whip (literally):--scourge.
BiblicalUsage: mastízō is to scourge, and it occurs once, in Acts 22:25. There, as they bind Paul with thongs to scourge him, he asks the centurion whether it is lawful to scourge a man who is a Roman and uncondemned. The word is the whip stopped by a question.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe mastízō shows me that Paul knew his rights and used them, and that a Roman scourging was no small thing to face.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from the base of G3145; a (properly, female) breast (as if kneaded up):--pap.
BiblicalUsage: The word is the breast, named in the most human moments of the Gospels. A woman in the crowd blesses the breasts that nursed Jesus, and Jesus Himself says the barren will be called blessed in the days of judgment. In Revelation the risen Christ is seen girded across His chest with a golden girdle, the breast named as the place of His strength and honour.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word reminds us that Christ took a real human body, nursed as a child and pierced as a man, and that the risen Lord still wears that body in glory.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a delicacy
BiblicalUsage: A delicacy is the rich food a father asks for or a ruler sets before you. Isaac sends Esau out for the savoury meat he loves, and Proverbs warns not to crave a ruler's dainties, because they are deceitful food.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that appetite is a small door for big trouble: what tastes rich can still be a trap, and the blessing Isaac meant for Esau was nearly lost over a meal.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a broom (as removing dirt (compare English 'to dust', i.e. remove dust))
BiblicalUsage: The word is a broom, and it appears once, in God's sentence on Babylon: He will sweep the city with the besom of destruction until nothing is left.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the picture is deliberate: the God who made all things can sweep a proud empire away like dust, and no power on earth can stand when He decides to clean house.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3151; random talk, i.e. babble:--vain jangling.
BiblicalUsage: Vain jangling is empty talk, the sound of people who have left the faith's plain teaching and wandered off into arguments that go nowhere.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that words without truth are worse than silence: they fill the room, stir up strife, and leave everyone further from God than before.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3152 and G3004; an idle (i.e. senseless or mischievous) talker, i.e. a wrangler:--vain talker.
BiblicalUsage: A vain talker is someone whose words are empty and unruly, and Paul warns Titus that there are many of them, especially among those who insist on the old law.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the warning still stands: a teacher is known by whether his words build up the church or only fill the air, and the church must be able to tell the difference.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3152; to render (passively, become) foolish, i.e. (morally) wicked or (specially), idolatrous:--become vain.
BiblicalUsage: The word means to become vain, and Paul uses it once, of people who knew God but would not honour Him: their thinking went empty, and their foolish hearts were darkened. It is the picture of a mind that trades the truth of God for its own imaginations.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this is how idolatry starts, not with a carved image but with a mind that stops thanking God, and once the thinking goes vain the heart follows.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from the base of G3155; empty, i.e. (literally) profitless, or (specially), an idol:--vain, vanity.
BiblicalUsage: Vain means empty, profitless, and the New Testament uses it for everything that promises life and delivers nothing. Paul says faith is vain if Christ was not raised, and Peter says we were redeemed from the empty way of life handed down by our fathers. Paul tells the crowd at Lystra to turn from these vanities to the living God, and James warns that a man who cannot bridle his tongue has a vain religion.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word draws a line between what is real and what only looks real. An empty faith, an empty tradition, an empty religion all share the same flaw: they have no living God at the centre. That is why the gospel matters so much — Christ risen is the one thing that is not vain, and everything else is measured against Him.
RelatedPeople: Paul; Simon Peter; James, Brother of Jesus
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3152; inutility; figuratively, transientness; morally, depravity:--vanity.
BiblicalUsage: Vanity is the emptiness and fading of everything that does not last. Paul says the whole creation was made subject to vanity, and he warns believers not to walk as the Gentiles do, in the vanity of their minds. Peter describes false teachers who speak great swelling words of vanity and lure the unstable back into sin.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that vanity is the Bible's word for the hollowness of life apart from God: the world promises fullness and gives only wind. But creation was subjected to vanity in hope, and that hope is the gospel — God will fill what is empty.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: rain
BiblicalUsage: Rain is God's gift and God's tool in Israel's story. Moses promises the early rain and the latter rain in their season if Israel obeys, and Solomon prays that when heaven is shut up for sin, God will hear and send rain again. Elijah announces the end of three years without rain, Zechariah tells the people to ask the LORD for rain, and the psalm pictures the king coming down like rain on mown grass.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe rain teaches us how dependent we are: no one in Israel could make it rain, and no one can make grace fall either. When God withholds rain it is a call to repent, and when He sends it, it is a reminder that He alone opens heaven. I hold that the latter rain is still the picture of what God does when His people ask.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: rain
BiblicalUsage: Rain is God's gift and God's tool in Israel's story. Moses promises the early rain and the latter rain in their season if Israel obeys, and Solomon prays that when heaven is shut up for sin, God will hear and send rain again. Elijah announces the end of three years without rain, Zechariah tells the people to ask the LORD for rain, and the psalm pictures the king coming down like rain on mown grass.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe rain teaches us how dependent we are: no one in Israel could make it rain, and no one can make grace fall either. When God withholds rain it is a call to repent, and when He sends it, it is a reminder that He alone opens heaven. I hold that the latter rain is still the picture of what God does when His people ask.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: slaughter
BiblicalUsage: Slaughter is the word for the killing prepared for Babylon's children, because of the iniquity of their fathers, so that they do not rise and fill the earth with cities.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the verse is a hard reminder that sin has consequences down the generations, and that God's judgment on a proud empire is thorough, not partial.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: accusative case of a derivative of the base of G3145 (through the idea of tentative manipulation, i.e. unsuccessful search, or else of punishment); folly, i.e. (adverbially) to no purpose:--in vain.
BiblicalUsage: In vain means to no purpose, and Jesus uses it once in each Gospel for the same charge: the Pharisees worship God in vain, teaching the commandments of men as doctrine. Their worship looks right, but it is empty because it honours tradition over God's word.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that worship is only real when it follows what God actually said, and any rule we add to His word turns the whole thing vain.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, an adult (as of full length); by implication, a man (only in the plural)
BiblicalUsage: The word means men, and it is almost always used of fewness: the LORD will scatter Israel so that only a few men are left, and the psalm remembers when they were but a few in number. Jacob says the same of his household when he fears the Canaanites: we are few in number, and they will gather against us.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word keeps showing up where God's people are small and outnumbered, and that is the point: God has always done His greatest work with a few.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to stretch out
BiblicalUsage: The word means to stretch out, and Isaiah uses it once, of God who stretches out the heavens as a curtain and spreads them out as a tent to dwell in.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the picture is meant to humble us: the sky we live under is something God stretched out like cloth, and the God who did that is not small.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a dainty, i.e. (generally) food
BiblicalUsage: The word is used once, in Job's picture of the wicked man's end: the womb forgets him, and the worm feeds sweetly on him. It is the sweetness of decay, the grave taking what it is owed.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the verse is Job at his bleakest, and it is honest: a life built on wrongdoing ends forgotten, and even the worm finds it sweet.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to suck, by implication, to relish, or (intransitively) be sweet
BiblicalUsage: To be sweet covers the waters at Marah, which God made sweet when Moses cast in the tree, and the stolen waters that taste sweet to the fool. David remembers the sweet counsel he took with a friend who turned against him, and Job says wickedness is sweet in the mouth of the wicked, though it turns to gall inside.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe sweetness is a test, not a proof: the waters at Marah were sweet because God healed them, but stolen waters are sweet only to the tongue. The Bible keeps asking whether what tastes good is actually good, and the answer is never in the taste alone. I hold that God's word is the sweetness that never turns bitter.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, extent (of time); but used only adverbially (especially with other particle prefixes), when (either relative or interrogative)
BiblicalUsage: When is the cry of a believer who cannot see the end: David asks how long the LORD will wait, and when he will come and appear before God. Isaiah asks the same after his vision of the throne: Lord, how long?
TheologicalSignificance: I believe 'how long' is one of the most honest prayers in the Bible, and God never rebukes it: He answers it in His own time, and the waiting itself is part of the faith.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: straw in the heap
BiblicalUsage: Straw in the heap is the picture Isaiah uses for Moab's judgment: Moab will be trodden down under God as straw is trodden down for the dunghill.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the image is meant to be humiliating: a proud nation ends up as refuse underfoot, and no one remembers the straw once the threshing is done.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3129; a learner, i.e. pupil:--disciple.
BiblicalUsage: A disciple is a learner, and Jesus defines the word by the life that goes with it: the disciple is not above his master, and anyone who will come after Him must deny himself, take up his cross, and follow. John says the mark of a real disciple is continuing in His word, and that the world will know His disciples by their love for one another. At Antioch the disciples were called Christians first, because the learning had become a life.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a disciple is not someone who merely agrees with Jesus, but someone who follows Him where He goes, even to a cross. The test is not what we know but whether we keep His word and love each other when it costs us something. That is why the name Christian stuck at Antioch: the disciples looked like their Master.
RelatedEvents: The Calling of the First Disciples; The Great Commission
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3101; intransitively, to become a pupil; transitively, to disciple, i.e. enrol as scholar:--be disciple, instruct, teach.
BiblicalUsage: To disciple means to make learners, and it is the last command Jesus gave: go and make disciples of all nations. A scribe who has been discipled in the kingdom is like a householder bringing out things new and old, and Paul and Barnabas made many disciples at Derbe before they returned. Joseph of Arimathea, a rich man who had become a disciple, is the one who buried Jesus.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that making disciples is the church's real work: not gathering crowds, but teaching people to follow Jesus until His ways become theirs. Joseph shows the other side of it — a disciple is known in the end by what he does with Jesus when it costs him.
RelatedPeople: Jesus; Paul; Barnabas; Joseph of Arimathea
RelatedEvents: The Great Commission; The Burial of Jesus
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: feminine from G3101; a female pupil:--disciple.
BiblicalUsage: The word is the feminine of disciple, and it is used once, for Tabitha at Joppa, a disciple full of good works and almsdeeds. When she died, the widows showed Peter the coats and garments she had made, and Peter prayed and raised her.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Tabitha is the proof that a disciple is measured by a life of quiet good works, and that God notices the coats sewn for widows as surely as any sermon.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: proportion (in size, number or ingredients)
BiblicalUsage: Proportion is the measured amount, and it appears where God fixes the measure: the holy anointing oil must not be made in any other proportion, and Pharaoh demands the same tale of bricks with no straw given. The word is about what is owed in full, whether to God or to a tyrant.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the contrast is the lesson: God fixes His measure in holiness, and Pharaoh fixes his in cruelty, and the same word shows which master you serve.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H4968); Mathusala (i.e. Methushelach), an antediluvian:--Mathusala.
BiblicalUsage: Methuselah's name reaches the New Testament in Luke's genealogy of Jesus, where he stands between Enoch and Lamech, the link back to the man who lived longer than anyone in Scripture. Luke traces Jesus through him to show that the Saviour belongs to the whole line of Adam, not only to Abraham.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the genealogy is the point: Jesus is not a late idea in God's plan, but the heir of the oldest line on earth, and Methuselah's long life is part of the road that leads to Him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: sweet
KeyPassages: Psalms 19:10; Proverbs 16:24; Judges 14:14; Song of Solomon 2:3
BiblicalUsage: Sweet is the word for what delights the taste, and the Bible uses it for God's word, for kind words, and for riddles. The psalm says God's judgments are sweeter than honey, and Proverbs says pleasant words are as a honeycomb, sweet to the soul. Samson poses the riddle of the sweetness that came out of the strong, and the bride in the Song sits under her beloved's shadow and finds his fruit sweet to her taste.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe sweetness is the Bible's picture of delight that is also good for you: God's word tastes sweet because it is true, and kind words heal because they are true too. Samson's riddle warns the other side of it — sweetness can come out of violence, and what tastes sweet is not always safe. I hold that the test is the source: sweetness from God endures, and sweetness from anywhere else fades.
RelatedBooks: Psalms; Proverbs; Judges; Song of Solomon
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a secret storehouse; hence, a secreted valuable (buried); generally money
BiblicalUsage: Hidden treasure is wealth buried out of sight, and the Bible uses it for wisdom, for God's secret provision, and for the things men chase in vain. Proverbs tells the young man to seek wisdom as silver and search for her as for hid treasures, and Isaiah promises Cyrus the treasures of darkness. Joseph's brothers find their money returned in their sacks, and Job says men dig for death as for hid treasures.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word asks what we are digging for: wisdom is the one treasure that repays the digging, because it is God who hides it and God who gives it. The treasures of darkness belong to the LORD too — He gives them to whom He chooses, even to a pagan king. And Job's line is the warning: men will dig just as hard for death, and find it.
RelatedPeople: King Solomon; Joseph, Son of Jacob; Job; Cyrus the Great
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Matred, an Edomitess
BiblicalUsage: Matred is named as the mother of Mehetabel, the wife of Hadar the last king of Edom, and the daughter of Mezahab. Her name is kept in the record of Edom's kings, the line that stood against Israel from Esau's day.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe her name matters because the Bible keeps the names of the mothers too, and the line of Edom is traced as carefully as the line of Israel, even when it stands against God's people.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Matri, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Matri is the family of Benjamin from which Saul was taken to be king: when the tribe was brought near by families, the family of Matri was taken, and Saul the son of Kish was taken. It is the only place the name appears, at the very moment Israel gets the king it asked for.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the detail matters: God chose the king from a named family, in the open, by lot, so that no one could say Saul took the throne for himself.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, to come forth to, i.e. appear or exist; transitively, to attain, i.e. find or acquire; figuratively, to occur, meet or be present
BiblicalUsage: To find is the word for what happens when seeking meets grace: Noah found grace in the eyes of the LORD, and Moses promises that if Israel seeks God with all its heart it will find Him. Isaiah calls the people to seek the LORD while He may be found, Jeremiah promises that those who search with all their heart will find Him, and Wisdom says those who seek her early shall find her.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe finding is never an accident in Scripture: God is found by those who seek Him, and He is found because He wants to be found. Noah did not earn grace by searching, but grace found him searching, and that is the pattern for us. I hold that the promise still stands — seek Him with all your heart, and you will find Him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to suck out; by implication, to drain, to squeeze out
BiblicalUsage: To drain or squeeze out is the word for wringing the last drop from something: Gideon wrings a bowl full of water from the dew-soaked fleece, and the priest wrings the blood of the bird offering out at the side of the altar. The psalm says the wicked will wring out the dregs of the LORD's cup and drink them, and Isaiah says Jerusalem drank the cup of trembling and wrung it out.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word is about getting everything out: God's judgment is not a sip but the whole cup, drained to the dregs. Yet Gideon shows the other side — God lets His servant wring out a sign, and the same hands that pour judgment also pour mercy.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to suck
BiblicalUsage: The word means to suck, and Isaiah uses it once, of Jerusalem's children nursing at her consolations: they will suck and be satisfied, and milk out and be delighted with the abundance of her glory.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the picture is deliberately tender: God comforts His people the way a mother feeds a child, and the satisfaction He gives is complete, not partial.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a whinnying (through impatience for battle or lust)
BiblicalUsage: The word is the neighing of horses, and it appears twice, both times in Jeremiah's warnings: the snorting of the enemy's horses is heard from Dan, and the whinnying of Judah's lust is the sound of a people chasing other gods.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the sound is the point: a nation gone after idols does not creep away quietly, it neighs like a stallion, and the whole land trembles at the noise.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a net (for capturing animals or fishes); a fastness or (beseiging) tower
BiblicalUsage: A net is a hunter's trap, and the Bible uses it for the snare that catches the unwary: the Preacher says a woman whose heart is snares and nets is more bitter than death, and that a man does not know his time, but is suddenly taken like fish in an evil net. Proverbs says the wicked are caught in the net of their own transgression, and Isaiah and Ezekiel use the net for nations taken in war.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the net is the Bible's honest picture of how sin works: it is set quietly, it looks like nothing, and then it closes. The escape is not cleverness but pleasing God, and the Preacher says plainly that the sinner is taken by it while the godly escape.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a narrow place, i.e. (abstractly and figuratively) confinement or disability
BiblicalUsage: Straitness is the crushing pressure of a siege, and the word is used for the worst of it: in the siege the people eat the flesh of their own children, and Jeremiah says the same of Jerusalem's last days. The psalmist says trouble and anguish took hold of him, and men in distress gathered to David in the cave of Adullam.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word names what happens when a people will not listen: the walls close in, and the pressure does what warnings could not. But the psalmist shows the other use of it — trouble took hold of him, and he took hold of God's commandments, and that is the way through.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Egypt (as the border of Palestine)
BiblicalUsage: The word is the name for Egypt as the hemmed-in land, the besieged place on Israel's border. Isaiah says the brooks of defence shall be emptied and dried up, Sennacherib boasts that he has dried up all the rivers of besieged places, and Micah pictures the day when men come from the fortress city even to the river.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the name is a warning in itself: Egypt looked strong and walled, but God calls it the besieged place, because no wall keeps Him out. The powers that hem God's people in are the ones He hems in.
RelatedPeople: Isaiah; King Hezekiah; Sennacherib, King of Assyria
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Egypt (as the border of Palestine)
BiblicalUsage: The word is the name for Egypt as the hemmed-in land, the besieged place on Israel's border. Isaiah says the brooks of defence shall be emptied and dried up, Sennacherib boasts that he has dried up all the rivers of besieged places, and Micah pictures the day when men come from the fortress city even to the river.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the name is a warning in itself: Egypt looked strong and walled, but God calls it the besieged place, because no wall keeps Him out. The powers that hem God's people in are the ones He hems in.
RelatedPeople: Isaiah; King Hezekiah; Sennacherib, King of Assyria
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a couch
