BiblicalUsage: A couch is a bed, and Isaiah uses the word once, in the warning that the bed is shorter than a man can stretch himself on: the covering is too narrow to wrap in, and the resting place is no rest at all.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the picture is of a people trying to rest on their own arrangements, and finding the bed too short: only God's provision fits, and everything else leaves you uncovered.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a fixed spot; figuratively, an office, a military post
BiblicalUsage: A garrison is a military post, and the word is used where the post changes hands: Jonathan goes over to strike the Philistines' garrison, and the LORD tells Shebna that He will drive him from his station and pull him down from his state.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that a post is only as secure as the God who gives it: Jonathan takes a Philistine garrison by faith, and Shebna loses his own post by pride.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a military guard
BiblicalUsage: A guard is the armed watch at a post, and the word appears twice: the Philistines challenge Jonathan to come up to them where the guard stands, and the LORD promises to encamp about His house because of the army.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the two verses belong together: men set a guard to keep others out, and God sets His own guard to keep His people safe.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a quarrel
BiblicalUsage: Strife is the quarrel that pride starts, and Proverbs names the cause plainly: only by pride cometh contention. Loving strife is loving transgression, and Isaiah says the people fast for strife and debate, striking with the fist of wickedness.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe strife is never an accident: it grows where pride is fed, and it shows up even in religion, where people fast and still fight. The cure is not a better argument but a humbler heart.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a quarrel
BiblicalUsage: Strife is the quarrel that pride starts, and Proverbs names the cause plainly: only by pride cometh contention. Loving strife is loving transgression, and Isaiah says the people fast for strife and debate, striking with the fist of wickedness.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe strife is never an accident: it grows where pride is fed, and it shows up even in religion, where people fast and still fight. The cure is not a better argument but a humbler heart.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: something stationed, i.e. a column or (memorial stone); by analogy, an idol
BiblicalUsage: A pillar is a standing stone, and the Bible uses it for memorials, for worship, and for idols. Jacob sets up the stone at Bethel and pours oil on it, and again at the place where God spoke to him; Moses builds twelve pillars at the foot of Sinai; and Hezekiah breaks the images and cuts down the groves, because pillars meant for memory had become idols.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a pillar is a marker of what a man decided to remember, and the Bible shows both sides of it: Jacob's stone marks the place God met him, and the pillars Hezekiah broke mark the places men met their idols. What we set up to remember will shape what we worship.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: something stationary, i.e. a monumental stone; also the stock of a tree
BiblicalUsage: The word is a standing stone, used for Absalom's pillar in the king's dale, which he raised because he had no son to keep his name in remembrance, and for the pillar Jacob set over Rachel's grave. Isaiah uses the same word for the stock of a tree that remains after it is cut down.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the word is about what remains after a life: Absalom built a stone to keep his name alive, and Rachel's pillar still marks a grave, but only the stump Isaiah saw carries the promise of new life.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a quarrel
BiblicalUsage: The word means strife or contention, and Isaiah uses it once, of the enemies who contend with God's servant: they shall be as nothing, and as a thing of nought.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the promise is complete: those who strive against God's people do not merely lose, they come to nothing, because the fight was never really against us.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a net, or (abstractly) capture; also a fastness
BiblicalUsage: A stronghold is a fortress and a hiding place, and the psalms make it a name for God Himself: the LORD is my rock and my fortress, and my deliverer, and David says the same in his song of deliverance. The word is also used for the holds where David hid from Saul, and for the fortresses where Ezekiel's exiles take refuge.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word teaches us where to run: David hid in real strongholds, but the psalms say the LORD Himself is the fortress, and no stone wall ever kept a man the way God does. I hold that the safest place on earth is not a cave or a castle, but the name of the LORD.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: something narrow, i.e. a column or hilltop
BiblicalUsage: The word is a narrow crag or column, and it appears once, at the pass where Jonathan climbed to the Philistine garrison: one sharp rock on one side, and another on the other, and the way between them was the only way through.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the narrow place is the picture of faith: Jonathan did not wait for a wide road, he climbed the crag that was there, and God gave him the victory on the far side.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: something planted, i.e. the place (a garden or vineyard), or the thing (a plant, figuratively or men); by implication, the act, planting
BiblicalUsage: A planting is what God plants, and the prophets use it for His people: Isaiah says the righteous are the branch of God's planting, the work of His hands, and the trees of righteousness, the planting of the LORD. Ezekiel promises a plant of renown, and Micah says Samaria will be made a heap, its stones poured down like a vineyard on a slope.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word is about ownership: God's people are His planting, and He tends what He plants. A vineyard He did not plant gets torn down, but the branch of His planting is never uprooted, because His hands are on it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: downward, below or beneath; often adverbially with or without prefixes
BiblicalUsage: Below or beneath is the word for the low place, and Moses uses it for the curse and the blessing together: if Israel obeys, it will be above only and not beneath, and if it disobeys, the stranger will get above it. Proverbs says the way of life is above to the wise, that he may depart from hell beneath.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that above and beneath are not about geography but about who rules: obedience lifts a people up, and disobedience puts them under, and the wise man walks the way that leads up.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Mattan, the name of a priest of Baal, and of an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Mattan is the priest of Baal whom the people slew before the altars when Joash was crowned, breaking down the house of Baal in Judah. A later Mattan is the father of Shephatiah, one of the princes who heard Jeremiah's words and wanted him dead.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the two Mattans show the two sides of a name: one served a false god and died at his own altar, and the other raised a son who tried to silence God's prophet. A name is not a destiny, but the choices attached to it are.
RelatedPeople: Joash, King of Judah; Jeremiah; Mattan, Priest of Baal
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a present
BiblicalUsage: A gift is a present, and Proverbs says a man's gift makes room for him and brings him before great men, while a gift in secret pacifies anger. Shechem offers any dowry and gift for Dinah, and the LORD gives the heave offerings to Aaron as His gift to the priests.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that a gift is a test of the heart: given openly it opens doors, given in secret it can buy silence, and given to God it becomes an offering. The gift itself is neutral — the motive is what makes it holy or corrupt.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Mattanah, a place in the Desert
BiblicalUsage: Mattanah is a station on Israel's wilderness journey, where the princes dug the well with their staves. The people sang the song of the well: spring up, O well, sing ye unto it.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the place matters because it is a well in the desert: Israel sang at a hole in the ground, because God gave them water there, and the song is still the right response to provision in a dry place.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a present; specifically (in a good sense), a sacrificial offering, (in a bad sense) a bribe
BiblicalUsage: A gift is a present or offering, and the Bible shows it in every light: Moses says every man shall give as he is able, according to the blessing of the LORD, and the Preacher warns that a gift destroys the heart. Proverbs says he that hates gifts shall live, the psalm says God received gifts for men, and at Purim the Jews sent portions to one another.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe gifts reveal what we trust: given freely they are worship, given to buy favour they are a bribe, and the line between them runs through the heart. The gift that destroys the heart is the one that buys a man, and the gift that blesses is the one that costs him nothing but love.
RelatedPeople: Moses; King Solomon; Queen Esther; Mordecai
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Mattanjah, the name of ten Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Mattaniah is the name of several men, and the most famous is the king: Nebuchadnezzar made Mattaniah king in Zedekiah's place and changed his name to Zedekiah. Another Mattaniah sang in the temple choirs, and another stood among the Levites who taught the people.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the name change is the story: a king who owed his throne to Babylon took a new name with it, and the kingdom that traded its identity for survival lost both. The singers named Mattaniah kept the older calling, and that is the better half of the name.
RelatedPeople: Mattaniah; Zedekiah, King of Judah; King Nebuchadnezzar
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a jail (as a guard-house); also an aim (as being closely watched)
BiblicalUsage: The word is the prison and the mark, and Jeremiah knows both: he is shut up in the court of the prison while Jerusalem falls, and the LORD tells him the city is given into the enemy's hand. Job says God has set him up for His mark, and Lamentations says the same of Jerusalem, set as a mark for the arrow.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word holds the two hardest pictures of the faithful life together: the prison cell and the target. Jeremiah was locked up for telling the truth, and Job was set up as a mark, and neither of them was abandoned — God was in the cell with Jeremiah and behind the shield with Job.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a present
BiblicalUsage: A gift is a present, and the Preacher says the gift of God is that a man should eat and drink and enjoy the good of his labour. The same word is used for the reward Jeroboam offers the man of God, which he refuses, and for the false gift of a man who boasts of giving and never gives.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the gift of God is not a thing but a capacity: the power to enjoy what you have is itself the gift, and the man who cannot enjoy his labour has missed it, whatever he owns. The gift that costs nothing to receive still costs everything to refuse, because it is the joy itself.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably a shortened form of G3161 (compare H4992); Mattatha (i.e. Mattithjah), an Israelite:--Mattatha.
BiblicalUsage: Mattatha stands in Luke's genealogy of Jesus, between Menan and Nathan. He is on the line that runs from David through Nathan rather than Solomon.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the line through Nathan matters: Jesus is David's son by a road the kings never walked, and the genealogy keeps the names of men history forgot.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H4993); Mattathias (i.e. Mattithjah), an Israelite and a Christian:--Mattathias.
BiblicalUsage: Mattathias appears twice in Luke's genealogy, once as the son of Amos and once as the son of Semei. Two men of the same name stand on the long road from David to Jesus.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that a repeated name is not a mistake but a reminder: ordinary men, named twice over the generations, are the links in the chain that brings the Saviour.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Mattattah, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Mattattah is one of the sons of Hashum who had taken foreign wives. He put them away at Ezra's command after the return from exile.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the single mention is enough: a man who obeyed a hard command is remembered, and the putting away of what God forbade is still the shape of repentance.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a branch (as extending); figuratively, a tribe; also a rod, whether for chastising (figuratively, correction), ruling (a sceptre), throwing (a lance), or walking (a staff; figuratively, a support of life, e.g. bread)
BiblicalUsage: A rod is a branch, a staff, and a tribe, and the word covers all three in Israel's story. Moses' rod becomes a serpent before Pharaoh and opens the sea when it is lifted over the waters, and Aaron's rod buds and blossoms to prove whom God has chosen. The same word names the tribes of Israel, and the psalm promises a rod of strength out of Zion.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the rod is the picture of authority that comes from God and not from men: a shepherd's stick in Moses' hand did what Pharaoh's army could not. And a dead stick that buds is the sign of the priesthood itself — life where there should be none, because God chose it. I hold that the rod of strength out of Zion is Christ, ruling in the midst of His enemies.
RelatedEvents: The Burning Bush; The Exodus and the Red Sea; Moses and Aaron Confront Pharaoh
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: what a trouble!
BiblicalUsage: The word is an exclamation, what a trouble, and Malachi uses it once, of priests who call God's service a weariness and offer Him the lame and the sick.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the sigh is the sin: when God's service feels like trouble, the heart has already left, and the offering that follows will be as cheap as the attitude.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {a present; specifically (in a good sense), a sacrificial offering, (in a bad sense) a bribe}
BiblicalUsage: The word is the Aramaic for a gift, and Daniel uses it where gifts are offered to buy what only God can give. Nebuchadnezzar promises gifts and rewards to whoever tells his dream, and Daniel refuses the king's gifts and reads the writing anyway.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Daniel's refusal is the whole lesson: the gifts of a king cannot buy the interpretation, because the interpretation belongs to God. A prophet who takes the gift stops being a prophet.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Mattenai, the name of three Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Mattenai is the name of three men after the exile: two who had taken foreign wives and put them away. A third Mattenai served as a priest of the course of Joiarib in Nehemiah's day.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the name shows both sides of the return: men who repented of mixed marriages, and a priest who served in the restored temple, and the same name covers the sorrow and the rebuilding.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a shorter form of G3161; Matthæus (i.e. Matthitjah), an Israelite and a Christian:--Matthew.
BiblicalUsage: Matthew is the apostle who sat at the receipt of custom when Jesus called him, and followed at once. He is named among the twelve, and he is there in the upper room after the ascension, waiting with the rest for the promise.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Matthew is the proof that Jesus calls the unlikely: a tax collector left his table the moment he was told to follow, and the man who took Rome's money became the one who wrote the gospel for the Jews.
RelatedEvents: The Calling of the First Disciples
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H4977); Matthan (i.e. Mattan), an Israelite:--Matthan.
BiblicalUsage: Matthan stands in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus, between Eleazar and Jacob. He is the father of Jacob and the grandfather of Joseph.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the quiet names in the genealogy are the point: Jesus comes through men nobody preached about, and God builds His greatest work on ordinary fathers.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably a shortened form of G3161; Matthat (i.e. Mattithjah), the name of two Israelites:--Mathat.
BiblicalUsage: Matthat appears twice in Luke's genealogy of Jesus, once as the son of Levi and once as the son of Jorim. Both stand on the line that runs back to David.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a name repeated across the generations is a thread God never dropped: two men named Matthat, centuries apart, both carrying the line toward the Christ.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: apparently a shortened form of G3161; Matthias (i.e. Mattithjah), an Israelite:--Matthias.
BiblicalUsage: Matthias is the man the apostles chose by lot to take Judas's place. He had been with them from John's baptism to the ascension, and the lot fell on him, and he was numbered with the eleven.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Matthias is the apostle nobody remembers, and that is his glory: he was faithful for years without a title, and when the lot fell on him he was ready. God keeps the faithful in reserve.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Mattithjah, the name of four Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Mattithiah is a Levite musician who played before the ark when David brought it to Jerusalem. He also stood beside Ezra on the wooden pulpit when the law was read to the returned exiles.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Mattithiah's life is the shape of a Levite's calling: he made music for the ark, and he stood by the preacher, and the same man served the worship of God in both ages.
RelatedEvents: David Brings the Ark to Jerusalem
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: something spun
BiblicalUsage: The word is something spun, and it appears once, of the wise-hearted women who spun blue and purple and scarlet and fine linen for the tabernacle.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the spun thread matters: the tabernacle was built by hands that knew their craft, and God counts women's spinning as worship.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: death (natural or violent); concretely, the dead, their place or state (hades); figuratively, pestilence, ruin
KeyPassages: Deuteronomy 30:19; Isaiah 25:8; Hosea 13:14; Proverbs 18:21; Song of Solomon 8:6
BiblicalUsage: Death is the end of life and the shadow over it, and the Bible uses the word for both the fact and the fear. Moses sets life and death before Israel and tells them to choose life, Isaiah promises that God will swallow up death in victory, and Hosea hears God say He will be death's plague. Proverbs says death and life are in the power of the tongue, and the Song says love is strong as death.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe death is the enemy God names plainly and then promises to destroy: He sets it before us as a choice, and He answers it with a victory. Love is strong as death, and the grave is not the last word — God swallowing death in victory is. I hold that every verse about death in the Old Testament is waiting for the empty tomb.
RelatedBooks: Deuteronomy; Isaiah; Hosea; Proverbs; Song of Solomon
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: water; figuratively, juice; by euphemism, urine, semen
BiblicalUsage: Water is life and judgment and cleansing in the Bible, and the word runs through the whole story. The Spirit moves on the waters at creation, the sea stands as walls on either side at the Red Sea, and Moses strikes the rock and water comes out for a thirsty people. David is led beside still waters, and Isaiah calls everyone who thirsts to come to the waters and buy without money.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe water is the Bible's picture of what only God can give: no man makes a sea stand up, or draws water from a rock, or stills a soul beside quiet waters. The call to come to the waters is the gospel itself — life is free, but it is only found where God gives it. I hold that every well in the Bible is a signpost to Christ, who gives living water.
RelatedEvents: Creation; The Exodus and the Red Sea; Water from the Rock at Meribah
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: exhausted
BiblicalUsage: The word means exhausted, and Moses uses it once, in the curse on a disobedient Israel: they shall be burnt with hunger, and devoured with burning heat, and with bitter destruction.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the verse is meant to frighten: a people that turns from God ends up burnt out and devoured, and the exhaustion is the fruit of its own choosing.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a belt (as movable)
BiblicalUsage: A belt is the girdle a man wears, and the word is used where God loosens the belts of the strong and where a curse clings like a girdle: Job says God loosens the girdle of the strong, and the psalm says let the curse be a girdle the wicked is girded with continually.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that a girdle is a man's strength and dignity, and God can loosen it in a moment: the strong are unbelted, and the curse a man chose fits him like a belt he cannot take off.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a fork
BiblicalUsage: A fork is a fleshhook, one of the tabernacle's tools, and it appears where the priests take their portion: the priest's servant thrusts the fleshhook into the pan, and whatever it brings up belongs to the priest.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the fleshhook is a small warning about the priesthood: the tool was God's, but Eli's sons used it to take more than their share, and the same utensil that served the altar became the sign of their greed.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a pruningknife
BiblicalUsage: A pruning knife is the tool that turns a sword into a farming blade, and the prophets use it for the age of peace: they shall beat their swords into plowshares and their spears into pruning hooks. Joel turns the picture around for the day of war: beat your plowshares into swords, and your pruning hooks into spears.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the two pictures belong together: God will one day make the tools of war into tools of peace, and until that day the nations will keep turning the tools of peace into weapons, but the pruning hook is the promise that the war will end.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {food}
BiblicalUsage: The word is the Aramaic for food, and Daniel uses it twice, of the great tree whose meat was for all: the beasts found shadow under it, and the birds lodged in its branches, and all flesh was fed from it.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the tree is Nebuchadnezzar himself: a king who fed the whole world forgot who gave him the food, and God cut the tree down to teach him that provision comes from heaven.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {food}
BiblicalUsage: The word is the Aramaic for food, and Daniel uses it twice, of the great tree whose meat was for all: the beasts found shadow under it, and the birds lodged in its branches, and all flesh was fed from it.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the tree is Nebuchadnezzar himself: a king who fed the whole world forgot who gave him the food, and God cut the tree down to teach him that provision comes from heaven.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a bandage, i.e. remedy; hence, a sore (as needing a compress)
BiblicalUsage: The word is a bandage or a sore, and it appears twice, both times of a wound no one will heal: Ephraim saw his sickness and went to Assyria for a cure, and Jeremiah says there is no one to plead the cause or give medicine for the bruise.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word is about wounds we take to the wrong doctor: Ephraim's sore could only be healed by the God he had left, and no bandage from Assyria would hold.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a bandage, i.e. remedy; hence, a sore (as needing a compress)
BiblicalUsage: The word is a bandage or a sore, and it appears twice, both times of a wound no one will heal: Ephraim saw his sickness and went to Assyria for a cure, and Jeremiah says there is no one to plead the cause or give medicine for the bruise.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word is about wounds we take to the wrong doctor: Ephraim's sore could only be healed by the God he had left, and no bandage from Assyria would hold.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a constellation, i.e. Zodiacal sign (perhaps as affecting the weather)
BiblicalUsage: The word is a constellation, and it appears once, when Josiah puts down the idolatrous priests who burned incense to the sun and the moon and the planets and all the host of heaven.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the planets are a warning about worshipping the creation instead of the Creator: the stars are God's servants, and bowing to them is treason against the One who hung them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: some noted constellation (only in the plural), perhaps collectively, the zodiac
BiblicalUsage: The word is a constellation, and God uses it once, when He asks Job whether he can bring forth Mazzaroth in his season, or guide Arcturus with his sons.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the question is the answer: no man orders the stars in their seasons, and Job's silence is the right response to a God who does.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Meah, a tower in Jerusalem
BiblicalUsage: Meah is the tower in Jerusalem's wall, named where the priests rebuilt the wall under Nehemiah: they sanctified the sheep gate and built even to the tower of Meah. The tower is named again in the procession at the dedication.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that a tower named in the rebuilding is a sign of a people coming home: the wall went up stone by stone, and the tower of Meah stood where the priests had set their hands to the work.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a hundred; also as a multiplicative and a fraction}
BiblicalUsage: The word is the Aramaic for a hundred, and it appears where the numbers of the exile are counted: Darius sets a hundred and twenty princes over the kingdom, the returned exiles offer a hundred bullocks, and Ezra is given a hundred talents of silver.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the counting is the point: God numbers the princes, the offerings, and the silver, and nothing in the exile is too small for Him to count.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: only in plural the bowels
BiblicalUsage: The word is the bowels, used once in the Aramaic of Daniel, for the belly of the great image: its head was gold, its breast and arms silver, and its belly and thighs brass.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the belly of brass is the third kingdom in the dream, and the image stands as a warning: empires look splendid from the head down, and they all fall to a stone cut without hands.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: the belly, i.e. (figuratively) interior
BiblicalUsage: The word is the belly or the inward parts, and Isaiah uses it once, in God's promise to Israel: if they had listened, their seed would have been as the sand, and the offspring of their bowels like the gravel of the sea.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the verse is a lament as much as a promise: God shows Israel what might have been, and the children who were never born are the measure of what disobedience cost.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a hundred; also as a multiplicative and a fraction
BiblicalUsage: A hundred is the number of fullness in counting: Adam lived a hundred and thirty years and begat a son, the children of Israel came out of Egypt six hundred thousand men on foot, and the census of the tribes is counted in hundreds.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the counting is God's way of saying He knows His people one by one: a hundred years of a life, six hundred thousand men on the march, and not one of them is lost in the number.
RelatedEvents: The Exodus and the Red Sea; Creation
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: (only in plural as singular) the setting (of the sun)
BiblicalUsage: The word is the setting of the sun, and Daniel uses it once, of the king who laboured till the going down of the sun to deliver Daniel from the lions' den.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the sunset is the measure of a king's love: Darius worked all day to save one man, and the sun went down on his failure — but God kept Daniel, and the den could not hold him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Mearah, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Mearah is a place on the coast beside the Sidonians, named in the land still to be taken. Joshua lists it among the towns the tribes had yet to possess when he divided Canaan.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the places named and not yet taken are part of the promise: God counts the land His people have not reached yet, and the map of what remains is still His.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a cavern (as dark)
BiblicalUsage: A cave is a hiding place and a grave in the Bible, and the word runs through the stories of the fugitives: Lot dwelt in a cave with his daughters after Sodom, David hid in the cave of Adullam and the men in distress gathered to him, and Saul went into a cave to cover his feet while David stood behind him. Abraham bought the cave of Machpelah for a burial place, and five kings hid in a cave at Makkedah.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the cave is where God's people learn to hide in Him rather than in the rock: Lot's cave ends in shame, David's cave gathers the distressed into an army, and Abraham's cave becomes the family grave where faith waits for the resurrection. The rock can hide you, but only God can keep you.
RelatedPeople: Lot; King David; King Saul; Abraham; Sarah
RelatedEvents: Destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah; Abraham Buys the Burial Cave; David Spares Saul at En Gedi
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a little or few (often adverbial or compar.)
BiblicalUsage: A little is the small amount, and the Bible uses it to measure what matters: better is little with the fear of the LORD than great treasure with trouble, and better is a little with righteousness than great revenues without right. The widow of Zarephath has only a little meal in the barrel, and Abraham asks for a little water to wash the angels' feet.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that little with God is more than much without Him: the widow's little meal fed three people through a famine, and the proverb says the same in a sentence — a little with the fear of the LORD is enough.
RelatedEvents: Elijah and the Widow of Zarephath
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: used only in plural the intestines, or (collectively) the abdomen, figuratively, sympathy; by implication, a vest; by extension the stomach, the uterus (or of men, the seat of generation), the heart (figuratively)
BiblicalUsage: The bowels are the inward parts, and the Bible makes them the seat of the deepest feelings: God promises Abraham a son who will come out of his own bowels, Jeremiah says his bowels are troubled for Ephraim, and Jonah prays from the fish's belly. The psalm says God's law is within the heart, and God promises David a son out of his bowels to sit on his throne.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the bowels are the Bible's word for the place where love hurts: God says His bowels are troubled for His people, and that is not sentiment but the heart of the Father. When the law is within us, the same inward place holds both His word and His compassion.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: refractory
BiblicalUsage: The word means refractory, stubborn, and Jeremiah uses it once, of an evil people who refuse to hear God's words and walk in the imagination of their own hearts.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that refusal is the heart of rebellion: the people did not fail to hear, they refused to hear, and that choice is what makes a people evil.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an execration
BiblicalUsage: A curse is the judgment God pronounces on disobedience, and the word is used where the curse falls: Moses says the LORD will send cursing and vexation on a people who forsake Him, and Proverbs says the curse of the LORD is in the house of the wicked. Malachi says the priests will be cursed for despising God's name, and that the whole nation is cursed with a curse for robbing God.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the curse is the other side of the blessing: God sets both before His people, and the curse is not spite but the honest consequence of turning from the One who blesses. The way out is the same in every verse — return to Him, and the curse is lifted.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a primary particle of qualified negation (whereas G3756 expresses an absolute denial); (adverb) not, (conjunction) lest; also (as an interrogative implying a negative answer (whereas G3756 expects an affirmative one)) whether:--any but (that), X forbear, + God forbid, + lack, lest, neither, never, no (X wise in), none, nor, (can-)not, nothing, that not, un(-taken), without. Often used in compounds in substantially the same relations. See also G3362, G3363, G3364, G3372, G3373, G3375, G3378.
BiblicalUsage: The word is the small negative, not, and it runs through the whole New Testament as the word of qualified denial: Jesus says take no thought for your life, and God so loved the world that whosoever believeth in Him should not perish. Paul says let not sin reign in your mortal body.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that this little word carries the gospel's hardest commands and its greatest promise in the same breath: do not worry, do not let sin reign, and the one who believes shall not perish.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a pile of rubbish (as contorted), i.e. a ruin
BiblicalUsage: The word is a pile of rubbish, a ruin, and Isaiah uses it once, of Damascus: it shall be taken away from being a city, and it shall be a ruinous heap.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the heap is the end of every city that trusts in itself: Damascus was a great city, and God says it will be a pile of rubbish, and the ruin is the sermon.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a robe (i.e. upper and outer garment)
BiblicalUsage: A robe is the outer garment, and the Bible uses it for priests, for kings, and for righteousness itself: the robe of the ephod is made of blue with bells of gold, Hannah makes Samuel a little coat every year, and Saul catches Samuel's skirt and tears it. Tamar wears a garment of divers colours, and Job says he put on righteousness and it clothed him like a robe.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the robe is the picture of being clothed by another: Samuel's mother made his coat, the priest's robe was God's design, and Job's righteousness was a garment he put on. The best robe in the Bible is the one God gives, and it fits because He made it.
RelatedPeople: Aaron; Samuel; Hannah; King Saul; Job
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {something (authoritatively) said, i.e. an edict}
BiblicalUsage: The word is the Aramaic for a decree, an authoritative word: the matter is by the decree of the watchers, says Daniel, and Ezra is given whatever he needs by the king's decree.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the decree of the watchers is higher than the decree of any king: Nebuchadnezzar learned that the Most High rules in the kingdom of men, and His decree stands when every other falls.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, vehemence, i.e. (with or without preposition) vehemently; by implication, wholly, speedily, etc. (often with other words as an intensive or superlative; especially when repeated)
BiblicalUsage: The word means very, exceedingly, and might, and it is used where the measure is the whole heart: love the LORD thy God with all thy heart and with all thy soul and with all thy might. God saw everything He had made, and behold, it was very good, and the psalm says His testimonies are very faithful.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the word is a demand for everything: not some of the heart, but all of it, and all of the soul, and all of the might — because the God who made all things very good deserves nothing less.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: may ook i.e. G3361 and G3756; as interrogative and negative, is it not that?:--neither (followed by no), + never, not. Compare G3364.
BiblicalUsage: The word is two negatives together, not, and it is the question that expects no for an answer: Paul asks, have they not heard, and have we not power to eat and to drink, and to lead about a sister, a wife. The two words stand side by side in the Greek, and together they ask the question that answers itself.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the double negative is Paul at his most human: he asks the question and knows the answer, and the church is left to admit that the gospel's messengers have every right to live by the gospel.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {an abode, of God (the Tabernacle or the Temple), men (their home) or animals (their lair); hence, a retreat (asylum)}
BiblicalUsage: A dwelling is a home, and the Bible uses it for God's house and for the lair of wild beasts: Moses says the eternal God is thy refuge, and underneath are the everlasting arms, and the psalm says God's tabernacle is in Salem. Job says the lions lie in their dens, and the Song pictures the mountains of the leopards.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word is about where you live: the eternal God is a dwelling, not a visit, and underneath the life lived in Him are everlasting arms. The lions have their dens, but God's people have a home that cannot be taken.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Meonothai, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Meonothai is named once, in the genealogy of Judah, as the father of Ophrah. His grandsons were the craftsmen of the valley.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that a single line in a genealogy is still a life: Meonothai raised a son whose sons were craftsmen, and the family trade is remembered alongside the name.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, a speck or point, i.e. (by implication) something; with negative, nothing
BiblicalUsage: The word means anything, and with a negative it means nothing, and it is used where the test is total: Joseph's master kept back nothing from him except his wife, and the dead know not anything. Balaam says he has no power at all to speak beyond God's word, and Israel testifies that Samuel took nothing from any man.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word is a measure of a whole life: nothing kept back, nothing taken, nothing spoken beyond God's word — and the man who can say that has kept himself clean.
RelatedPeople: Joseph, Son of Jacob; King Solomon; Balaam; Samuel
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a Meunite, or inhabitant of Maon (only in plural)
BiblicalUsage: The Meunites are a people of the desert, named where Judah fought them: God helped Uzziah against the Meunim, and the Simeonites smote their tents and destroyed them. The name also appears among the Nethinim who returned from exile.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the Meunites are a reminder that God fights for His people against enemies history barely remembers, and that the victory belongs to Him whether the enemy's name survives or not.
RelatedPeople: Uzziah, King of Judah; King Hezekiah
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: something lighted, i.e. an aperture; by implication, a crevice or hole (of a serpent)
BiblicalUsage: The word is a hole or aperture, and Isaiah uses it once, in the picture of the age of peace: the sucking child shall play on the hole of the asp, and nothing shall hurt or destroy in all God's holy mountain.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the child at the serpent's hole is the promise that peace will reach the most dangerous places: where death used to live, a child will play, and nothing will hurt.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a shorter (and probably original) form of G1691; me:--I, me, my.
BiblicalUsage: The word is the enclitic me, the small word for myself, and it is everywhere in the Gospels: come unto me, says Jesus, and the leper says, if thou wilt, thou canst make me clean. It is the word of the one who comes to Christ with nothing but need.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that this little word is the whole gospel in miniature: come unto me, make me clean — the sinner brings nothing but himself, and Christ is enough.
RelatedEvents: Jesus Heals a Man with Leprosy
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: fat; figuratively, rich
BiblicalUsage: Fat is the rich part of the sacrifice and the pasture, and the word is used for both: David offers burnt sacrifices of fatlings with the incense of rams, and Isaiah says the lambs shall feed in the fat pastures of the waste places.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe fat is the Bible's picture of the best portion: God is given the richest part, and the flock feeds where the land is fat — because the LORD provides the best for His own.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a cooking hearth
BiblicalUsage: A cooking hearth is a boiling place, and Ezekiel uses the word once, in the vision of the temple: there were boiling places under the rows, where the ministers of the house would boil the sacrifice of the people.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that even the kitchens of the temple are holy: God provides a place for every part of the service, and nothing in His house is beneath His care.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a haven
BiblicalUsage: A haven is a harbour, a mart, and Ezekiel uses the word once, of Tyre, the merchant city that was a mart of the peoples for many isles.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Tyre's haven is the picture of a city that trusted its trade: the ships came from every isle, and the wealth could not save it when God's judgment came.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Mebunnai, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Mebunnai the Hushathite is named once, among David's mighty men. He is one of the warriors who stood by David through the wars with the Philistines.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the mighty men are remembered by name because loyalty has a name: Mebunnai stood with David when it cost him, and the Bible keeps the record.
RelatedEvents: David's Mighty Men and the Philistine Giants
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a trampling
BiblicalUsage: A trampling is the treading down of a nation, and Isaiah uses it where the proud are trodden: a nation meted out and trodden down, and a day of trouble and of treading down in the valley of vision.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the trampling is what pride earns: the nations that marched over others are marched over themselves, and the valley of vision becomes the valley of treading down.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: perplexity
BiblicalUsage: Perplexity is the confusion of a people with no way out, and Isaiah calls the day of Jerusalem's siege a day of perplexity, while Micah says the day of the watchmen shall be their perplexity.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that perplexity is the judgment that fits the sin: a people who would not listen is left without an answer, and the confusion is the consequence of its own choices.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: emptiness
BiblicalUsage: Emptiness is the word for a city stripped bare, and Nahum uses it once, of Nineveh: she is empty, and void, and waste, and the heart melteth, and the knees smite together.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the three words together are the whole sentence on Nineveh: empty, void, and waste — a city that was full of plunder ends with nothing, and the knees that once marched now smite together in fear.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a divan (as enclosing the room); abstractly (adverbial) around
BiblicalUsage: The word is the round about, the circle around the king's table, and the Song says while the king sits at his table, the spikenard sends out its smell. The psalm uses it for the mischief of the lips that comes round about the wicked, and the temple walls were carved with figures round about.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that what is round about us is what we become: the king's table smells of spikenard, and the wicked man's lips return on his own head — the circle always closes.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a mixture, i.e. of wine with spices
BiblicalUsage: A mixture is wine mixed with spices, and the psalm uses it once, of the cup in the LORD's hand: the wine is red, it is full of mixture, and He pours out the same to the wicked.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the mixed wine is judgment made strong: God does not dilute His cup, and the wicked drink it to the dregs.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to strike in pieces; also to arrest; specifically to impale
BiblicalUsage: To smite is the Aramaic word for striking down, and Daniel uses it for the stone cut out without hands that smote the image and became a great mountain. The same word is used for God doing according to His will among the inhabitants of the earth, and for the man hanged on timber for altering the king's decree.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the stone is the whole gospel in a dream: a kingdom not made by hands smites every kingdom men have built, and the smiting is not the end but the beginning — the stone becomes a mountain that fills the earth. The kingdoms of men are all images with feet of clay, and the stone is still falling.
RelatedEvents: Nebuchadnezzar's Dream of the Image; Nebuchadnezzar's Humbling
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a joiner, i.e. brace or cramp
BiblicalUsage: A joiner is a brace or cramp, the iron that holds the work together, and it appears where David prepares iron for the temple and where the workmen repair the house in Josiah's day.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the joinings are the hidden work of the temple: nobody sees the cramps, but without them the stones fall, and God counts the unseen fastenings as worship too.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a halving
BiblicalUsage: A halving is the half of the spoil, and Numbers uses it twice, for the half that pertained to the congregation after the war with Midian: the half of the sheep, and the half of the persons.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the halving is God's order in the spoil: half to those who fought, half to the congregation, and the division itself is an act of worship, because the victory belonged to the LORD.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a window
BiblicalUsage: A window is an opening, and the word is used for the windows of Solomon's house, set in three rows, light against light, in the palace he built for himself.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the windows in three rows are the mark of a house built with care: light against light, in order, and the king's house was made to be lived in, not only looked at.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a cavern (as if excavated)
BiblicalUsage: A cavern is a hole dug out of the rock, and Isaiah uses the word once, of men going into the holes of the rocks and the caves of the earth to hide from the terror of the LORD in the day He arises to shake the earth.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the caves are the last hiding place of the proud: when the LORD arises, the rocks will not cover them, and the holes they dug to hide in become their graves.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, a dissolution; concretely, a ruin, or (abstractly) consternation
BiblicalUsage: Destruction is the ruin that follows folly, and Proverbs says the mouth of the foolish is near destruction, and the way of the LORD is destruction to the workers of iniquity. The fool's mouth is his own destruction, the psalm says God cast the king's crown to the ground, and Jeremiah prays that God would not be a terror to him in the day of evil.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe destruction is usually self-inflicted: the fool's mouth destroys him, the worker of iniquity walks into it, and the crown cast down is the end of a covenant broken. Jeremiah's prayer is the way out — make God your hope, not your terror, and the day of evil will not destroy you.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a stroke, i.e. battering-ram
BiblicalUsage: A stroke is a battering ram, and Ezekiel uses the word once, of the engines of war set against the walls of Tyre: he shall set engines of war against thy walls, and with his axes he shall break down thy towers.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the battering ram is the end of a city that trusted its walls: Tyre was strong on the sea, and God brought the ram to its gates, and no wall stands when He sends the breaker.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Mechida, one of the Nethinim
BiblicalUsage: Mechida is a family of the Nethinim, the temple servants who returned from exile with Zerubbabel. The name is kept in the lists of Ezra and Nehemiah.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the Nethinim are the quiet proof that God keeps His servants: a family that carried water for the temple is named in the record of the return, and no service is too low to be written down.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Mechir, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Mechir is named once, in the genealogy of Judah, as the father of Eshton. He is the son of Chelub the brother of Shuah.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that a single line is still a life: Mechir raised a son, and the son's name is kept, and the genealogy is God's way of saying that fathers matter.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: price, payment, wages
BiblicalUsage: Price is what a thing costs, and the Bible uses it for buying, for wages, and for the truth itself: Isaiah says buy wine and milk without money and without price, and Proverbs asks what good is a price in the hand of a fool who has no heart for wisdom. Ahab offers a price for Naboth's vineyard, David insists on buying the threshing floor at its full price, and Micah says the priests teach for hire.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe price is the test of what we value: the gospel is without price because Christ paid it, wisdom is priceless to the man who has a heart for it, and David would not offer God what cost him nothing. The price in a fool's hand is wasted, but the price paid in faith is never lost.
RelatedPeople: Isaiah; King Solomon; King Ahab; King David; Naboth the Jezreelite
RelatedEvents: David's Census and the Plague; Naboth's Vineyard
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a dance
KeyPassages: Exodus 15:20; 1 Samuel 18:6; Judges 11:34; Song of Solomon 6:13
BiblicalUsage: A dance is the movement of joy before God, and the Bible uses it at the great moments of deliverance: Miriam takes a timbrel and leads the women in dances after the sea closes over Pharaoh, the women come out with dances to meet Saul after David kills Goliath, and Jephthah's daughter comes out with timbrels and dances to greet her father. The Song pictures the dance of the two camps, the company of two armies.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe dancing is the body's way of saying what words cannot: Miriam danced because the sea had closed, the women danced because Goliath had fallen, and the joy was too big to stand still for. I hold that the dance of the two camps is the church itself — two armies, one joy, moving together before God.
RelatedBooks: Exodus; 1 Samuel; Judges; Song of Solomon
RelatedPeople: Miriam; Moses; King David; King Saul; Jephthah, Judge of Israel
RelatedEvents: The Exodus and the Red Sea; David and Goliath
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a Mecholathite or inhabitant of Abel-Mecholah
BiblicalUsage: A Meholathite is a man of Abel-meholah, and the word appears twice, for Adriel, who married Saul's daughter Merab when she should have been given to David, and whose sons were later given up to the Gibeonites.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Adriel's story is a warning about marrying into a king's bargains: he gained a princess and lost his sons, and the house of Saul kept paying for its broken promises.
RelatedPeople: Adriel the Meholathite; King Saul; King David; Merab
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, scrutinized, i.e. (by implication) a recess
BiblicalUsage: The word is a recess, a deep place, and the psalm uses it once: in His hand are the deep places of the earth, and the strength of the hills is His also.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the deep places belong to God as much as the heights do: the recesses no man has seen are in His hand, and the hills are His strength, not ours.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: or μεχρίς from G3372; as far as, i.e. up to a certain point (as a preposition, of extent (denoting the terminus, whereas G891 refers especially to the space of time or place intervening) or conjunction):--till, (un-)to, until.
BiblicalUsage: The word means as far as, until, and it marks the end of a road: Capernaum is told it shall be brought down to hell, though exalted to heaven, and death reigned from Adam until Moses. Paul says the gifts of the church will remain until we all come to the unity of the faith.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that until is the word of a limit: death reigned until Moses, judgment waits until the end, and the church's gifts last until unity comes — and every until in Scripture has a God who set it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an instrument for marking a circle, i.e. compasses
BiblicalUsage: A compass is the tool for marking a circle, and Isaiah uses it once, of the carpenter who marks out his idol with a line and a compass, shaping it with planes until it looks like a man.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the compass is the mockery of idolatry: a man measures out his god with a tool, and the god he makes is the size of his own hands — too small to save him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Mechujael or Mechijael, an antediluvian patriarch
BiblicalUsage: Mehujael is the son of Irad and the father of Methusael, on the line of Cain. The line runs from Enoch to Lamech, building cities and making swords while Seth's line called on the name of the LORD.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Cain's line is the record of a world getting on without God: cities, music, and metal, all of it real, and all of it ending in Lamech's boast — while the other line simply called on the LORD.
RelatedPeople: Enoch; Irad; Lamech, Son of Methusael; Cain
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a thoroughfare (as turnpiked), literally or figuratively; specifically a viaduct, a staircase
BiblicalUsage: A highway is the raised road, and the Bible uses it for the way God makes for His people: prepare the way of the LORD in the wilderness, says Isaiah, and the highway of the upright is to depart from evil. The stars fought from their courses in the highway of heaven, and the psalm says blessed is the man in whose heart are the ways to Zion.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the highway is the way God builds through the wilderness: it is raised above the flood, it is straight where the desert wanders, and the man whose heart is set on it is blessed. The stars themselves fought from their courses for Israel, because the road was God's.
RelatedPeople: Isaiah; King Solomon; Deborah; King David
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a covering, i.e. garniture
BiblicalUsage: A covering is a garniture of precious stones, and Ezekiel uses the word once, of the king of Tyre in Eden: every precious stone was thy covering, the sardius, topaz, and diamond.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the covering is the tragedy of Tyre: a king dressed in Eden's stones forgot the God who dressed him, and the beauty became the reason for the fall.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a hedge
BiblicalUsage: A hedge is a thorn fence, and Micah uses the word once, of a people whose best men are as a brier and whose most upright is sharper than a thorn hedge.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the hedge is the picture of a nation turned against itself: the men who should have been a wall of protection became the thorns, and the hedge that should have kept danger out became the danger.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a push, i.e. ruin
BiblicalUsage: The word is a push, a thrust toward ruin, and the psalm uses it once, of the violent man whom evil hunts to overthrow him.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the push is the end of the violent man's own road: evil hunts him as he hunted others, and the overthrow he planned for his neighbour falls on him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: adverb from a compound of G3361 and ἀμός (somebody); by no means:--not so.
BiblicalUsage: The word means by no means, not so, and it is Peter's answer twice, when he is told to eat what the law calls unclean: not so, Lord, for I have never eaten anything common or unclean.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Peter's refusal is the honest voice of a man who loved the law: he said not so to God Himself, and God had to tell him three times that what He has cleansed is clean.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Medan, a son of Abraham
BiblicalUsage: Medan is a son of Abraham by Keturah, named with his brothers Zimran, Jokshan, Midian, Ishbak, and Shuah. He is named again in the genealogy of the nations in Chronicles.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the sons of Keturah are the loose ends of Abraham's story: they were given gifts and sent away eastward, and their names are kept even though the promise went through Isaac.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {a contest or quarrel}
BiblicalUsage: Strife is the quarrel that hatred starts, and Proverbs uses it three times for the same truth. He devises mischief continually and sows discord, the false witness speaks lies and sows discord among brethren, and hatred stirs up strifes while love covers all sins.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe strife is always sown, never accidental: somebody plants it, and the harvest is a house divided. Love is the only cover for it, and the love that covers sins is the love that stops the sowing.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {a Midjanite or descendant (native) of Midjan}
BiblicalUsage: A Midianite is a descendant of Midian, and the word appears once, where the Midianites sold Joseph into Egypt to Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the sale is the hinge of Joseph's life: his brothers sold him to the Midianites, and the Midianites sold him to Egypt, and God used every sale to save the family that sold him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Medatha, the father of Haman
BiblicalUsage: Hammedatha is named as the father of Haman the Agagite, the enemy who plotted to destroy all the Jews in the days of Esther. His ten sons were hanged with him.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the father's name is kept because the hatred was inherited: Haman was the son of Hammedatha, an Agagite, and the old enmity of Amalek came back in his generation — and God turned it back on his own head.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3361 and G1161; but not, not even; in a continued negation, nor:--neither, nor (yet), (no) not (once, so much as).
BiblicalUsage: The word means neither, nor, and it carries the continued negation through a sentence: Jesus says take no thought for your life, and provide neither gold nor silver for the journey. He also says let not your heart be troubled, neither let it be afraid.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the neither is God's way of closing every door to worry: neither gold nor silver, neither trouble nor fear — the list is shut, and the peace that remains is His.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: , including the irregular feminine μηδεμία, and the neuter μηδέν from G3361 and G1520; not even one (man, woman, thing):--any (man, thing), no (man), none, not (at all, any man, a whit), nothing, + without delay.
BiblicalUsage: The word means no one, nothing, and it is the absolute negative of the New Testament: Jesus tells the healed leper to tell no man, and the demon is commanded to hold its peace and come out of the man. Paul says recompense to no man evil for evil.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word draws a line with no exceptions: tell no man, and pay back no man evil for evil — because the God who commands it is the one who provides for it.
RelatedEvents: Jesus Heals a Man with Leprosy
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3366 and G4452; not even yet:--not yet.
BiblicalUsage: The word means not even yet, and it appears once, of Noah: by faith he prepared an ark for the saving of his house, moved with fear, for things not seen as yet.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that not yet is the whole of faith: Noah built for a flood he had not seen, and the ark was the answer to a warning, not to a sight.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3366 and G4218; not even ever:--never.
BiblicalUsage: The word means never, not even ever, and Paul uses it once, of the men of the last days: ever learning, and never able to come to the knowledge of the truth.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the verse is a warning about learning without truth: a man can study for ever and never arrive, if he will not submit to what he learns.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, extent, i.e. measure; by implication, a dress (as measured)
BiblicalUsage: The word is a measure, a dress, and it appears where Hanun shames David's servants: he shaved off half their beards and cut off their garments in the middle, even to their buttocks, and sent them away.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the cut garment is the picture of calculated insult: Hanun measured out the shame exactly, and the war that followed was the price of a joke told at the wrong men.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {properly, a judgeship, i.e. jurisdiction; by implication, a district (as ruled by a judge); generally, a region}
BiblicalUsage: A province is a district under a ruler, and the Aramaic word is used where empires count their lands: Daniel is made ruler over the whole province of Babylon, Shadrach and his friends are set over the affairs of the province, and the enemies of the Jews warn the king that Jerusalem has made insurrection in times past.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the province is where God puts His people to work: Daniel ruled a pagan province without bowing to it, and the same God who set him over Babylon kept him through the furnace.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {properly, a judgeship, i.e. jurisdiction; by implication, a district (as ruled by a judge); generally, a region}
BiblicalUsage: A province is a district under a ruler, and the Aramaic word is used where empires count their lands: Daniel is made ruler over the whole province of Babylon, Shadrach and his friends are set over the affairs of the province, and the enemies of the Jews warn the king that Jerusalem has made insurrection in times past.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the province is where God puts His people to work: Daniel ruled a pagan province without bowing to it, and the same God who set him over Babylon kept him through the furnace.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a mortar
BiblicalUsage: A mortar is a bowl for beating grain, and the word appears once, of the manna in the wilderness: the people ground it in mills, or beat it in a mortar, and baked it in pans, and made cakes of it.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the mortar is the daily work of grace: the manna fell from heaven, but the people still had to grind it and bake it, and God's provision has always asked for our hands as well as our trust.
RelatedEvents: Manna and Quail in the Wilderness
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of foreign origin (compare H4074); a Median, or inhabitant of Media:--Mede.
BiblicalUsage: A Mede is a man of Media, and the word appears once, at Pentecost. Medes are named among the nations who heard the apostles speak in their own tongues the wonderful works of God.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the Mede at Pentecost is the sign of the gospel's reach: a man from the old empire of the east hears the gospel in his own tongue, and the nations God once scattered are gathered again.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a dwelling
BiblicalUsage: A dwelling is a home, and the Aramaic word is used where the gods cannot live: the Chaldeans tell Nebuchadnezzar that none can show the dream except the gods, whose dwelling is not with flesh. The king is told his dwelling shall be with the beasts of the field, and his heart shall be made like the beasts' heart.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word turns on the king: the gods whose dwelling is not with flesh cannot help him, and the king who thought his dwelling was a palace learns it is with the beasts. God dwells with flesh after all — He came down and lived among us.
RelatedEvents: Nebuchadnezzar's Dream of the Image; Nebuchadnezzar's Humbling
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a threshing, i.e. (concretely and figuratively) down-trodden people
BiblicalUsage: The word is a threshing, the trodden-down people, and Isaiah uses it once, in the lament over Babylon: O my threshing, and the corn of my floor, that which I have heard of the LORD of hosts I have declared unto you.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the threshing floor is where God separates the wheat from the chaff: His people are the corn of His floor, and the treading is not the end but the harvest.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a pile of fuel
BiblicalUsage: A pile of fuel is the wood laid for the fire, and the word is used for Tophet, the place of burning: the pile is made deep and large, and the breath of the LORD kindles it. Ezekiel says the same of the city under judgment: I will make the pile for fire great.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the pile is the picture of judgment prepared: the wood is laid, the fire is ready, and the breath of the LORD kindles it — because He does not bluff about what sin earns.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a compound of G3173 and αὐχέω (to boast; akin to G837 and G2744); to talk big, i.e. be grandiloquent (arrogant, egotistic):--boast great things.
BiblicalUsage: The word means to talk big, to boast, and it is used once, of the tongue: it is a little member, and it boasteth great things, as a small fire kindles a great forest.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the little member is the most dangerous part of the body: it boasts great things, and the forest it kindles is a life, a church, or a family.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3173; magnificent, i.e. (neuter, plural as noun) a conspicuous favor, or (subjectively) perfection:--great things, wonderful works.
BiblicalUsage: The word means magnificent things, and Luke uses it once, at Pentecost, where the crowd hears the apostles speak in their own tongues the wonderful works of God.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the wonderful works are the sign of the new age: the Spirit gives plain men the words of God, and the crowd hears the greatness of God in its own tongue.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3167; superbness, i.e. glory or splendor:--magnificence, majesty, mighty power.
BiblicalUsage: Majesty is the splendour of God, and the word is used where men see it and fall back: the crowd is amazed at the mighty power of God when Jesus heals the boy, and Paul warns that Diana's magnificence will be destroyed. Peter says the apostles were eyewitnesses of Christ's majesty on the mount.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe majesty is what happens when the veil lifts: the crowd sees God's power in a healed boy, the silversmith fears for his goddess, and Peter never forgot the mountain. The majesty of Christ is not an idea but a sight, and those who saw it could not keep quiet.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3173 and G4241; befitting greatness or magnificence (majestic):--excellent.
BiblicalUsage: The word means excellent, befitting majesty, and Peter uses it once, of the voice from heaven: there came such a voice to him from the excellent glory, saying, This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the excellent glory is the Father's own voice naming the Son: no greater honour exists than to be called beloved by God, and the mountain heard it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: adverb from G3173; much:--greatly.
BiblicalUsage: The word means greatly, and Paul uses it once, of his joy at the Philippians' care: I rejoiced in the Lord greatly, that now at the last your care of me hath flourished again.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Paul's greatly is the measure of a grateful heart: he rejoiced not in the gift but in the care behind it, and the flourishing of love is worth more than the money.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3173; greatness, i.e. (figuratively) divinity (often God himself):--majesty.
BiblicalUsage: Majesty is the greatness of God Himself, and Hebrews uses it for the place of Christ: He sat down on the right hand of the Majesty on high, and we have a high priest set on the right hand of the throne of the Majesty in the heavens. Jude closes his letter with glory and majesty to the only wise God.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the Majesty on high is the throne Christ sits on: He purged our sins and sat down, because the work was finished, and the high priest who sits is the proof that the way to God is open. I hold that majesty is not distance but the glory of a Saviour who reigns.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3173; to make (or declare) great, i.e. increase or (figuratively) extol:--enlarge, magnify, shew great.
BiblicalUsage: To magnify is to make great, and the Bible uses it for God and for men: Mary says my soul doth magnify the Lord, and Elizabeth's neighbours magnify God for the mercy shown to her. The Pharisees enlarge their phylacteries to be seen, and Paul says Christ shall be magnified in his body, whether by life or by death.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe magnifying is the choice every life makes: Mary magnified the Lord, the Pharisees magnified themselves, and Paul magnified Christ in his body. What we make great is what we worship, and the soul that magnifies God finds itself made great by Him.
RelatedPeople: Mary, Mother of Jesus; Elizabeth; Jesus; Paul
RelatedEvents: The Birth of John the Baptist
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, accumulation, i.e. impulse or direction
