BiblicalUsage: The word is an impulse, a direction, and Habakkuk uses it once, of the Chaldeans: they shall come all for violence, and their faces shall sup up as the east wind.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the faces set forward are the picture of an army with no doubt and no mercy: the Chaldeans came for violence, and the direction of their faces was the direction of God's judgment on His people.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to overthrow
BiblicalUsage: To overthrow is the Aramaic word for destroying, and Darius uses it once, in the decree for the temple: God destroy all kings and people that put their hand to alter and destroy this house which is at Jerusalem.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the decree is God's protection written in a king's hand: whoever touches His house will be overthrown, and the empire that signed it did not know it was signing its own warning.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: (including the prolonged forms, feminine μεγάλη, plural μεγάλοι, etc.; compare also G3176, G3187); big (literally or figuratively, in a very wide application):--(+ fear) exceedingly, great(-est), high, large, loud, mighty, + (be) sore (afraid), strong, X to years.
BiblicalUsage: Great is the word for what is large in size, in power, and in worth, and the New Testament uses it for the kingdom, the seed, the mystery, and the voice: the least in the kingdom is great, the mustard seed grows greatest among herbs, great is the mystery of godliness, and John hears a great voice on the Lord's day. The angel promises that Jesus shall be great.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe great is the word the gospel keeps for what God does: the kingdom makes the least great, the smallest seed becomes the greatest herb, and the mystery of godliness is great because God was manifest in the flesh. I hold that the greatness of Christ is the measure of all other greatness — everything else is small beside Him.
RelatedTopics: Kingdom of God; Faith; Jesus Christ
RelatedPeople: Jesus; Paul; Mary, Mother of Jesus
RelatedEvents: The Sermon on the Mount; The Birth of Jesus
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, a distinguished thing; hence something valuable, as a product or fruit
KeyPassages: Deuteronomy 33:13; Deuteronomy 33:14; Song of Solomon 4:13; Song of Solomon 7:13
BiblicalUsage: Precious things are the best fruits of the land, and Moses blesses Joseph with the precious things of heaven and earth, the dew and the deep, the sun and the moon. The Song pictures the garden as an orchard of precious fruits, and the mandrakes give their smell at the gates.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the precious things are God's way of blessing the whole of life: heaven and earth, sun and moon, garden and field — and the blessing of Joseph is the picture of a life God fills from top to bottom. The mandrakes at the gates are the small sign of it: even the road home smells of the garden.
RelatedPeople: Moses; Joseph, Son of Jacob; King Solomon
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a saw
BiblicalUsage: A saw is the tool for cutting stone and men, and the word is used where the cutting is done: the temple stones were sawed with saws, and David put the Ammonites under saws and harrows of iron.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the saw cuts both ways: it dressed the stones of God's house, and it judged the enemies of God's people, and the same tool serves the building and the breaking.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3173; magnitude (figuratively):--greatness.
BiblicalUsage: The word means greatness, magnitude, and Paul uses it once, of the power of God toward believers: the exceeding greatness of His power to us-ward who believe, according to the working of His mighty power.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the greatness of God's power is not a doctrine to admire but a power toward us: the same working that raised Christ works in those who believe.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Megiddon or Megiddo, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Megiddo is a city on the plain of Jezreel, named where the tribes failed to drive out the Canaanites, and where Josiah was slain by Pharaoh Necho. Zechariah says the mourning in Jerusalem will be as the mourning of Hadadrimmon in the valley of Megiddon.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Megiddo is the battlefield of the Bible: the kings fought there, the righteous king died there, and the last mourning will be like the mourning there — because the plain of Megiddo is where the wars of men keep ending, and where God's war will end.
RelatedPeople: Joshua; King Josiah; Zechariah the Prophet
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {a roll}
BiblicalUsage: A roll is a scroll, and the Aramaic word is used once, where the decree of Cyrus is found: there was found at Achmetha, in the palace of the Medes, a roll, and therein was a record thus written.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the roll in the archive is God's providence in a drawer: a forgotten record, found at the right moment, turned the whole empire toward rebuilding His house.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {a roll}
BiblicalUsage: A roll is a scroll, and the Aramaic word is used once, where the decree of Cyrus is found: there was found at Achmetha, in the palace of the Medes, a roll, and therein was a record thus written.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the roll in the archive is God's providence in a drawer: a forgotten record, found at the right moment, turned the whole empire toward rebuilding His house.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a covering (in a bad sense), i.e. blindness or obduracy
BiblicalUsage: The word is a covering in a bad sense, a blindness or hardness of heart, and Jeremiah uses it once, in the prayer that God would give the persecutors sorrow of heart and His curse.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the covering is the judgment that fits the crime: men who hardened their hearts against God are given the hardness they chose, and the sorrow of heart is the fruit of it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: plural from G3176; grandees:--great men, lords.
BiblicalUsage: The word is the plural of grandees, the great men, and it is used where the powerful gather: Herod's birthday feast is kept with his lords and high captains, the kings and great men of the earth hide in the caves from the wrath of the Lamb, and the merchants of Babylon were the great men of the earth.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the great men are the proof that greatness without God is nothing: they feast with Herod, they hide from the Lamb, and their merchandise cannot buy them out of the judgment.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: superlative of G3173; greatest or very great:--exceeding great.
BiblicalUsage: The word is the superlative, greatest, and Peter uses it once, of the promises: God has given us exceeding great and precious promises, that by these ye might be partakers of the divine nature.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the promises are exceeding great because they are God's own word, and they are precious because they make us partakers of His nature — the greatest gift is not a thing but a share in Him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: affright
BiblicalUsage: The word is fear or affright, and it is used where fear comes true and where fear is taken away: the fear of the wicked shall come upon him, says Proverbs, and the psalm says the LORD delivered David from all his fears.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the two verses are the two ends of fear: the wicked man's fear finds him, and the righteous man's fear is taken from him, and the difference is who they trusted.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a fright; also a granary
BiblicalUsage: The word is a fright, and also a granary, and it is used where God chooses what men fear and where He asks whether the seed is yet in the barn: Isaiah says God will choose their delusions and bring their fears upon them, and Haggai asks if the seed is yet in the barn, before the blessing comes.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word holds the two sides of fear together: God brings on men the very things they feared, and He asks whether the seed is in the barn — because the harvest depends on what was sown, not on what was feared.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, a hurry; hence (adverbially) promptly
BiblicalUsage: Quickly is the word for what God does without delay: His word runs very swiftly, the light of the righteous breaks forth speedily, and the spies run quickly to take the city. Moses tells Aaron to make atonement quickly, because the plague has begun.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that quickly is the speed of mercy: God's word runs swiftly, His light breaks forth speedily, and when the plague begins, the atonement must not wait — because delay is death.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Mehetabel, the name of an Edomitish man and woman
BiblicalUsage: Mehetabel is the name of two people: the wife of Hadar, the last king of Edom, and the daughter of Matred. A second Mehetabel is the father of Shemaiah, who tried to frighten Nehemiah into hiding in the temple.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the two Mehetabels show how a name travels: one is a king's wife in Edom, the other a father in Jerusalem, and the same name covers a queen and a plotter — the Bible keeps both.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: confusion or uproar
BiblicalUsage: Confusion is the uproar God sends on His enemies, and the word is used where the confusion does His work: the LORD destroys the nations with a mighty destruction, the Philistines turn their swords on each other, and in the last day a great tumult from the LORD will fall on every man. The chronicler says there was no peace in those days, but great vexations upon all the inhabitants.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe confusion is God's weapon when men will not listen: He turns their swords on each other, and the tumult they meant for His people falls on them. The confusion of the enemy is the deliverance of the righteous.
RelatedPeople: Moses; King Saul; Jonathan; Zechariah the Prophet
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Mehuman, a eunuch of Xerxes
BiblicalUsage: Mehuman is one of the seven chamberlains of King Ahasuerus, named on the seventh day of the feast. The king's heart was merry with wine when he commanded them to bring Queen Vashti before him.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the chamberlain's name is kept because the feast is where the story turns: a king's merry command sets in motion the fall of a queen and the rise of Esther, and the servants who carried the order are part of the record.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: irregular comparative of G3173; larger (literally or figuratively, specially, in age):--elder, greater(-est), more.
BiblicalUsage: Meizon is the comparative word for greater, and 2 Peter 2:11 uses it of angels, who are greater in power and might than the false teachers they refuse to accuse. Even beings that strong hold back where God has not given them leave to speak.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe strength that restrains itself is the mark of those who know their place before God.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: neuter of G3187; (adverbially) in greater degree:--the more.
BiblicalUsage: Meizon is the neuter form of the word for greater, and it turns up wherever one thing is weighed against another. Matthew 12:6 has Jesus say that one greater than the temple is in this place, and Matthew 13:32 calls the grown mustard seed the greatest among herbs. James 3:1 warns teachers that they shall receive the greater condemnation.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that greatness in Scripture is always measured against something, and Christ is the measure that outranks them all.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: continued comparative of G3187; still larger (figuratively):--greater.
BiblicalUsage: Meizoteros is the stronger comparative, still greater, and John uses it once, in 3 John 1:4, where he says he has no greater joy than to hear that his children walk in truth.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a pastor's greatest joy is not a growing church but children who keep walking in the truth.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a covering, i.e. garment; specifically, a coverlet (for a bed), an awning (from the sun); also the omentum (as covering the intestines)
BiblicalUsage: Mekasseh is a covering, whether a garment, a bed coverlet, an awning against the sun, or a sail spread over a ship. Ezekiel 27:7 pictures Tyre's fine linen spread forth to be her sail, and Isaiah 14:11 turns the word into judgment, where the fallen king's covering is worms spread under and over him.
TheologicalSignificance: I take it as a sober picture: what covers us in pride will not cover us in judgment.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an assessment (as based upon a census)
BiblicalUsage: Mekes is the assessment, the tribute levied as a share of the spoil. Numbers 31:28 orders a tribute unto the LORD from the men of war, one soul of five hundred, and Numbers 31:37 counts the LORD's tribute of the sheep at six hundred and threescore and fifteen.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the tribute teaches that even the spoils of victory belong to God first, not to the men who won them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: merchandise; also value
BiblicalUsage: Meker is merchandise, the ware that is bought and sold, and the price it fetches. Nehemiah 13:16 finds men of Tyre selling fish and all manner of ware in Jerusalem on the sabbath, and Numbers 20:19 has Israel offer to pay for any water they drink on the way through Edom.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that honest trade is no sin, but selling on the sabbath showed where Tyre's merchants and Judah's buyers had put their hearts.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a sword
BiblicalUsage: Mekerah is the sword, and its one appearance is dark: Genesis 49:5 calls Simeon and Levi's weapons instruments of cruelty in their habitations, as Jacob rebukes the violence they did at Shechem.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a weapon is judged by what it is used for, and Jacob names his own sons' swords cruel.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a Mekerathite, or inhabitant of Mekerah
BiblicalUsage: Mekerathiy names a man by his home, a Mecherathite, an inhabitant of Mecherah. 1 Chronicles 11:36 lists Hepher the Mecherathite among David's mighty men.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God keeps the names of men the world would forget, even down to the village they came from.
RelatedEvents: David's Mighty Men and the Philistine Giants
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3361 and G2089; no further:--any longer, (not) henceforth, hereafter, no henceforward (longer, more, soon), not any more.
BiblicalUsage: Meketi means no longer, not henceforth, and it draws the line between the old life and the new. 1 Peter 4:2 says the believer should no longer live the rest of his time in the flesh to the lusts of men, but to the will of God. 1 Thessalonians 3:1 has Paul say he could no longer forbear, and so sent Timothy to the Thessalonians.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that 'no longer' is the gospel in two words: the old master has lost his claim.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a fracture
BiblicalUsage: Mekittah is a fracture, the breaking of a thing already broken. Isaiah 30:14 pictures judgment as the breaking of a potter's vessel, smashed so thoroughly that no sherd is left to take fire from the hearth or water from the pit.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the verse warns that trusting in anything but God ends not in repair but in shards too small to use.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Mekonah, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Mekonah is a town in the land of Judah, named once in the list of places settled after the return from exile. Nehemiah 11:28 places it beside Ziklag, among the villages where the returned families lived.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe even a town named once matters, because it marks a family that came home.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably akin to G3173; length (literally or figuratively):--length.
BiblicalUsage: Mekos is length, and it stretches both ways, from the measure of a city to the measure of God's love. Ephesians 3:18 prays that believers may comprehend the breadth and length and depth and height of Christ's love, and Revelation 21:16 measures the new Jerusalem, its length as large as its breadth.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the love of Christ is the one length no reed can measure, and the city built on it is foursquare and sure.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a pedestal, also a spot
BiblicalUsage: Mekownah is the base, the pedestal on which the temple's lavers stood. 1 Kings 7:27 describes the ten bases of brass Solomon made for the temple, and 2 Chronicles 4:14 says the lavers were made upon the bases.
TheologicalSignificance: I take it as a plain reminder: holy things stand on something solid, and God gave the pattern for the base as well as the vessel.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a spot
BiblicalUsage: Mekunah is a base, a resting place, and Zechariah 5:11 sets it in a vision: the woman in the ephah is carried to the land of Shinar, where a house is built for her and she is set upon her own base.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe wickedness gets a house built for it only to be left there, far from God's people.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: origin (as if a mine)
BiblicalUsage: Mekuwrah is origin, the place a thing comes from, as if from a mine. Ezekiel 16:3 traces Jerusalem's birth to the land of Canaan, her father an Amorite and her mother an Hittite. Ezekiel 21:30 sends the sword's judgment back to the place where Ammon was created, the land of its nativity, and Ezekiel 29:14 promises Egypt a return to Pathros, the land of its habitation, as a base kingdom.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe where we come from shapes us but does not excuse us: Jerusalem's low birth makes God's choosing of her all grace, and Egypt's return to its origin is judgment measured out. My position is that God judges every nation in the place it began, and He alone decides where it ends.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3372; to lengthen, i.e. (middle voice) to enlarge:--grow up.
BiblicalUsage: Mekyno means to lengthen, to grow up, and its one appearance is in the parable of the seed. Mark 4:27 says the seed should spring and grow up, night and day, while the sower sleeps and rises and knows not how.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe growth in God's kingdom is His work more than ours: we sow, and He lengthens what we cannot explain.
RelatedEvents: The Parable of the Growing Seed
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, deputyship, i.e. ministry; generally, employment (never servile) or work (abstractly or concretely); also property (as the result of labor)
BiblicalUsage: Mela'kah is work in the widest sense: employment, business, ministry, and the thing made by labour. Genesis 2:2 says God ended His work which He had made and rested on the seventh day, and Exodus 20:9 commands six days of labour to do all our work. Exodus 31:3 shows the other side, where God fills Bezalel with His Spirit for all manner of workmanship, and 1 Kings 5:16 sets officers over Solomon's workmen.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe work began with God, not with the fall: He worked first, and He rested, and He still gives skill for the work He asks of us. My position is that ordinary labour is holy when it is done as service to Him, whether it is building a temple or earning a living.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to fill
BiblicalUsage: Mela' is the Aramaic word to fill, and Daniel uses it both for a kingdom and for a king's rage. Daniel 2:35 says the stone that smote the image became a great mountain and filled the whole earth, and Daniel 3:19 says Nebuchadnezzar was full of fury against Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe what fills a man rules him: the stone fills the earth with God's kingdom, and fury fills a king who will not bow.
RelatedEvents: Nebuchadnezzar's Dream of the Image; Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego in the Fiery Furnace
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: salt
BiblicalUsage: Melach is the Aramaic word for salt, and in Ezra it means both the seasoning and the salary. Ezra 4:14 has the king's enemies say they have maintenance from the king's palace, the salt that kept them in his service, and Ezra 6:9 orders salt to be given day by day for the burnt offerings at Jerusalem.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe salt here shows how service binds a man: those who eat the king's salt defend the king's honour.
RelatedEvents: Cyrus's Decree and Return from Exile
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, powder, i.e. (specifically) salt (as easily pulverized and dissolved)
BiblicalUsage: Melach is salt, the common mineral that preserves, flavours, heals, and marks a covenant. 2 Chronicles 13:5 calls God's gift of the kingdom to David a covenant of salt, a bond that does not rot. 2 Kings 2:20 has Elisha ask for salt in a new cruse to heal the waters of Jericho, and 1 Chronicles 18:12 and 2 Samuel 8:13 both name the Valley of Salt, where Abishai and David struck down the Edomites.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe salt is the right picture for God's covenant because salt keeps what it touches from going bad. My position is that a covenant of salt is one God will not let spoil, and the same salt that heals a spring can mark a battlefield.
RelatedEvents: Elisha Heals the Waters of Jericho
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: salt
BiblicalUsage: Melach is the Aramaic word for salt, and in Ezra it means both the seasoning and the salary. Ezra 4:14 has the king's enemies say they have maintenance from the king's palace, the salt that kept them in his service, and Ezra 6:9 orders salt to be given day by day for the burnt offerings at Jerusalem.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe salt here shows how service binds a man: those who eat the king's salt defend the king's honour.
RelatedEvents: Cyrus's Decree and Return from Exile
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: advice
BiblicalUsage: Melak is advice, counsel given to a king who needs it. Daniel 4:27 has Daniel plead with Nebuchadnezzar: let my counsel be acceptable unto thee, and break off thy sins by righteousness, and thine iniquities by shewing mercy to the poor.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe good counsel is plain and costly, and Daniel gave it to a king who could have killed him for it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to speak
BiblicalUsage: Melal is the Aramaic word to speak, and Daniel uses it for words that carry weight. Daniel 6:21 has Daniel answer the king from the lions' den, O king, live for ever, and Daniel 7:8 sees a little horn with a mouth speaking great things.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe speech shows the speaker: Daniel's words honour the king, and the horn's words honour itself.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: neuter of G3189 as noun; ink:--ink.
BiblicalUsage: Melan is ink, the fluid that carries words onto the page. 2 Corinthians 3:3 contrasts letters written with ink against believers written by the Spirit of the living God on fleshy tables of the heart, and 2 John 1:12 says John would not write with paper and ink but hoped to speak face to face, that their joy might be full.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that ink is a good servant but a poor substitute: the living letter is a person, not a page.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: apparently a primary word; black:--black.
BiblicalUsage: Melas is black, the colour of hair no man can change and of the horse that rides at the third seal. Matthew 5:36 says no one can make one hair white or black, and Revelation 6:5 shows a black horse whose rider carries a pair of balances.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe black here marks what is beyond our control and what is coming in judgment, and both belong to God alone.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Melatjah, a Gibeonite
BiblicalUsage: Melatiah is a Gibeonite who came home from exile and put his hands to the wall. Nehemiah 3:7 says he repaired the wall next to Jadon the Meronothite, men of Gibeon and Mizpah, working up to the governor's seat on this side of the river.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the wall went up because returned exiles and old neighbours worked side by side, each in his own stretch.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H4428 with pronominal suffix, my king); Melchi (i.e. Malki), the name of two Israelites:--Melchi.
BiblicalUsage: Melchi is a name carried by two men in Luke's genealogy of Jesus, one the son of Janna and one the son of Addi. Luke 3:24 names Melchi the son of Janna, and Luke 3:28 names Melchi the son of Addi, both links in the line that runs back to David.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the genealogy is the gospel in names: every link, even one we know nothing else about, holds the line to Christ.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H4442); Melchisedek (i.e. Malkitsedek), a patriarch:--Melchisedec.
BiblicalUsage: Melchisedek is the king of Salem and priest of the most high God, and Hebrews holds him up as the pattern of Christ's priesthood. Hebrews 7:1 tells how he met Abraham returning from the slaughter of the kings and blessed him, and Hebrews 5:6 and Hebrews 7:17 both quote the promise, Thou art a priest for ever after the order of Melchisedec.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Melchizedek matters because he shows a priesthood older than Aaron and higher than Levi: a king who is also priest, with no beginning of days in the record, pointing straight to Christ. My position is that Hebrews is right to rest everything on him, because a priest who lives for ever is the only priest we need.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: something fulfilled, i.e. abundance (of produce)
BiblicalUsage: Mele'ah is fulness, the full produce of a field or a harvest. 2 Samuel 23:11 sets it in a field full of lentiles where Shammah stood his ground, and Amos 2:13 pictures God pressed under His people as a cart pressed full of sheaves.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a full field is a gift and a weight at once: plenty that God gives, and plenty His people can crush Him under by their sin.
RelatedEvents: David's Mighty Men and the Philistine Giants
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain origin; Meleas, an Israelite:--Meleas.
BiblicalUsage: Meleas is a name in Luke's genealogy, one link between Nathan and David. Luke 3:31 names Melea the son of Menan, in the line that runs from David through Nathan to Jesus.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe no link in the line to Christ is wasted, even the names we meet only once.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, salted (i.e. land), i.e. a desert
BiblicalUsage: Melechah is salt land, ground so salted that nothing grows there. Jeremiah 17:6 says the man who trusts in man shall inhabit the parched places in the wilderness, in a salt land and not inhabited, and Job 39:6 makes the barren land the home of the wild ass.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe salt land is the picture of a life cut off from God: parched, empty, and unfit for dwelling.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Melek, the name of two Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Melek is a man's name, the son of Micah, and the name also hides inside Hammelech, son of the king. 1 Chronicles 8:35 and 1 Chronicles 9:41 both list Melech among the sons of Micah in Benjamin's line, and Jeremiah 36:26 names Jerahmeel the son of Hammelech, sent to seize Baruch and Jeremiah.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that names carry their meaning with them: Melech means king, and the king's own men were sent against God's prophet and failed.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a king
BiblicalUsage: Melek is the Aramaic word for king, and it runs through Daniel and Ezra as the title of the rulers who held God's people. Daniel 2:4 has the Chaldeans answer the king in Syriack, O king, live for ever, and Daniel 2:37 calls Nebuchadnezzar a king of kings, given kingdom and power and strength and glory by the God of heaven. Daniel 7:17 turns the word to prophecy, where four great beasts are four kings, and Ezra 7:12 shows Artaxerxes, king of kings, writing to Ezra the priest.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the Aramaic chapters of Daniel make one point plain: kings rise and fall by God's hand, and the king of kings answers to the God of heaven. My position is that no throne is final except His, and every king in Daniel proves it, whether he bows or is broken.
RelatedEvents: Cyrus's Decree and Return from Exile
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a king
BiblicalUsage: Melek is the Aramaic word for king, and it runs through Daniel and Ezra as the title of the rulers who held God's people. Daniel 2:4 has the Chaldeans answer the king in Syriack, O king, live for ever, and Daniel 2:37 calls Nebuchadnezzar a king of kings, given kingdom and power and strength and glory by the God of heaven. Daniel 7:17 turns the word to prophecy, where four great beasts are four kings, and Ezra 7:12 shows Artaxerxes, king of kings, writing to Ezra the priest.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the Aramaic chapters of Daniel make one point plain: kings rise and fall by God's hand, and the king of kings answers to the God of heaven. My position is that no throne is final except His, and every king in Daniel proves it, whether he bows or is broken.
RelatedEvents: Cyrus's Decree and Return from Exile
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a queen
BiblicalUsage: Meleketh is a queen, but in Jeremiah the word belongs to one queen only, the queen of heaven. Jeremiah 7:18 shows whole families at work for her, children gathering wood, fathers kindling fire, women kneading dough to make cakes for her. Jeremiah 44:17 has the people vow to keep burning incense to her as their fathers did, and Jeremiah 44:18 and Jeremiah 44:19 record their excuse: since they left off, they have wanted all things.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the queen of heaven shows how idolatry works: it is a family trade, passed down, and its worshippers credit it with every full cupboard. My position is that plenty is no proof of God's blessing when the plenty came from bowing to a false queen.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: cement (from its plastic smoothness)
BiblicalUsage: Melet is cement, the clay mortar of the brickkiln, and Jeremiah 43:9 has the prophet hide great stones in the clay in the brickkiln at the entry of Pharaoh's house in Tahpanhes, in the sight of the men of Judah.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God hid His sign in the very clay of Egypt's building yard: the place Judah trusted would be the place Babylon broke through.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a presumed derivative of G3199; to take care of, i.e. (by implication) revolve in the mind:--imagine, (pre-)meditate.
BiblicalUsage: Meletao means to meditate, to turn a thing over in the mind until it takes hold. 1 Timothy 4:15 commands Timothy to meditate upon these things and give himself wholly to them, that his profiting may appear to all, and Acts 4:25 quotes the psalm asking why the heathen rage and the people imagine vain things.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe meditation is a choice of what to turn over: truth that profits, or vain things that rage against God.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: apparently a primary word; honey:--honey.
BiblicalUsage: Meli is honey, the sweet food of the wilderness and the picture of God's word on the tongue. Mark 1:6 and Matthew 3:4 both describe John the Baptist eating locusts and wild honey in the desert, and Revelation 10:9 and Revelation 10:10 have John eat the little book, sweet as honey in his mouth, but bitter in his belly.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe honey tells the truth about God's word twice over: it is sweet to receive and it can be bitter to carry. My position is that a prophet eats the whole book, not only the sweet part, and the bitterness is part of the calling.
RelatedTopics: Prophecy; Enjoying God's gifts; Word of God
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3192; relating to honey, i.e. bee (comb):--honeycomb.
BiblicalUsage: Melissios is the honeycomb, and its one place in the King James Bible is Luke 24:42, where the risen Jesus is given a piece of a broiled fish, and of an honeycomb. The Greek text behind the modern editions does not carry the word here, so the study rests on the King James reading alone.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the risen Christ eating with His friends is proof He was no spirit, and the honeycomb is part of that homely proof.
RelatedEvents: Jesus Appears to the Disciples on Easter Evening
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain origin; Melita, an island in the Mediterranean:--Melita.
BiblicalUsage: Melite is the island where Paul's ship broke apart and the crew came safe to land. Acts 28:1 says that when they were escaped, then they knew that the island was called Melita.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God names the place after the rescue, not before: the island is Melita because Paul's company lived to learn its name.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a head of grain (as cut off)
BiblicalUsage: Meliy lah is the head of grain, the ear of wheat as it is cut off. Deuteronomy 23:25 lets a man pluck the ears with his hand as he walks through his neighbour's standing corn, but not put a sickle to it.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the law is generous and firm at once: a hungry man may eat, but the harvest still belongs to its owner.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an aphorism; also a satire
BiblicalUsage: Meliytsah is a taunting proverb, a satire, and also the dark saying that needs understanding. Habakkuk 2:6 says the oppressed shall take up a taunting proverb against the proud man who increases what is not his, and Proverbs 1:6 says wisdom is for understanding a proverb and the interpretation, the words of the wise and their dark sayings.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that a proverb can cut two ways: it mocks the proud and it trains the wise, and the difference is whose side you are on.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a strengthened form of G3199 (through the idea of expectation); to intend, i.e. be about to be, do, or suffer something (of persons or things, especially events; in the sense of purpose, duty, necessity, probability, possibility, or hesitation):--about, after that, be (almost), (that which is, things, + which was for) to come, intend, was to (be), mean, mind, be at the point, (be) ready, + return, shall (begin), (which, that) should (after, afterwards, hereafter) tarry, which was for, will, would, be yet.
BiblicalUsage: Mello means to be about to do a thing, to intend it, to have it coming. 1 Corinthians 3:22 counts things to come among all the things that are yours in Christ, and 1 Peter 5:1 looks to the glory that shall be revealed. 1 Thessalonians 3:4 recalls that Paul told the church beforehand that they should suffer tribulation, and 1 Timothy 1:16 says Christ showed longsuffering in Paul as a pattern to them which should hereafter believe.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe 'about to' is the tense of hope and of warning together: glory is about to be revealed, and suffering is about to come, and both are certain. My position is that the Christian lives between two certainties, and the word mello names them both.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a primary verb; to be of interest to, i.e. to concern (only third person singular present indicative used impersonally, it matters):--(take) care.
BiblicalUsage: Melo means to care, to be of interest to someone, and it is almost always used of God or of Jesus caring when no one else does. Matthew 22:16 has the Pharisees admit that Jesus carest for no man, and Mark 4:38 has the disciples cry, Master, carest thou not that we perish? 1 Peter 5:7 answers them both: cast all your care upon Him, for He careth for you.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the question the disciples asked in the storm is the question every frightened heart asks, and Peter's answer is the one that holds.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: fulness (literally or figuratively)
BiblicalUsage: Melo' is fulness, the whole contents of a thing and everything it holds. Psalms 24:1 says the earth is the LORD's, and the fulness thereof, and Psalms 50:12 says the world is Mine, and the fulness thereof. Deuteronomy 33:16 blesses Joseph with the precious things of the earth and the fulness thereof, and Isaiah 6:3 has the seraphim cry that the whole earth is full of His glory.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe fulness is the word for a world that belongs to God down to the last handful: nothing in it is empty of Him. My position is that the earth is full of His glory whether we see it or not, and the blessing is to live like it is true.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain affinity; a limb or part of the body:--member.
BiblicalUsage: Melos is a member, a limb or part of the body, and Paul makes it the picture of the church. 1 Corinthians 6:15 asks whether our bodies are the members of Christ, and Colossians 3:5 commands us to mortify our members which are upon the earth. Ephesians 4:25 says we are members one of another, and James 3:5 warns that the tongue is a little member that boasts great things.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the body is the honest picture of the church: no member stands alone, and a small one can set the whole on fire. My position is that what I do with my members is what I do with Christ's, and that thought should steady my tongue.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from μῆλον (a sheep); a sheep-skin:--sheepskin.
BiblicalUsage: Melote is a sheepskin, the rough cloak of the persecuted. Hebrews 11:37 says the faithful wandered about in sheepskins and goatskins, being destitute, afflicted, tormented.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a sheepskin in that list is an honour, not a disgrace: the world was not worthy of the ones who wore them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: (only in dual) tweezers
BiblicalUsage: Melqach is the tongs, the snuffers of gold that tended the temple lamps. 1 Kings 7:49 lists the tongs of gold among the vessels before the oracle, and 2 Chronicles 4:21 counts them again among the things made of perfect gold.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe even the tongs were gold, because nothing that served the light was too small to be made well.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a wardrobe (i.e. room where clothing is spread)
BiblicalUsage: Meltachah is the vestry, the wardrobe room where the vestments were kept. 2 Kings 10:22 has Jehu call for the man over the vestry to bring forth vestments for all the worshippers of Baal, so that every one of them could be dressed for his own destruction.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the vestry shows how religion can dress itself up for judgment: Baal's worshippers came in their robes and never left.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: the butler or other officer in the Babylonian court
BiblicalUsage: Meltsar is the steward, the officer set over Daniel and his friends in Babylon, the man the King James Bible calls Melzar. Daniel 1:11 has Daniel appeal to Melzar for a trial of pulse and water, and Daniel 1:16 says Melzar took away their meat and wine and gave them pulse.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God can turn even a king's steward into a quiet helper of the faithful, and Melzar's small consent kept four young men clean.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: something ruled, i.e. a realm
BiblicalUsage: Meluwkah is a kingdom, a realm, the thing a king rules. 1 Chronicles 10:14 says God turned the kingdom unto David the son of Jesse, and 1 Kings 1:46 says Solomon sitteth on the throne of the kingdom. 1 Samuel 10:16 has Saul keep silent about the matter of the kingdom Samuel spoke of, and 2 Kings 25:25 shows the kingdom's end, when Ishmael slew Gedaliah at Mizpah.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe kingdoms are given and taken by the same hand: God turned Saul's kingdom to David, set Solomon on its throne, and let it fall at Mizpah when the people would not listen. My position is that no kingdom stands on its own strength, and the only throne that never moves is God's.
RelatedPeople: King David; King Solomon; King Saul
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a hut, a hammock
BiblicalUsage: Meluwnah is a lodge, a hut, the flimsy shelter left standing in a field. Isaiah 1:8 leaves the daughter of Zion as a cottage in a vineyard, as a lodge in a garden of cucumbers, and Isaiah 24:20 says the earth shall be removed like a cottage, and fall, and not rise again.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a lodge is the picture of what is left when judgment has passed: a shelter that cannot shelter anyone.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a measure
BiblicalUsage: Memad is a measure, and Job 38:5 puts it in God's mouth: who hath laid the measures of the earth, if thou knowest, or who hath stretched the line upon it?
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the question answers itself: the One who measured the earth is the only One who can judge it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Latin origin ("membrane"); a (written) sheep-skin:--parchment.
BiblicalUsage: Membrana is a parchment, a sheet of prepared skin for writing, and Paul's last letter asks for one. 2 Timothy 4:13 has him ask Timothy to bring the cloke left at Troas with Carpus, and the books, but especially the parchments.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the parchments matter because a dying apostle still wanted the written word beside him, and he asked for it plainly.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: sorrow
BiblicalUsage: Memer is bitterness, the sorrow a child brings a parent. Proverbs 17:25 says a foolish son is a grief to his father, and bitterness to her that bare him.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe bitterness here is not anger but grief: the sorrow of a mother watching a son waste himself.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: middle voice of an apparently primary verb; to blame:--find fault.
BiblicalUsage: Memphomai means to find fault, to blame, and it cuts both ways in the New Testament. Hebrews 8:8 says God found fault with the people, and promised a new covenant, and Romans 9:19 has the objector ask, why doth He yet find fault, for who hath resisted His will?
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the difference is who is doing the blaming: God finds fault to make a new covenant, and man finds fault to excuse himself.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a presumed derivative of G3201 and μοῖρα (fate; akin to the base of G3313); blaming fate, i.e. querulous (discontented):--complainer.
BiblicalUsage: Mempsimoiros is a complainer, one who blames his fate, and Jude 1:16 puts him among the murmurers, walking after their own lusts, with mouths speaking great swelling words.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe complaining is not a small sin: it blames God's providence for what our own lusts have chosen.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: rule; also (concretely in plural) a realm or a ruler
BiblicalUsage: Memshalah is dominion, rule, the reach of a king or of God. Genesis 1:16 gives the greater light dominion over the day and the lesser light dominion over the night, and 1 Kings 9:19 counts the cities Solomon built in all the land of his dominion. 2 Chronicles 32:9 sends Sennacherib against Judah with all his power, and Daniel 11:5 promises a king of the south whose dominion shall be a great dominion.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe dominion belongs first to the lights God set in the sky, and every king after them rules on loan. My position is that the greatest dominion in Daniel is still a borrowed one, and it ends where God's begins.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Memucan or Momucan, a Persian satrap
BiblicalUsage: Memucan is one of the seven princes of Persia and Media who saw the king's face and sat first in the kingdom. Esther 1:14 names him among them, and Esther 1:16 has him answer before the king and the princes, charging that Vashti wronged not the king only but all the people. Esther 1:21 says his word pleased the king, and the king did according to the word of Memucan.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Memucan shows how a courtier's counsel can harden into law: one man's advice about a queen became a decree for an empire.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a primary particle; properly, indicative of affirmation or concession (in fact); usually followed by a contrasted clause with G1161 (this one, the former, etc.):--even, indeed, so, some, truly, verily. Often compounded with other particles in an intensive or asseverative sense.
BiblicalUsage: Men is the little particle that sets up a contrast, the 'indeed' that waits for its 'but'. 1 Corinthians 1:12 shows it at work in the divisions at Corinth, where every one saith, I am of Paul, and I of Apollos, and I of Cephas, and I of Christ, and 1 Peter 1:20 uses it of Christ, verily foreordained before the foundation of the world.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the smallest words carry the argument: Paul's 'indeed' divides the factions, and Peter's sets Christ before the world began.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a stronger form of G3303; a particle of affirmation (only with G2229); assuredly:--+ surely.
BiblicalUsage: Men is the stronger particle, assuredly, surely, and it only ever stands beside its partner. Acts 7:20 says Moses was born in the time when he was exceeding fair, and Galatians 4:10 rebukes the church for observing days, and months, and times, and years.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a particle this small still matters, because it marks the places where the writers lean hard on what they are saying.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a stronger form of G3303; a particle of affirmation (only with G2229); assuredly:--+ surely.
BiblicalUsage: Men is the stronger particle, assuredly, surely, and it only ever stands beside its partner. Acts 7:20 says Moses was born in the time when he was exceeding fair, and Galatians 4:10 rebukes the church for observing days, and months, and times, and years.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a particle this small still matters, because it marks the places where the writers lean hard on what they are saying.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a musical chord (as parted into strings)
BiblicalUsage: Men is the string of a harp, the chord that sounds when it is touched. Psalms 150:4 calls for praise with stringed instruments and organs, and Psalms 45:8 sets the music in the ivory palaces, where the king is made glad.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe strings were made to praise with, and the king's gladness and the people's praise belong in the same song.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a sistrum (so called from its rattling sound)
BiblicalUsage: Mena'na' is a sistrum, a rattle used as a musical instrument, and it sounds once, in the noisiest worship in the Bible. 2 Samuel 6:5 has David and all the house of Israel playing before the LORD on harps and psalteries and timbrels and cornets and cymbals, and on rattles besides.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God loves a loud, glad noise when His people bring the ark home, and even a rattle has its part in it.
RelatedEvents: David Brings the Ark to Jerusalem
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to count, appoint
BiblicalUsage: Mena' is the Aramaic word to count and to appoint, and it runs through Daniel and Ezra as the word for putting the right man in the right place. Daniel 2:24 says Arioch was the man whom the king had ordained to destroy the wise men of Babylon, and Daniel 2:49 has Daniel set Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego over the affairs of the province. Daniel 3:12 shows the same appointments turned into an accusation, and Ezra 7:25 has Artaxerxes tell Ezra to set magistrates and judges over the people beyond the river.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe appointing is God's work done through kings and priests: Daniel appoints faithful men, and Ezra appoints judges, and the same word covers both. My position is that who is appointed matters as much as what is decreed, because a faithful appointee can save a province.
RelatedEvents: Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego in the Fiery Furnace
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Menachem, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Menahem is the son of Gadi, who took the throne of Israel by the sword and held it ten years. 2 Kings 15:14 says he went up from Tirzah to Samaria and smote Shallum and slew him and reigned in his stead, and 2 Kings 15:16 records the cruelty of his campaign at Tiphsah. 2 Kings 15:17 dates his reign to the nine and thirtieth year of Azariah king of Judah.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Menahem is a warning written in a reign: a king who comes by murder rules by cruelty, and the ten years are remembered for both.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a sacrificial basin (for holding blood)
BiblicalUsage: Menaqqiyth is the sacrificial basin, the bowl that held the blood. Exodus 25:29 orders the bowls of pure gold for the table of shewbread, and Jeremiah 52:19 lists the basons and bowls among the gold and silver the captain of the guard carried away from the temple.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the basin's story is the temple's story: made of pure gold for holy use, and carried off when the people forgot why it was holy.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Menashsheh, a grandson of Jacob, also the tribe descended from him, and its territory
BiblicalUsage: Manasseh is the name of Joseph's firstborn, of the tribe that came from him, and of the king of Judah who bore his name. Genesis 41:51 says Joseph called him Manasseh, for God hath made me forget all my toil and all my father's house, and 2 Kings 21:1 says the later Manasseh was twelve years old when he began to reign, and reigned fifty and five years in Jerusalem. 2 Chronicles 33:13 tells the end of that reign, when Manasseh prayed and God was intreated of him, and brought him again to Jerusalem.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Manasseh holds both sides of the name: forgetting, and being remembered. My position is that the king who caused the exile is the same man who prayed his way home, and that is why his story is in the Bible at all.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a Menashshite or descendant of Menashsheh
BiblicalUsage: Menashshiy names the Manassites, the descendants of Manasseh, and it marks the half-tribe that stayed east of the Jordan. 1 Chronicles 26:32 counts the men of valour David made rulers over the Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half tribe of Manasseh, and 2 Kings 10:33 names the Manassites among the lands east of Jordan.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the half-tribe shows how one family can live on both sides of a river and still be one people.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an allotment (by courtesy, law or providence)
BiblicalUsage: Menath is a portion, an allotment given by courtesy, by law, or by providence. 2 Chronicles 31:3 gives the king's portion of his substance for the burnt offerings, and 2 Chronicles 31:4 commands the people to give the portion of the priests and the Levites. Nehemiah 12:44 sets men over the chambers to gather the portions of the law for the priests, and Psalms 11:6 turns the word to judgment, where fire and brimstone are the portion of the wicked's cup.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a portion is whatever God allots, and the same word covers the priest's food and the wicked's cup. My position is that I would rather have the portion God gives than the portion I take, because His portion feeds and theirs burns.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: numbered
BiblicalUsage: Mene is the word of the writing on the wall, numbered. Daniel 5:25 gives the writing itself, MENE, MENE, TEKEL, UPHARSIN, and Daniel 5:26 gives the reading: MENE, God hath numbered thy kingdom, and finished it.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God numbers kingdoms the way He numbers days, and when the count is finished the kingdom is finished too.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: the Apportioner, i.e. Fate (as an idol)
BiblicalUsage: Meni is the Apportioner, the god Fate, whom the Jews in Babylon worshipped. Isaiah 65:11 rebukes those who forsake the LORD and prepare a table for that troop, and furnish the drink offering unto that number, the King James rendering of the god's name.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Fate is the poorest god of all: it promises nothing, gives nothing, and takes the worship that belongs to the LORD.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a primary verb; to stay (in a given place, state, relation or expectancy):--abide, continue, dwell, endure, be present, remain, stand, tarry (for), X thine own.
BiblicalUsage: Meno means to abide, to stay, to remain where you were put, and it is the word John builds his gospel on. John 15:4 commands, Abide in me, and I in you, as the branch cannot bear fruit except it abide in the vine, and John 6:56 promises that he that eateth My flesh and drinketh My blood dwelleth in Me, and I in him. 1 John 4:16 says he that dwelleth in love dwelleth in God, and God in him, and 1 John 2:6 says he that saith he abideth in Him ought to walk even as He walked.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe abiding is not a feeling but a staying: in the vine, in the love, in the walk. My position is that fruit comes from staying put, not from striving, and the one who abides in Christ has Christ abiding in him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3303 and G3767 and G1065; so then at least:--nay but, yea doubtless (rather, verily).
BiblicalUsage: Menounge means yea doubtless, nay but, the word Paul uses when he will not be argued with. Philippians 3:8 opens with it, Yea doubtless, and I count all things but loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord, and Romans 9:20 answers the objector with it, Nay but, O man, who art thou that repliest against God?
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word is Paul drawing a line: some things are not up for debate, and God's right to make as He pleases is one of them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a chandelier
BiblicalUsage: Menowrah is the lampstand, the chandelier of the tabernacle and the temple, and its light never went out in God's house. 1 Chronicles 28:15 weighs the gold for every candlestick by its use, and 1 Kings 7:49 sets five candlesticks of pure gold on the right and five on the left before the oracle. 2 Chronicles 4:7 makes ten candlesticks of gold according to their form, and 2 Kings 4:10 puts a candlestick in the little chamber the Shunammite built for Elisha.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the lampstand is the picture of a light that is kept, not made: gold by weight, set in its place, burning where God said. My position is that the church is that lampstand now, and its job is still to hold the light where people can see it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3303 and G5104; indeed though, i.e. however:--also, but, howbeit, nevertheless, yet.
BiblicalUsage: Mentoi means nevertheless, yet, howbeit, the word that holds the line when everything else gives way. 2 Timothy 2:19 says, Nevertheless the foundation of God standeth sure, and James 2:8 says, If ye fulfil the royal law according to the scripture, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself, ye do well.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe 'nevertheless' is the believer's hinge: the foundation stands sure whatever else shakes.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: retreat
BiblicalUsage: Menuwcah is flight, retreat, the running away that fear makes. Isaiah 52:12 promises the exiles they shall not go out with haste, nor go by flight, for the LORD will go before them, and Leviticus 26:36 warns the disobedient that the sound of a shaken leaf shall chase them, and they shall flee as fleeing from a sword.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the contrast is the whole point: God's people leave in order, not in flight, because He goes before them.
RelatedEvents: Cyrus's Decree and Return from Exile
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: repose or (adverbially) peacefully; figuratively, consolation (specifically, matrimony); hence (concretely) an abode
BiblicalUsage: Menuwchah is rest, repose, the place where a weary people can settle. Deuteronomy 12:9 says Israel had not yet come to the rest and to the inheritance the LORD would give, and 1 Kings 8:56 blesses the LORD that He hath given rest unto His people Israel, according to all that He promised. 1 Chronicles 22:9 names Solomon a man of rest, and promises him peace and quietness, and 2 Samuel 14:17 has the wise woman of Tekoah call the king's word comfortable, as rest to her soul.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe rest in Scripture is a place before it is a feeling: an inheritance to come to, a promise kept, a son named for peace. My position is that God gives rest the way He gives land, as a gift to be entered, not a mood to be chased.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably from the same base as G3145 and G3415 (i.e. μάω, to strive); to disclose (through the idea of mental effort and thus calling to mind), i.e. report, declare, intimate:--shew, tell.
BiblicalUsage: Menyo means to show, to disclose, to tell what was hidden. 1 Corinthians 10:28 says if any man say unto you, This is offered in sacrifice unto idols, eat not for his sake that shewed it, and Acts 23:30 has the chief captain write that it was told him how the Jews laid wait for Paul.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe showing is a small act with a large result: one word about idol meat, and one warning about a plot, each changed what happened next.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Mephibosheth, the name of two Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Mephibosheth is the son of Jonathan, lame of his feet from the day his nurse fled with him at five years old, and the man David sought out to show kindness to. 2 Samuel 4:4 tells how he became lame, and 2 Samuel 9:6 has him fall on his face before David and answer, Behold thy servant. 2 Samuel 9:10 gives him a place at the king's table always, with Ziba's sons and servants tilling his land.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Mephibosheth is the gospel in a life: a lame son of a dead king, sought out, seated at the table, and fed for his father's sake. My position is that David's kindness to him is the clearest picture of grace in the Old Testament.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a breaker, i.e. mallet
BiblicalUsage: Mephiyts is a maul, a mallet, a breaker, and Proverbs 25:18 makes it a picture of a lying tongue: a man that beareth false witness against his neighbour is a maul, and a sword, and a sharp arrow.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a false witness is a weapon, not a mistake, and the proverb names all three edges of it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3361 and G4452; not yet:--not yet.
BiblicalUsage: Mepo means not yet, and it marks the things God has promised but not yet shown. Hebrews 9:8 says the way into the holiest of all was not yet made manifest while the first tabernacle was yet standing, and Romans 9:11 says the twins were not yet born, neither having done any good or evil, when God's purpose in election stood.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe 'not yet' is God's patience in two words: the way was coming, and the choice was already made.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: or μή πως from G3361 and G4458; lest somehow:--lest (by any means, by some means, haply, perhaps).
BiblicalUsage: Mepos means lest somehow, lest by any means, and it carries Paul's fear for the churches. 2 Corinthians 11:3 says, I fear, lest by any means, as the serpent beguiled Eve through his subtilty, so your minds should be corrupted from the simplicity that is in Christ. The Greek text behind the modern editions writes the word as two, lest and somehow, so the study rests on the joined form.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Paul's fear is a pastor's fear, and it is still mine: that clever words would steal a simple faith.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: or μή ποτε from G3361 and G4218; not ever; also if (or lest) ever (or perhaps):--if peradventure, lest (at any time, haply), not at all, whether or not.
BiblicalUsage: Mepote means lest at any time, if peradventure, and it guards both a hope and a warning. 2 Timothy 2:25 hopes that God peradventure will give repentance to those who oppose themselves, and Acts 5:39 warns the council, lest haply ye be found even to fight against God.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word holds the door open both ways: repentance may yet come, and fighting God is still possible.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, something meeting, i.e. a frame (of timbers)
BiblicalUsage: Meqareh is the frame of timbers, the meeting of the beams in a house. Ecclesiastes 10:18 blames slothfulness when the building decayeth and the house droppeth through.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a house falls slowly before it falls suddenly, and the frame rots while the owner idles.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a cooling off
BiblicalUsage: Meqerah is the summer parlour, the cool upper room where a king sat alone. Judges 3:20 has Ehud come to Eglon in his summer parlour with a message from God, and Judges 3:24 has the servants find the doors locked and think the king is covering his feet in his summer chamber.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the cool room is the picture of a king at ease who never saw the judgment coming through his own door.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an angle
BiblicalUsage: Mequts'ah is the corner, the angle where two sides of the tabernacle meet. Exodus 26:23 orders two boards for the corners of the tabernacle in the two sides, and Exodus 36:28 says Bezalel made them just so.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the corners matter because God gave their measure too: nothing in His house was left to guesswork.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, a headpiece, i.e. (plural for adverbial) at (or as) the head-rest (or pillow)
BiblicalUsage: Mera'ashah is the place at the head, the pillow or head-rest where a sleeper's head lies. 1 Kings 19:6 finds Elijah with a cake baken on the coals and a cruse of water at his head, and 1 Samuel 19:13 has Michal put a pillow of goats' hair for David's bolster to trick Saul's men.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the head-place is where God meets tired men and where a wife's quick wit buys a husband time.
RelatedEvents: Elijah at Horeb: The Still Small Voice
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: used as (abstract) noun, wickedness
BiblicalUsage: Mera' is wickedness, the mischief two kings plot together. Daniel 11:27 says both these kings' hearts shall be to do mischief, and they shall speak lies at one table, but it shall not prosper.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe lying at the same table is the picture of wickedness at its most polite, and it still does not prosper.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Merab, a daughter of Saul
BiblicalUsage: Merab is Saul's firstborn daughter, promised to David and then given to another. 1 Samuel 14:49 names her first among Saul's daughters, and 1 Samuel 18:17 has Saul offer her to David if he will fight the LORD's battles. 1 Samuel 18:19 tells the end of the promise: when the time came, Merab was given to Adriel the Meholathite.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Merab is a warning about promises made as bait: Saul offered his daughter to get David killed, and the promise was never his to keep.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: rebellion
BiblicalUsage: Merad is rebellion, the Aramaic word for rising against a king. Ezra 4:19 records the search of the records: this city of old time hath made insurrection against kings, and rebellion and sedition have been made therein.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the charge was true of Jerusalem's past and false as a reason to stop the rebuilding, and that is how old sins get used as new weapons.
RelatedEvents: Cyrus's Decree and Return from Exile
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a Merarite (collectively), or decendants of Merari
BiblicalUsage: Merariy names the Merarites, the family of Merari among the Levites. Numbers 26:57 counts them after their families, of Merari, the family of the Merarites, alongside the Gershonites and the Kohathites.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the census kept every family, because every family had its burden to carry for the tabernacle.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a Merarite (collectively), or decendants of Merari
BiblicalUsage: Merariy names the Merarites, the family of Merari among the Levites. Numbers 26:57 counts them after their families, of Merari, the family of the Merarites, alongside the Gershonites and the Kohathites.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the census kept every family, because every family had its burden to carry for the tabernacle.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to pull off
BiblicalUsage: Merat is the Aramaic word to pull off, to pluck away. Daniel 7:4 sees the first beast like a lion with eagle's wings, and watches till the wings thereof were plucked.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the plucked wings are the picture of a proud kingdom brought low before it is given a man's heart.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Merathajim, an epithet of Babylon
BiblicalUsage: Merathayim is the name God gives Babylon in judgment, the land of double rebellion. Jeremiah 50:21 commands, Go up against the land of Merathaim, and against the inhabitants of Pekod, waste and utterly destroy after them.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God names Babylon for what it is before He judges it: a land of rebellion twice over, and its end is already written.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Merajah, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Meraiah is a priest named among the chief of the fathers in the days of Joiakim. Nehemiah 12:12 lists him of Seraiah, in the register of the priests who served after the return.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the register keeps priests we know nothing else about, because faithful service is worth recording even when it is not worth a story.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Merajoth, the name of two Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Meraioth is the name of two priests in the line of Aaron, one in the early genealogy and one in Ezra's own line. 1 Chronicles 6:6 names Meraioth the son of Zerahiah, and Ezra 7:3 names Meraioth the son of Azariah in Ezra's descent. Nehemiah 11:11 names him again among the fathers of Seraiah, the ruler of the house of God.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the priestly line is kept name by name because the priesthood itself was kept that way, one faithful father at a time.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: enlargement, either literally (an open space, usually in a good sense), or figuratively (liberty)
BiblicalUsage: Merchab is breadth, enlargement, an open space, and the freedom that goes with it. 2 Samuel 22:20 has David sing that God brought him forth into a large place, because He delighted in him, and Habakkuk 1:6 has the Chaldeans march through the breadth of the land to possess dwellingplaces that are not theirs.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe breadth is both gift and threat: God brings His own into a large place, and the proud march through the breadth of the land to take it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: remoteness, i.e. (concretely) a distant place; often (adverbially) from afar
BiblicalUsage: Merchaq is remoteness, a distant place, and being from afar. Ezekiel 23:40 says Jerusalem sent for men to come from far, and Isaiah 8:9 calls the peoples of far countries to hear that they shall be broken in pieces.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe distance is no safety: the men from far came at Jerusalem's call, and the far countries are still within God's reach.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a friend
BiblicalUsage: Mere' a is a friend, a companion, the one who stands beside you. Genesis 26:26 brings Ahuzzath, one of Abimelech's friends, to Isaac at Beersheba, and Judges 14:11 brings thirty companions to be with Samson at his wedding. 2 Samuel 3:8 has Abner boast of his kindness to Saul's house, to his brethren and to his friends, and Proverbs 19:7 warns that the friends of the poor go far from him.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe friendship is proved where it costs something: Abimelech's friend walked to Beersheba, Samson's companions came to the feast, and the poor man's friends went far from him. My position is that a friend who stays when the money is gone is the only kind worth the name.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Meres, a Persian
BiblicalUsage: Meres is one of the seven princes of Persia and Media who saw the king's face. Esther 1:14 names him among them, the men who sat first in the kingdom under Ahasuerus.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the princes who sat first in the kingdom are the ones God used without their knowing it, to make room for Esther.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Mered, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Mered is an Israelite of Judah's line, named twice in the same genealogy. 1 Chronicles 4:17 lists Mered among the sons of Ezra, and 1 Chronicles 4:18 says his wife Jehudijah bare sons, and that these are the sons of Bithiah the daughter of Pharaoh, which Mered took.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Mered's house is a quiet picture of grace: a daughter of Pharaoh married into Judah, and her sons are counted in Israel.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: rebellion
BiblicalUsage: Mered is rebellion, and Joshua 22:22 puts it on the lips of the eastern tribes at their own altar: if it be in rebellion, or if in transgression against the LORD, save us not this day.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the tribes knew the weight of the word they used, and they staked their lives on not being guilty of it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Meremoth, the name of two Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Meremoth is the name of two Israelites, a priest who weighed the temple treasure and a man who put away a foreign wife. Ezra 8:33 has Meremoth the son of Uriah weigh the silver and gold in the house of God, and Nehemiah 3:4 has Meremoth the son of Urijah repair the wall. Ezra 10:36 lists a second Meremoth among those who had taken strange wives.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the two Meremoths show both sides of the return: one weighed the gold faithfully, and one had to put away what did not belong.
RelatedEvents: Nehemiah Rebuilds the Wall; Ezra's Journey to Jerusalem
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: bile (from its bitterness)
