BiblicalUsage: Mererah is bile, gall, the bitter fluid poured out in suffering. Job 16:13 says God's archers compassed him round about and poured out his gall upon the ground.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Job's gall is the picture of suffering that goes all the way through a man and leaves nothing inside unpoured.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3307 (through the idea of distraction); solicitude:--care.
BiblicalUsage: Merimna is care, the anxious solicitude that divides the mind. 1 Peter 5:7 commands us to cast all our care upon Him, for He careth for you, and 2 Corinthians 11:28 shows Paul carrying the care of all the churches daily. Luke 8:14 and Mark 4:19 both warn that the cares of this world, with riches and pleasures, choke the word and make it unfruitful.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe care is a burden with two owners: mine to carry until I cast it, and His to carry once I do. My position is that anxiety is not a small fault but a choking weed, and the cure is not trying harder but handing it over.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3308; to be anxious about:--(be, have) care(-ful), take thought.
BiblicalUsage: Merimnao is the verb, to be anxious, to take thought, to care. Matthew 6:25 commands, Take no thought for your life, what ye shall eat or drink, and Luke 10:41 has Jesus say to Martha, thou art careful and troubled about many things. 1 Corinthians 7:32 says the unmarried care for the things of the Lord, and Philippians 2:20 praises Timothy, who will naturally care for the Philippians' state.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word is neutral until you see what it is aimed at: care for the Lord's things is devotion, and care for tomorrow's bread is anxiety. My position is that Jesus does not forbid caring, He forbids the kind of caring that forgets who provides.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: feminine of G3313; a portion, i.e. province, share or (abstractly) participation:--part (X -akers).
BiblicalUsage: Meris is a part, a portion, a share, and it is used where belonging is decided. Luke 10:42 says Mary hath chosen that good part, which shall not be taken away from her, and Colossians 1:12 thanks the Father who made us meet to be partakers of the inheritance of the saints in light. 2 Corinthians 6:15 asks what part hath he that believeth with an infidel, and Acts 8:21 tells Simon he hath neither part nor lot in the matter.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a part is the whole question of belonging: Mary's part cannot be taken, Simon's part was never his, and the believer's part is an inheritance. My position is that I want the part Mary chose, the one that lasts.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3307; a separation or distribution:--dividing asunder, gift.
BiblicalUsage: Merismos is a dividing asunder, a distribution, a gift handed out. Hebrews 4:12 says the word of God pierces even to the dividing asunder of soul and spirit, and Hebrews 2:4 says God bore witness with gifts of the Holy Ghost, according to His own will.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word cuts both ways: God's word divides what man cannot, and God's gifts are distributed where He wills.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3307; an apportioner (administrator):--divider.
BiblicalUsage: Meristes is a divider, one who apportions an inheritance between brothers. Luke 12:14 has Jesus refuse the office: Man, who made Me a judge or a divider over you?
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Jesus refused the divider's seat because He came to give an inheritance, not to split one.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Meri-Baal, son of Jonathan
BiblicalUsage: Meri-baal is the name of Jonathan's son, the boy also called Mephibosheth. 1 Chronicles 9:40 says, And the son of Jonathan was Merib-baal, and Merib-baal begat Micah.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the name means contender with Baal, and the boy who bore it was lame and hidden and still kept in the king's house for his father's sake.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: stall-fed; often (as noun) a beeve
BiblicalUsage: Meriy' is the fatling, the stall-fed animal kept for feasting and sacrifice. 1 Kings 1:9 has Adonijah slay sheep and oxen and fat cattle by the stone of Zoheleth, and 2 Samuel 6:13 says David sacrificed oxen and fatlings when the ark had gone six paces.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a fatling shows what a feast costs: Adonijah's was for a stolen crown, and David's was for the ark coming home.
RelatedEvents: David Brings the Ark to Jerusalem
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: bitterness, i.e. (figuratively) rebellion; concretely, bitter, or rebellious
BiblicalUsage: Meriy is rebellion, bitterness made into a way of life. 1 Samuel 15:23 says rebellion is as the sin of witchcraft, and Deuteronomy 31:27 has Moses say he knows Israel's rebellion and stiff neck. Ezekiel 2:5 names them a rebellious house, and Isaiah 30:9 calls them a rebellious people, lying children, that will not hear the law of the LORD.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe rebellion is bitterness with a will behind it: it hears the word and refuses it, and calls the refusal freedom. My position is that God names it witchcraft because it trades His voice for another master's, and the price is always the throne.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: quarreller of Baal, Merib-Baal, son of Jonathan
BiblicalUsage: Merib-baal is the name of Jonathan's son, the boy also called Mephibosheth. 1 Chronicles 8:34 and 1 Chronicles 9:40 both say the son of Jonathan was Merib-baal, and Merib-baal begat Micah.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the name is a small puzzle the verses solve plainly: the lame boy at David's table and the father of Micah are one and the same.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Meribah, the name of two places in the Desert
BiblicalUsage: Meribah is the place of strife, named for the water where Israel strove with God. Exodus 17:7 says Moses called the place Massah and Meribah, because of the chiding of the children of Israel, and because they tempted the LORD. Numbers 20:13 says, This is the water of Meribah, because the children of Israel strove with the LORD, and Deuteronomy 33:8 recalls that Levi's holy one was proved at Massah and striven with at the waters of Meribah.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Meribah is the name of a place no one should want to revisit: the water came, and the striving is what the place is remembered for. My position is that God gives water even to a striving people, and the mercy is greater than the name.
RelatedEvents: Water from the Rock at Meribah
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: quarrel
BiblicalUsage: Meriybah is strife itself, the quarrel, the contention. Genesis 13:8 has Abram plead, Let there be no strife, I pray thee, between me and thee, and between my herdmen and thy herdmen, for we be brethren. Deuteronomy 32:51 and Numbers 27:14 both recall the waters of Meribah-Kadesh, where Moses and Aaron trespassed and did not sanctify God, and Ezekiel 47:19 names the waters of strife in Kadesh as the border of the promised land.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe strife is the sin that follows God's people everywhere, from Abram's herdmen to Moses at the water. My position is that Abram's answer is still the right one: we be brethren, so let there be no strife.
RelatedEvents: Abram and Lot Part Ways; Water from the Rock at Meribah
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: bitter, i.e. poisonous
BiblicalUsage: Meriyriy is bitter, poisonous, the bitterness that destroys. Deuteronomy 32:24 warns of bitter destruction, with the poison of serpents of the dust sent upon the disobedient.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe bitter destruction is the end of a bitter heart: what is sown in rebellion is reaped in poison.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: bitterness, i.e. (figuratively) grief
BiblicalUsage: Meriyruwth is bitterness, grief made audible. Ezekiel 21:6 commands the prophet to sigh with the breaking of his loins, and with bitterness sigh before their eyes.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God asked Ezekiel to carry the grief in his own body, so the people would see the judgment coming before they felt it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3313; to part, i.e. (literally) to apportion, bestow, share, or (figuratively) to disunite, differ:--deal, be difference between, distribute, divide, give part.
BiblicalUsage: Merizo means to divide, to apportion, to share out, and it is used for inheritances, for gifts, and for Christ Himself. Luke 12:13 has a man ask Jesus to tell his brother to divide the inheritance with him, and 1 Corinthians 1:13 asks, Is Christ divided? 2 Corinthians 10:13 says God distributed to Paul a measure to reach the Corinthians, and Hebrews 7:2 says Abraham gave Melchizedek a tenth part of all.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe dividing is right when God does the apportioning and wrong when man does the splitting: Abraham's tenth honoured a priest, and a divided Christ would honour no one. My position is that the church divides only what God has already joined.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a chariot; also a seat (in a vehicle)
BiblicalUsage: Merkab is a chariot, and also the seat or saddle a man rides upon. 1 Kings 4:26 counts Solomon's forty thousand stalls of horses for his chariots, and Leviticus 15:9 calls the saddle unclean when a man with an issue rides upon it.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the chariot shows both sides of power: Solomon's glory in the stalls, and the law's reminder that even a saddle can defile.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a chariot
BiblicalUsage: Merkabah is a chariot, the war machine and the royal carriage, and it runs through the histories. 1 Samuel 8:11 warns that a king will take their sons for his chariots, and 2 Chronicles 1:17 prices a chariot out of Egypt at six hundred shekels of silver. 1 Kings 7:33 makes the temple's wheels like the work of a chariot wheel, and 1 Chronicles 28:18 gives the pattern of the chariot of the cherubim that spread their wings over the ark.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the chariot is the picture of a king's strength and of God's: man's chariots take sons and cost silver, and God's chariot is cherubim over the ark. My position is that the chariot Israel wanted for safety became the warning Samuel gave, and the one God showed David was not for war at all.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Merodak-Baladan, a Babylonian king
BiblicalUsage: Merodach-baladan is the king of Babylon who sent letters and a present to Hezekiah. Isaiah 39:1 says he had heard that Hezekiah had been sick, and was recovered.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a get-well letter from Babylon was the beginning of the end for Judah's treasures, and Hezekiah showed them all.
RelatedEvents: Hezekiah Shows His Treasures to Babylon
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Merodak, a Babylonian idol
BiblicalUsage: Merodak is the Babylonian god, the idol whose name is the city's pride. Jeremiah 50:2 proclaims that Babylon is taken, Bel is confounded, and Merodach is broken in pieces.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the broken idol is the whole sermon: the god Babylon trusted could not keep its own city standing.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a Meronothite, or inhabitant of some (otherwise unknown) Meronoth.
BiblicalUsage: Meronothiy names a man by his town, a Meronothite. 1 Chronicles 27:30 has Jehdeiah the Meronothite over the asses, and Nehemiah 3:7 has Jadon the Meronothite repair the wall beside Melatiah the Gibeonite.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the Meronothites are remembered for ordinary faithfulness: one kept the asses, and one kept the wall.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a bitter herb
BiblicalUsage: Meror is the bitter herb eaten at the Passover. Exodus 12:8 commands the lamb to be eaten roast with fire, with unleavened bread, and with bitter herbs, and Lamentations 3:15 has the prophet say God filled him with bitterness and made him drunken with wormwood.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the bitter herb belongs on the Passover table on purpose: freedom tastes of bitterness remembered.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, bitterness; concretely, a bitter thing; specifically bile; also venom (of a serpent)
BiblicalUsage: Merorah is bitterness itself, gall and venom, the bitter thing in the body and in the soul. Deuteronomy 32:32 says the vine of Sodom bears grapes of gall, and Job 13:26 says God writest bitter things against me. Job 20:14 turns a rich man's meat to the gall of asps within him, and Job 20:25 brings the glittering sword out of his gall, with terrors upon him.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe gall is what sin turns into inside a man: sweet going down, poison in the bowels, and terror at the end. My position is that Job's bitter things are not God's cruelty but the truth about what his accusers' plenty really was.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: perhaps a primary word; a thigh:--thigh.
BiblicalUsage: Meros is the thigh, and Revelation 19:16 sets it in the last picture of the returning King: He hath on His vesture and on His thigh a name written, KING OF KINGS, AND LORD OF LORDS.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the name is written where a sword hangs, because the King who returns is the King who judges.
RelatedEvents: The Rider on the White Horse
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from an obsolete but more primary form of μείρομαι (to get as a section or allotment); a division or share (literally or figuratively, in a wide application):--behalf, course, coast, craft, particular (+ -ly), part (+ -ly), piece, portion, respect, side, some sort(-what).
BiblicalUsage: Meros is a part, a share, a division, and it is used for everything from geography to doctrine. Acts 2:10 names the parts of Libya about Cyrene, and 2 Corinthians 1:14 says the Corinthians acknowledged Paul in part. 1 Corinthians 11:18 says Paul hears there are divisions among the church, and believes it in part, and Colossians 2:16 warns not to let any man judge in meat or drink, or in respect of a holyday or new moon or sabbath.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe 'in part' is the honest measure of this life: we know in part, we are acknowledged in part, and the whole is still coming. My position is that a church that knows it only sees in part will be slower to judge and quicker to wait.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: bruised, i.e. emasculated
BiblicalUsage: Merowach is a blemish, a man with his stones broken, and Leviticus 21:20 bars him from the priest's office, alongside the crookbackt and the dwarf and the scabbed.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the bar was not cruelty but a picture: the priest who stood for a perfect people had to be without blemish, and the blemish pointed to the need for a better priest.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Merom, a lake in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Merom is the waters where the northern kings gathered to fight Israel. Joshua 11:5 says they pitched together at the waters of Merom, and Joshua 11:7 says Joshua came against them by the waters of Merom suddenly, and they fell before him.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Merom is the picture of a battle God wins suddenly: the kings gathered in one place, and Joshua fell on them there.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a run (the trial of speed)
BiblicalUsage: Merowts is the race, the trial of speed, and Ecclesiastes 9:11 says the race is not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong, nor bread to the wise, but time and chance happeneth to them all.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the race is not won by the fastest because God is the one who orders the outcome, and time and chance are His servants, not His rivals.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Meroz, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Meroz is a place whose people stayed home when the battle came, and Deborah cursed them for it. Judges 5:23 says, Curse ye Meroz, said the angel of the LORD, curse ye bitterly the inhabitants thereof, because they came not to the help of the LORD against the mighty.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Meroz is the warning for everyone who watches a battle and does nothing: the curse fell not for fighting on the wrong side but for not coming at all.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a spicy herb
BiblicalUsage: Merqach is a spicy herb, a bed of spices, and Song of Solomon 5:13 pictures the beloved's cheeks as a bed of spices, as sweet flowers, his lips like lilies dropping sweet smelling myrrh.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the spice bed is love's own garden: sweet, tended, and meant to be come near to.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: abstractly, a seasoning (with spicery); concretely, an unguentkettle (for preparing spiced oil)
BiblicalUsage: Merqachah is a seasoning, and also the kettle where spiced oil was prepared. Ezekiel 24:10 commands the cauldron to be spiced well and the bones burned, and Job 41:31 says Leviathan maketh the sea like a pot of ointment.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the kettle shows two fires: the city's judgment, spiced and boiling, and the sea creature God alone can master.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: oppression
BiblicalUsage: Merutsah is oppression, the crushing of the poor by power. Jeremiah 22:17 says the king's eyes and heart are not but for covetousness, and for shedding innocent blood, and for oppression, and for violence.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe oppression is the sin of a heart that wants and a hand that takes, and God names it plainly against a king.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a race (the act), whether the manner or the progress
BiblicalUsage: Meruwtsah is a running, a race, the act of running itself. 2 Samuel 18:27 has the watchman say the running of the foremost is like the running of Ahimaaz the son of Zadok, and Jeremiah 8:6 has every man turn to his course, as the horse rusheth into the battle.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe running shows the heart: Ahimaaz ran with good tidings, and Judah ran headlong into battle without repenting.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3319 and G2250; midday; by implication, the south:--noon, south.
BiblicalUsage: Mesembria is midday, noon, and by extension the south, where the sun stands at noon. Acts 8:26 sends Philip toward the south, to the desert road from Jerusalem to Gaza, and Acts 22:6 has Paul struck by the light from heaven about noon on the road to Damascus.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe noon is the hour God chooses for turning points: a desert road and a Damascus road, both in the full light of day.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Mesha, a place in Arabia
BiblicalUsage: Mesha is a place in Arabia, named once as a boundary of the sons of Joktan. Genesis 10:30 says their dwelling was from Mesha, as thou goest unto Sephar, a mount of the east.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the table of nations keeps even the boundary towns, because every family had its dwelling from God.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: oil
BiblicalUsage: Meshach is the Aramaic word for oil, the oil for the offerings and the lamps. Ezra 6:9 orders oil to be given day by day without fail for the burnt offerings, and Ezra 7:22 allows a hundred baths of oil, and salt without prescribing how much.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the oil was given without fail because the worship was daily, and God's house was never to run dry.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a waste or amazement
BiblicalUsage: Meshammah is desolation, a waste, an amazement at what judgment leaves behind. Ezekiel 5:15 says Jerusalem shall be a reproach and a taunt, an instruction and an astonishment unto the nations, and Ezekiel 6:14 promises to make the land desolate, more desolate than the wilderness toward Diblath. Isaiah 15:6 and Jeremiah 48:34 both say the waters of Nimrim shall be desolate, with the hay withered away and no green thing.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe desolation is meant to be seen: a reproach and an instruction to the nations round about, so that they shall know that I am the LORD. My position is that God makes a land desolate not to end the story but to prove He is the one writing it.
RelatedEvents: Fall of Jerusalem and the Exile
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Meshek, a son of Japheth, and the people descended from him
BiblicalUsage: Meshek is a son of Japheth and the people that came from him, traders and warriors in the north. Genesis 10:2 and 1 Chronicles 1:5 both list Meshech among the sons of Japheth, and Ezekiel 27:13 has Javan, Tubal, and Meshech trading persons of men and vessels of brass in the market of Tyre.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the nations of the table are real peoples with real trades, and Tyre's market bought men as well as brass.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a sowing; also a possession
BiblicalUsage: Meshek is a sowing, the seed scattered, and also the price a thing is worth. Psalms 126:6 pictures the sower going forth and weeping, bearing precious seed, and coming again with rejoicing, bringing his sheaves, and Job 28:18 says the price of wisdom is above rubies.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the sower and the price belong together: what is sown in tears is reaped in joy, and wisdom is worth more than the seed.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Meshelemjah, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Meshelemiah is a Korahite porter, a gatekeeper of the tabernacle, and the father of porters. 1 Chronicles 26:1 names Meshelemiah the son of Kore, of the sons of Asaph, and 1 Chronicles 26:2 lists his sons, Zechariah the firstborn, Jediael the second, Zebadiah the third. 1 Chronicles 9:21 says Zechariah the son of Meshelemiah was porter of the door of the tabernacle.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the gatekeepers are the quiet faithful: a father and his sons, keeping the door so worship could go on inside.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: possession
BiblicalUsage: Mesheq is possession, the steward of a house, the one who holds what belongs to another. Genesis 15:2 has Abram say, Lord GOD, what wilt Thou give me, seeing I go childless, and the steward of my house is this Eliezer of Damascus?
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Abram's complaint is the prayer of every childless believer: the house is full, but the heir is missing, and only God can fill it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Meshezabel, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Meshezabeel is an Israelite of the return, a father whose sons built the wall and served the king. Nehemiah 3:4 says Meshullam the son of Berechiah, the son of Meshezabeel, repaired the wall, and Nehemiah 10:21 lists Meshezabeel among those who sealed the covenant. Nehemiah 11:24 says Pethahiah the son of Meshezabeel was at the king's hand in all matters concerning the people.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe one family can span the whole return: a son on the wall, a name on the covenant, and a grandson at the king's hand.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: plunder
BiblicalUsage: Meshiccah is plunder, spoil, the prey taken from a conquered people. 2 Kings 21:14 says God will deliver the remnant into the hand of their enemies, and they shall become a prey and a spoil, and Habakkuk 2:7 warns the plunderer that those he bit shall rise up and he shall be for booties unto them.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe plunder turns on the plunderer: the spoil God gives to judgment becomes the spoil of the next judgment.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Meshillemith, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Meshillemith is a priest in the line of Immer, named once in the register. 1 Chronicles 9:12 traces Maasiai through Meshullam, the son of Meshillemith, the son of Immer.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that being named once among the priests who served is honour enough: Meshillemith stood in the line, and the line is what God remembered.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Meshillemoth, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Meshillemoth is the name of two Israelites, a father in Ephraim and a father in the priestly line. 2 Chronicles 28:12 names Berechiah the son of Meshillemoth among the heads of Ephraim who stood against the captives being brought in, and Nehemiah 11:13 traces Amashai through Meshillemoth the son of Immer.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the two Meshillemoths show the same name in two callings: one who stood for mercy, and one who fathered priests.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: silk (as drawn from the cocoon)
BiblicalUsage: Meshiy is silk, the fine cloth drawn from the cocoon, and Ezekiel uses it to dress Jerusalem. Ezekiel 16:10 says God covered her with silk, and Ezekiel 16:13 says her raiment was of fine linen, and silk, and broidered work.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe silk on Jerusalem is grace you can touch: God clothed the foundling in the finest cloth He had.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a satire
BiblicalUsage: Meshol is a satire, a byword, the taunt a broken man becomes. Job 17:6 says, He hath made me also a byword of the people, and aforetime I was as a tabret.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a byword is the cruellest wound of all: not the loss, but being made into a saying for others to repeat.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: (a) ruin, abstractly (the act) or concretely (the wreck)
BiblicalUsage: Meshow'ah is ruin, desolation and waste, the wreck of a land. Job 30:3 has the solitary fleeing into the wilderness in former time desolate and waste, and Job 38:27 has God satisfy the desolate and waste ground and cause the bud of the tender herb to spring forth. Zephaniah 1:15 makes it the day itself, a day of wasteness and desolation, a day of darkness and gloominess.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe desolation is not the last word: the same God who names the waste ground satisfies it with rain and makes the tender herb spring. My position is that ruin is real and judgment is real, and so is the watering that follows them both.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Meshobab, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Meshobab is a Simeonite prince named in the list of the chiefs. 1 Chronicles 4:34 names Meshobab, and Jamlech, and Joshah the son of Amaziah, among the princes of Simeon.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the list keeps princes we know nothing else about, because their tribe's story was worth telling in full.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Meshullam, the name of seventeen Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Meshullam is the name of seventeen Israelites, and three of them stand out in the record. 1 Chronicles 3:19 names Meshullam the son of Zerubbabel, and 2 Chronicles 34:12 names Meshullam of the Kohathites, an overseer who set the temple work forward. 2 Kings 22:3 names a third Meshullam as the grandfather of Shaphan the scribe, sent by Josiah to the house of the LORD.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe one name can hold many faithful men: a son of the governor, an overseer of the work, and the grandfather of a scribe, all counted.
RelatedEvents: Josiah Finds the Book of the Law
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Meshullemeth, an Israelitess
BiblicalUsage: Meshullemeth is the mother of King Amon, named once in the record of his reign. 2 Kings 21:19 says Amon was twenty and two years old when he began to reign, and his mother's name was Meshullemeth, the daughter of Haruz of Jotbah.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a mother's name in a bad king's record is no blame on her: the record keeps her because she was his mother, and his sins were his own.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: apostasy
BiblicalUsage: Meshuwbah is apostasy, backsliding, the turning away of a people who knew better. Hosea 11:7 says God's people are bent to backsliding from Him, and Jeremiah 2:19 says their backslidings shall reprove them, for it is an evil thing and bitter to have forsaken the LORD. Proverbs 1:32 warns that the turning away of the simple shall slay them, and Hosea 14:4 promises the healing: I will heal their backsliding, I will love them freely.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe backsliding is a bending, not a single fall: a people leaning away until they cannot stand straight. My position is that the promise is greater than the bending, because the God who names the sin also promises to heal it freely.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: spoilation
BiblicalUsage: Meshuwcah is spoilation, the stripping of a people left defenceless. Isaiah 42:24 asks, Who gave Jacob for a spoil, and Israel to the robbers? Did not the LORD, He against whom we have sinned?
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the question answers itself: the spoil was God's judgment, and the robbers were His instrument, not His rivals.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: mistake
BiblicalUsage: Meshuwgah is a mistake, an error, and Job 19:4 owns it plainly: And be it indeed that I have erred, mine error remaineth with myself.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe owning an error is the beginning of wisdom, and Job's words are the opposite of his friends' certainty.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3319; a go-between, i.e. (simply) an internunciator, or (by implication) a reconciler (intercessor):--mediator.
BiblicalUsage: Mesites is a mediator, a go-between, one who stands between two parties and reconciles them. 1 Timothy 2:5 says there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, and Hebrews 8:6 says He is the mediator of a better covenant, established upon better promises. Galatians 3:19 says the law was ordained by angels in the hand of a mediator, and Galatians 3:20 adds that a mediator is not a mediator of one, but God is one.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the mediator is the whole gospel in one word: God and men needed a go-between, and the go-between is a man. My position is that there is one mediator because there is one God, and no other name can stand in the middle.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3316; to interpose (as arbiter), i.e (by implication) to ratify (as surety):--confirm.
BiblicalUsage: Mesiteuo means to interpose, to step between as arbiter, and so to confirm. Hebrews 6:17 says God, willing to show the heirs of promise the immutability of His counsel, confirmed it by an oath.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God confirmed His promise the way men confirm theirs, and then went further: He swore by Himself, because there was no greater to swear by.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: neuter of compound of G3319 and G3571; midnight (especially as a watch):--midnight.
BiblicalUsage: Mesonyktion is midnight, the middle watch of the night. Acts 16:25 says at midnight Paul and Silas prayed and sang praises unto God, and the prisoners heard them, and Luke 11:5 has a man go to his friend at midnight to ask for three loaves.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe midnight is when prayer sounds loudest: prisoners heard it, and a friend at midnight still opens the door.
RelatedEvents: Paul and Silas in the Philippian Prison
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3319; to form the middle, i.e. (in point of time), to be half-way over:--be about the midst.
BiblicalUsage: Mesoo means to be half-way over, about the midst, and John 7:14 uses it of the feast: Now about the midst of the feast Jesus went up into the temple, and taught.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Jesus came at the middle of the feast because He is the middle of it: the teaching the feast was pointing to all along.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3319 and G4215; Mesopotamia (as lying between the Euphrates and the Tigris; compare H763), a region of Asia:--Mesopotamia.
BiblicalUsage: Mesopotamia is the land between the rivers, the Euphrates and the Tigris, where Abraham began. Acts 7:2 says the God of glory appeared unto our father Abraham when he was in Mesopotamia, before he dwelt in Charran, and Acts 2:9 lists the dwellers in Mesopotamia among those who heard the gospel at Pentecost.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Mesopotamia holds the whole story in miniature: the call began there, and the gospel returned there at Pentecost.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3326; middle (as an adjective or (neuter) noun):--among, X before them, between, + forth, mid(-day, -night), midst, way.
BiblicalUsage: Mesos is the middle, the midst, among, between, and it is the word for where Jesus stands. Matthew 18:20 promises that where two or three are gathered in His name, there am I in the midst of them, and Luke 24:36 has Jesus Himself stand in the midst of them and say, Peace be unto you. John 1:26 has John say there standeth one among you, whom ye know not, and 2 Thessalonians 2:7 says the restrainer will be taken out of the way.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the middle is where Jesus puts Himself: among the gathered, among the frightened, among those who do not know Him yet. My position is that the church is not built around an empty centre but around a present Lord.
RelatedEvents: Jesus Appears to the Disciples on Easter Evening
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3319 and G5109; a partition (figuratively):--middle wall.
BiblicalUsage: Mesotoichon is the middle wall, the partition between Jew and Gentile. Ephesians 2:14 says Christ is our peace, who hath made both one, and hath broken down the middle wall of partition between us.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the wall is down because Christ is the peace: the partition fell when He made the two into one.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a presumed compound of G3319 and G3772; mid-sky:--midst of heaven.
BiblicalUsage: Mesouranema is the midst of heaven, the mid-sky where angels fly with their message. Revelation 8:13 has an angel flying through the midst of heaven crying Woe to the inhabiters of the earth, and Revelation 14:6 has another angel fly in the midst of heaven, having the everlasting gospel to preach to every nation and kindred and tongue and people.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the mid-sky is the pulpit of the last days: woe to the earth, and gospel to every nation, from the same height.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H4899); the Messias (i.e. Mashiach), or Christ:--Messias.
BiblicalUsage: Messias is the Hebrew name for the Anointed One, the Christ. John 1:41 has Andrew find his brother Simon and say, We have found the Messias, which is, being interpreted, the Christ, and John 4:25 has the woman of Samaria say, I know that Messias cometh, which is called Christ, and when He is come, He will tell us all things.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the name is the confession: Andrew found Him, and the Samaritan woman waited for Him, and both were right.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3324; to replenish, i.e. (by implication) to intoxicate:--fill.
BiblicalUsage: Mestoo means to fill, to replenish, and in its one use it is mockery. Acts 2:13 says, Others mocking said, These men are full of new wine.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the mockers got it backwards: the men were full, but not of wine, and the filling they mocked was the Spirit.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain derivation; replete (literally or figuratively):--full.
BiblicalUsage: Mestos is full, replete, filled to the brim, and it is used for eyes, tongues, and hearts alike. 2 Peter 2:14 has eyes full of adultery, and James 3:8 has a tongue full of deadly poison. John 19:29 sets a vessel full of vinegar at the cross, and Matthew 23:28 says the Pharisees outwardly appear righteous, but within are full of hypocrisy and iniquity.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe 'full' is the most honest word in these verses: what fills a man is what comes out of him. My position is that the cure is not to be emptied but to be filled with something better, because a full vessel is never neutral.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a hedge
BiblicalUsage: Mesuwkah is a hedge, the fence that keeps a vineyard safe. Isaiah 5:5 has God say He will take away the hedge of His vineyard, and it shall be eaten up, and Proverbs 15:19 says the way of the slothful man is as an hedge of thorns, but the way of the righteous is made plain.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the hedge is God's protection, and losing it is the judgment: a vineyard without a hedge is food for anything that passes.
RelatedEvents: The Parable of the Wicked Tenants
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a measure (for liquids)
BiblicalUsage: Mesuwrah is a measure, a portion measured out for food or drink. 1 Chronicles 23:29 puts the Levites over all manner of measure and size for the offerings, and Ezekiel 4:11 measures the prophet's water by measure, the sixth part of an hin, from time to time.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe measured bread and water are the discipline of the siege: God counts what His prophet eats, and the counting is part of the message.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a primary preposition (often used adverbially); properly, denoting accompaniment; "amid" (local or causal); modified variously according to the case (genitive association, or accusative succession) with which it is joined; occupying an intermediate position between G575 or G1537 and G1519 or G4314; less intimate than G1722 and less close than G4862):--after(-ward), X that he again, against, among, X and, + follow, hence, hereafter, in, of, (up-)on, + our, X and setting, since, (un-)to, + together, when, with (+ -out). Often used in composition, in substantially the same relations of participation or proximity, and transfer or sequence.
BiblicalUsage: Meta is the preposition with, among, amid, the word that puts one thing beside another. 1 John 1:3 says our fellowship is with the Father, and with His Son Jesus Christ, and 1 Corinthians 6:6 shows the other side, where brother goeth to law with brother, and that before the unbelievers.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe 'with' is the whole of the Christian life in one small word: fellowship with the Father, or quarrel with a brother, and the preposition tells which.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to arrive, extend or happen
BiblicalUsage: The Aramaic word for arriving or reaching shows up in Daniel, where a tree's height reaches to heaven and where one like the Son of man comes to the Ancient of days. It marks the moment something gets where it was headed, whether a growing tree or a person brought near before God.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Daniel 7:13 is the verse that gives this plain word its weight: the Son of man does not merely appear, He comes to the Ancient of days and is brought near before Him.
RelatedTopics: Messiah; Son of Man; God's Sovereignty
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3326 and the base of G939; to change place:--depart, go, pass, remove.
BiblicalUsage: Metabaino means to change place, to move on from where you were. John uses it for the greatest move of all, passing from death to life, and for Jesus departing out of this world to the Father. Matthew and Acts use it more plainly, of Jesus leaving a town and Paul leaving a synagogue.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this word draws the line between two kinds of leaving: the world asks Jesus to depart from its coasts, but the believer passes from death to life and never goes back. Jesus' own departing was not an escape; it was His hour, the way home to the Father.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3326 and G906; to throw over, i.e. (middle voice figuratively) to turn about in opinion:--change mind.
BiblicalUsage: The islanders watching Paul after the snakebite changed their minds about him, first expecting him to swell up and die, then deciding he must be a god. The word is the turning of an opinion, and Luke uses it for a crowd that got the man completely wrong in both directions.
TheologicalSignificance: I take this as a warning about crowds: the same people who were sure Paul would drop dead were just as sure, minutes later, that he was a god, and both judgments were hasty.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3326 and G1325; to give over, i.e. share:--give, impart.
BiblicalUsage: To share is the plain sense here, and the New Testament makes it practical. John the Baptist tells the man with two coats to give one to the man with none, Paul counts giving among the gifts of grace, and Ephesians tells the reformed thief to work so he has something to give to the needy.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe sharing is the test of whether grace has reached our hands: we do not give to earn God's favour, we give because we have received, and the gift counts most when it costs us something we could have kept. That is the shape of grace in the hands: received freely, given freely, and the giving itself is the proof it was received.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3326 and G718; to lead over, i.e. transfer (direct):--turn about.
BiblicalUsage: James uses this word twice in one breath, for the bit that turns a horse and the rudder that turns a ship. A small thing steers a great body, and James is building his case that the tongue does the same to a life.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that James chose his pictures well: if a bit and a rudder can turn what is far bigger than they are, then the tongue is not a small matter, and neither is the grace that tames it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3326 and G142; to betake oneself, i.e. remove (locally):--depart.
BiblicalUsage: Matthew uses this word at the seams of Jesus' teaching, when He finished one set of parables and departed, and again when He finished His sayings in Galilee and went toward Judea. It is the ordinary word for moving on after the teaching is done.
TheologicalSignificance: I notice that Jesus never lingered where His word had been given: He taught, and then He departed, and the teaching went with Him to the next place that needed it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3326 and G2564; to call elsewhere, i.e. summon:--call (for, hither).
BiblicalUsage: Joseph sent and called his father Jacob down to Egypt, the angel told Cornelius to send to Joppa and call for Peter, and Felix told Paul he would call for him at a more convenient season. The word is always a summons, someone sent for from somewhere else.
TheologicalSignificance: I see two kinds of calling here: Joseph's call brought his whole family to safety, and Cornelius's call brought Peter to preach, while Felix's call was a delay dressed up as a promise.
RelatedPeople: Joseph, Son of Jacob; Simon Peter; Paul
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3326 and G2795; to stir to a place elsewhere, i.e. remove (figuratively):--move away.
BiblicalUsage: Paul warns the Colossians not to be moved away from the hope of the gospel. The word pictures a building shifted off its foundation, and Paul's point is that the gospel is the ground we stand on, not a view we hold lightly.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe steadfastness is not stubbornness: it is staying grounded where God put us, because the hope of the gospel is the only foundation that holds when everything else shifts.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3326 and G2983; to participate; genitive case, to accept (and use):--eat, have, be partaker, receive, take.
BiblicalUsage: This word covers both taking and sharing: the earth receives blessing when it drinks in the rain, the believer is made a partaker of God's holiness, and Paul urges hungry sailors to take food after fourteen days without eating. Receiving and participating turn out to be the same motion.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the Christian life is mostly receiving well: the earth does not earn the rain, the child does not earn the discipline, and we do not earn holiness — we take part in what God gives. The earth drinks the rain, the child takes the discipline, and we take part in holiness — all of it received, none of it earned.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3335; participation:--taking.
BiblicalUsage: Paul names the false teachers who forbid marriage and command abstaining from meats, which God created to be received with thanksgiving. The word is the taking itself, and Paul's argument is that what God made for receiving should be received, not refused in the name of holiness.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the test of true holiness is gratitude: God made food to be received with thanksgiving, and the teachers who forbid it are not more holy than God, only more severe.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3326 and G236; to exchange:--change.
BiblicalUsage: Paul says men changed the truth of God into a lie, and in the next breath that women changed the natural use into what is against nature. The word is exchange, and Romans 1 uses it for the trade at the root of idolatry: God's truth swapped for a lie.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe every false worship starts with an exchange like this one: we trade what God said for what we prefer, and then we worship the thing we made in the trade.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3326 and the middle voice of G3199; to care afterwards, i.e. regret:--repent (self).
BiblicalUsage: The son who said no and then repented and went, Judas who repented himself and brought back the silver, and Paul who says he did repent of his sharp letter — this word is the afterthought that changes the deed. It is regret that turns into a different course, and it is not the same in every man who feels it.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Judas is the warning here: he felt the regret and returned the money, yet never turned back to Christ, while the son in the parable repented and went, and that going is what made his repentance real. Repentance that never turns the feet is only regret, and regret alone saved no one.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3326 and G3445; to transform (literally or figuratively, "metamorphose"):--change, transfigure, transform.
BiblicalUsage: Jesus was transfigured before His disciples, His face shining like the sun; Paul tells believers to be transformed by the renewing of the mind; and we are changed into the Lord's image from glory to glory. The same word covers the glory on the mountain and the slow change in a believer's life.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe transformation is God's work from the inside out: the mind renewed by truth, the face turned toward His glory, until the change that began on the mountain finishes in us. No man transforms himself; the Spirit does the changing as we behold the Lord.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3326 and G3539; to think differently or afterwards, i.e. reconsider (morally, feel compunction):--repent.
BiblicalUsage: John the Baptist and Jesus both open with the same cry, repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand. Luke says heaven rejoices over one sinner who repents, Peter tells the crowd at Pentecost to repent and be baptized, and the risen Lord tells Ephesus to repent and do the first works.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe repentance is not a single act but the doorway of the whole Christian life: we enter by turning from sin to God, and we stay on the road by turning again whenever we wander, because the kingdom is still at hand. The kingdom is still at hand, so the turning is never finished in this life.
RelatedPeople: John the Baptist; Jesus; Simon Peter
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3326 and G3992; to send from elsewhere, i.e. (middle voice) to summon or invite:--call (send) for.
BiblicalUsage: Cornelius is told to send men to Joppa and call for Peter, Paul calls the disciples together after the uproar at Ephesus, and Felix sends for Paul to hear him concerning the faith in Christ. The word is a summons from elsewhere, and Luke uses it whenever the gospel is about to cross a boundary.
TheologicalSignificance: I notice that every one of these sendings opened a door: Cornelius's household heard the gospel, the Ephesian disciples were embraced and sent on, and even Felix, who kept delaying, heard the faith in Christ.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3326 and a derivative of G4976; to transfigure or disguise; figuratively, to apply (by accommodation):--transfer, transform (self).
BiblicalUsage: Paul says he transferred his teaching to himself and Apollos as a figure, warns that false apostles transform themselves into apostles of Christ, and promises that Christ will change our lowly bodies to be like His glorious body. The word is a change of form, and Paul uses it for honest illustration, for deceit, and for resurrection hope.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the difference between the two transformations in this word is everything: Satan's servants disguise themselves to deceive, while Christ changes His people to make them truly like Him. One change hides the truth, the other reveals it, and the difference is the Spirit.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3326 and G4762; to turn across, i.e. transmute or (figuratively) corrupt:--pervert, turn.
BiblicalUsage: Peter quotes Joel: the sun shall be turned into darkness before the day of the Lord. Paul uses the same word for men who would pervert the gospel of Christ. One turning is God's sign in the sky, the other is man's corruption of the good news.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the gospel is not ours to turn: the sun turned to darkness is God's doing at His appointed day, but a perverted gospel is man's doing, and Paul says there is no other gospel to turn it into.
RelatedTopics: Truth; False Teaching; Day of the Lord
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3346; transposition, i.e. transferral (to heaven), disestablishment (of a law):--change, removing, translation.
BiblicalUsage: Hebrews uses this word three times for three great changes: the priesthood being changed brings a change of the law, Enoch was translated so he did not see death, and the shaking removes what can be shaken so the unshakable remains. Removal and transfer are the same word, and Hebrews makes them the shape of God's new covenant.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Hebrews is telling us that God removes what is temporary on purpose: the old priesthood gives way, Enoch is taken, the shaken things fall, and what cannot be shaken — His kingdom — is what remains. What cannot be shaken is what remains, and that is the kingdom itself.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3326 and G5087; to transfer, i.e. (literally) transport, (by implication) exchange, (reflexively) change sides, or (figuratively) pervert:--carry over, change, remove, translate, turn.
BiblicalUsage: Enoch was translated by faith, certain men turned the grace of God into lasciviousness, and the Galatians were being removed from Him who called them into the grace of Christ. The word is transfer, and it swings both ways: God transfers His saints, and men transfer themselves away from grace.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Galatians 1:6 is the verse that should frighten us most here: the Galatians were not dragged away, they were removing themselves, and the grace they left was the grace that had called them. The grace they left was the grace that had called them, and there is no other gospel to turn to.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3326 and a form of G4862; betwixt (of place or person); (of time) as adjective, intervening, or (by implication) adjoining:--between, mean while, next.
BiblicalUsage: Peter slept between two soldiers the night before Herod would bring him out, and John's disciples asked Jesus to eat in the meanwhile. The word is the space between, whether two soldiers in a prison or the pause between one thing and the next.
TheologicalSignificance: I notice that God does His quietest work in the meanwhile: Peter asleep between soldiers, the church praying, and by morning the chains are off.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3361 and G5037; not too, i.e. (in continued negation) neither or nor; also, not even:--neither, (n-)or, so as much.
BiblicalUsage: Paul piles up the neither-nors: teachers of the law who understand neither what they say nor what they affirm, and a day of Christ that is not at hand, neither by spirit, nor by word, nor by letter. The word chains denials together, and Paul uses it to fence off error from every side at once.
TheologicalSignificance: I take Paul's doubled negatives as a model for discernment: error rarely comes from one direction, so the truth has to be guarded on every side, neither by spirit, nor by word, nor by letter.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3326 and G2192; to share or participate; by implication, belong to, eat (or drink):--be partaker, pertain, take part, use.
BiblicalUsage: Christ took part in flesh and blood so He could destroy the devil through death, believers are partakers of one bread at the Lord's table, and they cannot partake of the Lord's table and the table of devils. Sharing is the heart of this word, and Paul draws the line at what we share in.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe partaking is never neutral: we share in Christ's flesh and blood, we share in one bread as one body, and the table we sit at decides whose we are. The table we sit at decides whose we are, and there are only two tables.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a compound of G3326 and a collateral form of G142 or perhaps rather G109 (compare "meteor"); to raise in mid-air, i.e. (figuratively) suspend (passively, fluctuate or be anxious):--be of doubtful mind.
BiblicalUsage: Jesus tells His disciples not to seek what they will eat or drink, and neither to be of doubtful mind. The word pictures a man raised in mid-air, suspended and unsettled, and Jesus' cure for that anxiety is trust in the Father who knows what we need.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that anxiety is a kind of suspension: we hang in mid-air between what we fear and what we cannot control, and Jesus brings us down to solid ground by pointing us to the Father.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3326 and G1899; thereafter:--afterward.
BiblicalUsage: Esau found no place of repentance afterward, though he sought it with tears. The word is simply afterward, but Hebrews loads it with the weight of a missed chance: the blessing had passed, and tears could not call it back.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this one verse is a sober warning: repentance has its season, and Esau's tears were real, but they came after the door had closed.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: apparently a primary word; a "mother" (literally or figuratively, immediate or remote):--mother.
BiblicalUsage: Mary the mother of Jesus stands at the cross, Mary and the brethren wait outside while Jesus teaches, the church prays with Mary the mother of Jesus after the ascension, and Paul says the Jerusalem above is the mother of us all. The word stretches from one woman to the whole people of God.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe motherhood in Scripture is bigger than biology: Mary bore the Lord, the church bears His children, and the Jerusalem above mothers us all until we come home. That is why motherhood is holy ground in Scripture, not just biology.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, a biter, i.e. a tooth
BiblicalUsage: Job broke the jaws of the wicked and plucked the spoil out of their teeth, and Joel pictures a nation whose teeth are the teeth of a lion, with the cheek teeth of a great lion. The tooth is the biter, the weapon of the devourer, and both writers use it for power that tears.
TheologicalSignificance: I take Job's picture as the pattern for God's justice: the wicked hold their prey in their teeth, and God breaks the jaws and takes the spoil back.
RelatedTopics: Justice; God's Power; Evil and Suffering
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: apparently a primary word; an intoxicant, i.e. (by implication) intoxication:--drunkenness.
BiblicalUsage: Paul lists drunkenness among the works of the flesh that shut men out of the kingdom, Jesus warns against hearts overcharged with drunkenness when that day comes unawares, and Romans tells believers to walk honestly, not in rioting and drunkenness. Scripture never treats it as a small vice.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe drunkenness is named so plainly because it steals exactly what the Spirit gives: self-control, watchfulness, and a clear mind for the day of the Lord. A clear mind for the day of the Lord is worth more than any drink.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Metheg-ha-Ammah, an epithet of Gath
BiblicalUsage: David took Metheg-ammah out of the hand of the Philistines after he smote them and subdued them. The name is an epithet of Gath itself, the bridle of the mother city, and its capture marks David's victory over the Philistine stronghold.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the taking of Gath's bridle says what David's reign would be: the Philistines who had held Israel's bridle would hold it no longer.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a bit
BiblicalUsage: God tells Sennacherib He will put His bridle in his lips and turn him back by the way he came, and Isaiah repeats the word to the same king. The bit is God's restraint on a raging power, and the verse is a promise that no enemy runs loose beyond God's hand.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the bridle is one of Scripture's kindest pictures of sovereignty: even the proudest king is steered, and God turns him home by the road he came.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: figuratively, pleasantness (of discourse)
BiblicalUsage: The sweetness of the lips increases learning, and the sweetness of a friend's hearty counsel rejoices the heart like ointment and perfume. Proverbs uses pleasantness for words that do good, and the word is the flavour of speech that teaches and comforts.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that sweet speech is not flattery: it is truth made pleasant to receive, and Proverbs says it both teaches the hearer and gladdens the heart.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3326 and G2059; to explain over, i.e. translate:--(by) interpret(-ation).
BiblicalUsage: The apostles explain that Barnabas means the son of consolation, and the disciples explain that Rabbi means Master. The word is the work of translation itself, and the New Testament pauses to translate names so the reader knows what they mean.
TheologicalSignificance: I notice that Scripture never leaves a name unexplained when its meaning matters: Barnabas is the son of consolation because his life consoled, and Rabbi is Master because Jesus is one.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: , or (1 Cor. 13:2) μεθιστάνω from G3326 and G2476; to transfer, i.e. carry away, depose or (figuratively) exchange, seduce:--put out, remove, translate, turn away.
BiblicalUsage: God translated us into the kingdom of His dear Son, Paul says faith could remove mountains and still be nothing without love, and God removed Saul and raised up David. The word is a transfer, and Colossians uses it for the greatest one: out of darkness and into the kingdom.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Colossians 1:13 is the whole gospel in one transfer: we did not move ourselves out of darkness, God delivered us and translated us, and the kingdom we now live in is His Son's. We did not move ourselves; God delivered us and translated us into His Son's kingdom.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a compound of G3326 and G3593 (compare "method"); travelling over, i.e. travesty (trickery):--wile, lie in wait.
BiblicalUsage: Paul warns of the sleight of men and cunning craftiness that tosses believers about, and then tells them to put on the whole armour of God to stand against the wiles of the devil. The word is a method, a planned way of deceiving, and Paul answers method with armour.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that deception always has a method, and so does standing firm: the devil's wiles are planned, and the armour of God is given on purpose, piece by piece, so we can stand.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: wholesomeness; also (adverb) completely
BiblicalUsage: Isaiah says the whole head is sick and there is no soundness in the nation from foot to head, only wounds and bruises. Judges uses the same word for the completeness of the slaughter at Gibeah, everything that came to hand. Soundness and completeness are one word, and Isaiah shows what happens when both are gone.
TheologicalSignificance: I take Isaiah 1:6 as a diagnosis of a whole people: no soundness anywhere, only wounds, and no one had bound them up.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3326 and G3725; bounded alongside, i.e. contiguous (neuter plural as noun, frontier):--border.
BiblicalUsage: Jesus went into the borders of Tyre and Sidon, seeking a quiet house where no one would know Him, but He could not be hid. The word is the borderland itself, the edge where one country meets another, and it stands in the Received Text where the older Greek reads simply the region.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the borderland suits this story: Jesus crossed into Gentile country and could not be hidden, because even at the edges of the map, His fame went ahead of Him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Methusael, an antediluvian patriarch
BiblicalUsage: Methusael appears once, in the genealogy from Enoch to Lamech: Enoch begat Irad, Irad begat Mehujael, Mehujael begat Methusael, and Methusael begat Lamech. He is a link in the line of Cain, named only as a father and a son.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that even a single-verse name matters: Methusael stands in the line that leads to Lamech, and his place in the genealogy is the whole of what Scripture tells us about him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Methushelach, an antediluvian patriarch
BiblicalUsage: Enoch lived sixty-five years and begat Methuselah, and all the days of Methuselah were nine hundred and sixty-nine years, the longest life in Scripture. The chronicler names him again in the genealogy from Adam, the son of Enoch.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Methuselah's long life is a quiet sermon on God's patience: he lived longer than any man, and still he died, because even the longest life ends and only the promise lives on.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from another form of G3178; to drink to intoxication, i.e. get drunk:--drink well, make (be) drunk(-en).
BiblicalUsage: Paul says one man at the Lord's table is hungry while another is drunken, warns that the drunken are drunken in the night, and Peter answers the crowd at Pentecost that the disciples are not drunken. John adds the wedding at Cana, where men have well drunk before the good wine is served. The word is drinking to excess, and Scripture ties it to the night and to shame.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that drunkenness is the opposite of watchfulness: the night is when men get drunk, and the morning of Pentecost is when God pours out His Spirit on sober men. The morning of Pentecost belongs to sober men, and the Spirit fills those who watch.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a prolonged (transitive) form of G3184; to intoxicate:--be drunk(-en).
BiblicalUsage: The unfaithful servant eats and drinks and gets drunk while his lord delays, Paul says be not drunk with wine, wherein is excess, but be filled with the Spirit, and the Thessalonians hear that they that be drunken are drunken in the night. The word is the same as getting drunk, and Paul sets the Spirit against the wine as the true filling.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Ephesians 5:18 draws the line plainly: wine fills and wastes, the Spirit fills and builds, and a man cannot be filled with both at once.
RelatedTopics: Temptation; Fruit of the Spirit; Worship
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3184; tipsy, i.e. (as noun) a sot:--drunkard.
BiblicalUsage: Paul tells the Corinthians not to eat with a brother who is a drunkard, and says plainly that drunkards shall not inherit the kingdom of God. The word names the person, not just the act, and Paul treats the drunkard's company as a danger to the church.
TheologicalSignificance: I take Paul's bluntness as love for the church: a brother given to drink is not to be eaten with, not because he cannot repent, but because the church must not pretend his sin is harmless.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3361 and the neuter of G5100; whether at all:--not (the particle usually not expressed, except by the form of the question).
BiblicalUsage: Paul asks whether he used lightness in his plans, and tells married couples not to defraud one another except for a time of prayer, lest Satan tempt them. The word is a little particle, usually left untranslated, that turns a sentence into a question expecting the answer no.
TheologicalSignificance: I notice how much work one small word does: it lets Paul question himself in public, and it lets him warn married couples that even prayer has its season, and the tempter waits for the gap.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3385 and G1065; not at all then, i.e. not to say (the rather still):--how much more.
BiblicalUsage: Paul asks the Corinthians whether they do not know they shall judge angels, and how much more the things of this life. The word is a stronger form of the question particle, and Paul uses it to press the point: if the greater is true, the lesser follows.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Paul's argument from the greater to the lesser still stands: if we shall judge angels, we can settle the small disputes of this life without dragging each other before unbelievers.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: or μή τις from G3361 and G5100; whether any:--any (sometimes unexpressed except by the simple interrogative form of the sentence).
BiblicalUsage: The disciples ask whether any man has brought Jesus something to eat, and whether any of the rulers have believed on Him, and Jesus asks the children whether they have any meat. The word is two words in the Greek, whether any, joined into one question, and it stands where the answer is hoped for but not certain.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe these three questions show how the word works: the disciples wonder, the rulers are weighed, and the children answer no, and in each case the question itself does the work.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an iron bar (as forged)
BiblicalUsage: Job pictures Behemoth's bones as bars of iron, strong pieces of brass. The word is a forged bar, and Job uses it for strength no weapon can break.
TheologicalSignificance: I take the iron bar as Job's picture of a creature beyond man's taming: God made bones like bars of iron, and no hunter's snare will hold him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3348; participation, i.e. intercourse:--fellowship.
BiblicalUsage: Paul asks what fellowship righteousness has with unrighteousness, and what communion light has with darkness. The word is participation itself, the sharing of a life, and Paul uses it to forbid the unequal yoke.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe fellowship is the test of a yoke: righteousness and unrighteousness share nothing, light and darkness have no communion, and the believer must not pretend otherwise.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3348; participant, i.e. (as noun) a sharer; by implication, an associate:--fellow, partaker, partner.
BiblicalUsage: Hebrews calls believers partakers of the heavenly calling and partakers of Christ, and partakers of the Holy Ghost, while Luke calls the partners in the other ship at the miraculous catch. The word is the sharer, the one who has a part in something, and Hebrews makes it the highest honour a believer can hold.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that partaking is the heart of the gospel: we are not spectators of Christ, we are partakers of Him, and if we hold our confidence steadfast to the end, the part we hold is real. If we hold our confidence steadfast to the end, the part we hold is real.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a derivative of a compound of G3326 and G3624; a change of abode, i.e. (specially), expatriation:--X brought, carried(-ying) away (in-)to.
BiblicalUsage: Matthew's genealogy turns on this word three times: the carrying away into Babylon, the generations until the carrying away, and the generations from the carrying away unto Christ. The exile is the hinge of Israel's history, and Matthew counts his generations by it.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Matthew counts by the exile because it is the wound that proves the promise: fourteen generations to the carrying away, fourteen more to Christ, and the God who sent them away is the God who brought them home. The God who sent them away is the God who brought them home.
RelatedEvents: Cyrus's Decree and Return from Exile
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from the same as G3350; to transfer as a settler or captive, i.e colonize or exile:--carry away, remove into.
BiblicalUsage: Abraham leaves the land of the Chaldeans and dwells in Haran, and later Stephen says God will carry the people away beyond Babylon. The word is the settling of a people in a new land, whether by God's leading or by His judgment.
TheologicalSignificance: I notice that God moves His people both ways with this word: Abraham is carried into the land of promise, and Israel is carried beyond Babylon, and in both cases the move is God's doing.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3326 and ops (the face); the forehead (as opposite the countenance):--forehead.
BiblicalUsage: John seals God's servants in their foreheads, spares those with the seal, and shows the Lamb's company with the Father's name written in their foreheads, while the beast marks his followers in the same place. The forehead is where belonging is written, and Revelation makes it the mark of whose we are.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the forehead is the right place for the seal: it is the most visible part of a man, and God writes His name there so that all heaven can see whose servant stands before Him. God writes His name where all heaven can see it, so that no one mistakes whose servant stands there.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3384; the matrix:--womb.
BiblicalUsage: Every male that opens the womb shall be called holy to the Lord, and Abraham considered not the deadness of Sarah's womb. The word is the womb itself, and Scripture uses it where life begins and where faith must reckon with a body past bearing.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Sarah's womb is the verse that makes this word matter: Abraham believed against a dead womb, and Isaac was born, because God's promise does not wait on the body.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3384 and the base of G257; a mother-thresher, i.e. matricide:--murderer of mothers.
BiblicalUsage: Paul lists murderers of mothers among those the law is made for: the lawless and disobedient, the ungodly and sinners, the unholy and profane. The word is the murderer of a mother, and Paul puts it in the darkest company, beside murderers of fathers and manslayers.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Paul lists this sin to show what the law is for: it was not made for the righteous man, but for those who break even the bonds of blood, and the law names them plainly.
