Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3358; to measure (i.e. ascertain in size by a fixed standard); by implication, to admeasure (i.e. allot by rule):--figuratively, to estimate:--measure, mete.
BiblicalUsage: Jesus says with what measure you mete it shall be measured to you again, and to give with good measure, pressed down and shaken together. John shows the same word at the temple, where the angel tells him to measure the temple of God and the altar. Measuring is both a warning and a calling.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the measure we use is the measure we will be judged by: give generously and it comes back pressed down and running over, judge harshly and the same measure finds us. The measure is in our hands every day, and God will use the one we choose.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3354; a measurer, i.e. (specially), a certain standard measure of capacity for liquids:--firkin.
BiblicalUsage: At Cana there were six waterpots of stone containing two or three firkins apiece. The word is the measure itself, a firkin, and John names it so the reader can picture the scale of the wine Jesus was about to make.
TheologicalSignificance: I notice John counts the waterpots and their measure for a reason: six stone jars, two or three firkins each, is a great deal of water, and the miracle would need every drop of it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a compound of the base of G3357 and G3806; to be moderate in passion, i.e. gentle (to treat indulgently):--have compassion.
BiblicalUsage: The high priest can have compassion on the ignorant and on those out of the way, because he himself is compassed with infirmity. The word is a measured gentleness, a middle path between harshness and softness, and Hebrews makes it the fitness of a priest.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a priest who has never been weak cannot be gentle with the weak: Christ's priesthood is compassionate because He knows infirmity from the inside.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: adverb from a derivative of G3358; moderately, i.e. slightly:--a little.
BiblicalUsage: The young man Eutychus was brought alive, and the believers were not a little comforted. The word is a small adverb, moderately, a little, and Luke uses it to measure a comfort that was larger than the word itself.
TheologicalSignificance: I take Luke's understatement as the mark of true comfort: they were not a little comforted, because the boy who fell from the window was alive again.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an apparently primary word; a measure ("metre"), literally or figuratively; by implication, a limited portion (degree):-- measure.
BiblicalUsage: With what measure you mete it shall be measured to you again, God gives not the Spirit by measure to His Son, and grace is given to each of us according to the measure of the gift of Christ. The word is the standard itself, and Scripture uses it for judgment, for the Spirit, and for grace.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the measure of grace is the verse that settles the question: Christ gives as He wills, and every one of us has received according to the measure of His gift, not according to our deserving. Every one of us has received according to the measure of His gift, not according to our deserving.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3384 and G4172; a mother city, i.e. "metropolis":--chiefest city.
BiblicalUsage: This word never appears in any verse of the New Testament. Its only place in the Received Text is the subscription at the end of 1 Timothy, where Laodicea is called the chiefest city of Phrygia Pacatiana, so I cite no verse for it.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that honesty matters more than a forced verse: the word is a real Greek word for a mother city, but Scripture itself never uses it, and I will not pretend otherwise.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: the forehead (as open and prominent)
BiblicalUsage: David sank the stone into Goliath's forehead, leprosy rose up in Uzziah's forehead as he burned incense, the golden plate rested on Aaron's forehead to bear the iniquity of the holy things, and Ezekiel was told Israel was impudent and hardhearted, hard of forehead. The forehead is where defiance and holiness both show.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the forehead tells the truth about a man: Goliath's fell to a stone, Uzziah's broke out in leprosy, Aaron's bore the holy plate, and Israel's was hard against God. A hard forehead against God is the most dangerous place a man can stand.
RelatedPeople: King David; Aaron; Uzziah, King of Judah
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a fastness (as a covert of ambush)
BiblicalUsage: David dwelt in the castle at Jerusalem, hid in the strong holds of the wilderness of Ziph while Saul sought him daily, and Isaiah promises the righteous a place of defence in the munitions of rocks. The word is the fastness, the stronghold where a man hides and holds.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the stronghold is where David learned to trust: Saul sought him every day and God delivered him not into his hand, because the true fastness was the Lord Himself. Saul sought him every day, and God delivered him not into his hand.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: something tight, i.e. (figuratively) trouble
BiblicalUsage: Judah went into captivity because of affliction and found no rest, the sorrows of death compassed the psalmist and he found trouble and sorrow, and in distress he called on the Lord, who set him in a large place. The word is the strait, the narrow place where trouble closes in.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the strait is where prayer is born: the psalmist called on the Lord in distress, and the Lord answered him and set him in a large place. The Lord answered him and set him in a large place, and that is what He still does.
RelatedEvents: Fall of Jerusalem and the Exile
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: (only dual) double tinklers, i.e. cymbals
BiblicalUsage: David and all Israel played before God with cymbals and trumpets, and the Levites stood at the east end of the altar with cymbals and psalteries and harps while a hundred and twenty priests sounded with trumpets. The word is the cymbal itself, always in pairs, always in worship.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the cymbals belong where David put them: before God, with all their might, in the worship of the people He had chosen.
RelatedEvents: David Brings the Ark to Jerusalem
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a tinkler, i.e. a bell
BiblicalUsage: In that day there shall be upon the bells of the horses, Holiness unto the Lord. The word is the small bell, and Zechariah hangs it on the horses of the day when even the common things are made holy.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Zechariah's bell is a promise for ordinary life: in that day holiness will reach the horses' harness, and nothing will be too common for the Lord.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Metsobajah, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Jasiel the Mesobaite stands in the list of David's mighty men, named only once and only by the place he came from. Metsobayah is the town itself, and the man is remembered as the one from there.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that a name like this still counts: Jasiel is remembered because he stood with David, and the place he came from is part of how Scripture remembers him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a deep place (of water or mud)
BiblicalUsage: The depths covered Pharaoh's army, Leviathan makes the deep boil like a pot, Jonah was cast into the deep in the midst of the seas, and God promises to cast all our sins into the depths of the sea. The word is the deep place itself, and Scripture moves from the sea that drowns armies to the sea that drowns sins.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Micah 7:19 is the verse that turns this word into gospel: the same depths that swallowed Pharaoh's host swallow our iniquities, and God casts them where no man can fish them out again. God casts our sins where no man can fish them out again.
RelatedEvents: The Exodus and the Red Sea
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: shade
BiblicalUsage: Zechariah saw a man riding a red horse standing among the myrtle trees in the bottom, with red horses behind him. The word is the shady hollow, the low place, and the vision begins there, in the quiet dark where the Lord's riders wait.
TheologicalSignificance: I take the bottom as the place where God starts His visions: not on the heights, but down among the myrtles, where a man on a red horse stands ready.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: narrowness, i.e. (figuratively) trouble
BiblicalUsage: Trouble and anguish make the wicked afraid, the psalmist asks God to bring him out of the distresses of his enlarged heart, Zephaniah calls the day of the Lord a day of trouble and distress, and the wandering people cried to the Lord in their trouble and He delivered them. The word is the narrow strait where pressure closes in from every side.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Psalm 107:6 is the pattern for every trouble in this word: they cried to the Lord in their trouble, and He delivered them out of their distresses. That is the pattern for every trouble: cry to the Lord, and He delivers.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a hemming in, i.e. (objectively) a mound (of siege), or (subjectively) a rampart (of protection), (abstractly) fortification
BiblicalUsage: The fenced cities of Judah included Zorah and Aijalon and Hebron, and Isaiah says God will lay siege against Jerusalem with a mount and raise forts against her. The word is the siege mound or the rampart itself, the hemming in of a city.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that a siege work is a warning in stone: the same mound that protects a city can be raised against it, and only the Lord is a defence that cannot be turned.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Me-haj-Jarkon, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Me-jarkon is named once, in the border list of Dan, beside Rakkon and the border before Japho. It is a place on the edge of the tribe's land, and its name means the waters of yellowness, or the yellow water.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that even a border town in a list matters: Dan's inheritance reached to Me-jarkon, and God gave His people land down to its last stream.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Me-Zahab, an Edomite
BiblicalUsage: Mezahab is named twice, as the father of Matred and grandfather of Mehetabel, the wife of Hadar king of Edom. He is an Edomite remembered only through his daughter and granddaughter, in the genealogy of Edom's kings.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a name kept only in a genealogy still testifies: Mezahab's line reached the throne of Edom, and Scripture keeps the record even when the man himself is silent.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a portico (as covered)
BiblicalUsage: Ahaz turned the covert for the sabbath from the house of the Lord for the king of Assyria. The word is the covered porch, and the verse shows a king stripping God's house to please a foreign power.
TheologicalSignificance: I take Ahaz's porch as a picture of compromise: he took the covering God had given His house and turned it aside for Assyria, and the house was poorer for it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Medad, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Eldad and Medad stayed in the camp when the seventy went out, and the Spirit rested on them, and they prophesied in the camp. A young man ran to tell Moses, and Moses answered that he wished all the Lord's people were prophets.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Medad is the proof that God's Spirit is not confined to the tabernacle: He fell on two men who stayed in the camp, and Moses rejoiced instead of envying.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Medeba, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Israel laid Medeba waste in the song of victory, Moab howls over Medeba in Isaiah's burden, and the plain of Medeba marked the border of Reuben's land. It is a city of Moab on the high plain, taken and lost and mourned in turn.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Medeba shows how the cities of Moab passed between hands: Israel sang over it, Isaiah wept over it, and the land itself kept the record.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Mesha, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Mesha was the firstborn son of Caleb, the brother of Jerahmeel, and the father of Ziph. He is named once, in the genealogy of Judah, as the head of a family in the line of Caleb.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a single verse can still honour a man: Mesha is the firstborn of Caleb, and his sons carried the name of Ziph into the story of Judah.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Mesha, a Moabite
BiblicalUsage: Mesha king of Moab was a sheepmaster who paid the king of Israel a hundred thousand lambs and a hundred thousand rams with the wool, until Ahab died and he rebelled. His rebellion brought the kings of Israel, Judah and Edom against Moab, and Elisha with them.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Mesha's tribute is the measure of Moab's bondage: a hundred thousand lambs a year, until the yoke broke and the war came, and even then the prophet had the last word.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Mesha, a place in Arabia; also an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Mesha is named once, among the sons Shaharaim begat of Hodesh his wife, beside Jobab and Zibia and Malcham. The name covers both a place in Arabia and a man of Benjamin, and here it is the man, in the genealogy of Benjamin.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the genealogy keeps Mesha because every name in Benjamin's line mattered to the tribe that kept it, even the ones we know nothing else about.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Meshak, the Babylonian
BiblicalUsage: Daniel set Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego over the affairs of Babylon, the Chaldeans accused them of refusing the king's gods, and the three answered that they were not careful to answer the king in the matter. Meshach is the Babylonian name given to Mishael, and it stands in the story wherever the three stand together.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Meshach matters because of the company he kept: he would not bow with his friends, and the furnace could not separate what faith had joined.
RelatedEvents: Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego in the Fiery Furnace
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Meshak, the Babylonian
BiblicalUsage: Daniel set Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego over the affairs of Babylon, the Chaldeans accused them of refusing the king's gods, and the three answered that they were not careful to answer the king in the matter. Meshach is the Babylonian name given to Mishael, and it stands in the story wherever the three stand together.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Meshach matters because of the company he kept: he would not bow with his friends, and the furnace could not separate what faith had joined.
RelatedEvents: Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego in the Fiery Furnace
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: evenness, i.e. (figuratively) prosperity or concord; also straightness, i.e. (figuratively) rectitude (only in plural with singular sense; often adverbially)
BiblicalUsage: The Lord judges the world in uprightness, the just man's way is uprightness, and the sons of men are asked whether they judge uprightly. The word is evenness, the straight and level path, and Scripture uses it for God's judgment and for the life that walks straight.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe uprightness is the shape of God's own justice: He weighs the path of the just, He judges the people in uprightness, and the straight way is the safe way. The straight way is the safe way, and the upright path is the one God weighs.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: the best part
BiblicalUsage: Saul spared the best of the sheep and oxen when he should have destroyed them utterly, and the law says a man who lets his beast eat another's field must pay of the best of his own field. The word is the best part, and both verses show what men do with it.
TheologicalSignificance: I take Saul's best as the warning: he kept the best for himself and called it sacrifice, and Samuel told him obedience is better than sacrifice.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a cord (of a tent); or the string (of a bow)
BiblicalUsage: The tabernacle had its cords and pins, and Isaiah tells Zion to lengthen her cords and strengthen her stakes. The word is the cord itself, and it holds the tent up and holds the bowstring taut.
TheologicalSignificance: I notice that Isaiah's cords are a promise of growth: lengthen them, spare not, because the tent is going to get bigger, and the God who stretches it will hold it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: something founded, i.e. a foundation
BiblicalUsage: Ezekiel saw the height of the house round about, and the foundations of the side chambers were a full reed of six great cubits. The word is the foundation itself, and the prophet measures it because the house of God stands on what is laid underneath.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that foundations are worth measuring: the side chambers of the house stood on a full reed of foundation, and nothing in God's house is built on less.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a tweezer (only in the plural)
BiblicalUsage: The temple's bowls and snuffers and basons and spoons were of pure gold, and the chronicler lists the snuffers again among the gold vessels of the house. The word is the tweezer, the small tool that trims the lamps, and it was made of gold like everything else in the holy place.
TheologicalSignificance: I take the golden snuffers as a small sign of how God is served: even the tool that trims the wick is pure gold, because nothing in His house is common.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, a scatterer, i.e. the north wind (as dispersing clouds; only in plural)
BiblicalUsage: Out of the south comes the whirlwind, and cold out of the north. The word is the scatterer, the north wind that disperses the clouds, and Elihu names it in his speech about the weather of God.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Elihu's north wind is a reminder that God rules the weather: the cold comes from the north at His word, and no man orders it.
RelatedTopics: Nature and Creation; God's Power; Wisdom
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: tempered wine
BiblicalUsage: Her navel is like a round goblet which wants not liquor, says the Song, and the word is the tempered wine itself. It is the one place the word appears, in the praise of the beloved.
TheologicalSignificance: I take this single verse as it stands: the Song praises the beloved with the picture of a goblet never empty, and the wine is tempered, mixed well, and full.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a granary
BiblicalUsage: That our garners may be full, affording all manner of store, prays the psalmist, and the word is the granary itself. It is the storehouse of the harvest, and the prayer is for fullness.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that a full garner is a picture of God's provision: the storehouse full, the sheep bringing forth thousands, and the people blessed in the field and in the fold.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a plan, usually evil (machination), sometimes good (sagacity)
BiblicalUsage: Proverbs gives discretion to the simple, says discretion shall preserve and understanding shall keep, calls the young man to regard discretion, and says wisdom dwells with prudence and finds out knowledge of witty inventions. The word is a plan, usually evil, sometimes good, and Proverbs turns it to the good: discretion, the plan that keeps a man safe.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe discretion is the plan that saves: the same word that names the schemes of the wicked names the prudence of the wise, and the difference is whose counsel the plan follows. The difference is whose counsel the plan follows, and wisdom follows the Lord's.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a door-post (as prominent)
BiblicalUsage: Write the words on the posts of your house and on your gates, Moses says twice, and at the Passover the blood was struck on the two side posts and the upper door post of the houses where they ate the lamb. The doorpost is where the word of God and the blood of the lamb both belong.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the doorpost is the most ordinary holy place in Israel: the words on the posts of the house, the blood on the posts of the door, and every going out and coming in under God's word. The doorpost is where the word of God meets daily life, and that is where it belongs.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: irregular feminine of G1520; one or first:--a (certain), + agree, first, one, X other.
BiblicalUsage: Not one jot or one tittle shall pass from the law till all is fulfilled, Jesus says, and the women came to the tomb very early on the first day of the week. The word is the feminine of one, a single one or the first one, and it carries the smallest mark of the law and the first morning of the week.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that one jot is the measure of God's faithfulness: if not even the smallest stroke of the law falls, then not one of His promises will fail either.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: perhaps a primary verb; to sully or taint, i.e. contaminate (ceremonially or morally):--defile.
BiblicalUsage: To the pure all things are pure, but to the defiled and unbelieving nothing is pure, and even their mind and conscience is defiled. Hebrews warns that a root of bitterness springing up defiles many, and Jude says the filthy dreamers defile the flesh. The word is the stain itself, and Scripture traces it from the conscience to the flesh.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe defilement spreads the way Hebrews says it does: a root of bitterness springs up, and many are defiled by it, because no sin stays where it starts. No sin stays where it starts, and a bitter root defiles many.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3392 ("miasma"); (morally) foulness (properly, the effect):--pollution.
BiblicalUsage: Peter warns that if men escape the pollutions of the world through the knowledge of the Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, and are again entangled and overcome, their latter end is worse than the beginning. The word is the foulness itself, the effect of the stain, and Peter says escaping it is not enough without staying free.
TheologicalSignificance: I take Peter's warning as the sober end of the matter: to know the way out of the world's pollution and then go back into it is worse than never having escaped.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3392; (morally) contamination (properly, the act):--uncleanness.
BiblicalUsage: Peter names chiefly those who walk after the flesh in the lust of uncleanness, presumptuous and self-willed, not afraid to speak evil of dignities. The word is the contamination itself, the act of defiling, and Peter puts it first among the sins of the false teachers.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that uncleanness is not a private matter in Peter's eyes: it walks after the flesh, despises government, and speaks evil of dignities, and the church must name it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Mibchar, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Mibchar the son of Haggeri stands in the list of David's mighty men, and the King James spells his name Mibhar. He is named once, and his whole story is that he stood with David.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that a single verse can still honour a man: Mibchar is remembered among the mighty because he was there, and David's list keeps his name.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: select, i.e. best
BiblicalUsage: Sennacherib boasted he would cut down the choice fir trees of Lebanon, the king of the north took the most fenced cities and the chosen people could not withstand him, the Lord chose a place for His name and Israel's choice vows, and Pharaoh's chosen captains drowned in the Red Sea. The word is the select, the best, and Scripture uses it for trees, cities, vows, captains and peoples.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that chosen is a word with two edges: Pharaoh's chosen captains sank, and God's chosen people stood, because the difference is not in being chosen but in who chose them. God's chosen stand because He chose them, and Pharaoh's chosen sank because a man did.
RelatedEvents: The Exodus and the Red Sea
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: select, i.e. well fortified
BiblicalUsage: Elisha tells the kings to smite every fenced city and every choice city of Moab. The word is the select city, the well-fortified one, and the command is to leave Moab no strong place standing.
TheologicalSignificance: I take Elisha's command as the measure of the judgment: every fenced city and every choice city, because Moab's strength was in its walls, and God would have none of it left.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a separation, i.e. (concretely) a separate place
BiblicalUsage: The separate cities for the children of Ephraim lay among the inheritance of Manasseh, all the cities with their villages. The word is the separation itself, a place set apart, and Joshua uses it for cities that belonged to one tribe while standing inside another's land.
TheologicalSignificance: I notice that God's inheritance is not always tidy: Ephraim's cities stood inside Manasseh's land, and the separation was kept by the record, not by a fence.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a building
BiblicalUsage: Ezekiel was set on a very high mountain, by which was as the frame of a city on the south. The word is the building itself, and the prophet's vision begins with a structure he cannot yet name.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the frame of the city is a promise in outline: Ezekiel saw the building before he saw its measurements, and God shows the shape before He fills it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a refugee
BiblicalUsage: All the fugitives of Zedekiah's house shall fall by the sword, and those who remain shall be scattered toward all winds. The word is the refugee, the one who flees, and Ezekiel says the flight will not save them.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the fugitive's fate is the last word on running from God: the sword finds those who flee, and the winds scatter those who remain, because there is no refuge outside His word.
RelatedEvents: Fall of Jerusalem and the Exile
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Mibsam, the name of an Ishmaelite and of an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Mibsam is named twice, in the generations of Ishmael: the firstborn Nebaioth, then Kedar, Adbeel and Mibsam. He is a son of Ishmael, remembered in the genealogy of the twelve princes.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Mibsam's place in Ishmael's line matters: he is one of the twelve princes God promised to Abraham's son, and the promise was kept to the letter.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a rash utterance (hasty vow)
BiblicalUsage: If a woman vowed or uttered ought out of her lips while she had a husband, and he disallowed it on the day he heard it, the vow was of none effect and the Lord forgave her. The word is the rash utterance itself, the hasty vow spoken before it was weighed.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this law is kinder than it looks: the hasty word is not held against her, the husband's word releases her, and the Lord forgives her.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, a refuge, i.e. (objective) security, or (subjective) assurance
BiblicalUsage: Blessed is the man who makes the Lord his trust, the psalmist says the Lord has been his trust from his youth, Proverbs says trust in the Lord is the reason the word is taught, and Jeremiah blesses the man whose hope the Lord is. The word is trust itself, the refuge a man puts his weight on.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe trust is the one refuge that never gives way: the proud turn aside to lies, but the man who makes the Lord his trust is blessed, and his hope is the Lord Himself. The proud turn aside to lies, but the man who makes the Lord his trust is blessed.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Mibtsar, an Idumaean
BiblicalUsage: Mibzar stands in the list of the dukes of Edom, beside Kenaz and Teman, in Genesis and again in Chronicles. The King James spells him Mibzar, and he is remembered only as a duke of Edom.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that even a duke named twice in a list is kept for a reason: Edom's chiefs are recorded, and Mibzar's name stands among them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a fortification, castle, or fortified city; figuratively, a defender
BiblicalUsage: The golden mice were counted according to all the cities of the Philistines, both of fenced cities and country villages, and the king's men waited beside those he put in the fenced cities throughout Judah. The word is the fortification itself, and it stands for every walled town in the land.
TheologicalSignificance: I take the fenced city as the picture of man's defence: the Philistines counted theirs, Judah garrisoned hers, and both learned that walls without the Lord are no defence at all.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a balustrade (for stairs)
BiblicalUsage: The king made pillars of almug trees for the house of the Lord and for the king's house, and the word is the balustrade itself, the stair rail of the temple. It is named once, among the wonders of Solomon's building.
TheologicalSignificance: I notice that even a stair rail in Solomon's temple is worth naming: the house of the Lord was finished down to the last rail, and no part of it was left plain.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: abundance, i.e. (adverbially) liberally
BiblicalUsage: The feast of weeks was kept with a freewill offering, according as the Lord had blessed the giver. The word is the sufficiency itself, the measure of the blessing, and the offering was given in proportion to it.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that giving by the measure of the blessing is the right rule: the Lord blesses, and the hand gives according as He has blessed, neither more nor less.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: trade
BiblicalUsage: Solomon's revenue came beside what he had of the merchantmen and the traffick of the spice merchants, and of all the kings of Arabia. The word is trade itself, and the verse shows a kingdom grown rich on the roads of the merchants.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Solomon's traffick is a quiet warning: the richest king in the land grew rich on trade, and the trade brought the gold and the wives and the gods with it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a colonnade or internal portico (from its rows of pillars)
BiblicalUsage: Ehud went out through the porch after he had killed Eglon, shut the doors of the parlour and locked them. The word is the colonnade, the porch itself, and the verse turns on a man walking out through it with a king dead behind him.
TheologicalSignificance: I take Ehud's porch as the edge of the story: he went forth through it, shut the doors, locked them, and left the servants to find what he had done.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: something enclosing, i.e. a margin (of a region, of a panel); concretely, a stronghold
BiblicalUsage: The bases of the temple had borders between the ledges, and Ahaz cut off the borders of the bases and took down the sea from the brazen oxen. The word is the enclosing margin, the rim that holds a panel in place, and Ahaz cut it off in his remodelling of the house.
TheologicalSignificance: I notice what Ahaz cut: the borders that held the bases together, and the sea that stood on the oxen, and each cut made the house a little less than Solomon built it.
RelatedPeople: King Solomon; Ahaz, King of Judah
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H4317); Michael, an archangel:--Michael.
BiblicalUsage: Michael the archangel contended with the devil about the body of Moses, and would not bring a railing accusation but said, The Lord rebuke thee. In Revelation he fights with his angels against the dragon, and the dragon is cast out. The archangel is named only twice in the New Testament, and both times he is at war.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Michael is the pattern for how God's servants fight: he does not rail, he does not boast, he says, The Lord rebuke thee, and he lets the Lord do the rebuking.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: preservation of life; hence, sustenance; also the live flesh, i.e. the quick
BiblicalUsage: The Ethiopians were overthrown and could not recover themselves, and Ezra says God gave His people a little reviving in their bondage. The word is the preservation of life itself, the recovery, and it swings from a defeated army that could not recover to a remnant that was revived.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that reviving is God's gift to a remnant: a nail in His holy place, light for the eyes, and a little reviving in bondage, and it is enough.
RelatedEvents: Cyrus's Decree and Return from Exile
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: indigent
BiblicalUsage: Better is a poor and wise child than an old and foolish king who will no more be admonished, and a poor wise man delivered a city by his wisdom, yet no man remembered him, and his wisdom was despised and his words were not heard. Ecclesiastes keeps returning to the poor wise man, and the world keeps forgetting him.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the poor wise man is the preacher's portrait of wisdom itself: it delivers the city and is despised for it, and the world remembers the king who would not listen. The world remembers the king who would not listen, and forgets the poor man who saved the city.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a magazine
BiblicalUsage: Solomon had cities of store for his chariots and horsemen and for all he desired to build, and he built Tadmor in the wilderness and all the store cities in Hamath. The word is the magazine itself, the store city, and it marks a kingdom with more than it needs.
TheologicalSignificance: I take the store cities as the sign of Solomon's strength and his danger: he had room for everything, and the room itself became the temptation.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: indigence
BiblicalUsage: The land is one where you eat bread without scarceness and lack nothing, where the stones are iron and the hills yield brass. The word is indigence itself, or rather its absence: without scarceness is the promise, and the land is rich enough to keep it.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe without scarceness is the promise of the land in one phrase: bread enough, iron in the stones, brass in the hills, and nothing lacking.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a veil (as spread out)
BiblicalUsage: Woe to the women who sew pillows to all armholes and make kerchiefs upon the head of every stature to hunt souls, God says through Ezekiel, and then He says their kerchiefs will be torn and His people delivered out of their hand. The word is the veil itself, the kerchief spread to hunt.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the kerchief is a picture of false prophecy at its worst: it hunts souls with a veil, and God tears the veil to set His people free.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: scruf (as spreading over the surface)
BiblicalUsage: The priest looks again on the seventh day, and if the plague is somewhat dark and has not spread, it is but a scab, and the man is clean. But if the scab spreads much abroad after the cleansing, the priest sees it again, and if it spreads in the skin, he pronounces the man unclean. The word is the scab itself, and Leviticus watches it day by day.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the scab is a picture of sin in miniature: it looks small on the seventh day, and if it spreads, it is leprosy, and the priest must call it what it is. The priest must call it what it is, and leprosy by any other name still spreads.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Mispar, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Mispar came with Zerubbabel, in the list of the men who returned: Jeshua, Nehemiah, Seraiah, Reelaiah, Mordecai, Bilshan, Mispar, Bigvai, Rehum, Baanah. He is named once, among the first to come home from Babylon.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Mispar's place in the return list is honour enough: he came home with Zerubbabel, and his name stands among the builders of the second temple.
RelatedEvents: Cyrus's Decree and Return from Exile
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a number, definite (arithmetical) or indefinite (large, innumerable; small, a few); also (abstractly) narration
BiblicalUsage: Take the number of all the congregation, God tells Moses, with the number of their names, every male by his polls. The psalmist says He tells the number of the stars and calls them all by name, and the chronicler counts the sons of Tola, whose number in David's days was two and twenty thousand and six hundred. Numbering runs from the census to the stars.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the number of the stars is the verse that makes counting holy: He who counts the stars calls them by name, and the God who numbers the host of heaven numbers His people too. The God who numbers the host of heaven numbers His people too.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a lamentation
BiblicalUsage: Jacob's sons mourned their father seven days with a great and sore lamentation, the Jews in every province mourned with fasting and weeping and wailing, and Amos says the Lord will call the husbandman to mourning and those skilful of lamentation to wailing. The word is the lament itself, and Scripture gives it its own skilled mourners.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that lamentation is a holy work: seven days for a father, wailing in every province, and men skilled in lamentation called to mourn, because grief that is not mourned turns bitter. Grief that is not mourned turns bitter, so Scripture gives it its own skilled mourners.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Mispereth, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Mispereth came with Zerubbabel, in the list of those who returned: Jeshua, Nehemiah, Azariah, Raamiah, Nahamani, Mordecai, Bilshan, Mispereth, Bigvai, Nehum, Baanah. He is named once, in Nehemiah's copy of the return list.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Mispereth's single verse still counts: his name stands in the list of those who came home, and the return was made of men like him.
RelatedEvents: Cyrus's Decree and Return from Exile
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: fodder
BiblicalUsage: Rebekah told the servant they had both straw and provender enough, and the Levite at Gibeah said there was straw and provender for the asses. The word is fodder itself, the feed for the beasts, and it marks a household that is ready to receive a guest.
TheologicalSignificance: I notice that provender is the sign of a ready house: straw and feed enough, room to lodge, and no want of anything, and the guest is welcomed.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, a concealer, i.e. a covert
BiblicalUsage: God promises the treasures of darkness and hidden riches of secret places, and asks whether any man can hide in secret places where He will not see him, and Habakkuk sees the enemy rejoicing as if to devour the poor secretly. The word is the covert itself, the hiding place, and it hides both God's treasure and man's sin.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the secret place cuts both ways: God keeps His treasures there for those who seek Him, and no man hides his sin there from the God who fills heaven and earth. No man hides his sin in the secret place from the God who fills heaven and earth.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a refuge
BiblicalUsage: There shall be a tabernacle for a shadow in the daytime from the heat, and for a place of refuge, and for a covert from storm and rain. The word is the refuge itself, and Isaiah sets it in the day when the Lord's glory covers Zion.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the covert is the promise for the stormy day: shade from the heat, refuge from the storm, and a tabernacle over the people of God.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a pasture (i.e. open field, whither cattle are driven); by implication, a desert; also speech (including its organs)
BiblicalUsage: God led the people about through the way of the wilderness of the Red Sea, their children wandered forty years in the wilderness, Moses told them to remember all the way the Lord led them forty years to humble and prove them, and Isaiah heard the voice crying in the wilderness to prepare the way of the Lord. The word is the wilderness itself, and it is where God leads, tests, and speaks.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the wilderness is God's school: forty years to humble and prove, a voice crying to prepare the way, and a people led about until they learned to follow. A people led about for forty years learned to follow, and the wilderness taught them.
RelatedEvents: The Exodus and the Red Sea
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: overthrow
BiblicalUsage: A lying tongue hates those it has afflicted, and a flattering mouth works ruin. The word is the overthrow itself, and the proverb puts lying and flattery together as the two ways a tongue destroys.
TheologicalSignificance: I take the flattering mouth as the worse of the two: the lying tongue hates openly, but the flattering mouth works ruin while it smiles.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: flight
BiblicalUsage: Job says he is full of tossings to and fro until the dawning of the day. The word is flight itself, the restless turning of a man who cannot sleep, and Job uses it for a night that will not end.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Job's tossings are the picture of a night without comfort: he lies down, and the night is gone, and the dawning is still far off.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: tribute in money
BiblicalUsage: The enemies of the Jews warned the king that if Jerusalem was rebuilt, the city would pay no more toll, tribute and custom, and the king's own letter remembers the mighty kings who once took toll and tribute from all beyond the river. The word is the tribute itself, the money tax, and it stands in the argument against rebuilding.
TheologicalSignificance: I notice that the enemies' case was all about money: rebuild the wall and the tribute stops, and they were right about the money and wrong about everything else.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: tribute in money
BiblicalUsage: The enemies of the Jews warned the king that if Jerusalem was rebuilt, the city would pay no more toll, tribute and custom, and the king's own letter remembers the mighty kings who once took toll and tribute from all beyond the river. The word is the tribute itself, the money tax, and it stands in the argument against rebuilding.
TheologicalSignificance: I notice that the enemies' case was all about money: rebuild the wall and the tribute stops, and they were right about the money and wrong about everything else.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {Midjan, a son of Abraham; also his country and (collectively) his descendants}
BiblicalUsage: Middin is named once, in the list of the wilderness cities of Judah: Beth-arabah, Middin and Secacah. It is a town in the wilderness, and its name is the whole of what Scripture tells us.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that even a wilderness town in a list is part of the inheritance: Judah's border ran through Middin, and God gave His people the wilderness too.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a treading, i.e. a place for stepping on
BiblicalUsage: God tells Israel not to meddle with Edom, for He will not give them of their land, no, not so much as a foot breadth. The word is the treading itself, the place where a foot steps, and the verse measures God's gift by a single step.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the foot breadth is a measure of God's restraint: He gave Mount Seir to Esau, and not one step of it to Israel, and His people were to respect the boundary.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, an investigation, i.e. (by implication) a treatise or elaborate compilation
BiblicalUsage: The rest of Abijah's acts are written in the story of the prophet Iddo, and the greatness of the burdens on Joash and the repairing of the house are written in the story of the book of the kings. The word is the treatise itself, the written investigation, and the chronicler points to it as his source.
TheologicalSignificance: I take the story of the prophet Iddo as a reminder that Scripture quotes its sources: the chronicler did not invent the acts of the kings, he wrote from the records.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Midjan, a son of Abraham; also his country and (collectively) his descendants
BiblicalUsage: Midian was the fourth son of Keturah, born to Abraham after Sarah's death. Moses fled to the land of Midian and sat down by a well, and in the days of the judges the Lord delivered Israel into the hand of Midian for seven years. The name covers the man, the land, and the people.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Midian's story is the story of a kinsman turned enemy: Abraham's son became the land where Moses hid, and the people who oppressed Israel until Gideon.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {a contest or quarrel}
BiblicalUsage: The lot causes contentions to cease and parts between the mighty, a brother offended is harder to win than a strong city and his contentions are like the bars of a castle, and it is better to dwell in the corner of a housetop than with a brawling woman in a wide house. The word is strife itself, and Proverbs keeps showing its cost.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Proverbs names the price of strife plainly: it bars the castle against a brother, it drives a man to the housetop, and only the lot, cast before the Lord, can end it. Only the lot, cast before the Lord, can end a strife that men cannot.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a Midjanite or descendant (native) of Midjan
BiblicalUsage: Midianite merchantmen bought Joseph out of the pit and sold him into Egypt, Hobab the Midianite was Moses' father-in-law and was asked to journey with Israel, and a Midianite woman was brought into the camp in the sight of Moses while the congregation wept. The word names the people of Midian, and their story runs from Joseph's sale to the plague at Baal-peor.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the Midianites show how a people can be both kin and snare: Hobab was family and guide, the merchants sold Joseph, and the women of Midian brought the plague. A people can be both kin and snare, and Israel learned it from Midian twice over.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: reproof (i.e. curse)
BiblicalUsage: The Lord shall send upon the disobedient cursing, vexation and rebuke, in all they set their hand to, until they are destroyed and perish quickly, because they have forsaken Him. The word is the reproof itself, the curse that follows forsaking God.
TheologicalSignificance: I take this verse as the plain end of disobedience: cursing, vexation and rebuke, not because God is cruel, but because His people forsook Him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a cap (as hemispherical)
BiblicalUsage: Aaron's sons were given coats and girdles and bonnets for glory and for beauty, and Moses put the bonnets on them at their consecration. The word is the cap itself, the linen bonnet of the priest, and it was made for glory and for beauty.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the bonnet matters because God dresses His priests: glory and beauty, not rags, because the service is His.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a border
BiblicalUsage: Two chains of pure gold at the ends, of wreathen work, were fastened to the ouches of the breastplate. The word is the border itself, the wreathen edge, and it is named once, in the making of the high priest's garments.
TheologicalSignificance: I notice that even the chains have their border: gold, wreathen, fastened to the ouches, because the breastplate that bore the tribes was finished in gold.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Migdal-Eder, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Israel journeyed and spread his tent beyond the tower of Edar, after burying Rachel. The name is the tower of the flock, and it stands at the edge of the story where Jacob becomes Israel.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the tower of Edar marks a turning: Rachel buried, the tent spread beyond the tower, and Jacob's house moving on toward Bethlehem.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Migdal-El, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Migdal-el is named once, among the nineteen cities of Naphtali: Iron, Migdal-el, Horem, Beth-anath and Beth-shemesh. It is a fortified town, the tower of God, and its name is the whole of what Scripture tells us.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that a tower named for God in Naphtali's list still preaches: the tower of God stood among the cities of the tribe, and the name was the sermon.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Migdal-Gad, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Migdal-gad is named once, among the cities of Judah: Zenan, Hadashah and Migdal-gad. It is a town in the lowland, the tower of Gad, and its name is the whole of what Scripture tells us.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the lowland towns count as much as the great cities: Migdal-gad stands in Judah's inheritance, and God gave the tower with the rest.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a tower (from its size or height); by analogy, a rostrum; figuratively, a (pyramidal) bed of flowers
BiblicalUsage: Men built a city and a tower whose top would reach to heaven, and the Lord came down to see the city and the tower. Gideon threatened to break down the tower of Penuel, the psalmist tells Zion to count her towers, and the name of the Lord is a strong tower the righteous run into and are safe. The word is the tower itself, and it stands for man's pride and God's refuge at once.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the two towers in this word are the choice every man faces: Babel's tower, built to make a name, and the name of the Lord, the strong tower where the righteous run and are safe. One tower fell by confusion, the other stands forever, and every man must choose his tower.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: preciousness, i.e. a gem
BiblicalUsage: Their father gave them great gifts of silver and gold and precious things, with fenced cities in Judah, and the neighbours of the returned exiles strengthened their hands with vessels of silver and gold and goods and precious things. The word is the precious thing itself, the gift that marks a father's love and a neighbour's help.
TheologicalSignificance: I notice that precious things are given twice in this word: once by a dying king to his sons, and once by neighbours to exiles coming home, and both gifts were real.
RelatedEvents: Cyrus's Decree and Return from Exile
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Migdol, a place in Egypt
BiblicalUsage: Israel encamped before Pi-hahiroth, between Migdol and the sea, and the Jews in Egypt dwelt at Migdol and Tahpanhes and Noph. At Ezekiel the same word is the tower of Syene, where the land of Egypt will be made desolate. Migdol is the place on the edge of the sea, and the word is the tower itself as well.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Migdol stands at the edge of the Exodus for a reason: between Migdol and the sea, with Pharaoh behind and the water before, Israel learned that God makes a way where there is none.
RelatedEvents: The Exodus and the Red Sea
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3396; a compound:--mixture.
BiblicalUsage: Nicodemus brought a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about a hundred pound weight, for the burial of Jesus. The word is the compound itself, and John names it at the burial, where the spices were the last honour given to the Lord.
TheologicalSignificance: I take Nicodemus's mixture as the measure of his love: a hundred pounds of myrrh and aloes, brought in the night, for the body of the Lord.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a primary verb; to mix:--mingle.
BiblicalUsage: Pilate had mingled the blood of the Galileans with their sacrifices, and the soldiers gave Jesus vinegar mingled with gall, which He tasted and would not drink. The word is the mixing itself, and it stands at a massacre and at the cross.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the two mixings in this word could not be further apart: Pilate mingled blood with sacrifices in cruelty, and the soldiers mingled gall with vinegar in mockery, and Jesus would not drink.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a ledge or offset
BiblicalUsage: The nethermost chamber was five cubits broad, the middle six, and the third seven, for in the wall of the house he made narrowed rests round about, so the beams would not be fastened in the walls. The word is the ledge itself, the offset in the wall, and it is named once, in the building of the temple.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the narrowed rests show how carefully God builds: the beams rest on ledges, not in the walls, and the house stands because every part bears its own weight.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: something thrown off (by the spade), i.e. a clod
BiblicalUsage: The seed is rotten under their clods, the garners are laid desolate, the barns are broken down, for the corn is withered. The word is the clod itself, the lump the spade throws off, and Joel uses it for a land where nothing grows.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the rotten seed under the clod is Joel's picture of a ruined harvest: the seed is there, the clod covers it, and nothing comes up, because the rain has not fallen.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a suburb (i.e. open country whither flocks are driven from pasture); hence, the area around a building, or the margin of the sea
BiblicalUsage: The Levites dwelt in Gilead and in all the suburbs of Sharon, and the Levites left their suburbs and their possession and came to Judah and Jerusalem when Jeroboam cast them off. The word is the suburb itself, the open pastureland around the Levitical cities, and it marks the land the Levites lived on.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the suburbs of the Levites show what God gave His servants: no inheritance of land, but pastureland around the cities, and a portion among His people.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Migron, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Saul tarried in the uttermost part of Gibeah under a pomegranate tree in Migron, with about six hundred men, and the Assyrian's march passed to Migron and laid up his carriages at Michmash. It is a town near Gibeah, on the road of armies.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Migron is the place where two armies waited: Saul under the pomegranate tree with six hundred men, and the Assyrian on his march to Jerusalem.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an enumeration; by implication, a valuation
BiblicalUsage: If the household is too little for the lamb, the neighbour next to the house shall take it according to the number of the souls, and the priest shall reckon the worth of the estimation unto the year of jubilee. The word is the counting itself, the enumeration, and it fixes what a man owes.
TheologicalSignificance: I take the counting as the measure of fairness: every man according to his eating, every estimation unto the jubilee, and no man asked for more than the number allows.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a covering, i.e. weatherboarding
BiblicalUsage: A covering of rams' skins dyed red was made for the tent, with a covering of badgers' skins above, and Noah removed the covering of the ark and looked, and the face of the ground was dry. The word is the covering itself, and it shelters the tent and the ark alike.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the covering is the sign of a finished work: the tent covered, the ark uncovered, and in both cases the shelter did its work and was lifted.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a pen (for flocks)
BiblicalUsage: Though the fig tree shall not blossom and the flock shall be cut off from the fold, and there shall be no herd in the stalls, yet the psalmist says God will take no bullock out of his house nor he-goats out of his folds. The word is the pen itself, the fold where the flock is kept.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Habakkuk's empty fold is the test of faith: no flock, no herd, no fruit, and yet I will rejoice in the Lord, the God of my salvation.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: completion (in plural concrete adverbial, wholly)
BiblicalUsage: The flowers and the lamps and the tongs were made of gold, and that perfect gold. The word is completion itself, wholly, and the chronicler uses it for gold that is perfect through and through.
TheologicalSignificance: I notice that the temple's gold is described as perfect, not merely pure: the flowers, the lamps and the tongs were all of that perfect gold, because God's house is finished in gold.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: perfection (of beauty)
BiblicalUsage: Out of Zion, the perfection of beauty, God has shined. The word is perfection itself, and the psalmist puts it on Zion, the place God chose for His name.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Zion is called the perfection of beauty because God shines from it: the beauty is not the city's, it is the light of the God who dwells there.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: perfection (i.e. concrete adverbial, splendidly)
BiblicalUsage: Oholibah doted on the Assyrians, captains and rulers clothed most gorgeously, and Gog's army comes clothed with all sorts of armour. The word is perfection itself, splendidly, and Ezekiel uses it for clothing that dazzles and armies that terrify.
TheologicalSignificance: I take the gorgeous clothing as Ezekiel's warning: the Assyrians dazzled Oholibah with splendour, and the splendour was the snare.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: something perfect, i.e. a splendid garment
BiblicalUsage: The merchants of Tyre traded in all sorts of things, in blue clothes and broidered work and chests of rich apparel, bound with cords and made of cedar. The word is the splendid garment itself, and it stands in the cargo list of the richest city on the sea.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Tyre's rich apparel is the measure of her pride: blue clothes and broidered work in chests of cedar, and the whole cargo going down with the city.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Mikmas or Mikmash, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Saul chose three thousand men, two thousand with him in Michmash and a thousand with Jonathan in Gibeah, and the Philistines were smitten from Michmash to Aijalon. After the exile the children of Benjamin dwelt at Michmash again. It is a town of Benjamin on the ridge, fought over and lived in again.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Michmash is the town that keeps coming back: Saul held it, Jonathan fought from it, and after the exile Benjamin dwelt there again.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: treasure (as hidden)
BiblicalUsage: The word is treasure, hidden away and hoarded. It appears once, in Daniel's vision of the king of the north, who will seize the treasures of gold and silver and all the precious things of Egypt.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the verse is a warning: treasures men hide away are the very things a conqueror seizes first, and no hoard is safe from God.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a (fisher's) net
BiblicalUsage: The net is the fisherman's dragnet, and Habakkuk uses it for the wicked who haul whole nations in and then worship the net itself. Isaiah has the same picture at the Nile, where the fishers cast their nets into the river and the work fails when God dries it up.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the net is a picture of power that forgets God: men who catch everything soon start worshipping the catching, and the Lord will not let that stand.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Mikmethath, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Mikmethath is a place on the border of Ephraim's allotment, named twice as Joshua marks out the land. It stands on the north side of the boundary, facing Shechem, and its name survives only in those two boundary lists.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the boundary stones matter: God gave His people a real land with real borders, and even a name that appears only twice is part of the inheritance He measured out.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: (only in dual) drawers (from concealing the private parts)
BiblicalUsage: The breeches are the linen drawers the priests wore beneath their robes, from the waist to the thighs, so that no nakedness showed when they served at the altar. God commanded them for Aaron and his sons, and Ezekiel still requires them of the priests in the restored temple.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that God cares about modesty in worship: the priests were covered even where no one could see, because holiness reaches the parts of life nobody watches.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a pit (for salt)
BiblicalUsage: The word is a salt pit, a hollow where salt is dug, and it appears once, in the sentence on Moab: the proud nation will become a breeding of nettles and salt pits, a waste place forever.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the picture is exact: pride dries a nation out until nothing grows there but salt.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Mikri, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Mikri is named once, in the register of the families who lived in Jerusalem after the return. Elah the son of Uzzi, the son of Mikri, is counted among the Benjamites who settled the city.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a name kept in the register is honour enough: Mikri's grandson came home to Jerusalem, and the record kept his father's name with him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: masculine or neuter singular of G3398 (as noun); a small space of time or degree:--a (little) (while).
BiblicalUsage: The word is 'a little', and in the New Testament it almost always measures time: a little while. Jesus tells His disciples 'a little while, and ye shall not see me', and Hebrews answers the waiting with the same phrase — yet a little while, and He that shall come will come.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the phrase is meant to steady us: the waiting is real, but it is only a little while, and the coming is certain.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: , including the comparative μικρότερος apparently a primary word; small (in size, quantity, number or (figuratively) dignity):--least, less, little, small.
BiblicalUsage: The word is 'small', and it runs from size to standing: Zacchaeus was little of stature and could not see over the crowd, a cup of cold water given to one of the little ones is never forgotten, and a little leaven leavens the whole lump.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that smallness is no small thing in the kingdom: God notices the little ones, the little gifts, and the little sins that spread.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a stumbling-block, literally or figuratively (obstacle, enticement (specifically an idol), scruple)
BiblicalUsage: A stumbling block is anything set in the path that makes a person fall, and Scripture uses it both literally and for sin itself. The law forbids putting one before the blind, Isaiah calls the LORD Himself a stone of stumbling to those who refuse Him, and Ezekiel names the idols in the heart as the stumbling block of iniquity.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word is a warning in both directions: I must not set a trap in another person's path, and I must not let my own heart keep the idol that trips me. Christ is the stone the builders rejected, and He is either the foundation or the fall.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a thing written, the characters, or a document (letter, copy, edict, poem)
BiblicalUsage: The word is a writing, a document, and it carries both the highest and the most ordinary uses. The tables of stone were the writing of God, graven upon the tables, and centuries later Cyrus's decree went out through his kingdom put also in writing.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the contrast is the point: God's writing endures on stone, and even a pagan king's decree is preserved when it serves His purpose.
RelatedEvents: Cyrus's Decree and Return from Exile
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an engraving, i.e. (techn.) a poem
BiblicalUsage: Miktam is the heading set over six psalms — Psalms 16, 56, 57, 58, 59 and 60 — and it appears nowhere else in Scripture, only in those titles. The psalms under it run from quiet trust to cries for deliverance, and the word itself is a poem or an engraving, a thing cut deep so it lasts.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the heading is part of the gift: these are psalms carved like inscriptions, meant to be remembered word for word when trouble comes.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a burn
BiblicalUsage: The word is a burn in the skin, and it belongs to the priest's examination in Leviticus: when a burn heals and a white or reddish spot rises in it, the priest must look and say whether the plague of leprosy has taken hold there.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that even a burn is watched by God: nothing on the skin is too small for His law, and the priest's careful look is the people's protection.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Milalai, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Milalai is named once, among the musicians who walked in the procession when the wall of Jerusalem was dedicated. He carried the instruments of David the man of God, and his name is kept with the music of that day.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the single mention is enough: Milalai played his part on the day the city sang again, and his name is kept with the music.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a battle (i.e. the engagement); generally, war (i.e. warfare)
BiblicalUsage: War is the word for battle, and Scripture never treats it as an ordinary human quarrel. The song at the sea calls the LORD a man of war, the law of Deuteronomy tells Israel how to go out to battle, and Ecclesiastes sets a time for war beside a time for peace. David says God taught his hands to war, and his fingers to fight, and Isaiah promises a day when the nations shall learn war no more.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe war is real because evil is real, and God does not pretend otherwise. He fights for His people, He judges nations by it, and He promises a day when swords are beaten into ploughshares and war is learned no more.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain origin; Miletus, a city of Asia Minor:--Miletus.
BiblicalUsage: Miletus is the port city on the coast of Asia where Paul stopped on his way to Jerusalem and sent for the elders of Ephesus to meet him there. Years later he writes that he left Trophimus sick at Miletus, a plain line that shows even the apostle's companions were not always healed.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Miletus is remembered for the farewell: Paul told the elders he would see their faces no more, and the church at Ephesus wept over the parting.
RelatedEvents: Paul's Farewell to the Ephesian Elders
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Latin origin; a thousand paces, i.e. a "mile":--mile.
BiblicalUsage: The mile is the Roman thousand paces, and it appears once, in the Sermon on the Mount: if anyone compels you to go a mile, go with him two. The Roman soldier could lawfully press a man into carrying his pack for one mile, and Jesus doubles it.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the second mile is the whole sermon in miniature: love does not stop at what is demanded, it goes further.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Milcah, the name of a Hebrewess and of an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Milcah is the name of two women. The first is Nahor's wife, the mother of Bethuel and the grandmother of Rebekah, so the family of the promise runs through her. The second is a daughter of Zelophehad, who stood with her sisters before Moses to claim their father's inheritance.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Milcah's two lives show the same faithfulness: one kept the family line alive, and the other stood up for what God had promised her family.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a word, command, discourse, or subject
BiblicalUsage: Millah is the Aramaic word for a word, a matter, a thing said. In Daniel it carries the king's demand — the thing is gone from me — and Daniel's answer, and at the end it carries the great words of the horn that speaks against the Most High.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word shows whose words last. Kings lose their words and forget their dreams, but the words of God stand, and the boasting words of the horn are cut short.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a word, command, discourse, or subject
BiblicalUsage: Millah is the Aramaic word for a word, a matter, a thing said. In Daniel it carries the king's demand — the thing is gone from me — and Daniel's answer, and at the end it carries the great words of the horn that speaks against the Most High.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word shows whose words last. Kings lose their words and forget their dreams, but the words of God stand, and the boasting words of the horn are cut short.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: fulness, i.e. (concretely) a plump socket (of the eye)
BiblicalUsage: The word is the setting of a jewel, and it appears once, in the bride's praise of her beloved: his eyes are like doves by the rivers of waters, washed with milk and fitly set, like stones set in their sockets.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the picture is of a beauty that fits: every part in its place, nothing forced, and the beloved described as a work of art.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a rampart (as filled in), i.e. the citadel
BiblicalUsage: Millo is the citadel, the filled-in rampart at Jerusalem, and it marks the building of the city. David built around it when he took the stronghold, Solomon raised it higher with his labour force, and Jeroboam's rebellion began over the burden of that very building.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Millo is a warning in stone: the walls that made Jerusalem strong were built on forced labour, and the same walls helped break the kingdom apart.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a filling, i.e. setting (of gems)
BiblicalUsage: The word is the setting of a gem, and it belongs to the breastplate of judgment: four rows of stones, each one set in gold, with the names of the tribes of Israel engraved upon them and carried over Aaron's heart.
