TheologicalSignificance: I believe the setting is the sermon: God's people are not loose stones but set jewels, each one held in place and carried before the Lord.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a fulfilling (only in plural), i.e. (literally) a setting (of gems), or (technically) consecration (also concretely, a dedicatory sacrifice)
BiblicalUsage: Millu is the filling of the hands, the consecration of the priests. The ram of consecration was offered when Aaron and his sons were set apart, and the filling lasted seven days, with the priests kept at the door of the tabernacle until their consecration was complete.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe consecration still means filled hands. God does not send empty-handed servants, He fills their hands with His work and keeps them near His house until they are ready.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: middle voice from μῖμος (a "mimic"); to imitate:--follow.
BiblicalUsage: The word is to imitate, to follow a pattern, and the New Testament uses it for the faith itself. Hebrews tells the church to remember their leaders and follow their faith, Paul tells the Thessalonians to imitate his working with his own hands, and John warns against imitating what is evil.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe imitation is how faith is passed on. Doctrine is taught in words, but the life is taught by watching someone live it, and the church needs examples worth copying.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3401; an imitator:--follower.
BiblicalUsage: The imitator is the follower, and Paul uses the word as a chain: be followers of me as I am of Christ, and be followers of God as dear children. The Thessalonians became followers of the Lord and of Paul, and Hebrews holds up those who through faith and patience inherit the promises.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the chain must not break. Christ is the pattern, the apostles copied Him, and the church copies them, so that the next generation can still see what the life looks like.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: merchandise; abstractly, a selling
BiblicalUsage: The word is a selling, the merchandise and the bargain itself. Leviticus governs it — when you buy or sell, you shall not oppress one another — and Nehemiah finds merchants lodging outside the wall on the Sabbath, waiting to sell.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the market is a moral place: a fair price is a matter of justice, and the Sabbath sets a limit even on honest trade.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a sale
BiblicalUsage: The word is a sale, and it appears once, in the law that forbids selling an Israelite as a slave: they are My servants, whom I brought out of Egypt, and they shall not be sold as bondmen.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the verse is the foundation of freedom: God bought His people out of Egypt, so no man may buy them back.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a prolonged form of G3415 (from which some of the tenses are borrowed); to remind, i.e. (middle voice) to recall to mind:--be mindful, remember.
BiblicalUsage: The word is to remember, and it carries both the sting and the comfort of memory. Peter remembered the word of Jesus and went out and wept, the angels told the women to remember what He had said in Galilee, and God promises that their sins and iniquities will He remember no more.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe memory is a gift God uses both ways: it convicts the sinner who forgot, and it frees the forgiven, because God Himself chooses to forget.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: outspread (i.e. with outstretched wings)
BiblicalUsage: The word is the outspread wings of the covering cherub, and it appears once, in the lament over the king of Tyre: thou art the anointed cherub that covereth, with wings spread wide over the holy mountain of God.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the wings tell the story: the cherub was set to cover and guard, and the fall came when the guardian wanted the throne for himself.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a ruler or (abstractly) rule
BiblicalUsage: The word is rule, dominion, and Daniel uses it for the kings who rise and fall: a mighty king shall stand and rule with great dominion, and the king of the south shall be strong and have dominion greater than his. The Chronicler uses the same word for the sons of Shemaiah, who ruled throughout their father's house.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that dominion is always borrowed: kings rule for a season and their dominion passes, but the kingdom that shall not be destroyed belongs to God.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a possession
BiblicalUsage: The word is a breeding of nettles, a thicket of weeds, and it appears once, in the sentence on Moab: surely Moab shall be as Sodom, a breeding of nettles and salt pits, a perpetual desolation.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the nettles are the picture: a nation that was once a garden becomes a weed patch, and the residue of God's people will possess it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a bolt
BiblicalUsage: The word is a shoe, or a bolt, and it appears once, in Moses' blessing on Asher: thy shoes shall be iron and brass, and as thy days, so shall thy strength be.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the promise is for every day: God fits the strength to the day, and the shoes to the road.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {properly, a part of; hence (prepositionally), from or out of}
BiblicalUsage: The word is the little Aramaic 'from', and it does the quiet work of Daniel's story: the king's word is gone from him, the three friends trust God to deliver them from the furnace, and the officials remind the king of the decree that no man shall ask a petition of any god or man except the king.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the little words carry the big story: from the king, from the furnace, from every god but the King, and God is the one who delivers.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {properly, a part of; hence (prepositionally), from or out of}
BiblicalUsage: The word is the little Aramaic 'from', and it does the quiet work of Daniel's story: the king's word is gone from him, the three friends trust God to deliver them from the furnace, and the officials remind the king of the decree that no man shall ask a petition of any god or man except the king.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the little words carry the big story: from the king, from the furnace, from every god but the King, and God is the one who delivers.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a sacrificial offering
BiblicalUsage: The word is the Aramaic offering, and it appears twice: once when Nebuchadnezzar falls on his face and commands an offering to be made to Daniel, and once when Artaxerxes sends money for the offerings of the temple in Jerusalem.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the two offerings show the difference: one is offered to a man by mistake, and the other to God by command, and only the second belongs on an altar.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a sacrificial offering
BiblicalUsage: The word is the Aramaic offering, and it appears twice: once when Nebuchadnezzar falls on his face and commands an offering to be made to Daniel, and once when Artaxerxes sends money for the offerings of the temple in Jerusalem.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the two offerings show the difference: one is offered to a man by mistake, and the other to God by command, and only the second belongs on an altar.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: the driving (of a chariot)
BiblicalUsage: The word is the driving of a chariot, and it appears once, on the watchman's lips at Jezreel: the driving is like the driving of Jehu the son of Nimshi, for he driveth furiously.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the watchman saw what Jehu's pace meant: judgment was coming fast, and it was not slowing down.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, a channel or fissure, i.e. (by implication) a cavern
BiblicalUsage: The word is a den, a fissure in the rock, and it appears once, when Midian oppressed Israel so hard that the people made themselves dens in the mountains and hid in caves and strongholds.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the dens tell the story of fear: a people who forget God end up hiding in the rocks, and Gideon found them there.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: completion, i.e. (in produce) wealth
BiblicalUsage: The word is the completion of a harvest, the wealth of produce, and it appears once, in Eliphaz's warning that the wicked man's riches will not last: he shall not be rich, neither shall his substance continue.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the warning stands even when the speaker is wrong about Job: wealth that is not rooted in God does not continue.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a prince
BiblicalUsage: The word is a prince, a captain, and it appears once, in Nahum's picture of Nineveh's leaders as locusts: they camp in the hedges in the cold day, but when the sun rises they flee away, and no one knows where they have gone.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the picture is deliberate: princes who serve only themselves scatter like insects when the heat comes.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Minni, an Armenian province
BiblicalUsage: Minni is a province of Armenia, named once. Jeremiah summons the kingdoms of Ararat, Minni and Ashchenaz to march against Babylon.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the summons shows God's reach: He calls nations from the far north to do His judging, and no empire is beyond His word.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Minnith, a place East of the Jordan
BiblicalUsage: Minnith is a place east of the Jordan, named twice. Jephthah's pursuit of the Ammonites ran from Aroer to Minnith, and centuries later Ezekiel lists the wheat of Minnith among the goods traded to Tyre.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that a place known for war and for wheat tells the truth about the land: it was fought over because it was worth farming.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Minjamin, the name of two Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Minjamin is the name of two Israelites, both priests of the later years. One stands in the courses of the priests after the return, and the other helps distribute the offerings under Hezekiah.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the name is kept because the work was kept: the courses of the priests and the sharing of the offerings both needed faithful men, and Minjamin was one of them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: enumeration
BiblicalUsage: The word is a numbering, and it appears once, at the dedication of the second temple: twelve he-goats for a sin offering, according to the number of the tribes of Israel.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the number is the point: twelve goats for twelve tribes, because the whole house of Israel was being brought back, not only Judah.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a performance
BiblicalUsage: The word is a work, a deed done, and all three of its uses belong to the works of God. Wisdom says the LORD possessed her before His works of old, and the psalms call the people to come and behold the works of the LORD and to see how awesome He is in His doing toward the children of men.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the works are the evidence. God is known by what He has done, and the call is not to argue about Him but to come and look.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an object of attack
BiblicalUsage: The word is a mark, a target set up to be struck, and it appears once, in Job's cry: why hast Thou set me as a mark against Thee, so that I am a burden to myself?
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Job's question is honest, not faithless: he feels singled out by God, and he takes the feeling straight to God instead of hiding it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a miracle
BiblicalUsage: The word is a wonder, a miracle, and it appears once, when Elihu asks Job whether he knows the balancings of the clouds, the wondrous works of Him which is perfect in knowledge.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the question is the answer: the clouds are balanced by a wisdom we cannot weigh, and that is enough.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a classification
BiblicalUsage: The word is a division, a classification, and it appears once, at Josiah's Passover, when the burnt offerings were set aside according to the divisions of the families of the people.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that order is part of worship: every family had its place at the Passover, and no one was left out.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a poising
BiblicalUsage: The word is a poising, a balancing, and it appears once, in the same verse as the wondrous works: dost thou know the balancings of the clouds, the wondrous works of Him which is perfect in knowledge?
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the balancing is the wonder: clouds that weigh tons hang in the sky without falling, and the God who poises them knows how to hold my life too.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an escape
BiblicalUsage: The word is an escape, and it appears once, in David's cry to be far away from the storm: I would hasten my escape from the windy storm and tempest.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the escape David wanted was not from God's will but from men's violence, and God is the shelter he was running toward.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a terror, i.e. an idol
BiblicalUsage: The word is a horror, an idol, and it appears twice, in the same story told twice: Maachah the queen mother made an idol in a grove, and her son Asa cut it down and burned it at the brook Kidron.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Asa did right even against his own mother: no family tie protects an idol, and the grove must be cut down.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Miphkad, the name of a gate in Jerusalem
BiblicalUsage: Miphkad is the name of a gate in Jerusalem, the Muster Gate, and it appears once in the record of the wall's rebuilding. Malchiah the goldsmith's son repaired the stretch over against the gate Miphkad.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the gate's name fits the work: muster means gathering for inspection, and the whole wall was built by neighbours mustered side by side.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an appointment, i.e. mandate; concretely, a designated spot; specifically, a census
BiblicalUsage: The word is an appointment, a muster, a numbering. Joab brought David the sum of the muster of the people, and Ezekiel was told to burn the sin offering in the appointed place of the house.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that numbering is never neutral in Scripture: David's census brought a plague, and the lesson is that counting what God has given can turn into trusting the count instead of Him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an expansion
BiblicalUsage: The word is a spreading out, an expansion, and its two uses could hardly differ more: Tyre spread fine linen from Egypt to be her sail, and Job is asked whether any man can understand the spreadings of the clouds.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the contrast is the sermon: men spread their sails and call it power, but God spreads the clouds, and no one understands how.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a break (in the shore), i.e. a haven
BiblicalUsage: The word is a haven, a break in the shore where ships rest, and it appears once, in Deborah's song: Dan stayed in his ships and Asher sat still in his havens while the battle was fought without them.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Deborah's question still stings: comfort is a haven, and a haven can keep you out of the fight God called you to.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, a fracture, i.e. joint (vertebrae) of the neck
BiblicalUsage: The word is the joint of the neck, and it appears once, at the death of Eli: when the messenger told him the ark of God was taken, he fell backward from his seat by the gate, his neck broke, and he died.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the fall is the judgment: Eli's sons had despised the offerings, and the old priest who would not restrain them broke under the news.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a stride, i.e. (by euphemism) the crotch
BiblicalUsage: The word is a stride, named by euphemism for the crotch, and it appears once, when Hanun shamed David's ambassadors by cutting off their garments in the midst and sending them away.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the shame was deliberate: Hanun wanted the whole region to see that he despised David, and the war that followed was the price of the insult.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an aperture, i.e. (figuratively) utterance
BiblicalUsage: The word is an opening, and its two uses open two different doors: the Levites lodged around the house of God because the opening of its gates every morning belonged to them, and Wisdom says the opening of her lips shall be right things.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the two openings belong together: gates opened for worship in the morning, and lips opened for truth through the day.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a stretcher, i.e. a sill
BiblicalUsage: The word is the threshold, the sill of the door, and it keeps appearing where God and idols meet. Dagon fell with his head and hands broken off on the threshold, and his priests never trod on it again, while the glory of God stood at the threshold of the house.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the threshold is where the contest happens: Dagon could not stand in God's presence, and the sill of the house is no place for an idol.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an augury
BiblicalUsage: The word is a divination, an augury, and it appears twice in Ezekiel's sentence on the false prophets: there shall be no more any vain vision nor flattering divination in Israel, and those who spoke lying divinations are exposed.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the end of divination is good news: God's people do not need fortune-tellers, because God speaks plainly to His prophets.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a consecrated thing or place, especially, a palace, sanctuary (whether of Jehovah or of idols) or asylum
BiblicalUsage: The sanctuary is the holy place where God dwells among His people, and the word runs from the tabernacle to the temple and beyond. God said, let them make Me a sanctuary that I may dwell among them, and He planted His people on the mountain of His inheritance; and when they were carried into exile, He promised to be to them as a little sanctuary in the countries where they went.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the sanctuary was always a promise, not a building. God dwells with His people, and when the building is gone, He Himself is the sanctuary, until the day the dwelling of God is with men.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a sculpture (probably in bas-relief)
BiblicalUsage: The word is a carving, probably in bas-relief, and it belongs to Solomon's temple: the cedar within was carved with knops and open flowers, and the walls were carved with cherubim and palm trees and open flowers, all covered with gold.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the carving is worship in wood and stone: the house of God was made beautiful because the God who dwells there is beautiful.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an asylum (as a receptacle)
BiblicalUsage: The refuge is the city appointed for the manslayer who killed without intent, and the word belongs to the cities of refuge. God told Moses to give six cities where the slayer could flee from the avenger of blood, and Joshua set them apart, three on each side of the Jordan, so that the congregation could judge between the slayer and the avenger.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the cities of refuge preach the gospel before the gospel: a man who did not mean to kill could run to safety and live, and the congregation, not the avenger, decided his case. Christ is our city of refuge, and the gate is still open.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Mikloth, a place in the Desert
BiblicalUsage: Mikloth is named in the registers of Benjamin, where he is counted among the sons of Jeiel who lived in Jerusalem. He is named again among the rulers of David's monthly courses, where he served under Dodai in the second month.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the two mentions show a man who was both a father in the city and a ruler in the army, and the record keeps both.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, a buying, i.e. acquisition; concretely, a piece of property (land or living); also the sum paid
BiblicalUsage: The word is a purchase, a thing bought with money, and it belongs to the covenant and to Jeremiah's field. Every man-child born in Abraham's house or bought with his money was circumcised, and Jeremiah bought a field and sealed the deed, because the purchase was proof that the land would be bought again.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that a purchase is a promise in this story: Abraham's bought servants were brought into the covenant, and Jeremiah's deed was a down payment on the return.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: something bought, i.e. property, but only livestock; abstractly, acquisition
BiblicalUsage: The word is cattle, livestock, the property that walks. The hand of the LORD falls on the cattle of Egypt in the field, and all the cattle of Egypt die of the murrain, while Job's wealth is counted in sheep and camels and oxen before the day it is all taken away.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe cattle are the measure of wealth in the old world, and the measure shows how quickly wealth goes: the same word that counts Job's thousands counts their loss.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Miknejah, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Mikneiah is a Levite musician, named twice in the procession that brought the ark to Jerusalem. He played the harp on the Sheminith, among the singers and the gatekeepers who served before the ark.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the harp is the honour: Mikneiah's name is kept with the music that went up with the ark, and the song is part of the story.
RelatedEvents: David Brings the Ark to Jerusalem
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: reception
BiblicalUsage: The word is a taking, the receiving of a gift, and it appears once, in Jehoshaphat's charge to the judges: there is no iniquity with the LORD our God, nor respect of persons, nor taking of gifts.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the charge is for every judge still: God takes no bribes, and neither may the man who judges in His name.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: something called out, i.e. a public meeting (the act, the persons, or the place); also a rehearsal
BiblicalUsage: The convocation is the called assembly, the holy gathering, and the word runs from the feasts to the reading of the law. The first and seventh days of unleavened bread were holy convocations, the appointed feasts were proclaimed as holy convocations, and when Ezra read the law the Levites caused the people to understand the reading.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the gathering is the point of the feast. God calls His people together to hear His word, and a people that stops assembling stops hearing.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: something met with, i.e. an accident or fortune
BiblicalUsage: The word is a chance, a hap, a thing that happens, and Scripture uses it to test whether anything happens by chance at all. Ruth's hap was to light on the part of the field belonging to Boaz, the Preacher says one event happens to the wise and to the fool alike, and the Philistines called the plague a chance — but the ark went up to Beth-shemesh by the hand of God.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe there is no such thing as chance in God's world. What looks like a hap is providence wearing work clothes, and Ruth's chance meeting was the way God brought the Messiah's grandmother home.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: literally a cucumbered field, i.e. a cucumber patch
BiblicalUsage: The word is a cucumber patch, a garden of cucumbers, and it appears once, in Isaiah's picture of a desolate Jerusalem: the daughter of Zion is left as a lodge in a garden of cucumbers, a lonely hut in a field after the harvest.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the lodge is the warning: a city that forgets God is left standing alone like a watchman's hut in an empty field.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: literally a cucumbered field, i.e. a cucumber patch
BiblicalUsage: The word is a cucumber patch, a garden of cucumbers, and it appears once, in Isaiah's picture of a desolate Jerusalem: the daughter of Zion is left as a lodge in a garden of cucumbers, a lonely hut in a field after the harvest.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the lodge is the warning: a city that forgets God is left standing alone like a watchman's hut in an empty field.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: something turned (rounded), i.e. a curl (of tresses)
BiblicalUsage: The word is a curl, the well-set hair of the daughters of Zion, and it appears once, in the sentence on their pride: instead of well-set hair there shall be baldness, and burning instead of beauty.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the judgment fits the sin: hair dressed for show is shaved away, and the beauty that was worn for men is replaced by sackcloth.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: something to fume (incense) on i.e. a hearth place
BiblicalUsage: The word is the altar of incense, the hearth place for burning, and it appears once, when God commands Moses to make an altar of shittim wood for burning incense before the veil.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the incense altar is the prayer of the people made visible: the smoke rose morning and evening, and so must prayer.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: something to fume (incense) in, i.e. a coal-pan
BiblicalUsage: The word is a censer, the coal-pan for burning incense, and its two uses both end in judgment. Uzziah took a censer to burn incense in the temple and leprosy rose in his forehead, and Ezekiel saw seventy elders with censers filling the temple with the smoke of their idols.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the censer shows that worship is not safe when it is self-appointed: the same fire that carries prayer can carry idolatry, and God knows the difference.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a collection, i.e. (of water) a reservoir
BiblicalUsage: The word is a reservoir, a gathering of waters, and it appears once, when Jerusalem dug a ditch between the walls for the water of the old pool and forgot to look to the Maker who had fashioned it long ago.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the reservoir is the rebuke: they stored the water and forgot the God who sends it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: something waited for, i.e. confidence (objective or subjective); also a collection, i.e. (of water) a pond, or (of men and horses) a caravan or drove
BiblicalUsage: The word is a gathering, and it gathers two meanings: the gathering together of the waters which God called Seas, and the hope of Israel, the LORD Himself. Jeremiah calls Him the hope of Israel and the Saviour in time of trouble.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the two meanings are one: hope is a gathering, the waters gathered into seas and the people gathered to God, and the LORD is the hope because He is the One who gathers.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: pasture (the place or the act); also the haunt of wild animals
BiblicalUsage: The word is pasture, the place where flocks feed, and it moves from need to promise. Jacob's sons ask Pharaoh for pasture because their cattle have none, Joel laments that the pastures of the wilderness are dried up, and God promises to feed His flock in a good pasture on the high mountains of Israel.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that pasture is the promise of a shepherd: the flock does not find its own grass, the Shepherd leads it there, and the good pasture is His gift.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: pasturage; concretely, a flock
BiblicalUsage: The word is the pasturage, the flock's grazing ground, and the psalms use it for the people themselves: we are His people, and the sheep of His pasture, and Jeremiah pronounces woe on the shepherds who destroy and scatter the sheep of God's pasture.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word makes the people the pasture: God feeds His flock, and the shepherds who scatter it will answer to Him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: abundance, i.e. a great quantity
BiblicalUsage: The word is abundance, a great quantity, and it appears once, in the cup of judgment: thou shalt drink of thy sister's cup deep and large, and it containeth much.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the cup is full because the sin was full: judgment is measured to match what was done.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: abasement (the act or the thing)
BiblicalUsage: The word is a trampling, the act of treading down, and it belongs to judgment: the vineyard's wall is broken down and it is trodden under foot, the Assyrian is sent to tread down the nations like mire, and Daniel asks how long the sanctuary and the host shall be given to be trodden under foot.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the trampling is never the last word: God lets His vineyard be trodden down for a season, but the treader is judged too, and the sanctuary is raised again.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Mirmah, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Mirmah is named once, among the sons of Shaharaim. Shaharaim was a Benjamite who had sons by his wives in the country of Moab.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the single line is enough: Mirmah was a head of his father's house, and the record keeps his name with his brothers.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: fraud
BiblicalUsage: The word is deceit, fraud, and it runs from the first family to the last Servant. Jacob came with subtlety and took his brother's blessing, the sons of Jacob answered Shechem with deceit, and the Proverbs say the counsels of the wicked are deceit — yet of the suffering Servant it is written that there was no deceit in His mouth.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe deceit is the old family sin, and Christ is the end of it. He took no blessing by a trick, and the mouth that never deceived is the mouth that speaks for us.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: muddled water
BiblicalUsage: The word is fouled water, water muddled by feet, and it appears once, in God's charge against the fat shepherds: My flock eats what you have trodden with your feet and drinks what you have fouled.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the charge is about leaders who spoil what they were meant to guard: the flock goes thirsty while the shepherds muddy the water.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an aromatic unguent; also an unguent-pot
BiblicalUsage: The word is the compounding of ointment, the apothecary's art, and it belongs to the holy anointing oil and to the sweet spices. The oil was compounded after the art of the apothecary, the priests' sons made the ointments, and Asa was laid in a bed filled with spices prepared by the same art.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the compounding shows care: holy things are not thrown together, they are measured and mixed by skilled hands, and the same care goes into honouring the dead.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a female wicked doer
BiblicalUsage: The word is a wicked woman, a female doer of wickedness, and it appears once, for Athaliah: her sons had broken up the house of God and bestowed its dedicated things upon Baal.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the word is a warning, not an insult: a mother who leads her sons into idolatry breaks more than a house, she breaks a generation.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Mirjam, the name of two Israelitesses
BiblicalUsage: Miriam is the prophetess, the sister of Aaron and Moses, and her name runs through the whole wilderness story. She took a timbrel and led the women in song at the sea, and she spoke against Moses and was struck leprous for seven days, shut out of the camp until she was received again.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Miriam shows both sides of leadership: the song at the sea is the high point, and the leprosy is the warning that even a prophetess must not speak against God's chosen servant.
RelatedEvents: The Exodus and the Red Sea
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a cry, i.e. (of job), a revel
BiblicalUsage: The word is a revel, a banquet of those who stretch themselves out at ease, and it appears once, in Amos's sentence on the rich of Samaria: they shall go captive with the first that go captive, and the banquet of them that stretched themselves shall be removed.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the banquet is the indictment: they feasted while the nation rotted, and the feast was the first thing taken away.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a laughing-stock
BiblicalUsage: The word is a laughing-stock, a scorn, and it appears once, in Habakkuk's picture of the Chaldeans: the princes shall be a scorn unto them, and they shall deride every stronghold, heaping up dust and taking it.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the scoff is God's judgment on pride: kings who trust in walls become a joke to the army that takes them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a primary μῖσος (hatred); to detest (especially to persecute); by extension, to love less:--hate(-ful).
BiblicalUsage: The word is to hate, and the New Testament uses it in both directions. Jesus quotes the old saying, love your neighbour and hate your enemy, and then overturns it; He says a disciple must hate his own life by comparison with Christ; and He warns that the world hated Him first, so it will hate His people too. John presses it further: whoever hates his brother is a murderer.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe hatred is the test of love. We cannot claim to love God while hating our brother, and the only hatred Christ commands is the hatred of our own life when it competes with Him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: defence, high fort (tower), refuge, Misgab, a place in Moab
BiblicalUsage: The word is a high tower, a defence, a refuge, and David uses it for God Himself. The LORD is my rock and my fortress and my deliverer, the God of Jacob is our refuge, and He only is my rock and my salvation.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the tower is the right picture. A refuge is not a hiding place you dig, it is a height you run to, and the God who is my defence cannot be taken.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Mishal, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Mishal is a city of Asher given to the Levites, named twice in the allotment of the land. It is named once in the border of Asher's inheritance, and once in the list of the cities the Levites received.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the Levites' cities show God's provision: the tribe with no land of its own was given homes in every tribe's land, and Mishal was one of them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a request
BiblicalUsage: The word is a request, a petition, and its two uses are both prayers answered: the LORD fulfil all thy petitions, and delight thyself in the LORD and He shall give thee the desires of thine heart.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the two verses belong together: the petitions are fulfilled for the heart that delights in the LORD first.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Misham, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Misham is named once, among the sons of Elpaal. Elpaal was a Benjamite whose sons built Ono and Lod with their towns.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe builders are remembered: Misham's name is kept with the towns his family raised, and the work outlasted the man.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a support (concretely), i.e. (figuratively) a protector or sustenance
BiblicalUsage: The word is a stay, a support, and David uses it for God in the day of calamity: they prevented me in the day of my calamity, but the LORD was my stay. Isaiah turns it around: God takes away from Jerusalem the stay and the staff, the whole stay of bread and the whole stay of water.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the stay is the test of trust. When God is my stay, nothing can shake me, and when He takes the stay away, nothing else can hold the city up.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: support (abstractly), i.e. (figuratively) sustenance or (concretely) a walking-stick
BiblicalUsage: The word is a staff, a walking-stick and a support, and its uses run from comfort to false trust. The shepherd's staff comforts in the valley of the shadow of death, Isaiah says God will take away the stay and the staff from Jerusalem, and Egypt is called a staff of reed that breaks in the hand of any man who leans on it.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the staff is only as strong as the hand that holds it: lean on the Shepherd's staff and it comforts, lean on Egypt's reed and it breaks in your hand.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a kneading-trough (in which the dough rises)
BiblicalUsage: The word is a kneading-trough, the bowl the dough rises in, and it appears in the exodus and in the blessing. The people took their dough in troughs on their shoulders when they left Egypt, the frogs came up into the troughs in Pharaoh's house, and the blessing promises that the basket and the store shall be blessed.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the trough is a sign of daily bread: God provides the dough and blesses the bowl, and even the plagues reach into the kitchen.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: inspection
BiblicalUsage: The word is a washing, a cleansing, and it appears once, in the picture of the newborn Jerusalem: in the day thou wast born thy navel was not cut, neither wast thou washed in water to supple thee, nor salted at all.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the washing is the mercy: God found a child unwashed and unloved, and He washed her and took her for His own.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a hollow, i.e. a narrow passage
BiblicalUsage: The word is a hollow, a narrow passage, and it appears once, on the road to Moab: the angel of the LORD stood in a path of the vineyards, with a wall on this side and a wall on that side, and there was no way to turn.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the narrow place is God's mercy: Balaam could not go around the angel, and the donkey that stopped saved his life.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a breaker (of the sea)
BiblicalUsage: The word is a breaker, a wave of the sea, and it is always God's waves. David says the waves of death compassed him, the psalmist says all Thy waves and Thy billows are gone over me, and Jonah, in the belly of the fish, says the same.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the waves are His: the sea that overwhelms is the sea He commands, and the man under the waves is still in His hand.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: cessation, i.e. destruction
BiblicalUsage: The word is a cessation, a rest, and it appears once, at the end of the verse where Jerusalem remembers her affliction: the adversaries saw her, and did mock at her sabbaths.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the mockery is the wound: the enemies laughed at the very rest God had given her, and the city that broke the sabbaths lost them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: the orifice of the womb (from which the fetus breaks forth)
BiblicalUsage: The word is the breaking forth, the opening of the womb, and Hezekiah uses it in his darkest hour: the children are come to the birth, and there is not strength to bring forth. Hosea turns it into judgment: Ephraim is an unwise son who will not stay in the place of the breaking forth of children.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the picture is of a crisis that cannot deliver itself: the birth is ready and the strength is gone, and only God can bring it forth.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a brocade; by analogy, a (reticulated) setting of a gem
BiblicalUsage: The word is a setting, a brocade, the gold work that holds a stone or clothes a queen. The stones of the breastplate were set in ouches of gold like a signet, and the king's daughter is clothed in wrought gold within.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that gold is the frame, not the jewel: the setting serves the stone, and the clothing serves the daughter, and both are made to be seen.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: unction (the act); by implication, a consecratory gift
BiblicalUsage: The word is the anointing, the oil and the act, and it runs through the whole setting apart of the tabernacle. Moses poured the anointing oil on Aaron's head, the oil itself was compounded as a holy anointing oil, and the tabernacle and all its vessels were anointed with it.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the anointing is the mark of being set apart. Oil on the head means God has chosen this man and this place for His own, and the same Spirit anoints His people still.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: dawn
BiblicalUsage: The word is the dawn, the breaking of morning, and it appears once, in the psalm of the King: from the womb of the morning thou hast the dew of thy youth.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the dawn is the promise: the King's people come willingly like dew at first light, fresh and without number.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: disfigurement
BiblicalUsage: The word is a disfigurement, a marring, and its two uses face each other: the Servant's visage was so marred more than any man, and the law forbids offering an animal whose corruption is in it.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the two verses are one story: the perfect offering was marred for us, and the marred Servant is the only offering God accepts.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an err or
BiblicalUsage: The word is an error, an oversight, and it appears once, when Jacob sends his sons back to Egypt with double money: the money that was brought again in the mouth of your sacks, carry it again, peradventure it was an oversight.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the oversight is the test: Jacob would rather overpay than be found keeping what was not his, and honesty is the first step home.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a bed (figuratively, a bier); abstractly, sleep; by euphemism, carnal intercourse
BiblicalUsage: The word is a bed, and it keeps appearing at the turning points of sin. Reuben defiled his father's bed and lost the excellency, David rose from his bed in the evening and saw Bathsheba, and Ish-bosheth was murdered lying on his bed at noon.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the bed is where private sin begins: what is done in the bedroom does not stay in the bedroom, and the house of David never forgot it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a bed
BiblicalUsage: The word is the Aramaic bed, and in Daniel it is where the visions come: the visions of thy head upon thy bed, the thoughts that came into the king's mind upon his bed, and the dream that troubled Nebuchadnezzar while he lay upon his bed.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God speaks in the night: kings dream on their beds and cannot rest until Daniel tells them what the dreams mean.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a residence (including a shepherd's hut, the lair of animals, figuratively, the grave; also the Temple); specifically, the Tabernacle (properly, its wooden walls)
BiblicalUsage: The tabernacle is the dwelling, the tent where God lived among His people, and the word runs through the whole story of the wilderness. God showed Moses the pattern of the tabernacle on the mountain, the curtains were woven for it, and when it was set up the glory of the LORD filled it; and David remembered that God had gone from tent to tent and from one tabernacle to another.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the tabernacle is the gospel in canvas. God would rather pitch a tent among sinners than stay in heaven without them, and the tent became flesh and dwelt among us.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: residence
BiblicalUsage: The word is the Aramaic dwelling, a residence, and it appears once, when Artaxerxes sends silver and gold to the God of Israel, whose habitation is in Jerusalem.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the line is the confession of a pagan king: the God of Israel has a habitation, and even Artaxerxes sends gifts to it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a mission, i.e. (abstractly and favorable) release, or (concretely and unfavorable) an army
BiblicalUsage: The word is a sending out, a release, and its two uses are both about what cannot be stopped: there is no discharge in the day of death, and God cast upon Egypt the fierceness of His anger by sending evil angels among them.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the warning cuts both ways: death takes us and we cannot buy a discharge, and God's judgment, once sent, does its work.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a sending out, i.e. (abstractly) presentation (favorable), or seizure (unfavorable); also (concretely) a place of dismissal, or a business to be discharged
BiblicalUsage: The word is a sending out, a putting forth of the hand, and it covers both work and gifts. God blesses all that the hand is put to, and the Jews of the villages made Purim a day of sending portions one to another.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the open hand is blessed twice: God blesses the work of the hand, and the hand that sends portions to a neighbour is blessed again.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: audience, i.e. the royal court; also obedience, i.e. (concretely) a subject
BiblicalUsage: The word is the royal audience, the guard, the men who stand near the king. Ahimelech asks who is so faithful among all the servants as David, who goes at the king's bidding, and Benaiah is set over David's guard, the men who heard the king's word first.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the guard is the picture of faithfulness: David's men stood close and obeyed at a word, and the servant who goes at the King's bidding is honourable in His house.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Mishma, the name of a son of Ishmael, and of an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Mishma is the name of two men. One is a son of Ishmael, counted among the twelve princes of his house, and the other is a Simeonite whose sons are listed down to Shimei.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the two lists keep the promise straight: Ishmael's sons became princes as God said, and the sons of Simeon are counted too, because every family is remembered.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a report
BiblicalUsage: The word is a hearing, a report, and it appears once, in the promise of the coming King: He shall not judge after the sight of His eyes, neither reprove after the hearing of His ears.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the verse is the test of every ruler: sight and hearsay are not enough, and only the King who judges by the Spirit judges true.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Mashmannah, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Mishmannah is named once, as the fourth of the Gadite captains who came to David at Ziklag. They were men of might and men of war fit for the battle.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the fourth name matters: David's army was built one faithful man at a time, and Mishmannah was one of them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a guard (the man, the post or the prison); a deposit (figuratively); also (as observed) a usage (abstractly), or an example (concretely)
BiblicalUsage: The word is a guard, a watch, a ward, and it runs from prison to the heart. Joseph was put in ward and kept there, Nehemiah set a watch against the enemy day and night, and the Proverb says to keep the heart with all diligence, for out of it are the issues of life.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the heart is the ward that matters most: prisons hold the body, but the watch over the heart holds the life.
RelatedPeople: Joseph, Son of Jacob; Nehemiah; King Solomon
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: watch, i.e. the act (custody), or (concretely) the sentry, the post; objectively preservation, or (concretely) safe; figuratively observance, i.e. (abstractly) duty or (objectively) a usage or party
BiblicalUsage: The word is the charge, the keeping, and it belongs to obedience itself. Abraham kept God's charge, His commandments and His laws; the lamb was kept up until the fourteenth day; the people kept the charge of the LORD when the cloud tarried; and Aaron and his sons were told to keep the charge of the LORD at the door of the tabernacle, that they die not.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the charge is the shape of faithfulness. Keeping is not a single act but a watch, held day after day, until the cloud moves or the seven days are done.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, a repetition, i.e. a duplicate (copy of a document), or a double (in amount); by implication, a second (in order, rank, age, quality or location)
BiblicalUsage: The word is the second, the double, the copy, and it shows up in the king's copy of the law, in the second quarter of Jerusalem where Huldah lived, and in the order of Jesse's sons who followed Saul to the battle.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the copy is the point: the king was to write his own copy of the law and read it all his life, because a ruler who copies God's word will not be ruled by his own.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a family, i.e. circle of relatives; figuratively, a class (of persons), a species (of animals) or sort (of things); by extension a tribe or people
BiblicalUsage: The word is a family, a clan, a kindred, and it is the way God counts His people. The nations were divided after their families, the promise was that in Abraham all the families of the earth would be blessed, and Israel was numbered and judged family by family.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the family is God's unit. He blesses families, He numbers families, and He judges families, because the promise runs through the house, not only the man.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a stall for cattle (only dual)
BiblicalUsage: The word is a sheepfold, a stall for cattle, and it appears twice at the edges of a battle: Issachar couches between the burdens like a strong ass, and Deborah asks Reuben why he stayed among the sheepfolds listening to the bleating of the flocks while the battle was fought.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the sheepfold is the temptation of comfort: the fold is warm and the flocks are bleating, and the battle goes on without you.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a settling place (of water), i.e. a pond
BiblicalUsage: The word is a settling place of water, a pond, and it appears once, in God's charge against the fat shepherds who drank of the deep waters and fouled the rest with their feet.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the pond is the picture of greed: the shepherds drank the clear water and left the flock the mud.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: weight (numerically estimated); hence, weighing (the act)
BiblicalUsage: The word is a weight, the measure in shekels and talents, and it weighs the famous things: Goliath's coat of mail weighed five thousand shekels of brass, the crown of the Ammonite king weighed a talent of gold, and Solomon's yearly revenue was six hundred and sixty-six talents.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the scales tell the story: the giant's armour was weighed and found wanting, the crown was taken from a conquered king, and the gold that weighed Solomon down was the beginning of his fall.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a weight, i.e. a plummet (with line attached)
BiblicalUsage: The word is a plummet, the weight on a line that shows whether a wall is true, and its two uses are both judgments: God will stretch the plummet of Ahab's house over Jerusalem, and He will lay judgment to the line and righteousness to the plummet.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the plummet is the mercy in the judgment: God measures before He strikes, and the wall that is not plumb is the wall that falls.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: weight
BiblicalUsage: The word is a weight, and it appears once, in the sign of the siege: Ezekiel's bread was weighed out at twenty shekels a day, eaten from time to time, while he lay on his side for the iniquity of the house.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that weighed bread is the picture of siege: when God measures the food, the city knows it is under judgment.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a Mishraite, or inhabitant (collectively) of Mishra
BiblicalUsage: The word is a Mishraite, a man of Mishra, and it appears once, in the families of Kirjath-jearim, where the Mishraites are counted with the Ithrites and the Puhites and the Shumathites.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the list is the point: God counts the families of a small town by name, and the Mishraites are not lost in the crowd.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: maceration, i.e. steeped juice
BiblicalUsage: The word is steeped juice, the liquor of grapes, and it appears once, in the law of the Nazarite: he shall drink no liquor of grapes, nor eat moist grapes or dried, for all the days of his separation.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the grape juice is the test of the vow: the Nazarite gives up even the harmless fruit, because separation means separation, not moderation.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: jurisdiction
BiblicalUsage: The word is a jurisdiction, a dominion, and it appears once, when God asks Job whether he knows the ordinances of heaven and can set their dominion in the earth.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the question settles it: the heavens have a government, and it is not mine to set.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a banquet
BiblicalUsage: The word is the Aramaic banquet, and it appears once, when the queen came into the banquet house at Belshazzar's feast, where the king had drunk wine from the vessels of the temple.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the banquet is the setting of the judgment: they feasted with God's vessels, and the writing was already on the wall.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a banquet
BiblicalUsage: The word is the Aramaic banquet, and it appears once, when the queen came into the banquet house at Belshazzar's feast, where the king had drunk wine from the vessels of the temple.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the banquet is the setting of the judgment: they feasted with God's vessels, and the writing was already on the wall.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a spreading-place
BiblicalUsage: The word is a spreading-place, where nets are spread to dry, and Ezekiel uses it for Tyre and for the river of life: Tyre shall become a place to spread nets upon in the midst of the sea, and the fishers shall stand by the river from En-gedi to En-eglaim spreading their nets.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the nets tell both stories: a proud city becomes a drying ground for fishermen's nets, and the river of life makes the same ground fruitful again.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: slaughter
BiblicalUsage: The word is oppression, and it appears once, in the wordplay of the vineyard song: God looked for judgment, but behold oppression — for righteousness, but behold a cry.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the wordplay is the judgment: the word for justice and the word for oppression sound alike, and Israel gave God the wrong one.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: empire
BiblicalUsage: The word is a government, an empire, and it appears twice, in the promise of the Child: the government shall be upon His shoulder, and of the increase of His government and peace there shall be no end.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the government on His shoulder is the only one that never fails: every empire ends, but His government increases and His peace has no end.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: combustion, i.e. cremation (of a corpse), or calcination (of lime)
BiblicalUsage: The word is a burning, the calcining of lime or the burning of spices for a dead king, and its two uses are opposite ends: the peoples shall be as the burnings of lime, and Zedekiah is promised the burnings of his fathers, with odours burned for him.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the two burnings show the two ends: the wicked are burned like lime, and the king who surrenders is honoured with the burnings of his fathers.
RelatedPeople: Isaiah; Jeremiah; Zedekiah, King of Judah
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Misrephoth-Majim, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Misrephoth-maim is a place on the northern coast, the burnings of waters, named twice in the conquest. Joshua chased the northern kings as far as Misrephoth-maim, and God promised to drive out all who lived from Lebanon to Misrephoth-maim.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the name is a landmark of the promise: the land was given as far as the waters, and Joshua's victories ran to the very edge of it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3406; requital (good or bad):--recompence of reward.
BiblicalUsage: The word is a recompense, a repayment, and Hebrews uses it for both sides of the ledger. Every transgression received a just recompense of reward, confidence has a great recompense of reward, and Moses chose the reproach of Christ over the treasures of Egypt because he had respect unto the recompense of the reward.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the recompense is the reason to hold on. God pays every debt, the punishment and the reward alike, and Moses was right to count the reward greater than Egypt.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3409 and G591; a renumerator:--rewarder.
BiblicalUsage: The word is a rewarder, and it appears once, in the verse that defines faith: he that cometh to God must believe that He is, and that He is a rewarder of them that diligently seek Him.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the rewarder is the heart of faith: we do not seek God for nothing, we seek Him because He rewards the seeking.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3408; a wage-earner:--hired servant.
BiblicalUsage: The word is a hired servant, and it appears twice in the prodigal's speech: how many hired servants of my father's have bread enough and to spare, and I am no more worthy to be called thy son — make me as one of thy hired servants.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the hired servant is the measure of the father's house: even the lowest place there has bread enough, and the son who comes home finds more than he asked for.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3409; a rented building:--hired house.
BiblicalUsage: The word is a hired house, and it appears once, at the end of Acts: Paul dwelt two whole years in his own hired house, and received all that came in unto him, preaching the kingdom of God.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the hired house is the last picture of the mission: Paul in chains, in a rented room, and the gospel still going out to everyone who came.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3408; to let out for wages, i.e. (middle voice) to hire:--hire.
BiblicalUsage: The word is to hire, to take on labourers for wages, and it appears twice in the parable of the vineyard: the householder went out early in the morning to hire labourers, and the men standing idle in the marketplace answer, because no man hath hired us.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the hiring is the grace of the parable: the householder goes out again and again, and no one who wants work is left standing idle.
RelatedEvents: The Parable of the Workers in the Vineyard
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: apparently a primary word; pay for service (literally or figuratively), good or bad:--hire, reward, wages.
BiblicalUsage: The word is wages, hire, reward, and it runs through the teaching of Jesus and Paul alike. Great is your reward in heaven, says the Sermon on the Mount, and the same sermon warns that alms done to be seen have no reward of the Father; the labourers are called at evening to receive their hire, and every man shall receive his own reward according to his own labour.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the wages are the measure of the heart. God pays what is promised, and the reward He gives is never for show — it is for the work done where only the Father sees.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3409; a wage-worker (good or bad):--hired servant, hireling.
BiblicalUsage: The word is a hireling, a wage-worker, and its uses draw the line between the hired and the called. James and John left their father in the ship with the hired servants, and Jesus says the hireling is not the shepherd: he sees the wolf coming and flees, because he cares not for the sheep.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the hireling is the warning to every leader: the shepherd stays because the sheep are his, and the hireling flees because they are only his wages.
RelatedPeople: Jesus; James, Son of Zebedee; John the Apostle
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: (used as abstractly) supreme exaltation
BiblicalUsage: The word is exaltation, a lifting up, and its two uses are the two directions of pride: David ascribes the greatness and the majesty to the LORD, and Adonijah exalts himself, saying, I will be king.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the contrast is the whole story: God is exalted because He is God, and the man who exalts himself is brought low.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a Mithnite, or inhabitant of Methen
BiblicalUsage: The word is a Mithnite, a man of Methen, and it appears once, in the list of David's mighty men: Joshaphat the Mithnite stands among the thirty.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the list is the honour: the mighty men are named one by one, and the Mithnite's home town is kept with his name.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Mithkah, a place in the Desert
BiblicalUsage: Mithkah is a station in the wilderness journey, named twice in the record of the march. They removed from Tarah and pitched in Mithkah, and they removed from Mithkah and pitched in Hashmonah.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the stations are kept because the journey was kept: every camp is named, and no step of the wilderness is forgotten.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Mithredath, the name of two Persians
BiblicalUsage: Mithredath is the name of two Persians. The first was the treasurer who handed the temple vessels back to Sheshbazzar by the order of Cyrus, and the second wrote to Artaxerxes with the enemies of Judah to stop the building.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the two men show the two hands of empire: one hand returns what was stolen, and the other writes letters to stop the work, and God uses both.
RelatedEvents: Cyrus's Decree and Return from Exile
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a wide cloak (for a woman)
BiblicalUsage: The word is a wide cloak, a veil, and its two uses are opposite ends of a woman's life: Boaz measured six measures of barley into Ruth's veil, and Isaiah lists the wimples among the finery that will be stripped from the proud daughters of Zion.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the veil carries the story: Ruth's veil held the barley of a kinsman's kindness, and the wimples of Zion held only pride.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a step; figuratively, companionship
BiblicalUsage: The word is a step, and it is always God's step or man's step measured against His. The steps of a good man are ordered by the LORD, man's goings are of the LORD, and the king of the north has the Libyans and Ethiopians at his steps.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the steps are ordered, not random: I do not understand my own way, but the LORD orders it, and that is enough.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Mitsar, a peak of Lebanon
BiblicalUsage: Mitsar is the little hill, the hill Mizar, named once, in the psalmist's cry from the land of Jordan. My soul is cast down within me, therefore will I remember Thee from the land of Jordan and of the Hermonites, from the hill Mizar.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the little hill is the point: the psalmist remembers God from the smallest height, and no place is too low for remembrance.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: petty (in size or number); adverbially, a short (time)
BiblicalUsage: The word is little, petty, small in size or number, and it marks the small things God uses: a little city to flee to, a small beginning that greatly increases, and a small company of Syrians that overcame a great host.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that little is the measure God loves: the little city saved Lot, the small beginning grew, and the small company won because the LORD was with it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a shinpiece of armor (as prominent), only plural
BiblicalUsage: The word is a greave, the brass shinpiece of armour, and it appears once, on Goliath: he had greaves of brass upon his legs, and a target of brass between his shoulders.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the greaves are the measure of the giant: all that brass, and a single stone from a shepherd's sling brought him down.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a tiara, i.e. official turban (of a king or high priest)
BiblicalUsage: The word is the mitre, the turban of the high priest, and it belongs to the holy garments: the plate of pure gold was fastened upon the mitre, and the mitre was put upon Aaron's head at the consecration.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the mitre is the crown of the priest: holiness to the LORD was written on the gold, and the priest wore it on his forehead where all could see.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Mitspah, the name of two places in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Mizpah is the watchtower, the place of watching, and its name runs through the whole story of Israel. Jacob and Laban raised a heap there and said, the LORD watch between me and thee; Samuel gathered all Israel to Mizpah to pray and to choose a king.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Mizpah is the promise of the heap: when two men part and cannot watch each other, the LORD watches between them, and that is enough.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Mitspeh, the name of five places in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Mizpeh is the name of several places, all of them watchtowers. Joshua chased the northern kings to the valley of Mizpeh, one city of Judah bears the name, and Jephthah passed through Mizpeh of Gilead on his way to the Ammonites.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the name fits the land: a hill country needs watchtowers, and the places that watch are the places where the battles are decided.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an observatory, especially for military purposes
BiblicalUsage: The word is a watchtower, an observatory, and its two uses both end in looking: Judah came to the watchtower in the wilderness and looked, and the multitude was dead bodies, and the watchman cries that he stands continually upon the watchtower day and night.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the watchtower is the place of faith: the army is already dead before Judah lifts a sword, and the watchman sees it first because he is watching.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a secret (place or thing, perhaps, treasure)
BiblicalUsage: The word is a secret, a hidden treasure, and it appears once, in Obadiah's sentence on Edom: how are the things of Esau searched out, and how are his hidden things sought up!
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the secret is the judgment: what Esau hid is dragged into the light, and nothing stays hidden from God.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Mitsrajim, i.e. Upper and Lower Egypt
BiblicalUsage: Egypt is the land of bondage and the land of refuge, and its name runs through the whole of Scripture. Abram went down into Egypt in the famine, God says He has seen the affliction of His people which is in Egypt, and the firstborn of Egypt were smitten in one night.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Egypt is the picture of the world: it feeds you in the famine and enslaves you after, and the God who brought His people out of it is the God who brings His people out still.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a crucible
BiblicalUsage: The word is a crucible, the fining pot, and its two uses are both about testing: the fining pot is for silver and the furnace for gold, but the LORD trieth the hearts, and a man is tried by his praise as silver is tried by the pot.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the crucible is God's method: He does not guess at the heart, He refines it, and what comes out is what was really there.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a Mitsrite, or inhabitant of Mitsrajim
BiblicalUsage: The word is an Egyptian, a man of Egypt, and it runs from the first murder to the last mercy. Moses slew the Egyptian who smote a Hebrew, God promised to deliver His people out of the hand of the Egyptians, and David's men found an Egyptian servant left to die in the field and fed him.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the Egyptian is the reminder that Egypt is not only a nation but a people: God judges the nation and feeds the servant, and the same hand that smote Egypt saved the Egyptian.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, littleness; concretely, diminutive
