BiblicalUsage: The word is littleness, a diminutive, and it appears once, for the little horn: out of one of them came forth a little horn, which waxed exceeding great toward the south and the east and the pleasant land.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the little horn is the warning: the smallest power can grow exceeding great, and the pleasant land must watch for it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a command, whether human or divine (collectively, the Law)
BiblicalUsage: The commandment is the word for God's orders, and it runs through the whole law. God shows mercy to thousands who love Him and keep His commandments, Moses sets the commandments before Israel to teach them, and the psalmist says he shall not be ashamed when he has respect unto all God's commandments.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the commandments are not a burden but a mercy. They show the way, they are given to be taught to the children, and the man who respects them all is the man who is not ashamed.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a bed (as extended) for sleeping or eating; by analogy, a sofa, litter or bier
BiblicalUsage: The word is a bed, a couch, a bier, and it marks the ends of lives and the kindness of strangers. Jacob strengthened himself and sat upon his bed to bless his sons, David followed Abner's bier weeping, and the Shunammite set a bed and a table and a stool and a candlestick for Elisha in the little chamber on the wall.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the bed is where the story turns: the dying bless from it, the dead are carried on it, and the prophet is welcomed to it, and God is present at all three.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: for μυτιλήνη (abounding in shellfish); Mitylene (or Mytilene), a town on the island of Lesbos:--Mitylene.
BiblicalUsage: Mitylene is the town on the island of Lesbos, named once. Paul met his companions at Assos and they sailed on to Mitylene on the way to Jerusalem.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the single mention is enough: the journey to Jerusalem passed through Mitylene, and Luke kept the name because he was there.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: who? (occasionally, by a peculiar idiom, of things); also (indefinitely) whoever; often used in oblique construction with prefix or suffix
BiblicalUsage: The word is 'who?', the question that opens the Bible's great conversations. Who told thee that thou wast naked, God asks in the garden; who am I, Moses asks at the burning bush; and who is this that darkeneth counsel, God asks Job out of the whirlwind.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the question is the doorway: every honest 'who?' leads back to God, who knows the answer before we ask.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Mijamin, the name of three Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Mijamin is the name of three Israelites, all priests of the return. One gave his name to the sixth course of the priests, one is listed among those who had taken strange wives, and one went up with Zerubbabel.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the three men show the priesthood whole: the course, the failure, and the return, and God keeps all three in the record.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Mikael, the name of an archangel and of nine Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Michael is the archangel, the great prince who stands for the children of God's people, and Daniel's visions are where he appears. He came to help the angel who was withstood by the prince of Persia, he alone held with the messenger in the things of the prophecy, and at the time of the end he shall stand up for Daniel's people.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Michael is the proof that the war is real and the help is real: princes of darkness withstand God's messengers, and the chief prince stands for us.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Mica, the name of two Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Micha is the name of two Israelites. The first is the young son of Mephibosheth, kept at David's table with his father, and the second is a Levite whose son Mattaniah oversaw the singers at Jerusalem.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the boy at the table is the point: Mephibosheth's son ate at the king's table because of Jonathan, and grace runs to the children too.
RelatedPeople: Mephibosheth, Son of Jonathan; King David
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Micah, the name of seven Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Micah is the name of seven Israelites, and the three that matter most could hardly differ more. One was the man of Mount Ephraim who made an ephod and teraphim, set up a house of gods, and hired a Levite for his shrine, one was the son of Mephibosheth, and one was the prophet Micah the Morasthite, who prophesied in the days of Hezekiah that Zion would be plowed as a field.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the name is a warning in itself: the same name belongs to a prophet and to an idol-maker, and what matters is not the name but the God served.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Mikehu, a man of Mount Ephraim
BiblicalUsage: Michah is the man of Mount Ephraim who stole his mother's silver and confessed it. He watched her give it to a founder to make a graven image and a molten image for his house.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the story is the whole book of Judges in miniature: a stolen blessing, a mother's gift turned into an idol, and a house that became a shrine to a god of its own making.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Mikal, Saul's daughter
BiblicalUsage: Michal is Saul's daughter, who loved David and became his wife, and her story runs from love to contempt. She warned David of her father's plot and let him down through a window by night, and years later she looked out and saw the king dancing before the ark and despised him in her heart.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Michal's story is the saddest in David's house: she saved his life and lost her own place, and the woman who loved the shepherd came to despise the king.
RelatedPeople: Michal, Daughter of Saul; King David; King Saul
RelatedEvents: David Brings the Ark to Jerusalem
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, a container, i.e. a streamlet
BiblicalUsage: Michal is the brook of water, a streamlet, named once. Absalom's servants came hunting for Ahimaaz and Jonathan, and the woman at the house told them they were gone over the brook of water.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the brook is the hiding place God gave them: a little stream between the runners and the rebels, and the message got through.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Micajah, the name of two Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Three different men answer to this name, and the Bible keeps them apart by their stories. One is the royal official Josiah sends to consult Huldah when the Book of the Law is found, one is the prophet Micah whose words Jeremiah's elders quote a century later, and one is a priest who sounds a trumpet at the dedication of Jerusalem's wall.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the shared name is a small warning against blurring people together: each Micajah stands in his own place, and God deals with each one there.
RelatedEvents: Josiah Finds the Book of the Law; The Dedication of Jerusalem's Wall
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Mikajah, the name of an Israelite and an Israelitess
BiblicalUsage: Michaiah is the name of a queen mother, the daughter of Uriel, and also of a prince Jehoshaphat sends out to teach the law in the cities of Judah. The two bearers could hardly be more different — one stands beside a king, the other carries God's teaching into the towns.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that God uses both stations: a name can sit on a throne and walk a teaching road, and neither place is wasted.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Mikajah, the name of three Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Micaiah son of Imlah is the prophet Ahab hates because he never tells the king what he wants to hear. Summoned to bless a war, he first repeats the court prophets' lie and then speaks the truth plainly: Israel scattered on the hills, without a shepherd. Ahab has him fed on bread and water until he returns in peace — and Micaiah answers that if Ahab returns in peace, the LORD has not spoken by him.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Micaiah is the test of a true prophet: he would rather sit in prison on God's word than stand in the palace on the king's.
RelatedEvents: Micaiah and Ahab's Death at Ramoth-Gilead
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a sort, i.e. species
BiblicalUsage: Min is the word for a kind — the plants and animals God made to reproduce after their own kind, and the clean and unclean birds sorted by theirs. Creation does not blur its edges: each living thing bears seed within itself, after its kind, and the ark takes them in by the same rule, two of every sort.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the kinds tell us God loves order and fruitfulness together. He did not make a shapeless mass; He made families of living things, each able to go on being what He made it to be.
RelatedTopics: Creation; Goodness of Creation; Nature and Creation
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Mishael, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Mishael is one of Daniel's three companions in Babylon, the young man the king's court renames Meshach. In this verse Daniel goes home and tells Mishael, Hananiah and Azariah what the king has demanded, so they can seek mercy from God together before the night is out.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Mishael matters here because he prays with his friends: the wisdom that saves them all comes to men who seek God together, not alone.
RelatedTopics: Faithfulness in exile; Prayer; Friendship with Christ
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Mishael, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Mishael is one of Daniel's three companions in Babylon, the young man the king's court renames Meshach. In this verse Daniel goes home and tells Mishael, Hananiah and Azariah what the king has demanded, so they can seek mercy from God together before the night is out.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Mishael matters here because he prays with his friends: the wisdom that saves them all comes to men who seek God together, not alone.
RelatedTopics: Faithfulness in exile; Prayer; Friendship with Christ
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a level, i.e. a plain (often used (with the article prefix) as a proper name of certain districts); figuratively, concord; also straightness, i.e. (figuratively) justice (sometimes adverbially, justly)
BiblicalUsage: Mishor is a level place, a plain — and in the mouth of the psalmist and the prophet it becomes the road God makes straight. David asks to be led in a plain path because of his enemies, and Isaiah promises the rough places made plain when the LORD comes.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God levels the ground His people must walk: the way is not easy because the world is flat, but because He makes it so.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: pressure
BiblicalUsage: Mits is pressure — the squeezing that brings something out. The proverb stacks three pictures: churning milk brings butter, wringing a nose brings blood, and forcing wrath brings strife.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe pressure always produces something, so I watch what I am pressing.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: fewness; by implication, as superl. diminutiveness
BiblicalUsage: Miz'ar means a little while, a smallness of time. Isaiah uses it for how briefly Moab's glory will last, and for how soon Lebanon will turn into a fruitful field.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God's 'little while' is a mercy and a warning at once: judgment does not linger forever, and neither does the wait for His turning.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an altar
BiblicalUsage: The altar is where Israel meets God — earth or stone, built where He puts His name, with fire that never goes out. Noah and Abraham build them on the road, Moses builds one of acacia wood for the tabernacle, and Elijah repairs the broken one on Carmel before he calls down fire.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the altar is the heart of the whole old covenant: God comes down to a place, and sin is dealt with there, by blood, before anyone draws near. That is why the altar never stands empty for long.
RelatedEvents: The Binding of Isaac; The Tabernacle Is Built; Elijah on Mount Carmel
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, instrumental music; by implication, a poem set to notes
BiblicalUsage: Mizmor is the word in the heading of fifty-seven psalms — 'a psalm', a song set to music. It never appears in the body of a psalm at all; it stands at the door, telling the reader this is a song to be sung, not only read.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the headings matter: God gave His people songs, not just sayings, and singing them is part of how the truth gets into the heart.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a planted field
BiblicalUsage: Mizra is a sown field, a planted strip of ground — here, the fields along the Nile that wither when Egypt is judged. What men planted with care dries up in a day when God withdraws His hand.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word is a quiet warning: our plantings only stand while He waters them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: sunrise, i.e. the east
BiblicalUsage: Mizrach is the sunrise, the east — the direction the sun comes up and the quarter from which God's people look for Him. As far as the east is from the west, so far does He remove our transgressions; from the rising of the sun His name is great among the nations, and He promises to gather His children from the east.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the east is Scripture's picture of distance and of dawn together. Our sins are carried as far as the sun travels, and His mercy rises like the morning.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a bowl (as if for sprinkling)
BiblicalUsage: Mizraq is a bowl for sprinkling — one of the plain, working vessels of the tabernacle and the temple, made to carry blood and offerings to the altar. Princes bring silver bowls at the dedication, and Zechariah sees a day when even the bowls before the altar will be holy to the LORD.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe even the bowls are consecrated: nothing that serves God in His house is common.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a winnowing shovel (as scattering the chaff)
BiblicalUsage: Mizreh is a winnowing shovel, the tool that tosses grain into the wind so the chaff blows away. Isaiah pictures cattle eating winnowed grain in a restored land, and Jeremiah turns the tool into judgment: God will fan His people with a fan at the gates of the land.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the winnowing is honest work — the wind keeps what is solid and carries off what is not.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Mizzah, an Edomite
BiblicalUsage: Mizzah is a son of Reuel, a grandson of Esau, named among the chiefs of Edom. He appears only in the genealogies, twice in Genesis and once in Chronicles, a name carried down so the family line is not lost.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that even a name in a list is remembered by God: Mizzah's place in the record is his whole story, and it is enough.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Latin origin; a mna (i.e. mina), a certain weight:-- pound.
BiblicalUsage: A mna is a mina, a weight of silver and a sum of money — the nobleman in Jesus' parable gives one to each of ten servants with the order to trade until he returns. One turns it into ten, one into five, and one hides his in a cloth and hands it back untouched.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the mina is a test of faithfulness, not of talent: what matters is whether I put what He gave me to work.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: middle voice of a derivative of G3306 or perhaps of the base of G3145 (through the idea of fixture in the mind or of mental grasp); to bear in mind, i.e. recollect; by implication, to reward or punish:--be mindful, remember, come (have) in remembrance. Compare G3403.
BiblicalUsage: Mnaomai means to remember — to call something back to mind. At the altar a worshipper remembers his brother has something against him, and Peter remembers the Lord's word the moment the cock crows. In the Greek text behind the King James Version these forms stand under the verb numbered G3403, which the next study covers; Strong's splits the two numbers, the text does not.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe remembering is the hinge of repentance: Peter's tears begin the instant the word comes back to him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain origin; Mnason, a Christian:--Mnason.
BiblicalUsage: Mnason is an early disciple from Cyprus who opens his house to Paul and his companions on the road to Jerusalem. Luke calls him a disciple of long standing, and his hospitality carries the whole party through the last night before the city.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Mnason's welcome is the gospel in miniature: an old disciple, a door open, and travellers kept safe for one more night.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3415 or G3403; recollection; by implication, recital:--mention, remembrance.
BiblicalUsage: Mneia is mention, remembrance — the word Paul uses when he tells the churches he carries them in his prayers. Without ceasing he makes mention of Rome, he does not cease to give thanks for Ephesus, and every time he remembers Philippi he thanks God.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe prayer that remembers people by name is the plainest love the letters show.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3415; a memorial, i.e. sepulchral monument (burial-place):--grave, sepulchre, tomb.
BiblicalUsage: Mnema is a tomb, a grave — the new tomb where Joseph lays the body of Jesus, the tomb the women find empty on the first day of the week, and the tombs among which the possessed man of Gadara lives.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word gathers the whole gospel into one place: a man living among the dead, and a dead man who leaves His tomb empty.
RelatedEvents: The Burial of Jesus; The Resurrection
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3403; memory:--remembrance.
BiblicalUsage: Mneme is remembrance — Peter's promise that he will take care, even after his death, that his readers will always be able to call these things to mind.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Peter's last care is a pastor's care: truth that stays put after the teacher is gone.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3420; a remembrance, i.e. cenotaph (place of interment):--grave, sepulchre, tomb.
BiblicalUsage: Mnemeion is a tomb, the burial place — the cave where Lazarus lies four days, the garden tomb where Joseph rolls the stone over Jesus, and the tomb Mary finds empty while it is still dark.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe no word is more hopeful in the Gospels: the tombs keep opening, and the dead keep coming out.
RelatedEvents: Raising of Lazarus; The Burial of Jesus; The Resurrection
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a derivative of G3420; to exercise memory, i.e. recollect; by implication, to punish; also to rehearse:--make mention; be mindful, remember.
BiblicalUsage: Mnemoneuo means to remember on purpose. Paul tells Timothy to remember Jesus Christ raised from the dead, Hebrews tells the church to remember the leaders who spoke God's word to them, the risen Lord tells Ephesus to remember where it fell, and Jesus tells His hearers to remember Lot's wife.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe remembering is not nostalgia; it is how faith stays on the road. Forget what God did and who He is, and the next step goes wrong.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3421; a reminder (memorandum), i.e. record:--memorial.
BiblicalUsage: Mnemosynon is a memorial, a reminder kept before God. Cornelius's prayers and alms go up as a memorial before Him, and the woman who pours ointment on Jesus is promised that wherever the gospel is preached, what she did will be told for a memorial of her.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that God keeps memorials. Prayers and quiet acts of love are not forgotten, they are kept before Him like a record.
RelatedEvents: Peter and Cornelius; The Anointing at Bethany
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a derivative of G3415; to give a souvenir (engagement present), i.e. betroth:--espouse.
BiblicalUsage: Mnesteuo means to betroth — to be pledged in marriage. Mary is betrothed to Joseph when she is found with child of the Holy Spirit, and the angel Gabriel is sent to a virgin betrothed to a man named Joseph, of the house of David.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the betrothal is where the whole story turns: God's promise arrives inside an ordinary engagement, and two ordinary people carry it.
RelatedEvents: The Annunciation to Mary; The Angel Appears to Joseph
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a raising (of the hands)
BiblicalUsage: Mo'al is the lifting up of the hands — Ezra blesses the LORD, and all the people answer Amen, Amen, with lifting up their hands, and bow their heads and worship.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe lifted hands are the body's Amen: the whole person agrees with what the mouth has said.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: literally a foothold
BiblicalUsage: Mo'omad is a foothold, a place to stand — and the psalmist cries that he has none: he sinks in deep mire where there is no standing, and the floodwaters are come in over him.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the psalm names the worst kind of trouble honestly: not pain, but nowhere to stand — and it still turns the cry toward God.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {(only in the dual) a pair of scales}
BiblicalUsage: Mozen is a pair of scales — the balances in which Belshazzar is weighed on the night Babylon falls: 'Thou art weighed in the balances, and art found wanting.'
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God still weighs kings and kingdoms, and the scales do not lie.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {(only in the dual) a pair of scales}
BiblicalUsage: Mozen is a pair of scales — the balances in which Belshazzar is weighed on the night Babylon falls: 'Thou art weighed in the balances, and art found wanting.'
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God still weighs kings and kingdoms, and the scales do not lie.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: fat, i.e. marrow
BiblicalUsage: Moach is marrow, the fat richness inside the bones — Job uses it for the wicked man's easy prosperity: his breasts are full of milk, and his bones are moistened with marrow.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the picture is meant to sting: a man can be full of marrow and empty of God.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: admonition
BiblicalUsage: Mosar is instruction, admonition — Elihu says God opens the ears of men in the night and seals their instruction, warning them away from what they plan.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God still speaks in the dark hours: instruction sealed in a dream is still His voice.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: the morrow or (adverbially) tomorrow
BiblicalUsage: Mochorath is the morrow, tomorrow — Lot's daughters act the next day, the LORD strikes Egypt's cattle on the morrow, and a worm eats Jonah's gourd the next morning.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe tomorrow belongs to God in a way today does not: it arrives with His doing, not mine.
RelatedEvents: Destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah; The Ten Plagues
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from the base of G3425; toil, i.e. (by implication) sadness:--painfulness, travail.
BiblicalUsage: Mochthos is toil, hard labour. Paul reminds the Thessalonians that he worked night and day so he would not burden them, and he lists weariness and painfulness among the marks of his apostleship.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Paul's toil is the shape of love that refuses to be a burden. He works with his hands so the gospel comes free.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Latin origin; a modius, i.e. certain measure for things dry (the quantity or the utensil):--bushel.
BiblicalUsage: A modios is a bushel measure, a basket for grain — and Jesus uses it for a lamp: no one lights a candle and puts it under a bushel, but on a candlestick, so it gives light to all in the house.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the bushel is a warning against hidden faith: light is given to be set out, not stored.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3425 and G2980; hardly talking, i.e. dumb (tongue-tied):--having an impediment in his speech.
BiblicalUsage: Mogilalos means speaking with difficulty, tongue-tied — the deaf man they bring to Jesus, who has an impediment in his speech, and whom Jesus heals with a touch and a word.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the healing is the whole gospel in one touch: the man who could hardly speak is given a tongue, and the first thing he does with it is speak plainly.
RelatedEvents: Jesus Heals a Deaf and Mute Man in the Decapolis
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: adverb from a primary μόγος (toil); with difficulty:--hardly.
BiblicalUsage: Mogis means hardly, with difficulty — the spirit that seizes the boy 'hardly departeth from him', bruising him as it leaves.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word is honest about deliverance: some bondage leaves hard, and still it leaves.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a price (for a wife)
BiblicalUsage: Mohar is the bride-price, the payment a man offers for a wife — Shechem names any dowry for Dinah, the law sets the price when a maid is not given in marriage, and Saul asks a hundred foreskins of the Philistines for Michal.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the price shows how seriously marriage was weighed: a wife was not taken lightly, and the cost said so.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: the simpler form of G1698; to me:--I, me, mine, my.
BiblicalUsage: Moi is the plain word for 'to me', the unaccented form of the pronoun — Herod says 'bring me word again', and Jesus says not everyone who says to me 'Lord, Lord' will enter the kingdom.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the little word carries the whole question of the Gospels: what is said to me, and what is done about it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a prolonged form of the feminine of G3432; an adulteress (literally or figuratively):--adulteress(-ous, -y).
BiblicalUsage: Moichalis is an adulteress — and Jesus turns the word on His own generation: an evil and adulterous generation seeks a sign. James goes further and calls worldly believers adulterers and adulteresses, friends of the world and enemies of God, while Paul uses the married woman to teach how death ends a bond.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word is meant to hurt. Unfaithfulness to God is not a mistake, it is adultery, and naming it plainly is the first step back.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3432; (middle voice) to commit adultery:--commit adultery.
BiblicalUsage: Moichao is the middle-voice form of committing adultery — whoever puts away his wife and marries another commits adultery, and so does the man who marries her that is put away. In the Greek text these middle forms stand under the lemma μοιχάομαι, spelled differently from this study's headword.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Jesus draws the line where the heart draws it: adultery is not only the act, it is the breaking of the bond.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3431; adultery:--adultery.
BiblicalUsage: Moicheia is adultery itself, named among the evils that come out of the heart — out of the heart proceed evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, fornications, thefts. Jesus puts it in the list of what defiles a man, not what goes into him.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the list is the diagnosis: the heart is where adultery starts, long before the bed.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3432; to commit adultery:--commit adultery.
BiblicalUsage: Moicheuo is to commit adultery, and Jesus takes the commandment deeper than the act: whoever looks on a woman to lust after her has committed adultery with her already in his heart. The command stands in the law, in the Sermon on the Mount, and in Paul's summary of the whole law in love.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Jesus does not relax the commandment, He presses it home. The law reaches the eyes and the heart, and that is exactly where I need grace.
RelatedEvents: The Sermon on the Mount; The Ten Commandments
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: perhaps a primary word; a (male) paramour; figuratively, apostate:--adulterer.
BiblicalUsage: Moichos is an adulterer. Paul lists adulterers among those who will not inherit the kingdom of God, Hebrews says marriage is honourable and God will judge adulterers, and the Pharisee in the temple thanks God he is not like other men, extortioners, unjust, adulterers.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word stands as a boundary stone. God honours marriage, and He judges what breaks it, and the Pharisee's prayer shows I can be guilty of the same pride while naming the sin in others.
RelatedEvents: The Pharisee and the Tax Collector
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Molek (i.e. king), the chief deity of the Ammonites
BiblicalUsage: Molek is the god of the Ammonites, the idol to whom children were passed through the fire — and the law forbids it in the plainest words, on pain of death. Solomon, in his old age, builds Molek a high place east of Jerusalem for his foreign wives, and the kingdom pays for it.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Molek is the worst of idolatry because it takes the most precious thing — children — and calls it worship.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Moleketh, an Israelitess
BiblicalUsage: Moleketh is a daughter of Machir, named once in the genealogy of Manasseh, beside her brothers Gilead and Peresh. Her name appears nowhere else in Scripture.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that a single line in a genealogy is still a place in God's record: Moleketh is remembered, and that is her story.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably by variation for G3425; with difficulty:--hardly, scarce(-ly), + with much work.
BiblicalUsage: Molis means hardly, scarcely, with difficulty — the crowd at Lystra is hardly restrained from sacrificing to Paul and Barnabas, the ship sails slowly and with difficulty toward Cnidus, and Paul says scarcely for a righteous man will one die.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word keeps me honest about how hard things are: hardly restrained, hardly sailing, hardly dying for another — and grace does it anyway.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H4432); Moloch (i.e. Molek), an idol:--Moloch.
BiblicalUsage: Moloch is the Greek form of Molek, and Stephen throws it in the Sanhedrin's face. Their fathers carried the tabernacle of Moloch and the star of their god Remphan, and God carried them away beyond Babylon.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Stephen names the old idolatry because it never died: the same worship that followed Israel into the wilderness was still standing in the room.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from μῶλος ("moil"; probably akin to the base of G3433) and probably ὤψ (the face; from G3700); a mole ("black eye") or blow-mark:--stripe.
BiblicalUsage: Molops is a bruise, a weal, the mark of a blow — Peter says Christ bore our sins in His own body on the tree, that we should live unto righteousness, by whose stripes ye were healed.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the bruise is the price written on His body: healing comes through wounds, not around them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably from G3189; to soil (figuratively):--defile.
BiblicalUsage: Molyno means to defile, to soil. A weak conscience is defiled by eating food offered to idols, and yet Sardis has a few names who have not defiled their garments, and the redeemed are those who were not defiled with women.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe defilement is a matter of the conscience and the garment both. What touches me leaves a mark, and keeping clean takes watching.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3435; a stain; i.e. (figuratively) immorality:--filthiness.
BiblicalUsage: Molysmos is filthiness, a stain — Paul tells the Corinthians to cleanse themselves from all filthiness of the flesh and spirit, perfecting holiness in the fear of God.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the cleansing is a work I am told to do: God gives the promises, and I wash.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3470; to carp at, i.e. censure (discredit):--blame.
BiblicalUsage: Momaomai means to find fault, to blame — Paul gives no offence in anything, that the ministry be not blamed, and he takes care with the collection so no one can blame him over the money.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the care is part of the ministry: a blameless life keeps the gospel from being blamed.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: perhaps from G3201; a flaw or blot, i.e. (figuratively) disgraceful person:--blemish.
BiblicalUsage: Momos is a blemish, a blot — Peter calls the false teachers spots and blemishes, revelling in their own deceivings while they feast with the church.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the blot is the tell: what looks like fellowship but feeds itself is a stain on the table.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3201; blame, i.e. (by implication), a fault:--quarrel.
BiblicalUsage: Momphe is a quarrel, a complaint — Paul tells the Colossians to forbear one another and forgive one another, if any man have a quarrel against any.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the quarrel is the test of forgiveness: it is easy to forgive no one in particular, and hard to forgive the one with a name.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3306; a staying, i.e. residence (the act or the place):--abode, mansion.
BiblicalUsage: Mone is an abode, a dwelling place — in My Father's house are many mansions, Jesus says on the night before the cross, and He promises that He and the Father will come and make their abode with the one who loves Him and keeps His word.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the promise runs both ways: there is a room for me in His house, and a home for Him in mine.
RelatedTopics: Heaven; Presence of God; Love for God
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, something weighed out, i.e. (figuratively) a portion of time, i.e. an instance
BiblicalUsage: Moneh is a reckoning, a portion of time — Jacob tells Laban he changed his wages ten times, and counts the years: fourteen years for his two daughters, six years for his cattle, and twenty years in his house.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Jacob's counting is the patience of a man who was cheated and kept working: God kept the account, even when Laban did not.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3441 and G1096; only-born, i.e. sole:--only (begotten, child).
BiblicalUsage: Monogenes means only-begotten, the only one of its kind — John says the Word became flesh and we beheld His glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father, and no man has seen God, but the only begotten Son has declared Him. God so loved the world that He gave His only begotten Son, and Abraham offered up Isaac, his only begotten son.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this is the deepest word about Jesus in the whole New Testament. He is not one son among many, He is the only one, and the giving of Him is the measure of God's love.
RelatedTopics: Son of God; Love of God; Faith
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: neuter of G3441 as adverb; merely:--alone, but, only.
BiblicalUsage: Monon means only, merely, alone — whoever gives one of these little ones a cup of cold water only, in the name of a disciple, shall not lose his reward, and to the Philippians it is given not only to believe on Christ but also to suffer for His sake.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the small word guards the big promises: a cup of water counts, and suffering counts, and neither is lost.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3441; to isolate, i.e. bereave:--be desolate.
BiblicalUsage: Monoo means to leave desolate, to bereave — Paul's true widow is the woman left alone, desolate, who trusts in God and continues in supplications and prayers night and day. In the Greek text the form stands under the lemma μονόομαι, spelled differently from this study's headword.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the desolate widow is the church's charge precisely because she has no one else: God counts her prayers as her standing.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3441 and G3788; one-eyed:--with one eye.
BiblicalUsage: Monophthalmos means one-eyed — Jesus says it is better to enter into life with one eye than to be cast into hell fire with two.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the hard saying is a mercy in disguise: whatever costs me the kingdom is not worth keeping, even if it is my own eye.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably from G3306; remaining, i.e. sole or single; by implication, mere:--alone, only, by themselves.
BiblicalUsage: Monos means alone, only, single — this is life eternal, to know the only true God, and man shall not live by bread alone, and to the only wise God our Saviour be glory and majesty.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word draws a circle round God alone: only He is God, only His word feeds, only His glory lasts.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Moph, the capital of Lower Egypt
BiblicalUsage: Moph is Memphis, the capital of Lower Egypt, named as the place where the fugitives of Israel will be buried. Egypt shall gather them up, Memphis shall bury them.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the place-name is a judgment in one word: the people who ran to Egypt for safety will find only graves there.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: myrrh (as distilling in drops, and also as bitter)
BiblicalUsage: Mor is myrrh, the bitter, fragrant resin — the chief spice of the holy anointing oil, the bundle the beloved carries between her breasts, and the perfume on the garments of the king.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe myrrh is the scent of both worship and burial: it anoints the tabernacle and it will anoint the body, and love carries it close.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: bitterness, i.e. (figuratively) trouble
BiblicalUsage: Morah is bitterness, trouble of mind — Esau's Hittite wives were a grief of mind unto Isaac and to Rebekah.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the verse is a plain warning: a marriage outside God's way does not stay private, it grieves the whole house.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3474; to become insipid; figuratively, to make (passively, act) as a simpleton:--become fool, make foolish, lose savour.
BiblicalUsage: Moraino means to become insipid, to lose savour. Salt that has lost its savour is good for nothing but to be cast out, and Paul says God has made foolish the wisdom of this world, while men professing themselves wise became fools.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word cuts both ways. Salt can go flat, and wisdom can go foolish, and in both cases the loss is the loss of what the thing was for.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Mordecai, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Mordecai is the Jew of the captivity who raises his cousin Esther and uncovers the plot against the king. He ends the book second to the king himself, seeking the wealth of his people and speaking peace to all his seed.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Mordecai is the quiet man of the whole story: he does the faithful thing in the shadows, and God turns it into the saving of a nation.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: softness, i.e. (figuratively) fear
BiblicalUsage: Morek is softness, faintness of heart — God warns that He will send a faintness into the hearts of those left in the land of their enemies, and the sound of a shaken leaf shall chase them.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the faint heart is its own punishment: guilt makes a leaf sound like an army.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3474; silliness, i.e. absurdity:--foolishness.
BiblicalUsage: Moria is foolishness. The preaching of the cross is foolishness to them that perish, the world by wisdom knew not God, and the natural man cannot receive the things of the Spirit of God, for they are foolishness unto him.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the foolishness of God is wiser than men. The cross looks weak and it saves, and the world's wisdom looks strong and it misses God entirely.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a compound of G3474 and G3004; silly talk, i.e. buffoonery:--foolish talking.
BiblicalUsage: Morologia is foolish talking, silly talk — Paul puts it beside filthiness and jesting, and says none of these things should be named among saints, but rather giving of thanks.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the verse sets the standard plainly: the mouth of a saint is for thanksgiving, not for talk that cheapens everything it touches.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably from the base of G3466; dull or stupid (as if shut up), i.e. heedless, (morally) blockhead, (apparently) absurd:--fool(-ish, X -ishness).
BiblicalUsage: Moros means foolish, dull, heedless — Jesus calls the man who hears His sayings and does them not a foolish man who builds on sand, and five of the virgins are foolish because they take no oil. Whoever calls his brother a fool is in danger of hell fire, and the foolishness of God is wiser than men.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the fool in Scripture is not the man who lacks brains but the man who hears and does not do. Hearing without doing is the whole definition.
RelatedEvents: The Sermon on the Mount; The Wise and Foolish Builders; The Wise and Foolish Virgins
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: perhaps from the base of G3313 (through the idea of adjustment of parts); shape; figuratively, nature:--form.
BiblicalUsage: Morphe is form, the outward shape that shows what a thing truly is. Christ, being in the form of God, thought it not robbery to be equal with God, but took upon Him the form of a servant, and after the resurrection He appeared in another form to two disciples on the road.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word guards the mystery. He did not cease to be God when He took the servant's form, and He did not cease to be the servant when He rose.
RelatedTopics: Christology; Hypostatic Union; Son of God
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from the same as G3444; to fashion (figuratively):--form.
BiblicalUsage: Morphoo means to form, to shape — Paul travails in birth again for the Galatians until Christ be formed in them.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the forming is slow, painful work, like birth: Christ takes shape in a person the way a child takes shape, over time and not without labour.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3445; formation, i.e. (by implication), appearance (semblance or (concretely) formula):--form.
BiblicalUsage: Morphosis is the form, the outward appearance — the Jew has the form of knowledge and of truth in the law, and in the last days men will have a form of godliness but deny its power.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the form without the power is the oldest counterfeit: it looks right and does nothing.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: trouble
BiblicalUsage: Morrah is bitterness, trouble of heart — the heart knows its own bitterness, and a stranger does not intermeddle with its joy.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the proverb respects the privacy of sorrow: no one else can fully know what my heart carries, and God knows it all.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3448 and G4160; to fabricate the image of a bullock:--make a calf.
BiblicalUsage: Moschopoieo means to make a calf — in those days they made a calf, and offered sacrifice to the idol, and rejoiced in the works of their own hands.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Stephen's charge still lands: the calf was not made by accident, it was made on purpose, and men rejoice in what their own hands made.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably strengthened for όσχος (a shoot); a young bullock:--calf.
BiblicalUsage: Moschos is a young calf — the father kills the fatted calf for the son who was dead and is alive again, and the blood of calves and goats could never take away sins, but Christ entered once into the holy place with His own blood.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the calf carries both stories: the feast of a father who forgives, and the blood that could never finish the work.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: or Μωσῆς, or Μωϋσῆς of Hebrew origin; (H4872); Moseus, Moses, or Mouses (i.e. Mosheh), the Hebrew lawgiver:--Moses.
BiblicalUsage: Moses is the lawgiver, and the Gospels never let him go: he appears with Elijah on the mount of transfiguration, the law came by Moses and grace and truth by Jesus Christ, and by faith Moses refused to be called the son of Pharaoh's daughter. In the Greek text these forms stand under the lemma Μωϋσῆς, spelled differently from this study's headword.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Moses matters because the law came by him and the story does not end with him: he stands on the mountain to see the One the law was pointing to all along.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {Mosheh, the Israelite lawgiver}
BiblicalUsage: Mosheh is the Aramaic form of Moses' name, used in the decree that sets the priests in their divisions and the Levites in their courses, as it is written in the book of Moses. The Aramaic spelling is the exile's spelling, carried home with the people.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that even the spelling carries the story: the lawgiver's name sounds in Aramaic now, because the people have come home from exile speaking it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: {Mosheh, the Israelite lawgiver}
BiblicalUsage: Mosheh is the Aramaic form of Moses' name, used in the decree that sets the priests in their divisions and the Levites in their courses, as it is written in the book of Moses. The Aramaic spelling is the exile's spelling, carried home with the people.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that even the spelling carries the story: the lawgiver's name sounds in Aramaic now, because the people have come home from exile speaking it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: empire; a parallel
BiblicalUsage: Moshel is an empire, a dominion — or a parallel, a thing made like another. Alexander's kingdom is broken and divided toward the four winds, leviathan has no equal made without fear, and the Messiah's dominion will reach from sea to sea.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word holds the two ends of power: empires that break apart, and a dominion that does not.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, the waist or small of the back; only in plural the loins
BiblicalUsage: Mothen is the loins, the waist — Israel eats the Passover with loins girded, shoes on feet and staff in hand, righteousness is the girdle of the Messiah's loins, and Elijah girds up his loins and runs before Ahab to Jezreel.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe girded loins are the Bible's picture of readiness: truth round the waist, and feet ready to move when God says go.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: sweetness
BiblicalUsage: Motheq is sweetness — the fig tree asks, should I forsake my sweetness and my good fruit, and go to be promoted over the trees?
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the fig tree answers for every gift that refuses to be misused: sweetness is for bearing fruit, not for ruling.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: chaff (as pressed out, i.e. winnowed or (rather) threshed loose)
BiblicalUsage: Mots is chaff, the husk the wind drives away. The ungodly are not so, but are like the chaff which the wind driveth away, the nations are chased like chaff before the wind, and Ephraim will be as the morning cloud and the chaff that is driven with the whirlwind.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe chaff is the Bible's picture of a life with no weight. It looks like grain until the wind comes, and then it is gone.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Motsah, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Motsah is a town in the lot of Benjamin, named among the cities given to the tribe when the land is divided. The town is counted among Benjamin's cities, and the counting is the record.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the town-names in the division are promises kept in detail: God does not give the land in general, He gives it town by town.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: the simpler form of G1700; of me:--I, me, mine (own), my.
BiblicalUsage: Mou is the plain word for 'my', the unaccented genitive of the pronoun — out of Bethlehem shall come a Governor that shall rule my people Israel, and on this rock I will build my church.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the little word is the claim of the whole gospel: His people, His church — mine because He says so.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from Μοῦσα (a Muse); "musical", i.e. (as noun) a minstrel:--musician.
BiblicalUsage: Mousikos is a musician — in fallen Babylon the voice of harpers and musicians and pipers and trumpeters shall be heard no more at all in her.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the silence is part of the judgment: when a city that lived for pleasure falls, the music is the first thing to stop.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Moab, an incestuous son of Lot; also his territory and descendants
BiblicalUsage: Moab is the son of Lot by his elder daughter, and the father of a nation that stands against Israel for a thousand years. Balak hires Balaam to curse them, and yet Ruth the Moabitess comes home with Naomi out of the country of Moab, and into the line of David.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Moab is the proof that no nation is written off: the enemy's daughter becomes the great-grandmother of the king.
RelatedEvents: Ruth's Loyalty; Destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a Moabite or Moabitess, i.e. a descendant from Moab
BiblicalUsage: Moabi means a Moabite, one of Moab — Ruth the Moabitess marries into the family, gleans in the field of Boaz, and the law says a Moabite shall not enter into the congregation of the LORD, even to the tenth generation.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the tension is the point: the law shuts the door, and grace walks Ruth straight through it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, an assembly figuratively, a troop
BiblicalUsage: Moad is an appointed time, a fixed season — howl, O gate, cry, O city, for there shall come from the north a smoke, and none shall be alone in his appointed times, when the muster is called.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the appointed times belong to God: He calls the muster, and no one stands alone in it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Moadjah, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Moadjah is a priest, the head of a father's house in the days of Joiakim, named in the list of those who serve when the wall is dedicated. His house stands in its course among the priests who return.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the priests in the lists are the quiet backbone of the return: named, counted, and standing in their course.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, an appointment, i.e. a fixed time or season; specifically, a festival; conventionally a year; by implication, an assembly (as convened for a definite purpose); technically the congregation; by extension, the place of meeting; also a signal (as appointed beforehand)
BiblicalUsage: Moed is an appointed time, a season, a feast. God sets lights in the firmament for signs and for seasons, He appoints the feasts of the LORD, the lamp burns before Him from evening to morning, and Israel keeps the Passover at its appointed season.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the appointed times are God's calendar, not man's. He fixes the meetings, and His people keep them.
RelatedEvents: Creation; The Tabernacle Is Built; The Passover
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a purpose
BiblicalUsage: Moetsah is counsel, purpose, a plan. Men eat the fruit of their own counsel, the king's excellent counsellors write truth, and Israel walks in the counsels of Omri and the works of Ahab's house.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe counsel decides a life. Good counsel leads to life, and the wrong counsel is a road to ruin that still feels like a plan.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an entrance
BiblicalUsage: Moba is an entrance, a coming in — Abner came to deceive, to know thy going out and thy coming in, and the prophet is told to show the house to Israel, its going out and its coming in, that they may be ashamed.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God watches the doorways: He knows my going out and my coming in, and the shame of it is meant to turn me back.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a foundation
BiblicalUsage: Mosad is a foundation — when God appointed the foundations of the earth, wisdom was there, and the psalmist says all the foundations of the earth are out of course when justice fails.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the foundations are moral before they are stone: when justice goes, the earth itself goes out of course.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a foundation
BiblicalUsage: Mosadah is a foundation. The foundations of the earth should have taught men God's ways from the beginning; the foundations of the hills move and tremble at His anger, and the strong foundations of the earth hear the LORD's controversy with His people.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the foundations of the earth are God's own work. They move when He is angry, and they stand to hear His case.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, chastisement, i.e. (by implication) a halter; figuratively, restraint
BiblicalUsage: Moser is a band, a bond, a restraint — the kings say, let us break their bands asunder and cast away their cords, and God answers that He will break the yoke from Jacob's neck and burst his bonds.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the bands men hate are the very ones God breaks: His yoke is not the one that chokes, it is the one that frees.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Moserah or Moseroth, a place in the Desert
BiblicalUsage: Moserah is a camp in the wilderness where Aaron dies and is buried. From the wells of the children of Jaakan they journeyed to Moserah, and there Aaron died, and there he was buried.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the camps are remembered by their griefs as much as by their miles: Moserah is where Israel buried its priest and walked on.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: acquaintance
BiblicalUsage: Modaath is a kinswoman, an acquaintance of the family — is not Boaz of our kindred, Naomi asks Ruth, with whose maidens thou wast?
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the kinswoman's question opens the whole redemption: a relative is near, and nearness is what saves.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an acquaintance
BiblicalUsage: Moda is a kinsman, an acquaintance — Boaz is a mighty man of wealth, of the family of Elimelech, and wisdom says, call understanding thy kinswoman.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the kinsman is the Bible's picture of the redeemer: near enough to help, and willing to pay.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Moladah, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Moladah is a town in the south of Judah, given first to Judah, then to Simeon within Judah's lot, and settled again after the exile. The town outlasts every division that moves it from tribe to tribe.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that a town held through three divisions is a promise that survives exile: given, kept, and settled again.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: nativity (plural birth-place); by implication, lineage, native country; also offspring, family
BiblicalUsage: Moledeth is kindred, native country, the family and land a person comes from. Get thee out of thy country, and from thy kindred, God says to Abram, and Abraham sends his servant back to his country and his kindred for a wife for Isaac, and Ruth leaves her own land and kindred for Naomi's God.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe leaving kindred is the first act of faith in the Bible. God calls Abram out of everything he knows, and the blessing follows the leaving.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Molid, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Molid is a son of Abishur, named once in the genealogy of Judah, in the line of Jerahmeel. One line carries his whole story.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that one line is enough: Molid is counted in the tribe, and the counting is the honour.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Mophaath or Mephaath, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Mophaath is a city of the plain given to the Levites. It is named again when Jeremiah pronounces judgment on Moab.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the city carries both stories at once: a home for priests, and a witness against the nation that would not listen.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a miracle; by implication, a token or omen
BiblicalUsage: Mopheth is a wonder, a sign, a token. God multiplies His signs and wonders in Egypt, Aaron's rod becomes a serpent before Pharaoh, and Joel promises wonders in the heavens and in the earth, blood and fire and pillars of smoke.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe wonders are God's signature. He does not argue His power in the abstract, He shows it, and the showing is the proof.
RelatedEvents: The Ten Plagues; Moses and Aaron Confront Pharaoh
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a fire or fuel; abstractly, a conflagration
BiblicalUsage: Moqed is a burning, a hearth, a fire that does not go out — who among us shall dwell with the devouring fire, Isaiah asks, and the psalmist says my bones are burned as an hearth.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the fire is both judgment and presence: the same flame that burns the bones is the fire of the God who dwells with His people.
RelatedTopics: Judgment; God's Holiness; Fear of God
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: fuel
BiblicalUsage: Moqdah is the hearth, the place of burning — the burnt offering shall be on the hearth upon the altar all night unto the morning, and the fire of the altar shall be burning in it.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the all-night fire is the picture of a sacrifice that never stops: the altar burns while Israel sleeps.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a noose (for catching animals) (literally or figuratively); by implication, a hook (for the nose)
BiblicalUsage: Moqesh is a snare, a trap. The gods of the nations will be a snare to you, the peoples left in the land will be thorns and snares, the fear of man brings a snare, and the psalmist prays to be kept from the snares of the workers of iniquity.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the snare is the Bible's plainest warning about compromise. What looks like a neighbour becomes a trap, and what looks like fear becomes a chain.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: fear; by implication, a fearful thing or deed
BiblicalUsage: Mora is fear, dread, a fearful thing. The fear and dread of man falls on every beast, God redeems Israel with a mighty hand and great terrors, Isaiah says sanctify the LORD and let Him be your fear, and Levi's covenant was life and peace, and he feared God and was afraid before His name.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe there are two fears and they are opposites. The fear of man is a snare, and the fear of God is the beginning of freedom.
RelatedTopics: Fear of God; Fear of the Lord; God's Power
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a descent; as architecture, an ornamental appendage, perhaps a festoon
BiblicalUsage: Morad is a descent, a going down — the Amorites flee down the descent of Beth-horon under hailstones from heaven, the men of Ai chase Israel down the same kind of slope, and the mountains melt beneath the LORD like wax.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the descents are where battles are decided: going down is easy, and God meets His people on the slope.
RelatedTopics: Victory; God Fights for Us; Judgment
RelatedEvents: The Sun Stands Still at Gibeon
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a threshing sledge
BiblicalUsage: Morag is a threshing sledge, a board studded with teeth that grinds the grain — God makes His servant a new sharp threshing instrument to thresh the mountains, and Araunah offers his threshing instruments as wood for David's burnt offering.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the sledge is the servant's calling in miniature: made sharp by God, and used to thresh what stands against Him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a razor
BiblicalUsage: Morah is a razor — no razor shall come on the child's head, for he shall be a Nazarite unto God from the womb, Samson tells Delilah, and Hannah vows the same over the son she has not yet borne.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the uncut hair is the sign of a life set apart: the razor stays away because the child belongs to God from the first day.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a possession; figuratively, delight
BiblicalUsage: Morash is a possession, a heritage. Babylon will be a possession for the bittern and pools of water, Job's purposes are broken off and the thoughts of his heart are his possession no more, and on Mount Zion there shall be deliverance, and the house of Jacob shall possess their possessions.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe possession runs both ways in Scripture. God gives a heritage, and He takes one away, and the difference is faithfulness.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a possession
BiblicalUsage: Morashah is a heritage, a possession given by covenant. I will bring you into the land and give it you for a heritage, Moses' law is the inheritance of the congregation of Jacob, and the ancient high places are become ours in possession, the enemy says, before God answers.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a heritage is not earned but given. The land is God's gift, the law is God's gift, and the gift is the proof of the covenant.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a Morashtite or inhabitant of Moresheth-Gath
BiblicalUsage: Morashti means a Morashtite, one from Moresheth — Micah the Morasthite is the prophet whose words Jeremiah's elders quote, and Micah's own book opens with the word of the LORD that came to Micah the Morasthite.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the hometown tag is a mark of the prophet's humility: he is named by his village, and his words outlive empires.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: obstinate, i.e. independent
BiblicalUsage: Morat is a word for what is polished, stripped bare, smooth — the messengers go to a nation scattered and peeled, a people terrible from their beginning, a nation meted out and trodden down.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the stripping is the judgment itself: a nation polished bare has nothing left to hide behind.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Moreh, a Canaanite; also a hill (perhaps named from him)
BiblicalUsage: Moreh is the name of the oak and the hill where Abram first stops in Canaan. Abram passes through the land to the place of Sichem, to the plain of Moreh, and the hill of Moreh watches over Gideon's camp by the spring of Harod.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Moreh marks the first footprint of faith in the land: Abram stands under its oak, and the promise is spoken there.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an archer; also teacher or teaching; also the early rain
BiblicalUsage: Moreh is the early rain, the teacher — God gives the former rain moderately and the latter rain in the first month, and the psalmist says the rain fills the pools for pilgrims passing through the valley of Baca. The same word elsewhere names a teacher, and an archer.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the rain and the teacher are one picture: God sends both in season, and both make the dry ground live.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Moresheth-Gath, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Moresheth-Gath is the prophet Micah's hometown, named in his lament over the cities of Judah. Thou shalt give presents to Moresheth-Gath, for the houses of Achzib shall be a lie to the kings of Israel.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the prophet names his own town first in the judgment: the word of God begins at home.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Morijah, a hill in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Morijah is the land where Abraham is told to offer Isaac, and the mountain where Solomon builds the temple. The place of the offering becomes the place of the house, and the mountain remembers both.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Moriah is the most hopeful ground in the Bible: where Abraham lifts the knife, God provides the lamb, and where the temple stands, God dwells.
RelatedEvents: The Binding of Isaac; Building of Solomon's Temple
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: deliverance
BiblicalUsage: Moshaah is deliverance, a going forth — blessed be the Lord, who daily loadeth us with benefits, the God of our salvation, and unto GOD the Lord belong the issues from death.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the deliverances are daily, not once: He loads us with benefits every morning, and death itself has its issues in His hand.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a seat; figuratively, a site; abstractly, a session; by extension an abode (the place or the time); by implication, population
BiblicalUsage: Moshav is a dwelling, a seat, a place where people sit and live. Blessed is the man that walketh not in the counsel of the ungodly, nor sitteth in the seat of the scornful, and the sojourning of Israel in Egypt is four hundred and thirty years, and the Sabbath is a holy convocation in all your dwellings.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe where I sit decides who I become. The seat of the scornful and the house of God are both dwellings, and I choose my seat every day.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: something drawing, i.e. (figuratively) a cord
BiblicalUsage: Moshkah is a cord, a drawing band — canst thou bind the sweet influences of Pleiades, or loose the bands of Orion, God asks Job from the whirlwind.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the question puts me in my place: the stars are bound by cords I cannot touch, and the God who tied them is the God I answer to.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a wavering, i.e. fall; by implication, a pole (as shaking); hence, a yoke (as essentially a bent pole)
BiblicalUsage: Mot is a pole, a staff, a thing that shakes — the spies carry the cluster of grapes on a pole between two men, and the psalmist says He will not suffer thy foot to be moved, and He holds our soul in life and suffers not our feet to be moved.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the pole and the promise belong together: what men carry shakes, and what God holds does not move.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a wavering, i.e. fall; by implication, a pole (as shaking); hence, a yoke (as essentially a bent pole)
BiblicalUsage: Mot is a pole, a staff, a thing that shakes — the spies carry the cluster of grapes on a pole between two men, and the psalmist says He will not suffer thy foot to be moved, and He holds our soul in life and suffers not our feet to be moved.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the pole and the promise belong together: what men carry shakes, and what God holds does not move.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a pole; by implication, an ox-bow; hence, a yoke (either literal or figurative)
BiblicalUsage: Motah is a yoke, the bar across the oxen's neck — I have broken the bands of your yoke, God says, and made you go upright, and the fast He chooses looses the bands of wickedness and undoes the heavy burdens, and Hananiah breaks the yoke from Jeremiah's neck.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the yoke is the picture of everything that bows a person down: God breaks it, and the false prophet breaks the sign of it, and the difference is everything.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: death
BiblicalUsage: Moth is death, in Aramaic — the king's decree says whoever will not do the law of God and the law of the king, let judgment be executed speedily upon him, whether it be unto death, or to banishment, or to confiscation of goods, or to imprisonment.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the decree shows how seriously the return was guarded: the law was not advice, and death stood at the edge of disobedience.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: literally gain; figuratively, superiority
BiblicalUsage: Mothar is gain, profit, the advantage — man has no preeminence above a beast, for all is vanity, and in all labour there is profit, but the talk of the lips tendeth only to penury, and the thoughts of the diligent tend only to plenteousness.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word is the Preacher's question to every worker: what do you actually gain, and is it worth the labour?
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a family descent; also a sewer
BiblicalUsage: Motsah is a going forth, an origin — out of Bethlehem Ephratah shall He come forth unto Me that is to be ruler in Israel, whose goings forth have been from of old, from everlasting, and the house of Baal is broken down and made a draught house unto this day.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the goings forth are the point: the ruler's origin is from everlasting, and that is how you know Him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Motsa, the name of two Israelites
