BiblicalUsage: Motsa is the name of two Israelites. One is a son of Zimri in the line of Saul, and the other is a son of Caleb's concubine Ephah, and both are carried in the genealogies so their families are counted.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that two men sharing one name, both counted, is the record's honesty: the lines are kept straight even when the names repeat.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Motsa, the name of two Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Motsa is the name of two Israelites. One is a son of Zimri in the line of Saul, and the other is a son of Caleb's concubine Ephah, and both are carried in the genealogies so their families are counted.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that two men sharing one name, both counted, is the record's honesty: the lines are kept straight even when the names repeat.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Muppim, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Muppim is a son of Benjamin, named among the sons who go down into Egypt with Jacob. The whole house, seventy souls, is carried into the land of their sojourning.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Muppim's one line is the promise in seed form: a family goes down into Egypt, and a nation will come up out of it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: something conspicuous, i.e. the craw of a bird (from its prominence)
BiblicalUsage: Mur'ah is the crop of a bird, the craw — the priest takes away the crop of the burnt offering with its feathers, and casts it beside the altar on the east, by the place of the ashes.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the detail is the point: even the crop is taken away, and nothing of the offering is left unhandled by the priest.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: persecuted
BiblicalUsage: Murdaph is persecuted, pursued — he who smote the people in wrath with a continual stroke, he that ruled the nations in anger, is persecuted, and none hindereth.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the reversal is complete: the persecutor becomes the persecuted, and no one lifts a hand to stop it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a station, i.e. military post
BiblicalUsage: Mutstsab is a station, a post — I will camp against thee round about, and will lay siege against thee with a mount, and I will raise forts against thee.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the siege is the picture of judgment that does not rush: it camps, it posts, and it waits until the city falls.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: expansion
BiblicalUsage: Muttah is an expansion, a spreading out — the stretching out of his wings shall fill the breadth of thy land, O Immanuel, as the flood of Assyria sweeps through Judah.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the spreading wings are both threat and promise: the enemy spreads, and Immanuel's land still stands.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a stretching, i.e. distortion (figuratively, iniquity)
BiblicalUsage: Mutteh is a stretching out, a distortion — the iniquity of the house of Israel and Judah is exceeding great, and the land is full of blood, and the city full of perverseness.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the stretched-out sin is the measure of the judgment: what is bent far enough breaks.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an appointed place, i.e. asylum
BiblicalUsage: Muadah is an appointed place, a city of refuge — these were the cities appointed for all the children of Israel, and for the stranger that sojourneth among them, that whosoever killeth any person at unawares might flee thither.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the appointed cities are the mercy built into the law: a place to run, before the avenger catches up.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, covered, i.e. dark; abstractly, obscurity, i.e. distress
BiblicalUsage: Muaph is darkness, obscurity, gloom — nevertheless the dimness shall not be such as was in her vexation, when at the first He lightly afflicted the land of Zebulun and Naphtali, and afterward did more grievously afflict her.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the gloom is not the last word: the verse opens with 'nevertheless', and the light is coming behind it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: pressure, i.e. (figuratively) distress
BiblicalUsage: Muaqah is pressure, distress — Thou broughtest us into the net, the psalmist says, Thou laidst affliction upon our loins.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the pressure is named as God's own doing: He brought us into the net, and He brought us out into a wealthy place.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, made to slip, i.e. dislocated
BiblicalUsage: Muedeth is a foot slipped out of joint, dislocated — confidence in an unfaithful man in time of trouble is like a broken tooth, and a foot out of joint.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the picture is exact: a faithless friend in trouble does not just fail, he hurts to lean on.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a turn, i.e. circuit (of a building)
BiblicalUsage: Musab is a turn, a circuit — the side chambers of the temple widen as they go round, with a winding stair that turns upward from level to level.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the winding way is the temple's own logic: the higher you climb, the wider the room grows.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a reversal, i.e. the backside (of a gem), fold (of a double-leaved door), transmutation (of a name)
BiblicalUsage: Musabbah is a setting, a reversal, the back of a stone turned to show its face — the names of the sons of Israel are engraved on onyx stones, set in ouches of gold, and the rows of the breastplate are set in gold.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the setting is the honour: the names are not loose, they are set in gold and carried over the priest's heart.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a foundation
BiblicalUsage: Musad is a foundation — behold, I lay in Zion for a foundation a stone, a tried stone, a precious corner stone, and the house of the LORD is prepared and perfected from its foundation to its finishing.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the foundation is laid once and stands: a tried stone, and a house finished on it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a foundation; figuratively, an appointment
BiblicalUsage: Musadah is a foundation, an appointment — every place where the grounded staff passes, which the LORD lays upon the Assyrian, it shall be with tabrets and harps, and the prophet sees the foundations of the side chambers round about the house.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the grounded staff and the foundation are one word: God's appointment stands, and His judgment falls where He appointed it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, chastisement; figuratively, reproof, warning or instruction; also restraint
BiblicalUsage: Musar is discipline, instruction, correction. The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge, but fools despise wisdom and instruction; despise not the chastening of the LORD, for whom the LORD loveth He correcteth; he that spareth his rod hateth his son; and happy is the man whom God correcteth.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that discipline is love with its sleeves rolled up. God corrects the ones He loves, and the correction is the proof of the love, not the absence of it.
RelatedTopics: Wisdom; Obedience; Fear of the Lord
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to shake
BiblicalUsage: Mud is to shake, to measure out — He stood, and measured the earth, He beheld, and drove asunder the nations, and the everlasting mountains were scattered.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the shaking is the measure: God stands still, and the nations fall apart at a look.
RelatedTopics: God's Sovereignty; Judgment; Majesty of God
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to melt, i.e. literally (to soften, flow down, disappear), or figuratively (to fear, faint)
BiblicalUsage: Mug means to melt, to flow down, to faint — the heathen raged, the kingdoms were moved, and the earth melted at God's voice; the inhabitants of Canaan melt away at the news of the Red Sea; and Rahab says all the inhabitants of the land faint because of you.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the melting is the fear of God doing its work: kingdoms melt, and the earth itself cannot stand before His voice.
RelatedTopics: God's Power; Fear of God; Victory
RelatedEvents: The Exodus and the Red Sea
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to become thin, i.e. (figuratively) be impoverished
BiblicalUsage: Mukh means to grow poor, to become thin — if thy brother be waxen poor and hath sold away some of his possession, his kinsman shall redeem it; and if he be waxen poor and fallen in decay with thee, thou shalt relieve him; and if he be waxen poor and sold unto thee, he shall not serve as a bondservant.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the law's care for the poor brother is the test of Israel's heart: poverty is not a crime, and the poor are to be held up, not pushed down.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, abrupt, i.e. a precipice; by implication, the front; used only adverbially (with prepositional prefix) opposite
BiblicalUsage: Mul means in front of, over against, before — hearken now unto my voice, Jethro says to Moses, I will give thee counsel, and God be with thee; Balak sends for Balaam who dwells over against the river; and Moses speaks to all Israel on this side Jordan, in the wilderness, over against the Red Sea.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the little word is the Bible's way of saying where things stand: before God, before the river, before the people — and the standing is the story.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, abrupt, i.e. a precipice; by implication, the front; used only adverbially (with prepositional prefix) opposite
BiblicalUsage: Mul means in front of, over against, before — hearken now unto my voice, Jethro says to Moses, I will give thee counsel, and God be with thee; Balak sends for Balaam who dwells over against the river; and Moses speaks to all Israel on this side Jordan, in the wilderness, over against the Red Sea.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the little word is the Bible's way of saying where things stand: before God, before the river, before the people — and the standing is the story.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: circumcision
BiblicalUsage: Mulah is circumcision — then Zipporah takes a sharp stone and cuts off the foreskin of her son, and casts it at Moses' feet, and says, a bloody husband art thou to me, because of the circumcision.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the verse is one of the strangest in the Bible, and the point is plain: the covenant sign cannot be neglected, even on the road to deliver the people.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to jeer, i.e. (intens.) blaspheme
BiblicalUsage: Muq means to mock, to jeer, to blaspheme — they are corrupt, and speak wickedly concerning oppression, they speak loftily.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the jeer is the last refuge of the wicked: when they cannot answer, they mock, and the mockery is counted against them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to alter; by implication, to barter, to dispose of
BiblicalUsage: Mur means to change, to barter, to exchange — hath a nation changed their gods, which are yet no gods, but My people have changed their glory for that which doth not profit, and they changed their glory into the similitude of an ox that eateth grass.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the exchange is the tragedy of Israel in one word: glory traded for nothing, and the trade made willingly.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to withdraw (both literally and figuratively, whether intransitive or transitive)
BiblicalUsage: Mush means to depart, to withdraw, to move away — the pillar of cloud by day and the pillar of fire by night departed not from before the people, this book of the law shall not depart out of thy mouth, and the mountains shall depart but My kindness shall not depart from thee.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word draws the line between what leaves and what stays: pillars and mountains depart, and His kindness does not.
RelatedTopics: Faithfulness of God; Presence of God; Covenant
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to withdraw (both literally and figuratively, whether intransitive or transitive)
BiblicalUsage: Mush means to depart, to withdraw, to move away — the pillar of cloud by day and the pillar of fire by night departed not from before the people, this book of the law shall not depart out of thy mouth, and the mountains shall depart but My kindness shall not depart from thee.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word draws the line between what leaves and what stays: pillars and mountains depart, and His kindness does not.
RelatedTopics: Faithfulness of God; Presence of God; Covenant
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a Mushite (collectively) or descendants of Mushi
BiblicalUsage: Mushi means the Mushites, the descendants of Mushi — of Merari comes the family of the Mahlites and the family of the Mushites, the Levites counted by their families.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the Levite families are counted because the service is counted: every family has its charge, and the charge is the honour.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a Mushite (collectively) or descendants of Mushi
BiblicalUsage: Mushi means the Mushites, the descendants of Mushi — of Merari comes the family of the Mahlites and the family of the Mushites, the Levites counted by their families.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the Levite families are counted because the service is counted: every family has its charge, and the charge is the honour.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: 'To die for the son', probably the title of a popular song
BiblicalUsage: Muth is death, as a noun — for this God is our God for ever and ever, He will be our guide even unto death. The same word stands in a psalm heading, Muth-labben, the title of a song whose words are lost to us now.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the promise is the whole psalm in one line: the God who guides through life guides through death too, and the guiding does not stop at the grave.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to die (literally or figuratively); causatively, to kill
BiblicalUsage: Muth is to die. In the day that thou eatest thereof thou shalt surely die, God says, and the serpent says ye shall not surely die, and the soul that sinneth, it shall die, and Job asks, if a man die, shall he live again?
TheologicalSignificance: I believe death is the Bible's first warning and its last enemy. It enters through one act of disobedience, it falls on every soul that sins, and it is the question Job asks that only the resurrection answers.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to press, i.e. (figuratively) to oppress
BiblicalUsage: Muts means to press, to oppress — let Mine outcasts dwell with thee, Moab, be thou a covert to them from the face of the spoiler, for the extortioner is at an end, the spoiler ceaseth, the oppressors are consumed out of the land.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the oppressor's end is promised in the same breath as the outcast's shelter: God hides His people, and the pressing stops.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, fusion, i.e. literally, a casting (of metal); figuratively, a mass (of clay)
BiblicalUsage: Mutsaq is a casting, a thing poured and hardened — the molten sea is cast in one piece, ten cubits from brim to brim, the ten bases are of one casting, and the dust grows into hardness when the clods cleave fast together.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the casting is the picture of work done once and done well: poured, hardened, and standing for generations.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: narrowness; figuratively, distress
BiblicalUsage: Mutsaq is narrowness, distress — nevertheless the dimness shall not be such as was in her vexation, and God would have removed Job out of the strait into a broad place, and by the breath of God frost is given, and the breadth of the waters is straitened.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the narrow place is where God does His best work: the strait is not the end, it is the passage into the broad place.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, something poured out, i.e. a casting (of metal); by implication, a tube (as cast)
BiblicalUsage: Mutsaqah is a casting, a thing poured out — under the brim of the molten sea are knops compassing it, ten in a cubit, cast when it was cast, and Zechariah sees a candlestick of gold with a bowl upon the top of it, and seven pipes to the seven lamps.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the cast work is the temple's quiet witness: even the ornaments are made to last, because the house is God's.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: perhaps a primary word; the marrow:--marrow.
BiblicalUsage: Myelos is marrow — the word of God is quick and powerful, and sharper than any two-edged sword, piercing even to the dividing asunder of soul and spirit, and of the joints and marrow.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the marrow is the deepest place the word reaches: it does not stop at the skin, it divides what nothing else can divide.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from the base of G3466; to initiate, i.e. (by implication) to teach:--instruct.
BiblicalUsage: Myeo means to be initiated, to be taught by experience — Paul says, I am instructed both to be full and to be hungry, both to abound and to suffer need. In the Greek text the form stands under the lemma μυέομαι, spelled differently from this study's headword.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Paul's instruction is the whole Christian life in one verse: taught by plenty and by want, and content in both.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a presumed derivative of μύζω (to "moo"); to bellow (roar):--roar.
BiblicalUsage: Mykaomai means to roar, to bellow — the mighty angel cries with a loud voice, as when a lion roareth, and when he cries, seven thunders utter their voices.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the roar is the sound of a God who is not tame: the angel cries like a lion, and the thunders answer.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a derivative of the base of G3455 (meaning snout, as that whence lowing proceeds); to make mouths at, i.e. ridicule:--mock.
BiblicalUsage: Mykterizo means to mock, to turn up the nose at — be not deceived, God is not mocked, for whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the mockery is the self-deception: men think they can sow one thing and reap another, and God is not mocked.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3458; belonging to a mill:--mill(-stone).
BiblicalUsage: Mylikos means belonging to a mill, millstone — it were better for him that a millstone were hanged about his neck, and he cast into the sea, than that he should offend one of these little ones.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the millstone is the weight of the warning: harming the little ones is a sin too heavy to carry.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3458; a mill-house:--mill.
BiblicalUsage: Mylon is a mill-house, the place of grinding — two women shall be grinding at the mill, the one shall be taken, and the other left. In the Greek text behind the King James Version the mill-house stands where the later text reads the millstone's mill, and this study follows the King James reading.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the mill is the picture of ordinary life interrupted: two women grinding together, and one taken, and the readiness that makes the difference.
RelatedTopics: Waiting on God; Second Coming; Judgment
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably ultimately from the base of G3433 (through the idea of hardship); a "mill", i.e. (by implication), a grinder (millstone):--millstone.
BiblicalUsage: Mylos is a millstone — whoever offends one of these little ones, it were better a millstone were hanged about his neck and he were drowned in the depth of the sea, and two women shall be grinding at the mill when one is taken.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the millstone is the measure of the sin: what is done to the little ones is weighed, and the weight is terrible.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a compound of the base of G3466 and ὤψ (the face; from G3700); to shut the eyes, i.e. blink (see indistinctly):-- cannot see far off.
BiblicalUsage: Myopazo means to be short-sighted, to shut the eyes — he that lacketh these things is blind, and cannot see afar off, and hath forgotten that he was purged from his old sins.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the short sight is forgetfulness: he cannot see far because he has forgotten what was done for him close at hand.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain derivation; Myra, a place in Asia Minor:--Myra.
BiblicalUsage: Myra is a port in Lycia where Paul's ship touches on the voyage to Rome. They sail over the sea of Cilicia and Pamphylia, and come to Myra, and there the centurion finds a ship of Alexandria sailing into Italy.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Myra is the hinge of the voyage: the change of ships there carries Paul one step closer to Rome, and to the end of his road.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3463; a ten-thousand; by extension, a "myriad" or indefinite number:--ten thousand.
BiblicalUsage: Myrias is a myriad, ten thousand — an innumerable multitude of people gathers to hear Jesus, the church comes to Mount Sion and to an innumerable company of angels, and John hears the voice of many angels round about the throne, ten thousand times ten thousand.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the myriads are the measure of heaven's crowd: uncountable, and every one of them looking at the same throne.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: plural of an apparently primary word (properly, meaning very many); ten thousand; by extension, innumerably many:--ten thousand.
BiblicalUsage: Myrioi means ten thousand — a servant owes his lord ten thousand talents, Paul says though ye have ten thousand instructors in Christ, yet have ye not many fathers, and he would rather speak five words with understanding than ten thousand words in an unknown tongue.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the ten thousand is the number for 'more than you can pay': the debt no servant can settle, and the words no one can understand.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from G3464; to apply (perfumed) unguent to:--anoint.
BiblicalUsage: Myrizo means to anoint with perfumed oil — she hath done what she could, Jesus says, she is come aforehand to anoint My body to the burying.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the anointing is the act that understands what the disciples do not: she sees the burial coming, and she honours it beforehand.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably of foreign origin (compare H4753, G4666); "myrrh", i.e. (by implication) perfumed oil:--ointment.
BiblicalUsage: Myron is the perfumed ointment poured out in love and in grief, and all four Gospels bring it to the same table. A woman in Bethany breaks her alabaster box over Jesus in Mark 14:3, and Mary anoints His feet in John 12:3 until the house is filled with the smell. The sinful woman in Luke 7:37 brings the same costly ointment, and in Matthew 26:12 Jesus says it was poured for His burial.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the ointment matters because it was poured before anyone understood the cross, and Jesus received it as worship anyway. Costly love does not wait until it can explain itself, and what looks like waste to onlookers smells like devotion to Him. My position is simple: pour out the best you have on Jesus now, because the moment to honour Him is the moment you are in.
RelatedEvents: The Anointing at Bethany; The Sinful Woman Anoints Jesus; The Burial of Jesus
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of uncertain origin; Mysia, a region of Asia Minor:--Mysia.
BiblicalUsage: Mysia is a region on the north-west edge of Asia Minor, and it shows up at a turning point in the mission to the Gentiles. Paul and his companions come to Mysia in Acts 16:7 and try to go into Bithynia, but the Spirit does not let them. They pass by Mysia in Acts 16:8 and go down to Troas, where the vision of the Macedonian man sends them into Europe.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Mysia teaches me to trust a closed door as much as an open one, for the Spirit who stopped Paul from going one way was the same Spirit who sent him another, and the gospel reached Europe because he listened. A no from God is still guidance.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a derivative of μύω (to shut the mouth); a secret or "mystery" (through the idea of silence imposed by initiation into religious rites):--mystery.
BiblicalUsage: Mysterion is a secret that has been kept hidden and is now made known by God, and the New Testament uses it for the deepest things of the faith. Jesus says the mysteries of the kingdom are given to His disciples in Matthew 13:11, and Paul writes of the mystery of His will made known to us in Ephesians 1:9. The wisdom of God in a mystery is spoken in 1 Corinthians 2:7, and the mystery of Christ is revealed to Paul in Ephesians 3:3.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a mystery in Scripture is not a puzzle God hides from us, but a truth He kept until the right time to tell it. The cross, the church, the calling of the Gentiles — all of it was hidden in God and is now spoken plainly in Christ. That is why I never treat the gospel as my discovery; I treat it as His gift, revealed.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: perhaps from the same as G3453 (through the idea of tuition); a tale, i.e. fiction ("myth"):--fable.
BiblicalUsage: Mythos is a made-up tale, a fable, and the New Testament warns against trading truth for it. Paul tells Timothy not to give heed to fables and endless genealogies in 1 Timothy 1:4, and to refuse profane and old wives' fables in 1 Timothy 4:7. In 2 Timothy 4:4 people turn away their ears from the truth and are turned to fables, while Peter insists in 2 Peter 1:16 that the apostles did not follow cunningly devised fables when they told of Christ's power and coming.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the danger of a fable is not that it is boring, but that it is interesting enough to replace the truth. A good story that flatters the ear can crowd out the gospel that saves, and the church has to keep choosing the plain truth over the tale. My position is that eyewitness truth beats a clever story every time.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a home; figuratively, a pasture
BiblicalUsage: Na'ah is a home, a dwelling place, and by extension the pastures where shepherds keep their flocks. In Amos 1:2 the habitations of the shepherds mourn when the Lord roars from Zion, and in Jeremiah 9:10 the habitations of the wilderness are burned up so that no one passes through them.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that even a word as plain as home can carry judgment when the people who live there have turned away; God notices the places where ordinary life goes on, and when He speaks, the pastures hear it first.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a home; figuratively, a pasture
BiblicalUsage: Na'ah is a home, a dwelling place, and by extension the pastures where shepherds keep their flocks. In Amos 1:2 the habitations of the shepherds mourn when the Lord roars from Zion, and in Jeremiah 9:10 the habitations of the wilderness are burned up so that no one passes through them.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that even a word as plain as home can carry judgment when the people who live there have turned away; God notices the places where ordinary life goes on, and when He speaks, the pastures hear it first.

Definition: properly, a sandal tongue; by extension a sandal or slipper (sometimes as a symbol of occupancy, a refusal to marry, or of something valueless)
BiblicalUsage: Na'al is the sandal, the ordinary footwear of the ancient world, and it turns up in two hard places. In 1 Kings 2:5 David remembers blood shed in war, down to the shoes on Joab's feet, and in Amos 2:6 the Lord charges Israel with selling the righteous for silver and the poor for a pair of shoes.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a pair of shoes is a small price, and that is exactly the point; when a neighbour's life is worth less than footwear, the whole society has lost its way.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, to fasten up, i.e. with a bar or cord; hence, to sandal, i.e. furnish with slippers
BiblicalUsage: Na'al as a verb means to fasten up or furnish with sandals, and it also means to bolt a door shut. In 2 Chronicles 28:15 the men of Judah take the captives, clothe them, and shod them before sending them home, and in 2 Samuel 13:17 Amnon orders the door bolted after Tamar.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the same word can dress a wound or slam a door, and the difference is the heart behind it; kindness puts shoes on bare feet; cruelty bolts the door on the one it has hurt.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Naam, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Naam is a son of Caleb named once in the genealogies, and that single mention is all Scripture gives him. In 1 Chronicles 4:15 he stands among the sons of Caleb the son of Jephunneh, listed with Iru and Elah.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a name written once in the record is still written by God, and that is enough. Naam did not need a story to be counted among the people of God.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, to whisper, i.e. (by implication) to utter as a oracle
BiblicalUsage: Na'am means to whisper or to utter as an oracle, and its one occurrence is a rebuke of false prophets. In Jeremiah 23:31 the Lord says He is against the prophets who use their tongues and say, He saith, putting His name on words He never spoke.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that claiming God said what He did not say is one of the oldest sins in the book; a whisper dressed up as an oracle is still a lie, and the Lord answers it Himself.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Naamah, the name of an antediluvian woman, of an Ammonitess, and of a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Naamah is the name of three different bearers in Scripture, and the best known is the Ammonitess who became the mother of a king. In 1 Kings 14:21 Rehoboam the son of Solomon reigns in Judah, and his mother is named as Naamah the Ammonitess, and 2 Chronicles 12:13 names her again at the same point in his story. The name also belongs to a daughter of Lamech in the earliest generations and to a town in Judah.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Naamah is a reminder that God writes outsiders into the royal line. An Ammonite woman stands at the head of Judah's kings, and her son's story is told with her name attached, and God does not erase where a person came from when He gives them a place in His story.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Naaman, the name of an Israelite and of a Damascene
BiblicalUsage: Naaman is the Syrian commander who came to Israel a leper and went home clean. In 2 Kings 5:1 he is introduced as a great man and a mighty man of valour, but a leper, and in 2 Kings 5:11 he is angry at first because Elisha will not come out to him. In 2 Kings 5:17 Naaman asks for two mules' burden of earth, so that he may worship the Lord on Israel's soil from then on.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Naaman's healing came the moment he stopped dictating how God should heal him. He wanted a ceremony and got a command to wash, and the washing did what the ceremony never could; my position is that obedience in the plain thing is where the miracle lives, and another Naaman, a son of Benjamin, carries the same name in the genealogies.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: pleasantness (plural as concrete)
BiblicalUsage: Na'aman is pleasantness, and its only occurrence turns the word into a warning. In Isaiah 17:10 the people have forgotten the God of their salvation, so they plant pleasant plants and set strange slips, tending a garden while forgetting the Rock of their strength.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe pleasant things make a poor substitute for the God who saves; a garden planted in forgetfulness is still a garden, but it will not hold.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a Naamathite, or inhabitant of Naamah
BiblicalUsage: Naamathite is the name for a person from Naamah, and it belongs to Zophar, one of Job's three friends. In Job 2:11 Eliphaz the Temanite, Bildad the Shuhite, and Zophar the Naamathite come together to mourn with Job and to comfort him, and in Job 11:1 Zophar the Naamathite answers Job.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Zophar came as a friend and spoke as a judge, and the label that follows him is a warning to me; sitting with a sufferer is right; answering for God when you do not know is not.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a Naamanite, or descendant of Naaman (collectively)
BiblicalUsage: Naamite is the family name for the descendants of Naaman, a son of Bela. In Numbers 26:40 the census lists the sons of Bela, and among them the family of the Naamites, counted with the rest of Benjamin in the wilderness.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a family name in a census is a quiet promise that God counts His people one by one; the Naamites are not famous, but they are numbered.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to commit adultery; figuratively, to apostatize
BiblicalUsage: Na'aph means to commit adultery, and the Bible uses it for the act and for the unfaithfulness it pictures. The command is plain in Exodus 20:14, and the penalty is stated in Leviticus 20:10. Proverbs 6:32 says the adulterer destroys his own soul, and in Jeremiah 3:8 the Lord says backsliding Israel committed adultery and was put away.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe adultery is never only about a body, because God calls His own people adulterers when they chase other gods. The marriage bed and the covenant with God break in the same place: a promise kept only while it is easy. I hold that keeping faith in both is what a faithful life is.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: adultery
BiblicalUsage: Na'aphuph is adultery, the noun, and its one occurrence is God speaking to faithless Israel. In Hosea 2:2 the Lord tells the people to plead with their mother, to put away her adulteries from between her breasts, because she is not His wife and He is not her husband.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the harshest word in Hosea is also the most honest one, because God names the sin before He offers the return; He will not call it anything softer than it is.
RelatedEvents: Hosea Marries Gomer and Names the Children
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to groan
BiblicalUsage: Na'aq means to groan, and it is the sound of the wounded, not the sound of complaint. In Ezekiel 30:24 Pharaoh groans before the king of Babylon with the groanings of a deadly wounded man, and in Job 24:12 men groan from out of the city while the wounded cry out.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that God hears a groan as a prayer, even when the groaning one has no words left; the wounded do not have to explain themselves to be heard.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to growl
BiblicalUsage: Na'ar means to growl or roar, and its only occurrence is a picture of proud enemies brought low. In Jeremiah 51:38 the people of Babylon roar together like lions and yell as lions' whelps, loud and sure of themselves just before the fall.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a roar is not strength when God has already spoken; Babylon sounds like a lion in Jeremiah 51:38, and the verse itself is the sentence.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to growl
BiblicalUsage: Na'ar means to growl or roar, and its only occurrence is a picture of proud enemies brought low. In Jeremiah 51:38 the people of Babylon roar together like lions and yell as lions' whelps, loud and sure of themselves just before the fall.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a roar is not strength when God has already spoken; Babylon sounds like a lion in Jeremiah 51:38, and the verse itself is the sentence.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: (concretely) a boy (as active), from the age of infancy to adolescence; by implication, a servant; also (by interch. of sex), a girl (of similar latitude in age)
BiblicalUsage: Na'ar is a boy, a lad, and by extension a young servant, and it follows some of the best-known young men in Scripture. In Genesis 37:2 Joseph is seventeen years old, a lad feeding the flock with his brothers, and in Exodus 33:11 Joshua is called a young man, the servant who does not depart from the tabernacle.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that God trusts young people with real work, and the lad in the field is not a footnote; joseph the lad and Joshua the young man both grew into the men God used, and neither started by being important.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: (concretely) a boy (as active), from the age of infancy to adolescence; by implication, a servant; also (by interch. of sex), a girl (of similar latitude in age)
BiblicalUsage: Na'ar is a boy, a lad, and by extension a young servant, and it follows some of the best-known young men in Scripture. In Genesis 37:2 Joseph is seventeen years old, a lad feeding the flock with his brothers, and in Exodus 33:11 Joshua is called a young man, the servant who does not depart from the tabernacle.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that God trusts young people with real work, and the lad in the field is not a footnote; joseph the lad and Joshua the young man both grew into the men God used, and neither started by being important.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to reject
BiblicalUsage: Na'ar as a verb means to reject or cast off, and it falls on the holiest things when God judges. In Lamentations 2:7 the Lord has cast off His altar and abhorred His sanctuary, giving its walls into the hand of the enemy, and in Psalm 89:39 the psalmist cries that God has made void the covenant of His servant and profaned his crown.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the hardest verses in the Bible are the ones where God Himself seems to cast off what He loved; they are not the end of the story, but they are honest about what sin costs.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Naarah, the name of an Israelitess, and of a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Naarah is a wife of Ashur the father of Tekoa, and the name also marks a place on the border. In 1 Chronicles 4:5 Ashur has two wives, Helah and Naarah, and in 1 Chronicles 4:6 Naarah bears him four sons. The place appears as Naarath in Joshua 16:7, on the way down from Janohah to Jericho.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a name that belongs to both a mother and a town is a small picture of how the Bible works. People and places carry the same words, and the family line runs through both.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a girl (from infancy to adolescence)
BiblicalUsage: Na'arah is a girl, a young woman, and it is the word for the damsel at the well and the maid in the field. In Genesis 24:14 the damsel who offers water to the servant and his camels is the one God has appointed for Isaac, and in Ruth 2:5 Boaz asks his servant whose damsel Ruth is.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that God watches the ordinary kindness of a young woman at a well and builds a family on it; rebekah's offer of water and Ruth's work in the field are both small acts, and both carry the story forward.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Naaran, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Naaran is a town in the territory of Ephraim, named once in the list of possessions. In 1 Chronicles 7:28 the possessions and habitations of Ephraim are listed, and eastward Naaran stands among them with Bethel and Gezer and Shechem.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a town named once in a list is still part of the inheritance God gave. Naaran is not a famous place, but it is counted land.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Naarai, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Naarai is one of David's mighty men, named once in the list of the warriors. In 1 Chronicles 11:37 he stands as Naarai the son of Ezbai, counted among the men who stood with David.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the mighty men are remembered by name because loyalty is worth naming. Naarai has one verse, and that verse puts him beside the king.
RelatedEvents: David's Mighty Men and the Philistine Giants
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to scorn;
BiblicalUsage: Na'ats means to scorn, to despise, to provoke, and it is what Israel does to the Lord again and again. In Numbers 14:11 the Lord asks how long this people will provoke Him, and in Deuteronomy 31:20 He says they will turn to other gods and provoke Him when they are full. Psalm 10:3 says the wicked bless the covetous whom the Lord abhors, and Isaiah 1:4 calls them children that have provoked the Holy One of Israel.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe scorn is the sin underneath the other sins, because it treats God as if He does not matter. Israel did not fall in a day; they provoked the Lord a little at a time until the provoking became their life. I hold that the cure is the fear of God, which is the opposite of scorn.
RelatedEvents: The Twelve Spies and Israel's Unbelief
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably a brier; by implication, a thicket of thorny bushes
BiblicalUsage: Na'atsuts is a thorn or a brier, a thicket of thorny bushes, and it marks places left desolate. In Isaiah 7:19 the thorns and bushes are where the enemy comes to rest in the desolate valleys, and in Isaiah 55:13 the promise is that instead of the thorn shall come up the fir tree, and instead of the brier the myrtle tree.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the brier is the picture of what sin leaves behind, and the myrtle is the picture of what God plants in its place; He does not just clear the thorns; He grows something better where they were.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to be agreeable (literally or figuratively)
BiblicalUsage: Na'em means to be agreeable or pleasant, and it holds some of the tenderest words in Scripture. In 2 Samuel 1:26 David says of Jonathan, very pleasant hast thou been unto me, and in Ezekiel 32:19 the question is asked, whom dost thou pass in beauty, in a taunt over the fallen.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that pleasantness is a gift when it is real, and a trap when it is only appearance; david's lament shows what true affection sounds like, and Ezekiel shows what happens when beauty is trusted instead of God.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, tough, i.e. uncooked (flesh)
BiblicalUsage: Na means raw or uncooked, tough flesh, and its only occurrence is at the Passover table. In Exodus 12:9 the people are told not to eat the lamb raw, nor sodden at all with water, but roast with fire, head with legs and all.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God cares about the details of obedience, even down to how the lamb is cooked; the Passover was not a suggestion, and the roast was part of the remembering.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: delightful (objective or subjective, literal or figurative)
BiblicalUsage: Na'im means delightful or pleasant, and it describes friendship, prosperity, and the love of brothers. In 2 Samuel 1:23 Saul and Jonathan are lovely and pleasant in their lives, and in their death they are not divided, and in Job 36:11 those who obey and serve God spend their years in pleasures.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that delight is not a small thing to God, because He made friendship and obedience to be pleasant; the word holds both the love of Jonathan and the reward of the obedient, and both are good.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: (only in plural collectively or emphatic form) youth, the state (juvenility) or the persons (young people)
BiblicalUsage: Na'ur is youth, the days of being young, and the Bible ties it to remembering God early. In Psalm 25:7 David asks God not to remember the sins of his youth, nor his transgressions, and in Psalm 71:5 the psalmist says the Lord has been his trust from his youth.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe youth is not a waiting room for faith, it is the time to start it; the God who is trusted from youth is the God who holds through old age, and I would rather begin early than repair late.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: suitable, or beautiful
BiblicalUsage: Na'veh means suitable or beautiful, comely or delicate, and it is used for a woman and for speech. In Jeremiah 6:2 the daughter of Zion is likened to a comely and delicate woman, and in Proverbs 17:7 excellent speech is said to become a fool no more than lying lips become a prince.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that beauty without truth is only decoration, and the proverb proves it; fine words sound wrong in a fool's mouth because the life does not match the language.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, tough, i.e. uncooked (flesh)
BiblicalUsage: Na means raw or uncooked, tough flesh, and its only occurrence is at the Passover table. In Exodus 12:9 the people are told not to eat the lamb raw, nor sodden at all with water, but roast with fire, head with legs and all.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God cares about the details of obedience, even down to how the lamb is cooked; the Passover was not a suggestion, and the roast was part of the remembering.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H5177); Naasson (i.e. Nachshon), an Israelite:--Naasson.
BiblicalUsage: Naasson is the Greek form of Nahshon, and he stands in the line that leads to David and to Christ. In Matthew 1:4 Naasson is the son of Aminadab and the father of Salmon, and in Luke 3:32 he appears again in the genealogy, the son of Aminadab.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the genealogies are not filler, because every name in them is a link in a promise. Naasson sits between Aminadab and Salmon, and the line runs straight through him to the King.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to gush forth; figuratively, to utter (good or bad words); specifically, to emit (a foul odor)
BiblicalUsage: Naba means to gush forth or pour out, and it is used for words, for wisdom, and for stinking savour alike. In Proverbs 1:23 Wisdom says, I will pour out my spirit unto you, and in Psalm 19:2 day unto day uttereth speech. In Proverbs 15:2 the mouth of fools poureth out foolishness, and in Ecclesiastes 10:1 dead flies cause the ointment to send forth a stinking savour.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe what pours out of a person shows what is inside them, whether it is wisdom or folly. The same mouth can pour out the Spirit's words or a fool's, and the difference is what fills the heart first. I hold that I want my words to be the kind that pour out life.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to prophesy, i.e. speak (or sing) by inspiration (in prediction or simple discourse)
BiblicalUsage: Naba means to prophesy, to speak by inspiration, and it runs from the elders in the wilderness to the promise of the Spirit. In Numbers 11:25 the Spirit rests on the seventy elders and they prophesy, and in 1 Samuel 10:5 Saul meets a company of prophets coming down from the high place. In Ezekiel 37:9 the prophet is told to prophesy to the wind, that the breath may come upon the slain, that they may live, and in Joel 2:28 sons and daughters shall prophesy when the Spirit is poured out.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe prophesying is not guessing the future, it is speaking what God has given to speak. The Spirit that rested on the elders and told Ezekiel to prophesy to the wind is the same Spirit Joel promised to pour out on all flesh, and I hold that God still speaks through His word today.
RelatedTopics: Prophecy; Prophets; Outpouring of the Spirit
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to pierce; to be hollow, or (figuratively) foolish
BiblicalUsage: Nabab means to pierce or to be hollow, and its four occurrences are mostly about things made hollow. In Exodus 27:8 the altar is to be made hollow with boards, as it was shown to Moses on the mount, and in Jeremiah 52:21 the bronze pillars of the temple are described as hollow, four fingers thick.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a hollow altar still holds the fire, and that is the point; God does not need solid bronze to receive a sacrifice; He needs a people who build it the way He showed them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to bark (as a dog)
BiblicalUsage: Nabach means to bark like a dog, and its only occurrence is a rebuke of watchmen who will not bark. In Isaiah 56:10 the watchmen are blind and ignorant, dumb dogs that cannot bark, sleeping and loving to slumber while danger comes.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a watchman who will not bark is worse than no watchman at all; silence looks peaceful until the enemy is inside the gate.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Nabal, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Nabal is the churlish rich man of Carmel whose name means fool, and his story is told in full in one chapter. In 1 Samuel 25:3 he is introduced as churlish and evil in his doings, while his wife Abigail is a woman of good understanding, and in 1 Samuel 25:25 Abigail tells David that as his name is, so is he, and folly is with him. In 1 Samuel 25:38 the Lord smites Nabal about ten days after, and he dies.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Nabal is the warning label on the whole book of Proverbs: a man can be rich, well-fed, and a complete fool at the same time. His wife's wisdom saved his household once, but no one else could save him from himself, and my position is that a name lived down to is still a choice, and Nabal chose his.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: stupid; wicked (especially impious)
BiblicalUsage: Nabal as an adjective means foolish or stupid, and in its worst sense wicked and impious. In Psalm 14:1 and Psalm 53:1 the fool says in his heart, There is no God, and they are corrupt and have done abominable works. In Proverbs 17:21 the father of a fool has no joy, and in Isaiah 32:6 the vile person speaks villany and works iniquity against the Lord.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the fool in the Bible is not a person with a low score on a test, but a person who has decided God does not matter. Saying there is no God in the heart is where the corruption starts, and everything else follows from it. I hold that wisdom begins where folly ends, with the fear of the Lord.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to scan, i.e. look intently at; by implication, to regard with pleasure, favor or care
BiblicalUsage: Nabat means to look intently, to scan or regard with care, and it is used for God looking down and for men looking up. In Genesis 15:5 the Lord tells Abram to look toward heaven and count the stars, and in Exodus 3:6 Moses hides his face because he is afraid to look upon God. In Psalm 33:13 the Lord looketh from heaven and beholds all the sons of men, and in Isaiah 5:12 the people regard not the work of the Lord.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe looking is never neutral in Scripture, because what we look at shapes what we become. Abram looked at the stars and believed a promise, Moses feared to look at God and was sent, and the Lord looks at all of us and sees truly. I hold that I want my looking to be the kind that notices the work of the Lord.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to wilt; generally, to fall away, fail, faint; figuratively, to be foolish or (morally) wicked; causatively, to despise, disgrace
BiblicalUsage: Nabel means to wilt or wither, to fall away and fail, and it is the word for grass in the sun and for a leaf in autumn. In Isaiah 40:7 and Isaiah 40:8 the grass withereth and the flower fadeth, but the word of our God shall stand for ever, and in Psalm 1:3 the righteous man's leaf shall not wither. In Jeremiah 8:13 the leaf shall fade and the things God gave shall pass away from the faithless.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the withering grass is the Bible's gentlest warning and its firmest comfort at once. Everything green fades, and that is exactly why the word that does not fade matters so much. I hold that my life is grass, and His word is the only thing in it that will not wither.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a prophet or (generally) inspired man
BiblicalUsage: Nabi is a prophet, a person who speaks for God, and the word covers nearly three hundred occurrences from Abraham to Malachi. In Genesis 20:7 Abraham is called a prophet who shall pray for Abimelech, and in Deuteronomy 18:18 the Lord promises to raise up a Prophet like Moses and put His words in his mouth. In 1 Kings 18:22 Elijah stands alone as a prophet of the Lord against the prophets of Baal, and in Jeremiah 1:5 Jeremiah is ordained a prophet to the nations before his birth.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a prophet is not a fortune teller but a mouthpiece, and the test is whether the words are God's or his own. Abraham prayed, Moses spoke, Elijah stood alone, and Jeremiah was chosen before he could choose. I hold that the Prophet like Moses has come, and His words are the ones I live by.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, disgrace, i.e. the (female) pudenda
BiblicalUsage: Nabluth is disgrace or lewdness, and its only occurrence is God uncovering faithless Israel. In Hosea 2:10 the Lord says He will discover her lewdness in the sight of her lovers, and none shall deliver her out of His hand.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the uncovering is judgment, but it is also honesty, because God will not let a people pretend; what is hidden will be shown, and the showing is the first step back.
RelatedEvents: Hosea Marries Gomer and Names the Children
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Naboth, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Naboth is the Jezreelite whose vineyard cost him his life and cost Ahab his house. In 1 Kings 21:1 Naboth has a vineyard in Jezreel, hard by the palace of Ahab king of Samaria, and in 1 Kings 21:13 false witnesses say he blasphemed God and the king, and he is stoned. In 2 Kings 9:26 the Lord says He saw the blood of Naboth and the blood of his sons, and will requite it in that same plot of ground.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Naboth's vineyard is the clearest picture in the Bible of what happens when a king wants what is not his. Naboth would not sell his inheritance, and that refusal cost him everything in this life, but God saw the blood and answered for it, and my position is that an inheritance kept is worth more than a king's price.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, to pull up, especially the tent-pins, i.e. start on a journey
BiblicalUsage: Nasa means to pull up the tent-pins and set out on a journey, and it is the great travel word of the Exodus. In Genesis 12:9 Abram journeyed, going on still toward the south, and in Exodus 13:20 Israel took their journey from Succoth and encamped in Etham. In Numbers 10:12 the children of Israel took their journeys out of the wilderness of Sinai, and in Exodus 12:37 the children of Israel journey from Rameses to Succoth, about six hundred thousand on foot.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the journey is the shape of the life of faith, because God rarely lets His people settle where they start. Abram pulled up his tent, Israel pulled up theirs forty years running, and the cloud told them when to move. I hold that a Christian is a traveller, and the tent-pins are never in for good.
RelatedEvents: The Exodus and the Red Sea; Wilderness Wanderings
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to raise a beacon
BiblicalUsage: Nasas means to raise a beacon or lift up a standard, and its only occurrence is a promise of rescue. In Zechariah 9:16 the Lord their God shall save His people in that day as the flock of His people, for they shall be as the stones of a crown, lifted up as an ensign upon His land.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a lifted ensign is a promise you can see from a long way off; God raises His people like a standard on a hill so that everyone knows whose they are.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to raise a beacon
BiblicalUsage: Nasas means to raise a beacon or lift up a standard, and its only occurrence is a promise of rescue. In Zechariah 9:16 the Lord their God shall save His people in that day as the flock of His people, for they shall be as the stones of a crown, lifted up as an ensign upon His land.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a lifted ensign is a promise you can see from a long way off; God raises His people like a standard on a hill so that everyone knows whose they are.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to tear away
BiblicalUsage: Nasach means to tear away or pluck up, and it is used for the wicked being rooted out of the land. In Deuteronomy 28:63 the Lord says He will rejoice over the disobedient to destroy them and bring them to nought, and to pluck them from the land, and in Proverbs 2:22 the wicked shall be cut off from the earth and the transgressors rooted out of it.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that being rooted out is the end of a long road, not a sudden accident; the tearing away comes after the warnings, and the land itself is better off without the wicked in it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to retreat
BiblicalUsage: Nasag means to retreat or to move a boundary back, and it is used for landmarks and for borders. In Deuteronomy 19:14 no one shall remove his neighbour's landmark, which they of old time set in the inheritance, and in Hosea 5:10 the princes of Judah are like those who remove the bound, so the Lord pours out His wrath on them like water.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a moved landmark is a quiet theft, because nobody sees the fence walk a few feet in the night; God sees it, and Hosea says His wrath follows it like water.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to test; by implication, to attempt
BiblicalUsage: Nasah means to test or try, and it is used for God testing His people and for people testing God. In Genesis 22:1 God did tempt Abraham, asking for Isaac, and in Exodus 15:25 He proved Israel at the bitter waters of Marah. In Deuteronomy 8:2 the forty years in the wilderness were to humble them and prove them, to know what was in their heart, and in Psalm 26:2 David asks the Lord to examine him and prove him.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe God's testing is not a trap but a revealing, because He already knows what is in the heart and wants us to know it too. Abraham was tested and trusted, Israel was proved and grumbled, and David asked for the test himself. I hold that a test passed is worth more than a test avoided.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to interweave, i.e. (figuratively) to overspread
BiblicalUsage: Nasak means to interweave or overspread, to cast a covering over, and its only occurrence is a veil over the nations. In Isaiah 25:7 the Lord will destroy in His mountain the face of the covering cast over all people, and the veil that is spread over all nations.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the veil over the nations is the darkness that keeps people from seeing God, and Isaiah says the Lord Himself will destroy it; the covering is not lifted by us; it is torn by Him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to interweave, i.e. (figuratively) to overspread
BiblicalUsage: Nasak means to interweave or overspread, to cast a covering over, and its only occurrence is a veil over the nations. In Isaiah 25:7 the Lord will destroy in His mountain the face of the covering cast over all people, and the veil that is spread over all nations.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the veil over the nations is the darkness that keeps people from seeing God, and Isaiah says the Lord Himself will destroy it; the covering is not lifted by us; it is torn by Him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to go up
BiblicalUsage: Nasaq means to go up or ascend, and its only occurrence is the psalmist's wonder at a God who is everywhere. In Psalm 139:8 David says if I ascend up into heaven, thou art there, and if I make my bed in hell, behold, thou art there.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that there is no going up high enough to get away from God, and no going down low enough either; the verse is a comfort, not a threat, because the God who is everywhere is the God who knows me.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to guide; by implication, to transport (into exile, or as colonists)
BiblicalUsage: Nachah means to guide or lead, and it is most often God leading His people by hand. In Exodus 13:17 God led the people not through the way of the Philistines, though it was near, and in Psalm 23:3 He leadeth me in the paths of righteousness for His name's sake. In Psalm 31:3 David asks God to lead and guide him for His name's sake, and in Exodus 15:13 He in His mercy has led forth the people He has redeemed.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the difference between wandering and travelling is the guide, and Israel had the best one. God led them the long way on purpose, and He leads me the same way, in mercy and by His own hand. I hold that being led is better than being left to choose my own road.
RelatedEvents: The Exodus and the Red Sea
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a stream, especially a winter torrent; (by implication) a (narrow) valley (in which a brook runs); also a shaft (of a mine)
BiblicalUsage: Nachal is a stream or a winter torrent, and by extension the narrow valley the stream runs through. In Deuteronomy 8:7 the good land is a land of brooks of water, of fountains and depths that spring out of valleys and hills, and in 1 Samuel 17:40 David chooses five smooth stones out of the brook before he faces Goliath.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that water in a dry land is the Bible's plainest picture of provision; the brook does not ask to be noticed; it just runs where God sends it, and the valley is glad of it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to inherit (as a (figurative) mode of descent), or (generally) to occupy; causatively, to bequeath, or (generally) distribute, instate
BiblicalUsage: Nachal as a verb means to inherit or to take possession, and it is the word for entering the land. In Deuteronomy 12:10 the people are told they will go over Jordan and dwell in the land the Lord gives them to inherit, and in Deuteronomy 1:38 Joshua shall cause Israel to inherit the land. in Isaiah 49:8 the Servant is given to cause the people to inherit the desolate heritages, and in Isaiah 57:13 the one who trusts in the Lord shall inherit His holy mountain.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe inheritance in the Bible is received, not earned, because the land was a gift before it was a possession. Israel inherited Canaan for the same reason the trusting inherit the mountain: God gives it to those who trust Him. I hold that my inheritance is not a place I buy, but a promise I receive.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, something inherited, i.e. (abstractly) occupancy, or (concretely) an heirloom; generally an estate, patrimony or portion
BiblicalUsage: Nachalah is the inheritance itself, the portion, the land, or the people God calls His own. In Numbers 18:20 the Lord tells Aaron He is the priests' part and their inheritance, and in Deuteronomy 4:21 Moses is barred from the good land God gives Israel for an inheritance. In Joshua 13:33 the Lord God of Israel is the inheritance of Levi, and in Psalm 127:3 children are an heritage of the Lord.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the greatest inheritance in the Bible is not land but the Lord Himself. Levi had no fields because God was their portion, and children are called an heritage because people, not acres, are what God treasures. My position is that if God is my inheritance, I am rich already.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Nachaliel, a place in the Desert
BiblicalUsage: Nahaliel is a place in the desert on Israel's march, named once in the list of stopping places. In Numbers 21:19 the people go from Mattanah to Nahaliel, and from Nahaliel to Bamoth, on the road through the wilderness.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a stopping place in the wilderness is still part of the journey God led. Nahaliel is one camp among many, and the march went on.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Nacham, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Nacham is a man named once in the genealogy of Judah, and that single mention is all we know of him. In 1 Chronicles 4:19 he is the father of Keilah the Garmite, named among the sons of Hodiah's sister.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a man named once is still named, and the record keeps him. Nacham fathered Keilah, and that is enough for the book to remember him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, to sigh, i.e. breathe strongly; by implication, to be sorry, i.e. (in a favorable sense) to pity, console or (reflexively) rue; or (unfavorably) to avenge (oneself)
BiblicalUsage: Nacham means to be sorry, to repent, to sigh deeply, and it is used for God relenting and for people turning. In Genesis 6:6 it repented the Lord that He had made man, and it grieved Him at His heart, and in Exodus 32:14 the Lord repented of the evil He thought to do to His people after Moses prayed. In 1 Samuel 15:11 it repenteth the Lord that He set up Saul as king, and in Joel 2:13 the people are told to rend their hearts and turn to the Lord, for He is gracious and repenteth Him of the evil.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe repentance is the hinge of the whole Bible, because God relents when His people turn, and He grieves when they will not. The Lord's repenting is not Him changing His mind like a man, but His mercy answering a prayer and a turned heart. I hold that Joel's call still stands: rend your heart, not your garments, and turn.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Nachamani, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Nahamani is one of the leaders who came back from exile with Zerubbabel, named once in the list of returnees. In Nehemiah 7:7 he stands among the men who came with Zerubbabel and Jeshua and Nehemiah, counted with Mordecai and Bigvai and the rest.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the return from exile was made of names like this, ordinary people who came home. Nahamani is not a hero of the story, but he is on the list, and the list is the story.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a snorting
BiblicalUsage: Nachar is a snorting, the sound of a horse ready for battle, and it is used for warhorses and for the snorting of the sea beast. In Jeremiah 8:16 the snorting of the enemy's horses is heard from Dan, and the whole land trembles at the sound, and in Job 39:20 the glory of the warhorse's nostrils is terrible.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the snort of a horse is the sound of war coming, and the prophets use it because everyone in their day knew it; when the horses are heard, the time for talking is over.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Nacharai or Nachrai, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Naharai is the armourbearer of Joab, named twice in the lists of David's mighty men. In 1 Chronicles 11:39 he stands as Naharai the Berothite, the armourbearer of Joab the son of Zeruiah, and in 2 Samuel 23:37 the same title and the same name appear again.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the armourbearer is the quiet half of the hero's story, because the man who carries the shield never gets the song. Naharai stood beside Joab, and the book remembers him for it.
RelatedEvents: David's Mighty Men and the Philistine Giants
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: an incantation or augury
BiblicalUsage: Nachash as a noun means an enchantment or augury, a forbidden way of seeking knowledge, and it belongs to Balaam's story. In Numbers 23:23 Balaam says there is no enchantment against Jacob, neither any divination against Israel, and in Numbers 24:1 he goes not, as at other times, to seek for enchantments, but sets his face toward the wilderness.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that enchantment is the search for power without obedience, and Balaam learned it does not work against a people God has blessed; no spell can curse what God has decided to bless.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a snake (from its hiss)
BiblicalUsage: Nachash is the serpent, and it runs from the garden to the end of the age. In Genesis 3:1 the serpent is more subtil than any beast of the field, and speaks to the woman, and in Numbers 21:9 Moses makes a serpent of brass and sets it on a pole, so that whoever looks on it shall live. In Psalm 58:4 the wicked have poison like the poison of a serpent, and in Isaiah 27:1 the Lord will punish leviathan the piercing serpent with His sore and great sword.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the serpent is the Bible's oldest enemy and its strangest picture of salvation at once. The same shape that brought death in the garden is lifted on a pole to give life in the wilderness, and the sword in Isaiah is the promise that the serpent does not win. I hold that the seed of the woman has crushed the serpent's head.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Nachash, the name of two persons apparently non-Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Nachash is also the name of two men, and the best known is Nahash the Ammonite who besieged Jabesh-gilead. In 1 Samuel 11:1 Nahash the Ammonite comes up and encamps against Jabesh-gilead, and in 2 Samuel 10:2 David shows kindness to Hanun the son of Nahash, as his father showed kindness to David. In 2 Samuel 17:25 Abigail is called the daughter of Nahash, the sister of Zeruiah, Joab's mother.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Nahash shows how one name can hold both an enemy and a friend, because the Ammonite king who threatened Israel is also the father remembered with kindness. David did not forget the kindness, and the book does not forget the siege.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, to hiss, i.e. whisper a (magic) spell; generally, to prognosticate
BiblicalUsage: Nachash as a verb means to practise divination or enchantment, to whisper a spell and watch for signs, and the law forbids it outright. In Genesis 30:27 Laban says he has learned by experience that the Lord blessed him for Jacob's sake, and in Genesis 44:5 Joseph's steward asks if his lord does not divine with the cup. In Leviticus 19:26 the people are told not to use enchantment nor observe times, and in Deuteronomy 18:10 no one among them shall use divination or be an observer of times.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe divination is the sin of wanting to know the future without trusting the God who holds it. Laban learned by experience and called it wisdom, but the law calls it forbidden, and I hold that the difference matters. God's people do not need spells; they have His word.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a descent, i.e. imposition, unfavorable (punishment) or favorable (food); restfulness
BiblicalUsage: Nachath is a descent or an imposition, and in its good sense it means restfulness and quietness. In Ecclesiastes 4:6 a handful with quietness is better than both hands full with travail, and in Isaiah 30:15 the Lord says in returning and rest shall ye be saved, and in quietness and in confidence shall be your strength.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that quietness is not laziness, it is trust with its hands open; the handful with quietness feeds a person better than two fists full of worry.
