Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a descent, i.e. imposition, unfavorable (punishment) or favorable (food); restfulness
BiblicalUsage: Nachath is a descent or an imposition, and in its good sense it means restfulness and quietness. In Ecclesiastes 4:6 a handful with quietness is better than both hands full with travail, and in Isaiah 30:15 the Lord says in returning and rest shall ye be saved, and in quietness and in confidence shall be your strength.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that quietness is not laziness, it is trust with its hands open; the handful with quietness feeds a person better than two fists full of worry.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to sink, i.e. descend; causatively, to press or lead down
BiblicalUsage: Nachath as a verb means to sink or descend, and to press or break down, and it is used for enemies broken and bows bent. In 1 Samuel 2:10 the adversaries of the Lord shall be broken to pieces, and out of heaven He shall thunder upon them, and in 2 Samuel 22:35 David says God teaches his hands to war, so that a bow of steel is broken by his arms.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the same word that breaks the enemy's power also bends the bow in the warrior's hand; God presses down the proud and presses strength into His own, and both are His work.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to be urgent
BiblicalUsage: Nachats means to be urgent or to press hard, and its only occurrence is David in a hurry. In 1 Samuel 21:8 David asks Ahimelech for a spear or a sword, because the king's business required haste, and he has brought neither sword nor weapons with him.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe urgency shows what a person trusts, because David in a hurry runs to the priest and not to his own sword; haste is not the same as panic when the errand is the king's.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Nachbi, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Nahbi is one of the twelve spies, named once in the list of the men Moses sent. In Numbers 13:14 he stands as Nahbi the son of Vophsi, of the tribe of Naphtali, sent to search the land.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the spies are remembered by name because the mission mattered, even when ten of them failed it. Nahbi went, and his name is on the list.
RelatedEvents: The Twelve Spies and Israel's Unbelief
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: descending
BiblicalUsage: Nacheth means descending or coming down, and its only occurrence is a warning from the man of God. In 2 Kings 6:9 Elisha sends word to the king of Israel, saying beware that thou pass not such a place, for thither the Syrians are come down.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a single warning can save a king, and Elisha's word did it more than once; the Syrians came down to the place, and the king did not, because God told him first.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: we
BiblicalUsage: Nachnu is the pronoun we, and it is the voice of people speaking together about who they are. In Exodus 16:7 Moses asks, what are we, that ye murmur against us, when the people complain in the wilderness, and in Genesis 42:11 Joseph's brothers say, we are all one man's sons, we are true men, and not spies.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that we is the hardest word in the Bible to say honestly, because it ties my name to my neighbour's; the brothers said we and meant it, and the murmurers said we and blamed Moses for it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H5152); Nachor, the grandfather of Abraham:--Nachor.
BiblicalUsage: Nachor is the Greek form of Nahor, and he stands in the genealogy of Jesus. In Luke 3:34 he appears as the son of Thara, the father of Abraham, in the line that runs from Adam to Christ.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the genealogy is the proof that the promise travelled through real families. Nachor is one link in a chain that ends at Bethlehem, and the chain holds.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Nochor, the name of the grandfather and a brother of Abraham
BiblicalUsage: Nachor is Nahor, the brother of Abraham and the father of Terah's other line, and his name runs through the family story. In Genesis 11:22 Serug begets Nahor, and in Genesis 11:24 Nahor lives nine and twenty years and begets Terah, and in Joshua 24:2 the Lord reminds Israel that Terah, the father of Abraham and the father of Nachor, dwelt on the other side of the flood in old time.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Nahor matters because the family of promise did not start with Abraham alone. The same house that produced the father of the faithful also produced the father of the other branch, and God chose one and blessed the line through him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Nachshon, an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Nachshon is the prince of Judah, the man who led his tribe out of Egypt and into the promised land. In Numbers 1:7 he is named as Nahshon the son of Amminadab, of Judah, and in Ruth 4:20 Amminadab begat Nahshon, and Nahshon begat Salmon, and in 1 Chronicles 2:10 Amminadab begat Nahshon, prince of the children of Judah.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a prince is measured by where he leads, and Nachshon led Judah first in the march and first in the line to David. He led Judah in the march, and the tribe followed him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Nachum, an Israelite prophet
BiblicalUsage: Nahum is the prophet of the burden of Nineveh, and his whole book is one verse of introduction and three short chapters of judgment. In Nahum 1:1 the burden of Nineveh is called the book of the vision of Nahum the Elkoshite, and the vision that follows is the fall of the city Jonah once warned.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Nahum is the other half of Jonah, because the city that repented once fell later when it went back to its cruelty. God's patience is long, but it is not endless, and Nineveh learned both.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: coppery, i.e. (figuratively) hard
BiblicalUsage: Nachush means coppery or brazen, hard like brass, and its only occurrence is Job measuring his own strength. In Job 6:12 Job asks, is my strength the strength of stones, or is my flesh of brass, as he tells his friends he is not made of metal.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that Job's question is the right one for every sufferer: I am flesh, not brass, and I break; God does not ask us to be metal; He asks us to be honest.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Nadab, the name of four Israelites
BiblicalUsage: Nadab is the name of two men who both died for getting worship wrong and for getting power wrong. In Exodus 6:23 Nadab is the firstborn son of Aaron, born to Elisheba, and in Leviticus 10:1 Nadab and Abihu offer strange fire before the Lord, which He commanded them not, and are consumed. In 1 Kings 15:25 another Nadab, the son of Jeroboam, begins to reign over Israel and walks in the way of his father.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the two Nadabs are one warning told twice: nearness to God is not a licence to invent worship, and a throne is not a licence to invent a religion. The priest's son and the king's son both learned that God is holy, and neither lived to use the lesson.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to impel; hence, to volunteer (as a soldier), to present spontaneously
BiblicalUsage: Nadab as a verb means to volunteer, to give willingly because the heart is stirred, and it built the tabernacle. In Exodus 25:2 the Lord says to take an offering from every man that giveth it willingly with his heart, and in Exodus 35:21 every one whose heart stirred him up and whose spirit made him willing brought the offering. In 1 Chronicles 29:5 David asks who is willing to consecrate his service to the Lord, and in 2 Chronicles 17:16 Amasiah willingly offered himself to the Lord with two hundred thousand mighty men.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe willing giving is the only kind God asks for, because a forced gift is not a gift at all. The tabernacle was built by stirred hearts, and the temple was supplied the same way, and I hold that God still works that way. A willing heart is the offering He wants first.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to push off; used in a great variety of applications, literally and figuratively (to expel, mislead, strike, inflict, etc.)
BiblicalUsage: Nadach means to be driven away or pushed off, and it is the word for exile and for straying sheep. In Deuteronomy 30:1 the Lord says the people will call the blessing and the curse to mind among all the nations where He has driven them, and in Jeremiah 23:2 the pastors have scattered the flock and driven them away. In Ezekiel 34:4 the shepherds have not brought again that which was driven away, and in Deuteronomy 30:4 even if the driven ones are at the outmost parts of heaven, the Lord will gather them from there.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe being driven away is the Bible's picture of what sin does to a people, but Deuteronomy 30:1 holds the way back in the same breath. The driven ones are told to call it all to mind, and remembering is the first step home. I hold that no exile is too far for the God who drove them to bring them back.
RelatedEvents: Fall of Jerusalem and the Exile
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, to wave to and fro (rarely to flap up and down); figuratively, to rove, flee, or (causatively) to drive away
BiblicalUsage: Nadad means to wander or flee, to wave to and fro like a bird from its nest, and it follows the restless from Cain onward. In Job 15:23 the wicked wanders abroad for bread, and knows the day of darkness is ready at his hand, and in Psalm 55:7 the psalmist says he would wander far off and remain in the wilderness. In Proverbs 27:8 a man that wandereth from his place is like a bird that wandereth from her nest, and in Hosea 7:13 woe is pronounced on those who have fled from the Lord, though He redeemed them.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe wandering is what happens when a person leaves the place God gave them, and the bird out of the nest is the truest picture of it. The wicked wanders abroad for bread, the psalmist longs to wander far off and remain in the wilderness, and Hosea pronounces woe on those who flee from the God who redeemed them. I hold that the cure for wandering is not a map, but a return.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, to toss; figuratively, to exclude, i.e. banish, postpone, prohibit
BiblicalUsage: Nadah means to toss aside or banish, to drive away from following the Lord, and it is used for a king who leads a people astray. In 2 Kings 17:21 Jeroboam drave Israel from following the Lord and made them sin a great sin, and in Amos 6:3 the people put far away the evil day while they bring the seat of violence near.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe putting the evil day far away is how people live with sin today and judgment tomorrow; jeroboam drove a whole nation from following the Lord, and the nation followed him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a sheath (of a sword)
BiblicalUsage: Nadan is the sheath of a sword, and its only occurrence is the angel putting his sword away. In 1 Chronicles 21:27 the Lord commands the angel, and he puts up his sword again into the sheath, and the plague on Jerusalem stops.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the sword going back into the sheath is one of the kindest moments in the Bible; judgment stops when God says stop, and the sheath is the sign of it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a sheath (of a sword)
BiblicalUsage: Nadan is the sheath of a sword, and its only occurrence is the angel putting his sword away. In 1 Chronicles 21:27 the Lord commands the angel, and he puts up his sword again into the sheath, and the plague on Jerusalem stops.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the sword going back into the sheath is one of the kindest moments in the Bible; judgment stops when God says stop, and the sheath is the sign of it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to shove asunder, i.e. disperse
BiblicalUsage: Nadaph means to shove asunder or disperse, to drive away like chaff, and it is used for reeds and for leaves. In Isaiah 19:7 the paper reeds by the brooks shall wither and be driven away and be no more, and in Job 13:25 Job asks if God will break a leaf driven to and fro and pursue the dry stubble.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Job's question is the cry of everyone who feels small and scattered; a leaf driven to and fro is not worth pursuing, and yet God does pursue us, not to break us but to gather us.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to promise (pos., to do or give something to God)
BiblicalUsage: Nadar means to make a vow, to promise something to God, and the Bible treats a vow as a debt. In Genesis 28:20 Jacob vows that if God will be with him and keep him, the Lord shall be his God, and in Numbers 30:2 a man who vows a vow to the Lord shall not break his word. In Deuteronomy 23:21 he shall not slack to pay it, for the Lord will surely require it, and in Ecclesiastes 5:4 when you vow a vow to God, defer not to pay it, for He has no pleasure in fools.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a vow is a promise made to the one Person who never forgets, and that is why the Bible is so strict about it. Jacob vowed on the road and kept it, and the law says the keeping is the point. I hold that it is better not to vow than to vow and not pay.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, voluntary, i.e. generous; hence, magnanimous; as noun, a grandee (sometimes a tyrant)
BiblicalUsage: Nadib means generous or willing, and as a noun it means a prince or a grandee, because generosity was the mark of nobility. In Exodus 35:5 whoever is of a willing heart is to bring an offering to the Lord, and in Isaiah 32:5 the vile person shall no more be called liberal, nor the churl said to be bountiful. In Psalm 51:12 David asks God to uphold him with a free spirit, and in Isaiah 32:8 the liberal deviseth liberal things, and by liberal things shall he stand.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe generosity is nobility in the Bible, because the willing heart is the prince's heart. David's free spirit and Isaiah's liberal man are the same person: one who plans to give and then stands by it. I hold that a generous life is a steady life.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, tossed; abstractly, a rolling (on the bed)
BiblicalUsage: Nadud is a tossing to and fro, a rolling on the bed, and its only occurrence is a sleepless night. In Job 7:4 Job lies down and asks when he shall arise and the night be gone, and he is full of tossings to and fro unto the dawning of the day.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the longest night in the Bible is Job's, and the word for it is a tossing; He does not sleep through his suffering, and God does not ask him to pretend he does.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, to touch, i.e. lay the hand upon (for any purpose; euphemistically, to lie with a woman); by implication, to reach (figuratively, to arrive, acquire); violently, to strike (punish, defeat, destroy, etc.)
BiblicalUsage: Naga means to touch, to lay the hand upon, and it runs from a wrestling match to the cleansing of a prophet's lips. In Genesis 32:25 the man touches the hollow of Jacob's thigh as they wrestle, and in Exodus 19:12 whoever touches the mount shall surely be put to death. In Ruth 2:9 Boaz charges the young men not to touch Ruth, and in Isaiah 6:7 the live coal touches the prophet's lips, and his iniquity is taken away and his sin purged.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a touch in the Bible is never small, because the same hand can wound and can cleanse. Jacob is touched and walks lame for life, the mountain must not be touched at all, and Isaiah is touched and made clean. I hold that what touches me matters, and who touches me matters more.
RelatedEvents: Jacob Wrestles with God; Isaiah's Vision and Call
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to butt with the horns; figuratively, to war against
BiblicalUsage: Nagach means to butt with the horns, and it is used for false prophets who promise victory with iron horns. In 1 Kings 22:11 Zedekiah the son of Chenaanah makes horns of iron and says, with these shalt thou push the Syrians until thou have consumed them, and in 2 Chronicles 18:10 the same words are spoken again before the king.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe iron horns make a good show and a bad prophecy; zedekiah pushed with horns he had made himself, and the battle went the other way.
RelatedEvents: Micaiah and Ahab's Death at Ramoth-Gilead
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, to front, i.e. stand boldly out opposite; by implication (causatively), to manifest; figuratively, to announce (always by word of mouth to one present); specifically, to expose, predict, explain, praise
BiblicalUsage: Nagad means to tell or declare, to make a thing known plainly, and it is used for news from the road and for the heavens themselves. In 1 Kings 18:13 Obadiah says, was it not told my lord what I did when Jezebel slew the prophets of the Lord, and in Psalm 19:1 the heavens declare the glory of God. In Psalm 22:31 a people yet to be born shall be told of His righteousness, and in Isaiah 40:21 the prophet asks, hath it not been told you from the beginning.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe declaring is the work of everyone who has heard good news, because the heavens do it without being asked and Moses did it over a meal. What God has done is not a secret to keep but a story to tell, and I hold that the telling is part of the worship.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to glitter; causatively, to illuminate
BiblicalUsage: Nagah means to glitter or shine, and to give light, and it is used for the lamp of the Lord and the light of the world. In 2 Samuel 22:29 David says, thou art my lamp, O Lord, and the Lord will lighten my darkness, and in Isaiah 9:2 the people that walked in darkness have seen a great light, and upon them hath the light shined.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that light in the Bible is always a gift before it is a command; the lamp is the Lord's, the shining is His, and the people walking in darkness did not light it themselves.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, to thrum, i.e. beat a tune with the fingers; expectation. to play on a stringed instrument; hence (generally), to make music
BiblicalUsage: Nagan means to play a stringed instrument, to thrum a tune with the fingers, and it is used where music meets the Spirit. In 1 Samuel 16:16 the servants look for a cunning player on the harp to play when the evil spirit is upon Saul, and in 2 Kings 3:15 Elisha says, bring me a minstrel, and when the minstrel played, the hand of the Lord came upon him.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe music can open a door for the word of the Lord, because Elisha asked for a player before he asked for a prophecy; the harp does not replace the word, but it can quiet the room for it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to push, gore, defeat, stub (the toe), inflict (a disease)
BiblicalUsage: Nagaph means to smite or strike, to push against and bring down, and it is used for the Passover, for plague, and for stumbling. In Exodus 12:23 the Lord will pass through to smite the Egyptians, but will not suffer the destroyer to come into the houses with the blood on the door, and in 2 Chronicles 21:18 the Lord smote Jehoram in his bowels with an incurable disease. In 1 Samuel 7:10 the Lord thunders with a great thunder on the Philistines and discomfits them, and in 1 Samuel 25:38 the Lord smites Nabal about ten days after, and he dies.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the smiting in this word always has a purpose, whether it is judgment on Egypt, disease on a wicked king, or the thunder that routs an army. The blood on the door in Exodus 12:23 is the difference between the smiting that passes over and the smiting that falls. I hold that the Lord who smites also shields, and the door marked with blood is the sign of it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to flow; figuratively, to stretch out; causatively, to pour out or down; figuratively, to deliver over
BiblicalUsage: Nagar means to flow or pour out, and it is used for water spilled on the ground and for blood shed by the sword. In 2 Samuel 14:14 the wise woman says we must needs die, and are as water spilt on the ground, which cannot be gathered up again, and in Ezekiel 35:5 Edom is charged with shedding the blood of Israel by the force of the sword in the time of their calamity.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that spilled water is the Bible's picture of a life that cannot be put back, and the woman who said it knew it; what is poured out is gone, which is why the blood shed in anger is so terrible.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to drive (an animal, a workman, a debtor, an army); by implication, to tax, harass, tyrannize
BiblicalUsage: Nagas means to drive or oppress, to tax and harass, and it is the word for the taskmasters of Egypt. In Exodus 3:7 the Lord says He has heard the cry of His people by reason of their taskmasters, and in Isaiah 9:4 the rod of the oppressor is broken as in the day of Midian. In Isaiah 14:2 Israel shall rule over their oppressors, and in Zechariah 9:8 the Lord promises no oppressor shall pass through His house any more.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe oppression is the sin God hears first, because the cry of the oppressed reaches Him before the prayer of the comfortable. He saw the taskmasters, He broke the rod, and He promises a day with no oppressor at all. I hold that standing with the oppressed is standing where God stands.
RelatedEvents: The Exodus and the Red Sea
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to be or come (causatively, bring) near (for any purpose); euphemistically, to lie with a woman; as an enemy, to attack; religious to worship; causatively, to present; figuratively, to adduce an argument; by reversal, to stand back
BiblicalUsage: Nagash means to draw near or come close, and it is the word for Abraham pleading and for Moses alone on the mountain. In Genesis 18:23 Abraham draws near and asks if God will destroy the righteous with the wicked, and in Exodus 24:2 Moses alone shall come near the Lord, but the people shall not come nigh. In Joshua 3:9 the people are told to come hither and hear the words of the Lord, and in Isaiah 41:1 the nations are called to come near together to judgment.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe drawing near is the whole of prayer in one word, because Abraham drew near to argue for a city and Moses drew near alone to hear God. Nearness is not a privilege for the few; it is an invitation with a warning, since the people could not come nigh in Exodus 24:2. I hold that Christ has opened the way I could never open myself.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: butting, i.e. vicious
BiblicalUsage: Naggach means butting or vicious, an ox that is known to push with its horn, and it is used for the law of the goring ox. In Exodus 21:29 if the ox were wont to push with his horn in time past, and it has been testified to the owner, and he has not kept him in, and the ox kills a man or a woman, the ox shall be stoned and the owner also put to death, and in Exodus 21:36 if it is known the ox has used to push, the owner shall surely pay ox for ox.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the law of the butting ox is a law about responsibility, not about cattle; a known danger left unguarded is the owner's fault, and God holds the owner to it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a commander (as occupying the front), civil, military or religious; generally (abstractly, plural), honorable themes
BiblicalUsage: Nagid is a commander or ruler, one who stands at the front, and it is the word for Saul, for David, and for the Messiah. In 1 Samuel 9:16 Saul is to be anointed captain over Israel to save the people from the Philistines, and in 1 Samuel 13:14 the Lord has sought a man after His own heart and commanded him to be captain over His people. In 1 Chronicles 11:2 David is told he shall feed God's people and be ruler over Israel, and in Daniel 9:25 the Messiah the Prince is promised from the going forth of the commandment to restore Jerusalem.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the ruler in the Bible is measured by whether he saves the people or uses them, and the line runs from Saul to David to the Messiah. Saul was anointed and failed, David was chosen after God's own heart, and the Prince in Daniel 9:25 is the one who does not fail. I hold that every captain points to the one Captain who saves for good.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to drive forth (a person, an animal or chariot), i.e. lead, carry away; reflexively, to proceed (i.e. impel or guide oneself); also (from the panting induced by effort), to sigh
BiblicalUsage: Nahag means to drive or lead forth, to carry away people or cattle or a cart, and it is used for armies and for a woman on an ass. In 1 Chronicles 13:7 Uzza and Ahio drave the cart that carried the ark of God, and in 1 Samuel 23:5 David brought away the cattle of the Philistines and saved Keilah. In 2 Chronicles 25:11 Amaziah led forth his people to the valley of salt and smote the children of Seir, and in 2 Kings 4:24 the Shunammite says to her servant, Drive, and go forward, and slack not.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that driving and leading are the same word because the work is the same: getting people and things where they need to go. The cart, the cattle, the army, and the ass all move because someone drives them, and the Bible notices who is holding the reins.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to groan, i.e. bewail; hence (through the idea of crying aloud), to assemble (as if on proclamation)
BiblicalUsage: Nahah means to groan or bewail, to cry aloud in grief, and it is used for a nation lamenting and for a prophet wailing. In 1 Samuel 7:2 all the house of Israel lamented after the Lord while the ark abode in Kirjath-jearim for twenty years, and in Ezekiel 32:18 the son of man is told to wail for the multitude of Egypt and cast them down to the pit.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that lamenting after the Lord is the beginning of return, because Israel's grief in 1 Samuel 7:2 is what brought Samuel back to lead them; grief that turns toward God is not despair; it is prayer.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, to run with a sparkle, i.e. flow; hence (transitively), to conduct, and (by inference) to protect, sustain
BiblicalUsage: Nahal means to lead gently, to conduct with care, and it is the shepherd's word. In Psalm 23:2 He leadeth me beside the still waters, and in Isaiah 40:11 He shall gently lead those that are with young, carrying the lambs in His bosom. In Isaiah 49:10 He that hath mercy on them shall lead them, even by the springs of water shall He guide them, and in Genesis 33:14 Jacob says he will lead on softly, according as the cattle and the children are able to endure.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe gentle leading is how God treats His people, because He leads at the pace of the lambs and the children. Jacob led softly so the little ones could keep up, and the Lord does the same for me. I hold that the still waters are not an accident; they are where the Shepherd leads.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Nahalal or Nahalol, a place in Palestine
BiblicalUsage: Nahalal is a town of Zebulun, named in the division of the land and again in the failure to drive out the Canaanites. In Joshua 19:15 Nahallal stands among the cities of Zebulun with Kattath and Shimron and Idalah, and in Judges 1:30 Zebulun did not drive out the inhabitants of Kitron nor the inhabitants of Nahalol, but the Canaanites dwelt among them.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a town given and not taken is the story of Zebulun in one verse. Nahalal was theirs on paper and shared in fact, because they would not finish the work.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: pasture
BiblicalUsage: Nahalol is pasture or a meadow, and its only occurrence is among the places where the enemy rests. In Isaiah 7:19 they shall come and rest in the desolate valleys and in the holes of the rocks, and upon all thorns and upon all bushes, and the pastures are named among the places left empty.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that a pasture with no flock in it is a picture of a land under judgment; the grass grows, but no one is there to feed on it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a snarl
BiblicalUsage: Naham as a noun is a snarl or a roar, the sound of a king's wrath, and it is used for a lion. In Proverbs 19:12 the king's wrath is as the roaring of a lion, but his favour is as dew upon the grass, and in Proverbs 20:2 the fear of a king is as the roaring of a lion, and whoever provokes him sins against his own soul.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the proverbs pair the roar with the dew on purpose, because a king can do both; wrath roars like a lion, and favour falls like dew, and a wise person knows which one they are standing under.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to growl
BiblicalUsage: Naham as a verb means to growl or roar, and to mourn aloud, and it is used for lions and for a people who will not weep. In Ezekiel 24:23 the people are told they shall not mourn nor weep, but shall pine away for their iniquities and mourn one toward another, and in Isaiah 5:29 the enemy's roaring shall be like a lion, and they shall roar and lay hold of the prey.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that a roar can be grief or it can be threat, and the Bible uses the same sound for both; the people in Ezekiel are forbidden the mourning they need, and the enemy in Isaiah roars because he can.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to bray (as an ass), scream (from hunger)
BiblicalUsage: Nahak means to bray like an ass or to scream from hunger, and it is used for the complaints of the empty. In Job 6:5 Job asks if the wild ass brays when he has grass, or the ox lows over his fodder, and in Job 30:7 the outcasts bray among the bushes and gather under the nettles.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Job's point is simple: a creature cries out because it lacks something, and so does a man; the bray is not the problem; the hunger behind it is.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a stream (including the sea; expectation the Nile, Euphrates, etc.); figuratively, prosperity
BiblicalUsage: Nahar is a river, a stream, and it runs from Eden to the city of God. In Genesis 2:10 a river goes out of Eden to water the garden, and from there it is parted into four heads, and in Psalm 46:4 there is a river, the streams whereof shall make glad the city of God.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the river is the Bible's picture of life that comes from God and cannot be dammed; it watered Eden, it gladdens the city, and it still runs.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to sparkle, i.e. (figuratively) be cheerful; hence (from the sheen of a running stream) to flow, i.e. (figuratively) assemble
BiblicalUsage: Nahar as a verb means to sparkle or to flow, to be cheerful and bright, and it is used for nations coming to the Lord. In Isaiah 2:2 all nations shall flow unto the mountain of the Lord's house in the last days, and in Jeremiah 31:12 they shall come and sing in the height of Zion, and shall flow together to the goodness of the Lord.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe flowing to God is the right picture of worship, because water does not climb, it runs downhill to where it belongs; the nations flow to the mountain because the goodness of the Lord draws them.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a primary particle of strong affirmation; yes:--even so, surely, truth, verily, yea, yes.
BiblicalUsage: Nai is the strong yes, the word of affirmation, and Jesus and Paul both build on it. In Matthew 5:37 Jesus says let your communication be, Yea, yea, and Nay, nay, for whatever is more than these comes of evil, and in 2 Corinthians 1:20 all the promises of God in Him are yea, and in Him Amen, unto the glory of God.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a plain yes is a Christian duty, because a yes that means yes needs no oath behind it; God's promises are yea in Christ, and my word should be yea in the same way.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably of Hebrew origin (compare H4999); Nain, a place in Palestine:--Nain.
BiblicalUsage: Nain is a city in Galilee, and it is known for one morning when death was turned back at its gate. In Luke 7:11 Jesus goes into a city called Nain, with many of His disciples and much people, and at the gate He meets a widow carrying out her only son.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Nain is remembered because Jesus stopped a funeral there, and the whole town watched Him do it. A city no one would have named is named forever for what happened at its gate.
RelatedEvents: The Raising of the Widow's Son at Nain
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to smite, i.e. drive away
BiblicalUsage: Naka means to smite or drive away, and its only occurrence is a scornful word about the lowly. In Job 30:8 the children of fools, children of base men, are described as viler than the earth, smitten down below the standing of men.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the verse is Job's complaint, not God's verdict, because Job is saying how the world treats the lowly; the smitten are not vile to God, even when men call them so.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to strike (lightly or severely, literally or figuratively)
BiblicalUsage: Nakah means to strike or smite, and it covers everything from a blow in a fight to the wounding of the Servant. In Exodus 2:11 Moses sees an Egyptian smiting a Hebrew, one of his brethren, and in 1 Samuel 17:50 David smites the Philistine with a sling and a stone and slays him. In Isaiah 53:4 the Servant is esteemed stricken, smitten of God, and afflicted, and in Amos 4:9 the Lord says He has smitten Israel with blasting and mildew, yet they have not returned to Him.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the smiting that matters most is the one in Isaiah 53:4, because the Servant was smitten in our place. Moses struck an Egyptian, David struck a giant, and God struck His own Son so that the smitten would not have to be struck forever. I hold that the wound of Christ is the end of my wounding.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to defraud, i.e. act treacherously
BiblicalUsage: Nakal means to act treacherously, to defraud or deal subtilly, and it is used for brothers, for priests, and for whole peoples. In Genesis 37:18 Joseph's brothers conspire against him before he comes near to them, and in Numbers 25:18 the Midianites vex Israel with their wiles in the matter of Peor. In Psalm 105:25 God turns the Egyptians' hearts to deal subtilly with His servants, and in Malachi 1:14 cursed is the deceiver who has a male in his flock and vows and sacrifices a corrupt thing.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe treachery is the sin that hides behind a smile, because the brothers waited until Joseph was close, and the deceiver brings a corrupt thing to the altar with a vow on his lips. God sees the wiles, and the curse in Malachi 1:14 falls on the one who thought no one was watching. I hold that plain dealing is the only safe dealing.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, to scrutinize, i.e. look intently at; hence (with recognition implied), to acknowledge, be acquainted with, care for, respect, revere, or (with suspicion implied), to disregard, ignore, be strange toward, reject, resign, dissimulate (as if ignorant or disowning)
BiblicalUsage: Nakar means to recognise or discern, to know again what was hidden, and it turns on a coat, a blessing, and a face. In Genesis 27:23 Isaac discerns Jacob not, because his hands are hairy like Esau's, so he blesses him, and in Genesis 37:33 Jacob knows the coat and says, it is my son's coat, and Joseph is without doubt rent in pieces. In Deuteronomy 33:9 Levi says of his father and mother, I have not seen him, and does not acknowledge his brethren, and in 1 Kings 20:41 the king of Israel discerns the prophet when he takes the ashes away from his face.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe recognition is the hinge of so many stories, because Isaac failed to discern and blessed the wrong son, and Jacob recognised a coat and believed a lie. The same word covers the prophet recognised too late, and I hold that the danger is not in seeing but in seeing what we want to see.
RelatedEvents: Joseph and His Brothers; Jacob Receives Isaac's Blessing
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: smitten, i.e. (figuratively) afflicted
BiblicalUsage: Nake means smitten or afflicted, broken in spirit, and it is used for a nation and for a heart. In Isaiah 16:7 Moab shall howl for Moab, and the foundations of Kir-hareseth shall be stricken, and in Proverbs 15:13 by sorrow of the heart the spirit is broken.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that a broken spirit is not a ruined one, because the proverb pairs it with a merry heart and lets both stand; sorrow breaks, and God is near to the broken.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: smitten, i.e. (literally) maimed, or (figuratively) dejected
BiblicalUsage: Nakeh means smitten or maimed, and in its tenderest use it means poor and contrite in spirit. In 2 Samuel 4:4 Jonathan's son is lame of his feet, five years old when the tidings came of Saul and Jonathan, and his nurse took him up and fled, and he fell and became lame, and in Isaiah 66:2 the Lord says He will look to the one who is poor and of a contrite spirit, and trembles at His word.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the lame child and the contrite heart belong together in this word, because both are smitten and both are seen by God; mephibosheth fell and was lame for life, and the Lord looks to the one who trembles at His word.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: straightforward, i.e. (figuratively), equitable, correct, or (abstractly), integrity
BiblicalUsage: Nakoch means straightforward or upright, equitable and correct, and it is used for a case and for a walk. In 2 Samuel 15:3 Absalom tells a man that his matters are good and right, but there is no man deputed of the king to hear him, and in Isaiah 57:2 the one walking in his uprightness shall enter into peace and rest in his bed.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that uprightness is a road, not a pose, because Isaiah's walker enters peace by walking in it; absalom could call a matter good and right and still use it for his own ends.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Nakon, probably an Israelite
BiblicalUsage: Nakon is the owner of the threshingfloor where Uzzah reached out to steady the ark, and his name marks the place of that judgment. In 2 Samuel 6:6 when they come to Nachon's threshingfloor, Uzzah puts forth his hand to the ark of God and takes hold of it, because the oxen shook it.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the threshingfloor of Nachon is a warning about holy things handled carelessly. Uzzah meant well, and the ark still struck him down, because God's holiness is not steadied by a human hand.
RelatedEvents: David Brings the Ark to Jerusalem
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to complete
BiblicalUsage: Nalah means to complete or to finish, to bring a thing to its end, and its only occurrence is a spoiler being spoiled. In Isaiah 33:1 woe is pronounced on the one that spoils and was not spoiled, and that deals treacherously when none dealt treacherously with him, for when he shall cease to spoil, he shall be spoiled.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the spoiler's end is written into the spoiling itself; what goes around in Isaiah 33:1 comes around, and the finishing belongs to God.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to become clipped or (specifically) circumcised
BiblicalUsage: Namal means to cut off or clip, and to circumcise, and the Bible uses it for both the covenant sign and the cutting down of the wicked. In Genesis 17:11 Abraham is told to circumcise the flesh of the foreskin as the token of the covenant, and in Job 14:2 a man comes forth like a flower and is cut down. In Psalm 37:2 the evildoers shall soon be cut down like the grass, and in Job 24:24 the wicked are cut off as the tops of the ears of corn.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the cutting in this word cuts both ways, because the same knife that marks the covenant also cuts down the grass. Circumcision says this child belongs to God, and the cutting off says the wicked will not stand, and both are His doing. I hold that I want the mark, not the cutting off.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a leopard (from its stripes)
BiblicalUsage: Namer is a leopard, spotted and swift, and it is used for the speed of an army and the watchfulness of a judge. In Habakkuk 1:8 the horses of the Chaldeans are swifter than the leopards and more fierce than the evening wolves, and in Hosea 13:7 the Lord says He will be to Israel as a leopard by the way, watching them.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the leopard is feared for the same reason in both verses: it is fast, it is spotted, and it is already watching; an enemy you cannot outrun and a God you cannot hide from wear the same picture.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: probably of Hebrew origin (compare H5052); Nangæ (i.e. perhaps Nogach), an Israelite:--Nagge.
BiblicalUsage: Nangai is a name in the genealogy of Jesus, and it appears once in Luke's line. In Luke 3:25 the line runs from Mattathias through Amos and Naum and Esli down to Nagge, in the generations between David and Christ.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a name in the genealogy is a link, and the chain is only as strong as its links. Nagge holds his place at the foot of that little run, the father of Esli, and the line goes on through him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: from a primary ναίω (to dwell); a fane, shrine, temple:--shrine, temple. Compare G2411.
BiblicalUsage: Naos is the temple, the inner sanctuary where God dwells, and the New Testament uses it for a building, for a body, and for Christ Himself. In Matthew 23:16 Jesus rebukes the blind guides who swear by the temple and by its gold, and in John 2:19 He says, destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up. In 1 Corinthians 3:16 believers are told they are the temple of God and the Spirit dwells in them, and in Revelation 11:1 John is told to measure the temple of God and the altar.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the temple is the place where God meets His people, and the wonder of the gospel is that the meeting place moved. It was a building, then it was a body raised in three days, and now it is the people in whom the Spirit dwells. I hold that my body is the temple now, and I should live like it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of Hebrew origin (H5151); Naum (i.e. Nachum), an Israelite:--Naum.
BiblicalUsage: Naoum is the Greek form of Nahum, and he appears once in the genealogy of Jesus. In Luke 3:25 he stands as the son of Esli and the father of Amos, in the line that runs from David to Christ.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the genealogy carries more than one Nahum, because the prophet of Nineveh and the man in Luke's line share a name and a place in God's story. This Naum holds his link, and the chain goes on.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to puff, in various applications (literally, to inflate, blow hard, scatter, kindle, expire; figuratively, to disesteem)
BiblicalUsage: Naphach means to blow or breathe, and it is the word for God breathing life into man and into dry bones. In Genesis 2:7 the Lord God breathes into man's nostrils the breath of life, and man becomes a living soul, and in Ezekiel 22:21 the Lord says He will blow upon them in the fire of His wrath. In Ezekiel 37:9 the breath is told to breathe upon the slain that they may live, and in Malachi 1:13 the people snuff at God's table as if it were weariness.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the breath of God is the difference between dust and a living soul, and between dry bones and an army. The same wind that drowned Egypt gives life to the slain, and the same mouth that received life can snuff at the table. I hold that every breath I take is borrowed from the One who breathed first.
RelatedEvents: Creation; The Valley of Dry Bones
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a height; also a sieve
BiblicalUsage: Naphah is a height or a sieve, a high place or a tool for sifting, and it is used for both. In 1 Kings 4:11 the region of Dor is called a height, the district given to Solomon's officer, and in Isaiah 30:28 the Lord's breath sifts the nations with the sieve of vanity.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that a height and a sieve do opposite work: one lifts you up and one shakes you out; God puts His people on the heights and sifts the nations through the sieve, and both are His doing.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to fall, in a great variety of applications (intransitive or causative, literal or figurative)
BiblicalUsage: Naphal means to fall, and it covers a deep sleep, a righteous man stumbling, and an angel cast from heaven. In Genesis 2:21 the Lord causes a deep sleep to fall upon Adam, and in Psalm 37:24 though he fall, he shall not be utterly cast down, for the Lord upholds him with His hand. In Proverbs 24:16 a just man falleth seven times and riseth up again, but the wicked shall fall into mischief, and in Isaiah 14:12 Lucifer falls from heaven, cut down to the ground.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe falling is not the end of the story for the righteous, because the same word that drops Lucifer from heaven catches the just man by the hand. Adam falls asleep and wakes to a wife, the just man falls seven times and rises seven times, and only the wicked fall and stay down. I hold that the difference is not whether I fall, but whose hand holds me when I do.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to breathe; passively, to be breathed upon, i.e. (figuratively) refreshed (as if by a current of air)
BiblicalUsage: Naphesh as a verb means to breathe again or be refreshed, to take a breath after weariness, and it is the Sabbath word. In 2 Samuel 16:14 the king and all the people with him come weary and refresh themselves, and in Exodus 23:12 the seventh day is for rest, so that the ox and the ass may rest and the stranger may be refreshed.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that refreshment is God's idea, not man's luxury, because He built it into the week; the weary king and the stranger at the gate both get the same rest, and the rest is holy.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to dash to pieces, or scatter
BiblicalUsage: Naphats means to dash to pieces or scatter, to break like a potter's vessel, and it is the word for God's judgment and for His weapon. In Psalm 2:9 the Son shall break the nations with a rod of iron and dash them in pieces like a potter's vessel, and in Jeremiah 13:14 the Lord will dash fathers and sons one against another without pity. In Jeremiah 51:20 Babylon is called God's battle axe, with which He will break in pieces the nations, and in Psalm 137:9 happy shall he be that takes and dashes the little ones against the stones.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the dashing in pieces is the end of every power that sets itself against God, because a potter's vessel does not argue with the rod. Babylon was the axe and then became the clay, and Nineveh heard the dasher coming. I hold that the only safe place is on the side of the One who holds the rod.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Naphish, a son of Ishmael, and his posterity
BiblicalUsage: Naphish is a son of Ishmael, named in the list of the twelve princes of his line. In Genesis 25:15 Naphish stands among Hadar and Tema and Jetur and Kedemah, the sons of Ishmael, and in 1 Chronicles 1:31 the same names are listed again as the sons of Ishmael.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the sons of Ishmael are remembered because God keeps His promises to the children of the bondwoman too. Naphish is a prince of a line God said He would bless, and the book counts him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Naphtali, a son of Jacob, with the tribe descended from him, and its territory
BiblicalUsage: Naphtali is the sixth son of Jacob, born to Rachel through Bilhah, and the tribe that bears his name. In Genesis 30:8 Rachel says she has wrestled with her sister and prevailed, and calls his name Naphtali, and in Genesis 49:21 Jacob blesses him as a hind let loose, giving goodly words. In Deuteronomy 33:23 Moses blesses Naphtali as satisfied with favour and full with the blessing of the Lord.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Naphtali's name is a wrestling match turned into a blessing, because Rachel's struggle became her son's name and Jacob's blessing turned it into praise. The hind let loose and the tribe full of favour are the same story: God takes a wrestling and makes it a blessing.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: Naphtuchim, an Egyptian tribe
BiblicalUsage: Naphtuhim is an Egyptian tribe descended from Mizraim, named in the table of nations. In Genesis 10:13 Mizraim begets Ludim and Anamim and Lehabim and Naphtuhim, and in 1 Chronicles 1:11 the same list is given again in the genealogy of the nations.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the table of nations is God's census of the whole world, not just of Israel. Naphtuhim is counted among the peoples, and the counting means they matter to Him.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: properly, wrestled; but used (in the plural) transitively, a struggle
BiblicalUsage: Naphthul is wrestling or a struggle, and its only occurrence is the naming of Naphtali. In Genesis 30:8 Rachel says, with great wrestlings have I wrestled with my sister, and I have prevailed, and she calls his name Naphtali.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the struggle in the name is honest, because Rachel did not hide the wrestling that gave her a son; a name that remembers a fight is a name that remembers God heard it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to feel aversion
BiblicalUsage: Naqa means to feel aversion, for the mind to be alienated from someone, and it is used for God's own mind turning from faithless Judah. In Ezekiel 23:18 the Lord says His mind was alienated from Oholibah, like as His mind was alienated from her sister, and in Ezekiel 23:22 He will raise up her lovers against her, from whom her mind is alienated.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that alienation is the saddest word in Ezekiel, because it is God saying His mind has turned from His own people; the lovers she chased are the ones who will come against her, and the turning away is complete.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to puncture, literally (to perforate, with more or less violence) or figuratively (to specify, designate, libel)
BiblicalUsage: Naqab means to pierce or to bore, and in its sharpest use it means to blaspheme, to pierce the Name with a curse. In Leviticus 24:11 the Israelitish woman's son blasphemes the name of the Lord and curses, and is brought to Moses, and in Leviticus 24:16 whoever blasphemes the name of the Lord shall surely be put to death. In Numbers 23:8 Balaam asks how he shall curse whom God has not cursed, and in 2 Kings 18:21 the staff of Egypt is a bruised reed that will pierce the hand of any man who leans on it.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the word pierces in both directions, because a curse pierces the Name and a false trust pierces the hand. The blasphemer is stoned because words against God are not small, and the reed is a warning that leaning on Egypt cuts. I hold that my mouth should bless the Name it once could have cursed.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to be (or make) clean (literally or figuratively); by implication (in an adverse sense) to be bare, i.e. extirpated
BiblicalUsage: Naqah means to be clean or clear, to be held guiltless, and it is the word for innocence before God and before men. In Genesis 24:8 Abraham's servant is told he shall be clear from the oath if the woman will not follow, and in Exodus 20:7 the Lord will not hold him guiltless who takes His name in vain. In Numbers 14:18 the Lord is longsuffering and forgiving, and by no means clearing the guilty, and in Psalm 19:12 David asks God to cleanse him from secret faults.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe being clear is the question every conscience asks, because the servant wants to be clear of his oath and David wants to be clear of his secret faults. God clears the guilty only through forgiveness, and He never clears the guilty without it. I hold that my clearance is in the mercy of Numbers 14:18, not in my own record.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: revenge
BiblicalUsage: Naqam as a noun is vengeance, the repayment due to the wronged, and the Bible keeps it in God's hands. In Ezekiel 25:12 Edom deals against the house of Judah by taking vengeance, and greatly offends, and in Psalm 58:10 the righteous shall rejoice when he sees the vengeance. In Proverbs 6:34 jealousy is the rage of a man who will not spare in the day of vengeance, and in Ezekiel 25:15 the Philistines take vengeance with a despiteful heart, to destroy for the old hatred.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe vengeance belongs to God because only He can repay without becoming what He repays. Edom took vengeance and the Philistines took vengeance, and the Lord answers both in Ezekiel. I hold that my neighbour is to be loved, and my enemy is to be left to God.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to grudge, i.e. avenge or punish
BiblicalUsage: Naqam as a verb means to avenge or take vengeance, to grudge and repay, and it is claimed by God for Himself. In Numbers 31:2 the Lord tells Moses to avenge the children of Israel of the Midianites, and in Judges 16:28 Samson asks to be avenged of the Philistines for his two eyes. In 1 Samuel 24:12 David says the Lord shall judge between him and Saul, and avenge him of Saul, and in Nahum 1:2 God is jealous and the Lord revengeth, and He reserves wrath for His enemies.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the Bible gives vengeance to God and takes it from me, and that is a mercy, not a loss. Samson asked for it once and died with the asking, and David leaves his cause with the Lord in 1 Samuel 24:12. I hold that the God who reserves wrath is the God I can trust with my wrongs.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to strike with more or less violence (beat, fell, corrode); by implication (of attack) to knock together, i.e. surround or circulate
BiblicalUsage: Naqaph means to strike around or compass about, and it is used for the knops that ring the great sea in the temple. In 1 Kings 7:24 under the brim of the sea there are knops compassing it round about, ten in a cubit, cast in two rows, and in 2 Chronicles 4:3 the same oxen compass it round about in the same pattern.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the compassing knops are a picture of worship that goes all the way around; the sea is ringed on every side, and the work is finished on every side.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to bore (penetrate, quarry)
BiblicalUsage: Naqar means to bore or dig out, to pierce or quarry, and it is used for eyes and for rocks. In 1 Samuel 11:2 Nahash the Ammonite offers peace on condition that he may thrust out all their right eyes, and lay it for a reproach upon all Israel, and in Isaiah 51:1 the people are told to look to the rock whence they are hewn, and to the hole of the pit whence they are digged.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the same verb that gouges out an eye also digs a people out of a rock, because the digging is either cruelty or creation; nahash would dig out eyes for spite, and the Lord digs a people out of the pit for salvation.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to entrap (with a noose), literally or figuratively
BiblicalUsage: Naqash means to entrap with a noose, to lay a snare, and it is used for idolatry and for a king's trap. In 1 Samuel 28:9 the woman of Endor asks Saul why he lays a snare for her life, when he himself cut off those with familiar spirits, and in Deuteronomy 12:30 the people are warned not to be snared by following the gods of the nations after they are destroyed.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that a snare is always set where you are already walking, because Saul finds his in the very place he once cleansed, and Israel is warned about the gods of the land they are about to enter; the way out of a snare is to see it before you step in it.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: to loathe
BiblicalUsage: Naqat means to loathe, for the soul to be weary of its own life, and its only occurrence is Job at his lowest. In Job 10:1 Job says, my soul is weary of my life, and I will leave my complaint upon myself, and speak in the bitterness of my soul.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe Job's weariness is the honest end of suffering without answers, and the Bible does not soften it; He loathes his life and still speaks to God, and that is the prayer.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: innocent
BiblicalUsage: Naqi means innocent or clean, clear of guilt, and it is the word for hands and hearts that can stand before God. In Genesis 24:41 the servant shall be clear from the oath when he comes to Abraham's kindred, and in Deuteronomy 19:10 innocent blood must not be shed in the land, lest blood be upon the people. In 1 Samuel 19:5 Jonathan asks why Saul would sin against innocent blood by slaying David without a cause, and in Psalm 24:4 he that hath clean hands and a pure heart shall ascend into the hill of the Lord.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe innocence in the Bible is not naivety but a clean record, and the clean hands of Psalm 24:4 are the hands that have not taken what is not theirs. The servant is clear, the blood is innocent, and David is innocent of the charge, and the one who climbs the hill is the one whose hands match his heart. I hold that my clean hands are washed, not earned.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a cleft
BiblicalUsage: Naqiq is a cleft or a hole in the rock, and it is used for hiding places and for the enemy's rest. In Isaiah 7:19 they shall come and rest in the desolate valleys and in the holes of the rocks, and upon all thorns and upon all bushes, and in Jeremiah 13:4 the Lord tells Jeremiah to hide the girdle in a hole of the rock by the Euphrates.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that a hole in the rock can be a hiding place or a grave, depending on who sends you there; Jeremiah hides a girdle and finds it ruined, and the enemy rests in the holes of a desolate land.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: spotted
BiblicalUsage: Naqod means speckled or spotted, and it is the word for the marked sheep in Jacob's bargain with Laban. In Genesis 30:32 Jacob will pass through the flock and remove all the speckled and spotted cattle, and the spotted and speckled among the goats, and in Genesis 30:33 his righteousness shall answer for him in time to come, when every one that is not speckled and spotted among the goats shall be counted stolen.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the spotted sheep are the picture of a bargain God honoured, because Jacob's wages were the marked animals and the Lord multiplied them; Laban changed the wages ten times, and the spots still belonged to Jacob.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: of foreign origin (compare H5373); "nard":--(spike-)nard.
BiblicalUsage: Nardos is nard, the costly spikenard poured on Jesus in the last week before the cross. In John 12:3 Mary takes a pound of ointment of spikenard, very costly, and anoints the feet of Jesus, and wipes His feet with her hair, and in Mark 14:3 a woman in Bethany breaks an alabaster box of ointment of spikenard, very precious, and pours it on His head.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe nard is the smell of worship that costs something, because a pound of it was a year's wages and it was poured out in a single evening; the house was filled with the odour, and the act is remembered wherever the gospel is told.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: a flower of the same name, from νάρκη (stupefaction, as a "narcotic"); Narcissus, a Roman:--Narcissus.
BiblicalUsage: Narcissus is a Roman Christian whose household Paul greets, and his name is all we know of him. In Romans 16:11 Paul says, greet them that be of the household of Narcissus, which are in the Lord, and the greeting is the whole record.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe a household in the Lord is a church in miniature, and Narcissus is remembered for the people around his table. Paul does not greet the man himself, which may mean he is already gone, but his household is still in the Lord.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)

Definition: the crimson-grub, but used only (in this connection) of the color from it, and cloths dyed therewith

The eggs deposited beneath her body were thus protected until the larvae were hatched and able to enter their own life cycle. As the mother died, the crimson fluid stained her body and the surrounding wood. From the dead bodies of such female scarlet worms, the commercial scarlet dyes of antiquity were extracted. What a picture this gives of Christ, dying on the tree, shedding His precious blood that He might "bring many sons unto glory" (Heb 2:10)! He died for us, that we might live through him! Ps 22:6 describes such a worm and gives us this picture of Christ. (cf. Isa 1:18) (from page 73, "Biblical Basis for Modern Science", 1985, Baker Book House, by Henry Morris)
